en: The First Chapter of the Sūtrasthāna: He by whom all diseases of the world— passion and the rest, which are innate and rooted— have been swiftly and entirely cast away.
I bow my head to that one Physician and to the ancestral sages, such as the Grandfather (Brahmā), who are knowers of the medical scriptures.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "Seeking Longevity" (*Āyuṣkāmya*); thus indeed said the great seers, Ātreya and the others.
By one desiring long life, [the means] for accomplishing dharma, wealth, and pleasure [should be sought]. AS.Sū.1.2–1.3.
The highest respect should be accorded to the instructions of Āyurveda;
Āyurveda is the nectar of immortality, universal, and eternal Brahman.
He gave it to Dakṣa; he [gave] those two to the Aśvins; then [he gave it] to Śatakratu.
[Thus, one is freed] from diseases that cause obstacles to virtue (dharma), wealth (artha), pleasure (kāma), and liberation (mokṣa).
When men were being afflicted, Dhanvantari, Bharadvāja, Nimi, Kāśyapa, and Kaśyapa placed Punarvasu at their head.
The great-souled ones of great power, such as Lambāyana and others,
approached Śatakratu, the lord of the immortals and the refuge.
Upon seeing them, the Thousand-eyed One spoke according to the tradition:
"The preservation of life is the Veda and the Upaveda of Atharvan."

He understood that merit, which the Grandfather (Brahmā) recognized as possessing eight limbs through [the removal of] bodily ailments, seizing spirits, diseases of the upper body, thorns, fangs, old age, and vices.
Having received that sacred tradition and having revealed it to one another,
those supreme ṛṣis returned to the world of men filled with joy.
Then, for the sake of the preservation of Āyurveda, they composed these treatises after having [instructed] Agniveśa, Hārīta, Bhela, Māṇḍavya,
and Suśruta.
And with great devotion, they caused Karāla and the others, his disciples, to grasp [the teachings]; thereafter,
they too composed their own respective tantras, and those [tantras] were thus established.
The wise ones reported this to their gurus and the assemblies of sages;
praised by them, these [teachings] attained a firm foundation on earth.
Each one of these is insufficient for the treatment of all diseases; however, by devoting oneself to each individual system, one's entire lifespan would be exhausted.
Since it has been stated again and again by the authors of the tantras that "the very same meaning [is found] through study alone," in some cases it is explained with a certain degree of specificity.
Since they have not been respected in their speech, being intent on conveying mere literal meaning,
I have therefore for the most part condensed all the treatises into this *Aṣṭāṅgasaṅgraha*.
It avoids irrelevant digressions, objections, and repetitions;
it is composed solely as a compendium of the three aggregates of causes, symptoms,
and medicines.
It elucidates those passages whose true meaning is concealed,
and it most effectively dispels contradictions with one's own and other systems.
The composition shall be arranged according to the [successive] ages through systematic division;
it is eternally useful, difficult to comprehend, and pervades all its constituent parts by its very nature.
In this [treatise], the science of medicine (kāyacikitsita) has been specifically compiled; herein,
there is not even a single measure that is devoid of scriptural authority.
Those meanings and that arrangement of the text are for the sake of brevity; otherwise, the order would be different. Briefly stated, there are three humors: wind, bile, and phlegm.
Each of these is threefold, through the distinctions of increase, decrease, and equilibrium;
and increase and decrease are also each threefold, by way of being superior, middling, or slight.
These [doshas], when either morbidly transformed (*vikṛta*) or untransformed (*avikṛta*), destroy the body and sustain it;
though all-pervasive, they reside respectively below, in the middle, and above the heart and navel.
These [doshas] occupy the end, middle, and beginning of life, day, night, and mealtime respectively; by them,
the digestive fire (agni) becomes irregular, sharp, or dull, and when they are in equilibrium, it is balanced.
The digestive tract may be harsh, soft, or moderate; it becomes moderate even when these [humors] are equal, just as a poison-ant is neutralized by the presence of its own poison at birth.

And by these [three factors], three types of constitutions—inferior, middling, and superior—are distinguished separately. Among all of them, the constitution with balanced elements (samadhātu) is the best; those born from two humors are to be censured.
In that regard, vāyu (wind) is dry, light, cold, rough, subtle, and mobile;
pitta (bile) is slightly unctuous, sharp, hot, light, foul-smelling, flowing, and liquid.
Unctuous, cold, heavy, dull, smooth, soft, and stable;
their combinations (saṃsarga) and their simultaneous aggravation (sannipāta) arise from the increase and decrease of two or three [humors] respectively.
These two are said to be sixfold and tenfold according to the distinctions of excellence and so forth. The bodily constituents (dhātus) are chyle, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen.
The seven impurities to be corrupted are urine, feces, sweat, and so forth; furthermore,
whatever diseases arise when the *doṣas* are located within the *rasa* and other tissues.

They are called "born from that" by way of metaphorical designation, like [the term] "clarified butter-burner" (ghṛtadāha). Satisfying, sustaining, smearing, lubricating, supporting, and filling— these are their functions.
The wise know that the elements arise in succession through the processes of conception and karma;
they constantly sustain the body and serve as the nutriment for the elements.
The increase of all [humors] occurs through similar [qualities], while the opposite occurs through contrary ones. The tastes are sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, and astringent.

These six substances are based on the [six] elements and, as previously stated, they bring about strength. Among them, the first three [sweet, sour, and salty] subdue wind (māruta), while the three beginning with bitter (tikta) subdue phlegm (kapha).

Astringent, bitter, and sweet [tastes] pacify pitta, while others aggravate it. Substances are of three types: pacifying (śamana), aggravating (kopana), and beneficial for those in good health (svasthahita).
Due to the predominance of the qualities of heat and cold, potency (vīrya) is traditionally held to be twofold therein;
the post-digestive transformation (vipāka) of a substance is threefold, consisting of sweet, sour, and pungent.
Heavy, mild, cold, unctuous, smooth, dense, soft, and stable— these ten qualities,
along with the subtle and clear, and their opposites, constitute the twenty [qualities].
The sense objects, the pervasive, and other qualities such as the expansive;
the pervasive, having permeated the entire body, is capable of digestion.
"Vikāṣī," while drawing out the elements, loosens the bonds of the joints;
"Sara," however, is proclaimed by some to be characterized by sharpness and excellence.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas— these three are declared to be the great qualities (mahāguṇa). The application of time, purpose, and action may be deficient, improper, or excessive.
And right application (samyagyoga) should be understood as the sole cause of both disease and health;
for disease is the disharmony of the humors (doṣa), while health is the equilibrium of the humors.
Diseases are considered to be of two kinds through the division into endogenous and exogenous; their substratum is also twofold due to the distinction between body and mind.
Rajas and tamas are declared to be the two defects of the mind;
one should examine the patient through observation, palpation, and questioning.

Disease [is diagnosed] by means of its etiology, prodromal signs, symptoms, therapeutic suitability, and manifestation. Here, they say that location is twofold, distinguished as the site (bhūmi) and the body (deha).

One should designate the three types of terrain as follows: the arid (jāṅgala) is predominant in wind (vāta), the marshy (ānūpa) is characterized by an excess of phlegm (kapha), and the intermediate (sādhāraṇa) has balanced humors.
Time consists of the states of moments and so forth, which effect the application of medicine;
and medicine is, in brief, of two kinds: purificatory and palliative.
Enema, purgation, and emesis are the supreme medicines for the bodily humors (doṣas) in their respective order;
likewise, oil, ghee, and honey [are so].
The knowledge of wisdom, fortitude, the self, and so forth, is the supreme medicine for the defects of the mind; therefore,
the summary of the chapters of this treatise will hereafter be declared.
Those concerning longevity, the disciple, the day, the season, and the non-occurrence of disease; those concerning liquids, food, knowledge, protection, incompatible foods, and drinks.
The collection [of topics] beginning with moderation in eating, knowledge of medicinal substances, excellence, and purification (AS.Sū.1.50);
and the various classifications of the tastes of great decoctions, diverse medicinal ingredients, and so forth (AS.Sū.1.50).
The knowledge of the humors (doṣa) and so forth, their classifications, and their actions constitute disease and its medicine.
[These consist of] the examination of the body, emetics, purgatives, oleation, sudation, purification, non-unctuous enemas, and nasal drops.
The procedures for bloodletting— namely, smoking, gargling, cupping, irrigation, saturation,
and the use of syringes and leeches— as well as the surgical procedure for extracting foreign bodies, and the applications of instruments, caustics, and thermal cautery. (AS.Sū.1.52)
These forty chapters are called the *Śārīra-sūtra*.
They concern the descent of the embryo for the sake of obtaining a son, the conduct [during pregnancy], abnormalities, and those born of the body.

The twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of the Vessels and Vital Points" (sirāmarmaprakṛtyākhyā), which deals with diseases caused by bodily distortions and their remedies, along with the messenger (sadūta), constitutes the section on Diagnosis (nidāna) concerning all diseases.
For those suffering from fever, hemorrhagic diseases, asthma, consumption, intoxication, and the like;
for those with hemorrhoids and diarrhea; for those with urinary obstruction and polyuria; and for those with abscesses and abdominal enlargements. (AS.Sū.1.55)
There are sixteen [chapters] on the treatment of those afflicted by pale leprosy and wind-diseases, as well as wind-blood disorders;
and [sixteen] on the treatment of fever and blood-disorders, cough, dyspnea, and consumption.

Vamau (vam and au) are used in cases of intoxication, hemorrhoids, diarrhea, and urinary disorders; and two each are used in cases of abscesses, abdominal tumors, abdominal enlargement, anemia, edema, and erysipelas.
The treatment for leprosy (kuṣṭha), vitiligo (śvitra), diseases of wind (anila), and blood-wind disorders (vātāsra) [is covered in] twenty-four chapters; after this follows the Kalpasiddhi.

The preparation (kalpa) for the enema (vasti) is the purification (vireka); its successful administration is the formulation of the enema (basti-kalpanā). Furthermore, there is the preparation of proven enemas (siddha-basti), as well as the successful application of both the decoction enema (basti) and the oil enema (anuvāsana).

The eighth section is on pharmaceutical preparations; from this point onward, each subsequent section concerns the treatment of children, the knowledge of disease-causing spirits, and their expulsion.
When there is a separate perception during bathing, there are two [types of *sannipāta*]; in insanity and loss of memory, there are two;
and in cases of the eyelid, the junction, and the destruction of vision, there are two for each.

In cases of the ripening of a discharge from all the eyes, as well as in wounds of the ears, nose, and mouth, on the head, in cases of immediate fracture, and in fistula-in-ano, two [mātrās] each [should be applied]. As.Sū.1.62.
There are two [chapters] for tumors and the like, minor diseases, and diseases of the private parts;
two for poison from snakes and insects, and two for spider and rat poisons.
The fifty-fifth chapter, which completes the eight sections, is dedicated to poison and the administration of poisons, as well as to rejuvenation (rasāyana) and aphrodisiacs (vājīkaraṇa). AS.Sū.1.64.
"One hundred and fifty chapters are proclaimed through six sections.
Thus ends the first chapter;
now the second chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the initiation of the student;
thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
Devoted to his teacher, diligent, and intensely applied with sharpness of intellect, memory, and recitation;
possessing a straight face, nose, and eyes, and having slender, smooth, and clear nails.
A celibate student who has conquered the pairs of opposites, who is wise, of good conduct, and steadfast;
who has resided [there] for six months, who is capable, and endowed with modesty, purity, and noble lineage.
A student who has reached the end of the study of the meaning and practice of the Tantras is to be taught; however,
this should not be done during a lightning strike at an improper time, during thunder, an earthquake, or during an eclipse.

On the fifteenth day when the moon is absent, or in the absence of the teacher, one should recite [the text] with words that are neither too clipped nor too slow, and neither too high nor too low in pitch.
With humble appearance, he should attend upon his teacher like a king;
while the teacher is still asleep, he should lie down, and he should rise before him.
One should not utter merely a name, nor should one mock even that which is improper;
one should be indivisible, free from arrogance, not stubborn, truthful, and pleasant to behold.
One who is learned, knows the proper time, has mastered the texts, understands the treatises on meaning,
and who attends to the helpless and the sick like his own children.

AS.Sū.2.9: Only when authorized by his teacher does one acquire the title of "physician. However, he who knows the scriptures alone but is not fully proficient in clinical practices [is not a true physician].
Having encountered a patient, he becomes bewildered like a coward entering a battlefield;
yet he who performs medical treatment with audacity, disregarding the scriptures, [is likewise lost].
He incurs reproach among the virtuous and faces execution by the king,
[if he fails] regarding the cause, the symptoms, the pacification, and the non-recurrence of diseases.
He who possesses this fourfold knowledge is a king-worthy physician, the best among healers; for him,
the surgical instruments, the treatises, and water serve to manifest both virtues and defects.
Therefore, one who regards the bowl [as the primary concern] should augment wisdom through extensive learning;
for the scripture is like a lamp, providing vision and broadening the mind.
A physician who treats with these two properly applied does not commit an error.
He who, being summoned, goes forth well-attired and with auspicious omens; AS.Sū.2.14 AS.Sū.2.14.
Having gone [to the patient], he does not direct his mind elsewhere for any reason other than the sake of the patient;
he examines the diseases correctly, according to the specific distinctions of the etiological factors (*nidāna*) and so forth.
He does not publicly disclose her shameful condition, nor does he neglect the proper time for action regarding her.
And he who knows how to apply [the treatment] is a physician who attains success. One should not accept meat from women when their supervisor is absent or has turned away.
And with them, one should avoid staying in private and engaging in jesting;
likewise, one should avoid those who are afflicted, those who are disliked by the king, good physicians, and those who hate them or are themselves hateful.

One who is fierce, afflicted by grief, timid, ungrateful, or conceited regarding their medical knowledge; one who lacks necessary equipment, is distracted, disobedient, or whose life-force has departed— [these should not be treated].
Even one who wishes to live, though afflicted by disease, should avoid physicians who lack the previously mentioned qualities and who sell their treatments; for they are the precursors of death.
The physician, the medicinal substances, the attendant, and the patient constitute the four pillars of medical treatment; each of these has been specified as possessing four qualities.

A physician who is skillful, has grasped the meaning of the scriptures from authoritative sources, has observed clinical practice, and is pure, [should provide] medicine that is prepared with many methods, possesses many qualities, is effective, and is appropriate.
The attendant should be devoted, pure, skillful, and intelligent; the patient should be wealthy, compliant with the physician, communicative, and endowed with courage.
When the physician is deficient, even if his four components are excellent, they are useless;
yet a physician who possesses those qualities can sustain even those who are suffering and lack even one of those components.

Therefore, they know that among the factors of medical treatment, this [the physician] alone is the primary cause. Disease is of two kinds: curable and incurable; these two, moreover, are each further divided into two types.
[The diseases] are easy to cure, difficult to cure, manageable, or incurable; [however],
all medicines act upon the body of a young man who has self-control.
When it does not strike a vital spot (*amarmaga*), when its causes, premonitory signs (*pūrvarūpa*), and symptoms (*rūpa*) are mild, when it is without complications (*anupadrava*),

when the affected humor (*dūṣya*), location (*deśa*), season (*ṛtu*), and constitution (*prakṛti*) are dissimilar [to those that would normally cause harm], and when the four factors [of physician, medicine, attendant, and patient] are complete— this is the perfection of the quarters (*pādasampat*).
When the *grahas* (humors) are concordant, the disease follows the path of a single humor; it is new, easy,
easily curable, and accomplished by easy means in a short time.
AS.Sū.2.29: That which is achieved through difficult means, with great hardship, over a long period of time,
that which possesses symptoms of the incurable type, and likewise that which requires surgical instruments and other such interventions [is considered difficult].
Because his lifespan is residual, he may be maintained by wholesome means; generally, however, in the opposite case,
having given a small amount of happiness for a small cause, that [disease] is extended.
In one whose lifespan is fixed by past karma, a disease does not reach total destruction;
like a falling man supported by pillars, the patient is held back here by beneficial treatments.
One who is incurable transcends all medical treatments and must be rejected;
therefore, one who remains in a state of absolute perversion should simply be disregarded.
Causing delusion, confusion, and aversion, it is seen as a fatal sign that destroys the senses;
having first thus examined the diseases, one should then begin the treatment.
Otherwise, one will certainly incur the loss of one's own purpose, knowledge, and fame;
even the union of two strong [factors] that are curable becomes incurable.
Therefore, one should recognize that the union of the curable and the incurable is itself incurable;
the incurable does not become curable, nor does the curable turn into the incurable.
Diseases pass into other stages due to the neglect of treatment or through fate;
yet, even the venom of a poisonous serpent or blazing fire would be better [than such a state].
One should not consume meat obtained from a distressed person or a wretched individual; rather,
compassion for living beings is the superior dharma— this is the teaching of the best of physicians regarding those in distress.
"But he who proceeds having achieved his goal transcends everything.
Thus ends the second chapter.
The Third Chapter. Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "Daily Regimen."
Thus indeed said the great sages, such as Ātreya and others:
"One should rise during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, examining whether one's food has been digested or not."
For the sake of protecting his life, one who is healthy and has experienced the urge should void urine and feces facing north during the day, and facing south at night.
Restraining his speech, self-controlled, with his limbs covered and his head veiled,
he should move about; he should not utter words with effort when they are prompted by agitation.
On a path strewn with impurities, corpses, ashes, cow-pens, and dung; near a village, fire, or an anthill; or on a pleasant, elevated place, a burial mound, or at the foot of a tree.
One should not void [urine or excrement] facing a woman, a deity, a cow, the moon, wind, food, fire, or water;
nor should one do so without first covering the ground, except out of fear or incapacity, or by choice.

One should not engage in other activities until this incurable disease has been conquered; [the patient] should have the openings of the channels cleansed by rubbing with a lump of pure, flawless clay.
One should employ pure water that has been drawn out and earth that removes stains and odors, using drops that do not splash upward.
Having touched bodily constituents, impurities, tears, fat, hair, or nails that have been cast off;
having bathed with the intention to eat; after eating; after sleeping; after sneezing; and during the worship of the gods—AS.Sū.3.9.
Having stepped onto a path, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) while seated,
facing either north or east, staying in a secluded place, with the knees not exposed and the gaze not directed elsewhere.
Without speaking, with his upper garment arranged, using [water] that is clear, taken from the base of the thumb,
not drawn up [from a vessel], not bent down for, not heated by fire, and not putrid— AS.Sū.3.11.
Not with foam, bubbles, or alkaline water; not with water held in a single hand; not with wet hands; not with hands or feet soiled by impurities; nor [should one sip] with noise.
[It is] produced from the *vaṭa*, *asana*, *arka*, *khadira*, *karañja*, and *karavīra* trees;
[and] produced from the *sarja*, *arimeda*, *apāmārga*, *mālatī*, and *kakubha* trees.
A root that is astringent, bitter, or pungent, or any other such [root],
from a tree that is well-known, whose tip is crushed, which has straight joints, and which grows in good soil.
Having a thickness equal to the tip of the little finger, with a beautiful tuft at the end, and twelve finger-breadths in length,
one should eat the tooth-stick after breakfast, while restraining one's speech.
Or, one should gently rub [the teeth] with this, which has been moistened with honey and the three-fold group of the three aims (trivarga),
thereby cleaning the teeth without harming the gums.
One should gently scrape the tongue with a tongue-scraper;
thus, the impurities, bad tastes, and odors arising from the tongue, mouth, and teeth will be removed.
Appetite, clarity of the senses, and lightness do not arise [in one who eats improperly], nor do they arise [in one who eats at the wrong time].
One should not eat when suffering from indigestion, vomiting, dyspnea, cough, fever, or facial paralysis.

It also causes thirst and diseases of the mouth, stomach, heart, eyes, head, and ears; however, [these ailments do not arise from] those produced by *śleṣmātaka*, *ariṣṭa*, *bibhītaka*, *dhava*, and *dhanvana* trees.
Bilva, vañcula, nirguṇḍī, śigru, tilvaka,
tinduka, kovidāra, śamī, pīlu, pippala, iṅguda, and gulgulu. (AS.Sū.3.20)
Pāribhadraka, amlīkā, mocaka, śālmalī, and śaṇa;
that which is sweet, sour, salty, dry, hollow, putrid, and slimy.
One should discard a seat made of *pālāśa* wood, a tooth-stick, and sandals;
one should first scrub the teeth from the bottom upward and sprinkle the eyes in the morning.
With his mouth full of water during the summer and autumn seasons, [he should rinse] with cold water;
having prostrated before the gods and the elders, he should recite the auspicious "One Hundred and Eight Blessings."
Immediately after hearing [the recitation], one should look at ghee placed in gold;
thereafter, one should constantly apply *sauvīra* collyrium, which is beneficial for the eyes.
Therefore, your eyes are charming and possess subtle vision;
they are pure, clearly displaying three colors, and have very smooth, thick eyelashes.

The eye consists of fire; therefore, there is specifically fear for one afflicted by śleṣman (phlegm). For this reason, one should apply *rasāñjana* for seven nights for the purpose of draining [the humors].

Then follows the administration of *aṇutaila* as nasal drops (*nasya*), and then the holding of it as a gargle (*gaṇḍūṣa*). [The patient] possesses thick, elevated, and clear skin on the neck, shoulders, throat, face, and chest.
Those who habitually use nasal medication will have fragrant breath, a pleasant voice, and pure senses; they will be free from wrinkles, gray hair, and freckles.
Cracking and roughness of the lips, dryness of the mouth, diseases of the teeth,
and impairments of the voice shall not occur from holding oil-gargles (sneha-gaṇḍūṣa).
A gargle consisting of water from *khadira*, *kṣīravṛkṣa*,
and *arimedā* overcomes anorexia, bad taste in the mouth, impurities, fetid breath, and excessive salivation. (AS.Sū.3.30)
Lightness of the mouth arises from rinses of lukewarm water;
thereafter, one should employ medicinal smoke and perfumes, garlands, and so forth.

By means of this smoke, diseases of vāta and kapha arising above the clavicle shall not occur. [The doshas] provoked by collyrium are pacified by nasal drops (nasya), gargles (kavala), and errhines (nāvana).

By means of smoke, one should gradually conquer wind and phlegm that have been provoked by food morsels. Perfumes, garlands, and the like are aphrodisiacs, destroyers of misfortune, and means of adornment.
One should not wear clothing that is worn out, soiled, blood-stained, or gaudy.
One should not wear a garland that hangs down, nor one that is outside [the body], nor one that is red, except for a water-born flower.
One should not hold a garment, a flower,
or a sandal with one's mouth; rather, desiring beauty, clarity, and fragrance, one should wear them [properly].
The fresh sprouts of betel vines, combined with nutmeg, cloves, camphor, kaṅkola, and black pepper, along with areca nuts, are pleasing to the heart.

It is unwholesome for those suffering from hemorrhaging, bile disorders, chest wounds, emaciation, or irritated vision; it is also unwholesome for those afflicted by poison, fainting, or intoxication, as well as for those with wasting diseases.
For a person who has just woken from sleep, after eating, or after bathing or vomiting,
two betel leaves, one areca nut, along with powdered khadira, are wholesome. (AS.Sū.3.38)
One should exert oneself excessively toward goals that lead to further prosperity; for even a long life, if censured, lacks the means to achieve its purpose.

One who desires wealth should resort to agriculture, trade, and cattle-rearing— activities that do not conflict with the two worlds— as well as to a virtuous king through appropriate means. (AS.Sū.3.40)

Having released his momentum, he should exit after touching with his hand one who has traveled, slept, eaten, or been in an assembly, as well as women, jewels, objects of worship, clarified butter, and auspicious things. (AS.Sū.3.41)
Wearing a sunshade and footwear, he should walk [only] as far as the length of a yoke;
at night, or when there is an urgent matter, he should go with a staff, wearing a head-covering, and accompanied by an attendant.

One should wander at night with [the upper robe] wrapped around oneself, but not with the head covered during the day; one should avoid the shadows of shrines, objects of worship, banners, and ill-omened things, as well as ashes, chaff, and impurities.
One should not step on ground containing gravel, clods of earth, offerings, or bathing sites; nor should one go to a crossroads at midday, during the two twilights, at night, or at midnight.
One should not frequent a tree-shrine or a crossroads at night,
nor should one frequent slaughterhouses, forests, empty houses, or cemeteries even during the day.
One should not utter the sound "huṃ" toward a corpse, an object of worship, or auspicious and praiseworthy things;
one should not circumambulate them keeping them to the left, nor should one circumambulate other [objects] by turning away from the right.
One should pay homage to crossroads and to well-known trees;
one should not [travel] with those who are predatory beasts, the diseased, or the accursed, nor with those who are blind, hungry, or thirsty.
One should not travel with animals whose tails have been cut off, nor with those that are one-eyed, nor on the back of a cow;
nor should one travel too early in the morning, too late in the evening, or when the sun is at the zenith.
One should not [cross] where water is not nearby, nor too quickly, nor continuously;
nor with an enemy, nor with strangers, nor alone, nor with those who are unrighteous.
One who is aged, afflicted, a woman, pregnant, or a member of a royal retinue or the twice-born should give way;
one should not precede draft animals in matters of bathing, eating, or drinking.
One should not cross a river by means of one's arms, nor should one walk toward a mass of fire; one should not climb a treacherous mountain, a precarious boat, or a tree.
One should not strike down a fruit from a tree with a clod of earth or with another fruit;
nor, when being restrained, should one enter, nor by a non-doorway, nor onto a seat.
One should stay in another's house oneself, sleeping moderately and not waking [the host];
one should not practice restlessness of the hands, speech, feet, face, genitals, or stomach.
Every three fortnights, one should have the hair of the head, the beard, the nails, and the body hair trimmed;
one should not do so with one's own hand or with the teeth, and one should perform the bath immediately thereafter.
Then, having developed a desire for food and drink, one should perform an oil massage with fragrant oils that ward off wind and provide pleasant sensations according to the season.
Oil massage (abhyaṅga) alleviates Vāta, promotes nourishment, induces sleep, strengthens the body, and makes the skin firm;
it removes pain from burns, fractures, and wounds, as well as exhaustion, fatigue, and old age. (AS.Sū.3.56)
Qualities arise from massage like the lubrication of the axle and leather of a chariot;
in the sense of touch, Vāyu is predominant, and touch has its locus in the skin.
Since an excellent oil massage is beneficial for the skin, one should therefore practice it;
one should practice it especially on the head, ears, and feet.
Keśya, when applied to the head, nourishes the sense organs; filling the ears with it cures pain in the jaw, neck, head, and ears.
Anointing the feet, moreover, brings stability to them, induces sleep, clarifies vision, and dispels numbness, fatigue, stiffness, contraction, and cracking of the feet. (AS.Sū.3.60)

Oil massage (abhyaṅga) is contraindicated for those afflicted by phlegm (kapha), those who have undergone purification therapies (saṃśuddhi), and those suffering from indigestion (ajīrṇin). Physical activity that produces exertion in the body is called exercise (vyāyāma).
Lightness, capacity for action, a blazing digestive fire, the reduction of fat,
and the distinctness and firmness of the limbs arise from physical exercise.
One suffering from disorders of wind or bile, a child, an elderly person, or one with indigestion should avoid it; however,
those who are strong and eat unctuous food may consume it in half-doses.
During the cold season and in spring, one should do so only slowly; at other times, having done that, one should massage the body all over for its comfort.
From excessive physical exertion, thirst, consumption, fainting, internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta), fatigue, exhaustion,
cough, fever, and vomiting arise. (AS.Sū.3.65)
Exertion, staying awake, travel, women, laughter, talk, and other such rash acts—
as one who draws a lion toward himself like an elephant, he perishes by indulging in them excessively. (AS.Sū.3.66)
Udvartana (massage with medicinal powders) alleviates kapha, dissolves fat,
stabilizes the limbs, and is supreme for clarifying the skin.
Bathing is illuminating, aphrodisiac, life-prolonging, and bestows vigor and strength;
it conquers itching, impurities, fatigue, perspiration, drowsiness, thirst, burning sensations, and evil influences. (AS.Sū.3.68)
Sprinkling the lower part of the body with warm water bestows strength; sprinkling the head with that same water, however, takes away strength from the hair and the eyes.

One should not bathe the head without having first bathed the whole body; nor should one bathe in water that is shallow or cold. One should not enter the water, sleep, or perform any action while naked.
One should not bathe in the water of another without first removing five lumps [of earth]; one should not look at oneself in the water, nor at the reservoir while standing on its bank.
One should not splash water with the hand or the foot;
having bathed, one should not wipe the limbs nor shake the hair.
One should quickly put on two washed garments along with a turban while they are still damp;
one should not wear a garment previously worn, nor should one touch oil or fat.
One should change one's garment for sleeping, for departing, and for the worship of deities; likewise,
one should bathe in cases of eye disease, facial disease, ear disease, or dysentery.
It is forbidden for those suffering from flatulence, catarrh, or indigestion, as well as for those who have already eaten;
one should eat food according to the rules for food and drink, except in cases of necessity.
Having rejoiced with a serene mind, having offered oblations and given gifts according to his ability, he should listen to the teaching "Cooking with water in a secluded place at one's ease."
One should give everything intended for others; one should not cook food for oneself alone.
One should not eat the food of those who are about to die, of the dead, or of those living in misery.

One should not [accept food] from those conquered by women, eunuchs, outcasts, or those who commit cruel and evil deeds; nor from members of a hostile group, courtesans, those who run eating-houses, rogues, or shopkeepers.
One should not eat foods from one's lap, nor should one drink water with cupped hands; furthermore,
one should not consume anything mixed with sesame seeds after the sun has set.
One should not eat immediately after a meal, nor should one indulge in forbidden pleasures; rather,
one should engage in conversations that are superior in virtue, meaningful, and characterized by the three qualities.
One should pass the middle of the day accompanied by beloved and virtuous companions;
one should not associate with those who are hated by the world and the king, nor with nihilists.
A steadfast person should have no taste for the enmity of the Kali age amidst prosperity and adversity;
they should be content with anything other than what is heard [of worldly affairs] and find their curiosity directed toward that alone.
Patient, upright, and skillful, he performs his duties with careful deliberation;
modest, wise, and full of great energy, he shares his wealth and is fond of guests.
Of noble conduct, profound, virtuous, and affectionate toward those who depend on him;
a giver of funeral cakes to his ancestors, a performer of sacrifices, an offerer of oblations, and compassionate by nature.
He is authorized by those of good reputation; he is compassionate toward the wretched; he provides comfort to the frightened; and he is a conciliator of the angry.

One should be the first to speak, pleasant-faced, of good character, and a worshiper of those worthy of worship; those worthy of honor— wealth, kinsmen, age, learning, and conduct— are to be honored in ascending order.
One should feel even greater compassion for the fool who harms himself, who is devoid of moral restraint, who has abandoned the true path, and who serves as fuel for the flames of hell.
One should speak words that are righteous, meaningful, pleasant, true, measured, and beneficial;
one should not despise oneself, nor praise oneself, nor cause oneself harm.

One should not despise those who are inferior on account of their conduct, wealth, limbs, strength, or learning; one should not be a wounder of others' vitals, nor cruel, nor sharp-tongued, nor a scorcher of others.
One should be envious of the cause, but not of the fruit; one should not commit evil even toward an evildoer.
One should not raise a rod against another, nor, when angry, should one strike them down.
Except for a son or a disciple worthy of the teaching,
one who intends their welfare should not perform such actions as dancing, instrumental music, singing, and the like, nor should one engage in ostentatious conduct.
Having assumed a well-known appearance as Keśava and being devoted to peaceful conciliation,
he should touch the part of the body above the navel with his lower garment.
One should not delay regarding purification after having engaged in sexual intercourse (AS.Sū.3.93). One should not laugh, sneeze, belch, or yawn with the mouth uncovered (AS.Sū.3.93).
One should not scratch one's own head simultaneously with both hands;
nor should one carry a load on the head while simultaneously carrying fire.
One should not pick the nose nor grind the teeth;
one may perform scraping, cutting, piercing, tearing, and rubbing.
One should not step with one foot upon the other, nor should one scratch or cleanse oneself;
nor should one perform these acts while seated in a bronze vessel.
One should constantly keep [the sacrificial fires] stainless, with nails, feet, and inner disposition purified;
one should not attend to a fire that is not kindled, nor while being impure.

One should not blow [the conch] with the wind at one's back, nor while unclothed, nor when fatigued, nor with a distracted mind; one should not blow it with the mouth, nor leap, nor place it below, nor underfoot.
One should not constantly look at things that are moving, subtle, or unpleasant;
nor at anything inauspicious, nor at feces or urine, nor at an unpolished mirror.
One should not look at the sun when it is rising or setting, when it is scorching hot, when reflected in an image,
when eclipsed, or when obscured by a cloth.
Nor should one look at anything else that is exceedingly brilliant, nor the face of a guru when he is angry;
nor a woman who is discharging [fluid], nor one in her courses, nor one who is naked, nor one engaged with another.
One should not lie down with one's wife while eating, sleeping, sneezing, yawning, or on an uncomfortable seat; nor should one lie down on the same bed, nor eat together with her.
One should protect her without envy and should not tolerate a wanton woman; nor, while still impure from a meal, should one gaze at the stars, the moon, the snow, the moonlight, or the sun.
One should not look at, walk toward, recite over, sleep near, or touch the head of a cow that is suckling or wandering; nor should one offer such a cow to anyone else.
One should not perform any other ritual action for the worship of the gods when there are halos around the sun or moon, meteors, or Indra’s bow (a rainbow); nor should one run while it is raining.

One should not speak of the lunar day of the fortnight, nor should one point out the constellations; one should not disclose the strength of one's own birth-lagna or constellation, nor the impurities in one's house.
One should not manifest contempt nor a lack of affection toward the Lord;
one should [endure] headwinds, heat, dust, frost, and harsh winds.
Crookedness, sneezing, eructation, coughing, sleep, food, and sexual intercourse;
making noise, being unclean, and the raising of the hands, eyebrows, and eyes, as well as playing musical instruments—
The shadow of a riverbank, drinking liquor, [avoiding] beasts of prey, fanged animals, and horned creatures;
service to the base, the ignoble, and the overly clever; and conflict with the most excellent.
Eating during the twilights, sleeping with women, studying, and brooding [over worldly matters] (AS.Sū.3.110);
as well as prideful stability regarding health, life, power, and knowledge (AS.Sū.3.110).

One should avoid traveling through the midst of water, fire, or worship; one should avoid smoke from a corpse, excessive addiction to liquor, and the granting of undue confidence or independence to women.
One should not dwell for even a single day in a location condemned by the scriptures;
nor in a place abounding in disease, nor one without a physician, nor one without a leader.
One should not dwell in a place abounding in non-Dharmic people, nor in one that is afflicted, nor on a mountain, even if it is rich in water, medicines, firewood, flowers, grass, and fuel.
In a city that was abundant in food, secure, delightful, and adorned by the wise,
he was one who held in high regard men, gods, perfected beings (siddhas), and the scriptures.
He is the support of the three aims of life and of the people as appropriate; protecting the ten spheres of action and conquering internal enemies.
Violence, theft, sexual misconduct, slander, harsh speech,
falsehood, idle chatter, malice, covetousness, and wrong view.
One should abandon evil action of ten kinds through body, speech, and mind;
one should avoid harming others while acquiring wealth.
Since it is impossible for him not to give away riches acquired through dharma,
he effortlessly presides over the splendors of heaven and liberation.
Having eaten a light and wholesome meal in the evening, being pure and with a concentrated mind,
one should lie down after recollecting the Teacher and one's own proper conduct.
In a clean place free from clutter, with two or three trusted attendants,
he should lie down comfortably on a spacious, level, well-spread bed provided with suitable pillows.
One should use a bed and seat that is soft, auspicious,
and knee-high; placing the head toward the east or south, one should direct the feet toward the teachers.
Constantly reflecting upon the Dharma alone during the periods of both the forenoon and afternoon,
one should always extract the essence from the body and other things that lack essence.
Fearing at every moment death and its improper conduct,
[one should reflect] upon health, wealth, wisdom, youth, and the performance of dharma.
It is said that [a king] brings happiness, long life, and welfare, while the opposite occurs in the reverse case. For on this earth, a king is called a treasury of all splendor.
Therefore, one who possesses devotion should attend upon him without defiling his mind.
[One should avoid] reclining with crossed legs, using a seat, laughing, disputing, spitting, and yawning.
One should avoid all activities that are by nature excessive in his presence;
having carefully observed those various states of the elements (sattva) and so forth, one should act for one's own welfare. (AS.Sū.3.126)

Furthermore, whatever other path exists here for the instruction of what is beneficial, one should follow that as well; thus, having entered upon this conduct, it becomes a livelihood for all living beings, a mass of renowned and vast virtues protected by the deities.
One who lives for more than a hundred years, having attained liberation through meritorious deeds, goes toward a happy rebirth; even at the dissolution of the body, he finds contentment.
Thus ends the third chapter.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
"Now, therefore, we shall explain the seasonal regimen," so said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
Time, indeed, is the Blessed One, without beginning or end, which follows the karma accumulated [by beings].

In accordance with it, the sun and other luminaries, as well as the specific great elements such as space and so forth, undergo various transformations; thus acting as conditions, they become the causes for the birth and death of living beings, and for the seasons, juices, potencies, humors, physical bodies, strengths, calamities, and prosperities.

It (time) is divided twelvefold by way of the distinctions of *mātrā*, *kāṣṭhā*, *kalā*, *nāḍikā*, *muhūrta*, *yāma*, day-and-night (*ahorātra*), fortnight (*pakṣa*), month (*māsa*), season (*ṛtu*), half-year (*ayana*), and year (*varṣa*).

In this system, the twinkling of an eye (*akṣinimeṣa*) consists of *mātrās*; fifteen of those are a *kāṣṭhā*; thirty of those are a *kalā*; twenty of those, each divided into sixteen parts, are a *nāḍikā*; two *nāḍikās* are a *muhūrta*. When day and night are equal, four [muhūrtas] less a quarter constitute a watch (*yāma*). Four such watches make a day and night. Fifteen days and nights make a fortnight (*pakṣa*). Two fortnights make a month; that month ends with the bright half. By these months, beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa and occurring in pairs in succession, there arise the six seasons known as Hemanta (winter), Śiśira (dewy season), Vasanta (spring), Grīṣma (summer), Varṣā (rainy season), and Śarad (autumn). Among these, the three beginning with Śiśira are the sun’s northern course (*udagayana*) and its period of accumulation (*ādāna*); the remaining three are the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*) and its period of emission (*visarga*). These two, the period of accumulation and the period of emission, constitute a year (*varṣa*).

AS.Sū.4.4–5: Of these two, the extraction [of the essence] belongs to Agni. Indeed, at that time, the sun—encompassed by the nature of the season and its path—is a mass of intensely hot rays; through contact with it, the winds become sharp and harsh. Drying up the qualities born of Soma and taking away the moisture of the world, they produce dryness according to the sequence of the seasons. Strengthening the dry tastes—bitter, astringent, and pungent—they bring about weakness in human beings.
AS.Sū.4.5

The summer season, however, is mild (*saumya*). Even during that time, when the power [of the sun] is struck down by the path of the seasons, clouds, winds, and rains; when the sun is in its southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*); when the moon possesses unimpeded strength and constantly nourishes [the world] with cool rays; and when the heat on earth is pacified by the waters of Mahendra—the juices (*rasa*) increase, becoming non-arid, and they become sour, salty, and sweet respectively, while the strength of human beings also increases. Regarding this, there is a verse: AS.Sū.4.7 There is also a verse here:

In the winter and the cool season, the strength of the exhalation and inhalation is at its peak; it is moderate in autumn and spring, and diminished during the rainy season and the summer heat. (AS.Sū.4.7) The circles of the sky are smoky-grey with dust, dim, and obscured by frost. (AS.Sū.4.8)
From the quarters, the sun, the wind, and the coolness, there arises a hair-raising [sensation] superior [to all]. Lodhra, priyaṅgu, punnāga, and lavali are radiant with flowers.
AS.Sū.4.9 Elephants, goats, buffaloes, horses, crows, and pigs become arrogant.
AS.Sū.4.10 [The waters] are covered by masses of ice, and fish and birds are hidden within them.
AS.Sū.4.10 At the onset of winter, the rivers are tearful and the wells are steaming.
AS.Sū.4.11 Struck by the cold winds, the bodily vapors enter within and become chilled.
In the stomach, they produce a concentrated heat and a powerful digestive fire;
in the process of excretion, they generally tolerate heavy substances due to their inherent nature and other factors.
One should administer nourishing foods and drinks for the sake of its proper management;
otherwise, being without fuel, it may either sink away or, due to excessive excitation, flare up.
One should also cook the bodily elements (dhātus) for this person; then, due to their depletion, the wind (marut),
accompanied by heat, becomes aggravated, especially when it is cold.
Therefore, in this condition, one should partake of unctuous substances and tastes that are sweet, sour, and salty (AS.Sū.4.14),
as well as the flesh of animals that dwell in holes, aquatic creatures, marsh-dwellers, and those that eat raw meat (AS.Sū.4.15).
Meats, fresh wines produced from molasses and flour,
and [fresh] preparations of black gram, sugarcane, milk, fat, oil, and newly cooked rice.
Physical exercise, dry massage, oil massage, sudation, medicinal smoking, collyrium, and exposure to sunlight;
lukewarm water for the rules of purification, and underground chambers.
He lies upon a bed provided with charcoal and prepared with rugs and woolen blankets;
his limbs are anointed with saffron or even with costly aloe-wood.
One should sleep covered with light, warm garments at the proper time, having perfumed oneself with incense,
while warding off the cold wind by the contact of the limbs of a full-bodied woman.
In the winter season, cold is excessive due to clouds and rain;
and because of the dryness born of the period of withdrawal (ādāna), the aforementioned regimen should be followed even more strictly.
In spring, the southern wind blows and the sun possesses ruddy rays;
the trees and the *kakubha* shrubs are stainless, with fresh sprouts, bark, and leaves.
Adorned with rows of forests of *kiṃśuka*, *aśoka*, mango trees, and others,
they were filled with the sweet, tumultuous clamor of the songs of cuckoos and swarms of bees.
In the winter, the phlegm (śleṣman) that has accumulated is stirred up by the rays of the sun;
then, obstructing the digestive fire (agni), it produces many diseases.

Therefore, in this condition, one should employ strong emetics, medicated smoke, gargles, and nasal drops; as well as physical exercise, dry massage, honey, barley, wheat, and the meat of wild animals.
One should associate with friends, gardens, and charming young women;
having bathed, well-adorned, wearing garlands, and anointed with sandalwood and agallochum.
And various necklaces arranged upon jeweled ornaments, marked with mangoes and blue lotuses;
and [various] liquors: *āsava*, *ariṣṭa*, *śīdhu*, *mārdvīka*, and *mādhava*.

One should drink water boiled with musta and śuṇṭhī, or water infused with heartwood (sāra), or honey-water. One should avoid heavy foods, cold things, daytime sleep, unctuous substances, sour tastes, and sweet tastes.

In summer, the sun has sharp rays and resembles the flax flower; the quarters of the sky blaze as if set on fire by forest fires, and the earth is parched, yet the wind from the southwest is pleasant.
By winds, heat, and fogs, living beings are as if afflicted by fever;
they are made turbid by elephants and buffaloes distressed by the heat.
The rivers have their banks swollen high, their waters exhausted by the mass of coals that are the rays of the sun; the trees are devoid of shade.
With their leaves shattered and withered, and marked by dry bark and creepers,
they draw away the splendor of the world, because at that time the sun is exceedingly intense.
Therefore, one should avoid physical exertion, exposure to the sun, and pungent, sour, salty, or hot foods.
Alcohol should not be consumed; if it must be used, it should be taken in very small quantities or diluted with a great deal of water.
Otherwise, it causes swelling, laxity, burning sensations, and delusion.
Those [medicines] kept in new earthen vessels are pleasing to the heart and fragrant.
Drinks that are stirred, rich in sugar, and cold;
food that is sweet, cool, and liquid; and meat from wild animals and birds.
Rice, milk, ghee, grapes, coconut water, and sugar;
palm-leaf fans, breezes, pearl necklaces, and garlands with lotuses and water-lilies.
Slender women with bracelets of lotus stalks, lovely and anointed with sandalwood paste;
lakes, ponds, rivers, and snow-capped forests.
One should wear fragrant and very light garments;
one should sleep during the day in a fountain-house with water flowing from mechanical devices.
And at night, on the surface of the open sky strewn with fragrant flowers,
with his body moistened by camphor and sandalwood, he engages in sparse sexual union.
In the rainy season, the wind is of Varuṇa, causing the emergence of all crops;
the sky is dimmed by dense masses of clouds as dark as split sapphire.
The rows of steps in the long ponds were submerged by the unrestrained torrent of water,
and the lotuses were made to bloom by the forceful impact of the streams of water.
The rivers take on the appearance of oceans; the earth has its waters and dry lands indistinguishable;
and it resounds with the deep thundering of clouds and the cries of peacocks and frogs.
AS.Sū.4.41 Illuminated by the glow of lightning, with *indragopa* insects and fragments of rainbows; AS.Sū.4.42 Surrounded by dark green grass, and radiant with *śilindhra* and *kuṭaja* flowers.
When the body is weakened by the force of that [excessive] intake, and the digestive fire is sluggish and impaired,
[diseases arise] due to rain, earth-moisture, water, sourness, improper digestion, and the corruption of the mobile elements (vāyu) and the rest.
One who has completed the sequence of purification should employ enema therapy (bastikarma),
consuming aged śāli rice, wheat, and barley prepared with vegetable soups and meat broths.
AS.Sū.4.44 Nigada, madirāriṣṭa, mārdvīka, or a small amount of water;
AS.Sū.4.45 celestial water, water from a boiled well, cauṇḍa, or indeed sārasa [water].
When [the weather] is agitated by rain and wind, food that overcomes moisture and wind is beneficial.
One should partake of food that is dried, light, unctuous, hot, sour, and salty.
Generally, food and drink prepared with honey should be consumed at the onset of the rainy season,
avoiding snakes, damp ground, mist, cold winds, and spray.
His dwelling is provided with fire and free from gadflies, mosquitoes, and rats;
he is fond of rubbing the body, anointing it, bathing, incense, perfumes, and aloe-wood.
Adorned with variegated garlands, garments, and ornaments, he should travel on excellent female elephants.
[He should avoid] river water, churning, day-sleep, excessive running, and sexual intercourse.
In autumn, one should avoid frost, walking on foot, physical exercise, and the rays of the sun; the sky is bright with white clouds, and the earth is slightly marked by mud.
AS.Sū.4.50 The sun, illuminating the seven-day lily and the night-lily, shines resplendently upon the rice fields.
AS.Sū.4.51 The sun, having dispersed its sharp rays due to the departure of the mass of clouds, [shines forth].
The quarters of the sky were tawny-hued and exceedingly clear, filled with rows of cranes;
[the waters] were stirred by the friction of the shoulders of fish and swans nestled within the lotuses.
The lakes, pure and with their waves breaking,
[are seen] by those whose bodies have been accustomed to the cold of the rains, suddenly [struck] by the rays of the sun.
AS.Sū.4.53 When that previously accumulated *pitta* becomes aggravated by heat,
AS.Sū.4.54 the drinking of bitter medicinal ghees (*havis*), purgation, and bloodletting are always recommended.
Cold food and drink that is light, and having an astringent, sweet, or bitter taste; rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, wheat, barley, mung beans, sugar, and honey.
Patola, āmalaka, and grapes are highly beneficial for those who eat sparingly;
[the former] by the rays of the sun during the day, and [the latter] by the rays of the moon at night.
Water that has been heated, refreshed, and consecrated by Agastya—
pure, clean, and ripened by time— is like nectar when drunk.
And he should swim in lakes that are frequented by beautiful lotuses and where rows of bees hover, whirling as they are tossed by the flapping wings of flocks of swans.
Wearing light, clean garments, adorned with garlands, and anointed with cool ushira paste,
one should resort to the moonbeams at twilight while staying upon a palace roof.
One should avoid curd that causes satiety, exposure to the sun, alkaline substances, muscle fat, oil, rice-cakes, and meat; one should also avoid strong liquor, sleeping during the day, and frost.

AS.Sū.4.60 The habitual consumption of all tastes [is recommended], each being predominant in its respective season. AS.Sū.4.61 The period of seven days at the end and the beginning of the seasons is known as the junction (sandhi) between seasons.
In that regard, the former rule is to be abandoned and the latter is to be practiced in due order;
for diseases born of unwholesome habits arise from sudden abandonment and practice.

This procedure is prescribed for embodied beings during such seasons and when they are in a state of health; in other conditions, the procedure is one that counteracts the specific disorder and ignorance.
Regarding the three characteristics of the season known as the nature of the heap of months (māsarāśi),
one should engage in the conduct therein according to their strength in successive order.
Thus ends the fourth chapter;
[now begins] the fifth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter entitled "The Prevention of Disease.
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
One should not suppress the urges of flatus, feces, urine, semen, thirst,
hunger, sleep, cough, fatigue, dyspnea, yawning, tears, vomiting, or the emission of semen.
By the suppression of downward wind (adhovāta), there arise abdominal tumors (gulma), upward movement of wind (udāvarta),
pain, exhaustion, obstruction of flatus, urine, and feces, impairment of vision, loss of digestive fire, and diseases of the heart.
From [excessive] feces arise scrotal swelling, headache, catarrh, and pain in the head; upward-moving wind causes cutting pain and oppression of the heart.
The discharge of feces through the mouth and the aforementioned diseases are recorded;
as well as aching of the limbs, urinary calculi, and pain in the bladder, penis, and groin.
AS.Sū.5.6 Due to the suppression of urine, various diseases generally arise; their treatment consists of suppositories,
massage, immersion baths, sudation, and enema therapy (basti).
In cases of consumption (yakṣma) arising from the provocation of feces, food and drink that loosen the stool are recommended;
however, in those arising from urine, ghee is praised as a drink to be taken before a meal.
And when it reaches the end of digestion, one should administer two *yojanas* at the maximum dose; furthermore,
this is designated as *avapīḍaka* because of its retention.
In that condition [of vomiting], there is eructation, anorexia, trembling, and obstruction of the heart and chest, as well as flatulence,
cough, and hiccup; the treatment for it is the same as for hiccup.
Headache, weakness of the senses, and facial paralysis result from suppressing the urge to sneeze;
[these are also caused by] sharp smoke, collyrium, snuffing, nasal drops, and gazing at the sun.
One should induce a persistent sneeze and practice sweating and oil massage; furthermore,
food that subdues Vāta and ghee taken after meals should be employed.
From the suppression of thirst arise emaciation, weakness of the limbs, deafness, delusion, vertigo, and heart disease;
in such cases, every cooling regimen is beneficial.
AS.Sū.5.13 Breaking pain in the limbs, loss of appetite, lassitude, emaciation, colic, and vertigo result from hunger.
AS.Sū.5.13 In that case, light, unctuous, warm, and small quantities of food should be administered.
In sleep, delusion, heaviness of the head and eyes, lassitude, yawning, and aching of the limbs are observed; therein, dreaming and being massaged are desired.
From the suppression of cough, its aggravation occurs, as well as dyspnea, anorexia, heart disease,
emaciation, and hiccups; therefore, a treatment that specifically overcomes cough should be administered here.
From suppressing [the breath] during fatigue-induced dyspnea, abdominal tumors (gulma), heart disease, and fainting may arise;
in such cases, rest is beneficial, as is a therapeutic regimen that subdues Vāta.
From yawning arise diseases similar to those of sneezing, and every procedure that conquers Vāta [is indicated].
From it also arise chronic rhinitis (pīnasa), pain in the eyes, head, and heart, stiffness of the neck (manyāstambha), loss of appetite, and vertigo.
Accompanied by swellings and tears, there occurs dreaming, intoxication, and pleasant conversations;
[as well as] erysipelas, urticaria, leprosy, eye-itching, jaundice, and fever.
AS.Sū.5.19 Throat irritation, dyspnea, nausea, deformities, and swelling are symptoms of vomiting.
AS.Sū.5.19 Vomiting occurs after gargling, inhaling smoke, eating food that causes flatulence, or consuming dry (rough) food.
Physical exercise, the discharge of blood, and purgation are recommended here;
furthermore, oil mixed with alkali and salt is praised for the purpose of massage.
From the semen, there occurs its discharge, as well as pain in the genitals,
swelling, fever, distress in the heart, retention of urine, breaking pain in the limbs, hernia, urinary calculi, and impotence.
One should resort to bloodletting, crest-ornaments, wine, meat broth, enemas, massage,
and immersion baths; one should consume milk prepared with enema-purifying drugs and enjoy the company of beloved women.
In that case, one should attend to him in every way, avoiding anyone who suppresses natural urges,
who has suppressed feces, who is exhausted, emaciated, or afflicted by thirst and colic.
All diseases arise from the suppression or the excessive provocation of natural urges; the primary remedy for those [diseases] has been specified therein.
Therefore, when the wind (vāyu) generally becomes aggravated in many ways,
one should administer food, drink, and medicine that facilitate its downward movement (anulomana).
In due course, even in a jewel, a stain inevitably arises from water; therefore,
one should rise up at the proper time for the purification of impurities.
Having reached the ultimate limit of decline,
those who have become indifferent generally develop an aversion toward medicines even after a very long time.
Excessive corpulence, loss of digestive fire, urinary disorders, leprosy, and loss of vitality;
obstruction of the channels, impairment of vision, dyspnea, edema, and jaundice.
It [causes] swelling of the thighs, stiffness, abdominal distress,
dysentery, colic, vomiting, glandular swellings, worms, tumors, drowsiness, and the seeing of bad dreams.

Even for one who is satisfied by nourishing foods, [these may cause] diseases of the throat, headache, and the loss of intellect and sleep, as well as the depletion of vitality, complexion, and strength. (AS.Sū.5.30)
Moreover, even when consuming accustomed foods,
the taste-carrying vessels (rasavahāḥ sirāḥ) do not convey the flavor to him, because their openings are smeared by the humors (doṣa).
Therefore, even a person in good health should employ emesis and the other therapies according to the prescribed rules;
for the *doṣas*, though subdued by fasting and digestive treatments, may sometimes become aggravated again.
But for those who have been purified by the purificatory therapies (saṃśodhana), there is no recurrence [of the disease];
henceforth, one should apply [the treatments] in due order and according to what is appropriate.

One who knows the proper time should prescribe proven elixirs (*rasāyana*) and aphrodisiac formulations (*vṛṣyayoga*) for those emaciated by medicinal therapy; subsequently, nourishing food should be administered as a wholesome regimen.
Through rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, wheat, meat, milk, ghee, and so forth,
combined with heart-pleasing and digestive medicinal substances, these provide relish and promote digestion.
Through massage, dry powdering, bathing, non-unctuous enemas, and unctuous enemas,
he thus obtains relief as well as the full digestive power of the fire.
The clarity of intellect, complexion, and the sense faculties; virility and longevity;
and those [diseases] arising from spirits, poison, wind, fire, wounds, fractures, and so forth.
Desire, anger, fear, and the like are the adventitious diseases;
their abandonment, the restraint of the senses, and mindfulness are the remedies for errors of judgment.
Knowledge of place, time, and the self; following the conduct of the virtuous;
the pacification rites prescribed in the Atharva Veda; and the worship of adverse planets.
The means for perceiving the elements and so forth have been indicated individually;
this rule has been set forth in brief for the purpose of their non-arising.
For the pacification of both innate and adventitious disorders that have arisen,
one should purify the accumulation of *doṣas* produced in the cold season during spring, and those produced in the summer during the rainy season.
At the end of the rainy season, one who has properly and quickly [adopted these measures] never suffers from diseases born of the season (AS.Sū.5.62).
One who constantly practices wholesome diet and conduct, acts with circumspection, and is unattached to the objects of the senses [is likewise free from such ailments] (AS.Sū.5.63).
AS.Sū.5.63 One who is generous, impartial, devoted to truth, patient, and a servant of the wise becomes free from disease.
AS.Sū.5.64 One should never exert effort toward unattainable objects, but always show respect for those things that are subject to loss.

Diseases do not afflict one who has conquered the senses, provided that there is no adverse fate at that time. When the season is favorable, sense-objects are pleasing, and actions are righteous, then one's work results in happiness.
"The mind is to be disciplined and the intellect made clear; for the wise man, these always lead to happiness.
Thus ends the fifth chapter.
The Sixth Chapter. Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "Knowledge of Mobile Substances."
Thus have the great sages, Ātreya and others, said:
"It is life-sustaining, satiating, pleasing to the heart, refreshing, and an awakener of the intellect. (AS.Sū.6.2)
Thin, with its flavor unmanifest, refined, cool, pure, and like nectar; light due to being drawn up and released by the sun, it removes wind and phlegm.
Ganges water, fallen from the sky, conquered by the sun, moon, and wind, overcomes the afflictions of bile, blood, and poison through its coolness, life-sustaining power, and gentleness. (AS.Sū.6.4)
Regarding the state of being beneficial or harmful, that [food] further depends upon place and time;
for instance, pure rice-gruel, when showered [with milk], remains as radiant as silver.
That water from the Ganges should be drunk while it is neither turbid nor discolored; otherwise,
it is of the sea and must not be drunk, except during the month of Āśvayuja.
One should always drink water that has fallen from the surface of a dug well, a stone slab, or a cloth, provided it is contained in a vessel made of gold or clay and remains unspoiled. (AS.Sū.6.7)
In the absence of that [color], that which is situated on the ground and resembles the atmosphere—
whether it be white, yellowish (kaṣāya), sweet, black, or pale— is [to be understood accordingly]. AS.Sū.6.8 AS.Sū.6.8

In a dark-blue region it is astringent and sweet; in a saline, alkaline soil it is salty; in a tawny soil it is alkaline; and in a mixed soil, it is mixed; furthermore, in a soil where the qualities of water predominate, it is so too.
It is sweet, salty, and sour when the quality of earth predominates;
it is bitter, pungent, and astringent when fire predominates; and it is [bitter, pungent, and astringent] when wind predominates.

In a place that imitates the divine, where the subtle flavors are unmanifest, which abounds in the qualities of space, and which is pure, broad, dark, and white, it should be struck by the sun and wind.
That [water] is further remembered as being of eight kinds: from wells, springs, lakes, ponds, streams, cascades, springs,
and from tanks or rivers (AS.Sū.6.12).
Well water is alkaline, increases bile, stimulates digestion, and is not excessively wind-increasing.
Lake water is sweet and light; pond water is heavy and increases wind.
The water from a spring is pungent, increases bile, and removes the [other] humors;
water from a well is sweet and subdues bile; and the water of a pond is sweet and fragrant.

One should prescribe that [water] which is not river-born (nādeya) as being wind-increasing (vātala), dry (rūkṣa), and pungent (kaṭuka). Regarding the heaviness or lightness [of water], it depends on its proximity to desert lands (dhanvan), marshy regions (anūpa), or mountains (mahīdhra).
Those rivers that flow toward the western ocean, those that flow swiftly, and those with pure water are generally wholesome; others are the opposite.

The waters of the rivers originating from the Himalayas and Malaya mountains— though their waters have been exhausted by the tossing, splashing, and breaking against rocks— remain wholesome when they reach the path.
Those originating from Mahendra cause worms, elephantiasis, and diseases of the heart, throat, and head; those arising from Prācya, Avanti, and Aparānta cause hemorrhoids.

Furthermore, those originating from the Sahya and Vindhya mountains cure abdominal diseases and elephantiasis; those born in the Pāriyātra mountains destroy the humors and cure skin diseases, anemia, and diseases of the head.

The waters of the ocean, produced by the strength and prowess [of the gods], cause the three humors; they are turbid with the putrefaction of insects, snakes, urine, and feces, as well as weeds and masses of grass.
Covered with mud, lotuses, moss, thick leaves, and so forth,
unseen by the sun, the moon, or the wind, and infested by small creatures. (AS.Sū.6.21)
It is excessively rained upon, discolored, turbid, and thick with foam;
it is tasteless, foul-smelling, and heated, being so cold that it can be grasped by the teeth. (AS.Sū.6.22)
That which is non-seasonal, that which is celestial, and that which is the first menstrual flow;
as well as that which is defiled by contact with the threads of spiders and other insects, or by feces, urine, and poison.
One should administer that [medicine] through bathing and drinking to alleviate thirst, flatulence, abdominal enlargement,
fever, cough, weak digestion, ophthalmia, itching, swellings, and other such ailments. (AS.Sū.6.24)
One should avoid that; however, in the absence of water, another [liquid] is recommended. By straining it through thick cloth, one protects against tiny living beings.
For one who has become putrid, there is heating with fire, the sun, or iron balls;
[and treatment] with *parṇī*, roots, lotus stalks, knots, pearls, *kataka* nuts, and *śaivala* moss.
Or one should effect its purification with cloth or *gomeda* stone;
the destruction of foul odors is achieved with *pāṭalā*, *karavīra*, and other flowers.
Water is not [suitable] water if it comes from another region while one's own water has not been digested;
nor is boiled water [suitable] when there is undigested matter (āmadoṣa), nor other [water] when it is digested or even when it has been fully processed.
This procedure is for cold; however, when there is heat or indigestion, one should avoid the cold. Water is the life-force of living beings, and the entire universe is composed of it.
Therefore, by means of absolute negation, water is not prohibited anywhere; otherwise,
there would be dryness of the mouth, weakness of the limbs, and so forth, or even death from the lack of it.
For neither one who is healthy nor one who is diseased can subsist without water; it alone, when prepared with medicinal herbs, whether cooked or raw, warm and wholesome, is beneficial.
Having observed that nectar [is beneficial] when administered in the proper measure, whereas poison is otherwise; even water, when administered in excess to one who is thirsty, acts as such.
In one afflicted by fever, especially, it turns into a state of phlegm and bile;
it increases undigested matter (āma), thirst, sleep, drowsiness, flatulence, and heaviness of the limbs.

It cures cough, weak digestion, nausea, excessive salivation, dyspnea, and catarrh. Though it is sweet in its digestive transformation (pāka) and cold in potency (vīrya), when administered, it is hot.

Therefore, one should not separate [the patient] from the administration of non-unctuous enemas due to lightness; in cases of undigested matter (āma) and constipation, one should drink lukewarm water even if not thirsty.
To whatever extent they moisten the food, excessive moisture destroys the digestive fire;
obstructed by phlegm and wind, it releases its binding upon the stomach.
Food liquefied with lukewarm water is digested quickly,
as is the case for one whose doshas and digestive fire are unstable, or whose strength is depleted by disease.

Even a small amount of unboiled water is not beneficial, for it aggravates the three *doṣas*; because it is an adversary to the digestive fire (*tejas*), one with weak digestion should avoid such water.

All those suffering from splenic disorders, abdominal tumors, abscesses, or gulma; those with anemia, abdominal enlargement, diarrhea, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), emaciation, or edema—[should all be treated in this manner].
If one is unable [to fast], one may certainly drink a small amount of food prepared with medicinal herbs; even a healthy person should drink only a little, except during autumn and the summer heat.

Water drunk at the beginning of a meal causes loss of digestive fire and emaciation of the body; when drunk at the end, it causes corpulence and the upward movement of phlegm from the stomach. (AS.Sū.6.41)
It brings about a moderate state of the bodily constituents, equilibrium of the elements, easy digestion, and comfort;
it also cures coldness, intoxication, exhaustion, fainting, vomiting, fatigue, and dizziness. (AS.Sū.6.42)
It destroys thirst, burning heat, pitta, blood disorders, and poisons;
it should be reduced by one-third or one-half depending on the location, season, and the relative heaviness or lightness [of the patient's condition].
Water that has been boiled until it is free of scum, devoid of bubbles, pure, and wholesome is beneficial for hiccups,
flatulence, wind-disorders, phlegm, thirst, cough, dyspnea, and chronic rhinitis.
In cases of pain in the flanks, absence of fat, recent purification,
and acute fever, [the diet] is digestive-stimulant, carminative, beneficial for the throat, light, and a cleanser of the bladder (AS.Sū.6.45).
Water that has been heated over stone, silver, earth, gold, tin, or copper,
whether hot or cold, destroys the three *doṣas* and conquers thirst and diarrhea.
Water that has been boiled and then cooled is light, non-greasy, and removes fatigue;
it is recommended in cases of the combination of pitta and kapha, as well as in sannipāta.
Water that has lost its fiery quality becomes sour upon boiling and aggravates all the *doṣas*;
this remains true even for water produced from snow that has stood overnight.
That which is produced from moonstone (candrakānta) removes phlegm and wind through its extreme coldness, heaviness, and stability; it also wards off demons, poisons, and bile-fevers.
Coconut water improves vision, intellect, complexion, and stability; it is sweet, cooling, light, unctuous, aphrodisiac, and refreshing.
Divine water, excellent in the rainy season, removes thirst, bile, and wind, stimulates digestion, and cleanses the bladder; non-rainwater is inferior— thus ends the section on water.
It has a sweet taste and post-digestive effect, is unctuous, provides ojas, increases the bodily tissues (dhātus),
alleviates vāta and pitta, is aphrodisiac, increases kapha, and is heavy and cold.
Generally, milk here is that of the cow; it is vitalizing, a rejuvenative (rasāyana),
beneficial for those suffering from chest wounds or emaciation, intellect-promoting, strengthening, galactagogue, and laxative.
It destroys fatigue, giddiness, intoxication, misfortune, dyspnea, cough, excessive thirst, hunger, chronic fever, difficulty in urination, and hemoptysis.

Cold buffalo [milk] is more harmful than [cold] water, fire, or lack of sleep; it becomes light when accompanied by drinking little water, physical exercise, and the consumption of pungent and bitter substances.
Goat’s meat conquers wasting diseases, fever, dyspnea, hemorrhagic disorders, and diarrhea.
Camel’s meat is slightly dry, hot, and salty; it stimulates the digestive fire and is light.
Human flesh is recommended for [the treatment of] disorders caused by vāta and kapha, abdominal distension, worms, swelling, abdominal enlargements,
and hemorrhoids; it also conquers diseases of the eyes caused by vāta, pitta, and blood.
AS.Sū.6.57 Through saturations, drops, and nasal administrations, the warm woolen [blanket] is unwholesome;
it cures diseases of Vāta, yet it produces hiccups, dyspnea, pitta, and kapha.
The milk of a female elephant produces stability; that of a solid-hoofed animal is very hot and light;
[the milk of] a tree-branch [animal] removes wind, is slightly sour and salty, and causes dullness.

Milk causes excessive secretions and is heavy when raw; however, when boiled with skill, it becomes otherwise. If over-boiled, it becomes even heavier; but when warm from the milk-pail, it is like nectar.
For those who eat oil-cake and sour substances, that [food] is extremely heavy and causes excessive secretions; moreover,
due to lack of physical activity, the food taken at dawn is considered more harmful than that taken at nightfall.
By this, "levity" (laghimā) has been explained; it is like movement even in [inert] natures,
and in short things, as well as in bodies larger than oneself, and even in flesh— one should understand it in this way and so forth.
Curd (dadhi) has an acidic post-digestive taste (pāka-rasa), is constipating (grāhin), heavy, and hot; it conquers vāta but produces fat (medas),
semen (śukra), strength (bala), phlegm (śleṣman), bile (pitta), blood (rakta), digestive fire (agni), and swelling (śopha).
Rociṣṇu is recommended for loss of appetite, cold fever, irregular fever, catarrh,
and difficulty in urination; however, it is parching in cases of malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī-gada).
One should not eat at night, nor should one eat hot food during the spring, summer, or autumn;
nor should one eat without mung bean soup, nor without honey, nor without ghee, nor without rock salt.
A fever that is neither free of impurities, nor constant, nor mild, but otherwise,
brings about blood-bile fever, erysipelas, leprosy, and anemia.
Buttermilk is light, astringent and sour, digestive, and it conquers kapha and vāta; it cures swelling,
abdominal enlargement, hemorrhoids, disorders of the duodenum, urinary retention, and anorexia.

It overcomes abdominal tumors (gulma), splenic disorders, complications from medicated ghee, artificial poisons (gara), and anemia (pāṇḍvāmaya). Likewise, whey (mastu) that has been strained is light, cleanses the channels, and conquers constipation (viṣṭambha).
Freshly extracted butter is cool, sweet, astringent, and sour;
it conquers consumption, hemorrhoids, sciatica, blood-bile disorders, and wind-diseases, while being constipating and digestive-stimulant.
That which originates from milk is astringent, conquers hemorrhagic disorders and eye diseases,
