and is recommended for the intellect, memory, intelligence, digestive fire, strength, longevity, semen, and vision.
For those desiring the luster and delicacy of youth, old age, progeny, or a beautiful voice;
and for those whose bodies are exhausted by wounds, emaciation, creeping diseases, weapons, or fire.
Ghee is the best among unctuous substances; it is cooling, restores youthfulness, and removes wind, bile, poison, insanity, emaciation, misfortune, and fever.
Boiled with the prescribed rites, this [preparation] possesses a thousandfold potency and performs a thousandfold actions;
it cures intoxication, epilepsy, fainting, and diseases arising from the head, ears, eyes, and the female reproductive tract.
The ancient [oil] overcomes diseases and cleanses and heals wounds;
it performs the aforementioned qualities and more, being like nectar itself.
And likewise, the scum of clarified butter (ghṛtamaṇḍa) is also dry, sharp, and thin.
Kilāṭa, dadhikūcīkā, takrapiṇḍaka, and moraṭā [are also similar].
Sakṣīra, śāka, pīyūṣa, rocanā, and vahnisādana increase the semen,
induce sleep, and produce kapha; they cause constipation and aggravate the heavy doṣas.
One should understand the qualities and defects of curd, clarified butter, and so forth, just as one does for milk:
cow's milk and its clarified butter are excellent, whereas those from a goat are censured.
Thus ends the section on milks (kṣīravarga). The juice of sugarcane is heavy, unctuous, nourishing, and it produces phlegm and urine.
The meat of the *vṛṣa* (bull) is aphrodisiac, cooling, and subdues *vāta*; however, it aggravates *vāta* after eating.
It pacifies *rakta-pitta*, and its taste is sweet both in its post-digestive effect (*pāka*) and its flavor (*rasa*).
That [food], even if initially salty, becomes like sugar-candy when bitten by the teeth,
due to the crushing pressure from the roots and tips of the teeth, the gnawing of insects, and the admixture of impurities.
And because it undergoes transformation after being held for some time, the *yāntrika* [variety] is burning, heavy, and constipating; therefore, among those, the *pauṇḍraka* is such.
The best [bamboo] possesses coolness, clarity, and sweetness; it is a portion following that [quality].
Then, in sequence, there are the Śātaparvaka, Kāntāra, Nēpāla, and others. (AS.Sū.6.80)
Phāṇita (unrefined treacle) is salty, astringent, warm, and slightly burning;
it is heavy, causes secretions to accumulate, promotes the accumulation of bodily waste, and cleanses the urine.
Washed jaggery (dhautaguḍa) does not cause excessive phlegm and promotes the evacuation of urine and feces; other types of jaggery, however, abound in worms, marrow, blood, fat, flesh, and phlegm.
They are pleasing to the heart, wholesome when old, and beneficial when fresh; they increase phlegm and diminish the digestive fire.
They are aphrodisiac, beneficial for those with emaciation or chest wounds, and they alleviate bleeding disorders (raktapitta) and wind (vāta).
Matsyaṇḍikā, khaṇḍa, and sitā are progressively more excellent in their qualities; yaṣa-śarkarā possesses those same qualities and is bitter, sweet, and astringent.
Sugar derived from *kāśa* and *darbha* leaves destroys the three *doṣas*. All types of sugar destroy burning sensations, thirst, vomiting, fainting, and hemorrhaging.
Among the products of sugar and sugarcane, unrefined treacle is the best;
it is beneficial for the eyes, acts as a laxative, and alleviates thirst, phlegm, poison, hiccups, and blood-bile disorders.
Honey conquers skin diseases, urinary disorders, worms, vomiting, dyspnea, cough, and diarrhea; it cleanses, heals, and promotes the healing of wounds, yet it increases wind (vāta).
It is dry, astringent, and sweet; honey-sugar is similar to it. When hot, it destroys heat, and when combined with hot substances, it overcomes that which is afflicted by heat.
Because they produce honey even from poisonous flowers due to their poisonous nature,
those bees and other insects are themselves poisonous.
In the case of emesis and non-unctuous enema (nirūha), honey mixed with warm [liquids] is not prohibited;
for in those two procedures, it is withdrawn quickly even before the medicine has reached digestion.
Honey is beneficial only in small quantities because of its heavy, rough, and astringent qualities, as well as its coldness;
for there is nothing more difficult to digest than it, which [leads to] indigestion and other ailments in a person.
Because it is antagonistic to [therapeutic] interventions, it kills instantly, like poison;
and because it consists of various substances, honey is the supreme "carrier" (yogavāhin) of medicinal properties.
*Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha*, Sūtra 6.92.

Therefore, when combined with aphrodisiac formulations, it follows the state of virility. Honey is of four types— *bhrāmara*, *pauṣpika*, *kṣaudra*, and *mākṣika*— each subsequent one being superior to the preceding.
"Among these, one should employ only the last two when they are old;
thus ends the section on Sugarcane (Ikṣu-varga).
In that [group], oil is primary because it is like its own source (the sugarcane), being sharp and pervasive. (AS.Sū.6.94)
It causes skin diseases, is detrimental to the eyes, is subtle and hot, and does not increase *kapha*.
It is capable of nourishing those who are emaciated and reducing those who are corpulent.
AS.Sū.6.95 It cures constipation and destroys worms; through its processing, it conquers all diseases.
AS.Sū.6.96 Through the application of this oil, one becomes free from old age, free from defects, and has overcome fatigue.
In ancient times, the lords of the Daityas possessed exceedingly great strength in battle. Oil extracted from the *satikta*, *uṣaṇa*, and *airaṇḍa* plants is sweet, laxative, and heavy.

It conquers abdominal tumors, glandular swellings, disorders of wind and phlegm, abdominal enlargement, and intermittent fevers; it also overcomes pain and swelling localized in the waist, genitals, abdomen, and back.
That which is produced from the castor-oil plant (raktairaṇḍa) is sharp, hot, slimy, and foul-smelling;
that produced from hemp (umā) and safflower (kusumbha) is hot and causes skin diseases, phlegm, and bile.
The root of *dantī*, *karañja* which destroys demons, *ariṣṭa*, and *śigru*;
and that which originates from *suvarcalā*, *iṅgudī*, *pīlu*, *śāṅkhinī*, and *nīpa*.
That which is produced from the heartwood of *sarala*, *agaru*, *devāhva*, and *śiṃśapā* (AS.Sū.6.100),
as well as that derived from *tuvara* and *āruṣkara* (AS.Sū.6.101), is sharp, pungent, and sour, and it generates *pitta*.
It cures hemorrhoids, skin diseases, worms, phlegm, semen disorders, fat, and wind.
One should prescribe the bitter fruits of *karañja* and *nimba*, which are not excessively hot.

Astringent, bitter, and pungent substances that are fibrous are for the cleansing of wounds. Those produced from *tuvara* and *aruṣkara*, being extremely hot, sharp, and pungent, [are used for cauterization].
Specifically for the destruction of worms and skin diseases, as well as for purgation from above and below,
[the fruit] derived from *akṣa*, *atimuktaka*, *akṣoḍa*, coconut, and *madhūka* [is used].
That which is produced from cucumber (*trapusa*), gourd (*urvāruka*), bottle-gourd (*kūṣmāṇḍa*), *śleṣmātaka*,
and *priyāla* (AS.Sū.6.104) removes wind and bile, is beneficial for the hair, increases phlegm, is heavy, and is cold. (AS.Sū.6.105)
That which originates from *śrīparṇī* and *kiṃśuka* pacifies *pitta* and *śleṣman*.
Among these, sesame oil is the best, while safflower oil is the lowest.
Fat and marrow subdue wind (vāta) and bestow strength, bile (pitta), and phlegm (kapha);
one should know that fat is similar in its essential nature to these two.
Fat derived from the owl, the pig, the domestic goose,
and the cock is excellent within its own respective groups; likewise, that derived from the crocodile and the buffalo is preeminent among its own kind.
The fat of the kākamadgu bird is like that; likewise, the fat derived from the kāraṇḍa bird is censured.
Alcohol (madya) is digestive, appetizing, sharp, pungent, and bestows satisfaction and nourishment.
AS.Sū.6.109 It is pungent and bitter in taste, sour in its post-digestive transformation (pāka), and laxative.
AS.Sū.6.110 It is slightly astringent, and it promotes voice, health, intelligence, complexion, and lightness.
It is beneficial for those who have lost their sleep or suffer from excessive sleep; it vitiates pitta and blood,
is wholesome for the lean and the obese, is dry, subtle, and cleanses the channels (srotas).
When drunk according to the proper method, it removes wind and phlegm; otherwise, it is like poison. Fresh [alcohol] is heavy and generates those [same] doshas, whereas old [alcohol] is the opposite.
This drink should not be administered to those who have undergone hot treatments, nor to those who have been purged, nor to those suffering from hunger;
it should not be excessively sharp, soft, clear, or thick, nor should it be spoiled.
AS.Sū.6.113 It removes abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), and emaciation; it is unctuous and heavy.
AS.Sū.6.114 It subdues wind and bile, and promotes fat, blood, breast milk, urine, and phlegm.
Vāruṇī liquor possesses those same qualities; it is pleasing to the heart, light, and sharp,
and it destroys colic, cough, vomiting, asthma, constipation, flatulence, and chronic rhinitis.
It is beneficial for colic, dysentery, thirst, swelling, and hemorrhoids.
Jagala is digestive and constipating, and medaka is likewise dry.

Bakkaśa liquor, because its essence has been extracted, causes constipation and provokes the bodily humors (doṣas). Sura liquor made from vibhītaka fruits is not excessively intoxicating, is light, and is wholesome.
In cases of ulcers, anemia, and skin diseases, it is not excessively contraindicated.
Yavasurā causes constipation, is heavy, dry, and aggravates the three doṣas.
Kauhalī is nourishing and heavy, while madhūlaka increases phlegm.
Ariṣṭa possesses the qualities of its constituent ingredients and is superior to all other alcoholic liquors in its properties.
It cures malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), anemia (pāṇḍu), skin diseases (kuṣṭha), hemorrhoids (arśas), consumption (śoṣa), edema (śopha), abdominal enlargements (udara), and fever (jvara);
it also destroys abdominal tumors (gulma), worms (krimi), and splenic enlargement (plīha). It is astringent, pungent, and increases vāta.
Wine made from grapes (mārdvika) is scraping, pleasing to the heart, not excessively hot, sweet, and laxative;
it diminishes pitta and vāta slightly, and destroys anemia, urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, and worms.
Date-palm liquor (khārjūra) has qualities slightly inferior to this [grape wine], is wind-increasing, and heavy.
Sugar-cane liquor (śārkara) is fragrant, pleasant to the palate, agreeable to the heart, not excessively intoxicating, and sweet.
Gauḍa [liquor] promotes the passage of urine, feces, and flatus; it is nourishing and digestive. Śīdhu increases vāta and pitta, and it removes disorders of fat and phlegm.
It destroys fat, swelling, abdominal enlargements, and hemorrhoids; among these, the fermented juice (pakvarasa) is the best.
AS.Sū.6.124: Honey-ferment (madhvāsava) is excising, sharp, and overcomes urinary disorders, chronic rhinitis, and cough.
Surāsava is sharp in its intoxication, sweet, pungent, and dispels vāta.
Maireya is sweet, exhilarating, laxative, nourishing, and heavy.
Wine fermented from dhātakī that has aged is dry, appetizing, and digestive. Grape wine is equal to honey; indeed, it is an excellent digestive stimulant.

AS.Sū.6.126 A fermented liquor made from grape juice (*mṛdvīka-ikṣurasa-āsava*) is said to be similar to *mārdvīka*. AS.Sū.6.127 A fermented liquor prepared by combining [ingredients] is pleasing to the heart, increases wind (*vātala*), and follows the properties of the medicinal herbs used.
Grapes, sugarcane, honey, and the five types of grain beginning with *śāli* and *vrīhi* are the sources of intoxicants;
anything other than these is a counterfeit intoxicant.
One should recognize wine as being of various types according to its predominant qualities resulting from the mixture of its ingredients.
Śukta (fermented gruel) increases blood, pitta, and kapha, and it facilitates the downward movement of vāta.
It is burning, extremely sharp, pungent, beneficial for the heart, appetizing, and laxative; it stimulates digestion, has a cooling touch, and destroys anemia, eye diseases, and worms.
Jaggery, sugarcane juice, wine, *mārdvīka* liquor, and fermented gruel (*śukta*) are progressively lighter in the order mentioned.
One should know that bulbs, roots, fruits, and so forth, when fermented in the same manner, are likewise [lighter].
Fermented grain water (śāṇḍākī) and other sour liquids made from unfermented grains are appetizing and light.
Fermented rice water (dhānyāmla) is purgative, sharp, hot, increases bile, and is cool to the touch.
It removes fatigue and exhaustion, is appetizing, stimulates digestion, and alleviates pain in the bladder.
It is recommended for non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana), is beneficial for the heart, light, and dispels wind and phlegm.
Sauvīraka and tuṣodaka, when endowed with these very same qualities,
destroy worms, heart disease, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, and anemia.
One should know that these are prepared respectively with husked and unhusked barley;
thus ends the section on intoxicating drinks (madyavarga).
The urine derived from cows, goats, sheep, buffaloes, elephants, horses, camels,
and donkeys is bilious (pittala), dry, sharp, hot, with a salty after-taste, and pungent.
The light [formulation] conquers worms, edema, abdominal enlargements, constipation, colic, anemia,
kapha, and vata; it also overcomes Gulma, anorexia, poison, vitiligo, leprosy, and hemorrhoids.

In purgation, non-unctuous enemas, external applications, sudation, and so forth, cow’s urine is highly esteemed; it is the best among those [substances] that stimulate digestion, promote digestion, and act as a laxative.

Goat's [milk] removes dyspnea and cough; through filling the ears with it, it conquers earache. One should apply the [urine] derived from elephants and horses for [the treatment of] kilāsa (vitiligo) and kṣāra (alkaline preparations).
The dung of the donkey (rāsabha), which is astringent and bitter, cures insanity, epilepsy, worms, and urinary disorders; it also removes hiccup and dyspnea.
The meat of birds (vaiṣkira) removes the exhaustion of strength on long journeys and cures wind diseases;
the meat of beasts of prey (prasaha) subdues epilepsy and insanity.
The bile produced by large deer removes skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*),
cures eye diseases of aquatic creatures, and subdues even aggravated *pitta*.
Bile is bitter, antidotal to poison, and a digestive stimulant; it conquers phlegm and wind.
The bitter *rocanā* removes evil, while human urine destroys poison.
"By means of the groups of water, milk, sugarcane juice, oil, and liquor, respectively—
thus has this one portion of liquids been illustrated in a general manner. (AS.Sū.6.143)
Thus ends the sixth chapter.
The seventh chapter:
Now we shall expound the chapter entitled "The Knowledge of the Nature of Food."
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:
"The *rakta*, *mahān*, *sakalama*, *atūrṇaka*, and *śakunāhṛta* [are the types of *mudga*]."
Śārāmukha, dīrghaśūka, lodhraśūka, sugandhika;
puṇḍra, pāṇḍu, puṇḍarīka, pramoda, and gaura-śārivā.
The *kāñcana*, *mahiṣa*, *śūka*, *dūṣaka*, and *kusumāṇḍaka*;
the *lāṅgala* and those called *lohavāla*— these are the *kardama* [fevers], which fear the cold.
The *pataṅga*, *tapanīya*, and other auspicious varieties of *śāli* rice are sweet in both digestion and taste; they are unctuous, aphrodisiac, and cause the feces to be formed and scanty.
AS.Sū.7.5 Those [lotuses] that have an astringent aftertaste are wholesome, light, diuretic, and cooling.
AS.Sū.7.6 Among those growing on stalks, the red variety is the best; it cures thirst and the three doṣas.
The *mahān* is greater than that, and the *kalama* is greater than that;
beyond those are the *yavaka*, *hāyana*, *pāṃsuvāpya*, *naiṣadhaka*, and so forth.
Sweet, warm, heavy, unctuous, sour in digestion, and increasing *kapha* and *pitta*,
they facilitate the passage of urine and feces; yet each preceding one among these is more censured than the next.
AS.Sū.7.8:
*Ṣaṣṭika* rice is unctuous, absorbent, light, sweet, pacifies the three *doṣas*, is stable, and cold.
AS.Sū.7.9: Among *vrīhi* grains, *ṣaṣṭika* is the best; among those, the white is superior to the black-white.
Then, in sequence: mahāvrīhi, kṛṣṇavrīhi, and jatūmukha;
(AS.Sū.7.10) kukkuṭa, aṇḍaka, lāba, akṣa, pārāvataka, and sūkara.
Varaka, koddālaka, ujjāla, cīna, śārada, and dardura;
as well as gandhana and kuruvinda— these are considered to differ only slightly in their qualities.
Another variety of rice, *vrīhi*, is sweet with a sour post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), increases bile (*pitta*), and is heavy.
The *pāṭala* rice, however, causes excessive urine, feces, and heat, and aggravates all three humors (*tridoṣa*).
Kaṅgu, kodrava, jūrṇāhva, gadī, varuṇapādikā;
śyāmāka, toyaśyāmāka, hastiśyāmāka, and śilbikā.
Śiśiroddālanī, nīvāra, varūka, baraka, and utkaṭā;
madhūlikā, anta, nirgaṇḍī, veṇuparṇī, and praśāntikā.
Gavethu, kāṇḍalauhitya, toyaparṇī, mukunda,
and rāsnā remove phlegm and bile; they are dry, astringent-sweet, and cooling.
[The Priyaṅgu group] increases vāta, binds feces and urine, is light, and has a scraping (lekhanā) nature.
Among them, Priyaṅgu promotes the healing of fractures, is nourishing (bṛṃhaṇī), and is heavy.
Koradūṣa is most palatable, cooling to the touch, and removes poison. Uddālaka, however, is hot in its potency, while nīvāra increases phlegm.
Madhūlikā is especially cooling in potency, unctuous, and aphrodisiac.
Barley is dry, cold, heavy, sweet, laxative, and produces feces and wind.
It is aphrodisiac, promotes stability, and overcomes urine disorders, fat, bile, and phlegm;
it also conquers chronic rhinitis, dyspnea, cough, stiffness of the thighs, and diseases of the throat and skin.
Those called *anuyava* should be known as inferior in quality to *yava*.
Bamboo-barley (*veṇuyava*) is hot, laxative, astringent, and increases wind and bile.
Wheat is aphrodisiac, cooling, heavy, unctuous, life-sustaining, and it subdues wind and bile;
it promotes healing, is sweet, provides stability, and is laxative.
Pathyā, nandīmukhī, śītā, kaṣāyā, madhurā, and laghu—
this is the group of awned grains (śūkadhānyavarga).

AS.Sū.7.22 Legumes such as *śimbija*, mung beans (*mudga*), *maṅgalya* beans, forest mung beans (*vanamudga*), and *makuṣṭha*; as well as lentils (*masūra*), *kaphala*, *āḍhakī*, and various kinds of chickpeas (*caṇaka*).
Astringent, sweet, and light, they cause constipation and flatulence;
being dry, with bound feces, and cold, they are beneficial when pungent in their post-digestive transformation (vipāka).
In cases of bile, blood, phlegm, and fat, [these are used] by application as soups, ointments, and so forth.
Among pulses, mung beans (*mudga*) are the best; they are light and produce little wind (*vāta*).
Among those, the green varieties are superior; makuṣṭhas cause worms.
Masūras are highly praised for external applications and the like, and they are extremely astringent.
Rājamāṣa beans are heavy, produce abundant feces, are coarse, and are excessively wind-increasing (vātala).
Kulattha pulses are astringent-sweet, coarse, and hot; they increase blood and bile (raktapitta).
They destroy chronic rhinitis, dyspnea, cough, hemorrhoids, hiccups, flatulence, and disorders of kapha and vāta;
they also cure seminal disorders, urinary calculi, semen, visual impairment, swelling, and abdominal enlargement.
The *niṣpāva* (flat bean) is constipating, light, sharp, sour in its post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*),
and causes a burning sensation; however, it is laxative, dry, astringent-sweet, and heavy.
When ripe, it is sour, causes wind and flatulence, and produces breast milk, urine, blood, and bile; it is hot,
causes a burning sensation, and removes defects of vision, semen disorders, phlegm, swelling, and pain.
Black gram (māṣa) is unctuous, promotes strength, phlegm, impurities,
and bile; it is laxative, heavy, hot, subdues wind (vāta), is sweet, increases semen, and acts as a purgative.
One should know the fruits of *kākāṇḍolā* and *ātmaguptā* to be possessed of excellent qualities;
those of *kuśa*, *āmra*, and *śimbī* are sweet, alleviate wind and bile, and are cooling.
Various types of pulses (śimbijātayaḥ) are sweet, cooling, heavy, strength-depleting, and parching by nature; they are rich in oil and should be eaten by those who possess strength.
Sesame is unctuous, hot, bitter, pungent, astringent, and sweet;
it promotes intelligence, improves the hair, is heavy, improves the complexion, is cool to the touch, and subdues *vāta*.
AS.Sū.7.34 It produces little urine, is pungent in its post-digestive effect, and increases intellect, digestive fire, kapha, and pitta.
AS.Sū.7.34 Black salt is highly praised; next to it is white salt, and after that, red salt.

The seed of the safflower (kusumbha) is unctuous, sweet, bitter, and hot; it increases phlegm and bile, is heavy, impairs vision and semen, and is pungent in its post-digestive effect (pāka). In this context, the black gram (*māṣa*) is the lowest among all [legumes], and the barley (*yavaka*) is the lowest among those produced from stalks.
Fresh grain, as well as that which is grown in irrigated fields or in paddy fields, causes excessive secretions (*abhiṣyandi*).

Light [food] is that which has been stored for a year, grown on burnt earth, or produced on dry land; likewise, legumes that have sprouted quickly, are dehusked, and have been roasted by the proper method.
Thus ends the section on leguminous grains (śimbidhānyavarga). Lightness of maṇḍa, peyā, vilepī, and odana [is also to be understood].

As before, the *maṇḍa* (gruel) prepared with *śiva* (ginger) there promotes the downward movement of wind (*vāta*), destroys thirst, exhaustion, and residual morbid humors, acts as a digestive stimulant, and restores the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*).
It softens the channels, induces perspiration, and kindles the digestive fire;
it removes hunger, thirst, exhaustion, debility, abdominal diseases, and fever. (AS.Sū.7.40)
Emulsive food mixed with *pathyā* is wholesome, stimulating digestion and promoting maturation;
thin gruel is astringent, pleasing to the heart, quenches thirst, stimulates digestion, and is beneficial.
For one who has been purified of wounds and eye diseases and is weak after drinking oil,
rice that is well-washed, drained, steamed, and cooled of its heat is light.
That rice which is prepared with a decoction of fiery medicinal herbs and then fried is light; conversely, that which is prepared with milk, meat, and similar substances is heavy.

Thus, one should prescribe everything for those who are emaciated, those freed from disease, those who are pure, and those desiring purification, by means of substances, actions, combinations, measures, and so forth. (AS.Sū.7.44)

For those who are emaciated, wasted, and with injured chests, whose tissues, sense-faculties, and vitality are diminished; for those desiring [improvement in] vision, hearing, digestive fire, longevity, strength, complexion, and voice.
For those with fractured or dislocated joints, for those with wounds, and for those suffering from disorders of Vāta,
meat broth is highly beneficial; it is pleasing to the heart, wholesome, supremely aphrodisiac, nourishing, and invigorating.
Maudga (mung bean) is wholesome for those with cleansed wounds, throat diseases, and eye diseases; kaulattha (horse gram) promotes the downward movement of vāta and conquers gulma, tūnī, and pratūnī.

Bean soup (māṣasūpa) is considered best when its internal impurities have been thoroughly removed; likewise, *khalaka* and *āmbalika* soups are pleasing to the heart, digestive, and should be prepared with their appropriate medicinal herbs.
In that context, *rasa* is made with meat, *yūṣa* with grains, and *khala* with fruits;
while *kāmbalika* is known to consist primarily of roots, sesame paste, and sour ingredients. (AS.Sū.7.49)

They should be known as prepared or unprepared, according to whether they are possessed of or devoid of oil and other such ingredients; those with little meat and so forth are considered to be clear and salted with water.

In the case of gruel, meat broth, soup, and vegetables, there is an increasing degree of heaviness in each subsequent one; likewise, there is a distinct heaviness in thin, thick, sour, and sweet [preparations] respectively.
Preparations of sesame oil-cake, dried vegetables, sprouted grains,
*caṇḍākī-vaṭaka*, *dṛghna*— these are defective, debilitating, and heavy. (AS.Sū.7.52)
Parpaṭas are light and appetizing, while kṣāraparpaṭa is even lighter; rāgaṣāḍavas are pleasing to the heart, aphrodisiac, appetizing, yet heavy.

They provide nourishment and alleviate thirst, vomiting, diarrhea, wasting, fainting, and fatigue. Cold *mantha* (a churned drink) relieves thirst, vomiting, and fatigue, and bestows immediate strength.
For those who drink *mantha*, urinary disorders, wasting diseases, and skin diseases do not occur.
*Rasālā* is nourishing, aphrodisiac, unctuous, strengthening, and provides relish.
This drink relieves fatigue, hunger, thirst, and exhaustion; it is nourishing, heavy, constipating, diuretic, and beneficial for the heart, possessing the qualities of its constituent ingredients.
Parched grains (lāja) cut through thirst, vomiting, diarrhea, urinary disorders, fat, and phlegm;
they pacify cough and bile, stimulate digestion, and are light and cooling. (AS.Sū.7.57)
Pṛthuka (puffed rice) is heavy, strengthening, and causes the retention of phlegm and wind.
Dhānā (fried grain) is constipating, parching, satiating, scraping, and heavy.
Barley meal (saktu) removes throat ailments, eye diseases, worms, hunger, thirst, fatigue,
vomiting, and ulcers; it is light when drunk and bestows strength immediately.
A solid mass is said to be hard and heavy, while a lump is soft and light; due to its connection with fluidity, a bolus of parched grain flour is even lighter.
The same conceptualization applies to *śaṣkulī*, *modaka*, and so forth; and it has been explained that one should not eat them when separated by water, nor twice, nor at night, nor alone.

One should not eat groats after having already eaten other food, nor should one cut them with one's teeth; nor should one eat too many of the *karkandhu* and *badara* fruits, which alleviate fatigue, thirst, and exhaustion.

Roasted grain flour (saktu) has a sour taste, is pleasing to the heart, and possesses the qualities of its constituent ingredients; oil-cake (piṇyāka), however, causes emaciation, is parching, causes constipation, and impairs the eyesight.
Veśavāra is heavy, unctuous, and increases strength and nourishment.
Those made from mung beans and other such pulses are heavy, following the specific qualities of their constituent substances.
One should know that cakes cooked in glowing embers, earthen pans, frying pans, pits, and on coals—
though all of a single origin— are progressively lighter as they ascend; such is the section on prepared foods.
The hariṇa, eṇa, kuraṅga, ṛśya, gokarṇa, mṛgamātṛkā,
kālapucchaka, cāruṣka, varapota, śaśa, and oraṇa.
The śvadaṃṣṭra, aśarabha, koḍa, kāraka, śambara, karāla,
kṛtamāla, and pṛṣata are recorded as the deer species.
Lāvaka, vārtika, vartīra, raktavartmaka, and karkara;
kapiñjala, upacakra, cakora, and rurubāhu.
The vartaka, the vartikā, the tittiri, the krakara, and the śikhī; the one called tāracūḍa, the varaka, the gona, the girivartikā— these are [the birds].
Likewise, the *śārapada*, *indrāhva*, and *vāraṭa* are the *viṣkira* (scattering) birds;
as are the *śatapatra*, *bhṛṅgarāja*, *koyaṣṭi*, and *jīvajīvaka*.
The *khañjarīṭaka*, *hārīta*, *durnāmāri*,
*kṛśāgra*, *hā*, *laṭvā*, *laḍūṣa*, *vaṭahā*, *rokṣvela*, and *ḍiṇḍimāṇava*.
The Jaṭī, Dundubhi, Pārkāra, Lohapṛṣṭha, Kuliṅgaka,
Śārikā, Śuka, Śārṅga, Cirīṭī, Kakubha, and Yaṣṭika.
The mañjarīyaka, the dātyūha, the godhāputra, the priyātmaja,
the kalaviṅka, the parabhṛta, the kapota, and the aṅgāracūḍaka.
The pigeon, the francolin, and others are called "pecking birds" (pratudāḥ) among the twice-born.
The white, the dark, the variegated-backed, the black, the kākulī, and the mṛga [are also included].
The frog, cillaṭa, kūcīkā, iguana, porcupine, and śāṇḍaka;
the male snake, plantain tree, dog, mongoose, and so forth— these are the hole-dwellers.
Cows, donkeys, mules, camels, horses, leopards, lions, bears,
monkeys, cats, mice, tigers, wolves, brown bears, and hyenas.
The fox, jackal, hawk, blue jay, owl, dog, and crow; the rabbit-killer, vulture, osprey, bearded vulture, heron, and sparrow.
The *dhūmikā* and the *madhuhā* are among the predatory beasts and birds; [so too are] the buffalo, the *nyaṅku*, the *rohīta*, the boar, the *ruru*, and the elephant.
The *sṛmara*, the *camara*, the rhinoceros, and the *gavaya* are the great wild animals (*mahāmṛga*).
The *haṃsa*, *sārasa*, *kādamba*, *baka*, *kāraṇḍava*, and *plava* are [the water birds].
The Mṛṇālakaṇṭha, Cakravāka, Balākā, and Raktaśīrṣaka;
the Utkrośa, Puṇḍarīkākṣa, Śarārī, and Maṇituṇḍaka.
The kākatuṇḍa, ghanārāva, madgu, krauñca, ambukukkuṭa,
nadyākhya, mallikā, and other such water-dwelling birds; AS.Sū.7.80.
Fish: the Rohita, Pāṭhīna, tortoise, Kumbhīra, crab, pearl-oyster,
conch, Udru, Śambūka, Śapharī, Vartmi, and Candrikā.
The *bulūkī*, the crab, the crocodile, the *śiṃśumāra*, the *timiṅgila*, the *rājī*, the *cilicima*, and so forth— these they call the eight kinds of meat.
Regarding the origins (yoni), because the goat and the sheep have mixed habitats, they are considered indeterminate;
the first two are known as *jāṅgala* (arid) and *anūpa* (marshy), while the middle two are considered *sādhāraṇa* (intermediate).

They are called *viṣkira* (scattering) and so forth because they are associated with actions such as scattering [grain] and because they are eaten [in that manner]. Among them, those that have bound impurities (*baddhamala*) are the best meats for those who desire relish; they are cooling (*hima*).
Meat from wild animals, which is astringent, sweet, clear, and light,
is beneficial in cases of *sannipāta* where *pitta* is predominant, *vāta* is moderate, and *kapha* is subordinate.
Among these, the *tāmra* (red deer) is *hariṇa* (the spotted deer), while the *eṇa* (black antelope) is black; it is pleasing to the heart and subdues the three *doṣas*.
The *śaśa* (hare) is lighter than that, possesses all six tastes, is constipating, dry, and cold.
AS.Sū.7.87: That which has a pungent post-digestive effect (kaṭupāka), stimulates the digestive fire (agnikṛt), and is wholesome (pathya) when vāta is predominant in a sannipāta disorder;
likewise, the common quail (lāva) is not dry, whereas the grey partridge (kapiñjala) is slightly dry.
Doves and pigeons, as well as other wild birds, are highly esteemed; likewise,
quails and similar birds are nourishing, slightly warm, heavy, and unctuous.

Among those [birds], the partridge is the best; it promotes intelligence, digestive fire, strength, and semen; it is astringent, improves the complexion, and is supreme in alleviating disorders of wind and the combined humors (sannipāta).
Because it roams through arid and marshy lands, the peacock is unctuous, hot, heavy, and nourishing;
yet it is not very wholesome, though it is beneficial for the ears, the voice, youth, and the eyes.
And likewise, the wild cock is aphrodisiac; however, the domestic one increases phlegm and is heavy.
Karakaras and upacakrakas are beneficial for the intellect, stimulate the digestive fire, and are pleasing to the heart.
The *kāṇakapota* pigeon is heavy, salty, and causes all the [three] *doṣas*.
From this point on, the groups [of substances] are increasingly heavy, hot, unctuous, and sweet.

The meat of large animals produces urine and semen, is strengthening, subdues wind (vāta), and increases phlegm (kapha) and bile (pitta). Among these, the carnivorous and the predatory animals are cold-natured.

They are beneficial for the eyes, promote the easy passage of feces and urine, are fleshy, and have a pungent post-digestive effect; they are supremely beneficial for those afflicted by chronic hemorrhoids, disorders of the duodenum (grahaṇī), and consumption (śoṣa).
The iguana neutralizes poison, and the rat increases semen;
[these cure] dry cough, exhaustion, excessive digestive fire, intermittent fever, and chronic catarrh.
Cow's meat cures emaciation and pure disorders of wind (*vāta*); sparrows are phlegm-forming (*śleṣmala*), unctuous, subdue wind, and are excellent for increasing semen.
The buffalo is heavy, hot, unctuous, and produces sleep, firmness, and large skin;
likewise, the boar removes fatigue and bestows relish, semen, and strength.
The swan (*haṃsa*) produces a sweet voice, conquers bile and blood, is nourishing, and is cooling. Fish produce phlegm and bile, but are supreme destroyers of wind (*vāta*).
Because they move against the current and leap through the air,
Rohita is the foremost among them, while Cilicima is the lowest.
Because it wanders outside its proper range, it indeed produces all kinds of defects.
The crab is supremely aphrodisiac, nourishing, pleasing, and heavy.
Meat from a goat that is neither too cold, heavy, nor unctuous is free from defects;
because it shares similar properties with the bodily tissues (*dhātu*), it is non-obstructive and nourishing.
The opposite of this should be known as the sheep's [meat], for it is nourishing. One should avoid meat that is excessively fatty, or that has been killed by disease or poisoned by water.
A cow that has died naturally, is full of smoke, has not been kept in its usual pasture, and is emaciated;
or one that has been recently killed and is in the prime of its youth— such meat is praised as pure and fragrant.
The black antelope, the kuraṅga deer, the hariṇa deer, the hare, the quail, the kapiñjala partridge,
the tittiri partridge, the krakara, the monitor lizard, the porcupine, the vulture, and the lord of beasts (the lion).
Likewise, the śārika, the nyaṅku, the haṃsa, the rohitaka, the tortoise,
and the vartman are recorded as the foremost among their respective species, and even among those, they are considered the most excellent.
The common quail, the grey partridge, the iguana, the lion, the condemned cow,
the frog, the ruru deer, and the one-eyed pigeon— these are forbidden; the rest have been explained as appropriate.
The eggs of young animals are heavy, while those of old animals are predominantly composed of sinews, weak, and heavy with impurities. They are astringent and sweet in taste.
In the case of males and females, the first half and the latter half [of the body] are heavy when pregnant;
in the case of females among quadrupeds and birds, however, the male is light.
One should diagnose heaviness of the head, shoulders, thighs, back, waist, and legs,
as well as of the stomach and the large intestine, in the order mentioned.
And among the bodily constituents beginning with blood, each subsequent one is more significant than the preceding;
[more significant] than flesh are the testicles, the penis, the kidneys, the liver, and the rectum.
Thus ends the section on meat (Māṃsavarga). Pāṭhā, śaṭī, śrūṣā, suniṣaṇḍa, and satīnaja constitute the vegetables (śāka).
Rājakṣava and vāstuka destroy the three doṣas, are light,
and are astringent; suniṣaṇḍa kindles the digestive fire and is aphrodisiac, but among these, rājakṣava is the best.
Vāstuka destroys disorders of the digestive tract and hemorrhoids, and it is a laxative;
it cures the three doṣas, leprosy, and is aphrodisiac, hot, and a rejuvenative (rasāyana).

Kākamācī is laxative, beneficial for the voice, sour, and a stimulator of the digestive fire (agni-dīpanī); it is beneficial for malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), hemorrhoids (arśas), wind (vāyu), and phlegm (kapha), is heating, constipating, and light.
Paṭola, saptalā, ariṣṭa, śārṅgāṣṭhā, valguja, and amṛtā; vetrāgra, bṛhatī, vāśā, kuntalī, and tilaparṇikā.
Maṇḍūkaparṇī, karkoṭaka, kāravella, and parpaṭa; nāḍī, kalāya, gojihvā, vārttāka, and vanatiktaka.
Karīra, kūlaka, nandī, kuvelā, śakulādanī,
kaṭhilla, kembuka, kośātaka, and karkkaśa are cooling. (AS.Sū.7.117)
Bitter in digestion, pungent, constipating, increasing wind, and conquering phlegm and bile;
palatable, curing worms, sweet in digestion, and providing relish— such is the *paṭola* (AS.Sū.7.118).
The two types of *bṛhatī* are bitter, digestive, carminative, and subdue wind;
*vṛṣa*, however, is an excellent remedy for vomiting and cough, and it removes *rakta-pitta*.
Kāravella is pungent, digestive, and conquers phlegm and bile. Vārttāka is pungent, bitter, hot, and sweet; it conquers phlegm and wind.
Karīra is alkaline, generates fire, is beneficial for the heart, appetizing,
and does not increase pitta; it causes flatulence and is astringent with a sweet-bitter taste.
Kośātaka and avalguja are purgative and stimulate the digestive fire. Śyāmā, śālmalikā, kāśmarya, bhañjakī, rṇakā, and yūthikā [are likewise used].
The *vṛkṣādinī*, milky trees, the *bimbī*,
the *tanikā* tree, the *lodhra*, hemp, the *kacchudāra*, the *saśelu*, and the *vṛṣamuṣṭikā*.
Bhallātaka, kovidāra, kamala, utpala,
and kiṃśuka possess qualities similar to those of the paṭola group; they are sweet, astringent, and excellent for conquering pitta.
Karīra (Capparis spinosa) relieves suppressed urine and diarrhea;
it is slightly bitter, light, beneficial for the eyes, aphrodisiac, and subdues the three doṣas.
Tanduliyaka is cooling, dry, sweet in its post-digestive taste and juice, and light; it destroys intoxication, bile, poison, and blood disorders. Munjata overcomes wind and bile.
Pālakya is unctuous, cold, heavy, sweet, highly nourishing, and a supreme promoter of semen; it is slimy, heavy, increases phlegm, is laxative, and cooling.
Madaghnyā, upodakā, and cuñcu are grasping [plants]; these two are as described previously. Vidārī destroys wind and bile, promotes urination, and is sweet and cold.
Jīvantī is life-sustaining, nourishing, beneficial for the throat, heavy, aphrodisiac, and a rejuvenative;
it is good for the eyes, destroys all the doṣas, and is sweet and cooling. (AS.Sū.7.129)
Among leafy vegetables, *bhaṇḍī*— also known as *parvaṇī* or *parvapuṣpikā*— is the foremost; it is slightly inferior to the second [best] and subdues wind and bile.
Kūṣmāṇḍa, tumba, kāliṅga, karkāru, ervāru, tiṇḍiśa,
as well as trapusa, cīnāka, and cirbhiṭa increase phlegm and wind.

The kūṣmāṇḍa (pumpkin gourd), the best among the fruits of climbing vines, is laxative, constipating, and causes secretions; it is heavy, sweet in taste and post-digestive effect, and subdues vāta and pitta.
Trapusa (cucumber) cleanses the bladder, is aphrodisiac, and excessively increases urine;
tumba is more parching and constipating; while kāliṅga, urvāru, and cirbhiṭa are similar [in action].

One should know that the unripe [fruit] is cooling and removes pitta; the ripe fruit is the opposite. However, when its stalk has withered, it contains alkali, increases pitta, and conquers kapha and vāta.
Mṛṇāla, bisa, śālūka, śṛṅgāṭaka, and kaśeruka are pleasing to the taste, digestive stimulants, beneficial for the heart, alleviate aṣṭhīlā and abdominal distension, and are light. (AS.Sū.7.135)
Nandī, māṣaka, kelūṭa, krauñca, ādana,
kaloḍyaka, satarūḍha, and kadamba are dry, constipating, cooling, and heavy.
Kalambu, nālikā, māṣa, kaṭhiñjara, and kutumbaka;
cillī, laṭvāka, niṣpāva, kurūṭaka, and gavedhuka.
Yātukā, sālakalyāṇī, śrīparṇī, pīluparṇikā,
kumārī, jīvaloṇīkā, yavaśāka, and suvarcalā. (AS.Sū.7.138)
Kuṣmāṇḍa, nīlinī, svarcā, vṛkadhūmaka, and lakṣmaṇā;
all types of ālūpa as well as all pulses (sūpya) [should be prepared] with lakṣmaṇā.
Jīvantikā, cuñcuparṇī, prapunnāṭa, and kuberaka are sweet, dry, salty, heavy, and increase vāta and śleṣman. (AS.Sū.7.140)
Cold food that has been processed with feces and urine generally digests slowly by causing constipation; however,
when it is steamed, its juice is squeezed out, and it is rich in unctuousness (sneha), it does not cause excessive morbidity.
The *cillī* with small leaves is considered equal to *vāstuka*. *Takkārī* and *varaṇa* are sweet and slightly bitter, and they conquer phlegm and wind.
Varṣābhū, kālaśāka, and substances that are alkaline, pungent, or bitter are digestive stimulants and carminatives; they destroy artificial poisons, edema, phlegm, and wind.
The sprouts of *ciribilva* are digestive stimulants, destroyers of phlegm and wind, and laxative;
likewise, *sorupūkā* and *lāṅgalī* are light, hot, laxative, and bitter.
Sesame and vetasa are wind-increasing, pungent, bitter, and sour, and are laxatives;
likewise, pañcāṅgula is so, while bamboo shoots cause a burning sensation.
The Bilva, Rāsnā, and Balā vegetables increase wind and bile, are dry, have a pungent post-digestive effect (vipāka), and subdue phlegm; they destroy wind and cure diarrhea.
Vatsādanī destroys wind; gaṇḍīra and citraka destroy phlegm. Pattūra is digestive, bitter, and overcomes spleen disorders, hemorrhoids, phlegm, and wind.
Kāsamarda overcomes worms, phlegm, expectoration, and excessive secretions; it is laxative.
Kusumbha is dry, hot, sour, heavy, increases pitta, and is laxative.
Mustard greens are alkaline, sweet, unctuous, hot, and heavy;
among vegetables, they are the lowest, binding the feces and urine, and producing all the *doṣas*.
The young radish (mūlaka), which has an unmanifest taste, is slightly alkaline and bitter; it removes the bodily humors (doṣa), is light, and being warm, it subdues [the diseases].

Furthermore, it cures gulma, cough, consumption, dyspnea, ulcers, diseases of the eyes and throat, as well as hoarseness of voice, loss of digestive fire, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), and chronic rhinitis (pīnasa). As.Sū.7.151–152.

That which is heavy, hot, and pungent, yet sweet in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), produces all the doṣas; however, when prepared with unctuous substances, it is heavy and causes internal secretions (abhiṣyandi), yet it conquers vāta.
Dried [piṇḍālu] removes wind and phlegm, whereas all raw [piṇḍālu] aggravates the humors.
Piṇḍālu is pungent and hot; it subdues wind and phlegm but increases bile.
Kuṭhera, śigru, surasa, sumukha, asurī, bhūstṛṇa,
dhānya, tumbaru, śaileya, yavānī, and śṛṅgaveraka.
Parṇāsa, gṛñjana, ajājī, jīraka, and gajapippalī; phaṇijjārjaka, jambīra, kharāhva, and kālamālikā. (AS.Sū.7.155)
Dīpyaka, kṣavaka, dvīpin, bastagandhā, and others bind the feces; they are pungent in taste and post-digestive effect, provoke the doṣas, and are light.
This group known as the Haritaki category is burning, dry, sharp, and hot; it destroys vision, semen, and worms, and is employed in conjunction with foods (as an upadaṃśa).
It is fragrant, pleasant to the palate, appetizing, and digestive;
it cures hiccups, cough, poisoning, asthma, pain in the flanks, and foul odors.
Surasa, sumukha, śophagandhahā,
and dhānakā are astringent, bitter, and sweet; they promote urination and do not produce pitta.
Kharāhvā (Trivṛt) destroys pain in the bladder; Citraka is an excellent digestive stimulant.
Its leaf is alkaline and sweet, while its middle portion is sweet and slimy.
Garlic is sharp and hot; its bulb is pungent in taste and post-digestive effect, and it is laxative (AS.Sū.7.161).
It is beneficial for the heart, promotes hair growth, is heavy, aphrodisiac, unctuous, and improves the relish for food and stimulates digestion (AS.Sū.7.161).
It heals broken joints, is strengthening, but vitiates blood and bile; it cures leucoderma, skin diseases, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, urinary disorders, worms, phlegm, and wind disorders.
This elixir destroys hiccup, chronic rhinitis, dyspnea, and cough; however,
the onion is slightly inferior in its qualities, though it is sweet in its post-digestive effect.
It produces phlegm but not bile; it is a destroyer of wind alone.
Sūraṇa is a digestive stimulant, appetizing, a destroyer of phlegm, clear, and light.
The *viśeṣādarśa* is wholesome, whereas the *bhūkanda* is excessively dosha-inducing. Among leaves, flowers, fruits, and tubers, heaviness increases in that order.
Among leafy vegetables (*śāka*), *jīvantī* is the best, while mustard (*sārṣapa*) is the very worst;
thus ends the section on leafy vegetables (AS.Sū.7.166).
*Drākṣā* (grape) is the best of fruits; it is aphrodisiac, beneficial for the eyes, and promotes the passage of urine and feces.
Sweet in digestion and taste, unctuous, slightly astringent, cold, and heavy,
it destroys disorders of wind, bile, and blood, as well as a bitter mouth and alcoholism.
Sweet pomegranate (*dāḍima*) overcomes thirst, cough, fever, dyspnea, hoarseness of voice, chest wounds, and wasting, as well as conditions of excessive *pitta* and the three *doṣas*.
AS.Sū.7.168 [It is] not antagonistic to pitta, not excessively hot, and sour; it removes vāta and kapha.
AS.Sū.7.169 All [these qualities] are beneficial for the heart, light, unctuous, constipating, appetizing, and digestive-stimulating.
AS.Sū.7.169 [The fruits of] the *mocaka* date palm, the *kharjūra* date palm, the breadfruit tree (*panasa*), the coconut palm (*nālikera*), and the *parūṣaka*;
AS.Sū.7.170 [the fruits] produced from the *āmrātaka*, the *tāla* palm, the *kāśmarya*, the *rājādana*, and the *madhūka*.
AS.Sū.7.170 [The fruits] originating from sauvīra, badara, aṅkola, phalguna, and śleṣmātaka;
AS.Sū.7.171 vātāma, abhiṣuka, akṣoḍa, mukūlaka, and nikocaka.
The *ūrumāṇa* and *priyāla* are nourishing, heavy, and cooling;
they alleviate burning sensations, injuries from wounds, and consumption, and they purify the blood and bile (*raktapitta*).
AS.Sū.7.172 Sweet in digestion and taste, unctuous, causing constipation, and increasing phlegm and semen. AS.Sū.7.173 The coconut is heavy, unctuous, pacifies pitta, and is sweet and cold.
The *moca* (plantain) is said to provide strength and flesh, be beneficial for the heart, nourishing, a cleanser of the bladder,
sweet in taste, slightly astringent, and not excessively cold.
The fruit of the rājādana (pomegranate) removes blood-bile, is aphrodisiac, improves the appetite, increases phlegm,
is heavy, unctuous, sweet, and astringent.

The fruit of the palmyra palm (*tāla*) increases *pitta*, while that of the *kāśmarya* is cooling; it removes obstructions of feces and urine, promotes the hair, enhances intellect, and acts as a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*).
Madhūka fruit is beneficial for the heart, while jamba is laxative; badara is heavy,
and vātāma is hot in potency, increases kapha and pitta, and is laxative.
The fruit of the *priyāla* is excellent for removing wind (*vāta*), is unctuous (*snigdha*), and is not hot (*anuṣṇa*).
The pulp of the *priyāla* is sweet, aphrodisiac (*vṛṣya*), and alleviates *pitta* and *anila*.
The kernel of the *kola* fruit possesses similar qualities; it conquers thirst, vomiting, and coughing.
[One may take] rice cooked with *tinduka*, *aśmantaka*, *āsīna*, *phalinī*, and *bimbī*.
Taṅka, aśvakarṇa, bakula, gāṅgeruki, dhava, dhanvana,
śvetapāka, kapittha, siñcatī, bhavya, and jāmbava.
Seeds originating from milky trees and the seeds of the lotus (pauṣkara) conquer phlegm and bile;
they are astringent and sweet, dry, cooling, heavy, and scraping.
AS.Sū.7.181 It causes constipation, flatulence, and stiffness, and provokes vāta.
AS.Sū.7.182 Raw kapittha is harmful to the throat; it is astringent-sour and aggravates the three doṣas.

Matured [liquor] that is appetizing, astringent-acidic, and sweet dispels hiccup and vomiting; it destroys the humors (doṣas) and is highly esteemed for its use in ṣāḍava, ariṣṭa, and rāga preparations.
One should prescribe both types of wood-apples (*kapittha*) and the like as antidotes to poison and as astringents; the fruit of the *siñcatikā* is nourishing, subdues wind and bile, and is unctuous.

The fruit of the *jāmbava* tree is wholesome, clear, and sour, yet it is excessively wind-increasing (vātala). That which is produced from milk-exuding trees (*kṣīrivṛkṣa*) is slightly sour, causes constipation, and is harmful to the throat.
The fruit of the *akṣakī* is sour, which destroys bile and phlegm, yet increases wind;
when young, it is astringent, pungent, and sour, dry, and it produces wind, blood disorders, and bile.
A fully ripe mango that is sour increases blood, bile, and phlegm.
One that is sweet and sour is heavy, unctuous, subdues wind, and does not increase bile.
The juice of the *sahakāra* (mango) is beneficial for the heart; it is fragrant, unctuous, and appetizing, and it bestows phlegm, muscle tissue, semen, and strength. (AS.Sū.7.187–188)
The lavalī fruit is digestive, pacifies pitta and vāta, purifies semen and blood,
is astringent, appetizing, beneficial for the heart, and increases vāta.

The bilva fruit that is heavy, burnt by fire, or over-ripe is harmful to the humors and causes putrid flatulence. However, when it is ripe or young, it is sharp, increases bile, is light, and stimulates digestion.
Both [types of] *vṛkṣāmla* are excellent for subduing wind (*vāta*) and phlegm (*śleṣman*), are hot, unctuous, and astringent.
*Vṛkṣāmla* is astringent, dry, hot, light, and stimulates digestion and the appetite.
The fruit of the *kośāmra* is slightly inferior to that in removing wind and phlegm;
the *karañja* fruit causes constipation and is not antagonistic to bile and phlegm.
The fruit of the *śamī* is heavy, hot, sweet, dry, and hair-destroying.
The *pīlu* is pungent in both taste and post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), sharp, hot, a laxative, and increases *pitta*.
AS.Sū.7.193 It conquers worms, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, hemorrhoids, spleen disorders, phlegm, and wind.
AS.Sū.7.194 The *pīlu* fruit that is slightly bitter, sweet, and not excessively hot conquers the three *doṣas*.
Nīpa, śatākṣika, prācīnāgara, and that which is produced from tṛṇaśūlya;
the fruit of iṅguda and vikaṅkata possess qualities only slightly different from these.
The skin of the mātuluṅga is bitter and pungent, unctuous, and overcomes vāta.
Its flesh is nourishing, sweet, heavy, and removes vāta and pitta.
That light kesara [medicinal substance] cures cough, dyspnea, hiccups, intoxication, and diarrhea;
it also treats dryness of the mouth, disorders of wind and phlegm, constipation, vomiting, and anorexia.
It destroys abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, hemorrhoids, colic, and weak digestion. The bark and pulp of *bhallātaka* are nourishing, sweet, and cooling.
Its bone is like fire, pure, and is excellent for removing phlegm and wind.
The pigeon is heavy and is of two types: sweet-sour and cold, and [the other] hot.
AS.Sū.7.199 It is appetizing and pacifies even excessive fire; it is appetizing and sweet.
AS.Sū.7.200 When cooked, the *māruka* fruit is quickly digested, but if not too hot, it is heavy and increases the *doṣas*.
Fresh grapes and *parūṣaka* fruit increase pitta and kapha due to their acidity;
they are heavy, hot in potency, subdue vāta, and are laxative, as is the *karamarda*.
Likewise, sour [fruits] such as the *kola*, *karkandhu*, *likuca*,
*āmrātaka*, *ārūka*, *airāvata*, *dantaśaṭha*, *satruḍa*, and *mṛgalaṇḍika*.
Ripe and dried *karamardaka* does not excessively increase *pitta*. The dried fruits of *amlīkā* and *aṅkola* are digestive stimulants (*dīpana*) and carminatives (*bhedana*).
It relieves thirst, fatigue, and exhaustion; it is light and desired for disorders of kapha and vāta.
Among fruits, the *likuca* is the best; however, it aggravates all the doṣas.
Water that is defiled by frost, wind, heat, foul breezes, or the saliva of serpents;
that which is inhabited by living creatures; that which is submerged in water; that which does not originate from the earth; and that which is out of season—[such water should be avoided].
One should discard grain that is mixed with other types, lacks potency, or is spoiled by age; likewise, one should discard vegetables that have been prepared dry or are not tender.

AS.Sū.7.206 That which has not yet developed its flavor, as well as dried [vegetables], except for radish; AS.Sū.7.207 likewise, fruit is generally [forbidden] in this way when raw, with the exception of the *bilva*.
Thus ends the section on fruits (AS.Sū.7.207),
which consists of preparations based on awned grains, pods, flour-cakes, cooked foods, meat, vegetables, and fruits.
This section on specific food items, which is for the most part highly practical,
has been described according to their respective tastes, potencies, and so forth, for the purpose of accomplishing their specific actions.
It is not possible to explain everything in full detail; moreover,
because of this, there is no absolute certainty regarding what is beneficial or harmful.
AS.Sū.7.210 Due to differences in dosage, application, method of administration, location, time, state, and so forth,
AS.Sū.7.210 those various substances are observed to produce their respective effects in those very ways.
Wine, when consumed in the proper measure, destroys diseases arising from it;
even poison, when consumed bit by bit, acts as nectar.
Food that is either deficient or excessive provokes the collection of the bodily humors (*marut*);
however, when honey and clarified butter are taken in equal proportions, they possess the nature of a poison.
Alkali, when combined with a sour juice, becomes sweet in an instant;
the bitterness of the *uttuṇḍakī* fruit is rendered sweet by the *tinduka*.
As.Sū.7.214 Assafoetida, red ochre, and rock salt possess superior fragrance, color, and taste;
[the excellence] of betel nut, betel leaf, and conch shells arises from their color, fragrance, and taste.
Kodrava destroys blood and bile, yet it causes a burning sensation;
likewise, kuṣṭha and tila seeds, when combined with bhallātaka, perform that same function.
Jaggery is the cause of the digestion of fire; it destroys [the fire] through fearlessness and other factors.
When there is excessive thirst due to the fire, even clarified butter (sarpis) mixed with Madana is prescribed.
Even life-sustaining milk leads to death through even a trace of poison; likewise,
between the two types of poison— stationary (vegetable/mineral) and mobile (animal)— each destroys the other despite being equal [in potency].
Barley flour (saktu) increases wind and is dry, yet when drunk, it provides satisfaction;
even without being consumed, gems, mantras, and the like perform their intended effects.
From fresh ginger, dried ginger (*śuṇṭhī*) is produced, which becomes lighter through processing; for even from light roasted flour (*saktu*), prepared balls (*piṇḍikā*) are heavy.
Even when parched and crushed, the light red rice (raktaśāli) pṛthuka becomes heavy;
ground rice attains a heaviness even greater than that of wheat.

Parched rice (lāja) is light and pacifies pitta, whereas rice is heavy and increases pitta; fermented grain-water (kulmāṣa) is heavy and causes purging, whereas green gram (mudga) is light and constipating.
Raw buttermilk prepared with ginger and fresh ginger is highly effective for inducing the evacuation of undigested matter (āma).
A drink made from jaggery and water is even more effective for increasing urination, yet it is heavy to digest.
Rasālā made from thickened curd and jaggery is heavy and highly nourishing; however, when thick curd is churned with a stick, it causes excessive swelling and is very heavy.
Buttermilk, even when its fat has not been removed, alleviates swelling and is light;
clarified butter, being more unctuous, destroys [diseases] such as facial paralysis, just like fresh butter.
Wheat is indeed beneficial for the eyes; however, when cooked in oil, it destroys vision.
Radish generates the bodily humors (doṣas), yet when prepared [properly], it is free from such faults.
Honey, even when it is an antidote to poison, turns into poison itself if it is heated; likewise,
grapes placed in a poor-quality vessel become sour and cause harm.
A thick, smooth, and dry ointment of sandalwood causes burning;
conversely, that of aguru causes coldness because it obstructs the heat residing in the skin.
The sesame seed is pure, cool to the touch, and pure; its oil is pure, and its dregs are cold.
It is these [dregs] that cause phlegm, not the oil or the dregs.
Curd causes swelling, whereas buttermilk and fresh butter do not;
curd, milk, and karīra are wholesome for those dwelling in Maru and Vāsi.

In the eastern regions, pickled fish (kṣāra) is used; among the Saindhavas and Aśmakas, however, it is oil and sour gruel (tailāmla); in Malaya, it is tubers and roots; and in Koṅkaṇa, moreover, [the same].
In the northern regions, they consume gruel and parched flour; in the lands of Avanti, wheat is eaten.
The Bālhīkas, Bāhavas, Cīnas, Śūlikas, Yavanas, and Śakas [are also mentioned].
Meat, wheat, grape wine, weapons, and fire are appropriate for some;
likewise, ghee, milk, liquor, and meat constitute bodily suitability for certain individuals.

For some, gruel, broth, or the juice of other [meats] is beneficial; for others, wheat or rice. Even those things which are unwholesome may become wholesome when prepared with those very same ingredients.
Food, drink, and medicine, when administered with due regard for the humors (doṣas), their quantity, the time, and other factors,
provide suitability (sātmya); indeed, such food quickly bestows strength and does not cause excessive disorder, even if it is abundant.
Fresh cow’s milk is laxative, yet for some it is constipating;
generally, during the winter, the digestive fire becomes weak when phlegm and wind are predominant.
Even with poison-neutralizing milk, the poison increases in the body for a day;
emesis and other such treatments are prohibited for those who are obese, elderly, or young.
Buttermilk destroys undigested phlegm in the stomach, yet it produces [phlegm] in the throat;
while grapes and dates alleviate wind, they nevertheless produce wind in the stomach.
A peacock is not excessively wholesome, yet it is beneficial for the ears, voice, youth, and eyes;
when applied as a contact-remedy, a cold substance is recommended for the eyes, whereas a warm one is esteemed for the ears.
Milk is sweet, laxative, and cold; curd is the opposite of that. From it, [butter] is produced in due time, and from that again, ghee is produced like milk.
Milk and curd that have not been churned are pacifiers of wind (*vātaghna*), whereas those that have been churned increase wind (*vātala*).
Buttermilk (*takra*) is astringent and sour; it is constipating (*grāhin*) when slightly sour, but purgative (*bhedana*) when very sour.
Dhātakī, jaggery, and water are the causes for the fermentation of wine and vinegar;
however, when cold, substances that are unctuous, sour, and salty are beneficial at the beginning and end of that process.
Consuming food with parched grain (udamantha) and sleeping during the day are censured except in the summer season;
even when occurring at the appropriate time, [excessive] heat and other factors are causes for the accumulation of wind and the other humors.
In the seasons, in tastes, in dryness, in oiliness, and in strength, there is a gradual progression.
Kākāmācī is a rejuvenative (rasāyana); it is like poison when consumed fresh or the day after being gathered.
AS.Sū.7.244 Radish is a child-like remedy that conquers the *doṣas*, whereas the tuberous root (*kanda*) acts in the opposite manner.
In cases of fever, gruel, decoctions, clarified butter, milk, and purgatives [should be administered].
One should administer [emetics] every six days, having observed the relative strength and weakness of the doshas;
and for those afflicted by vomiting, heart disease, or abdominal tumors, emesis is prescribed in medical treatment.
Even though it is prohibited, enema (basti) is prescribed for those suffering from hemorrhoids and skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
In fever, there is similarity of season and doṣa; in urinary disorders (prameha), there is similarity of the vitiated element (dūṣya).

In the case of a blood-gulma (raktagulma), chronicity is a factor that makes it easily curable. One should employ eye-drops (āścyotana) for ophthalmia with excessive secretions (abhiṣyanda) after three days have passed.
Collyrium is prescribed for one whose humors have been ripened, and nasal drops for coryza;
when cataract has not excessively increased, venesection is ordained.

Even when there is an excess of vitiated blood, venesection is not desired in cases of asrapitta; furthermore, for those suffering from eye diseases, even wholesome food is unwholesome if consumed at night.
For those suffering from urinary disorders (*pramehin*), roasted barley flour (*saktu*) that is dry is beneficial, whereas it is harmful when moist.
For those suffering from abdominal tumors (*gulmin*), milk, curd, and similar substances combined with *hapuṣā* and other such drugs are beneficial.
Honey is recommended during the rainy season even when there is a provocation of vāta;
that same [honey] is like wine for wine, but for poison, it is another form of antidote.
Ghee produced from marshy regions is highly strengthening during the winter; moreover,
lassitude and heaviness appear as premonitory symptoms even in fever born of Vāta.
A burning sensation arising generally from the consumption of garlic is pacified by sudation;
that which arises from sleeping during the day reaches old age, while food eaten on one day does not [digest] until the next.
When obstructed in the abdominal cavity by fat and hemorrhoids, the digestive fire is seized by the wind;
clarified butter is difficult to drink and difficult to digest, whereas milk acts as a digestive stimulant.
Scorpions arise from the putrefaction of the corpses of snakes and other creatures;
when they are bitten by those very same [scorpions], they lose their lives instantly.
Even a potent poison does not afflict them excessively;
for them, the poison pervades all limbs and circulates like semen.
That meat is listed for consumption in the section on meats; furthermore,
fly dung cures vomiting, yet the fly itself causes vomiting.
In the case of fever and abdominal tumors caused by kapha,
even when both are curable by fasting (laṅghana) and the factors of place and time are identical, fasting is not considered to have the same effect in both conditions.
In every respect, *doṣajittakra* is praised as proven effective for disorders of the *grahaṇī*, for wounds caused by the *doṣas*, and for chronic rhinitis, dyspnea, cough, and similar ailments.
These and many other subtle phenomena, whose causes are difficult to perceive, are diverse among existing things; only a small portion of them has been illustrated here.
By this method, the wise person should also infer the specific location for themselves;
they should not rely solely on the treatise, nor should they fail to examine the traditional scripture.
Thus ends the section on the mother and others;
thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Knowledge of the True Nature of Food.
Thus ends the seventh chapter.
Now begins the eighth chapter. Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the rules for the protection of food; thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
AS.Sū.8.2: Among lords, and especially among kings who possess great wealth, those who are enemies generally outnumber even their friends.
Consequently, those acting under their influence, being close attendants, administer poison in food, drink, and other such things.
And women, impelled by that same aspiration and out of a desire for good fortune, [should likewise act].

Therefore, the king should appoint a physician who is of noble birth, affectionate, trustworthy, devoted to his duty, free from deceit, skillful, dexterous, discreet, pure, not arrogant, diligent, free from vice, without egoism, not prone to anger, not reckless, skilled in understanding the meaning of speech, proficient in the eight branches of the science of life (Āyurveda) according to the sacred tradition, one who has secured both yoga and kṣema, who keeps medicines and other remedies at hand, who knows what is wholesome for each individual, and who is a protector of life.

One should honor that person with wealth and respect at the proper time, as a disciple honors a teacher or a son honors his father; even if their words are contrary, one should consider them timely and wise. For even a noble lordly elephant is not to be praised by people if it is unrestrained.
Therefore, one should make oneself dependent upon that [medicine] regarding food and conduct;
for even life, once acquired, one maintains by oneself through the power of skillful means. Moreover, kings have many dependents.

Furthermore, there are conditions such as acute pain and the application of surgical instruments that require examination at every moment; and among patients, kings in particular are subject to such states.

For they are overcome by negligence and unable to endure suffering; they themselves have a taste for unwholesome things and are attended by servants who mostly speak pleasant words while promoting what is harmful. Therefore, the physician should have his residence built near the royal palace, so that he may have direct supervision over all the utensils used for the king’s body.

When the food is properly prepared, well-examined, pure, first offered to the fire and other deities, inspected by the priest (*śikhin*), and sprinkled with consecrated water (*prokṣaṇa*), the physician, standing before the king who holds medicinal gems in his hands, should feed him.
And while he is eating, one should cause drums smeared with *nāgadapa* to be sounded.
In that case, poisoned food, when being boiled,
does not boil properly and takes a long time to cook.
Even when cooked, it becomes as if stale immediately; lacking heat, it becomes rigid and undergoes corruption according to its own color, smell, and taste,
becoming excessively moist.
And it becomes covered with mold,
and the bodily excretions quickly become dry.

There is a decoction-like appearance, a dark or blackish hue, and the visibility or invisibility of shadows that are deficient, excessive, or disfigured; furthermore, there is the emergence of masses of froth, hairline patterns, various upward streaks, threads, and bubbles—
especially in preparations where salt predominates— and a garland of foam on the surface with a blue streak in the middle of the liquid.
The [color] of milk is copper-red; that of wine and water is black; and that of curd is dark-brown.
The color of buttermilk is blue-yellow; that of whey is like the color of a pigeon; and that of fermented grain-water is black.
The color of liquid medicine is tawny;
that of ghee is tawny-hued; and that of honey is greenish-yellow.
The marrow of fat has a reddish hue and the smell of grease;
this is the ripening of raw fruits.
AS.Sū.8.8:
The putrefaction of cooked items;
the sudden wilting and appearance of being overcooked in fresh, moist substances.
The darkening or discoloration of dry [flesh],
the softening of hard [flesh], or the hardening of soft [flesh].
The fading of garlands, the loss of fragrance, the withering of their tips, the darkened circles on bedspreads and coverlets, the shedding of threads, hair, and down,
and the coating of rust and grime upon objects made of metal and gems.
There is the destruction of affection, passion, respect, power, complexion,
and touch; however, one who is suspicious of his own faults is terrified.
Terrified, with perspiration and trembling, his face parched and darkened.
He looks about in every direction with agitation and embarrassment;
and where he had administered the poison, he especially hides himself behind pillars, walls, and the like, with his upper garment slung down over him.
With faltering gait, dejected, ashamed, and laughing at the wrong time, even when questioned he gives an irrelevant answer;
or else, not wishing to speak, he becomes confused and snaps his fingers.
He touches his neck, scratches his head,
and licks his lips.
He yawns,
scratches the ground,
and hastens in his actions.
They act contrary [to what is right] and do not abide in their own proper sphere;
some, due to the haste of a king's command or because of another offense, being unstable in character, act in this very manner.
Therefore, one should also examine the fire and other elements;
for when fire encounters poisoned food, it turns into a single-eddied flame that is dry and dull, with many-colored tongues of fire like a rainbow, and it crackles intensely.

The smoke from this [fire] smells like a corpse and produces fainting, salivation, horripilation, headache, catarrh, and agitation of the vision. In that case, one should administer nasal drops (nasya) and collyrium (añjana) made from *nalada*, *kuṣṭha*, and *lāmajjaka* mixed with honey.
Or one should drink the smoke itself, prepared from apāmārga, viḍaṅga, the two types of balā, citraka, meṣaśṛṅgī, flowers of sumana, kṣāra, drākṣā, ghee, and jaggery; furthermore,
by the addition of unctuous substances and salt, the digestive fire will become thus [strengthened].
Therefore, one should examine it by means of birds:
in that case, crows become weak-voiced from consuming food tainted with poison,
and flies do not alight upon poisoned food.
They perish while still hidden;
indeed, as soon as this [moon] is seen, the eyes of the cakora bird lose their luster and the voice of the cuckoo undergoes a transformation.
The gait of the swan falters,
the king of bees hums,
and the crane becomes intoxicated.
The cock crows,
the parrot and the maina shriek,
and the golden [cock] vomits gold.
The kāraṇḍava bird flies away elsewhere;
the jīvañjīvaka dies or grows weary.
The mongoose's hair stands on end,
the monkey voids excrement,
and the spotted deer weeps.
The peacock rejoices at the mere sight of it, and its poison becomes mild; furthermore,
the heat of food that has been vitiated by poison rises up with the color of a peacock’s throat.
Even by its vapor, [it produces] fainting and so forth, like smoke;
their proof is exactly like that.
Food touched by the hand causes burning, swelling, numbness, and cracking of the nails, like poison;
for this, an ointment made of *śyāmā*, *indragopa*, *soma*, and *utpala* is the remedy.

Food being eaten [while poisoned] causes a tingling sensation in the lips, burning within the mouth, heaviness at the root of the tongue, lockjaw, chattering of the teeth, salivation, and a loss of the sense of taste.
In that regard, the action described for smoke and the action described for the tooth-stick,

when it has reached the stomach (āmāśaya), produces sweating, intoxication, fainting, vomiting, discoloration, flatulence, horripilation, burning sensations, loss of appetite, impairment of vision, and constriction of the heart, as well as the accumulation of spots on the limbs.
In that case, one should quickly administer emesis using the fruits of *madana*, *āmalaka*, *bimba*, and *kośātakī* combined with curd and honey,
or else with the water of *niṣpāva* beans.

Then, once the body has been lubricated, one should administer a purgative consisting of the powder of *triphalā*, *trikaṭu*, *nāgapuṣpa*, *madhuka*, *barhiṇaparṇī*, and the two types of *bṛhatī*, combined with the bile and fat of any one of the following: lion, tiger, wolf, hyena, leopard, cat, jackal, deer, or monitor lizard, mixed with honey. This is the elixir named *Jīvana*, the supreme medicine for all poisons.

When that has been digested, one should feed the patient soft rice with a small amount of salt and ghee, along with *mudga* bean soup, supported by milk or ghee prepared with *śyāmā*, *vyoṣa*, and *ativiṣā*.

One should smear him with madhuka, śirīṣa, and candana. When it has reached the colon (pakvāśaya), it produces thirst, burning sensations, fainting, diarrhea, agitation, drowsiness, impairment of the senses, loss of strength, emaciation, pallor, and abdominal enlargements.
In that case, one should administer a purgative with ghee mixed with *nīlinī* fruit and honey, and give *dūṣīviṣāri* with curd.

When the poison is introduced by means of a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*), there occurs a shredding of the gums, a medicinal odor, dryness, and swelling of the palate, teeth, tongue, and lips; in such a case, after applying an astringent wash, one should perform rubbing (*pratisāraṇa*) with the powder of *dhātakī* flowers, *jāmbava* stones, and *harītakī*, along with honey, or with a paste of *saptacchada*.
A gargle (*gaṇḍūṣa*) consisting of the juices of pomegranate, *karamarda*, *bibhītaka*, *āmrātaka*, *kola*, and *badara*, combined with honey, should also be used.
By this, the tongue-scraper, gargles, and mouth-rinses are explained.
(AS.Sū.8.17) When collyrium is improperly applied, there occur lacrimation, inflammation of the eyelids, discharge, redness, pain, distortion of vision, and even blindness.
In that case, the drinking of ghee should be administered; one should saturate long peppers (*pippalī*) seven times with boiled milk,
and then ghee cooked with their paste is used as an eye-satiation (*netratarpaṇa*).

One should prepare a collyrium from the flowers of *kapittha*, *meṣaśṛṅgī*, and *bhallātaka*, or with the resin of *varaṇa*. Then, one should saturate the powder of *bṛhatī*, *śirīṣa* seeds, *prapauṇḍarīka*, and *nāgabalā* seven times with honey.
This collyrium, combined with *sroto'ñjana* and gold dust, should be applied.

[It cures] headache, discharge from the ears, nose, or eyes, bleeding from the channels, and impairment of the sense organs resulting from the improper administration of nasal medication or fumigation.
In that case, one should administer ghee prepared with milk and a paste of ativiṣā, śvetā, kākamācī, and madayantikā for both nasal drops (nasya) and internal consumption (pāna).
If burning of the skin, sweating, suppuration, eruptions, or cracking occur due to the application of an oil massage (abhyaṅga),
then, after sprinkling the patient with cold water, one should apply an ointment consisting of candana, tagara, uśīra, kuṣṭha, veṇupatrikā, amṛtā, somavallī, śvetā, padmaka, and kāleyaka.
These same substances—kapittha juice and cow urine—are for drinking;
the roots of girikarṇikā, white mūla, priyaṅgu, sārivā, madhuka, sarpasugandhā, amṛgī, urvāru, and kataka, ground with a decoction of śelu, are for external application.
By this, the methods for rubbing, friction, sprinkling, anointing, as well as ornaments, vehicles, beds, coverlets, garments, armor, sandals, shoes, and footstools, are explained.
Specifically, for a deformity caused by jewelry, an ointment should be applied using the pastes of *aśvagandhā*, *apāmārga*, *kiṇihī*, *khadira*, and *śirīṣa* mixed with cow bile.
For a deformity caused by a footstool, a paste of *śleṣmātaka*, *sarpa*, *sugandhā*, and *āmra* mixed with honey should be used.
When caused by a bite from a *chatra* spider, there appears an eruption of painful vesicles that ripen quickly and resemble ripe *jāmbava* fruits;

in such a case, one should apply an ointment to all parts of the body made from the pastes of *madhuka*, *pāṭalā*, *kaśeruka*, *lodhra*, *añjana*, *kuṣṭha*, *sarpasugandhā*, *khadira*, and *śirīṣa*. By this, the treatment for the *amara* spider is also explained.
AS.Sū.8.19 When head massage is improperly applied, it causes headache, the formation of nodules, and the falling out of hair. In that case,
a plaster should be applied using black earth well-saturated with the powders of *śyāmā*, *pālindī*, and *taṇḍulīyaka*, along with clarified butter and bear bile.

Alternatively, a decoction of either cow dung, *mālatī* root, or *mūṣikakarṇī*, or house-soot, or a wash with goat’s milk mixed with the bark of *śleṣmātaka*, *pāṭalā*, *śirīṣa*, *madhuka*, and the two types of *haridrā*, should be used for sprinkling.
By this, the methods for head-bathing water, combs, garlands, and turbans are explained.
When ear-filling is applied [inappropriately], swelling, pain, suppuration, and impairment of hearing may occur.
In that case, for filling [the ear], a decoction of *bahupatrā* mixed with ghee and honey, or a well-cooled decoction of *somavalka*,
should be used; when applied as a facial plaster, it causes darkening of the face and the appearance of lotus-stalk-like eruptions (*padmakaṇṭakā*), as well as disorders arising from massage.
In that case, an ointment made of madhuka, payasyā, bandhujīva, bhañjī, punarnavā, and candana mixed with ghee, along with the internal consumption of honey and clarified butter,
[is the remedy]. From smelling poisonous flowers, there arises headache, lacrimation of the eyes, and loss of the sense of smell.
In this regard, there is the procedure just mentioned and that which arises from tears; and here there is also [this verse]: AS.Sū.8.21.
One should untiringly provide water for washing fruits, roots, leaves, and so forth, as well as for the vessels and condiments; likewise,
having caused those things to be smelled to be smelled, one should also touch those things that are to be touched.
Then, having added the medicinal addition and waited for exactly one nāḍikā,
he should ascertain the purity of both the vessel and the water.
The lord of the earth should consume his food properly;
for poison becomes greatly attenuated by the habitual use of mild and sharp [medicines].
Therefore, a skilled physician should bind a potent poison upon his hand;
for the retention of poison is auspicious, a destroyer of demons, and an increaser of joy.
Moreover, a medicine storehouse is desired that is protected from the northeast direction, with medicines placed upon a wooden board covered by a sealed jar.
AS.Sū.8.26 High up, in a praiseworthy direction, with many windows, and spacious; AS.Sū.8.27 the kitchen should be well-swept and attended by trustworthy persons.
The dwelling should have its doors guarded by honest men, possess inner courtyards with well-constructed awnings,
contain well-washed sturdy jars and other vessels, and be supplied with pure water and fuel.
The cooks there were skilled in their own work, dexterous, and vigilant;
they had trimmed their hair and nails, were fit for ancestral rites, and were uninvolved in the king's affairs.
Their leader should be a learned man of noble birth, well-examined,
one who shares his wealth, devoted, pure, and obedient to the physician.
AS.Sū.8.30 All such kings who are situated nearby are always praised.
AS.Sū.8.31 Those who are free from mutual conflict and alliance are beneficial to the king.
A single physician, endowed with virtuous qualities, should remain mentally vigilant toward them,
being intent upon protecting the king’s body and his requisites.
Now, when one desiring victory marches against an enemy, the physician should be well-equipped with medicines, surgical instruments, and appliances.
One who knows the location of the residence called Tuṅgadhvaja should treat the warriors who have come for battle;
[he should provide] a path, water, shade, food, fodder, and fuel.
Since enemies cause corruption, one should recognize them and eliminate them;
one should not undertake a military expedition or the settling of a colony without having ascertained [the situation].
The earth, water, grass, wood, stones, paths, by-paths, and trees [are affected];
the ground poisoned by poison appears in some places as if it were scorched. (AS.Sū.8.36)
