The grass, shrubs, and other vegetation wither; dead insects and reptiles appear; and the hooves and claws fall away, accompanied by burning, itching, and pain.
Vomiting, fainting, fever, delusion, and headache arise;
in that case, [one should use] the root of *saubhañjana*, *somavallī*, and *uśīraka*.

One should cause [the patient] to drink the juice of *mātuluṅga* with asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) mixed with a measure of curd; likewise, the urines of goats, sheep, and elephants, as well as their meats and bloods.
One should cook it by combining it with all the fragrant substances (sarvagandha); once cooked,
one should add somarājī, that which is called sunandā, sarala, and gandhanākulī.
One should sprinkle that ground with *cāraṭī* and *trāyamāṇā*; [thereby] the water becomes free of poison, no longer foul-tasting, and not merely lukewarm, but marked with stripes.
Water that is frothy, heavy, disturbed by birds, unappreciated by them,
filled with dead or distressed fish, and which causes pain, swelling, and itching upon touch— AS.Sū.8.42.
The rice-gruel prepared by him, even when merely consumed, causes a burning sensation;
it is digested with difficulty as if it were partially burnt, and once fully cooked, it induces fainting and fever.
One should observe [the urine] as being blue, yellow, variegated, or red on all sides;
in that case, one should drink an anti-poison medicine (agada) such as Śigru and others, which counteracts the defects of the soil.
Having burnt ajaśṛṅgī, the plant known as viśālā, viṣaghnī, uttamāraṇī,
phaṇijjaka, and prativiṣā, one should strain that ash. (AS.Sū.8.45)

Having strained that [mixture] many times, one should cook it and add to it the paste (kalka) of *sarala*, the two types of *rajanī* (turmeric and *daruharidrā*), and the medicinal additives (*pratīvāpa*).
Elā, udīcya, mañjiṣṭhā, sunandā, and bākucī are also administered;
therefore, drops [of the medicine] fall where it shall become free of poison.
Having burned *pāṭalā*, *pāribhadra*, *aśvakarṇa*, *śamyāka*, and *sidhraka* inside a water-pot, one should throw them into poisoned water.
In cold weather, heat [is applied], and in hot weather, snow; and when there is wind mixed with poison,
Śigru and other such remedies are desired to cause dizziness, fainting, and so forth.
One should sprinkle the finely powdered paste of *devadāru*, *nata*, *anantā*, *madhuka*, *arjuna*, *gairika*, *vajrakanda*, *latā*,
and *lodhra*. (AS.Sū.8.50)
On the tops of trees, on banners, on cotton cloths, and on very large [objects],
the wind becomes free from poison through contact with these powders in every respect.
The shadow of a tree corrupted by poison becomes distorted;
its flowers become scentless or excessively fragrant, causing pain in the heart and head.
One should employ fruits, leaves, and so forth, which cause itching, suppuration, or diarrhea;
whatever has been prescribed with reference to the soil is all desired to be used there as well. (AS.Sū.8.53)
One should not touch a maiden who is unknown or unexamined; indeed,
skilled men employ various stratagems.
From birth, through contact with poison, a girl is rendered poisonous;
she kills by touch, exhalation, and so forth. This, however, is the method for examining her.
It withers through contact with his hands and hair, as if by flowers and sprouts; on the bed, it is infested with bedbugs, and in the clothes, with lice, as well as in the bathing water.
One dies because of insects; knowing this, one should avoid [the food] from afar.
It should not be un-sprinkled, nor unknown to the physician, nor un-inspected.
The king should not consume anything that has not first been tasted by the cooks and others;
it is auspicious, known as Sarvārthasiddha, and removes sins, demons, and poisons.
Now, an eye-salve that is beneficial for the eyes, conducive to longevity, and destructive of enemies will be described.

Then, during the bright fortnight, on an auspicious day, when the moon—the lord of medicinal herbs—has entered into conjunction with any one of the following asterisms: Puṣya, Punarvasu, Hasta, Citrā, Mṛgaśiras, Śravaṇa, Revatī, Śatabhiṣaj, Rohiṇī (the Prājāpatya), or any of the three Uttarās, and at a praiseworthy moment, one should procure eye-salve produced from the waters of the Indus, which is glossy, radiant, and possesses the fragrance, color, and appearance of a blue lotus.
One-eighth part each of gold, silver, and udumbara wood constitutes eight portions;

having placed all of these into a crucible, and having first performed the bali and auspicious rites, one should kindle a fire by adding fuel from any of the woods—khadira, kadara, dhava, or syandana—or else with cow-dung.

Then, having worshipped Āryāvalokiteśvara and Āryatārā, as well as Brahmā, Dakṣa, Aśvin, Rudra, Indra, Aditya, Soma, Varuṇa, Vaiśvānara, Vāyu, Viṣṇu, Janaka, Bharadvāja, Dhanvantari, Suśruta, Bhavya, Sukanyā, Skanda, Cyavana, Vainateya, and other deities mentioned according to the ritual rules—having honored them with flowers, unbroken rice, parched grain, svastikas, boiled milk-rice, husked barley, and prepared milk-porridge mixed with jaggery and ghee—and having honored elderly physicians and Brahmins clad in white garments with great sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), one should repeatedly blow upon that ointment in that fire and then pour it out separately into individual vessels.

Having bound [the substance] in a white cloth, one should let it soak in the waters of the atmosphere for twelve nights in the following liquids: cow-dung juice, urine, ghee, curd, honey, fat, marrow, oil, wine, water with all perfumes (*sarvagandha*), sugar-water, and sugarcane juice; likewise in decoctions of *harītakī*, *āmalaka*, *bibhītaka*, *kāśmarya*, *mṛdvīkā*, *śṛṅgāṭaka*, *kaśeruka*, *utpala*, *nalina*, *saugandhika*, and lotus stalks (*mṛṇālikā*); likewise in the juices of the common quail (*lāva*), the grey partridge (*kapiñjala*), the black antelope (*eṇa*), the rabbit (*śaśa*), the deer (*hariṇa*), and the crab (*kulīra*); and likewise in water containing *madhuka*, sandalwood, *kālānusārya*, *analada*, *padmaka*, *uśīra*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *anantā*, red ochre (*gairika*), and saffron (*kuṅkuma*).

Then, having dried it in the shade, and having added crystal, pearl, coral, and *kālanusāryā* as an after-throw, a learned Brahmin—having performed the rites of offering and auspiciousness once more—should have a maiden wearing unwashed garments grind it upon a stone. He should then place it in a collyrium box fashioned from any one of the following: gold, silver, copper, conch-shell, stone, ivory, the tusk of a gavaya, *vaiḍūrya*, crystal, *meṣaśṛṅgī*, or the heartwood of *snuhi*.
Then, as before, having performed the propitiatory rite (*svastyayana*), the twice-born man, knowing all the sciences, should duly consecrate it with the ritual dedicated to Sāvitrī.

Then, having mounted him upon the back of an elephant, followed by white umbrellas, chowries, and fly-whisks, accompanied by the sounds of conchs and drums, and by the auspicious proclamations of "Auspicious Day" (*puṇyāha*) uttered by the best of the twice-born interspersed with Vedic recitations, and having offered flowers as an oblation, he should cause him to enter from the physician’s house into the house of the leader.

Immediately thereafter, having performed worship to cows and Brahmins, being pure and observant of the precepts, and reciting this *dhāraṇī*—this *vidyā*—one should, with that ointment which was previously instructed by the Lord of Videha and perfected for all purposes, apply it to the right eye first with a stick made from any one of the aforementioned materials for an ointment-container, while remaining purified.
Now follows the mantra: *Namaś-cakṣuḥ-pariśodhana-rājāya tathāgatāya arhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya. Tadyathā: Oṃ cakṣuḥ prajñācakṣur jñānacakṣur vijñānacakṣur viśodhaya svāhā.*

Thereafter, remembering that very *dhāriṇī* [formula], every day at dawn and dusk, a physician with a serene mind should prescribe this supreme, purifying, health-giving, strength-bestowing, and all-poison-destroying collyrium, which was prepared of old for the Aśvins when Indra was intent on slaying Vṛtra. Therefore, it should be prescribed by the physician for kings and royal ministers desiring to conquer the earth, as well as for Brahmins engaged in the study of the Vedas or delving into other great treatises.
And there are verses on this subject: Now, the auspicious yogas composed by Bṛhaspati shall be proclaimed.
A king who serves these does not meet his death at the hands of enemies. Bilva, āḍhakī, barley-alkali, pāṭalī, bālhika, and black pepper.
A decoction prepared with *śrīparṇī* and *sallakī* is the supreme sprinkling;
anything poisoned that is sprinkled with it immediately becomes free of poison.
Grass, fuel, water, weapons, beds, seats, and drinking water; armor, ornaments, umbrellas, fly-whisks, and dwellings.
Śelu, pāṭalī, ativiṣā, śigru, gopī, punarnavā, samaṅgā, the root-bark of vṛṣa, kapittha, and the blood of a vṛṣa (AS.Sū.8.66).
Likewise, sprinkling it with *dantaśaṭha* destroys poison.
(AS.Sū.8.67) *Lākṣā*, *priyaṅgu*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *samaṅgā*, and *lahareṇukā*— (AS.Sū.8.67)
The paste of yaṣṭīmadhu combined with honey and mixed with blood and bile should be placed inside a cow's horn and buried in the ground for seven nights. (AS.Sū.8.68)
Then, having had the gem set in gold, one should wear it on the hand;
by its touch, that which is possessed of poison immediately becomes free of poison.
Manohvā, śamī flowers, bark [of the śamī], niśā, white mustard,
kapittha, kuṣṭha, and mañjiṣṭhā, finely ground into a paste with bile.

This excellent, harmless remedy called Saumya, prepared from the [milk] of a dog, a cow, and a Kapilā cow, should be administered as the supreme antidote for poison; and a precious gem should be worn as before.
Alternatively, *mūṣikā* and *ajaruhā*, when bound to the hand, remove poison; likewise,
*hareṇu*, *māṃsī*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *rajanī*, *madhuka*, and honey [are so used].
A gemstone made from the bark of the *akṣa* tree, *rasa*, lac, and dog bile, as described previously;
likewise, musical instruments and banners carved from these same ground substances.
AS.Sū.8.73 AS.Sū.8.73

Having heard, seen, or smelled it, one immediately becomes free from poison. [The remedy consists of] the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), the five salts (pañcalavaṇa), mañjiṣṭhā, and the two types of turmeric (rajanīdvaya).
One should place small cardamom, trivṛt, leaves, viḍaṅga, indravāruṇī, and madhuka, along with honey, inside a cow's horn. (AS.Sū.8.75)
Therefore, one should administer a dose of warm water before a meal;
poison consumed thus reaches digestion, and even if it is not poisonous, it causes no harm.
Lac, resin of the *sarja* tree, *uśīra*, mustard seeds, with *patra*, *vālaka*, vella, *aruṣkara*, *pura*, and the flowers of the *arjuna* tree.
Incense in the bedchamber destroys all poisons, both stationary and mobile.
Therein, there are no venomous insects, no mongooses, and no reptiles.

Where this incense— consisting of a peacock feather, crane bone, mustard seeds, sandalwood, and ghee— is burned, there no magical spells (*kṛtyā*), sorcery (*karṣaṇa*), or other such rites shall prevail. (AS.Sū.8.79)
Incense containing *viśālā*, the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), *mañjiṣṭhā*, *yaṣṭīmadhu*, and the five salts, when placed in the bed, clothing, seat, or house, destroys poison. (AS.Sū.8.80)
O King, a powder of *dviniśā*, *patra*, *vellī*, *elā*, and *trivṛt*, mixed with honey and placed in a cow's horn, should be added to the bathing water. (AS.Sū.8.81)

One should add the previously mentioned tri-kaṭu (three pungents) and other ingredients to the bathing water; alternatively, a decoction may be made from arka flowers, śvetā, apāmārga, and mustard seeds.
It should be prepared with *katakā*, the two types of *ākulī*, and clarified butter constantly applied;
or else as a paste made from sandalwood and the bark of milk-exuding trees and *palāśa*.
A decoction made from mūrvā, elavāluka, surasā, kulī,
and taṇḍulīyaka, combined with kākamācī, is beneficial for all purposes requiring water.
Wearing forehead marks made from *rocanā*, *patra*, *naipālī*, and saffron,
one is not harmed by poisons and becomes beloved by women, men, and kings. (AS.Sū.8.85)
Gautama stated that a body smeared with powders derived from *haridrā*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *kiṇihī*, *kaṇā*, and *nimba* becomes free from poison. (AS.Sū.8.86)
One should administer life-restoring remedies consisting of nasal drops, potions, collyriums,
and ointments to one who has consumed poison, as well as sharp emetics. (AS.Sū.8.87)
Pippalī, madhuka, honey, sugar, and sugarcane juice, together with the powder of the two types of niśā (dūrvā and haridrā), patra, vella, elā, and trivṛt, mixed with honey.
If purgation, bloodletting,
or venesection is indicated, one should first provide protection for the heart even while in the midst of enemies.
One who has not eaten should drink the ghee known as Ajeya, or even the nectar;
[one may also take] ghee, honey, curd, milk, and finally cold water.

Meat is desired [as a vehicle] with a paste of sugar, licorice, and *pālindī*, as in the case of the iguana, the deer, and the mongoose; likewise, the meat of the spotted deer is taken with long pepper and dry ginger.
With long pepper, ativiṣā, and the meat of a peacock,
along with sugar-candy— these soups (rasas), prepared according to their respective requirements, should be very cold and mixed with ghee. (AS.Sū.8.92)
One should give fine copper powder with honey at the proper time for the purification of the heart to one who has drunk poison and has been purified, both above and below. (AS.Sū.8.93)
Then, when the heart is purified, one should apply an abrasive of gold powder;
like water on a lotus leaf, poison does not adhere to that which has the quality of gold.
And a long life is produced; this procedure is prescribed even for one who has swallowed poison. Thus should the physician protect the person from poisons in the womb and so forth.

From the destruction of that [mind], there would be the annihilation of all actions of living beings. Wisdom, fortitude, patience, and renunciation— though existing in human form, they are superhuman.
Because he is [known] through the king's actions, he is to be propitiated by means beyond the senses;
where the king is present, the physician should enter having been introduced.
Even if authorized, one should not resort to an improper vehicle, standing place,
or seat; when it is appropriate, one should stand before the king and not interrupt his speech.
At the proper time, for the sake of the king, for his own sake, and for the benefit of those he holds dear,
he should speak— conjoined with righteousness and purpose— at the right place and the right time, also for the sake of others.
One should not instruct one who does not ask, for that is a great act of rashness;
nor should one act against his welfare, for that would bring about the destruction of the very root.

One should speak what is agreeable and beneficial, and should privately restrain [the patient] from what is harmful; if there is a fault, one should address it with noble and consoling words, or else overlook it.
One should either remain silent in response or avoid conversation with those who are disliked;
for even a wise person may be ignorant of the mind, whereas a fool may understand the inner disposition.
Even one who is very dear may become hateful, and even one who is hateful may quickly become dear; having informed the king, one should carry out even the most minor tasks.
He should neither travel nor remain for long in the treasury or the inner apartments;
even when there is only a small gain, he should show satisfaction with a mind free from arrogance.
One should avoid mutual gossip with others, slander, and speaking ill of others in pairs;
one should also avoid wearing clothing and other items similar to those of the king, as well as royal pastimes. (AS.Sū.8.105)
Whatever is given by the king must be accepted for the sake of increasing his satisfaction. When it is appropriate to laugh, one should maintain restraint out of deference to the master alone.
When [another] speaks, one should resort to silence regarding the vital secrets of others,
but maintain deafness toward one's own vital secrets; for this is the excellence of fortitude and sweetness.
One should not, through excessive exertion, make oneself too elevated;
for just as a fall leads to suffering, so an elevation does not produce happiness.
Service to the king involves [risk from] playthings, weapons, snakes, and fire;
that [danger] is warded off by well-trained [servants] through great skill.
Having attained sovereignty difficult to obtain and the high esteem of the king,
one should remain vigilant so that one may enjoy these for a long time.
One should arrange a bed all around, consecrated with protective mantras;
at night, one should provide white mustard seeds and auspicious unhusked rice grains to the pure person.
Likewise, at the head of the bed, one should place a protective power [symbol] made of barley sprouts and lac, along with *dūrvā* grass,
a full water-jar, flowers, fruits, and shoots.
Having offered oblations at twilight and having eaten at the end of the night,
this rite of auspiciousness (svastyayana) should be performed by one who is pure for one who is pure.

This is the summary taught for the purpose of protecting against poison— a practice that bestows longevity, promotes nourishment, and overcomes spirits, poisons, sorcery, and evil; however, the detailed procedure is given further on in the Uttara-tantra.

"Having thoroughly examined everything, one who acts with deliberation should apply that [treatment] after diagnosing the signs of the disorder. Thus, the king who is ever vigilant receives instruction for protection against poison, disease, and malevolent spirits.
The Great-Souled One, unassailable by the hosts of his own and his enemies, brings about the welfare and prosperity of the people for a long time.
Thus ends the eighth chapter;
here begins the ninth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the knowledge of incompatible foods;
thus said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
One should not eat together village, marshy, or aquatic meats with honey, molasses, sesame, milk, beans, radish, lotus stalks, or sprouted grains;
especially not fish with milk.
For both of these [fish] are *abhiṣyandi* (secretory) because they ripen into a sweet taste, yet they are mutually contradictory due to their cold and hot potencies (*vīrya*).
Among them, the *cilicima* is particularly so;

it has scales, red eyes, red stripes all over its body, and emits a red luster. It generally moves on the ground. Because it is extremely *abhiṣyandi*, it generates diseases even more intensely than others, as well as the poison of raw meat (*āmaviṣa*).
All sour substances taken together with milk are incompatible (viruddha).

Furthermore, [substances] taken subsequently [to milk] are also incompatible, as are the fruits [of the following], as well as *kaṅgu*, *varaka*, *makuṣṭha*, *vella*, *kulattha*, *māṣa*, and *niṣpāva*.
Having consumed green vegetables such as *namūlaka* and others, one should drink milk out of fear of the affliction of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*).
One should not eat *pauṣkara*, *rauhiṇīka*, or *jātuka* potherbs together with honey and milk; nor should one eat pigeons fried in mustard oil together with those two.
Likewise, one should eat jujubes fried in mustard oil together with fish and jujubes; porcupine and boar meat together with raw meat and bile;
chicken and *pṛṣata* deer with curd; mutton with *kusumbha* greens; sesame cakes with sour gruel (*sauvīraka*);
salt with milk; and black-gram soup with radish.
One should eat leafy vegetables with fresh butter;
*upodakā* with *maireya* wine and *ārdvīka* liquor;
and *pīlu* fruits with *karīra* sprouts.
One should take *virūḍhaka* sprouts with curd, black-gram soup, jaggery, honey, or ghee;
or *lakucaphala* with curd, buttermilk, or jaggery; or *kākamācī*.
That very [substance] cooked in a vessel used for frying fish or for cooking ginger, or cooked elsewhere, having been kept overnight;
or clarified butter kept for ten nights in a bronze vessel; or anything hot among wine, curd, honey, or *bhallātaka*; or *kāmpillaka* prepared with buttermilk—these are incompatible.
AS.Sū.9.4:
Roasted meat on a spit,
fried quail, liquor, rice-and-pulse porridge, and milk-rice are incompatible when consumed together.
Honey, ghee, muscle fat, oil, and water, taken in equal parts, or in pairs, or in threes, or all together;
or honey and ghee in unequal proportions, followed by a drink of rainwater.
Madhupushkara seeds, the potherb padmottarikā, sugar-candy, meat prepared with sour gruel, and honey, when consumed together, are incompatible and excessively aggravate vāta; likewise,
yellow mustard fried in mustard oil is incompatible.
Milk-rice with churned curd as a drink excessively aggravates bile, and it is incompatible;
it also excessively aggravates phlegm.
Upodakā prepared with sesame paste is a cause of dysentery;
likewise, balākā is incompatible with vāruṇī liquor and kulmāṣa grains,
and that same bird, when fried in the fat of a boar, causes instantaneous death.

The flesh of the monitor lizard, quail, partridge, and peacock, prepared with castor root, *dāruharidrā*, and fire, and saturated with castor oil; likewise, the flesh of the green pigeon (*hārīta*), roasted on a spit over turmeric-colored fire,
scorched by that same turmeric fire, and then covered with its own ashes and dust, served with honey.
Likewise, long peppers (pippalī) prepared with oil extracted from fish should be consumed;
one should not eat cold and hot foods, new and old foods, raw and cooked foods, or various types of food together at once.
Immersion in water by one who has been suddenly afflicted by heat causes injury to the skin and the eyes,
as well as an increase in thirst; likewise, the drinking of milk leads to the aggravation of *rakta-pitta*.
For one who has exerted himself with the body, sudden ingestion [of food] leads to vomiting or abdominal tumors;
for one who has exerted himself with speech, it leads to loss of voice.
Thus, a portion of the incompatibilities among food and drink substances, which are frequently encountered, has been described.
Regarding medicinal substances, however, their application strictly according to the instruction is the most reasonable course;
any contradiction thereof has not been stated here for fear of excessive prolixity,
nor is such knowledge exclusively beneficial.
Furthermore,
one should not administer a medicinal substance in brief until the humors have been first provoked.
For that is contradictory because it exists as an adversary to the elements;
it is so both through the inequality and the equality of the powerful mutual qualities.
Furthermore, due to the influence of the *saṃskāras* and other factors, there is also natural incompatibility:
milk with horse-gram (*kulattha*), jackfruit (*panasa*), fish, heated curd, honey, and ghee in equal parts. (AS.Sū.9.9)
Water in saline soil, roasted barley flour during the nights, and likewise *yavaka* grains with water in between—
this is merely an illustration for those whose intellects are as sharp as the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass.
Because it pierces the accumulated impurities and pervades everywhere,
[it destroys] eruptions, swellings, intoxication, abscesses, tumors, consumption, as well as vitality, strength, memory, intelligence, the sensory faculties, and the mind.

One who consumes incompatible food may incur fever, internal hemorrhage (raktapitta), and eight other great diseases, as well as death like [the effects of] poison. In such cases, one should quickly administer purification or pacification with substances antagonistic to those [diseases].
Or first, by means of those very substances, there is the refinement of the body (AS.Sū.9.13) for those who possess physical exertion, unctuousness, a stimulated digestive fire,
youth, and strength (AS.Sū.9.13).
Even if it is contrary [to the patient's habit], food that is wholesome and taken in small quantities does not cause affliction;
by acting in opposition to the humors (*doṣa*) and other factors, it removes the disease of the sick. (AS.Sū.9.14)
The combination of curd, milk, and so forth at one time is not contradictory; however,
due to differences in application and other factors, even wholesome things may become unwholesome.
Likewise, through the distinction of its specific varieties, even that contradiction is removed.
One should abandon what is unwholesome by degrees and practice what is wholesome.
Thereafter, skipping one stage, then two stages, and likewise three stages—
in this sequence, the defects are abandoned and the qualities are increased.
They do not lead to affliction; they attain a state of stability. These three are the supports for that: food, sleep, and celibacy.
Supported by these pillars of reasoning, the body—endowed with strength, complexion, and growth—persists as long as the force of its vital impressions (*saṃskāra*) lasts for life.
In this regard, food has been described and will be further discussed [in the following].
It originates from the creation of the world and other such phenomena; it is rooted in *tamas* and consists of *tamas*.
AS.Sū.9.19 Due to the abundance of darkness, sleep generally arises at night.
AS.Sū.9.20 When the channels are obstructed by phlegm and when one has ceased from physical exertion, [sleep arises].
AS.Sū.9.20 Sleep enters the embodied being through the sense-faculties due to their respective functions.
AS.Sū.9.21 When all the sense-faculties have ceased, yet the mind has not ceased;
At that time, one perceives dreams of various forms arising from the sense objects;
pleasure and pain, nourishment and emaciation, strength and weakness are all dependent upon sleep.
Masculinity and impotence, knowledge and ignorance, and life itself— these do not exist apart from the proper time; nor is sleep indulged in at an improper time due to excessive attachment.
Sleep may deprive one of happiness and long life, like another Night of Doom;
yet that same sleep, when properly employed, endows the body once again with happiness and long life.

The intellect of one devoted to yoga becomes stainless through ascetic practice, just as [the intellect] is purified by heat. Staying awake at night is parching, while sleeping during the day is oily.
AS.Sū.9.25 One should remain seated and avoid drowsiness while practicing that which is non-rough and non-obstructive.
AS.Sū.9.26 This is because in the summer, due to the accumulation of wind (vāyu), dryness, and the shortness of the nights, [the body becomes parched].
Day-sleep is beneficial at other times, for it produces phlegm and bile;
except when one is exhausted by excessive talking, traveling, walking, wine, women, carrying loads, or physical labor.

Those exhausted by anger, grief, and fear; those suffering from dyspnea, hiccups, and diarrhea; the elderly, children, the weak, the emaciated, the wounded, and those afflicted by thirst and colic—[these should not be treated with emetics].
For those afflicted by indigestion, those who are intoxicated, and even those accustomed to sleeping during the day,
there is indeed equilibrium of the bodily constituents (dhātus), as phlegm (śleṣman) nourishes their limbs in such a state.
Those with an abundance of fat and phlegm, as well as those who require constant oleation therapy, should not sleep during the day;
nor should one afflicted by poison or suffering from throat diseases ever sleep at night.
Halīmaka is characterized by heaviness of the head, a sense of numbness,
lassitude of the limbs, fever, vertigo, loss of mental clarity, obstruction of the bodily channels, and dullness of the digestive fire.
Swelling, anorexia, nausea, catarrh, hemicrania,
itching, urticaria, eruptions, pustules, cough, drowsiness, and diseases of the throat.
Furthermore, there may be the onset of the force of poison due to unwholesome sleep; moreover,
because it is not properly digested, the phlegm (kapha) excessively obstructs the channels.
Then, when the channels are obstructed, heaviness of the limbs arises;
for one with heavy limbs there is lassitude, and from lassitude comes excessive sleepiness.
Purgation, emesis of the body and head,
bloodletting, medicated smoking, and [avoidance of] hunger, thirst, physical pain, exhilaration, grief, sexual intercourse, fear, and anger.
Thought, longing, a comfortable bed, nobility of character, and victory over darkness—
these ward off unwholesome, coarse food and excessive sleep.
These very factors should be understood as the causes of insomnia:
the loss of time and of wholesome habits, as well as disease and the aggravation of vāta and pitta.
From the loss of sleep arise body ache, heaviness of the head, yawning, dullness,
exhaustion, giddiness, indigestion, drowsiness, and diseases born of Vāta.
When phlegm is diminished and stirred up by wind, it obstructs the channels and produces a severe lethargy that robs one of consciousness and causes delusion.
In that case, the eyes are wide open and bulging, with the pupils turned upward; they are tearful and have disheveled eyelashes.
It can be cured within two and a half nights, but it cannot be cured beyond that. Therefore,
one should habitually resort to sleep at night according to the proper time and according to what is wholesome for oneself.
AS.Sū.9.41 Due to unwholesome habits or excessive wakefulness, one should sleep for half the night; in the morning, one who has not eaten should sleep.
However, one who suffers from insomnia should habitually consume milk, sugarcane juice, or meat broths.
Meat from marshy and aquatic animals, edible foods made of molasses and flour,
*śāli* rice, intoxicants, mung beans, inspissated milk, and buffalo curd.
Anointing with oil, rubbing with unguents, bathing, filling the ears,
pouring [medicinal liquids] into the eyes, and applying ointments to the head and the face.
In a fragrant place with a pleasant breeze, upon a comfortable bed as is appropriate,
he receives massages and pleasant touch from attendants who understand his mind.
One should drink ghee with milk as an after-drink, boiled with the *jīvanīya* (life-promoting) drugs.
Embracing the vine-like arms of a beloved woman is true bliss; it is the fulfillment of all that needs to be done.
For one who delights in celibacy and whose mind is free from desire for vulgar pleasures, objects that are agreeable to the mind merely provide the comfort of sleep.
Sleep does not bypass its own time for one who is content and satisfied; moreover,
a person prone to sleep should avoid these very things to the greatest extent possible.

Sleep arises from time, natural constitution, disease, mental state, physical exhaustion, phlegm, external factors, and darkness. Of these, the first sustains the body; the others, which end with sin, have disease as their cause.

AS.Sū.9.49: However, when engaging in sexual intercourse, one should not approach a woman who is menstruating, one who is disliked, one of improper conduct, one who is ill-omened, one who is excessively stout, one who is excessively thin, one who is pregnant, one who has recently given birth, one who is not lying on her back, one with deformed limbs, a prostitute, one who is childless, one of a defective womb, one of another caste, or another man’s wife; and especially one who is advanced in age or caste, one of the same lineage (*sagotrā*), the wife of a teacher, a friend, a kinsman, or a servant, or a female ascetic (*varṇinī*). Likewise, one should not go at a sacred tree, a crossroads, a meeting of four roads, a grove, a cemetery, a slaughterhouse, near water, among medicinal herbs, or in the presence of Brahmins, teachers, gods, or the king's palace; nor during the day, at the time of releasing cattle, at midday, at midnight, on festival days, or when one is thirsty or has not formed a firm resolve.
And one should not engage in perverse sexual intercourse,
especially with a woman who is excessively exhausted, pregnant, recently delivered, menstruating, or whose vagina is constricted.
One should avoid striking the head and should not restrain the semen when it is about to be emitted; thus,
one should engage in sexual intercourse only for the sake of maintaining the stability of the mind and body.
"One should not be intent upon that," it is said;
and here there is a verse (AS.Sū.9.50):
A young man, confident and joyful, desiring her in private, with his limbs well-poised, fragrant, having voided urine and other waste,
free from distress, neither hungry nor overfed, and satiated for three days with aphrodisiacs— AS.Sū.9.51.
One should approach a woman, or women endowed with good qualities, who has previously been with him;

during the spring, one may do so every two days, at its end [one day] every fortnight, and likewise during the rainy season; however, during the winter and the cool season, a man of strength may indulge in desire according to his wish.
Bath-pastes, body-unguents, fans, moonlight, meat, spirituous liquors, milk, meat-broths, *rasālā*,
various foods rich in sugar, and very cold water.
One who is exhausted at the end of sexual intercourse should indulge in sleep;
for through contact with women, even the strong may instantly become impotent.
In this way, their semen and vital essence (dhātu) are quickly replenished;
[this also serves] to counteract the depletion of vision, lifespan, ojas, and semen, as well as diseases localized in the penis.
AS.Sū.9.55 Otherwise, the fool incurs provocation of the wind (*vāyu*) and unrighteousness.
AS.Sū.9.56 Or, by suppressing the urge while lying on one's back, there occurs an increase [of urine], urinary disorders, stones, and gravel.
The onset of diseases such as *timira* (visual impairment) certainly results from striking the head and other parts of the body.
Dizziness, fatigue, weakness of the thighs, and the depletion of strength, the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), and the sense faculties (*indriya*) [arise from the same].
AS.Sū.9.57 There may also be untimely death, especially from excessive sexual intercourse. AS.Sū.9.58 [A child] born before sixteen years or after seventy years is not [viable].
A man who desires long life should not engage in sexual union with women. For a very young boy, whose bodily constituents (*dhātus*) are not yet fully developed, incurs harm by approaching a woman.
AS.Sū.9.59 It is suddenly scorched like a pond whose water has been drained.
AS.Sū.9.60 It is as dry and withered as wood that has been gnawed by insects and is decayed.
AS.Sū.9.60 Just as something touched quickly falls apart, so does an old man when approaching a woman.
AS.Sū.9.61 For the semen is the supreme vital energy (*tejas*) of the body; it is the very essence even of the essence of food.
One who has conquered the self must protect that [body], for from it comes a noble lineage; being vigilant, one should pursue those states known as pleasant for the present moment.

One might become attached to things that appear pleasant but have a painful outcome; this is merely harmful to the body. (AS.Sū.9.62) Intellectual error, contact with unsuitable objects, and seasonal abnormalities [are the causes of disease]. (AS.Sū.9.63)
Even when a person is intent on wholesome food, they may be afflicted by diseases;
at that time, the morbid humors (malas) do not immediately oppress one who consumes unwholesome things.
When [the humors] obstruct the provocation [of one another] by means of corrupted tissues (*dūṣya*) and so forth,
then not even every therapeutic measure (*upacāra*) is effective against all disorders at all times.
For not all unwholesome things have equal defects,
nor indeed are all defects of equal strength, nor are all bodies alike.
In the state of resistance to disease, those very things which are unwholesome become the most unwholesome when they are increased by factors such as similar [aggravated] doshas.
Furthermore, those very same disorders, accumulated through many causes,
mutually contradictory, powerful, and persisting for a long time, [arise].
All [the humors], when equally provoked, even upon encountering a slight cause,
resort to the seats of the vital breaths (prāṇāyatana), becoming deep-seated and pervading all pathways.
Even those things that are unwholesome for the body may, after a long time, become quickly acting [in their harm].
AS.Sū.9.70: Furthermore, other things that are unwholesome [for one person] may, through habituation, become tolerable for others.
Furthermore, their humors (doṣas) undergo depletion through [the effects of] karma, wind, sun, and so forth.
For those whose diet, age, suitability, and constitution differ, [a single regimen] may be equally beneficial.
A disease arises from the simultaneous affliction by one or more of the deranged *vāyu* and other humors.
AS.Sū.9.72: Furthermore, the derangement of *vāta* and the other humors results from the abnormal movement of the planets (*graha*).
Furthermore, the occurrence of these [calamities] arises from terrestrial, atmospheric, and celestial portents,
as well as from the collective karma [of beings].
The vitiated wind is obstructive, stagnant, excessively hot or cold, coiled, making a terrifying sound, harsh, appearing out of season, and powerful.
With its movement obstructed by one another, filled with dust, tears, and distress,
its taste, color, and other qualities altered, and abandoned by birds.
Water that originates from a blameworthy source, from a depleted reservoir,
or which is defiled by the presence of many flies, mice, and snakes; AS.Sū.9.75.
The place abounds in unwholesome food and has lost its great medicinal herbs of righteousness; and the time is adverse, exhibiting signs of extreme deficiency as appropriate.
AS.Sū.9.77 Because these are difficult to avoid, they lead to ever-increasing harm;
for those whose actions are not restrained during that most terrible time, AS.Sū.9.77.
The fivefold regimen for them should be applied in the same manner as for rejuvenation (rasāyana);
the growth of the body is commended through the medicines previously extracted.
Celibacy, compassion, generosity, delight in right conduct,
tranquility, the true Dharma, excellent discourse, and worship of the gods and the self-conquered sages.
Residing in regions that are not afflicted and associating with virtuous people,
as well as performing rituals based on divine intervention, are desired actions for the preservation of life.

One should perform the respective practices during the winter and other seasons, even when they are not the prescribed times, because the practice of those [meditations] is caused by the dualities such as cold and so forth.
AS.Sū.9.82: The seasonal regimen and so forth, as well as the remedies for the humors caused by cold, heat, and rain;
and for this very reason, in the conduct [of life], the *hemanta* and *śiśira* seasons are treated as equal.
For all living beings, lifespan always depends upon a combination [of factors];
its strength or weakness is established in both destiny (*daiva*) and human effort (*puruṣakāra*).

One should know that actions performed in another birth are destiny (*daiva*), while those performed in this life are human effort (*pauruṣa*); these two types of action are further divided into three categories according to whether they are superior, middling, or inferior.
The application of these two [types of conduct] is the cause of a long life that is very happy and fixed; the opposite is the cause of its contrary.
The intermediate [result] belongs to the intermediate [cause], which is mixed and blended; hear another [point]:
divine power is indeed weakened and overcome by human effort.
Likewise, seeing that human effort is weak when confronted by powerful destiny,
some believe that the measure of one's lifespan is fixed.
Some karma is fixed as to its maturation at a certain time and is great;
some is fixed as to its time and is awakened by conditions.
Thus, death is taught to be of two kinds, distinguished by timely and untimely; and from that follows this sequence of beneficial and harmful practices.
The exponents of the Vedas declare that there are one hundred and one types of death;
among these, one is associated with time (natural), while the remainder are considered adventitious.
And by means of sacrifices such as the Śyena, one [slays] an enemy; likewise, according to them,
the slaughter of oneself was ordained through the Dīrghaśravasa-soma and other rites.
For one who desires long life, there is the attainment of it through that [rite], as well as by means of the Mitravindā sacrifice; moreover,
one should protect oneself from everything— such is the traditional teaching (smṛti).
Likewise, death is taught by the followers of the Sugata to be of four kinds;
for those whose lifespan is fixed, it occurs through the failure to avoid the uneven (dangerous conditions).
For others, illness is certain; however,
death at an improper time [occurs] through such things as sudden blows from weapons, whereas otherwise death is not manifest.
The encounter with wildly agitated and fierce elephants, horses, and the like;
and the consumption of food accompanied by the violence of hostile winds and other such elements.
The sages endowed with divine vision would not say that one should avoid the methods of Rasāyana therapy, such as those based on divine means (daivavyapāśraya).
Moreover, even they would not obtain the maintenance of their lifespan according to their desire;
and for the wise, there would be no fear of snakes, lions, elephants, and the like.
For one who desires long life, there are false walls and fortresses, false protection against death, and the mere avoidance of the wives of others and so forth.
Summoned by the deity of the mantra, the great serpents do not speak;
they remain as if asleep from poison, yet they indicate the presence or absence of one's life-force.
For one seized by Sanyāsa, Rohiṇīkā, and the like, death may occur suddenly;
however, through indifference there is no death, nor is there life through medical treatment.
The lifespan of one who lives according to the righteous path would not be equal to that of a thousand men striking one another daily in battle.
Indra and the other gods would not approach their enemy with weapons, nor would the Aśvins approach one afflicted by disease,
if untimely death were not to occur.
Through the preservation or lack of preservation of unbaked and baked jars,
their duration for a long or short time is observed, as is the case with those situated in various places.
Even though untimely death is extremely well-known and established by all the scriptures, how could a wise person have any doubt regarding it when it is actually observed?
When a physician or other [factors] possessing excellence are available,
yet death occurs, they call that "timely death" (kālaja); the opposite of this is otherwise.
Just as a chariot being driven correctly undergoes gradual wear,
so too does the lifespan of those who possess self-mastery; for others, it is the reverse.
A lamp with pure oil and a clean wick, untroubled by insects, wind, or other disturbances,
burns brightly and properly as long as its fuel is not exhausted.
Therefore, just as it would be otherwise in the case of the opposite,
so too by means of the application of what is beneficial and what is harmful, a person certainly becomes [so].
Having abandoned everything else, one should therefore protect the body;
for in its absence, there is the total non-existence of all things for embodied beings.
Just as one who knows a city is attentive to the city, or as a charioteer is attentive to his chariot,
so should the wise man be attentive in the duties concerning his own body.
Having specifically examined the causes for the preparation of food, such as their inherent nature and so forth, one should eat what is beneficial; for the body is indeed produced from food.
One who has fallen under the sway of fear, shame, constraint, greed, joy, or sorrow should never suppress the natural urges; for that is the source of all calamities.
For a man who practices what is beneficial, there arises no premature encounter with the fangs of Time (Death) regarding his strength,
enthusiasm, sensory faculties, and lifespan.
Even if one incurs blame by abandoning things that are harmful,
a self-possessed person nevertheless attains freedom from debt toward the virtuous.
And whatever origin of disease cannot be altered here by anyone,
having encountered that, a wise person should not grieve.
For those who consume wholesome food and engage in wholesome activities, who practice virtuous conduct,
and who have regard for both worlds, life indeed becomes like nectar.
Greedy for the pleasures of the village, subject to the afflictions, and having destroyed the true path,
the deluded person lives for no purpose, increasing his own miserable rebirths.

A wise person who desires to live for a long time should conquer those enemies residing within the body that are ever-present, and should avoid both what is to be avoided and what is not to be avoided.
Therefore,
remembering the words of Ātreya, a wise person should not perform an action that results in unwholesome consequences, whether in the present or in the future.
Thus ends the ninth chapter.
Now begins the tenth chapter.
AS.Sū.10.1: Hereafter, we shall expound the chapter on the rules for food and drink.
Thus have the great seers, Ātreya and others, declared:
they say that food and drink prescribed by rule, which provide the objects of the desired senses, are the basis for life.
For vitality, radiance, the elements, the sense faculties, strength, contentment, nourishment, eloquence, health, and so forth depend upon it;
and the maintenance of the internal fire has that as its fuel.

"The maintenance of the body has fire as its root" (AS.Sū.10.3). Now, a self-possessed person, having examined the seven specific preparations of food—which result in health or ill-health and which have as their causes the conditions of inherent nature, combination, processing, quantity, place, time, and application—should pursue only that which is beneficial. (AS.Sū.10.3)
In that regard, by way of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), divine water, red rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, mung beans, antelopes, quail, and so forth are light;
whereas milk, sugarcane, *vrīhi* rice, black gram, meat from marshy regions, and so forth are heavy.
Indeed, these [substances] undergo a change of state through specific combinations (*saṃyoga*) and other factors.
In that context, conjunction (saṃyoga) is the state of aggregation of two or more substances;
it initiates a specific quality which the individual substances do not possess singly.

The *saṃskāra* (processing) is produced by water, fire, contact, cleansing, churning, place, time, mental disposition (*bhāvanā*), the vessel, and so forth; whereas the *mātrā* (measure), however, is the quantity of the food-mass according to the size of the lump, in its totality, and in relation to each individual substance,
while *deśa* (place) refers to the location of the substance and the consumer at the time of its production.
Furthermore, in that regard, [the patient] is to be examined according to the user's state of health or illness and according to the distinction of their constitution;
time, however, is to be examined with respect to the season and the disease, as well as by the signs of digestion or indigestion.
Even when indigestion is present, the undigested essence (*rasa*) of a previous meal, being mixed with a subsequent one, quickly provokes all the *doṣas*.

However, when the food has been digested, when the *doṣas* have returned to their own seats, when the downward movement of wind (*vātānulomya*) is restored, when the urges for urine and feces have been discharged, when belching and the openings of the channels of the heart are purified, when the sense organs are clear, when the body is light, when the digestive fire (*agni*) is kindled, and when hunger has arisen—food consumed at such a time does not corrupt the *doṣas*, but rather increases longevity, strength, and complexion;
this alone is the proper time for eating.
Furthermore, that which has been delayed in time, being obstructed by wind (vāta), undergoes digestion with great difficulty; it causes emaciation and further destroys the appetite for food.

Regarding the rules for consumption: one should not eat while naked, nor while wearing only a single garment, nor while dressed in dirty clothes; nor without having offered oblations, nor without having recited prayers, nor without having made offerings to the deities, nor to the ancestors, nor without first giving the *agra-anna* (the first portion) to the fire, nor to the teachers, nor to guests, nor to those who have arrived; nor without having looked after even the animals that depend on or dwell near him, provided they are his own property. One should eat while endowed with a commendable place, time, and utensils; wearing a garland and being well-adorned; with hands and feet fragrant and moistened; with a very clean face; accompanied by a desired companion; [eating food] that is free from hair, flies, and the like; blameless; not blaming [others]; blameless; not reheated; neither too hot nor burnt; well-cooked; without greed; not unwholesome (*asātmya*); not unknown; not of unknown origin; not too late in the evening, nor too early in the morning; not in the open air, not in the heat of the sun, nor in the dark; not beneath a tree; not lying down; not leaning forward; not from a broken vessel; not in an uncovered or dirty place, nor in one defiled by disposition; not while standing on a seat; not while holding it in the hand; not while the hand is raised; facing the east; with a cheerful mind; eating wholesome food provided by pure, hungry, and agreeable people.
He should not eat stale food, except for meat served as a side dish or other solid foods;
nor should he leave any remainder, except for curds, honey, ghee, water, parched grain flour, fermented gruel, and milk-rice.

Furthermore, he should eat what is unctuous, light, warm, without delay, neither too quickly, and while not talking, laughing, or distracted, but with full attention, having properly observed himself.

For substances that are unctuous, light, and hot kindle the digestive fire within the abdomen, cleanse the gastrointestinal tract, do not disturb the bodily tissues (*dhātu*), cause rapid digestion, and direct the vital wind (*anila*) in its natural downward course.
Likewise, the unctuous [substance] strengthens the sense organs, builds up the body, diminishes old age, increases strength, and brings about clarity of complexion.
Furthermore, food that is light by nature and so forth undergoes transformation without oppressing the bodily constituents (*dhātus*) or agitating the humors (*doṣas*);
even when it has gone bad, it causes little harm.
Moreover, heat generates appetite, dries up phlegm (*śleṣman*), and [subdues] it.
One who eats too slowly does not achieve satiety, eats excessively, and the food becomes cold, resulting in irregular digestion.

However, for one who eats too quickly, while talking or with the mind elsewhere, there may be spitting out, depression, lack of stability in the food, and an inability to discern its qualities and defects.
Having thus correctly examined oneself, thinking "this is suitable for me" and "this is unsuitable," one should always remain vigilant and reflect upon this.
In this context, "sātmya" (habituation) is that which exists together with one's own self and has been practiced; some say it is that which is beneficial due to its suitability.
That which is contrary to sātmya is asātmya, because it does not provide benefit.

Others, however, maintain that suitability (sātmya) is manifold according to the influence of constitution, age, season, humor (doṣa), and disease; for they accept mere relief (upaśaya) as the criterion and designate even that which possesses contrary qualities as suitable through its therapeutic application,
while they consider that which possesses similar qualities to be unsuitable because it does not provide relief.
Suitability (*sātmya*), moreover, is of three kinds according to the division of superior, inferior, and middling:
among these, that which contains all tastes is superior, that which has a single taste is inferior, and that which is of a middling taste is middling;
of these, they prescribe the superior for one whose *doṣas* are in equilibrium.
It has been stated previously that one should gradually become accustomed to other things as well, or else avoid even wholesome items by one-quarter [of the usual amount];
therein, that collection of foods which maintains the equilibrium of the *dhātus* and restores those that are disturbed is, in brief, wholesome (*hita*), while the opposite is unwholesome (*ahita*).

Furthermore, although that [diet] is not fixed due to the variety of factors such as the individual's constitution and the application of yoga, one should practice it according to the instruction and according to what is most prevalent,
and one should avoid it; likewise, one should specifically avoid eating at the same time every day, eating between meals, eating in improper measure, and eating irregularly.
In that context, eating wholesome and unwholesome foods together is "equal eating" (samaśana); eating after what has already been eaten is "intermediate eating" (madhyaśana);
and immoderate eating will be taught separately.
However, eating at an improper time or when one has not yet reached the right state of digestion is called "irregular eating" (viṣamāśana).
While eating, one should place the drinks, soups, meat-broths, and side dishes in silver vessels;
furthermore, very hot milk that is neither parched nor overly greasy should be placed in golden vessels.

In bronze vessels, there were *khalakhaṭvaraka* and *kāmbalika* dishes, along with *rāga*, *ṣāḍava*, and *saṭṭaka* condiments; ghee was served in vessels variegated with diamonds and lapis lazuli, and very cold milk in iron ones; water and beverages were served in copper vessels; and rice was served in vessels made of clay, gold, crystal, and glass, in a spacious and delightful place.
For otherwise, due to the difference in color, fragrance, and taste, it would be harmful.
Moreover:
One should place solid foods on the right side, and drinks, foods to be licked, and mouth-cleansing boluses on the left; hard foods to be chewed should be placed in the middle.
According to one's digestive temperament (*agni-sātmya*), one should first eat liquids or semi-dry foods.
But even more so, [the food] should be heavy, sweet, and unctuous at the beginning;
sour and salty in the middle; and dry, liquid, and combined with other tastes at the end.

In that regard, for one with weak digestive fire whose heat has been stimulated by warm liquids, other food consumed will undergo proper digestion (AS.Sū.10.11). However, water alone is best as a post-drink (anupāna), because it is the source of all tastes, because it is compatible with all living beings, and because it possesses qualities such as sustaining life (AS.Sū.10.11).
That [cold] diet is indicated for curd, honey, barley, wheat, and various types of wine, as well as for all burning (vidāhin) substances during autumn and summer;
whereas a hot diet is indicated for flour-based foods and other indigestible items during the winter,
and one should observe the principles regarding liquid substances accordingly.

Milk is [beneficial] for śāli and ṣaṣṭika rice; likewise, meat broth is for those exhausted by fasting, travel, speaking, sexual intercourse, or physical exercise, as well as for children, the elderly, and those suffering from consumption (śoṣa) and similar ailments;
however, sour substances are for [those with] vāta disorders.
In cases of pitta, sugar-water;

in cases of kapha, decoction of triphalā with honey; and in diseases of the eyes and throat, curd-whey, or the supernatant liquid of curd (mastu), or the cream of curd (kūcikā), or the thickened cream (kīlāṭa).

One should employ fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla), whey (mastu), or buttermilk (takra) with vegetable-based foods; wine with meats; and various fruit-acidulated waters or fermented liquors (āsava) with fruits.
Specifically, one should use honey-based liquors (madhvāsava) with domestic animals and sharp, triphalā-based liquors with wild animals.

For birds of prey (*viṣkira*), one should provide fermented liquors made from the fruits of the *nyagrodha* and other trees; for hole-dwellers (*bileśaya*) and those killed by poisoned weapons, fermented liquors made from *arka*, *śelu*, *śirīṣa*, and *kapittha*; for beasts of prey (*prasaha*), fermented liquors made from sour fruits; for large wild animals (*mahāmṛga*) and aquatic creatures, fermented liquors made from *kāśa*, sugarcane, lotus seeds, *śṛṅgāṭaka*, *kaśeruka*, grapes, and *khadira*, or cold water mixed with honey, or whey (*udaśvit*);
and for those that scratch with their claws (*pratuda*), as well as for those exhausted by fatigue or emaciated, [one should provide] liquor (*surā*).
Honey-water for those with thickened secretions;
wine for those accustomed to wine and meat who have weak digestive fires; and likewise [other remedies].

In brief, a post-prandial drink (anupāna) that is not contrary to the food and is non-contradictory [to the bodily elements] satisfies, gladdens, invigorates, and nourishes; it brings about the fullness of the body, settles what has been eaten, breaks up the mass of food, produces softness, moistens, and generates easy digestion and rapid movement of the food.

However, it should be avoided by those suffering from diseases of the supraclavicular region, dyspnea, cough, spitting, hiccups, hoarseness of voice, or chest injuries, as well as by those habitually addicted to singing and speaking;

for in them, the *āmāśaya* being vitiated, having encountered the oily essence of food situated in the chest and throat, produces diseases such as excessive secretions (*abhiṣyanda*), loss of digestive fire (*agnisāda*), vomiting, and so forth.
Furthermore, after drinking it, one should not engage in speaking, singing, walking long distances, or sleeping.
And [those suffering from] excessive drinking, a moist body, consumption, eye disease, or ulcers [should not eat at night].

(AS.Sū.10.13) Thereafter, having had the food in his hand removed by another, and having gradually cleansed what remains between his teeth by means of cleaning, he should rinse his mouth to remove any smear, odor, or oiliness. Having sipped water so that drops fall from the tips of his fingers over his eyes, and having cleared his mouth with betel and the like, and having dispelled the upward pressure of phlegm through the inhalation of medicinal smoke (*dhūma*), he should walk about one hundred paces and then lie down on his left side. (AS.Sū.10.13)
One who has consumed a meal that is predominantly liquid should not indulge excessively in lying down;
after eating, one should avoid vehicles, swimming, riding animals, fire, and exposure to the sun.
Furthermore, these are the factors that facilitate the digestion of food:
Namely: heat, wind, moisture, humidity, time, and their proper combination.
Therein, heat digests; wind draws away [waste]; moisture produces softness; humidity brings about relaxation; time effects the pervasion throughout the entire body;
and the proper combination of these results in the transformation of food and the equilibrium of the elements (*dhātu*).
Furthermore, the causes for proper digestion are the appropriate and beneficial refinement of the body, diet, physical activity, sleep, and cheerfulness.
As the food is being digested, its qualities attain the state of bodily qualities, provided they are non-contradictory according to their respective natures;
however, those that are contradictory, or are impaired by opposing factors, will afflict the body.
And there are these verses on this subject:
"Parched grain, black pepper, and flattened rice, as well as rice-grains that have been well-ground... (AS.Sū.10.14)
One who desires happiness should never eat today what he has already eaten; one should eat in moderation food that is dominated by vegetables,
and that which is pungent, sour, astringent, or salty.
One should abandon food that is unwholesome to the body's tastes, as well as heavy and dry food;
for that which aggravates all the *doṣas* will be described in the section on etiology (*nidāna*) and elsewhere.
Kilāṭa, curd, kūcikā, fish, dried meat, and radish are excessively moistening, constipating, burning, heavy, and parching. (AS.Sū.10.17)
One should not habitually consume all such things as alkaline preparations, flour-based foods,
or sprouted grains; rather, one should habitually consume rice, wheat, barley, ṣaṣṭika rice, and the meat of wild animals.
Suniṣaṇṇaka, jīvantī, bāla, mūlaka, and vāstuka; AS.Sū.10.19 pathyā, āmalaka, mṛdvīkā, paṭolī, mudga, and śarkarā.
Clarified butter with divine water, milk, honey, pomegranate, and rock salt;
and triphalā with honey and clarified butter at night, for the strengthening of the eyes.
That which maintains health and that which eradicates disease [arise] through the natural state, the proper measure, and their conjunction, as well as through their mutual opposites. (AS.Sū.10.21)
Those foods which are incompatible should be avoided by the wise;
for by abandoning the causes of imbalance and by consuming those that are harmonious, [health is maintained].
Imbalanced [humors] do not persist; the constituent elements arise in equilibrium.
One should fill two parts of the stomach with food and one part with drink.
One should leave the fourth [element] as the remaining substratum for the winds and so forth, for the sake of a mild digestive fire, strength, health, sovereignty, happiness, and the self.

This sequence should be applied constantly, though not necessarily in other cases. [Excessive use] causes dryness, loss of strength and complexion, roughness of the skin, and the obstruction of flatus and feces.
Excessively unctuous food causes the accumulation of phlegm, excessive salivation, heaviness of the heart, lassitude, and loss of appetite (AS.Sū.10.26).
Excessively hot food causes intoxication, burning sensations, thirst, loss of strength, vertigo, and internal hemorrhaging (rakta-pitta) (AS.Sū.10.26).
Cold [food], however, causes loss of appetite, impairment of the digestive fire, nausea, constipation, horripilation,
excessive hardness of stool and urine, lack of satiety, lack of pervasion [of nutrients], and slow digestion. (AS.Sū.10.27)
Excessively liquid food causes chronic rhinitis, urinary disorders, cough, and discharge, and it destroys the strength of the digestive fire.
Excessively sweet food pacifies the fire; when consumed as unwholesome (asātmya), it does not lead to the nourishment of the body.
Excessive salt is harmful to the eyes; that which is too pungent or too pure leads directly to old age.
Without even contracting a slight physical ailment, such a man reaches the end of his hundred-year lifespan.
Thus ends the tenth chapter.
Now begins the eleventh chapter.
11.1: Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "On Eating in Moderation" (Mātrāśitīya).
"Thus have the great seers, Ātreya and the others, said:
one should be a consumer of measured food. (AS.Sū.11.2)

Furthermore, the definition of *mātrā* (proper quantity) is as follows: it depends on the digestive fire (*agni-bala*) and the nature of the food substance; it consists of not compressing the abdomen with food, not obstructing the heart, not distending the sides, and no excessive heaviness of the stomach; it brings satisfaction to the sense organs, cessation of hunger and thirst, and a state of comfort during standing, sitting, lying down, walking, breathing in and out, and during conversation and discourse; it involves easy digestion in the evening and morning, and it promotes strength, complexion, and corpulence. This is the characteristic of *mātrā*.
It is taught that for heavy foods, one should eat until three-quarters full or half-full; even for light foods, one should not eat to complete satiety.

For those foods that abound in the qualities of air and fire are light; because their qualities are similar [to fire], they kindle the digestive fire, yet when consumed improperly, they cause little harm.
Others, however, which abound in the qualities of earth and water, are the opposite due to their dissimilarity [to fire], except for the power of physical exercise and the digestive fire.
Furthermore, immoderation in eating consists of either deficiency or excess.

In this regard, food taken in insufficient quantity causes the impairment of strength, complexion, nourishment, mind, intellect, and the sense organs; it acts as an obstruction, is non-aphrodisiac, lacks vitality, expels the essential nutrients (*sāra*), generates misfortune, and is the abode of eighty types of wind disorders (*vāta-vikāra*).
Furthermore, they say that food taken in excess provokes all the *doṣas*.

For by that [excessive food], the *vāta* and other *doṣas*, being simultaneously aggravated and confined to one part of the abdomen, enter that very undigested matter (*āma*) and, causing distension, bring about *alasaka* (intestinal torpor).
Furthermore, by suddenly reversing the flow through both the upper and lower pathways, one brings about *viṣūcikā*.
(AS.Sū.11.4) Moreover, (AS.Sū.11.4)
It moves neither upward nor downward, and food is not digested;
having become stagnant in the stomach, it is therefore known as *alasaka* (intestinal obstruction).
It is characterized by various piercing pains due to the intense provocation of the *vāyu* and other humors.
AS.Sū.11.5 Viṣūcikā is so called because it pierces the limbs as if with needles.

AS.Sū.11.6 In that condition, Vāta produces colic, abdominal distension, body ache, dryness of the mouth, delirium, trembling, fainting, vertigo, yawning, convulsions, inward turning of the eyes, and excessive pain in the head and heart, as well as the contraction and stiffness of the vessels.
Pitta, moreover, produces fever, diarrhea, internal burning, discoloration, thirst, intoxication, vertigo, fainting, and exhaustion.

Kapha, however, produces vomiting, anorexia, salivation, malaise, indigestion, cold-fever, and heaviness of the limbs. Specifically, in a person who is weak, has a low digestive fire, and an abundance of kapha, or one who suppresses the urges of flatus, urine, and feces, food and drink—oppressed by the wind (vāyu) and its path obstructed by kapha—fails to move outward due to its sluggish nature; consequently, it generates the aforementioned symptoms such as colic and others in excessive measure, with the exception of vomiting and diarrhea.
In that condition of alasaka, the excessively aggravated doshas paralyze the body like a staff; therefore, they declare this alasaka to be incurable.
Furthermore, those who habitually consume incompatible foods, eat before previous meals are digested, or eat while still hungry, consider the resulting āma-dosha to be "āma-poison" (āmaviṣa).
Because their symptoms resemble those of poison,
they are ultimately incurable.

Because of its lack of promptness and because it involves contrary applications, one cannot obtain the entire fruit of food through the dosage alone; for the factors such as nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth have distinct results.
Thus it is said:

AS.Sū.11.8: Food and drink that is consumed when it is heavy, rough, dry, cold, disliked, constipating, burning, impure, incompatible, or excessively watery; or when taken at the wrong time or out of season; or by one who is afflicted by desire, anger, greed, envy, pride, grief, agitation, fear, or hunger—even that causes the *āma* (undigested matter) to become corrupted. AS.Sū.11.9: In that case, while the corruption is being treated, one should induce vomiting with salted warm water once the morbid matter has become thick and sluggish.

AS.Sū.11.9 Likewise, one should cause the patient who is vomiting with excessively suppressed morbid humors (doṣas) to drink a decoction of *madanaphala* mixed with a paste of *kṛṣṇā* and *nāgadantī*,
or [the same] mixed with a paste of *pippalī* and *siddhārthaka*.

Alternatively, one may administer the juice of *kośātakī* mixed with the powder of *dantī* and *māgadhikā*, or, depending on the patient's condition, the strong emetics described in the section on emetics; thereafter, one should treat the patient with sudation and the application of suppositories.
Moreover,
for one who has been immediately and correctly purified, those afflictions are stilled.
In the case of colic with an empty stomach, one should drink the powder of asafoetida,
prativiṣā, vyoṣa, sauvarcala salt, vacā, and abhayā, mixed with lukewarm water.
Alternatively, one may take the root of Pippalī, Trivṛt, Dāru, Saindhava salt, Śuṇṭhī, along with milk, salt, Pippalī, and Marica.
Or [one may take] pāṭhā, amlavetasa, kṣāra, yavānī, and pauṣkara; or twice as much [of the following]: hiṅgu, vacā, agni, kuṣṭha, suvarcikā, kṣāra, biḍa salt, and ajamodā.

Mustā, ajamodā, pūtikā, vacā, śuṇṭhī, agni, and dhānyaka destroy splenic disorders, abdominal enlargement, flatulence, choleraic symptoms, piles, heart disease, abdominal tumors, and upward-moving wind. (AS.Sū.11.14)
One suffering from thirst and colic should drink a decoction made of *savalaka*, *śaṭī*, and *bilva*;
[or one made] with *rāsnā*, *kaṭphala*, *ṣaḍgranthā*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, and *joṅgaka*.

One should perform an ointment, a rubbing powder, or an incense fumigation with guggulu, ativiṣā, kuṣṭha, patra, vyāghranakha, and ambuda— either dried or mixed with urine (AS.Sū.11.16). Furthermore, one should apply a plaster made of sour substances ground together to an abdomen that is painful and distended.
A preparation of *dāru*, Himalayan *kuṣṭha*, *śatāhvā*, asafoetida,
rock salt, barley flour, alkali, and buttermilk is supreme for overcoming pain in the digestive tract.
In cases of retention of feces and urine, one should apply a suppository made with rock salt and other ingredients; furthermore, one should wrap the limbs that have been thoroughly fomented and bent.
When *viṣūcī* has become excessively aggravated, cauterization of the two heels is recommended with a paste made from the two types of alkali (*kṣāra*),
aged oil-cake (*piṇyāka*), *kuṣṭha*, *aruṣkara*, and *citraka*.

Oil cooked with fermented gruel and rock salt is beneficial for massage (AS.Sū.11.19). For one who has properly undergone emesis and purgation, when there is extreme stiffness of the limbs (AS.Sū.11.20), [this oil is recommended].
One should cook ghee and oil with bhallātaka, beeswax, aged oil-cake, and ginger, along with sour liquids; this is an excellent remedy for khalli.
A rubbing paste made from cinnamon bark, *rāsnā*, eaglewood, drumstick tree, costus, vacā, and *śatāhvā*, ground with sour liquids,
cures abdominal tumors and cholera; likewise, oil cooked with these same ingredients serves the same purpose.
Having fasted on that day, one should treat the patient as if they have undergone purgation; thus,
the treatment for *viṣūcī* and *alasaka* has been stated in general according to the established tradition.

In cases of disorders arising from undigested food (āmadoṣa), however, having observed that the patient has digested his meal at the time of eating, that the stomach (āmāśaya) is smeared with morbid humors (doṣa), that the abdomen is numb and heavy, and that there is no desire for food, one should administer medicine for the purpose of digesting the remaining morbid matter and for the purpose of kindling the digestive fire.
One should not, however, administer medicine again while the previous meal is still undigested.
For when the digestive fire is weakened by the defect of undigested matter (*āma*), it is incapable of simultaneously digesting the undigested matter, the medicine, and the various types of food;
moreover, because of its extreme force, this disorder suddenly overwhelms the patient whose digestive strength has been suppressed.
Furthermore, disorders arising from the defects of undigested food (āmadoṣa) are pacified by fasting alone;
that [fasting] is of three kinds.
Therein, fasting, digestive therapy, and depletion are the treatments; among these, fasting is for those with minor morbid humors (doṣas),

for by it, through the increase of wind and fire, the person with minor humors undergoes desiccation, just as a small reservoir of water, when overwhelmed by wind and sun, reaches a state of drying up.

In the case of moderate doshas, one should employ fasting and digestive treatments, or exposure to wind and sun, as well as sprinkling with dust and ashes—just as a very large reservoir of water is managed.
However, for those with excessive doshas, the primary task is the drainage of the doshas;
for indeed, there can be no growth of rice and other crops as long as the flood of water in a pond has not been drained away.
Therefore, for those conditions caused by over-satiation, there is no pacification without under-nutrition;
and for those caused by under-nutrition, there is no pacification without over-satiation.

In this same manner, for other diseases as well, one should administer medicine that is contrary to their respective etiological factors (*nidāna*). However, if there is a persistent residual connection (*anubandha*), one should set aside what is contrary to the etiology and instead apply what is contrary to the disease itself, or that which serves its purpose. For one whose humors have been released, whose remaining humors are fully ripened, and whose digestive fire is kindled, one should appropriately employ oil massages (*abhyaṅga*), non-unctuous enemas (*āsthāpana*), unctuous enemas (*anuvāsana*), and various drinks of medicated fats (*sneha-pāna*).
Having carefully examined the various stages of the doshas, medicines, and so forth, it is said here (AS.Sū.11.27):
"He whose teeth, lips, and nails are blackish, who has diminished consciousness, who is afflicted by vomiting, and whose eyes have turned inward and become copper-colored..."
A man whose voice is weak and whose joints are all slackened should depart for the sake of returning again.
Having added the three pungents (vyoṣa), the fruit of *karañja*, the two types of *haridrā*, and the root of *mātuluṅgī*, [one should prepare a remedy].
Pills made from these [substances] dried in the shade, when used as an ointment for the eyes, destroy *viṣūcī*.
A wick (varti) may also be prepared from *śirīṣa*, *naktāhva*, seeds of *phaṇijjaka*, *trāyantī*, and the fruits of *apāmārga*.
A preparation of goat’s urine cures *viṣūcikā* (choleraic pain) through applications as a paste, fumigation, collyrium, and nasal drops.
AS.Sū.11.30: Indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) arises from phlegm as undigested matter (*āma*), while that which is obstructed (*viṣṭabdha*) arises from wind.
That which is burnt by the provocation of bile is known to be of three types.
AS.Sū.11.31: Among these, in the case of undigested matter (āma), there is heaviness, excessive moisture, and swelling of the cheeks and eye-sockets.
AS.Sū.11.31 And eructation occurs as undigested food is expelled exactly as it was eaten.
AS.Sū.11.32 In Viṣṭabdha (obstipation), there is colic, flatulence, and various types of Vāta-pain.
AS.Sū.11.32 When [the food] is undigested, there is the non-passage of feces and flatus, stiffness, delusion, and pain in the limbs.
AS.Sū.11.33 When it is partially digested (vidagdha), there is vertigo, thirst, fainting, and pitta, along with various types of pain.
AS.Sū.11.33 There is eructation accompanied by foul-smelling, sour gas, and perspiration and a burning sensation arise.
AS.Sū.11.34 In the case of *āmadoṣa*, fasting (*laṅghana*) should be performed; however, in the case of *viṣṭabdha* (obstruction), strong sudation (*svedana*) is required.
If there is burning, emesis is indicated, or whatever else may be beneficial according to the specific condition.
From undigested matter (*āmāśaya*) that has become excessively thin and dissolved, *vilambikā* arises.

AS.Sū.11.35 A vomiting characterized by symptoms of both phlegm (kapha) and wind (vāta) is treated with remedies appropriate for those two. AS.Sū.11.36 A distaste for food after the meal is finished, as well as impurity and heaviness of the heart, [indicate the presence of undigested matter].
In that case, one who is hungry should sleep during the day without eating; when hunger is slight, one should eat light food.
During four watches or two watches of the night, there is an equal amount of time for food and medicine.
Digestion occurs quickly when [the digestive fire] is strong and properly applied, but slowly when it is weak;
therefore, one should administer medicine with food to a person with a weak digestive fire. (AS.Sū.11.37–38)
A meal taken in the forenoon should be wholesome, light, digestive, and nourishing. However, if the morning meal has not yet been digested, an evening meal does not cause harm.
If the evening meal has not been digested, the morning meal indeed causes harm.
By day, the heart is awakened by the sun like a lotus.
When that [mind] has awakened, the channels everywhere attain a state of clarity,
due to physical exertion, mental investigation, and the scattering of the mind.
By day, his bodily constituents do not undergo moistening;
when they are not moistened, food poured into them does not become excessively corrupted.
Just as fresh milk mixed with other [substances] remains [unspoiled] when the milk is not yet scorched;
but at night, when the heart is languid and the channels are constricted.
All the bodily constituents (dhātu) undergo putrefaction within the enclosed abdominal cavity;
when they are moistened and undigested, anything else poured into them becomes corrupted.
When milk is scorched, it is like milk poured into [fire] that has already been heated;
therefore, one should not eat another meal while the food from the previous night remains undigested.
Cleanliness of eructation, vigor, timely evacuation of the natural urges,
lightness of the body, and hunger and thirst are the signs that food has been digested.
Generally, the multitude of diseases arises through intellectual error,
especially cholera among men who are greedy for food.
If food that is obstructed by the *doṣas* becomes stagnant and fails to reach the digestive fire because it is overwhelmed by an excess of *pitta*,
then a corrupted hunger arises which destroys those of dull intellect like poison.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter.
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
12.1: We shall now expound the chapter on the knowledge of the two types of medicinal herbs.
Thus said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:
medicine is of two kinds— vitalizing and disease-destroying.
Both [the internal and external] possess both natures; however,
the designation is made according to their predominance.
Among these, that which promotes vigor (ūrjas-kara) is of two kinds: rejuvenation (rasāyana) and aphrodisiac therapy (vājīkaraṇa).
The destruction of disease is also of two kinds:
the pacification of disease and its prevention from recurrence.
Furthermore, substance is of two kinds: with substance and without substance;
therein, that which has substance is of three kinds.
