Regarding the categories "earth-born," "sprout-born," and "mobile," among those to be described, [substances] beginning with gold and ending with salt are generally earth-born;
furthermore, the sprout-born is fourfold, distinguished as trees (*vanaspati*), shrubs (*vānaspatya*), creepers (*vīrudh*), and medicinal herbs (*oṣadhi*).
Among these, a fruit-bearing tree is a *vanaspati*;
one possessing flowers and fruit is a *vānaspatya*; and [the others are] creepers, shrubs, and climbing plants.
Since medicinal plants end with the ripening of their fruit,

they say that substances derived from mobile beings— such as honey, clarified butter, and so forth— are "mobile substances" (jaṅgamadravya). Furthermore, non-substances (adravya) include fasting, wind, sunlight, shade, mantras, soothing words, giving, fear, startling, agitation, exhilaration, scolding, laughing, sleep, staying awake, massage, and so on.
Furthermore, [treatment] is of three kinds: recourse to divine power (*daivavyapāśraya*), recourse to rational means (*yuktivyapāśraya*), and the conquest of the mind (*sattvāvajaya*).

Among these, recourse to divine power consists of mantras, medicinal herbs, gems, auspicious rites, offerings, oblations, burnt sacrifices, observances, expiations, fasting, benedictions, prayers, pilgrimages, and so forth.
Relying on reasoning consists of the application of diet, medicine, and so forth;
the subduing of living beings, moreover, is the restraint of the mind from what is harmful;
and again, it is threefold.
Extraction, suppression of the natural state, and abandonment of the cause—
these, moreover, are of two kinds, distinguished as external and internal.

In that regard, external extraction refers to the removal of knots, tumors, stye-like growths, parasites, foreign bodies, and the like, by means of surgical instruments, hands, and mechanical devices; internal [extraction], on the other hand, is performed by means of emetics, purgatives, and so forth;
while the alleviation of the natural state of the humors is pacification (*saṃśamana*).
That [treatment] is external, such as massage, sudation, plasters, affusions, and rubbing;
internal is that which, having entered within, pacifies the *doṣas* without causing agitation— namely,

the avoidance of etiological factors according to the specific *doṣa*, the renunciation of cold, heat, fasting, physical exercise, and so forth, and the non-consumption of unctuous, dry, and other such substances.

In that regard, surgical instruments and the like are employed for conditions treatable by them, but not for those treatable by medicine; whereas medicine is employed for conditions treatable by it, but not for those treatable by instruments and the like.
Furthermore, [the treatment] is of three kinds: contrary to the cause, contrary to the disease, and accomplishing both purposes.
In that regard, the opposite of the cause consists of light, dry, and hot qualities and so forth in a disease born of heavy, unctuous, and cold factors; likewise,
in the other type of disease, the opposite consists of the other [qualities].

There are two primary therapeutic approaches: lightening (laṅghana) and nourishing (bṛṃhaṇa); five procedures beginning with emesis (vamana); treatments including fumigation, medicinal smoking, and collyrium;
as well as measures such as scarification, poulticing, and incision.

AS.Sū.12.6 And that which is specifically beneficial even when fever persists despite the pacification of the *doṣas*— namely, *mustā*, *parpaṭaka*, and gruels (*yavāgū*) in urinary disorders (*prameha*), as well as turmeric (*rajanī*) and barley-based food (*yavānna*) and so forth;
and in cases of internal hemorrhage (*raktapitta*), purgation for upward-moving [blood] and emesis for downward-moving [blood].
Furthermore, medicine that relies upon fate (divine intervention) serves both purposes:

for example, emesis in cases of vomiting, purgation in cases of diarrhea, the drinking of wine in alcoholism, cauterization with fire in burns caused by *tuttha*, fomentation (*sveda*) when bile is deeply internalized or has gone astray, and the consumption of pungent, sour, salty, sharp, and hot foods—these are for the purpose of discharging [the humor] externally and restoring it to its own path;
likewise, when phlegm (*śleṣman*) is deeply internalized and stagnant, cold external treatment is applied, whereby the phlegm dissolves through the inward penetration of heat that oppresses it.
For such medicine, being non-perverted and truly existent, performs its purpose by counteracting the cause and the disease;
moreover, non-medicine is of two kinds: that which causes affliction and that which follows upon affliction.
In that regard, there is affliction that takes life immediately and affliction that manifests after a lapse of time;
furthermore, based on the distinctions of taste, potency, and so forth, a portion of medicine is taught here in its general outlines.
Gold is nourishing, unctuous, and sweet in both its taste and post-digestive effect;
it removes the defects of poison, is cooling, slightly astringent, and is a rejuvenative elixir.
Silver is unctuous; it is astringent and sour in taste, and sweet in its post-digestive transformation (vipāka).
It stabilizes youth, is cooling, scraping, and conquers wind and bile.
Copper is slightly bitter and sweet, astringent, scraping, and light;
it has a pungent post-digestive taste (vipāka) and flavor (rasa), is cooling, caustic, and conquers phlegm and bile.
Bitter (tikta) [taste] has an astringent aftertaste; it is clear, scraping, light,
clarifies the vision, is dry, and removes pitta and kapha.
Tin and lead are slightly astringent and salty, are purgative, alleviate jaundice, worms, and wind, are scraping,
and increase bile; they possess qualities similar to those [of tin].
Black iron (kṛṣ� aṇaloha) is beneficial for the eyes, astringent, sweet and bitter;
it is scraping, increases vāta, is cold, and destroys worms, skin diseases, and phlegm.
It relieves flaccidity of the limbs, graying of the hair, and paleness; it conquers wasting and swelling.
Likewise, it is sharp, specifically emetic, and very difficult to digest.
Rubies, sapphires,
topazes, and emeralds; pearls, coral, diamonds, indranīlas, lapis lazuli, crystal, and so forth.
The *maṇiratna* is cooling, astringent, sweet, and scraping;
it is beneficial for the eyes, and by wearing it, it removes evil, misfortune, and poison.
Beneficial, life-prolonging, invigorating, producing joy and enthusiasm, and auspicious is glass (kāca), which, being alkaline and hot in potency, restores vision when used as a collyrium.
Conch and sea-foam are cold, astringent, and scraping; *tutthaka* is pungent, alkaline, astringent, clarifying, and light.
Gairika is scraping, purgative, beneficial for the eyes, and removes itching, worms, and poison;
it is clear, unctuous, astringent-sweet, and cold.
Manohvā destroys phlegm, is bitter and pungent, scrapes the tissues, and is laxative;
haritāla is unctuous, astringent, and pungent, and it destroys poison.
Collyrium that is astringent, sweet, cold, scraping,
and unctuous destroys hemorrhagic disorders, bile, poison, vomiting, and hiccups, and it clarifies the vision.
Among these, *srotoñjana* is the best, followed by *sauvīrāñjana*;
*rasāñjana* destroys *kapha*, is bitter and pungent, excising, and warm.
Śilājatu is sweet, pacifies hiccup, cures cough, urinary disorders, and consumption; it destroys phlegm, is hot and pungent, and is a rejuvenative elixir.
Bitter [taste] is scarifying and, due to its capacity for combination (*yogavāhitva*), it conquers all diseases; specifically,
it removes difficult urination (*kṛcchra*), urinary disorders (*meha*), hemorrhoids (*arśas*), anemia (*pāṇḍu*), edema (*śopha*), and phlegm (*kapha*).
Bamboo manna (vaṃśarocanā) is astringent, sweet, dry, and cures cough.
Tugākṣīrī is sweet, cooling, and cures consumption, dyspnea, and cough.
All dissolving salt is known to be subtle, laxative, and impure;
it subdues Vāta, is digestive, sharp, hot, appetizing, and increases Kapha and Pitta.

The water from a bow-strap well (saidhanva) is sweet, aphrodisiac, beneficial for the heart, and alleviates the three doṣas; it is light, non-hot, wholesome for the eyes, non-burning, and stimulates the digestive fire.

Sauvarcala salt is light, beneficial for the heart, fragrant, and it purifies the eructation; it is pungent in its post-digestive effect, relieves constipation, stimulates digestion, and promotes appetite.
AS.Sū.12.29 It facilitates the downward movement of phlegm and wind, stimulates digestion, promotes the passage of feces,
and destroys constipation, flatulence, obstruction, colic, and heaviness.
Sea salt is sweet in its post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), heavy, and increases phlegm (*śleṣman*).
Salt from saline soil (*audbhida*) is slightly bitter, pungent, alkaline, sharp, and causes moistening.
The qualities of black salt (kṛṣṇa-lavaṇa) are like those of sauvarcala, except it is devoid of fragrance.
Romaka salt is light; that which arises from dust (pāṃsūttha) is alkaline, increases phlegm, and is heavy.
Regarding the application of salts, one should employ rock salt (*saindhava*) and others;
they remove abdominal tumors (*gulma*), disorders of the *grahaṇī*, anemia (*pāṇḍu*), splenic enlargement (*plīha*), flatulence (*ānāha*), and diseases of the throat.
That produced from barley awns pacifies dyspnea, hemorrhoids, phlegm, and wind;
svarjikā possesses qualities slightly inferior to it, while kṣāra is superior to that.
All alkaline substances (kṣāra) are supremely sharp and hot; they destroy worms, are light,
vitiate the bile and blood, are digestive, excise, are pleasing to the heart, and are fissuring.
It is unwholesome for semen, vitality, hair, and eyes because of its pungency and salinity;
it is astringent, sweet in its post-digestive effect (pāka), dry, slightly salty, and light.
It is illuminating, digestive, purifying, and supremely stabilizing for youth; it is hot in potency, promotes longevity, and bestows strength upon the intellect and the senses. (AS.Sū.12.36)
It cures leprosy, discoloration, hoarseness, chronic and irregular fevers,
as well as diseases of the head, eyes, anemia, heart disease, jaundice, and disorders of the small intestine (grahaṇī).
It [treats] emaciation, swelling, diarrhea, urinary disorders, delusion, vomiting, worms, dyspnea,
cough, salivation, hemorrhoids, splenic disorders, flatulence, and abdominal enlargement.

Harītakī overcomes obstructions of the channels, abdominal tumors (gulma), stiffness of the thighs (ūrustambha), and loss of appetite, as well as those various diseases born of kapha and vāta. (AS.Sū.12.39)
Similarly, the āmalaka fruit is cooling and, due to its sweetness, is the best for conquering pitta;
it conquers kapha because of its pungent post-digestive transformation (vipāka), and it conquers vāta because of its acidity.
Furthermore, it is beneficial for the throat, pleasing to the eyes, heart-pleasing, and removes burning sensations and fever;
however, the *akṣa* fruit is slightly inferior in those qualities and is astringent-sweet and cooling.
It alleviates cough, dyspnea, phlegm, and bile in the throat; it is light and promotes the hair. However, its marrow is an excellent promoter of hair, while its collyrium (añjana) destroys semen.
This Triphalā is the best elixir; it removes diseases of the eyes, promotes healing, and conquers skin disorders, moisture, obesity, urinary disorders (meha), phlegm, and blood disorders.
Caturjātaka consists of saffron along with cinnamon, cardamom, and patchouli; trijātaka consists of cinnamon, cardamom, and patchouli.
Black pepper (marica) aggravates bile, is sharp and hot, dry, and promotes digestion and the digestive fire;
it is pungent in taste and post-digestive effect, subdues phlegm, and is light.

Pippalī is phlegm-increasing (śleṣmalā), sweet, cold, moist, heavy, and unctuous (AS.Sū.12.44). When dried, it is the opposite of that; it is unctuous, aphrodisiac, and pungent in taste (AS.Sū.12.45).
It is sweet when cooked, subdues wind (vāta), phlegm (kapha), dyspnea, and cough,
and is laxative; one should not consume it excessively except according to the prescribed method for rejuvenation (rasāyana).
AS.Sū.12.46 Ginger is digestive-stimulant, aphrodisiac, constipating, cordial, and relieves obstructions.
AS.Sū.12.47 It is appetizing, light, sweet in its post-digestive effect, unctuous, hot, and conquers phlegm and wind.
In the same way, this triad— ginger and the three pungents (trikaṭuka)— overcomes obesity,
weak digestion, dyspnea, cough, elephantiasis, and chronic rhinitis.
Cavikā and pippalīmūla are slightly inferior to marica in their qualities.
Citraka is equal to fire in its digestive power (pāka) and destroys swelling, hemorrhoids, worms, and skin diseases.
This group of five spices (pañcakolaka) is traditionally defined as being without black pepper;
it destroys abdominal tumors, splenic disorders, abdominal distension, and colic, and is a supreme digestive stimulant.
One should conquer the great bitter and hot decoction [of the five roots] along with *bilva*, *kāśmarya*, *tarkārī*, *pāṭalā*,
and *ṭuṇṭuka* to overcome *kapha* and *vāta*.

The *hrasva-bṛhatyaṃśumatī-dvaya-gokṣuraka* [decoction] is traditionally known to be sweet in post-digestive taste (*pāka*) and flavor (*rasa*), neither too cold nor too hot, and it conquers all the *doṣas*.
Balā, punarnavā, eraṇḍa, and the two types of śūrpaparṇī constitute a moderate [decoction] that destroys kapha and vāta, does not excessively increase pitta, and is light.
The group known as Jīvana, consisting of abhīru, vīrā, jīvantī, jīvaka, and ṛṣabhaka,
is traditionally held to be beneficial for the eyes, aphrodisiac, and a destroyer of pitta and vāta.
Tṛṇa grass, śara, darbha, sugarcane, rice, and kāśa conquer pitta; likewise do ajaśṛṅgī, haridrā, vidārī, sārivā, and amṛtā.
The two [decoctions] known as *balya* and *kaṇṭaka*, prepared with *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *abhīru*, *sairya*, *sahi*, *trāyamāṇā*,
and *karamardī*, remove all the *doṣas*.
Kāravī, kuñcī, vājājī, kavarī, dhānya,
and tumbaru remove the odor of food, improve the appetite, stimulate digestion, and conquer kapha and vāta.
Vāṣpikā is pungent, bitter, and hot; it is an excellent destroyer of worms and phlegm.
Dīpyaka relieves colic and flatulence, improves the appetite, and conquers pain in the digestive tract.
Sesame seeds that are unpalatable and oily are said to be like *bāṣpikā*.
Asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) destroys wind, phlegm, abdominal distension, and colic, but it provokes bile.
That which has a pungent post-digestive taste and flavor is appetizing, digestive, carminative, and light;
it is beneficial even for those with pitta and blood disorders, and that which originates from the region of Bōṣkāṇa is especially excellent.
Then, another substance with lesser qualities for the purpose of flavoring and fumigation consists of śatāhvā,
kuṣṭha, tagara, suradāru, and hareṇu.
Elā, elavāluka, sarala-bark, vyāghra-nakha,
and coraka are light, hot, pungent in their post-digestive effect (pāka), and they subdue kapha and vāta.
Sairyaka is bitter and sweet, unctuous and hot; it conquers kapha and vāta, destroys urinary obstruction and retention, is aphrodisiac, and is cooling. Gokṣuraka is cooling.
The two types of *viṣā* are digestive, destroy *kapha* and *pitta*, and are bitter and cold.
*Musta* destroys *kapha*, is bitter and pungent, is astringent, and is digestive.
Tiktāmṛtā destroys the three doṣas, is astringent, hot, and an elixir; it stimulates digestion and cures fever, thirst, burning sensations, jaundice, and vātarakta.
Bhūnimba and Parpaṭaka are bitter and cold; they alleviate fever and are light.
Nimba is bitter and cooling; it removes skin diseases, worms, bile, and phlegm.
Mahānimba is highly astringent, dry,
and cold; guggulu is slimy to the touch but clear when consumed.

It is sweet, pungent, bitter, and astringent; it is a rejuvenative (rasāyana), beneficial for wounds, and beneficial for the voice. It is pungent in its post-digestive effect (pāka), dry, subtle, and a stimulator of the digestive fire (agnidīpana).
Warm, laxative, and light, it destroys moisture, fat, wind, phlegm, scrofula, urinary disorders, apacī, worms, pustules, glandular swellings, and edema.
Śaṅkhapuṣpī is laxative, bitter, promotes intelligence, and destroys worms and poison.
Aguru is pungent, bitter, hot, unctuous, and removes wind and phlegm.
All varieties of sandalwood, being bitter and sweet, are extremely cooling; they destroy bile, hemorrhage, poison, thirst, burning sensations, and fatigue, and are heavy and parching.
Laghu-rakta, uśīra, and vālaka are likewise digestive;
they alleviate fever, diarrhea, vomiting, internal hemorrhage, and chest wounds.
Madhuka destroys rakta-pitta (bleeding disorders), cleanses wounds, and promotes healing; it is heavy, sweet, cooling, aphrodisiac, beneficial for the eyes, and improves the voice and complexion.
The two types of *niśā* (turmeric and *dāruharidrā*), which are pungent and bitter, remove leprosy, urinary disorders,
pitta, and kapha; through external application, they conquer itching, swelling, malignant ulcers, and poison.
Prapauṇḍarīka is beneficial for the eyes, cooling, and promotes the healing of wounds; it is astringent, bitter, and sweet, and it clarifies the blood and bile.
The three *balās* are sweet, aphrodisiac, unctuous, cooling, and strength-giving. Among them, *nāgabalā* is strengthening, beneficial for those with chest wounds or wasting, and heavy.
Betel leaf is pungent, alkaline, appetizing, hot, and dispels phlegm;
areca nut is a laxative, causes delusion, and is astringent, sweet, and appetizing.
Jātipatrī, kaṭuphala, kaṅkolaka,
and lavaṅgaka are light, they alleviate thirst, are pleasing to the heart, and destroy foul odors of the mouth.
Camphor is sweet and bitter, it destroys thirst, is digestive, and is cooling;
likewise, *latākastūrikā* is supreme for removing dryness of the mouth.
The lotus is astringent-sweet and cold; it conquers pitta, kapha, and blood disorders.
Bakula, punnāga, kumuda, utpala, and pāṭala possess the same properties.
The *koraṇḍa* and *kiṃśuka* flowers are inferior to the *campaka* in their qualities;
the *mālatī* and *mallikā* flowers, being bitter, overcome the wind (*māruta*).
Sinduvāra, which grows on poison, bile, phlegm, or food, possesses those same qualities; kaitaka destroys phlegm and is bitter, while śairīṣa removes poison.
The astringent decoction of *āgastya* flowers is wind-increasing, yet it conquers phlegm and bile; when administered as nasal drops (*nāvana*), it removes quartan fever.
Bandhūka is phlegm-increasing and constipating; yūthikā is exactly like that. Saffron destroys phlegm, is hot in potency, and purifies wounds.
The seed of *avalveḍaka* cures wind and phlegm in the waist;
otherwise, remaining seated [in that posture] produces complexion, phlegm, fat, and delicacy.
Therefore, one should prepare broth from the meat of animals that are young, of the road, or strong; this provides comfort during walking,
promotes the downward movement of wind (māruta), and removes lameness, stiffness, and fatigue.

Footwear, which has a name corresponding to its purpose, increases strength, vision, and semen; an umbrella, which improves the complexion and is beneficial for the eyes, wards off wind, rain, and heat.
A windy place causes dryness, discoloration, stiffness, burning sensations, thirst, vertigo, exhaustion,
and loss of digestive fire; therefore, one should overcome these by staying in a non-windy place, as the opposite effects arise from the latter.

The eastern wind is hot and causes secretions; it aggravates skin diseases, hemorrhoids, poisons, and worms, as well as fever caused by the combination of all three humors (sannipāta), dyspnea, undigested matter (āma), and wind (vāyu).
The western wind destroys fainting, burning sensations, thirst, and poison. The southern wind is excellent; it is beneficial for the eyes and increases the strength of the limbs.
It pacifies *raktapitta* (blood-bile) and does not provoke *vāta*. The northern wind is unctuous, mild, and indeed sweet.
It has an astringent aftertaste, is cooling, and does not aggravate the bodily humors (doṣas). Sunlight causes vertigo, thirst, perspiration, burning sensations, fainting, and discoloration.

By means of the distinctions of taste and so forth, only a mere indication of medicinal substances has been stated; for there is no substance here that is not medicinal. Their understanding of these forms [is derived] from those who frequent the forests.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
AS.Sū.13.1: Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the collection of the foremost [substances].
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:
water is the best among [substances] for soothing, restraining, and moistening.
Among those things that remove fatigue, bathing and wine are the foremost;
among those that promote vitality, milk is the foremost.
Meat is the foremost among nourishing substances; meat broth is the foremost among invigorating substances;
and salt is the foremost among substances that stimulate the appetite for food.

Among substances that serve as food, *tinduka* is the best; among sour things, [pomegranate] is the best; among heart-pleasing things, [mango] is the best; and among strengthening foods, the cock is the best.
Oil is for the pacification of vāta and kapha; ghee is for the pacification of vāta and pitta;
honey is for the pacification of kapha and pitta.
Sudation is for those things that cause softness;
physical exercise is for those that cause firmness;
alkali is for those that destroy virility.
Unripe wood-apple for those with throat ailments;
sheep's ghee for those with heart ailments;
and buffalo milk for those who suffer from insomnia.
Curdled milk is the foremost among things that cause secretions;
sugarcane juice is the foremost among things that produce urine; and barley is the foremost among things that produce feces.
Jāmbava is among those that generate vāta; horse-gram (kulattha) is among those that generate amlapitta;
black gram (māṣa), fried cakes (śaṣkulī), and sheep's milk are among those that generate pitta and śleṣman.
Durālabhā is the best among those that dry up bile and phlegm; fasting is the best among those that alleviate fever;
and vṛṣa is the best among those that pacify raktapitta.
Kaṇṭakārikā is the best among those that cure cough;
lac is the best among those that cure fresh wounds;
and the practice of Nāgabalā is the best among those that cure chest-wounds and consumption.

Puṣkaramūla is for the alleviation of hiccups, dyspnea, cough, pain in the flanks, and loss of appetite; goat’s milk is for the destruction of wasting, the promotion of breast milk, and the checking of hemorrhaging; the clear liquid from a clod of earth roasted in fire is for the alleviation of vomiting and excessive thirst.
Aruṣkara and the root of citraka are for the alleviation of dry hemorrhoids; kuṭaja is for the alleviation of bleeding hemorrhoids;
and parched grain (lāja) is for the suppression of vomiting.
The habitual consumption of *yavaśūka* (barley-germ) is for those [remedies] that cause laxation, digestion, and cure hemorrhoids;

the habitual consumption of buttermilk is for the pacification of hemorrhoids, edema, disorders of the *grahaṇī*, and complications of *ghṛta*; and the habitual consumption of the meat of carnivorous animals is for the destruction of hemorrhoids, wasting, and disorders of the *grahaṇī*.
Musta is the best among those that are astringent, digestive stimulants, and carminatives;
ativiṣā is the best among those that are astringent, carminative, and eliminators of all the doṣas;
and bilva is the best among those that are astringent, digestive stimulants, and pacifiers of vāta and kapha.
Udīcya is the best among those that cause purging, stimulate digestion, and cure vomiting and diarrhea;
kaṭvaṅga is the best among those that are astringent and stimulate digestion;
and kuṭaja bark is the best among those that are astringent for kapha, pitta, and blood, and are drying agents.
The filaments of the blue lotus (*utpala*) and the white water lily (*kumuda*), along with *anantā*, are for the collection of blood and the pacification of *rakta-pitta*;
the fruit of *kāśmarya* is for the collection of blood, the management of diarrhea, and the pacification of *rakta-pitta*;
and *gandhapriyaṅgu* is for the pacification of excessive hemorrhaging from blood and bile.
Pṛśniparṇī is the best among those that are astringent for blood, digestive stimulants, carminatives, pacifiers of Vāta, and aphrodisiacs;
Sālaparṇī is the best among those that are aphrodisiacs and removers of all the doṣas;
and Balā is the best among those that are astringents, strength-promoters, and pacifiers of Vāta.

Pippalīmūla is the best among those that stimulate digestion, promote digestion, and relieve abdominal distension; Citrakamūla is the best among those that stimulate digestion, promote digestion, and cure swelling and pain of the rectum;
Gokṣuraka is the best among those that cure dysuria and disorders of Vāta;
and Haridrā is the best among those that cure urinary disorders (prameha).
Bloodletting is for those who remove abscesses, erysipelas, pustules, and cervical lymphadenitis;
the habitual use of castor oil is for those who remove intestinal obstruction, abdominal tumors, and wind-pain;
and garlic is for those who remove abdominal tumors and wind.

Asafoetida resin is the best among those that are laxative, digestive, carminative, and pacifiers of wind and phlegm; sour sorrel is the best among those that are breaking-up agents, digestive stimulants, carminatives, and pacifiers of wind and phlegm;
and camel’s milk is the best among those that destroy abdominal swelling.
Iron filings are the best among those that cure anemia;
khadira is the best among those that cure skin diseases; and viḍaṅga is the best among those that kill worms.
Rāsnā is the best among those that remove vāta;
the root of eraṇḍa is the best among those that are aphrodisiacs and remove vāta; and guggulu is the best among those that remove fat and vāta.
Amṛtā is the best among those that are astringent, digestive stimulants, and pacifiers of disorders of wind, phlegm, and blood;
madanaphala is the best among those used for emesis, non-unctuous enemas, and unctuous enemas;
and trivṛt is the best among those that cause easy purgation.
Caturaṅgula is for mild purgatives;
snuk-milk is for sharp purgatives;
and pratyakpuṣpī is for head-purgatives (errhines).
Among those that destroy cataracts, triphalā is the best;
among those that heal wounds, guggulu; and among those that counteract poisons, śirīṣa.
The āmalaka fruit is the best among those that maintain youth; the harītakī is the best among wholesome things;
and the habitual use of milk and ghee is the best among elixirs.
The habitual consumption of equal parts of ghee and roasted grain flour (*saktu*) is the best among aphrodisiacs that cure *udāvarta*;
the mental resolve and the semen of a crocodile are the best among aphrodisiacs;
and despondency is the worst among non-aphrodisiacs. (AS.Sū.13.3)
Oil gargles with *abhayā* are the best among those things that strengthen the teeth and improve the relish for food;
sandalwood and *udumbara* are the best among ointments for quenching burning sensations.
Rāsnā and agaru are for cooling ointments to remove heat; lāmajjaka and uśīra are for ointments to remove burning sensations, skin disorders, and perspiration;
and kuṣṭha is for use in massage and poultices that alleviate vāta.

Madhuka is the foremost among those that are beneficial for the eyes, aphrodisiacs, promoters of hair growth, beneficial for the throat, strengthening, purgative, and healing; it is the foremost among those that cause indigestion when eaten, those that corrupt the digestive tract (grahaṇī), and those that produce censurable diseases by eating substances of incompatible potencies.
Eating in moderation is the foremost among things that have a wholesome ripening;
eating in excess is the foremost among causes of the disorder of undigested food (āmadoṣa);
and consuming food according to one's digestive fire is the foremost among things that kindle the fire.
Diet and lifestyle activities should be followed according to what is suitable for one's constitution;
eating, sleeping, and sitting alone cause the destruction of happiness,
while irregular eating causes imbalance of the digestive fire.
Eating at the proper time produces health; well-prepared food generates faith;
and the suppression of natural urges produces ill health.
Satiety is the foremost among the qualities of food;

fasting is the foremost among things that cause the decline of life; eating in measured quantity is the foremost among things that promote emaciation; and food made from *gavedhuka* grass is the foremost among such things.
Food made from *uddālaka* is the foremost among things that cause dryness; wine is the foremost among things that produce mental elation;
the excessive consumption of wine is the foremost among things that destroy intelligence, fortitude, and memory;
and excessive indulgence with women is the foremost among things that cause emaciation.

The suppression of the urge of semen is among those things that cause impotence; rubbing the feet [with unguents] is among those things that generate an appetite for food; seeing a slaughterhouse is among those things that destroy the appetite for food;
and improper application is among the gateways to disease.
Sexual intercourse with a woman during her menses is the foremost among the causes of misfortune; celibacy is the foremost among the factors that promote longevity.
Adultery is the foremost among things that shorten life;
the unnecessary exertion of vital force is the foremost among things that obstruct life;
and despondency is the foremost among things that increase disease.
Joy is the foremost of things that gladden; sorrow, of things that wither;
and consolation, of things that bestow strength.
Nirvṛti is for those things that cause nourishment; puṣṭi is for those things that cause sleep; and svapna is for those things that cause drowsiness.

The practice of all tastes [is indicated] for those things that produce strength; the practice of a single taste [is indicated] for those things that cause weakness, anorexia, or the provocation of any one of the humors; and the fetus is [the foremost among] those foreign bodies to be extracted.
Agni is the foremost among those that pacify stiffness, cold, colic, and convulsions;
Āma is the foremost among those things to be expelled as indigestion; and a child is the foremost among those who require mild remedies.

Among those who are palliative, the elderly; among those for whom sharp medicines, sexual intercourse, and physical exercise must be avoided, the pregnant woman; and among those for whom mental cheerfulness is required, she who is carrying a fetus.
Dejection is the gathering of those who produce suffering; it is the confluence of those difficult to treat and those incurable due to undigested toxins.
Fever is the foremost among acute diseases;
leprosy is the foremost among chronic diseases; and consumption is the foremost among collections of diseases.
Prameha is the foremost among chronic diseases;
leeches among surgical instruments; and the enema among mechanical devices.
The Himalayas are the foremost among lands of medicinal herbs; Soma is the foremost among herbs; and the desert region is the foremost among lands conducive to health.

The presence of lands devoid of marshy terrain is a quality of those who can provide instruction; the absence of such lands is a quality of those who cannot provide instruction, which constitutes a sign of impending death.
The physician is the success of the components of medical treatment;
the physician is the success of the components of the science of medicine;
and the nihilist is the one to be avoided among those things to be shunned.
Lust is for those who cause affliction;
self-possession is for those who provide assistance;
and reasoning accompanied by scripture is for those who seek realization.
The visible results of actions produce certainty;
the incapacity of those who cause fear is terrifying;
and conversation with those possessing such knowledge increases the intellect.

The teacher is the foremost among the causes for the mastery of the scriptures; Ayurveda is the foremost among the nectars; and hatred toward a good physician is the foremost among the causes for the loss of life.
Truthful speech is the foremost among things to be practiced;
vital breath is the foremost among the causes that bestow life;
and the renunciation of everything is the foremost among pleasures.

In that regard, the determination [of the specific cause] occurs through water, fire, earth, heated clods of earth, clarified butter, buttermilk, repeated application, blood-letting, the application of castor oil, camel’s milk, madana fruit, wine, akṣepa, one-sensed organisms, and pregnant women—either individually or from their combination; however, in the case of the *puṣkaramūla* group and others, it occurs only from their combination. And there is a verse on this point: AS.Sū.13.5: "And here there is a verse. (Note: The provided text fragment for the verse is incomplete; the standard version of this verse in the *Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha* Sūtrasthāna 13.5 is as follows: "Water, fire, earth, heated clods, ghee, buttermilk, repeated application, blood-letting, castor oil, camel’s milk, madana fruit, wine, akṣepa, one-sensed organisms, and pregnant women—by these, individually or collectively, the determination [of the cause] is made. (Note: The term *akṣepa* refers to a type of seizure or convulsion; *ekarasāḥ* refers to single-sensed organisms such as insects or plants; *garbhiṇī* refers to a pregnant woman.)
One hundred and fifty-five [verses] have been declared for the foremost [treatises];
one should know that this alone is sufficient for determining what is beneficial and what is harmful.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
14.1: Now we shall expound the chapter on the collection of groups [of drugs] beginning with those for purification (śodhana).
Thus indeed said the great seers, Ātreya and the others.

AS.Sū.14.2 The fruits, flowers, and leaves of *madana*, *nīpūraka*, *ikṣvāku*, and the two types of *kośātakī*; the fruits of *kuṭaja*, *karañja*, *trapusa*, *sarṣapa*, *pippalī*, *viḍaṅga*, *elā*, *pratyakpuṣpī*, *hareṇu*, *pṛthvīkā*, *kustumbaru*, and *prapunnāṭa*; the autumnal fruits of *hastiparṇī*; and the roots of *kovidāra*, *karbudāra*, *ariṣṭa*, *śvagandhā*, *nīpa*, *vidula*, *bilva*, *bimbī*, *bandhujīvaka*, *śvetā*, *śaṇapuṣpī*, *sadāpuṣpī*, *vacā*, *citrā*, *citraka*, *mṛgendravāruṇī*, *suṣavī*, *caturaṅgula*, *svādukaṇṭaka*, *pāṭhā*, *pāṭalī*, *śārṅgeṣṭā*, *madhuka*, *mūrvā*, *saptaparṇa*, *somavalka*, *dvīpi*, *śigru*, *sumanā*, *saumanasyā*, *yavānī*, *vṛścīva*, *punarnavā*, *mahāsahā*, *kṣudrasahā*, *ikṣukāṇḍa*, *ālaktā*, *pippalīmūla*, *cavikā*, *nalada*, *uśīra*, and *hrībera*.

The bark of *śālmalī*, *śeluka*, *bhadraparṇī*, *airāvatī*, *āvartakī*, *upodakā*, *uddāla*, *dhanvana*, *rasāñjana*, *rājādana*, *upacitrā*, *gopaśṛṅgāṭikā*, and *picchā*, as well as the flower of *priyaṅgu*.
Tālīsapatra, haridrā, the tubers of śṛṅgavera,
madhuyaṣṭī, dāruharidrā, and sāsa.
Tagara, guḍūcī, honey, molasses, milk, alkali, and salt—these are for use in emesis (vamanopayogīni).

Trivṛt, śyāmā, dantī, dravantī, śaṅkhinī, saptalā, jagandhā, ajaśṛṅgī, vacā, gavākṣī, chagalāntrī, suvarṇakṣīrī, citraka, kiṇihī, the small five roots (hrasvapañcamūla), vṛścīva, punarnavā, palaṅkaṣā, vāstuka greens, and sāla roots—[these are for use in purgation].

The barks of *tilvaka*, *aramyaka*, *kāmpilyaka*, and *pāṭalī*; the fruits of *triphalā*, *pīlu*, *priyāla*, *kuvala*, *badara*, *karkandhu*, *kāśmarya*, *parūṣaka*, *drākṣā*, *nīlinī*, *klītanaka*, *udakīryā*, *viḍaṅga*, *pūga*, and *pañcāṅgula*;
and the fruits and leaves of *caturaṅgula*.
The bark, fruit, and leaves of *pūtīka*, as well as the milky sap of *mahāvṛkṣa*, *saptacchada*, and *jyotiṣmatī*,
along with milk, wine, whey, curd, fermented grain-water (*dhānyāmla*), and urine, are substances used for purgation.
The fresh juices of *kośātakī*, *devadālī*, *saptalā*, and *kāravellikā*, along with *arka* milk and warm water, constitute the two types [of enemas].
However, because they are innumerable, those substances which are employed in various specific conditions during those respective enema procedures are not enumerated here.
One should administer [these] from the groups of medicinal juices (rasaskandhas) according to the specific humor (doṣa) and the stage of the disease;

however, for all [conditions], one generally uses the fruits of *madana*, *kuṭaja*, *jīmūtaka*, the two types of *ikṣvāku*, *kośātakī*, *trapusa*, *siddhārthaka*, and *śatāhvā*, along with the roots of *balā*, the ten roots (*daśamūla*), *eraṇḍa*, *trivṛt*, *vacā*, *yaṣṭyāhva*, *kuṣṭha*, *rāsnā*, *punarnavā*, and *kattṛṇa*.

Sarala, devadāru, hapuṣā, hiṅgu, rasāñjana, vyoṣa, patra, elā, amṛtā, yava, kola, kulattha, guḍa, lavaṇa, mastu, dhānyāmla, mūtra, sneha, kṣīra, and kṣaudra— these are the ingredients used for nirūha enemas.
Apāmārga, viḍaṅga, marica, pippalī, śirīṣa, bilva, ajājī, ajamoda, vārtāka, pṛthvīkā, elā, and hareṇuphala— [these are also used].
The leaves of the *tālīsa*, *tamāla*, *tarkārī*, and *harītaka* group;
the fruits, leaves, and bark of the *śigru*; and the fruits and leaves of the mustard plant.
The roots of turmeric, radish, and ginger; the leaves of *nāgarakaṇda*;
the tubers of *ativiṣā*; and the roots of *kuṣṭha*, *vacā*, *bhārṅgī*, *śvetā*, *kiṇihī*, *nāgadantī*, *jyotiṣmatī*, *gavākṣī*, *vayasthā*, *vṛścikālī*, *bambī*, and *karañja*.
The flowers and roots of *arka* and *alarka*, *lodhra*, *madana*, *saptaparṇa*, *nimba*, and *pīlu* seeds, as well as *muruṅgī*, *mātuluṅgī*, and clove (*lavaṅga*) flowers.
Agaru, suradāru, sarala, sallakī, jiṅginī, asana, rasāñjana, hiṅgula, akṣa,
niryāsa, tamāla, sāla, tāla, madhūka, dārvīsāra,
tejasvinī, meṣaśṛṅgī, varāṅga, iṅgudī, the two types of bṛhatī, and coca-bark.

Rājādana pith, honey, salts, fermented liquors, the juices of cow dung and the like, urine, bile, and other such substances that are beneficial to the senses; likewise, oleaginous substances, milk, blood, meat broth, grain-water, and water—these are for use as head-purgatives (śirovirecana).

AS.Sū.14.6: Madhuka, padmaka, mañjiṣṭhā, sārivā, mustā, punnāga, nāgakesara, elavāluka, suvarṇatvak, tamāla, pṛthvīkā, hareṇu, lākṣā, śatapuṣpā, sallakī, sugar, madanaka, marubaka, nyagrodha, udumbara, aśvattha, plakṣa, lodhra-bark, and the lotuses—padma and utpala—as well as all fragrant substances with the exception of kuṣṭha and tagara, are suitable for use as habitual medicinal smoke (prāyogika-dhūma). Agaru, guggulu, sallakī, śaileya, nalada, hrībera, hareṇu, uśīra, mustā, adhyāmaka, varāṅga, śrīveṣṭaka, sthauṇeyaka, paripelava, elavāluka, kunduruka, sarjarasa, yaṣṭyāhva, fruit-essences, fats, beeswax, the marrow of bilva fruit, barley, sesame, black gram, saffron, and the fats of fat, marrow, muscle, and clarified butter are suitable for use as unctuous medicinal smoke (snaihika-dhūma).

AS.Sū.14.6 The substances for head-purgation (*śirovirecana*) and pungent aromatic substances (*gandhadravya*), namely *manohvā* and *haritāla*, are used for strong fumigation (*tīkṣṇadhūma*). AS.Sū.14.7 *Bhadradāru*, *kuṣṭha*, *tagara*, *varuṇa*, *balā*, *atibalā*, *ārtagala*, *kacchurā*, *ahlādinī*, *kuberākṣī*, *vatsādinī*, *arka*, *alarka*, *kataka*, *bhārṅgī*, *kārpāsī*, *vṛścikālī*, *pattūra*, and so forth; the *vidārigaṇa* group, the *vīratarādi* group, the six groups of roots (*pañcamūla*) excluding those called *tṛṇa*, and others—these are the pacifiers of *vāta*.
AS.Sū.14.7: "Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking a new existence."

Dūrvā, anantā, mocarasa, mañjiṣṭhā, paripelava, kālā, kālīyaka, kadalī, kandalī, payasyā, ātmaguptā, coconut, date-palm, grape, vidārī, badarī, balā, nāgabalā, nāgapuṣpa, śatāvarī, śītapākī, odanapākī, tṛṇaśūlya, aṃśumatī, the two types of ariṣṭa, kāriṣṭa, āṭarūṣa, ketkaṭa, priyaṅgu, dhātakī, dhava, dhavan, dhanvana, syandana, khadira, kadara, priyāla, tāla, sāla, sarja, tiniśa, aśvakarṇa, gundrā, vānīra, padmā, padmaka, lotus seeds, mṛṇāla, kumuda, nalina, saugandhika, puṇḍarīka, śatapatra, śaivāla, kalhāra, utpala, kākoli, utpalikā, śalūka, śṛṅgāṭaka, kaśeruka, krauñcādana, and others of similar cooling potency; the Sārivādi group, the Padmakādi group, the Paṭolādi group, the Nyagrodhādi group, the great astringent decoction (mahākaṣāya) which removes burning sensations, and the grass pentad (tṛṇapañcamūla)—these are the pacifiers of Pitta.

Śītaśiva, śatapuṣpā, sarala, suradāru, rāsnā, iṅgudī, sātalā, sumanaḥ, kākādanī, lāṅgalikā, hastikarṇa, muñja, tāla, majjaka, and others—likewise those belonging to the āragvadhādi, rasanādi, arkādi, surasādi, muṣkakādi, vatsakādi, mustādi, and śītaghna groups; the great decoctions (mahākaṣāya); and the five roots of the creepers and the thorny shrubs (vallī- and kaṇṭaka-pañcamūla)—these are the pacifiers of phlegm (śleṣman).
And there is a verse on this point:

"Having carefully examined the defects (doṣas), the tissues affected (dūṣyas), and so forth, these groups, when properly combined, are sufficient for the conquest of all diseases for those of self-restraint. Thus ends the fourteenth chapter.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter. Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the compendium of major decoctions (mahākaṣāyasaṅgraha); thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
AS.Sū.15.2 Because medicinal herbs and diseases are infinite, decoctions (kaṣāya) are likewise infinite.
However, those which are most useful or possess superior qualities are designated by names such as "vitalizing" (jīvanīya), and so forth.
For each [of these], forty-five great kaṣāyas will be described through the combination of ten kaṣāyas;
this is for the sake of their comprehension by those of dull intellect,
and merely to provide illustrative examples for those who are intelligent.

For it is possible for the intelligent, having observed common qualities such as being sweet, cool, and unctuous in substances like *jīvanti* and others, to determine that even milk, sugarcane, grapes, *akṣoṭa*, *vidārī*, tubers, and so forth—possessing those same qualities—are "vitalizing" (*jīvanīya*) and the like;
however, for one of dull intellect, it is better simply to follow what has been stated.
Furthermore, when these are enumerated individually, their designations amount to fifty-four.

Although there is a commingling of substances (dravya-saṅkara) in decoctions (kaṣāya) because those very same substances are present, there is nevertheless no contradiction regarding their designation,

since even a single substance may perform multiple functions; in this context, the tastes (rasa), with the exception of salt, are called "decoctions" (kaṣāya) when they are prepared for medicinal formulation.
Because it originates from that [salt],
there is no possibility of designating it by names such as "exudation" (niryāsa) and so forth;
furthermore, because it lacks distinct utility or benefit, it is purposeless.
And on this point there is a verse:
"Jīvantī and Kākolī, the two types of Medā, and Mudgaparṇī and Māṣaparṇī."
Ṛṣabhaka, jīvaka, and madhuka constitute the group known as the vitalizers (jīvanīya). Vātyā, balā, payasyā, kākolī, ikṣu, and vājigandhā [also belong to this group].
Kṣīriṇī, rājakṣavaka, and bhāradvājī— this is a nourishing [formula].
Haimavatī, ciribilva, mustā, kuṣṭha, vacā, and the two types of haridrā.
This group consisting of *citraka*, *kaṭukā*, and *ativiṣā* is known as the scraping (lekhana) group.
*Arka*, *eraṇḍa*, *citrā*, *citraka*, *ciribilva*, *śaṅkhinī*, and *saralā*.

Hemakṣīrī, kaṭukā, and vahnimukhī are purgatives; this is [the group] that causes evacuation. Honey, madhuka, pṛśniparṇī, kaṭphala, lodhra, priyaṅgu, and dhātakī [are the group that causes constipation].
Ambaṣṭhakī, samaṅgā, and mocarasa constitute the *sandhāna* (binding agent). From the combination of hiṅgu, marica, amlavetasa, dīpyaka, and the fruit of bhallātaka, [the *saṃyoga* is formed].
This group, known as Sapañcakola, is prescribed as digestive (dīpanīya). It consists of aindri, atirasā, payasyā, ṛṣyaproktā, sthirā, balā, and atibalā.
Thus ends this tenth section on strengthening [therapies]: *hayagandhā*, *rohiṇī*, *ṛṣabha*,
*candana*, *tuṅga*, *payasyā*, *sitālatā*, *madhuka*, *padmaka*, and *uśīra*.
This group of drugs, praised for its qualities, is declared to consist of mañjiṣṭhā together with sārivā,
haṃsapādī, the two types of bṛhatī, mṛdvīkā, sārivā, and the roots of ikṣu.
Kaiḍarya, madhuka, kṛṣṇā, and vidārī produce phlegm; so too do vṛkṣāmla, badara, dāḍima, kuvala, āmra, āmrātaka, likuca, and karamarda.
Know this group— consisting of ginger, *cavikā*, *citraka*, *viḍaṅga*, *mūrvā*, *amṛtā*, *vacā*, and *mustā*— to be beneficial for the heart, along with *mātuluṅga* and *amlavetasa*.

This group, including long pepper and bitter gourd, is renowned as a destroyer of satiation (appetite-suppressant). [The group consists of: *kuṭaja* fruit, *bilva*, *citraka*, *mahauṣadha*, *prativiṣā*, *vacā*, and *cavikā*.
Dhanvayavāsa, pathyā, and the group beginning with dāruharidrā destroy hemorrhoids (arśas). Khadira, āmalaka, aruṣkara, niśā, abhayā, saptaparṇa, and karavīra [are likewise used].
Kuṣṭha-destroying [substances] include catuṅgula, viḍaṅga, jāti, and pravāla; as well as nalada, kṛtamāla, candana, sarṣapa, ghana, nimba, kuṭaja, and madhuka.
Dāruharidrā, asana, and naktamāla destroy itching (kaṇḍū); so too do akṣīva, marica, kebuca, viḍaṅga, gaṇḍīra, kiṇihī, and nirguṇḍī.
Śvadaṃṣṭrā, viṣā, and ākhuparṇī likewise kill worms before long; so too do mañjiṣṭhā, śleṣmātaka, rajanī, suvahā, śirīṣa, and pālindī.
The powders of *sailā*, *candana*, and *katkā*, together with *sinduvāra*, destroy poison; as do [the powders] of *śāli*, *kuśa*, *kāśa*, *ṣaṣṭika*, *vīraṇa*, *darbha*, *ikṣuvālikā*, and *ikṣu*.
Similarly, for the generation of breast milk in women with an abundance of *guṇa* and *rasa*, [one should use] the roots of *mala*;
[and] *pāṭhā*, *nāgara*, *surataru*, *ghanāmṛtā*, *sārivā*, *indrayava*, and *mūrvā*.
Kaṭukā, kirātatikta— this group [of drugs] purifies the breast milk. Medā, the two types of kākolī, vṛkṣaruhā, jīvaka, ṛṣabha, and kuliṅga.
This is the semen-producing group [of drugs], together with jaṭilā, śūrpaparṇī,
kuṣṭha, elavāluka, kaṭphala, kāṇḍekṣu, ikṣu, abdhiphena, and kośīra.
Semen is purified by *vasuka*, *ikṣuraka*, and the exudations of *kadamba*;
likewise by *drākṣā*, the two types of *kākolī*, *madhuparṇī*, *madhuka*, *jīvaka*, and *vidārī*.
Medicated oils containing ghee, jīvantī, śāliparṇī,
saubhañjanaka, punarnavā, vṛścīka, kulattha, māṣa, and badara.
One should know that [these] are conducive to sudation: barley, sesame, arka, uru, and pūga (AS.Sū.15.25);
as well as parched grain, mango, jujube, pomegranate, barley, ṣaṣṭika rice, mātuluṅga, and sevya (AS.Sū.15.25).
Jambu, mango sprouts, emetic nut, and clay; as well as ginger, dhanvayavāsaka, vālaka, parpaṭaka, sandalwood, and guḍūcī.
Bhūnimba, ghana, paṭolī, and kustumburī destroy thirst;
so too do the two types of bṛhatī, vṛkṣaruhā, puṣkaramūla, abhayā, kaṇā, and śṛṅgī.
Śaṭī, durālabhā, and the seed of badara destroy hiccup; likewise, śyāmā, anantā, padmā, kaṭvaṅga, the filaments of the lotus, and lodhra [are used for the same].
The decoction of *dhātaki*, *kusuma*, *samaṅgā*, *mocarasa*, *āmrāsthi*, and *viḍ* is for the treatment of constipation (*viḍgrahaṇa*).
[Also] *jambū*, *sallakī*, *madhuka*, *nīlotpala*, *kacchurā*, *tila*, and *śryāhva*.
Fried clay, milk, śālmalī, viḍsalt, and virajana;
Jambu, āmra, udumbara, vaṭa, kapītana, plakṣa, pippala, and aśmantaka.

Bhallātaka and somavalka are prescribed for the retention of urine (AS.Sū.15.31). The flowers of the kamala, nalina, kumuda, madhuka, saugandhika, dhātakī, and latā, along with utpala, śatapatra, and puṇḍarīka, lead to the discharge of urine and restore its natural color (AS.Sū.15.31).
Vṛkṣādanī, īśvadaṃṣṭrā, darbha, eṭaka, vaśira, kuśa, kāśa,
gundrā, and pāṣāṇabheda should cause the urine to flow and act as purgatives.
Grapes, *āmalaka*, *punarnavā*, *vṛścīva*, *durālabhā*, *abhayā*, *kṛṣṇā*,
along with *śṛṅgī*, *tāmalakī*, and *kaṇṭakārī*, destroy cough.
Caṇḍā, amlavetasa, śaṭī, tāmalakī, surasā, hiṅgu,
jīvantī, puṣkaramūla, and elā— this group, along with aguru, is for the pacification of dyspnea.
Grapes, *pīlu*, *parūṣaka*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *sārivā*, *amṛtā*, *pāṭhā*,
and *triphalā*— this group is prescribed for the pacification of fever.
One should know that pomegranate, phalgu, parūṣaka, priyāla, barley, ṣaṣṭika rice,
sugarcane, jujube, along with grapes and dates, are destroyers of fatigue.
Padmaka, kalāya, uśīra, madhuka, utpala, sārivā, sita, udīcya,
kāśmarya fruit, and candana— this group is declared to be a destroyer of burning sensations.
Nata, nāgara, aguru, vacā, dhānyaka, bhūtīka, pippalī, vyāghrī, and syonāka,
together with agnimantha, quickly pacify cold [fevers].
Tinduka, priyāla seed, saptacchada, khadira, kadara, and badara;
arimeda and vājikarṇa, and kakubha— these are the remedies for urticaria (udarda).
Kākoli, elā, sevya, the two types of nidigdhikā, śāliparṇī, and pṛśniparṇī,
as well as candana, madhuka, and urubūka, quickly destroy bodily aches.
Dīpyaka, marica, ajāji, gaṇḍīra, along with ajagandha and pañcakola, pacifies colic; and likewise, the first daśamūla pacifies swelling.
Honey, madhuka, parched grain, red ochre, phalinī, mocarasa, earth,
and potsherds— these [substances] cause blood to flow, as does lodhra together with sugar.
Śaila, elavāluka, kaṭphala, mocarasa, aśoka, padmaka, śirīṣa,
along with sthāpanī, saha, tuṅga, kadamba, and vidula, alleviate pain.
Kaidera, hiṅgu, coraka, palaṅkaṣā, aśoka, rohiṇī,
vayasthā, pūti, arimedas, jaṭilā, golomī, and vacā are the inducers of consciousness.
Aindrī, dūrvā, amoghā, viṣvaksenā, vyathā, śivā,
ariṣṭā, brāhmī, savātyapuṣpī, and śatavīryā— one should establish the embryo.
Amṛtā, pathyā, dhātrī, jīvantī, śreyasī, and sthirā,
along with maṇḍūkaparṇī, atirasā, and punarnavā, restore youth.
Thus, these formulations have been set forth for the purpose of destroying various kinds of diseases;
one should adapt them according to the requirements of the patient suffering from illness.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
16.1: Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the collection of various groups of substances.
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:
Vidārī, pañcāṅgula, vṛścikālī, vṛścīva, devāhvaya, and śūrpaparṇī.
Kaṇḍūkarī, Jīvanī, Hrasvā—these two groups of five; Gopasutā and Tripādī.
This group beginning with Vidārī is pleasing to the heart, nourishing, and subdues Vāta and Pitta.
This group [of drugs] cures emaciation, abdominal tumors, body aches, upward breathlessness, and cough.
It consists of Sārivā, Uśīra, Kāśmarya, Madhūka, and the two types of Śiśira.

Yaṣṭī and parūṣaka destroy burning sensations, hemorrhaging from pitta, thirst, and fever. Padmaka, puṇḍraka, vṛddhi, tugākṣīrī, ṛddhi, śṛṅgī, and amṛtā— these ten are known as the "vitalizers" (jīvana).

AS.Sū.16.5 Those which increase breast milk, destroy hemorrhaging and bile, and are nourishing, bulk-promoting, vitalizing, and aphrodisiac; AS.Sū.16.6 *parūṣaka*, *varā*, grapes, *kaṭphala*, and the fruit of *kataka*.
Pomegranate leaves and pomegranate fruit are a vegetable that conquers thirst, urinary disorders, diseases, and wind;
likewise, *añjana*, *phalinī*, *māṃsī*, and the juices of *padma* and *utpala*.
Sailā, madhuka, and nāgāhva remove poison, internal burning, and pitta;
likewise, paṭola, kaṭurohiṇī, candana, together with madhusrava, guḍūcī, and pāṭhā [achieve the same].
Guḍūcī, padmaka, āriṣṭa, dhānakā, and red sandalwood destroy phlegm, bile, skin diseases, fever, poison, vomiting, loss of appetite, and jaundice. (AS.Sū.16.8)

[This group] destroys bile-fever, phlegm-fever, vomiting, burning sensations, and thirst, and it stimulates the digestive fire. Āragvadha, indrayava, pāṭalī, kākatiktā, nimba, amṛtā, madhurasā, sruvavṛkṣa, and pāṭhā [are these].
Bhūnimba, sairya, paṭola, the two types of karañja, saptacchada, agni, suṣavī-phala, bāṇa, and ghoṇṭā—
this group beginning with āragvadha conquers vomiting, skin diseases, poisons, and fevers.
[This group] purifies Kapha, itching, urinary disorders (prameha), and malignant ulcers.
AS.Sū.16.11: Asana, tiniśa, bhūrja, śvetavāha, prakīryā, khadira, kadara, bhaṇḍī, śiṃśapā, and meṣaśṛṅgī.
The groups beginning with *trivṛt*— namely *trivṛt*, *nimba*, *palāśa*, *jyotiṣmatī*, *śāka*, *sāla*, *dhava*, *kavaka*, *kaliṅga*, *chāgakarṇa*, and *aśvakarṇa*—
are victorious over leucoderma, skin diseases, phlegm, and worms. (AS.Sū.16.12)
This [decoction] destroys anemia, urinary disorders, and defects of the fat tissue. (AS.Sū.16.13) Varana, the two types of Sairiya, Shatavari, Dahanamula, Morata, Bilva, and Vishanika— (AS.Sū.16.13)
The group beginning with *varaṇa*— consisting of *dvibṛhatī*, two types of *karañja*, the two types of *jayā*, *bahalapallava*,
*darbha*, and *rujākara*— subdues phlegm, fat, and sluggish digestion. (AS.Sū.16.14)
It cures Āḍhyavāta, headache, abdominal tumors (gulma), and internal abscesses (vidradhi).
[The ingredients are] ūṣaka, tutthaka, hiṅgu, the two types of kāsīsa, and saindhava salt.
Śilājatu, when combined with [other substances], removes urinary disorders (kṛcchra), stones, abdominal tumors (gulma), obesity, and phlegm (kapha).
Regarding this, there are also [the following verses]:
Vīratara, araṇika, naga, guccha, moraṭa, tuṇṭuka, the pair of sairyaka,
mustaka, mañjarī, karkaśa, and pārtha— this group of ten, beginning with vīratara, induces urination and cures diseases caused by vāta.
[This] removes urinary calculi, gravel, dysuria, and the pain of urinary obstruction.
Lodhra, śābaraka-lodhra, palāśa, ajīṅgiṇī, sarala, and kaṭphala [are used together].
AS.Sū.16.18 Kutsitāmra, kadalī, gataśoka, selu, bāluka, paripelava, and moca;
AS.Sū.16.19 this group of drugs beginning with lodhra is known as the one that removes fat and phlegm.
[This group] removes defects of the womb, is a styptic, improves the complexion, and destroys poison. Arka, alarka, nāgadantī, viśalyā, bhārṅgī, rāsnā, vṛścikālī, and prakīryā [are these herbs].
Pratyakpuṣpī, Pītataila, Udakīryā, Śvetāyugma, and the tree of the ascetics (Tāpasavṛkṣa)—
this group beginning with Arka removes phlegm, fat, and poison.

AS.Sū.16.21 It pacifies worms and skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*) and especially purifies wounds (*vraṇa*). AS.Sū.16.22 *Surasā*, the two types of *yavānī*, *phaṇijjaka*, *kālamālā*, *viḍaṅga*, *kharabu*, *vṛṣakarṇī*, *kaṭphala*, and *kāsamarda*.
Kṣavaka, sarasī, bhārṅgī, and kārmuka; kākamācī, kulahala, viṣamuṣṭi, bhūstṛṇa, and bhūtakeśī—
this is the surasādi group, which destroys phlegm, fat, and worms.
[This group] destroys coryza, anorexia, dyspnea, and cough, and cleanses wounds:
*muṣkaka*, *snuh*, *varā*, *dvīpī*, *palāśa*, *dhava*, and *śiṃśapā*.
Vatsaka overcomes abdominal tumors, urinary disorders, urinary calculi, anemia, obesity, hemorrhoids, kapha, and seminal defects.
Madhurasā, truṭi, vacā, dīrghavṛnta, phala, vellaka, and sarṣapa [are used for this purpose].

The group of ten beginning with *rohiṇī*, *stapanī*, *hiṅgu*, and *bhārṅgī* destroys colic; *ghuṇapriyā* [is used for] wind-disorders; and the group beginning with *vatsaka* cures wind, phlegm, obesity, anorexia, and chronic catarrh.
It destroys colic, hemorrhoids, fever, and abdominal tumors, while acting as a digestive stimulant and a promoter of digestion.
Vacā, jalada, devāhva, nāgara, ativiṣā, and abhayā [are used for this purpose].
The two types of *haridrā*, *yaṣṭyāhvā*, *kalaśī*, and that which arises from *kuṭaja* (AS.Sū.16.27),
as well as the *vacā* and *haridrādi* groups of drugs, destroy diarrhea caused by wind (vāta). (AS.Sū.16.28)
Priyaṅgu, the two types of añjana, padmā, the pollen of lotus, yojanavallī, and anantā destroy fat, phlegm, wind, and defects of breast milk.
Sāla wood, mocarasa, samaṅgā, punnāga, and śīta are the causes for aphrodisiacs.
Ambaṣṭhā, madhuka, namaskarī, nandīvṛkṣa, palāśa, and kacchurā [are used for similar purposes].
Lodhra, gāṭakī, the pulp of bilva, vaṭa-bark, and the pollen of the lotus;
the two groups beginning with priyaṅgu and ambaṣṭha destroy chronic diarrhea.
These two are healing for pitta, beneficial, and also promote the healing of wounds.
Mustā, vacā, agni, the two types of niśā, the two types of tiktā, bhallātaka, pāṭhā, triphalā, and viṣā— these are [the ingredients].

Kuṣṭha, truṭī, and haimavatī destroy diseases of the female reproductive tract and breast milk, and they also digest impurities. Nyagrodha, pippala, sadāphala, the two types of lodhra, the two types of jambu, arjuna, kapītana, and somavalka— [these are used for the same purposes].

The Nyagrodhādi group consists of *plakṣa*, *āsrava*, *vañjula*, *priyāla*, *palāśa*, *nandī*, *kolī*, *kadamba*, *viralā*, *madhuka*, and *madhūka*. This group is wound-healing (*vraṇya*), astringent (*saṅgrāhī*), and a remedy for fractures; it destroys fat, bile, blood, thirst, burning sensations, and diseases of the female reproductive tract.

Cardamom, the two types of *elā*, *turuṣka*, *kuṣṭha*, *phalinī*, *māṃsī*, *jalada*, *dhāmakā*, *spṛkkā*, *coraka*, *coca*, leaves, *tagara*, *sthauṇeya*, and *jātī*— these are the aromatic substances.

The group beginning with *śukti*— namely *śukti*, tiger-claw (*vyāghranakha*), *surāhva*, *aguru*, *śrīvāsaka*, saffron (*kuṅkuma*), *caṇḍā*, *guggulu*, *devadhūpa*, *khapura*, *punnāga*, and *nāgāhvaya*—
subdues wind (*vāta*), phlegm (*kapha*), and poison. (AS.Sū.16.36)
It clarifies the complexion and destroys itching, pustules, and skin eruptions.
[The plants] Śyāmā, Dantī, Dravantī, Kramuka, Kuṭharaṇā, Śaṅkhinī, Carmasāhvā, Svarṇakṣīrī, Gavākṣī, Śikhari, Rajanikā, Chinnarohā, and Karañja [are used for this].

The bastāntrī, vyādhighāta, and the fruits of the *tīkṣṇavṛkṣa*—which are thick and possess many tastes—as well as the *śyāmā* and other such plants, destroy abdominal tumors (*gulma*), irregular appetite, phlegm, heart disease, and dysuria.

Pippalī, pippalīmūla, cavya, citraka, śṛṅgavera, marica, hastipippalī, hareṇuka, kailā, jamoja, indrayava, pāṭhā, jīraka, sarṣapa, mahānimba-phala, phalgu, hiṅgu, bhārṅgī, vacā, mustā, madhurasā, ativiṣā, viḍaṅga, and kaṭurohiṇī. (AS.Sū.16.38)

The Pippalyādi group alleviates phlegm and cures catarrh, wind-disorders, and loss of appetite; it is digestive-stimulant, destroys abdominal tumors (gulma) and colic, and promotes the digestion of undigested food (āma).

The groups have been declared as twenty-five; among them, one should employ that which is appropriate according to what has not been obtained, and one should discard any substance that is unsuitable for application.

These groups [of drugs], when combined with medicinal pastes (kalka), decoctions (kvātha), fats (sneha), electuaries (leha), and so forth, according to the requirements of the humors (doṣa) and the affected tissues (dūṣya),
destroy even most difficult diseases— whether administered internally or externally through drinking, nasal medication (nasya), non-unctuous enema (anvāsana), plasters (lepa), or massage (abhyaṅga).
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
AS.Sū.17.1: We shall now expound the chapter on the knowledge of substances and so forth.
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and others:
"In this world, substance consists of the five great elements."

Its substratum is earth; its source is water; and through the combination of space, air, and fire, specific manifestations arise, though the designation is made according to whichever element is predominant.
Therefore, because of the impossibility of the combination of the elements (*bhūta-samavāya*), there is no substance (*dravya*) that possesses a single taste;
consequently, there are no diseases caused by a single humor (*doṣa*).
In this regard, the taste is manifest.
But because it is overwhelmed by the taste, the after-taste (anurasa) is either unmanifest or slightly manifest;
furthermore, the two functions of taste are cutting (chedana) and pacifying (upaśamana).

The beneficial and harmful potencies reside in their substrates, which are designated as substances such as earth and the rest; furthermore, qualities such as heaviness and so forth—governed by nature, transformation, processing, place, and time—are metaphorically attributed to the tastes through association. Among these, a substance that abounds in the qualities of heaviness, hardness, clarity, slowness, density, grossness, stability, and smell is of the earth element (*pārthiva*), and it effects accumulation, heaviness, cohesion, and stability.

That which is characterized by the qualities of liquidity, unctuousness, coldness, heaviness, slowness, thickness, mobility, softness, and黏滑ness (slipperiness), and is abundant in the taste-quality of water, is watery; it produces moisture, lubrication, cohesion, exudation, softness, and refreshment.

That which abounds in the qualities of sharpness, heat, roughness, subtlety, lightness, and clarity is of the fiery (āgneya) nature; it produces burning, digestion, illumination, radiance, and coloration.

That which abounds in the qualities of roughness, subtlety, lightness, clarity, expansion, pervasiveness, coldness, and harsh touch is of the windy (vāyya) nature; it produces dryness, lightness, clarity, exhaustion, and movement.
That which abounds in the qualities of sound— subtle, light, clear, smooth, pervasive, and distinct— is of the nature of space; it produces porosity and lightness.
And thus, there is no substance whatsoever in the world that does not become a medicinal drug through the application of various purposes; among these,
those consisting primarily of fire and wind are generally "upward-acting" (ūrdhvabhāgika).
For, due to their lightness and because fire moves upward while wind possesses the quality of blowing,
those consisting of earth and water generally tend toward the lower parts.
For, due to the heaviness of those two [earth and water] and the downward-flowing nature of water,
their combined essence consists of both parts.
Pacification (śamana), however, has been previously described as having qualities opposite to those of the humors (doṣas).
And when there is a mixture of these, since the performance of a function occurs predominantly through one element, that which is more predominant is designated as the performer of that function;
thus, that which consists of air is the grasper, while that which consists of fire performs digestion and transformation.
The application of both types [of substances]—consisting of earth and water—is nourishing (bṛṃhaṇa).
Among them, pungent, sour, and salty [tastes] are increasingly hot in their potency (vīrya) in successive order. (AS.Sū.17.14)
Those that are bitter, astringent, and sweet are cold;
those that are bitter, pungent, and astringent are dry and cause the retention of feces, urine, and flatus.
[Foods that are] salty, sour, and sweet, as well as unctuous, promote the evacuation of feces, urine, and flatus.
AS.Sū.17.16: [Foods that are] salty, astringent, and sweet are heavy.
In the same way, sour, pungent, and bitter [tastes] are light;
others, however, maintain that salt is common to both heavy and light, as well as to unctuous and dry.
Regarding potency (*vīrya*), some say it is of eight kinds, distinguished by being heavy, light, unctuous, dry, sharp, dull, cold,
and hot; others, however, recite [the following]:
The potency of a substance is to be known as that by which, through its conjunction, an action is produced;
that which lacks potency performs nothing, for every [action] is indeed produced by potency.

Furthermore, by them [the authors of the treatises], even though the designation *vīrya* (potency) for the eight qualities beginning with heaviness— which are endowed with extremely superior power and constitute the essence of all medicinal properties— is established according to specific traditional injunctions (*viśiṣṭāmnāya*), it is nevertheless presented as being worldly (*laukika*).

For, by means of that [designation], many qualities that are both abundant and preeminent, which overcome other qualities such as taste and post-digestive transformation (*rasavipāka*), are thereby subsumed.
Furthermore, in those various instances where the essential nature of a substance (*dravya*) is described, linguistic usage proceeds by way of its specific function;
for this very reason, the inherent nature of a substance that transcends all others is traditionally designated as "potency" (*prabhāva*).

And although there is a commonality in the accomplishment of action (*kriyānirvartana*), tastes (*rasa*) and the like—which are the opposite of that [specific function]—are not referred to by the name "potency" (*vīrya*) or by the designation "potency" (*prabhāva*).

Others, however, because the preceptor and the rest consist of Agni and Soma, and because time consists of heat and cold through the division of grasping and releasing, maintain that [time] is twofold;
and they say this:
Even though a substance consists of diverse elements, it never transcends the two great powers, Agni and Soma,
just as the manifest and unmanifest world does not transcend them.
Among these, the hot [quality] performs burning, cooking, sweating, liquefying, and the pacification of wind and phlegm;
the cold [quality] performs refreshing, stabilizing, vitalizing, and the purification of blood and bile, and so forth.
Thus vigor has been explained; now its maturation is being described.
The post-digestive effect (vipāka), however, is generally sweet for the sweet and the salty, sour for the sour, and pungent for the others;
it yields results similar to its [original] tastes.
One should observe its mildness, medium intensity, or abundance according to the specific qualities of the substance.
But Parāśara recites: AS.Sū.17.26. AS.Sū.17.26. AS.Sū.17.25.

There are three post-digestive transformations (vipāka) of tastes: the sour taste transforms into sour, and the pungent into pungent; the other four [tastes] transform into sweet, while those of mixed tastes transform into mixed. Regarding the pungent, bitter, and astringent tastes, there is the view that their post-digestive transformation is pungent.

AS.Sū.17.27 When pitta is diminished, how do bitter and astringent [tastes] act? AS.Sū.17.28 In that regard, one should understand that for those substances which are sweet in both taste and post-digestive effect (*vipāka*) and cold in potency (*vīrya*), as well as those which are sour and hot in potency, or those which are pungent, their qualities and their capacity to pacify the aggravation of the *doṣas* should generally be known according to their respective tastes.
For example, as in the case of milk, wine, black pepper, and so forth,
there occurs a change [of state] through the blending of tastes and other qualities.
Just as honey, being sweet, pacifies phlegm, yet generates wind due to its pungent post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), its astringency, its dryness, and its cold potency (*vīrya*).
Likewise, even barley produces bile despite being cold because it possesses a hot potency (*uṣṇavīrya*);
similarly, oil obstructs the feces and urine due to its pungent post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*), and indeed by that very transformation.

Sour *kāñjika* conquers *kapha* due to its dryness and heat; *kapittha*, however, conquers *pitta* due to its dryness, while *āmalaka* conquers *pitta* due to its cold potency and *kapha* due to its sweet post-digestive effect (*pāka*). It does not aggravate *vāta* because of its coldness, dryness, and lightness. *Saindhava* salt conquers *pitta* due to its sweet post-digestive effect and conquers *kapha* due to its lightness.
Kaṭukā and śuṇṭhī also subdue vāta through their oiliness, heat, and sweet post-digestive effect; so too do pippalī, garlic, and onion through their oiliness, heat, and heaviness.
However, due to its oiliness and heaviness, it generates phlegm; furthermore, the radish, because it is sweet when cooked,
increases phlegm, while tiger’s claw, viśalyā, arka, and agaru generate bile because they possess a hot potency and are unctuous and bitter.

The great *pañcamūla*, being astringent and bitter, overcomes *vāta* but not *pitta* because of its hot potency (*uṣṇavīrya*); likewise, *kulattha* is astringent yet has an acidic post-digestive transformation (*amlapāka*). This has been stated merely as an illustration (AS.Sū.17.30). Therefore:
Some [substance] performs its action through its taste (rasa), another through its post-digestive transformation (pāka),
some through its specific property (guṇa), its potency (vīrya), or indeed through its sovereign power (prabhāva).
When, in a substance, one among the tastes and so forth exists with greater strength,
it overpowers the others and attains the status of being the cause for that [substance].
When there is a combination of contradictory qualities, the lesser is indeed overcome by the greater.
Taste, post-digestive effect, potency, and specific action— each of these overcomes the preceding one.
When there is equality of strength among the tastes (rasa) and so forth, this refers to their innate strength.
AS.Sū.17.34: Furthermore, even tastes and other factors that are mutually contradictory [can act] in accomplishing an effect.

Qualities and defects do not necessarily counteract one another, just as the tastes, potencies, and other properties [of substances] do not, depending on the predominance or subordination of the constituent elements.
AS.Sū.17.35 Whether uniform or diverse, they rest upon the substance.
AS.Sū.17.36 Sweetness, coldness, sliminess, unctuousness, heaviness, and dullness [are their qualities].
The qualities that have been described for substances existing together with milk, as well as those for marshy and aquatic meat, apply likewise to [substances] that are slightly deficient in quality.
Therefore, their stability, increase, and decrease are caused by substances (dravya). One should know the taste (rasa) by its falling [into the body] and by its subsequent permeation (adhivasana).
The potency and maturation of substances [are determined] by the completion of their action,
as illustrated among the sweet groups by ghee, oil, molasses, and so forth.
The sixfold division of tastes based on distinctions such as the relish of qualities (*guṇāsvāda*) and so forth is not tenable.
AS.Sū.17.40: Let there be either an incalculable number [of tastes] due to their distinction, or unity based on the characteristic of being a relish (*āsvāda*).

The distinction that is postulated on the basis of a slight difference in the excellence or deficiency of the elements (bhūta) is not intended to be expressed, because of the confusion [of categories] and because the fruit is equal.

AS.Sū.17.41: Even though there are distinctions among heavy and other qualities, because one does not overstep one's own genus (svajāti), there is no difference in number; that same principle applies to the tastes as well. AS.Sū.17.42: Just as there is no difference in number [among the tastes], such is their sequence.

The coating of the mouth and other such effects observed in all [substances] such as clarified butter are not present in pomegranates and the like; therefore, only six tastes are traditionally recognized.

AS.Sū.17.43 Furthermore, in the case of infinity and unity, there would be no coordination of diverse purposes. AS.Sū.17.44 The qualities beginning with weight (gurutva) are called "potencies" (*vīrya*); otherwise, they are merely "qualities" (*guṇa*).

Because they lack the capacity to produce other [tastes], the other [qualities] are indeed merely qualities (guṇas). AS.Sū.17.45: Some have stated that the six types of digestion (pākas) correspond to the tastes; that is incorrect.
That rice which is sweet does not attain acidity, nor does the pomegranate, though acidic, become bitter;
and oil attains pungency, yet the long pepper, though pungent, does not.
AS.Sū.17.46 Just as there would be no reversal in the case of the ripening of tastes, so it is here. AS.Sū.17.47 For barley is observed to be heavy and yet to increase the wind (vāta).

Clarified butter, though cold, is an appetizer; cow's urine, though hot, is a quencher of fire. Green gram (mudga), though having a pungent post-digestive effect, destroys pitta, whereas black gram (māṣa) increases pitta.
Phāṇita, though sweet when cooked, is laxative; it is unctuous, hot, and heavy.
Just as its taste is sweet, so too are other qualities observed in it.
The fruit of the *ākṣakī* tree, though sour, increases wind (*vāta*) and subdues phlegm (*kapha*) and bile (*pitta*).
Curd indeed produces heaviness and diminishes the digestive fire (*vahni*), but the pigeon (*pārāvata*) does not.
The wood-apple (*kapittha*) and the sour pomegranate are constipating, as is the *āmalaka* fruit. Dhātakī is astringent, constipating, and cooling, but not so the *harītakī*.
Therefore, the tastes and other qualities are secondary and are dependent upon it separately;
since the specific potency (prabhāva) resides in the substance, the substance is considered the most important.
AS.Sū.17.52 When the taste and other qualities are equal, that action which is distinguished arises from its specific power (prabhāva).
AS.Sū.17.53 Although dantī is equal to citraka in terms of taste and the rest, it is a purgative [only] because of its own power.
Madhuka, grapes, ghee, and milk are digestive stimulants (dīpana).
Due to their pungent post-digestive taste (pāka), pungent flavor (rasa), unctuousness, and heaviness, they conquer kapha and vāta.

Garlic produces wind and phlegm, yet it does not possess those same qualities [as its opposites]. Since blood and other elements conquer the mutually contradictory [doshas] such as wind and the rest, [garlic is not subject to that rule].
The effects of barley and other such substances are the manifestation of that [poison's] power;
while the *śirīṣa* and other plants destroy the poison, sleep and the like serve to increase it.
And whatever action consists of various types involving gems, mantras, and medicinal herbs—
such as the extraction of foreign bodies, the accumulation [of merit], protection, longevity, wisdom, subjugation, and so forth.
Furthermore, that which neutralizes poison even by mere sight and other such means is an *agada* (antidote);
that which causes purgation, is aphrodisiac, or quickly produces semen [is also such].
Whatever substance acts as a purgative or emetic, and whatever [remedy] effects pacification and so forth— each of these,
having attained its proper dose and other conditions, is described in detail.
And all that is born of its power; therefore, it is called inconceivable.
Whatever action a substance may perform through its taste, potency, qualities, and post-digestive transformation (vipāka), [it is due to this power].
"Otherwise, it produces that immediately through its power; therefore, there is no scope for a cause in that regard.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter. Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the classification of tastes.
Thus indeed said the great seers, Ātreya and others:
"The rasa, moreover, is composed of water and is initially unmanifest."

Because time consists of six seasons, it becomes mixed with the qualities of the great elements in states of deficiency or excess; thus, being improperly transformed and digested, it undergoes a sixfold change according to the distinctions of sweet and so forth. Among these, the sweet taste arises from the predominance of the elements earth and water.
Sourness belongs to earth and fire;
salinity to water and fire;
and bitterness to air and space.
The pungent [taste] belongs to wind and fire;
the astringent belongs to wind and space.
Among these, the sweet, when tasted, smears the mouth and clarifies the sense faculties.
It refreshes the body and is most beloved even to six-legged insects, ants, and the like.
Sour [taste] causes the tongue to recoil, burns the chest and throat, causes salivation from the mouth, contracts the eyes and eyebrows, makes the teeth tingle, and causes the body hair to bristle;
salt [taste] causes the mouth to flow with saliva, burns the throat and cheeks, and stimulates the appetite for food.
The bitter [taste] clarifies the mouth, cleanses the throat, and suppresses the sense of taste;
the pungent [taste] intensely agitates the tip of the tongue, causes a tingling sensation in the throat and cheeks, causes secretions from the mouth, eyes, and nose, and burns the body;
whereas the astringent [taste] numbs the tongue, constricts the throat, and afflicts the heart.

AS.Sū.18.5 Among these, the sweet taste (*madhura-rasa*), due to its wholesomeness (*sātmya*) from birth onwards, increases all the bodily constituents (*dhātu*); it promotes longevity; it is beneficial for children, the elderly, those with chest wounds, those who are emaciated, and for strength, complexion, the sense organs, skin, hair, and the throat; it is pleasing, nourishing, life-sustaining, satiating, stabilizing, and healing; it increases breast milk and pacifies wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), poison, burning sensations, fainting, and thirst; it is unctuous (*snigdha*), cold, soft, and heavy. AS.Sū.18.5 AS.Sū.18.6 Even though it possesses such qualities, when used excessively and constantly, it causes obesity, loss of digestive fire (*agni*), heaviness, intestinal torpor (*ānāha*), and impairment of the sense organs.
It brings about dyspnea, urinary disorders, diseases of the throat, loss of consciousness, sweetness in the mouth, tumors of the eyes and throat, and cervical lymphadenitis (gaṇḍamālā);
it also causes vomiting, urticaria, headache, cough, catarrh, worms, elephantiasis, fever, abdominal enlargement, and spitting.

Sour [taste] subdues *vāta*, promotes the downward movement of *vāyu*, causes burning in the digestive tract (*koṣṭha*), produces *rakta-pitta*, is hot in potency (*uṣṇa-vīrya*), is cold in touch (*śīta-sparśa*), and awakens the sense organs. (AS.Sū.18.7–8)
It is clarifying, digestive, appetizing, nourishing, satiating, pleasing, moistening, pervasive, light, unctuous, and beneficial for the heart.
When consumed in excess, it produces flaccidity in the body and causes the dissolution of *kapha*, itching, pallor, and similar disorders.

Salt [tastes] removes spreading infections caused by wounds, hemorrhagic disorders (raktapitta), thirst, edema, and even delusions in emaciated persons because of its fiery nature (taijasa). It loosens stiffness, bonds, and accumulations; it is antagonistic to all other tastes; it stimulates digestion, improves appetite, promotes digestion, moistens, dries, lubricates, induces perspiration, breaks up masses, and cuts through obstructions. It is mobile, pervasive, and causes dilation; it carries away the wind (pavana), liquefies phlegm (kapha), and purifies the channels. It is not excessively heavy, and it is unctuous, sharp, and hot. AS.Sū.18.10
