It causes baldness, graying hair, thirst, burning sensations, fainting, erysipelas, swelling, skin eruptions, abdominal enlargements, convulsions,
and blood-bile (asrapitta); it produces wounds, irregular growths, and gout (vatarakta), while the consumer of it [or its use] destroys strength.

Bitter (tikta) is itself unpalatable; it removes anorexia, poison, worms, fainting, excessive secretions, fever, burning sensations, thirst, skin diseases (kuṣṭha), and itching. It dries up moisture, fat, muscle-fat, marrow, feces, urine, bile, and phlegm; it stimulates digestion, promotes maturation, is scarifying, purifies the breast milk and the throat, is beneficial for the intellect, is not excessively dry, and is cold and light. [It causes] the depletion of the elements and strength, fainting, exhaustion, giddiness, wind diseases, and roughness.

When excessively consumed with qualities that are harsh, clear, and rough, it produces alasaka (intestinal torpor), swelling, urticaria, obesity, ophthalmia, worms, diseases of the mouth, poison, skin diseases, and itching. It is a healer of wounds, a desiccant of unctuousness and moisture, appetizing, digestive, stimulant, scraping, and purifying. It dries up food, clarifies the sense organs, breaks up the accumulation of blood, cuts through bonds, opens the channels, and diminishes phlegm; it is light, dry, sharp, and hot.
Being excessively oppressed by it, he brings about thirst, intoxication, fainting, delusion,
and physical exhaustion.
The loss of strength and semen, emaciation, trembling, vertigo, fever, exhaustion, and extreme leanness;
and an exceedingly intense provocation of the wind (vāyu) in the hands, feet, sides, back, and other parts.
Through contraction, piercing, or by virtue of its predominance in the qualities of wind and fire,
astringent (kaṣāya) quickly destroys phlegm (balāsa), bile, and blood; being extremely dry, it binds the feces.
Ghee has a color like that of its source (the cow), it provides moisture and dryness, and it is cooling, nourishing, healing,
and scraping. However, through excessive use, even it causes the obstruction of semen, thirst, flatulence, stiffness, constipation, and emaciation.
It causes obstruction of the channels, retention of flatus, feces, and urine, and conditions such as hemiplegia and convulsions.

AS.Sū.18.19 Now, the sweet group (*madhuraskandha*) consists of: ghee, honey, oil, milk, fat, marrow, products of sugarcane, grapes, *kṣoḍa*, dates, *moca*, *coca*, jackfruit, *siñcatikā*, *priyāla*, *rājādana*, *kharyūrī*, the heartwood of *tāla*, *kāśmarya*, *madhūka*, *parūṣaka*, *āmalakī*, *vīrā*, *vidārī*, *śatāvarī*, *tugākṣīrī*, *jīvaka*, *ṛṣabhaka*, *kṣīraśuklā*, *madhūlikā*, *ātmaguptā*, *balā*, *atibalā*, *viśvadevā*, *sahadevā*, *sālaparṇī*, *mudgaparṇī*, *pṛśniparṇī*, *maṣaparṇī*, *mahāsahā*, *kṣudrasahā*, *ṛddhi*, *vṛddhi*, *śrāvaṇī*, *chatrā*, *aticchatrā*, *ṛṣyaproktā*, and *aśvagandhā*.

The group of vitalizing (jīvanīya) substances consists of *gandhāśvadaṃṣṭrā*, *mṛṇālikā*, lotus seeds (*puṣkarabīja*), *śṛṅgāṭaka*, *kaśeruka*, *takakanaka*, *bimbī*, *prapauṇḍarīka*, and so forth, as well as the five roots of grasses (*tṛṇapañcamūla*). The category of sour substances (*amladravyaskandha*) includes pomegranate, *āmalaka*, mango, *āmrātaka*, *kośāmra*, citron (*mātuluṅga*), *amlīkā*, *āmlavetasa*, *sakuvala*, *lakucha*, *pārāvata*, *bhavya*, *karamarda*, *dhava*, *dhanvana*, *kola*, *badara*, *airāvataka*, *kapittha*, *dantaśaṭha*, *prācīnāmalaka*, orange (*nāraṅga*), *tilakaṇṭaka*, silver-leaf fig (*rūpya*), whey (*dadhimastu*), buttermilk (*takra*), fermented grain water (*dhānyāmla*), wine (*madya*), vinegar (*śukta*), and so forth.
The aggregate of saline substances consists of those beginning with rock salt (*saindhava*) and ending with alkaline salts (*kṣāra*), as well as tin, lead, and so forth.

AS.Sū.18.22 The group of bitter substances (*tiktadravyaskandha*) consists of agaru, tagara, uśīra, bālaka, candana, nalada, kṛtamāla, naktamāla, apāmārga, the two types of haridrā, musta, mūrvā, madanaphala, ajaśṛṅgī, trāyamāṇā, kaṭukā, kirātatiktaka, karavīra, viśālā, suṣavī, ativiṣā, yavāsaka, jyotiṣmatī, pāṭhā, vikaṅkata, arka, kākamācī, vacā, varaṇa, vatsaka, vaijayantī, vetasa, saptaparṇa, somavalka, sumanaḥ, kāṃsya, loha, and so forth, as well as the vegetable group beginning with *paṭola*.

The pungent substance group consists of black pepper, asafoetida, *tejovatī*, long pepper, elephant pepper, *viḍaṅga*, marking-nut seeds, radish, mustard, garlic, onion, *karañja*, realgar, *ālā*, deodar, costus, cardamom, *surasa*, *coraka*, *hareṇukā*, urine, bile, and so forth; as well as the *kuṭhera* group of herbs and the five spices (*pañcakola*).

AS.Sū.18.24 The group of astringent substances (*kaṣāyadravyaskandha*) consists of: *harītakī*, *priyaṅgu*, *anantā*, honey (*kṣaudra*), *lodhra*, *kaṭphala*, *dhava*, *dhanvana*, the fruits of *dhātrī*, the flowers of *dhātakī*, *padmā*, *padmaka*, the flowers of *padma*, *nāgakesara*, *kumuda*, *utpala*, *tuṅga*, *tinduka*, *kadamba*, *udumbara*, *jambu*, *āmra*, *plakṣa*, *vaṭa*, *bibhītaka*, *vikaṅkata*, the seeds of *jambu* and *āmra*, *āmalaka*, *kapittha*, *aśvattha*, *mocarasa*, *samaṅgā*, *somavalka*, *saptaparṇa*, *syandana*, *āsana*, *sallakī*, *sāla*, *tāla*, *priyāla*, *elā*, *vāstukā*, *paripelava*, *jiṅgiṇī*, *badarī*, *khadira*, *kadara*, *arimeda*, *kāśa*, *kaśeruka*, bamboo (*vaṃśa*), *aśmantaka*, *aśoka*, *śirīṣa*, *śiṃśapā*, *palāśa*, *śamaśiṇa*, *śaṅkhanābhi*, *meṣaśṛṅgī*, young *kharjūra*, *sphūrjaka*, *bhūrja*, *arjuna*, *ajakarṇa*, *varaṇa*, *priyāla*, *muktā*, *añjana*, *garika*, lotus stalks (*bisamṛṇāla*), and so forth.
In that regard, for the most part, sweet food increases phlegm (*śleṣman*), with the exception of aged *śāli* rice, barley, wheat, mung beans, honey, sugar, and the meat of wild animals.
Generally, that which is sour increases pitta, except for pomegranate and āmalaka; generally, that which is salty is detrimental to the eyes, except for rock salt (saindhava);
generally, that which is bitter and pungent increases vāta and is non-aphrodisiac, except for amṛtā, paṭolī, ginger, long pepper, and garlic.
"Generally, [these] are astringent, cooling, and styptic, with the exception of *harītakī*" (AS.Sū.18.26);
thus, there is a summary of those most essential and constantly used items according to their general characteristics (AS.Sū.18.26).
Ghee, āmalaka, rock salt, paṭolī, ginger,
and abhayā are excellent for their respective [doshas] in the [three] pillars; however, the specific locations of the tastes shall be explained later.

Now, that region which is delightful, strewn with lotuses, lilies, blue water-lilies, and *avakīrṇa* flowers from ponds, lakes, pools, and wells, as well as from various forest thickets on cool mountains; where the ground is firm and moist, the green grass is abundant, and trees are covered with widely spreading creepers and tender shoots; which is teeming with crops, reptiles, and birds; where phlegm and bile predominate, and the waters and medicinal herbs are heavy; and where the people are afflicted by diseases such as elephantiasis (*ślīpada*), throat ailments, abdominal dropsy (*āpīna*), and fever—that is the marshy (*anūpa*) region, the source of sweet tastes.

AS.Sū.18.29 That country which abounds in uneven, vast tracts of sand, where the water is extremely deep and tasteless, where the people are generally enduring of hardship, free from disease, long-lived, and dwell in arid lands (anūpa), is a *jāṅgala* region; it is the source of pungent tastes.
For this very reason, one must distinguish between what is common to the marshy (*anūpa*) and what is common to the arid (*jāṅgala*).
Of these two [categories], the first is the source of salt and sour, while the other is the source of the remaining two;
their combinations, however, amount to fifty-seven, and there are verses on this point: [The verses follow.]
Among the pairs [of tastes], the sweet one goes with five; the sour, with four; the salty, with three;
the bitter and the pungent, with two; and the astringent, with one. Thus, they total exactly fifteen.
Among the triads, one should consume the sweet with the sour, the four [sweet, sour, salty, and bitter] combined with the salty,
three [sweet, sour, and bitter] joined with the bitter, two [sweet and salty] with the pungent, and one [the pungent] alone.
The sweet [taste] thus possesses ten [qualities], and the sour possesses six; the actions [of these] are as previously described.
The salty possesses three, and the bitter possesses one; in this way, there are twenty [qualities].
Among the groups of four, the sweet and sour tastes each reach three [others]; the salty taste follows three;
that accompanied by the bitter reaches one; thus, the sweet taste reaches ten [others].
There are four sour [tastes] and one pungent; thus, there are fifteen varieties. By the omission of each one individually, there are six combinations within the group of five.
There is one [type] consisting of six tastes, and six that are distinct; thus, there are sixty-three varieties of these taste-differences,
both by way of primary and secondary tastes and through the conceptualization of their relative degrees.
They arise in numbers beyond calculation and are to be employed according to the specific faults and medicines;
thus ends the eighteenth chapter.
Now begins the nineteenth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the knowledge of the humors and so forth;
thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
For the body has its roots in the humors (doṣas), the constituent elements (dhātus), and the waste products (malas);
therefore, we shall describe their characteristics.
Among these, vāyu sustains the body through such functions as inhalation and exhalation, exertion, pulsation, the sharpness of the sense organs, and the initiation of movement.
Pitta is characterized by digestion, heat, desire, hunger, thirst, luster, clarity, vision, intelligence, heroism, and softness;

Śleṣman by stability, unctuousness, firmness of the joints, virility, forbearance, intellect, fortitude, strength, and lack of fickleness; while Rasa is characterized by contentment, nourishment, and the nourishment of the blood.
Vitality is nourished by the purification of the complexion; blood by the nourishment of flesh;
and flesh by the nourishment of the body's unctuousness, impurities, and fat.
Fat (medas) [is known] by the oiliness of the eyes and limbs, firmness, and nourishment of the bones;
marrow (majjā) [is known] by the upward support of the body and the nourishment of the bones;
and bone-marrow (asthi-majjā) [is known] by oiliness, strength, filling of the bones, and the nourishment of semen.
It produces joy, strength, and the fetus; it supports the semen; it sustains the wind and fire;
it carries away feces through the moistening of food, and urine.

Sweat is characterized by moisture, skin-softness, oiliness, and the maintenance of body hair (AS.Sū.19.3). When increased, Vāyu afflicts [the body] with emaciation, blackish discoloration, trembling of the limbs, twitching, a desire for warmth, loss of consciousness, loss of sleep, impairment of the sense organs, pain in the bones, drying of the marrow, retention of waste matter, flatulence, distension, delusion, dejection, fear, grief, delirium, and so forth (AS.Sū.19.3).

Pitta is [known] by yellowness of the skin, impairment of the sense organs, weakness, loss of vitality (*ojas*), desire for cold, a burning sensation, a bitter taste in the mouth, thirst, fainting, and sleepiness; and by anger and so forth. Kapha is [known] by whiteness, coldness, heaviness, lassitude, heaviness of the limbs, obstruction of the channels, fainting, drowsiness, sleep, labored breathing, cough, salivation, nausea, loss of digestive fire, and dislocation of the joints; and so forth. Rasa (the nutrient fluid) is [known] by salivation, anorexia, a bad taste in the mouth, nausea, obstruction of the channels, aversion to flavors, aching of the limbs, and other such conditions characterized primarily as disorders of kapha.

[One should avoid] leprosy, erysipelas, pustules, menorrhagia, burning sensations in the eyes, mouth, penis, and anus, abdominal tumors, abscesses, splenic disorders, freckles, jaundice, loss of digestive fire, fainting, redness of the limbs and eyes, and other conditions predominantly caused by pitta such as vātarakta;

[and one should avoid] goiter, scrofula, tumors, nodules, diseases of the palate, tongue, and throat, heaviness and swelling of the buttocks, lips, arms, abdomen, thighs, and shanks, and other conditions predominantly caused by kapha and blood disorders affecting the flesh.
By the premonitory symptoms of urinary disorders (prameha), complications such as obesity and other conditions predominantly consisting of disorders of phlegm (śleṣman), blood, and muscle;

by the presence of excessive fat, excess bone, and extra teeth; and by heaviness of the bones, eyes, and limbs, as well as large-rooted ulcers on the joints—these indicate the involvement of marrow (majjā).

Excessive semen results from excessive desire for women or the occurrence of seminal calculi; excessive feces is characterized by abdominal pain, flatulence, and heaviness; and excessive urine is characterized by piercing pain in the bladder and distension.
Through itching and foul odors, perspiration,
and other impurities such as rheum of the eyes, [the body suffers from] excess,

liquidity, itching, and heaviness; furthermore, when diminished by excessive salivation, loss of appetite, nausea, loss of consciousness, delusion, reduced speech and movement, lack of joy, exhaustion of the limbs, irregularity of the digestive fire, and so forth, the *vāyu* afflicts [the person].

Pitta is [diagnosed] by stiffness, coldness, irregular piercing pain, loss of appetite, indigestion, roughness of the limbs, tremors, heaviness, whiteness of the nails and eyes, and so forth; Kapha is [diagnosed] by giddiness, twisting sensations, sleeplessness, aching of the limbs, a burning sensation, pricking pain, a feeling of being scorched, eruptions, trembling, a sensation of fuming, looseness of the joints, a sense of melting in the heart, and emptiness in the seat of phlegm (āmāśaya), and so forth.

Rasa [is known] by its inability to withstand sound, by the melting of the heart, trembling, emaciation, piercing pain, emptiness, throbbing, and aching, as well as by even slight exertion, fatigue, and thirst.
Blood [is known] by dryness of the skin, a desire for sour and cold things, and flaccidity of the vessels.

Fat (*medas*) [is diminished] by dryness of the buttocks, cheeks, and so forth, as well as by emaciation of the thighs, roughness, lassitude of the eyes, cracking of the joints, and laxity of the vessels; and by those symptoms mentioned for the depletion of muscle (*māṃsa*), such as enlargement of the spleen, numbness of the waist, pain in the joints, dryness of the limbs, emaciation, exhaustion, wasting, and a craving for fatty meat. Bone (*asthi*) [is diminished] by the falling out of teeth, nails, body hair, and head hair, as well as by dryness, coarseness, laxity of the joints, pain in the bones, and a craving for meat that is firm in bone.

Marrow is characterized by aching in the hollows of the bones, weakness, giddiness, and the appearance of darkness; semen is characterized by exhaustion, weakness, dryness of the mouth, seeing darkness (timira), body ache, pallor, prostration, impotence, pricking pain in the testicles, a sensation of fuming in the penis, and delayed ejaculation, or ejaculation accompanied by blood,
or the sound of wind moving obliquely or upward within the abdomen due to the twisting of the intestines, with pressure on the sides and heart, and scanty feces.
Urine [is affected] by pricking pain in the bladder, dryness of the mouth, difficulty in urination, scanty or discolored urine, or by the presence of blood in the urine;

sweat [is affected] by stiffness of the hair follicles, loss of body hair, cracking of the skin, numbness, roughness, and loss of perspiration; and other impurities likewise [are affected] by their respective channels being parched, empty, and light.
One should observe the increase and decrease [of the humors] through the opposite qualities and their respective diminution or augmentation; furthermore,
one should observe the increase and decrease of the impurities (malas) through their excessive retention or discharge.
But when the impurities increase, their destruction causes extreme pain due to its impropriety;
among them, the wind resides in the bone, while the bile resides in the blood and sweat.
In the remaining [elements], phlegm [predominates];
therefore, these [elements] possess the quality of increasing or decreasing by one at a time,
but this is not the case for bone and wind.
For virtually all increase [of bodily constituents] is generally accompanied by *śleṣman* (phlegm), being caused primarily by over-nutrition;
conversely, decrease is accompanied by *vāyu* (wind) due to the opposite conditions.
Therefore, one should treat disorders arising from increase and decrease through lightening (*laṅghana*) and nourishing (*bṛṃhaṇa*) therapies, respectively.
In the case of wind (vāyu), however, [it is balanced] by nourishing and lightening therapies;

and in all cases, the bodily elements (dhātavaḥ) indeed increase when they are treated with food and lifestyle habits that are non-contradictory, being either similar to them or predominantly possessing similar qualities, through the application of substances whose properties and actions are the opposite of those [of the aggravated element]. (AS.Sū.19.9)
But there is a decrease [of the humors] through the opposite factors, or by those characterized by an abundance of opposite qualities;
for thus, those bodily constituents (*dhātu*) which are heavy are increased by being brought into union with other heavy substances.
Light substances, however, are diminished by light ones that possess contrary qualities and cause separation;

therefore, blood is replenished even more effectively by other substances. From blood comes flesh, from flesh fat, from fat bone, from young bone marrow, from marrow semen, and from semen the embryo in its unformed stage.

However, where there is an absence of food and lifestyle habits possessing these general characteristics that correspond to the [deficient] qualities, or where it is impossible to consume those that are available due to incompatibility, loathing, lack of appetite, or some other intervening cause—

In that regard, it is best to consume foods and activities belonging to other temperaments (prakṛti) that are predominantly characterized by similar qualities. For example, in the case of a deficiency of semen (śukra), the use of milk and ghee, as well as other substances that are sweet, unctuous, and cold, is recommended.

Furthermore, whatever action increases a particular element by virtue of having a similar function, that very action should be cultivated by one who desires the increase of that element; likewise, that which causes its decrease through a similar function should be avoided by one seeking that same result.
Moreover—
Specifically, those arising from an increase in blood should be treated by bloodletting and purifying body-cleansing therapies;

those arising from an increase in muscle tissue by purification, surgical instruments, caustic applications, and thermal cautery; and those arising from fat by means of the therapeutic procedures for obesity and emaciation.
Those caused by the depletion of rasa should be treated with meat broth, wine, and milk;
those caused by the depletion of bone with enemas containing bitter substances and milk enemas;
and those caused by the increase of feces according to the procedure for diarrhea.
Those arising from the depletion of feces [are treated] with barley, black gram, fermented gruel, and the meat of goat, sheep, and other animals;
those arising from the depletion of urine [are treated] by the therapeutic measures for urinary disorders (meha) and dysuria (kṛcchra);
and those arising from the depletion of sweat [are treated] with massage, exercise, wine, sleep, shelter from the wind, and sudation.
And there is a verse on this point:
"Those portions of the digestive fire that reside in the bodily constituents [become unbalanced] through their dullness or excessive sharpness."
The increase and decrease of the bodily constituents (dhātus) occur; hear another [point]:
even in the case of a forest fire, the flame reaches various pieces of fuel in succession.
Just as increase and decrease occur, so too does the succession of the bodily constituents (dhātus);
for each constituent is specifically conducive to its own increase or its own depletion.
The preceding element, whether increased or diminished, produces the subsequent one; that which is determined by its own individual seed arises very swiftly and intensely.
The doshas, when vitiated by the tastes, corrupt the dhatus; both types [of doshas] corrupt the malas.
There are two apertures below, seven in the head, and those that carry sweat.
The humors (mala) and their respective seats (malāyana) exist according to their own nature; therefore,
diseases arising from them will be described therein, specifically those born of Vāta in the section on Vātaroga.
Pitta located in the skin produces eruptions (visphoṭaka) and smallpox (masūrikā);
when located in the blood, it causes erysipelas (visarpa) and a burning sensation; and when located in the flesh, it causes the sloughing away of the flesh.
When [the poison] is in the fat, it causes burning sensations and glandular swellings; in the sweat, excessive vomiting and thirst;
in the bones, intense burning; and in the marrow, a yellowish discoloration of the nails and eyes.

Semen that is foul-smelling, yellowish, or pale, when located in the semen itself, leads to anger; when located in the vessels, it leads to delirium; and when located in the tendons, it leads to thirst.
Kapha located in the visceral cavities causes intoxication, thirst, and burning sensations; when it pervades the body, it causes other symptoms of consumption (yakṣman).
Kapha situated in the skin produces stiffness and a whitish appearance.
Pāṇḍu, vāta-roga, blood-disorders, those located in the flesh such as arbuda and apacī, the appearance of limbs covered like moist leather, and excessive heaviness.
When located in the fat, it causes obesity; when in the urine, it causes urinary disorders (meha); when in the bones, it causes stiffness of the bones;
when in the marrow, it causes whiteness of the eyes; and when situated in the semen, it causes the accumulation of semen.
When located in the vessels, it causes obstruction, excessive heaviness, and stiffness of the limbs;
when in the tendons, it causes pain in the joints; and when in the abdominal cavity, it causes distension of the belly.
Anorexia and indigestion, as well as those various disorders arising from phlegm,
will be taught there and there along with their respective bases, namely feces and urine.
Affliction and injury, however, are impurities residing in one's own physical basis and sense faculties,
resulting from physical exertion, the sharpness of heat, and the practice of what is unwholesome.

Due to the rapid movement of the wind (māruta), the humors (doṣas) move from the visceral cavities to the peripheral branches, bones, and vital points (marmans); likewise, they are expelled from those locations through the purification of the openings of the channels (srotas).
Due to swelling, oozing, suppuration, and the suppression of the bodily wind (vāyu),
they remain localized within the visceral cavity (koṣṭha) and linger there, awaiting further causes.

Having obtained the strength of time and other factors, they become provoked even toward other substrates; however, when those [humors] are situated in other locations that are weak, they do not [become provoked].
One should administer one's own treatment by force against those [diseases] that overcome others; or, one should pacify an adventitious disorder after having counteracted the resident [dosha].
That which is the brilliance (*tejas*) of all the elements is said to be the supreme vitality (*ojas*);
it is soft, lunar in nature, pure, red, and slightly yellowish. It is the essence at the beginning of the embryo, and that which is the essence derived from the embryonic fluid.
That which was formerly the heart, as it undergoes dissolution, takes refuge [in that state];
it is the essence of the body, the moisture, and where the vital breath (prāṇa) is established.
That which, by its non-destruction, there is no destruction, and by which embodied beings are nourished; though situated within the heart, it is all-pervading— that is the supreme abode of life.
Vital energy (*ojas*) is diminished by anger, hunger, anxiety, grief, fatigue, and the like.
One who is weak fears constantly, and with his sense faculties distressed, he broods.
When that [blood] is diminished, one becomes ill-favored, dejected, rough, and emaciated; in that case,
the remedy consists of vitalizing (jīvanīya) herbs, milk, meat broth, and the like.
For when the *ojas* (vital essence) of the body increases, there occurs satisfaction, nourishment, and the arising of strength.
Whatever food one dislikes and whatever one desires, provided it is not contradictory [to one's health], [should be consumed].

By abandoning that [which causes increase] and consuming that [which causes decrease], one should conquer those two states of increase and decrease. The *doṣas* produce a preference for things that are either contrary to or similar to themselves.
The wise observe that [the humors] are mostly increased or diminished, yet the ignorant do not perceive this;
the humors, having increased according to their respective strengths and natures, spread throughout the body.

When the humors have become depleted, they abandon their forms and perform their own specific functions. Those very same humors that are balanced lead to the growth of the body; those that are unbalanced lead to its destruction.
Therefore, because they must be protected from decline and for the sake of their growth through beneficial conduct alone,
[this concludes] the nineteenth chapter.
Now begins the twentieth chapter. Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "The Classification of the Doṣas."
Thus indeed said the great sages, such as Ātreya and others:
from the elements of air and space, [the wind arises], and from fire, pitta.
From water and earth comes phlegm;

therein are the receptacle for digested food (pakvāśaya), the hips, the thighs, the feet, the bones, the ear, and the sense of touch. These are the seats of wind (vāta), and among them, the receptacle for digested food is particularly so.
The navel, the stomach, sweat, lymph, blood, the eyes, and the skin are the seats of pitta;
here, the navel is particularly [prominent].
The chest, throat, head, kloma, joints, stomach, plasma, fat, the nose, and the tongue are the seats of kapha.
Here too, specifically regarding the chest,
the body is stabilized— like a house by a tripod of pillars— by the three *doṣas* situated respectively below, in the middle, and above; therefore,
because they provide stability to the body, the *doṣas* are called "pillars."
They are called *dhātus* because they sustain [the body];
they are called *malas* because they cause impurity and consist of the impurities of food;
and they are called *doṣas* because their intrinsic nature is to corrupt.
Each of these is further divided fivefold;
for example, wind is divided by the distinctions of prāṇa, udāna, vyāna, samāna, and apāna.

Therein, *prāṇa* is situated in the head; it moves through the throat and chest, and its functions consist of supporting the sense organs, the heart, the mind, and the vessels, as well as spitting, sneezing, belching, exhaling, inhaling, and the intake of food.

*Udāna* is situated in the chest; it moves through the throat, nose, and navel, and its functions consist of the exertion for speech, vigor, strength, the clarity of the voice, nourishing the channels, and the awakening of intelligence, fortitude, memory, and the mind.

Vyāna is situated in the heart and moves throughout the entire body with extremely rapid speed. Its functions include movement, extension, contraction, raising, lowering, closing and opening the eyes, yawning, tasting food, purifying the channels, inducing perspiration, and the flow of blood; it also conveys semen to the female organ and, having separated the essence from the waste of food, gradually nourishes the bodily constituents (dhātus). Samāna is located near the internal fire (antaragni) and kindles it; it carries the humors, wastes, semen, menstrual blood, and water between the stomach and the colon. Moving through the channels, its functions—by supporting them—include the retention of food, digestion, separation [of nutrients], and the downward expulsion of waste.

Apāna, however, is situated in the apāna region; it governs the bladder, the pelvic region, the penis, the testicles, the groins, the thighs, and the hips, and its functions include the expulsion of feces, urine, semen, and the fetus (AS.Sū.20.3).
Pitta is divided into the categories of *pācaka*, *rañjaka*, *sādhaka*, *ālocaka*, and *bhrājaka* (AS.Sū.20.3).

In that context, when *pitta*—which resides between the stomach (*āmāśaya*) and the small intestine (*pakvāśaya*), and although composed of the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūta*), has its lunar qualities (*somaguṇa*) diminished due to the predominance of the fiery quality (*tejoguṇa*) and has consequently abandoned its liquid nature—is aided by auxiliary causes such as wind (*vāyu*) and moisture (*kleda*), it acquires the designation "fire" through functions such as burning and digestion. This *pitta* digests food, separates it into essence (*sāra*) and waste (*kiṭṭa*), and supports the other seats of *pitta* while remaining located there; this is called the "digestive" (*pācaka*) *pitta*. However, that which is situated in the stomach (*āmāśaya*) is called the "coloring" (*rañjaka*) *pitta* because it colors the nutrient fluid (*rasa*).
Residing in the heart, it is the accomplisher because it brings about the desired object through intelligence, memory, self-confidence, and energy;
residing in the eyes, it is the perceiver because it perceives forms;
residing in the skin, it is the illuminator because it gives luster to the skin.
It digests ointments, affusions, plasters, and so forth, and it reveals shadows and light. Kapha is characterized by its functions of supporting, moistening, awakening, satisfying, and binding.

Situated in the chest, by its own power and in conjunction with the power of the triad [of wind, bile, and phlegm], as well as that of the heart and the remaining seats of phlegm, it is called the "supporter" (*avalambaka*) because, while staying right there, it supports [the body] through its watery function.
Situated in the stomach (*āmāśaya*), it is the "moistener" (*kledaka*) because it moistens the mass of food;
situated in the tongue, it is the "awakener" (*bodhaka*) because it correctly awakens the perception of taste.

Located in the head, it is the *tarpaka* (nourisher) because it nourishes the sense organs such as the eyes; located in the joints, it is the *śleṣaka* (uniter) because it binds the bones together (AS.Sū.20.5).
Thus, in these locations, vāta, pitta, and śleṣman exist predominantly in their unmodified states, even though they pervade the entire body.
The cause of their increase will be explained in the section on etiology (Nidāna),
and the general characteristics of increase and decrease were already stated in the previous chapter.
For increase is twofold, distinguished by accumulation (*caya*) and provocation (*prakopa*).
Among these, qualities such as dryness (*rūkṣa*), when associated with the quality of heat (*uṣṇa-guṇa*), bring about the accumulation of Vāyu;

those associated with the quality of cold (*śīta-guṇa*) bring about its provocation; and qualities such as unctuousness (*snigdha*), when associated with the quality of heat, bring about its pacification (*praśama*).

Sharp qualities and others accompanied by the quality of cold cause the accumulation (*caya*) of *pitta*; those accompanied by the quality of heat cause its provocation (*kopa*); and dull qualities and others accompanied by the quality of cold cause its pacification (*praśama*). Similarly, unctuous qualities and others accompanied by the quality of cold cause the accumulation of *kapha*; those accompanied by the quality of heat cause its provocation; and likewise, dry qualities and others cause its pacification.
Accumulation (*caya*) means increase within its own seat, while aversion toward the causes of increase [indicates] provocation.

AS.Sū.20.6 Furthermore, there is a desire for contrary qualities, anger, and straying onto wrong paths. AS.Sū.20.7 There is the perception of one's own [physical] signs, a lack of well-being, and the onset of disease.
AS.Sū.20.7 Equilibrium when situated in its own place is the absence of morbid change; this is tranquility (*śama*).
AS.Sū.20.8 [This occurs] in the body—whether in its entirety, in half, or even in a single part—without being provoked by the wind (*anila*).
The *doṣa* produces a disorder, just as a rain-cloud produces rain in the sky.
Then, the *vāta* and other *doṣas*, having become aggravated, afflict the body with various kinds of disorders.
AS.Sū.20.9 However, the eighty transformations of wind are most clearly manifest, as follows:

Splitting of the nails, cracking of the feet, pain in the feet, drooping of the feet, numbness of the feet, vāta-khuḍatā (lameness), stiffness of the ankle, cramps in the calf muscles, sciatica (gṛdhrasī), splitting of the knee, dislocation of the knee, weakness of the thighs, stiffness of the thighs, lameness, prolapse of the rectum, pain in the rectum, upward jerking of the testicles, stiffness of the penis, distension of the groin, splitting of the spinal column, diarrhea, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), limping, kyphosis, dwarfism, stiffness of the sacrum (trika), stiffness of the back, crushing pain in the sides, constriction of the abdomen, fainting of the heart, palpitations of the heart, rubbing sensation in the chest, as well as obstruction in the chest, piercing pain in the chest, wasting of the arms, stiffness of the neck, stiffness of the nape (manyā), hoarseness of the voice, stiffness of the jaw, splitting of the palate and lips, splitting of the teeth, looseness of the teeth, muteness, obstruction of speech, delirium, astringent taste in the mouth, dryness of the mouth, loss of the sense of taste, loss of smell, earache, absence of hearing, hyperacusis, deafness, stiffness of the eyelids, contraction of the eyelids, darkness before the eyes (timira), pain in the eyes, displacement of the eyeball, displacement of the eyebrows, splitting of the temples, splitting of the forehead, headache, cracking of the scalp, facial paralysis (ardita), disease of a single limb, disease of all limbs, convulsions (ākṣepaka), rigidity like a staff (daṇḍaka), fatigue, vertigo, trembling, yawning, exhaustion, despondency, dryness, roughness, a dusky-red complexion, insomnia, and instability of the mind.

Furthermore, the disorders of *pitta* are: burning (*ūṣa*), scorching (*ploṣa*), forest-fire-like heat (*dava*), distress (*davathu*), internal burning (*vidāha*), internal burning sensation (*antardāha*), burning of the skin (*tvagdāha*), burning of the shoulders (*aṃsadāha*), a sensation of fuming (*dhūmaka*), sour eructation (*amlaka*), excessive heat (*ūṣmādhikya*), excessive perspiration (*atisveda*), body odor (*aṅgagandha*), exhaustion of the limbs (*avayavasadana*), putrefaction of the blood (*śoṇitakleda*), putrefaction of the flesh (*māṃsakleda*), cracking of the skin and flesh (*tvaṅmāṃsāvadaraṇa*), cracking of the skin (*carmadaraṇa*), red urticaria (*raktakoṭha*), red vesicles (*raktavisphoṭa*), red circular patches (*raktamaṇḍala*), hemorrhagic bile (*raktapitta*), greenish discoloration (*haritatva*), yellowish discoloration (*hāridratva*), bluish discoloration (*nīlikā*), axillary patches (*kakṣyā*), jaundice (*kāmalā*), a bitter taste in the mouth (*tiktāsyatā*), a blood-like odor in the mouth (*lohitagandhāsyatā*), fetid breath (*pūtimukhatva*), excessive thirst (*tṛṣṇādhikya*), lack of satiety (*atṛpti*), inflammation of the mouth (*āsyapāka*), inflammation of the throat (*galapāka*), inflammation of the eyes (*akṣipāka*), inflammation of the anus (*pāyupāka*), inflammation of the penis (*meḍhrapāka*), loss of vitality (*jīvādāna*), entering into darkness (*tamaḥpraveśa*), and greenish or yellowish discoloration of the eyes, urine, and feces.

The disorders of *śleṣman* (phlegm), however, are: satiety, drowsiness, excessive sleep, stiffness, heaviness of the limbs, lassitude, sweetness in the mouth, salivation, expectoration of phlegm, excess of waste products, *balāsa*, coating of the heart, coating of the throat, thickening of the vessels (*dhamanī*), goiter (*galagaṇḍa*), obesity, coldness of the digestive fire, urticaria (*udarda*), a whitish complexion, and whiteness of the eyes, urine, and feces.
In that case, there is a sharp, all-pervading heat throughout the body, a burning sensation,
and an aversion to sweating.
A localized burning devoid of sweat, like a flame of fire, is *ploṣa*;
a burning in the mouth, lips, and palate is *dava*;
and a burning in the sense organs such as the eyes is *davathu*.
Various types of burning sensations occur in the hands, feet, and shoulders;
a burning sensation in the digestive tract is internal heat (antardāha);
and a sensation of fuming in the head, neck, throat, and palate is called "fuming" (dhūmaka).
There is internal burning, heartburn, upward eructation, and sour belching; there is blackness and foul odor of the blood,
and moisture, blackness, and foul odor of the flesh.
The external combination of the skin is *carma-kotha*;
due to heaviness of the digestive tract (*koṣṭha*), there is a lack of desire for food, which is satiety (*tṛpti*).
Others, however, say that satiety is like a state of being sated toward food that one does not enjoy, which is anorexia (*arocaka*).
Tandrā is the non-perception of objects, like that of one afflicted by sleep;
however, others have read *staimitya* as *pramīlaka*. *Upalepa* is like a coating or smearing.
Its excessive accumulation is its overfilling;
it causes extreme dullness of the digestive fire, coldness, congestion in the chest, and urticaria.
Some experience shivering from the cold and urticaria;
others, however, say that it is especially due to contact with cold water during the winter season.
Itching accompanied by redness and swelling is udarda, which arises from kapha. AS.Sū.20.14: Major disorders, however, will be taught according to their respective [sections].
Furthermore, minor disorders (kṣudravikāra) receive their names based on the very limb they affect,
such as nail-lesions, temple-lesions, forehead-lesions, internal burning, throat-coating, heart-coating, and so forth.
For their essential nature has been taught in that very same way;

among all those [humors], even when not explicitly mentioned, and among other modifications which are innumerable, these alone are the self-characteristics of the defects (*doṣas*), pervading the entire body and never deviating from them.
Likewise, the actions and the preliminary signs therein, which are indicated in the *Āyuṣkāmayya* chapter (AS.Sū.20.16) as the marks of the self (*ātman*), are as follows:

the actions of Vāyu consist of falling, extension, obstruction, piercing pain, pricking, tearing, itching, thirst, movement, body ache, trembling, distress, convulsions, breaking pain, colic, emaciation, numbness, roughness, porosity, contraction, and throbbing; its taste is astringent, and its color is dusky-red.

The characteristics of *pitta* are burning, heat, suppuration, sweating, moisture, putrefaction, discharge, and redness; its tastes are pungent and sour; and its color is everything except white and reddish.
The characteristics of *śleṣman* are itching, stability, heaviness, coating, unctuousness, coldness, binding, and slowness; its tastes are sweet and salty; and its color is white.
Kapilabala, however, described their specific characteristics according to their tastes:
bile (pitta) is pungent, sour, and salty; phlegm (kapha) is sweet, sour, and salty.
Vāyu is observed through inference to be astringent, bitter, and pungent;
furthermore, Suśruta recites [as follows]:
Bile, when heated, attains acidity; phlegm attains salinity.
Thus, one should attentively and correctly observe these functions of wind and the other humors through scripture, direct perception, and inference.
Thereafter, taking into account the factors of place, time, dosage, and so forth, one should immediately begin treatment.
And there are verses on this: "Hereafter, the disorders will be described according to their divisions of increase and decrease.

Know that the three [humors] are distinct; their combination is threefold, and thus there are nine types therein. When all three increase equally, there are three; when one exceeds the others, there are six.
There are thirteen when all are combined; however, there are six by way of exceeding two, one, or one [by one];
one by way of being equal or greater; and six by way of the differentiation of degrees of excellence.
Thus, there are twenty-five [stages] according to the elders; likewise, there are that many [stages] for those who have diminished [faculties].
Through the increase, equality, and decrease of each one, there are six, and again another six.

Through the decrease of one and the increase of two, and also through their reverse, those sixty-two divisions are taught; [these], together with the sixty-three, are the causes for one's own welfare.

In states of disease, the simultaneous occurrence of increase, equilibrium, and decrease [of the humors] is difficult to comprehend; indeed, this group of six will be taught through its various transformations.
When pitta is situated in its natural state and vāyu increases due to the depletion of kapha,
it seizes [pitta] from its site and spreads through the limbs wherever it goes; at those places, piercing pain and burning sensation occur, shifting from one location to another.
In such cases, loss of strength and exhaustion may occur in the region of the limbs.
When pitta is diminished and vāyu becomes powerful, it displaces the kapha from its natural state (prakṛtistha).
Then one should draw out [the vāta]; [otherwise] there will be pain accompanied by coldness, stiffness, and heaviness.
When the vāta is in its natural state and the pitta is increased while the kapha is diminished— AS.Sū.20.27.
Then a burning sensation and pain arise for him,
when the naturally situated kapha has increased and the pitta remains while the vāyu is diminished.
Then one should suppress it; it produces lassitude, heaviness, and fever. When the wind is in its natural state and kapha has increased due to the depletion of pitta...
Then one should suppress it; it produces coldness, heaviness, and fever. When the pitta is in its natural state and the phlegm is increased while the wind is diminished— AS.Sū.20.30.
At that time, one should restrain [the breath]; otherwise, it may cause weak digestion,
stiffness of the head, sleepiness, lassitude, a coating sensation, heart disease, and heaviness of the limbs.
Spitting, yellowness of the nails and other parts,
and those disorders which have been described separately as resulting from the increase or decrease of the *doṣas*— [these occur in bile and phlegm].
But in the remaining cases as well, one should apply those very same principles as appropriate;
likewise, through their association with rasa, blood, and so forth, there arise the various distinctions of the decrease, equilibrium, and increase of these humors (doṣas).

One should understand that those who have attained [the realms] reach infinity through the application of degrees of intensity, according to their respective states; thus ends the twentieth chapter with a focused mind.
Now begins the twenty-first chapter. "We shall now expound the chapter on the treatment of the *doṣas*," so said Ātreya and the great sages.

The treatment for Vāta consists of oleation (sneha), sudation (sveda), mild, unctuous, warm, sweet, sour, and salty substances; purificatory measures (saṃśodhana); dietary regimens; and procedures such as massage (abhyaṅga), poultices (upanāhana), bandaging (upaveṣṭana), rubbing (unmardana), affusion (pariṣeka), immersion baths (avagāha), gentle pressing (saṃvāhana), squeezing (pīḍana), frightening (vitrāsana), blowing air (vidhmāpana), and diversion (vismaraṇa). It also includes the preparation of fermented liquors (surā) and spirits (āsava), various types of fats (sneha) enriched with digestive (dīpanīya), carminative (pācanīya), Vāta-alleviating (vātahara), and purgative (virecanīya) substances, as well as those processed a hundred or a thousand times (śatapāka/sahasrapāka). Furthermore, enemas (basti) for all purposes, specific rules for enema administration, especially oil-based ones, meat broth, unctuous enemas (anuvāsana), a pleasant lifestyle, avoidance of sexual intercourse, and the winter regimen (haimanta-vidhi).

For pitta, [the treatment consists of] drinking ghee, oleation with ghee, the downward elimination of morbid humors, the consumption of sweet, bitter, and astringent medicinal herbs and foods, the enjoyment of soft, fragrant, cool, and pleasing scents, and immersion in extremely cold and fragrant water.

Wearing upon his chest garlands fashioned from various colored flowers—such as jasmine, *mallikā*, and others—which are pleasing to the mind through their touch and fragrance, and which include pearls, gems, lapis lazuli, emeralds, conch shells, crystals, rubies, moonstones, and strings of shimmering, most beautiful jewels;

and sprinkling at every moment with cool, clear, fragrant waters scented with the finest sandalwood, *priyaṅgu*, *kāleyaka*, lotus stalks, and camphor, along with lotuses, water lilies, and blue lotuses, upon the ground, floors, doors, windows, and palace walls.

Listening to songs and instrumental music that are pleasant to the ear, soft, sweet, and agreeable to the mind; sitting together with friends who are unrestrained in their dress, conduct, and shared interests, and who delight in mutual glances during festivities;

and the compassionate embrace of beloved children, whose bud-like faces are made fragrant by the natural absence of falsehood, who do not speak too clearly, and whose utterances are sweet, tender, and free from artifice.

And there was an embrace with women who were utterly devoid of pity; who wore garments that were exceedingly thin, soft, and fragrant; whose ornaments consisted mostly of pearls resembling jasmine buds; whose speech was charmingly sweet, gentle, and affectionate, following them as they moved to the accompaniment of the tinkling of their girdles and anklets which echoed the cries of *kalahaṃsas* excited by the chatter of their female companions; whose waists trembled from the exertion of bearing the heavy burden of ornaments upon their own broad hips and breasts, and whose lotus-eyes were half-closed; who, though their fresh youth had slightly faded, were melting away the single garment through the excessive savoring of the pleasure of union with their lovers; who, displaying a mixture of modesty, embarrassment, boldness, dejection, joy, despair, wonder, smiles, anger, favor, and trepidation, had all their limbs moistened and liquefied by perspiration which washed away their cooling unguents; who, being the delighters of the entire body and heart, bore with their slender forms a force of Love (*Anaṅga*) that seemed to possess four divisions, like an army of the God of Desire.

The floors of the palace were like sandy beaches with waters cooled by the scattering of all the rays of the moon; there was a fountain-house where pure streams of water issued from mechanical devices shaped like swans, their surfaces spread over with exceedingly white sand.

It was a place where the surface of the water was covered with the thick shade of a multitude of various trees—tall, broad, and flowering—with many branches well-situated along the banks, their waters resembling the ocean; its entire vast sandy bed was pervaded by the pollen of white, red, and blue lotuses; one part of the ground was infused with the fragrance of the mud by the streams of water flowing from swinging leather bags, large skins, jars, and water-vessels held by groups of people; it was draped with clusters of sprouts and blossoms from hanging mangoes, rose-apples, kadambas, vidulas, and niculas; it was constantly sprinkled with droplets of water resembling pearls that fell after being expelled from the mouths of jars moved by human effort, mixed with ushira and sandalwood and failing to stick; it allowed the entry of cool breezes spreading unimpeded over a great distance; it utterly dispelled heat, burning, delusion, fatigue, exhaustion, and thirst through the constant showering of cool water spray; it possessed a beauty of the highest degree, rivaled the coolness of the Himalayas, and mocked the playful appearance of the rainy season.

The pleasure-pools are delightful with the sweet warbling of flocks of water-birds colored by the pollen of blooming lotuses, blue lilies, white lilies, fragrant lilies, red lilies, and hundred-petaled flowers; the groves have gentle breezes occupied with arranging beds from heaps of various flowers fallen from the spreading creepers shaken by swarms of bees alighting out of greed for honey-drinking;
furthermore, ghee, milk, purgatives, all mild substances, and avoidance of sleeping during the day constitute the regimen for the summer season.

Furthermore, for phlegm (śleṣman), the prescribed treatments are sharp purificatory measures; foods consisting mostly of dry substances seasoned with pungent, bitter, and astringent flavors; sharp wines that have stood for a long time and are pleasing to the heart; running, fasting, swimming, staying awake, wrestling matches, sexual intercourse, physical exercise, dry massages, bathing, and anointing.

In particular, honey, vegetable broth, emetics, and fasting at all times; the use of medicinal smoke and gargles; easy restraints; and the regimen appropriate for the spring season are intended solely for the purpose of alleviation.
And there are these verses on this subject: "The therapeutic treatment which has been proclaimed here with reference to each of the individual doṣas...
In cases of combined or aggregated disorders, one should differentiate them according to their respective natures:
the summer [season] is generally [indicated] for wind and bile, while the spring is for phlegm and wind.
The Maruta [season] is to be employed because of its capacity for mobilization; however, the Śarad [season] is used for Kapha and Pitta.
When Vāyu is provoked, the tastes—pungent, sour, and sweet—are to be applied in that order.
In a disorder of pitta, a sweet and astringent taste is beneficial at first;
thereafter, a pungent, bitter, and finally an astringent taste are beneficial in a disease of kapha.
The accumulation, provocation, and pacification of *vāyu* occur during the three seasons beginning with summer;
those of *pitta* during the seasons beginning with the rainy season; and those of *śleṣman* during the seasons beginning with winter.
The wind is accumulated by light and dry medicinal herbs;
being of such a nature, it does not become provoked in a body of similar nature due to the heat of the season.
Pitta undergoes accumulation and provocation through water and herbs that have an acid post-digestive transformation (vipāka), but not due to the coldness of the season.
Kapha is accumulated by water and herbs that are unctuous and cold;
even when the time and the body are similar [to those conditions for provocation], it does not become aggravated because it has become congealed.
Thus, this is the nature of time; however, due to the influence of food and other factors,
the *doṣas* undergo accumulation (*caya*) and so forth either immediately or even after a lapse of time, but not otherwise.
The provoked impurity suddenly pervades the body from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head, but it then subsides like a small stream of water.
One should conquer the accumulated humor (caya) while not provoking that which is already aggravated;
when all humors are provoked, one should conquer the strongest, provided it does not conflict with the remaining humors.
In all cases where their strength is equal, wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (kapha) follow this sequence;
for the natural strength of these humors, beginning with wind, is as previously stated.
Parāśara also spoke, citing this very same point as authoritative:
"Just as that which is initially obtained from the presentation [of the case] is the physician's conquest of the disease."
For it is observed that by the breaking of the leader, the defeat of the entire army occurs simultaneously.
Some authorities maintain that, first of all, the destruction of phlegm (śleṣman) should take place from its location.
AS.Sū.21.18 When [the poison] has smeared the head, the chest, and the throat, how can there be an appetite for food?
AS.Sū.21.19 In its absence, how could there be the consumption of food and drink?
And if there is no ingestion [of food], how can there be the suppression of the humors?
Therefore, at the outset, *kapha* must be destroyed, for it is the bolt on the door of the body.
Since pitta is considered to reside in the middle part [of the body] and acts swiftly,
one should therefore apply its suppression following that [pitta], for this [vāta] is the companion of pitta.
For this very reason, another sequence beginning with bile (pitta) and ending with phlegm (kapha) has been recorded by others;
however, Suśruta does not state this view in all cases.
One should conquer pitta, kapha, and vāta respectively in cases of fever and diarrhea.
Because fever generally consists of the nature of heat, the element of fire (tejas) predominates therein.
There is frequent evacuation of the bowels due to pitta, as well as a soft bowel habit; furthermore,
the secondary kapha in that condition causes heaviness, indigestion, and lethargy.
Furthermore, the wind (vāyu) necessarily increases during those days when fever and diarrhea subside; therefore,
this is the procedure for overcoming the [residual] humors (doṣas).
Others say that for those two as well,
[the causes] are phlegm, bile, and wind, respectively.
Because their origin is for the most part from the agitation of the stomach (āmāśaya),
they arise in that [stomach] through the first stage; even there, they increase gradually while remaining within their own substratum.
For the swiftness of action remains inherent in those who are corrupted within their own bases,
once they have recognized the excess of their respective humors through their own various actions according to their strength.
One should administer each specific medicine and apply it as a continuous treatment, rather than following a sequential order;
for such application may pacify one disease while provoking another.
That which is not pure is not truly pure; rather, that which pacifies without provoking anger is pure.
Both [anger and the pacifier] are impure stains, for one cannot conquer the enraged stain through a state of insignificance.
Because they consist of the *doṣas*, the *doṣas* do not neutralize one another even when present in equal proportions;
nor is there an equality of qualities such as cold, liquid, sour, salty, or pungent [among them].
And since their defects are seen to be mutual, they do not overcome one another;
for even when there is mutual opposition, each of the three qualities acts as an initiator [of its own effects].
In all cases, the three doshas are seen to be involved simultaneously in a disease. Vata associated with ama causes pain, flatulence, and a lack of movement.
Bile (pitta) is foul-smelling, blackish, pungent, thick, and heavy; phlegm (kapha) is turbid, fibrous, dense, adhesive, and slimy.
In the opposite case, however, it is ripe; likewise, bile is copper-colored or blackish-yellow and clear, while phlegm is clear or else thick and lumpy.
It is clear, frothy, white, and sweet in taste;
because of the weak strength of the digestive heat (ūṣman), the primary constituent (dhātu) is not properly cooked.
Some declare that the vitiated rasa located in the stomach (āmāśaya) is *āma*;
others [declare it] to be from the excessively vitiated *doṣas* themselves through their mutual intensification (*mūrcchana*).
Just as poison arises from *kodrava* grain, they say that [the disease] originates from raw meat;
by that raw meat, the *doṣas* and the *dūṣyas* are corrupted.
Those diseases and those arising from them are taught as being "sāma";
one should not eliminate the *doṣas* that are *sāma* and have spread throughout the entire body.
Those [defilements] that are latent within the elements, unagitated like juices from raw fruit,
would lead to the destruction of the body because they are difficult to extract.
Once they have been prepared with digestive, appetizing, oleating, and sudorific therapies,
one should purify them at the appropriate time using purification treatments, according to the proximity [of the disease] and the patient's strength.
A properly applied medicinal substance kills the impurities located in the stomach through the mouth;
those arising above the clavicle through the nose; and those from the receptacle of digested food (the colon) through the anus. (AS.Sū.21.42)
One should not hold back the aggravated humors (doṣas) by means of medicines when they are moving upward or downward on their own, for if they are thus suppressed, they cause harm.
One who eats wholesome food should not neglect the diseases that have arisen from previous humors— such as those described as the non-occurrence of illness, excessive corpulence, and so forth.
"One should eliminate obstructed [doshas] by digesting them with various digestive remedies.
This is the twenty-first chapter.
Now begins the twenty-second chapter.
"Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the classification of diseases," so said the great seers, Ātreya and the others.
Indeed, diseases are of seven types.
Those [afflictions] arise from being born together with the embryo, from the time of birth, from the power of [external] conditions, and from their own nature;
they are, however, each of two kinds therein.
Among them, those that are innate (sahaja) are derived from defects in the semen and the menses.
Diseases such as leprosy, hemorrhoids, and urinary disorders are born of the father;

those born of the mother include conditions arising from the fetus's distress within the womb, such as hunchback, clubfoot, lameness, and vitiligo; and those born of the essence of food or from the neglect of the mother’s cravings during pregnancy.
Those born of [past] births arise from one's own misconduct; those born of nourishment and those born of depletion;

those caused by pain such as wounds, fractures, blows, anger, grief, fear, and so forth; those physical and mental [diseases] born of time such as fevers caused by cold and other factors; and those born of corruption and those born of lack of protection.

Fever and other ailments produced by supernatural power (*prabhāva*)—such as those resulting from the transgression of a divine teacher or a curse—are of this type; those caused by *piśācas* and the like are also included.

Fever and other ailments arising from one's own nature (*svabhāva*), such as hunger, thirst, and fever, are likewise categorized here. These include both those produced by time (*kāla*) and those not produced by time (*akāla*); among these, those produced by time are those brought about by the *rakṣas* spirits.
Those born from lack of protection and those born out of season are,
in brief, further divided into two types:
those produced by present karma and those produced by past karma.

In that regard, concerning the arising of disease, there is present karma— that which, with reference to this very body, consists of the non-performance or performance of prescribed or prohibited acts taught by authoritative persons, whether seen or unseen; whereas that which belongs to a past life is called "fate" (*daiva*), as previously stated, distinguished by being either determinate or indeterminate.

Therefore, those diseases whose causes are visible arise from present actions; those that are contrary [to this] are born of fate (*daiva*); and those of both natures have small origins but cause great suffering. Among these, the subsiding of the former diseases occurs through the cultivation of their respective remedies.
AS.Sū.22.2 Even while there is the practice of opposing factors, [liberation occurs] for some through the exhaustion of undesirable karma,
and for others through the exhaustion of the karma of faults caused by fate.

Others, however, describe present action as being performed by another, and they call that the "instigation by another"; and they say this: if the accomplishment of an effect were to arise solely from action performed by oneself...

Why does even a wise person, out of regard for the pleasure and pain resulting from benefits or harms performed by others, undergo satisfaction or anger, or develop a mind intent on retaliation— merely because those acts were committed by another person?
Thus, these two kinds of diseases become threefold.
Furthermore, these defects are of seven kinds; moreover,
this entire collection of diseases, though remediable, requires the instruction prescribed by Āyurveda for their counteraction.

For even a disease that has a fixed cause, through the proper execution of a physician’s instructions, may—despite the non-exhaustion of the appropriated life-formations (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*)—attain a state of bearable sensation; yet, if left untreated, almost every such disease generally bursts forth unexpectedly on its own. Furthermore, even if it subsides spontaneously due to the slightness of its primary cause, it departs most rapidly for one who is not afflicted, provided there is the perception of treatment endowed with the sixteen qualities.
However, when fate yields uncertain results, disease finds no opportunity for one who is devoted to the practice of what is beneficial;
therefore, in no state whatsoever should a self-possessed person view the beneficial and the harmful as equal.
Furthermore, diseases are of three kinds, distinguished as mild, moderate, and severe.
Among these, those with few symptoms are mild, those with moderate symptoms are moderate, and those with complete symptoms are severe;
furthermore, they are of four types according to the distinctions of being easily curable and so forth, as previously taught.
Even when diseases are divided into many more categories, they do not deviate from the classification of being either endogenous (*nija*) or exogenous (*āgantu*).
Among those, the endogenous [diseases] arise from the humors (*doṣa*).
In these cases, first the wind (*vāta*) and the others fall into a state of imbalance, and subsequently the affliction is produced.
But those [diseases] born of external causes are adventitious; in them, pain first arises through the trauma, and thereafter the imbalance of the *doṣas* occurs.
It is precisely by means of this imbalance of the *doṣas* that the disease, in its many forms, is followed and increases.
And this being so, there is no persistence of disease apart from the *doṣas*; the only difference lies in the sequence of priority and posteriority.

Therefore, diseases, though uniform in their nature due to the commonality of "sickness," are innumerable in their divisions; each will be taught according to its own specific characteristics— whether gross or subtle— based on the distinctions of their origin, location, shape, color, name, pain, and power, as well as whether they are mature or immature.
Furthermore, because they are innumerable, one should classify the incurability of diseases by means of the very signs of the *doṣas*;
for the *doṣas* alone are the cause of all diseases.
Just as a bird, flying about in every direction throughout the day, never transcends its own shadow;
or just as the entire range of modified phenomena, established in their manifold forms, does not exist apart from the three qualities (guṇas);
even so, this entire range of modified phenomena does not transcend the three defects (doṣas).

Just as lightning, rain, and so forth occur in the sky but not necessarily due to a specific cause, and likewise waves, bubbles, and so forth occur in water, so too do diseases arise from the bodily humors (*doṣas*). Their causes are threefold: unwholesome contact between the senses and their objects, intellectual error (*prajñāparādha*), and the effects of time (*pariṇāma*). Each of these, moreover, is divided into three types based on the distinctions of excessive application (*atiyoga*), deficient application (*ayoga*), and improper application (*mithyāyoga*).

In that regard, excessive contact (atiyoga) consists of the eyes and other sense faculties coming into too much contact with their respective objects, such as forms; whereas lack of contact (ayoga) consists of having too little contact or no contact at all.
The perception of things that are subtle, extremely distant, extremely near, excessively brilliant, or intensely loud; the hearing of things that are disagreeable, distorted, and so forth;
and the smelling of things that are foul-smelling, impure, acrid, pungent, or repulsive.

The improper application [of regimen] (*mithyāyoga*) consists of the consumption of unwholesome tastes through specific dietary preparations based on their inherent nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth; likewise, it includes the inappropriate utilization of bathing and other such acts, as well as contact with cold or heat and other tactile objects, and contact with impure substances, injury, poison, wind, and so on. Furthermore, unwholesome action (*ahita-karman*)—whether of body, speech, or mind—is also [considered] intellectual error (*prajñāparādha*).

In that context, excessive engagement in physical and other actions is *atiyoga* (over-application); lack of engagement or very little engagement is *ayoga* (non-application). This includes [faults such as] the forceful arousal or suppression of vital energies (*vega*), irregular movements of the limbs, stumbling, scratching, striking, and the practice of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
Likewise, hunger, thirst, speaking while half-eaten, fear, sorrow, envy, and malice— these and the ten kinds of unwholesome actions constitute their respective false applications.
Transformation is called time;
that too is threefold according to the distinctions of cold, heat, and rain. Among these, time characterized by excessive brevity is over-action (atiyoga).
Deficiency of specific characteristics is *ayoga* (non-application), while its opposite is *mithyāyoga* (false application); these,
namely *atiyoga* and the others, are generally characterized by the absence of therapeutic suitability (*anupaśaya*).
Or rather, this failure to avoid them is entirely a transgression of wisdom (*prajñāparādha*).
Furthermore, objects, activities, and time—when properly engaged with—become causes of health for the most part due to their therapeutic effect (*upaśaya*).
Even among these, the sense objects, with the exception of taste, either afflict or favor the respective sense organs accordingly.

The remaining [topics], namely taste, action, and time, as well as the entire body and all states of being— without these, one cannot determine the presence or absence of all conditions, nor can one ascertain [the states of] proper application (*yoga*), excessive application (*atiyoga*), and so forth. (AS.Sū.22.8)

Furthermore, among all disorders, specific variations in their manifestation—whether they occur or do not occur—arise from the particularities of the etiological factors (*nidāna*), the *doṣas*, and the affected tissues (*dūṣya*).

For when these three [factors] do not mutually reinforce one another due to such particularities, or if they do so only slightly or weakly, then the diseases do not manifest; or if they do manifest, they are either mild or possess incomplete symptoms.

In the case of the opposite, however, the three paths of diseases are reversed: external, internal, and intermediate. Among these, the external consists of the bodily constituents such as blood and the skin.

Furthermore, that which is called the "branches" (śākhā) consists of external parts such as swellings, carbuncles, abscesses, alajī, apacī, skin tags, warts, tumors, fleshy growths, moles, and freckles; the middle part consists of swellings, hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, erysipelas, and abscesses; and the "roots" (mūla) consist of the vital points (marman) such as the head, heart, and bladder, as well as the bones and joints.

Attached therein are the tendons, vessels, ligaments, and so forth; and dependent upon them are hemiplegia, seizures, facial paralysis, consumption, pain in the bones and joints, prolapse of the rectum, and diseases of the head and other regions.

The internal [space]—synonyms for which are *mahāsrotas* (the great channel), the middle of the body, the great depression, and the *koṣṭha* (visceral cavity) based on the receptacles of the raw and cooked food (*āmāśaya* and *pakvāśaya*)—is the interior. Dependent upon it are fever, diarrhea, vomiting, indigestion, choleraic dysentery, dyspnea, cough, hiccups, flatulence, abdominal enlargement, splenic disorders, and other internal conditions; as well as erysipelas, swelling, hemorrhoids, abscesses, and tumors.
And those diseases are either independent or have other [diseases] as their retinue; they are designated respectively as primary (anubandhya) and secondary (anubandha).
Among them, the first are autonomous, with distinct forms and specific etiological factors and palliative measures.
The others, however, are the opposite of that; likewise, the defects there are also of two kinds, having other attendants, and the diseases are also twofold:
those that precede and those that follow.
Among these, the former are designated as premonitory symptoms (pūrvarūpa),
while the others are complications (upadrava); one should recognize them exactly as they will be described below.

When the primary [enemy] has been pacified, their pacification occurs; or, if they do not subside, one should subsequently attack them, or swiftly deal with a powerful adversary without contradicting the primary objective,
for that [secondary threat] becomes more painful due to the body being afflicted by disease, like a case of urinary disorder (prameha) accompanied by carbuncles.
Likewise, one primary disease becomes the cause of another primary disease;
for example, fever is the cause of internal hemorrhage (raktapitta), or internal hemorrhage is the cause of fever, and both are causes of dyspnea (śvāsa).
It [is the remedy] for splenic disorders, abdominal swelling,
hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, ascites, diarrhea, and malabsorption syndrome.
Coryza is the precursor of cough and fever; those two are the precursors of wasting,
and wasting is the precursor of consumption.

A single transgression is the cause of a single disease, and likewise many [transgressions] are the cause of many; similarly, a single symptom [indicates one], and in the same way, there is a single means for its pacification, yet that very same [means] may lead to the provocation of another.
Therefore, one should examine those [transgressions and symptoms] with care, by means of the scriptures and other methods.

In that regard, based on authoritative tradition (āgama), one should understand the disease as being thus, its provocation thus, its source thus, its location thus, its nature thus, its deity thus, its form, sound, smell, taste, and touch thus, its premonitory symptoms thus, its complications thus, its increase, stability, and decrease thus, its sequelae thus, and its name thus.
In this respect, there is the application of treatment; otherwise, there is its cessation.

Through direct observation with one's own senses, one should examine the patient according to their specific condition: the color, shape, proportions, and bulkiness; the complexion, feces, urine, and excessive vomiting; the rumbling in the intestines; the cracking of the fingers and other joints; the color and odor of the bodily excretions; and the touch of the body—whether it is numb, cold, hot, stiff, throbbing, smooth, or rough—as well as its natural or morbid state. Furthermore, one should ascertain the tastes in the mouth through questioning, as well as whether there has been easy or difficult vomiting, the softness or hardness of the digestive tract (koṣṭha), dreams, intentions, the onset of birth and disease, the stars [at birth], aversions, likes, and experiences of pleasure and pain.
Likewise, age is known through direct perception; moreover,
it is inferred by the crawling away of lice, while bodily distaste is indicated by the swarming of flies and bodily sweetness by their absence.

Likewise, one should examine the digestive fire by the power of digestion, strength by the capacity for exertion, and a disease with hidden signs by means of therapeutic suitability and unsuitability.

The measure of the doshas [is determined] by specific transgressions, the depletion of lifespan by fatal signs (riṣṭas), and the lack of cultivation regarding constitution, mental disposition, essence, suitability, and strength; and on this matter,
there is also this verse:
He who, like a yogin, does not enter the inner self of the patient with the lamp of knowledge and wisdom, does not truly treat that person's ailments.
AS.Sū.22.13 These two types of diseased persons do not manifest the true nature of their illness: namely,
one who has a severe illness [but does not appear so] due to the strength of their mental constitution (*sattva*) and physical body.
A light disease appears as such, while another [severe] disease appears otherwise;
the fool is deluded by these two based merely on external symptoms.
Therefore, if one administers medicine that is deficient in quantity or potency, or conversely,
contrary to what is wholesome, it robs the patients of their lives.
Knowledge does not operate upon the entirety of the object of knowledge through its constituent part alone; therefore,
a physician who desires to know should seek the truth through the thorough study of the treatise.
But one who is constantly diligent and reflects upon everything in every way,
that wise person never falters, even on a difficult path of action.
The adventitious disorder follows the innate one, and likewise the innate disorder, when greatly aggravated, follows the adventitious one.
Having correctly understood the secondary association (*anubandha*) and the primary nature (*prakṛti*) in that case, one should then commence the treatment.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter.
Now begins the twenty-third chapter.
23.1. Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the conduct regarding medicinal substances (*bheṣajāvacaraṇīya*).
"Thus indeed said the great sages, such as Ātreya and others,
when administering medicine: first of all, one should examine the patient in this manner."

In what region was this person born and raised, or in what region do humans have such a variety of food, such a variety of recreation, such strength, such a temperament, such a nature, such tastes, such diseases, such things that are beneficial and harmful, and by what specific cause has his *doṣa* been provoked? (AS.Sū.23.2)
For indeed, there are many causes for the provocation of even a single *doṣa*;
therefore, having understood it by its specific characteristics and actions, the physician should discern the *doṣa* in this manner,
as follows:
By what cause is the *vāyu* provoked? Is it by diet, or by conduct that is dry, light, cold, or violent; or by the suppression of natural urges, or by fear, or by grief?
Thereupon, the medicine applied as an antidote to that [provocation] quickly leads to success.
In this regard, the tastes—sweet, sour, and salty, as well as pungent, bitter, and astringent—are mutual opposites.
Immediately thereafter, one should investigate by means of the classification of mild, moderate, and excessive degrees: how was the causal factor (nidāna) indulged in?

For even from a single type of cause, there arises a distinction in the strength or weakness of a disease due to the specific variations in the proportional power of the individual humors (doṣas), whether they are combined separately or collectively, according to their division into mild and so forth.

In that regard, among diseases consisting of many defects and medicines possessing many tastes, one should determine the true nature of the power of diseases and medicines by observing individually the influence of each taste and defect;
however, this is not possible in all cases.

For it is not possible to ascertain the true nature of the power of a whole through inference from the power of its parts, when those parts are combined in an irregular transformation, are of diverse natures, mutually supported, impaired by other factors, and further differentiated by various permutations.
For when such a collection [of factors] is present, one should understand the true nature of the disease and the medicine by perceiving the power of that very collection; likewise,
one should determine which specific substratum this disease is occupying.
For a humor that has spread, occupying its own location and causing distress to the head and other parts, becomes difficult to overcome;
therefore, one must seek a specific remedy according to the specific location,
and thus one should reflect as follows:
To whom does this disease belong that is afflicted by it, or who is suitable for it, and of what quantity is it?

For the variation in the potency and dosage of medicine corresponds to the specific humor involved, taking into account the strength of both the disease and the patient; [otherwise], purificatory drugs that are excessively fiery or airy, or those that are excessively mild or administered in excessive doses, may lead to sudden and extreme force.

Likewise, if physicians administer caustic, fire, or surgical treatments to a patient of weak constitution or little strength who has been given excessive purgatives, they may suppress the disease with sedative measures; however, when the body is already exhausted by the disease, these [sedatives] quickly bring on other complications—
such as exhaustion, fainting, intoxication, delusion, and loss of strength— if they are stronger than the bodily strength.
There is an excess of digestive fire, as well as exhaustion and loss of appetite.

One who is excessively obese, excessively emaciated, weak, whose limbs and body parts have poorly formed flesh, blood, bone, and marrow, who has a low digestive fire, eats little, is nourished by unwholesome food, or is devoid of essential strength (sāra), is simply unable to withstand the force of a disease, let alone such a medicine of such intensity.
