Therefore, one should treat such a person with medicines that do not cause despondency, which are mild, pleasant, progressively more substantial, and free from complications— especially in the case of the weak.
Thus, children in particular— whose hearts are generally unstable, tender, and timid, and who are mostly delicate and dependent— are especially [vulnerable]; likewise,
when one is afflicted by a powerful disease, medicine that is weak or insufficient is ineffective, as it merely agitates the humors further and exacerbates the illness.
One should also examine even a suitable medicine in this way:

"This [medicine] has such a taste, potency, post-digestive effect, quality, substance, and action; it has such a specific power; it was born in this region, gathered in this season, collected in this manner, stored in this manner, prescribed in this manner, prohibited in this manner, processed in this manner, compounded with this, and administered in this dose; for a person of such a type, at such a time, it eliminates or pacifies this much of a disorder."

Furthermore, there was another such medicine which, when administered with that specific measure or distinction, produced this effect; for indeed, the subtle variations in the humors, the medicines, the affected tissues, place, time, strength, digestive fire, food, taste, suitability, mental constitution, physical nature, and age—
when these are not carefully considered— can destroy the patient.
When examined, however, these [symptoms] would confound even a physician of vast intelligence,
let alone one of small intellect;
therefore, one should constantly refine one's judgment through the repeated study of the meaning of the scriptures and practical application.
Moreover,

there are diseases for which treatment has been specified in the treatises through general rules and exceptions; in such cases, only a wise person can correctly determine the final course of action by weighing the relative gravity or lightness of the humors and other factors.
Time also bestows suitability upon the medicine;
it has been described in two ways— by the divisions of *kṣaṇa*, *lava*, *muhūrta*, and so forth, and by the state of the patient— as was previously stated.
Time is threefold, characterized by cold, heat, and rain.
Among these, the periods between heat and cold, and between rain and cold, are designated as the common seasons of spring (*vasanta*) and the end of autumn (*atyāyu*).
However, the commencement of the rainy season during the summer and monsoon periods is specifically conceptualized as the "rainy season" (*prāvṛṭ*).
During those common days, the administration of emetics and other therapies proceeds; on other days, it is withheld for fear of under-dosage or over-dosage.
For these common days are free from complications because they are pleasant due to moderate cold, heat, and rain, being thus suitable for the body and the medicines;
the others, however, are the opposite.
For instance, during the cold season, because the body is afflicted by excessive cold, it becomes extremely constricted by cold winds and characterized by excessively rigid and heavy humors (*doṣa*).

Consequently, even a medicinal substance intended for purification that possesses a hot nature becomes weak in its potency due to being overwhelmed by the cold, and thus results in improper administration (*ayoga*).
The body is also subject to disorders dominated by *vāta* during the rains;

likewise, when the sky is overspread on all sides by an exceedingly thick and dense downpour, and the rays of the sun are obstructed by a mist of spray, the earth becomes a mass of mud from the flooding of water-layers, and the body—being excessively moistened, its digestive fire weakened, and its strength diminished due to the difficulty of procuring food—becomes afflicted.

Furthermore, when a cluster of medicinal plants has its root-network, core, and branches inundated by a mass of water brought down by the falling torrents released from the belly of a rain-cloud, and its trunk and branches are covered with a profusion of tender young shoots, it becomes as if it had returned to a state of infancy and possesses little potency.

Furthermore, because it is not properly prepared, the earth becomes impure; and when water—sour in its digestion and defiled by contact with the carcasses, bodily fluids, urine, and excrement of birds, wild animals, reptiles, and the like—is combined with the heat of the rain-clouds and mingled with a cool breeze charged with sprays of cool water, it causes an excessive burning sensation in this [patient] who is tender and whose [digestive fire] is not yet matured.

Consequently, having become unwholesome, it certainly leads to a lack of efficacy, for even medicine collected at the outset fails when the earth is afflicted by winds following the waters of the clouds.

Furthermore, in the summer, because it has been depleted by repeated depletion, the body becomes parched by hot, dry winds and sunlight; it is excessively perspiring, extremely flaccid, and its humors (doṣas) are greatly diminished.
Meanwhile, even though the medicine is not inherently hot, it acquires heat and sharpness from the falling rays of the sun and thus leads to excessive administration (atiyoga).
Furthermore, the body is susceptible to the afflictions of thirst, giddiness, and exhaustion;
therefore, one should administer emesis and other therapies only during those intermediate periods that are common to all seasons, unless the disease is urgent.

In the case of an urgent disease, however, one should carefully apply the medicine itself, having prepared it by superimposing artificial qualities that are contrary to the seasonal qualities, through various combinations, processing methods, and dosages.
In the various conditions of the patient, however, the parts [of time] are designated as "time" (kāla).
For example, in this particular condition, this medicine is either timely or untimely.
For medicine that has not reached its proper time or has passed its proper time does not become effective;
however, its administration is of eleven kinds, as follows:
Without food, before food, between meals, after food, with food, during food, in a bolus, repeatedly, with morsels, between morsels, and at night— among these,
"without food" means the medicine is taken as a pure substance alone, which possesses extreme potency due to being administered without any solid food.

One who is strong should consume [the medicine] in the morning when the channels of the stomach (āmāśaya) are free from the excess of phlegm; however, for others, it is beneficial to take it before a meal or with food, as this avoids excessive exhaustion. "Prāgbhakta" means that which is taken immediately after a meal.

AS.Sū.23.14 That [emetic] should be administered for the purpose of strengthening the lower part of the body when it is afflicted by disorders of the *apāna* wind, for the pacification of diseases located therein, and for the purpose of causing emaciation. AS.Sū.23.15 "Mid-meal" means in the middle of the meal; that [purgative] is used when there is a disorder of the *samāna* wind.
In diseases located in the visceral cavities and in those of the Pitta type,
[the medicine] should be taken after food (adhobhakta), that is, immediately following a meal.

In the case of a disorder of the *vyāna*, it ends with breakfast; in the case of a disorder of the *udāna*, it ends again with dinner. This is for the purpose of strengthening the upper body, for the pacification of diseases located therein, for the alleviation of disorders characterized by *śleṣman* (phlegm), and for the purpose of causing bulkiness.
That which is prepared with food at the same time as the meal,
or mixed in afterwards, is suitable for children, those who are delicate, those who dislike medicinal drugs, those suffering from loss of appetite, and for diseases affecting the entire body.
Regarding *antarābhakta*: when medicine is administered at midday after the morning meal has been digested,
and once that medicine has been digested, a meal is taken again in the afternoon.
By this, the night [treatment] is explained;

it is for one whose digestive fire is inflamed, in cases of diseases arising from the *vyāna* wind, and for that which is taken both at the beginning and at the end of a meal. (AS.Sū.23.19) *Sāmudga* [is so called because it is applied] like a pair of cymbals.

AS.Sū.23.19 That [treatment], however, consisting of light food in small quantities, digestive remedies, electuaries, powders, and so forth, is indicated in cases of hiccups, tremors, convulsions, and when the *doṣas* are located in the upper or lower parts of the body.
AS.Sū.23.20 Furthermore, it is administered repeatedly, whether after eating or on an empty stomach.
AS.Sū.23.20 In cases of dyspnea, cough, hiccups, thirst, vomiting, and disorders caused by poison;
AS.Sū.23.21 That which is taken with a morsel, being mixed with a morsel of food.
That which is the interval between morsels—the space between each pair of morsels—both of these [periods] involve a modification of the vital breath (*prāṇānila*);
therefore, one should employ substances that stimulate the digestive fire (*agnidīpana*), aphrodisiacs (*vājīkaraṇa*), and powders, electuaries, boluses, and so forth, together with the food morsels.

In cases of heart disease, one should administer emetics between meals; in diseases above the clavicles, one should employ fumigation at night. Regarding the first [of these], one who is thirsty, has drunk cold water, suffers from indigestion, is hungry, or is emaciated should avoid taking medicine.
In the remaining cases, [the causes] are that which is unwholesome to the heart, unwholesome to one's constitution, excessively sharp, hot, of pungent odor, and in excessive quantity.
And on this matter, there is a verse:
The physician should first examine the disease, and immediately thereafter the medicine; then, following that, he should perform the treatment preceded by knowledge.
Even when a disease has subsided, it may recur due to even a slight cause,
for the bodily channels have been prepared by the humors (doṣas), like a residual subtle fire.
Therefore, one should pursue that through practice that is never-failing,
thereby bringing about the firmness of even those previously accomplished yogas.
If wholesome food becomes loathsome due to constant consumption or its inherent nature,
one should once again render it palatable through various methods of preparation.
Through the mind's conformity with its objects, there arises satisfaction, vigor, relish, strength,
and the enjoyment of happiness; furthermore, from this, disease is completely destroyed.

That appetite which arises from greed, the depletion of the bodily constituents (*doṣa*), or an imbalance of disease— the one who knows the application of wholesome treatments should, through appropriate methods, modify the diet in those cases.
In the cold, hot, and rainy seasons— corresponding respectively to the months of Caitra, Śrāvaṇa, and Kārtika—
one should quickly eliminate phlegm, wind, and bile through their respective treatments.
Or one may remove the impurities during these months— those of the rainy season, autumn, and spring— according to the prescribed rule, at intervals of three months, when they are common to all.
Having provided appropriate remedies for cold, heat, and rain,
one should administer the treatment that is indicated and not let the proper time for action pass by.
AS.Sū.23.32: If the desired quality is not obtained within seven days, one should employ another [treatment] after the previous one has ceased its activity;
when the force of the former has subsided, a confusion of treatments is not beneficial.

Even when the quality is slight, one should indeed employ that very [remedy] in order to attain excellence and preeminence; for a king, a pure physician should prescribe a medicine that is pleasing to the heart, administered in small doses, and with minimal side effects.
Having repeatedly employed this pure tradition, which possesses many virtues, one who is free from other tasks, attentive, and likewise approved by those ministers—
One should cause it to be tasted by attendants and administer it oneself.
Whatever region is suitable for a particular person, medicine produced from that region is beneficial for him.
Even when dwelling in another land, there arises in him a birth of qualities equal to those [of his former teacher]; it is cultivated with vigor, correctly, repeatedly, naturally, and easily.
Medicine endowed with the proper taste, smell, and other qualities, taken at the right time, in the proper dose, after digestion,
and with a concentrated mind, acts like nectar;
thus ends the twenty-third chapter.
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter. Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "The Two-fold Approach to Treatment."
Thus indeed said the great seers, Ātreya and the others:
"Since the object of treatment is twofold, treatment itself is considered to be of two kinds.
In that context, nourishing (*santarpaṇa*) is the first and depleting (*apatarpaṇa*) is the second;
"nourishing" (*bṛṃhaṇa*) and "lightening" (*laṅghana*) are cited as their synonyms (AS.Sū.24.3). That which leads to bulkiness is nourishing, and that which leads to lightness is lightening.
For you, the bodily [humors] are for the most part composed of earth and water, and so too are the others; therefore,
there is the action of oleation, drying, sudation, and astringency.
AS.Sū.24.4 Furthermore, because of the twofold nature of living beings, [treatment] does not exceed two types.
AS.Sū.24.5 These are purification (śodhana) and pacification (śamana); therein, lightening therapy (laṅghana) is also included.
If one should expel the external humors, that is the fivefold purification (śodhana):
purgation (nirūha), emesis (vamana), oleation of the body and head (kāya- and śiro-reka), and bloodletting (asravi-sruti).
That which does not purify the humors, nor excites those that are balanced,
but equalizes those that are discordant— that is pacification (śamana), and it is of seven kinds.
Digestion-stimulating, appetite-inducing, hunger, thirst, physical exercise, sunlight, and wind are [therapies]; however,
nourishing therapy and pacification are for vāyu, pitta, and anila.
One should nourish those emaciated by disease, medicine, wine, women, or grief;
as well as those exhausted by carrying loads or travel, those wasted by chest wounds, those who are parched, weak, or dominated by vāta.

In the summer, one should also provide nourishment for pregnant women, those who have recently given birth, children, and the elderly with meat, milk, sugar, ghee, sweet substances, and unctuous enemas.

Those suffering from urinary disorders, intoxication, excessive unctuousness, fever, thigh-stiffness (ūrustambha), or leprosy (kuṣṭha) [should avoid] sleep, comfortable beds, oil massage, bathing, relaxation, and exhilaration.
Those suffering from erysipelas, abscesses, splenic disorders, diseases of the head, throat, or eyes,
as well as those who are corpulent, should always undergo fasting; in the winter season, others may do so as well.

In that regard, one should treat with purification therapies those patients who suffer from obesity, excessive strength, or a predominance of pitta and kapha, as well as those afflicted by disorders of undigested matter (āmadoṣa), fever, vomiting, diarrhea, heart disease, constipation, heaviness, eructation, nausea, and so forth. (AS.Sū.24.12)

For those suffering from moderate obesity and similar conditions, one should generally first employ digestive and appetizing treatments; likewise for those afflicted by low obesity, weakness, and so forth, using these very same methods.

Those who are afflicted by the defects of hunger, thirst, and suppression [of natural urges], even if they are of moderate strength, are weakened; how much more so those men of little strength who are further afflicted by wind, heat, and exhaustion?
One should not administer nourishing therapy to those who require lightening therapy; however, one should apply lightening therapy mildly to those who require nourishing therapy,
or treat them with skillful means according to the strength of the patient, the place, the time, and other factors.
When there is *bṛṃhaṇa* (nourishing therapy), there shall be strength, nourishment, the destruction of diseases treatable by it,
clarity of the sense organs, the expulsion of impurities, lightness, and relish for food.
One who fasts experiences the simultaneous onset of hunger and thirst, a pure heart, belching, a clear throat,
mildness of disease, enthusiasm, and the disappearance of drowsiness.
When food and other necessities are consumed without due regard [to proper measure],
they cause excessive corpulence, extreme emaciation, and so forth; these, along with their medicinal treatments, will now be explained.
And form (rūpa) is to be known by those very [senses], yet it transcends them due to its extreme magnitude;
in that regard, with reference to purification, coarseness and other qualities have been previously illustrated.

The nutrient fluid (*rasa*) produced from food, when mixed with phlegm (*śleṣman*) accumulated by the guru and other elders, remains in an undigested state (*āma*) and, loosening the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), leads to corpulence (*staulya*).
From excessive corpulence arise excessive hunger and thirst, perspiration, labored breathing, drowsiness,
intolerance of exertion, dullness, short life, and sluggishness of strength and speed.

From excessive nourishment of the fat (medas), foul odor and stammering occur; moreover, when the channels are obstructed by fat, the wind (vāyu) becomes particularly aggravated in the abdominal cavity (koṣṭha).
While moving about, it kindles the fire; hunger and thirst exist there even more intensely than that.
When they increase, the fire and wind burn that [body], which is thick like a hollow tree trunk.
Excessive perspiration occurs due to the presence of sweat-carrying vessels at its root, the liquefaction of fat, and its association with phlegm (śleṣman),
when the rasa has been digested within the digestive tract (koṣṭha) and its channels are obstructed. (AS.Sū.24.23)
AS.Sū.24.23 Because it does not find its functional outlet everywhere, the *praya* (chyle) accumulates.
AS.Sū.24.24 Its remnant is of little flavor; due to its smallness, it is not sufficient for the nourishment of the blood and other tissues.
Even when the accumulation of wind and the other elements is equal, that which was previously accumulated accumulates even more;
thus, by means of that unequal [accumulation], it brings about [the predominance] of the bodily constituents (dhātus).
AS.Sū.24.25 [It cures] dyspnea and other such ailments, as well as fever, abdominal diseases, fistula-in-ano, urinary disorders,
stiffness of the thighs, pustules, abscesses, and similar maladies.

One who has excessive accumulation [of fat], lacks enthusiasm, and has unstable buttocks, belly, and breasts is known as excessively obese (*atisthūla*); in such a case, food that subdues *vāta* should be administered.
Kulattha, yavaka, and barley remove phlegm and fat; likewise,
jūrṇa, śyāmāka, mudga, and others [are beneficial], as are ariṣṭa and honey-water when drunk.
Whey and buttermilk are sharp, hot, dry, and liquefying medicinal substances;
one should employ them along with mental exertion, sexual intercourse, physical exercise, purification therapies, and staying awake at night.
Depending on the state of the body, one should likewise perform dry bathing, rubbing with unguents, and so forth.
One should lick a paste of *triphalā* with honey, as well as *guḍūcī*, *abhayā*, and *ghana*.
The application of *rasāñjana*, the great *pañcamūla*, *guggulu*, and *śilāhvaya* is beneficial, as is the juice of *agnimantha*. (AS.Sū.24.30)
Viḍaṅga, ginger, alkali, iron filings, honey,
and the powder of barley and āmalaka constitute a formulation that overcomes the defect of excessive corpulence.
Madana, triphalā, mustā, saptāhva, ariṣṭa, vatsaka, along with pāṭhā and āragvadha— when drunk, this [decoction] conquers diseases characterized by excessive corpulence.
Similarly, vatsaka, śamyāka, devadāru, the two types of niśā,
mustā, pāṭhā, khadira, triphalā, nimba, and gokṣura— AS.Sū.24.33.

One should also employ madana and other such substances as a paste for bathing and similar purposes; [the ingredients include] asafoetida, gomedaka, the three pungents (vyoṣa), kuṣṭha, krauñca-bone, and gokṣura.
Elavāluka, vacā, khara, aśvagaṇḍā, and bhedaka,
drunk with buttermilk, whey, or the juice of kola (AS.Sū.24.35).
It cures dysuria, worms, urinary disorders, and obesity.
[This is prepared] with anti-worm drugs, the three myrobalans (triphalā), oil, roasted flour (saktu), the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), and dīpyaka. (AS.Sū.24.36)
A stirred drink (mantha) soaked in iron-water is recommended for those suffering from wasting diseases (bṛṃhaṇa).
[The herbs used are: vyoṣa, kaṭvī, varā, śigru, viḍaṅga, ativiṣā, and sthirā.
Asafoetida, black salt, cumin, yavānī, coriander, and chitraka;
the two types of niśā, the two types of bṛhatī, hapuṣā, pāṭhā, and the root of kembuka.
The powder of these [drugs], mixed with honey, ghee, and oil in equal parts,
and combined with sixteen times its weight of roasted grain flour (saktu), when drunk, destroys that [disease].
It cures all diseases such as excessive corpulence and others of that kind,
as well as heart disease, jaundice, vitiligo, asthma, cough, and throat obstructions;
it promotes intelligence, intellect, and memory, and stimulates a sluggish digestive fire.
Likewise, sudation and bloodletting should be applied according to the specific disease.
[The symptoms include] excessive emaciation, vertigo, cough, excessive thirst, and loss of appetite.
There is a depletion of oils, digestive fire, sleep, vision, hearing, semen, vitality, hunger, and voice;
as well as pain in the bladder, heart, head, calves, thighs, sacrum, and flanks, along with fever.
Excessive fasting gives rise to incoherent speech, upward movement of wind, exhaustion, vomiting, splitting pain in the joints and bones,
and the retention of feces and urine.

Due to excessive emaciation, one cannot endure exertion, rain, cold, heat, thirst, or hunger; because of this diminished strength, one cannot withstand satiety, disease, or the administration of medicine.
Dyspnea, cough, consumption, splenic disorders, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, and weak digestive fire— these,
as well as diseases of blood-bile and wind, generally afflict those who are emaciated.

Emaciation is indeed better than obesity, for there is no medicine for the obese; neither nourishing therapy nor fasting is sufficient to conquer excessive fat, impaired digestion, and wind disorders.
Emaciation is destroyed by things that are sweet, unctuous, and satiating, as well as by comfort;
while corpulence is destroyed by the excessive indulgence in things that are the complete opposite of those.

One whose buttocks, abdomen, and neck are withered, whose joints are thick, and who is covered with visible veins is said to be excessively emaciated; for such a person, the previously mentioned nourishing regimen (*bṛṃhaṇa*) should be applied.
Medicinal plants such as *aśvagandhā* and *vidārī*, which are aphrodisiacs, are beneficial; likewise,
through freedom from anxiety, exhilaration, and constant nourishment [the vital essence is increased].
And due to the habit of sleeping, one who is emaciated thrives like a boar;
this should also be prescribed for the remaining diseases arising from excessive fasting.
That which is effective at the time [of administration], and that which, through practice, leads to nourishment;
for one who has suddenly wasted away is immediately replenished by nourishing therapy.
When [the affliction] has been gradually diminished over a long period through that practice,
one should apply nourishing therapy there, having observed the body's dimensions, digestive fire, strength, and other factors.
Indeed, there is nothing else that increases the bulk of the body as much as meat;
for the meat of a meat-eater is especially so, because it is composed of meat. Therefore, one should consume the light meat-juices of carnivorous animals, seasoned with salt.
Likewise, one should provide meat soups prepared with dried meat (veśavāra) or wild game (jāṅgala), both seasoned and unseasoned, as well as milk and other nourishing drinks that provide satiation.
One should administer [this] to those who are emaciated, those suffering from fever, those with cough, those with dysuria,
those who are thirsty, those with upward-moving wind (udāvarta), and those with obstructed flatus and feces.
With equal parts of black sesame oil, dark sesame oil, honey, and other such substances, one should prepare a satiation-drink (*tarpaṇa*);
likewise, a churned drink (*mantha*) may be prepared by combining sugar, honey, wine, and parched grain flour (*saktu*).
Treacle, roasted grain flour, ghee, whey,
and sour gruel constitute a nourishing drink (tarpaṇa) that cures dysuria and is supreme for alleviating upward movement of wind (udāvarta).
A churned drink (mantha) made with dates, grapes, vṛkṣāmla, amlīkā, pomegranate,
parūṣaka, and āmalaka immediately overcomes diseases such as thirst.
Sweet and sour, prepared with water, and either unctuous or dry,
*mantha* provides immediate nourishment and bestows stability, complexion, and strength.
For one who is obese, heavy and non-satiating food is beneficial; for one who is emaciated, the opposite is beneficial.
For both, preparations of barley and wheat are appropriate and wholesome when administered correctly.
Fatness and emaciation may occur even by nature; in those cases as well, this same procedure should be applied,
constantly according to the state of the disease, and after due differentiation.

He who employs lightening and nourishing therapies according to the proper measure and other factors will have balanced bodily constituents and digestive fire, and his physical frame will be well-proportioned.

And because of the firmness of his sensory faculties, he is not overcome by the pairs of opposites (dvandva). The [doshas] exceed [their normal state] according to their movement, through the distinctions of being grasping, piercing, and so forth.
The twenty-fourth chapter: "Upakramas are not distinct from the [two] types [of treatment], even as diseases are distinct from each other.
Now begins the twenty-fifth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the procedure for oleation therapy (sneha-vidhi).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
For the purpose of employing unctuous substances and the like, and for alleviating their complications,
one should collect the necessary medicinal materials in advance.

Medicinal substances that are heavy, cold, slow, unctuous, mild, subtle, soft, and liquid generally promote oleation (snehana), while those with opposite qualities generally promote drying (virūkṣaṇa).
Among unctuous substances, ghee, marrow, fat, and oil are considered the best;
among these, ghee is the most excellent because it conforms to the requirements of processing.
Because they are sweet, non-irritating, and because one practices them from birth onwards,
they subdue pitta in the order mentioned first; the others [subdue it] in the reverse order.
Oil is heavier than ghee; muscle fat is heavier than oil, and marrow is even heavier than that.
A *yamaka* (combination of two) is heavy with three [substances], and a *trivṛt* (combination of three) is great with four.
Those with a desire for unctuous substances, curd, milk, meat, bones, fruits, or wood;
those fit for sudation or purification; and those addicted to wine, women, physical exercise, or excessive anxiety.

The elderly, children, those who are pale, emaciated, or rough, those with diminished blood and semen, those afflicted by Vāta, those suffering from ophthalmia (timira), and those with severe insomnia; AS.Sū.25.8 AS.Sū.25.8

Those who should be given unctuous therapy (snehya) are as follows; however, those with extremely weak digestion, sharp digestion, obesity, or weakness, as well as those suffering from stiffness of the thighs (ūrustambha), diarrhea, acute diseases of the throat, poisoning, abdominal enlargement (udara), fainting (mūrchā), vomiting (chardi), anorexia (aruci), phlegm disorders (śleṣma), thirst, and intoxication (madya), should not be treated with it. *Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha*, Sūtrasthāna 25.9.
AS.Sū.25.9 When [the patient] has been delivered and when nasal medication, enema, or purgation have been administered;
AS.Sū.25.10 in those cases, ghee is recommended for those desiring intelligence, memory, intellect, and digestive fire.
Oil [is indicated] for those suffering from diseases of knots, channels, worms, phlegm, fat, and wind,
as well as for individuals who desire lightness and firmness and possess a hard bowel.
In those whose bodily constituents (*dhātu*) are depleted by wind, heat, travel, carrying loads, women, or physical exercise;
and in those who are susceptible to dryness, affliction, excessive digestive fire (*atimagni*), or those traveling on paths obstructed by wind.
The remaining two [fats] are used for pain in the joints, bones, vital points (*marmans*), and the abdominal cavity;
likewise for pain in the vagina, ears, and head caused by burns, injuries, or displacement.

One should use oil during the rainy season and ghee at the end of the rains; however, during the month of Mādhava, one should use all other fats. Furthermore, one may employ any unctuous substance for anyone when the sun is bright and clear.
During the fertile period (ṛtu), when the doshas are balanced, [one should avoid intercourse] if vāta and kapha are predominant; during the day, if vāta and kapha are predominant;
at night, if pitta is predominant; and likewise in cases of combined doshas (saṃsarga) where pitta is the dominant factor.
If the patient is in a hurry, one should administer oil during the day even in the cold season,
and ghee at night even in the heat; however, this may be done otherwise after considering the humors (*doṣa*) and other factors.
One may suffer from diseases caused by *vāta* and *kapha* at night, and by *pitta* during the day;
therefore, one should administer unctuous substances (*sneha*) appropriately through food such as edibles, or via enemas (*basti*).

Through nasal administration, massage, gargling, and the saturation of the head, ears, and eyes— with variations in taste, by way of single or combined applications— there are sixty-four modes of consideration.

Because the oil is overcome by other substances and because it is small in quantity, they are prescribed in sequence; and due to the absence of the aforementioned causes, there is no deliberation regarding the drinking of clear [oil].
That is the best method for oleation (sneha-kalpa), because it quickly accomplishes the action of oleation. Those [substances] are digested in two, four, and eight watches (yāma) respectively.
There are short, medium, and superior measures; among these,
one should determine the shortest measure after considering the humors and other factors, but it should indeed be the shortest from the very beginning.
For if it is administered into an unknown stomach, it may cause great danger to life; therefore,
it should be used by those who are weak, have a sluggish digestive fire, are children, the elderly, or those who prioritize comfort.
For those suffering from indigestion, an empty stomach, fever, diarrhea,
or cough, thin gruel (peyā) is beneficial; for it is easy to digest and can be continued during the period of convalescence.
After a long time, it becomes strengthening and does not cause harm even when it has gone bad; [this is] for those afflicted by urinary disorders, swellings, pustules, leprosy, and vāta-śoṇita.
For those with moderate constitutions and mild digestive fire, this [enema] is easily unctuous;
it does not deplete strength, causes only slight displacement [of doshas], and is sufficient for purification.
For those who endure the afflictions of great thirst, hunger, and the heat of digestion, and for those tormented by abdominal tumors, upward-moving wind, erysipelas, or bites,
as well as for the insane and those with difficult urination— that [treatment] is indeed great and acts very quickly. (AS.Sū.25.25)
One should conquer diseases by following all the prescribed paths when properly administered. Indeed,
when the previous meal has been digested, a large quantity of unctuous substances should be given for the sake of purification.
A pacifying (śamana) diet is recommended when one suffers from hunger and thirst, provided it is without food and taken in a moderate amount.
A nourishing (bṛṃhaṇa) diet, consisting of meat broth, wine, and similar substances, is beneficial even in small quantities when accompanied by food.

In children, the elderly, those suffering from thirst, those who consume fats, excrement, or wine; in women, those constantly using unctuous substances, those with weak digestion, those accustomed to comfort, and those who fear hardship.
For those with a soft digestive tract, few bodily humors, during hot weather, and for those who are emaciated,
one should take unctuous substances before a meal; this bestows strength upon the thighs, calves, and waist.
AS.Sū.25.29 The downward movement of the bodily urges, health, and the non-depletion of diseases from the lower body;
AS.Sū.25.30 In the middle [part of the body], the largeness, strength of the digestive fire (*agni*), stability, and the alleviation of pain in the abdomen.
For stability of the sense organs, [one should use] ghee prepared with the drugs of the ūrdhvajatrūgada group; for vāta, ghee with salt is desired, while for pitta, it is desired plain.
The physician should administer [medicines] combined with alkali and the three pungents (trikaṭuka) for one with excessive phlegm;
one should drink hot, clear water after the oily substance (sneha) for its easy digestion.
For the purification of the coating in the mouth, one should use *tuvara* and *āruṣkara*; however,
there should be no application of heat during the administration of unctuous substances (*sneha*), for what is unctuous is indeed antagonized by hot things.
Then, wearing heavy upper garments and lying in a windless place, he should await the end of old age, drinking only small amounts of warm water when thirsty.

One should recognize that the medicine is being digested by the presence of headache, giddiness, spitting, fainting, exhaustion, restlessness, and fatigue; once it is digested, one knows it by the subsiding of those symptoms and a sense of lightness.

AS.Sū.25.35: When there is doubt as to whether food has been digested or not, one should drink warm water again, [judging] by the downward wind, well-being, hunger, thirst, belching, and purification.
Through that, may there be purity of digestion, as well as lightness and a relish for food;
one who intends to eat food in moderation tomorrow, or has drunk, or is drinking [liquids], [should practice this].
One should consume liquids that are warm, non-obstructive to the channels, not excessively unctuous, and free from admixture;
one should use warm water for all purposes, observe celibacy, and sleep at night.

Excessive physical exertion, suppression of natural urges, grief, rain, cold, and heat; exposure to strong winds, riding in vehicles, walking long distances, excessive talking, and remaining in improper postures— these [are causes of disease].
One should avoid those days on which one sleeps with a low or very high pillow, or during the hours of sleep, or when there is smoke or dust; one should likewise avoid other such days as well.
In all procedures, this is generally the sequence when diseases have been diminished; however,
in the case of pacification through oleation, the regimen should be like that for one who has undergone purgation.
Before the drinking of the unctuous substance, mild medicine should be administered;
it stimulates the digestive fire and brings about lightness of the gastrointestinal tract.
One should drink [the unctuous substance] for three days if the digestive tract is soft, and for seven days if it is hard. (AS.Sū.25.41)
When properly lubricated, it becomes thoroughly accustomed to the non-emission [of semen]; for once it has become so accustomed, it does not cause the arousal of impurities.
Or, by excessive application, one may overcome diseases just as water flows out from a reservoir when its dam is breached,
washing away the earth.
In the same way, even oil, having suppressed the digestive fire, flows through and emaciates the body.
When the fire is kindled, there is downward movement of the wind (vāta), and the feces are unctuous and non-hardened.

Softness and smoothness of the limbs, absence of exhaustion, lack of craving for unctuous substances, and lightness [of the body]— these are the signs when [the body] is properly oleated; in the case of dryness, the opposite occurs, as well as turbidity of the sense organs.
Anemia, loss of digestive fire, discharge from the nose, mouth, and anus,
burning in the anus, loss of appetite, vomiting, fainting, thirst, and dysentery.
Acid eructation, dizziness, dyspnea, and cough result from the excessive consumption of unctuous substances,
or from food and lifestyle habits that are unwholesome due to improper quantity, untimely intake, or incorrect application.
Unctuous substances (sneha) cause swelling, hemorrhoids, drowsiness, sleepiness, loss of consciousness,
itching, skin diseases, fever, nausea, colic, abdominal distension, and loss of strength. (AS.Sū.25.47)

[One should avoid] weakness of the stomach and sense organs, dullness, yawning, stiffness, and speech impediments arising from one's own [excessive] doshas, as well as diseases such as anemia (pāṇḍu) resulting from excessive application [of physical exertion].
Hunger, thirst, physical exertion, sweating, and dry food, drink, and medicines; buttermilk, *ariṣṭa*, *khala*, *uddāla*, barley, *śyāmāka*, and *kodrava*;
long pepper, the three myrobalans, honey, *pathyā*, cow’s urine, and *guggulu*.

AS.Sū.25.49 The treatment for complications arising from oleation (sneha) should be applied according to the specific disease and its own requirements. AS.Sū.25.50 Regarding the signs of insufficient or excessive dryness (virūkṣaṇa), they are the same as those for insufficient or excessive fasting (laṅghana).
When the digestive fire of one with a pitta constitution is further intensified by unctuous substances, it quickly digests that unctuousness and, circulating again toward the *ojas*, [causes harm].
A severe thirst accompanied by complications may arise and afflict him;
he would lose his life if he did not quickly drink cool water.
Or one afflicted by that thirst, burning with the fire of unctuousness like a serpent by its own venom, should resort to cold sprinklings or immersion baths.
If there is indigestion but the patient is strong, one should apply cold plasters to the head and face; if the vomiting does not cease, one should induce emesis by drinking cold water again.
After eating dry food when kapha and vāta are likewise provoked, one should scrape the tongue; furthermore, if the doṣas are balanced, one should completely expel the oil with warm water.
Then, one should resort to the previously mentioned procedure according to the strength of the *doṣas* and other factors;
however, ghee alone should not be drunk in cases of *pitta*, especially when it is associated with *āma*.
For one should follow the entire body, destroy its consciousness, and cause its death;
one should practice sudation while consuming the juices of unctuous, liquid, warm, and desert-originated foods.
Having remained lubricated for three days, one should perform purgation and then emesis again;
after another day, having agitated the phlegm by means of those [emetic] agents, one should proceed.
By means of sesame, mung beans, curd, milk, jaggery, fish broth, and so forth,
they become fleshy, corpulent, possessed of abundant phlegm, and have irregular digestive fires.
Those who are accustomed to oleation and require it should first be treated with drying therapies;
once they have been oleated, they should then be purified. In this way, complications arising from improper oleation do not occur.
It is sufficient to remove impurities; furthermore, unwholesome affection has become prevalent among children, the elderly, and others who are unable to endure the avoidance of oily substances.
One should employ these non-stimulating, immediately unctuous applications:
decoctions of abundant meat, and the broths (rasas) of wild and marshy animals. (AS.Sū.25.61)
Or, when those [grains] have been fried in oil, one should prepare a gruel that is not too thick,
along with sesame powder mixed with fat, molasses, and likewise *kṛsarā*.

One should drink lukewarm *peyā* (gruel) prepared with sesame and wool-cloth (*tilakāmbalika*), containing abundant fat and clarified butter, either in a vessel mixed with sugar and ghee, or as a dish made with milk (*kṣaireyī*).
Or fresh milk mixed with ghee and salt,
as well as gruel (*peyā*) consisting of five *prasṛta* measures of rice and five [measures] of fats.
One who has digested [the meal] should eat milk-rice mixed with black gram and abundant fat, along with oil, ginger, and molasses juice, followed by meat broth;
or one may take a single type of unctuous substance (sneha) with sour wine, or curd with molasses and sugar.
Boar fat, ghee, long pepper, salt, and sesame seeds;
AS.Sū.25.66: Long pepper, salt, the four unctuous substances, curd-whey, and buttermilk.
Ghee prepared with curd, containing the three pungents (vyoṣa), and cooked in the juice of *dhātrī* and grapes;
[as well as] water, alkali, milk, wine, and curd from *yava*, *kola*, and *kulattha*.

Ghee prepared with equal parts [of the aforementioned drugs] is an excellent immediate unctuous agent (sadyaḥsnehana). Furthermore, four types of unctuous substances (snehas) should be prepared with the decoctions of jujube (badara) and triphalā.

One should employ immediate unctuous therapies (sadyaḥsneha) that remove disorders of the female reproductive tract and seminal impurities; unctuous substances mixed with salt cause a person to become unctuous very quickly.
For that [unctuous substance] is indeed liquefying, non-dry, subtle, hot, and pervasive.
[It is increased by] jaggery, meat from marshy regions, milk, sesame, mung beans, wine, and curd.
In cases of skin diseases (kuṣṭha), swellings (śopha), and urinary disorders (prameha), one should not administer [medicines] for the purpose of oleation (sneha),
except for those prepared with triphalā, pippalī, pathyā, guggulu, and similar substances.

AS.Sū.25.71 One should administer these unadulterated fats according to their respective [dosages]. AS.Sū.25.72 However, for those whose digestive fires have been diminished by diseases, one should employ those capable of kindling the fire of the body.

A man who consumes fats is declared to have a kindled internal fire, a purified digestive tract, fresh bodily tissues, and to be endowed with strength and complexion; he possesses firm sense organs, is slow to age, and lives for a hundred years.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter.
Now begins the twenty-sixth chapter.
26.1: Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "The Procedure for Fomentation" (Svedavidhi).
"Thus indeed said the great seers, Ātreya and others:
there are four types of thermal sudation (agni-sveda), distinguished by heating, poultices, liquids, and steam."
AS.Sū.26.2 Therein, *tāpasveda* (steam-sudation) should be administered by means of the palms of the hands, bronze bowls, sand, cloth, small jars, and so forth, as well as direct application of fire.

AS.Sū.26.3 *Upanāhasveda* (poultice-sudation), however, consists of powders of all types of fragrant substances, grains, mustard seeds, *kiṇva* (ferment), *vacā*, *devadāru*, *rāsnā*, roots of *eraṇḍa*, *madhuka*, *śatāhvā*, the dregs of liquor (*surākiṭṭa*), and other wind-alleviating (*vātahara*) materials; as well as fragments of barley and wheat, and *veśavāra* (minced meat) prepared from the blood, bile, heads, feet, and flesh of animals from marshy regions (*ānūpa*).
Likewise, when the wind is associated with phlegm, [it should be treated] with *surasā* and other such [herbs], and when associated with bile, with *padmaka* and other such [herbs].

The limb should be repeatedly plastered with these substances—either individually or combined—with milk, fermented gruel (*śukta*), fermented rice-water (*dhānyāmla*), salt, and whey, mixed with plenty of fat and made pleasantly warm; this preparation is known as *sālvaṇa*. It should be bound with skins that are thick, heat-inducing, non-putrid, and soft-haired, or in their absence, with leaves that dispel wind, or with woolen or silk cloths. To avoid burning, it should be released at night while remaining on the hand during the day, or bound both day and night as required.
Alternatively, according to the strength of the doshas, the time,
and the patient's own strength, sudation with liquids is of two kinds.
Regarding sprinkling (*pariṣeka*) and immersion (*avagāha*):

there, one should fill water-jars, rain-pits, or conduits with decoctions made from *śigru*, *varaṇa*, *āmrātaka*, roots of *mūlaka*, mustard, *surasa*, *arjaka*, *vāsā*, bamboo, *aśmantaka*, *aśoka*, *śirīṣa*, *arka*, *karañja*, castor-oil plant, *mālatī* leaves, *pūtīka*, the "ten roots" (*daśamūla*), and other wind-alleviating (*vātahara*) substances, along with whey, water, wine, milk, vinegar, and so forth, as previously mentioned; these may be used individually or combined according to the specific dosha. Then, having anointed the patient with oil prepared with wind-alleviating drugs—or leaving him unanointed—one should sprinkle him while he is seated on a mat or lying down, either on a single limb or the whole body, covered with a cloth.
One should immerse [the patient] in a large cauldron, vessel, or trough filled with those very waters;
furthermore, steam-sudation (ūṣmasveda) is divided into eight types.
The bolus (piṇḍa), the bed (saṃstara), the tube (nāḍī), the solid stone (ghanāśman), the pot (kumbhī), the pit (kūpa), the hut (kuṭī), and the jentāka bath are the types of fomentation.

Among these, one should take lumps of clay, potsherds, stones, clods of earth, or iron balls heated to the color of fire and immerse them in water or sour gruel. With these, wrapped in a moist cloth, one should apply sudation to a limb that is predominantly composed of phlegm and fat, or to one that is painful or knotted.
Alternatively, one may use dust, sand, cow dung, horse dung, chaff of grain, husks, or raw meat paste, boiled with sour liquids and wrapped as before, to apply sudation.

In cases of wind diseases (*vātaroga*), *piṇḍasveda* (bolus fomentation) is performed using moist cow-dung and similar substances formed into balls, or with poultices (*upanāha-dravya*), poultice-masses (*utkārikā*), *kṛsara* (rice and pulse porridge), or meat-balls; this same [method] is called *saṃkara-sveda* (mixed fomentation).

*Saṃstara-sveda* (bed fomentation) is as follows: having properly heated the appropriate fomentation materials in a furnace with its mouth covered, one should spread out a bed of straw (*kiliñja*) in a windless shelter for the patient to lie upon. Then, having covered it with a woolen blanket, silk cloth, or any other wind-warding leaf as an upper cover, and further concealed by a cloak of human skin (*raurava-ajina*) and so forth, one should apply the fomentation.
Having warmed it as before, one places another [pot] over the mouth of the *ukhā*.

Having joined and sealed a side-opening of the size of the opening at the base of a tube, one should apply steam to the patient—who is seated comfortably with his limbs well-anointed and covered—using a tube made from either *śaroṣikā*, bamboo, *kiliñjaka*, or *karañja* leaves; shaped like an elephant’s trunk, two or three *vyāmas* long, with a circumference at its base and tip equal to one-fourth or one-eighth of its own length, its openings covered on all sides by leaves that ward off the wind, and bent twice or thrice.
For steam, moving in a curved path and having its fierce velocity checked, causes sweating comfortably without burning the skin; this is *nāḍīsveda* (tube-fomentation).

AS.Sū.26.8 Having heated a solid, level stone slab or a patch of ground to the height of a man or more with a fire lit by wood that dispels wind, and having removed the fire and sprinkled it with warm water, sour gruel, and so forth, one should foment [the patient] upon a bed covered as prescribed; this is *ghānāśmasveda* (fomentation with a stone slab).
AS.Sū.26.8
AS.Sū.26.9 As before, having boiled the sudorific substances in a pot, one should sit close by and inhale the steam in that manner.

Alternatively, having dug that [pot] into the ground and placed above it a seat or a bed covered with a moderately thick coverlet, with rugs (*kutha*), blankets (*kambala*), and woolen cloths (*goṇikā*) hanging down all around, one should inhale the steam while staying there; meanwhile, iron balls and stones heated to the color of fire should be slowly immersed in the pot—this is *kumbhīsveda* (pot-sudation).

AS.Sū.26.10: One should cause [the patient] to sweat while situated on a well-spread bed inside a pit dug twice as deep as the width of the bed, which has been filled with either wind-dispelling wood or dried cow dung, set on fire until the smoke has vanished; this is *kūpasveda* (pit-sudation).

Having constructed a hut that is neither too high nor too wide, circular, without gaps, and whose walls are thickly plastered with a paste of *upanāha* (poultice) materials, and having surrounded it on all sides with a cluster of *hasantikās* (fire-pits) filled with glowing *khadira* charcoal from which the smoke has been removed, one should cause [the patient] to sweat while situated on a bed in its center; this is *kuṭīsveda* (hut-sudation).
Now,
one desiring to construct a steam-bath house (jentāka) should first examine the ground.
In the eastern or northern direction, in a virtuous region with an excellent portion of ground,
on soil that is either black or golden-colored, on the bank of any one of the water reservoirs such as a moat or a lotus pond;
To the south or west, at a good bathing place (sutīrtha) on a level and well-proportioned plot of ground,
one should have a gabled pavilion (kūṭāgāra) constructed facing east or north, directed toward the bathing place, having receded seven or eight ratnis from the water;
its height and width shall not exceed sixteen ratnis.
It should be well-rounded on all sides, finished with plaster work, and provided with many windows.

Inside this gabled chamber (kūṭāgāra), one should have a circular base (piṇḍikā) constructed against the walls on all sides, equal in width and height to the wall-jewels, extending from the door-frame to the door-leaf.

And in the center of this gabled chamber, one should have a charcoal-receptacle pillar made of clay, shaped like a ball, measuring two men's heights and one cubit in width, provided with many minute holes and fitted with a lid.

Having filled it with wood of *khadira* or *aśvakarṇa*, one should set it ablaze. When he knows that the wood is well-burnt, smokeless, and entirely heated by the fire, and that the fire-chamber is endowed with the heat suitable for sudation,
then he should have the patient— whose body has been anointed with wind-alleviating unguents and covered with a cloth— enter therein.
He should instruct him thus: "My dear friend, enter for the sake of prosperity and health;
having entered, ascend this platform and lie down comfortably on either side as you please.
Even if you are overcome by haste, sweat, or fainting, this platform must not be abandoned until your final breath."
For if you were to fall from this pedestal and fail to reach the door, you might lose your life immediately due to being overcome by perspiration and fainting;
therefore, you must not let go of this pedestal under any circumstances.

You should know that you have reached the state when you perceive yourself to be free from congestion, with the thick secretions of sweat properly discharged, all channels unobstructed, and the body light, devoid of obstruction, stiffness, numbness, pain, and heaviness.

Then, you should enter the door following the lead of the *piṇḍikā*. Having emerged, even if you are excessively perspiring, you should not suddenly enter cold water for the sake of protecting your eyes.

Rather, once you have been properly sweated and are free from feverish distress and fatigue, you should eat after being sprinkled with pleasantly warm water according to the proper rule; this is the *jentāka* (sauna) method of sudation.
For those [patients], one should specifically apply heat, fomentation, and sudation in cases of kapha,
and poultices in cases of vāta.
When one [of the humors] is slightly mixed with bile, it becomes liquid (AS.Sū.26.14).

Furthermore, when vāyu is enveloped by medas and kapha, it is non-fire-like (anāgneya); [this state arises] through staying in a windless dwelling, wearing heavy garments, drinking excessive alcohol, physical exercise, hunger, exposure to heat, wrestling, walking on a journey, carrying heavy loads, indignation, and fear (AS.Sū.26.14).
And for an internal abscess (upanāha) associated with pitta, it should be performed without fire according to the very procedure previously mentioned; and on this point there is this [verse]:
"In a windless place, having applied unctuous substances internally and externally, and after the food has been digested, one should apply sudation."
AS.Sū.26.15 [The strength of a person] is middling, inferior, or superior depending on the influence of disease, the country, and the season.
AS.Sū.26.16 One afflicted by *kapha* requires drying therapy; one who is already dry requires both drying and oleation therapies for *kapha* and *vāta*.
When the vāyu is located in the stomach (āmāśaya) and the kapha is situated in the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya),
[treatment] should first be dry (rūkṣa) or first involve oleation (sneha), according to the respective location.
There is little [pain] in the groins, very little in the eyes, ears, and heart, or none at all.
Having covered the eyes with lotuses, water-lilies, and the like, or with a ball of roasted flour (saktu), [one should proceed].
With cool vessels containing pearl necklaces and lotuses— *padma*, *kumuda*, and *utpala*— and repeatedly with hands moistened by water, one should touch the sweating heart.
When the cold and the pain have subsided, once the patient has been fomented and softness has arisen in the limbs,
he should be gently massaged, bathed, and thereafter follow the regimen for oleation therapy.
From the provocation of bile and blood arise thirst, fainting, weakness of voice and limbs, vertigo,
pain in the joints, fever, and the appearance of dark-red circular patches.
From excessive sudation, vomiting occurs; in that case, a stabilizing medicine is indicated.
This also applies to those suffering from poison, alkali, fire-injury, diarrhea, vomiting, or urinary disorders.
Sudation is heavy, sharp, and hot; generally, the opposite [of these qualities] is astringent.
Medicines are also characterized by being liquid, stable, mobile, unctuous, dry, or subtle.
Sudation, astringency, smoothness, dryness, subtlety, mobility, and fluidity;
in brief, [these qualities] generally belong to the bitter, astringent, and sweet tastes.
When strength has been regained through the destruction of the aforementioned diseases, the patient may become paralyzed (stammita),
characterized by stiffness of the skin and tendons, contraction, tremors, and impairment of the heart, speech, and limbs.
One should diagnose excessive stiffness by the dark discoloration of the feet, lips, skin, and hands;
one should not apply sudation to those who are excessively obese, dry, weak, or fainting.
Those who require sedation, those suffering from wounds, emaciation, or exhaustion, those afflicted by the disorders of alcohol,
and those with cataracts, abdominal diseases, erysipelas, leprosy, consumption, or obesity; (AS.Sū.26.26)
Those who have undergone purgation with yellow milk, curd, fat, or honey;
those suffering from prolapsed or burnt rectums; and those afflicted by exhaustion, anger, grief, or fear. (AS.Sū.26.27)

One should administer mild [therapies] to those suffering from hunger, thirst, consumption, anemia, urinary disorders, and afflictions of bile; likewise to pregnant women, those with uterine bleeding, those who have recently given birth, and those with acute (vātyayika) diseases.
In cases of dyspnea, cough, catarrh, hiccups, flatulence, constipation, hoarseness, diseases of wind (vāta), hemiplegia, facial paralysis,
body aches, and stiffness of the waist, sides, back, abdomen, and jaw; [these are the indications for the use of oil].

In cases of enlargement of the scrotum, inguinal hernia, intestinal obstruction, and vātakaṇṭaka; in dysuria, tumors, glandular swellings, seminal disorders, and conditions characterized by excessive wind (vāta).
Trembling, swelling, numbness, stiffness, yawning, heaviness of the limbs,
and pain in the ears, neck, head, abdomen, calves, feet, and thighs [are the symptoms].

One should apply sudation appropriately according to the specific classification of the medicinal substances. Once fomented, one should eat wholesome food in accordance with the nature of the *doṣas* and the disease.
On that day, one whose entire body has been subjected to sudation should especially avoid physical exercise.
[One should observe] the radiance of the digestive fire, softness of the skin, clarity of the complexion, a desire for food, and the purity of the bodily channels.

Sudation (sveda) removes dullness and drowsiness, and it quickly restores movement to stiffened joints. Whether they are located in the digestive tract (koṣṭha), the tissues (dhātu), the channels (srotas), or situated in the limbs and bones, [the doshas] become moistened by oleation (sneha).
The humors (doṣas), having been liquefied by sudation and brought to the gastrointestinal tract (koṣṭha), are properly expelled through purificatory procedures (śuddhi).
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter.
Now begins the twenty-seventh chapter.
27.1. Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "The Procedure for Emetics and Purgatives."
Thus said the great sages, beginning with Ātreya:

"That which removes the *doṣas* from the upper part is called emesis (*vamana*); that from the lower part is called purgation (*virecana*); or both are termed 'purgation' (*virecana*) because they purge the impurities. (AS.Sū.27.2)

In this regard, medicinal substances that are hot (*uṣṇa*), sharp (*tīkṣṇa*), subtle (*sūkṣma*), pervasive (*vyavāyin*), and dispersing (*vikāṣin*) reach the heart by their own potency; then, due to their subtlety and pervasiveness, they follow the channels (*dhamanī*). When the interior of the body has been softened by their unctuousness (*sneha*), they cause the entire mass of morbid humors (*doṣasaṅghāta*) to liquefy through the heat of perspiration—just as moist wood is split—by means of the sweat-heat from both the gross and subtle channels.
Furthermore, by virtue of their heat, sharpness, and dispersing nature, they break apart [the humors].

That mass of morbid humors (doṣasaṅghāta), having been dissolved and broken up, becomes mobile like a handful of water in an oiled vessel; not adhering due to its state of flowing upward, it reaches the stomach (āmāśaya) and, impelled by the upward-moving breath (udāna), moves upward because the medicine consists of the nature of fire and air and possesses the power of the upper part.
Because the medicine consists of the nature of water and earth and possesses the power of the lower part, it moves downward.
And because it consists of the qualities of both and possesses the power of both parts, it moves in both directions.

In that regard, when phlegm (śleṣman) is predominant, or when it is associated with bile (pitta), or when bile is located in its own site, or when wind (anila) is associated with a predominance of phlegm, one should administer emesis (vamana). However, when bile is associated with phlegm, or when phlegm is located in its own site, one should administer purgation (vireka).

AS.Sū.27.5 Among these, those treatable by emesis include: those who have ingested poison, those bitten by venomous creatures, those pierced by poisoned arrows, those suffering from incompatible food, indigestion, acute fever, consumption (rājayakṣman), diarrhea, severe internal hemorrhage (raktapitta), choleraic syndrome (viṣūcikā), intestinal torpor (alasaka), indigestion (avipāka), anorexia, wasting (apacī), tumors (granthi), swellings (arbuda), elephantiasis (ślīpada), diseases of fat, chronic poisoning (gara), insanity (unmāda), epilepsy (apasmāra), dyspnea, cough, nausea, erysipelas (visarpa), urinary disorders (prameha), leprosy (kuṣṭha), anemia (pāṇḍu), diseases of the eyelids, mouth, nose, or skull, ear obstruction, edema, defects of breast milk, and especially the Kapha-related diseases mentioned in the chapter on the classification of humors (doṣabheda).
AS.Sū.27.5
For these indeed reach destruction through vomiting, just as unripened rice and other grains perish when the water is drained away.

AS.Sū.27.6: The following persons are not to be treated [with purgatives]: pregnant women; those who are delicate; those preoccupied with other tasks; those who have consumed dry food in excess; those with excessively stimulated digestive fire; those exhausted by the labor of carrying heavy loads or traveling long distances; those constantly fatigued; those suffering from chest wounds or wasting diseases; those who are very obese, emaciated, old, or young; those who are weak; those afflicted by fatigue, fear, grief, anger, intoxication, fainting, hunger, thirst, or fasting; those engaged in sexual intercourse, physical exercise, Vedic study, or anxious reflection; those suffering from vomiting; those with upward-moving hemorrhage (ūrdhvaraktapitta), wind disorders, or those who have undergone non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana) or unctuous enemas (anuvāsana); those with a constricted bowel, difficult vomiting, heart disease, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), urinary obstruction, abdominal tumors (gulma), splenic enlargement, abdominal dropsy, prostate enlargement (aṣṭhīlā), hemorrhoids, loss of voice, cataracts, vertigo, or wind disorders; those suffering from facial paralysis (ardita), convulsions (ākṣepaka), eye pain, or pain in the head, temples, ears, or sides; and those whose bowels have not been prepared for a non-unctuous enema or who suffer from intestinal worms.
Except in cases of food that is incompatible with one's constitution or habituated intake, because of their rapid action,
in those instances for a pregnant woman there may be miscarriage, loss of the fetus, or the onset of severe diseases.
In a delicate person, due to the agitation of the heart, there may be an upward or downward discharge of blood;
in one distracted by other tasks, the medicine does not take effect,
or if it takes effect with difficulty, it may produce the defects of improper administration.
In one who is dry, there is a seizing of the limbs by Vāyu;

in one whose body has been depleted by Vāyu due to a diet consisting mostly of dry food, there is a loss of strength. Likewise, for those with an excessively kindled digestive fire, or for those exhausted by the constant labor of carrying loads, traveling on roads, and riding vehicles, there occurs an excessive discharge of blood due to further injury from exertion.

In those with diminished digestive fire (*kṣīṇāgni*) and others, due to the body's inability to withstand the strength of the medicine, there occurs obstruction of bodily strength and the danger of internal injury.
Furthermore, in cases of persistent vomiting or upward-moving *raktapitta*, the *udāna* wind may toss up the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and cause excessive discharge of blood.
In those who have undergone non-retentive enemas (*āsthāpana*) or oil enemas (*anuvāsana*) while suffering from upward-moving wind (*ūrdhvavāta*), there is an excessive upward movement of the wind.

In one whose bowels are constricted or who has vomited poorly, excessive purging causes the humors (doṣas) within the abdominal cavity to become agitated, resulting in erysipelas, stiffness, numbness, and confusion, or even death; in those suffering from heart disease, it causes cardiac obstruction;
and in those afflicted by upward-moving wind (udāvarta) and the like, or by facial paralysis (ardita) and the like, it leads respectively to the aggravation of their ailments or to death.

In one whose abdomen is infested with worms, if the enema is administered first, there may be excessive vomiting because the worms, having not been expelled previously from below, are too numerous and, failing to exit completely, pull excessively upon the heart. Furthermore, in this context, all the treatments to be described— beginning with those for pregnant women and ending with those involving medicinal smoke— should generally be avoided.

However, one who suffers from indigestion (*ajīrṇin*) should avoid all [therapies] except for emesis (*vamana*), out of fear of the complications of *āma* and out of fear that the *doṣas* of acute fever (*navajvara*) might become stagnant (AS.Sū.27.8).

Now, those conditions curable by purgation (*virecana*) include chronic fever (*jīrṇajvara*), upward-moving hemorrhage (*ūrdhvaraktapitta*), abdominal tumors (*gulma*), abscesses (*vidradhi*), splenic disorders (*plīha*), hemorrhoids (*arśas*), fistula-in-ano (*bhagaṃdara*), abdominal enlargement (*udara*), intestinal worms (*kṛmi*), scabies (*koṣṭhaka*), urinary retention (*mūtrāghāta*), seminal disorders of the female genital tract (*reto-yonidoṣa*), gout (*vātaśoṇita*), chlorosis (*halīmaka*), freckles (*vyaṅga*), partial blindness (*timira*), cataracts (*kāca*), ophthalmia (*abhiṣyanda*), inflammation of the eye (*akṣipāka*), burns from alkali or fire, leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), ulcers (*vraṇa*), colic in the head or the large intestine (*śiraḥ-pakvāśaya-śūla*), upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*), constipation (*vibandha*), vomiting (*chardi*), eruptive boils (*visphoṭa*), and so forth; as well as the diseases caused by *viṣūcikā* mentioned among those to be vomited upon, and the bile-related diseases mentioned in the chapter on the differentiation of *doṣas*.

AS.Sū.27.8 For these [doshas] are especially destroyed by strong purgation, just as the heat of a fire-house is removed by extinguishing the fire. AS.Sū.27.9 Those who should not be purged are: those suffering from acute fever (navajvara), diarrhea, severe internal hemorrhage (raktapitta), ulcers of the anus, those who have undergone fasting, those who have stayed awake all night, those with weak digestion, those afflicted by consumption (rājayakṣman), alcoholism (madātyaya), flatulence, those with foreign bodies (śalya), those who have been wounded, those who are excessively unctuous, dry, or have a hard bowel (krūra-koṣṭha). Among these, one should not eliminate the undigested doshas in the case of acute fever.
Furthermore, one should not provoke the wind (vāta),
for it may destroy a patient suffering from severe diarrhea or hemorrhaging due to excessive blood-bile (raktapitta) by causing their further aggravation.

In one with a perforated anus, there occurs an obstruction of the vital breath (prāṇa) within the rectum; in one afflicted by pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman), due to the depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātu), the waste products gain strength, and from their presence, the destruction of the body would follow;
in one afflicted by alcoholism (madātyaya), when the body is depleted by liquor, the wind (vāyu) leads to the obstruction of the vital breath.
In one who is distended, the wind accumulated in the receptacle of feces, spreading suddenly, may produce an extremely severe distension or even death;
in those with a wound from a splinter or a blow, the wind residing in the injury may destroy life;
and in one who is excessively oleated, there may be an excessive application [of oil].

In one with a cruel digestive tract (krūrakoṣṭha), the morbid humors (doṣas) excited by the medicine, failing to be expelled, may produce heart pain, piercing pain in the joints, abdominal distension, vomiting, fainting, and exhaustion, and thus destroy life;
in those such as pregnant women, the previously mentioned complications would occur.

AS.Sū.27.10 Now, at an appropriate time, for one who has been properly oleated and sudated, whose mind is unafflicted, and who is to vomit the next day—having increased the *śleṣman* (phlegm) with liquid substances such as the meat-broth of domestic, marshy, or aquatic animals, milk, curd, *māṣa*-beans, sesame paste, vegetables, and so forth; having been made to sleep comfortably after his food is digested; having bathed and anointed himself in the forenoon, wearing garlands and new clothes; having honored the deities, fire, the twice-born, teachers, elders, and physicians; having performed the *homa*, offerings, auspicious rites, expiations, and recitations of blessings; seated upon a stool provided with a cushion and a backrest at the level of his knees; having fasted or having drunk a small amount of unctuous gruel, or a measure of ghee with gruel-scum (*maṇḍa*); or for those who are timid, emaciated, young, old, or delicate, according to the nature of the *doṣas*—having drunk up to the throat any one of milk, buttermilk, broth, sugarcane juice, meat-broth, wine, fermented grain-water, or gruel-scum; on an auspicious rising of a constellation, lunar day, *karana*, and *muhūrta*; the physician, having administered the medicinal dose prescribed according to the disease, the *doṣa*, the affected tissue (*dūṣya*), and other factors—mixed with honey and rock salt, lukewarm, and consecrated by the benedictions uttered by Brahmins—[should proceed].
Furthermore,
[the deities] Brahmā, Dakṣa, the Aśvins, Rudra, Indra, Earth, Moon, Sun, Wind, and Fire.
May the sages, along with the multitude of medicinal herbs and the hosts of living beings, protect you. May the elixir of the immortals, which bestows the state of the ageless gods, [protect you].
AS.Sū.27.12 May this medicine be for you like nectar among the most excellent of beings.
AS.Sū.27.13 Oṃ! Homage to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Bhaiṣajyaguruvaiḍūryaprabharāja.
It is as follows:
Oṃ.
Having consecrated [the medicine] with the mantra: "Bhaiṣajye bhaiṣajye mahābhaiṣajye bhaiṣajyasamudgate svāhā," one facing north should cause the patient, who is facing east, to drink it.
Then, once he has drunk it, with his arms resting on his thighs and his mind intent on vomiting, he should be warmed for a moment by hands heated over a fire while being observed.
When he should perceive that the disorder is undergoing dissolution through the appearance of perspiration,
and has been displaced from its locations by horripilation;
By the distension of the abdomen, it gradually spreads through the belly; and by the oppression of the heart, nausea, and salivation, it moves upward toward the upper part of the body.

Then, with several attendants present to support his sides, forehead, and neck, and to massage his abdomen and back in an upward direction, the patient—free from shame—should open his lips, palate, and throat; expelling the *vegas* (bodily discharges) without excessive exertion, neither failing to discharge those not yet discharged nor continuing those already discharged, he should vomit while stroking the throat with fingers having well-trimmed nails, or with the stalks of blue lotuses, white lotuses, or castor seeds.
He should do so neither too erect, nor too bent forward, nor leaning to the side.
In that regard, for one who is excessively extended, there is pain in the back and the heart; for one who is excessively bent forward, there is pain in the head and the thorax;
and for one whose sides are twisted, there is pain in the lateral thorax, the heart, and the upper trunk.
In this way, one should induce vomiting in cases of *kapha* with pungent, sharp, and hot substances;
when associated with *pitta*, one should use sweet substances.

When [the doshas] are associated with Vata, one should administer sour substances with fats until there is the elimination of Kapha, or until the manifestation of Pitta occurs, at which point the application of pure medicine alone is required (AS.Sū.27.16).
However, if the force of the movement is weak, one should induce it again and again with warm water mixed with the paste of Pippali, Āmalaka, and mustard seeds, along with salt.
One who is unable to tolerate a profuse emesis should rest for two or three days and then administer emetic therapies that are unwholesome, loathsome, unsightly, or foul-smelling.
However, the purgatives may be contrary [to the desired effect];
therefore, in all emetic procedures, one should administer rock salt and honey for the purpose of dissolving and breaking up the phlegm (kapha),
and one should observe the urges as they reach the receptacle.

In that regard, the non-occurrence of the medicine alone, or its occurrence with obstruction of the natural urges, is the characteristic of improper administration (ayoga). From that, there arise anorexia, heaviness, flatulence, itching, eruptions, urticaria, lassitude, colic, coryza, horripilation, excessive salivation, swelling, cold fever, and so forth.

Furthermore, the characteristic of balanced *yoga* (proper administration) is that the aggravation of *kapha*, *pitta*, and *vāyu* occurs gradually at the appropriate time, the pain is not excessive, and there is spontaneous subsiding followed by restoration of health, clarity of mind, purity of voice, and the reversal of conditions such as loss of appetite. However, in the case of excessive administration (*atiyoga*), there is the emergence of frothy, blood-streaked, and moon-like (white) matter.

Consequently, there arise emaciation, loss of voice, fever, burning sensations, dryness of the throat, vertigo, delusion, insanity, fainting, a sense of emptiness in the head, a sensation of smoke in the heart, body aches, numbness, thirst, aggravation of the upward-moving wind (*ūrdhvānila*), earache, facial paralysis (*ardita*), obstruction of speech, lockjaw, inability to protrude or retract the tongue, rolling of the eyes, loss of consciousness, sleepiness, and the loss of strength and digestive fire; or, due to the discharge of vital blood (*jīvaśoṇita*), death occurs.

The method for achieving these successes will now be explained. When he has been made to vomit by means of yoga, and his hands, feet, and mouth have been thoroughly cleansed, one should comfort him for a moment, administer whichever of the three types of smoke is appropriate according to his capacity, and after he has again sipped water and been honored with fragrant betel, while he is lying on a bed in a windless room, one should instruct him according to the rules of conduct prescribed for oleation therapy.

Then, having considered the strength of the digestive fire and the degree of hunger, at evening or on the following day, one who has been bathed with comfortable water should consume, in the evening and in the morning, well-cooked food made from old red *śāli* rice—either without fat, salt, or pungent spices, or with little fat, salt, and pungency—and consisting mostly of liquid, followed by warm water. One should observe this regimen for the sequence beginning with *peyā*.
*Peyā*, *vilepī*, unseasoned and seasoned broth (*yūṣa*), meat broth (*rasa*)—these three, both types [of broth], and likewise the single [meat broth]—[should be consumed in succession].
A person who has been purified by superior, middling, or inferior degrees of purification should gradually observe the times for eating;
just as a tiny spark of fire, when fanned by grass, cow dung, and other fuels, grows progressively larger.
The internal fire of a pure person is likewise great, stable, and capable of digesting everything; [it is nourished] by drinks and other such things.
AS.Sū.27.24: Regarding emesis, four, six, and eight urges are desired for the inferior, middling, and superior [patients], respectively.
These same ten [pala] should be doubled or tripled for purgation; likewise, a *prastha* should be double or fourfold [of that].
They say that emesis ends with the elimination of *pitta*, while purgation ends with the elimination of *kapha*.
Having removed two or three urges accompanied by feces, one should measure [the output]; in the case of purgation, however, it is measured when the medicine has been expelled.
In the case of emesis, it is measured when the medicine has been vomited.

AS.Sū.27.26 Now, once he has vomited, having again treated him with oleation and sudation, one should administer a purgative on the following day. One should feed him light-to-digest, non-phlegmatic, unctuous food that is sour with fruits and warm, followed by a drink of warm water, along with wild-rice meat broth.

Then, after he has slept comfortably, when the time for phlegm has passed, one should administer the appropriate dose of medicine according to the previously mentioned procedure, having divided the stomach while fasting.
However, one who has not undergone emesis— unless they have an extremely harsh digestive tract—
should not [administer the medicine], for in one who has not undergone emesis, the medicine, being obstructed by phlegm, moves upward.
Or, being obstructed in the chest, it remains there; consequently, it is not capable of inducing purgation.
Even in one who has been properly purged, the phlegm (śleṣman) may descend downward and, by covering the grahaṇī, brings about heaviness of the body.
Or there may be dysentery;

however, this fault does not apply to one with a non-cruel (soft) bowel, because [the disease] is of a windy nature. But during the period of phlegm (kapha), if emesis has not been performed, the aforementioned defects—namely colic, flatulence, and heaviness—will arise; therefore, once the phlegm has been diminished by vomiting, one should administer a purgative in the afternoon or at night.
Therefore, even though it is not covered by food, it is the same;
moreover, it produces vomiting again.

However, for one who has not been purged, emesis should be administered without food during the period of increased *śleṣman*, because [the substance] is then easily expelled from above. Furthermore, the digestive tract (*koṣṭha*) is of three types. (AS.Sū.27.29)
It is mild, cruel, and moderate; among these,
one with an abundance of bile is mild.

One who has excessive vāta and hard bowels may be purged even by milk, sugarcane juice, sour liquids, buttermilk, meat-broth, jaggery, rice-and-pulse porridge (kṛsara), ghee, fresh wine, warm water, or pīlu, grape, betel nut, and similar substances;
yet such a person is difficult to purge even with triphalā, tilvaka, trivṛt, nīlinī fruit, and other such drugs.
One with excessive phlegm (śleṣman) and balanced humors (sāmadoṣa) is moderate; such a person is considered "ordinary" (sādhāraṇa).
