Those who generally become unctuous by drinking clear liquids after three, seven, or five nights [are also ordinary]. In that regard, purgation (virecana) for pitta is performed with substances that are astringent and sweet.
In cases of *kapha*, [one should use] urine that is pungent and hot;
in cases of *vāta*, [one should use] substances that are unctuous, hot, and salty.
As soon as the medicine has been swallowed, one should suddenly sprinkle his face with cold water to prevent vomiting;

then, having cleansed the interior of the mouth with warm water, he should smell pleasant fragrances such as moist, fragrant earth, *mātuluṅga*, *jambīra*, *sumanas*, *saugandhika*, and other such delightful scents.

Remaining on a comfortable bed in a windless place, he should drink small amounts of warm water from time to time to prevent constipation, being attentive to it and not suppressing the urges when they arise. And while being moved about, he should void himself into a receptacle kept near the bed that is neither too cold nor too hot.
Just as in emesis, sweat, saliva, the medicinal drug, phlegm, bile, and wind emerge in succession, so too in purgation do wind, urine, feces, bile, and phlegm [emerge],
followed finally by wind;
for such is the arrangement of the humors within the body and because of the reversal of their paths in the two types of purification.
If there is no movement [of the bowels], however, one should have the patient drink warm water to stimulate the medicine and should foment the abdomen with the heat of the palms.

When the purgative has begun to act in one with a stimulated digestive fire and an unctuous body, even if the morbid humors (doṣas) are numerous, or when it has not acted at all in one with few humors, or when the medicine has been digested, one should administer a further dose after considering the remainder of the day and the patient's strength; however, this must not be done while the medicine is undigested for fear of excessive action (atiyoga). Alternatively, one may administer it again on that same day if the patient has eaten, or on the following day if the unctuousness is not yet firm, or after ten days have passed, provided the body has been prepared and the physician is attentive.
Women who serve near kings and merchants are generally of a nature characterized by the suppression of their natural impulses through shame, fear, and greed. (AS.Sū.27.32–33)
Therefore, because their bodily air (vāta) has increased due to the suppression of natural urges, these persons are constantly afflicted and difficult to purge;
one should purify them after they have been well-oleated,
as well as others who engage in untimely evacuation, physical exertion, or dietary habits.

Consequently, because they are always afflicted by disease, even a minor ailment becomes difficult to cure for them; furthermore, the therapeutic procedure for such cases will be explained in the section on the successful treatment of complications arising from oleation therapy (*snehavyāpatsiddhi*).

AS.Sū.27.35 Therein, from improper purgation (asamyag-vireka), there arise impurity of the abdomen and heart, flatulence, anorexia, salivation, provocation of *kapha* and *pitta*, vomiting, vertigo, itching, eruptions, burning sensation, heaviness, loss of digestive fire, drowsiness, numbness, coryza, and retention of flatus, feces, and urine. From proper purgation (samyag-vireka), there occurs the alleviation of disease and the opposite of what was stated [for improper purgation].
Due to excessive purgation, however, only water free from impurities, or blood, or something resembling the wash-water of fat and flesh, or black matter may be discharged.

There is cutting pain (parikartikā), a twisting sensation in the heart, prolapse of the rectum, the sensation of the eyes bulging out, a feeling as if ants are crawling over the body, and symptoms similar to those of excessive emesis.
One who has been properly purged should be treated according to the procedure prescribed for emesis, with the exception of the use of medicinal smoke.
AS.Sū.27.36 Now, as if he has vomited, by gradually consuming foods he should return to his normal diet;
and regarding this, there is also [this verse]:

When the food is digested, emesis should be administered; when the phlegm is digested, purgation should be administered. [One should treat] one who has weak digestive fire, is impure, is not emaciated, and is weakened by the doshas.
One should cause the patient who has drunk the medicine to fast until signs of digestion are observed;
thus, he will not be afflicted by the complications arising from the agitation caused by oleation, sudation, and medicinal drugs.

The digestive fire becomes weak through purification therapies, bloodletting, the administration of fats, and fasting; therefore, one should follow the sequential regimen beginning with thin gruel (peyā).

One should not administer gruel (peyā) to those who have discharged a small amount of bile and phlegm, nor to a habitual drinker of alcohol, nor to one with a predominance of vāta and pitta; for them, a regimen beginning with nourishing drinks (tarpaṇa) is beneficial.
An unripened emetic expels the *doṣas*, whereas a ripening one acts as a purgative; therefore, one should not wait for the ripening of an emetic.
When the downward evacuation occurs upward and the upward evacuation occurs downward due to such a reversal,
one should cause the patient to vomit or sprinkle them with warm water.
In the case of purgation, the feet should be treated with cold and the upper body with the opposite;
likewise for one who is weak yet has abundant morbid humors, provided those humors are spontaneously ripening.
One should administer purgatives that cause evacuation;
for a weak man who has been previously cleansed, whose doshas are minimal, and who is emaciated, one should provide him with such food.
One who does not know the proper dosage should drink a mild medicine in small quantities;
it is better for that to be drunk repeatedly, as otherwise it brings about danger. One should remove many unstable humors (doṣas) in small amounts again and again.
In one who is weak, those [doshas] should be pacified with mild substances in small doses; for if they are not eliminated, they cause suffering for a long time or may even kill him.
One should purify a patient with weak digestion and a harsh bowel by means of ghees containing alkali and salt,
once the digestive fire has been kindled and the phlegm and wind have been subdued.
In those who have a rough, predominantly vāta, or cruel constitution, in those habituated to physical exercise,
and in those with a keen digestive fire, medicine is digested even without being purged.
To them, one should first administer an enema, followed by an unctuous purgative;
or, after expelling some feces, [one should give a purgative] with sharp medicinal suppositories (phalavarti).
For an unctuous purgative easily eliminates the morbid matter that has already set in.
[It is indicated for] those suffering from poisoning, trauma, pustules, leprosy, edema, and erysipelas.
One should purify those afflicted by jaundice, anemia, and urinary disorders who have not been excessively oleated,
using all types of unctuous purgatives; however, those who have already been prepared with oleation should be purified with dry purgatives.
Between the intervals of emetic and other such procedures,
one should again apply oleation and sudation; and at the end, one should administer oleation for the sake of strengthening the body.
Just as the dirt of a garment is removed by first causing it to come loose with alkaline substances and the like,
so too is the oil and sweat of the body removed by means of black gram, sesame seeds, and other such ingredients.
If one undergoes purification therapy without having practiced oleation and sudation,
his body will break apart like dry wood being split with an axe.
That which proceeds easily, swiftly, with great force, and without obstruction,
does not cause excessive exhaustion, nor does it produce pain in the heart or the rectum.
That which expels the entire morbid humor (doṣa) accumulated within the internal channels and the moist tissues—
whether it be a purgative or a non-unctuous enema (nirūha)— should be designated as "sharp" (tīkṣṇa).
[The medicine] should be untouched by water, fire, or insects; endowed with the qualities of place and time; fresh;
slightly exceeding the proper measure; and well-processed with substances of equal potency.
Medicine administered to one who has undergone oleation and sudation attains sharpness;
conversely, in the opposite case, it becomes weak and reaches a state of dullness.
Disease is sharp, moderate, or mild, characterized by all, intermediate, or slight symptoms; for these,
treatment that is sharp, moderate, or mild is beneficial according to the strength [of the patient].
A substance does not undergo digestion unless the impurities have been expelled; for it is only when they have become integrated with the self that [the body] decays.
Therefore, one should not employ emesis or purgation as a habitual practice.
The improper administration of [medicine] is like poison, whereas its correct application is like nectar;
since it must necessarily be administered at the right time, one should drink it with great care.

When properly administered, purificatory therapy brings about clarity of intellect, strength of the sense organs, equilibrium of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), radiance of the digestive fire, and a delayed onset of aging.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter.
Now begins the twenty-eighth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the chapter titled "The Procedure for Enemas" (Bastividhi).
"Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and others:
'Enema therapy (basti) is employed when the humors (doṣas) are dominated by vāyu.'"

AS.Sū.28.2 It is administered by means of an enema (*basti*), or because it follows after [the treatment] previously mentioned, it is called *basti*. AS.Sū.28.3 And it is the most preeminent among all therapeutic measures, because it quickly effects nourishment and the like, and because it eradicates deranged *vāyu*.
For wind is indeed the leader of the humors (doṣas).
He is the sole cause of all bodily movements,
pervading the limbs and minor members through his fivefold nature;
he is the ordainer and the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of various external and internal entities, as well as of the diseases arising from the three pathways.

Moreover, because it is pleasant, enema (basti) is prescribed for children, the elderly, the emaciated, the obese, and those whose tissues (dhātu) and sense organs (indriya) are depleted; for women who have not conceived due to the affliction of wind (anila), and for those with difficult childbirth.

Likewise, it bestows digestive power (agni-bala), complexion (varṇa), intelligence (medhā), voice (svara), longevity (āyus), and happiness; it maintains youth and is beneficial in cases of lameness, stiffness of the thighs (ūrustambha), fractures, contractions, wind disorders, flatulence, colic, anorexia, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), and cutting pain (parikartikā).
That enema, however, is of three types:
the non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana), the unctuous enema (anuvāsana), and the urethral/vaginal enema (uttarabasti).
In that regard, non-unctuous enema (*āsthāpana*) is prepared through the combination of various substances according to the specific humors (*doṣa*), affected tissues (*dūṣya*), and other factors.

Its varieties include: provocation (*utkleśana*), purification (*saṃśodhana*), pacification (*saṃśamana*), scraping (*lekhana*), nourishment (*bṛṃhaṇa*), aphrodisiac therapy (*vājīkaraṇa*), slimy enema (*picchābasti*), honey-and-oil enema (*mādhutailika*), and so forth.
The synonyms for *mādhutailika* are *yāpana*, *yuktaratha*, *doṣahara*, and *snigdhabasti*;

their essential nature is explained by these very names (AS.Sū.28.7). It is called *āsthāpana* because it establishes [the patient] in youth or because it establishes the *doṣas* [in their proper state]. It is called *nirūha* because it ascends into the body, because it eliminates the *doṣas*, and because its power is inconceivable, such that no [logical] inference (*ūha*) can be applied to it.
Anuvasana is an unctuous enema prepared with appropriate medicinal drugs for the purpose of oleation; it is described as being of four types in the section on oleation.
Its variety is the *mātrāvasti*; it is equal in quantity to a small dose of oil for drinking and should be used constantly, like the *mādhutailika* regimen.

AS.Sū.28.9: For children, the elderly, those exhausted by travel, carrying loads, or riding vehicles; those engaged in physical exercise or anxious thought; those constantly occupied with women; and for kings, lords, delicate persons, the weak, and those whose digestive fire is impaired by wind—[this oil] is beneficial when used without restriction. It is pleasant, strengthening, improves the complexion, promotes the evacuation of waste, and pacifies the *doṣas*. Nevertheless, these two [types of enema] should not be administered during indigestion, nor should one indulge in daytime sleep;
because it does not cause harm even when administered daily following a meal, or because it is given every day (*anuvasanam*), it is called *anuvāsana* (daily enema).

AS.Sū.28.10: Some say that the *uttarabasti* (urethral/vaginal enema) is like an oil enema (*anuvāsana*) in its lubrication and like a decoction enema (*nirūha*) in its cleansing; it is called *uttarabasti* because it is administered after (*uttara*) a *nirūha*, or because it is given through the upper (*uttara*) passage.

AS.Sū.28.11 In these cases, enemas are to be administered for: abdominal tumors (gulma), splenic disorders, distension, colic, diarrhea, chronic fever, coryza, obesity, diseases of the heart, abdomen, and flanks; for conditions involving stiffness in the joints, burning sensations in the sides, pain in the flanks and vagina, numbness of the limbs, emaciation, tremors, heaviness, excessive lightness, rumbling in the intestines, and retention of flatus, feces, urine, and semen; for urinary calculi, gravel, scrotal enlargement, and the loss of semen, menstrual blood, breast milk, or the cessation of menstruation; for insanity, seminal defects, intestinal worms, and digestive disorders; and especially for the various wind-diseases (vātavyādhi) described in the *Doṣabhedīya* chapter, such as those characterized by sounds, scanty emissions, or foul odors. Indeed, these reach their ultimate destruction through enemas, just as a tree is destroyed by cutting its roots.

Those who should not be administered an enema (anāsthāpya) are: those who are excessively unctuous, those with aggravated doshas, those with chest wounds, those who are extremely emaciated, those who have fasted, those who have undergone emesis, purgation, or nasal therapy, those suffering from persistent vomiting, spitting, cough, dyspnea, hiccups, emaciation, intestinal obstruction, perforation, or edema; and those afflicted by flatulence, alasaka, visūcikā, diarrhea, anorexia, weak digestion, swelling of the rectum, leprosy, or diabetes mellitus.
A pregnant woman whose eighth month has not yet arrived should not undergo this procedure;

for in her case, a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) administered when the doshas are excessively unctuous or aggravated may cause abdominal enlargement, fainting, or edema by provoking the underlying doshas.
Furthermore, in one with a chest injury or who is extremely emaciated, the enema—having caused agitation—may quickly afflict the body.

It will be explained that for one who has not eaten, or for one who has undergone emesis and purgation, the body is empty; in such a state, an unctuous enema (snehabasti) would burn like caustic alkali (kṣāra) upon a wound,
immediately suppressing the digestive fire (agni) and leading to diseases of phlegm (śleṣman).
One should prevent the downward displacement of the enema by means of upward-moving [drugs] that cause the channels to open;
however,
an oil enema (anuvāsana) causes the provocation of the humors (doṣas).
In those suffering from persistent vomiting and other such conditions, the vāyu may carry the nirūha upward;
furthermore, in one with hemorrhoids (arśas), the enema (basti) may fail to return because its path is obstructed, and thus it may injure the vital breaths (prāṇa).
Furthermore, oleation (sneha) may cause the obstruction of the channels (abhiṣyanda) and flatulence (ādhmāna) in those with hemorrhoids;
for those suffering from conditions beginning with intestinal obstruction (baddhodara) and ending with flatulence, death results from excessive distension,
as does death from the complications of alasaka and other disorders arising from undigested matter (āmadoṣa).
For those suffering from loss of appetite and similar ailments, there is an increase of their respective morbid humors;
for a pregnant woman, the previously mentioned defect applies.
Those who are eligible for non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana) are the same as those eligible for unctuous enemas (anuvāsana).
Those whose digestive fires are parched or excessively kindled, and those especially afflicted by wind alone, are nourished most effectively even by means of a non-unctuous enema (anuvasana).
Like a tree nourished by watering its roots, those who are unfit for enemas (anuvāsana) are likewise unfit for non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana).

These include: those fasting; those suffering from acute fever, anemia (pāṇḍuroga), jaundice (kāmalā), urinary disorders (prameha), coryza, splenic enlargement, abdominal diseases caused by kapha, obesity, flatulence with loose stools, or pain from ingested poison, artificial poison, or bile; those with excessive secretions (abhiṣyanda), a heavy digestive tract, extreme obesity, elephantiasis (ślīpada), goiter, scrofula (apacī), intestinal worms, or a condition of the abdomen characterized by parasites.
In that regard, the specific defects for those who are excessively unctuous and so forth have been stated individually;
furthermore, AS.Sū.28.15 states: "An oil enema administered to one who has not eaten and whose stomach is empty..."
AS.Sū.28.15 Through [its] speed, distance, and subtlety, it quickly ascends upwards. AS.Sū.28.16 Because of that, there would be no mastery over the wind for one who remains in the place of the wind.
AS.Sū.28.16 There is also the rapid destruction of the bodily fire (*kāyāgni*), especially because [the disease] does not recede.
AS.Sū.28.17 However, when the wind (*anila*) is obstructed in the stomach (*āmāśaya*) by the unctuousness (*sneha*) and the food recently consumed, [it causes distress].

When it is situated in the digested food (*pakvastha*), it kills; when situated in the digested food, it causes one to fall away from the digestion of food. Both the *nirūha* enema and the wind (*samīra*) possess sharp force.
As long as those two sharp [humors] have not become delirious, they may be present together with food in the lower part of the body,
or situated above it along with the feces, or even remaining within the digestive tract itself.

When obstructed by impure food, these two [conditions] may quickly take away one's life. One who has eaten should not be given an oil enema (anuvāsana), nor should one who has eaten be given a decoction enema (nirūha).
In those afflicted by jaundice and similar conditions, an unctuous enema (snehabasti), having provoked the humors (doṣas), may produce abdominal enlargement;
in those of low status and the like, it would further increase the morbidity.

The nozzle (netra) for those two, however, should be made of gold or other metals, gems, conch, horn, ivory, bone, bamboo, reed, khadira, kadara, tiniśa, tinduka, or other heartwood; it should be straight, smooth, and have a globular tip like a cow’s tail. Its length shall be five, six, seven, eight, nine, twelve, or sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgula), respectively, for those who are less than a year old, one year old, two years old, seven years old, twelve years old, sixteen years old, and twenty years old and above.

At the base and the tip, it should have a circumference equal to four thumbs and little fingers; the root-opening should be three finger-breadths in depth, increasing by half a finger-breadth from that point up to its maximum; the openings at the tips for the bamboo sprout, the *mudga* bean, the *māṣa* bean, the *kalāya* pea, the *klinna-kalāya*, the *arka-kandhu*, and the *vāhya* should be sized accordingly; at the tip, one should fashion *karṇikās* (protruding rims) according to the dimensions of the finger-breadths of the root-opening; inside these *karṇikās*, one should fix a thread through which a thick cloth wick is drawn, and between the two *karṇikās* at the base, separated by a distance of two finger-breadths, one should cause two *karṇikās* to be made.
In subsequent years, one should increase the size of the nozzle (netra) after considering the patient's age, strength, and physique.

(AS.Sū.28.22) Then, having prepared a bladder made from the hide of a goat, sheep, boar, deer, cow, or buffalo—any one of these—soaked in oil, with its pores, veins, and shoulder-knots removed, neither too round, soft yet firm, dyed with an astringent decoction (kaṣāya), easy to position, and of a size appropriate for the medicinal dose; and having placed it face down with its opening exposed, tied it firmly and evenly at the two ear-loops with a strong thread, turned it over, and again applied another thread for binding the mouth of the bladder, one should store it in a protected place.
In the absence of a bladder, one should insert any one of the following: a piece of leather from a swimming animal, the leg of a goat, beeswax, or a thick,
fine cloth.
The dose for the non-unctuous enema (*āsthāpana*) in the first year is one *prakuñca*;
thereafter, one should increase it by one *prakuñca* each year until it reaches six *prasṛta*.
Thereafter, the increase continues upward;
for one who has reached an age of eighteen or seventy years, twelve finger-breadths [of growth] have passed,
and beyond that, only ten remain.
Others, however, desire even twelve *prasṛta* for the eight [types of non-unctuous enemas];
the dose for the *mādhutailika* should be applied as one-fourth less than the respective dose for the *āsthāpana*.
"In the case of an oil enema (*anuvāsana*), it is exactly like this; for a non-unctuous enema (*āsthāpana*), it is one-quarter [of that].

(AS.Sū.28.26) Now, a patient who is fit for a non-unctuous enema—one who has undergone oleation and sudation, has performed emesis and purgation, has followed the sequential regimen of thin gruel (*peyā*) and so forth, and has regained strength—is fit for an oil enema and should first be treated with an oil enema.

In the seasons of winter and spring, [the regimen] is otherwise during the day; at night it is otherwise, having considered the *doṣas* and other factors, for otherwise there would be the manifestation of diseases mentioned in this treatise.
Furthermore, the followers of Dhanvantari say:
One should not administer an enema at night, for the aggravation of *sneha* (unctuous substances) occurs during the night;
[it should be done] during the day when the *doṣas* are situated in their proper locations and the digestive fire is endowed with the essence of food.
When the body has open channels and orifices, and the unctuous element (sneha) flows through them,
it is characterized by diminished bile and phlegm, dryness, and is severely afflicted with diseases of Vata.

AS.Sū.28.29 One may administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) at will even at night, provided the food has been digested. However, one should administer it even to a patient who is afflicted solely by Vāta, is impure, or whose strength has not yet been restored, because of the critical nature of the disease.

The procedure for that [purgation] is as follows: having performed more auspicious rites than for emesis, one should have the patient comfortably anointed and bathed with warm water; then, having administered the appropriate unctuous substance, one should have him eat a meal consisting mostly of liquids, light and warm, followed by a post-prandial drink, reduced by one-quarter from his usual amount; after he has walked about and voided feces and urine, with his hand moistened by food and attended by trustworthy caregivers, one should have him lie down on a continuous bed in a windless room—neither too high nor too low, well-spread, with the foot-end slightly raised, lying on his left side with his head toward the east.
For one who eats excessively unctuous food, the unctuousness, due to its contact with both pathways, produces oiliness, intoxication, fainting, impairment of the digestive fire, and nausea;
for one who eats dry food, it causes constipation or loss of strength and complexion;
and for one who eats liquids in small quantities or whose feces and urine have been discharged, it causes disorder because the [unctuousness] remains uncovered where it ought to be covered.
If one has eaten for a long time and the food is about to cause a burning sensation (vidāha), it may induce fever;

furthermore, because the mouth of the fire, the grahaṇī, and the rectum are situated on the left side, they become depressed when the patient lies on that side, so that the medicine reaches them without obstruction during both entry and exit. Therefore, once he is lying down, one should have him keep his body straight, use his own arms as a pillow, extend his left thigh, bend the other, and likewise extend his right arm over it.

First, the physician, having placed the nozzle—its tip and opening well-sealed with a wick—over the vessel, should press upon the perineum with the big toe and toes of his right foot to prevent obstruction. Having sprinkled it with a powder of *śatāhvā* and rock salt, and having consecrated it as before by touching it at dawn, he should pour lukewarm oil—prepared with appropriate medicinal drugs—into the bladder. After removing air bubbles by means of the *avalīka* (bladder-vent) and exhalation, and at the end of the medicinal infusion, he should wrap the mouth of the bladder two or three times with thread. Placing the nozzle upon his right hand, he should stand ready.

AS.Sū.28.30 Then, having smeared the anus with ghee, one should insert the nozzle— its entry point likewise smeared, its tip covered by the palm of the upturned left hand with the thumb pressed against it, its "pericarp" (the handle) grasped by the middle and index fingers, straight, following the spinal column, comfortable, and single-mindedly— swiftly, without trembling, neither too fast nor too slow, inserting it as far as the pericarp with lightness. The patient, for his part, should support it while remaining in alignment with it.

Then the physician, not releasing the nozzle with the thumb and index finger of the right hand and not moving the tube, should hold it with both hands turned upward and grasp it firmly; leaving only a small portion remaining which is governed by the vital air (*vāyu*), he should slowly and steadily squeeze it without causing agitation.
Otherwise, complications arise, which, along with their treatments, will be described in the *Siddhisthāna*.
Others, however, say that the duration for administering the enema is thirty mātrās; furthermore,
while the enema is being administered, one should not perform sneezing, coughing, laughing, yawning, or shaking.
When there is an urge for feces, urine, or flatus, one should pull back the eyelids; once the urge has subsided, one should discharge the remainder.
At the end, while the patient is lying supine, one should strike the temples three or four times with the palm of the hand, and likewise with the heels.
One should lift the bed three times from the foot-end; then, while the person lies with all limbs extended along with the pillow, one should strike the two heels with the fist,
as well as the heels, the toes, the soles of the feet, and the calves.
One should gently massage the painful limb with oil in the direction opposite to the hair for about a hundred words;
in this way, the oil quickly does not recede but follows along and permeates the veins on all sides.
Thereafter, however, one should follow the conduct prescribed out of affection; and when the digestive fire is kindled, one should eat light food in the evening.
One should certainly not entertain affection for the future, nor should one let the patient remain overnight;
however, the time for his return is at most three watches of the night.
Thereafter, if it does not come out even after a day and night, one should wait;
if it still does not return, one should purge the patient with sharp enemas consisting primarily of *phalavarti* or salt and sour gruel (*lavaṇāranāla*),
and one should observe the treatment for complications arising from oleation (*snehavyāpad*).

If [the oil] does not come out due to excessive severity, it might cause complications such as stupor; nevertheless, it should be ignored. However, once it has been quickly expelled without impurity, one should apply another unctuous substance (sneha) alone;
for if it remains stagnant, it does not perform its function.

Once he has rested comfortably, one should generally have him drink either a decoction of *śuṇṭhī* and *dhānyaka*, or simply warm water, following any of the aforementioned procedures of emesis, purgation, or non-unctuous enema (*āsthāpana*), for the purpose of digesting the residual unctuous substance (*sneha*) and pacifying the *vāta* and *kapha*. Then, at the time of eating, he should consume food as prescribed.
And one should not give gruel to a patient who has already undergone an oil enema, for that would cause further secretions in his already lubricated digestive tract;
rather, one should administer an oil enema again on the third or fifth day.

Or when the digestion of the unctuous substance has occurred, and the digestive fire is thus kindled, one should administer non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana) daily for three or four days according to this sequence and in accordance with the state of the *doṣas* and other factors, for the purpose of purifying the channels, to those who are habitually dry, have aggravated *vāta*, or engage in constant physical exercise— provided they have been sufficiently lubricated by these unctuous enemas (*snehabasti*).
However, if there is a predominance of *vāta* and they remain insufficiently lubricated, one should first treat them with further oleation (*snehana*).

AS.Sū.28.34 Then, on the third or fifth day, when midday has slightly passed, having observed that the patient—whose body has been anointed with oil, sweated, and cleansed of impurities, who has not yet eaten but is not excessively hungry—has had auspicious rites and blessings performed for him, one should regard Āryāvalokita as the Protector, Āryatārā as the Self-born Creator, and [worship] Dhātṛ, the Aśvins, Ātreya, the Seven Sages, Kāśirāja, the Lord of Videha, and other such authors of treatises beginning with Agniveśa, offering them shares like those prepared in a sacrifice with lamps, perfumes, fruits, oblations, and incense. Having honored the physicians who have mastered medicinal herbs and the twice-born, accompanied by those learned in the science, one should administer the enema (vasti) appropriately according to the strength of the humors (doṣa), the drugs, and other factors.
In that case, one should boil twenty palas of medicinal herbs together with eight *madana* fruits according to the method for preparing a decoction.

One should add oil equal to one-fourth of the decoction in cases of Vāta, one-sixth in Pitta, and one-eighth in the case of a healthy person or in Kapha; the paste (kalka) should also be one-eighth of the entire quantity, with consistency being such that it is neither too thin nor too thick. One *pala* of jaggery, honey, and rock salt should be added according to the requirements, and the remaining ingredients should be prepared accordingly.

AS.Sū.28.36 All these ingredients, having been heated together by the steam from a pot of hot water and stirred with a churning stick, should be placed in a bladder and administered as a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) according to the procedure for an unctuous enema (anuvāsana).

It should be neither too hot nor too cold, neither too mild nor too sharp, neither too unctuous nor too dry, neither too thin nor too thick, neither deficient nor excessive in quantity, and neither saltless nor excessively salty, nor excessively sour.
In that case, due to remorse consisting of mere tears, there is no burning from the medicine;
however, through the churning by the *khaja* (whisk), the decoctions, fats, and other ingredients, when properly combined, initiate the application correctly.
Otherwise, one or another of the decoctions and so forth, becoming excessive, would aggravate its respective *doṣa*.
Furthermore, the specific complications and their treatments for excessive heat and other such conditions will be taught later in the section on successful therapies (siddhi).
AS.Sū.28.37. Moreover, AS.Sū.28.37.
For if the nozzle is directed obliquely, the stream does not enter; if the anal canal is injured, an ulcer may form;
and if the nozzle is moved, the enema, even if administered slowly, fails to reach its destination. If pressed too forcefully, it may rush up into the throat;
if too soft or cold, it causes rigidity; and if hot, sour, or sharp, it produces vertigo, burning sensations, and delusion. (AS.Sū.28.38)
An unctuous enema causes excessive dullness, while a dry one causes wind (vāta). One that is thin, administered in a small dose, or deficient in salt causes improper action (ayoga).
An enema that is excessive in dose causes over-action (atiyoga), whereas a thick one causes agitation and takes a long time to pass.
Excessive salt causes both burning sensations and diarrhea; therefore, one should apply it properly in equal measure. One should take a dose of three *palas* each for both the oil and the honey.
For one who is healthy, half a *karṣa* of *māṇimantha* and two *palas* of paste should be used;
for all the remaining liquid ingredients, one should prepare ten *palas*.
Honey, salt, unctuous substance, paste, and decoction— these should be added in this order;
this is the procedure for the preparation of non-unctuous enemas (nirūha).
Immediately after it has been administered, the patient should lie on his back with a pillow and remain focused on that [medication] until its potency has pervaded the body.
If his urge is intense, he should release while squatting;
however, the time for returning is another muhūrta,
for if he does not return then, he will quickly fall into the power of death.

Therefore, in that case, one should administer other unctuous, sharp, and hot substances that are compatible— such as fats, alkalis, urine, and sours— as well as fruit-suppositories, sudation, and frightening or startling measures; furthermore, one should consult the chapter on the successful management of complications arising from enemas.
But when [the disease] has subsided on its own, one should administer the second, third, and fourth [applications], as before, until it is well-established.
Among these, the first draws the wind (vāyu) away from its own path.
The second [wind] is for bile, and the third is for phlegm.
In that case, deficient, correct, or excessive administration [of the enema] should be treated like [the management of] purgation.
However, once the enema has been properly retained, one should bathe the patient with lukewarm water and feed him a thin broth of wild game meat.
When he has bathed and eaten, his remaining morbid humors (doṣas), being mobile, return to their own locations.

Thereafter, one should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) using oil prepared with the ten roots (daśamūla) and other ingredients in appropriate waters to the patient who is afflicted by vāta, after he has eaten either nourishing food or another similar meal, or again in the evening after eating a small amount of light food.
For those with inferior application of the correct method, it is like drinking oil; however,
the distinction is that when the enema is correctly administered, after remaining for a short time, the oil, along with the feces and followed by the vital air (vāyu), is expelled.
And there is a verse on this point:
"In the case of kapha, one should thus administer an unctuous enema once or three times."

In cases of *pitta*, five or seven enemas should be administered; in cases of *vāyu*, nine or eleven. After that, one should again administer an uneven number [of enemas], followed by a second *āsthāpana* (non-unctuous enema).
In cases of kapha, pitta, and vāta, food should be taken respectively with vegetable broth, milk, and meat juice;
[the latter] combined with a decoction of vāta-alleviating herbs, trivṛt, and rock salt.
In the case of Vata, a single unctuous enema (basti) should be prepared with sweet, sour, and warm substances combined with meat broth,
along with a decoction of the *Gnyagrodhadi* group and *Padmakadi* group, mixed with sugar. (AS.Sū.28.52)

In cases of pitta, three [decoctions]— sweet and cold, combined with ghee, milk, sugarcane juice, and honey, and those containing a decoction of the āragvadhādi group along with vatsakādi— are beneficial. (AS.Sū.28.53)

In cases of *kapha*, [medicines] that are dry, mixed with honey and cow’s urine, and sharp, hot, and pungent are used; furthermore, these three [types of treatment] destroy the *doṣas* even in *sannipāta* (combined disorders) by means of their respective sequences.
Therefore, according to Ācārya Caraka, an enema is not considered appropriate beyond three;
for there is no fourth humor (doṣa) against which it might be administered again. [It acts] successively as an exciter, a purifier, and a pacifier of the humors. (AS.Sū.28.55)
Others also declare that one should prepare the enema in three ways; all of this should be determined according to the strength of the humors, the medicine, and other factors.
However, once the signs [of successful treatment] have been correctly established, one should not discontinue [the therapy] without considering the possibility [of further benefit].
First, there is one application of oleation; at the end, there are twelve applications of non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana).
Thus, including the preliminary treatments (anvāsana), thirty types of enemas (basti) have been described.
Fifteen of these are administered with oil first, while three are given at the end.
There are six and five intervals between the enemas; however, in this [treatment], there are eight enemas in the regimen.

There are three types of decoction enemas (nirūha) and three types of unctuous enemas (sneha); these two [categories] should be used at the beginning and at the end [of a course of treatment]. One should not habitually employ either the unctuous enema (snehavasti) or the decoction enema (nirūha) exclusively.

From oleation (sneha), there is the danger of aggravating the humors (utkleśa), increasing the fire (agni), and causing injury; from non-unctuous enemas (nirūha), there is the danger of wind (maruta).
Therefore, one who has received a non-unctuous enema should receive oleation, and one who has been oleated should receive a non-unctuous enema.
Thus, through the very method of purifying with unctuous substances, the enema therapy (bastikarma) conquers the three doṣas. He who employs eighteen sets of eighteen enemas [attains mastery].
By means of the procedure as it has been described, he shall become free from old age and disease;
he shall have a lifespan of a thousand years, retain what he has heard, be cleansed of all evil, and possess the radiance of an immortal.
Possessing the speed of a horse, the strength of an elephant, and a steady fire of intellect and senses,
[he is effective] against diseases of the bladder in women, as well as those of the womb and the uterus.

One should administer the subsequent enema (uttaravasti) to those who have been purified by two or three non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana). Its nozzle should be twelve finger-breadths in length, measured by the patient's own fingers.
It is circular like a cow’s tail, with a *karṇika* (protuberance) fashioned at the base and middle;
its tip is shaped like a mustard seed, smooth, and made of gold or other [precious materials].
His bladder should be firm, resembling the stalk of a jasmine flower;
its enema nozzle should be soft and light, with a capacity determined according to the patient's strength, or measured at one *śukti*.
Then, for this person who has bathed and eaten, according to the procedure for administering oleation therapy,
he should sit straight and comfortably on a soft seat at the level of the knees.

When the penis is erect and steady, one should slowly insert a straight, thick catheter, with a circumference equal to the tip of the stalk of a *mālatī* flower, for the purpose of purifying the channels.
One should insert a smooth probe; once it has cleared the anus, one should then insert the tube steadily, like the rectum, up to the end of the urethra.
When the oil has been administered and has entered [the channels], the procedure for an oil enema (sneha-basti) is beneficial;
by this method, one should administer three or even four enemas.
One should consider all the remaining points for this [treatment] to be the same as those for an oil enema (anuvāsana). However,
during a woman's menstrual period, the vagina remains open and does not retain [the medicine].
Therefore, one should administer it even during the non-seasonal period (anṛtu) or in times of distress (ātyaya),
as well as in cases of vaginal displacement, vaginal pain, gynecological disorders, and menorrhagia.
The nozzle should be ten finger-breadths long, with an opening for a mung bean that is four finger-breadths wide.

In cases of urinary disorders (mūtrakṛcchra), a [tube] two fingers long should be applied to the path of the offspring (the vaginal canal), while for children, it should indeed be a bamboo splinter (śukti).
For a woman lying on her back with her thighs properly drawn together,
one should join [the penis] for three or four times within a day and night, with her knees raised.
In this manner, one should increase the dose of oil for three days;
then, having rested for three days, one should administer it again for another three days.
After emesis, purgation occurs after a fortnight; thereafter, a non-unctuous enema (nirūhaṇa) is administered after a fortnight.
One who has received a non-unctuous enema may receive an unctuous enema (anvāsya) immediately, while one whose bowels have been purified by purgation may do so after seven nights.
Just as a cloth removes the dye from water mixed with safflower and other substances,
so does enema (basti) extract impurities from the body once it has been softened.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter.
Now begins the twenty-ninth chapter.
29.1: Hereafter, we shall explain the chapter titled "The Procedure for Nasal Administration" (Nasyavidhi).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:
"Medicine administered through the nose is called *nasya*."
AS.Sū.29.2 It receives the designations "nasal drops" (nāvana) and "nasal therapy" (nastaḥkarma),
for the nose is indeed the gateway to the head.

Therein, the administered medicine, having reached and pervaded the channels, the *śṛṅgāṭaka*, and the head, as well as the openings of the vessels of the eyes, ears, throat, and so forth, quickly extracts from the upper part of the body the entire collection of morbid humors (*doṣa*)—which have ascended above the clavicle and are firmly attached like the fibers of a *muñja* reed—thereby removing all pathological conditions.
That purgative therapy is threefold: nourishing (*bṛṃhaṇa*), pacifying (*śamana*), and evacuating (*virecana*).

For those [patients], purgation of the head (śirovirecana) should be administered with a sharp unctuous substance or with drugs proven effective for head-purgation, prepared with their decoctions, powders, or fresh juices; or else, they should be applied as appropriate, mixed with liquids and fine pastes, along with honey, rock salt, fermented liquors (āsava), bile, or urine, as specifically prescribed for conditions such as heaviness, swelling, coating, itching, stiffness, excessive lacrimation, suppuration, salivation, bad taste, anorexia, hoarseness of voice, worms, catarrh, epilepsy, loss of the sense of smell, tumors, warts, ringworm, urticaria, and other disorders born of phlegm (śleṣman) located above the clavicles.
In that regard, oleation (sneha) is indicated for those who are fearful, impotent, emaciated, or delicate;

while the drying therapies (śoṣa) are indicated for those afflicted by throat diseases, disorders of the three humors (sannipāta), fever, excessive sleep, mental derangement, worms, or poison, as well as for those with secretions, snakebites, or loss of consciousness.

When those very [conditions] involve excessive doshas and require rapid action, a powder applied to the tip of the nose becomes even more intensely stimulating. For nourishing treatments (*bṛṃhaṇa*) in cases arising from Vāta— such as *sūryāvarta*, *ardhāvabhedaka*, head diseases caused by parasites, contraction of the eyes, twitching, timira, difficulty in waking, toothache, earache, ringing in the ears, dryness of the nose and mouth, obstruction of speech, impairment of the voice, torticollis (*manyāroga*), facial paralysis (*apatānaka*), hemiplegia (*apabāhuka*), insomnia, and so forth— one should employ unctuous and sweet substances processed with them, as well as appropriate prescribed fats, exudates, and the blood and meat-juices of animals from arid lands (*dhanva*).

The pacification [of disorders] such as wrinkles, gray hair, baldness, severe redness, rashes, freckles, dark spots, and internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta), and so forth, should be performed with unctuous substances, medicinal juices, and the like, as prescribed for each specific case; or, when the *doṣas* are in equilibrium, with *aṇutaila* mixed with milk and water.
In that regard, oleation (sneha) is of two kinds according to the difference in dosage:
enema (marśa).
A paste (kalka) administered through the nose as a purgative, a laxative, or a pacifier is termed an *avapīḍa*; however, a powder for purging administered in this manner is called a *pradhamana*.
The remainder, which is an ointment for the nose, is designated as an *avapīḍaka*.
Others maintain that the juice squeezed out from medicinal herbs that have been ground into a paste is called *avapīḍa*;
furthermore, when this is sharp, it has the specific designation of *śirovirecana* (head-purgative).
Likewise, others say that all purgatives may be administered as a nasal medication (*nasya*).
Because it shares the common property of being an immediate purgative of phlegm (śleṣman),
the procedure for Aṇutaila is now stated.

As for the procedure for *aṇutaila*: one should cook oil—or ghee, if the humors (*doṣa*) are dominated by pitta—with eight times the quantity of water and six times the quantity of milk, along with well-ground pastes of mañjiṣṭhā, madhuka, prapauṇḍarīka, jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, the two types of kākolī, payasyā, sārivā, anantā, nīlotpala, añjana, rāsnā, viḍaṅga, taṇḍula, madhuparṇī, śrāvaṇī, medā, kākanāsā, sarala, sāla, bhadradāru, and candana.

Alternatively, one should boil sandalwood, agallochum, *patra*, *dārvī*, cinnamon bark, *madhuka*, the two types of *balā*, *bilva*, blue lotus, lotus filaments, *prapauṇḍarīka*, *viḍaṅga*, *uśīra*, *hrīvera*, wild cinnamon bark, *mustā*, *sārivā*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, the two types of *aṃśumatī*, *jīvantī*, *devadāru*, *surabhi*, and *śatāvarī* in a divine liquid ten times their quantity until only one-tenth remains as a decoction; then, one should prepare oil with an equal portion of that decoction and one-tenth part of the decoction’s weight.
Furthermore, during this tenth boiling, one should add goat’s milk equal in measure to the oil.

This *aṇutaila* as well, by virtue of its specific qualities, is superior to the former [in that it] strengthens the sense organs, is beneficial for the hair, skin, and throat, is nourishing, bulk-promoting, and destroys the three *doṣas*. Those who are unfit for [the administration of] oil are: one who has just eaten a meal, one who has consumed fats, wine, or poison, one who has drunk water, one desiring to drink, one who has bathed the head, one desiring to bathe, one from whom blood has flowed due to venesection, one who has urinated or evacuated, one who has undergone emesis, purgation, or enema therapy, a pregnant woman, a woman recently delivered, one suffering from acute coryza, dyspnea, or cough, and even during non-seasonal bad weather.
In that regard, the dosha provoked by nasal medication (nasya) in one who has already eaten may obstruct the upward channels and produce vomiting, dyspnea, cough, and coryza;
in those who have consumed oily substances or are desirous of drinking, it produces discharge from the eyes, nose, and mouth, as well as amblyopia (timira) and diseases of the head;

and in one who has bathed the head, it produces pain in the head, eyes, and ears, diseases of the throat, chronic rhinitis (pīnasa), stiffness of the jaw and neck (hanu-manyā-stambha), facial paralysis (ardita), and tremors of the head.

For one desiring to bathe, [suppression of the urge causes] numbness and heaviness of the head, loss of appetite, catarrh, and discharge of blood; for one who has urinated or defecated, it causes emaciation, loss of appetite, and loss of digestive fire— these being the disorders arising from excessively suppressing the natural urges.
For one who has been struck, it causes more intense pain;
for those who have undergone emesis and other such procedures, it results in dyspnea, cough, loss of the senses, heaviness of the head, itching, and disorders caused by worms.
In a pregnant woman, it may cause aversion to food, fever, fainting, and hemicrania, while the offspring may be born deformed, with impaired senses, or afflicted by insanity or epilepsy.
The defects mentioned for a woman who has suffered blood loss during childbirth also apply here;
furthermore, due to the obstruction of the channels in acute coryza, there arise malignant coryza, hair loss, lice, itching, eczema,
and an increase in the severity of diseases such as dyspnea and cough.

In unseasonable weather or during foul days, due to sudden cold, there arise headache, shivering, a sense of heaviness, itching and inflammation of the palate and eyes, stiffness of the neck (manyā), throat diseases, catarrh, and facial eruptions (arūṣikā). In these conditions, one should administer oleation, sudation, nasal drops (nasya), facial plasters, affusions, sharp pressed-out juices (avapīḍa), medicinal smoke, gargles, and so forth, after considering the respective sites of the affliction and the aggravation of the specific doṣas.
Specifically for a pregnant woman suffering from dryness during nasal therapy (nasya), she should drink milk boiled with *varṣābhū*, *kākolī*, and *kapikacchu*;
or alternatively, milk boiled with *balā*, *vidārī*, *aṃśumatī*, and *medā*.

Likewise, clarified butter (*havis*) cooked with these same herbs, or unctuous substances (*sneha*) prepared with Vata-alleviating drugs, should be employed for head-pouch enemas (*śirobasti*) and ear-filling treatments (*karṇapūraṇa*).
And all nourishing food and drink—
even when one has already eaten— should be considered for those suffering from urgent diseases;
however, the measure of a *marśa* is a drop that falls from the two joints of the index finger when dipped into and withdrawn from clarified butter or similar substances.
AS.Sū.29.12: These eighteen drops— ten, eight, and six— are the superior, middling, and inferior measures of decoctions and the like, consisting of eight, six, and four [parts] respectively.

Regarding *pradhamana* (blowing [medicine] into the nose), it should be administered repeatedly, as required by the nature of the *doṣas*, using a tube with two openings six finger-breadths long, until the air impelled from the mouth reaches the throat.

(AS.Sū.29.13) Now, for a man fit for *nasya* (nasal therapy), whose vigor is unimpeded, whose internal and external orifices have been cleansed, whose head has been lubricated and fomented, who is not excessively hungry, whose channels have been purified by the practice of medicinal smoking (*prāyogika-dhūma*), and who lies supine on a well-spread bed in a windless place with his head slightly elevated and his feet raised, with his hands and feet extended—one should repeatedly foment the region above the clavicle with the heat of the palms.

Then, one-third of the medicinal substance to be administered—placed in a shell made of gold, silver, or copper—should be heated with warm water. While the patient’s head is slightly inclined forward, the practitioner should press the left thumb and little finger against the base of the nose; cover the eyes with a fourfold cloth; lift the tip of the nose with the middle fingers; and, closing each nostril alternately with the index and ring fingers, pour the liquid continuously into the other nostril using the right hand, either through a tube or a cotton swab.

In cases of diseases caused by wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (kapha), [the enema should be administered] respectively in the afternoon, at midday, and in the forenoon; in cases of excessive salivation, drooling, sleepiness, delirium, grinding of the teeth, choking, difficult opening of the eyes, fetid breath, ringing in the ears, thirst, headache, dyspnea, cough, and insomnia, it should be administered at night.

For one in good health, the five therapeutic procedures (*pañcakarma*) should be administered following the enema (*basti*), specifically at midday during the cold season, in the forenoon during autumn and spring, in the afternoon during summer, and when the sun is visible during the rainy season.

Furthermore, they should not be given in deficient or excessive doses, nor all at once, nor while the substance is excessively hot or cold, nor to one with the head excessively raised or bent, nor to one whose limbs and body parts are contracted. *AS.Sū.29.15*
In that case, if one excites a mild morbid humor (doṣa) but does not eliminate it,
it will cause heaviness, anorexia, cough, excessive salivation, rhinitis, vomiting, and diseases of the throat.
The defects of excessive administration of *atiyoga* (over-application) include:
when administered all at once, it causes excessive oleation (*utsnehanam*), headache, catarrh, nasal discharge, and obstruction of the breath;
whereas if it is excessively hot, it causes burning sensations, suppuration, fever, hemorrhaging, headache, weakness of vision, fainting, and vertigo.
Excessive coldness [of the nozzle] causes those very same defects—

fainting, numbness, itching, burning, and fever— to arise in those with diminished humors even when their heads are held too high, because the head is not properly reached; and in those with excessively lowered heads, they arise due to traveling too far [into the passage].

If, while the patient's limbs are contracted, the morbid humors (doṣas) fail to properly pervade the vessels, causing agitation, pain, or stiffness; or if, during the administration of the nasal medication (nasya), fainting occurs due to the intensity of the drug or its unwholesome nature—then one should sprinkle cold water on the body, excluding the head.
Furthermore, while the nasal medication is being poured, one should not engage in anger, laughter, speech, trembling, or sneezing.
For indeed, there arises the occurrence of headache, catarrh, cough, blurred vision, baldness, graying hair, freckles, moles, warts, and impurities of the face; however,
as soon as the nasal medication has been administered, one should massage the ears, forehead, scalp, cheeks, neck, shoulders, hands, and soles of the feet at ease.
One should expectorate slowly,
neither swallowing nor inhaling; one should spit out the medicine from both the left and right sides along with the phlegm, for if it is swallowed, it would diminish the digestive fire.
And one should increase the [expectoration of] morbid humors by spitting from one side; all the vessels are properly pervaded by the medicine.

One should foment this patient repeatedly until the appearance of the medicine, but one should not pull it out; he should spit, and then in the same manner, one should pour the second portion, and likewise the third, according to the strength of the humors and other factors.
In the case of an avapīḍa used for purgation, however, one should subsequently sprinkle oil after considering the strength of the doṣas.
Once the nasal medication has ceased its action, the patient—now awake and lying on his back—should be kept there for about a hundred words' time.
Then, to pacify the remaining aggravated doṣas, one should have him inhale a purgative smoke as appropriate, or hold warm water gargles (gaṇḍūṣa).
Then one should prescribe for him the regimen prescribed for oleation therapy,
and he should avoid drinking excessively liquid substances;
furthermore, on the third day, one should administer nasal drops and perform bloodletting.

In cases of hiccups, impairment of voice, stiffness of the neck, facial paralysis, or when the head is afflicted by disorders of Vāta and the like, one should administer this [oil] daily in the morning and evening, or at both times, for five, seven, or nine days, or until the proper application is achieved (AS.Sū.29.17). When the head has been properly oleated or purged, there occurs easy inhalation and exhalation, sneezing, sleep, and awakening, as well as clarity of the head and the sense organs.

There is also the alleviation of the aforementioned diseases; however, regarding deficient (ayoga) and excessive (atiyoga) administration, one should treat the respective disorders of vāta and kapha according to their own specific [therapeutic] principles.

Furthermore, regarding the other previously mentioned complications [AS.Sū.29.18], massage (pratimarśa), however, may be administered even to those who are emaciated, wounded, thirsty, or suffering from dryness of the mouth, as well as to the elderly, children, the timid, and the delicate, and even during unseasonable rain or foul weather. [AS.Sū.29.18]
However, it should not be used in those with malignant catarrh, excessive morbidity, worms in the head, those who have drunk alcohol, or those with weak hearing;
for in these cases, because the humors are aggravated, that much [treatment] causes further provocation of the humors.
There are fifteen times [for its application], and their qualities are as follows:

When administered in the morning after one has eaten, it results in purification of the channels, lightness of the head, and clarity of the mind; at the end of voiding feces and urine, of anointing the head, or of gargling, it results in clarity of vision;
and at the end of cleaning the teeth, it results in firmness of the teeth and a pleasant fragrance.

At the end of travel, physical exertion, or sexual intercourse, there is the destruction of fatigue, exhaustion, perspiration, and stiffness; at the end of daytime sleep, there is the removal of residual drowsiness and heaviness as well as clarity of mind;
and at the end of excessive laughter, there is the pacification of wind (vāta).
At the conclusion of vomiting, there is the removal of phlegm accumulated in the channels;
at the end of the day, there is purification of the channels as well as pleasant sleep and awakening.
And on this point, it is said:
The measure for the massage is considered to be two drops;
or it may be a single drop, by which no agitation arises in one who is not already agitated.
When phlegm has been expectorated, or where oil is not directly perceived,
nasal therapy (*nasya*) should not be administered to those under seven years of age nor to those over eighty years.
There is no smoke until the eighteenth year; no morsel of food until the forty-fifth;
no purification until the hundredth; and none after the seventieth has passed.
From birth until death, the *pratimarśa* enema is recommended, just like the *basti*;
for by its constant use, it produces qualities similar to those of the *marśa*.
In this case, there is no restriction, nor is there any fear of complications as with *marśa*; indeed,
oil alone is recommended for nasal administration through constant practice.
Because the head is a seat of phlegm (śleṣman), unctuous substances (sneha) are [indicated] for a healthy person, and no others; [furthermore,
there is] the quality of acting quickly or slowly, and the state of being superior or inferior in quality.
If there were no distinction between *marśa* and *pratimarśa*,
then who would resort to *marśa*, which involves complications and dangers?
[The other two types of treatment] are called *acchapāna* and *vicāra*, while staying in a small hut (*kuṭī*) and exposure to wind and sun (*vātātapasthiti*).
And one should prescribe an enema of the same measure as the after-drink;
thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter.
Now begins the thirtieth chapter. Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "The Procedure for Smoking."
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and others:

"Smoking (dhūma) is employed for the pacification of diseases of the wind and phlegm located above the clavicle, such as pain in the head, eyes, and ears; ophthalmia (abhiṣyanda); heaviness; hemicrania (ardhāvabhedaka); catarrh (pīnasa), cough, and dyspnea; bad taste in the mouth, excessive salivation, and hoarseness; foul-smelling breath, nasal disorders, and mouth diseases; hiccup; throat diseases and toothache; weakness, anorexia, lockjaw, torticollis, worms, itching, pallor, defects of the hair, excessive sneezing, drowsiness, excessive sleep, and snoring. (AS.Sū.30.2)
Likewise, for the purpose of nourishing and clarifying the head, skull, sense organs, and mind,
even a substance prepared from cool ingredients becomes incompatible with pitta and blood due to its heat resulting from contact with fire.
It is of three types:
pacifying (śamana), nourishing (bṛṃhaṇa), and purifying (śodhana);
likewise, there are those that cure cough, induce emesis, and serve as fumigation for wounds.
In this context, "śamana" (pacifying) is a synonym for "prāyogika" (preparatory), "madhyama" (moderate),
"bṛṃhaṇa" (nourishing), "snehana" (oleating), and "mṛdu" (mild);
whereas "śodhana" (purifying) is a synonym for "virecana" (purgative) and "tīkṣṇa" (sharp).

AS.Sū.30.4 However, those for whom smoke is contraindicated are: one who has undergone purgation or received an enema; one who has stayed awake all night; one whose head has been injured; those who have consumed curds, sour milk, milk, wine, fats, gruel, poison, or water; one who has eaten fish; and those suffering from anemia, urinary disorders, abdominal enlargement, flatulence, upward-moving wind (udāvarta), blindness (timira), Rohiṇikā, or hemorrhaging (raktapitta).

For these, as well as others, very hot smoke produces vertigo, fever, headache, impairment of the sense organs, dryness and inflammation of the palate, a sensation of fuming, vomiting, fainting, hemorrhaging, facial paralysis (ardita), or even death.
Furthermore, in other cases as well,

having identified pitta as being combined with either vāta or kapha, one should administer, according to the specific condition, ghee, decoctions, potions, nasal drops, mouth-washes, ointments, collyriums, and affusions— whether oleaginous, dry, or cooling.

By this, the remedies for all injuries caused by smoke are explained. Specifically, however, when smoke enters all the channels, there occur heat, flatulence, eye diseases, dyspnea, cough, catarrh, weakness of the limbs and voice, and acid eructations.

In that case, the use of ghee, milk, sugarcane juice, grapes, and sugar is indicated; emesis should be induced with similar substances, as well as pungent and bitter agents used as nasal drops (nasya) and mouth-rinses (gaṇḍūṣa).

There are eight times for the administration of the habitual dose (prāyogika): at night, after voiding urine, after voiding feces, after brushing the teeth, after sweating, after eating, and after surgical procedures.

AS.Sū.30.7 There are eleven [occasions for cleansing] with earth: after sneezing, sexual intercourse, laughing, sitting for a long time, yawning, urination, defecation, cleaning the teeth, sipping water, applying a poultice, and at the conclusion of surgical procedures.

For one who is sharp [of constitution], there are five times for [administering] nasal drops, collyrium, emesis, bathing, and sleeping at the end of the day; for during these times, there is an aggravation of *vāta* and *kapha*. As for the nozzle (*netra*), it should be made from the materials used for enema nozzles, shaped like a cow’s tail, with a circumference at its tip and base equal to that of the little finger and the thumb respectively. Its aperture should be such that it allows the passage of a *rājamāṣa* bean and a smoking wick (*dhūmavarti*). It should be straight, provided with three sheaths, smooth, and containing a loose internal rod (*śalākā*). For pacification and other treatments, one should make it forty, thirty-two, or twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length, according to the patient's own finger measurement.
For cough and emesis, [the nozzle] should be ten finger-breadths long;
for fumigating wounds, it should be eight finger-breadths long, with a circumference like a pea and a channel as wide as a horse gram.

For in this way, smoke that has issued from afar, by cutting off the eyelid and adhering slowly due to its thinness, becomes non-irritating to the eye (AS.Sū.30.9). However, in the case of *kāsaghna* and other [medicines], in the absence of a tube, one should apply a tube made from any one of the following: reed, bamboo, castor-oil plant, or similar materials (AS.Sū.30.9).

AS.Sū.30.10 Having prepared a smooth paste of the appropriate medicinal substances for fumigation in a quantity of one *akṣa*, one should soak a twelve-finger-long reed (*iṣīkā*) in water for a day and night and then coat it with the paste.

Therein, having fashioned a wick (*varti*) nine fingers long, five layers thick, as stout as a thumb, with a barley-corn diameter in the middle, dried in the shade, and with the central reed removed, one should dip it in oil, ignite it over charcoal embers, place it into the opening at the base of the nozzle, and administer it for drinking as required.

Then, one fit for the practice of smoke-inhalation (*dhūma*), being cheerful and sitting upright, having previously regulated his inhalation and exhalation, with lips and teeth parted and the gaze fixed on the bridge of the nose, should alternately close one nostril and draw [the air] in through the other,
then expel it through the mouth; but when using the mouth, he should do so only through the mouth.
Not out of a desire for destruction, nor out of fear of obstructing one's vision;
therein, the preparatory [mind] occurs for two or three breaths and three cycles.
When the *doṣa* has risen above the throat, one should first drink through the nose and then through the mouth;
however, when it is in the throat, one should first drink through the mouth and then [through the nose].
One should drink this twice during the day and night.

The unctuous [nasal medication] should be administered three or four inhalations at a time, as many times as necessary until the discharge of mucus occurs, once every day and night. The sharp [nasal medication] should be administered through the nostrils alone, four inhalations at a time, as many times as necessary until lightness of the channels is achieved.
Likewise, three or four times a day and night,
they say that there is therein inhalation, exhalation, and retention.

AS.Sū.30.15 For the cough-destroying powder or pill, one should place it into a well-positioned shallow bowl filled with smokeless, glowing, steady charcoal; having covered it with another bowl that has a hole made in its top, and having placed a tube at that opening, one should inhale the smoke through the mouth alone.
When it reaches the chest, one should exhale it through the mouth alone.
When the smoke has subsided, one should again inhale and drink [the medicated oil] until the elimination of the *doṣas* is achieved or until lightness [of the body] occurs;
likewise, for the purpose of emesis, one should drink a very thick *kṛsarā* and then drink [the oil].
In the same manner, one should fumigate the ulcer for the sake of clarity and to alleviate moisture and pain;
if the fuming is not applied, there will be an increase in the disease due to the provocation of the *doṣas*.
Regarding excessive application, it has been stated previously;
and there is also this [verse]:
Purification of the heart, throat, and sense organs, lightness of the head,
and tranquility are the signs of one who has properly drunk [the emetic] for the aforementioned diseases.
In the combination of vāta and kapha, pacifying (śamana) medicated smoking is recommended for the maintenance of health;
in the case of vāta alone, nourishing (bṛṃhaṇa) smoking is praised, while in the case of kapha, purificatory (saṃśodhana) smoking is indicated.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter.
Now begins the thirty-first chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the procedure for gargling and related treatments (gaṇḍūṣādividhi).
"Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:
'The gargle (gaṇḍūṣa) is of four kinds.'"
Oleaginous, pacifying, purifying, and healing— of these, the first three respectively destroy diseases caused by vāta, pitta, and kapha.

*ropaṇa*, *āsyavraṇaghna*, *śamana*, *stambhana*, *prasādana*, and *nirvāpaṇa* are synonyms [of healing]. Among these, an unctuous substance (*sneha*) prepared or combined with sweet, sour, salty, and hot medicinal herbs, which is not excessively hot— such as meat broth, sesame paste water, or milk— is *snaihika* (unctuous).

The pacifying [therapy] is performed with bitter, astringent, sweet, and cold substances, such as decoctions of *paṭola*, *ariṣṭa*, *jambu*, mango, and *mālatī* sprouts, as well as blue lotus (*utpala*), licorice (*madhuka*), black water, honey, milk, sugarcane juice, ghee, and so forth.

The purifying [therapy] is performed with head-evacuants (*śirovirecana*) that are pungent, sour, salty, and hot, stirred into a paste dissolved in any one of fermented gruel (*śukta*), wine, fermented rice-water (*dhānyāmla*), or urine.
Healing, however, is achieved by means of astringent, sweet, and cold substances, as well as those specifically prescribed for each case;
moreover—
In cases of hypersensitivity of the teeth, looseness of the teeth, and wind-type (vātika) diseases of the mouth,
lukewarm or cold water mixed with ground sesame paste is beneficial; furthermore,
oil or meat broth should always be used for holding in the mouth as a gargle (gaṇḍūṣa).
In a suppurating ulcer associated with burning from alkali, in a wound caused by a foreign body,
in cases of poisoning, and in burns from alkaline substances or fire, clarified butter or milk should be applied.
Holding honey as a mouth-rinse produces clarity in the mouth, heals wounds in the oral cavity, and alleviates burning sensations and thirst. (AS.Sū.31.6–7)
Fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla) destroys bad taste in the mouth, impurities, and foul odors. That same liquid, when cooled and made salt-free, is an excellent remedy for dryness of the mouth.
AS.Sū.31.8 A gargle of quick-acting alkaline water breaks up the accumulation of phlegm.

AS.Sū.31.9 Then, sitting comfortably in a windless place with sunlight, being single-minded and having sweated and massaged the regions of the throat, cheeks, and forehead, one should hold [the medicine]— either a liquid dose filling half, a third, or a fourth of the mouth, or a paste the size of a jujube fruit— without swallowing it, with the face slightly tilted upward.
In the case of the "mouthful" (kavala) method, one should move it alternately between the two cheeks and the throat;
this indeed is the distinction between the mouthful (kavala) and the gargle (gaṇḍūṣa).
That measure which is moved about in the mouth is known as a *kavala*;
however, that measure which is not moved about is proclaimed a *gaṇḍūṣa*.
Furthermore, one should perform sudation and massage;
thus provoked, the phlegm moves toward the mouth.
It should be retained for as long as there is fullness of the cheeks with phlegm, discharge from the nose and eyes, or until the medicine is not overwhelmed by phlegm;
in this manner, one should hold three, five, or seven mouthfuls,
or until the signs of having properly inhaled the smoke have arisen.
One should recognize its proper application by its own natural state; its deficient application by dullness, lack of relish for tastes, lack of knowledge, excessive salivation, and coating;

and its excessive application by mouth-dryness, burning sensation, fatigue, loss of appetite, fluidity in the heart region, hoarseness of voice, and ringing in the ears. One should treat these conditions according to their respective requirements.
Pratisāraṇa, however, is of three kinds,
consisting of substances prescribed for gargling.
Rasa-kriyā, kalka, and cūrṇa should be applied appropriately in cases such as abhiṣyanda, adhimantha, and galaśuṇḍikā; however,
from excessive rubbing, complications such as ulceration, burning, inflammation, suppuration, and dryness may arise.
Facial ointment (mukhālepa) is also of three types: that which subdues the *doṣas*, that which neutralizes poison, and that which improves the complexion.
It is of three measurements, with a thickness of one-fourth, one-third, or half a finger-breadth.
One should not speak excessively, nor indulge in laughter, anger, weeping, eating, fire, sunlight, or sleeping during the day with an unwashed face,
for fear of itching, dryness of the skin, catarrh, and impairment of vision; furthermore,
one who is becoming dehydrated must not be neglected.
For dryness indeed vitiates the skin;
one should remove it by moistening it, and at the conclusion of the application, one should anoint the face.
However, it should not be administered to those suffering from insomnia, lack of appetite, nasal catarrh, or inflammation of the throat.
When properly applied, it pacifies wrinkles, gray hair, cataracts, freckles, moles, and other such conditions caused by the passage of time.
Oil for the head, moreover, when applied by one in good health, bestows the strength of vision and a face as beautiful as the *puṇḍarīka* lotus; furthermore, it is divided into four types.
Anointing (abhyaṅga), affusion (pariṣeka), poultice (picu), and enema (vasti) are more effective in that successive order; among these, the nature of anointing and the others is well known.

Regarding the procedure for the head-enema (śirobasti): one should prepare an enema bag that is well-softened, double-mouthed, the size of the head, reaching up to the ears, and twelve finger-breadths in width.

AS.Sū.31.16 Now, for one whose body is purified, either in the evening or at night, having been well-anointed and fomented, seated on a stool with a support at the level of the knees, one should bind a cloth band smeared on both sides with a smooth, three-finger-wide strip of very fine bean flour that has been freshly moistened with warm water, applied to the hairline.

Then, having placed the bladder over it, having secured the base of the bladder firmly with a strong cloth-wick, and having made it non-leaking by applying a paste of black gram (māṣa), one should pour in a well-heated, medicated oil—prepared as is beneficial for the specific disease, humor (doṣa), and affected tissue (dūṣya)—until it reaches one finger-breadth above the hairline.
It should be retained until there is discharge from the ears, mouth, or nose, or until the pain subsides;
especially in disorders born of Vāta, it may be retained for ten thousand mātrās.
Eight [applications] are for disorders born of pitta and blood,
six for those born of kapha, and one thousand for the act of curing disease.

Then, once the oil has been removed, one should release the enema and gently massage the head, shoulders, neck, back, forehead, and other areas. After the patient has bathed with warm water, one should feed them a suitable meal and instruct them in the conduct prescribed for oleation therapy.

In this manner, one should apply [the treatment] for three, five, or seven days; and regarding this, it is said in the *Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha*, Sūtrasthāna 31.17: "In cases of dryness, itching, impurities, and so forth, an oil massage (*abhyaṅga*) should be employed there."

In cases of arūṃṣikā (scaly patches on the scalp), itching of the head, burning sensation, suppuration, and ulcers, however, [the treatments are] affusion, cotton pads, hair-cutting, incision, and fumigation. (AS.Sū.31.17–18)
In cases of paralysis of the eyes, numbness, affliction from sleeplessness, dryness of the nose and mouth, blindness, and severe diseases of the head, an enema (basti) should be administered.

Oil for the head (mūrdhataila) conquers the graying, yellowing, and flaking of the hair, as well as wind-related diseases of the head; it produces clarity of the sense organs and strength in the voice, jaw, and head.
One should maintain the filling in the ear while massaging the root of the ear;
pain will persist until softness occurs after a hundred measures, provided there is no sensation.
The time it takes for the tip of the hand to circle the right knee-joint,
equal to the duration of a blink of an eye, is known as one *mātrā*.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter.
Now begins the thirty-second chapter.
32.1: Hereafter, we shall explain the chapter on the procedure for eye-drops and collyrium.
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:
"The application of eye-drops (*āścyotana*) is the primary treatment for all diseases of the eye."

AS.Sū.32.2 Furthermore, by means of a preparation of various substances, an ointment for the eyelashes— which destroys redness, tearing, itching, pain, burning, piercing, suppuration, swelling, and itching—
should be applied to the eyes while avoiding the eyelashes; it possesses these very qualities when prepared in this manner.
Furthermore, that which is known as the "cat-like" [state] is the improper time for those two:
namely, the night.

As for the time: it is at the moment when all great sensations arise, or when one is lying in a sheltered place protected from the wind; having cleansed the eye and placed a vessel at the outer corner, one should open the eye with the left hand and, using a cotton wick attached to a mother-of-pearl shell with the right hand, pour eight, ten, or twelve drops near the inner corner, two finger-breadths away.
In this way, by not letting the drops fall directly onto the eye, no afflictions such as passion (rāga) will arise from the striking of the eye.
One should cleanse the instilled drops with a soft cloth or with another cloth soaked in warm water; in cases of wind and phlegm, one should apply fomentation,
and the eye-drops for those two conditions should be lukewarm.
It is very cooling for pitta, blood disorders, and poisons;
