however, one should not apply it if it is excessively sharp, hot, cold, too abundant, too scanty, or if it has not been properly strained.
Or, if it is excessively sharp or hot, it causes burning sensations, redness, suppuration, and weakness of vision.
Excessive coldness causes stiffness, lacrimation, friction, and pricking pain;
excessive [cold] causes astringent-ness of the eyelids, contraction, throbbing, opening [of the eyes], intolerance of wind, and roughness of the skin;
and insufficient quantity does not bring about the pacification of disease.

It prevents the flow of tears and relieves the pain of eye-grinding; furthermore, medicine applied to the eyes, having traveled through the sockets, joints, veins, *śṛṅgāṭaka*, and the channels of the nose and mouth, turns back the humors that have moved upward.

When, in cases of eye diseases arising from bile (*pitta*), phlegm (*śleṣman*), or blood (*śoṇita*), the signs of ripeness (*pakvaliṅga*) are observed in one whose eyes have been purified by cleansing treatments through the thickening, sliminess, excessive itching, swelling, flaccidity, and loss of color of the eye-secretion (*dūṣikā*),
then collyrium (*añjana*) should be applied for a disease localized in the eye itself.
It should not be done when the force of the humors (doṣa) has arisen, nor when the humors have not been eliminated;
for in those cases, due to the agitation of the humors, there is an increase of passion and other afflictions, as well as the onset of eye diseases such as timira.
That [treatment] is of four kinds: scraping (*lekhana*), healing (*ropaṇa*), oleation (*snehana*), and clarification (*prasādana*).
Among these, scraping is performed with the five tastes beginning with sour for conditions such as *śuklārma* (white pterygium).
In cases of abhiṣyanda (ophthalmia), healing is achieved with bitter and astringent substances combined with fats;
in cases of vāta-timira (blindness caused by vāta) and similar conditions, oleation is performed using ghee and other such substances.

At the end of excessive secretions (abhiṣyanda), one should apply clear, cool, and unctuous [medicines]; likewise, for vision impaired by solar eclipses, lightning, thunderbolts, the falling of meteors, or the sight of terrifying beings such as piśācas, and for those with normal vision, one should apply clarifying [therapies].
Furthermore, a soothing powder, when applied to an eye inflamed by sharp collyrium, receives the designation of a counter-collyrium (*pratyañjana*);
or else, collyrium is of six kinds according to the distinction of its counter-agents (*pratirasabheda*).
The faculty is indeed of two kinds: sharp and dull;
however, the conceptualization is of three kinds.

The bolus (piṇḍa), the medicinal extract (rasakriyā), and the powder (cūrṇa) are, in order from first to last, more potent; therefore, one should employ them respectively for diseases that are strong, moderate, and weak.
Among these, the bolus for a sharp (tīkṣṇa) medicine should be the size of a hareṇu seed.
The dose of *rasakriyā* is one part of *viḍaṅga*, twice that amount of powdered clay,
and two *śalākā*s [of the resulting mixture].
For a soft [substance], one should use a three-pronged instrument; however, for a golden vessel, one should use a sweet [instrument].
Sourness shines forth in salt made from sheep's horn;
bitterness [shines forth] in [salt] in a bronze vessel.
In one made of vaidūrya or stone, it is pungent;
in one made of copper or iron, it is astringent;
and in one made of any of the following—nalada, plakṣa, lotus, crystal, or conch—it is cold.
Thus it possesses unimpaired qualities.

Furthermore, for the purpose of rubbing the wick, there is a grinding stone that is very smooth, with a hollowed center, non-emitting [of dust], five finger-breadths in length, and three finger-breadths in width.
There are also five applicator-sticks made of gold, silver, copper, iron, and wood, as well as the fingers.
In that regard, for the first [type of collyrium], namely the soothing, lubricating, and emollient types, the medium dose is used; for the scraping type, the medium dose is also used.
In the final stage of healing,
because of its softness, the finger is most important here; therefore, it alone should be employed when the eye is painful.

The remaining [teeth] should be ten finger-breadths long, as thick as a *rājamāṣa* bean, very smooth, slender in the middle, bud-shaped at their two ends, and as round as a *kalāya* pea. Now, collyrium (*añjana*) should be applied twice daily at a time when it is neither too cold, nor too hot, nor cloudy, nor windy.
Likewise, one should [apply it] constantly, or not at all;
and when the eye is diseased, first on the affected one and afterwards on the other.
Otherwise, when the eye is constricted by irritation from the collyrium, the medicine will not properly enter within;
likewise, in cases of extreme cold and so forth, there is an increase in the disorder due to the provocation of the respective humors (doṣas).

One should not apply [collyrium] to those who are angry, frightened, apprehensive, grieving, exhausted, or who have just eaten, vomited, smoked, drunk alcohol, received an enema, or been purged; nor to those who have stayed awake at night, whose natural urges are suppressed, who have wept, or who are thirsty; nor to those suffering from fever, vomiting, pain, fatigue, eye disease, head injury, or headache; nor to those who have just bathed their heads or when the sun has not yet risen.

For if applied to these, the collyrium may rise as steam and produce agitation, tearing, pain, turbidity, redness, discharge, pricking, difficulty opening the eyes, swelling, discharge of semen, cataracts, and other such ailments.

Then, having sat down comfortably while the patient is likewise seated, one should lift the upper eyelid with the left thumb and apply collyrium from below the black portion of the eye, starting from the inner corner (kanīnakā) as far as the outer corner (apāṅga). It should be applied in quantity that is neither too little nor too much, and it must not be excessively sharp, clear, thick, rough, rapid, slow, applied with a sidelong glance, trembling, rubbing, or interrupted.
In the case of powder collyrium (cūrṇa), however, one should perform repeated strokes back and forth.
Otherwise, there would be the production of passion, tears, semen, and so forth; therefore, following the collyrium, one should move the eye slowly inward without opening it,
and in this way, one follows the eye [of the deity].
One should move the eyelids slightly,
but one must not perform sudden opening, squeezing, or washing,
for fear of the obstruction caused by morbid humors aggravated by tears.
Moreover,
when the eye is free from the agitation caused by medicinal applications and has become tranquil;

Then, one should wash [the eyes] with water appropriate for the disease, the bodily humor, and the season; subsequently, with the right thumb, one should wash the right eye while wearing one's clothes.
Having grasped [the eye] on the upper eyelid, one should gently cleanse it all around;
in this manner, the right eye should be cleansed with the right thumb, and likewise the left eye.

If collyrium is applied to the eyelids, it may cause disorders; otherwise, it will produce diseases. Therefore, at the conclusion of using sharp collyrium, one should have the patient inhale medicinal smoke.
If itching, heaviness, or coating should occur after the application of collyrium, one should again apply a sharp collyrium or smoke;
this same procedure is the remedy for the symptoms of eyes that have been excessively purged.

From excessive purgation, there arise exhaustion, burning sensations, pricking pain, colic, stiffness, friction, lacrimation, severe awakening of the eyes, turbidity of the visual pathways, headache, and weakness of vision; in such cases, cold eye-drops, or collyrium applied as an antidote (pratyañjana),
lead to the alleviation of the respective disorders through proper purgation.
And there is the capacity for the opening and closing of the eyes, and for enduring wind and sun;
and in this regard,
one should likewise contemplate the applications [of treatment] such as healing ointments and so forth.
And one should treat those [afflictions] according to the emergence of their specific doshas.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter.
Now begins the thirty-third chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "The Procedure for Tarpaṇa and Puṭapāka.
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.

AS.Sū.33.2 When the eye is fatigued, parched, dry, stiff, distorted, sunken, turbid, or obstructed; when the eyelashes are withered; or when it is afflicted by diseases such as difficult opening (*kṛcchronmīla*), protrusion of vessels (*sirōtpāta*), twitching of vessels (*sirāharṣa*), *arjuna*, dryness (*śuṣka*), darkness (*timira*), ophthalmia (*abhiṣyanda*), *adhimantha*, wind from elsewhere (*anyatōvāta*), shifting wind (*vātaparyaya*), dryness with slight swelling (*śuṣkālpasōpha*), and so forth; and when it is devoid of its natural color, tears, and discharge—then one should apply *tarpaṇa* (soothing saturation).
However, it should not be applied when complications have not subsided, nor during extreme cold, heat, rain, or cloudy weather, nor in those for whom nasal therapy (*nasya*) is contraindicated.

Similarly, regarding *puṭapāka* (AS.Sū.33.3): Now, when the eighth part of the day has passed or remains, in a room protected from wind and sunlight and free of smoke, having hung a curtain of either blue or yellow cloth, one who has finished his meal and is lying comfortably on his back should have two circular, non-constricting, even, and well-draining supports made of crushed *māṣa* flour paste, two finger-breadths in height, placed outside the eye sockets. Then, while the eyes are closed, he should pour into them milk, ghee, or the scum of ghee (*sarpirmaṇḍa*) that has been cooked with the appropriate medicinal herbs and dissolved in warm water.

One should count the measures while the patient slowly opens his eyes until the eyelashes and the hairs of the eyebrows are submerged; for disorders arising in the eyelids, one should count a hundred measures; for those arising at the junctions, three hundred; for those arising in the white part (śukla), five hundred; for those arising in the black part (kṛṣṇa), seven hundred; for those arising in the pupil (dṛṣṭi), eight hundred; and for cases of adhimantha, ten thousand.
However, for each disorder, one should apply one thousand [drops] in the case of vāta, six hundred in pitta, five hundred in kapha, and the same amount for the maintenance of health (svasthakarma).
Then, having made an opening at the corner of his eye with a probe, one should let the oil flow into a vessel.

Having removed the supports and cleansed the eye sockets with a paste of barley, one should administer medicated smoke as appropriate to pacify the deranged fat and phlegm; then, after the patient has rinsed his mouth with lukewarm water, one should feed him according to the specific disease,
while he avoids exposure to sunlight, open air, and the sight of bright objects.

By this method, one should administer [the medicine] every other day for vāta, with an interval of one day for raktapitta and pitta, and with an interval of two days for kapha, as well as for those in a healthy state;
for combinations of two doṣas (saṃsarga) and all three doṣas (sannipāta), it should be according to the predominance of the specific doṣa.
In this manner, one should administer it for one day, three days, or five days, or until satiety is reached;

the signs of being satisfied, unsatisfied, or excessively satisfied should be indicated respectively by health, or by disorders of *vāta* and *kapha*. When the saturation has been properly achieved, then one should apply *puṭapāka* in those very same diseases.
It is of three types:
oleating (snehana), scraping (lekhana), and clarifying (prasādana).

AS.Sū.33.7 Therein, one should apply an unctuous (*snehana*) collyrium to a dry eye using the meat, fat, marrow, and lard of animals from marshy or common habitats, as well as with sweet substances ground with milk.

AS.Sū.33.8 One should apply a scraping (*lekhana*) collyrium to an oily eye using the meat and liver of wild animals and birds, along with scraping substances such as pearl, coral, conch-shell, copper, iron, sea-foam, green vitriol (*kāsīsa*), realgar (*srotoja*), rock salt (*saindhava*), and so forth, ground with curd-whey, honey, and flour.
However,

for the purpose of inducing clarity [of the mind], one should use the liver, heart, marrow, and fat of wild animals and birds, along with sweet substances ground with women’s breast milk and clarified butter.
It destroys wind, bile, blood, impaired vision, and ulcers, but it is contraindicated for those with phlegm disorders.

Now, one should take a lump of meat the size of a *bilva* fruit, prepare it as *veśavāra*, mix it with an equal amount of medicinal paste, wrap it sequentially with leaves of castor, *vaṭa*, and blue lotus for the purpose of oleation and so forth, and bind it with either a cord of *kuśa* grass or *muñja* reed.

In this case, having applied a coating of clay two finger-breadths thick, one should cook [the vessel] over wood of any of these—dhava, dhanvana, madhūka, nyagrodha, kāśmarya, rājādana, arjuna, naktamāla, or pāṭalī—or with the dung of a cow or a buffalo.
Once it has reached the color of fire, one should remove it, strip away the clay, threads, and leaves, and squeeze it with a cloth.
With that juice, one should fill the eyes in the evening, like a satiation treatment (tarpaṇa).
One should maintain two hundred measures for oleation, one hundred for scraping, and three hundred for soothing;
the inhalation of smoke is to be performed in the same manner as the heating [of the pipe], with the exception of the soothing [smoke].
The first two types of *puṭapāka* should be lukewarm,
while the clarifying type should be cold; it should be applied for one day, two days, or three days.
The period of avoidance for *tarpaṇa* and *puṭapāka* is double [that of the primary treatment];
one should dwell wearing a bandage over the eyes and using *mālatī* and *mallikā* flowers;
furthermore, this same procedure applies to *puṭapāka* even in cases of chronic diarrhea (*pakvātisāra*).
And there is a verse on this matter: "Regarding those diseases [treated] by irrigation, collyrium, saturation, and *puṭapāka*..."
"One should rectify those [defects] according to their respective natures whenever they arise due to a deviation from the prescribed rules.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter.
Now begins the thirty-fourth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter titled "The Procedure for Surgical Instruments and Tools" (Yantra-śastra-vidhi).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.

AS.Sū.34.2: "Painful shafts" (śalya) are those things that cause affliction to the mind and body. Regarding the extraction of these various shafts situated in diverse locations, the means employed are surgical instruments (yantra); furthermore, they are used for the application of surgical tools, alkali, and fire in cases such as hemorrhoids and fistula-in-ano, as well as for the protection of the remaining parts of the body.

Likewise, in the administration of enemas and similar procedures, there are instruments such as horns, gourds, and jars, as well as others like the "Jāmbavauṣṭha" (bear-lipped) and so forth; since these various forms serve many purposes for both the healthy and the sick,
it is impossible to determine their exact number based on their functions.
Others, moreover, declare that there are one hundred and one yantras;
here, however, they are briefly indicated as being of six kinds.
They are as follows: the *svastika*, the forceps (*saṃdaṃśa*), the *tāla*, the tube (*nāḍī*), the probe (*śalākā*), and other minor instruments (AS.Sū.34.4).

Among these, the *svastika* instruments have various animal-head shapes such as those of the heron, lion, vulture, and osprey; their names correspond to these forms, they are generally made of iron, and they measure eighteen finger-breadths in length (AS.Sū.34.4).

These [instruments] have edges shaped like lentils (*masūra*) and are bound at the neck with spikes; their handles are curved at the base like a hook for the purpose of extracting splinters that have become embedded in bone.
One should employ those with mouths resembling lions, tigers, serpents, crocodiles, and so forth, when the visible handles are suitable for the splinters;
for other cases, however, one should use instruments with mouths like those of herons, crows, ospreys, and the like, according to the requirements and conforming to the shape of the wound.
There are two types of forceps, each sixteen finger-breadths in length: those with a handle and those without.
These two are taught for the purpose of extracting foreign bodies lodged in the skin, flesh, vessels, or ligaments.

Likewise, there is another type of forceps (*sandaṃśa*) six finger-breadths long and half a finger-breadth wide, with two curved arms, shaped like the meeting of the tips of the thumb and fingers; it is used for extracting fine splinters, eyelashes, wounds, and excess flesh, and the *mucuṭī* is similar to it.

That [instrument], however, is fine, with narrow openings, and two-armed; it is bound at its base with a ring (rucaka) due to the pressure of the bandage, and is used for extracting the excess flesh from deep wounds where the wound edges have been severed.

There are also two *tālayantra* instruments, twelve finger-breadths long, shaped like the gullet of a fish—one with a single blade and one with two blades—used for extracting foreign bodies from the ear canals.
AS.Sū.34.8 Tubular instruments are hollow, of many kinds, and serve many purposes; they may have openings at one end or on both ends.
They are used for the purpose of visualizing foreign bodies located within the channels, for their extraction, for facilitating surgical procedures, and for suction.
One should make those [tubes] with openings the width of a stream and likewise elongated according to their application.

For the purpose of viewing a foreign body in the throat, one should make a tube ten finger-breadths long and five finger-breadths in circumference. However, for the purpose of grasping a double-pronged hook, one should make a tube of that same measurement with a three-holed opening at its mouth.

Likewise, the instrument for hemorrhoids (*ārśoyantra*) is of three types: one with four ears, one with five openings and faces for extracting foreign bodies (*śalyanirghātinī*), and one shaped like the pericarp of a lotus with a twelve-finger-length head and a three-finger-length aperture. (AS.Sū.34.10)

Made of copper, iron, gold, ivory, horn, or wood, shaped like a cow’s teat, four finger-breadths long—or one as long as the palm of the hand—and five finger-breadths in circumference for men, or six finger-breadths for women;
it has two apertures for inspection and one aperture for practical use.
For thus, the visualization is comfortable, and there is no excessive penetration by the knife, caustic, or fire;
the opening, however, is three finger-breadths long and as wide as the belly of the thumb.

Of the remaining one finger-breadth, below it is half a finger-breadth, and above it likewise half a finger-breadth, with a raised and rounded *karṇikā* (pericarp) extending half a finger-breadth in height.

The third [instrument] is similar to that, called *śamyā*, but it is without lateral openings for the purpose of compression; however, in the case of fistula-in-ano (*bhagaṇḍara*), one should remove the upper lip from the opening and fashion it accordingly.

Likewise, the instrument for nasal polyps (*ghrāṇārśas*) and tumors (*arbuda*) is shaped like a tube, two finger-breadths in length, with a single opening and a circumference equal to the index finger.

Likewise, the finger-guard (*aṅgulītrāṇaka*)— which is inserted onto the fingers, has slightly thick and rounded lips, upper and lower openings, is shaped like a cow’s udder, measures four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*), and is made of ivory, horn, or wood—
is fastened with a firm thread to the wrist and should be employed for draining the mouth.
AS.Sū.34.12 For the examination of vaginal ulcers, there is an instrument sixteen finger-breadths long,
with a hollow in the middle, four-sided, and having four sliding rods; it is fixed above by two movable seals, has a face like a lotus bud, and expands upward when the rods are inserted at the base.

The instruments for washing and anointing sinus ulcers (*nāḍīvraṇa*) are six finger-breadths long, shaped like enema tubes (*bastiyantra*), with no rim at the opening; they have channels at both the base and the mouth for the insertion of a thumb or a pea, respectively.
For abdominal dropsy (*dakodara*), one should employ a tube with openings at both ends, or a brush-tube (*picchanāḍī*).

Instruments appropriate for their specific purposes have been described for oil enemas (*snehabasti*), urethral/vaginal enemas (*uttarabasti*), insufflation (*pradhamana*), medicated smoke (*dhūma*), urinary retention, hydrocele (*mūtravṛddhi*), and obstructed penis (*niruddhamaṇi*), among others.

The syringe (śṛṅga), however, is of short, medium, or long size, measuring eighteen, twelve, or [ten] finger-breadths in length; its opening has an entry of three finger-breadths and a tip with a hole like a mustard seed or a stone;
it is bound with thin leather and has a nipple-shaped mouth, intended for sucking out wind, poison, blood, water, or corrupted breast milk.
For the purpose of sucking out phlegm and blood, a gourd (*alābu*) should be employed;

it should be twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length, eighteen finger-breadths in circumference, with an opening three or four finger-breadths in diameter and height, and its interior should be wrapped with blazing *kuśa*, *balvaja*, or *picu* grass. A water-pot (*ghaṭī*) should be used in exactly the same manner, according to the same measurements and functions.
Furthermore, for the purpose of elevating and dissolving tumors (gulma),
various types of probe-instruments (śalākā-yantra) exist, which serve diverse purposes and possess corresponding lengths and circumferences as required.

For their probing and extraction, there are two instruments with the mouth of an earthworm for the purpose of extracting foreign bodies from the channels; two with the mouth of a lentil petal, measuring eight and nine finger-breadths respectively;
and six probes.
For the purpose of spreading them out, there are two [needles] twelve and sixteen finger-breadths long with faces like the hoods of snakes;
likewise, for the purpose of moving them, there are two with faces like the nocks of arrows, ten and twelve finger-breadths long;
and for the purpose of extracting them, there are two with faces like fish-hooks.
Likewise, the *garbhaśaṅku* is equal in size to a surgical probe (*śaṅku*), measuring eighteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) with a curved tip; it is used for extracting dead fetuses.
Similarly, the instrument called *sarpaphaṇa* has a tip bent like a serpent’s hood and is used for removing urinary calculi (*aśmarī*).
Furthermore, the *dantanirghātana* measures four finger-breadths, has a mouth like the feathered end of an arrow (*śarapuṅkha*), and has a thick, rounded edge.
Six turbans made of cotton are for the purpose of wiping away various wounds, exudations,
and caustic applications; of these, two measuring six and seven finger-breadths respectively are suitable for wounds on the nose, whether distant or near.
The enema nozzle is ten or twelve finger-breadths long;
the ear-cleanser is shaped like the mouth of a *sruva* ladle with the tip of an *aśvattha* leaf;

likewise, for the purpose of cauterization (*kṣāra-agni-karma*), there are instruments with lips like those of a *jāmbava* fruit, measuring twelve, eight, and two finger-breadths respectively, with tips of two, one, and half a finger-breadth.
The probes (śalākā) are of various sizes— thick, thin, long, short, and medium; however,
in cases of intestinal hernia (āntravṛddhi), they should be curved like a half-moon with the tip protruding upward from the middle.

For cauterization, nasal polyps, and tumors, there are three types of spoons: those with mouths the size of a jujube stone fragment, those with curved handles for the application of alkali, poisons, or medicinal drugs, and those shaped like a ladle. These are eight finger-breadths long, shaped like spoons, and have depressions at their mouths the size of the nails of the little, ring, and middle fingers respectively;
they are prescribed for such purposes as the urethral enema (*uttarabasti*) and collyrium (*añjana*), according to their specific requirements.

AS.Sū.34.17 The instruments [of restraint] are: magnets, ropes, leather, intestines, cloth, stones, hammers, the palms of the hands, the soles of the feet, the fingers, the tongue, the teeth, the mouth, the branches [of trees], the nails, hair, horses, time, digestion, and joy or fear.
AS.Sū.34.18 These are applied to the entire body or even to a single part of the body.
AS.Sū.34.18 One should employ [the instruments] appropriately at the joints and in the abdominal vessels.

AS.Sū.34.19 The functions of the instruments, however, are for the most part twenty-fourfold: striking, filling, binding, expanding, turning back, moving, opening, pressing, clearing the passage, pulling out, extracting, causing pain, elevating, depressing, breaking, churning, suctioning, probing, tearing, straightening, washing, blowing, applying collyrium, and wiping.
Because it turns around, plunges well, and, having grasped what is to be grasped, draws it out.
Therefore, among instruments, the *kaṅkamukha* is the foremost; and that which is authoritative in all locations consists of twenty-six surgical instruments.

They are as follows: the tooth-scaler, the circular-tipped, the *vṛddhipatra*, the lotus-leaf, the one-and-a-half-edged, the ring, the scissors, the snake-mouth, the saw, the *kuśā*-leaf, the *aṭīmukha*, the internal-mouth, the *śarārīmukha*, the triple-brush, the small axe, the rice-mouth, the probe, the *vetasapatra*, the arrow-head, the ear-piercing needle, the needle-brush, the *khaja*, the *eṣiṇī*, the hook, and the nail-scraper.

Generally, these [instruments] are six finger-breadths long, well-forged by skilled smiths, as blue as the petal of a blue lotus, easy to grasp, well-formed, with excellent edges and well-aligned tips, and not jagged; each one usually has a blade measuring two or three times the width of its own circumference, or even one-fourth more than that, and they should be employed according to the specific disease and location.
Their shapes are generally explained by their very names, much like [the description of] surgical instruments.
Among those, the first three instruments are for incision;
the three beginning with the *vṛddhipattra* are for excision.
There are four [types of blades] for splitting, beginning with the maṇḍalāgra; eight for cutting, beginning with the kuśapatra; and five for scraping.
The six instruments beginning with the *kuṭhārika* are for piercing;
among them, the *ārā* and *vrīhimukha* are for splitting and incising,
while the *sūcīs* are for suturing.
The *sūcīkūrca* is for pounding; the *khaja* is for churning;
and the *eṣiṇī* is for searching and piercing.
The hook is for seizing; the claw-blade is for extracting, and for cutting, piercing, scraping, and scarifying.

Thus is the application of the twelve types of surgical instruments. Specifically, for scraping dental tartar, the *dantalekhana* instrument should be well-joined, quadrangular, and single-edged. (AS.Sū.34.23)

The *maṇḍalāgra* has a blade as wide as the nail of the index finger; it is to be employed for scraping and excising [lesions] such as diseases of the eyelids, decayed teeth and gums, ill-placed wounds, and tonsillitis (*galagaṇḍikā*).
The *vṛddhipatra* is shaped like a razor; it is desired for elevated or deep swellings, with its tip being straight and needle-like.

In the opposite case, however, the *aṅguliśastraka* (finger-sword) is used for throat diseases; it has its blade bent backward, its tip emerges from a ring, its blade is equal in length to half a finger-breadth—being similar to one of the types such as the *vṛddhipatra*, *maṇḍalāgra*, or *adhyardhadhāra*—it has a circular ring for insertion the size of the first joint of the index finger, and it is secured with a firm thread.
The *kartarī* (scissors) has a noose at three parts of its length and is for the purpose of cutting wounds, sinews, hair, and threads.
The *sarpavaktra* (snake-mouthed) is curved with a blade half a finger-breadth wide, for the purpose of excising nasal polyps, ear tumors, hemorrhoids, and growths (*arbuda*).
The saw (karapatra) is ten finger-breadths long, two finger-breadths wide, with fine teeth and a sharp edge; it is provided with a handle for the purpose of cutting bone.
The probe (kuśapatrāṭī) has a tip like a leaf, a fruit [or head] of two finger-breadths, and an internal opening shaped like a half-moon with a fruit of one and a half finger-breadths.
The *kuṭhārikā* has a broad handle, is shaped like a cow’s tooth, and has a blade half a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) long; it is for the purpose of piercing vessels located within bone.

The *vrīhimukha* has a blade of one and a half fingers; it is for the purpose of piercing vessels in fleshy areas, and for the purpose of lancing and incising [affections of] the abdomen, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), abscesses (*vidradhi*), and so forth.
The *śalākā* (probe) is double-faced, with a tip like the bud of a *kurabaka* flower, made of copper, and intended for piercing the *liṅganāśa* (optic nerve).

The *ārā* (scalpel) is square, with a circular opening half a finger-breadth wide, penetrating to that same depth; it is intended for causing pain to thick earlobes and for incising swellings (*śopha*) when there is doubt as to whether they are suppurated or not.
The ear-piercing instrument (karṇavyadhana) is three finger-breadths in length, with a hole one finger-breadth wide, solid, and shaped like the tip of a jasmine bud;
there are three needles, circular, with hidden and firm loops.

In that regard, for wounds involving joints and bones in fleshy areas, the *tryaṅgulā* (three-finger) instrument is triangular; for those with little flesh, the *dvyaṅgulā* (two-finger) is circular; and for the vital points (*marmans*) of the stomach and large intestine, the *vrīhimukhā* (rice-mouth) is a half-and-two-fingers long and curved like a bow.

The *sūcīkūrca* (needle-cluster) has a single circular base, is well-fastened at the tip with seven or eight needles, and is used for leprosy, vitiligo, freckles, alopecia, numbness, and similar conditions.
The *khaja* is eight *kaṇṭakas* long and half a finger-breadth wide, made of copper or iron; it is used for draining blood from within the nose.
There are two types of *eṣaṇī*, both having a very smooth surface; one is eight fingers long and is used for searching for cavities in wounds containing foreign bodies or pus.

Another [instrument] is shaped like a needle, bound with a thread smeared with alkali, for the purpose of incising the channels and the tracts of fistula-in-ano; the *baḍiśa* has a downward-pointing face, a needle-sharp tip, and is used for grasping the uvula, hemorrhoids, and so forth;
the *nakhaśastra* measures eight finger-breadths, having the shape of a horse’s ear on one side and the shape of a calf’s tooth on the other, for the extraction of minute foreign bodies.

AS.Sū.34.31 Minor instruments, however, include leeches, alkali, fire, sun-crystals (*sūryakānta*), glass, rock-crystal, *kurucindana*, nails, *śāka*, *śophālikā*, and the like, as well as thorny leaves, sea-foam, dried cow dung, and so forth;
and one should prepare various mechanical instruments and their respective applications by means of one's own ingenuity.

In this context, the hand itself is the most important [instrument], because surgical instruments and machines are dependent upon it (AS.Sū.34.32). Regarding that, there are eight defects of the machine: being too long, too short, too thick, too thin, crooked, uneven, difficult to grasp, and loose (AS.Sū.34.32).
In this regard, there are exactly eight defects of surgical instruments: the blunt, the chipped, and the rough-edged, with the exception of the saw;
among these, an instrument that has been tempered with alkali is used for cutting arrows, splinters, and bone, while one tempered with water is used for cutting flesh.
One should employ oil in cases of incision and splitting, as well as in venesection and the excision of tendons.
Furthermore, for cutting instruments, the blade should be the size of a māṣa grain; for scraping instruments, it should be half the size of a māṣa grain.
Among the instruments for piercing (vyadhana) and draining (visrāvaṇa), the kaiśikī [instrument] is used.

One should grasp them with the index finger, middle finger, and thumb— keeping the hand well-composed— at the portion common to the handle, for the purposes of cutting (chedana), splitting (bhedana), and scraping (lekhanā).

AS.Sū.34.35: For bloodletting at the tip of the pedicle, one should use the index finger and thumb with the palm covering the tip of the pedicle; for the *vrīhimukha* (rice-mouth) instrument, it is placed in the mouth.
At the base, for the purpose of gathering [the net],
there should be a small pair of tongs and a pair of scissors above the middle of the net;
the remaining parts should also be arranged as appropriate for the ease of operation.
The whetstone for them should be very smooth, with the luster of a bean or mung bean; and for establishing the edge, a slab of śālmalī wood is used.
Furthermore, even one who has mastered the teachings should not engage in surgical procedures unless he has undergone proper training or has repeatedly observed the practice,
for the body is pervaded by veins, ligaments, vital points (*marmans*), and other such structures.

Therefore, one should prepare [the instruments] as appropriate for extraction and other procedures from things such as hairy skins, flowers, fruits, gourds, cucumbers, water-filled leather bags, bladders, intestines, pieces of flesh, and lotus stalks; likewise, one should prepare those suitable for bladder compression using a tube filled with water through a side-opening vessel, those suitable for the application of fire or caustic on soft pieces of flesh,
and those suitable for binding the limbs and members of a mannequin.
Furthermore,

a physician who wishes to be skillful should cause a man with a complete body— neither emaciated nor afflicted by a long-standing disease— to be placed in a flowing river, his entrails drawn out and bound with muñja and balbaja grass, enclosed in a cage, and allowed to soak in a secluded place. (AS.Sū.34.38)

Having properly extracted that [body] once it has thoroughly decomposed and having made its body elongated, one should gently rub it with a brush made of *uśīra*, bamboo, *kūrca* grass, or similar materials. Then, one should examine all the external and internal parts—the skin and so forth, as well as the limbs, vessels, tendons, and other components—according to the scripture shown by the teacher and with the eye.
Thus, that which is seen through the treatise (*śāstra*) and that which is seen through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
When those two have come together, it should further increase one's knowledge;
it should be nine finger-breadths in width and twelve finger-breadths in thickness, and very solid.
Made from linen, bark-fiber, wool, silk, fine cotton cloth, or soft leather; with its loops well-arranged, well-sewn, and containing a blade within the inner wool.
And the well-stocked sheath for surgical instruments, its opening closed with a probe—
thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter.
Now begins the thirty-fifth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter titled "The Procedure for Leeches.
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
One should employ leeches for the purpose of bloodletting in the case of kings, the wealthy, the timid, the delicate, children, the elderly, and women.
These [leeches] are of two kinds: venomous and non-venomous.

AS.Sū.35.3 Among those, the poisonous [leeches] are born from foul water, corpses, frogs, fish, and the like, or from urine and excrement; they are reddish, white, or very black, thin or thick, restless, and slimy; their middles are thick and hairy, and they are covered with various upward-pointing stripes like the rainbow (Indra’s weapon).
From their bite, there arises burning, swelling, suppuration, itching, pustules, erysipelas, fever, fainting, and the appearance of vitiligo.
In that regard, one should perform treatments that remove poison, bile, and blood.

Those [stones] produced from fragrant, pure, and abundant water containing lotuses, blue lotuses, saugandhika lilies, and other such plants, which are dark like moss or have vertical streaks as dark as moss, and are round, are non-poisonous.
Furthermore, the maximum measurement for all of them is eighteen finger-breadths.
In that regard, one should apply [the measures] of four, five, or six finger-breadths for humans; for elephants and horses, other [proportions] should be used.

Among them, women have delicate bodies, thin skin, small heads, and large lower trunks; men are the opposite, and they stand facing forward with the shape of a half-moon. In cases of diseases characterized by many defects and those that have been long-standing, men should be employed [as donors].
Women [should catch] leeches from stagnant waters by means of moist hides; having caught them, one should place them in a new jar containing fragrant mud.

For their food and drink, one should give them sweet, cool, and clear water, along with a powder made of *śṛṅgāṭaka*, *kaśeruka*, *śālūka*, *śaivāla*, lotus stalks, *vallūra*, fine clay, and the seeds of the lotus.
For the purpose of removing the accumulation of saliva and other secretions, one should likewise remove the previous food and drink every three days and thereafter provide different ones;
after five days, one should transfer them into another jar of the same kind.
However, fainting occurs for these [women] due to the improper vomiting of vitiated blood and its continuous discharge.

Having recognized that those [leeches] which remain in vessels filled with water due to their lack of movement and their lack of desire for food, one should discard them. As for the others, once they have voided their excrement into a solution of turmeric and mustard paste, or into *avantisoma*, or buttermilk, and have been revived again in water, one should apply them to the site of the bite while the patient is seated comfortably or lying down. After lubricating the site of the bite with the powders of clay and cow dung in a manner agreeable to the patient, one should apply them. If they do not attach themselves, one should drop drops of milk, ghee, fresh butter, or blood upon them, or else one should incise them.
When they bite with their mouths placed like the hoof of a horse and with raised shoulders,

or when they breathe like infants and drink [the blood] with the force of head-shaking and wave-like movements of the arms, one should cover them with a wet cloth and sprinkle them with water sparingly.
Just as a swan takes milk from a mixture of milk and water, so too, when the blood is agitated, the leeches first draw out the vitiated blood;
and when there is a pricking sensation or itching at the site of the bite, one should then remove them for the sake of preserving the pure blood.
If, due to greed, the leech does not release its hold, one should place honey or salt powder in its mouth.

Once it has fallen off, its body should be smeared with rice-husks, and its mouth anointed with oil and salt; then, pressing slowly from the tail toward the mouth in the direction of the hair, one should properly expel it.
Then, as before, one should apply [the paste],
and for seven nights one should not let those [leeches] fall again.
However, if the blood is impure, one should cause it to flow by gently rubbing from the bite with honey or jaggery.
Immediately after blood has flowed, one should wash the bite with cold water and cover it with a cotton pad soaked in ghee.
Once the bleeding has ceased, one should apply plasters made of astringent, sweet, and cooling substances mixed with ghee, in order to clarify any remaining disturbed blood.
In this regard, one should observe the application of medicinal formulations and other procedures as in the case of venesection (sirāvyadha).
And one should treat it so that, upon the removal of the vitiated blood, there occurs a softening of the swelling and the subsiding of the burning sensation, redness, and pain.
One should not extract [the blood] vitiated by *raktapitta* using two gourd-spoons (*alābughaṭikā*), nor should one extract that which is vitiated by the combination of *vāta* and *kapha*;
likewise, one should not extract [blood] vitiated by *kapha* using a horn because of its coagulating nature, but rather one should extract that which is vitiated by *vāta* and *pitta*.
Then, having covered the limb with the tip of a horn whose end is bound with a layer of fine cloth, one should suck [the poison];
likewise, one may use two hollow gourds filled with burning cotton.
On this subject, there are these verses:
Having firmly bound the limb above with a rope or a cloth bandage evenly,
one should perform the incision while avoiding the sinews, joints, bones, and vital points (*marmans*).
With footprints extending downward and moving upward,
neither too deep nor thick nor horizontal, he should not place one footprint upon another.

One should remove blood that is localized in one part while the patient is asleep by means of leeches and the like; however, blood that is diffused throughout the body should be removed with leeches, or where it pervades the vessels, by venesection.
For blood that has clotted, one should use a lancet; for deep-seated blood, leeches;
for blood located in the skin, a gourd, a tube, or a horn; and for pervading blood, a vein.

Alternatively, for one whose blood has flowed [due to a wound] caused by wind (vāta), cooling applications such as plasters and the like should be used; this may be done using horns, leeches, or gourds, respectively, depending on whether the site is a seat of wind or other humors.
When there is itching with pain and swelling, one should sprinkle it with warm clarified butter.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter;
now begins the thirty-sixth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter titled "The Procedure for Venesection.
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.

Indeed, many methods for bloodletting were previously described, as well as other therapeutic procedures such as purgation; however, among these, venesection is the primary treatment for diseases curable by them.
For by this means, those diseases are eradicated along with their roots, just as rice and other crops are destroyed by breaking the embankment of a field.
And likewise,
in the *Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha*, Sūtra 36.3, it is stated: "Venesection is half of medical treatment, or medical treatment in its entirety."
Just as the enema (basti) is prescribed in the Śalyatantra for the treatment of the body, so too is blood the substrate for both the disorders and those who suffer from them.
Indeed, nothing else is so much to be condemned as this first [of the humors].

In that regard, they say that blood is the bodily fluid derived from the essence of food, known as *rasa*, which is unvitiated and colored by unvitiated *tejas*. It has the appearance of an *indragopa* insect, and its color resembles rabbit's blood, the *guñjā* berry, lac, a lotus, or gold. When washed, it becomes free of impurities; it is sweet, slightly salty, unctuous, non-congealed, neither cold nor hot, heavy, and it causes the accumulation, provocation, and pacification of *pitta* alone. By nature, it is both *saumya* (cooling) and *āgneya* (fiery). Thus they describe blood.
Likewise, some say that the fault (doṣa) and the object of the fault (dūṣya) are distinct, while others say they are both of the same nature.
And this very [body], when purified through the proper practice of diet and lifestyle, becomes the source of strength, complexion, happiness, and longevity.

Otherwise, however, due to the very nature of the autumn season, [the eyes] become afflicted with excessive secretions, *abhiṣyanda*, *adhimantha*, *śuklārma*, *timira*, red streaks (*raktarājī*), aching and piercing pain in the head, burning, itching, diseases of the ears, suppuration of the mouth, putridity, coating of the mouth and nose, skin diseases, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), splenic disorders, abscesses, erysipelas, fever, hemorrhaging (*rakta-pitta*), leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), pustules, elephantiasis (*ślīpada*), venereal sores (*upadaṃśa*), swelling of the temples (*śaṅkha-śopha*), gout (*vāta-śoṇita*), urinary disorders (*rakta-meha*), minor ailments, loss of appetite, hoarseness of voice, heaviness and exhaustion of the limbs, anorexia, sour eructations, salivation, anger, delusion, sweating, intoxication, fainting, epilepsy (*apasmāra*), tremors, drowsiness, and so forth.

Furthermore, those who, though properly treated with remedies that counteract all the *doṣas*—such as cold, hot, unctuous, or dry—and who are otherwise curable, do not recover, have their conditions arisen from the provocation of blood (*rakta*). Therefore, in such cases, one should pierce the appropriate vein (*sirā*) to drain the excessively aggravated blood.

AS.Sū.36.7 However, [venesection] should not be performed on those who have consumed fats, those who have undergone any of the five purificatory procedures (*pañcakarma*), pregnant women, women who have recently given birth, those with indigestion, jaundice, impotence, those under sixteen years of age, those over seventy, those injured by trauma, those with excessive hemorrhaging, those with vitiated blood, those who are unoleated, excessively oleated, or unsweated, nor those afflicted by convulsions (*ākṣepaka*), hemiplegia (*pakṣāghāta*), diarrhea, vomiting, dyspnea, cough, abdominal enlargement, internal hemorrhage (*raktapitta*), hemorrhoids, anemia, or generalized edema.

AS.Sū.36.7 Furthermore, veins should not be pierced if they are not suitable for venesection, nor if they are unrestrained, nor if they are not raised; nor should one perform it obliquely, nor during extreme cold, heat, rain, wind, or cloudy weather.

In those cases such as after drinking oleaginous substances, even though the veins have been properly pierced, they may not bleed or may bleed excessively; however, in one who has been properly lubricated and fomented, the humors (doṣas), having become liquefied and entered the blood, are properly expelled. Yet this prohibition does not apply to diseases involving poison, complications, or acute emergencies, for regarding the venesection in each of these specific diseases, there is a distinct classification.

In diseases of the head and eyes, [the vein] at the forehead, the bridge of the nose, or near the outer corners of the eyes; in ear diseases, all around the ears; and in nasal diseases, at the tip of the nose.
In cases of coryza, however, [the veins] are located in the nose and forehead;
in diseases of the mouth, they are situated in the tongue, lips, jaw, and palate;
and in glandular swellings above the clavicle, they are found in the neck, ears, temples, and head.
In epilepsy, they are located in the middle of the jaw-joint;

in insanity, in the eyebrows, the outer corners of the eyes, and the forehead; and in internal abscesses and pain in the flanks, they reside in the sides, the armpits, and the space between the breasts.
In the fourth [case], it is located below the aggregate of the [vertebral] column, resting on one side;
in the third, it is situated in the middle of the sacroiliac joint between the two shoulders;
in dysentery and colic, it is two finger-breadths all around the hips.
In cases of seminal disorders caused by the consumption of cooked meat as a side dish,
a goiter (galagaṇḍa) may appear on the penis;
or, in cases of Gṛdhrasī, it occurs four finger-breadths above or below the knee joint, localized at the root of the thigh.

One should apply [the treatment] two finger-breadths below the base of Indra’s bladder for apacyā; for pain in the thighs and knee-joints, at the "jackal's ear" (kroṣṭukaṇīrṣa); and for elephantiasis (ślīpada), four finger-breadths above the ankle—each according to its respective location as will be described.

In diseases of the feet such as burning sensation, itching, fissures, wind-disorders, blood-disorders, *vātakaṇṭaka*, *vidārikā*, and *pādadārī*, [the vein] is located two finger-breadths above the *kṣipra* marman;
by this, the other thigh and arm are explained.
Specifically, however, for enlargement of the spleen (*plīhodara*), it is on the inner side of the left half, in the middle of the arm.
In the same way, they prescribe [treatment] for the liver (yakṛt) in the right arm,
as well as for cough and dyspnea, just as in cases of gṛdhrasī and viśvācī.
Some authorities maintain that this applies even to *bāhuśoṣa* (wasting of the arm) and *apabāhuka* (paralysis of the arm);

however, when these [specific vessels] are not visible, one should perform venesection on whichever vessel is closest to the site of the disease mentioned for other ailments, especially in the case of a patient with a severely advanced condition. Furthermore, one should prepare in advance a bed, a seat, a water-pot, cloth, bandages, and so forth.
Likewise, according to availability, a powder of tagara, elā, śītaśiva, kuṣṭha, pāṭhā, viḍaṅga, bhadradāru, trikaṭu, agāradhūma, haridrā, and arka shoots is for the purpose of causing blood to flow;
and a powder of lodhra, madhuka, priyaṅgu, pattaṅga, gairika, rasāñjana, śālmalī, conch-shell, barley, wheat, and māṣa beans is for the purpose of stabilizing the blood.
The powder of the bark, sprouts, and resin of the *vaṭa*, *aśvattha*, *aśvakarṇa*, *palāśa*, *bibhītaka*, *sarja*, *arjuna*, *dhanvana*, *dhātakī*, *sālasāra*, *arimeda*, and *tinduka* trees;
or the powder of linen, lampblack, lac, and sea-foam; or whatever else is required as an instrument for counteracting the complications of excessive hemorrhage.

For a physician who has prepared his equipment does not fall into delusion. (AS.Sū.36.10) Then, having performed the auspicious rites for the patient and having observed the strength of the disease, the patient's constitution, and other factors, he should have the patient drink either unctuous meat broth from wild animals or gruel. Once the patient has been comforted for a mere moment, he should be fomented in the forenoon or afternoon with either heated coals, warm steam, or hot water. He should then be made to sit facing the sun on a soft seat raised to the height of the knees, with his elbows resting on his knees and his feet placed flat on the ground.
At the hairline, one should bind [the head] with one of the following: a cloth, skin, bark, or a woven band;
then, the patient, using two fists with the thumbs tucked inside the long cloth, should press upon the temples as appropriate, clench the teeth against each other, and puff out the cheeks.

A person standing behind him, with his body clothed between the patient's garment and the nape of his neck, should restrain him without obstructing the vital breaths; this is the method of restraint for piercing veins, excluding those that face inward. Then, the physician, having steadied the vein with his thumb and striking it with his middle finger, should wait until it has risen, is throbbing, or is sensitive to touch. Having placed an upward-pointed lancet (*kuṭhārikā*) in his left hand and positioned it over the middle of the vein, he should strike it with the middle finger in the same manner, or press it with the pad of his thumb.
One should observe the swelling [of the vein] upon pressing with the thumb, as it is covered by thick, hidden skin;
the veins are filled by coughing and by the agitation of anger.
Having raised the tip of the nose with the thumb, one should pierce the subnasal area with a *vrīhimukha* needle.
When the tongue is raised and its tip bitten,
[the physician should examine] below the tongue, as well as the palate and the roots of the teeth of one whose mouth is opened wide.
One should apply pressure on the vessels of the neck above the breasts while the patient has his chest extended, his head raised,
and is supported by both arms at his sides.
For one with an elevated penis, the physician should sit with his back raised and head lowered upon the patient’s penis, hips, back, and shoulders;

for one suffering from *viśvācī* or *gṛdhrasī*, he should sit comfortably with the patient’s elbows and knees extended; and for one with hidden thumbs and clenched fists, having bound the vessel four finger-breadths above the site to be incised with a cloth or similar material, [he should proceed] with the hand-vessel (*hastasirā*).

Having thus firmly positioned one foot and placed the other foot slightly contracted upon it, one should press down with both hands from below the knee-joint as far as the ankles, bind it as before, and then pierce the vein of the foot;

in each case, one should apply various methods and adjust the instrument accordingly. In fleshy areas, one should insert [the needle] to the depth of a barley grain using the *vrīhimukha* (rice-mouth) instrument.
Otherwise, [he should cut] from the top of the bones a piece the size of half a barley grain or the size of a rice grain with a small knife.

In every case, one should swiftly apply the surgical instrument into the middle of the vein, avoiding the vital spots (*marmans*) and other sensitive areas, ensuring the incision is not too shallow, is deep enough, is straight, and is not confused with adjacent vessels;
[the incision] struck by a single blow should flow with a continuous stream of blood.
One should wait for a moment once it has been properly pierced; they know this as "well-pierced.
If it flows only slightly for a short time, it is "badly pierced" and should be treated with oil and powders.
If pierced with a loud crackling sound, however, it bleeds painfully and must be held with effort.

Furthermore, even when veins have been properly pierced, the causes for the failure of blood to flow are: fainting, fear, looseness of the instrument, excessive tightness, overeating, emaciation, piercing with a blunt instrument, passing urine or having evacuated the bowels, insufficient fomentation, and the wound opening being obstructed by phlegm.
Then, having identified the specific cause for the lack of flow, one should treat it accordingly;
one should dust the opening of the vein with a powder of tagara and other ingredients mixed with an abundance of oil and salt,
and one should press the patient on the middle of the back.

When the blood flows well in this manner, one should sprinkle the opening of the vein with drops of warm oil mixed with salt for the purpose of pacifying the phlegm and wind and preventing the cessation of the flow;
at first, the vitiated blood flows out like yellow dye from a *kusumbha* flower.
Having heard correctly, one should remain personally [attentive]; if it is pure, one should not extract it.

However, for one from whom blood flows and fainting occurs, one should release the instrument and, while comforting them with the touch of hands moistened with cold water, with the breeze of a fan, and with pleasant words to the ears, and having thus allayed the fainting, one should cause the blood to flow again.
He faints again on the following day, or even after three days; however, the maximum quantity of blood that may be let is one *prastha*.

Otherwise, one must consider the strength of the disease, the body, and the season (AS.Sū.36.18). Among these, blood that is frothy, reddish, dark-brown, clear, dry, non-clotting, astringent in aftertaste, smelling of iron, flowing with force, and cold is due to Vāta (AS.Sū.36.18).

Due to *pitta*, [the discharge] is black like house-soot or collyrium, yellow, green, foul-smelling, fishy-odored, and—because of its pungency—is disliked by flies; because of its heat, it does not congeal, and it resembles cow’s urine with a shimmering appearance. Due to *kapha*, it is pale like the flower of the *kovidāra* tree or water mixed with red ochre (*gairika*); it is cold, unctuous, congealing, thick, slimy, stringy, and exudes from the opening of the ulcer; it has a salty taste and the smell of fat (*vasā*). When there is a combination of two or more doshas, the symptoms are a mixture of these.
If the blood is copper-colored, dark-blue, turbid, and foul-smelling due to a derangement of the humors (sannipāta),

it should first be purified and released; then, once the blood has flowed out, one should press the site with the thumb to ensure the vein remains open, slowly remove the instrument, and comfort the patient.
Having placed a cloth soaked in oil over the opening of the vein,
one should bind it and cause the patient to lie down. If the blood does not stop, one should dust the opening of the vein with the previously mentioned powders and press it with the tip of a finger.
Having placed either *śālmali*, *upodaka*, or *āpiccha* at the opening of the wound, one should bind it firmly;
or else, a cloth smeared with beeswax (*madhūcchiṣṭa*) should be applied.

One should sprinkle [the patient] with cold water, or treat him for the purpose of inducing sweating by means of cold, sweet, and astringent food and drink, affusion, ointments, exposure to wind, or staying in a cool room.

One should administer a decoction of the *padmakādi* group made sweet with sugar and honey, or milk, or sugarcane juice; or, having pierced a vein in any one of the following—deer, antelope, goat, sheep, buffalo, or boar—one should give the raw blood, or blood fried in ghee, as a drink.
Or one should administer an enema using that same [blood] which has been purified by being rubbed with *darbha* grass;
one should feed the patient with unctuous soups and broths,
or else, immediately after the venesection, one should pierce that same vein again.
If the blood does not stop in any way, one should apply an alkaline solution for coagulation,
or cauterize the opening of the vein with a heated probe;
nor should one neglect it for even a moment.

For when the blood is depleted, the *vāyu* seizes the vital points (*marmans*) and produces fainting, loss of consciousness, trembling of the head, vertigo, stiffness of the neck, facial paralysis, drooping of the jaw, hiccups, pallor, deafness, depletion of the bodily constituents,
convulsions, and so forth, or even death; for blood is the life-force (*prāṇa*) of living beings, and through its depletion, the digestive fire (*anala*) is extinguished.
Since the wind (vāyu) causes increase, one should therefore administer nourishing therapy (bṛṃhaṇa) with due method.
However, if the blood is impure, one should drain it again in the afternoon or on the following day.
Then, in every way, one should pacify the remaining blood that cannot be drained by means of cold affusions, plasters, purgation, fasting, and unctuous, sweet foods and drinks; or,
after treating it with oleation and other measures for about a month, one should puncture again.

One should treat according to their respective natures those complications (*vyāpada*) that may arise from defects of piercing (*vyadhadoṣa*), such as piercing too high, piercing too low, piercing with a curved needle, or piercing obliquely. Regarding this, there is a verse here (AS.Sū.36.22): "As long as [the humors] moving out of their path do not return to their own locations by means of pressure from the instrument..."
When the humors (doṣas) have become aggravated and have entered the blood, one should partake of wholesome diet and conduct;
once the blood has been removed, food and drink that are neither too hot nor too cold, light, and digestive-stimulating (dīpanīya) are beneficial.
At that time,
because the blood and the digestive fire (agni) are particularly unstable, the body must be protected;
[one should protect it] when the complexion and the sense faculties are clear, when one desires the objects of the senses, and when the force of digestion is unimpeded.
"They say that a man endowed with happiness, possessed of nourishment and strength, and having pure blood [is healthy]. Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter.
Now begins the thirty-seventh chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "The Procedure for the Extraction of Foreign Bodies."
Thus indeed said the great seers, Ātreya and others:
"For the movement of foreign bodies (śalya) is of three kinds: upward, downward, and transverse."

Furthermore, that [wound] is of two kinds, each distinguished by being straight or crooked (AS.Sū.37.3). Among these, one should recognize a wound with a foreign body as being dark-colored, covered with pustules, accompanied by swelling and pain, repeatedly discharging blood, protruding like a bubble, and having soft flesh (AS.Sū.37.3).
Specifically, when the foreign body (śalya) is located in the skin, there occurs a discolored swelling that is elongated and hard.

When it is located in the muscle (māṃsa), there is an increase in swelling, non-healing along the path of the foreign body, intolerance to pressure, a sucking sensation (coṣa), and suppuration (pāka).
When [the dosha] is located within the muscle tissue (peśī), it is like that which has reached the flesh, except for swelling;
when it has entered the vessels (sirā), there is distension of the vessels and pain.
When [the vāta] has entered the sinews, there is the tossing about of the network of sinews and violent pain;
when it has entered the channels, there is the loss of the specific functions and qualities of the channels.
When [the vāta] is located in the vessels (dhamanī), the wind, impelling blood mixed with froth, exits with a sound; there is pain in the limbs and nausea.
When it has entered the bones, there are various types of pain and swelling.
When it has entered the joints, there is an obstruction of movement, just as when it is in the bones.
AS.Sū.37.7 When [the poison] has reached the joints of the bones, there is a fullness of the bones, friction, and great strength.
AS.Sū.37.8 But when it has reached the internal cavities, flatulence, abdominal distension, and the appearance of urine, feces, and food occur from the opening of the wound.

If it reaches a vital spot (*marman*), one should treat it as if it were pierced in a vital spot; furthermore, one should identify a foreign body (*śalya*) in the skin or other tissues by means of the discharges (*parisrāva*) taught according to their respective locations.
AS.Sū.37.9 In the case of arrows with subtle trajectories, these very same signs become indistinct.
AS.Sū.37.10 In those whose bodies are pure, they are extracted when positioned in the direction of the hair (anuloma).

Furthermore, those [diseases] that have been displaced by the provocation of the *doṣas*, sexual intercourse, physical exercise, or trauma, cause affliction once again. In that regard, when the skin has disappeared, one should apply a paste of earth, black gram, barley, wheat, and cow-dung powder to the area where there is swelling or pain after the skin has been lubricated and fomented.
Or where clarified butter placed there solidifies quickly, or a medicinal plaster dries up rapidly.
In that case, one should recognize the presence of a foreign body (śalya) when it is hidden within the flesh; one should treat the patient with oleation and other procedures.
Furthermore, in a person who has been emaciated, the foreign body becomes loosened and unattached; wherever it causes agitation, pain, or swelling, there the foreign body is located.
In the same way, even when the cavities of the abdomen, the bones, and the flesh are involved,
and the channels, veins, arteries, and ligaments are destroyed, one should place the patient on a chariot with broken wheels yoked to donkeys and carry him quickly along a rough road.

Then, one should determine [the condition] through agitation and other such signs. When a joint has become displaced, one should treat it with oleation and sudation, and by means of stretching, flexing, binding, and pressing, one should recognize it as before.

AS.Sū.37.14 When [the arrow] has entered the bone, one should treat the bones by means of oleation and sudation, and by applying firm pressure and binding; thus one should observe it. AS.Sū.37.15 But when it has entered a *marman*, because there is no other [visible] state apart from the flesh and so forth, the examination of the *marmans* is as previously described.

The general characteristic [of injury], however, is that where there is agitation or pain resulting from physical exercises such as mounting the shoulders of an elephant or a horse with the hands raised, rapid movement, leaping, jumping, or swimming; or from belching, vomiting, coughing, sneezing, spitting, laughing, or breath-control (prāṇāyāma); or from the discharge of waste or semen. (AS.Sū.37.15–16)
Or, where even with very slight exertion there occurs sleepiness, heaviness, a tingling sensation, or swelling, one should diagnose a *śalya* (foreign body) there.
In brief, a *śalya* is of four kinds.
When it is not visible, one should infer its presence from its circular shape, according to the distinctions of circular, triangular, or quadrangular forms (AS.Sū.37.18).
For the extraction of all large foreign bodies, there are only two methods: the reverse and the direct.
In that regard, one should lead it back toward oneself in reverse order, and forward away from oneself in direct order.
Since a foreign body (śalya) that has moved horizontally is easily extracted, one should cut it out from that direction.

One should extract a foreign body by cutting it against the grain, provided it is not protruding at the tip; likewise, one should extract a foreign body that requires excision or one that has a broad opening.

Likewise, one should not extract arrows that have fallen into the armpits, the groins, the chest, or the intercostal spaces; nor should one extract an arrow that has entered a vital point (*marman*), or one that is without swelling or pain, provided it does not cause suppuration.
Now,
if a foreign body is within reach of the hand, one should extract it with the hand.
If it is impossible [to remove] by means of a mechanical instrument according to its specific nature,

yet remains impossible even after dissecting with a blade, then one should make the wound bloodless, apply heat with fire, ghee, honey, and so forth, cauterize it, satisfy it with ghee and honey, bandage it, and prescribe the regimen of conduct (*ācārika*). If it is lodged in a vein or a ligament, one should extract it by releasing it with the tip of a probe.

One should extract a splinter lodged in the heart by means of cold water and other such methods for one who has been agitated; likewise, one should extract it from elsewhere even if it is difficult to remove along its natural path.
If it is lost within the cavities of the bones or trapped by the crushing of the bone, one should hold the person down with the feet and pull it out with a mechanical instrument.

It is indeed impossible [to control] it in this way; rather, having secured it with a strong harness, or having bent back the tip of the arrow-shaft, or having tied one end with bowstrings and the other with a five-strand rope so that the horse is well-restrained, one should bind it to the horse's muzzle-ring.
Then, one should strike it with a whip in such a way that it raises its head with speed.
One extracts the splinter;
or, having bent down a sturdy tree branch, one should extract it after binding [the patient] to it as previously described.
Having bound a weak splint with *kuśa* grass,
one should press upon the swelling of a splint seized by edema.
If it is displaced in an improper direction, one should move it by striking with a stone mallet and then,
having crushed the ear with a forceps like that for the ears, [remove it] exactly along its natural path.

Having grasped [the foreign body] as appropriate with a multi-mouthed tube-instrument (*nāḍīyantra*) or another probe-instrument (*śalākāyantra*), one should extract it as before, using a magnet for those located in the ear, provided the wound-opening is not too small.
[One removes] what has entered the colon by means of purgation;
obstruction of flatus, feces, urine, or the fetus by means of enemas; and corrupted wind, poison, breast milk, and so forth, by means of suction with the mouth, teeth, or a horn.
When a foreign body has entered the throat passage, one should insert a lotus fiber with a thread attached into the throat. Then,
once it is known that the foreign body has been grasped, one should pull out both the thread and the lotus fiber simultaneously.
In the absence of lotus fibers, this same procedure applies even to lotus stalks.

However, if a wax [plug] is stuck in the throat, one should then insert a tube into the throat; once that has been heated by fire, one should insert a fine-tipped probe. Then, having sprinkled it with cold water once the foreign body has been grasped and it has become stable, one should extract it.
Even in the case of non-wax [materials], the procedure is exactly the same, using a probe smeared with either heated lac or beeswax.
If a fish-bone or any other similar bone-thorn has become stuck in the throat, one should remove it by means of a finger wrapped with a thread or a cord;
or else, one should have the patient drink a mass of hair tied with a firm, long thread and mixed with a liquid, and cause them to vomit, and as they vomit,
one should suddenly pull out the thread that remains attached to a portion of the foreign object.
One should remove it with a soft tooth-cleaning brush, or push it out from the other side; likewise, when a fish-hook is stuck, one should treat a thorn in the same manner.
One with a sore throat should lick a powder of the three myrobalans (triphalā) mixed with honey, ghee, and sugar, while gently gargling. Alternatively,
one should press down on a person standing waist-deep in water with their head hanging downward, or shake them, or cause them to vomit, or bury them up to the mouth in a heap of ashes.

For otherwise, disorders of phlegm (śleṣma) such as abdominal distension, cough, dyspnea, chronic rhinitis, impairment of the sense organs, fever, and even death may occur due to water moving along the wrong channels; in such cases, one should treat the phlegm according to its specific nature.
One should cause a morsel-thorn to enter with water,

or strike it on the shoulder with the fist; likewise, having straightened the eyelid and removed the foreign body from the eye, one should apply a fomentation of warm water and steam, followed by a sprinkling with honey, madhuka decoction, and clarified butter.
AS.Sū.37.32 A foreign body may also fall out by itself from the eyes or other parts of the body through tears, sneezing, coughing, eructation, urine, feces, or flatus.
AS.Sū.37.33 When an insect has entered the ear canal, there is a pricking sensation, heaviness, and a buzzing sound; furthermore, when it moves, there is increased pain.
In that case, there should be filling with lukewarm water mixed with salt and madhuka, or with wine;
and once the insect has emerged, there should be the removal of it.

If, however, it has died right there, suppuration, putrefaction, and moistening occur; in such cases, one should perform the treatments prescribed for ear-discharge (karṇasrāva) and those prescribed for nasal obstruction (pratīnāha).
One should fill the ear, which is full of water, with oil-water churned by the hand;
or, having tilted the head to one side, one should strike it with the hand or suck it out with a tube.
Regarding this, there are the following verses:
A foreign body made of gold, silver,
or other minerals that has remained for a long time generally melts away through the heat generated by the body.
Horn, bamboo, wood, bone, ivory, hair,
stone, and those made of clay— these are shafts that do not disintegrate within the body.
A foreign body made of horn, bamboo, iron, palm-wood, or wood is generally extracted even after a long time,
for it quickly digests the flesh and blood.
If the site where a foreign body is deeply embedded in the flesh does not become inflamed,
then it should be treated with massage, fomentation, purification, emaciation, and nourishment.
Having caused suppuration through sharp irritants, drinks, food, pressure, weapons,
or branding with a hot iron, one should extract the foreign body by means of incision, probing, and compression.
Having observed the manifold forms of surgical instruments for extracting foreign bodies, a wise physician should identify the foreign body through various means and extract it accordingly.
When the ulcer has subsided, when its edges are no longer excessively sensitive to touch,
and when there is only slight swelling and heat, one should declare it to be free of the foreign body (*niḥśalya*).
The body itself is the supreme thorn, defiled by its own impurities and faults;
whereas a thorn [from] arrows and the like is considered a thorn only in a specific sense.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter.
Now begins the thirty-eighth chapter:
We shall now expound the chapter titled "The Procedure for Surgical Operations" (Śastrakarmavidhi).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and others:

"For when two types of disease— endogenous (*nija*) or exogenous (*āgantu*)— require a therapeutic intervention and have transcended the scope of medicinal treatment, surgical procedure (*śastrakarman*) is employed."

Furthermore, that inflammation generally begins with swelling; therefore, having observed that the state of swelling itself consists of combinations of Vāta, Pitta, Kapha, blood, or their collective derangement (Sannipāta), one should, out of fear of suppuration, apply fasting, plasters, affusions, bloodletting, decoctions, drinking of ghee, and purification therapies appropriate to each specific case.
Even so, if it does not subside, there should be application of caustic;
and if it does not dissolve, there should be application of poultice.

In that regard, the characteristic of a non-suppurated swelling (śopha) is its small size, mild heat and pain, coloration identical to the skin, and stability. However, when it is suppurating, it becomes discolored and distended like a bladder.

Accompanied by agitation, piercing pain, redness, burning, distress, loss of appetite, thirst, fever, restlessness, and intolerance to touch, [the patient] exudes fluid; he dries up the medicinal plaster; he experiences a tingling sensation as if smeared with mustard paste; he feels as if crawling ants are moving over him; he feels as if being pressed by the hand, crushed by a finger, struck by a staff, pricked by needles, pierced by spears, cut by a weapon, bitten by scorpions, burned by fire or caustic alkali, and churned by a firebrand.

When [the ulcer] has ripened, however, there is an absence of forceful discharge, flaccidity of the skin, looseness of the skin, the appearance of wrinkles, pallor, elevation in the center, rebounding upon being pressed with the fingers and released, the movement of pus like water in a bladder, itching, and the subsiding of inflammation, pain, and other such symptoms.
(AS.Sū.38.7) Pain arises without wind; burning arises from bile; swelling arises from the manifestation of phlegm. (AS.Sū.38.8)
There is redness and suppuration from the blood; thus, due to the humors (doṣas) along with the blood,
when suppuration has set in excessively, it becomes hollow, with thin skin, and consumed by the humors.
Covered with folds, dark-brown, and with the body hair falling out;
however, in certain swellings caused by phlegm (kapha), because of their deep-seated nature, it is the blood itself that suppurates.
Thereafter, the signs of ripening become indistinct,
wherein there is a similarity of color to the skin, coldness, swelling, tenderness to touch, and a hardness like that of stone.
One should not fall into confusion regarding that;
they call it *raktapāka*.

Then, having determined that it is properly ripened, one should perform incision with sharp and hot substances in cases of those who are timid, the elderly, children, the weak, the impotent, the emaciated, pregnant women, those afflicted by poison, those debilitated by weapons, those whose humors (*doṣas*) have been brought out by ripening, those with consolidated swellings, those where the swelling is located at joints or vital spots (*marmans*), or when the swellings are small.
AS.Sū.38.11 In other cases, however, incision [is required].
AS.Sū.38.12 In the case of incising an unripe [abscess], there may be injury to vessels and ligaments, excessive hemorrhage, increased pain, tearing, or erysipelas at the site of the wound.
And there is a verse on this:
When it is cooked by being ground, it becomes pus, vessels, ligaments, blood, and flesh.

When it has grown large, it quickly consumes [the body] as fire consumes grass and weeds; he who, out of ignorance, cuts down that which is not yet ripe, and he who neglects that which is already ripe.
Those two who act indecisively should be understood as being like dog-cookers (outcastes).
Before [administering] the surgical instrument, one should feed the desired food and cause them to drink strong liquor.
One does not faint from contact with food, nor does a weapon fail to strike one who is intoxicated,
except in cases of obstructed labor, abdominal stones, and diseases of the mouth.

AS.Sū.38.16: At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada. Then, the venerable Mahākāśyapa approached the Blessed One, paid homage with his head at his feet, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the venerable Mahākāśyapa said this to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, it would be well if the Blessed One would teach the Dharma discourse on the seven treasures, so that the monks, having heard it, might dwell with their minds well-established in the seven treasures. The Blessed One replied: “Kāśyapa, listen well and attend closely; I shall speak. “So be it, Blessed One,” the venerable Mahākāśyapa replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then spoke thus: “Kāśyapa, what are the seven treasures? They are the treasure of faith, the treasure of ethical discipline, the treasure of learning, the treasure of generosity, the treasure of wisdom, the treasure of shame, and the treasure of moral dread. Kāśyapa, these are called the seven treasures. Kāśyapa, what is the treasure of faith? Here, a noble disciple possesses unwavering faith in the Tathāgata’s enlightenment: “Thus is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly awakened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, well-gone, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. This, Kāśyapa, is called the treasure of faith. Kāśyapa, what is the treasure of ethical discipline?
