Here, a noble disciple dwells restrained by the restraint of the Prātimokṣa, possessed of right conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and trains himself by undertaking the training rules. This, Kāśyapa, is called the treasure of ethical discipline. Kāśyapa, what is the treasure of learning? Here, a noble disciple has learned much, remembers what he has heard, and accumulates what he has heard; those teachings which are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, and which set forth the perfectly pure holy life, he learns much of them, retains them in mind, recites them verbally, and penetrates them with his view. This, Kāśyapa, is called the treasure of learning. Kāśyapa, what is the treasure of generosity? Here, a noble disciple dwells as a giver, one who opens his hands, one who delights in renunciation, one who is generous, one who is free from the stinginess of mind, one who gives to those who come, and one who shares his possessions. This, Kāśyapa, is called the treasure of generosity. Kāśyapa, what is the treasure of wisdom? Here, a noble disciple is wise; he possesses the wisdom that discerns the arising and passing away of phenomena, the wisdom that is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. This, Kāśyapa, is called the treasure of wisdom. Kāśyapa, what is the treasure of shame? Here, a noble disciple is possessed of shame; he feels shame regarding unwholesome, evil qualities that have not yet arisen, thinking, ‘How may these unwholesome, evil qualities not arise in me? and likewise regarding those that have already arisen. This, Kāśyapa, is called the treasure of shame. Kāśyapa, what is the treasure of moral dread? Here, a noble disciple is possessed of moral dread; he feels dread regarding unwholesome, evil qualities that have not yet arisen, thinking, ‘How may these unwholesome, evil qualities not arise in me? and likewise regarding those that have already arisen. This, Kāśyapa, is called the treasure of moral dread. Kāśyapa, these are the seven treasures. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having spoken, the Well-Gone One rose from his seat and departed for the forest. Then, the venerable Mahākāśyapa followed the Blessed One from behind, calling out, “Wait, Blessed One! Wait, Well-Gone One! The Blessed One stopped and said, “Kāśyapa, why do you follow me from behind, calling out, ‘Wait, Blessed One! Wait, Well-Gone One!’? “Blessed One, I am following the Blessed One because I wish to hear the Dharma discourse on the seven treasures. “Kāśyapa, did you not hear the Dharma discourse on the seven treasures while I was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada? “I did not hear it, Blessed One. “Kāśyapa, go to the village of Nādikā; there, the Blessed One will teach the Dharma discourse on the seven treasures. “It is well, Blessed One,” the venerable Mahākāśyapa replied to the Blessed One. Then, the venerable Mahākāśyapa, having risen from his seat, paid homage with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed. Then, the Blessed One, having stayed at Śrāvastī for as long as he wished, set out to wander toward the village of Nādikā together with a great community of monks. When the Blessed One had traveled by stages and arrived at the village of Nādikā, he stayed there in the Brick House. Then, the venerable Mahākāśyapa approached the Blessed One, paid homage with his head at his feet, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the venerable Mahākāśyapa said this to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, it would be well if the Blessed One would teach the Dharma discourse on the seven treasures, so that the monks, having heard it, might dwell with their minds well-established in the seven treasures. “Kāśyapa, listen well and attend closely; I shall speak. “So be it, Blessed One,” the venerable Mahākāśyapa replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then spoke thus: “Kāśyapa, what are the seven treasures? They are the treasure of faith, the treasure of ethical discipline, the treasure of learning, the treasure of generosity, the treasure of wisdom, the treasure of shame, and the treasure of moral dread. Kāśyapa, these are called the seven treasures. [The rest of the discourse follows the same structure as above. Kāśyapa, these are the seven treasures. Then, the venerable Mahākāśyapa, having heard the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dharma discourse on the seven treasures, was filled with joy and delight. He rose from his seat, paid homage with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed. Then, the venerable Mahākāśyapa, having spent the rainy season retreat in the village of Nādikā, set out to wander toward Śrāvastī together with a great community of monks. When the venerable Mahākāśyapa had traveled by stages and arrived at Śrāvastī, he stayed there in the Jeta Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada. Then, the venerable Mahākāśyapa approached the Blessed One, paid homage with his head at his feet, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the venerable Mahākāśyapa said this to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, I have taught the Dharma discourse on the seven treasures to the monks in the village of Nādikā, so that they, having heard it, might dwell with their minds well-established in the seven treasures. “Well done, Kāśyapa! Well done, Kāśyapa! It is excellent that you have taught the Dharma discourse on the seven treasures to the monks in the village of Nādikā, so that they, having heard it, might dwell with their minds well-established in the seven treasures. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having spoken, the Well-Gone One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, the venerable Mahākāśyapa, having spent the rainy season retreat in Śrāvastī, set out to wander toward the village of Pāṭaligrāma together with a great community of monks. When the venerable Mahākāśyapa had traveled by stages and arrived at the village of Pāṭaligrāma, he stayed there in the Brick House. Then, the venerable Mahākāśyapa approached the Blessed One, paid homage with his head at his feet, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the venerable Mahākāśyapa said this to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, I have taught the Dharma discourse on the seven treasures to the monks in the village of Pāṭaligrāma, so that they, having heard it, might dwell with their minds well-established in the seven treasures. “Well done, Kāśyapa! Well done, Kāśyapa! It is excellent that you have taught the Dharma discourse on the seven treasures to the monks in the village of Pāṭaligrā

Then, having prepared all the instruments necessary for treating wounds—such as surgical instruments, weapons, alkali, cautery, *jāmbavauṣṭha*, cotton swabs, pads, leaves, thread, leather straps, honey, oils, decoctions, ointments, pastes, sprinkling vessels, water jars, cold and warm water, cauldrons, fans, and so forth—and having arranged a bed with a steady, strong, and reliable person to hold the patient; on an auspicious day and at a favorable hour, after honoring Brahmins with curd, unbroken rice, food, drink, gold, and gems, and having worshipped his chosen deities and performed auspicious rites; once the patient has eaten and is seated or laid down facing east, the physician, facing west, should secure the patient and apply the instrument in the direction of the hair, avoiding vital spots (*marman*), veins, ligaments, joints, bones, and arteries, until the pus is seen.
One should draw the instrument out only once and quickly;
even in large incisions, the length of the surgical opening is said to be two finger-breadths.

Having observed a space of two finger-breadths or three finger-breadths, and having probed with the left index finger in a region that is not too open, but deep and fleshy— avoiding a region that is the opposite, or one that is excessively constricted by the stalk of a *karīra* plant or the bristle of a boar—
one should know the direction in which it has gone and where its opening (*utsaṅga*) lies.
In each respective place, one should make an incision that is well-proportioned, free of pockets, long, and wide, so that the morbid humor does not remain.
Bravery, swiftness of action, a sharp instrument, absence of perspiration and trembling,
and lack of confusion in the physician are praised during surgical procedures.
In that regard, oblique incision is desired for the eyebrows, cheeks, forehead, bridge of the nose, lips, gums, neck, throat, collarbones,
armpits, abdomen, and groins; however, elsewhere, injury to the vessels and ligaments, excessive pain, slow healing of the wound, and the formation of a mass of flesh result from oblique incision.

Then, having applied the surgical instrument and comforted the patient with cold water, one should press all around and wash the wound with the finger; having removed the blood from the wound with a cloth after rinsing it with a decoction (kaṣāya), one should fumigate the wound with guggulu, agaru, sarjarasa, vacā, white mustard, hiṅgu, salt, and neem leaves mixed with ghee—substances that alleviate pain and ward off demons. Then, having inserted a wick smeared with its appropriate medicinal paste along with honey, ghee, and sesame paste, and having filled [the cavity] with the paste, one should cover it at the edge of the vessel with barley flour (saktu) slightly roasted and mixed with ghee, using the right fingers well-moistened with water. Having applied a thick compress (kavalikā), one should place a soft bandage straight, unknotted, and without constriction on either the left or right side, and then bind it.
In those cases arising from wind and phlegm, one should bandage the wounds two or three times.
In cases arising from bile, blood, or injury, one should sprinkle [the area] once all around; however,
when the pain from a surgical wound is persistent, one should sprinkle the ulcer with warm liquorice (yaṣṭīmadhuka) and ghee.
Taking water from a water-pot, one should sprinkle it around while scattering leaves, *śabarī* grass, and other materials, performing protection for him to prevent the assault of demons; furthermore,
one should offer them a sacrificial oblation (*bali*) and carry [the vessel] upon one's head.
Lakṣmī, Guhā, Atiguhā, Jaṭilā, and Brahmācāriṇī;
Vacā, Chatrā, Aticchatrā, Dūrvā, and also Siddhārthakas.

AS.Sū.38.25 One should fumigate the bed, seat, and other such items twice a day with guggulu and similar substances; likewise, one should follow the conduct prescribed for oleation therapy and that prescribed for the daily regimen.

Furthermore, specifically from sleeping during the day, there occurs swelling, itching, redness, pain, and an increase in pus in the ulcer. In the case of women, however, when [the semen] has been moved or discharged through memory, touch, or sight—
In the case of *śukra* (semen), one may incur the defects arising from sexual intercourse even without physical contact.

One should feed the patient according to their suitability (*yathāsātmya*) with any one of the following: well-aged *śāli*, *ṣaṣṭika*, barley, or wheat; accompanied by soups of *mudga*, *masūra*, *āḍhakī*, or *satīna*; combined with the meat-broth of wild animals (*jāṅgala*); mixed with *jīvantī*, *suniṣaṇṇaka*, *taṇḍulīyaka*, *vāstuka*, eggplant (*vārtāka*), *paṭola*, *kāravella*, young roots, and *śaśāka*; seasoned with pomegranate, *āmalaka*, and rock salt (*saindhava*); made unctuous with clarified butter (*sarpiḥ-snigdha*); light and small in quantity; and followed by an abundance of warm water.
In this way, what has been properly eaten undergoes digestion for him;
from indigestion, however, a powerful derangement of the wind and the other humors may arise.
Thereafter, one may suffer from swelling, pain, suppuration, burning, and flatulence.

One should avoid fresh grain, black gram, kalāya, horse gram, niṣpāva, and śimbī; cold water, wine, sugarcane juice, milk, flour preparations, sesame products, dried vegetables, meat, green potherbs, sour, salty, pungent, and alkaline substances; and the flesh of animals from marshy regions.
This group of nine grains and so forth causes all the [three] doṣas in one suffering from a wound.
Alcohol— being sharp, hot, dry, and sour— would quickly destroy the wound.
One should fan him with young *uśīra* stalks, but one should not shake him;
one should not prick him nor scratch him, and while he is moving about, one should protect him.
Listening to pleasant stories told by affectionate and elderly members of the twice-born,
one who possesses hope for liberation from disease quickly heals the wound.
Furthermore, on the third day, one should perform the treatment of the wound as before, beginning with the washing;
for if it is not bound after being released on the second day, the wound will heal slowly and become intensely painful.
And one should not administer a medicinal preparation that has disheveled hair, nor one that is excessively unctuous or dry, too loose or too tight, rough, or poorly applied;
for from excessive unctuousness, moistening occurs.
From excessive harshness there is cutting and pain; from excessive looseness there is impurity;
from excessive tightness there is inflammation; and from roughness and improper application there is friction of the wound edges.
In a wound that is inevitably accompanied by pus, one should apply a probe;
[the wound] being characterized by putrid flesh, a cavity, sinus tracks, and filled with pus.
For if a vikeśikā (gum) remains inside, it quickly purifies the wound; however,
one should treat an opened swelling that is not yet suppurated with digestive (pācana) measures.
With foods and poultices that do not excessively aggravate the wound, one should treat a wound that requires suturing as follows:

having removed loose bone, foreign bodies, dust, grass, hair, dried blood, and the like; having properly repositioned the torn and hanging flesh and the joints and bones to their respective places; and once the bleeding has ceased, one should suture it appropriately with a needle using either tendon, thread, or hair.
Alternatively, one may use the bark of hemp, *aśmantaka*, *mūrvā*, or flax;
in brief, there are four varieties of stitching.
For example, there are the "cow-hood" (goṣphaṇika), the "tunnasīvana," the "winding rope-knot" (vellitakarajjugranthi), and the "binding" (bandhana);
their specific forms are distinguished by these very names, and they are employed according to the nature of the strike.
One should not insert the needle too close, nor too far away, nor one that grasps too little or too much;

having thus observed that it is properly sewn, one should sprinkle it with honey, ghee, and the powders of *añjana*, *madhuka*, *nimba*, *lodhra*, *priyaṅgu*, *sallakī* fruit, and *kṣauma* bark, and then apply the bandage and other treatments as before.

Wounds that should not be sutured include those in the groin, chest, and armpits, those that are unstable, those with little flesh, those from which wind escapes, those containing internal foreign bodies or blood, and those caused by poison, fire, or alkali.
Sutures are indicated for wounds arising from fat, those with ruptured or scarred edges, ears with small flaps, and fresh traumatic wounds.

On the head, forehead, bridge of the nose, ears, nostrils, cheeks, lips, nape of the neck, arms, abdomen, buttocks, anus, genitals, scrotum, and other such firm and fleshy regions, there are fifteen specific types of binding:
*kośa*, *dāma*, *utsaṅga*, *svastika*, *anuvelita*, *muttolī*, *maṇḍala*, *sthavikā*, *ayamaka*, *khaṭvā*, *cīnavibandha*, *vitāna*, *goṣphaṇā*, and *pañcāṅgī*.
Their forms are for the most part explained by their very names.
Among them, one should place the *kośa* on the joints of the fingers.
The *dāma* [arrangement] is on the constricted parts of the body;
the *utsaṅga* on the hanging [parts];
the *svastika* on the joints, the beard, the space between the eyebrows, the breasts, the abdomen, the eyes, the cheeks, and the ears.
An *anuvellita* occurs when the hair is curled upon the limbs; a *muttolī* when it is on the neck or the private parts; and a *maṇḍala* when it is on a rounded limb.
The *sthavikā* bandage is used for the thumb, fingers, penis, tip of the scrotum, and scrotal hernia;
the *yamaka* bandage for twin ulcers;
and the *khaṭvā* bandage for the jaw, temples, and cheeks.
A dark mark at the outer corners of the eyes,
a band-like mark on the abdomen, thighs, or back, a canopy-like mark on the head and so forth, or a large mark on a broad limb.
One should apply the *goṣphaṇa* bandage at the joints of the nose, lips, and chin;
the *pañcāṅgī* above the collarbone;
and whichever [bandage] is most suitable for whichever specific region, one should apply it there.
However, the bandage should not be placed directly over the ulcer, nor should it be so tight as to cause pain; indeed,
bandaging is recommended when vāyu is vitiated, in cases of fracture, and in ulcers.
In that regard, for the last two [types of yoga], bondage is twofold according to the distinction between left and right; however,
it is threefold everywhere according to being tight, loose, or moderate.

In cases of *kapha* and *vāta*, the binding is thick and firm; in cases of *pitta* and *rakta*, it is thin and loose. In cases of *vāta* and *pitta*, the binding is moderate, as it is also in wounds caused by *kapha* and *pitta*.
Likewise, one should bind it firmly on the buttocks, armpits, groins, thighs, and head;
and evenly on the branches (limbs), face, neck, ears, penis, scrotum, back, sides, abdomen, and chest;
and loosely at the joints of the eyes.
In cases arising from wind and phlegm (vāta-śleṣma), [the bandage] should be applied evenly on a loose spot; on a firm spot, it should be tight.
In cases where the site of the disease is severe, one should apply stronger treatment; likewise, in cases of pitta and rakta during the winter and spring seasons, one should act after three days.
However, in cases of pitta and rakta where the site is moderate, one should act immediately.
In a state of equanimity, one should be relaxed;
in a state requiring relaxation, one should not be so;
likewise during autumn and summer, and in the evening and morning.

Furthermore, if not properly protected, the ulcer becomes afflicted by various complications due to contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, grass, wood, dust, cold, wind, heat, and so forth; it thus assumes the state of a malignant wound,
and in such a case, the oil does not remain for long and the medicinal application dries up quickly.
It heals with difficulty, and once healed, discoloration occurs.
A wound that is crushed, churned, fractured, dislocated, or lacerated,
and where bones, ligaments, or vessels have been severed, heals quickly through proper bandaging.
In all activities such as rising and lying down, he is not afflicted;
[the tongue] has upturned lips, is swollen, uneven, hard, and extremely painful.
A wound that is even, soft, and painless heals quickly and becomes clean;
however, for firm wounds with little flesh that do not heal due to dryness, [remedies must be applied].
The medicinal drug should be covered with leaves— according to the specific disorder and the season— using leaves that are not decayed, young, and without holes, and which are well-fitted all around.
With clean, non-rough leaves from the *kṣīrī*, *bhūrja*, *arjuna*, and *kadamba* trees,
[one should treat] those suffering from leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), those burned by fire, those with carbuncles (*piṭaka*), and those with diabetes (*madhumeha*).

In cases of rat poison, the *karṇikā* (fleshy growths) should be cauterized with alkali; they are toxic and must not be bound together during the cooking of the flesh, nor in severe anal inflammation (*gudapāka*).
When wounds are disintegrating, accompanied by pain and burning, spreading through the stages of swelling,
and when flies deposit worms into them due to lack of protection—
While consuming [these], they cause pain, swelling, and the discharge of blood;
in such cases, one should employ the *surasādi* group for washing and filling [the wound].
A plaster made from the barks of *saptaparṇa*, *karañja*, *arka*, *nimba*, and *rājādana*, ground with cow’s urine, is beneficial; likewise, irrigation with alkaline water is beneficial.
Or, having covered the wound with a strip of flesh, one should quickly extract them;
and as those various stages arise, one should treat them with appropriate therapeutic measures, taking into account the humors (*doṣa*) and other factors.
One should not, in haste, cause it to heal while internal defects remain;
for even with a slight application [of medicine], having created an internal cavity, it undergoes further transformation.
Therefore, one should cause a perfectly clean wound to heal;
even when it has healed, one should avoid indigestion, physical exercise, sexual intercourse, and similar activities.
"For six or seven months for men— this rule is praised.
Thus, with reference to this ulcer, only a mere indication has been shown.
"The detailed explanation regarding its practice will be stated further on"—
thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter.
Now begins the thirty-ninth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the method for cooking alkaline preparations (kṣārapāka).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.

Alkali (kṣāra), being produced from the combination of various medicinal herbs, is the substratum of all tastes, yet it is predominantly pungent and salty. It is sharp, hot, caustic, digestive, fissuring, liquefying, purifying, and healing; it destroys worms, pus, fat, and poisons, and is the best among all primary and secondary surgical instruments. Because it performs cutting, piercing, lancing, and scraping, it is employed when instruments are difficult to apply due to congestion or lack of space—such as in the nose, hemorrhoids, tumors, and the like—or when surgery has failed, and in malignant ulcers that are frequently aggravated. (AS.Sū.39.2)

It is of two kinds, distinguished by external and internal cleansing (AS.Sū.39.3). Among these, in cases such as hemorrhoids, tumors, fistulas, cysts, malignant ulcers, sinus tracts, warts, eyelid diseases, mouth diseases, leprosy, vitiligo, moles, and dark spots, [cleansing] is performed through external purification (AS.Sū.39.3).

However, regarding internal cleansing (*antaḥparimārjana*), it will be prescribed specifically for each case in instances such as tumors, abdominal diseases, loss of digestive fire, accumulation of impurities, colic, constipation, urinary stones, and gravel. But neither [type of cleansing] should be applied to those who are fearful, weak, emaciated, or afflicted by vāta-pitta; nor to those suffering from fever, diarrhea, anemia, diseases of the head or heart, urinary disorders, ophthalmia, or timira; nor to those afflicted by anorexia; nor to those who have undergone emesis or purgation, those who are fasting, pregnant women, those with displaced fetal parts, those with pain throughout the entire body, or those who have consumed poison or alcohol.

One should avoid [administering] [medicines or treatments] at vital spots (*marmans*), veins (*sirās*), ligaments (*snāyus*), joints (*sandhis*), cartilage (*taruṇāsthi*), sutures (*sevanīs*), arteries (*dhamanīs*), the throat, the navel, the interdigital spaces, the scrotum, the penis, the urinary passages, and in regions with little flesh; nor on the eyes, except for diseases of the eyelids (*vartma-rogas*);
likewise, one should avoid [doing so] during cold, heat, rain, cloudy weather, or when there is a strong wind.
(AS.Sū.39.5) Now, external cleansing (*parimārjana*) is of three kinds: moderate (*madhya*), mild (*mṛdu*), and sharp (*tīkṣṇa*).

The method for its preparation is as follows: Having fasted and purified oneself in the autumn, wearing white garments on an auspicious day, one should perform an offering (*bali*) in the four directions with liquor, meat-paste, flowers, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), and so forth, for a large, undamaged *kālamuṣkaka* tree grown in a commendable location and of middle age. After circumambulating it and worshipping it, one should consecrate it (*adhivāsayet*) with the words:
"Homage to those deities who dwell here, having taken refuge in this place."
"Free from anger, they ought to depart, leaving behind this imperishable dwelling.
For the sake of medicine, I shall take this [body] for all living beings."
"Neither out of greed nor out of anger [should one cut down] a tree, especially for the sake of a Brahmin. Thus [it is said].

AS.Sū.39.8 Then, on the following day, if no portent or abnormality whatsoever is seen there, then when the sun has risen to the height of a yoke, having caused the Brahmins to recite auspicious prayers, one should cause that tree to fall with its top toward the east or toward the north.

And in this manner, having collected in the spring the *pāribhadra*, *palāśa*, *aśvakarṇa*, *rājavṛkṣa*, *mahāvṛkṣa*, *vṛkṣaka*, *indravṛkṣa*, *āsphota*, *saptacchada*, *naktamāla*, *tilvaka*, *kadalī*, *bibhītaka*, *aśvamāraka*, *pūtīka*, *citraka*, *arka*, *kākajaṅghā*, *pāmārga*, and *agnimantha*—along with barley stalks including their awns, four types of *kośātakī*, and *savā* trees—all cut into pieces with roots, fruits, leaves, and branches, neither too dry nor placed on a stone surface in a windless spot, one should heap them separately; and into the heap of *muṣkaka* wood, having added lime-dust, one should set fire to it using sesame twigs.

Having burned [the wood] and once the fire has subsided, one should separately prepare the ashes of *sudhā* and sugar; then, having mixed all the other alkaline substances along with an additional *droṇa* of *uṣkaka* in a thousand *pala* of water and a thousand *pala* of the urine of cows and other animals, one should strain it through a large cloth until it becomes clear, red, sharp, and slimy. Then, having taken that alkaline extract and discarded the ash, one should cook it according to the procedure for cooking medicinal fats (*sneha*).

While that is being cooked, one should take those alkali ashes and sugar, heat them in an iron vessel until they are fire-colored, and pour them into a copper vessel containing milk-alkali (kṣīravaka) in a quantity of one kuḍava. Having ground that lye very finely with that [liquid], one should add it as an additive; then, stirring constantly with a ladle, one should cook it until it rises with steamy bubbles and becomes thick enough to coat the ladle. Then, having removed it from the fire, one should store it well-sealed in a jar or a barley-sack.
This is the medium-strength alkali.

In a mild [preparation], one should add grits and similar substances by pouring them in and then removing them, but one should not throw them in after grinding them. In a sharp [preparation], however, one should give an after-addition (*prativāpa*) consisting of *dantī*, *citraka*, *lāṅgalikā*, *pūtīka*, sprouts, *tālapattrī*, *viḍa*, *svarjikā*, *kanakakṣīrī*, asafoetida, *vacā*, *ativiṣā*, and burnt conch and oyster shells, all finely powdered, as previously described.
One should administer those [alkalis] after seven nights for those with strong disease-force;
however, for one whose strength is diminished, one should again add alkaline water for the purpose of restoring strength.
In this regard, there are ten qualities of alkali: it is neither too sharp nor too mild, white, smooth, swift, slimy, peaked, easy to extinguish, causing little pain, and non-obstructive.
And there are exactly ten defects,
namely: too hot, too cold, too sharp, too mild, too thin, too thick, too slimy, spreading, having inferior medicinal ingredients, and having insufficient cooking.

In that regard, for the procedure of cauterization with alkali (*kṣārakarman*), one should have ready at hand cotton-wool swabs (*picu*), wicks (*varti*), probes (*śalākā*), spoons (*darvī*), *añjalikā* vessels, clarified butter (*ghṛta*), honey (*madhu*), fermented gruel (*śukta*), *tuṣodaka*, buttermilk (*mastu*), milk-water (*kṣīrodaka*), cold poultices (*śītapradeha*), beds, seats, and so forth. Then, for the patient who is fit for alkali therapy— whether seated or lying down and supported by attendants— the physician, having incised, scraped, or scarified the disease, should apply the alkali using a probe wrapped in either cotton-wool or a cloth.

Then, one should disregard a hundred *mātrās* in the case of eyelid diseases; however, having everted the eyelids and covered the dark portion with a cotton pad or beeswax, one should apply a thin paste of alkali on a lotus leaf for fifty *mātrās*. In the case of hemorrhoids or tumors arising in the nose, one should raise the nose while facing the sun and disregard [the count] for fifty *mātrās*.
Similarly, in cases of hemorrhoids arising in the region of the ears, one should close the opening of the instrument with the hand and retain [the caustic] for exactly one hundred mātrās;

then, having wiped it clean with a cloth and observed that the caustic has been properly burnt, one should extinguish it with clarified butter, honey, sour gruel (śukta), fermented rice-water (tuṣodaka), buttermilk (mastu), milk, and so forth.
Thereafter, one should apply a cooling and sweet plaster mixed with ghee.

For the purpose of moistening, foods that cause secretions (abhiṣyandi) should be consumed. However, if the area does not slough off due to its deep-rooted nature after being cauterized with alkali (kṣāra), then one should apply a paste made of sesame seeds combined with fermented rice-water (dhānyāmla), liquorice (madhuyaṣṭikā), and *suvarṇakṣīrī*, or alternatively, with *trivṛt* and the essence of *viḍaṅga*.
The wound should be washed with a decoction of *mālatī*, *vṛṣāṅkola*, *nimba*, *āsphota*, *paṭolī*, and *karavīra* leaves;
furthermore, ghee or oil prepared from the paste and decoction of these same ingredients serves as a healing agent.
Alternatively, [ghee or oil] may be prepared from *nāgapuṣpa*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *candana*, and *tilaparṇikā*.
One should treat the ulcer according to the specific nature of the disease and the involved *doṣa*. For its healing, sesame seeds together with *yaṣṭimadhu* (liquorice) are highly recommended.
Among these, when the area resembles a ripe *jāmbava* fruit, has subsided, and the respective symptoms have slightly subsided, it is considered properly cauterized (*samyagdagdha*).
By the opposite of that, if there is pricking, itching, numbness, and so forth, it is poorly cauterized;
in that case, one should apply [the cautery] again.
Furthermore, when the eyes are excessively burnt by alkalis, bloodletting, redness, swelling, fever, suppuration, erysipelas, diseases of the head, or the provocation of vāta and pitta,
there occurs a loss of visual faculty due to the bursting of the eyelids from over-application.

In the nose, there is cracking of the nasal bridge and the young bones, contraction, and loss of the sense of smell; likewise, in the ears and other senses, there is impairment according to their respective functions.

In the anus, there is obstruction of feces and urine, diarrhea, impairment of virility, and death due to the tearing of the rectum, or else constant swelling, pricking pain, distressing sensations, and discharges.
If there is an inability to restrain feces, urine, or flatus,
or if the fire spreads excessively, one should repeatedly extinguish it with the aforementioned cooling measures; therefore, one should not cauterize an excessively large area all at once.
And there is a verse on this point:
"For sourness is cold to the touch; therefore, it is combined with alkali."
Therefore, one should quickly bring it to a state of sweetness and thoroughly allay it with sour substances,
[especially] when afflicted by fever, diarrhea, thirst, delusion, fainting, and pain in the heart.
If there is an excessive administration [of emetics], it burns the body like fire burning dry grass;
therefore, one should quickly have the patient drink curd mixed with ghee.
Curd-whey with jaggery, or oil with sugar-candy; or ghee prepared in the fresh juice of *dhātrī*, *kapittha*, sour *dāḍima*, and *amlavetasa*.
When doubled, it is prepared with sprays of juice; it overcomes excessive pain from alkaline disorders. [One should use] pomegranate, *āmalaka*, *āmrātaka*, wood-apple, and *karamardaka*.
One should cook the juice of mango and citron over a gentle fire;
then, once the alkaline potency has subsided, one should administer a dose according to the patient's strength.
By that, the caustic is neutralized and the skin attains clarity;
however, in the case of excessive hemorrhage, cooling measures should be applied both externally and internally.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter.
Now begins the fortieth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the chapter on the procedure for cauterization (agnikarma).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:

"Fire is even more powerful than caustic alkali (*kṣāra*); for where medicines, surgical instruments, and caustic alkali have failed, it succeeds through burning, and because its effects are irreversible."

AS.Sū.40.2 Therein, thermal cautery (*agnikarma*) is applied to the skin, flesh, vessels (*sirā*), ligaments (*snāyu*), joints (*sandhi*), and bones. Among these, for cases of moles, freckles, dark spots (*alakā*), warts (*carmakīla*), painful growths (*saruka*), stiffness, flaccidity of the limbs, ophthalmia (*abhiṣyanda*), conjunctivitis (*adhimantha*), and pain in the head, eyebrows, temples, forehead, or facial paralysis (*ardita*), one performs skin-cauterization (*tvagdāha*) using a sun-crystal (*sūryakānta*), long pepper (*pippalī*), goat dung, cow-tusk, or an arrow-shaft, according to the specific condition such as ophthalmia and the like, in the regions of the eyebrows, temples, and forehead.

In cases of cysts, tumors, hemorrhoids, fistula-in-ano, scrofula, elephantiasis, hernia, malignant ulcers, sinus tracts, fistulous channels, and deep-seated suppuration or sloughing, cauterization with *jāmbavauṣṭha*, needles, probes, ghee, molasses, honey, beeswax, oil, muscle fat, or metals such as gold, copper, iron, silver, and bell-metal is indicated for the purpose of cauterizing the flesh. In cases of excessive discharge from veins, ligaments, joints, bones, or membranes; in sinus tracts of the teeth; and in conditions involving the eyelids, eyelashes, or the loss of vision due to improper venesection, cauterization of the veins and other structures is performed using *jāmbavauṣṭha*, needles, probes, honey, beeswax, molasses, and fats.

One should not apply cauterization (agnikarma) to a patient whose internal organs are ruptured, who has internal hemorrhaging, whose foreign body (śalya) has not been extracted, who is afflicted by many wounds, during the hot season, or to one unfit for alkaline treatment (kṣāra). However, in an emergency condition, one may perform cauterization on a patient who has received cooling countermeasures and has eaten slimy food.

AS.Sū.40.4 Now, having prepared the patient who requires cauterization by performing rites for well-being (*svastyayana*), providing all necessary implements, and having him lie down facing east with his head supported by trusted attendants, the physician—using smokeless, large, steady, and blazing embers of *khadira*, *badara*, or other woods, fanned by bellows or a fan until they reach the color of fire, glowing and radiant as they emit upward flames according to the method of application—should cauterize the diseased area using the *jāmbavauṣṭha* and other instruments, according to the requirements of the disease, in the form of rings, half-moons, svastikas, chessboard patterns, dots, lines, or scarification, while repeatedly encouraging the patient with beneficial words and water. He should continue until the signs of successful cauterization appear.
In cases of swellings, hollows, decayed teeth, sinus tracts, infestation by worms, or malignant ulcers, one should fill them with oil, beeswax, honey, and molasses and then cauterize them;
once properly burnt, one should apply honey and ghee, as well as cold and unctuous plasters.
When the *liṅga* (penis) is properly cauterized, there is burning accompanied by sound; when the skin is burnt, there is a foul odor and contraction of the skin.
When the flesh is burnt, there is a pigeon-like color, slight swelling and pain, and the wound becomes dry and shriveled.

When blood remains, there is blackness, elevation, and ulceration, along with the discharge of lymph; when a vein is burnt, there is a blackish-red, rough, and firm ulcer; and when a ligament or similar tissue is burnt, the symptoms of the "badly burnt" (durdagdha) and "excessively burnt" (atidagdhā) types are like those of the "accidentally burnt" (pramādadagdhā).
And medical treatment (cikitsita) for one consumed by negligence is again fourfold.
Regarding these, that which is scorched (tuttha), badly burnt (durdagdha), properly burnt (samyagdagdha), and over-burnt (atidagdha):

therein, that which becomes discolored and excessively emits vapors is scorched; that wherein eruptions arise accompanied by intense burning, heat, and pain, and which subsides only after a long time, is badly burnt.
When the area has the color of a ripe *tāla* fruit, is evenly leveled, and possesses all the previously mentioned characteristics, it is properly cauterized.

However, in the case of excessive burning (*atidagdha*), there is intense pain, smoking, hanging down of the flesh, complications involving the veins and other structures, deep ulceration, fever, burning sensations, thirst, fainting, vomiting, excessive hemorrhage, and the various afflictions resulting from that; furthermore, healing occurs with great difficulty, and even when healed, there is discoloration.
Indeed, burning by means of oil (*snehadāha*) is even more painful.
For that [fever], because it follows the subtle channels of the bodily humors (*sneha*), enters deeply;
and in this regard, it is said:
"For one who is afflicted by it, treatment with fire and heating, as well as warm medicine, should be administered. (AS.Sū.40.7)

AS.Sū.40.7 When the blood has congealed, heat does not emerge from it to the exterior; therefore, pain increases and the blood becomes inflamed. AS.Sū.40.8 Because of that, the blood is further scorched.

When applying heat, one should remove it once the steam has subsided and the pain has diminished; in the case of a bad burn, one should apply both cold and hot treatments, and then repeat the procedure again.
One should apply only cool ointments and affusions of ghee;
when properly cauterized, [one should treat it] with *tavakṣīrī*, *plakṣa*, sandalwood, and *gairika*.
AS.Sū.40.10 A plaster made from the pastes of the meat of marshy animals, combined with honey and ghee, [should be applied].
AS.Sū.40.11 Once the heat has subsided, one should further employ the treatment for pitta-type abscess (pittavidradhi).
If it is excessively burnt, one should remove the shattered flesh and then perform a cooling treatment, followed by an application of rice-paste made from the pounding of *śāli* rice grains.
Or one should apply a plaster made of ground decoctions of *tindukī* bark mixed with clarified butter; or else,
one should cover the ulcer with leaves of *guḍūcī* or *aupodaka*.

One should administer for him all medicinal treatments as in the case of *pitta-visarpa*. However, in the case of a burn caused by fats (*sneha-dagdha*), one should apply even more intensely dry (*rūkṣa*) remedies.
Since surgical instruments, caustics, and fire are the supreme weapons of Death,
the physician, remaining vigilant, should therefore apply them correctly.
Thus ends the Sūtrasthāna, the heart of the treatise (tantra).
Herein, the subtle meanings that have been briefly indicated (sūtrita) are indeed expanded upon in every respect.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter;
the Sūtrasthāna is completed. [Now begins] the Śārīrasthāna.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the desire for a son;
thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.

Now, indeed, a man twenty-one years of age should marry, according to the irreproachable rite, a maiden who is not of the same lineage (*gotra*), but of equal birth, born into a family free from hereditary diseases, endowed with beauty, character, and auspicious marks; one whose teeth, lips, ears, nose, nails, hair, and breasts are neither deficient nor deformed; who is gentle, healthy by nature, and not brownish or reddish-brown; whose limbs are neither too small nor too large; who is about twelve years old; and whose name does not contain terms associated with gods, serpents, rivers, mountains, trees, birds, constellations, outcasts, or terrifying things; one who is faultless and beyond reproach.
When she has reached sixteen years of age, a man of twenty-five years should strive for the sake of a son;
for at that time, having both attained their full vigor, they will procreate offspring endowed with vitality.

If a man less than twenty-five years of age impregnates a woman less than sixteen years of age, the embryo, while still within the womb, may perish; or [the child] may have a short lifespan, lack strength, health, or wealth, or possess impaired faculties. This is because, as stated in the *Abhidharma-samuccaya-śāstra* (AS.Śā.1.4), "if the semen and ovum are corrupted during the first three nights of the fertile period.
In that regard, when food has been properly digested and has sequentially reached the marrow, its essence acquires the designation of "semen" (*śukra*).
That [essence], however, like ghee from milk or molasses from sugarcane juice, having settled by relying upon the semen-bearing portion within the body, remains pervading all the limbs,
and especially in the marrow, the testicles, and the breasts.
That which is emitted through excitement by means of friction, having become concentrated from the heart’s involvement and flowing forth from limb after limb—

being gentle, unctuous, heavy, white, honey-scented, sweet, slimy, abundant, thick, and possessing a color like any one of ghee, oil, or honey— is the semen (*śukra*) fit for conception (AS.Śā.1.5). Likewise, it is said that the very blood of women, reaching the womb every month and flowing for three days, is called the menstrual flow (*ārtava*).

Due to excessive indulgence, whether out of season or during the fertile period, that very condition becomes known as *asṛgdara*, *pradara*, *vyāpad*, or *raktayoni*. In its treatment, one should observe the therapeutic measures for *raktapitta* and the prohibitions regarding diseases of the private parts.
In those whose channels are obstructed by wind (vāta) and phlegm (kapha), one should treat the non-flowing [menstrual blood] with pitta-alleviating measures.

For that [blood], whether accompanied by semen or devoid of semen, or even lifeless, if it remains increasing within the womb of a woman who indulges in wind-increasing substances, manifests the signs of pregnancy and becomes a *gulma* (abdominal tumor).
In that regard, one should observe the treatment for gulma (AS.Śā.1.7); sometimes, however, vātodara occurs like a pregnancy, and it is pacified by means of pacifying vāta (AS.Śā.1.7).
That very [menstrual blood], when at times suppressed by mild and nourishing diet and lifestyle, produces a disorderless abdominal enlargement that resembles a pregnancy; because of this,
the ignorant call her "pregnant" even though she is not pregnant.

Then, when the blood has been discharged due to perverted conditions or by chance, those who do not perceive the embryo-body say, out of ignorance, that it has been "carried off by spirits" (*bhūta-hṛta*).

This is because the removal of vital energy (*ojas*) occurs through the *rakṣas* demons, but not the removal of the body itself—either because [the demons] do not desire it or because they lack the power;
for the activity of both desire and power is what is observed.

Furthermore, the removal of anyone's body by non-human beings is never observed. And if some beings possessed of extraordinary power were to disregard even what is seen and proceed to cast away the body of the embryo, then how could they possibly neglect its mother when the opportunity had presented itself?
Furthermore, menstrual blood that resembles the juice of lac or the blood of a rabbit is said to be pure when it is washed and becomes free from impurity.

Just as the scent of flowers or fruits is not perceived on a young or withered tree, or of such [trees] themselves, so too the semen, body hair, and so forth are not perceived in a man less than sixteen years old or more than seventy years old, nor are the menses, breast milk, and so forth perceived in a woman less than twelve years old or more than fifty years old.
Now,

when the semen and menstrual blood are pure and free from disease, and the couple are mutually enamored, one should treat them by first applying oleation and then performing purification according to the rules, followed by non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) and unctuous enema (anuvāsana).
Specifically, however, by means of preparations of sweet medicinal herbs mixed with ghee and milk for a man,
and with oil and bile-increasing meats for a woman,
the semen and the menstrual blood are thus nourished through the similarity of their qualities.

AS.Śā.1.13 Wind, bile, phlegm, the odor of a corpse, knots, pus, diminished urine, feces, and semen are the seeds of the skin. Among these, [semen] discharged by wind is thin, dry, frothy, reddish, scanty, interrupted, and painful, and it is emitted after a long time; that which is discharged by bile is slightly yellow, slimy, blue-black, or as if burning.
When mixed with marrow, it is abundant and obstructed; when mixed with water, a small portion floats;
through phlegm (kapha), it has the foul odor of a corpse and is not small; through blood, it becomes knotted; and through wind (vāta) and phlegm, it is likewise affected.
That which resembles putrid pus is caused by bile and phlegm;
that which is emaciated is caused by wind and bile, as was previously stated along with its treatment.
When vitiated by the combination of the humors (sannipāta), the menstrual blood has the odor of urine and feces; even though it resembles semen, it is rendered non-seed (abīja) by the defects.
Its symptoms and names are as previously described.

Among those, cases involving *kuṇapa* (corpse-like), *granthi* (nodular), *pūya* (pus-like), and diminished semen are curable with difficulty; however, those involving urine, feces, semen, or menstrual blood—specifically when the menstrual blood is *kuṇapa*, *granthi*, or *pūya*—are incurable.

Among those, one should treat the first three types of defects of semen and menses according to the therapeutic measures for their respective doshas, and both types [of defects] by means of the prevention of diseases of the genitals and the female reproductive tract (AS.Śā.1.15).

Furthermore, in the case of a vātika defect of semen, one should administer a drink of ghee prepared with *vasuka*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and sour fruits, with the addition of barley alkali (*yavakṣāra*).
An enema (āsthāpana) prepared with *bilva* and *vidārī* combined with milk,
and an oil for unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*) prepared with *madhuka* and *bhadradāru*.
Oil prepared with the juice of *kṣīrakulīra* should be administered as an enema (*uttarabasti*) in the Pitta-type [hemorrhoids];
ghee prepared with *kāṇḍekṣu*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, and *guḍūcī*, with the addition of *mūrvā* and *madhūka*, should be drunk;
and purgation should be induced with the powder of *trivṛt* mixed with ghee.
For the Kapha-type [hemorrhoids], an asthāpana enema prepared with *payasyā* and *śrīparṇī*, combined with milk;
an oil for anuvasana enema and uttarabasti prepared with *madhuka* and *mudgaparṇī*;
and the drinking of clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) prepared with a decoction of *pāṣāṇabheda*, *aśmantaka*, and *āmalaka*, with the addition of a powder of *pippalī* and *madhuka*.
An emetic is a decoction of *madanaphala*;
a purgative is the powder of *dantī* and *viḍaṅga* licked with oil;
and a non-unctuous enema (*āsthāpana*) is one strongly charged with a decoction of *rājavṛkṣa* and *madanaphala*.
Oil prepared with madhuka and pippalī is used for anuvasana enema and uttarabasti;
in cases of vāta-type menstrual disorders, one should drink ghee prepared with bhārgī, madhuka, and bhadradāru.
One should apply to the vagina milk boiled with *kāśmarya* and *kṣudrasahā*, or a paste of *madhuka* and *sṛgālavinnā* combined with milk and ghee, or a paste of *priyaṅgu* and sesame; furthermore,
a decoction of *sarala* and *mudgaparṇī* should be used for washing.

In cases arising from Pitta, one should drink a decoction of the two types of Kākolī and Vidārī root, or a decoction of Utpala and Padmaka, or a decoction of Madhūka flowers and Kāśmarya fruit, mixed with sugar;
or a decoction of Śvetacandana mixed with honey;
or a paste of Dhava and Dhātakī with ghee; or a paste of Madhuka, Madhurasā, and Mṛdvīkā with ghee.
The milk of *śamyāka* and *gavākṣī* is a purgative;
one should apply a paste of *candana* and *payasyā* to the vagina,
and use a decoction of *gaurī* and *ariṣṭaka* for washing.
In cases of the phlegmatic type (ślaiṣmika), one should drink a decoction of *kuṭaja*, *kaṭukā*, and *aśvagandhā* mixed with honey;
or a decoction of the tender leaves (*pravāla*) of milk-exuding trees (*kṣīrivṛkṣa*); or one should lick the powder of these very same drugs with honey and ghee.
Emesis may also be induced with a decoction of *madanaphala*.
One should place that very paste into the vagina; the decoction of *lodhra* and *tinduka* is for washing, or alternatively, goat or ram urine may be used.
In the case of a fetid discharge (*kuṇapa-retas*), one should administer ghee prepared with *dhātakī* flowers, *khadira*, *arjuna*, and *dāḍima*, or with *asanā* and other such ingredients.
If there is a knot in the semen, it should be treated with *pāṣāṇabheda* and the ashes of *palāśa*;
if the semen is putrid, with *parūṣaka* and the group beginning with *nyagrodha*.

If the urine, feces, or semen are excessively vitiated by wind (vāyu), one should take asafoetida (hiṅgu), uśīra, and citraka; or else, a preparation of citraka, vitunnaka, priyaṅgu, hiṅgu, samaṅgā, and lotus stalks (mṛṇāla) with an addition of powdered elā and mocarasa.
Likewise, in cases of discharge from a tumor (granthi) or menstrual blood (ārtava), one should drink a decoction of pāṭhā, trikaṇṭaka, and vṛkṣaka;
and in cases of discharge resembling a corpse or pus, one should drink a decoction of sandalwood (candana).

In this case, the paste and decoction of triphalā should be used for holding in the mouth and for rinsing (AS.Śā.1.18). In all disorders of semen and menstrual blood, both the woman and the man should be treated repeatedly with oleation and other therapies, and especially with urethral enemas (uttarabasti) (AS.Śā.1.18).

And according to their respective origins, using medicinal pastes and cotton swabs, those whose semen and menstrual blood have been thus purified should follow the previously mentioned regimen (AS.Śā.1.19). The fertile period (*ṛtu*), characterized by the appearance of menses, lasts for twelve nights.
Others say it is sixteen nights; some say even a month for one who has a pure womb, uterus, and menses.
Similarly, others say that there is also a woman whose menses have not yet appeared;
she has a thin and serene face and swelling hips and breasts.
One should know that a woman who desires a man and has her menses has sunken eyes and a sunken belly;
just as a lotus closes when the day has passed, so does she.
When the proper time has passed, the womb does not receive the semen;
the blood accumulated over a month is [only] received again through the two channels during the fertile period.

The wind may expel from the opening of the birth canal something slightly black and foul-smelling. Then, from the first day of the appearance of the [menstrual] blood, she should remain celibate for three nights, avoiding bathing and ornaments, and sleeping on a bed of *darbha* grass.

On the fourth day, having been massaged with unguents, bathed in cold water, anointed, adorned, and wearing white garlands and garments, she— having performed auspicious rites and prayers for well-being— should look upon her husband with undistracted mind, while he eats a small amount of barley-gruel prepared with milk from one of the vessels made of leaves or from the palm of his hand for the purpose of emaciation, and avoids pungent, hot, sour, and salty foods. (AS.Śā.1.24)
For at that time, she gives birth to exactly what she sees or thinks; therefore,
after the bath, one who desires a virtuous son should wait for three more nights.
Having seen the flower, for seven nights, or on the eighth, the tenth, or the twelfth night, one desiring a son should cohabit.
One desiring a daughter should perform [the rite] on the fifth, seventh, or ninth [lunar day];
in those cases, there is an ever-increasing perfection of longevity, health, sovereignty, good fortune, strength, complexion, and sensory faculties for the offspring;
beyond this, however, there is a progressive decline of longevity and the other qualities.
In that regard, during even nights the menstrual flow diminishes, while during odd nights it is replenished;
therefore, from these [nights] in succession, the birth of a son or a daughter occurs.
For this very reason, one desiring a son should not approach a woman who has not ceased to experience her menstrual flow, even on distant days; however,
if due to dietary factors there is an excess of semen on odd days and a deficiency on even days, then a male child is born with a female form,
or is weak or deficient in limbs, and a female child is born with a male form, or is weak or deficient in limbs.
If the eleventh and thirteenth lunar days coincide, the child will be a eunuch (AS.Śā.1.27).
Then the preceptor should perform the rite for obtaining a son (AS.Śā.1.27).
But for a Śūdra woman, [the rite] is performed without mantras;

she should be told, "Contemplate the regions that possess the form, complexion, and conduct of the son you desire," and she should conform herself to the food, recreation, behavior, and attire of those regions.

And at the conclusion of his work, for one month, the man should remain celibate (*brahmacārī*), consuming *śāli* rice with clarified butter and milk, neither overeating nor remaining hungry; being happy, wearing garlands, cheerful, with limbs refreshed, dressed in white garments, and with the approval of the astrologers, he should—during the auspicious portion of the night, contemplating auspicious things and desiring [conception]—ascend a well-spread bed with his right foot first, facing east. And the woman, likewise prepared, having had her body massaged and having consumed food consisting primarily of sesame oil and black gram, should first ascend the bed from the north with her left foot, positioned to the right of the man.
Therein one should employ the mantra:
"Thou art life; thou art the support from all sides. May Dhātṛ establish thee; may Vidhātṛ establish thee. Be possessed of Vedic splendor! [And he says:
"Brahmā, Bṛhaspati, Viṣṇu, Soma, Sūrya, and likewise the two Aśvins."
"May Bhaga, Mitra, and Varuṇa bestow upon me a heroic son," [he says].
Then, having comforted one another with Sāman chants, they should lie down together joyfully and in harmony.
And once she has eaten her fill, one should suddenly sprinkle her with cold water.

In that regard, a woman who is overfed, hungry, thirsty, frightened, dejected, afflicted by grief, angry, excessively obese, desiring another man, or desiring sexual intercourse does not conceive a fetus, or conceives one that is defective.
Likewise, a person does not remain as they are;
for thus a man is born with the behavior of a woman, or a woman with the behavior of a man.
One should not lie prone or on one's side;
for in a woman lying prone, the wind becomes powerful and afflicts the womb,
while in one lying on her right side, the phlegm, being afflicted, flows out and obstructs the uterus.
Similarly, when the woman is on her left side, the bile burns the blood and semen;
therefore, she should receive the seed while lying on her back,
for in this way the humors remain in their proper places.
Having recognized that she has conceived, one should administer the *puṃsavana* rites during the *puṣya* asterism before the fetus becomes manifest;
others say [one should do so] for twelve nights.
Regarding that, some say "on even days," while others say "every day" (AS.Śā.1.32).
It is as follows:
Having infused one of these— lakṣmaṇā, avaṭaśṛṅga, sahadevā, or viśvadevā— with milk, one should oneself sprinkle three or four drops into the right nostril using a cotton swab;
however, if one desires a daughter, one should do so into the left.
One should not spit upon these;
likewise, one should cause [the patient] to inhale the juice from the root-paste of white bṛhatī grown under the Puṣya asterism.
Likewise, one should cause [the patient] to drink eight [leaves of] blue lotus petals, white water-lily petals, the root of *lakṣmaṇā*, and banyan shoots (AS.Śā.1.33). Furthermore,

a woman wearing white garlands and garments should drink, with milk, a paste of the root of *lakṣmaṇā* extracted under the Puṣya asterism, in a quantity the size of an udumbara fruit, for the sake of producing and maintaining a son (AS.Śā.1.33).

In the same manner, one should cause [the patient] to inhale the vapors of gauradaṇḍa, apāmārga, jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, śaṅkhapuṣpī, madhyadaṇḍā, sahacara, nagnajita, agnijihvā, or eight shoots of the vaṭa tree, while standing at the threshold; and having smelled the steam of boiling rice-flour, one should have them drink its juice as previously described.
Furthermore, whatever else the Brahmins or elderly women may say, that too one should do.
Then, one should hold with one's head and right hand the ten medicinal herbs known as the *prajāsthāpanā*;
one should drink milk or ghee prepared with these,
bathe during each *puṣya* asterism using these very herbs, and always apply them [to the body].
Likewise, there is the constant administration of all life-sustaining medicinal herbs according to their respective prescriptions for the stabilization of the embryo (AS.Śā.1.35);
and there are attendants who follow what is pleasant and beneficial, possessing gentle appearance, speech, conduct, and gestures, as well as the husband himself (AS.Śā.1.35).

Furthermore, one should approach her again after a month. In that regard, if the semen is white or resembles the surface of clarified butter (*ghṛtamaṇḍa*), there will be fairness of complexion for the embryo; if it resembles oil, there will be blackness; if it resembles honey, there will be a dark-brown complexion.

Likewise, from the consumption of sweet substances such as milk and from dwelling in water, a mother’s offspring may have a fair complexion; from sesame and heating foods, a dark complexion; and from a mixture of these, a swarthy complexion; furthermore, differences in complexion arise from the customs of one's country and family.
Likewise, from the contact of the fire element with the water and space elements, there is whiteness;
from the contact with earth and wind, there is blackness.

When all the elements are in equilibrium, there is a dark complexion (AS.Śā.1.38). Furthermore, the factors that produce distinctions among sentient beings are the mother, the father, the sentient being [in the womb], and so forth; the teachings heard repeatedly by the pregnant woman, and one's own accumulated karma (AS.Śā.1.38).
"And there is previous practice" (AS.Śā.1.39), and regarding this, there are [verses]:

In women who are constantly supplied with ghee, milk, and other such [nourishment], who are joyful, and whose nature is characterized by phlegm (kapha), the menstrual blood remains for a long time; in those of the opposite constitution, it is otherwise.
Just as a clean cloth takes on color immediately upon immersion, so too does [the embryo] take on passion (rāga) from the very moment of conception.
The embryo is certain [to develop], as are the seed and the prepared field; likewise,
when the divine [factors] are not adverse, the result of a well-applied action is certain at the proper time.
Since success [is achieved] through the *puṃsavana* and other rites, one should perform them prior to the manifestation [of the fetus].
And those born in this way will be handsome, full of vitality, and long-lived.
Those who liberate others from debt are considered good sons by those who possess sons; she who delights in devotion to the deities, proper conduct, and purity gives birth to one of great virtue.
Thus, due to the force of habitual practice in previous lives, this behavior continues to flow;
even in women, semen is indeed emitted during union with a man.
That [action] does nothing at all to the embryo; thus it is not considered [as a cause].
Now begins the second chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the section on the body concerning the descent of the embryo;
so indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.

When the old seed has passed away and the womb is established in its pure state, the semen—unadulterated, impelled by unadulterated wind, accompanied by the other great elements, and coagulated by the menstrual blood—immediately enters the womb. There, it is joined by the *jīva* (the life-principle), which follows the influence of afflictions such as passion, is impelled by its own karma, and moves with the speed of thought;
and because effects conform to their causes, it attains a state of similarity to that [semen].
And for that very reason, from the predominance of the semen (*śukra*) a male is born, from the predominance of the menses (*ārtava*) a female, and from the equality of the two a neuter.
When the semen and menses are divided into fragments by the wind (*anila*), offspring are produced according to those respective divisions.
Regarding abnormalities and those of non-human forms:
now, the signs of a woman who has recently conceived are the retention of the seed in the womb, satiety, heaviness, throbbing, and the binding together of the semen and the menses.
Likewise, there occur exhilaration, nausea, drowsiness, lassitude of the limbs, salivation, cardiac distress, exhaustion, and thirst;

and in due course, for one whose pregnancy has become manifest, there is heaviness of the abdomen alone, emaciation of the eyes and voice, disarrangement of the pubic hair, sleepiness, yawning, fainting, vomiting, loss of appetite, swelling of the feet, a craving for sour things, and a desire for various high and low objects (AS.Śā.2.5). Furthermore, the pathways of her channels that carry the *rajas* are obstructed by the fetus.
Therefore, after that, the menstrual flow is no longer seen;
consequently, it is obstructed below and, as it accumulates further and further downward, they call it "the lower [blood]."
Others say it is the placenta; while the blood remains, the line of body hair appears, and the remainder of the placenta passes upward into the blood.

Therefore, the fullness of the cheeks and breasts, as well as the blackness of the lips and nipples— which reside in the breasts themselves, are colored by *kapha*, and have attained the state of milk— become nourished by the essence of food once again in the woman who has given birth.
In that regard, in the first month, the *kalala* (embryonic mass) is produced.
In the second [week], it becomes a solid mass (*ghana*), then a *peśī*, and then an *arbuda*; from these, respectively, males, females, and neuters arise.
In the third [week], it develops fivefold.
For example, the thighs, arms, and head,

as well as all the limbs, parts, and sense organs, arise simultaneously at the very same moment as the growth of the thighs and so forth, with the exception of teeth and such which appear after birth;
these latter, however, become manifest gradually.
This is the primary nature; anything other than this is a transformation (vikṛti).
Furthermore, according to their respective [causes], states corresponding to whichever gender—male, female, or neuter—the embryo possesses, abide in both the mind and the body.
But when there is a confusion of specific characteristics (vaiśeṣikaliṅga), the intermediate states arise from whichever [characteristic] is more predominant.
For example:

Impotence, timidity, lack of confidence, delusion, instability, heaviness of the lower body, lack of firmness, laxity, softness, the portion of the seed within the womb, and other such factors that produce femininity;
the opposites of these produce masculinity; and those that are mixed produce neuter characteristics.
Then his sensation becomes manifest;
from that point onward, it throbbs and he forms a longing for the objects of the five sense-faculties.
For his heart is born of the mother, and it is connected with the mother’s heart by means of the channels that carry its essence;
therefore, through those [channels], faith arises in both of them.
And thus, they call a woman who has two hearts "dauhṛdinī" (one with pregnancy-longings);
others, however, say that the period of pregnancy-longings begins from the third fortnight until the fifth month.
When her longing is intense, one should give her even what is unwholesome, provided it is accompanied by something wholesome.
For if the longing is disregarded, the wind (vāyu), becoming agitated and circulating within the body, may cause the destruction or deformity of the fetus;
however, when the longing is fulfilled, she gives birth to a son who is vigorous and long-lived.
In the fourth month, the division of the major and minor limbs becomes distinct and the embryo becomes firm.

In the fifth month, the mind becomes more awakened and there is an accumulation of flesh and blood. In the sixth month, the hair of the head, body hair, nails, bones, tendons, and so forth become manifest, as do the accumulation of strength and complexion.

In the seventh [week], there is the completion of all limbs (AS.Śā.2.14). In the eighth, both the embryo and the mother repeatedly draw vitality from one another through the nutrient-carrying channels; therefore, at that time, the pregnant woman is alternately joyful and exhausted, and so too is the embryo (AS.Śā.2.14).
Thus, at that time, the birth of the embryo becomes accompanied by destruction because the vital energy (*ojas*) is no longer stable;
for even as it experiences the turning and other movements while intent on emerging, it is separated from its vital energy.
And although there may be some breathing for a short time, that is caused by the persistence of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the vital energy in a limb that has already been severed.

"However, because the mother possesses stable *ojas*, when it is transferred [to the fetus] only partially, there is indeed exhaustion (*glāni*)," so says [Vāgbhaṭa] in Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha Śārīrasthāna 2.15;
others, however, say:
Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha Śārīrasthāna 2.15.
Because that region belongs to Nairṛta, there is death for the embryo therein;
therefore, to prevent miscarriage, a woman who has bathed, being pure and observing celibacy, should be devoted to the propitiation of the deity,
and she should offer an oblation of meat and rice at this time.

They say that even if one day has passed beyond that [conception], the time for birth may last up to a year; beyond this, it becomes abnormal. However, the male fetus remains in the womb facing the mother's back, with its hands joined at the forehead, its limbs contracted, and resting against the right side of the womb (AS.Śā.2.16).
The left side is female, the middle is neuter;
and the embryo situated there awakens when the mother is awake, and sleeps when she is sleeping.
And regarding the development of the dependent [embryo], from the moment of conception (*niṣeka*), there occurs the moistening and warming of the womb by its secretions (*upasneha* and *upasveda*).

Then, as its major and minor limbs become manifest, a channel is connected to its navel; another channel is connected to that [first] channel, and to that [second] one is the mother’s heart. (AS.Śā.2.17)
Then, the essence of the food flowing from the mother's heart through the vessels reaches the other [side],
and from there it gradually reaches the navel.

Then, being cooked again within the receptacle of digested food (*pakvāśaya*) by the fire of its own body, it becomes nourishing for the elements (*dhātu*) and so forth due to its abundance of pure essence (*prasāda*). Likewise, through the pores of the skin, the moisture itself—having become like milk—is the nutrient-fluid (*rasa*). Because the unborn [embryo] does not directly receive food and drink, and because the nutrient-fluid is stainless, there is no production of gross waste in the embryo. Thus, while staying in the womb, at the time of birth, the embryo turns head-downward through the influence of the wind of delivery (*prasūtimāruta*) and emerges; immediately thereafter, another [wind] causes it to fall from the mother’s heart.

This is the natural state; otherwise, it is a transformation (AS.Śā.2.19). In that regard, if she moves her right foot first, her right arm is strong and active, milk appears in her right breast first, her right side is elevated, her abdomen is rounded, she delights in seeing, touching, and inquiring about things with masculine names, and she has a longing for things with masculine names, as well as dreams of such things, her facial complexion is bright, her hunger is keen, the line of hair on her body points upward, and she desires men—she gives birth to a son. In the opposite case, she gives birth to a girl; and in the case of a mixture [of these traits], a neuter.
At the time of questioning, whatever limb, organ, or external object a woman touches, one should predict that as the sign for her fetus.

AS.Śā.2.20: When the wind (vāta) moving along an improper path dries up the channels that carry the nutrient essence (rasa) of the fetus, then the child is born with a wind-related disease or with deficient limbs.
Or it remains in the womb for many years,
when the purpose of the woman and the man is accomplished simultaneously.
Or when the seed of those two is equal in quantity and present simultaneously,
and the seed is corrupted in its portion, then one of dual nature, a "double-seeded" (dviretas) hermaphrodite, comes into being.

AS.Śā.2.22 When the woman has first achieved her purpose, and subsequently the man emits semen, the wind (vāta) of the woman— whose mind is unsettled by passion— renders it defective and strikes down the channels that carry the male seed; then the organ becomes like that of a eunuch (vātendriya),
and during intercourse he emits only wind.
But when it does not obstruct [the flow] entirely, or while not obstructing it, closes the opening of the channel, then it becomes driven by *saṃskāra*.
In this context, *saṃskāra* refers to aphrodisiac enemas (*vājīkara-basti*) and foods that gladden the mind.
For those [semen-discharging substances], by bestowing strength upon the semen, nourish its channels (AS.Śā.2.24).

When a man who has little seed and little strength— being agitated, filled with aversion toward women, or desiring another woman— causes an obstruction to intercourse with a woman, or when a woman of that same description [causes an obstruction] for a man (AS.Śā.2.24).
Then it is called *āsekyam*,
for by tasting that semen, he attains the erection of the penis (*dhvaja*).
But when both [partners] are of such a nature— that is, both male and female— then it is *vakradhvaja*.
AS.Śā.2.25 His banner is never paralyzed.
AS.Śā.2.26 When a fetus arises from a woman of putrid womb, known as *saugandhika*, it gains strength through the scent of the odor of that womb-banner.
But when, overcome by envy and with diminished joy, they unite, that is known as the passion of envious delight (*īrṣyārati*).

Upon seeing another couple engaged in sexual union, a desire for sexual intercourse arises in him (AS.Śā.2.28). When a man or a fetus suffers the loss of the testicles due to a disorder of wind or fire, then he is known as a *vātaṣaṇḍaka* (one whose virility is destroyed by wind) (AS.Śā.2.28).
These eight types of eunuch births, distinct from one another, are said to arise from the diversity of karma (AS.Śā.2.29).

However, when the humors (*doṣa*) slightly corrupt the blood and the womb of a woman, whatever embryo is conceived therein, whichever part of the mother-derived portion of that embryo—whether in its seed or in a portion of the seed—the humor becomes provoked; then a deformity enters that very part.
For when the productive seed is corrupted within her seed known as blood (śoṇita), which resides in the womb (garbhāśaya), then it produces a barren woman;
when it is corrupted in her limbs, then it produces one whose offspring is putrid.

Whatever is born of it dies (AS.Śā.2.31). Furthermore, when that constituent part [is present], those portions of the seeds which produce the female characteristics residing in the body, such as the downward heaviness and so forth, constitute one portion [of the seed] (AS.Śā.2.31).
Then, when that which is primarily of female form produces a non-female offspring called *vārtā*, they call that a "female failure" (*strī-vyāpad*).

In the same way, one should apply this to the male: when the seed known as semen (*śukra*) is corrupted, it likewise produces a sterile offspring, or one with a putrid womb, or a non-male who is primarily of male form and has a mouth like grass; by this, the corruption of the parts derived from the mother and the father is explained.
By this,
the transformation of the constituent parts arising from habituation (*sātmyaja*), arising from taste (*rasaja*), and arising from the mind (*sattvaja*) is explained.

Whichever limb or part of a limb is afflicted within its seed or its germinal portion, a deformity arises in that very limb or part; however, through repentance, it does not arise (AS.Śā.2.34). Furthermore, when a woman who has conceived immediately indulges in wind-increasing (vātalā) substances, her wind becomes provoked and, spreading through the body and settling in the womb, produces in the fetus conditions such as being dull-witted, deaf, mute, nasal-voiced, stammering, lame, humpbacked, dwarfed, having missing limbs, or having extra limbs, or some other wind-related disorder.
Likewise, like wind, bile (pitta) causes baldness, graying of hair, loss of beard and mustache, discoloration of the skin, nails, and hair, and jaundice;
whereas phlegm (śleṣman) causes leprosy, vitiligo, dental disease, and so forth.
The three aims [of life] consist of mixed transformations (AS.Śā.2.35),
and furthermore, when the light has not reached the visual portion, it results in congenital blindness (AS.Śā.2.35).
That same [condition], when accompanied by vāta, has eyes that are distorted, rough, and reddish; when accompanied by pitta, it has tawny eyes;
when accompanied by śleṣman, it has white eyes.
"One who follows after red [desire] and has red eyes" (AS.Śā.2.36); for the pregnant woman shares the same welfare as the fetus (AS.Śā.2.36).

Therefore, one should protect her specifically with things that are pleasant and beneficial from those factors that cause injury to the fetus. As the fetus grows, the woman’s strength diminishes both because she must bear the burden of its weight and because the essence of her food is extracted by it. In this regard, these are the factors that cause injury to the fetus, namely: sexual intercourse, physical exercise, emaciation, trauma, excessive agitation, traveling in vehicles, staying awake at night, sleeping during the day, suppression of natural urges, indigestion, exposure to the sun, fire, anger, grief, fear, terror, fasting, sitting on high, uneven, or hard seats, falling into pits, wells, or precipices, and seeing or hearing unpleasant things.

In brief, all food and drink that is excessively hot, sharp, or dry, as well as violent physical activities [should be avoided]. Likewise, for the sake of protecting the deity and preserving his strength, one should not wear red garments, should not mount a vehicle, and should not consume wine or meat.

Furthermore, whatever else elderly women may say— that for a woman who lies constantly on her back, the umbilical cord attached to the fetus winds around its neck and causes harm; or that one who sleeps in an exposed position or wanders about at night gives birth to an insane child.
One who is prone to quarreling suffers from epilepsy;
one prone to sexual excess becomes deformed and shameless, or excessively devoted to women;
one constantly grieving becomes timid and emaciated, or short-lived.

A woman who covets, one who torments others, one who is envious, or one who is dominated by women; or a thief, one who is full of toil, one who is treacherous, or one who is lazy; or one who is intolerant, fierce, or deceitful.

One who is habitually sleepy, drowsy, dull-witted, or having weak digestion; one who is addicted to wine, thirsty, short-tempered, or unstable; or one who constantly eats the meat of iguanas, suffers from urinary calculi, or has slow urination.
One who constantly eats the flesh of boars will have bloodshot eyes and a snoring disposition with very coarse body hair; one who constantly eats fish will have a blinking gaze or fixed eyes;
and one who constantly eats sweets will suffer from urinary disorders or be mute and excessively corpulent.

One who constantly consumes sour [tastes] becomes afflicted with blood-bile (raktapitta), skin diseases, or eye diseases; one who constantly consumes salty [tastes] quickly develops wrinkles, graying hair, or baldness;
and one who constantly consumes bitter [tastes] becomes emaciated, weak, or wasted away.

A woman who habitually consumes pungent substances gives birth to a child who is weak, has scant semen, or is even sterile; one who habitually consumes astringent substances gives birth to a child who is dark-complexioned, prone to flatulence, or suffers from upward-moving wind (udāvarta). Furthermore, whatever constitutes the etiological factor for a particular disease, a pregnant woman who indulges in that very thing will give birth to a child abounding in that specific disorder.
By this, the defects of the semen derived from the father are also explained. Therefore, those desiring excellence of offspring should properly attend to their own bodies and their food.
In particular, one should treat a woman's diseases with medicines, diets, and regimens that are mild, sweet, cool, and pleasant;
one should not administer emetics or other such purificatory therapies to her.
One should not perform bloodletting alone;

rather, starting from the eighth month, one should administer non-unctuous enemas (asthāpana) or unctuous enemas (anuvāsana), or treat disorders curable by emesis and other means with mild measures that serve the same purpose. One should treat a pregnant woman just as one would a vessel full of oil, without causing agitation.
And there are verses on this point:
"In the case of a non-urgent illness, this is the procedure; but in the case of an urgent illness, [the following applies].
One should protect a woman with effort even by means of harsh disciplinary measures;
for a woman is the root of offspring, and a protected woman protects [the family].
