Of all the stages of life, the state of the householder is the first and is beyond reproach.
When the mouth is covered by the fetal membrane and the throat is constricted by phlegm, [one is still supported].
And because the passage of the wind is obstructed, the one staying in the womb does not cry out.
Now begins the third chapter:
"Next, we shall expound the chapter on the management of the fetus" (AS.Śā.3.1).
Thus said the great sages, Ātreya and others:
"In the first month, the pregnant woman should drink milk that is unseasoned, in the proper quantity, and cold, at the appropriate times."

During that period as well, for the first twelve nights, one should drink ghee produced from milk, boiled with *śāliparṇī* and *palāśa*, and processed with gold and silver, followed by a draught of cold water;
one should take food that is sweet, cool, predominantly liquid, and wholesome, both morning and evening.
One should not employ oil massages or dry body rubs,
and one should avoid those things that cause the humors to increase as previously described, especially until the fifth month;
in the second month, one should drink milk processed with sweet medicinal herbs.
In the third [period], that same [mixture] with ghee and honey;
in the fourth, it is joined with fresh butter in the amount of an akṣa.
In the fifth [month], milk-ghee;
in the sixth, that same [ghee] prepared with sweet medicinal herbs;
and in the seventh as well.
Regarding this, women say that the mother suffers a burning sensation due to the growth of hair on the fetus;
however, the Blessed Ātreya says "no.
Rather, due to the pressure of the fetus, the *doṣas* reach the heart and cause a burning sensation; from that, itching arises, and from the itching, *kikkisa* (scab) is produced.
In that case, one should give her a palmful of butter prepared with sweet medicinal herbs along with *kola*-water; furthermore,
one should massage her breasts and abdomen with a paste of sandalwood and lotus stalks.
Or with the powders of śirīṣa, dhātakī, mustard, and madhuka;
or with the pastes of kuṭaja, arjaka seeds, mustā, and haridrā; or with the pastes of nimba, kola, surasa, and mañjiṣṭhā.
Anointing [the area] with *triphalā* mixed with the blood of a hare, a deer, or a *pṛṣata* antelope, or with oil prepared from the paste of *karavīra* and *karañja* leaves,
and furthermore, pouring [water] over it that has been boiled with *mālatī* and *madhuka*.
One should avoid scratching in order to prevent skin lesions and disfigurement; one should practice bathing and dry massage,
and consume a sweet diet that is minimal in fat and salt, followed by a small amount of water as a drink.
On the eighth day, one should drink milk-gruel mixed with ghee;
Khaṇḍakāpya says "no," for fear of causing jaundice (paiṅgalya) in the fetus.

"Let there be the affliction of yellowish discoloration; nevertheless, one should proceed in this manner, for it produces offspring that is free from disease and endowed with strength, complexion, vitality, and firmness, and who becomes the foremost among kinsmen—so said the venerable Ātreya.
One should administer an enema using water boiled with *badara* fruits, mixed with minced meat, milk, curd-whey, oil, salt, fruit, ghee, and honey.

For the purpose of purifying the old feces (*purāṇaviḍ*), one should administer an oil enema (*anuvāsana*) with oil prepared from sweet medicinal herbs such as *madhuka* and others, in order to direct the wind (*vāyu*) downward; for when the wind is directed downward, she gives birth easily and without complications.
However, one should place a pregnant woman in a prone position or administer an oily enema (anuvasana);
thus, because her passage is opened, the medicine enters properly.

"From that point onward, one should treat her with unctuous gruels and meat broths from wild animals until the time of delivery," said the Blessed Dhanvantari. "In the ninth month, however, one should insert a tampon of oil from that same oil used for the oil enema into the vagina for the purpose of lubricating the birth canal and the uterus."
By this [method], beginning from the first month, gradually at the time of delivery, the womb, hips, flanks, and back of the pregnant woman become supple,
and the wind (vāyu) becomes favorable.
When the urine and feces have returned to their natural state and the placenta has entered its proper path,
she gives birth at the appropriate time, powerfully and with ease, to a desired son who is healthy, long-lived, and happy.

One should prescribe a daily bath for the pregnant woman using a decoction of the leaves of *bilva*, *kārpāsī*, *paphphaṇā*, *pāṭalī*, *picumanda*, *agnimantha*, *māsī*, and *vardhamānaka*, cooled down, or with water infused with all fragrant substances (*sarvagandha*).

And before the ninth month, one should have a maternity chamber constructed for her—its floor cleared of bones, gravel, and potsherds; located in an auspicious site recommended by the science of architecture (vāstuvidyā); pleasant in all seasons; supplied with all necessary utensils; provided with a ready fire; and having its door facing either east or north.

In that regard, when the lunar mansions and other astrological factors are favorable, having honored cows, Brahmins, and elders with the exclamation "Auspicious Day" (*puṇyāha*), she should enter [the lying-in chamber] while circumambulating it clockwise. Surrounded by women who have given birth many times, who are affectionate, undepressed, and capable of enduring hardship, she should await the time of delivery while intent on rites for well-being (*svastyayana*) and following a diet and lifestyle that is conducive and harmonizes the winds, urine, and feces.
Even if there is slight obstruction of feces and urine, she should apply medicinal suppositories (*phalavarti*).

In that regard, for a woman whose delivery is imminent, there occurs exhaustion and debility; the eyes appear as if their lids have been released from their fastenings; there is spitting, an abundance of urine and feces, looseness of the abdomen, and heaviness in the lower body; a lack of desire for food; and pains—characterized by piercing, splitting, aching, throbbing, and discharges—in the womb, as well as in the belly, heart, hips, bladder, and groins.
Immediately following that, the appearance of the *āvis* (birth-pains) and the flow of the amniotic fluids occur.

Then, when she has conceived and the auspicious rites for protection have been performed, one should have her drink gruel mixed with ghee— she having had her hands anointed, being sprinkled with warm water, and holding in her hand a fruit bearing a masculine name. Then,

as she lies on her back upon a soft bed on the ground covered with a well-dyed bull’s hide, with her thighs and back slightly bent, women who are trustworthy, pleasant to look at, mature in age, skilled in midwifery, experienced, and whose nails have been clipped, should attend her, comforting the woman in labor with kind and truthful words.

Then one should give her the powder of *kuṣṭha*, *elā*, *lāṅgalī*, *vacā*, *cavya*, *citraka*, and *cirabilva* to smell repeatedly. Likewise, from time to time, one should apply the smoke of *bhūrjapatra*, *śiṃśapā*, or *sarjarasa*— whichever is available— and, having anointed the regions of her sides, back, waist, and thighs with lukewarm oil, one should massage them comfortably for her.
The embryo turns face downwards;
this is its characteristic.
Having released the heart, it enters the abdomen,
seizes the head of the bladder,
and the attendants hasten her [delivery].
If it does not turn in this way, then one should repeatedly cause it to yawn and walk about according to the procedure just mentioned (AS.Śā.3.17).
Others, however, say that a mortar filled with grain should be struck with a pestle (AS.Śā.3.17).
But that is not correct;

for the constant avoidance of strenuous exercise is prescribed for a pregnant woman, especially at the time of delivery. Because all her bodily constituents (*dhātu*) and humors (*doṣa*) are agitated and because of her extreme delicacy, the wind (*vāyu*), impelled by the exertion of the pestle-like labor, might find an opening and destroy her life-force (*prāṇa*).

Then, having placed the woman whose pregnancy has turned upon a couch, a skilled woman, sitting at her feet while she is seated, should lubricate her vulva in the natural direction for her comfort, and press her buttocks with her two feet; furthermore,
she should repeatedly clear the birth canal.
And one should say slowly, "O fortunate lady, proceed gently; your facial complexion is very serene, so you shall give birth to a son.
Another [woman] should mutter this mantra into her left ear.
May earth, water, space, fire, wind, Viṣṇu,
and Prajāpati always protect you while you are pregnant, or may they even grant you freedom from suffering.
"Give birth, O lady of auspicious countenance,
to an unblemished son who possesses the splendor of Kārttikeya and is protected by Kārttikeya and the other gods."
Likewise:
"O beautiful lady, here are Amṛta, Soma, and Citrabhānu."
Let horses neigh loudly as they dwell within your palace;
let this woman release this nectar drawn from the waters, which is light within her womb.
"May Fire, Wind, Sun, and Indra, together with the salt-ocean, grant you peace"—thus one should instruct another:
"Do not flow away when sensation has not yet arrived.

For premature delivery is as harmful and detrimental as the sudden urge of feces, urine, and so forth; it causes the fetus to suffer from dyspnea, cough, emaciation, deformity, and other ailments. Likewise, like the suppression of those very urges, the failure to deliver during labor leads to injury. Therefore, act as instructed:
first, you should deliver very slowly and gradually.
When the fetus has begun to emerge, it is difficult; when it reaches the opening of the birth canal, it is even more difficult until delivery.
Therefore, as the woman is giving birth, they should make a sound, saying, "One born! One born! Blessed, blessed is the son!"

In this way, her vital breaths are nourished by joy (AS.Śā.3.26). However, if there is an obstruction of the fetus, one should fumigate the birth canal with the sloughed skin of a black cobra (AS.Śā.3.26).

Or one should bind the root of *hiraṇyapuṣpī* with *piṇḍītaka*, and one should also wear *suvarcalā* or *viśalyā* on the hands and feet (AS.Śā.3.27). Now, if after giving birth the placenta does not come out, then one should press firmly above the navel with the right hand, while grasping from behind with the other hand, and shake it.
Or he should strike her hip with his heel.
Or, grasping the buttocks, he should press them very firmly;
or he should touch the throat and palate with a braid or with a finger wrapped in hair.
He should also fumigate the vulva with birch bark, glass beads, and the sloughed skins of snakes. (AS.Śā.3.29)

Alternatively, having anointed the vagina with clarified butter prepared from *bhūrja* and *guggulu*, or with clarified butter processed with the roots of *śāli* rice, one should fumigate it with the smoke of *kaṭukālābu*, *jālinī*, *nimba*, and the sloughed skin of a snake.
Or, even if she has not been anointed, one should smear her with a paste mixed with pungent oils or with oil-soaked pastes;
or else, one should have her eat that same paste of jaggery and ginger.
Alternatively, one should smear the hand and the abdomen with a paste of *lāṅgalī* root, or pour the milk of the *mahāvṛkṣa* over the head (AS.Śā.3.30).

Or, one should have the patient drink a paste of *kuṣṭha* and *tālīsa* mixed with any one of the following: a decoction of *bilva* and *balvaja*, *maireya*, *āsava*, or the scum of *surā*; or with a sour preparation of *kulattha* pulse that is pungent, sharp, and hot; or with a syrup of *madhuka* and *pippalī*.

Alternatively, having prepared a paste of long pepper (*pippalī*), cardamom (*elā*), *kola*, *bibiḍa*, *cavya*, *citraka*, and *upakuñcikā*, one should cut off the right ear of a living donkey or bull, immerse it in any one of the broths such as those of *bilva*, horse-gram (*kulattha*), or *balvaja*, and after letting it remain for a moment, one should extract that broth and have the patient drink it.
Or one may take a paste of *kuṣṭha* and *elā* with wine,
or a decoction of *arka* and *alarka* mixed with wine for a woman who has recently given birth.
One should administer either a paste of *kuṣṭha*, *lāṅgalikī*, and *mūlaka* with any one of wine or urine;
or the powder of the *vatsakādi* group with wine;
or a wick of oil prepared with *śatapuṣpā*, *kuṣṭha*, *madana*, and *hiṅgu*.
Then, at the time of the non-unctuous enema (anuvāsana), one should administer it to her.

Furthermore, she should be given a decoction enema (āsthāpana) using a decoction of *bilva*, *balbaja* grass, and so forth, combined with the fruits of *jīmūtaka*, *ikṣvāku*, *dhāmārgava*, *kuṭaja*, *arka*, *kṛtavedhana*, *hastiparṇī*, and *abhīru*.
Or, one may use the scum of *surā* liquor mixed with *siddhārthaka*, *kuṣṭha*, *lāṅgalikī*, and the milky sap of *mahāvṛkṣa*;

or, having steamed and crushed the stalks of *śālmali*, one should macerate them in a decoction of the five roots (*pañcamūla*). Then, using that strained liquid, which is oily and combined with the fruits and other ingredients, [one should proceed].
One should administer an uttarabasti using pungent oil prepared with the aforementioned drugs for stabilization (asthāpana),
or one should perform an anuvāsana with pungent oil prepared with a paste of śigru, sumukha, marica, ajājī, and citraka, along with milk and cow’s urine.

One should fill the vagina with the feather of an *umā-śālmalī* bird mixed with ghee and shake it out; or, with a lubricated hand having trimmed nails, one should extract [the fetus] following the direction of the birth canal (AS.Śā.3.34).
If, after delivery, there is pain in the bladder, the umbilical region, or the abdomen known as *makkalla*, one should drink powdered barley-alkali with ghee or lukewarm water.
Or [a decoction] of *varaṇa* and so forth, with the addition (*pratīvāpa*) of five *kola*-berries and *melā*;
or alternatively, [a decoction] of *vīrataru* and so forth, with the addition of saline soil (*mūṣara*) and so forth.
Or salt powder with a decoction of the vatsakādi group,
or the vatsakādi group itself with wine.
One should consume either a paste of black pepper and *bhadradāru* with a decoction of the two *aṃśumatī*s;
or a paste of *bhārṅgī*, ginger, and *devadāru* with warm water;
or old jaggery mixed with the powders of the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), the three aromatics (*trijātaka*), and *dhanikā*.
If her vagina should slip from its natural position,
then a skilled woman, having lubricated the vagina with the blood of any [animal], should reinsert it into its proper place.

Once she has settled down, one should repeatedly foment her with oil cooked with the paste of *aśoka*, *rohiṇī*, *barhis*, *uśīra*, *priyaṅgu*, and *devadāru*, and fill [the vagina]; then one should say, "Go, O blessed lady, to your own place.
Likewise, another woman should attend to the infant immediately after birth according to the procedure for the care of infants.
This will be explained further among the subsequent [chapters]. Now, one should anoint the woman who has recently given birth with *balā* oil;

once she is hungry, one should have her drink a dose of unctuous substance that is suitable for her constitution, combined with the powder of the five pungent spices (*pañcakola*), or with the powder of *yavānī*, *upakuñcikā*, *cavya*, *citraka*, the three acrids (*vyoṣa*), and rock salt, to be digested over the course of a day.
Or, for one who is unfit for oleation, after she has drunk a decoction of Vāta-alleviating drugs or a decoction of the *hrasva-pañcamūla*,
one should anoint her abdomen with *yamaka* oil and wrap it with a cloth.
Likewise, the wind (vāyu) would not cause distension of the abdomen because there is no space [for it to accumulate].

However, when the unctuous substance (sneha) has been digested, one should administer a well-steeped, liquid gruel (yavāgū) prepared with the previously mentioned drugs, or with a decoction of the Vidārigandhādi group, or with milk, in the proper dose.
Prior to and after drinking the unctuous gruel, one should sprinkle the patient with warm water twice daily.

Having observed this for three nights, five nights, or seven nights, one should thereafter nourish the patient gradually with a light broth made of barley, jujube, and horse gram, along with light food and drink;
after twelve nights have passed, one should further strengthen them with the juices of wild animals and other such foods, taking into account the strength of their digestive fire and other factors.
One should have her drink water that has been boiled and then cooled;

likewise, one should treat her with massages, dry powders, affusions, and immersions prepared with drugs that are vitalizing (*jīvanīya*), nourishing (*bṛṃhaṇīya*), sweet, and wind-alleviating (*vātahara*), as well as with pleasant foods and drinks.

For in this way, she is restored to life from a body that has become depleted, with all its bodily constituents (*dhātu*) loosened by the growth of the fetus, and which is characterized by exhaustion, pain, moisture, discharge of blood, and extreme emptiness.
For this very reason, the disease of a woman who has recently given birth becomes difficult to cure or even incurable;
therefore, one should treat her with diligence according to the prescribed method.

Thus, having been prepared for half a month plus [the preceding period], she should gradually be released from the restrictions on food, movement, and conduct; once the trauma of childbirth has passed, she may again experience menstruation, according to some (AS.Śā.3.41). Beginning with this first month, she remains so until she is again capable of conceiving (AS.Śā.3.41).
Thus, the entire procedure for a woman has been correctly demonstrated in every respect.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
Hereafter, we shall explain the complications of pregnancy.
Thus indeed said the great seers, Ātreya and the others:
"If a woman has conceived a fetus, she should avoid those things that ought to be avoided."
Then, for a woman who experiences pain in the bladder, the sides of the abdomen, the hips, the vagina, and the vulva, as well as the appearance of [menstrual-like] blood,
one should treat her while she lies on a soft, comfortable, and cool bed, with her head slightly lowered, using cold applications, affusions, and other such measures.
For example:
one should smear [the area] all around below the navel with ghee that has been washed a thousand times.
Having soaked a tampon with well-cooled clarified butter prepared from madhuka, one should place it near the vagina;
one should sprinkle [the area] with cow's milk, a decoction of madhuka, or a decoction of the nyagrodhādi group;
and one should insert into the vagina oils that have been saturated with the expressed juice of those same [herbs].
Or, one should administer a handful of milk-ghee prepared with the horn of that [animal]; however,
if the blood flows excessively, one should have him consume from that same [mixture] a quantity equal to an akṣa.
Or one should have him lick pure milk-ghee mixed with the filaments of the lotus, blue lotus, and water lily, along with honey and sugar;
or the powder of dhātakī, red ochre, resin of the sarja tree, and añjana, with honey. (AS.Śā.4.5)
One should cause [the patient] to drink either a paste of the bark and tender leaves of the *nyagrodha* and other such trees, or the blood of a rabbit, a deer, or an antelope, mixed with honey.
Or [one may take] *ṛddhi*, *vidārī*, and *jīvantī* with milk;

or blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), white sugar, unripened fruit, clod of earth, sandalwood, and so forth; or rice, lotus-root, the unripe fruit of the *udumbara*, and the shoots of the *nyagrodha*; or with goat's milk; or with a decoction of *kaśeruka*, lotus-stalk, water-chestnut (*kaśṛṅgāṭaka*), *kāśmarya*, *aparūṣaka*, grapes, *sārivā*, *prapauṇḍarīka*, *anantotpala*, and *kadamba* seeds—sweetened with sugar and honey—with powdered *śāli* rice.

Or, one should feed [the patient] well-cooled red śāli rice with milk boiled with life-sustaining (*jīvanīya*) herbs, along with milk boiled with *balā*, *atibalā*, śāli rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, sugarcane root, and *kākolī*, mixed with honey and sugar.
One should employ treatments for blood-bile (raktapitta), excluding those that are purificatory, using the meat-juice of wild animals possessing a cooling potency; furthermore,
one should engage in gentle discourses that are pleasing to the mind.
However, for one who has not seen blood, one should have her drink milk prepared with madhuka, payasyā, and suradāru;
or alternatively, with tāmravallī, aśmantaka, śatāvarī, and payasyā.
Or one may take ghee prepared with the Vidāryādi group of drugs, or ghee cooked with the fresh juice of Śvadaṃṣṭrā and milk, or ghee cooked with the juice of onion, mixed with honey.

If flowers appear when less than three months have passed, the embryo generally does not remain, because its essential substance has not yet been formed; furthermore, in the case of a mother with a constitution of undigested matter (*āma*), it does not remain even after that time,
due to the administration of contrary treatments.
In that case, one should employ dry and cold [substances], as follows:
AS.Śā.4.10. For example:
First, one should observe a fast; thereafter, one should drink a decoction of *durālabhā*, *mṛdvīkā*, *uśīra*, *parpaṭaka*, *ghanasāracaṃdana*, *ativiṣā*, *balā*, *kaṭvaṅga*, and *dhānyaka*.
For food, one should consume gruels made from grass-grains, *śāli* rice, and *ṣaṣṭika* rice, along with soups of *mudga* beans and other pulses.

Once [the fetus] has been subdued, one should administer unctuous and cooling substances as before (AS.Śā.4.11). However, if the immature fetus has fallen, one should have her drink one of the various types of liquor according to its potency (AS.Śā.4.11).

For the purpose of purifying the womb-cavity and for the sake of forgetting the pain [of childbirth], one should treat those who do not drink alcohol with gruels made of wild barley (*uddālaka*) and other grains, mixed with digestive (*pācanīya*) substances and sesame seeds, while excluding fats and salts; this should continue for as many days as there were months of pregnancy.
Thereafter, until the purification of the impurities (*doṣa*), tissues (*dhātu*), and moisture, one should provide nourishing foods that preserve strength and are free of fats. *AS.Śā.4.12*
For if a residue of raw matter remains, unwholesome states would recur again and again;
therefore, one should treat the patient with sharp measures, leaving no residue behind.

Thereafter, [the patient] should be treated with the drinking of medicated fats, enemas, and diets that are digestive-stimulants, carminatives, vitalizers, nourishing agents, sweet, and wind-alleviating (AS.Śā.4.13). However,

for her whose fetus has become large and developed in essence, if there is the appearance of menses or other vaginal discharge due to the failure to avoid things that ought to be avoided (AS.Śā.4.13),
[the following applies].

On account of that [fetal movement], the wind (vāyu) becomes aggravated; seizing the bile (pitta) and phlegm (śleṣman), it remains pressing upon the nutrient-carrying channel (rasavahā nāḍī) of the fetus.

Consequently, because the channel is obstructed by the humors (doṣas)—just as a canal might be choked by grass, leaves, and the like—the nutrient fluid does not flow properly. Thus, failing to attain growth, the fetus either sinks down or withers away.

In such a case, where occasional bleeding or discharge is observed and the amount is small, yet the fetus continues to throb without falling below its expected size, [it is known as *mūḍhagarbha*]. (AS.Śā.4.14)
And his belly does not expand;
they call him "one who sits [without eating]."

But when there is a monthly flow of menses or a daily discharge that is not too slight, and the fetus, though long present, moves only slightly, while the abdomen, despite having increased, diminishes,
then it is *upaśuṣkaka* (withered) and *nāgodara* (serpentine).
But when those two, being nourished even by the slight strength of the mother’s food, become fully developed and endowed with hair, teeth, and so forth,
then the woman gives birth even after many years.

In that condition, when the downward wind (*vāta*) is obstructed by the upward-moving wind (*upaviṣṭaka*) and the parching wind (*śuṣkaka*), the wind strikes back and causes the excretion of feces that is accompanied by sound, frothy, and broken up; the urine is suppressed; there is pain in the hips, back, and heart; yawning; loss of sleep; frequent catarrh; dry cough; exhaustion; the ears seem to whistle; the temples seem to throb; the body feels as if covered with ants; the wind seems to move about in the belly as if cutting it; one feels as if entering darkness; digestion of food is difficult; there is daily emaciation; and the skin becomes cracked, discolored, and rough.

By bile (pitta), one voids stools that are copper-colored or green; there is fuming eructation, sour belching, vomiting, fainting, and a burning sensation in the abdomen and heart. The woman becomes yellowish-red in appearance like cow's urine, with eyes, urine, nails, and skin of a similar hue; she is dark-complexioned, weak, and constantly swollen.

Due to *śleṣman* (phlegm), there is sweetness in the mouth, nausea, vomiting of phlegm, aversion to food, whiteness of the hands, feet, and eyes, as well as cough and dyspnea. For these two [conditions], one should employ the application of gruels (*sāṃpiṣāḥ*) prepared with life-sustaining (*jīvanīya*), nourishing (*bṛṃhaṇīya*), and sweet medicinal herbs.

Likewise, it causes the growth of the fetus for those who consume milk, juices, and unripened fruits; likewise, there is nourishment through these very substances such as clarified butter and so forth.

The provision [of the patient] through frequent gifts of vehicles and carriages, and by means of nourishing [foods], during times of abundance. Furthermore, specifically regarding wind disorders, one should first administer a milk enema mixed with *saindhava* salt, and then, after she has bathed in cold water, feed her soft *śāli* rice.
Then, one should administer an unctuous enema (anuvasana) prepared with the Vidarigandhadi group of drugs;
one should also reside in a windless place.
In the case of Pitta, one should drink milk boiled with a decoction of Madhuka and Vidari.

Having crushed three *sthūla-kukkuṭī* plants and one *āḍhaka* of dehusked *māṣa* beans in a mortar with milk and water, one should cook the juice thereof with ghee and the broth of either a partridge (*tittiri*) or a grey partridge (*kapiñjala*). This should be administered for the purpose of increasing the "seated" (*upaviṣṭaka*) type of impotence and for nourishing those who are emaciated.
One should drink gruel prepared with goat’s milk, goat’s dung, and the *jīvanīya* drugs.
One should also cook ghee with milk and a paste of *payasyā*, the two types of *kākolī*, and *suniṣaṇṇaka*. (AS.Śā.4.21)
In the morning,
one should consume milk as a post-drink and eat with the juice of raw meat.
One should eat those very same roasted items there,
as well as the flesh of aquatic animals;
however, in the case of kapha, one should drink clear *surā* liquor with the meat of marshy or aquatic animals as a side dish for three nights, five nights, or seven nights.
AS.Śā.4.22 One should combine a vessel of ghee with five vessels of sesame, mung beans, black gram, salt, and wood-apple, and store it well-protected.
Then, in the morning, one should eat a bolus the size of a wood-apple, followed by a drink of boiled goat’s milk that has cooled.
In this very case, one may also place a vessel of jujube powder [near her];
thus, if there is no growth, one should purge her with strong purgatives and cause the fetus to fall with other means for inducing miscarriage.
Furthermore, when the fetus is lodged within the channels obstructed by wind (vāta), being dormant and not moving, they call that state "lodged" (līna).

In that case, one should feed [the patient] red *śāli* rice with the broth of any one of the following— hawk, osprey, cow, fish, iguana, peacock, cock, or partridge— prepared with abundant ghee; or alternatively,
one should have them drink barley meal (*saktu*) mixed with sesame, black gram, and the tender fruits of the *bilva*, along with milk.
Or she should frequently consume grape wine with an accompaniment of fat and meat, and she should repeatedly massage her abdomen, groin, thighs, hips, sides, and back with oil;
furthermore, she should be made to feel joy again and again.
One should also observe what was stated previously;
however, for a woman who suffers from upward movement of wind (udāvarta) and constipation, one should treat her with unctuous food and drink that pacify vāta.
In the eighth month, however, one should administer an oil enema (anuvāsana) using oil prepared with madhuka.

If that [unsuccessful enema] has not succeeded, one should administer a *nirūha* enema using the juice extracted from the roots of *vīraṇa*, *śāli*, *kuśa*, *kāśa*, *ikṣu*, *bālikā*, *vetasa*, and *parivyādha*, along with *bhūtīka*, *anantā*, *kāśmarya*, *parūṣaka*, *madhūka*, *madhuka*, and *mṛdvīkā*, mixed with milk and half as much water; this should be combined with the paste of the marrow of *priyāla* and *bibhītaka*, sesame, and a little salt, and administered while warm.
Once the obstruction has been removed, the patient should bathe and eat, and in the evening, one should administer an *anuvāsana* enema with that same oil.

For if Udāvarta (upward movement of wind) is neglected, it may suddenly cause the miscarriage of a pregnant woman carrying her fetus. Furthermore, when a fetus is released from its bond—either due to an excessive accumulation of humors (*doṣa*), or by the aforementioned sexual intercourse and other factors, or by other diseases, or by the previously accumulated karma of the mother and child—it falls like fruit from its stalk. Having been freed from its bond and having passed beyond the womb-bed, it causes agitation of the abdominal cavity as it slips down through the openings of the liver, spleen, and intestines.

Then, due to the agitation of the internal cavities, the apāna-vāyu becomes obstructed and causes pain in the abdomen, bladder, flanks, and womb, as well as constipation and retention of urine; having produced these, it causes the fetus to be expelled, which, being in a liquid state of blood,
was previously described as such.

When the fetus has become enlarged, the abdomen appears rigid, motionless, cold, and like a stone; excessive pain arises, yet the fetus does not move, the afterbirth does not emerge, and the vagina does not discharge. Furthermore, her eyes sink, she is overwhelmed by intense distress, suffers, moves about abnormally, faints, wanders, weeps day and night, and does not sleep. With fetid breath, she breathes with difficulty and lives in extreme agony; one should recognize such a woman as having a dead fetus (*mṛtagarbha*).

However, when that embryo has at some point entered the birth canal improperly in various ways, and is afflicted and deluded by vitiated wind (*vāyu*), they call it a "confused embryo" (*mūḍhagarbha*).
And due to the variety of afflictions caused by the vitiated wind, its positions are innumerable.
In brief, however, there are three types of [birth]: upward,
horizontal, and downward.
Furthermore, there are eight postures, which will be described later in this very work (AS.Śā. 4.30).

Among those various conditions, one should avoid a woman who has inverted sense-objects, who is afflicted by convulsions, fainting, or loss of restraint; who is covered in filth, seized by dyspnea or vertigo, whose limbs are cold, and who emits a putrid odor from her eructations.
But one should not neglect a fetus, which is like a thorn in the womb, even for a single moment.
For that [fetus], having rendered the mother breathless, would quickly kill her;
and if the fetus is conscious, being torn open by the instrument, it would convulse its limbs in a distorted manner.
Therefore, one should strive for union with that [reality], and one should employ the previously mentioned mantras and medicinal herbs. Furthermore,
that union is of three kinds.
[The physician should apply pressure] on the head, the shoulder, or the hips. However, some say that for a dead fetus, the procedure is the same as that for inducing the expulsion of the placenta.
Some say that the application of mantras and so forth is prescribed by the Atharvaveda;
others say it is like the extraction of a splinter by a surgeon who has mastered his craft.
However, there is no surgical procedure more difficult than this. (AS.Śā.4.35)

Since one must apply a sharp instrument that is smooth to the touch without harming the uterus, liver, spleen, intestines, womb, and other internal organs situated therein, and since drawing out, turning, excising, cutting, piercing, pressing, and straightening must be performed with a single hand, therefore,
having consulted the master and exerting the utmost effort, one should proceed with the treatment accompanied by those skilled in that science.
In the case of non-action, death is certain;
in the case of undertaking [surgery], there is doubt.
Likewise, in cases of abdominal stones and similar conditions (AS.Śā.4.37),

one should then place the woman on her back with her thighs flexed and her waist raised by a cloth-cushion; having then anointed her hand, the vagina, and the fetus with the marrow of the *dhanvana*, *agavṛntikā*, and the pulp of the *śālmalī* tree mixed with ghee, one should extract the fetus (AS.Śā.4.37).
In that case, for one who has arrived via the two thighs, there is simply a longitudinal stretching;
for one who has reached [the head] by one thigh, the other thigh is extended.
Having blocked the buttocks with his own buttocks, lifted [the fetus] upward, and extended the thighs;
having lifted the posterior half like a crossbar as it arrived transversely, he brought the anterior half straight toward the birth canal;
then, having pressed against the shoulder whose head was turned toward the side, he lifted it upward and brought the shoulder into the birth canal.
Having pressed upward on the two arms that have entered [the womb] and brought them to the base of the head,
he whose middle part is bent enters the birth canal with his hands, feet, and head. (AS.Śā.4.39)

If the fetus is not bent but has one foot [present] and the second [foot] at the birth canal (yoni) or the anus (pāyu), those two being "upside-down" (mūḍha) and impossible to extract by hand, one should employ a surgical instrument (śastra). Then, having comforted the woman and incised [the abdomen] with a scalpel (maṇḍalāgra) or a finger-scraper (aṅguli-śastra), one should remove the fetal head-bones after extracting them, seizing [the body] with a fetal hook (garbha-śaṅku) and pulling it out via the chin, the palate, the chest, or the armpit.

Or, having severed the arm at the level of the unseparated head, or at the eye-socket, or likewise at the shoulder region of one whose arm is stuck there; or, having opened the abdomen of one who is bloated like a leather bag filled with air, and having extracted the entrails, one should remove the body once it has become flaccid.
Having torn apart the pelvic bones of the one attached by the hips (jaghanasakta),
moreover, whatever limb of the fetus becomes stuck due to the force of the wind, [the practitioner] should cut it into pieces.
Having cut those [tissues] accordingly, the physician should extract [the foreign body] properly, while diligently protecting the woman;
then, the physician should cause any other [foreign body] that has not yet fallen out to fall, as previously described.
When the fetus has been thus extracted, one should sprinkle her with warm water; then, having anointed her body, one should insert a lubricated tampon into the birth canal.
The vagina becomes soft by this, and her colic is pacified.
[This is prepared] from *dīpyaka*, *ativiṣā*, *rāsnā*, asafoetida, *elā*, and the five *kolakas*.
Then one should cause [the patient] to drink either a powder, a paste with an unctuous substance, or a decoction of kaṭukā, ativiṣā, pāṭhā, śāka, tvak, hiṅgu, and tejana. (AS.Śā.4.45)
And likewise, for the purpose of discharging the morbid humors and for the pacification of pain,
one should drink oil in this manner for three nights, and then for seven days.
In the evening, one should drink the *ariṣṭa* as well as the well-prepared *āsava*; furthermore,
one should place cotton swabs (*picu*) soaked in a decoction of *śirīṣa* and *kakubha* into the vagina.
And whatever other complications may arise, one should treat them according to their respective natures.
Milk prepared with Vāta-alleviating herbs is beneficial for ten days as a dietary supplement.

For ten days one should consume the meat broth, while eating very light, wholesome, and small quantities of food. Devoted to oleation and massage, one should employ unctuous substances such as *balā*-oil and others.
After four months, she will gradually experience various pleasures.
Now, we shall explain *balā-taila*.
AS.Śā.4.51: The section on the four foundations of mindfulness.

Take six parts of the decoction of *balā* root and an equal amount of milk; one part of the decoction of *yava*, *kola*, *kulattha*, and the ten roots (*daśamūla*), and fourteen parts of oil. Having combined all these together, add the finely ground paste of the following: *kākolī*, *kṣīrakākolī*, *jīvaka*, *ṛṣabhaka*, *mudgaparṇī*, *māṣaparṇī*, *modā*, *mahāmedā*, *kṣīraśuklā*, *madhuka*, *devadāru*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *candana*, *sārivā*, *tagara*, *kuṣṭha*, *śatāvarī*, *aśvagandhā*, *punarnavā*, *śatapuṣpā*, *avarapatra*, *rasa*, *sarala*, *śaileya*, *elā*, *vacā*, *agaru*, *kālānusārī*, and rock salt (*saindhava*). Cook this slowly over a mild fire, and once prepared, store it well-protected in a suitable vessel. This is the "King of Oils" favored by the Blessed Dhanvantari; it should be employed for drinking, nasal drops, massage, and enemas for kings, royal officials, women who have recently given birth, the emaciated, infants, the elderly, the delicate, those suffering from colic, those possessed by great malevolent spirits, those whose bodies are exhausted by chronic diseases, and those with limbs pierced in vital spots, fallen, struck, or fractured; as well as for those afflicted by divine calamities, curses, mental distress, or fever.

By this, strength, manliness, memory, intelligence, wisdom, digestive fire, valor, and vitality increase; various disorders of wind such as hemiplegia, convulsions, facial paralysis, and others, as well as abdominal tumors, hiccups, dyspnea, and coughs, are cured. When used daily, intestinal hernia is pacified within six months, and even a barren woman obtains a virtuous son according to her desire. Regarding this, there are these verses:
If the womb of a woman who has expired at the opening of the bladder throbs at the time of birth,
one should quickly incise it and extract the infant.
Madhuka, śākabīja, payasyā, and suradāru;
aśmantaka, black sesame seeds, tāmravallī, and śatāvarī.
Vṛkṣādanī, payasyā, the creeper utpalasāribā,
anantā, sārivā, rāsnā, padmā, and madhuyaṣṭikā.
Ghee [prepared with] the two types of *bṛhatī*, *kāśmarya*, milky thorns, and bark;
*pṛśniparṇī*, *balā*, *śigru*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, and *madhuparṇikā*.
AS.Śā.4.56: Śṛṅgāṭaka, lotus stalk, grapes, kaśeru, madhuka, and balā—
these seven formulations, completed by half-verses, [are to be taken] with milk.
In the seventh month, if the fetus miscarries,
one should administer a compound of *kapittha*, *bilva*, *bṛhatī*, *paṭola*, *ikṣu*, and *nigdhikā*.
In the eighth month, one should administer milk boiled with roots; likewise, in the ninth month,
[milk boiled] with sārivā, anantā, payasyā, and madhuyaṣṭi.
In the tenth month, one should administer prepared milk with *payasyā*,
or alternatively, with *yaṣṭimadhuka*, *nāgara*, and *amaradāru*.
Now begins the fifth chapter. Now, therefore, we shall expound the section on the body concerning the division of its constituent parts.
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:

"The entire body is called an *aṅga* (limb). Furthermore, within that, there are six *aṅgas*: the head, the trunk, the two arms, and the two thighs; while the eyes, navel, hands, feet, and so forth, are its *pratyaṅgas* (minor limbs)."
Furthermore, the formation of a limb arises from the great elements— known as space, wind, fire, water, and earth— which consist of great qualities and are presided over by consciousness. Moreover,

through the power of various seen and unseen karmas of beings themselves, there is produced a vast variety of forms, distinguished by differences in subtle and gross degrees, such as specific arrangements, shapes, dimensions, moisture, brilliance, and voice, whether characterized by similarity or dissimilarity.
In that regard,
space consists predominantly of the element of being (sattva).
Air abounds in rajas;
fire abounds in both [rajas and tamas]; water abounds in sattva and tamas.
Earth abounds in *tamas*;
their specific characteristics are, respectively, non-obstruction, mobility, heat, fluidity, and solidity;
furthermore, they reside specifically within the sense organs, beginning with the ear.
The sequence [of elements] occurs through sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, each increasing one by one.
Among these, those born from space are the ear, sound, all the channels, and the void.
The qualities of air are touch, the sensation of touch, the movements of exhalation, inhalation, and so forth, and lightness.
The qualities of fire are vision, form, bile, heat, digestion, warmth, intelligence, complexion, radiance, splendor, and valor.
The qualities of water are the sense of taste, flavor, the collection of fluids such as sweat, moisture, fat, lymph, blood, semen, urine, and the like, coldness, and unctuousness.
The olfactory organ is composed of earth; odor, hair, nails, bones, and so forth constitute the collection of solid forms; and there is fortitude and stability.
Among these, those derived from the mother are soft, consisting of skin, blood, flesh, fat, marrow, heart, stomach, uterus, liver, spleen, *kloman*, intestines, anus, and so on.
The father-born [elements] are the stable ones: hair, nails, bones, semen, vessels, sinews, and so forth.

The self-born [elements] are: birth in various wombs, mind, consciousness, the sense-faculties, inhalation and exhalation, maintenance [of the body], specific features of form, voice, and complexion, desire, anger, greed, fear, joy, virtue, vice, immorality, memory, intelligence, will, aversion, effort, ego-sense, pleasure, pain, life-span, and self-knowledge.

Life span, health, freedom from laziness and greed, clarity of the senses, excellence of voice and complexion, abundance of vital energy (*ojas*), great joy, intelligence, and strength are born of suitability (*sātmyaja*).
Those born of *rasa* (nutritive essence) are: the formation, maintenance, growth, satisfaction, non-greed, nourishment, and vigor of the entire body.

Those born of pure *sattva* are: purity, faith in the hereafter, gratitude, courtesy, perseverance, heroism, profundity, intelligence, wisdom, memory, a bright appearance of the eyes, devotion, freedom from obsession, and the opposite of the quality of *tamas*.
The qualities belonging to *rajas* are: difficult behavior, ignoble valor, envy, excessive talkativeness, egoism, greed, hypocrisy, pride, anger, exhilaration, and lust.

Those characterized by *tamas* are ignorance, despondency, negligence, sleep, laziness, hunger, thirst, grief, envy, wrong-headedness, deception of others, and the opposition of the quality of *sattva*.
In this context, *sattva* is the mind (*manas*); its agitation consists of *rajas* and *tamas*, and they say that the body is composed of these very elements.
Furthermore, its detailed classification is as follows: AS.Śā.5.16. AS.Śā.5.16.

The layers of the skin, the humors (*doṣas*), the tissues (*dhātus*), the wastes (*malas*), the sense organs presided over by them, the organs of action, the supra-sensory receptacles (*āśayas*), the seats of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), the networks of tendons (*kaṇḍarā*), the tufts, cords, sutures, masses of bones, cranial sutures (*sīmanta*), bones, bone-joints, ligaments, muscles, arteries, veins, channels, heats, vital points (*marmans*), hair of the head and beard, body hair, and the various distinctions between normal and morbid states—
among these, as blood is being processed like milk, six layers of skin arise from the refinement of the skin, and from the refinement of the blood [arises the flesh].
Of these, the first is Udakadhārā,
and the second is Asṛgdharā.
The third has sidhma and kilāsa as its basis; the fourth has all types of kuṣṭha as its basis;
and the fifth again has alajī and vidradhi as its basis.
The sixth, however, is the *prāṇadharā* (life-sustaining);
when it is severed, one suffers as if entering blind darkness, and by presiding over which, formless growths arise at the joints—blackish-red, thick-rooted, and most difficult to treat.
Others speak of seven layers of skin.
Therein, the first is called Bhāsinī, which illuminates the colors and the five shadows beginning with space (khādi); it measures eighteen parts of a grain of rice.
The second is called Lohinī; it measures sixteen parts.
The third is named Śvetā, measuring twelve parts;
the fourth is named Tāmrā, measuring eight parts;
and the fifth is named Vedinī, measuring five parts.
The sixth is named Rohiṇī, the size of a grain of rice;

the seventh is named Māṃsadhara, the size of two grains of rice (AS.Śā.5.19). As for the moisture that remains within the receptacles of the elements, it is cooked by its respective internal heats and, being enveloped by sinews, phlegm, and the fetal membrane, becomes like the heartwood of wood—the residue of the essence of the elements. Because it is the residue of the nutrient fluid (*rasa*) and is so minute, it is designated as *kalā*.
These seven layers (kalā), which are the boundaries between the different dispositions of the elements (dhātu-āśaya), are as follows:

AS.Śā.5.20 Of these, the first is called *māṃsadhara* (the flesh-supporting layer); within it, upon the flesh, the veins, ligaments, arteries, and channels spread out like lotus roots and stalks in the mud of a pond.
The second is named Rakta-dharā; it is within the flesh, and in it blood is found, especially in the veins, spleen,
and liver.
From the flesh, when wounded, blood flows forth like sap from a milky tree;
this is the third [layer], called the fat-holder (medodharā).
AS.Śā.5.22 AS.Śā.5.22
For in that [fourth layer], there is fat within the abdomen and in the small bones, along with blood;

and that same substance, covered by the cranial bone in the head, is called the brain (*mastiska*) or the marrow of the skull (*mastulunga*); furthermore, in the large bones, there is marrow; this fourth layer is named *śleṣmadharā*.
For by the phlegm situated therein, all the joints are bound together and become firm, like axles with their side-pieces.
The fifth is named *purīṣadhara* (feces-bearing);
it is located there, resting upon the receptacles of undigested and digested food (*āmāśaya* and *pakvāśaya*), and it separates the waste matter situated within the abdominal cavity.

The sixth [channel], named Pittadhara, is situated between the stomach (*āmāśaya*) and the small intestine (*pakvāśaya*). For it, by virtue of being the seat of the internal fire, holds back with force the food directed from the stomach toward the small intestine; it dries it with the heat of bile, digests it, and releases what is digested. However, when presided over by the humors (*doṣa*), it releases even undigested food due to weakness.
Then, because it receives food, it is further designated as the *grahaṇī* (the "receiver");
its strength is indeed bile (*pitta*), which is synonymous with fire (*agni*). Therefore, supported, nourished, and sharing a single destiny with fire, it sustains the body.

(AS.Śā.5.24) The seventh [dhamanī], named *śukradharā* ("bearer of semen"), is located two finger-breadths on the right side below the opening of the bladder, resting upon the urinary passage; it pervades the entire body and brings forth semen.
The humors (doṣa), elements (dhātu), and impurities (mala) have been described previously.
The five sense-faculties are hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell;
their respective objects, by way of their homogeneity, are sound, touch, form, taste, and odor;
and their bases for the five sense-faculties are the two ears, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the two nostrils.
The five faculties of action (karmendriya), known as speech, anus, genitals, hands, and feet,
have as their purposes speaking, excretion, sexual pleasure, grasping, and locomotion.

The mind (*manas*), however, is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) because it pervades all objects; for it is through its conjunction that the five sense-faculties engage with their respective objects, and because it possesses the nature of both the cognitive and the active faculties.

(AS.Śā.5.27) There are seven receptacles (*āśaya*) in sequence: the receptacles of blood, phlegm, feces, bile, digested food, wind, and urine. In women, there is an eighth receptacle, the womb (*garbhāśaya*), located between the receptacles of bile and digested food. (AS.Śā.5.28)
The internal organs connected to those seven cavities— the heart, liver, spleen, lungs, *uṇḍuka*, kidneys, intestines, and so forth—
arise there from the clear blood of one whose body is inflated by the *samāna* wind and cooked by the heat of the body; from this, the liver and spleen are produced.
From the froth of the blood comes the lungs; from the waste of the blood comes the unduka;
and from the refined essence of the blood come the kidneys.
From the refinement of blood and flesh, the intestines arise;
they measure three and a half vyāmas in men and three vyāmas in women.

Due to the connection of blood with wind (*anila*), the heart becomes blackish; furthermore, from the refined essence of phlegm and blood, it arises resembling the interior of a lotus, hollow and downward-facing.
That is specifically the seat of consciousness and of all states that follow consciousness.

On its left side are the spleen and lungs, and on the right side are the liver and gallbladder (kloma). Likewise, the sense faculties arise from the refined essence (*prasāda*) of the channels carrying phlegm and blood, as well as from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Within those eyes, the white circle (śuklamaṇḍala) arises from the clarity of phlegm (śleṣman) and is born of the father;
the black circle (kṛṣṇamaṇḍala) arises from the blood (asṛj) and is born of the mother;
and the circle of vision (dṛṣṭimaṇḍala) in the center consists of both.
There are five circles known as the eyelashes, the white, the black, the pupil, and the vision;
there are four junctions between them.
And two at the corners of the eyes and the pupils; thus there are six [tears],
and there are six layers and two eyelids.
The external [elements] are fire and water;
the second is flesh, the third is fat, and the fourth is bone;
their thickness is one-fifth of what is seen.
The qualities of the binding structures (bandhana) are fourfold, consisting of the vessels (sirā), the tendons (kaṇḍarā), the fat (medas), and phlegm (kapha).
It was stated previously that phlegm, moreover, is the binding agent for all the joints.
The light residing in the eye, through its conjunction with external light which is of its own kind, becomes fit for action—just as a tool is sharpened by a stone;
yet, through excessive conjunction, it is impaired.
Furthermore, even when situated within water like lightning or the submarine fire (vaḍavāmukha), it does not lose its nature as light due to the excellence of its potency.

The tongue is produced from the refined essence of flesh, blood, and phlegm; the testicles are produced from the refined essence of flesh, blood, phlegm, and fat (AS.Śā.5.32). There are ten seats of the vital breath (*prāṇāyatana*): the head, the attachment of the tongue, the throat, the heart, the navel, the bladder, the rectum, semen, vitality (*ojas*), and blood.
Among those, the first seven are further designated as the great vital points (mahāmarmas),
and there are sixteen tendons (kaṇḍarās).
Of those [bones], there are two each in the hands and feet, and four separately in the neck and the back.

There are sixteen webs; four each in the ankles and the wrists, formed of flesh, veins, ligaments, and bones, and situated as mutually interlaced lattices. There are six tufts (kūrca) located in the hands, feet, neck, and genitals.
There are four muscle-tendons (māṃsarajju) on both sides of the spinal column for the purpose of binding the muscles; of these, two are external.
And two [veins] situated internally;
there are seven sutures.
These five [bones] are in the head; one each in the tongue and the penis are to be avoided by the surgeon with the instrument;
thus there are fourteen collections of bones.
Of those [channels], each one is located at the ankles, knees, groins, wrists, elbows, armpits, the sacrum, and the head; likewise,
there are the sīmanta-s (cranial sutures).
Those five [bones] in each head make eighteen;
there are three hundred and sixty bones in total.
Of these, there are one hundred and forty branches,
and one hundred and twenty intermediate sections.
"One hundred above" means that there are five toe-nails on each leg; since there are three bones in each toe, these amount to fifteen,
along with the five metatarsal bones.
There is one [bone] obstructing that [ankle], two each in the insteps, ankles, and shanks; one each in the heels, knees, and thighs;
and all the nails, bones, and so forth, as well as those of the arms, are like those of the legs.
There are twenty-four *paraśukas*,
and just as many *sthālakas* and *arbudas*.
Thirty on the back, eight on the chest,
and one each on the two sides of the hips.
Likewise, there are two in each of the hips,
as well as in the shoulders, the shoulder-blades, the cheeks, the ears,
the temples, the collarbones, and the palate. (AS.Śā.5.42)
There are thirteen in the neck and four in the throat-vessel.
There are two jaw-bands,
thirty-two teeth, and likewise [thirty-two] molar sockets.

There are three in the nose and six in the head. These, located in the knees, buttocks, shoulders, cheeks, palate, temples, groin, and the middle of the head, are designated as "skull-bones" (kapāla).
The ten *rucakas* are located in the nostrils, ears, neck, and eye-sockets; the *taruṇas* are in the hands, feet, sides, and back; and the *valayas* are likewise [in those same locations].
The remaining bones are called *nalaka*; these five types of bones have names that correspond to their shapes, for upon them the muscles are bound by means of veins and tendons.
There are two hundred and ten bone-joints;
of these, sixty-eight are in the limbs.
There are fifty-nine [joints] in the lower part and eighty-three in the upper part;
therein, for each leg and for each toe, there are three [joints].
There are two in the two thumbs, fourteen in each [of the other fingers], and one each in the ankles, knees, and groins.
There are three [vertebrae] in the pelvic bones and twenty-four in the spinal column;
likewise, there are the same number in the two sides.
Eight [bones] in the chest;
eight in the neck.
There are three in the throat channel;
eighteen are bound to the channels of the throat; thirty-two are in the channels of the heart, liver, and spleen; and [thirty-two] in the roots of the teeth.
There is one on each of the chin, the nose, and the crown; two each on the cheeks, the ears, the conch-shell area, the eye-paths, and the jaw-joints;
and two above the eyebrows.
There are five [bones] in the skull;
these are designated as *kora* in the fingers, ankles, knees, wrists, and elbows.
The *ulūkhalas* are located at the armpits, the groins, and the roots of the teeth;
the *sāmudgas* are on the shoulder-blades, the anus, the generative organ, and the hips;
and the *prataras* are on the neck and the spinal column.
In the skull and the pelvic bones, they are known as *tunnasevanī*;
on both sides of the jaw, they are *vāyasatuṇḍa*;
and in the throat, eyes, heart, liver, spleen, and the ducts of the *kloman*, they are known as *maṇḍala*.

In the auditory passages of the ears, there are conch-spiral joints; thus, bone-joints are of eight types (AS.Śā.5.48). However, as for the two thousand [joints] supported by ligaments, muscles, and vessels, since there is nothing to be said regarding the application of the surgical knife to them, they are not mentioned separately.
There are nine hundred sinews. There are nine hundred sinews.
Of these, six hundred are in the branches,
two hundred and thirty are in the intermediate sections, and seventy are above.
In that regard, there are six in each toe of every single leg;
thus there are thirty [in both legs], and ten each in the soles of the feet, the *kūrca* (ankle region), and the ankles.
There are thirty in the shanks, ten in the knees,
and forty in the thighs.
Ten in the groins;
forty in the hips.
There are twenty in the scrotum, penis, bladder, and intestines;
eighty in the back;
and sixty in the two sides.
There are eighteen on the chest, four on each shoulder,
and eight on the shoulders.
There are two each in the two carotid regions, the two eye-sockets, the two lips, and the palate;
there are thirty in the neck.
There are three clavicles,
four in the jaws, and five on the tongue.
In the twelve upper and lower gums,
in the six heads,
and there in the branches and joints, they are spreading.
The large sinews, however, are round; they are known as *kaṇḍarās*,
and they are hollow within the bladder, the stomach, the colon, and the intestines.
The sides, back, chest, and head are broad;
for by the firm binding of the tendons at the joints, the body strives properly like a boat.
Therefore, one should protect those [tissues] with great effort even more than the bones, veins, and so forth;
and he who correctly understands the external and internal ligaments becomes capable of extracting even a deeply hidden foreign body (śalya).
There are five hundred muscles (peśī). *Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha*, Śārīrasthāna 5.54.
Of these, four hundred are on the branches and sixty are in the inner frame.
Forty [veins] are above; there, in each leg and in each toe, there are three respectively, making fifteen.
Ten each are situated in the forepart of the foot, on the sole of the foot,
at the ankle, and likewise above the foot in the instep; there are twenty in the shank.
There are five in the knees, twenty in the thighs, and one each in the penis and the perineal raphe.
Two in the testicles; ten in the buttocks.
There are three folds in the rectum known as *valīs*,
two at the neck of the bladder, and four in the abdomen.
One [vein] arises from the navel; six are in the heart and the stomach; and [six] are in the liver, spleen, and gallbladder.
Five are situated vertically on the back, ten are long on the two sides,
and ten are on the chest.
There are three [fingers] above the shoulders and elbows; ten [fingers] in the neck.
There are eight [veins] in the two cheeks, eight in the two jaws, and one each in the throat, the Adam's apple, the tongue, and the head.
There are two [hair-tufts] each on the palate and the forehead, and on the nose, the lips, and the ears;
for women, however, there are twenty additional ones.
In that regard, there are ten [fingers] on the two breasts;
their full development occurs in youth.
Among those, ten are located within the womb; two are situated at the opening, and two are circular.
There are three pathways for the embryo; that in which the embryo resides is the womb (*yoni*), which is shaped like the interior of a conch shell and possesses three spirals.
In its third whorl, within the space between the bile and the receptacle for digested food, is the womb-bed;

therein are three muscular fibers (*peśya*) into which the semen and menses enter (AS.Śā.5.58). By means of these—[fibers] that are thin, thick, gross, minute, broad, round, short, long, firm, soft, smooth, and rough—the joints, bones, veins, and ligaments of the body are covered.
When the openings of the channels and vessels are divided minutely, they amount to twenty-nine hundred thousand nine hundred and fifty-six.
By these [pores], this [body] is latticed, covered, and spread;
and there are as many hairs on the head, beard, and body.
For their mouths are dependent upon it; therefore they are nourished by them, and through them they carry sweat [to the body].
Likewise, they bring into the interior the potency of unguents, ointments, and the like, which has been processed in the skin, and they perceive touch.
Furthermore, the channels (srotas) are indeed innumerable;
nevertheless, the veins (sirā) and other such structures will be taught elsewhere according to their grosser aspects and their practical utility.
Thus are enumerated the stable, embodied entities within the body;
as for the fluids, when they are in excess, they cause the falling away of feces to persist.
Likewise, it is the outer skin that supports the urine, blood, and other bodily constituents (dhātus) located throughout the entire body,
as well as that which is situated within the skin in the form of wounds and is designated by the term *lasīkā*.
And that which is bound with heat and issues forth from the pores of the skin, designated as sweat— that is water (AS.Śā.5.63).

Regarding that first essence of food called *rasa*, and [the subsequent elements] blood, feces, phlegm, bile, urine, fat, marrow, and bone-marrow, there is an increase in their respective measures of one *añjali* each, following the sequence starting from the first.
A half-handful of semen,
and an equal amount of brain matter and vital energy (ojas).
Women have four handfuls of menstrual blood and two of breast milk;
both of these consist of the essence of rasa.
This is the measure of the equilibrium of the elements; from this,
one should discern their respective increase and decrease through their characteristics, as well as other countless manifest and unmanifest states.

For example, the followers of Dhanvantari recite [the following]: "Just as [the body consists of] impurities such as flesh, ears, and so forth, [so too do it consist of] wind, intellect, mindfulness, and the rest. (AS.Śā.5.65)
For bodies are indeed diverse, and the humors (doṣas), elements (dhātus), and wastes (malas) are constantly fluctuating;
therefore, even for water and the other [elements], equality in terms of quantity— as in the case of flesh and so forth— cannot be specified.
"One should infer [the state] solely from health by means of inference" (AS.Śā.5.66);
however, all constituent parts indeed become innumerable due to their extreme subtlety when distinguished as atoms (paramāṇu) (AS.Śā.5.66).
Regarding the conjunction and disjunction of those atoms, the cause is wind impelled by karma (AS.Śā.5.67).
This very factor, when apprehended both non-differently and differently, leads to bondage and liberation respectively (AS.Śā.5.67).
And there is a verse on this point: "He who knows the body part by part...
Out of delusion, he never engages in what is harmful.
Now begins the sixth chapter:
Hereafter, we shall explain the chapter on the classification of the vessels (sirā).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:
"The ten root vessels, connected to the heart, carry *ojas* to all the limbs and minor parts of the body."
For bodily movements are dependent upon that [wind];

having moved two finger-breadths, one finger-breadth, half a finger-breadth, a barley-corn, or half a barley-corn, they become seven hundred in number, branching out like the veins and fibers of a tree leaf.
Among those, there are four hundred branches;
therein, sixteen are not to be pierced.
One hundred and thirty-six [yojanas] are the intermediate distance; therein, thirty-two [yojanas] are below,
and one hundred and sixty-four [yojanas] are above.
There too, there are fifty;
in each of their thighs, there are one hundred.
In that regard, one should not pierce the Jālandharā [veins],
nor the three located within the abdomen,
nor the thirty-two located in the hips, the anus, and the penis. (AS.Śā.6.5)
Of those [channels], two each at the groins and the iliac regions— making eight— one should protect from the surgical instrument;
sixteen are on the sides, of which one each, directed upward, is known as the side-junction (*pārśva-saṃdhi*).
There are twenty-four [ribs] on the back;
of these, two pairs on both sides of the spinal column extend upward, making four,
and there are twenty-four in the belly.
Of those [hairs], there are two on each side of the line of hair above the vulva, making four;
forty are on the chest;
and of those, two are on the heart, and two by two are on the roots of the breasts and the nipples.
In each of the individual pillars and supports there are fourteen;
in the neck there are twenty-four.
Among those, fourteen— namely four and eight known as vital points (*marmans*),
two in the nape of the neck (*kṛkāṭika*) and two in the temples (*vidhura*)— one should not touch with a surgical instrument.
There are sixteen [nerves] in the jaws; of these, two are connected to the joints, making sixteen in total.
In the tongue, there are two below them which perceive taste, and two which set speech in motion; those four together [with the others] constitute the total.
There are twenty-four in the nose— of those, two are perceivers of odor— and one in the palate; thus, there are three [additional channels],
making fifty-six in the eyes.
There are two for the actions of opening and closing each of those [eyes],
two for each of the outer corners, making six;
and those located on the nose and eyes are sixty on the forehead.
Following their hair-ends are four [channels], two in the two curls, and one in the *sthapanī*; thus there are seven in the ears, making sixteen in total,
of which two are sound-conductors.

One should avoid eight [of these] with a surgical instrument: those two located at the junctions of the conch-shells (*śaṅkha*), twelve on the head, two in the elevations (*utkṣepa*) of those [conch-junctions], one in each of the sutures (*sīmanta*), and one in the *adhipati* [suture].
Likewise, there are the small, crooked, mixed, and knotted [veins], which are not to be incised at their junctions (AS.Śā.6.7).
Among them, according to their respective fourfold division, one hundred and seventy-five carry wind and blood (AS.Śā.6.7).
This is the division [of the humors]; for even when residing in pure blood along with bile and phlegm, the *doṣas* thus sustain the body,
but by their reversal they cause affliction.
In that regard, those which are dark-red, throbbing, fine, and filling or emptying momentarily carry *vātarakta* (wind-blood disorder).
Those which are blue, yellow, or black, warm to the touch, and quickly discharging carry *pittarakta* (bile-blood disorder).
White, unctuous, stable, cold, and itchy eruptions indicate kapha and blood;
when there is a mixture of symptoms, they indicate a combination (saṃsarga) or all three humors (sannipāta); those that are level, deep-seated, unctuous, and red indicate pure blood.
There are twenty-four vessels;
by them this body is moistened, like a grove by water-carriers or like a field by irrigation channels.
And by those channels it is surrounded like the nave of a wheel by its spokes;
in that nave, the vital breaths (prāṇas) are especially established,
and because it is the locus of the internal fire.
Of those vessels, indeed, ten extend upward, ten downward, and four horizontally;
by them, the respective limbs and parts of the body are supported and nourished.
Of those [channels], the upward-moving ones, having reached the heart, each become threefold;
from among those thirty, two by two carry wind, bile, phlegm, blood, and nutritional essence.
By eight [elements] sound, form, taste, and smell are perceived;
by two each, one speaks, makes a sound, sleeps, and awakens;
and two carry the breath.
And two [channels] of a woman depend on the breasts for milk, while that of a man is semen;
thus, those moving downward and situated in the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya) arise in three ways. AS.Śā.6.12 AS.Śā.6.12
Therein, the first ten [channels] function as before; two carry food by means of the receptacle of the measure (mātrā), and two carry water.
Two [channels] carry urine and two carry semen, and those same two release it; in women, they likewise carry the menstrual flow.
Two of these are the *varconirasinī* (feces-carrying) channels, which are connected to the large intestine;
thus there are twelve.
The remaining eight are transverse vessels (*dhamanī*) that nourish the sweat.
It was stated previously that the four currents moving horizontally, when divided, become very many;
[thus] there are nine currents for men.
The ears, eyes, nostrils, mouth, anus, urinary passage, and three others— namely the two breasts and the blood-path in women—
as well as other internal channels, these thirteen are the bases of life; they are the conduits for the movement of breath, water, food, the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), and waste products.
In that regard, for those who carry the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the heart is the root and the great channel;
these are vitiated by the depletion of the constituent elements (*dhātu*), dryness, thirst, hunger, physical exertion, and the suppression of natural urges.
Then, when [the breath] is released, it is obstructed, becoming shallow or frequent, accompanied by sound and pain;
in that state, the treatment is like that for dyspnea (AS.Śā.6.16). Furthermore, the root of those [channels] carrying water is the *talu* and the *kloma*.
These [humors] become deranged by excessive sexual intercourse, exposure to heat, consumption of dry food, astringents, and the suppression of natural urges;
consequently, there arises excessive thirst, dryness of the mouth, ringing in the ears, and the perception of darkness.
In that regard, thirst has been described as the disease; its medicine is the stomach, which is the root of the food-carrying channels, and the left side of the body.

If these are impaired, one should understand everything that has been stated in the chapter on "The Measure of Food" (Mātrāśitīya). The heart and the ten vessels are the root of the nutrient-carrying channels.
The liver and spleen belong to those carrying blood;
the sinews and skin to those carrying flesh;
and the kidneys and flesh to those carrying fat.
The hips are nourished by the bone-carrying [channels],
the fat and marrow by the marrow-carrying [channels], the joints and bones by the semen-carrying [channels], and the breasts, testicles, and marrow by the [same].
The bladder is the receptacle for the urine-carrying channels, the groin for the feces-carrying channels,
and the colon and large intestine for the sweat-carrying channels; while the fat and the hair follicles are the receptacles for the [channels carrying] the lymph.

Their various complications arising from unwholesome diet and lifestyle, as well as their respective treatments, should be identified according to their specific characteristics of increase and decrease, following the chapter on the "Knowledge of the Doshas and so forth" (Doṣādivijñānīya). However, in the case of venesection, there may be vertigo, delusion, tremors, delirium, flatulence, colic, anorexia, thirst, vomiting, fever, excessive hemorrhage, and obstruction of urine and feces, leading even to death.

Therefore, one should treat a case where the channels have been pierced after rejecting [the possibility of healing], and likewise a case where the foreign body has been extracted, according to the procedure for fresh wounds (AS. Śā.
6.20). In that regard, the specific types of channels are the *sirās* (veins) and *dhamanīs* (arteries).
Others, however, maintain that there is a distinctness [of function] among the veins (sirā), arteries (dhamanī), and channels (srotas); yet,
due solely to their mutual proximity, their similar functions, and their subtlety, they appear as if non-distinct even though their functions are actually separate.
Others, however, say:

"Srotas, sirā-dhamanīs, rasa-vāhinīs, nāḍīs, paths, ayanas, gārgas, body cavities—whether closed or open—locations, āśayas, kṣayas, and niketas; these are the names for the perceptible and imperceptible spaces of the bodily constituents within the body."
And those cavities, when provoked, cause the *dhātus* situated in their own locations and those situated in the channels to become disturbed;
and they too, being disturbed, [disturb] those channels.
The channels corrupt the channels, and the humors corrupt the tissues;
thus, the vitiated doshas are the corrupters of all these.
And these [tissues] generally become impaired due to the defect of fire;
therefore, longevity, health, strength, growth, complexion, and vitality depend upon that [fire],
as do the *rañjaka* and other elemental fires, as well as the metabolic fires (*dhātu-agni*) of the tissues.

In the same way, food also, when cooked by that very [fire], attains the state of nectar, while uncooked, it becomes poison. (AS.Śā.6.23) In this regard, the specific type of *pitta* known as the "digestive fire" (*pācaka*) has been previously mentioned.

Others, however, say that the internal heat produced by the combination of humors (*doṣa*), elements (*dhātu*), and waste products (*mala*) is the fire whose locus and function have been described above.

Indeed, having been properly ingested, the mass of food is drawn into the stomach by the vital wind (*prāṇa-vāyu*); its consistency is broken up by liquids, softened by fats, and then, being ignited, the internal fire—fanned by the equalizing wind (*samāna*)—cooks it while located in the stomach, just as fire cooks rice and water in a pot.
Even though it contains all tastes, when being digested, it first becomes sweet and excites phlegm (kapha) in the form of froth;
then, having become sour through improper digestion (vidagdha), it moves from the stomach (āmāśaya) and excites clear bile (pitta).

And having reached the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya), the wind becomes pungent; then, while the food is thus moistened, the five fires of the fivefold great elements, being dispersed by the wind, cook the five elemental qualities residing in the food according to their respective natures.
Once digested, they nourish, each according to its own nature, the bodily constituents and the qualities of the elements that have become their transformations.

And thus, from food that has been digested, just as from oil containing various medicinal ingredients, there is produced a clear, essential substance called *rasa* (nutritive essence) and an impurity called *kiṭṭa* (waste).

And by those two, essence (*sāra*) and impurity (*mala*), the channels (*srotas*) belonging respectively to the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) that consist of them are filled through a continuous succession;
and from the channels, the constituents nourish themselves according to their respective divisions and in their proper order.

Furthermore, even as they enter into each subsequent stage, there is no depletion of the preceding channels, provided they are properly replenished by the timely and correct application of food during the process of transformation.
Consequently, the pure and impure constituents known as *dhātus* follow their own respective measures according to the age and body of the individual (AS.Śā.6.28).

In this regard, the essence of food (*āhārarasa*), propelled by the *vyāna* wind, is digested in succession within the seven fires of the *dhātus*; immediately upon its departure from its own original state, it acquires the designation of the *dhātu*s such as blood and so forth. In due time, possessing unimpeded strength and measure, it invigorates the body and nourishes both the *dhātus* and the *dhātumalas*.
Then,
the waste of food becomes clear urine and solid feces.
The essence of chyle is blood; its waste products are phlegm and lymph.
The essence of blood is flesh; its waste products are the tendons, veins, and bile.
The essence of flesh is fat; its waste products are the skin, muscle-fat, and the impurities of the ears, eyes, nose, mouth, hair-follicles, and the generative organ.
The essence of fat is the bones, sinews, and joints; its waste product is sweat.
The essence of bone is marrow; its waste products are hair, body hair, and nails.
The essence of marrow is semen; its waste products are the impurities of the eyes, feces, and the oiliness of the skin.
The essence of semen is *ojas*;
due to its extreme purity, it lacks impurities,
and for this very reason, others do not even admit that it undergoes digestion (*pāka*).

Others, however, maintain that the embryo consists of the essence of semen alone. Furthermore, due to the greater or lesser intensity of the wind, fire, and food, from those respective specific modes of condensation, there arises within the womb a fivefold [element]—formless yet possessing sound—that is slightly audible, whether abundant or slight.
And this being so, all states within the body consist of food alone;

for by that very [food], this machine of the body—both internally and externally—is pervaded in this manner over a long period, maintained through an uninterrupted flow until the exhaustion of karma, endowed with health and the accumulation of strength. Otherwise, however, due to the upward movement of the essence of food, either because the channels are obstructed or because the flow of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) is not properly directed, it is cut off in the interim.
Or it becomes a vessel for diseases;
others, however, describe it thus.

As soon as food has been swallowed, rolled down the throat-passage, and descended into the great abyss [of the stomach], whichever portion of it is licked by the bodily fire (*kāyāgni*) and brought to digestion, from that very portion a minute essence called *prasāda* (the refined extract) is produced. Immediately upon its production, this essence spreads equally throughout all the constituent elements (*dhātu*), following primarily and most extensively through the open, partially closed, and nearby channels (*srotas*) with their openings wide; subsequently, it follows the others in turn.
In this manner, the essence of food itself directly nourishes all the constituent elements at various different times.
Furthermore, the elements do not transition into the state of another element by means of the destruction of their own nature; rather,
fire becomes fourfold through a distinction of power.
It is even, uneven, sharp, and dull; therein, the "even" [agni] properly digests food that has been properly consumed,
while the "uneven" digests even improperly consumed food, and does not digest even properly consumed food.

The sharp [agni] digests even that which is improperly consumed quickly; that same [agni], when increased excessively, becomes "over-agni" (atyagni).
