The dull [agni], however, even when properly consumed, displays signs of undigested matter (āma) such as heaviness in the abdomen, flatulence, constipation, rumbling in the intestines, dryness of the mouth, and stiffness of the wind, and it digests only after a long time.
Moreover, even by an external fire consisting of flames and embers, cooking does not always take place in a uniform manner;
how much less so by that which has heat as its nature within the internal substratum?
Therefore, one should protect it with great effort.

In that regard, one should gradually bring the other [doshas] to a state of habituation using their respective superior and moderate [regimens], and then maintain them with the superior [regimen], as well as by the treatments for vāta and the others mentioned in the chapter on the management of doshas, and by the application of medicines and exercises prescribed for grahaṇī disease.
Regarding this, there is a verse here (AS.Śā.6.33): "The [folds] are of the same color as one's own dhātu, circular, thick, and fine."
The channels are long in shape and resemble spreading creepers; furthermore,
whatever food and conduct are consistent with the [patient's] humors and qualities [are beneficial].
That which is out of balance with the *dhātus* is a corrupter of the channels (*srotas*). There is either excessive flow, obstruction, or even knots in the vessels (*sirā*).
Going astray from the path is the characteristic of corruption in the streams (of consciousness).
Like lotus stalks, they are subtle and extend far.
The gates of the channels in the body are those by which the nutrient essence (*rasa*) is accumulated;
some say this occurs in a day and night, others in six days, and still others [in longer periods].
Through the process of digestion and so forth, food attains the state of semen after one month;
however, aphrodisiacs and similar substances produce semen and other fluids immediately by virtue of their potency.
Generally, one should administer other medicinal treatments after a day and night have passed.
[The bodily constituents include] phlegm, bile, excrement in the channels, sweat, nails, and hair.
Oiliness, unimpaired skin, moisture, and vigor are the impurities of the bodily constituents (dhātus) in their respective order.
When the fire resides in its proper place, it is balanced; when it moves to an improper path, the fire becomes irregular.

When the digestive fire is overwhelmed by bile, it becomes sharp; when it is afflicted by phlegm, it becomes dull. When the fire is extinguished, one dies; when it is properly balanced, one lives long and free from disease.
One would become diseased if that [element] were disturbed; therefore, one should protect it with great effort.
Now begins the seventh chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "The Classification of the Vital Points" (Marmavibhāga).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
There are one hundred and seven vital points (marmas); among them,
forty-four are located in the limbs.

There are twenty-six vital points in the lower trunk and thirty-seven above it (AS.Śā.7.3). Now, on one thigh, in the middle of the sole near the middle finger, there is a vital point named *talahr̥daya*; one pierced there dies from pain.
Between the thumb and the finger, death occurs quickly due to a convulsive seizure;
two finger-breadths above the *kṣipra* vein on both sides is the *kūrca*.
In that case, there is wandering and trembling of the foot; below the ankle joint is the *kūrcaśiras*, where there is pain and swelling;
the *gulpha* is at the junction of the foot and the calf.
In that regard, *ruk* (pain) refers to stiffness of the thighs or impotence.
The *indrabasti* is located at the midpoint of the shank, twelve finger-breadths from the heel and other points;
death occurs there due to the loss of blood.
The knee is at the junction of the shanks and thighs; there, lameness occurs.
(AS.Śā.7.4) The pin [of the knee] is three finger-breadths above the knee on both sides.
In that condition, there is an increase in swelling and stiffness of the thighs; in the middle of the thigh, due to the loss of blood, there is wasting of the thigh (sakthi-śoṣa);
above the urvī and below the groin-joint at the root of the thigh is the lohitākṣa.
In that case, due to the depletion of blood, there occurs hemiplegia; a "vitapa" (branch-like swelling) develops between the groin and the scrotum,
resulting in impotence or diminished semen.
The arms are like the thighs; however, the specific differences are the ankle and the wrist, as well as the knee and the elbow.
From piercing these, lameness results.

The armpit-supporter (kakṣādhara) is like a branch, located between the armpits and the eyes; therein lies lameness (AS.Śā.7.5). The anus (guda), which expels wind and feces, is connected to the large intestine (sthūlāntra) (AS.Śā.7.5).
In that regard, immediate death occurs in the case of the bladder,
which has little flesh and blood internally, is curved like a bow at the waist, possesses a single opening,
and is directed downward; even there, however, death is not instantaneous except from a wound caused by a urinary stone.
In that case as well, if pierced on both sides, the patient does not survive;
if pierced on one side, there occurs a wound with discharge of urine,
but if treated with effort, it heals.

The navel is situated between the receptacles of digested and undigested food; there too, death is instantaneous (AS.Śā.7.6). Between the trunk and the chest, and between the two breasts, is the heart—the gateway to the receptacle of undigested food and the locus of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas; there too, death is instantaneous (AS.Śā.7.6).
Two finger-breadths below the two breasts, at the roots of the breasts on both sides— there, death occurs for one whose internal cavity is filled with phlegm.
Two finger-breadths above the nipples of the two breasts, at the *stanarohita* (the areola) on both sides— there, death occurs for one whose internal cavity is filled with blood.
On both sides of the chest are the two *apastambha* vessels, which carry wind; death results from them due to the filling of the thoracic cavity with blood and the onset of cough and dyspnea.
Below the shoulder blades, on the upper portions of the flanks, are the two *apālāpa* vessels; death results from them when the blood therein turns into pus.
On both sides of the spinal column, at the level of the hips, are the two *kaṭīkataruṇa* bones.
Due to the loss of blood in those two [channels], one becomes pale, discolored, and deformed, and dies;
the *kukundara* are on both sides of the spinal column, at the outer part of the hips.
From the ignorance regarding these two [organs], there is loss of movement in the lower body;
the buttocks (*nitamba*) are the coverings for the hips and ears, connected to the other sides of the torso;
from ignorance regarding them, there is swelling in the lower body, weakness, and death.

The two side-joints (pārśvasandhi) are connected to the lower sides and the interior, situated between the hips and the sides, extending transversely and upwards; death results from their being filled with blood due to the filling of the thoracic cavity (koṣṭha).
The two *bṛhatī* vessels run straight from both sides of the root of the breasts toward the spinal column (pṛṣṭhavaṃśa).
Death results from complications caused by excessive hemorrhaging from those two [shoulder-blades], which are connected to the spine on both sides and to the roots of the arms.
The shoulder-blades (aṃsaphalaka) are attached to both sides of the spinal column and to the base of the upper arms.
The paralysis and wasting of their arms;
the shoulders, which are the binding points for the neck, arms, head, and the seat of the spine in the middle of the neck and arms;
and the stiffness of those arms.
At both ends of the throat-pipe are four vessels;
of these, two are the *nīlā* and two are the *manyā*.
In those [veins], muteness, impairment of voice, or loss of the sense of taste occurs;
on both sides of the neck, there are four mother-veins (*sirāmātṛkā*) separately, and injury to them results in immediate death;
at the junction of the head and neck are the *kukāṭika* [veins].
When the two [temporal bones] have unstable tops and the two [malleoli] are situated below the back of the ears,
there is deafness.
The two nostrils are connected on both sides to the two ear-paths within;
there is the non-perception of smell in them.
Below the two eyebrows, at the ends of the tail, are the two eyes; outside of them is the blindness.
If there are two conch-marks (*śaṅkha*) above the eyebrows at the ends of their tails, extending toward the ears on the forehead, death occurs immediately; likewise,
if there are two depressions (*āvarta*) above the eyebrows.
Blindness or impairment of vision in those two;
the two protuberances above the temples at the hairline.

Of these two, one with the arrow-head remains alive either because it has fallen out through suppuration or because it was never extracted; however, one with the arrow-head remaining in the middle of the eyebrows cannot survive. This [condition] is called *sthapanī*.
In that regard, there are five joints on the head, like those of a raised [limb], and the transverse and upward sutures called *sīmanta*;
death occurs through [disturbances in] these by means of insanity, dizziness, and loss of consciousness.
The convergence of the vessels that nourish the tongue, nose, eyes, and ears occurs at the palate;
their four openings are known as the *śṛṅgāṭakas*, and death occurs instantly upon injury to them.
Above the interior of the head, the convergence of vessels and joints is the *romāvarta*; it is named the *adhipati*.
In that case as well, death occurs immediately;
furthermore, the general characteristic of the *marmans* is that when they are afflicted, pain arises and there is irregular throbbing.
And generally, as stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* (AS.Bh.
7.12): "bodily numbness, heaviness, delusion, and a desire for cold."
Sweating, fainting, vomiting, and labored breathing are the symptoms of one pierced in a vital point (marmaviddha). Furthermore, it is called a "vital point" (marman) because it causes death.
Furthermore, that [body] is a collection of flesh, vessels, sinews, bones,
and joints; therefore, when it is afflicted, there is especially an obstruction of life-force,
though the designation is generally made in terms of its constituent parts.
Therefore, based on their respective substrates such as flesh and so forth, the vital points (*marmāṇi*) are divided into five types. As follows: [AS.Śā.7.14]
The eleven muscular *marmans* are the *tala*, *hṛdaya*, *indrabasti*, *guda*, *stana*, and *rohitā*.

The forty-one vascular *marmans* are the *urvī*, *lohitākhyā*, *nābhi*, *hṛdaya*, *stanamūla*, *apastambha*, *apālāpa*, *pārśvasandhi*, *bṛhatī*, *nīlā*, *manyā*, *mātṛkā*, *phaṇā*, *apāṅga*, *sthapanī*, and *śṛṅgāṭaka*.
The twenty-seven ligamentous *marmans* are the *kṣipra*, *kūrca*, *kūrcaśiras*, *viṭapaka*, *kakṣādhara*, *vasti*, *aṃsa*, *vidhura*, and *utkṣepa*.
The eight bone-marmans are the sacrum, the two young-of-the-hips (kaṭīkataruṇa), the two buttocks (nitamba), the two shoulder-blades (aṃsaphalaka), and the two temples (śaṅkha).

The twenty joint-marmans are the ankle (gulpha), the wrist (maṇibandha), the knee (jānu), the elbow (kūrpara), the two kukundaras, the two kṛkāṭikas, the two āvartas, and the two sīmanta-adhipatis. Furthermore, there are nineteen marmans that take life immediately, consisting of five types: the anus (guda), the bladder (vasti), the navel (nābhi), the heart (hṛdaya), the two mātṛkās, the two śaṅkhas, and the two śṛṅgāṭakas; because they are fiery (āgneyatva), their time limit is within seven nights.

The thirty-three vital points (*marmans*)— namely, the palms, the heart, the eyes, Indra (the forehead), the bladder, the chest, the waist, the ribs, the buttocks, the flanks, the joints, the *bṛhatīs*, and the sutures (*sīmanta*)— are fatal at intervals of time; because they possess both lunar (*saumya*) and fiery (*āgneya*) natures, their period of action is within half a month.

Among those, however, three— the two *utkṣepas* and the *sthāpanī*— are sometimes swift and quickly [effective] in extracting the arrow-head (*viśalyaghna*), because they belong to the wind element (*vāyavyatvāt*).

For as long as the wind remains here, obstructed by the opening of the *śalya*, so long does one live. The forty-four [points] that cause deformity— the *kūrca*, the knees, the elbows, the earth, the blood-named [region], the branches, the armpits, the lower parts, the *kukundara*s, the shoulder-blades, the *nīla* [veins], the *manyā*, the neck, the *vidhura*, the nape, and the whirls at the outer corners of the eyes— are [to be avoided] because of their gentle nature.
For *soma*, by means of its stability and coolness, sustains the vital breaths (*prāṇas*); yet these same breaths, when sometimes afflicted, cause death.
The eight locations—the armpits, the head, the ankles, and the wrists—cause pain due to the predominance of the qualities of fire, wind, and *soma*.
For it has been stated that fire and wind especially cause affliction, whereas soma supports the vital breaths.
But others say:
"The five [factors], beginning with flesh, when increased and combined together, cause the immediate loss of life."
Others say that for those [beings] who are deficient one by one and for those who are small, the others [arise] respectively by their very nature. AS.Śā.7.21 AS.Śā.7.21

Specific karmic functions are like the drawing of water by the moon, the ignition of fire by the sun, and the attraction of iron by a magnet; likewise, even when many vital points (*marman*) in the hands and feet are severed, death does not occur by its very nature.
Furthermore, others provide a reason for this as well.
For when the hands or feet are severed, the vessels contract; consequently, due to the minimal flow of blood, life is preserved.
However, in the case of piercing a vital point (*marman*), death occurs either from the excessive loss of blood or from the derangement of the bodily wind (*vāyu*).

Therefore, in one struck in a vital point (*marman*), that limb should be quickly incised at the joint region. However, for vital points that have been slightly or deeply struck, the respective treatments should be applied in their proper order, from the first to the last; or, for those struck very slightly, the subsequent treatments alone may be used.
Furthermore, they are divided into five types. *Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha*, Śārīrasthāna 7.23.
For example:
twelve [fingers] measured by one's own fingers are [the distance] from the base of the thighs to the top of the head, and from the branches to the armpits.
The two ankles, the two wrists, and the two roots of the breasts—these six are two finger-breadths (aṅgulas) wide;
the two knees and the two elbows are four finger-breadths wide;

the beard-region, the anus, the bladder, the navel, the heart, the two *nīla* vessels, the two *manye*, the *mātṛkā* channels, the *sīmanta* sutures, and the *śṛṅgāṭaka* junctions—these twenty-nine are equal in measure to the palm of the hand.
The remaining fifty-six [petals] have the measure of five finger-breadths;
others, however, say that the swift ones have the measure of a grain of rice.
Others maintain that there are vital points (marmas) the size of a pea (*kalāya*) located at the nipples of the breasts, as well as others the size of a sesame seed (*tila*);
and on this subject, there are these verses: [The verses follow.]
Even when this body is pervaded by vital points (*marmans*), it is the life-force that protects those vital points;
therefore, a wise person should always cultivate only those things that are conducive to longevity.

Even a very slight injury to a vital point (marman) generally causes much greater suffering; likewise, diseases that take refuge in the vital points, once they have set in, persist even with great effort.
Falling into despair, he is violently distracted; empty and delirious, he wanders and trembles.
He breathes heavily with great difficulty, his limbs repeatedly collapsing.
His heart palpitates and does not remain in one place;
due to the injury to his vital organs (marmans), he undergoes death through these symptoms.
Even if he is not pierced in a vital spot, a man who is afflicted by cutting, tearing, and so forth,
and whose blood has flowed excessively, will immediately lose his life.
But one who lives otherwise, even if pierced by hundreds of arrows,
a person of merit whose lifespan is fixed does not die under any circumstances.
Therefore, one should indeed strive to treat [the patient] until the very last breath;
having obtained the consent of the patient's kinsmen and friends, the physician should then decline the case.
Now begins the eighth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the section on the body concerning the classification of constitutions (prakṛti).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and others:
"There are seven constitutions (prakṛtis) [of humans], which arise from the humors (doṣas) individually, through their combination, and in a state of equilibrium."

In that regard, if at the time of the semen, the ovum, or the womb, there exists in the mother’s diet or conduct one or more *doṣas* in excess, then by that [excess], the constitution (*prakṛti*) of the being being born is produced through its own poison— just as a worm arising in a poisonous plant is [affected] by the poison, or like a scorpion and such [creatures] which are like venomous serpents [affected] by their own poison. Therefore, because the semen and ovum have been permeated by the body [of the mother] and because it is [thus] constituted by nature (*prākṛtatva*), it is not harmed by that *doṣa* to such an extent.
Furthermore, his body is refined by those very qualities,
and consequently, it is not suddenly afflicted by factors that are the opposites of those qualities.
In that state, however, when the humors (doṣas) have undergone morbid change, the embryo is either conceived only with extreme difficulty, perishes immediately upon conception,
or becomes deformed.
And likewise, some say:
"The [humors] such as wind (vāta) are of two kinds: natural (prākṛta) and modified (vaikṛta)."

Among them, the primary ones are of seven kinds; they serve as the causes of the [other] sevenfold primary constituents (*prakṛti*), are produced simultaneously with the body, and are designated as *dhātus* because they sustain the body;
they are the seeds of the morbid transformations known as *doṣas*.

In one who is about to die, all [the elements] deviate from their natural state even while remaining present within the body; the designation [of the disorder] is made according to whichever constituent of *prakṛti* is most predominant.
However, the morbid humors (*vaikṛta*) arise from the impurities of the essence of food after it has emerged from the womb.
They descend into the primary elements by the power of time and other factors; through their association with the increase and decrease of dreams and vital breaths, they sustain and afflict the body.
Similarly, *ojas* (vital essence) is also located in the heart; it is of the size of eight drops and serves as the substratum for the *rasa*-based *ojas*, which undergoes both decrease and increase.

Now, according to his own defects and qualities, one of a *vāta* constitution has a thin, dry, and stiff body; his limbs, teeth, nails, hair, eyes, and voice are small; he dislikes cold, suffers from flatulence, and has swollen calves; he walks with a clicking sound in his joints; he is quick to begin actions, prone to agitation, forgetfulness, and instability; his resolve, intellect, gait, and vision are fickle; his natural disposition is unfriendly; he is a thief, ignoble, envious, and lacks control over his senses; he delights in music, history, laughter, amorous play, quarrels, hunting, and garden excursions; and he finds relief through a desire for unctuous, hot, sweet, sour, and salty foods and drinks. Furthermore:

One who has little wealth, strength, life-span, or sleep; whose speech is feeble and whose body is covered with visible veins; who is unfortunate, eats excessively, speaks much, is an atheist, and has cracked hair, hands, and feet.
With his mouth slightly agape from sleep, he trembles, snorts, and gnashes his teeth;
he wanders through rivers that are dry, parched, and uneven, and across the sky and the peaks of mountains.

One of a pitta constitution has a body that is hot and fair-complexioned, with copper-colored nails, eyes, tongue, lips, palms, and soles; his joints, ligaments, and flesh are lax; his hair and body hair are like those of a camel—reddish-brown, sparse, and soft; he possesses moderate strength and vitality, but little semen, sexual desire, or offspring; he is brave and conceited; he develops wrinkles, baldness, graying hair, moles, and freckles early; he is quick to hunger and thirst; he is intelligent but ill-favored; and he finds relief and preference for things that are sweet, bitter, astringent, and cold. Furthermore:

Adorned with beloved garlands, ointments, and ornaments, well-conducted, pure, and affectionate toward those who depend on him, he is endowed with wealth, daring, intelligence, and strength; even among his enemies, he becomes a refuge in times of fear.

One who hates the heat, perspires excessively, has a foul odor, and is prone to frequent excretion, anger, drinking, eating, and envy; while asleep, such a person sees *karṇikāra* and *palāśa* trees, as well as conflagrations, meteors, lightning, the sun, and fire.

One of phlegmatic constitution (*kapha-prakṛti*), however, has a complexion like that of *dūrvā* grass, a blue lotus, or a reed stalk; his muscular joints are even, well-proportioned, smooth, firm, delicate, and closely knit; his limbs are full and beautiful; he has a broad forehead, thighs, and arms; his eyes are clear, wide, large, long, and thick-lashed, with distinct white and black parts; his voice is deep like that of a lion, a drum, or a cloud; he is patient with hunger, thirst, and heat; he possesses great vitality, strength, semen, sexual vigor, and offspring; he wears garlands and ointments for a long time without fading; he maintains enmity firmly and secretly; he is graceful, truthful, mindful, resolute, and free from greed; and even in childhood, he does not weep, and his relief comes from pungent, bitter, astringent, hot, and dry things.
Moreover,
furthermore.

One who speaks little, has little anger, and is moderate in drinking and eating; long-lived, wealthy, far-sighted, generous, faithful, profound, liberal, patient, noble, prone to sleep, slow to act, grateful, upright, learned, fortunate, modest, devoted to his teachers, and firm in friendship. (AS.Śā.8.14)
In a dream, he sees reservoirs of water with lotuses and flocks of birds, as well as rain clouds;
if there is a mixture of both characteristics, his nature is a combination (saṃsarga).
One who possesses all qualities and whose constitution has balanced humors (doṣa) is ideal;
however, among those, the first three types are chronically afflicted because their constitutions are permeated by the latent tendencies of the humors.
In particular, those whose nature is dualistic— since they produce modifications through a mixture of qualities, just as hunger, thirst, and so forth are designated as "health" [only when balanced]—
should be treated according to the method described in the chapter on the management of the *doṣas*, by means of a regimen possessing opposite qualities.
Through a balanced state of all tastes, through suitability, and through that which is prescribed according to the season,
there are seven constitutions (prakṛti), distinguished by the humors (doṣa) as well as by qualities such as the mental temperament (sattva) and others.

One should know those [qualities] by means of the aforementioned purities and so forth produced from them (AS.Śā.8.17). Furthermore, there are seven types of natures based on birth, family, region, time, age, strength, and the individual self (AS.Śā.8.17).

For various specific dispositions of persons are seen to be determined by birth and so forth. Furthermore, because of the varying degrees of the [three] constituents (*sattva* and so on), and because they mutually conform to one another through differences in the body, their distinctions become innumerable.
The body conforms to the *sattva* and other [qualities], and the *sattva* and others also conform to the body. Furthermore,

due to the penetration of the innumerable varieties of *sattva* and the other qualities, there arises an imitation of appearance, voice, and conduct, which is designated by the term *anūka* and possesses innumerable varieties.
That possession (*āveśa*), however, is produced by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) resulting from practice in an immediately preceding birth;
therefore, one should observe the person’s inclination (*anūka*) exactly according to the respective specificities of gods, humans, animals, ghosts, and denizens of hell.
Age is threefold: childhood, middle age, and old age.
Among these, one is a child until the sixteenth year.
Up to the sixth month it is middling, and beyond that it is advanced;
among these, the infant is of three types according to whether its subsistence is on breast milk, solid food, or both.
In that [stage], there is an increase in the size of the body and an excess of phlegm (*śleṣman*); by means of that, a child possesses oiliness, softness, delicacy, little anger, and good fortune.
(AS.Śā.8.21) Youth is also threefold: middling, fullness, and non-decline.
In that [state], there is an increase of bile (pitta);
by that, there is a keen digestive fire, the maturation of superior wisdom, and perseverance.

Therein, from thirty until forty years of age, there is the full perfection of the elements, faculties, powers, vigor, manliness, mindfulness, speech, consciousness, humility, and virtues; beyond this, however, there is decline. But the aged person—whose qualities such as the elements and faculties are constantly wasting away, and who is overcome by wrinkles, gray hair, coughing, asthma, loss of digestive fire, and so forth—succumbs like an old house battered by rain.

In that state, there is an excess of wind (*māruta*); by this, the skin remains upon joints where the flesh has become lax and its substance diminished, resulting in roughness of the skin, stooping of the body, trembling, coughing, labored breathing, the provocation of phlegm and nasal mucus, and the depletion of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*).
Others, however, say:
Childhood, growth, luster, intellect, skin, semen, eyes, tears, and the sense organs—
these ten depart in succession during each decade, as do the mind and all the senses.
Thus, in this era, the measure of the maximum lifespan is one hundred years.

Furthermore, there are humans who, due to specific differences in their karma, live for less than or more than a hundred years; having ascertained the measure of their lifespan through the aforementioned specific natures, one should divide their age into three parts.
Moreover,
every year the lifespan of men diminishes by one hundred years.
Due to the abundance of demerit regarding one's lifespan, whatever measure of it is desired,
there is also a threefold strength.
It is innate, produced by time, and produced by application;
therein, the innate is the natural state of the body and the sentient being,
while that produced by time consists of what arises from the divisions of seasons and what is produced by age.
Furthermore, that which is produced through proper application arises from diet, conduct, strengthening practices, and yoga; and these are the factors that increase it,
namely:

Birth in a region inhabited by strong people and at a time of similar character, as well as an auspicious conjunction of time; the excellence of seed, field, body, food, and mental disposition (*sattva*); natural constitution (*svabhāva*), youth, physical exercise, and joy—these are the factors [of strength].

Furthermore, the eight essential constituents (*sāra*)—skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, semen, and *sattva*, which are progressively superior—are taught for the purpose of knowing the measure of one's strength.
Furthermore,

a physician should not be deluded by the mere observation of the body, thinking, "This person is strong because of his physical development or large stature," or "This person has little strength because of his leanness or small stature";
for both of these cases are seen to be otherwise in the instance of the elephant and the lion.

In that case, one who is endowed with all essential qualities (*sāra*) becomes exceedingly strong, possessed of supreme dignity, capable of enduring afflictions, confident in himself regarding all undertakings, intent upon what is auspicious, firm of body, with perfectly composed gait, and possessing a great voice that is resonant, smooth, and deep; he partakes in happiness, sovereignty, wealth, enjoyments, and honor; he is subject to slow aging and few illnesses; his offspring are generally widespread and of equal virtue; and he is long-lived.
One who is the opposite of this, however, lacks essential quality (*asāra*).

The medium [type] has medium qualities (AS.Śā.8.29). Furthermore, the measurement is by one's own fingers: the big toe and the forefinger are two finger-breadths in length; the other three are respectively shorter by one-fifth each, or else they are without their nails (AS.Śā.8.29).

The forefoot, the sole of the foot, and the heel are each four finger-breadths long; they are five, six, and four finger-breadths wide respectively; the foot is fourteen finger-breadths in length and likewise fourteen in circumference;
similarly, the ankles and the middle of the shank are four finger-breadths in height; such is the foot.
The shank is eighteen finger-breadths in length, and the thigh is four finger-breadths [longer];
the knee is thirty finger-breadths in circumference, and the thigh is [thirty-two finger-breadths].
The six āyāmas [are mentioned] in AS.Śā.8.30; the scrotum and penis have a circumference of sixteen and five [aṅgulas] respectively in AS.Śā.8.30.
The hips are sixteen finger-breadths in width and fifty in circumference;
the bladder-head is ten finger-breadths,
and the abdomen is twelve finger-breadths.
It is ten [yojanas] in width and twelve in length; on the sides, the three [joints] are twelve in height,
and the back is eighteen in height.
The space between the breasts is twelve finger-breadths;
the area extending to the edges of the breasts is twenty-four finger-breadths in width and twelve finger-breadths in height; such is the chest.
The heart is two finger-breadths [in width];
the shoulders and armpits are eight [finger-breadths], and the shoulder-blades are six.
The upper arms are sixteen [finger-breadths] long,
the forearms fifteen,
and the hands twelve finger-breadths.
There too, the middle finger is five finger-breadths long; the index and ring fingers are each half a finger-breadth less than that;
and the little finger and the thumb are each three and a half finger-breadths long.
The neck is four finger-breadths in height and twenty-two in circumference;
the face is twelve finger-breadths in height and twenty-four in circumference;
the mouth is five finger-breadths wide. (AS.Śā.8.31)
The distance between the chin and the lips, the nose and the eyes, and the ears and the forehead is four finger-breadths (caturaṅgula) each;
the boundary of the nostrils is three parts of a finger-breadth (tribhāgāṅgula) in width.
The eye is two finger-breadths long and as wide as the belly of the thumb; therein, the black portion is one-third of the white,
and the pupil is one-ninth of the black, the size of a lentil seed.
The head is six finger-breadths in height and thirty-two in circumference; thus,
the entire body measures eighty-four finger-breadths,
and it is said to be "even" when its length and breadth are equal.
In that regard, it is as previously stated: [the body] may be of such dimensions, desirable or undesirable, inferior or superior;

likewise, short or long, fair or dark-haired, hairy or hairless, stout or lean. Furthermore, the desirable [body] is one where the large frame, the appearance of the face, jaws, nipples, back, voice, thighs, hips, waist, chest, neck, and palate are prominent, as are both qualities of the hands, feet, chin, ears, and forehead. (AS.Śā.8.32)
Having fine bones, teeth, nails, finger-joints, and hair;
long fingers, thighs, and arms; and [long] breath, eyes, and tongue when gazing.

One whose mouth, lower lip, tongue, forehead, ears, temples, and chest are broad; whose penis, neck, hair, skin, teeth, eyes, voice, sense organs, nails, and sides of the body are small; and whose skin, teeth, nails, and hair are glossy—[such a person is long-lived].
He possesses a voice with profound underlying intention, concealed joints, and hidden spinal column and roots of the teeth;
his palate, lips, nails, and corners of the eyes are red, and the tongue, palms, and soles of the feet are copper-colored.
With black hair, eyebrows, eyelashes, and pupils;
with white, bright circles of the teeth, a high forehead, chest, neck, face, nails, and feet;
and with ears, breasts, and the tip of the nose set low as he walked.
The affection for his thick shoulders, neck, teeth, fingers, skin, thin nails, tongue,
rounded buttocks, neck, and nails.
He has even backs, teeth, and forehead; likewise, his thighs are rounded and tapering,
and his navel spirals to the right.
Her breasts have a wide interval between them, her eyebrows are arched,
her nails are shaped like tortoises, and her feet,
face, and bridge of the nose are straight.
The jaws are not protruding, the facial appearance is smooth, the palate and tongue are neither too thick nor too thin, and the lips and the bodily frame are well-proportioned.
The heart is throbbing, the temples feel warm,
the palate, feet, and belly are heated, there is breath,
and the hair on the back and ears is bristling.
The eyebrows are slightly drooping; the forehead is wrinkled with well-knit joints in the shape of a half-moon; the head is like an umbrella;
the hair is soft with many roots; and the veins, bones, and joints are firm and well-concealed, as are the natural functions of wind, urine, feces, and the private parts.
There are smiles, cries, and various movements;

likewise, having been bathed and anointed, the body gradually extends downward and becomes parched until it is desired [to die]. And regarding this, there is a verse here (AS.Śā.8.33): "The womb becomes a progressively superior field for the birth of one who is free from disease."
Increasing gradually through the knowledge and discernment of the [proper] extent,
may there be a hundred autumns for this body endowed with all virtues.
Longevity, sovereignty, and all desired things are established therein;
it experiences neither pride nor dejection, and undergoes both pleasure and pain.
One who possesses *sattva* remains steadfast when being assailed, neither *rājasa* nor *tāmasa*.
Generosity, ethical discipline, compassion, truthfulness, celibacy, and gratitude— these are [the qualities of the virtuous].
Elixirs and loving-kindness: the group that increases merit and longevity. Now begins the ninth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the knowledge of morbid alterations (Vikṛtivijñānīya).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.

In healthy or diseased persons who desire another body, the doshas— which pervade the entire body and have transcended the scope of medicinal treatment— suddenly produce a reversal of their natural state, signaling like dense clouds the exhaustion of the lifespan;
this, in brief, they call *riṣṭa*.
In that regard, fair, dark, black, fair-dark, and black-dark are the colors of the body's natural constitution (*dehaprakṛti*),
along with their subdivisions such as lotus-fair and so forth.
Blue, dark, coppery, yellow, white, and so forth are the modifications (*vikṛti*).
Among these, when the primary color (*prakṛti-varṇa*) and the modified color (*vikṛti-varṇa*) appear simultaneously on the whole body or a part of the body, it indicates death.

By this, it is stated that exhaustion, growth, grief, joy, roughness, oiliness, and so forth—likewise the changes in the specific states of those mentioned in the "Chapter on the Differentiation of Temperaments" (*prakṛtibhedīya*), such as large, increased, subtle, and long, as well as all things determined by their respective divisions of *doṣas* and other factors—undergo alteration due to external causes.
There are five shadows in the body;
among them, the shadow of the void (ākāśa) is like a polished sword-blade, blue and stainless, oily, and as if possessing radiance.
From wind, it is rough with dust and ashes, reddish-brown or dark, lusterless, and smelling of sweat and impurities;
from fire, it is red like heated gold or lightning, pleasing to the sight;
and from water, it is as clear as lapis lazuli or sapphire, dense, and very glossy.
The earth possesses a brilliant luster; it is dense, stable, smooth, pure, dark, and white.
Among these, the wind-related [omens] lead to destruction and extreme suffering, while the remaining ones result in the arising of happiness.
There are seven rays: red, yellow, pale-white, white, black, dark-brown, and green.
These are glossy, expansive, stainless, and auspicious.
The impure [perceptions] are the opposite;
these are the distinctions between the two.
Shadow occupies the color and is perceived when near; it consists of the five elements.
Radiance, however, illuminates the color and is perceived from a distance; it arises solely from fire.
He in whose sight the maiden consisting of a reflected shadow is not seen is one whose life has departed.
If, in the sun, a mirror, or other such surfaces, a reflection is suddenly seen as severed, split, deficient, excessive, disordered, lost, distorted, or otherwise transformed or deformed;
AS.Śā.9.8.

He whose forehead does not perspire, whose hair and body hair appear as if oiled though they have not been oiled, and whose eyes are excessively sunken, protruding, dilated, narrowed, with arched brows, drooping brows, squinting, uneven, wandering in their gaze, lacking vision, resembling the color of a mongoose, a pigeon, a firebrand, or various discolored hues such as blue; or whose eyes are excessively mobile, fixed, drooping, watery, excessively open, excessively closed, or have disheveled eyelashes;
or whose nose is excessively open, excessively closed, crooked, cracked, covered in pustules, or dry—he has reached the end of his life.
If one's lower lip sinks downward and the upper lip moves upward, or if both are as dark blue as a ripe jambu fruit;
or if the teeth are excessively dry, copper-colored, blackish, stained with plaque, covered in spots, or if they suddenly fall out.
Or, one whose tongue is crooked, stiff, numb, coated, heavy, dark-brown, swollen, dry, or spreading, as if covered with thorns;
or one whose cheeks, forehead, and jaw-joints have fallen from their positions as if displaced;
or one who cannot support his head, neck, or back due to their own weight—[such a person is incurable].
Or he whose jaw or testicles are displaced,
whose urine is excessively hot,
or from whom blood flows from his own hair follicles despite the absence of any toxic disorder.

He whose limbs suddenly become either excessively light or excessively heavy without cause is about to die. He in whom one or more voices suddenly appear hoarse, indistinct, emaciated, or dejected is about to die.
Or he who, when wishing to speak, becomes confused; or for whom, while speaking, the chest aches intensely;
or whose breath is excessively long, excessively short, foul-smelling, or fragrant.
One whose fingers do not burst when being stretched;
one who, even in the act of coughing, passing wind, urinating, and so forth, produces a sound that transcends his natural state;
and one for whom pleasant or unpleasant odors—such as those of garlands, fruits, sandalwood, corpses, and the like—are perceived on his body, face, impurities, wounds, clothing, and so on.
The body of one from whom lice, flies, and other such creatures excessively abandon it due to its lack of relish, or conversely, resort to it due to its sweetness;

whose limbs and members, though constantly warm, exhibit coldness, or in the case of cold limbs, an extreme cold resembling that of the *kumuda* and *utpala* lotuses; who suffers from excessive perspiration, excessive rigidity, or a sagging as if the flesh and blood had vanished;
and in whose body both the proper application (*yoga*) and the excessive application (*atiyoga*) of the great elements are simultaneously observed.
"All of them are ripened by time"— and regarding this,
there is a verse in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* (AS.Śā.9.11): "He upon whose forehead appear unprecedented lines resembling the crescent moon..."
If [the breath] moves on the forehead or at the top of the bladder for six months, that person does not live.
For that embodied being whose water [in the body] is like that on a lotus leaf, [he does not live].
The life of one who floats while floating lasts for six months. He whose veins have a greenish luster and whose hair follicles are closed [will live for six months].
That man who craves sour things meets his death through bile (pitta),
if there is a powder on his head or even in his mouth that resembles cow-dung dust.
If there is smoke on the head accompanied by moisture, his life lasts until the end of the month.
Or, new whorls and curls appear on the head or between the eyebrows.
Death occurs within six nights for one who is healthy, but within three nights for one who is ill. However,
for one who has bathed and been anointed, if the chest dries up excessively first, death is imminent.
If all his limbs are moist, he does not live for half a month. He whose heat is in the chest and whose abdomen is excessively cold [will likewise perish].
With excrement broken up and thirst, he is just like a hungry ghost (preta).
Urine, feces, spittle, and semen sink into the water.
If one's phlegm is expectorated in many colors, he perishes within a month; likewise,
if there is a weakening of the voice or a loss of strength and complexion.
Having observed the increase of disease through improper treatment, one should predict death; likewise,
one who speaks with a discordant voice has reached the point of his own death.
One should keep the listener of this sound far away;
[he who is] gasping for breath, whose vital heat has departed, and whose groin is afflicted by sharp pain.
A wise person should avoid one who finds no relief;
one who, having developed cold sores, or whose limbs are cold, suffers from a burning sensation.
Averse to heat and afflicted by cold, he wanders within the domain of the lord of the departed;
his shadow appears like a rope clinging to his neck.
The living being is inevitably dragged away before long by the servants of Yama.
Thus ends the tenth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the diagnosis of complications;
thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
Like space that has become solidified, yet like space it is not solid;
it is as if formless, yet it possesses form, and though possessing form, it remains as if formless.
Luminous and yet devoid of light, white and black, non-existent and existent;
free from eye disease, he beholds the moon marked with many forms and stains.
He who sees demons, gandharvas, vanas, pretas, or others of that kind while awake,
as well as their forms and their descriptions, perishes.
He who does not see Arundhatī situated near the Seven Sages,
nor Dhruva, nor the celestial Gaṅgā, does not see that year.
He hears the sounds of clouds, torrents of rain, thunder, lutes, small drums, and flutes,
as well as other sounds, whether they be non-existent or existent.
Just as one who, pressing his ears, does not hear the *dhukadhuka* sound,
so too is he who perceives odors, tastes, and tangibles erroneously.
Or, in every respect, he who does not smell the fragrance of the lamp; for whom flavors lead to disorder when consumed according to rule, but to health when consumed contrary to rule.
He whose body is covered as if with dust, or who feels no pain in his limbs—
without intense austerity or yoga performed according to the prescribed rules— [he does not attain the goal].
He who knows that which is beyond the senses may predict their death:
the tongue becomes dark, the mouth putrid, and the left eye sinks.
One should avoid that person whose [excrement] dissolves upon his own head; likewise,
one who creeps along with shoulders drooping, as if scraping the ground with his feet.
One who eats much wholesome food constantly declines in strength;
whereas one who eats little has abundant feces and urine, and one who eats much has scanty feces and urine.
Or one who eats little, being afflicted by phlegm, breathes deeply and struggles;
or one who, having exhaled long, inhales short and becomes faint.
He who breathes out a short breath and trembles violently,
tossing his head while raising his hands with great difficulty; AS.Śā.10.15.
He whose sweat flows from the forehead, whose joints and ligaments are loosened,
and who faints when being lifted up— whether he be strong or weak— is one who will die.
One who falls asleep while still standing, or who moves his feet [while sleeping],
or who desires to grasp that which does not exist, such as a bed, a seat, or a wall; AS.Śā.10.17.

One who laughs when there is no reason to laugh, who is excessively joyful, who licks his lips, who licks his upper lip, and who makes blowing sounds— these are signs of one who will die within six months.
If a shadow that is black, yellow, or reddish pursues him, or if he has hatred toward physicians, medicines, drinks, food, teachers, and friends; AS.Śā.10.19 [he is in danger].
All these who are subject [to death] should be known as equal in their fate.
He whose neck, forehead, and heart become cold and perspire—
Another region is hot, and the deities are his refuge—
he who possesses but a minute light, whose attention is divided, and who is always ill-favored and dejected.
He whose offerings the scavengers do not consume, and who,
without cause, possesses intelligence, splendor, growth, and glory—
Therefore, he incurs ruin, or he goes to the abode of Yama—
whosoever, whether healthy or diseased, possesses a mind consisting of virtues and faults.
If one's nature undergoes a change within six months, that person does not live.
Devotion, character, mindfulness, renunciation, intelligence, and strength become causeless.
These six signs cease for one who will die within six months.
One who dies within a month exhibits intoxication-like gait, trembling of speech, and delusion.
One who is unaware [of the practice] loses [the merit] after six days due to the pain of plucking out the hair; likewise,
one whose food does not pass the throat [loses it], except in the case of a disease of the throat.
Servants act with hostility, and a corpse-like appearance arises;
he for whom sleep is constant or who has no sleep at all does not live.
The mouth is filled with tears, the feet perspire profusely,
and the eyes become agitated for one who is about to go to the realm of King Yama.
The physician should not live with those dispositions by which he formerly found pleasure;
nor, even when asked, should he speak of death, which is painful to hear.
When one has passed away, one's kinsmen and friends do not wish to treat them,
for that person whose life-force has departed is attended by the Piśācas and others who are the messengers of Yama.

Because they destroy the potencies of medicinal herbs, one should therefore avoid them. There is no death for one who is free from fatal signs (ariṣṭa), and there is life for one in whom fatal signs are observed.
"In the case of one who is not destined to die, there is the perception of death; yet even in the case of one destined to die, it may not occur due to lack of skill.
This is the statement of Caraka, which is recited by Suśruta as well.
For death is certain when one is struck by misfortune; however, it is said that this is averted by stainless Brahmins who are devoted to elixirs, asceticism, and charity.

Kṛṣṇātreya states that fatal signs (riṣṭa) are of two kinds, distinguished by being either stable or unstable. Furthermore, due to the abundance of the [doshas], a mere semblance of a fatal sign may arise.

When those defects are pacified, one may indeed remain stable; however, [if they persist], one will surely go to death. The entire fruit of Ayurveda is established in one who knows life (the physician).
Therefore, a physician should always remain intent on the knowledge of fatal signs.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the knowledge of modified diseases;
thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
When a disease arises due to all the causes, premonitory signs, and manifest symptoms being excessive according to their respective natures;
or when, in a person afflicted by disease, moles, freckles, lines, birthmarks, or dark spots suddenly appear on the face.
One whose nails and teeth have fallen out, or who has flowers on the abdomen or veins of various colors;
one who is wasting away and suffers from eye-secretion, swelling of either the eyelids or the nose, or drooping of the eyelids;
or one who is emaciated and for whom hunger and thirst are not relieved even by many heart-pleasing foods and drinks.
He whose blood is discharged with froth, and who suffers from pain in the abdomen or the chest, [is in danger].

He whose phlegm is blue, yellow, or red, and who frequently has powerful pain in the neck, dryness of the tongue, inflammation of the throat, mouth, and anus, as well as cutting pain arising from the stomach,
excessive thirst, and diarrhea— [such a person perishes].
For one who has cutting pain arising from the colon, excessive thirst, and extreme constriction of the anus;
for whom the Vāyu, having taken refuge in either the stomach or the colon, destroys consciousness and produces a gurgling sound in the throat;
and for one who is emaciated, whose thirst increases and who suffers from pain in the heart.
For instance, when there is hiccough with bloody diarrhea, or abdominal distension with diarrhea, accompanied by intense thirst and the departure of the life-force (*parāsu*), it is said here:
"A powerful, deep-seated, and chronic fever destroys [the patient]. (AS.Śā.11.3)

Accompanied by delirious speech and labored breathing, with diminished strength, swollen limbs, and impaired digestive fire; with unemaciated body, obstructed speech, bloodshot eyes, and pain in the heart.
A dry cough that occurs either in the forenoon or in the afternoon,
accompanied by phlegm, in one who is deprived of strength and flesh; AS.Śā.11.5.
In *raktapitta*, blood is discharged profusely— black, with the luster of a rainbow, copper-colored,
turmeric-yellow, or green; such are the forms it displays.
Spreading from the pores of the skin and clinging to the throat, mouth, and heart,
it is like a foul-smelling dye on a cloth— forceful and exceedingly abundant.
One who is aged and suffering from jaundice, fever, vomiting, cough, edema, and diarrhea;
one suffering from cough, dyspnea, fever, vomiting, thirst, diarrhea, and edema.
Consumption (yakṣmā) is characterized by pain in the sides, loss of appetite, vomiting of blood, and a burning sensation.
Vomiting occurs with forceful urges, has the odor of urine and feces, and is accompanied by a shimmering appearance (candrikā).
It is accompanied by impurities, pus, coughing,
and labored breathing; it is consumed by other diseases such as thirst, with the tongue protruding and consciousness lost.
One suffering from alcoholism, one afflicted by extreme cold, one who is emaciated, and one whose face has the luster of oil;
one with hemorrhoids, and one with swelling of the hands, feet, navel, anus, scrotum, and mouth.
One afflicted by pain in the heart, sides, and limbs, by vomiting, anal burning, and fever;
diarrhea characterized by stools as dark as liver-paste or the washing of meat.
It is equal to oil, ghee, milk, curd, marrow, fat, and fermented liquor;
it is equal to brain matter, soot, pus, minced meat, water, and honey.
Excessively red, black, oily, putrid, clear, thick,
or painful; variegated, discharging minerals, or devoid of feces, or excessively fecal.
It is covered with threads, infested by flies, marked with streaks,
and filled with spots; its anal folds are decayed, its stalk is severed, and it is painful with its joint-bones.
One should have the patient, whose anus is prolapsed and whose strength is exhausted, consume food alone.
[This applies to those suffering from] thirst, cough, fever, vomiting, burning sensations, abdominal distension, and dysentery.
One suffering from urinary calculi (aśmarī) has swollen testicles, suppressed urination, and is afflicted by pain;
one suffering from urinary disorders (meha) suffers from thirst, burning sensations, pustules, sloughing of the flesh, and diarrhea.
Swelling on the vital points, the heart, the back, the breasts, the shoulders, the anus, or the head,
or on the joints of the feet and hands, indicates that the patient suffering from urinary disease will have little strength to survive.
And [the patient] suffers from all [these]: putrefaction of the flesh, burning sensations, thirst, intoxication, fever, erysipelas,
obstruction of the vital organs (marmans), hiccups, labored breathing, vertigo, and exhaustion.
Gulma is a thick, broad, and dense mass, elevated like the shell of a tortoise;
it is bound by veins and accompanied by fever, vomiting, hiccups, flatulence, and pain.
One suffering from cough, catarrh, nausea, dyspnea, diarrhea, and swelling;
one with retention of feces and urine, dyspnea, swelling, hiccups, fever, and vertigo.
Through fainting, vomiting, and diarrhea, it destroys the weak abdominal region;
[the patient] has swollen eyes, a distorted perineum, and thin, moist skin.
One who suffers from abdominal distension repeatedly brought on by purgation,
as well as jaundice accompanied by swelling and yellowing of the eyes, nails, and vision;
Accompanied by lassitude, burning sensations, loss of appetite, vomiting, fainting, flatulence, and diarrhea,
and beset by many complications, [the disease] spreads from the two feet to the man.
In a woman, swelling from the mouth kills; from both the abdomen and the private parts, it kills as well.
One marked with streaks, when discharging [fluid], kills one suffering from vomiting, fever, dyspnea, and diarrhea.
Fever and diarrhea [occur] at the end of swelling, or swelling [occurs] at the subsidence of those two.
Especially for one who is weak, these signs arise as the end for the embodied being:
swelling located in the feet and drooping of the calves.
The physician should avoid treating one whose thighs sink down,
and especially one whose face, hands, and feet are withering away.
Or he swells even without [visible] bodily [swelling], and after a month he reaches his end;
likewise, one who has abdominal dropsy or edema does not see his own penis.
Or for one whose lower garment does not remain in place due to the distension of the abdomen;
[or] one suffering from erysipelas accompanied by cough, discoloration, fever, fainting, and a breaking pain in the limbs.
One suffering from dizziness, facial swelling, nausea, physical exhaustion, and diarrhea; one with leprosy characterized by disintegrating limbs, red eyes, and a lost voice.
It destroys those with weak digestion, those afflicted by living organisms, and those suffering from thirst and diarrhea;
it also [destroys] one whose skin is numb, who is bent, and who is tormented by tremors, swelling, and pain.
It is accompanied by wind-blood disorders (vātāsra), delusion, fainting, intoxication, sleepiness, and fever;
it involves stiffness of the head, loss of appetite, dyspnea, contraction, eruptions, and suppuration.
Headaches, loss of appetite, dyspnea, delusion, diarrhea, thirst, and vertigo—
these afflict all diseases when the voice, the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), strength, and the digestive fire have been depleted.
One suffering from gout, epilepsy, leprosy, hemorrhagic disease, abdominal dropsy, consumption,
abdominal tumors, or urinary disorders— these, even if their ailments are slight, should be rejected if they are emaciated.
If a patient exhibits severe loss of strength and flesh, an increase in disease, and a loss of appetite,
he will not live beyond three fortnights.
When a severe *vātāṣṭhīlā* (wind-tumor) has greatly increased and remains in the heart,
it instantly robs life from one who is overwhelmed by thirst.
If the wind causes laxity in the calves and bends the nose, or if it stretches the temples of one who is emaciated,
it immediately robs him of his life.
Having gone between the navel and the anus, or taking hold of the groins,
or seizing the anus and the heart, the powerful [wind] acts upon one whose body is wasted.
The impurities, having obstructed the bladder, the head of the rectum, and the navel, produce pain,
causing colic in the groins, thirst, and diarrhea.
Or the wind, producing breath, having seized the anus and the groins, having stretched out the tips of the ribs and seized the chest, [causes pain].
The fever that suddenly seizes one who is motionless and has fixed eyes robs him of his life instantly. It is accompanied by thirst, fainting, and the loss of strength.
The joints of one who is about to die become loosened;
and at the time of sunrise, excessive perspiration breaks out from his mouth and other parts of his body.
For one afflicted by a "lepajvara" fever, life is difficult to maintain;
for one on whose body there appear eruptions resembling coral beads.
Arising quickly, they perish; he does not perish for long. They resemble split lentils and are like coral.
Blisters resembling calluses, appearing within the folds of the skin, destroy the body;
the eyes become yellowish-red, the face becomes swollen, and the flesh of the temples wastes away.
One should avoid that person who experiences terror and heat in the limbs (AS.Śā.11.47),
and who suddenly runs about with the skin of the body excessively rubbed or irritated (AS.Śā.11.48).
They have the scent of sandalwood, ushira-root, wine, corpses, and crows;
they possess the luster of moss, a cock’s crest, saffron, and lamp-soot.
Wounds that have internal burning and lack heat are destroyers of life. A wound born of wind (vāta) does not cause pain, nor does one born of bile (pitta) cause burning.
That which is not born of phlegm, nor does it turn into pus, nor causes pain even though it arises from a vital spot (marman);
that which is not powdery yet appears as if strewn with powder, and where it is seen to appear suddenly— [that is the sign of death].
One should avoid all those types of wounds that have the appearance of a spear, a banner, and so forth;
as well as fistula-in-ano (bhagandara), which discharges feces, urine, and wind, and is infested with worms.
Striking knee against knee, he raised his feet and brought them down.
He who, being afflicted, repeatedly opens his mouth, does not live;
he who bites his fingernails with his teeth, or tears his hair or grass with them, [does not live].
Scratching the ground with a piece of wood, striking a clod of earth with another clod,
one whose body hair stands on end, who has thick urine, dry cough, and fever— AS.Śā.11.55.
He who laughs repeatedly, sneezes repeatedly, and strikes his bed with his foot;
he who repeatedly probes for his own vulnerabilities—such a patient does not survive.
The wise physician should avoid one who has labored breathing, whose body heat has departed, whose groin is afflicted with piercing pain,
and who finds no relief.
For one whose secondary humors increase while the primary constitution declines,
death suddenly and repeatedly carries away his life.
If a physician, striving to prepare medicine for a specific patient,
is unable to do so, that patient's life is difficult to sustain.
Even if it is well-known, proven many times, and administered according to the rules,
a medicine does not succeed for one who lacks proper medical treatment.
If, while medicine or food is being prepared,
there occurs an unexpected reversal of its color, smell, and so forth, then even if he appears healthy, that person will not live.
In a windless place, the fire of one whose light is extinguished even with fuel present;
or in the house of a sick person, that in which [the lamps] break or fall.
The life of that man is difficult to preserve, who is excessively lacking in the means of sustenance; yet even more rare is the life of that weak man whom disease suddenly releases.
Ātreya considers his life to have reached a state of uncertainty;
thus ends the twelfth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the knowledge of messengers and other [omens].
The fatal signs (*riṣṭa*) have been described as pertaining to the patient.

Furthermore, the caste, dress, speech, gestures, place, and time of the messenger, as well as the physician’s intentions regarding the meeting with him, his departure, journey, and entry, the movement of the planets, the occurrence of unusual events, and the patient's dreams— all these indicate good or bad fortune.

In that regard, a messenger from a patient who is inauspicious is one who belongs to a higher caste than the patient, is of another stage of life (*āśrama*), is a heretic (*pāṣaṇḍa*), is a eunuch, is shaven-headed, wears matted hair, is a woman, is diseased, is many in number, is suffering from indigestion, is discolored, dirty, or wears a single garment that is torn, wet, or stained with mud or oil; who wears red garlands and ointments; whose limbs and appearance are deformed by artificial means; who rides on a donkey, camel, or buffalo; who is agitated, panting, weeping, or speaking harsh and inauspicious words; who calls out from a distance; or who carries grass, clods of earth, husks, charcoal, ashes, chaff, lead, bones, hair, or a skull, forehead, nose, mouth, teeth, tongue, neck, nails, fingers, breasts, belly, navel, back, hips, genitals, calves, a skull, raw meat, a stone, a pestle, a winnowing basket, sandals, a broom, a weapon, the hem or fringe of a garment, cotton, something broken or fallen, a sprig, a stick, a scale, a rope, a noose, leather, bamboo, an empty vessel, or an oil-container; who touches or scratches the ground with his feet; or who, having grasped a ripe fruit, a spreading branch, or something similar, approaches the physician at a place or time possessing qualities corresponding to those deformities.
For example: AS.Śā.12.3 AS.Śā.12.4 AS.Śā.12.4.

Even when standing upon a vessel containing liquids such as ghee or water, if one is extremely cold and stiff at dawn, it is inauspicious in cases of phlegmatic diseases but auspicious in cases of bilious diseases;
likewise, in the event of a breach of a dam, or during vomiting, urinary disorders, dysentery, and the like, it is inauspicious, whereas in the case of constructing a dam, it is auspicious.

Likewise, it is inauspicious [for a patient] to approach a physician at midday, during either of the two twilights, at midnight, or on the fourth, sixth, ninth, or festival days; or when there is an eclipse, a portentous event, or the appearance of a comet; or under the asterisms of Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Ārdrā, Āśleṣā, Maghā, Mūla, or the three Pūrvās; or when the physician is asleep, naked, lying on the ground, anointed with oil, with disheveled hair, facing south, distressed, cutting, piercing, intent on fire-rites or ancestral rites, or contemplating or speaking of something inauspicious;
or when [the patient] stands with hands joined in reverence toward the southern direction, standing on one uneven foot.

If a messenger reports something inauspicious regarding the patient’s condition, the physician should observe the signs of the senses or form a judgment; he should not then follow that [ominous path].
Instead, with a mind tender with compassion, full of goodwill, and like that of a mother or father, he should set out, aspiring for the ultimate recovery of the patient.

AS.Śā.12.5: At the moments of setting out, departing, or entering, [one should see or encounter] curds, honey, clarified butter, parched grain, flowers, unbroken rice, *udumbara*, *aśvattha* trees, pearls, gems, an umbrella, sprouts of *dūrvā* grass, a mirror, a maiden, a banner, a chariot, a chessboard, dice, a king, a tree of fortune, an auspicious throne, crops, fish, horses, a swan and a blue jay, a bull, a lion, a right-spiraling conch, a lotus, white mustard seeds, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), a *svastika*, a gateway arch, bamboo flutes, a bride and groom, an elephant with temples dripping with rut, a cloud pouring rain, a full water-jar, turmeric, the three-eyed Śiva, Viṣṇu, Skanda, Brahmā, the world-protectors, the gods, the sky, the directions, fire, lakes, rivers, oceans, sacrifices, the wind, the luminaries, the treatises on Dharma, sacred fords, poetry, the nectar of Dharma, wealth, and pleasure; the Vālakhilyas and others, Vedic utterances, a treasure, the Kaustubha gem, gold, Maṇibhadra, Mount Sumeru, *priyaṅgu* seeds, a lamp, *vacā* root, perfumed sweets, Aditi, Arundhatī, Ṛddhi, Sāvitrī, Umā, the celestial Gaṅgā, Śacī, Devasenā, Svadhā, Peace, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, offspring, forgiveness, the word "Svasti," the *vaṣaṭ* call, the syllable *Oṃ*, and meritorious rites—this is the one hundred and eight auspicious things. By seeing, touching, or praising these, one dispels inauspiciousness and bestows supreme success in one's aims.
Moreover,
birds with male names that fly to the left are auspicious.

The female jackal, the dark-colored female, the tawny female, the cuckoo, the *kokilāralā*, the muskrat, the sow, the house-lizard, the one-hoofed animal, and those with feminine names are auspicious when on the right; so too are the peacock, the chickpea, the hawk, the elephant, the goat, and the monkey.
Upon entering, however, these effects are reversed;
in all cases, it is auspicious for a dog and a jackal to move from right to left, while for a deer and a bird, the opposite is desired.
In every respect, the sight of the bharadvāja, the blue jay, the partridge, and the mongoose is auspicious;
however, the mention of the hare, the snake, the goat, the sheep, the iguana, the ram, and the pig is desired [for its specific effects].
AS.Śā.12.7 AS.Śā.12.7
There was no sight or cry of bears or monkeys that was contrary [to auspiciousness], nor even of snakes; however, there were undesirable sights and sounds of lizards, cocks, cats, and owls.

Likewise, the word "cutting" (cheda) is desired in cases such as knots and tumors; the word "piercing" (bheda) in cases such as abdominal lumps and dropsy; the word "obstructed" (ruddha) in cases such as dysentery and hemoptysis; and the word "flowing forth" (pravartana) in cases such as urinary stones and abdominal enlargements.
In this manner, other sounds should also be applied accordingly.

Furthermore, in all instances, words such as "firm," "stationary," "increasing," "protected," "immovable," "constant," "secure," and "auspicious," as well as the sounds of auspicious musical instruments, are excellent.
Sounds such as "wounded," "struck," "fallen," "cursed," "blows," "cutting," "tearing," "burning," "alas! alas!", and "forbid! indicate that medical treatment should not be undertaken.

Furthermore, if in a direction that is ablaze there are harsh cries of birds and beasts, or if on a tree that is withered, dry, and covered in creepers and thorns [such sounds occur], [medical treatment is forbidden].

Or, in such a place, there is the sight of grass, straw, wood-carriers, potsherds, clods of earth, and so forth; as well as thorns, elevated footprints, broken utensils for walking or sitting, empty jars, liquor, fat, oil, sesame seeds, pregnant women, outcasts, those addicted to vice, and the dead.
Upon entering from the house of a person of the four classes, there is the previously mentioned emergence of auspicious signs;
however, for the physician who has entered, there is no hospitable reception, nor are gains, satisfaction, or praise— these being inauspicious.
If the planets are situated in censurable positions and act as crooked followers of the sick man's speech;

or if there is an eclipse of the birth star by Ketu, Śani, or Rāhu; or if inauspicious marks appear on his house, wife, bed, seat, vehicle, jewels, or utensils—these indicate a prohibition against medical treatment.
A dream, whether seen by oneself or by another, is the cause of good or evil; it is observed to be of seven kinds: seen, heard, experienced, desired, imagined, real, and born of a defect.
Among these, the first five kinds are fruitless.
Likewise, according to its own nature, when it is forgotten, it is very short by day, very long [at night], and not clearly seen when one is deeply asleep;
in the first part of the night, it produces fruit either little or after a long time.
At the release of cattle, at great festivals, and furthermore,
being unassailed by sleep, or by opposing words, or by acts of giving, restraint,
and observance— therein, he who drinks liquor together with the departed spirits is dragged away by dogs.

He who sees a garment with the hue of lac-dyed red, or he who is carried away laughing by noble women while his body, garlands, and clothes are red, is struck by fever; he is afflicted by *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic fever).
He who [dreams] of the southern direction with a donkey, camel, buffalo, or boar will suffer from consumption;
he in whose heart a thorny creeper, bamboo, or palm tree grows will suffer from a chronic enlargement of the spleen (gulma);
and he on whose head [these grow] will suffer from a disease of the head or from decapitation.
He who, naked and sprinkled with clarified butter, offers oblations into the blazing fire until lotuses grow upon his chest, is afflicted by leprosy;
he who drinks oil in the company of Caṇḍālas is afflicted by urinary disorder; and he who is intoxicated is afflicted by epilepsy.
He who beholds an eclipse of the moon or the sun will develop an eye disease;
he who sees their fall will suffer the destruction of his eyesight.

AS.Śā.12.15 One who, having consumed fried cakes or sweetmeats, vomits upon waking; one on whose head creepers and the like grow, or into whom birds settle; one who becomes dull-witted; one who is surrounded by vultures, owls, crows, and the like, or by hungry ghosts (*preta*), *piśācas*, *rākṣasas*, Dravidians, Andhras, women, *caṇḍālas*, and so forth; one who is dragged while dancing toward the south by a woman; one who goes naked toward the outcastes, or goes naked himself; one who enters a deserted forest, or is embraced by monkeys, chariots, hungry ghosts, or renunciants; one who, naked, wears a red garland, is smeared with mud, laughs, or dances; one who becomes entangled or falls into thickets of cane, bamboo, thorns, or grass; one who falls upon the ground covered with dust or onto anthills, ash, cremation grounds, pits, or dwellings; one who sinks into mud, wells, or turbid water, or is carried away by a current; one who enters a land of red flowers, a cave filled with darkness, the abode of evil deeds, a narrow pass, or his mother; or one who is swallowed by a fish—[such a person sees these omens].
AS.Śā.12.15: [The section on] the nature of the aggregates.

Furthermore, those who undergo shaving, experience the growth of body hair, or undergo marriage; who fall from or climb up the peak of a mountain or a palace; who [climb] *śālmalī*, *kovidāra*, *kiṃśuka*, or *pāribhadraka* trees adorned with sacrificial posts and flowers; or who are defeated, bound, vomit, purge, experience horripilation, or receive gold, iron, salt, oil, oil-cakes, or cotton; who eat cooked food, drink liquor or fats, or are anointed with them; who are reviled by angry ancestors (*pitṛs*); or who see the moon, sun, stars, lamps, or deities falling or perishing; or who see their own face, arm, or limb being split apart; or who see men who are naked, dressed in saffron robes, ungentle, holding staffs and nooses, black with red eyes; or who see a woman who appears black and white, with long hair and breasts, resembling the Night of Doom (*kālarātri*)—these diseased persons meet their death, while those who are healthy face a threat to their lives.
And there are verses on this point:
"Due to the channels carrying the mind being filled with powerful impurities...
Terrible dreams are seen by those whose lives are facing destruction.
Furthermore, even after seeing an inauspicious dream, he who [sees it] right there again... AS.Śā.12.17 AS.Śā.12.17
If he should see something gentle and auspicious, its fruit shall indeed be auspicious for him.
[He should see] gods, twice-born brahmins, bulls, living beings, friends, and kings.
He sees virtuous people, those of renown, fires well-kindled, clear reservoirs of water,
maidens, young boys, fair-complexioned men, those dressed in white garments, and those of great splendor.
Whoever should see a man-eater with a blazing body drenched all over with blood, or whoever should obtain an umbrella, a mirror, poison, or meat—
White flowers, garments, impure ointments, and fruit;
mountains, palaces, fruitful trees, lions, men, and elephants.

One may mount a vehicle drawn by oxen or horses, and cross over rivers, lakes, and oceans. Traveling toward the northeast portends death; likewise, approaching those who should not be approached leads to death.
Escape from confinement, the touch of the stars, mountains, and the sun; weeping, rising from a fall, and the crushing of enemies.
He who possesses long life, health, and wealth enjoys these manifoldly.
[One should give] to ancestors, gods, and the twice-born, and to those who are angry, terrified, or emaciated in spirit.
The sight of those with soiled garments and flowers is not praised; however,
it is [praised] when they themselves are content, possessing pure flowers and garments as their very nature.
Seeing [them] in a dream is praised, as is conversing with them;
having seen dreams, whether terrible or auspicious. (AS.Śā.12.26)
Having bathed in the morning and offered mustard seeds the color of fire, or sesame seeds smeared with ghee, while reciting the Sāvitrī mantra,
one who is purified is released from sins and diseases.
The patient, accompanied by a retinue endowed with auspicious conduct,
being faithful, compliant, and having gathered abundant materials; AS.Śā.12.27 AS.Śā.12.27.
Association with virtuous characteristics, devotion toward physicians and the twice-born,
and lack of despondency regarding medical treatment— these are the signs of recovery from illness.
Since birth and death are correctly explained here [in this section],
this section is therefore called the "Body" (śārīra) because it concerns the body.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter of the Section on Diagnosis (Nidānasthāna).
Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnosis of all diseases (Sarvaroganidāna).
"Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:

'In this Kṛta Yuga, there were men who were free from the dualities such as passion and aversion; they had conquered greed, anger, fatigue, exhaustion, indolence, and fear, and they were without possessions.'"
By the power of their merit, from the collection of all qualities in the earth and other elements, there arose crops and medicinal herbs endowed with inconceivable taste, potency, and so forth.

Consuming these at the proper time and in moderation, and due to their possession of virtues such as truthfulness, straightforwardness, and compassion, they became like gods in splendor, endowed with excellence of form, appearance, proportion, clarity, growth, firmness, courage, and vitality; they were long-lived and free from disease.

In the Kṛta Yuga, however, due to the inherent nature of the age, as the earth and other elements gradually lose all their qualities and as bodies likewise decline, diseases such as fevers—inevitable for men because of their transgression of dharma, characterized by indifference and harshness, and neglected by the gods—manifested themselves; such is the general origin of all diseases (AS.ni.1.3).

Now, as for the fever: during a sacrifice of Prajāpati—who had attained the state of Pracetas due to the curse of Sthāṇu—Paśupati, being incited by Rudrāṇī because she had been insulted in a previous birth, protected [the sacrifice] for a thousand divine years so that it would not be destroyed. At the conclusion of his vow, the fire of his wrath, accumulated over a very long time, emerged from his head in the form of a servant named Vīrabhadra; he was a massified embodiment of anger, with ashes as his weapon, possessing three heads, eyes, arms, and feet, tawny eyes, fangs, spike-like ears, and a dark body.

Surrounded by Bhadrakālī, who was manifested by the Goddess, and by infinite attendants emerging from every pore of his body—possessing various deformed shapes and terrifying speech, actions, and forms—he roared like a thousand clouds at the end of the four ages, making heaven and earth resound. Enveloped in a mass of flames and amidst a tumultuous clamor that causes the dissolution of the great elements, he performed the slaughter of the Dānavas and the destruction of the horse-sacrifice ritual; then, with palms joined in reverence, he addressed Śiva:
"O God of gods, you have become auspicious."
Being praised by the gods, beginning with the Grandfather (Brahmā), as well as by the Father of the World and the Creator (Dhātṛ),
the wielder of the trident commanded him, saying, "What shall I do now? and [thus] directed his wrath toward him.

"Since even the gods could not conquer my wrath when Dakṣa sought to obstruct my vow and consumed the sacrificial offering of Dakṣa, therefore, O Daitya, you shall become Jvara, the feverer of this world with its mobile and immobile beings.

For you are the first and foremost among the diseases of creation; through your nature of darkness, you are the Great Delusion (*mahāmoha*) amidst births and deaths; because you cause a burning heat during other transgressions, you are of the nature of torment (*santāpa*); thus, you shall certainly be Jvara in both states."
Thus favored by Umāpati, he wanders everywhere throughout the world under various names,

as follows: among elephants he is Pākala, among horses Abhitāpa, among dogs Alarka, among lotuses Indramada, among luminous plants Jyotis, among grains Cūrṇaka, in water Nīlikā, on the earth Ūṣara, and among men Jvara.
Simultaneous with that [fever] are anorexia, aching of the limbs, headache, vertigo, exhaustion, debility, thirst, burning sensations, and so forth;
and from that burning sensation arises *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic fever).

And at that very sacrifice, among those overcome by anger and fear who were fleeing in all directions, there arose abdominal tumors, abscesses, hernias, and enlargement of the belly through physical agitation such as leaping and jumping; urinary disorders, leprosy, hemorrhoids, swellings, and diarrhea from consuming the sacrificial oblation (havis);
