and insanity, epilepsy, and possession by spirits through fear, terror, grief, and contact with impurities.

Due to his excessive passion for Rohiṇī and his enjoyment of the remaining daughters, Prajāpati was struck by anger; consequently, the Moon, the King of the Constellations, was afflicted with consumption (rājayakṣmā), along with cough, dyspnea, and other ailments that arise simultaneously with it.
For he too does not manifest without fever; thus, the entire collection of diseases is preceded by fever, or is denoted by the word "fever.
Fever is darkness, a morbid transformation, affliction, evil, disease, illness, suffering, malady, consumption, and sickness—these are synonymous terms.

In this context, that which causes pain is *roga* (disease); its perception [is achieved] through its etiology (*nidāna*), premonitory symptoms (*pūrvarūpa*), manifest signs (*rūpa*), therapeutic suitability (*upaśaya*), and pathogenesis (*samprāpti*).
In that context, the primary cause (nidāna) is the provocation of the bodily humors such as wind (vāyu) and so forth;
furthermore, its [cause] is the indulgence in unwholesome diet and lifestyle (ahitāhāra-vihāra).

The synonyms for *nidāna* (etiology) are: cause (*hetu*), sign (*nimitta*), basis (*āyatana*), agent (*kāraka*), doer (*kartṛ*), instrument (*kāraṇa*), condition (*pratyaya*), origin (*samutthāna*), root (*mūla*), and source (*yoni*).
The so-called "premonitory symptom" (*pūrvarūpa*) is that by which a specific future disease is recognized, but not a specific [imbalance of the] *doṣas*.
For that [disease] which is about to arise has an unmanifest form due to its smallness,
whereas its form is manifest [once it has arisen].
Its synonyms are *liṅga*, *ākṛti*, *lakṣaṇa*, *cihna*, *saṃsthāna*, and *vyañjana* (AS.ni.1.10).
*Upaśaya* is the continuous experience of comfort through medicines, diet, and lifestyle that are contrary to the causes and the disease, and which produce contrary effects (AS.ni.1.10).
For that which is known as homologous (sātmya) to the disease is [the upaśaya],
while its opposite is non-homologous (anupaśaya);
by this, location (deśa) and time (kāla) are also explained.

AS.ni.1.11 Furthermore, *samprāpti* (manifestation) is as follows: the morbid humor (*doṣa*) is thus corrupted, and by that [corruption], the disease (*vyādhi*) is thus initiated; its synonyms are birth (*jāti*), arrival (*āgati*), completion (*nirvṛtti*), and accomplishment (*niṣpatti*).
AS.ni.1.12 It is differentiated by distinctions of number, classification, predominance, strength, and time.

In that regard, "number" refers, for instance, to the classification of eight types of fever, three types of internal hemorrhage (raktapitta), and five types of cough; this is the conceptualization of the respective portions of the combined humors (doṣas).
The predominance [of diseases] arises from the distinction between primary and secondary conditions or from the relative degrees of intensity among the *doṣas*;

the specific strength or weakness of the *doṣas* results from the discernment of whether the causes and other factors are complete or partial; furthermore, the specific timing of the provocation of the *doṣas* is determined by the seasons, day and night, and the time of eating.
By this much alone, the meaning of the nidāna has been briefly stated;
however, it will be taught in detail according to each respective disease.

Now, Vāyu becomes provoked by the excessive consumption of bitter, pungent, astringent, dry, light, and cold substances; by indigestible foods, sprouted grains, grasses, pulses, chickpeas, *karīra*, *tumbaka*, *kāliṅga*, *cirbhiṭa*, lotus stalks (*visa*), lotus roots (*śālūka*), *jāmbava*, *tinduka*; by eating when one is emaciated, dehydrated, overfed, thirsty, or hungry; by drinking water while hungry; by blood loss, purgation, and other such procedures performed in excess; by the suppression or premature arousal of natural urges; by staying awake at night, exposure to strong winds, physical exercise, wrestling, fighting with the strong, suppression [of urges], drawing a stiff bow too far, jumping from great heights onto uneven ground, traveling on foot, studying, running, crossing water, trauma, taming bulls, horses, or elephants, lifting or throwing stones, slabs, iron, or wood, whirling, shaking, tight bandaging, striking others, and other such rash acts; and by fear, grief, longing, and the like; as well as during the summer and rainy seasons, in the afternoon, during the latter part of the night, and at the end of the digestion of food.

Pitta is provoked by pungent, sour, salty, alkaline, hot, sharp, burning, fermented, *śāṇḍākī*, wine, urine, whey, curd, fermented grain-gruel, oil, horse-gram, black gram, flat beans, sesame, cooked rice, *kaṭvara*, *kuṭheraka* and similar groups of plants; by *āmrātaka*, *amlīkā*, *pīlu*, *bhallātaka*, the fruit-stone of *lāṅgalikā*, black pepper; and by exposure to sun, fire, dust, smoke, anger, envy, indigestion, sexual intercourse, and so forth; as well as during the rainy season, autumn, midday, midnight, and at times when food causes a burning sensation.

Kapha [is increased] by sweet, sour, salty, unctuous, heavy, cold, slimy, and obstructive substances; by fresh grain, flour-based foods, *pṛthuka*, thick edibles, *śaṣkulī* cakes, raw meat, milk, *kīlāṭa*, *morata*, *kūcīkā*, buttermilk, *piṇḍaka*, *pīyuṣa*, sugarcane juice, molasses, jaggery, meat from marshy regions, *moca*, dates, *bhavya*, coconut, drinking water at night, excessive drinking of water, over-nutrition, sleeping immediately after eating, sleeping during the day, sleeping for too long, lack of physical, vocal, or mental exertion, sleeping on a pillow, exposure to frost, joy, suppression of tears, and improper administration of purgatives and other therapies; and also during the winter and spring seasons, the forenoon, the evening, and immediately after eating.
Contact arises from the conjunction of two things. AS.ni.1.15–AS.ni.1.16. Contact arises from the conjunction of two things.

Sannipāta arises from the combination of all these factors: eating too much (adhyashana), eating in equal measure (samashana), eating irregularly (vishamashana), eating incompatible foods (viruddhashana), eating mixed foods (sankirna-shana), consuming spoiled water, wine, curd that has turned sour, barley-meal, fodder, *surā* liquor, oil-cakes, raw radish, mustard, dried vegetables, parched grain, lean meat, *lakucha* fruit, unripe fruit, or clay; from the rotation of food types, seasonal disturbances, smelling unwholesome medicinal odors, ingesting poisons, vatsanābha, or artificial poisons (*gāra*); from untimely bad weather, affliction by malevolent spirits (*graha*), possession by spirits, exposure to easterly winds or mountain slopes, and the improper application of rejuvenation therapies (*rasāyana*), oleation, sudation, purgation, and so forth; from the habitual performance of sinful deeds; from the ripening of past actions (*karma*); from difficult childbirth in women; and from the improper postnatal care of those who have given birth.

Thus, in the *Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha*, *Nidānasthāna* 1.17, the cause for the provocation of the *doṣas* in all diseases has been stated in general; and regarding this, there are [the following verses]: *Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha*, *Nidānasthāna* 1.17.
In each respective disease,
the humors (doṣas), having become aggravated, quickly enter the rejuvenating channels (rasāyanīs) located at the sites of the diseases and undergo transformation within the body.
If a disease arises under a lunar mansion (nakṣatra) that causes misfortune through conception, birth, death, or opposition, it leads to suffering or death.
Fever that has arisen ceases within six nights if it occurs under the Aśvinī constellation; however,
it ceases in five days under Bharaṇī, and in seven days under Kṛttikā.
After twenty-one nights, or after eight nights under the asterism Rohiṇī,
or after eleven days under Mṛgaśiras, or after six or nine nights.
If a fever begins under Ārdrā, death occurs after five days; under Punarvasu, there is doubt [of survival] after three fortnights, or the fever subsides after thirteen days.
Death occurs after twenty-seven days, or after two days, or after seven days; furthermore, death may occur even after a long time under the asterisms Puṣya or Śleṣā, but under Maghā it is certain.
One necessarily attains well-being within twelve days, provided one has not died; however,
death occurs on the eighth day during the first two Phālguna months, or otherwise at other times.
On the ninth, or on the twenty-first day from the fire-offering, the fever attains a state of calm;
or there is peace on the seventh day from the hand-constellation (hasta), or on the eighth from the citrā constellation.
Furthermore, if Citrā arises, one should predict death after ten days; if Svātī, after three fortnights;
and if Viśākhā, on the twenty-second day.
If there is no peace on the ninth day for one under Maitra, death follows thereafter;
if it is Jyeṣṭhā, death occurs on the fifth day, or after that, there is happiness until the twelfth.
Recovery occurs ten days after the onset if it falls under the root-nakṣatra (Mūla), or after three weeks; however,
if it occurs under Pūrvāṣāḍhā, recovery is in nine days, and under other nakṣatras, it takes one month.
Or else, within eight or nine months, there will be auspiciousness;
[this applies] from Āśleṣā through Dhaniṣṭhā, but in the case of the waters (Śatabhiṣaj), it takes twelve [months].
Death occurs within six or twelve days under the Bhādrapadās; however,
there is relief after three weeks under the Uttarās and also under the Revatīs.
"In four nights or eight nights [the sacrifice is] secure," so says Gautama.
Thus ends the first chapter.
Now begins the second chapter. Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnosis of fever.
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and others:
fever arises in human beings from eight causes— from the individual doṣas, from their combinations, from their simultaneous aggravation, and from exogenous factors.

AS.ni.2.3: Therein, the *doṣas*, provoked by the aforementioned specific aggravating factors, enter the stomach (*āmāśaya*), mingle with the heat (*ūṣman*), follow the course of the *āma*, and block the channels that carry rasa and sweat. Pitta, however, because of its liquidity, like heated water, overcomes the fire; and all the *doṣas*, having expelled the digestive fire (*paktṛ*) from its own seat, spread throughout the entire body along with it. Through contact with that [fire], they gain strength and, by their own heat, greatly increase the bodily heat. By blocking the openings of the internal channels, they produce stiffness; by removing sweat even from the exterior, and by afflicting all the sense organs, they bring about fever.

The following are its premonitory symptoms: a bad taste in the mouth, lack of desire for food, heaviness of the body, lassitude, diminished vitality, stumbling in gait, excessive sleep, restlessness, envy, aversion toward wholesome instructions, a fondness for children and sweet foods, a craving for sour, salty, and pungent tastes, body ache during indigestion, turbidity of the eyes, tearing, yawning, bending of the body, fatigue, horripilation, and sudden likes or dislikes for sound, fire, water, cold wind, shade, and sunlight. (AS.ni.2.4)
Immediately after that, the manifestation of the fever occurs; as it is said here (AS.ni.2.5):
"The arrival and departure, the agitation, and the mildness of the pain and the heat [are its signs]."
AS.ni.2.5 There, in various parts of the body, various shifting pains occur.
AS.ni.2.6 Numbness, stiffness, cramps in the calves, and exhaustion [occur] in the feet.
AS.ni.2.6 There is a sensation as if the joints are being dislocated, a sinking feeling in the thighs, and stiffness in the waist.
AS.ni.2.7 The back feels as if it is being crushed to powder, and the abdomen feels as if it is being squeezed.
The ribs, especially those on the sides, seem as if they are breaking;
there is a seizing and piercing pain in the heart, as if the chest were being prodded with a goad.
There is churning of the shoulders, separation and pressure of the arms, and the shoulders;
there is incapacity in the jaws for chewing, yawning, and a ringing sound in the ears.
Piercing pain in the temples and at the head, a sensation of distress in the mouth,
a bitter taste in the mouth, or the non-excretion of impurities.

AS.ni.2.10 Dryness, reddish discoloration of the skin, mouth, eyes, nails, urine, and feces; AS.ni.2.11 Excessive salivation, anorexia, lack of appetite, indigestion, absence of perspiration, and insomnia.
Drying of the throat and lips, thirst, parchedness, vomiting, coughing, despondency,
horripilation on the body and teeth, trembling, and suppression of sneezing.
In fever caused by Vāta, there is dizziness, delirium, a desire for warmth, and bending of the body (AS.ni.2.12).
There is simultaneous pervasion of the limbs, delirium, and a bitter taste in the mouth (AS.ni.2.13).
AS.ni.2.13 There is no ripening of food in the mouth, a desire for cold things, vertigo, fainting, intoxication, and restlessness.
AS.ni.2.14 There is discharge of feces, vomiting of bile, spitting of blood, and acid eructations.
In the Pittaja type, there is the eruption of red boils, a yellowish or greenish discoloration of the skin and other parts,
perspiration, foulness of breath, and excessive thirst. (AS.ni.2.14–15)
Aversion to specific objects, dullness, obstruction of the channels, and sluggishness of the flow [of the breath]. AS.ni.2.15–16.
Excessive salivation, sweetness in the mouth, nausea, dyspnea, and rhinitis;
nausea, vomiting, cough, stiffness, and whiteness of the skin and other parts [are the symptoms].

In cases arising from *kapha*, there are cold eruptions (*piṭaka*) on the limbs, itching, and urticaria (*udarda*). At the appropriate time, all [the symptoms] manifest according to their respective natures, or they simply increase.

AS.ni.2.19 Non-relief [of symptoms] by the factors mentioned as causes is the sign of non-beneficiality. AS.ni.2.20 When there is a combination of symptoms according to their respective [causes], that fever is also known as "combination-born" (saṃsargaja).
Headache, fainting, vomiting, burning sensation, delusion, dryness of the throat and mouth, restlessness, and pain in the joints. (AS.ni.2.20–21)
From Pitta associated with Vata, there arise sleeplessness, thirst, vertigo, horripilation, yawning, excessive speech, and restlessness;
from Pitta associated with Kapha, there arise burning sensations, loss of appetite, pain in the joints and head, catarrh, dyspnea, cough, and constipation.
Coldness, numbness, darkness of vision, giddiness, and drowsiness are the symptoms of fever produced by *kapha* and *vāta*.
Coldness, rigidity, perspiration, burning sensations, instability, thirst, cough, and the discharge of *kapha* and *pitta* [are the symptoms of mixed fever].

Delusion, drowsiness, and a coating of bitterness in the mouth are to be known as the symptoms of fever arising from phlegm and bile (śleṣmapittaja). The fever arising from all three doshas (sānnipātika) possesses all the symptoms, and in this case, there is frequent shivering.
Likewise, there is excessive cold or great sleep, or waking by day and sleeping at night;
or there is constant sleep or no sleep at all, and excessive perspiration or none at all.
The non-engagement in distorted behaviors such as singing, dancing, and laughing;
[the eyes] are tearful, turbid, reddened, squinted, and have disheveled eyelashes.
There is pain in the eyes, the calves, the sides, the head, the joints, and the bones, along with vertigo;
both ears feel as if they are being carried away by a living creature, and the throat feels as if it were covered with bristles.
The tongue is parched and rough; the joints of the limbs are heavy and lax;
there is spitting of blood, bile, and phlegm; excessive salivation, and great thirst in the head.
The appearance of dark-red pustules and circular patches (maṇḍala),
pain in the heart, and the retention or excessive discharge of impurities (AS.ni.2.29).
Glossiness of the mouth, loss of strength, weakness of voice, and delirious speech; delayed digestion of the humors (doṣas), drowsiness, and constant gurgling in the throat.
One should call that condition *sannipāta-abhinyāsa*, characterized by the loss of vital energy (*hṛtaujas*);
it occurs when pitta is intensely compressed within by vāyu obstructed by kapha.
And because of its penetrating nature and subtlety, it moves along the external pathways; by that,
there is yellowness of the eyes in a fever arising from the derangement of all three humors (sannipāta).
When the doshas are obstructed and the digestive fire is destroyed, it possesses all the symptoms [of death] and is incurable;
otherwise, it may be difficult to treat or result in disability.
Furthermore, in a fever arising from the combination of all three humors (*sannipāta*), where the *pitta* is situated separately,
it produces a burning sensation either on the skin or within the digestive tract (*koṣṭha*), whether preceding or following [the onset of the fever].
In the same way, wind (vāta) and phlegm (kapha) [cause] coldness; when these two [are provoked], burning sensations and other symptoms become difficult to overcome.
In that condition, when there is coldness and so forth, the phlegm is liquefied and dried up by the pitta.

When the cold has subsided, acidity, fainting, intoxication, and thirst arise. Furthermore, at the end of the burning sensation and other symptoms, drowsiness, spitting, vomiting, and exhaustion occur.
An external [fever] arises from injury, possession by spirits, a curse, or malevolent magic. (AS.ni.2.37–38)
In this case, [the disease] is of four types, arising from injury such as cuts, incisions, or burns;
and due to physical exertion, the wind (vāyu) therein generally vitiates the blood.
Accompanied by pain, swelling, and discoloration, it produces a fever that is attended by distress;
[this fever] arises from possession by spirits, medicinal drugs, poison, anger, fear, grief, or desire.
From possession by a spirit, there is sudden laughing and weeping;
from the smell of medicinal herbs, there is fainting, headache, swelling, and sneezing.
From poison arise fainting, diarrhea, a dark discoloration of the face, burning sensations, and heart disease;
from anger, trembling and headache; and from fear or grief, delirium.

From desire arise delusion, lack of relish, burning, yawning, sleep, and the loss of strength and fortitude (AS.Ni.2.43). In the [disorders] beginning with seizure, there is derangement of the three humors; in those beginning with fear, it is wind (marut) that is predominant (AS.Ni.2.43).

Anger is indeed the [cause] of bile (pitta) in cases of wrath; however, those two terrible fevers arising from curses and malevolent spells (abhicāra)—fevers born of the derangement of all three humors (sannipāta)—are considered most unbearable.
In that regard, one who is being offered into the fire with malevolent mantras suffers intensely.
First the mind [is affected], then the body; thereafter, for one seized by eruptions, thirst, vertigo, burning sensation, and fainting, the fever increases day by day. (AS.ni.2.44–45)
Thus, fever is seen to be of eight types; however, in brief, it is of two kinds:
bodily and mental. It is also classified as mild or sharp, and as having its seat internally or externally. (AS.Ni.2.45–46)

[Fever] is natural (*prākṛta*), modified (*vaikṛta*), curable (*sādhya*), incurable (*asādhya*), with undigested toxins (*sāma*), or without toxins (*nirāmaka*). AS.Ni.2.47: First, in the case of bodily fever (*śārīra*), there is heat in the body; in the case of mental fever (*mānasa*), there is heat in the mind.
In the case of vāyu, due to its quality of being easily directed by yoga, there is coldness; when combined with kapha, it becomes cold;
when combined with pitta, there is burning; when combined with both, it is mixed; and furthermore, when it resides internally, it is likewise.
AS.ni.2.48 When the downward movement is excessive, there may be disorders, internal agitation, and the retention of waste products.
AS.ni.2.49 When the upward movement is excessive, there is heat only externally, and it is easily curable.
In the rainy season, autumn, and spring, the natural [diseases] arise from wind and the other [humors] in their respective order.
The other type is *vaikṛta* (derivative), which is accompanied by both pleasure and pain and is generally curable; whereas the *prākṛta* (natural) type arises from *vāyu* (wind).
This is because there is a great danger resulting from the confusion of initiating treatment intended for one path [of dosha] in another.
In the rainy season, the vitiated wind (vāta), combined with bile (pitta) and phlegm (kapha),
produces fever; and in autumn, it is the bile that causes fever, with phlegm acting as its secondary force.
Due to that [seasonal] nature and because of the discharge [of humors], there is no danger from fasting therein;
in spring, phlegm increases, and subsequently wind and bile do so as well.
Fever caused by strong [doshas] with very slight [vitiation of] the tissues and without complications is curable; however,
when there is complete knowledge of the morbid transformation (vikṛti), it is declared incurable from the outset.
AS.ni.2.55: Intensity of the complications of fever, lack of exhaustion, frequent urination,
absence of bowel movement, undigested feces, and lack of hunger are the characteristics of *sāma-jvara* (fever with undigested toxins).
In fever, excessive thirst, delirium, labored breathing, and dizziness occur;
the discharge of impurities and nausea are the signs of the fever being in the process of maturation (pacyamāna).
Due to the absence of complications and because of fasting for seven nights, the fever becomes digested.
Fever is said to be of five types, according to the strength or weakness of the morbid humors (mala) and time (kāla).
For the most part, it is designated as arising from the combination [of all three humors] (sannipāta).
It is classified as continuous (santata), daily (satata), quotidian (anyedyuṣka), tertian (tṛtīyaka), and quartan (caturthaka).
The pervasive impurities of the channels that carry the bodily constituents, urine, and feces. (AS.ni.2.59–60)
Scorching the entire body, increased by similar [aggravating factors] such as unwholesome food and the like,
they are powerful, heavy, and rigid, especially when localized in the rasa-dhatu.
Constant and unopposed, they produce a most unbearable fever;
then, that heat of the fever quickly consumes the impurities or the bodily tissues (dhātus). (AS.Ni.2.62)
In every way, through the purification or impurity of the tastes and so forth,
[the doshas] of vāta, pitta, and kapha [manifest] for seven, ten, or twelve days respectively. (AS.Ni.2.63)
"Generally, one follows the boundary for both liberation and destruction"—
this is the opinion of Agniveśa; however, the traditional teaching of Hārīta is as follows.
The seventh stage is doubled, as are the ninth and the eleventh;
this is the limit of the three *doṣas* for both liberation and destruction.
Fever resulting from purity or impurity persists for a long time;
[it occurs] in those who are emaciated, those who have recently recovered from illness, and those who indulge in improper diet and other such habits.
Even a slight disorder, having gained strength from any one of the corrupted elements (dūṣya) and so forth,
becomes accompanied by its opposite and, characterized by increase and decrease, produces an imbalance.
In those that are extremely subtle and even more subtle, and in those that are extremely distant and even more distant.
Because the dosha moves slowly and in small quantities through the channels of blood and so forth over a long period,
it does not completely destroy the body even when there is an abundance of medicine.
Therefore, this fever is characterized by an interrupted course and a remission of the heat;
it is irregular, with an irregular onset, action, and timing, and it is persistent.
Just as the movement becomes slower and the power weaker in successive stages, so too,
over time, it attains qualities similar to those of the *rasa* and the other elements.
The provoked humor (doṣa) causes fever, sometimes after a long time and even after a much longer period;
it is like water sprinkled upon the ground, which awaits its own time [to evaporate].
Just as a seed is for a sprout, so is the seed of the *doṣas* for disease;
just as poison, having produced its impulse, becomes weak and settles in the internal receptacle (*āśaya*).
Just as the poison of a venomous creature becomes more active when provoked by the strength of its prey at the proper time,
so too do irregular fevers such as the *santata* (continuous) and others manifest.
The powerful dosha manifests in them at its own time, causing fever.
Furthermore, this fever, which fluctuates according to the relative strength of the opposing forces,
subsides; once the doshas have been diminished, the subtle fever dissolves into the rasa and other tissues.

Because it is excessively suppressed, it produces emaciation, discoloration, dullness, and other such symptoms; being overly suppressed, due to extreme weakness, it does not manifest on the fifth day.
The dosha residing primarily in the blood generally causes constant fever; when it has taken refuge in the tissues,
it occurs twice a day, and when it has taken refuge in the flesh, it occurs once every other day.
In that [third stage], the channels carrying flesh and the channels of fat [are affected] in the tertian [fever].
Grāhī arises from pitta and vāta in the head, and from kapha and pitta in the trika;
it occurs in the back due to vāta and kapha, and is known to recur with an interval of one day.
AS.ni.2.84: When the fourth [day] fever is located in the fat, marrow, or bone—
some say it is specifically located in the marrow— it manifests its characteristic power.
It is of two kinds: first from phlegm in the calves, and from wind in the head;
because it courses through the deep tissues and because it arises from the combination of all three humors (sannipāta).

And because the humors (doṣas) are of equal intensity, the quartan fever (caturthaka) is difficult to treat. When it has reached the bones and marrow, there occurs the "reverse quartan" (caturthaka-viparyaya).
It causes fever for three days in one way and releases it for one day,
due to the relative strength or weakness of the *doṣas* arising from food, activity, and other factors.
In that same way, there may be fever of the mind and of karma from time to time; [the symptoms are] nausea,
heaviness, dejection, a breaking sensation in the limbs, and yawning.

In a fever involving all the tastes, there is loss of appetite, vomiting, and exhaustion (AS.ni.2.89). In a fever involving blood, there is spitting of blood, thirst, and the eruption of red, hot pustules (AS.ni.2.90).
Burning sensation, redness, vertigo, intoxication, and delirium occur when [the fever] is located in the blood (AS.ni.2.90).
Thirst, exhaustion, loose stools, internal burning, giddiness, and darkness [occur] when it is located in the Pitta (AS.ni.2.91).
When fat is located in the flesh, there is foul odor and twitching of the limbs; when it is located in the skin,
there is sweating, excessive thirst, vomiting, and intolerance of one's own body odor.
In the case of [the fever] located in the bones, there is delirious speech, exhaustion, loss of appetite, and the breaking sensation in the bones; furthermore,
there is the downward or upward movement of the humors (doṣas), labored breathing, convulsions of the limbs, and moaning.
When [the *vāyu*] has reached the marrow (*majja*), there is an internal burning sensation, coldness on the outside, labored breathing,
and hiccups (AS.ni.2.93). There is the perception of darkness, a cutting pain in the vital organs (*marmans*), and stiffness of the penis (AS.ni.2.94).
The emission of semen and death arise when [the disease] is based in the semen;
among these five stages, each subsequent one is more difficult to cure, and one should avoid the last two.
AS.ni.2.95 As if smearing the limbs with phlegm and heaviness;
AS.ni.2.96 Mild fever accompanied by a coating— this is *pralepaka*, which is characterized by coldness.
One who has a constant mild fever, is emaciated, and feels cold, succeeds with difficulty. One whose limbs are stiff and in whom phlegm (śleṣman) predominates, suffers from vātabalāsaka.
One who passes urine that has the color of turmeric or a frog, being of that same color,
is known as the fatal variety of fever named Hāridraka.
In a person whose *kapha* and *vāta* are equal and whose *pitta* is diminished,
a nocturnal fever arises that is either intense or mild. (AS.ni.2.98–99)
When the strength has been drained by the sun during the day and further desiccated by physical exertion,
fever caused by Vāta will certainly arise in the body during the first part of the night.
When the phlegm and bile are vitiated and located in the stomach (āmāśaya),
then one half of the body becomes cold while the other half becomes hot.
When bile (pitta) is corrupted in the body and phlegm (śleṣman) is situated at the extremities,
because of that there is heat in the body and coldness in the hands and feet.
The affliction that agitates the elements dissolves at the time of liberation.
Then the person breathes heavily, perspires, makes moaning sounds,
vomits, moves about, trembles, and raves, with limbs that are alternately hot and cold and whose luster has been destroyed.
Unconscious and afflicted by the force of fever, he looks about as if angry;
with a sound indicating the presence of the *doṣas*, he voids liquid feces with great force.
The body becomes light; exhaustion, delusion, and fever depart; there is a sense of ripening in the mouth, excellence of the sense organs, and absence of pain;
perspiration and sneezing occur; the mind attains its natural state and desires food; and itching appears on the head—these are the signs of the departure of fever.
Thus ends the second chapter.
Now begins the third chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnosis of hemoptysis and cough.
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:
"By means of things that are excessively hot, sharp, pungent, sour, salty, and burning... (AS.ni.3.2)
When kodrava and uddālaka grains, or foods combined with them, are consumed in excess,
the pitta provoked by those pitta-inducing substances causes the blood to become liquefied, resulting in fainting.
Having attained a state of mutual similarity, they pervade the body;
bile [pervades] blood through its transformation, as well as through association and corruption.
And because it conforms to [the characteristics of] smell and color, it is designated by the term "rakta" (blood);
it originates from the site of blood, namely the spleen and the liver.
Heaviness of the head, loss of appetite, desire for cold things, a sensation of fumes, and sour eructations (AS.ni.3.5–6).
Vomiting, the sensation of having vomited something loathsome, cough, dyspnea, vertigo, and exhaustion;
a metallic or bloody smell and taste in the mouth, as well as the odor of raw fish, and loss of voice.
The appearance of red, yellow, and green colors in the eyes and other parts;
and the failure to distinguish between the colors blue, red, and yellow.
In this [state], there occurs the perception of their respective colors in dreams;
[the winds] move upward through the nose, eyes, ears, and mouth, and downward through the penis, vagina, and anus.
When provoked, it flows out through all the pores of the skin;
because it arises from phlegm (kapha) and other humors, it is curable by means of purgation.
There are many medicines for pitta, yet purgation is indeed the best medicine; furthermore, it effects the purification of that kapha which acts as a persistent sequela.
Even sweet astringents are beneficial for one whose phlegm is purified;
how much more so those astringents that are bitter, which by their very nature dispel phlegm?
AS.ni.3.13: Since that which is unstable and so forth is merely palliative for the downward [movement of doshas], emesis is the means for its expulsion;
however, emesis with only a small amount of medicine is not a superior remedy for pitta.
For one who is bound by latent tendencies and is fickle, even that which is peaceful does not belong to him;
for such a person, only bitter things are beneficial, while sweet things alone are harmful.
AS.ni.3.15 A fever involving both courses (the *ubhayāyana*) that is a combination of *kapha* and *māruta* is incurable,
because it is impossible to reverse [the doshas] and because of the absence of medicinal remedies.
Indeed, there is no purificatory therapy for this [condition] that acts as a reversal;
in cases of *raktapitta*, the physician's remedy consists of purification and reversal therapies.
In this very way, a complete pacification of it is not found;
for when the humors are combined, a total alleviation is beneficial.
In that regard, one should observe the progression of the doshas specifically in the channels and the blood,
as well as the complications through the knowledge of their morbid transformations, with particular attention paid to those [complications].
Since cough is a disease that acts rapidly, it will therefore be described [next]. There are five types of cough: those caused by vāta, pitta, śleṣman, chest injury (kṣata), and wasting (kṣaya).

All these [doshas], when neglected, lead to wasting (kṣaya) and become increasingly powerful one after another. The premonitory symptom (pūrvarūpa) of their impending manifestation is itching in the throat and anorexia.
AS.ni.3.21 A sensation as if the throat were filled with porcupine quills and a state of unease in the heart [result from improper diet].
AS.ni.3.22 [These arise] from astringent, slimy, unwholesome, pungent, sour, salty, and hot substances.
By consuming food that is dry, cold, heavy, unctuous, moistening, or stale;
and by the suppression of natural urges, exertion, and by day-sleeping or night-keeping awake.
And by other similar factors that cause the depletion of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) and create obstructions,
when the *apāna* wind is agitated and obstructed, it enters the *apāna*. (AS.ni.3.23–24)
AS.ni.3.24 When that [wind] remains in its place above the rasa, it is pressed upon in the chest.
AS.ni.3.25 There, conjoined with udāna, it fills the throat as well.
With the *vāhinī* [breath] situated at the root of the throat and the head, one should then, as it were, lift up the limbs,
cast the eyes about, and press upon the back, chest, and sides.
Because it passes through the mouth with the [lips] wide open, it produces a sound like that of a cracked bell-metal vessel;
therefore, it brings about the depletion of complexion, luster, strength, and flesh.
Due to the difference in causes, there is a difference in the resistance of the wind when it is gathered together. AS.ni.3.28.
From that, a discordance of pain, sound, and irregularity arises in the coughs;
then, the Vata wind, aggravated by Vata-inducing factors, causes dryness of the chest, throat, and mouth.
It causes pain in the heart, flanks, chest, and head, as well as delusion, agitation, loss of voice, dry cough, and intense forceful pain with a wheezing sound.
In that condition, characterized by horripilation, the patient discharges dried phlegm with difficulty and then recovers.
From pitta, there arises yellowness of the eyes and phlegm, a bitter taste in the mouth, fever, and vertigo.
Vomiting of bile and blood, thirst, hoarseness of voice, a sensation of fumes, intoxication,
and the constant perception of lights as if by the force of coughing (AS.Ni.3.32).
Due to kapha, there is slight pain in the chest, the head and heart feel numb and heavy,
there is a coating in the throat, lassitude, coryza, vomiting, and anorexia. (AS.ni.3.33)
Horripilation and the discharge of thick, unctuous, white phlegm [result] from various acts of rashness,
such as fighting, when practiced beyond one's physical capacity.
When the chest is wounded internally, the powerful Vāyu,
accompanied by Pitta and becoming aggravated, produces a cough that brings up phlegm along with blood.
One should expect to spit out phlegm that is yellow, dark-brown, dry, knotted, and copious;
while the throat is painful and the chest feels as if it were being torn asunder.
As if being pierced by sharp needles, the patient suffers from piercing pain,
fever, dyspnea, thirst, hoarseness of voice, and trembling.
Then, moaning like a pigeon, he suffers from pain in the sides; furthermore,
his vigor, appetite, digestion, strength, and complexion gradually decline.

In one who has been emaciated, there may be the presence of blood and urine, as well as stiffness of the back and waist; in a patient suffering from *rājayakṣman*, the bodily constituents (*dhātavaḥ*), dominated by *vāyu*, become aggravated.
They produce cough through the seats of consumption (yakṣman), and from that, one spits out phlegm that resembles putrid pus, yellow, foul-smelling, greenish, and reddish.
The sides seem as if they are being torn away and the heart seems as if it is falling; there is a sudden desire for heat and cold, excessive eating, and loss of strength.
The face becomes smooth and serene, and the teeth and eyes become magnificent;
thereafter, all his imperishable forms manifest.

Thus, this cough born of wasting (kṣayaja-kāsa) destroys the bodies of those who are already emaciated; however, it may be palliable (yāpya) in those who are strong. Similarly, the cough born of chest injury (kṣataja-kāsa) is likewise [palliable] when it is recent.
The three types of curable [diseases] may be cured through supportive treatment even when afflicted by various doshas;
those that are mixed are palliable, and all become incurable due to the two factors of old age and in the elderly.
Since diseases such as cough, dyspnea, consumption, vomiting, and loss of voice arise from neglecting [this condition],
one should therefore conquer it with haste.
Thus ends the third chapter.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
AS.Ni.4.1: We shall now expound the diagnosis of dyspnea (śvāsa) and hiccups (hidhmā).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and others:
"A cough may arise from an increase in [phlegm], or from the provocation of the humors by the factors previously mentioned."
Also from dysentery, diarrhea, vomiting, poison, anemia,
and fever; from dust, smoke, wind, injury to the vital organs (marmans), and excessive cold water.
The five types [of asthma] are the minor (kṣudraka), the tamaka, the interrupted (chinna), the great (mahān), and the fifth is the upward-moving (ūrdhva).
When the wind, its movement obstructed by phlegm, is situated throughout the body, it causes [these conditions].
Vitiating the channels that carry breath, urine, and food, the morbid [dosha],
situated in the chest, produces asthma originating from the stomach (āmāśaya).
Its premonitory symptoms are pain in the heart and the sides, and the upward movement of the vital breath (prāṇa).
In that condition, constipation and splitting pain in the temples occur;
there, the wind (marut), impelled by exertion and overeating, may propel the *kṣudra* [vātavyādhi], which subsides on its own.
Moving upward in a reverse direction through the channels, the wind (vāyu) excites the phlegm (kapha),
seizes the head, neck, chest, and sides, and causes pain therein.
It causes coughing, wheezing, delusion, loss of appetite, catarrh, and thirst,
as well as a violent onset of breathlessness that afflicts the vital breaths.
One may faint from its force; at the end of the spitting [of phlegm], one finds momentary relief.
Lying down, one breathes with difficulty, but upon sitting up, one attains ease.
With eyes bulging, forehead profusely perspiring, and in great pain, his mouth parched,
breathing repeatedly, trembling, and desiring warmth— AS.ni.4.11.

It increases due to clouds, rain, cold, and eastern winds, as well as substances that increase *śleṣman* (phlegm). This *tamaka* [asthma] is palliable; it may be curable if it is recent or if the patient is strong.

One afflicted by fever and fainting may be relieved by cold treatments; that condition is known as *pratamaka*. One suffering from the pain of a severed vital organ (*marman*) breathes with gasps interrupted by pauses.
[The patient] is covered in sweat, faints, suffers from abdominal distension, and experiences burning and obstruction in the bladder.
AS.Ni.4.15: His downward vision is impaired, his eyes are rolling, he is delirious, and one of his eyes becomes bloodshot.
With a parched mouth, prattling, dejected, his luster lost and consciousness gone,
he gasps with great, agonizing labored breaths.
Being shaken and agitated like a rutting bull incessantly,
his knowledge and discernment were lost, and his eyes and face were bewildered.
Contracting the chest, with suppressed urine and feces, his speech is broken; his throat is parched,
he faints repeatedly, and there is excessive pain in the ears, temples, and head.
He breathes out long and upward, and does not draw [the breath] back down again.
With the channels of the mouth obstructed by phlegm and afflicted by the enraged wind (vāyu),
he laments as his vital points (marmans) are being severed, his speech being suppressed.
These [diseases], whether unmanifest or manifest, will certainly lead to the loss of life;
they have a single cause— breathing— and are characterized by specific premonitory signs, numbers, and locations.
Hiccup (hidhmā) is of four types: that arising from food (bhaktodbhavā), the minor (kṣudrā), the twin (yamalā), and the great (mahatī), as well as the deep-seated (gambhīrā).
Among these, it is treated with urgency by means of improper applications [of breath control].
Afflicted by food and drink that is dry, sharp, rough, and unwholesome,
[the patient] produces hiccup that is painless, soft-sounding, and followed by sneezing.
That which subsides through wholesome food and drink is known as *annajā*. When the *vāyu* is provoked by physical exertion, it brings about the minor hiccough (*kṣudrā hidhmā*).
That [disease] which spreads to the base of the clavicle, has little force, and is soft,
will progress toward increase; furthermore, it becomes soft immediately after eating.
That which proceeds toward food with slow and twin-like impulses.
As it approaches transformation and reaches its full development,
it causes the head and neck to tremble in one who is bloated and excessively thirsty.
Accompanied by delirious speech, vomiting, diarrhea, turbid vision, and yawning,
that dyspnea (hidhmā) is known as yamalā; it is also characterized by forcefulness and is associated with the complications of digestive transformation (pariṇāmavatī).
When the pair of eyebrows and temples have fallen away, and the eyes are flooded with tears,
it paralyzes the body, robs one of speech and memory, and steals away consciousness.
Obstructing the path of food and causing a piercing pain in the vital organs,
great hiccup (mahāhidhmā) manifests by bending the back and producing emaciation.
Having great roots, great sounds, great velocity, and great strength,
it proceeds as before from either the receptacle of undigested food or from the navel.
Having that form, she should repeatedly perform yawning and the stretching of the limbs;
when there is a deep resonance, one should accomplish that [state] which is deep among those [states].
One should avoid the first two [types of women], as well as one who has all the signs of pregnancy, one who is in her courses, one who is pregnant, one who is elderly, and one who is promiscuous.
For one whose body is emaciated by diseases or weakened by the cessation of food,
all diseases lead to destruction, yet none act with such rapidity as this.
Hiccups and dyspnea, for these two indeed take up residence at the time of death.
Thus ends the fourth chapter.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnosis of consumption (rājayakṣma) and other diseases;
thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
Accompanied by many diseases and preceded by numerous ailments,
it is known as *rājayakṣmā*, *kṣaya*, *śoṣa*, and the "king of diseases" (*rogarāj*).
Because he was formerly the king of the stars and the twice-born,
and because he is both a king (*rājā*) and a wasting disease (*yakṣmā*), he is therefore considered *rājayakṣmā*.

It is called *kṣaya* (decay) because it causes the decay of the body, its medicinal remedies, and its lifespan; and it is called *śoṣa* (wasting) because it dries up the bodily fluids (*rasa*) and so forth. It is the king of diseases because it reigns over them.
Violence, suppression of natural urges, the depletion of semen, ojas, and unctuousness,
and the abandonment of the rules for food and drink— these four are its causes.
The wind (vāyu), provoked by those [factors], having provoked the bile (pitta) and phlegm (kapha) throughout the body,
enters the joints of the body and afflicts the channels (sirā).
By obstructing the openings of the channels, or likewise by leaving them excessively dilated, the [vital breaths] moving upwards,
downwards, or transversely produce diseases according to their respective locations.
In one who is about to develop this [disease], there will be a severe catarrh, frequent sneezing,
salivation, sweetness in the mouth, and a sense of exhaustion in both the digestive fire and the body.
AS.ni.5.9: Even in clean vessels, food, drink, and so forth, there is often the sight of impurities,
such as the falling of flies, grass, hair, and the like, into the food and drink.
Nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, and loss of strength even when eating; coldness of the hands, swelling of the feet, and excessive whiteness of the eyes.
AS.ni.5.11: A desire to know the measure of one's own arms; a perception of the loathsomeness of the body;
a fondness for women, wine, and meat; a state of disgust; and veiling the head.
AS.ni.5.12 There is excessive growth of nails and hair, and in dreams there is being overcome by moths, lizards, snakes, monkeys, beasts of prey, and birds.
AS.ni.5.13 Ascending onto a heap of hair, bones, husks, ashes, and so forth;
seeing empty villages and regions; and [seeing] water drying up.
From falling luminous mountains and from blazing trees,
there arise catarrh, dyspnea, cough, pain in the shoulders, head, and voice, as well as loss of appetite.
When located in the upper part of the digestive tract (koṣṭha), fever causes upward discharge, flaccidity, and dryness;
when located in the lower part, it causes downward discharge; when located obliquely, it causes pain in the sides; and when located in the joints, it produces fever.
AS.ni.5.16 These eleven symptoms arise in one suffering from *rājayakṣman*. AS.ni.5.17 One should recognize their complications as the destruction of the throat and pain in the chest.
Yawning, body aches, spitting, weakness of the digestive fire, and foul odor of the mouth [occur].
Among these, due to Vāta, there is pain in the head and sides, and aching of the shoulders and limbs.

Destruction of the throat and loss of voice [result] from pitta; burning sensation, diarrhea, vomiting of blood, foul odor of the mouth, fever, and intoxication [occur] in the feet, face, and hands. AS.ni.5.19: [These symptoms arise] in the feet, face, and hands.
AS.ni.5.19: Burning sensation, diarrhea, vomiting of blood, foul odor of the mouth, fever, and intoxication.
From *kapha* arise anorexia, vomiting, cough, heaviness of the head and limbs,
excessive salivation, chronic rhinitis, dyspnea, loss of voice, and diminished digestive fire. (AS.ni.5.19–20)
Due to the humors (doṣas), characterized by a weak digestive fire and associated with internal coatings, and with phlegm being predominant.
When the channels are obstructed and the heat of the bodily tissues is diminished, the rasa, being scorched in its own location, produces various complications. (AS.Ni.5.22)
If one does not go [to the physician], flesh and other tissues waste away, and blood flows upward;
food is digested only within the stomach, and his digestive fire itself is impaired.
For the most part, this [essence] has become impure and is not at all sufficient for the nourishment of the elements;
even its rasa is not fit for blood, much less for flesh. (AS.ni.5.24)
Obstructed by feces, he exists in a state of mere exhaustion;
even when the symptoms are slight, the patient is wasted and incapable of enduring the strength of the disease or the medicine. (AS.Ni.5.25)
One should avoid [these] and certainly accomplish [the treatment] in all cases; otherwise,
there will be complications from the humors, either individually or combined, as well as wasting and the sixth [type of complication], which arises from fat.
In that condition, there is loss of voice; the voice becomes weak, dry, and unstable.
Due to Vāta, there is a sensation in the throat as if it were filled with bristles, and it is relieved by unctuous and warm treatments.

From pitta, there is burning and dryness in the palate and throat, as well as a sensation of impatience; from kapha, the throat feels as if it were being smeared, and there is a dull, rattling sound in the chest.
The voice is obstructed by all [doshas] and exhibits all symptoms due to wasting;
it feels as if excessively smoking when caused by fat (medas), characterized by the signs of phlegm (kapha).
In this condition, the syllables are difficult to perceive, and one should avoid all [such words], including the final one;
loss of appetite occurs due to the humors (doṣas) localized in the tongue and the heart.
The fifth [type of taste] arises from a combination [of all three humors] and from mental distress.
Regarding the wind and the other humors, the mouth tastes astringent, bitter, and sweet respectively.
Vomiting that arises from all [doshas] is tasteless; that caused by grief, anger, and so forth is according to their specific impurity.
Vomiting due to the doshas individually or collectively is the fourth type, while the fifth is caused by disagreeable objects.
When the *udāna* humor is deranged, it casts up the humors (*doṣas*) through the various channels of the body;
among these, nausea, loss of taste, salivation, and loss of appetite are the primary symptoms.
The wind, causing pain in the navel, the back, and the sides, may force up food;
then one vomits it in small, broken fragments that are astringent and frothy. (AS.ni.5.34)
Accompanied by loud sounds, it is black and clear, occurring with great difficulty and force;
it is attended by coughing, dryness of the mouth, pain in the heart and head, impairment of the voice, and exhaustion. (AS.Ni.5.35)
Due to pitta, [the stool] resembles alkaline water, is smoky-colored, greenish-yellow, mixed with blood, sour, pungent, and hot; it is accompanied by thirst, fainting, burning sensations, and heat.
From *kapha*, [the discharge] is unctuous, thick, white, covered with *śleṣman* threads,
sweet, salty, copious, persistent, and causes horripilation. (AS.Ni.5.37)

One who suffers from swelling of the face, sweetness in the mouth, drowsiness, nausea, and cough; and one who possesses all the symptoms of the [fatal] signs described for the disorders caused by all the humors— such a person one should abandon.

When the mind is distressed and the heart is afflicted by the sight or hearing of things that are putrid, impure, foul, or loathsome, vomiting arises from contact with such disagreeable objects. (AS.ni.5.39)

One should examine [the causes] such as wind (vāta) and so forth; however, one should specifically declare [the condition] to be born of worms (kṛmi) when there is thirst, intoxication, lack of pregnancy-longing (dauhṛda),
colic, trembling, and nausea.
Heart diseases are known to be of five types, including those caused by worms and the symptoms of heart disease;
their origin arises from the same etiological factors described for *gulma*.
By means of wind (vāta), the heart is excessively pricked with pain, as if being pierced or bursting open; it is split, dried up, stiffened, empty, and flows [with fluids].
Sudden dejection, grief, fear, intolerance of sound,
trembling, convulsions, delusion, obstruction of breath, and scant sleep.
From pitta arise thirst, vertigo, fainting, perspiration, acid eructation, exhaustion,
vomiting of acidic bile, a sensation of fumes, yellowness, and fever.
Due to phlegm (śleṣman), the heart becomes stiff and heavy, like a vessel made of bronze or filled with stones;
it is accompanied by cough, loss of digestive fire, spitting, drowsiness, lethargy, anorexia, and fever.
The symptoms of all [three] doshas are present; with the three doshas and parasites, there is darkening of the eyes,
entry into darkness (loss of vision), nausea, emaciation, itching, and discharge of phlegm.
In this state, the heart is torn apart as if by a saw;
one should quickly treat that terrible disease with swift action.
Thirst arises from wind (vāta), from bile (pitta), from phlegm (kapha), from the combination of all three (sannipāta), from the depletion of the bodily fluids (rasakṣaya),
and as a sixth type, from external afflictions (upasarga); however, in the case of the first [type], wind and bile are the causes.
For when all [the bodily constituents] are provoked, it causes the drying up of the somatic (saumya) elements,
and produces dizziness, trembling, burning sensations, thirst, fever, and delusion throughout the entire body.
When the vessels (sirā) that carry [saliva] from the root of the tongue, the throat, the hair-follicles, the palate,
and water are dried up, thirst arises; its general characteristics are as follows:
Dryness of the mouth, lack of thirst for water, aversion to food, loss of voice,
roughness of the throat, lips, and tongue, protrusion of the tongue, and exhaustion.
Incoherent speech, mental derangement, thirst, seizures, and likewise various diseases [arise from this].
From the wind (māruta), there is emaciation, dejection, piercing pain in the temples, and vertigo of the head.
From pitta arise loss of the sense of smell, bad taste in the mouth, impairment of hearing, sleepiness, and loss of strength;
from drinking cold water, there is an increase [of these symptoms], as well as fainting and bitterness in the mouth.
Redness of the eyes, persistent emaciation, burning sensation,
and excessive tearing occur when the provoked *kapha* obstructs the wind (*vāta*) in the water-carrying channels. (AS.ni.5.54–55)
Because of that [phlegm], the channels become clogged with phlegm and are dried up as if by mud;
then the throat becomes as if covered with bristles, and there is sleep and a sweet taste in the mouth.
Distension of the abdomen, heaviness of the head, numbness, vomiting,
anorexia, laziness, and indigestion— these symptoms all arise when [the doshas] are present in their entirety.
Thirst arising from [the suppression of] natural urges, or that born from the obstruction of vāta and pitta,
occurs in one who is exhausted by heat and suddenly resorts to cold water.

AS.ni.5.58 That [fever] which occurs when the heat (ūṣman) is obstructed and has entered the abdominal cavity (koṣṭha) is born of bile (pittaja); so too is that which arises from excessive drinking or intoxication, and that which is produced by sharp fire or unctuous substances (sneha).
Thirst arising from phlegm (kapha) is caused by the consumption of unctuous, heavy, sour, and salty foods;
that which is characterized by the symptoms described for the depletion of rasa (rasakṣaya) is of the nature of depletion (kṣayātmikā).
The intense thirst that arises due to complications such as emaciation, urinary disorders, fever, and other chronic diseases is known as *upasargātmikā* (thirst resulting from secondary afflictions).

Thus ends the fifth chapter. Now begins the sixth chapter: We shall now expound the chapter titled "The Diagnosis of Alcoholism" (Madātyayanidāna). AS.Ni.6.1. 1. Now, therefore, we shall explain the chapter on the diagnosis of alcoholism.
"Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:
[Pitta] is sharp, hot, dry, subtle, sour, diffusive, quick-acting, and light. (AS.Ni.6.1–2)

Intoxicating liquor is expansive and clear; its opposite is vigor (*ojas*). The qualities beginning with "sharpness" (*tīkṣṇa*) are also said to exist in poison, as they cause the disturbance of the mind.
Poisons arise for the end of life through their state of extreme intensity;
wine, by its qualities such as sharpness and so forth, [destroys] the qualities of vitality such as dullness and so forth.
Agitating the mind with ten [objects], one leads it to transformation;
in the first intoxication, however, one stands in the second abode of negligence.
Struck by false conceptualization, the deluded person perceives what is not happiness as happiness;
having reached the junction between the middling and the superior, he is characterized by passion and darkness.
Like an unrestrained beast of prey, a fool would do nothing;
this ground is the locus of faults, the abode of immorality.
He alone is the guide for this [world] on its many paths toward miserable rebirth; yet,
remaining in the third intoxication, he lies motionless like a corpse.
Even after death, the evil-minded person goes to an even more wretched state.
Dharma and adharma, pleasure and pain, gain and loss, benefit and harm— [all these follow him].
AS.ni.6.9 When one who is attached does not know [the truth], how should the wise person practice that?
AS.ni.6.10 Delusion, fear, sorrow, anger, and death are all rooted in intoxication.
Insanity, intoxication, fainting, epilepsy,
and apatānaka— where there is a single loss of memory, everything therein is unwholesome.
Food that is unwholesome leads indeed to disease or death;
liquor is the destroyer even of the three aims of life, of intelligence, of fortitude, and of modesty.

Those who are strong, having eaten their fill, and who consume large quantities of food; those who are unctuous, endowed with vigor and youth, and whose lineage is devoted to liquor— these do not become excessively intoxicated.
Those with a predominance of fat and phlegm, with weak vāta and pitta, and possessing strong digestive fire,
as well as those who are overconfident and prone to anger, become excessively intoxicated when the opposite conditions prevail.

Through wine that is sour and parched, and when consumed during indigestion, in large quantities, or excessively, there arise four types of alcoholism (madātyaya): from vāta, from pitta, from kapha, and from all three combined.
All [of them] arise from all [causes], yet they are designated according to what is predominant;
their common characteristic is delusion and heartache.
Constant diarrhea, thirst, fever characterized by both cold and heat, and loss of appetite;
pain and trembling in the head, sides, and bones; piercing pain in the vital organs (marmans), and stiffness in the sacrum (trika).
Obstruction of the chest, blurred vision, cough, dyspnea, and insomnia;
excessive perspiration, constipation, swelling, and mental confusion.
Incoherent speech, vomiting, nausea, giddiness, and the sight of bad dreams;
specifically from *anila* (wind), there is wakefulness, dyspnea, trembling, and headache.
In dreams, one wanders, flies up, and converses with ghosts;
from pitta arise burning fever, perspiration, delusion, diarrhea, thirst, and vertigo.
The body becomes greenish-yellow, with redness of the eyes and cheeks;

due to phlegm (kapha), there is vomiting, nausea, drowsiness, urticaria-like eruptions, and heaviness of the limbs. In the case of the tri-discordant (sarvaja) type, all these symptoms appear together. One who drinks liquor [without moderation] [develops these]. *Aṣṭāṅga Saṃgraha*, Nidāna-sthāna 6.20.
If he performs another improper act with haste, there may occur destruction or emaciation caused by wind (māruta), which are especially painful for one who is weak.

In the case of *dhvaṃsaka* (destructive fever), there is spitting of phlegm, dryness of the throat, excessive sleepiness, intolerance of sound, and lassitude. In *vikṣaya* (wasting fever), there is extreme pain in the limbs and head.
Heartburn, constriction of the throat, delusion, cough, thirst, vomiting, and fever—
these afflict one who has turned away from intoxicants, who has mastered the self, and acts with conscious deliberation. (AS.ni.6.22–23)
He is never touched by physical or mental afflictions; however, for one who is intent on food that produces passion and delusion, the three diseases may arise.
Intoxication, fainting, convulsions, and death arise from the obstruction of the channels that carry rasa, blood, and consciousness, each succeeding one being more severe than the preceding.
In this context, intoxication (mada) arises from all [three] doshas as well as from blood, alcohol, and poisons;
it is characterized by speech that is persistent, copious, and rapid, and by movements that are restless and faltering.
In intoxication arising from wind (vāta), the body becomes rough, dark-gray, and reddish;
through bile (pitta), one is prone to anger, has a reddish-yellow complexion, and is fond of quarreling.

From phlegm (kapha), one speaks little and indistinctly, is pale, intent on meditation, and lazy; from the combination of all three humors (sannipāta), one possesses all these traits; and from blood (rakta), there is stiffness of the limbs and the gaze.
The symptoms of bile (pitta) are present, along with a change in appearance, loss of voice, and weakness of the limbs due to liquor;
from poison, there is trembling and excessive sleep, and it is more severe than all [the other poisons].

One should diagnose vāta and the other [doshas] among the blood and other tissues by observing the excellence of their specific characteristics. Seeing the sky as reddish, blue, or black, one enters into darkness.
In fainting caused by Vāta, there is rapid awakening, pain in the heart,
trembling, dizziness, emaciation, and a dusky-red complexion.
Seeing the sky as red or yellow due to bile, one enters into darkness;
upon awakening, one is afflicted by sweat, burning sensations, thirst, and heat.
With a complexion appearing variegated as blue and yellow, and with eyes agitated by red and yellow,
one who sees the sky resembling a cloud due to phlegm shall enter [the state of] space. (AS.ni.6.32)
After a long time, he awakens from that darkness, accompanied by nausea and salivation,
with his limbs heavy and motionless as if covered by wet leather.
Like another form of epilepsy, it possesses all the symptoms and three doshas;
it quickly casts the person down motionless, yet without the loathsome movements [of epilepsy].
(AS.Ni.6.34) When the doshas have completed their course in the bodies of living beings, intoxication and fainting occur.
The impurities subside by themselves, like a case of fever that abates without medicine; for these extremely powerful impurities seize the activity of speech, body, and mind.
When the vital breaths, having gathered together and taken refuge in the seat of the life-force,
cease their activity, the person becomes like a piece of wood, resembling one who is dead.
If medical treatment is not applied quickly, one may die very soon,
like one in a shoreless flood of water teeming with crocodiles.
One should quickly turn back a person who is sinking into renunciation (saṃnyāsa),
for there is an embrace by his own internal enemies, such as intoxication, pride, anger, and delight. (AS.ni.6.37–38)
That which is appropriate and inappropriate is equalized by liquor devoid of rational application (yukti).
AS.ni.6.39: [The factors to be considered are] strength (bala), time (kāla), place (deśa), suitability (sātmya), constitution (prakṛti), assistants (sahāya), disease (āmaya), and age (vayas).
If, having analyzed [the teachings] accordingly, one drinks [them], then one drinks the nectar;
thus ends the sixth chapter.
Now begins the seventh chapter. Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "The Diagnosis of Hemorrhoids" (Arśas).

Thus indeed said the great seers, Ātreya and others: "They tear like an enemy, therefore they are called *arśāṃsi* (piles). Furthermore, they are of many types and accompanied by very many complications; they are fleshy protuberances (*māṃsakīla*) located in the anus, the penis, and other areas.
In brief, hemorrhoids are of two types: congenital and those arising after birth;
furthermore, they are of two kinds: dry and moist.
Moreover, the substratum for all of them is fat, muscle, and skin.

The anus, attached to the large intestine, measures four and a half finger-breadths (aṅgulas). Within it, there are first three muscular folds known as *valīs*, each measuring one and a half finger-breadths;
these are the *pravāhiṇī*, the *visarjanī*, and the *saṃvaraṇī*.
They say the anal lip is one and a half barley-corns beyond the hair-line;
the first [lip] is one finger-breadth from the anal lip. Therein, the heating of the seeds of the innate anal folds is the locus [of hemorrhoids].
Its cause is twofold: the transgression of the mother and father, and destiny; through these two, there is the provocation of the humors (doṣas).
Therefore, these are incurable;
by this, all hereditary disorders (vikāra) are explained.

Specifically, however, those that are congenital (sahaja) are difficult to look at, rough, pale, thickened, and dreadful, with their openings turned inward, and they are afflicted by many complications.
Now,
the other six types [of hemorrhoids] arise from the individual humors, from their combinations, from their concerted action, and from blood.

In that regard, those [hemorrhages] in which vāta and śleṣman predominate are dry, while those in which rakta and pitta predominate are moist. The causes for the provocation of the doṣas have been stated previously.

When that [wind] accumulates waste matter—due to sitting on high, uneven, or hard seats; from traveling on unsteady vehicles such as camels; from excessive sexual intercourse; from improper insertion of the enema nozzle; from frequent contact with cold water; from friction caused by clothing, clods of earth, or grass; from constant straining; from the suppression of the urges of flatus, urine, and feces; or from women’s miscarriages, pressure on the fetus during pregnancy, or difficult labor—then this provoked *apāna* wind, having encountered that accumulated waste matter situated in the lower part of the body, deposits it within the folds of the rectum.
Thereafter, when those [doshas] have become excessively moistened, ulcers arise (AS.Ni.7.7).

Their premonitory symptoms are: difficult digestion, rumbling in the intestines, excessive belching, sour eructation, lack of appetite, constipation, a sensation as if the navel were filled with stones, flatulence, the downward movement of wind with difficulty and accompanied by sound, excessive urination, scanty feces, cutting pain in the anus, aching in the thighs, swelling of the eyes, turbidity of the sense organs, lassitude, drowsiness, emaciation, weakness, and apprehension regarding disorders of the *grahaṇī*, edema, abdominal enlargement, anemia, and abdominal tumors (AS.Ni.7.7).
And once they have arisen, these signs become even more manifest (AS.Ni.7.8). Indeed,

due to the obstruction of the downward path by these [signs], the apāna-vāyu, turning back, agitates the samāna, vyāna, udāna, and prāṇa vāyus as well as pitta and śleṣman, and destroys the digestive fire (agni) (AS.Ni.7.8).

Now, one who has hemorrhoids (arśas) becomes entirely emaciated, discolored, wasted, and dejected; he suffers from excessive retention of flatus, urine, and feces, as well as urinary stones and gravel. His stools are irregularly constipated or loose, undigested, broken, or dry. Furthermore, he voids stool that is alternately white, pale, green, yellow, red, or reddish-brown, thin yet thick, and slimy. He experiences severe cutting pain in the regions of the navel and groin, accompanied by anal pain, dysentery (pravāhikā), sexual excitement, and fainting. He has scanty semen and offspring, eats little, and his body is covered with visible veins. He is irritable and difficult to treat. He is afflicted by cough, dyspnea, chronic rhinitis, thirst, anorexia, and swelling of the hands, feet, face, and eye-sockets. He suffers from sneezing, shivering, vomiting, blurred vision, headache, a weak and broken voice, ear disease, fever, and body aches. He has pain in all the joints and bones, and is intermittently tormented by gripping pains in the heart, abdomen, sides, back, bladder, and the sacrum (trika). He is lost in deep thought and is extremely lethargic.

Among these, those caused by a predominance of *vāta* are dry, withered, hard, rough, parched, dusky, and reddish; they have sharp, cracked openings, irregular centers, and sizes ranging from those of the *kadamba* flower to the *tuṇḍikerī*, *karkandhu*, *siddhārtha*, *bimbī*, and dates; they are crooked, dissimilar to one another, and characterized by excessive pain in the waist, flanks, and other areas, causing colic and upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*), as well as abdominal tumors (*gulma*), prostate enlargement (*aṣṭhīlā*), splenic disorders (*plīhodara*), and abdominal dropsy (*udarā*) resulting from that very cause.
The skin, nails, eyes, face, and urine become black.

[In the case of] those dominated by pitta (pittolbaṇa), they have blue tips, are red, yellow, or black, soft, flaccid, intolerant to touch, foul-smelling, thin, exuding a small amount of blood, accompanied by burning and suppuration, causing fever, delusion, and anorexia, resembling the liver in appearance, similar to the tongue of a parrot or the mouth of a leech, thick in the middle like a barley grain, moist, discharging yellowish feces, and turning the skin, nails, and other parts yellow.

Those [diseases] dominated by *śleṣman* (phlegm) have large roots; they are firm, unctuous, pale, round, and thickened; heavy, rigid, smooth, and slimy; characterized by extreme numbness and sensitivity to touch; shaped like a *karīra* fruit, a jackfruit stone, or a cow's teat; accompanied by excessive discharge and diarrhea; causing pain in the groin, abdomen, and navel; associated with nausea, cough, dyspnea, catarrh, anorexia, vomiting, difficulty in urination, urinary disorders (*prameha*), cold fever, swelling, heaviness of the head, a coating over the sense organs, weak digestion, impotence, and severe disorders of *āmadoṣa*; they do not burst nor do they exude fluid; they are abundant in itching; they cause extremely loose stools mixed with phlegm and fat; and they produce whiteness of the skin, nails, and other parts.

AS.ni.7.12 One should distinguish those born from a combination of [humors] or their conjunction by the confusion of their symptoms. AS.ni.7.13 Those dominated by blood (rakta), however, resemble the shoots of the *vaṭa* tree, coral, or the fruit of the *kākanandikā*; they possess the characteristics of *pitta*, and when excessively oppressed by hard feces, they suddenly discharge a large amount of vitiated, hot blood.

If that [blood] flows excessively, complications arise from the depletion of blood; regarding this, there is a verse: AS.ni.7.13 *tasyātipravṛttau raktakṣayopadravā bhavantīti bhavati cātra ślokaḥ* (In case of its excessive flow, complications due to the loss of blood occur; and on this subject, there is a verse).
By means of dry and constipating substances such as mung beans, kodrava grain, jūrṇāhvaka, karīra, chickpeas,
and so forth, the wind (vāyu), provoked in its own location, becomes powerful.
The downward-flowing channels, becoming congested and drying up from below,
cause the retention of feces, flatus, and urine, which is agonizing.
Due to that, there occurs intense pain extending to the abdomen, back, heart, and sides;
as well as flatulence, distension of the abdomen, nausea, and cutting pain.
There is also intense pain in the bladder, swelling arises in the cheeks,
and due to the upward movement of the wind (vāyu), vomiting, loss of appetite, and fever occur.
Heart disease, disorders of the grahaṇī, retention of urine,
dysuria, deafness, blindness, asthma, headache, cough, and chronic rhinitis.
Mental disturbances such as thirst, bile-fever, abdominal tumors,
and stomach ailments arise, as well as various extremely severe diseases born of wind (vāta).
Among those with difficult names [of diseases], this upward movement of wind (udāvarta) is the supreme complication;
it arises even without those [other causes] in those whose internal cavities are overcome by Vāta.

Those innate (*sahaja*) disorders of the three humors (*tridoṣa*), as well as those situated within the *bala* (the vital essence), are incurable; they may only be palliated by means of digestive power (*agni-bala*) and other such factors.
Those diseases arising from the combination of two humors (*dvandva*), those located in the second layer (*balā*) of the body,
and those that have persisted for more than a year, are said to be difficult to cure.
However, hemorrhoids that have arisen from external causes, those dominated by a single *doṣa*,
and those that have not been present for long are easily curable.
They will also be described in their respective locations, such as the penis and other parts; however,
those born from the navel are shaped like earthworms, slimy, and soft.
The *vyāna* wind, having seized the phlegm (*śleṣman*), produces a growth on the exterior of the skin;
being like a wedge, firm, and rough, they know that as *carmakīla*.
From wind (vāta) comes pricking pain and roughness; from bile (pitta), blackish-red discoloration;
from phlegm (śleṣman), oiliness, a knotted consistency, and coloration matching the surrounding skin.
A wise person should quickly exert effort toward the pacification of hemorrhoids (arśas), for if left unchecked,
they may quickly obstruct the rectum and cause intestinal obstruction (baddhagudodara).
Thus ends the seventh chapter.
Now begins the eighth chapter.
8.1. Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnosis of diarrhea and disorders of the *grahaṇī*.
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and others:
"Diarrhea is produced especially by the excessive drinking of water. (Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha, Nidāna-sthāna 8.1–2)
Due to wine, parching foods, excessive eating, hemorrhoids, the improper administration of oleation,
worms, and the suppression of natural urges, the Vāyu becomes aggravated by these and similar factors.
It liquefies the lower element (feces) by destroying the digestive fire with that very [substance],
and having impaired the abdominal cavity along with the feces, it reduces the stool to a liquid state.
The symptoms of impending diarrhea manifest as a piercing pain in the heart, the rectum, and the abdomen, along with lassitude of the limbs and retention of the waste products.
There, due to Vāta, there is a lack of digestion and a watery discharge;
one voids stool that is scanty, accompanied by much noise and pain, and is obstructed.
It is rough, frothy, clear, or knotted, occurring repeatedly;
likewise, it resembles burnt jaggery and is accompanied by sliminess and cutting pain.
With a dry mouth, a prolapsed anus, bristling body hair, and groaning,
[the patient] has yellow, black, turmeric-colored, or grass-green feces due to bile (pitta).
Accompanied by blood, it is extremely foul-smelling and characterized by thirst, fainting, perspiration,
and a burning sensation; with Kapha, it is thick, accompanied by pain, heat in the anus, and suppuration.
It is slimy, stringy, white, unctuous, raw, and associated with phlegm;
it is frequent, heavy, foul-smelling, obstructed, and accompanied by persistent pain.
One who is drowsy, lazy, and averse to food, passing very little stool accompanied by dysentery,
experiencing horripilation, feeling a sense of nausea, and having heaviness in the bladder, anus, and abdomen (AS.Ni.8.12).
Even when something has been done, he perceives it as undone; he is the self of all and possesses all characteristics.
When the mind is agitated by fear, bile causes the feces to liquefy.
Then the wind (vāyu) causes excessive diarrhea of hot, liquid, and floating stools;
they say its symptoms are identical to those of vāta-pitta, and it is likewise caused by grief.

Diarrhea, in brief, is of two types: with undigested matter (sāma) and without undigested matter (nirāmaka). Among these, the first [type] is accompanied by blood; due to heaviness, the patient sinks in water.
Accompanied by foul-smelling feces, flatulence, constipation, pain,
and regurgitation— this is the opposite when free from *āmadoṣa*; however, even when fully ripened (*pakva*), if it is caused by *kapha*, it sinks [in water].

In cases of diarrhea, if one does not exert sufficient effort [in treatment], the disease of the *grahaṇī* may arise; this occurs either due to the consumption by another person of substances that destroy the digestive fire (*agni*), or through other causes.
Whether accompanied by mucus or free from it, that which causes diarrhea once food has been digested is called *atisāra* (diarrhea),
because it flows excessively and is rapid by its very nature.
If the stool is undigested when eaten, or if it is digested when the food has been digested,
or if it is neither; or if it is suddenly bound and suddenly loose again.
The grahaṇī disorder caused by delayed digestion may lead to the accumulation [of doshas] and cause diarrhea.
It arises in four ways: from each of the individual doshas and from their combination (sannipāta).
Its premonitory symptoms are a feeling of heaviness in the abdomen, delayed digestion, and sour eructations.
There is excessive salivation, a bad taste in the mouth, loss of appetite, thirst, exhaustion, and vertigo.
A distended abdomen, vomiting, ringing in the ears, and rumbling in the intestines (AS.ni.8.22);
emaciation, a sensation of smoke, catarrh, and fever (AS.ni.8.23) are the general symptoms.
Fainting, headache, constipation, and swelling of the hands and feet [occur].
Among these, from vāta there is dryness of the palate, darkness before the eyes, and ringing in the ears.

AS.ni.8.24 Pain in the sides, thighs, groins, and neck occurs frequently, as does choleraic pain (viṣūcikā). AS.ni.8.25 Greed for all flavors, along with hunger, thirst, and cutting pain in the bowels (parikartikā), [arise].
When digested, it causes flatulence; while being digested, it causes distension; and when food has been eaten, one attains normal health.
One who is afflicted by wind disorders, heart disease, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, splenic enlargement, or anemia [should take this].

AS.ni.8.26 After a long time, he passes stool that is painful, liquid, dry, thin, and frothy like foam accompanied by sound. AS.ni.8.27 He repeatedly voids feces, suffering from pain in the anus, dyspnea, and cough.
Due to bile (pitta), one who has a yellowish complexion produces blue-colored, yellowish, and liquid [stools];
he suffers from foul and sour eructations, burning sensations in the heart and throat, loss of appetite, and thirst.
Due to phlegm (śleṣman), food is digested with difficulty, and there is vomiting, anorexia,
a coating of the mouth, spitting, coughing, nausea, and catarrh.
One feels heaviness in the heart, the abdomen is numb and heavy;
there is a foul, sweet belching, lassitude, and a lack of desire for women.
AS.ni.8.30 The passing of stool that is broken up, mixed with mucus, and heavy;
