AS.ni.8.31 weakness even in one who is not emaciated; and in the case of all [three] doshas combined, there is a mixture of all these symptoms.
Regarding the classification of the vessels (sirā), those three fires beginning with Viṣama which were mentioned [in the previous section]— AS.ni.8.31,

These too may be disorders of the *grahaṇī*, whereas balanced [humors] are the cause of health. Vāta diseases, urinary stones, leprosy, urinary disorders, abdominal enlargements, and fistula-in-ano [are also caused by imbalance].
Hemorrhoids and *grahaṇī*—these eight are the great diseases that are very difficult to overcome.
Thus ends the eighth chapter.
Now begins the ninth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnosis of urinary obstruction;
thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
Difficulties caused by vāta, pitta, kapha, and their combination (sannipāta);
stones in the bladder formed from vāta, pitta, śleṣman, or semen;
vātabasti, aṣṭhīlā, kuṇḍalikā, mūtrātīta, abdominal enlargement (jaṭhara), utsaṅga, and granthi; obstruction of semen or feces; and uṣṇavāta, depletion of urine (mūtrakṣaya), and exhaustion.
Among those, the nine beginning with vātabasti are dominated by vāta;
following that, two are dominated by both vāta and pitta.
The last [type] is characterized by a predominance of phlegm and bile (AS.ni.9.4). Furthermore, the bladder is the site for all urinary diseases (AS.ni.9.4).

Though he was previously struck in his vital points (marmans), even while facing downward, the bladder—like a new jar submerged in water—is filled from its sides by the urine flowing incessantly through thousands of minute openings in the urine-carrying channels (nāḍīs). Furthermore, the vitiated *vāta* and other doshas enter the bladder through those very same channels and, according to their respective natures, produce afflictions and urinary disorders (*pramehas*). Among these, in *vāta-kṛcchra*, one urinates with great difficulty, characterized by intense pain in the bladder, penis, and groin, occurring frequently in small quantities.
In the case of *pitta*-dominant dysuria (*pittakṛcchra*), one always experiences pain, and the urine is red, yellow, or black;
there is heaviness in the bladder and penis, swelling, and one voids urine mixed with mucus. In the case of *kapha*-dominant dysuria (*kaphakṛcchra*), [the symptoms are as follows].
When all [the doshas] are combined, it is a complication arising from their combination (*sannipāta-kṛcchra*),
and that is the most difficult to treat (AS.Ni.9.6).

However, when the Vāyu, having obstructed the opening of the bladder, dries up the urine— whether accompanied by Pitta, Kapha, or semen— then, gradually, just as gallstone (*rocanā*) forms from bile in a cow, or as sediment (*paṅka*) forms from clear water in a jar, in the same way a urinary calculus (*aśmarī*) is produced.

And all that [disease] has its basis in phlegm (śleṣman); furthermore, its premonitory symptoms are fever, distension of the bladder, loss of appetite, difficulty in urination, pain in the bladder, head, scrotum, and penis, and a fishy odor of the urine.

The general signs [of obstruction] are as follows: when one urinates through the navel, the bladder, or the meḍhrī (urethra), there is pain due to the blockage of the passage, and the flow of urine is obstructed; upon its removal, however, one voids urine that is clear, black like a *gomedaka* gem, and very easy to pass.
Furthermore, due to the agitation of that [obstruction], the urine may be mixed with blood.
Furthermore, various pains arise for him through running, leaping, and other such activities;
and just as urine does not flow when the bladder is occupied by feces that have descended from the colon (pakvāśaya), so it is with a stone (aśmarī).
In that condition, afflicted by intense pain in the perineal raphe, the penis, and the urethra due to the wind (vāyu), he gnashes his teeth, presses upon his navel, and rubs his penis.
In this condition, the patient trembles repeatedly, voids feces with great difficulty accompanied by wind,
and passes urine in a broken stream; furthermore, his urinary stone becomes dark-brown, rough, irregular, and covered with thorns like the flower of the Kadamba tree.
As if being cooked by bile, the bladder feels as though it is burning;

the stone is reddish, yellowish, or black, and has the shape of a *bhallātaka* seed. Due to phlegm (*śleṣman*), the bladder feels heavy and as if pricked with needles, and the stone is cold, white, large, resembling a hen’s egg, or honey-colored.
Generally, these three types of calculi occur in children;
because of their small bladder and the paucity of muscular development, they are easily grasped and extracted (AS.Ni.9.9).
However, in adults, the seminal calculus (śukrāśmarī) arises with semen as its cause.

Due to the obstruction of sexual intercourse, the semen that has been excited but not discharged is seized by the wind (vāyu) moving through the wrong channels; it collects between the testicles and dries up. Thereupon, it becomes a dry calculus (aśmarī), which obstructs the path of the semen, causes painful urination (mūtrakṛcchra), pain in the bladder (bastivedanā), and swelling of the testicles.
As soon as it has arisen, the semen is expelled;
and as soon as that [expulsion] is pressed, it dissolves in that very same space.
However, when a stone (*aśmarī*) itself is broken into minute fragments by the wind, it is called gravel (*śarkarā*). (AS.ni.9.10)
When the downward-moving wind (anuloma-māruta) is present, that [semen] falls out along with the urine like sand;
however, due to the suppression of the urge to urinate, the wind obstructs the opening of the bladder.
Then it causes retention of urine, pain, and itching;
and sometimes, having displaced the bladder from its natural position, it makes it protrude like a fetus, swollen and fluctuating.

In that condition, there is pain, throbbing, burning, and cramping, along with the dribbling of urine drop by drop; when the bladder is pressed, the urine flows out in a stream. This two-fold *vātabasti* is difficult to cure; of these two, the second type, in which *vāyu* (wind) is predominant, is even more difficult to cure.

(AS.Ni.9.12) Furthermore, the *vāyu* forms a knot (*granthi*) between the urinary passage and the rectum, appearing like a stone (*aṣṭhīlā*), dense, elevated, immobile, and accompanied by intense pain.
Due to that, there occurs obstruction of flatus, feces, and urine, as well as abdominal distension; that is Vātāṣṭhīlā.

When the vitiated *vāyu* becomes coiled within the bladder (*basti*), accompanied by intense pain, stiffness, and heaviness, it churns the urine, causing it to flow only in small amounts; this condition is *vātakuṇḍalikā*.

When the urine is suppressed for too long and then released, it does not flow; however, while straining, it flows out with difficulty in small quantities—this is *mūtrātīta* (Asaṅga Saṃhitā, Nidāna-sthāna 9.13). Due to the obstruction of urine, the *apāna* wind causes intense pain and distension below the navel along with the retention of feces, filling the abdomen; this is *mūtrajaṭhara*.

When one urinates with a small amount of urine due to its being displaced by wind (māruta) or because of a defect in the channels (chidra-viguṇya), the residual urine remains in the bladder, the urethral tube, or the glans penis; this residue, heavy and either painful or painless, trickles out slowly—that is called *mūtrotsaṅga*.
A small, round mass at the opening of the bladder that arises quickly, having symptoms similar to a stone (*aśmarī*), is *mūtragranthi*.

AS.ni.9.14: In one who has been urinated upon, due to sexual intercourse, the semen—agitated by Vāyu and displaced from its natural location—is discharged along with the urine, either before or after it, appearing like ash-water; this is *mūtraśukra*.
When the urinary passage is compressed by Vāyu, it enters the fecal channel; consequently, one urinates with difficulty, accompanied by a fecal odor and mixed with feces; this is *viḍvighāta*.

When *pitta* is aggravated by excessive travel, exposure to heat, hot food, and so forth, and is impelled by *vāyu*, it causes burning in the bladder, penis, and anus, and may discharge urine that is green, yellow, red, or mixed with blood with great difficulty; this condition is called *uṣṇavāta*.
When *vāta* and *pitta* take refuge in the bladder, they deplete the urine accompanied by pain and burning; this is *mūtrakṣaya*.

When *pitta*, *śleṣman*, or both are congealed in the bladder by *vāta*, then the urine becomes accompanied by burning, reddish, yellow, white, thick, difficult to pass, and dry; it takes on the color of the powder of either conch-shell or *rocanā*, or it may possess all these colors.
This is *mūtrāvasāda*.
Thus, the diseases arising from the non-emission of urine have been described in detail. (AS.Ni.9.15)
"Those arising from excessive activity will be described hereafter by means of their causes and characteristics"—
thus ends the ninth chapter.
Now begins the tenth chapter. Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "The Diagnosis of Prameha."
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and others:
there are twenty types of *prameha*.
Namely:
from phlegm (kapha), there are ten types of urinary disorders—water, sugarcane juice, thick liquid, wine, flour-paste, semen, sand, cold, and saliva;
and from bile (pitta), there are six types—alkali, black, blue, turmeric-yellow, madder-red, and blood-colored.
There are four types of madhumeha: those arising from vāta, vasā, majjā, and fat (AS.Ni.10.3).
Whatever collection of diet and lifestyle produces *śleṣman*, fat, and urine is their cause (AS.Ni.10.3).

In that regard, *śleṣman* (phlegm) located in the bladder, combined with wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), fat (*medas*), moisture (*kleda*), flesh (*māṃsa*), semen (*śukra*), and nutrient essence (*rasa*), produces the [ten] types of *prameha*. Likewise, *pitta* joined with those same factors as well as phlegm and blood (*śoṇita*) produces [the six types],
and *vāyu* combined with those same factors plus muscle-fat (*vasā*), lymph (*lasīkā*), marrow (*majjā*), and vitality (*ojas*) produces [the remaining four].

Among all three doshas, kapha is the first to become aggravated in cases of prameha, because urine has kapha as its substrate (adhiṣṭhāna). Furthermore, due to the increase of that [kapha], medas (fat) alone is first vitiated by it, owing to their extreme similarity (atyanta-sabhāgatva).
Immediately thereafter, there is the drying up of the body and so forth;
then, upon the depletion of phlegm and other humors, the Pitta becomes dominant and vitiates the blood as well.

Upon the depletion of that too, the Vāyu draws the bodily tissues such as the muscle-fat (vasā)—which constitute the ultimate essence of the body—and having drawn them toward the bladder, expels them along with the urine.

Therefore, those [types of fever] arising from phlegm (kapha), bile (pitta), and wind (vāta) are, respectively, curable, manageable, and incurable. Likewise, those born of bile are incurable because they reside in the fat (medas) where the humors are combined, and because their treatment is contradictory.

Furthermore, the wind-born (vātaja) types [of prameha] occur when the bodily constituents (dhātus) have been depleted; due to their great severity and because they require contradictory treatments, they are difficult to cure.
However, if the fat (medas) is not excessively vitiated, even the bile-born (pittaja) types may become curable.
Moreover, due to contact with the bodily constituents, in all types of meha, the urine becomes turbid and copious.

AS.ni.10.6 Due to the combination of the humors (*doṣa*) and the bodily constituents (*dūṣya*) in varying degrees of intensity, specific types of *prameha* arise— such as *śabala*, *kalmāṣa*, and others— based on particularities of the urine's color, taste, touch, and smell, just as there are variations in colors such as white and black.
AS.ni.10.7 Their premonitory symptoms (*pūrvarūpa*) include the excessive growth of the nails and so forth, the matting of the hair, sweetness in the mouth, and dryness of the palate and throat.

AS.ni.10.7 Thirst, excessive impurity, a desire for coldness on the external body and in the bodily orifices, oiliness, perspiration, numbness in the limbs, the sensation of ants crawling due to excessive sweetness and a burning sensation in the hands and feet, a cadaverous (visra) odor in the urine and body, whiteness of the urine, and an excess of labored breathing, sleep, drowsiness, and laziness [occur]. AS.ni.10.8 In that condition, one who suffers from udakameha passes urine that is cold, white, odorless, and clear, like water.
One who has *ikṣumeha* passes urine that is extremely sweet like sugarcane juice, cold, slightly slimy,
and turbid; one who has *sāndrameha* passes urine that becomes thick after standing overnight.
In *surāmeha*, one passes urine that resembles wine—clear at the top and thick at the bottom;
in *piṣṭameha*, with hair standing on end, one passes urine that is thick and white like flour;
in *śukrameha*, the urine has the appearance of semen or is mixed with semen.
One who passes sand-like urine (sikatāmehī) generally voids it with pain and along with actual sand;
one who passes cold urine (śītamehī) voids what is sweet and extremely cold;
and one who passes slow urine (śanairmehī) voids it very slowly and gradually.
In *lālāmeha*, the urine is slimy and as if bound with threads;
in *kṣārameha*, it resembles flowing alkali in its color, smell, taste, and touch;
in *kālameha*, it is hot and black like soot.
In *nīlameha*, the urine is frothy, fishy-smelling, sour, and blue like the wing of a blue jay;
in *hāridrameha*, it is pungent, burning, and resembles turmeric; in *mañjiṣṭhāmeha*, it has a fishy odor and the color of madder-water.
One who passes urine resembling blood (śoṇitamehin) voids urine that is foul-smelling, warm, salty, and like blood;
one who passes fat (vasāmehin) voids urine mixed with fat or fat itself;
one who passes marrow (majjamehin) voids urine mixed with marrow or marrow itself.
One who has *hastimeha* urinates copiously like an intoxicated elephant; the urine is watery, sweet, and non-irritating, and being obstructed by that very lymph (*lasīkā*), it flows continuously.

One who has *madhumeha* urinates like honey; the vital essence (*ojas*) is oily and sweet, but due to its dryness, Vāyu imparts an astringent quality to it, whereby one with *madhumeha* urinates what is followed by astringency and sweetness, like honey.
That [madhumeha], however, is held by some to be of two types:
arising from the depletion of the bodily elements (*dhātu-kṣaya*) or from the obstruction of the humors (*doṣāvaraṇa*) due to the provocation of *vāyu*.

For when the *vāyu* is thus obstructed, it seizes the essence of the food (*āhāra-prasāda*) and repeatedly manifests symptoms of the humors and their increase or decrease without apparent cause, thereby bringing about the difficult-to-cure madhumeha.
All of these, when neglected, result in the condition of *madhumeha*;
therefore, all are designated by the term *madhumeha*, because in all cases one voids sweet urine as before, and the body itself becomes sweet-tasting.
In that regard, catarrh, looseness of the body, anorexia, indigestion, salivation, vomiting, excessive sleep, cough, and so forth are the complications arising from kapha-type [fevers].
Testicular tearing, urinary urgency, pain in the penis, acid eructation, thirst, fever, burning sensation, fainting, diarrhea, and jaundice are the complications arising from pitta-type [fevers].
Catching pain in the heart, restlessness, insomnia, trembling, colic, constipation, emaciation, cough, and dyspnea are the symptoms of those [types of prameha] born from Vāta (AS.Ni.

10.11). Now, when his body is thus excessively moistened by the vitiation of fat and other factors, and the bodily tissues are permeated by the doshas, ten types of carbuncles (*piṭaka*) arise—fatal to life and accompanied by most agonizing complications—due to their localization in specific regions such as fleshy parts, joints, and vital points (*marma*), as the prameha further progresses (AS.Ni.
Furthermore, in the lower part of the body,
the humors of those suffering from urinary disorders are indeed directed toward that [region],
as follows:
Śarāvikā, kacchapikā, jālinī, putriṇī, vidārikā, sarṣapikā, masūrikā, alajī, vinatā, and vidradhi (AS.ni.10.12).
Among these, śarāvikā is dark-brown, accompanied by moisture and pain, with a depressed center and elevated margins, and it has the shape and size of a shallow bowl (AS.ni.10.12).
*Kacchapikā* is deeply rooted, characterized by painful pricking sensations, smooth, and resembles the back of a tortoise;
*mahāśayā* involves intense pain and pricking, is stiff, exudes a glossy discharge, and is covered with a network of fine pores, muscles, and veins;
*jālinī* consists of large pustules covered with small ones; and *putriṇī* is likewise covered with numerous small pustules.
*Kaṇṭhinā* is hard and round like the tuber of the *vidārī* plant;

*vidārikā* ripens quickly and is accompanied by great pain; *sarṣapikā* is shaped and sized like a mustard seed and covered with pustules of that same kind; *masūrikā* is shaped and sized like a lentil (*masūra*).

Alajī is a large, painful swelling that arises suddenly, burning the skin, covered with vesicles, spreading, red or black, causing excessive thirst, delusion, and fever; it is characterized by a preponderance of burning sensation and is extremely distressing.
Vinatā, however, is a deep-seated ulceration located on either the back or the abdomen, accompanied by blue discoloration, intense pain, and discharge;
it will be described separately as Vidradhi (abscess).

Among these, the first five are difficult to endure because they arise from an excessive accumulation of phlegm (*śleṣman*) and fat (*medas*), sharing the same nature as the primary disease and causing its increase;
however, the others are not so, due to the predominance of bile (*pitta*) and the resulting smallness of phlegm and fat.
Furthermore, due to the influence of *prameha*, an aggravation of the respective *doṣas* occurs in the carbuncles (*piṭaka*).
On this subject, there is a verse:
"Even in the absence of *prameha*, these [carbuncles] arise in one whose fat (*medas*) is vitiated. (AS.ni.10.14)
And they are not perceived as such as long as there is no grasping of the object—
[namely,] that which is turmeric-colored or red, and devoid of the premonitory signs of *meha*.

If one urinates [a substance] that is not [the typical urine of] meha, they know that to be rakta-pitta (blood-bile). Having observed prameha that is sweet, slimy, and honey-like, there should be a twofold investigation.

From overfilling [of the channels], there arises a condition originating from phlegm (kapha); when the humors (doṣas) are diminished, it becomes characterized by wind (vāta). Those types of urinary disorders (meha) caused by phlegm and bile, as well as those caused by wind, occur sequentially along with their premonitory symptoms (pūrvarūpa).
Those [types of] hemorrhoids caused by pitta are palliable; however, they are curable if the fat (medas) is not excessively vitiated.
Thus ends the tenth chapter.
Now begins the eleventh chapter: We shall now expound the diagnosis of abscesses (vidradhi), swellings (vṛddhi), and abdominal tumors (gulma).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and others:
"By consuming foods that have been kept overnight, or those that are hot, dry, parched, or burning [in their effects]..."
Through lying on uneven beds, various physical movements, and various factors that vitiate the blood, [the disease] takes refuge in the skin, flesh, fat, bone, sinews, blood,
and tendons. (AS.Ni.11.3)
A swelling, whether external or internal, which has large roots and causes great pain— whether it be circular or elongated— is known as *vidradhi* (an abscess), and it is said to be of six types.
By the humors (doṣas), individually or combined, and by blood and trauma,
there occurs an external [growth] in various parts of the body that is severe, knotted, and elevated.
Internal, more terrible, deep-seated, and dense like a thicket;
rising up like an anthill; and like a fire or a weapon that strikes swiftly.
In the navel, bladder, liver, spleen, pleura, heart, abdomen, or groins,
or in the kidneys or the anus, there may be extremely intense pain due to vāta.
It is dark reddish-brown, slow to suppurate, and irregular in shape; it is accompanied by piercing pain,
cutting pain, vertigo, distension, throbbing, spreading, and a sound.
Due to pitta, it is reddish-copper or black, accompanied by thirst, delusion, fever,
and burning; due to kapha, it is pale, itchy, and characterized by rapid onset and suppuration.
Accompanied by nausea, coldness, stiffness, yawning, anorexia, and heaviness;
with delayed onset and a burning sensation, it is a mixed type arising from the derangement of all three humors (sannipāta).
By implication, one should here distinguish between the external and internal characteristics:
[the internal type] is covered with black vesicles, is dark-brown, and is accompanied by intense burning pain, agony, and fever. (AS.Ni.11.11)
The external [type] has the symptoms of pitta and blood, while the internal [type] occurs only in women;
it arises from injury by weapons and the like, or in one who consumes unwholesome food after being wounded.
The heat of the wound, scattered by the wind and impelling pitta along with blood,
produces an abscess (vidradhi) characterized by pitta and blood, accompanied by many complications.
The specific types of complications among them are recorded according to the difference in their locations:
hiccup occurs at the navel, and urine becomes foul-smelling and difficult to pass at the bladder.
In the case of obstruction in the liver, there is labored breathing; in the spleen, swelling and thirst;
furthermore, in the *kloman*, there is constriction of the throat; and in the heart, there is a seizing of all the limbs.
Diabetes, asthma, cough, a sensation of the heart being torn apart,
pain in the abdomen, flanks, chest, and shoulders, and the occurrence of flatulence in the abdomen.
There is stiffness of the thighs, groins, kidneys, waist,
and back, as well as pain in the sides and obstruction of flatus in the anus.
One should diagnose their states of being unripe, ripened, or suppurated as one does for swellings;
those ripened above the navel discharge through the mouth, while those below it discharge through the anus. (AS.Ni.11.18)
One should know that in a *vidradhi* (abscess), the humors arise from the anus, mouth, or navel due to moisture;
among these, the one born of the combination of all three humors (*sannipātaja*) should be avoided, just like [the incurable types of] ulcers.
When the abscess is suppurated and located in the heart, navel, or bladder, it may burst either internally or externally; or,
being suppurated, it may leak from the mouth in a person who is emaciated and afflicted by complications.
In the same way, when the veins of the breasts become distended upon reaching women who have recently given birth or those who are pregnant, a dense swelling may arise.
Because the openings of the channels are extremely subtle, [the flow] does not occur in virgins. When the wind moves with its passage obstructed, it becomes enraged and causes swelling and pain.
Reaching the testicles from the groin,
[the vāta] compresses the vessels that carry to the scrotum and causes enlargement of the two scrotal sacs.
That disease, Vṛddhi, is of seven types: caused by the humors (doṣas), blood, fat, urine, and the intestines.
Even those arising from urine and the intestines are due to the wind (vāta); the difference lies solely in their causes.
AS.ni.11.25 A sensation like touching a leather bag filled with air, being rough, and pain without a visible cause arises from wind (vāta).
AS.ni.11.26 Resembling a ripe udumbara fruit, accompanied by burning, heat, and suppuration, it arises from bile (pitta).
From *kapha*, [the swelling] is cold, heavy, unctuous, pale-yellow, hard,
and slightly painful; from blood, it is covered with black vesicles and exhibits the symptoms of increased *pitta*.

AS.ni.11.27 An increase of fat due to phlegm is soft and resembles the fruit of the palmyra palm. AS.ni.11.28 That which arises from urine occurs in one who habitually suppresses the urge to urinate and while passing urine.
Like a leather bag filled with water, it becomes agitated and tender;
there is difficulty in urination, and folds (valayas) appear at the base of the scrotum.

By foods that aggravate the wind (*vāta*), by immersion in cold water, by the suppression [of natural urges], by fighting, carrying heavy loads, traveling on foot, and by moving the limbs in an uneven manner;

AS.ni.11.29–30. By foods that aggravate the wind, by immersion in cold water, by the suppression [of natural urges], by fighting, carrying heavy loads, traveling on foot, and by moving the limbs in an uneven manner.
When the wind, agitated by other disturbing factors and having vitiated the small intestines, leads it downward from its own location; AS.ni.11.31.
Then,

situated at the groin joint, that Vāyu produces a swelling resembling a knot (granthi). If it is neglected, it causes enlargement of the scrotum (muṣkavṛddhi) characterized by distension, pain, and stiffness.

When pressed, it moves with an internal sound and causes distension; when released again, it returns. This intestinal hernia (āntravṛddhi), which has the same appearance as a flatulent hernia (vātavṛddhi), is incurable.

AS.Ni.11.33–34: Gulma is of eight types— arising from each of the doṣas individually, from their combinations, and from their collective accumulation— and it is characterized by a network of veins that are rough, black, or reddish, appearing like lattice windows.
And due to the disorder of the menstrual blood (ārtava), the eighth [type] arises in women.

Now, if one who has been emaciated by diseases such as fever or diarrhea, or by procedures such as emesis, being desirous of food, consumes foods that increase *vāta*, or drinks cold water immediately after eating and drinking, or indulges in activities that agitate the body—such as fasting, swimming, sexual intercourse, or traveling in vehicles—or if he provokes undigested hunger (*chardi*), or suppresses already provoked *vāta* and other humors, or holds his breath in inhalation and exhalation, or performs emesis and purgation without prior oleation; or if, having already been purified, he again indulges in excessively heating or obstructive substances—then the provoked humors, dominated by *vāta* according to their respective natures, whether individually, combined, or all together, or accompanied by blood, enter the great channels (*mahāsrotas*), block the upward and downward pathways, and inevitably producing pain, bring about the formation of a *gulma*.

AS.ni.11.35 Because one suffers there as if pierced by a stake, afflicted by intense pain, and breathes with difficulty, it is therefore called *śūla* (colic). AS.ni.11.36 In that condition, due to excessive emaciation, or because of the obstruction of the pathways by *kapha* and *pitta*, the *vāyu* (wind), having found a support, leaps up; becoming hardened through dryness, whether independent or dependent upon its own site or the sites of *pitta* and *śleṣman*, it becomes perceptible to touch. Although formless, because it is massed together, it assumes, as it were, a form and remains in the shape of a knot (*granthi*), thereby receiving the designation *gulma* (abdominal tumor).
AS.ni.11.36: Its five locations are the bladder, the navel, the sides, and the heart.

Now, its premonitory symptoms are: lassitude, impairment of the digestive fire and the body, lack of relish for food, intolerance of satiety, pain in the abdomen, flatulence, frequent belching, vomiting when food is undigested, abdominal distension, and the appearance of fecal matter without its normal evacuation.

AS.ni.11.37: Among these, due to Vāta, there is a piercing pain as if from a needle or a spike; stiffness of the neck, headache, pain in the temples, fever, body ache, splenic enlargement, flatulence, intestinal gurgling, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), obstruction of breath, dryness of the mouth, and rigidity of the limbs. During times when Vāta is aggravated, complications increase; there is irregularity of digestion, and the skin, nails, and other parts become blackish, reddish, or rough. Furthermore, because of the mobility of Vāta, the gulma (abdominal lump) arises and subsides at various locations with pains that may be slight or great. It feels as if covered by ants, characterized by much pricking and throbbing; it seems to stretch the skin over its own site and sometimes seems to contract it. It causes horripilation, and when the pain becomes intense, it generally affects the entire body, though it is often localized in the bladder region.

From pitta arise burning, a sensation of fuming, acidity, thirst, fever, perspiration, diarrhea, fainting, relief from cold applications, and a greenish or yellowish discoloration of the skin and other parts; furthermore, there is a *gulma* (abdominal tumor) that, like a heated iron ball, burns that location, causing pain, fuming, and heat, being as tender as a loose ulcer, hairless, and generally situated near the navel.

From *kapha* arise: numbness, anorexia, indigestion, a coating of the heart, cold fever, satiety, lassitude, cough, nausea, coryza, sleepiness, laziness, whiteness of the nails and other parts, and *gulma* that is numb, stable, heavy, hard, deep-seated, slightly painful, and generally located in the heart and flanks;
when these signs are combined, it is due to a combination [of doshas].
That [gulma] is of three types;
among all collections [of diseases], it is a collection-gulma (nicaya-gulma) and is incurable.

However, blood-gulma (rakta-gulma) occurs only in women, due to the specific nature of the womb and the menstrual flow, as well as dependence on others, lack of independence, and compliance with medical treatment.
In that regard,

when she is menstruating, has recently given birth, or suffers from a vaginal disease, if she indulges in vāta-aggravating substances, then her aggravated vāyu enters the opening of the vagina and obstructs the menstrual flow.

Being thus obstructed, it develops the abdomen month by month and manifests the signs of pregnancy, such as nausea, drowsiness, physical exhaustion, longing for specific things, and the appearance of breast milk.

Furthermore, due to the involvement of *vāyu* and the excessive aggravation of *pitta*, it gradually assumes the characteristics of a *vāta-pitta-gulma*, characterized by pain, stiffness, burning sensations, diarrhea, and so forth. There is especially intense pain in the uterus (*garbhāśaya*), which causes foul odor and discharge from the vagina.
Moreover, unlike a fetus, a *gulma* does not consist of distinct limbs; rather, it feels like a single mass and throbs with pain only after a long time.
Only the *gulma* (abdominal lump) increases, not the abdomen; furthermore,
every *gulma* is established upon its own specific *doṣa*.
Therefore, [other abscesses] ripen either after a long time or not at all;
however, because its seat is blood that is severely corrupted, a *vidradhi* (abscess) undergoes rapid suppuration.
And on this point, there is a verse:
In Gulma with internal localization, there is pain in the bladder, abdomen, heart, and spleen;
loss of digestive fire, complexion, and strength, and the non-occurrence of natural urges.
Conversely, in the external abdominal cavities, there is not much pain; rather,
there is discoloration and a marked protrusion of the space externally.
When there is distension of the abdomen accompanied by swelling, extremely severe pain,
and intense gaseous inflation due to the obstruction of flatus in both the upward and downward directions, they designate that condition as ānāha (intestinal obstruction).
A *ghana* is like a *aṣṭhīlā*; a *granthi* is a *aṣṭhīlā* that is elevated upward.
A *ānāha* has the same symptoms, whereas a *pratyaṣṭhīlā* is transverse and shaped like a *aṣṭhīlā*.
When the Vāyu moves from the colon (pakvāśaya) toward the anus and the perineum (gudopastha), causing intense pain,
it becomes *tūnī*; however, when that same [Vāyu] moves in the opposite direction, it becomes *pratūnī*.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter.
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
AS.Ni.12.1: Hereafter, we shall expound the chapter titled "The Diagnosis of Abdominal Enlargement" (Udaranidāna).
"Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and others:
'All diseases arise when the digestive fire is weak, but abdominal diseases especially do so. (AS.ni.12.1–2)
Due to indigestion and the consumption of impure foods, a collection of impurities arises;
obstructing the upward and downward flow of the bodily constituents, it blocks the channels that carry water.
Having vitiated the prāṇa, apāna, and agni [vātas], [the doṣas] located in the skin, flesh,
and joints cause distension of the abdomen; that abdominal enlargement (udara) is divided into eight types.
[The abdomen is afflicted] by the various doṣas individually and collectively, as well as by splenic enlargement, intestinal obstruction, perforation, and ascites.
Afflicted by that [condition], with parched palates, lips, feet, hands, and bellies, they lose their physical exertion, strength, and appetite; emaciated, their abdomens are distended.
Men may appear like hungry ghosts; this is the characteristic of one who is destined [to die].
There is a loss of appetite, and all food is digested only after a long time and with a burning sensation.
He does not distinguish between what is digested and what is undigested, nor can he endure satiety;
his strength constantly diminishes, and he pants even when performing slight exertion.
Swelling of the thighs, lack of movement, some edema in the feet,
pain in the bladder and joints, and distension even after eating only light and small amounts of food—

The appearance of lines [on the abdomen] and the destruction of folds occur in all types of abdominal enlargements; furthermore, there is drowsiness, lassitude, accumulation of waste, and diminished digestive fire.
There is burning, swelling, distension, and finally the appearance of water;
however, this [other type] is entirely without water, reddish, without swelling, and not very heavy.
The network of veins becomes like a lattice of windows and is constantly making a gurgling sound;
having obstructed the umbilical region and produced a forceful impulse, it then vanishes.
The Vayu (Māruta) causes pain in the heart, waist, navel, anus, and groin;
it issues forth with sound, while the feces are bound and urine and excrement are scanty.
The digestive fire is neither too weak nor excessive, and there is no greed or distaste in the mouth.
In that case of vātodara (wind-belly), swelling occurs in the hands, feet, scrotum, and joints.
Pain in the flanks, abdomen, waist, and back; breaking pain in the joints;
dry cough; aching of the limbs; heaviness in the lower body; and retention of waste products.

The abdomen becomes dark-brownish or reddish in color, with skin and other features that suddenly undergo fluctuating decrease and increase; it is accompanied by pricking pain and a sense of being split open, and is covered with thin, black veins.
It produces a sound like that of a bloated leather bag,
and the wind there moves in all directions with pain and noise.
In *pittodara* (bilious abdominal enlargement), there is fever, fainting, burning sensation, thirst, a bitter taste in the mouth, vertigo, diarrhea,
yellowness of the skin and other parts, and a greenish hue of the abdomen. (AS.ni.12.18)
Bound by yellowish-red vessels, perspiring, and hot, it burns;
it smokes, has a soft touch, suppurates quickly, and is intensely inflamed.

In *śleṣmodara* (abdominal enlargement caused by phlegm), there is lassitude of the limbs, drowsiness, swelling, and heaviness; as well as excessive sleep, nausea, loss of appetite, dyspnea, cough, and a pale complexion of the skin and other parts.
The abdomen is distended, steady, glossy, marked with white streaks,
and large; it increases slowly, is hard, cold to the touch, heavy, and stable.
By those various factors that aggravate the three *doṣas*, by the menstrual impurities provided by women,
and by poisons such as artificial and natural toxins, the *malas* (impurities) accumulate along with blood.

Having reached the abdominal cavity and undergoing transformation, they produce a most dreadful abdomen characterized by the three symptoms, accompanied by swelling, fainting, and vertigo, which suppurates quickly.
And that [disease] is especially aggravated by the sight of cold winds and clouds (AS.Ni.12.24),
and by the agitation of one who has overeaten, as well as by activities such as riding in vehicles (AS.Ni.12.24).
Due to excessive sexual intercourse, carrying heavy loads, traveling on foot, or emaciation from disease,
the spleen located on the left side becomes displaced from its position and increases in size.
Or, if the blood has increased from the lymph-chyle and other tissues, one should increase that [treatment];
it becomes extremely hard like a stone, elevated like the back of a tortoise.
Increasing gradually, it causes the abdomen to swell within the womb,
accompanied by dyspnea, cough, thirst, a bad taste in the mouth, flatulence, pain, and fever.
Accompanied by pallor, fainting, vomiting, burning sensations, and delusion;
it appears reddish, discolored, or marked with blue and yellow streaks.

One should recognize the presence of the doshas there in their respective order by upward movement of wind (udāvarta), pain, swelling, delusion, thirst, burning sensations, fever, heaviness, anorexia, and hardness.
One should treat splenomegaly arising from the right side, as well as a displaced liver;
and [treat] those with obstructed channels in the anus due to food eaten together with eyelashes and hair.
When provoked by dyspepsia-inducing foods, upward-moving disorders, or foods that cause coating of the stomach,
the wind (vāyu), becoming aggravated, obstructs the feces, bile, and phlegm. (AS.Ni.12.31)

The apāna [vāyu] moves toward the abdomen; by that, there may arise burning sensations, fever, thirst, and sneezing, as well as cough, dyspnea, weakness of the thighs, and pain in the head, heart, navel, and anus.
There is attachment to impurities, lack of appetite, vomiting, and a distended abdomen with obstructed wind;
it is firm, covered with blue or reddish veins, or devoid of such veins.
And above the navel, it generally takes on the shape of a cow's tail (gopuccha) due to bone fragments and other foreign objects, or by eating food containing such substances, or by overeating.
The intestines are torn and cooked, and [the contents] flow out through their openings;
the undigested matter (āma) itself passes from the rectum, followed by very small amounts of fecal matter and chyle.
Equal to the stench of a corpse, slimy, yellowish-red,
and filling the rest of the belly, it brings about a terrible abdominal disease.
It increases below the navel and quickly attains the nature of water;
it takes on the appearance of the aggravated *doṣas* and is pervaded by dyspnea, thirst, and vertigo.

They call this *chidrodara* (perforated abdomen), while others call it *parisrāvī* (effusive); it occurs in one who has suddenly drunk water after beginning the administration of oleation therapy and the like.
In one who drinks excessive water, whose digestive fire is weak, or who is emaciated or excessively thin,
the wind (vāyu) and phlegm (kapha), having obstructed the channels of water, become overwhelmed by the fluid.
Then that very water, having moved from its place and taken refuge in the abdomen, causes it to increase;
consequently, there arises abdominal enlargement (udara) accompanied by thirst, discharge from the anus, and pain.

Accompanied by cough, dyspnea, and anorexia, the abdomen is distended with prominent veins; it feels like a water-filled leather bag to the touch, and it emits sounds, trembles, and is subject to agitation.
Dakodara (ascites) is large, glossy, firm, and has a protruding navel; furthermore,
due to neglect, all the *doṣas* have shifted from their own locations.
Due to the process of digestion, the fluids liquefy even the openings of the joints and channels; furthermore,
external sweating is obstructed when it is directed obliquely.
Having replenished that very water, one should prepare a medicinal paste (picchā); at that time, there would be a heavy abdomen, firm, round, and not producing a sound when struck.
It is soft, free of lines, touched at the navel, and glides along;
it is born from water, and thereafter there is a further increase of the abdomen.
The signs described for abdominal dropsy arising from water, including the disappearance of veins,
apply to dropsy caused by vāta, pitta, kapha, the spleen (plīha), their combination (sannipāta), and water itself.

The difficulty increases progressively; beyond a fortnight, the patient is generally lost. Furthermore, all [such cases] where fluid has appeared and which are accompanied by the complications mentioned regarding fatal signs (riṣṭa) [are incurable].

Generally, all types of abdominal enlargement (udara) are considered most difficult to treat from the very moment of their onset. However, that which is caused by the absence of water (ajātāmbu), occurring in a strong person, and having recently arisen, can be cured with effort.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter.

Now begins the thirteenth chapter: We shall now expound the chapter entitled "The Diagnosis of Anemia (Pāṇḍu), Edema (Śopha), and Erysipelas (Visarpa). AS.Ni.13.1. 1. Now, therefore, we shall explain the chapter on the diagnosis of anemia, edema, and erysipelas.
"Thus indeed have the great sages, Ātreya and the others, declared:
when the impurities (malās), dominated by pitta, are provoked by the aforementioned provocative factors," *Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha*, Ni. 13.1–2.
There, the pitta situated in the heart, being driven by the powerful vāyu,
reaches the vessels (dhamanīs) and pervades the entire body. (AS.ni.13.2–3)
Having vitiated the phlegm, skin, blood, and flesh, it takes refuge within;
it produces various kinds of discolorations on the skin between the skin and the flesh.
Because the colors pale-yellow, turmeric-yellow, and green possess an excess of paleness (*pāṇḍutva*),
that disease is called *pāṇḍu*; due to it, there is heaviness (*gaurava*).
There would be a loosening of the bodily constituents (dhātus) and a depletion of the qualities of ojas;
consequently, one becomes deficient in blood and fat, devoid of essence, and has flaccid sense organs.
With limbs as if being crushed and a heart that does not soften,
with swollen eye-sockets and face, irascible, spitting, and speaking little.
One who hates food, hates the cold, has withered body hair, and has extinguished digestive fire;
one whose thighs are weak, who suffers from fever, labored breathing, ringing in the ears, exhaustion, and dizziness.
That [madatyaya] is of five kinds, caused by the humors individually or collectively, and from the eating of clay.
Its premonitory symptom is palpitation of the heart and dryness of the skin.
Loss of appetite, yellowish urine, absence of perspiration, and diminished digestive fire;
exhaustion and fatigue— these arise from Vāta, along with body ache, piercing pain, and trembling.
AS.ni.13.10 Blackness, roughness, and redness of the veins, nails, feces, urine, and eyes;
AS.ni.13.11 Swelling, abdominal distension, bad taste in the mouth, dryness of the stool, and pain in the flanks and head.
AS.ni.13.11 From pitta arise veins that appear greenish-yellow, fever, and darkness (delusion).
AS.ni.13.12 Thirst, perspiration, fainting, desire for cold things, foul odor, and a bitter taste in the mouth [also occur].
There is frequent discharge of feces, sour belching, burning sensation, and the appearance of white veins due to kapha.
AS.Ni.13.13: Drowsiness, a salty taste in the mouth, horripilation, and loss of voice [occur].
Cough and vomiting arising from the combination [of all three doshas] possess mixed symptoms and are extremely difficult to endure.
Earth is bitter and subdues wind; alkaline soil is pungent and subdues bile; and saline soil is sweet and subdues phlegm.

Having corrupted the tastes and other elements, and having dried up what has been eaten through its own dryness (raukṣya), it fills the channels with undigested matter and, by obstructing them, produces [disease] as described before.
Then, suffering from jaundice, with a swollen navel, feet, face, and penis,
the man voids stool that is broken up, mixed with blood and phlegm, like that of worms.
If one suffering from anemia (pāṇḍuroga) consumes substances that increase pitta, it may lead to jaundice (kāmalā).
Pitta, residing in the visceral tract and the peripheral tissues, having scorched the blood and flesh, brings about this condition.
Having yellow eyes, urine, skin, nails, face, and excrement; suffering from burning sensations, indigestion, and thirst; eating like a frog; and having impaired sense faculties.
This [jaundice] may occur even in one with a predominance of pitta, even apart from anemia (pāṇḍuroga).
Through neglect, it becomes characterized by swelling and is difficult to cure; this is Kumbhakāmala.
When a pale-yellow, dark-green, or yellowish discoloration occurs in cases of anemia (pāṇḍuroga),
there may be vertigo, thirst, lack of sexual desire for women, and mild fever arising from vāta and pitta.
Lassitude, loss of strength and digestive fire, *loḍhara*, that [condition] is called *halīmaka* and *alasa*; these are declared to be their premonitory symptoms (*upadrava*).
Those characterized primarily by swelling have been described; therefore, that [condition] itself is now being explained.
Vāyu, when vitiated, carries the vitiated pitta, rakta, and kapha into the external vessels (AS.ni.13.22).
Having been led there, their movement being obstructed, they take refuge in the skin and flesh;
this raised, compact swelling is called *utsedha* (elevated swelling) because it arises from a collection [of humors]. (AS.ni.13.22–23)
AS.ni.13.23 Everything consists of nine substances due to the distinctions of their causes and the variations in their forms.
AS.ni.13.24 [Diseases arise] from the humors individually, from pairs [of humors], from all [humors combined], from trauma, and also from poison.
Alternatively, [the swelling] is of two kinds: innate (*nijam*) and adventitious (*āgantum*); and it is further classified as affecting the whole body (*sarvāṅgaja*) or a single limb (*ekāṅgaja*).
They know it to be of three types according to the specific characteristics of being broad (*pṛthu*), elevated (*unnata*), or knotted (*grathita*).

The general cause of swellings arising specifically from the [vitiated] doshas is for one who has been quickly depleted by disease, physical labor, fasting, and so forth, yet continues to engage in such activities.
Furthermore, for another person, there may be an excessive intake of heavy, sour, unctuous, and cold foods;
or salt, alkaline, pungent, and hot substances; or [excessive consumption of] leafy vegetables, water, sleep, and staying awake.
Eating clay, village meat, or dried meat; indigestion, physical exhaustion, and sexual intercourse;
walking on foot along a path, or traveling in a vehicle that causes agitation—[these are to be avoided].
Dyspnea, cough, diarrhea, hemorrhoids, abdominal enlargement, menorrhagia, fever, cholera,
intestinal torpor, vomiting, erysipelas, and anemia.
Furthermore, other doshas, when improperly treated, remain situated in the chest;
those located in the middle part produce swelling in the upper body, in the bladder in the lower body, and in the middle part.
AS.ni.13.30: [The humors] pervade all limbs and reside within each individual part;
their precursors are burning sensations, stretching of the vessels, and heaviness of the limbs.
Swelling caused by Vata is mobile, dry, with rough hair, and reddish-black;
it is characterized by contraction, throbbing, horripilation, pain, piercing, tearing, and numbness.
AS.ni.13.32 Rapid arousal and subsidence: it rises quickly when pressed, and the body becomes thin;
it is pacified by unctuous, warm massages; it is slight at night and great during the day.
The skin becomes as if smeared with mustard seed, and it experiences a tingling sensation;
due to bile, there appears a yellowish, reddish, or blackish luster, and the body hair turns copper-colored.
In the middle [stage], the pacification of the rapid pursuit [of the breath] first arises in the body, characterized by thirst,
burning heat, fever, perspiration, dryness, moisture, intoxication, and dizziness.
It desires cold, causes diarrhea, is malodorous, intolerant to touch, soft, itchy,
has pale hair and skin, is hard, cold, and heavy.
Oily, smooth, stable, and thick, it causes sleep, vomiting, and loss of digestive fire; when suppressed, it does not rise, its onset is difficult to pacify, and it gains strength at night.
When wounded by a blade of *kuśa* grass or similar instruments, blood flows slowly or as a slimy discharge;
there is a desire for touch and warmth. These three types arise from *kapha* and so forth, and from their respective combinations (*dvandva*).
Due to the confusion of causes and signs, and from the accumulation [of various factors], it consists of a collection;
through impact by weapons and the like, there arise cutting, piercing, wounding, and so forth.
From contact with the cold winds, the ocean winds, the juices of *bhallātaka* and *pikacchu*,
or with [their] bristles, there occurs swelling of the ears accompanied by erysipelas (*visarpa*).
AS.ni.13.40 It is intensely hot, has a reddish luster, and is generally characterized by the symptoms of *pitta*.
AS.ni.13.41 That which arises from poison results from the crawling over or the urination of venomous creatures.
From the falling of the fangs, teeth, or claws [of venomous creatures], even those creatures that are not poisonous [become harmful];
and from contact with feces, urine, semen, or the mixing of soiled garments.
Due to contact with the wind from a poison-tree, or by the application of a toxic powder (garayoga),
[the bite] becomes soft, mobile, pendulous, and quickly produces burning and pain.
A swelling that is new and free from complications is curable; one that is not so has been described as incurable.
Visarpa (erysipelas) arises from the same causes—humors, affected tissues, and external trauma—as swelling.
They say that it has three bases, because it relies upon the external, the internal, and both;
and among these, the faults are increasingly difficult to remedy as one proceeds.
Aggravated by provocative factors, especially those that cause a burning sensation,
they spread rapidly through the body; remaining within, they move from the interior to the exterior.
One should know that those situated externally reside in both [the external and internal], while those residing within have their support therein.
This occurs due to the affliction of the vital points (marmans) and the obstruction of the channels (ayanas).
Due to excessive thirst, the irregular discharge of the bodily urges,
and the rapid loss of digestive fire and strength, [the disease] arises; in the external [type], it is the opposite of this.
Among these, *parīsarpa* caused by *vāta* has symptoms identical to those of *vāta-jvara*;
it is characterized by swelling, throbbing, pricking pain, piercing pain, stiffness, distress, and horripilation. (AS.ni.13.48–49)
From pitta, it moves rapidly, exhibits the symptoms of pitta-fever, and is excessively red; from kapha,
it is accompanied by itching, is unctuous, and has a pain similar to that of kapha-fever.

If neglected, all [these swellings] are covered with eruptions (sphoṭa) characterized by their own specific defects. AS.Ni.13.51: When they have ripened and burst open, they each bear the characteristic signs of a wound (vraṇa).

[The patient] suffers from fever, vomiting, fainting, diarrhea, thirst, and vertigo arising from wind and bile (vāta-pitta), as well as bone pain, loss of digestive fire, darkness before the eyes, and anorexia.
It makes every limb appear as if strewn with glowing embers;
whatever region the erysipelas (visarpa) spreads to, that very place becomes thus.
AS.ni.13.53 It is black like extinguished coals, or blue, or red, and it accumulates quickly.
AS.ni.13.54 Because of its rapid movement, it spreads swiftly like eruptions caused by a fire.
When Vāta becomes excessively powerful, it causes a spreading erysipelas (visarpa) that follows the vital points (marmas);
it then causes pain in the limbs, takes away consciousness and sleep, and provokes labored breathing.
Having fallen into such a state, he suffers from hiccups; indeed, there is no place where he is not seized by the torment of skin diseases while lying on the ground or sitting upon beds and seats.
Then, while moving about, the afflicted person experiences sleep arising from exhaustion of both mind and body; being difficult to awaken, this condition is called agnivisarpa.
The wind (pavana), obstructed by phlegm (kapha), having split that phlegm into many parts, [causes the disease].

Or, in one with increased blood (vṛddharakta), it affects the blood located in the skin, vessels, ligaments, and flesh; and having vitiated it, [it produces] elements that are long, minute, round, thick, and rough.
It forms a garland of red nodules accompanied by intense pain and fever, along with dyspnea, cough, diarrhea, dryness of the mouth, hiccups, vomiting, and vertigo. (AS.Ni.
Accompanied by delusion, discoloration, fainting, breaking pain in the limbs, and loss of digestive fire—
this is Granthivīsarpa, arising from the provocation of Kapha and Vāta.
From the combination of *kapha* and *pitta*, there arises fever, stiffness, drowsiness, sleepiness, headache,
exhaustion of the limbs, tossing about, delirium, anorexia, and vertigo.
Fainting, loss of digestive fire, splitting pain in the bones, thirst, heaviness of the sense organs,
evacuation of undigested matter (āma), and a coating of the channels— this [āmavāta] spreads throughout the body.
Generally seizing the seat of the stomach and only one part of it, it is not excessively painful,
and is covered with pustules that are very yellow, red, or pale-white.
It has a dark-blue luster, is black, glossy, dirty, swollen, and heavy;
it undergoes deep suppuration, is intensely hot to the touch, becomes moist when touched, and cracks open.
When the flesh has sloughed off like mud, the network of tendons and veins is clearly visible,
and there is a corpse-like odor, they call that type of erysipelas *kardama*.
Arising from all [causes] and possessing all symptoms, it is a mirror for all the bodily constituents (*dhātu*);
provoked by injury to an external cause, it agitates the *pitta* along with blood.
The Vāta humor may produce Visarpa (erysipelas), characterized by eruptions resembling Kulattha beans,
abounding in swelling, fever, pain, and burning sensations, and appearing dark-bluish or reddish.
Those arising from both wounds and systemic causes are incurable, as are all those that have invaded the vital points (marmas).
Those in which the tendons, vessels, and flesh are decayed, which are excessively moist, and which smell like a corpse, are likewise incurable.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter titled "The Diagnosis of Kuṣṭha, Śvitra, and Kṛmi.
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
Through improper diet and conduct, especially through that which is antagonistic, and by practicing such acts as censuring the virtuous, slandering others, and stealing their property;
The impurities, driven forth immediately by past sinful actions,
enter the obliquely coursing channels and settle in the skin, lymph, blood, and flesh.
Corrupting [the tissues], loosening them, and emerging from there outward,
they cause discoloration of the skin; the wise call that *kuṣṭha*.
Because it consumes that entire body when neglected over time,
having entered and pervaded all the internal elements, it brings about their complete putrefaction.
AS.ni.14.6 Through these [worms], which cause sweating, moistening, and putrefaction, and which are minute and extremely cruel,
the body hairs, skin, sinews, vessels, and young bones are gradually destroyed.
From this [treatment], one should consume [the remedy] for white leprosy (śvitra), which is declared to be external to [the major types of] kuṣṭha.
Kuṣṭhas are of seven kinds, arising from the doṣas individually, in combination, or when all have come together.

AS.ni.14.8: Although all [types of leprosy] involve the three doṣas, they are designated according to which one is predominant. From vāta arises the kāpāla type of kuṣṭha; from pitta, the audumbara; and from kapha, [the maṇḍala].
Maṇḍala, vicarcī, and that called ṛṣya arise from vāta and pitta;
carma, ekakuṣṭha, kiṭibha, sidhma, alasaka, and vipādikā [arise from kapha].
Those arising from wind and phlegm, as well as ringworm (*dadru*), *śatāruṣī*, *puṇḍarīka* with eruptions, *pāmā*, and *carmadala*, arise from phlegm and bile.
With all [the preceding symptoms] together, it is *kākaṇaka*; with the first three plus *kākaṇaka*, it is *dadru*.
*Puṇḍarīka*, *ṛṣyajihva*, and the others—these are the seven great leprosies (*mahākuṣṭha*).
Excessive smoothness or roughness of touch, perspiration or absence of perspiration, discoloration of the skin, burning sensation,
itching, numbness, pricking pain, elevation of urticarial patches (koṭha), and fatigue [are the signs].
In these cases, there is excessive pain in the ulcers, rapid onset, and long duration;
even when healed, they remain dry, and they undergo suppuration even with a slight cause.
Horripilation, blackness of the skin, and roughness— these are the primary symptoms of *kuṣṭha*.
It resembles a blackish-red skull, is dry, numb, harsh, and thin.
The *kāpāla* [type of leprosy] is extensive, with no distinct boundaries, covered with bristling body hair, characterized by intense pricking pain, accompanied by little itching, and spreads rapidly.
It has a copper-colored skin like that of a ripe udumbara fruit, with hair and veins as pale as gold;
it is thick, full of moisture, red, and causes burning sensations and pain.
One should know that the Udumbara worm causes rapid emergence and bursting;
it is firm, thick, heavy, unctuous, white or red in color, and slow-moving.
Mutually adhering, elevated, with much itching, discharge, and worms;
a circular patch with smooth, yellowish margins.
Vicarcikā is characterized by itching and pustules, is dark-brown in color, and abounds in serous discharge.
It is rough, has thin reddish margins, is dark-brown within, and is elevated.
AS.ni.14.20 Accompanied by pain, burning, and discharge, and covered with hard pustules;
AS.ni.14.21 That which has the shape of a deer's tongue is called *ṛṣyajihva*, and it is full of worms.

AS.ni.14.21 Kiṭibha is characterized by a rough touch like that of an elephant’s hide, is known as *camaka*, has a large base, and is free from perspiration; furthermore, it resembles a fragment of fish. Sidhma is rough, with a touch like that of calluses or coarse skin, itchy,
and harshly black; though dry on the outside, it is oily within and sheds dust when rubbed.
AS.ni.14.23 It has a smooth touch and is thin, white, and copper-colored, like the *dugdhika* flower.
AS.ni.14.24 It generally occurs on the upper part of the body and is covered with itchy eruptions (*gaṇḍa*).
Due to blood, there is alasaka, cracking of the hands and feet,
vipadika, intense pain, slight itching, and the body being covered with reddish pustules.
AS.ni.14.25 Long-spreading, with the hue of *dūrvā* grass or the *atasī* flower; AS.ni.14.26 *Dadru* has destroyed circular patches, is itchy, and is persistent.
Śatāru has a thick base, is accompanied by burning pain, is reddish-brown in color, and consists of many ulcers;
it is rich in moisture and parasites, and generally arises at the joints.
With reddened edges, pale in the center, and accompanied by itching, burning,
and pain; swollen and covered with red [spots] like the rays of a lotus petal.
Puṇḍarīka is characterized by an abundance of thick, flowing lymph and blood, is quickly suppurating, and is covered with white and reddish pustules on thin skin.
Eruptions, pustules, scabies, itching, exudation, and excessive pain; these [lesions] are small,
dark-brown or reddish, numerous, and generally appear on the buttocks, hands, and elbows.
Accompanied by cracking, unable to tolerate touch, and characterized by itching, piercing pain,
burning, redness, flaking skin, and peeling like a bark, it is called *kākaṇaka*, marked by intense burning and pain.
First it is red and black, resembling the *kākaṇantī* fruit; then,
endowed with all the symptoms of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), it becomes multicolored.

One should indicate the predominance of the doshas in skin diseases (kuṣṭha) by means of the signs and actions prescribed in the chapter on the classification of doshas; one should avoid treating those cases where all the doshas are excessively aggravated.
That which has been described as occurring in the *riṣṭha* (tendons), and that which resides in the bone, marrow, and semen, is palliable;
that which has reached the fat is difficult to cure, while that which involves the bile, the two-fold [humors], the blood, and the flesh is incurable.
That which is not difficult to treat is characterized by an abundance of *kapha* and *vāta*, and when the single *mala* (impurity) is located in the skin.
When *kuṣṭha* is situated in the skin, there occurs pricking pain (*toda*), discoloration (*vaivarṇya*), and dryness (*rūkṣatā*).

In the case of blood and muscle [vitiation], there is perspiration, numbness, and swelling (AS.ni.14.35). Furthermore, there are eruptions localized in the hands and feet, and excessive moisture in the joints (AS.ni.14.36).
When [vitiated] fat is present, there is deformity of the hands, loss of mobility, and cracking of the limbs;
when it resides in the bone and marrow, there is collapse of the nose, redness of the eyes, and loss of voice.
When the semen is afflicted by worms, there is injury to one's own wife and offspring;
and all the symptoms previously described for the [affliction of] blood and the other humors likewise occur.
That which arises solely from *kuṣṭha* is called *śvitra*, *kilāsa*, and *aruṇa*;
it is described as non-exuding (*aparisrāvi*) and as being dependent on the origin of three *dhātus*.
From wind (vāta), it is rough and reddish; from bile (pitta), it is copper-colored like a lotus petal.
I shall now describe [the symptoms] that destroy the body hair: it is white, thick, heavy, and itchy due to kapha;
one should recognize [these same characteristics] appearing successively in the blood, muscle, and fat.
By its very color, both of these are difficult [to treat], and each subsequent one is more so than the preceding;
[the first] has many non-white hairs that are not intermingled with one another and is new.
Leucoderma that has not been burnt by fire is curable; otherwise, it is to be rejected.
Even if it is recent, [it is incurable] when it arises on the private parts, the palms of the hands, or the lips.
From indulging in contact, food, bedding, and so forth, all diseases generally arise; in particular, disorders of the eyes and skin are mobile.
Worms are said to be of two kinds, distinguished by being external or internal;
they are of four types based on their origin from external impurities, phlegm, blood, or feces. (AS.Ni.14.45)
By name, there are twenty kinds of external [spirits] arising from impurity;
they are the size of sesame seeds in form and color, and they take refuge in hair and clothing.
Those known by the names *yūkā* (lice) and *likṣā* (nits) are many-legged and minute;
they produce two kinds of skin eruptions: pustules and itchy swellings.
Those born internally have kuṣṭha as their sole cause, and among them, those born from phlegm (śleṣman) predominate;
[these are caused] by sweet foods, jaggery, milk, curd, roasted barley flour, and fresh rice.
Born from phlegm (kapha) in the stomach (āmāśaya) due to the consumption of feces, various grains, leafy vegetables, sesame oil-cakes, and so forth, these [worms] grow large and crawl everywhere.
Some resemble broad beans, some are like earthworms;
others have the shape of sprouted grain, being thin, long, or minute.
White and copper-colored, they are sevenfold by name:
the entrail-eaters (antrādā), the belly-twisters (udarāveṣṭā), the heart-eaters (hṛdayādā), and the great-growers (mahāruhā).
Darbha flowers that are fragrant cause nausea,
salivation, indigestion, and anorexia.
Fainting, vomiting, fever, constipation, emaciation, sneezing,
and chronic rhinitis [are caused by] minute creatures born of blood that reside in the blood-carrying vessels.
Footless, with rounded copper-colored bodies, some are invisible due to their extreme minuteness;
they are the Keśādās, the Lomavidhvaṃsas, the Lomadvīpas, and the Udumbaras.
These six types of kuṣṭha, which share the same action and have the breast-milk as their mother,
arise from the feces in the colon and spread downwards.
When they become increased and turn toward the stomach (āmāśaya),
then his eructations and breaths will follow the odor of feces.
Broad, round, thin, and thick, and dark-brown, yellow, white, and black—
these five are the worms known by the names Kakeruka and Makeruka.
The sausurādā, known as salūna, and lelihā produce diarrhea,
colic, constipation, emaciation, roughness, and pallor. (AS.Ni.14.58)
The fourteenth chapter [ends] with "due to the emergence of horripilation, suppression of fire, and itching of the anus.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnosis of wind-diseases (vātavyādhi);
thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
In the accomplishment of all purposes and misfortunes, the wind is the sole cause of this entire universe; it is especially so for the body, whether it be healthy or diseased.
He is Viśvakarman, the soul of all, the universal form, the Lord of Creatures;
he is the creator, the sustainer, the pervasive Viṣṇu, the destroyer, death, and the ender.
Therefore, one should always strive with effort to avoid those two faults;
regarding the recognition of their defects, the natural and the unnatural [causes] have been previously described.
In this chapter on the classification of disorders (*doṣabheda*), both in brief and in detail, the names, locations,
individual fivefold movements, and functions of the morbid states (*vaikṛta*) are described.
Its classification is now stated, along with its causes and characteristics,
in order to enumerate what was previously mentioned as being beyond numbering by means of eighty [categories].

Vāyu becomes aggravated by those things that cause the depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātus) when they are excessively consumed; moving through the empty channels, it fills them intensely once again.
Having reached those [channels] which are filled with other defects, the powerful [Vāyu],
becoming enraged, produces colic, constipation, and intestinal distress in the colon (pakvāśaya).
It causes obstruction of the feces, urinary stones, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, and stiffness of the three [upper back], the back, and the waist,
as well as various other difficult complications in the lower part of the body.
In the stomach (āmāśaya), there arise thirst, nausea, dyspnea, cough, and choleraic pain (viṣūcikā);
also obstruction of the throat, eructations, and diseases located above the navel.
In the case of the ears and other sense organs, there is impairment of their function; in the skin, cracking and roughness;
in the blood, intense pain, numbness, burning heat, discoloration, and loss of its natural redness.
When it has reached the muscle and fat tissues, it causes obstruction of the channels, loss of appetite, emaciation,
giddiness, and hard, painful nodules accompanied by piercing pain and dizziness.
The limbs of the teacher become heavy, extremely painful, and stiff, as if struck by fists or clubs;
when located in the bones, it causes intense pain in the bones of the thighs and joints, along with a loss of strength.
When located in the marrow, it causes hollowness in the bones, sleeplessness, constant pain,
and either the rapid discharge, retention, or morbid alteration of semen.
Similarly, when located in the semen, it causes distension and depletion of the vessels;
when situated there [in the semen], being fixed in the sinews, it produces sciatica, stiffness, and hunchback.
When the *vāyu* has reached the joints, it causes swelling with a sensation like that of a leather bag filled with air,
as well as pain during the processes of extension and contraction.
AS.ni.15.17 It rests upon all the limbs and consists of pricking, piercing, throbbing, breaking, stiffening,
convulsing, numbness, joint-pain, contraction, and trembling.
But when the enraged [wind] repeatedly enters all the channels (dhamanī),
it then convulses the limbs; this disease is known as ākṣepaka (convulsive seizure).
The wind, struck below and moving upward, enters the channels situated in the heart and,
having entered them, afflicts the heart, the head, and the temples.
One should cause the limbs to contract all around and bend them like a bow;
thereafter, one breathes out with difficulty, the eyes being stiff, drooping, and closed.
If one coos like a pigeon and is unconscious, that is apatantraka; and that same condition is called apatānaka when the wind has been released from the heart.
One may repeatedly experience well-being and repeatedly experience ill-health when [the womb] is obstructed;
this [condition] arises from miscarriage or is produced by excessive bleeding.
And that which arises from trauma is indeed the most difficult to treat;
for I consider it so when the wind, having become obstructed within, blocks the channels.
Then it pervades the entire body and the collarbone is stretched;
the limbs become like a drawn bow, and there is rigidity and a fixed stare of the eyes.
He yawns, gnashes his teeth, and spits out phlegm; he experiences pain in the sides and suffers from stiffness of the speech, jaw, back, and head.
"Internal extension" (antarāyāma) is this [breath], and external extension (bāhyāyāma) is of that same kind. Due to the external extension of the body, the head is drawn backward.
If the chest is tossed about, the neck is crushed there;
there is discoloration of the teeth and the mouth, perspiration, and stiffness of the limbs.
They say that an external swelling which is accompanied by trembling and is forceful is a *dhanuṣkampa*;
this occurs when it reaches a wound situated at a vital point (*marman*) due to the agitation of the wind (*samīraṇa*).
The humors exert pressure upon the entire body from head to foot;
stretching for one who is thirsty and has pale limbs is prohibited.
When the force has subsided, there will be restoration of health in all cases of convulsions (ākṣepakas).
[From] scraping the tongue, eating dry food, or from injury— AS.Ni.15.31.
When the Vāyu, located at the root of the jaw, becomes aggravated, it causes the jaw to sag; furthermore,
it may cause the mouth to remain wide open or, conversely, to be tightly closed.

By that [condition], there would be drooping of the jaw, and chewing and speaking would be performed with great difficulty. When the Vāyu resides in the channels of the speech-carrying vessels, it causes the tongue to become stiff.

AS.ni.15.33 Tongue-tiedness is the inability to consume food, drink, or speak because of that [wind]. AS.ni.15.34 Carrying a heavy load on the head or speaking excessively with loud laughter [is the cause of this].
From terror, yawning, sneezing, and the drawing of a stiff bow,
from an uneven pillow, and from chewing hard things— AS.ni.15.35.
When the wind (vāyu) is aggravated by various wind-increasing factors and ascends upwards,
it causes the distortion of one half of the face, including the speech, laughter, and gaze.
Then his head shakes, there is a blockage of speech, fixedness of the eyes,
trembling of the teeth, loss of voice, loss of hearing, and suppression of sneezing.
AS.ni.15.37 There is loss of the sense of smell, confusion of memory, and fear arises in one who is asleep.
AS.ni.15.38 There is spitting, moving toward the side, and the closing of one eye.
Intense pain above the knees, or even in one half of the body,
some call that *ardita*, while others call it *ekāyāma*.
When the wind (vāyu), relying on the blood, affects the vessels of the head that support it,
making them rough, painful, and black, that condition is known as sirāgraha, which is incurable.
Having seized half of the body and having dried up the vessels and tendons, the wind strikes one side,
loosening the bonds of the joints.
His entire half-body would become incapacitated and devoid of sensation;
some call this condition "disease of a single limb," while others know it as "hemiplegia."
Likewise, when the wind (anila) is localized throughout the entire body, it causes diseases of all the limbs;
a hemiplegia (pakṣaghāta) caused by pure wind is considered the most difficult to cure.

But a fistula caused by injury that has become associated with another [type] is difficult to treat and should be avoided. One accompanied by *kapha* causes obstruction of the channels with undigested matter (*āma*) and produces stiffness of the limb.
The wind known as Daṇḍaka, having destroyed all vital functions, makes [the patient] incurable;
the wind situated at the base of the shoulder contracts the vessels located there.
That which causes the movement of the arms is called *apavāhuka*;
it is the tendon (*kaṇḍarā*) of the fingers that extends from the palm to the back of the arm.
That which removes movement from the arms is known as Viśvācī. When the Vāyu situated in the waist seizes the tendons of the thigh, [it causes the condition known as Akṣepaka].
Then the creature becomes lame; indeed, it becomes a cripple in both its legs. At the start of walking, it trembles and moves as if limping.
One should know that *kalāyakhañja* is characterized by the loosening of the binding of the joints.
It is caused by the excessive consumption of things that are cold, hot, liquid, dry, heavy, or unctuous.
In cases of indigestion, as well as through fatigue, agitation, sleep, and staying awake;
when phlegm, fat, and wind are excessively accumulated along with undigested matter (āma).
When one suppresses the other dosha and it becomes excessive,
it fills the interior of the thigh bones with stagnant phlegm.
Then he stiffens them with that [wind]; the thighs become rigid, cold, and insentient.
Like those belonging to another, they become heavy and extremely painful.
Accompanied by lassitude, numbness, drowsiness, vomiting, anorexia, and fever,
it is joined with weakness of the feet, difficulty in lifting them, and numbness. (AS.ni.15.52–53)
They call that ūrustambha; others, however, call it āḍhyavāta. It is a swelling arising from vāta and blood (vātaśoṇita) in the middle of the knee, accompanied by great pain.
AS.ni.15.54 The Kroṣṭuka-śīrṣa [fever] should be known as being thick like the head of a jackal.
AS.ni.15.55 When pain arises in the foot due to uneven standing or from fatigue, it is [the fever] called Ruk.

When the wind (vāta) takes hold of the ankle, they call that condition *vātakaṇṭaka*. When the tendons (*kaṇḍarā*) of the heels and the toes are afflicted by the wind, [that is known as *pārṣṇigraha*].
It suppresses the upward displacement of the thigh; that is called *gṛdhrasī*.
*Viśvācī* and *gṛdhrasī* are described as being accompanied by severe pain in the knee, which is termed *khallī*.
When both feet of a person feel as if they are numb and become swollen,
that condition should be known as *pādaharṣa*, arising from the provocation of *kapha* and *vāta*.
Vāyu, accompanied by pitta and blood, causes a burning sensation in the feet;
one should specifically diagnose that as *pādadāha* (burning of the feet), especially when it occurs while walking.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter [of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-nirdeśa*].
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnosis of vāta-śoṇita (blood disorders caused by wind);
thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
Food that is burning-hot, incompatible, and various other such things corrupt the blood;
as do sleeping, waking, and sexual intercourse when practiced contrary to the prescribed rules.
Generally, when the blood of men who are delicate by nature, who do not habitually practice walking,
and who have been afflicted by injury or impurity becomes vitiated;
When Vāyu is increased by vāta-aggravating factors or cold things, it becomes provoked and moves into wrong channels;
obstructed by such blood, it first vitiates that very blood.
Āḍhyaroga, khuḍa, vātabalāsa, and vātaśoṇita—
these are the names by which it is known; and it first attacks the feet.
Hanging [testicles] due to specific conditions such as riding on vehicles and the like are its characteristics;
likewise, there will be a wasting away similar to leprosy (kuṣṭha) as well as flaccidity of the limbs.
In the knees, calves, thighs, hips, shoulders, hands, feet, and the joints of the limbs,
there occur itching, throbbing, piercing pain, splitting pain, heaviness, and numbness.
Having come into being again and again, they perish; and having repeatedly manifested, they vanish.
Sometimes they take their stand at the base of the feet, and sometimes even at the hands.
Like the enraged venom of a rat, it spreads throughout the entire body;
first, it arises as a superficial swelling resting upon the skin and flesh.
In the course of time, it spreads deeply into all the tissues;
when accompanied by itching and other symptoms, the skin becomes raised and coppery, dark, or reddish.
In the deep [type of swelling], there is excessive pain greater than before, intense burning and heat at night,
a knotted swelling that suppurates, and it spreads into the joints, bones, and marrow.
Moving with speed, as if piercing within and making crooked gestures,
it moves everywhere throughout the body, causing one to become lame or crippled.
When Vata is predominant, there is excessive pain, throbbing, and pricking;
the swelling is characterized by dryness, blackness, or a dark-brown color, and it fluctuates in size.
Contraction of the vessels, joints, and fingers, stiffness of the limbs,
excessive pain, aversion to cold, lack of relief [from cold], rigidity, tremors, and numbness.
In the blood-type [inflammation], there is swelling, excessive pain, pricking, a coppery color, and a tingling sensation;
it is accompanied by itching and exudation, and does not subside with either unctuous or dry treatments.
In the case of pitta, there is a burning sensation, confusion, perspiration, fainting, intoxication, thirst,
intolerance to touch, pain, redness, swelling, suppuration, and intense heat.
In kapha disorders, there is rigidity, heaviness, numbness, unctuousness, and coldness;
