there is itching and dull pain, and when there is a combination [of doshas], all the symptoms appear together.
A case following from a single doṣa that is recent is curable; one arising from two doṣas is manageable (yāpya);
however, one arising from all three doṣas, which is discharging, rigid, and forms tumors (arbuda), should be abandoned.
The wind (māruta), having entered and obstructed one another within the branches and joints, quickly destroys the path of the blood and carries away the vital breaths (asūn) through intense pains.
In the fivefold wind, *prāṇa* [is aggravated] by dryness, physical exercise,
fasting, overeating, injury, travel, the urging of natural urges, and suppression [of those urges].
When aggravated, it may bring about the impairment of the eyes and other sense organs,
as well as many diseases such as chronic catarrh, thirst, cough, and asthma.

The udāna [vital air] is disturbed by the suppression of sneezing, eructation, vomiting, and sleep, as well as by heavy loads, excessive weeping, laughter, and other such factors; it then produces diseases.
It causes constriction of the throat, loss of consciousness, vomiting, anorexia,
and diarrhea, as well as diseases localized above the clavicles, such as goiter and others.
The *vyāna* [vital air], when vitiated by excessive walking, standing, playing, or uneven physical exertions,
as well as by opposing factors, dryness, fear, joy, grief, and so forth, [causes disease].
The loss of virility, enthusiasm, and strength; swelling, mental agitation, and fever;
diseases of the entire body, piercing pain, horripilation, and numbness of the limbs.
The Samāna [vāyu], through irregular, undigested, cold, or mixed foods, causes leprosy, erysipelas, and all other diseases that affect the entire body.
Furthermore, one who is corrupted by sleeping and staying awake at improper times brings about diseases such as colic,
abdominal tumors, and malabsorption syndrome, which arise in the regions of the small intestine and the stomach.
Apāna [vāyu] is provoked by dry and heavy food, suppression of natural urges, excessive straining,
and by the overuse of traveling in vehicles, sitting, standing, and walking.
When aggravated, it produces many difficult-to-cure diseases localized in the colon (pakvāśaya),
such as disorders of urine and semen, hemorrhoids, prolapse of the rectum, and others.
And all [disorders] caused by the wind (māruta) are accompanied by drowsiness, numbness, heaviness, oiliness, loss of appetite,
lethargy, coldness, swelling, and loss of digestive fire.

One should recognize that the condition is free from *āma* when there is a desire for pungent and dry things, as well as relief through similar [remedies], whereas the opposite of drowsiness and other such symptoms indicates its presence.

The obstruction of the *vāyu* by [other doshas] will now be described in its many varieties. When *vāyu* is obstructed by *pitta*, the symptoms are burning sensation, thirst, colic, giddiness, and darkness before the eyes.

Burning sensations caused by pungent, hot, sour, and salty substances; a desire for cold things; coldness, heaviness, and pain; and relief primarily from pungent and similar substances [are the symptoms].
In the case of [fever] covered by phlegm (kapha), there is a desire for fasting, physical exertion, and things that are dry and hot;
in the case of [fever] covered by blood, there is a burning sensation and pain, which is intense when located between the skin and the flesh.
There may be redness, swelling occurs, and circular patches appear;
furthermore,
there is a hard swelling of the flesh that is discolored, as well as pustules.
A sensation like the crawling of ants arises,
and there is a swelling in the limbs that is mobile, glossy, soft, and cold, accompanied by anorexia.
This should be known as "rich-vata" (āḍhyavāta); it is difficult to treat when vāta is occluded by fat (medas).
When occluded by bone (asthi), the patient welcomes contact that is extremely hot and pressure.
When [the body] is pervaded by marrow, the limb is excessively pricked as if by a needle; it becomes weary, suffers from piercing pain,
bends, yawns, and feels as if it is being constricted.
And when [the semen] is being pressed with both hands, one experiences relief from the pain;
when obstructed by the semen, there is either excessive force, or else it is fruitless.
When the wind (vāyu) is obstructed by food, there is pain in the stomach after eating, which subsides once the food is digested;
when it is obstructed by urine, there is non-emission of urine and distension of the bladder.
When obstructed by feces, there is constipation below, and it causes cutting pain in its own location;
the fatty substance (sneha) quickly undergoes decay, and the person feels bloated after eating.
When food is pressed down by feces, it causes pain; when dry, it is expelled only after a long time.
When the bodily wind (vāyu) is obstructed by all the constituent elements (dhātus), there is pain in the hips, the groins, and the back.
When the vital breath (prāṇa) is obstructed by bile (pitta), the wind moves in a contrary direction, there is physical discomfort, the heart is excessively pained,
and there is vertigo, fainting, pain, and a burning sensation. (AS.ni.16.43–44)
When food is improperly digested, emesis occurs if it resides in the udāna; there is confusion and other such symptoms.
If it resides in the samāna, there is internal burning and loss of strength; however, if it resides in the vyāna, the burning sensation is all-pervasive.
Fatigue, restriction of bodily movement, and a burning sensation accompanied by pain;
(furthermore,) the impairment of the digestive heat (*samāna-uṣman*), excessive perspiration, restlessness, and thirst.
There would be a burning sensation in the *apāna* [wind], and the feces would take on a turmeric-yellow color;
there is excessive pain and a feverish heat in the vagina, the urethra, and the anus.
But when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is obstructed by phlegm (*śleṣman*), exhaustion, anorexia, and vomiting occur.
The retention of spittle, sneezing, eructation, exhalation, and inhalation [is caused by the *udāna*];
heaviness of the limbs, loss of appetite, and obstruction of speech and voice [are also caused by the *udāna*].
In the case of Vyāna, there is loss of strength and complexion, stiffness of the joints, bones, and speech,
heaviness in all the limbs, and a marked faltering in gait.
When the *samāna* [vāyu] is obstructed, there is excessive coldness, absence of perspiration, and weak digestion;
when the *apāna* is obstructed by kapha, there is the discharge of urine and feces.
Thus, they know that there are twenty-two kinds of obstruction of the vital air (vāyu);
likewise, the prāṇa and the others obstruct one another in their respective order.
All these are the twentyfold obscuration of knowledge; [they include] the suppression of inhalation and exhalation, catarrh, and stiffness of the head.
When the udāna is obstructed by the prāṇa, there is heart disease and dryness of the mouth;
when the prāṇa is obstructed by the udāna, there is a loss of complexion, vitality, and strength.
Following this method, the physician should analyze all obstructions by observing the locations of the bodily winds (vātas) and their increase or decrease in functional activity.
And there is a mutual mixed obscuration among the five [breaths], beginning with prāṇa;
[this occurs] through the twelve [factors] beginning with pitta, and by those [factors] being mixed with one another.

Likewise, through various combinations of pitta and the other [doshas], the obstruction becomes manifold; and due to the variations in their relative proportions, the number of such obstructions becomes infinite.
One should observe that [disease] attentively, according to the arising of its respective signs, and repeatedly, even when it is hidden, by means of its gradual response to therapeutic measures.
Specifically, the *prāṇa* is said to be life and the *udāna* is said to be strength;
from the affliction of these two, there occurs the loss of both lifespan and strength.
If the obstructed vital winds remain for a year— whether unrecognized or recognized—
they become difficult to cure even with great effort, or they may become incurable.
Abscesses, splenic disorders, heart disease, abdominal tumors, loss of digestive fire,
and other such conditions arise as complications when those [vital breaths] are obstructed and neglected.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter; the third section, the Section on Diagnosis (Nidānasthāna), is completed. Now begins the Section on Therapeutics (Cikitsāsthāna).
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of fever;
thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.

When the dosha, accompanied by undigested matter (sāma), stays in the stomach (āmāśaya), it destroys the digestive fire and obstructs the channels; because it thereby produces fever, one should administer fasting (laṅghana).
In the premonitory symptoms of fever and other diseases, or during the onset itself, one should diligently preserve one's strength;
for health is the foundation of strength, and the entire course of medical treatment is for the sake of health.
When the doshas have been diminished by fasting, when the digestive fire is kindled, and when lightness has been attained,
health, hunger, thirst, relish for food, digestion, strength, and vitality arise.
In that case, when the humors are aggravated, excessively provoked, predominantly characterized by *kapha*,
and mobile, there occur nausea, excessive salivation, aversion to food, cough, and choleraic diarrhea (*viṣūcikā*).
In one who has just eaten and has developed a fever characterized by undigested matter (āmadoṣa),
emesis is especially recommended for those fit for emetics; otherwise, one should not perform it.
For dyspnea, diarrhea, fainting, heart disease, and irregular fever,
one should administer ghee combined with long pepper, or with *kaliṅga* fruits, or with licorice.
Having drunk warm water, one should induce vomiting with honey-water or salt-water,
or with the decoctions of *paṭola*, *nimba*, *karkoṭa*, *vetra*, and leaves.
One who understands the distinctions of strength and time should administer emetics consisting of thin gruel, scum, sugarcane juice, wine, or those [substances] prescribed in the [relevant] chapters.
Whether emesis has been performed or not, a patient suffering from fever should undergo depleting therapy (viśoṣaṇa) in order to digest and pacify the aggravated doshas.
Just as food does not digest when covered by raw matter or ashes in the fire, so too [the fever] does not subside;
therefore, one should fast those suffering from fever until the morbid humors have been digested.
In a fever caused by vāta and kapha, one should drink very small amounts of warm water when thirsty; this,
having dissolved the kapha, will quickly alleviate the thirst.
Having stimulated the digestive fire and softened the channels, one should purify them;
this promotes the downward movement of the obstructed pitta, vāyu, sweat, feces, and urine.
Cold [therapy] removes sleepiness, lassitude, and loss of appetite, and serves as a support for the vital breaths; the opposite of this increases the accumulation of the humors.
Although it possesses such qualities, one should employ heat [as a remedy] even when there is not an absolute predominance of pitta.

In cases of aggravated pitta characterized by irritation, burning sensations, delusion, and diarrhea; in disorders arising from poison or alcohol; in summer; in those emaciated by chest wounds; and in those suffering from internal hemorrhaging (asrapitta).
Water prepared with *ghanacandana*, ginger, *parpaṭa*, and *uśīra*—
this cold water is beneficial for them; it is digestive and removes thirst and fever.
Heat does not exist without bile, and fever does not exist without heat;
therefore, one should avoid things contrary to bile even more so when bile is predominant.
In the case of fever with acute pain caused by undigested matter (āmaja), one should avoid bathing, oil massage, ointments, residual food, and fasting—
just as one would avoid these when suffering from indigestion— to alleviate the colic.
One should not drink that medicine, for it would bring about even more *āma*;
for one whose digestive tract is overwhelmed by *āma*, milk is like the venom of a serpent.
In cases of swelling of the chest, nasal catarrh, and dyspnea, as well as pain in the calves, joints, and bones caused by vāta and śleṣman, sudation (sveda) is recommended;
it promotes the flow of sweat, urine, feces, and flatus, and brings about sharpness of the digestive fire.
One should observe everywhere the rules of conduct prescribed for oleation therapy (AS.Ci.1.22).
Fasting, sudation, time [of administration], barley gruel, and bitter tastes [are the remedies] (AS.Ci.1.23).
Digestive stimulants (pācana) should be administered for the various morbid humors (mala), either according to the specific stage of the disease or in their proper sequence.
Lightening therapy (laṅghana) is indicated in cases of pure vāta disorders, wasting (kṣaya), exogenous fevers (āgantujvara), and chronic fevers (jīrṇajvara).

For among those [fevers], that which is beneficial is desired as a pacifying (śamana) treatment rather than one that causes emaciation. One should recognize a fever caused by *sāma* (undigested toxins) by its symptoms, provided it has not yet undergone desiccation (*aviśoṣita*).
One should consider the two types of knowledge regarding therapeutic measures for fasting (laṅghana); when it is appropriate,
one should treat the patient who shows signs of having fasted with thin gruels (peyā).
From the beginning, one should administer [the decoctions] prepared with their respective medicinal herbs, preceded by a gruel (maṇḍa),
for six days, or until the fever attains mildness.
By these [foods], his digestive fire is kindled, just as a fire is by fuel-sticks;
and they stimulate the digestive fire because of their medicinal composition and lightness.
They facilitate the downward movement of flatus, urine, feces, and the bodily humors (doṣas).
Due to their liquid and warm nature, they promote sweating, and due to their softness, they alleviate thirst.
Because it serves as food, because it promotes life, and because of its lightness;
because it destroys fever and is wholesome for those suffering from fever, therefore one should first [treat] with gruels (peyā).
One should treat all fevers at their onset with the exception of those arising from alcohol; first,
one should administer easily digestible parched grain porridge (*lājapeyā*) mixed with ginger, coriander, and long pepper.
One who desires sourness should drink that [alkali] with rock salt and pomegranate; or, one who has passed stool and has excessive bile should drink it cold with dry ginger and honey.
One suffering from pain in the bladder, the flanks, or the head should take [milk] prepared with vyāghrī and gokṣura,
along with pṛśniparṇī, balā, bilva, nāgara, utpala, and dhānyaka.
One who suffers from fever and diarrhea should consume a prepared thin gruel (*peyā*) that is sour, digestive-stimulating, and carminative;
one suffering from hiccup, cough, asthma, or bronchial catarrh should do so with the *hrasva-pañcamūla* (the five roots of small stature).
One afflicted by *kapha* with constipated stools should drink barley prepared with the "great five roots" (*pañcamūla-mahat*), along with *yava*, *pippalī*, and *āmalaka*.
Barley gruel fried with ghee promotes the downward movement of impurities and morbid humors;
[it may be prepared] with *cavikā*, *pippalīmūla*, *drākṣā*, *āmalaka*, and *nāgara*.
When the abdominal cavity is obstructed, painful, and characterized by cutting sensations, one should drink a preparation made from *kola*,
*vṛkṣāmla*, *kalaśī*, *dhāvanī*, and *śrīphala*.
One afflicted by thirst and suffering from sleeplessness and lack of perspiration [should drink a decoction] of sugar, *āmalaka*, and ginger;
or [a decoction] of sugar, jujube, *mṛdvīkā*, *sārivā*, *musta*, and sandalwood.
One should prepare a drink mixed with honey that destroys thirst, vomiting, burning sensations, and fever; likewise,
one may prepare soups, meat broths, and other such preparations using these very same medicinal herbs.
In one who has developed an addiction to liquor, in whom the kapha has moved to the seats of pitta,
and who suffers from thirst, vomiting, and burning sensations during the summer when those two [pitta and kapha] are predominant; AS.Ci.1.40.
When blood flows upwards, they do not desire a gruel (peyā) for those [patients]; however, in such cases,
[one may use] grapes, pomegranate, kāśmarya, pathyā, pīlu, and parūṣaka.
One should prepare parched grain satiations (lājatarpaṇa) with madhūka and badara fruits, mixed with honey and sugar-candy,
either crushed in fever-alleviating water or taken with plain water.
Then, once the satiating drink has been digested, one should drink an extremely fine powder; or,
if hungry, one should eat barley gruel or boiled rice with fried grains.

This six-day regimen should be observed by one who seeks to protect both his strength and the [remaining] humors, using soups prepared with water and salt, or meat broths made from mung beans or wild grains.
Then,
once the humors (doṣas) have been ripened by fasting and other such measures,
a decoction (kaṣāya) is recommended for the remaining portion of the humors, as it either promotes their digestion (pācana) or pacifies them (śamana).
Bitter [taste] should be employed especially in cases of pitta, and pungent [taste] in cases of kapha;
although astringent [taste] also removes pitta and kapha, it is not recommended for that purpose.
In acute fever (navajvara), due to the stagnation of the impurities (mala), a decoction (kaṣāya) produces irregular fevers (viṣamajvara) as well as anorexia,
nausea, hiccups, flatulence, and other such symptoms.
The impurities (malas), congealed by the astringent tastes, neither fall away nor undergo digestion;
moving obliquely or along wrong paths, they even increase the fever.
Because of the binding of *āmadoṣa*, *kapha*, and *vāta*, it also causes pain,
abdominal distension, and other such symptoms; some say the medicine should be administered after seven days, while others say after ten days.

Some [authorities] maintain that this [emetic therapy] should be administered to one who has eaten light food when the [doshas] are aggravated, but not to one afflicted by a severe fever when the force of the doshas is rising; for [in such a case], it would cause harm.
Alternatively, when the *doṣa* is excessively accumulated and causes drowsiness and a sense of stiffness,
the medicine, instead of being digested, further inflames the fever.
When the fever has become mild, the body light, and the impurities (malas) have been mobilized,
then one should administer medicine even for a patient who has only recently suffered from fever.
Pāṭhā,
uśīra, and vālaka should be prepared as a decoction or a cold infusion, combined with parpaṭa, or with śuṇṭhī and duḥsparśā.
One should drink that, and likewise [a decoction of] bhūnimba, guḍūcī, musta, and nāgara;
these decoctions should be administered as appropriate to digest the doṣas.
Pāṭhā, indrayava, bhūnimba, musta, parpaṭaka, and amṛtā destroy fever, anorexia, thirst, bad taste in the mouth, and indigestion. (AS.Ci.1.54–55)
In Jayantī, the drugs combined with mahauṣadha cure diarrhea and fever.
For fever caused by vāta, [one should use] durālabhā, amṛtā, mustā, and nāgara.
Alternatively, pippalī root, guḍūcī, viśvabheṣaja,
and the minor pañcamūla, combined with honey, [are used] in cases of pitta.
Kaliṅga, mustaka, kaṭukā, mustā, parpaṭaka, as well as dhanvayāsa and bhūnimba—
this is the Vatsakādya group [of drugs] for kapha.
Alternatively, *vṛṣa*, *gāṅgeyī*, *śṛṅgī*, *eraṇḍa*,
and *durālabhā* constitute a digestive stimulant and carminative for cases associated with pain, obstruction, wind, and phlegm.
Abhayā, pippalīmūla, śamyāka, kaṭukā, ghanam,
kaliṅgakas, the leaf of paṭola, and kaṭukarohiṇī.
Paṭola, sārivā, mustā, pāṭhā, and kaṭukarohiṇī;
paṭola, nimba, triphalā, mṛdvīkā, mustā, and vatsaka.
Kirātatikta, amṛtā, candana, and viśvabheṣaja;
dhātrī, mustā, amṛtā, and honey— these constitute the completion of half-verse formulations.
AS.Ci.1.62 These five are considered the pacifiers for the five [types of] santata and the others. AS.Ci.1.63 Patola, indrayava, ariṣṭa, bhadramusta, amṛtā, and the two [types of] dvaya.
The two types of sārivā, pāṭhā, trāyantī, kaṭurohiṇī,
paṭola, ariṣṭa, mṛdvīkā, śamyāka, triphalā, and vṛṣa.
Candana, uśīra, dhānya, abda, guḍūcī, and viśvabheṣaja;
devadāru, sthirā, śuṇṭhī, vāsā, dhātrī, and harītakī.
These five formulations, consisting of *sārivā*, *drākṣā*, *śatāhvā*, *kaṇā*, and *reṇukā*, combined with honey and sugar (or molasses), destroy the five types of fevers. (AS.Ci.1.65–66)
Kāśmarya, sārivā, drākṣā, trāyamāṇā, amṛtā, and guḍa;
śatapuṣpā, vacā, kuṣṭha, devadāru, and hareṇukā.
Māṃsī, musta, and dhānyaka combined with sugar and honey; or kṛṣṇā, punarnavā, drākṣā, śatāhvā, guḍa, and sārivā [combined with sugar and honey].
Śāliparṇī, balā, drākṣā, sārivā, and chinnaruhā;
āragvadha, balā, rāsnā, kāśmarya, madhuka, and jaggery.
Either the fresh juice of śatāvarī or chinnaruhā mixed with jaggery,
or the juice of amṛtā combined with kṛṣṇājīra, sugar, and ginger.
The juice of *amṛtā* alone quickly conquers fever caused by *vāta*.
[AS.Ci.1.70] *Bhārṅgī*, *sarala*, *gāṅgeyī*, *dāru*, *kuṣṭha*, and *elavāluka*— [AS.Ci.1.71]
In fever caused by Vāta, one should drink lukewarm ghee mixed with jaggery;
in fever caused by Pitta, one should take the *paṭolādi* and *guḍūcyādi* groups as prescribed in the Sūtrasthāna.
The *añjanādi* group, along with *kāśmarya*; the *sārivādi* group with sugar; white sugar (*sitā*), *madhuka*, *kāśmarya*, *śīta*, *uśīra*, and *parūṣaka*.
Guḍūcī, sārivā, lodhra, kamala, utpala, and sugar; drākṣā, abhayā, atikta, ghana, śamyāka-phala, and parpaṭa.
Śyāmā, parpaṭa, duḥsparśa, tiktā, atiktā, sitā, and vṛṣā; śarkarā, tiktaka, kaṭukā, trāyamāṇā, and bibhītaka.
Parpaṭa, combined with guḍūcī and āmalaka, or even alone,
may be used as a decoction (kaṣāya) or as a cold infusion (hima); likewise, a decoction or cold infusion made from tiktā, drākṣā, madhuka, and nimba [may be employed].
Kaṭukā, ground finely and mixed with sugar, cures fever caused by pitta;
for fever born of kapha, ativiṣā, uśīra, paṭola, marica, and kṣapa [are used].
Samūla, indrayava, dvīpi, kuṣṭha, nimba, vacā, and jaggery; and saptacchada, amṛtā, nimba, sphūrjāta, combined with honey.
Niśā, trikaṭuka, tiktā, nāgapuṣpa, kaliṅgaka,
sārivā, ativiṣā, kuṣṭha, duḥsparśā, musta, and guggulu.
Parūṣaka, triphalā, tiktā, the seeds of vṛṣaka, and ghanā [are used];
likewise, nāgara, triphalā, mustā, mūrvā, and pāṭhā, combined with honey.
In cases of combined (saṃsarga) or aggregated (sannipāta) disorders, one should formulate these [medicines] in mixed combinations.
For a disorder arising from vāta and pitta, [the decoction of] gokarṇaka, balā, and darbha, mixed with sugar, should be used.
AS.Ci.1.81: Drākṣā, āmalaka, bhūnimba, along with guḍūcī, śaṭhī, and guḍa; AS.Ci.1.82: Trāyantī, sārivā, drākṣā, kāśmarya, chinnaruhā, and guḍa.
Drākṣā, amṛtā, trāyantī, guḍūcī, sārivā, and balā;
AS.Ci.1.83: Drākṣā, madhūka, madhuka, lodhra, kāśmarya, and sārivā.
Musta, āmalaka, drākṣā, padmaka, kesara, and padmaka;
mṛṇāla, candana, uśīra, nīlotpala, and parūṣaka.
A thick decoction (phāṇṭa) or a cold infusion (hima) of grapes and other such fruits,
scented with jasmine flowers and combined with honey, sugar, and parched grain, conquers diseases born of wind and bile.
Fever, alcoholism, vomiting, fainting, burning sensation, exhaustion, giddiness,
upward-moving hemorrhage (raktapitta), thirst, and jaundice— these too [are cured by it].
In cases of *kapha* and *vāta*, a decoction of *vacā*, *tiktā*, *pāṭhā*, *āragvadha*, and *vatsaka*, or a decoction of *chinnodbhava* (guḍūcī) combined with the powder of *pippalī*, [is recommended].
A decoction of *vyāghrī*, dry ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), and *amṛtā*, combined with the powder of long pepper (*pippalī*),
conquers fever caused by *vāta* and *kapha*, as well as dyspnea, cough, catarrh, and pain.
Pathyā, kustumburī, mustā, śuṇṭhī, kattṛṇa, parpaṭa,
along with kaṭphala, vacā, bhārgī, devāhva, honey, and hiṅgu.
It subdues fever caused by phlegm and wind, as well as spitting, pain in the abdomen, heart, and flanks,
diseases of the throat, swelling of the mouth, cough, and dyspnea.
The *āragvadhādi* group, when taken with honey, conquers fever caused by *kapha* and *pitta*.
Likewise, bitter vṛṣa, uśīra, trāyantī, triphalā, amṛtā, paṭola, ativiṣā, nimba, mūrvā, and dhanvayavāsaka [are used];
and the juice of the flowers and leaves of vṛṣa, combined with sugar and honey.
It destroys fever caused by *pitta* and *śleṣman*, as well as *asṛkpitta* (hemorrhagic disorders) and *kāmalā* (jaundice).
Anantā, viśvabheṣaja, kaṭukā, water, and *toyada* (musta)— these [are the ingredients].
[These] destroy fever, thirst, vertigo, delusion, the sensation of smoke, and acidity.
In the case of *sannipāta* fever, [one should use] *vyāghrī*, *devadāru*, and the two types of *niśā*.
Patola leaves and nimba bark combined with triphalā and kaṭukā;
mustā, parpaṭaka, pathyā, mṛdvīkā, and kaṭurohiṇī.
Trāyantī, kaṇā, its root, drākṣā, pathyā, and madhūlikā;
triphalā, uśīra, ṣaḍgranthā, yaṣṭīmadhu, balā, and ghanā.
Nāgara, the root of pauṣkara, guḍūcī,
and kaṇṭakārikā [are used] for fever characterized by a predominance of vāta and śleṣman, accompanied by cough, dyspnea, and pain in the flanks.
One should prepare a cooling preparation consisting of madhūkapuṣpa, mṛdvīkā, trāyamāṇā, parūṣaka,
uśīra, tiktā, triphalā, and kāśmarya.
Drinking that decoction at the proper time dispels all fevers;
likewise, [a decoction of] *jāti*, *āmalaka*, *mustā*, and *dhanvayavāsaka* [achieves the same].
When the medicine has bound the stool, one who has excess *kapha* should consume *kaṭukā*, grapes, *trāyantī*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*),
and jaggery; once the medicine is digested, he should eat food such as thin gruel (*peyā*), but not immediately.
Peyā increases kapha, just as rain increases mud among the dust.
AS.Ci.1.101: Therefore, one should administer it even before [the main treatment] for those whose bodies are saturated with phlegm.
Light soups made from horse gram, chickpeas, peas, and the like— dry, endowed with a bitter taste, heart-pleasing, appetizing, and pungent.
Red rice and other varieties, as well as aged *ṣaṣṭika* rice, are beneficial in fever; likewise, when phlegm is predominant, barley that has been dehusked and made into groats is recommended.

This decoction, prepared with fever-alleviating herbs according to the strength of the *doṣa*s, the affected tissues (*dūṣya*), and other factors, should be strained and used two or three times as appropriate, along with boiled rice.
Light soups made from mung beans and other such grains, as well as those from horse gram (*kulattha*), cure fever; so too do soups made from *kāravella*, *karkoṭa*, young radish, and *parpaṭa*.
Soups made from eggplant, neem flowers, patola fruits and shoots,
and extremely light meats of wild animals are beneficial.

These are prepared with *vyāghrī*, *parūṣa*, *tarkārī*, grapes, *āmalaka*, and pomegranate, along with long pepper (*pippalī*), ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), coriander (*dhānya*), cumin (*jīraka*), and rock salt (*saindhava*).
These may generally be prepared either mixed with sugar and honey or left unmixed;
they are appetizing side dishes cooked with non-sour buttermilk (takra).
One should administer clear, fire-perfected [medicines] even with non-decoction drinks;
these, along with water cooled after boiling and wine according to suitability, are used for ten days while fasting on a diet of decoctions and wholesome food. (AS.Ci.1.108)
One should administer ghee when kapha is diminished and vāta and pitta predominate in a fever;
it is like nectar when the doshas have ripened, but otherwise it is like poison.
If, even after ten days have passed, there is an increase in the complications of fever,
one should employ the sequence of treatments beginning with fasting (laṅghana) until the depletion of phlegm (kapha).
At the end of the day, one should feed the patient— whether still suffering from fever or recently freed from it— a light meal;
for at that time, the digestive fire is strong and the heat is increased due to the depletion of *śleṣman*.
Alternatively, at the appropriate time, in accordance with the nature of the bodily humors (*doṣa*) and one's suitability (*sātmya*),
even one with a weak digestive fire who eats is not afflicted by indigestion (*ajīrṇa*).
Thus ends the first chapter.
Now begins the second chapter.
Chapter 2.1: We shall now explain the treatment of chronic fever (jīrṇajvara).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and others:
"Due to the weakness of the bodily tissues (*dhātu*), fever persists even when it has become chronic (*jīrṇa*)."
For fire is dry; it produces fever in one who has been dried out by fire.
Through emesis, sudation, cold water, decoctions, and light meals,
that which is the exceedingly powerful element, the companion, and the ever-moving wind (vāyu) [is pacified].
Clarified butter is its pacifier, just as water is for a burning house;
it follows the processing that conquers vāta and pitta while being light for digestion.
Therefore, one should certainly administer that [remedy] prepared with its own appropriate medicinal drugs;
for by its coldness, it overcomes the feverish heat and the pitta, which are of the opposite nature.
Ghee, when prepared with appropriate medicinal formulations, pacifies Vāta through its unctuousness, and Kapha through its equalizing properties.
All the previously mentioned decoctions should be administered with ghee according to the specific Dosha involved.
A decoction of triphalā, the bark of picumanda, madhuka, the two types of bṛhatī, and an equal amount of mūradala,
taken with ghee, cures fever and cough. [AS.Ci.2.8] [Likewise, a decoction] of nidigdhikā, tāmalakī, trāyamāṇā, and kaliṅgaka...
[The oil] prepared with *kṛṣṇā*, *aṃśumatī*, *ativiṣā*, *kaṭukā*, *āsevyā*, and *candana*; and with *dhātrī*, *bilva*, *ghana*, *drākṣā*, and *sārivā*.
Ghee taken immediately destroys chronic fever, cough, halīmaka,
loss of appetite, irregular digestion, and newly arisen consumption (yakṣman).
One should cook ghee, which destroys fever, in a decoction of vāsā, guḍūcī, triphalā, trāyamāṇā, and yavāsaka, along with milk, using these as a paste.
Pippalī, musta, mṛdvīkā, candana, utpala, nāgara; balā, durālabhā, mustā, trāyantī, nimba, and parpaṭa.
Having boiled the two groups of five roots (pañcamūla), one should cook ghee with milk and a paste (kalka) of raisins, medā, āmalaka, pauṣkara, śaṭhī,
and tāmalakī; this is an excellent remedy for fever.
This [decoction] cures cough due to wasting (kṣayakāsa), pain in the head, flanks, and heart, as well as burning sensations in the shoulders.
One should boil horse gram (kulattha), jujube (kola), the three myrobalans (triphalā), the ten roots (daśamūla), and barley (yava).
Having ground two palas of akṣa fruits, one should add them to a droṇa of water that has been purified,
along with pañcakolaka, saptāhva, vayasthā, nimba, and tumburu.
Śaṭhī, puṣkaramūla, arka-mūla, prativiṣā, vacā,
kirātatiktaka, musta, karkaṭākhya, and durālabhā.
Naktamāla, ubhe (the two types), pāṭhā, kaṭukā, śigru, and tejanī; AS.Ci.2.16 somavalka, dvirajanī, kaṇṭakī, and kaṇṭakārikā.
One pala each of paṭola, hiṅgu, gojihvā, kebuka, madana,
and jhaṭā, along with half a pala each of the salts and the alkaline substances (kṣāra).
One *prastha* of clarified butter, when prepared with these [ingredients], is an appetizer that conquers *kapha* and *vāta*,
and is beneficial for disorders of the heart, spleen, *grahaṇī*, abdominal tumors, cough, dyspnea, and hemorrhoids.
For those suffering from chronic fever, this [preparation] is like nectar;
it consists of mañjiṣṭhā, ativiṣā, pathyā, vacā, nāgara, and rohiṇī.
One should boil one *pālika* each of *devadāru* and *haridrā* in one *droṇa* of water;
when it has been reduced to a decoction, one should prepare one *prastha* of ghee with these pasted ingredients in the measure of a *picu*.
A compound of ginger, long pepper, asafoetida,
the two alkalis, and the five salts is like nectar for those suffering from fevers arising from all [three doshas] when they are obstructed by kapha.
[This is indicated] for those suffering from goiter, hiccup, loss of appetite, dyspnea, cough, and disorders of jaundice;
for those with throat obstruction (or nodules), urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, splenic enlargement, epilepsy, and edema.
For those afflicted by upward-moving wind (udāvarta), those with weak digestive fire, and those with worms in the stomach,
[medicines] from the juice and paste of *guḍūcī*, *triphalā*, and *vṛṣa* [should be used].
Oils prepared with raisins and *balā* destroy fever;
once the ghee has been digested, one should eat rice with soft meat broth.
For that strength is indeed sufficient to remove the humors (doṣas), it is supreme, and it bestows strength;
the juices derived from mung beans, kāravella, and other such plants remove kapha and pitta.

Generally, therefore, [heavy foods] are not beneficial in a fever characterized by a predominance of Vāta when it has become chronic; they produce colic, upward movement of gases, and constipation, and they increase the fever.
If the fever is still not pacified even by this means, one should perform purification (śodhana).

For one who is fit for purification, one should administer emesis as previously described when the morbid humor (doṣa) has reached the stomach (āmāśaya), provided that the patient is strong and his strength is being preserved.
In fever arising from over-nutrition (*santarpaṇa*), emesis should be induced with water mixed with long pepper (*pippalī*) and salt;
in fever where burning sensation (*dāha*) and thirst (*tṛṣṇā*) predominate, it should be induced with water mixed with sugar (*śarkarā*) and honey (*mākṣika*).
But when the morbid humors (doṣas) have ripened and become lax, or in cases of fever caused by irregularity or alcohol,
one should administer a bolus (modaka) made of triphalā, śyāmā, trivṛt, pippalī, and kesara.
One should administer the *vyoṣādi* purgative mixed with sugar and honey;
or likewise, the juice of grapes and *dhātrī*, or *harītakī* together with grapes.
Or one should lick the juice of *āmalaka* fruits fried in ghee to remove fever; likewise, one may lick the powder of *trivṛt*, *kṛṣṇā*, and *triphalā*.
One should drink triphalā with ghee and honey, or with the juice of grapes;
or one may take āragvadha with milk or with the juice of raisins.
A person afflicted by fever should drink either triphalā or trāyamāṇā with milk;
or he should drink a decoction of triphalā mixed with ghee, or boiled with ghee.
One should drink milk as a post-drink, or warm grape juice; for those who have been purged, a restorative diet beginning with thin gruel should be administered in the proper sequence.
One should always observe the waste matter as it is being expelled, even when it is provoked by fever.

For even a humor (doṣa) that has reached maturity may undergo transformation once it has established a seat within the digestive tract; or, while being digested, it may lead to excessive discharge or to a state of stagnation.
The complications arising from the retention of *āma* and the therapeutic measures for those disorders have been described.
He who, out of delusion, administers a purgative to one suffering from undigested fever (āmajvara),
is like one who would touch a sleeping black cobra with the tip of his hand.
For one emaciated by fever, emesis or purgation is not beneficial; however,
one may remove the impurities at will using milk or non-unctuous enemas (nirūha).
For one accustomed to milk, whose phlegm has been depleted, who suffers from burning sensations and thirst,
and who is afflicted by bile and wind, milk is wholesome even if he is suffering from diarrhea.
That [divine water], like a forest scorched by fire, revives his body which has been heated by the exertion of leaping,
and it quickly subdues his fever.
Therefore, one should administer processed water— whether cold or hot— or even simply warm water from a stream,
having distinguished the appropriate time; otherwise, it kills the patient suffering from fever.
Milk boiled with dry ginger, dates, raisins, sugar, and ghee,
then cooled and mixed with honey, destroys thirst, burning sensations, and fever.
Similarly, one should drink [the juice] boiled with grapes (drākṣā), balā, yaṣṭī, sārivā, kaṇā, and candana,
along with four parts of water; or one may drink it boiled with pippalī and four parts of water.
One suffering from fever is freed from cough, dyspnea, headache, pain in the flanks,
and chronic fever by drinking milk boiled with the five roots (pañcamūlī).
For one whose wind and feces are obstructed, fever may be cured by drinking milk that has been boiled with the root of *Areṇḍa* or young *Bilva*,
or by drinking it while still warm from the milking vessel.
For one suffering from the discharge of blood-stained mucus, accompanied by thirst, colic, and dysentery,
milk prepared with ginger, *balā*, *vyāghrī*, *gokaṇṭaka*, and jaggery is effective. (AS.Ci.2.44)
It overcomes swelling, retention of urine and feces, wind, fever, and cough;
a decoction prepared with *vṛścīva*, *bilva*, and *varṣābhū* destroys fever and swelling.
Milk prepared with the essence of *śiṃśipā* quickly removes fever. A non-unctuous enema (*nirūha*), however, restores strength, digestive fire, freedom from fever, joy, and appetite.
When combined with the [appropriate] dosha, it quickly acts once the [dosha] has reached the matured state (pakvāśaya);
it removes either pitta or kapha-pitta that has entered the pakvāśaya.
Enema removes all three impurities located in the colon,
as well as stiffness in the neck, back, and waist in those whose kapha and pitta have been depleted.
For one with a burning sensation and bound feces, one should administer an oil enema (anuvāsana) prepared with the leaves of *paṭola* and *nimba*, along with *kaṭukā* and *caturaṅgula*.
A decoction made from *sthirā*, *abalā*, *gokṣuraka*, *madana*, *uśīra*,
and *vālaka* boiled with an equal amount of water until only the milk remains, should be mixed [with the aforementioned ingredients].
One should administer an enema (basti) using the paste of *mustā*, *madana*, *kṛṣṇā*, *madhuka*, and *vatsaka*,
along with honey and ghee, to destroy fever.
[One should also use] the four *parṇinīs*, *yaṣṭī*, *phala*, *uśīra*, and *nṛpadruma*.
One should boil *yaṣṭī*, *śatāhvā*, the fruit of *phalinī*, and *musta* as a paste;
this enema, combined with jaggery, honey, and ghee, destroys fever.
With *trāyamāṇā*, *amṛtā*, *yaṣṭī*, the two types of *aṃśumatī*,
*balā*, *candana*, and *vṛṣa*, along with the meat of wild animals and birds; AS.Ci.2.52.
When the decoction has been prepared, one should add [the paste of] madana fruit, yaṣṭīmadhu, pippalī, and musta, having ground them; this enema (basti),
containing ghee, honey, and a small amount of rock salt, immediately destroys fever.

The bark of mango and other trees, conch shell, sandalwood, madhuka, blue lotus, golden orpiment, madder, lotus stalks, collyrium, and padmaka— AS.Ci.2.54 AS.Ci.2.54 (continued) [These are used for the preparation of a medicinal paste.]
One should administer a cold enema (basti) prepared with milk and a paste (kalka) [of the aforementioned drugs], along with honey and sugar,
to alleviate burning sensations and fever; likewise, an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) prepared with those same ingredients should be given.
Jīvantī, madana, medā, pippalī, madhuka,
vacā, ṛddhi, rāsnā, bilva, śatapuṣpā, and śatāvarī.
Having ground [the drugs] together with milk, water, ghee, and oil,
one should prepare an *anuvāsana* enema for fever, administering the unctuous substance according to the nature of the morbid humors (*yathāmala*).
With *candana*, *agaru*, *kāśmarya*, *paṭola*, *madana*, and *utpala*;
or likewise with *paṭola*, *ariṣṭa*, *madana*, *guḍūcī*, and *madhuka*.
And those enemas which will be described among the Siddhis as destroyers of fever (AS.Ci.2.59) remove headache and heaviness, alleviate phlegm, and awaken the sense organs (AS.Ci.2.59).
In chronic fever, one should administer appetizing nasal medication (nasya) and purgation;
for one with an empty head, unctuous therapy; and for those suffering from burning sensations, pitta-alleviating treatments.
One should also prescribe medicinal smoke (dhūma), gargles (gaṇḍūṣa), and mouth-washes (kavala) according to the specific dosha involved. (AS.Ci.2.60)

[These] remove catarrh, bad taste in the mouth, and diseases of the head and throat (AS.Ci.2.60). For loss of appetite, the filaments of the citron (*mātuluṅga*) with clarified butter and rock salt [are used] (AS.Ci.2.61).
Alternatively, one should hold in the mouth a paste of *dhātrī*, grapes, and sugar;
or one should apply substances prepared with cold or hot ingredients according to what is comfortable to the touch.

When fever has become chronic and is localized in the skin, one should administer massages, ointments, affusions, and the like; these same measures, including collyriums and fumigations, should also be applied in cases of fever of exogenous origin.
In the event of burning sensations, one should perform an oil massage with ghee that has been washed a thousand times;
furthermore, one should apply various groups of drugs mentioned in the Sutra-sthāna, such as those that are sweet, sour, or astringent.
Alternatively, one should cook [the ointment] with *dūrvā* and other Pitta-alleviating herbs mentioned in the group of purificatory drugs (*śodhana-gaṇa*),
which possess cold potency and a cold touch, having been prepared as a decoction and paste.
Oil mixed with milk, when used for massage, immediately removes burning sensations and fever.
Chandana, madhuka, kālā, drākṣā, madhurasā, and niśā.
Thus, it is established that oil prepared as previously described is an excellent remedy for fever with burning sensations;
one should also apply a paste made from those same [drugs], not ground too finely, to the head and the body.
One should apply affusion and immersion with the decoction of that [AS.Ci.2.65–66], as well as with water containing *ārdraka* stalks, milk, sour gruel, ghee, and so forth.
[One may use] the foam produced from *kapittha*, *mātuluṅga*, sour *vidārī*, *lodhra*, and *dāḍima*,
or from the foam of *badarī* sprouts, or from *ariṣṭaka*.
With camphor, padmaka, uśīra, kālīya, ambu, and sandalwood;
with tuṅga, priyaṅgu, śaivāla, lotus, blue water-lily, and mud.
A paste made from the tips of vetra, lodhra, and puṇḍrāhvā, ground with sour gruel (āranāla),
applied either individually or combined, destroys burning sensations and restores the natural complexion.
With the bark of *dhātrī*, *patra*, *nalada*, conch shell, *vyāghranakha*, and *utpala*; with *candana*, *añjana*, *musta*, *vṛkṣāmla*, and *amlavetasa*.
When anointed with a paste made from *sajīvaka*, *madhuka*, *palāśa*, and *dāḍima*,
combined with the juice of *bījapūra*, honey, and vinegar; AS.Ci.2.72.
In the head and the limbs, thirst, vomiting, burning sensations, delusion, headache,
swellings, pustules, and the delirium born of the affliction of fever are destroyed.
A paste of *gaura* and *āmalaka*, combined with sour substances and clarified butter (*sājya*), possesses those same qualities. [Furthermore:
*madhūka*, *madhuka*, *udīcya*, *nīlotpala*, and *madhūlikā*.
Licked with honey and ghee, they conquer burning fever, vertigo, cough,
hemorrhagic disorders, erysipelas, dyspnea, hiccups, and vomiting.
One should quickly emetic a patient suffering from vomiting using cold honey-water;
this is the procedure for alleviating pitta described in the section on the management of the *doṣas*.
For one who practices this, the burning fever quickly perishes.
Sweet music from a lute, moonlight, and the roof-terrace of a palace—
Necklaces cool with yellow sandalwood remove the burning sensation,
as do streams garlanded with water stirred by gentle breezes.
The great trees seem to threaten with their trembling coral-like fingers;
the indistinct words of children and the speech of women afflicted by passion [are likewise heard].
The truthful words of the virtuous quickly dispel the burning heat [of passion],
for they possess various powers according to the differences in individual inclinations.
The embrace of the beloved’s lovely limbs removes burning and cold fevers;
once the burning and cold have subsided, one should then remove those [applications] with tagara,
agaru, and saffron, which are hot in potency and have a warm touch.
With *kuṣṭha*, *sthauṇeya*, *śaileya*, *sarala*, and *amaradāru*; with *nakha*, *rāsnā*, *pura*, *vacā*, *caṇḍā*, the two types of *elā*, and *coraka*.
With *pṛthvīkā*, *kāśīru*, *surasa*, *hiṃsrā*, *adhyāmaka*, and *sarṣapa*;
with the ten roots (*daśamūla*), *mṛta*, *eraṇḍa* (both types), *pattūra*, and *rohiṣa*.
With *tamāla* leaves, *pūtīka*, *sallakī*, *dhānyaka*, and *dīpyaka*;
with *miśī*, *māṣa*, *kulattha*, *agni*, *prakīryā*, and the two types of *nākulī*.
One should cook the oil for a fever characterized by coldness with other similar substances,
along with decoctions and medicinal pastes (kalpa), and with fermented liquors such as *surā* and *sauvīraka*.
One should massage [the area] with that [mixture] while it is comfortably warm, and apply a paste made from those same ingredients well-ground;
one should also employ sprinkling and immersion baths with them while they are lukewarm.
And likewise, with sour gruel, cow’s urine, and whey alone,
or with saffron, agallochum, musk, nakha, cardamom, and devadāru; AS.Ci.2.87–88.
Applications made from śaileya, caṇḍā, tvak, musta, rāsnā, kapikacchū, and vacā—
either individually or all together— well-ground into a paste, destroy coldness.
One should cook barley powder, anointed with ghee, in four times its amount of milk; this paste,
which adheres to the ladle, should be applied as an ointment for one suffering from fever.
The *āragvadha* group and others, as well as fumigations, incense, and other [remedies] produced from *agaru*, will be described for use in drinking, massage,
and external application in cases of irregular fever (*viṣamajvara*).
Sweating therapies involving both fire and non-fire methods, sudation-inducing medicinal drugs, and diet;
AS.Ci.2.91: And the elimination of Vāta and Śleṣman through the application of combined forces.
A bedchamber for the fetus, mattresses, blankets, and rugs; and warming-rooms laughing with smokeless, glowing coals.
One suffering from shivering (vepathu) should consume wine along with the three pungents (savyūṣaṇa), buttermilk, horse gram, rice, and kodrava;
as well as anything else that increases pitta.
One should drink the paste of *ajājī* with jaggery, or the juice of *amṛtā* with jaggery,
or the juice of the *vārtāka* fruit mixed with honey.
A paste of madhuka, aguru, kauntī, and vyāghranakha,
drunk with wine along with honey, removes even severe cold fever.
Beloved women, endowed with full breasts, adorned with graceful charms,
and intoxicated by the wine of youth, should embrace him.
Once one has ascertained that the cold has subsided, one should then remove those [purgatives] again;
in the case of constipation (ānāha), the physician who knows the proper time should perform the treatment prescribed for alasaka.
One should have him drink a gruel prepared with pippalī, pippalīmūla, yavānī, and citra,
which promotes the downward movement of vāyu.
If, even with such complications, this cold-fever does not subside,
it is because the Vāta and Kapha are excessively aggravated in their own seats, or the Pitta is in its own seat.
Having eaten cucumber with buttermilk as a post-digestive drink, one should resort to fire; likewise,
one should remain covered while standing in the sun until perspiration arises.
Then, having bathed after the rubbing [massage], one should be moderate in diet once the fever has subsided;
for those two [doshas] reach pacification through the very increase of pitta and return to their own source.
Thereupon, the fever arising from vāta and kapha is quickly averted.
[This is achieved] by means of svarjikā, kuṣṭha, mañjiṣṭhā, lākṣā, mūrvā, niśā, and auṣadha.
Oil prepared with *satakra* (sour gruel) relieves burning sensations and chills when used for massage; furthermore,
[these symptoms are treated] by means of emetics, purgatives, and enemas, respectively.

The wise physician should treat fevers arising from phlegm, bile, and wind— whether they are combined, aggregated, characterized by one or more predominant factors, or equal in strength— with the following measures. (AS.Ci.2.103–104)
One should conquer fevers by means of the aforementioned medicines, taking into account the sequence of the *doṣas*,
whether by increasing one *doṣa* or by suppressing that which has become predominant.
Or one may conquer the fever of the combined humors (sannipāta-jvara) by following the sequence of the seats of phlegm (kapha).
Regarding the means for warding off sleep, that which is described as "sanyāsa" is beneficial.
In the case of *sannipāta*, this complication is especially severe;
at the conclusion of *sannipāta* fever, there is a very terrible [pain] at the root of the ear.
Swelling arises because of that, and only some are liberated from it;
one should quickly conquer it by means of bloodletting and the drinking of clarified butter.

If a fever does not subside through applications of plasters that destroy *kapha* and *pitta*, nor through nasal drops (*nāvana*) or gargles (*kavalagraha*), nor by means of cold, hot, unctuous, or dry treatments and the like; AS.Ci.2.109 [then further measures are required].
One who follows the branch [of the treatise] should quickly release the vein of the arm in due order;
this same procedure should be performed appropriately even in the case of a *viṣama* (irregular) fracture.
In the chapter on fever (AS.Ci.2), after having distinguished [the types] according to Vāta and the other doshas,
that which is stated immediately thereafter (AS.Ci.2.111) consists of preparations made with *paṭola*, *kaṭukā*, *mustā*, *prāṇadā*, and *madhuka*.
Decoctions made from three, four, or five [herbs] destroy irregular fevers (viṣamajvara). One should employ triphalā, pathyā, guḍūcī, and pippalī individually.
On the day the fever is expected to arrive, one should administer either bhallātaka with jaggery according to various prescribed methods, or else fasting (laṅghana) or nourishing therapy (bṛṃhaṇa).
In the morning, one should consume garlic with oil, or likewise ghee before a meal;
similarly, one may take aged curd, milk, buttermilk, or *ṣaṭpala* ghee.
Kalyāṇaka-pañcagavya, that which is called Tikta, and Vṛṣa-prepared [pañcagavya];
and the great Mahā-pañcagavya according to the ritual procedure, as well as Pañcamāhiṣa.

The prepared ghee made from the five products of the cow (*pañcājya*) and that made from the four products of the camel (*caturauṣṭra*), as well as the prepared ghee [prepared] with *kaṭurohiṇī*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *vṛṣa*, *granthika*, and *citraka*.

Pāṭhā, svaguptā, and dviniśā, combined with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in five prasthas each, should be consumed; this is the supreme remedy for conquering irregular fevers (viṣamajvara).
It produces clarity of speech, voice, memory, intellect, digestive fire, strength, health, and virility.
One should cook ghee with curd in a decoction of *kola*, *agnimantha*, and *triphalā*.
This addition of *tilvaka* is a destroyer of irregular fevers (*viṣamajvara*).
Boiled milk, ghee, honey, sugar, and long pepper, when combined with their own juices, [are likewise effective].
These remove irregular fever, heart disease, chest wounds, cough, and wasting;
one should consume *surā* liquor and that which is sharp wine, along with the meat of peacock, partridge, and cock.
Having consumed meat— which is pure and hot in potency— to one's heart's content along with food,
one should sleep on that same day or otherwise undergo emesis.
Or, having drunk a large dose of clarified butter,
one should induce vomiting again with *nīlinī*, *ajagandhā*, *trivṛtā*, and *kaṭurohiṇī*.
When fever arrives, one who has been prepared with oleation and sudation should drink [the medicine];
or, on that same day, one who has undergone sudation should be given either an *āsthāpana* or a *yāpana* enema.
On that day, one should drink the dung of a bull with milk,
or the dung of a bull with buttermilk, or rock salt with wine.
Realgar, rock salt, and long pepper, mixed with oil, should be used as an eye-salve (añjana).
Likewise, the fat of a tiger, combined with asafoetida and rock salt in equal parts, should be administered as a nasal drop (nasya).
Old ghee, along with fat, should be taken together with rock salt; likewise, *palankaṣā*,
nimba leaves, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, and *harītakī*.
Mustard seeds with barley, ghee, and incense; or *viḍa* salt or that produced from cats;
with *puradhyā*, *vacā*, *sarja*, nimba, arka, agaru, and *dāru*.
This "Unconquered" (aparājita) incense should be administered in all types of fevers.
One should employ sahadevā, vacā, bhadrā, and nākulī [as an incense].
Inhalation, rubbing with powders, and ointments that destroy all fevers; and those fumigations, nasal medications, collyriums, and sudden alarms which have been prescribed for mental disorders.
Medicine based on fire (therapeutic heat) dispels all fevers,
especially irregular ones, for those [irregular fevers] are generally born from the association with exogenous factors.
In a case of irregular fever (viṣamajvara) that does not subside, one should pierce the vein appropriate to the specific type;
however,
when the entire [dosha] has reached the rasa-dhatu, one should administer emesis and fasting.
When blood is located [in the body], one should employ sprinkling, pacifying measures, ointments, bloodletting, and purgatives;
when it is located in the flesh, strong purgatives; and when it is located in the fat, measures that destroy the fat.
When the Vāta is located in the bones, treatments that pacify Vāta— such as massage, sudation, and rubbing—
alleviate the fever and the pain caused by Vāta; basti therapy (enemas) is particularly effective for this purpose.
In cases of fever caused by *visarpa*, eruptions, or trauma resulting from pure *vāta*,
one should administer ghee internally, apply cold ointments and affusions, and consume meat broth.
And one should perform the appropriate therapeutic measures, such as bloodletting, as prescribed;
in cases arising from planetary influences (*graha*), one should employ the remedies mentioned in *Bhūtavidyā*, such as gems and mantras.

In cases arising from the smell of medicinal herbs, [one should apply] a remedy that pacifies *pitta* and overcomes poison; in cases of poison [itself], one should employ desired and pleasing objects, as well as measures for the pacification of the specific *doṣa*.
One should conquer fever born of anger and other passions through the discernment of what is beneficial and what is harmful;
that which is born of anger finds peace through desire, and that which is born of desire through anger.
Those two [fevers] arise from fear and grief; likewise, the other two, arising from curses and Atharvaṇa mantras, are treated with measures relying on divine power (*daivavyapāśraya*).
Those fevers first manifest alone, and subsequently they are pervaded by the bodily humors (*mala*).
Therefore, one should prescribe diet and other treatments according to the [specific] doṣas;
for fever does not persist when it is devoid of vāta and the other [doṣas].

One should listen to diverse discourses connected with the three aims of life (trivarga) that dispel illness, sleep, and other such states; one should not listen to those concerning the dead or the diseased.
One should distract his memory of the time of the fever with captivating sensory objects;
and until strength is regained, one should avoid physical exercise, bathing, and sexual intercourse.
Even when free from fever, one who has consumed heavy, unwholesome, burning foods, or anything else that causes fever,
should not suddenly consume all types of food indiscriminately.
Since it is immediately life-threatening,
one should therefore specifically administer the appropriate remedy for that [disease] in each respective stage.
Objects pleasing to the mind, speech that is delightful and courteous,
and a heart pure and moist with compassion— this is the destroyer of all fevers.
One should honor one's mother, father, the gods, physicians, Brahmins, Hara, and Hari; and one should practice charity, self-restraint, truthfulness, compassion, and straightforwardness.
And one should always carry the mantra, the jewel-gem, and the great medicinal herbs;
[as well as] Āryāvalokita, Parṇaśabarī, and Aparājitā.
One should prostrate to Noble Tārā for the cessation of all fevers,
and likewise, while reciting the mantra, one should resort to the Uṣṇīṣa, which is the remedy for all diseases.
One is liberated from all diseases, whether adventitious or innate.
Thus ends the second chapter.
Now begins the third chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
One should successfully treat fresh *raktapitta* that flows upward, occurs in a strong person, follows a single *doṣa*, and is free from complications, provided it arises during a favorable season.
One should cause the blood that flows downward, as well as that which is accompanied by two *doṣas*,
to be expelled; for that [blood] repeatedly becomes aggravated even when pacified, and moves from one channel to another.
One should avoid administering [purgatives] when they have been excessively used, in cases of weak digestive fire, when all three *doṣas* are aggravated, or when two pathways are involved;
this should be done after considering the etiology, the route, the impurities, the secondary forces, and the strength [of the patient].
In cases of rakta-pitta, one should apply [therapies] according to the state of place, time, and other factors;
likewise, one should employ fasting or nourishing at the outset, as well as purification or pacification.
One should treat the upward-moving [doshas] arising from over-nutrition in a strong person with abundant doshas by means of purgation,
and those moving downward by means of emesis.
Furthermore, after considering whether a patient requires pacification (śamana) or nourishment (bṛṃhaṇa),
as well as whether they are fit for fasting (laṅghya) or nourishment, one should administer the two pacifying tastes— bitter (tikta) and astringent (kaṣāya)— when [the disease] has moved upward.

In cases of downward-flowing *raktapitta*, fasting and the consumption of water boiled with the six parts of *śuṇṭhī* (dry ginger) without the ginger itself are prescribed; furthermore, nourishing and sweet tastes are beneficial.
In cases of upward movement [of the doshas], saturation therapy (tarpaṇa) should be employed; in downward movement, gruel (peyā) should be given first.
For one who is strong and eating, an enema that has not been expelled should not be retained, as it indeed causes disease.
Otherwise, it would act as quickly as fire; therefore, one should administer it promptly. [The drugs are:
Trivṛt, Triphalā, Dhātrī, Trāyantī, Āragvadha, and Abhayā.

One should administer for the purpose of purgation preparations made from *gavākṣī*, sugarcane juice, milk, grapes, honey, and sugar in abundance, formulated according to their respective pharmaceutical methods; or [one may use] *trivṛt* with a decoction and paste of *śyāmāka* along with sugar.
One should prepare this electuary according to the prescribed method and then lick it in a dose of one *pāṇitala*.
It consists of *triphalā*, *trivṛtā*, *śyāmā*, *pippalī*, sugar, and honey.
This bolus (modaka) cures disorders of the *sannipāta* type, as well as upward-moving *raktapitta* and fever.
Similarly, [a bolus] consisting of equal parts of *trivṛt* and sugar, combined with one-fourth part of *pippalī*, [has the same effect].
Emetic therapy combined with fruit, or a satiating drink (tarpaṇa) with sugar and honey;
or water with sugar, or Madhuka-water mixed with honey.
Or one may take *phala*, *indrayava*, *gāṅgeyī*, and *madhuka* mixed with honey;
or milk, or sugarcane juice; for one who has been purified, the procedure described immediately following applies.
One who wishes to preserve their strength should employ the appropriate *mantha*, *peyā*, and so forth;
the *mantha* mentioned for fever should be prepared with grapes (*drākṣā*) and other fruits that subdue pitta.

Or one may take a churned drink (mantha) made with honey, dates, grapes, *parūṣaka* fruit, and sugar-water; or a churned drink made with the "five essences" (*pañcasāra*) along with parched rice flour and ghee.
Or, for one with weak digestion who desires sourness, [a preparation] with pomegranate and *āmalaka* made sour;
or *kamala*, *utpala*, *kiñjalka*, *pṛśniparṇī*, and *priyaṅgu*.
Uśīra, śābara, lodhra, śṛṅgavera, kucandana, hrībera,
dhātakī flowers, the pulp of bilva, and durālabhā.
Peyās prepared with half-and-half portions will now be described, as well as those compounded with one-quarter parts.

Bhūnimba, sevya, jalada, candana, ambu, and priyaṅgu— AS.Ci.3.19–20: Peyās prepared with half-and-half portions will now be described, as well as those compounded with one-quarter parts. [The ingredients are] bhūnimba, sevya, jalada, candana, ambu, and priyaṅgu.
Mudga beans combined with śāliparṇī; masūraka lentils with pṛśniparṇī; haraṇu beans with either tūvarī, vātibalā, or balā.
For one whose digestive fire is impaired by that [fever], gruels (peyā), meat-broths, and meat juices are beneficial;
these should be non-acidic or slightly acidic, and mixed with ghee, honey, and sugar.
Grain produced from the *śūkaśimbī* plant, as well as leafy vegetables and meat, are recommended;
that which was described as light and cooling in the section on the knowledge of the nature of food is [also advised].
The previously mentioned water may be drunk, either boiled with the five roots (*pañcamūla*),
or boiled with the light [group of] roots and then cooled, or as honey-water, or fruit-water.
One should prepare collyrium and other remedies from the *padmakādi* group, as well as from the *sārivādi* group;
likewise, one should employ the ten-fold group that destroys burning sensations in food and drink.
When [the fever] follows from *kapha*, vegetable soup (*yūṣa*) and greens are recommended; when it follows from *vāta*, meat broth (*rasa*) is used.
For one who is not timid, quail (*lāvā*) with sprouts of *mudga* beans and *paṭola* is beneficial.

In cases of *asṛkpitta* (hemorrhagic disorders), preparations derived from *makuṣṭha* and *dhanvayāsa* are considered excellent. For constipation (*vibandha*), rabbit meat with *vāstūka* greens is recommended, while partridge (*tittiri*) is likewise beneficial.
When wind (māruta) is predominant, a decoction prepared with the extract of *udumbara* is effective;
likewise, [decoctions] of *plakṣa*, *barhiṇa*, and *nyagrodha* are used for the [respective] *kukkuṭa* [fevers].
The vartaka and the krakara are beneficial for double lotuses and lotus stalks;
the vartikā, the lotus stalk, and the aśvattha tree are beneficial for the kapiñjala.
One should avoid whatever is a cause of raktapitta (hemorrhagic disorders).
[One should take] phalinī, mṛd, lodhra, and añjana with honey, along with the decoction of vāsā.
The resin of *vāṭarūṣaka*, when drunk, pacifies bile and blood;
it may be taken either combined with sugar and honey, alone, or even boiled.
The bull immediately conquers blood [in the form of hemorrhage], for he is indeed its supreme medicine.
One should drink *bhūnimba*, *kaṭukā*, and sugar with the juice of *vāsā*.
Or, with that same [milk], one may take lotus filaments and *padmaka* mixed with honey;
or *lodhra*, *nāgakusuma*, *śāḍvala*, blue lotus, and *vāstuka*.
Or one should lick the juice of cow and horse dung with honey and ghee;
or alternatively, *pathyā*, *rajanī*, and *ahiṃsrā*; or likewise, onion (*palāṇḍu*).
[The powder] produced from *phalinī*, *lodhra*, *khadira*, *śālmalī*, and *kovidāra*;
[and that] produced from *śirīṣa*, *śelu*, *kakubha*, *sinduvāra*, and *atimukta*.
The flowers of *palāśa*, *yūthikā*, *śigru*, *madhūka*, and *asana*,
ground into a powder with honey— either combined together or used separately— [should be applied].
One should consume buffalo ghee that has been processed with these flowers along with honey;
or one may lick harītakī with honey, or the filaments of a lotus with honey.
Popped rice, water chestnut, nut grass, dates, black earth,
sprouts of milk-exuding trees, grapes, bamboo manna, and white sugar.
Gairika, madhuka, lodhra, conch shell, śambūka, añjana,
or the root of taṇḍūlīyaka, or the seed of vāstuka.
Paṭola, mālatī, nimba, the two types of candana,
padmaka, lodhra, vṛṣa, taṇḍulīya, kṛṣṇā, mṛd, and madayantikā.
Śatāvarī, gopakanyā, the two types of kākolī, and madhuyaṣṭikā—
these three decoctions, taken with honey and sugar, cure raktapitta (hemorrhagic disorders).
If the blood is clotted, one should lick the excrement of a pigeon mixed with honey;
or, if the blood flows excessively, one should drink blood with honey.
One should eat the meat of wild animals, such as the vājā, along with its bile and liver for a month. [Then one should apply] lodhra, kālīyaka, uśīra, phalinī, śaṅkha, and gairika.
Patola leaves, duḥsparśā, samaṅgā, and the sārivā creeper;
[and] the bark of jambu, vetasa, aśvattha, hayāhva, udumbara, and arjuna.
Kirātatiktaka, kramuka, musta, kaṭphala, and padmaka;
prapauṇḍarīka, drībera, kamala, utpala, and parpaṭa.
Chandana, combined with sugar either separately or all together,
may be prepared as a cold infusion (phāṇṭa), boiled, cooled, or taken as a powder with rice-water.
When drunk, it quickly conquers hemorrhaging, as well as thirst, burning sensations, and fainting;
[this is prepared] with sandalwood, uśīra, lotus stalks, parched grain, mudga beans, kaṇā, and barley.
A decoction made from *balā* and water that has been left to steep overnight destroys *raktapitta*.
The clear supernatant liquid (*prasāda*) produced from sandalwood, lotuses, fragrant substances, clay, and heated clods of earth [is also effective].
Very cold, combined with sugar and honey, it overcomes excessive hemorrhaging;
likewise, a clear decoction of sugar, lodhra, madhuka, uśīra, and candana [is effective].
Water mixed with *mṛdvīkā*, *sārivā*, *mustā*, *dhātakī*, and *yaṣṭimadhu*; or water containing *vaiḍūrya*, pearl, conch shell, *gairika*, and *āmalaka*.
One should drink honey-water or the juice of sugarcane; this conquers [the disorder of] blood.
Alternatively, having crushed pieces of sugarcane, one should soak them in a new jar.
That [water] which remains hidden in the sky, having flowed during the night into the morning,
is endowed with those qualities when it forms a crest-ornament of blooming, honey-sweet lotuses.
Or one should drink the paste of *trapusī* root with honey and rice-water;
or one should drink *karañja* seeds combined with that [rice-water], honey, and sugar.
Lodhra, candana, and yaṣṭyāhva— or indeed yaṣṭyāhva alone;
or blue lotus, sugar, yaṣṭī, madhuka, and the filaments of the lotus.
The decoction of *chinnodbhava* is cooling and overcomes *raktapitta*;
one should also employ those decoctions that have been prescribed for *pitta-jvara*.
When the fire has been kindled by these various astringent decoctions and the kapha has been conquered,
if the raktapitta is not pacified, then milk [is indicated] in that case where vāta is predominant.
In the same manner, one should cook goat meat or beef in five times the amount of water;
or alternatively, it may be cooked with the "light" group of five roots (laghupañcamūla) along with sugar and honey.
Jīvaka, Ṛṣabhaka, Drākṣā, Balā, Gokṣura, and Nāgara—
each of these boiled separately and then cooled, [should be taken] with ghee or with sugar.

Vomiting may be induced with milk mixed with the flowers of the emetic plant (*vamanī*), licorice (*madhuka*), and honey-sugar; likewise, milk boiled with *gokaṇṭaka*, *abhīru*, and the *parṇinīs* may be used.
It quickly destroys blood accompanied by pain, especially when it is located in the urinary tract (AS.Ci.3.59); however,
it is particularly beneficial when located in the anal tract when combined with *mocarasa* (AS.Ci.3.60).
One should also prescribe here the treatment for bloody diarrhea and hemorrhoids using banyan shoots or buds, as well as ginger, udīcya, and blue lotus.
Having drunk the decoctions with milk, one should eat [food] with milk alone;
or one should cause [the patient] to drink ghee that has been cooked with these same decoction-formulations.
Having boiled vṛṣa, including its roots and head, in eight times its weight of water until one-eighth remains,
one should cook ghee with that decoction.
That [milk], containing the pollen of those flowers, being cold and mixed with honey, cures pitta and blood disorders,
pitta-gulma, fever, dyspnea, cough, heart disease, and jaundice.
One should also destroy timira, bhrama, visarpa,
and hoarseness; one should cook ghee with the juice of *palāśa* stalks and that [juice] as its internal ingredient.
That [milk], mixed with honey, destroys blood [disorders]; likewise, milk prepared with vatsaka, or similarly with lodhra, utpala, samaṅgā, and trāyamāṇā, has the same effect.
One should eat a *utkarikā* (a type of cake) made from the powder of parched grain, wheat, madhuka, and sugar,
moistened with milk and prepared with ghee; this is a destroyer of *pittāsra* (blood-bile).
When the throat passage is obstructed by blood, mucus,
phlegm, and thickened secretions, one should lick alkaline extract made from lotus stalks mixed with honey and ghee.
In the same manner, one should separately prepare a medicated ghee with milk using the alkali derived from lotus stalks, lotus filaments, śyāmā, āsana, and madhūka.
With the powders of abhīru, kākolī, medā, vṛkṣāmla,
and pomegranate, along with the root of bījapūra, vidārī, and madhuka; AS.Ci.3.69.

That [milk], prepared with the five *pañcamūla* groups beginning with the first [the minor group], conquers its respective afflictions: obstruction, fever, flatulence, colic, cough, and internal hemorrhage (*asrapitta*). It serves the same purpose as those [five groups].
In cases of hemorrhage, especially when it originates from the rectum, an enema (basti) is recommended using madhuka,
añjana, māñjiṣṭhā, mṛṇāla, utpala, and gairika.
With gold, *lodhra*, *kālīya*, *samaṅgā*, lotus,
sandalwood, *saugandhika*, white [lotus], and conch shell— these being ground together and combined with honey and ghee.
One should administer an enema (āsthāpana) with milk to this patient, and after he has bathed in cold water,
one should feed him śāli rice with honey and ghee.

In this manner, one should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) at the proper time even in cases of difficult-to-cure diarrhea; likewise, when blood is predominant after digestion, or when purgation has been excessive, one should proceed accordingly.
Milk boiled with the Vidāryādi group of drugs is desired for use in an asthāpana enema,
along with honey, sugar, and ghee; likewise, ghee itself is used in an anuvāsana enema.
One should pacify blood located in the bladder with urethral enemas (uttarabasti); likewise, this same procedure is prescribed for menorrhagia (pradara).
When the pure blood flows excessively due to cutting, piercing, and other such procedures,
this medicine specifically prescribed for *pradara* (menorrhagia) is also indicated for diseases of the female genital tract (*yoni-roga*).
When the blood has been purified from the nasal passages, one should administer nasal drops (nāvana) and post-nasal irrigation (anuṣecana),
using the previously mentioned decoction formulations saturated with milk, sugarcane juice, and other such liquids.
Milk and other such [substances], water with sugar, or plain wholesome water;
as well as the juice of pomegranate flowers, mango stones, and young grass— these are beneficial.
One should employ cooling measures in the form of plasters, ointments, and the like,
as well as whatever internal and external remedies have been prescribed for pitta-fever.
That which is beneficial for *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders) and that which is beneficial for *kṣatakṣīṇa* (wasting due to chest injury) [have been described].
Thus ends the third chapter;
now begins the fourth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of cough;
thus said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
In the case of cough arising solely from wind (vāta),
one should first treat it with unctuous substances (sneha) prepared with vāta-alleviating drugs, such as gruels (peyā), vegetable soups (yūṣa), meat broths (rasa), and the like.
Then, one should treat obstructed feces and flatus with linctuses, medicated smokes, massages, sudation,
affusions, immersions, and enemas; however, when pitta is present, these should be administered after a meal.
One *prastha* of ghee prepared in the decoction of thirty *palas* each of *guḍūcī* and *kaṇṭakārī* cures vāta-type cough and stimulates the digestive fire.
One should cook one *prastha* of clarified butter with two *śāṇas* each of alkali, *rāsnā*, *vacā*, asafoetida, *pāṭhā*, liquorice, and coriander, along with the five spices (*pañcakola*).
When drunk in a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla) with a thin gruel (maṇḍa) as an after-drink,
it cures cough, dyspnea, pain in the heart and flanks, disorders of the grahaṇī, and abdominal tumors (gulma).
Kāśmarya, triphalā, vyoṣa, śaṭhī, drākṣā, parūṣaka,
the two types of pāṭhā, devadāru, ṛddhi, svaguptā, agnika, and gokṣura.
Vyāghnī, āmalakī, medā, kākanāsā, śatāvarī,
and vidārī— each taken in the measure of one karṣa— should be boiled with one prastha of ghee.
And by means of milk, one quickly conquers fever, cough, and halīmaka, as well as abdominal tumors,
loss of appetite, and pain in the liver, spleen, head, heart, and flanks.
It [the decoction] cures jaundice, hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors (anila-aṣṭhīlā), wounds, swellings, and consumption.
One should prepare it by boiling rāsnā, daśamūla, and śatāvarī in one droṇa of water.
One *palā* each of *kulattha* pulse, *badara* fruit, and barley,
along with half a *tulā* of goat meat— these should be cooked in one *āḍhaka* of ghee.
Having considered it, that [milk] boiled with equal parts of the *jīvanīya* group of drugs, each weighing one *pala*, when administered through drinking,
nasal drops, or enemas, is effective for wind diseases (*vātaroga*).

One should conquer coughs, tremors of the head, pain in the female genital tract and groins, diseases of the entire body or of individual limbs, as well as splenic disorders and upward-moving wind (ūrdhvānila), by using a preparation prepared from the decoction and paste of the Vidāryādi group; this also overcomes cough. (AS.Ci.4.13)
Ghee prepared with aśoka seeds, kṣavaka, jantughna, añjana, padmaka,
and viḍa salt— either this ghee or the powder [of these drugs] saturated with ghee [is used].
One afflicted by cough should lick [the powder] and drink goat's milk after;
[one should also take] viḍaṅga, ginger, rāsnā, pippalī, asafoetida, and rock salt.
One should drink that powder with a dose of ghee, along with bhaṅgā and the milk of ṛkṣa,
in cases of cough caused by vāta associated with kapha, as well as in dyspnea, hiccups, and impaired digestive fire.
In cases of cough caused by Vāta, one should lick a paste of durālabhā, śṛṅgavera, śaṭhī, rāsnā, white sugar, and karkaṭaśṛṅgī, mixed with oil.
One should lick as an electuary the powdered pippalī, musta, bhārṅgī, karkaṭakī, and śaṭhī— each of which is difficult to touch—
mixed with old jaggery and oil.
In the same manner, one should drink long pepper (*pippalī*) together with dry ginger (*śuṇṭhī*) and *bhārgī*; likewise,
one should drink long pepper with rock salt (*saindhava*) along with lukewarm water.
One should drink ginger mixed with sugar and *musta*, or *kaṇā* and *reṇukā* with curd;
or else, one may take the pulp of jujube fruits with wine, curd, or whey.

Alternatively, one suffering from cough accompanied by nasal catarrh should inhale, according to the prescribed procedure, a lubricating (snaihika) medicinal smoke consisting of powdered long pepper fried in ghee and mixed with rock salt.

One who subsists on milk and meat broth should also inhale the medicinal smokes prescribed for hiccup and dyspnea; likewise, one should consume *śāli*, barley, wheat, and *ṣaṣṭika* rice along with the meat of domestic, marshy, and aquatic animals.
One should feed [the patient] beneficial foods with the juices of masha and atmagupta,
or with soups [prepared from them], along with yavani, pippali, bilva-pulp, nagara, and chitraka.
For a disorder born of Vāta, one should drink a gruel prepared with rāsnā, jīraka, pṛthakparṇī, palāśa, śāṭī, and pauṣkara, enriched with unctuous, sour, and salty substances.
[This preparation] destroys pain in the waist, heart, flanks, and abdomen, as well as dyspnea and hiccups;
likewise, [one may take it] with the decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla) combined with the five spices (pañcakola) and jaggery.

One should drink gruel made with sesame seeds, or milk-rice (kṣaireyī) with rock salt, or meat of fish, chicken, or boar accompanied by clarified butter and rock salt. Vāstuka, vāyasī-vegetable, suniṣaṇṇaka, and kāsaghna are [also] beneficial. AS.Ci.4.25
The fruit and leaves of *kaṇṭakārī*, as well as young and dried radish; oils such as sesame oil and the like; and foods prepared with milk, sugarcane juice, or molasses.
One should drink curd-whey, sour gruel, the juice of sour fruits, and wine.
In the case of pitta-type cough accompanied by phlegm, emesis induced with ghee is beneficial.
Likewise, [one may bathe] with water boiled with *madana*, *kāśmarya*, and *madhuka*,
or with a paste of *phala* and *yaṣṭyāhvā* saturated with the juices of *vidārī* and sugarcane.
In pitta-type cough with thin phlegm, one should administer *trivṛt* combined with sweet substances for purgation; if the phlegm is thick, it should be combined with bitter substances.
When the doshas have been removed from the heart, one should resort to a restorative diet that is cold, unctuous, and sweet; however,
when the kapha is thick, it should be cold, dry, and combined with bitter flavors.
Pippalī, musta, yaṣṭyāhva, drākṣā, mūrvā, and mahauṣadha;
lākā, amṛtā, phala, drākṣā, tvak, kṣīrī, pippalī, and sitā.
Dusparśā, karkaṭī, śuṇṭhī, śaṭhī, drākṣā, sitā, balā,
the root and fruit of nidigdhikā, vaṭa seeds, and rasāñjana.
Date palm, long pepper, bamboo manna, and gokṣura— these five,
combined with ghee and honey, are electuaries for those coughing from pitta, as described in the half-verses.

For one who drinks milk as an after-drink, one should lick *śṛṅgī* with ghee, sugar, and honey; for the pitta-type [fever], a linctus made of sugar, *dhātrī*, honey, grapes, camphor, and blue lotus [is prescribed].
With coffee-berries, long pepper, and black pepper, along with ghee and Anila, it is beneficial.
Fifty halves of grapes, thirty long peppers, and one pala of sugar.
