One should have the patient lick the juice of cow-dung from a milk-yielding cow mixed with honey;
[this is prepared] with cinnamon, cardamom, the three pungents (vyoṣa), raisins, long pepper root, and lotus seeds.
A linctus made from parched grain, musta, śaṭhī, rāsnā, dhātrī fruit, and bibhītaka,
combined with sugar, honey, and ghee, cures heart disease and cough.
Pippalī, āmalaka, drākṣā, lāja, lākṣā, and sitopalā [are also used for this purpose].
Having powdered these and cooked them with milk, one should lick [the mixture] with a portion of honey equal to one-eighth [of the total].
[One should also take] the juices of vidārī, sugarcane, and lotus stalks, along with milk and white sugar.
One should drink [this] mixed with honey; it removes cough caused by pitta (AS.Ci.4.37).
Barley, śyāmāka, and kodrava grains should be consumed with sweet meat broths from wild animals (jāṅgala) (AS.Ci.4.38).
In cases of thick phlegm, soups made from mung beans and other pulses, along with bitter vegetables taken in appropriate doses, are beneficial;
likewise, bitter electuaries mixed with honey are recommended.

For those with diminished phlegm, śāli rice and ṣaṣṭika rice are beneficial when accompanied by meat soups and similar broths; sugar-water, grape juice, sugarcane juice, and milk should be used as after-drinks (anupāna).
In cases of pitta-type cough, one should prepare meat broth, milk, gruel, and vegetable soups with kākolī, the two types of bṛhatī, the two types of medā, vṛṣa, and nāgara.
One should boil grapes, *kaṇā*, the five roots (*pañcamūla*), and the grass-root group (*tṛṇākhya*) in water;
with that decoction, one should drink milk that has been boiled and cooled, mixed with honey and sugar.
One should administer a gruel prepared by him, well-cooled and mixed with honey,
containing *śaṭhī*, *drībera*, *bṛhatī*, sugar, and *viśvabheṣaja*.
Having ground [the ingredients], one should drink the juice strained through a cloth and mixed with ghee,
along with equal quantities of buffalo milk, goat milk, sheep milk, cow milk, and the juice of *dhātrī* (myrobalan) fruits.
In the same manner, one should drink clarified butter prepared with the sweet group of drugs,
or that which has been cooked with sugarcane juice mixed with milk and reduced to a decoction.
One should drink it with sugar in the morning, or lick it mixed with honey;
or ghee cooked in a decoction of the sprouts of milk-exuding trees, mixed with an equal amount of milk.
One should have a patient suffering from pitta-type cough drink [this] with honey, or one should have them lick a linctus made of medā,
vidārī, kākolī, svayaṃguptā fruit, and balā.
Having made into a paste sugar, jīvaka, mudgaparṇī, māṣaparṇī, and durālabhā,
one should cook that ghee with eight times the amount of milk.
When applied to drinks, foods, or linctuses, it overcomes pitta-type cough;
one should either lick the powder of these [drugs] or drink their decoction. (AS.Ci.4.48)
One suffering from cough due to kapha should first drink the oil extracted from ignited pine wood (surakāṣṭha), strained and sprinkled with the three pungents (vyoṣa) and barley alkali (yavakṣāra).
One should administer unctuous purgation above, below, and to the head according to the proper method;
for a strong patient, one should employ sharp purgatives and also apply a *saṃsarga* (combined therapy).
With foods made from barley, mung beans, and horse gram, which are warm, dry, and intensely pungent,
combined with *kāsamarda*, eggplant, *vyāghrī*, alkali, and long pepper (AS.Ci.4.51).
One should drink a medicated oil prepared with the juices of *dhānvana*, *baila*, sesame, mustard, and *nimba*;
or one may drink water decocted with the ten roots (*daśamūla*), warm water, wine, or honey-water.
Or one should drink water mixed with the roots of puṣkara, śamyāka, and paṭola, along with niśā and honey, at the three times of the day for taking food.
Long pepper, long pepper root, ginger, and bibhītaka;
deodar, chebulic myrobalan, nut grass, long pepper, and dry ginger.
Guḍūcī, pippalī, bhārgī, śṛṅgī, and karkaṭaka;
as well as vyoṣa, dāru, citraka, ḍaṅga, triphalā, sugar, and balā.
The root-bark of *nidigdhikā* combined with black pepper,
along with the soot of peacock and cock feathers and alkaline ash derived from barley.
Viśālā, pippalīmūla, and trivṛt, mixed with honey as a liquid—
these seven linctuses, arranged in half-verses, cure cough caused by kapha.
One should lick black pepper with honey, and likewise *joṅgaka* with honey; one should also take the juices of *vyāghrī*, *vārtāka*, and *bhṛṅga* separately with honey.
Kāsaghnā, horse dung, surasā, and asitā;
devadāru, śaṭhī, rāsnā, karkaṭākhyā, and durālabhā.
Pippalī, nāgara, musta, pathyā, dhātrī, and sitopalā—
these two electuaries, combined with honey and oil, [are indicated] for kapha associated with vāta.
One should lick a paste of viḍaṅga, saindhava salt, hiṅgu, kuṣṭha, vyoṣa, and manaḥśilā,
saturated with honey and ghee, for cough, dyspnea, and hiccups. (AS.Ci.4.61)

Jaggery, alkali, *uṣaṇaka*, *kaṇā*, pomegranate, and *śvāsakāsajit* (the plant that conquers asthma and cough) are taken in the sequence of two *pala*s, half a *pala*, one *akṣa*, half an *akṣa*, and one *pala* respectively.
[In another formulation: two *pala*s of pomegranate, eight [parts] of jaggery, and three *pala*s of *vyoṣa*.

It is clarifying, digestive-stimulant, beneficial for the voice, and overcomes chronic rhinitis, dyspnea, and cough. (AS.Ci.4.62) Pāṭhā, ginger, śaṭhī, mūrvā, gavākṣī, long pepper, and musta— (AS.Ci.4.63)
Having ground these together with warm water, one should drink them combined with asafoetida and rock salt;
likewise, one may drink mustā, śaṭhī, śuṇṭhī, nāgara, ativiṣā, and bhayā prepared in the same manner.
One should drink the digestive (pācana) formulation for fever mentioned previously, along with *pathyā* and *śṛṅgī*;
or alternatively, a formulation consisting of *dīpyaka*, *trivṛt*, *viśālā*, *ghana*, and *pauṣkara*.
One suffering from cough due to phlegm (kapha) should drink long pepper (pippalī) boiled with honey in cow’s urine, or even in water; alternatively,
one may take a karṣa of long pepper paste fried in oil along with sugar-candy.
One should cause [the patient] to drink a decoction of horse gram (kulattha) that destroys cough caused by phlegm,
combined with black salt (sauvarcala), chebulic myrobalan (abhayā), emblic myrobalan (dhātrī), long pepper (pippalī), alkali, and ginger (nāgara).
One should drink this powder mixed with ghee to alleviate cough caused by Vāta and Kapha;
one *prastha* of ghee should be cooked with one *āḍhaka* of *daśamūla* decoction and [the powder] in doses of one *akṣa*.
A gruel taken as an after-drink with puṣkarāhvā, śaṭhī, bilva, surasā, vyōṣa, and hiṅgu removes all diseases caused by vāta and śleṣman.
Ghee prepared with the juice and exudate of *nirguṇḍī* leaves conquers cough;
likewise, ghee prepared with the juice of *viḍaṅga* and containing *vyoṣa* within it [is also effective].
Punarnavā, sitāṭikā, surasa,
kāsamarda, amṛtā, paṭola, bṛhatī, and phaṇijjaka— these, combined with their juices and mixed with milk, [are used as a purgative].
By consuming ghee prepared with the three pungents (trikaṭu),
one no longer has fear of cough, irregular fever, consumption, or hemorrhoids.
[One should take] the juice of Kaṇṭakārī, including its roots, fruits, and leaves, in a measure of one āḍhaka.
One *prastha* of clarified butter [should be cooked] with *balā*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), *viḍaṅga*, *śaṭhī*, and pomegranate;
with *sauvarcala* salt, alkali from barley (*yavakṣāra*), *mūlā*, *āmalaka*, and *pauṣkara*.
With vṛścīva, bṛhatī, pathyā, yavānī, citraka,
and ṛddhi; with mṛdvīkā, cavya, varṣābhū, durālambhā, and amlavetasa.
One should decoct śṛṅgī, tāmalakī, bhārṅgī, rāsnā, and gokṣuraka with their pastes;
this is recommended for all types of coughs, as well as for dyspnea and hiccups.
One should boil one *tulā* of crushed *kaṇṭakārī* in one *droṇa* of water.
With one āḍhaka of that decoction and one prastha of ghee,
[one should cook it] with a handful each of rāsnā, dusparśa, ṣaḍgranthā, the two types of pippalī, and citraka.
One should conquer cough, dyspnea, expectoration of phlegm, hiccup, anorexia, and chronic rhinitis with sauvarcala salt, yavakṣāra, and the root of kṛṣṇā.
One should place one *tulā* of crushed *pacedvyāghnī* into an *āḍhaka* of water on the fire;
once it has been strained, one should add the powdered *vyoṣa*, *rāsnā*, *amṛtā*, and *agnikā*.
Take half a pala each of śṛṅgī, bhārṅgī, ghanagranthi, and dhanvayāsa; [add] sixteen palas of ghee and forty palas of water.
Furthermore, one should place that purified sugar-candy on the fire; when it has cooled and becomes sticky enough to adhere to a ladle, one should add two *kuḍavas* each of the following separately:
This linctus made of long pepper, *bakuchi*, honey, and fresh ghee conquers abdominal tumors, heart disease, hemorrhoids, dyspnea, and cough.
Having boiled one akṣa each of triphalā, pippalī, pāṭhā, sārivā, the two types of bṛhatī,
marica, padmaka, musta,
and uśīra in one āḍhaka of water until one-fourth remains, [one should add] eight palas of milk.
Having added one pala of jaggery, one should cook it until it reaches the consistency of a paste that adheres to the ladle;
this linctus completely cures every type of cough characterized by a predominance of phlegm.
Or one should drink milk prepared with these [drugs], or mixed with sesame and honey;
and one should inhale pacifying smoke when there is excessive phlegm, or purificatory smoke.
Realgar, red ochre, licorice, spikenard, nut-grass, and the bark of *Aṅgudī*—these [are used].
Having drunk the smoke according to the procedure for curing cough, one should drink milk afterwards;
at the end of each expulsion [of phlegm], that lukewarm smoke mixed with jaggery destroys [the disease].
For coughs caused by an excess of vāta and śleṣman, whether recent or chronic,
[one should use] prapauṇḍarīka, madhuka, śārṅgeṣṭā, elā, and manaḥśilā.
Having prepared a wick from black pepper, long pepper, grapes, cardamom, and the flower-clusters of *surasā*, one should inhale the smoke using a cloth made of linen.
One should drink milk or jaggery-water following that [medicated ghee] smeared with ghee. Similarly, [one may use a preparation] with nepālī, tāla, black pepper, lākṣā, añjana, and kuṭannaṭa.
This fumigation, prepared according to the previous method with *uśīra*, *rohiṣa*, *phala*, *drāmilī*, and bamboo scrapings,
is prescribed along with its appropriate after-drink.
Smoke from cotton seeds and *aśvagandhā* destroys cough;
or one should drink [the juice] of the pulp of *kośātakī* fruits combined with *manaḥśilā*.
If, however, in a cough caused by phlegm, there is an association with pitta (*tamaka*), [this treatment should be applied]. (AS.Ci.4.91)
In that case, one should apply the treatment for pitta-type cough according to the specific stage of the condition; however,
if there is an association with kapha in a wind (vāta) disorder, one should perform kapha-alleviating therapy.

In cases where vāta and kapha are associated with pitta, one should administer a pitta-alleviating treatment (AS.Ci.4.92). In a dry condition characterized by vāta and śleṣman, an unctuous treatment is indicated; in a moist condition, a drying treatment is required (AS.Ci.4.93).
In cough associated with pitta, however, the treatment for kaphaja [cough] combined with bitter substances [should be applied].
Thus ends the fourth chapter.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of cough caused by chest injury and wasting (kṣatakṣayakāsacikitsita).
Thus indeed said the great seers, such as Ātreya and others:
"In the case of an internal chest wound, one should immediately drink lac mixed with honey."

When the milk has been digested, one should eat aged *śāli* rice with milk and sugar; for those suffering from pain in the flanks or bladder, or having diminished bile and digestive fire, that [milk] should be mixed with wine.
But for one with a perforated ulcer (bhinnaviṭ), [one should administer] a decoction of *samuṣṭā*, *ativiṣā*, *pāṭhā*, and *vatsaka*,
along with lac (*lākṣā*), ghee, beeswax (*madhūcchiṣṭa*), the group of life-promoting drugs (*jīvanīyagaṇa*), and sugar.

One with a stimulated digestive fire should drink *tvakkṣīrī* boiled in milk along with fuel-sticks (*samit*). [He should also use] *ikṣvālikā*, lotus root (*bisagranthi*), lotus filaments (*padmakesara*), and *candana*.
One suffering from chest wounds should drink boiled milk mixed with honey for the purpose of healing;
likewise, one should consume raw barley powder prepared with milk and combined with ghee.
In cases of fever with burning sensations, one should drink sugar, honey, and parched grain flour mixed with milk;
however, those suffering from cough should drink clarified butter prepared with sweet medicinal herbs.
Or boiled jaggery-water cooled with honey and black pepper;
or the powder of *āmalaka* fruits cooked in milk and mixed with ghee.
Or one may administer long peppers according to the procedure for elixirs (rasāyana); those suffering from cough or pain in the joints and bones should lick them mixed with ghee and honey.
Madhūka, madhuka, grape-skin, kṣīrī, pippalī, and balā;
trijāta in the amount of half a karṣa each, and one pala of white sugar along with half a pala of pippalī. (AS.Ci.5.10)
One pala each of raisins, madhūka, and dates, finely powdered and made into pills with honey, destroy [the disease] and are aphrodisiacs for pitta-blood disorders.
Cough, dyspnea, anorexia, vomiting, fainting, hiccup, intoxication, and vertigo;
chest injury, consumption, loss of voice, splenic disorders, wasting, and disorders of aggravated vāta—[these are cured by it].
In cases of excessive increase of blood, one should also treat hemoptysis, pain in the heart and flanks, thirst, and fever; furthermore,
one should drink goat's or wild animal blood.
One who spits blood should drink the powder made from *varṣābhū*, sugar, and red rice grains, prepared with grape juice, milk,
and ghee.
Or one should administer *taṇḍulīyaka* prepared with *madhūka*, *madhuka*, and milk;
and when blood has flowed out through its respective channels, one should apply the appropriate medicinal treatment.
One karṣa each of ground pippalī and madhuka, along with one upala of sugar,
and one prastha each of cow’s milk, goat’s milk, and sugarcane juice;
Powdered barley, wheat, and grapes, the juice of *āmalaka*, and oil— each in the measure of one *prasṛta*— all of this should be cooked over a gentle fire. (AS.Ci.5.17)
Pacelaka, combined with ghee and honey, cures cough due to chest wounds (kṣatakāsa);
it destroys dyspnea, heart disease, and cough, and is beneficial for the elderly and those with diminished semen.
Mūḍhavāta is treated with goat's fat fried in wine and mixed with rock salt;
this is for one who is emaciated, wasted, afflicted with chest wounds, suffering from poor sleep, yet possesses a stimulated digestive fire.
One should take [this] with milk and honey, along with ghee,
honey, and sugar; or sugar, barley, wheat, *jīvaka*, and *ṛṣabhaka* with honey.
One who is emaciated, suffering from chest wounds, or wasted away should lick [the medicine] with ghee and milk as an after-drink;
or he should drink a decoction of the flesh of carnivorous animals fried in ghee.
Combined with long pepper and honey, this increases muscle and blood.
[It is prepared] from nyagrodha, udumbara, aśvattha, plakṣa, sāla, and priyaṅgu.
One should consume ghee produced from milk boiled with *tālamastaka*, *jambū* bark, *priyāla*, *padmaka*, and *aśvakarṇa*.
For one with chest wounds, diminished semen, strength, and sensory faculties, rice gruel is prescribed;
for those afflicted by vāta and pitta, or suffering from a splitting sensation in the limbs, massage with clarified butters (ghṛta) is considered appropriate.
When one is afflicted by wind-diseases (mātariśvan), the drinking of *jīvanīya* ghee along with oils that destroy wind-disorders should be administered for pain in the heart and flanks.
Or one should prepare a ghee that destroys diseases of Vāta and is antagonistic to Pitta and blood,
by boiling it with an equal amount of milk in a decoction of Yaṣṭyāhvā and Nāgabalā.
Ghee prepared with the paste of *payasyā*, *pippalī*, and *vāṃśī*, along with eight times its quantity of milk and the juice of *kola* and *lākṣā*, is beneficial for wounds.
Ghee [should be prepared] with pastes of *kaṭvaṅga*, the bark of *dārvī*, the bark and leaves of *vatsaka*,
the *jīvanīya* group of drugs, *śuṇṭhī*, *varī*, *vīrā*, and *punarnavā*.
Balā, bhārgī, svaguptā, ṛddhi, śaṭī, āmalakī, kaṇā,
śṛṅgāṭaka, payasyā, and the light pañcamūla.
Fruits such as grapes and walnuts are sweet, unctuous, and nourishing.
One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with these [fruits] in the quantity of one *karṣa* each, having ground them into a fine paste.
One half-prastha of honey, when cooled, combined with milk, vidārī, sugarcane juice, and goat meat broth,
along with half a tulā of powdered sugar.
Having processed half a pala each of black pepper, cinnamon, cardamom, cinnamon leaves, and nāgakeśara,
one should lick a dose of that powder according to one's digestive fire.
This is called "the consumption of nectar" (*amṛtaprāśa*); ghee is the nectar for men. Having consumed the essence of the nectar of ambrosia, one should eat milk and meat broth.
One should nourish those whose semen is depleted, those suffering from chest wounds, those who are emaciated, the weak, those afflicted by disease,
those excessively addicted to women, the thin, and those deficient in complexion and voice.

Śvadaṃṣṭrā, uśīra, mañjiṣṭhā, balā, kāśmarya, and kattṛṇa cure cough, hiccup, fever, dyspnea, burning sensation, thirst, and blood-bile (raktapitta); they bestow progeny and remove vomiting, fainting, heart disease, and disorders of the female reproductive tract and urine. (AS.Ci.5.35)
One should boil one *pala* each of *darbhamūla*, *pṛthakparṇī*, *palāśa*, *ṛṣabhaka*,
and *sthirā* in their decoction with four times as much milk.
With the pastes of *svaguptā*, *jīvantī*, *medā*, *ṛṣabhaka*, and *jīvaka*;
and with *śatāvarī*, *ṛddhi*, *mṛdvīkā*, sugar, *śrāvaṇī*, and *bisā*.
One *prastha* of this prepared ghee cures diseases of the heart caused by vāta and pitta, as well as colic;
it also removes dysuria, urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, cough, emaciation, and consumption.
It bestows strength and flesh upon those exhausted by archery, women, wine, heavy loads, or travel on the road.
One should cook ghee in a decoction made from eight *palas* of *madhuka*, one *prastha* of grapes, and water.
When one *prastha* [of ghee] has been prepared with a paste of eight *pala*s of *pippalī*, and it has cooled,
one should mix it with eight *pala*s each of honey and sugar.
In cases of excessive hemorrhage, wasting due to injury, and blood-gulma,
that [medicated ghee] is beneficial when prepared from the juice of *dhātrī* fruit, *vidārī*, sugarcane, and the *jīvanīya* drugs, along with ghee. (AS.Ci.5.40–41)
One should boil one *prastha* each of cow’s milk and goat’s milk;
once it is prepared and cooled, one should then add two *prasthas* of sugar and honey.
It cures consumption, epilepsy, hemorrhagic disorders, cough, urinary disorders,
and wasting; it stabilizes youth, promotes longevity, and bestows muscle, semen, and strength.

If pitta is predominant, one should lick ghee; if vāta is predominant, one should drink it. Ghee, when licked, pacifies pitta, but because of its small quantity, it does not destroy the digestive fire.
It overcomes the wind and indeed obstructs the yellowed heat;
these very same ghees, moreover, [are prescribed] for those whose limbs are emaciated, wasted, and thin. (AS.Ci.5.44)

One should prepare thickened preparations with the powders of *tvakkṣīrī*, *pippalī*, and parched rice; having made these into ghee-balls (*sarpirguḍa*) mixed with honey, one should administer them along with milk.
By means of these, one shall very quickly attain semen, virility, strength,
and nourishment. Balā, vidārī, the short pañcamūla, and punarnavā— AS.Ci.5.46.
Likewise, the sprouts of the five milky trees (pañcakṣīrivṛkṣa) should be taken in the measure of one handful;
these, along with two parts of milk and one part of the juice of vidārī and ajarasā, [are used] in a decoction.

One should cook one āḍhaka of ghee with the life-promoting (jīvanīya) drugs ground to a paste in the measure of one akṣa; when it has been strained and cooled, one should add thirty-two palas of sugar.
One *kuḍava* each of the powders of wheat, long pepper, bamboo manna, and water chestnut,
all mixed with honey and stirred with a churning stick.
Having made boluses of clarified butter and jaggery, one should wrap them in birch bark;
having eaten those weighing one *pala* each, one should subsequently drink milk or wine in cases of phlegm (*kapha*).

In cases of wasting, cough, chest injury, emaciation, or exhaustion from physical labor, sexual indulgence, or carrying heavy loads; in cases of spitting blood, fever, chronic rhinitis, or when [the disease] is localized in the chest—
These are recommended for pain in the sides and head, and for disorders of the voice and complexion,
when three *āḍhakas* each of milk, ghee, and oil have been boiled with sugar and *sarjarasa*.
When the preparation has been cooked and thickened, one should add ten palas each of the following powdered ingredients:
grapes (*drākṣā*), *ātmaguptā*, *varṣābhū*, *samaṅgā*, *abhīru*, and long pepper (*pippalī*). (AS.Ci.5.53)
Similarly, having split open an *āmalaka* fruit, one should take half a *prastha* of *viśvabheṣaja* (dry ginger);
a person who is emaciated, wasted, wounded, or drying up should eat these with lumps of jaggery weighing one *pala* each.

Likewise, through the immediate increase of the *rasa* and other elements, one attains nourishment. (AS.Ci.5.55) Half an *āḍhaka* of cow’s milk, one *prastha* of ghee, and one *āḍhaka* of sugarcane juice— (AS.Ci.5.55)
One should add one *kuḍava* of the juice of *vidārī* and one *prastha* of the juice of the *taittira* bird;
when that has been prepared, one should grind the following ingredients with sugarcane juice:
One *kuḍava* of *madhūka* flowers, one *kuḍava* of *priyāla*,
two *palas* of *tvaṅkṣīrī*, and twenty *kharjūra* fruits.
One part each of vibhītaka and majña, one-fourth part of pippalī, thirty palas of sugar, and one handful of madhuka. (AS.Ci.5.58)
Likewise, one should add half-pala quantities of the vitalizing (jīvanīya) drugs here;
once the preparation is cooked, two kuḍavas of honey should be added when it has cooled, and then the boluses (modaka) should be prepared.
One should have them prepared sprinkled with a powder of one pala each of black pepper and cumin; they are used in diseases of wind-blood and bile, as well as in chest wounds, cough, and wasting.

It is beneficial for those whose ojas, voice, and semen are depleted, for disorders of the female reproductive tract, for excessive discharges, for women who have suffered fetal loss, for barren women, and for the miscarriage of a fetus.
One should boil one *tulā* of *kūṣmāṇḍa* (pumpkin gourd) from which the skin and seeds have been removed, after it has been steamed. AS.Ci.5.61
While stirring a *prastha* measure of clarified butter until it takes on the color of honey, one should add [the following] into it.
One hundred *kaṇa* from sugar candy, two *pala* each of *śuṇṭhī* and cumin, and half a *pala* each of the three aromatics (*trijāta*), coriander, and black pepper.
Once it has been cooled, one should add honey and half as much ghee, churn it with a churning-stick, and set it aside; when administered, it destroys [the disease].
It cures cough, hiccup, fever, dyspnea, hemoptysis, chest wounds, and wasting;
it promotes the healing of chest injuries and bestows intelligence, memory, and strength.
One should drink this heart-pleasing rejuvenative elixir (*kūṣmāṇḍaka-rasāyana*) prepared by the Aśvins, increasing the dose of *nāgabalā* root by half a *karṣa* at a time.

One pala [of this] taken with milk for a month, while subsisting on milk alone and abstaining from solid food— this application is supreme for promoting nourishment, longevity, strength, and complexion.

This is the procedure for *maṇḍūkaparṇī* and for *yaṣṭīmadhu*, which are known as the "wealth-giving" (*vittauṣadha*) drugs. One should boil one *tula* of *nāgabalā* in a *droṇa* of water until only a quarter remains.
One should prepare ghee and milk in equal proportions with that decoction,
along with half-pala quantities each of atibalā, balā, yaṣṭīmadhu, and punarnavā.
With *prapauṇḍarīka*, *kāśmarya*, *priyālaka*, and *kapikacchu*; with *aśvagandhā*, white *abhīru*, the pair of *medās*, and *trikaṇṭaka*.
With *kākolī*, *kṣīrakākolī*, *kṣīraśuklā*, the two types of *jīraka*,
lotus stalks (*mṛṇāla*), *bisā*, dates (*kharjūra*), *śṛṅgāṭaka*, and *kaśeruka* (AS.Ci.5.71).
This *nāgabalā* ghee conquers hemorrhaging due to pitta, chest wounds, and wasting; it also overcomes thirst, vertigo, and burning sensations, and is supreme for bestowing strength and nourishment.

When used for six months, this [preparation], which is described as improving complexion, longevity, and vitality, and destroying wrinkles and graying hair, causes even an old man to become like a youth.
It consists of sugar and powdered long pepper (pippalī) taken with ghee and honey.
One should drink milk either combined with [these] or boiled [with them], which removes cough and fever.
[Milk] prepared with sour fruits, fried in ghee, and processed with the juice of vidārī and sugarcane [is also beneficial].
A man who has been depleted by women should drink a broth that is supremely life-sustaining and nourishing (AS.Ci.5.74),
or he should consume a churned drink (mantha) made of flour strained through a cloth and mixed with honey and ghee (AS.Ci.5.75).

A person who is accustomed to a diet of barley, who has a stimulated digestive fire, and who is emaciated from chest wounds, should drink [milk] prepared with the *jīvanīya* (vitalizing) drugs; or alternatively, he may consume meat from wild animals fried in ghee and likewise prepared with the *jīvanīya* drugs.
One should administer the elixir (rasa) mixed with sugar as a condiment when [the patient] is emaciated;
likewise, it may be taken with the milk or meat-broths of cows, buffaloes, horses, elephants, or goats.
One should feed [the patient] barley-based food with soups or sour fruits soaked in ghee;
this regimen is for when the digestive fire is kindled, while for a weak fire, it serves as a digestive stimulant and promoter.
The decoction mentioned for consumption (yakṣman) is recommended for those with chest injuries; however, if the stool is liquid,
one should use a binding [decoction] of daśamūla, svayaṃguptā, śaṅkhapuṣpī, śaṭhī, and balā.
Take two *pala* portions each of *hastipippalī*, *apāmārga*, the root of *pippalī*, *citraka*, *bhārṅgī*, and *puṣkaramūla*, along with one *āḍhaka* of barley.
One should boil one hundred *harītakī* fruits in five *āḍhaka*s of water;
when it has been reduced to the consistency of a decoction for steaming barley, that strained liquid and those hundred *abhayā* fruits [are to be used].
Having added one *tulā* of sugar-candy and one *kuḍava* each of ghee,
oil, and powdered long pepper, [the preparation is cooked]; then, once it has cooled, honey is added.
From this elixir, one should always consume two *abhaya* fruits along with the linctus;
it destroys wrinkles and graying hair, and increases complexion, longevity, and strength.
[It cures] the five types of cough, wasting, dyspnea accompanied by hiccups, irregular fever, urinary disorders,
abdominal tumors, malabsorption syndrome, hemorrhoids, heart disease, loss of appetite, and chronic rhinitis.
This auspicious and excellent elixir (rasāyana) prescribed by Agastya [is as follows]:
daśamūla, balā, mūrvā, the two types of haridrā, and the two types of pippalī.
Pāṭhā, aśvagandhā, apāmārga, svaguptā, ativiṣā, amṛtā,
tender bilva, trivṛt, dantī root, and the leaf of citraka.
Payasyā, kuṭaja, hiṃsrā, the flower and the pith of bījaka; bolā, sthavira, bhallātaka, vikaṅkata, and śatāvarī.
One pala each of *pūtīkarañja*, *śamyāka*, *candralekhā*, *sahācara*, the bark of *saubhāñjanaka* and *nimba*, and *ikṣura*.

One thousand and one hundred *pathyā* fruits and two *āḍhaka*s of barley should be boiled in eight times as much water; once it has reached the consistency of boiled barley, one should remove it from the heat.

When it has been purified, one should add sugar and Pathyā; then, to that, one should add a *tulā* of aged jaggery, followed by one *prastha* each of oil, clarified butter (*ājya*), and the juice of *dhātrī*. AS.Ci.5.90. Then, once again—
One should cook it over a mild fire until it leaves a coating on the ladle, then remove it from the heat;
once cooled, one should add two *prasthas* of honey and one *kuḍava* of long pepper (*pippalī*).
Then,
one should bury three palas of powdered *trijātaka* in old grain kept in an earthen jar for one month; thereafter, one should consume it as previously described.

This elixir (rasāyana) spoken by Vasiṣṭha is superior to the previous one in its qualities; it is recommended for those in good health, requires no restrictive regimen, and is praised for all seasons.

One *pālika* of rock salt (*saindhava*), two *pala*s of ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), and two *pala*s of black salt (*sauvarcala*); one *kuḍava* each of wood-apple (*vṛkṣāmla*), pomegranate (*dāḍima*), and *ārjaka* leaves.
In this [preparation], one should provide one *karṣa* each of long pepper (*marica*) and cumin (*jājī*), two *caturthika* measures of coriander (*dhānyaka*),
and twelve *pala* of sugar (*śarkarā*).
Having prepared a powder from this, one should administer a dose with food and drink; it is appetizing, digestive, strengthening, and cures pain in the flanks, dyspnea, and cough.
Take one *ṣoḍaśikā* of *dhānya*, two each of *ajāji* and *dīpyaka*,
two each of *dāḍima* and *vṛkṣāmla*, and two *pala*s of *sauvarcala* salt.
One *karṣa* of ginger and five *palas* from the pulp of the *dadhittha* fruit—
this powder should be mixed with sixteen *palas* of sugar.
This ṣāḍava should be administered with food and drinks as before; furthermore,
the regimen prescribed for consumption (yakṣman), bile disorders (pitta), and blood diseases is recommended for a wound.

When the injury to the [vulnerable] tissues has subsided but the *kapha* has increased, for that patient of cough who experiences a tearing sensation in the chest and head, one should inhale these following medicinal smokes (*dhūma*).
Having prepared a wick from the pastes of the two types of medā, the two types of balā,
and yaṣṭīmadhu, well-soaked in linen cloth, one should inhale the smoke while following it with a drink of *jīvanīya* ghee.
Manahshila, bala, ajagandha, tvakshiri, and nagara—
these should be taken with a post-drink (anupana) of sugar-water, sugarcane juice, or molasses-water, just as before.
Having ground equal parts of realgar and fresh *vaṭa* sprouts,
one should drink the resulting smoke with ghee, followed by a meal consisting of partridge meat.

In the case of [fever] born of depletion (*kṣayaja*), one should first administer nourishing therapy (*bṛṃhaṇa*) and increase the digestive fire (*agni*). For a patient with abundant *doṣas*, one should administer a mild purgative (*virecana*) along with unctuous substances (*sneha*).
With *śamyāka*, with *trivṛt* combined with grape juice,
with a decoction of *tilvaka*, and with the fresh juice of *vidārī*.
One whose body is emaciated and who suffers from cough due to wasting (kṣayakāsa) should drink ghee prepared as a purificatory treatment with proper method,
when pitta, kapha, and the bodily tissues (dhātus) have been depleted.
One should drink ghee prepared with *karkaṭakī*, milk, and the two types of *balā*;
or [ghee] prepared with *vidārī*, *kadamba*, and the fruit of the *tāla* palm.

Ghee and milk [are used] when there is discoloration of the urine and difficulty in its passage; [they are also indicated] when the penis and anus are swollen and painful, along with the hips and groins.
One should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) with light ghee-scum or with a mixed preparation;
for one who has been given a supplementary meal of meat from wild animals, such as the quail or hole-dwelling creatures.
Likewise, carnivorous animals should be employed gradually;
due to their heat and their violent nature, they cause [the humors] to fall away from the channels.
With those [drugs] properly purified, one should bring about nourishment; when the nutrient fluid (rasa) flows correctly, one should use cavya, triphalā, bhārgī, daśamūla, and citraka.

In water boiled with horse gram (kulattha), long pepper root (pippalīmūla), pāṭhā, jujube (kola), and barley (yava), along with ginger (nāgara), dūsparśā, long pepper (pippalī), śaṭī, and puṣkara... [AS.Ci.5.111]
One should cook ghee with equal parts of the powders of *karkaṭaśṛṅgī*;
when this is prepared, one should add the two powdered alkalis and the five salts.
Having administered it according to the proper method, one afflicted by wasting cough (kṣayakāsa) should drink the appropriate dose.
[This is prepared] with kāsamarda, abhayā, mustā, pāṭhā, kaṭphala, and nāgara.
One *prastha* of ghee, along with one *akṣa* each of *pippalī*, *kaṭurohiṇī*, *kāśmarī*, and *surasā*, should be cooked with one *āḍhaka* each of milk and grape juice.
This auspicious preparation, derived from the leaves, roots, fruits, and sprouts of vṛṣa, vyāghrī, and guḍūcī, cures chronic fever, enlargement of the spleen, and all types of cough. (AS.Ci.5.115)
Ghee cooked with the juices and pastes [of these drugs] cures cough, fever, and loss of appetite;
or alternatively, ghee prepared with double the amount of pomegranate juice combined with the three pungents (vyoṣa).
A person should drink [this] after a meal, combined with barley-alkali (yavakṣāra),
or ghee prepared with long pepper (pippalī) and nut grass (musta), mixed with goat’s milk.
These ghees are for the purpose of increasing the digestive fire in those suffering from wasting and cough; they also serve to purify the throat, chest, and channels obstructed by the humors (doṣas).
Needles from the porcupine, when cauterized and mixed with ghee, honey, and sugar, [should be used].
The two [roots] of *barhipāda* (śyonāka) with honey and ghee cure dyspnea and cough;
or else, the alkali of castor leaves combined with *vyoṣa*, oil, and jaggery.
Alternatively, one should have the patient lick an alkaline preparation made from the leaves of *surasā* and *eraṇḍa*;
or one should have them lick the powder of the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*) with old jaggery and clarified butter.
One should lick a paste of citraka, triphalā, jīraka, karkaṭaśṛṅgī, and the three pungents (kaṭutrika), along with grapes, mixed with honey and ghee; or one may take it with jaggery.
Pāṭhā, madhuka, jīvantī, tvakkṣīrī, triphalā,
ghanam (musta), śaṭhī, the two types of bṛhatī, drākṣā, pippalī, elā, and vitunnaka.
Sārivā, the root of puṣkara, karkaṭa-khyā, rasāñjana, punarnavā,
iron filings, trāyamāṇā, and yavānikā.
AS.Ci.5.123: *Ṛddhi*, *tāmalakī*, *bhārṅgī*, *viḍaṅga*,
*dhanvayāsaka*, alkali (*kṣāra*), *citraka*, *cavya*, *amlavetasa*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), and *dāru*.
One should conquer all coughs by licking this powder with honey and ghee:
padmaka, triphalā, vyoṣa, viḍaṅga, and devadāru. (AS.Ci.5.124)
This powder of balārāsnā, mixed with an equal amount of sugar,
should be licked with honey and ghee for a delicious taste; it is an excellent remedy for cough.
Similarly, one may take the powder of *mārica* with ghee, honey, and sugar; or one should hold a pill made of *pathyā*, *śuṇṭhī*, *ghana*, and *guda* in the mouth.
In all types of cough and dyspnea, one may administer either *bibhītaka* alone,
or the paste of *tilvaka* leaves fried in ghee and mixed with sugar.
Alternatively, as a peyā (gruel), it conquers vomiting, thirst, cough, and diarrhea. [One should take] white mustard, gaṇḍīra, viḍaṅga, vyoṣa (the three pungents), and citraka.
One should prepare a gruel (yavāgū) with that water along with Abhayā; it should be taken with ghee and salt for cough,
hiccups, dyspnea, and catarrh.
Mung bean soup, well-prepared and cooked in the decoction of *kaṇṭakārī*, is recommended for anemia (*pāṇḍvāmaya*), wasting (*kṣaya*), swelling (*śopha*), and earache (*karṇaśūla*).
Amalaka with ghee and sour substances is a remedy for all types of cough;
likewise, milk, soups, and meat broths prepared in a decoction of Vata-alleviating herbs [are beneficial].

One should cause those suffering from wasting cough to eat birds that scratch with their claws, those that peck, and those that live in burrows; and those medicinal smokes along with their after-drinks which have been prescribed for cough due to chest injury (kṣatakāsa) [should also be used].
These [remedies] should also be applied in the case of consumptive cough (kṣayakāsa), as well as those which will be described for pulmonary consumption (yakṣman);
they are nourishing, digestive of the fire, and purifying of the channels.
In cases of wasting cough, all strengthening (balya) treatments are recommended when applied in alternation; for this reason,
wasting cough arising from the derangement of the three humors (sannipāta) is a formidable condition.
"Whatever is beneficial for a *sannipāta* [disorder] according to the strength of its respective humors is wholesome"—
thus ends the fifth chapter.
Now begins the sixth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of dyspnea and hiccup;
thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.

Since dyspnea (śvāsa) and hiccup (hidhmā) have identical causes and other factors, their treatment is likewise the same; therefore, one should first treat the afflicted patient with sudation therapies (sveda).

When the congealed *kapha* in the channels is treated with unctuous substances and smeared with salt and oil, it becomes liquefied even if it was previously adherent; having thus dissolved, it reaches the digestive tract (*koṣṭha*) and becomes easily expelled.
There should be softness in the channels and a downward movement of the wind;
once the patient has been fomented, one should feed them food that is unctuous and prepared with the juices of marshy animals.
Or one may administer it with curdled milk; thereafter, a mild emetic should be given to him,
especially for those suffering from cough, vomiting, cardiac oppression, or loss of voice.
When the corrupted body is cleared of phlegm, one attains comfort through the administration of long pepper, rock salt, and honey— provided it is not contraindicated by Vata.
When the channels have been purified, the wind moves unimpeded;
in cases of flatulence, upward-moving wind (udāvarta), and tamaka asthma, [one should treat with] mātuluṅga and sour vetasa.
Food combined with asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), *pīlu*, and *biḍa* salt acts as a downward-moving purgative;
or one should administer a lukewarm purgative consisting of sour fruits mixed with rock salt (*saindhava*).
For these [diseases] arise from the provocation of the vital breath (prāṇa) whose movement is obstructed by phlegm (kapha);
therefore, for the purpose of purifying that path, purification through the upper and lower routes is beneficial.
Just as water flowing with great force is stirred up even more by the obstruction of its path,
so too should one clear the patient's channel of that [obstruction] by means of air.
When [the patient] has not yet become tranquil despite having undergone purification, one should remove the latent impurity with medicated smokes (*dhūma*). [The ingredients for the smoke are:
turmeric leaves, *airaṇḍa* root, lac, and realgar.
One should grind devadāru, ela, and māṃsī together and prepare a wick;
one should inhale the smoke produced from that wick when smeared with ghee, or alternatively, consume barley grains mixed with ghee.
Beeswax, resin of the *sarja* tree, clarified butter, or *agaru*; or sandalwood, the horn of a goat, or the hair or sinews of cows.
Or the skins, horns, and hooves of a rishi-deer, a lizard, a kuraṅga deer, or an eṇa deer;
or guggulu, or realgar, or the resin of the sāla tree.
Sallakī, guggulu, loha, and padmaka, soaked in ghee, [should be applied]; indeed, for those who require sudation, even for those not fit for sudation, this may be used for a moment.
One should apply fomentation by sprinkling lukewarm unctuous substances mixed with sugar and milk,
and by means of *utkārikā* poultices and *upanāha* compresses using the medicinal drugs prescribed in the chapter on fomentation.
In the case of *āmavāta*, one should treat the chest and throat with mild measures according to the prescribed regimen (AS.Ci.6.17).
Having observed that the *vāta* has been aggravated by excessive treatment, one should pacify it with wind-alleviating therapies (AS.Ci.6.18).
One should bring [the condition] to subsidence by means of unctuous juices and other substances, and by massages that are not excessively hot;
for in those whose kapha is not provoked, who have not undergone sudation, and who are weak, purification [therapies] would lead to harm.
When the Vāyu has gained a foothold in the vital points (marmans), it quickly dries them up and takes away the life-breaths;
therefore, one should pacify those [Vāyu disorders] with decoctions, linctuses, unctuous substances, and so forth.
One should treat hiccup and dyspnea arising from the complications of diminished strength, wounds, diarrhea, blood disorders, pitta,
or burning sensations with sweet, unctuous, and cold remedies.
In a decoction of *kulattha* and the ten roots (*daśamūla*), there should be the meat-broths (*rasa*) of wild animals,
as well as soups (*yūṣa*) made from *śigru*, eggplant (*vārtāka*), *kāsaghna*, and radish (*vṛṣamūlaka*).
With the tender leaves of *nimba*, *kulaka*, *bṛhatī*, and *mātuluṅga*;
and with *vyāghrī*, *durālabhā*, *śṛṅgī*, the pulp of *bilva*, and *trikaṇṭaka*.

A soup should be prepared with water boiled with *sāmṛta*, *agni*, and *kulattha* pulses; likewise, [a soup] may be made with *rāsnā*, *bṛhatī*, and so forth, along with *balā*, green gram (*mudga*), and *citraka*.
A gruel prepared with citraka, ajājī, śṛṅgī, and sauvarcala,
or with daśamūla, is beneficial for curing cough, dyspnea, hiccup, and pain.
With the ten roots (daśamūla), śaṭhī, rāsnā, bhārṅgī, bilva, vṛddhi, and pauṣkara; with kulīraśṛṅgī, capalā, tāmalakī, and amṛtā.
When this has been digested, one should drink a decoction; thereafter, one should eat a gruel prepared with those same ingredients,
subsisting on *śāli* rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, wheat, barley, mung beans, and horse gram.
To alleviate cough, cardiac oppression, pain in the flanks, hiccups,
and labored breathing, one should take barley meal (saktu) soaked in milk and sun-grown sprouts, mixed with honey.
One should drink barley that has been stirred with a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla) and other herbs;
and one should add alkali, asafoetida, ghee, biḍa salt, and pomegranate to the food.
One should take puṣkara, śaṭhī, vyoṣa, mātuluṅga, and amlavetasa; or a decoction of daśamūla, or alternatively, of devadāru.
Or one suffering from hiccup and dyspnea who is thirsty should drink the scum of *vāruṇī* liquor;
[this is prepared] with *pippalī*, *pippalīmūla*, *pathyā*, *jantughna*, and *citraka*.

Once the wound has been smeared with these powdered ingredients and has healed, one should place it in a vessel of ghee; that [ghee], having been kept for a month in buttermilk, is indeed an appetizer and a conqueror of asthma and cough.
One should drink one *prasṛta* measure each of *pāṭhā*, *madhurasā*, *dāru*, and *sarala*, which have been soaked overnight, along with a small amount of salt, in the scum of *surā* liquor.
Śirīṣa, kunda, and kadalī flowers combined with pippalī and soaked in rice-water are a supreme remedy for hiccup,
dyspnea, and cough.
Or, having ground them with fermented rice-water (āranāla), they may be combined with the juice of citron (mātuluṅga);
or else, with water, they may be combined with asafoetida (hiṅgu), black salt (sauvarcala), long pepper (kaṇā), *kola*, and green gram (mudga).

One should administer either bhārgī, ginger, or alkali combined with black pepper, ground with their own decoction and kneaded into a warm poultice (bāṣpikā). Alternatively, one may cause the patient to drink it.
In cases of dyspnea accompanied by pitta and kapha, one should administer the fresh juice of *saptaparṇa* or the flowers of *śirīṣa*, combined with *madhuka* and *kaṇā*.
A poultice (utkārikā) made from *tugākṣīrī*, *pippalī*, honey, *madhūlī*, jaggery,
and *śuṇṭhī* should be applied when there is an association with pitta; however, it should be used when vāta is the associated secondary factor.
Milk combined with the flesh of a porcupine and a hare, fragments of meat, ghee, scorpions, and blood,
along with the juice of *suvarcalā*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), and clarified butter— [this is the remedy]. (AS.Ci.6.38)
In cases where vāta and pitta are persistent, one should administer rice gruel boiled with coriander as a drink;
or alternatively, goat's milk prepared with four parts water, along with jaggery and ginger.
One should lick the juices of pippalī root, madhuka, jaggery, and the dung of cows,

horses, and goats, combined with honey and ghee, to destroy hiccup, ophthalmia, and cough (AS.Ci.6.40); as well as the juices of the dung of cows, elephants, horses, boars, camels, donkeys, rams, goats, and sheep.
One who has an excess of phlegm should lick these [medicines] one by one at equal intervals, or otherwise drink them.
One suffering from dyspnea with an excess of phlegm should likewise lick the soot derived from the skin, hair, bones, hooves, and horns of quadrupeds, as well as that of *vājigandhā*.
Or an alkaline preparation derived from triphalā, pāṭhā, and the fruits and roots of bṛhatī; or [a collyrium made of] pearl, coral, lapis lazuli, conch shell, saugandhika, and añjana.
Masāragalla, crystal, glass, ilā, and the two types of salt;
the fruit of apāmārga, copper, iron, silver, and the fruit of śaṇa. (AS.Ci.6.44)
One should lick that with *jyotīrasa* mixed with honey and a liquid extract; or else, [one may take] *śaṭhī*, *pauṣkara*, and *dhātrī*, or *pauṣkara* combined with *kaṇā*.
Either red ochre, collyrium, or black [pigment], or the fresh juice of wood-apple (kapittha),
or emblic myrobalan, rock salt, and long pepper mixed with the juice of wood-apple.
Or one should lick a paste of *pathyā*, *viḍaṅga*, *uṣaṇa*, and *pippalī* with ghee and honey;
or alternatively, a paste of *pippalī*, *drākṣā*, *pathyā*, *śṛṅgī*, and *durālabhā*.
Or one may take *tryūṣaṇa* combined with alkali along with ghee, honey, and oil;
or the juices of *dhātrī* and *kapittha* mixed with *pippalī* and honey;
or sugar, *tvāmalakī*, and *drākṣā*, along with the juice of cow and horse dung.
Either kola, lāja, honey, drākṣā, pippalī,
and nāgara; or guḍa, oil, niśā, drākṣā, kaṇā, rāsnā, and uṣaṇa.
One should drink the medicinal powders with juices, water, wine, and so forth; or else, [one may take] the powders of jīvantī, musta, surasa, bark, the two types of elā, and pauṣkara.
Caṇḍā, tāmalakī, iron (loha), bhārṅgī, nāgara,
and vālaka; karkaṭākhya, śaṭhī, kṛṣṇā, nāgakesara, and coraka.
This powder, when consumed as desired with double the amount of sugar,
is an excellent remedy for pain in the flanks, fever, and cough, and it effectively cures hiccups and dyspnea.
Jīvantī, coraka, śṛṅgī, pauṣkara, surasa, śaṭhī,
pippalī, tvak, biḍa, kṣāra, śuṇṭhī, hiṅgu, and amlavetasa.
Elā, āmalakī, bhārṅgī, and vṛkṣāmla, powdered together,
[should be taken] with the juice of mātuluṅga, or with wine, or with clarified butter.
When licked, added to food, or used alone,
it cures hiccups, dyspnea, constipation, hemorrhoids, cough, and pain in the heart and flanks.
A powder made from *śaṭhī*, *tāmalakī*, *bhārṅgī*, *caṇḍā*, *vālaka*, and *pauṣkara*,
with eight times as much sugar, is an excellent remedy for hiccups and dyspnea.
One should eat equal parts of jaggery and ginger, or one should administer them as a nasal drop (nasya); likewise,
one may take the root of garlic, onion, or leek.
Alternatively, one should administer the juice of sandalwood with human breast milk as a nasal drop (nāvana);
or one may give long pepper (*pippalī*) with sugar, or licorice (*madhuka*) mixed with honey.
[One should apply] breast milk, or the excrement of flies, or the juice of lac;
or clarified butter (ghṛta) mixed with rock salt (saindhava), or clarified butter prepared with breast milk.
One should drink or apply as an ointment that [mixture] made into a paste with sweet substances,
once warm and once cold, alternately, along with sugar and honey.
In the same way, ghee prepared with milk and the drugs that act on the lower part of the body (purgatives) is established [as a remedy]; likewise,
[ghee prepared] with *kaṇā*, *sauvarcala* salt, alkali (*kṣāra*), *vayasthā*, *hiṅgu*, and *coraka*.
One should cook ghee and whey with the ten roots (*daśamūla*) in a decoction of *sakāya* (the body of the plant).
One should drink that, or one may lick it, prepared with the life-promoting (*jīvanīya*) drugs and mixed with honey.
Tejovatī, abhayā, kuṣṭha, pippalī,
kaṭurohiṇī, pūgīka, pauṣkara root, palāśa, citraka, and śaṭhī.
One should boil two parts each of *paṭu*, *tāmalakī*, *jīvantī*, and the pulp of *bilva*,
along with one *karṣa* each of *vacā*, *patra*, and *tālīsa*.
A *prastha* of ghee processed with the four parts of asafoetida, when drunk, quickly destroys asthma,
wind-disorders, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*), hiccups, and pains in the heart and flanks.
Alternatively,
one may drink clarified butter prepared with one *prastha* of ghee and a *picu*-measure each of *siddhārthaka*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, lac, and *sarjarasa*, along with *padmaka* and *manohvā*.
Clarified butter prepared with the *vatsakādi* group as a decoction additive, or clarified butter from the first group of drugs combined with the five salts, dispels both asthma and cough.

One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with one *āḍhaka* of water and the following ingredients, each in the measure of a *kola*: *hiṃsrā*, *viḍaṅga*, *pūtīka*, the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), the three fruits (*triphalā*), and *agnika*.
Combined with two *prasthas* of milk, it destroys cough, dyspnea, chronic rhinitis,
hemorrhoids, anorexia, abdominal tumors, consumption, and hiccups.
Or one should administer old ghee mixed with half a part of rock salt (saindhava),
or Dhānvantara-ghee, Vṛṣa-ghee, Dādhika-ghee, or [ghee prepared with] Tryūṣaṇa and other such ingredients.
The sudden sprinkling of cold water, terror, distraction,
fear, grief, exhilaration, envy, the suppression of breath, and being stung by insects are beneficial.
Whatever is hot, subdues phlegm and wind, and facilitates the downward movement of wind should generally be used, especially that which is most effective at removing wind.
That which produces Vāta while removing Kapha, or produces Kapha while subduing Vāta— such an action is not definitive; between these two, that which subdues Vāta is generally superior.
For in the nourishing therapy (br̥ṃhaṇa) of all [patients], the treatment is generally slight and feasible;
in the pacifying therapy (śamana), there is no excessive harm; and in the reducing therapy (karśana), it is neither too severe nor impossible.
Therefore, one should treat those [conditions] primarily with pacifying (śamana) and nourishing (br̥ṃhaṇa) therapies;
and cough, dyspnea, wasting, vomiting, and hiccups should be treated with the remedies for one another.
Thus ends the sixth chapter.
Now begins the seventh chapter.
Hereafter, we shall expound the chapter titled "The Treatment of Rajayakshma" (Phthisis).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:
"For one who is strong, whose doṣas are abundant, and who has been treated with oleation and sudation, purification [therapy] is indicated. (AS.Ci.7.1–2)
For a patient suffering from consumption (yakṣman), one should administer unctuous substances that do not cause emaciation,
either with milk mixed with *phala* (emetic nut) or with a sweet meat-broth. AS.Ci.7.2–3.
One should induce emesis with gruel mixed with ghee and prepared with emetic substances; one should administer purgation using trivṛt, śyāmā, and nṛpadruma.
These should be combined with sugar, honey, and ghee, or with milk, or with a nourishing draught (tarpaṇa),
or with the juices of grapes, vidārī, kāśmarya, and meat.
For one whose digestive tract has been purified, one should employ a regimen that is nourishing and digestive-stimulant,
as well as agreeable foods and drinks that alleviate vāta and are light.

Rice (*śāli*), sixty-day rice (*ṣaṣṭika*), wheat (*godhūma*), barley (*yava*), and mung beans (*mudga*), when properly prepared, are light, do not lose their potency, are easily digested, and provide strength.
Goat's milk, ghee, meat, and the flesh of carnivorous animals conquer wasting diseases (śoṣa),
as do [the flesh of] the raven, the owl, the wolf, the leopard, the cow, the horse, the mongoose, and the snake.
The flesh of vultures, hawks, donkeys, and camels is beneficial when administered under disguise;
for if it is known [to be such], it is loathsome and leads to vomiting rather than strength and vigor.

Deer and similar animals are beneficial for pitta and kapha, while the *prasaha* group and others are beneficial for vāta; these may be prepared as *veśavāra* or formulated within soups and other liquid preparations.
Fried in mustard oil or clarified butter as appropriate,
the *rasikās* should be tender, unctuous, and prepared with potent medicinal substances.
Likewise,
soups prepared from mung beans, horse gram, and kulattha, along with long pepper, barley, kulattha, and ginger, are beneficial.
One should drink the unctuous goat meat broth together with pomegranate and āmalaka;
by that, the six disorders beginning with chronic rhinitis (pīnasa) are eliminated.
With *drākṣā* (grape) that has been freed of its seeds and ground with the juice of *kola* and *dāḍima*,
mixed with a paste stirred in clear water from grain.
One should prepare [a powder] combined with sauvarcala salt, vyoṣa, patra, elā, and dīpyaka,
along with honey, camphor, lavaṅga, and kesara.
The *candrakānta* stone, which is true to its name, removes dryness and bestows the brilliance of fire;
one *pala* of it, ground into a paste with the juices of sour *śukti*, *amlavetasa*, and *dhātrī*, as well as *drākṣā*, [should be used].
Combined with six *pala*s of jaggery and mixed with one *karṣa* each of the following finely ground ingredients:
*vṛkṣāmla*, coriander, *drakṣā*, black mustard, pomegranate, and black pepper.
A decoction of *nāgapuṣpa* mixed with a small amount of *sauvarcala* salt,
along with the bark of *sevyapatra*, blended with the juice of *surasā*.
The *bhūribhūstṛṇaka* decoction, prepared with honey, is beneficial for the throat and appetizing; one should especially drink aged wine, which cleanses the channels.
In cases of Pitta and other [doshas], honey-wine (madhu-ariṣṭa), Āccha-wine, or Vāruṇī-wine are especially effective;
alternatively, water prepared with the five roots (pañcamūla) or with Tāmalakī may be used.
One should carefully prepare pure food for him using the four *parṇinī* herbs or with *dhānyanāgaraka*, according to what is suitable for him.
Ghee prepared with *daśamūla* and milk, or with meat broth,
or containing *balā* and the broth of the flesh of carrion-eaters, should be administered.
Ghee prepared with ten times the amount of milk and mixed with honey,
along with *jīvantī*, *madhuka*, *drākṣā*, and the fruits of *kuṭaja* [is beneficial].
Puṣkarāhvā, śaṭhī, kṛṣṇā, vyāghrī, gokṣuraka, balā, nīlī, utpala, tāmalakī, trāyamāṇā, and durālabhā.
Having made a paste of these, ghee is cooked; it is the supreme remedy for the king of diseases (fever).
[One should take] durālabhā, gokṣuraka, the four parṇinīs, and balā.
Having divided the parts into measures of one *pala* each, including one *pala* of *parpaṭaka*,
one should boil them in ten times the amount of water until only one-tenth remains.
When that [mixture] has been purified, one should cook one *prastha* of ghee with twice as much milk,
adding as an internal ingredient (*garbha*) *śaṭhī*, *kṛṣṇā*, *bhūnimba*, *utpala*, and *sārivā*.
One should conquer pain in the head, the sides, and the back by using the root of *trāyantī* along with its leaves and fruit, as well as the fruit of *kuṭaja*.
Ghee prepared with dates (*kharjūra*), raisins (*mṛdvīkā*), licorice (*madhuka*), and *parūṣaka* cures thirst, vomiting, diarrhea, cough, burning sensations, vertigo, and fever. (AS.Ci.7.28)
Ghee prepared from fresh milk boiled with *daśamūla* and mixed with long pepper (*pippalī*) removes disorders of the voice, cough, dyspnea,
and fever (AS.Ci.7.29).
That [mixture], combined with long pepper and honey, is supreme for restoring the voice;
it destroys pain in the head, the sides, and the chest, and removes cough, dyspnea, and fever.
The ghee that arises from being boiled with five [sets of] five roots,
or with the decoction of the five [sets of] five roots in four times the amount of milk.
This prepared ghee overcomes the sevenfold strength of consumption (yakṣman).
One should cook ghee with five parts of *pañcakola*, alkali of barley (*yavakṣāra*), and six *pala* [of other ingredients].
One *prastha* measure of this decoction, mixed with an equal amount of milk, purifies the channels and cures abdominal tumors,
fever, enlargement of the abdomen, splenic disorders, malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*), anemia, and chronic rhinitis.
One should conquer cough, dyspnea, loss of digestive fire, edema, and upward-moving wind by using water boiled with *rāsnā*, *balā*, *gokṣuraka*, *sthirā*, and *varṣābhū*.
Ghee prepared with *jīvantī* and *pippalī* as the internal ingredients along with milk conquers wasting diseases;
likewise, ghee prepared from milk boiled with *aśvagandhā*, combined with sugar and milk, [is effective].
One should boil one *tulā* of common meat in two *droṇas* of water.
With that [decoction] reduced to one-eighth part,
one should prepare one *prastha* of ghee along with one *pala* each of the *jīvanīya* (vitalizing) drugs; this cures diseases caused by *vāta* and *pitta*.
This meat and ghee, when drunk with meat broth,
conquers cough, dyspnea, loss of voice, emaciation, and pain in the heart and flanks.
One should boil one *tulā* each of yaṣṭī, balā, guḍūcī, and the minor *pañcamūla* in a winnowing basket until eight parts of the water remain; into that, one should cook a vesselful of ghee.
For the treatment of *arman* (corneal opacity), this Pārāśara ghee is prepared by mixing three vessels of milk with the juices of *dhātrī*, *vidārī*,
and sugarcane, along with the well-ground *jīvanīya* drugs.
A decoction of *mūrvā*, *haridrā*, and *khadira*, along with ghee and the juice of cow dung, when practiced regularly, uproots consumption (*rājayakṣman*) together with its army.
Ten equal parts of the ten liquids produced from cow, elephant, goat, sheep, and horse; the sweet group of drugs, the three pungents (trikaṭu) ground into a paste, and devadāru.
One should quickly cook that [milk] as a destroyer of wasting diseases; likewise, there is Vāsāvarī-ghṛta.
[The ingredients are: the two groups of five roots (pañcamūla), varaṇa, barley, bilva, and punarnavā.
Having added the inner pulp of *karañja*, *bola*, *sthavirakula*, *badara*, and *agnikā*,
along with the milk of *snuhī*, *śukākhyā*, *cavya*, and rock salt; AS.Ci.7.42.
One should drink a dose of *harītakī* with barley gruel to remove wasting, swelling, urinary disorders, and abdominal enlargement; or one should lick it mixed with honey.
One should administer these prepared ghees together with food,
or [the following powder]: cardamom, *ajamoda*, the three myrobalans, *saurāṣṭrī*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), and *citraka*.
[One should take] those produced from Sāra, Ariṣṭa, Gāyatrī, and Sālabījaka; and eight *pala* each of *bhallātaka* and *viḍaṅga*.
One should cook [the paste] in sixteen-fold water until it remains as a sixteenth part;
then, with that [decoction], one should cook one *prastha* of ghee, and when this is prepared, six *palas* [of the medicinal ingredients].

One should add thirty palas of *akṣīra* and double that amount of honey; then, three palas each of ghee and the three aromatics (*trijāta*), having been stirred with a churning-stick, should be licked from that mixture.
That [milk] taken with milk as a post-drink (anupāna) in the forenoon is a rejuvenative (rasāyana) that requires no restrictive regimen;
it promotes intelligence, vision, and longevity, stimulates digestion, and quickly destroys [diseases].
Those *sarpiguḍas* (medicated jaggery boluses) which have been prescribed for urinary disorders, tumors, wasting diseases, anemia, and fistula-in-ano,
should also be employed in cases of chest injury and wasting.
[These consist of] date-palm, long pepper, grapes, *pathyā*, *śṛṅgī*, and *durālabhā*.
Triphalā, pippalī, mustā, śṛṅgāṭa, jaggery,
and sugar; vīrā, śaṭhī, puṣkaramūla, surasā, sugar, and jaggery.
Long pepper, *citraka*, parched grain, long pepper, emblic myrobalan, and jaggery;
AS.Ci.7.51: the essence of *viḍaṅga*, *cavya*, and the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), all finely powdered.
These five linctuses (lehas), remembered in half-verses, are beneficial for the voice when taken with honey and ghee;
they destroy cough, consumption, dyspnea, pain in the flanks, and phlegm.
Cinnamon, cardamom, long pepper, and *kṣīrī* (milk-hedge plant), with sugar added in double the quantity of each in successive order—
these, powdered, one should eat or lick; their qualities are the same as those previously described.
Sesame, black gram, and *aśvagandhā*, when mixed with honey and ghee,
are highly recommended for the aforementioned diseases that are predominantly caused by *vāta*.

AS.Ci.7.54 [This condition] is not treated with a decoction; specifically, for one suffering from *svarasāda*, one should apply nasal drops (*nasya*), medicinal smoke (*dhūma*), and other such treatments.
In that case as well, for a disorder born of Vāta, one should drink lukewarm ghee after the meal,
prepared with the fresh juices of *kāsamarda*, *vārtāku*, and *mārkaṣa*.
This prepared remedy, conquered by Ārtagala, cures cough and improves the voice; or else,
the paste of *badarī* leaves fried in ghee with rock salt may be used.
Or one should administer oil prepared with madhuka, drākṣā, pippalī, kṛminud fruits,
and the root of haṃsapādī as a nasal irrigation (nastaḥ).
One should eat rice with jaggery along with warm water as a drink and ghee, as well as milk-rice (pāyasa); likewise, one should employ unctuous sudation.
In the case of a Pitta-originated fever, one should drink ghee followed by boiled, cooled milk.
One should eat milk-porridge (pāyasa) prepared with liquorice (yaṣṭīmadhuka), along with honey and ghee, which has been cooked with the decoction and paste of the sprouts of milky trees (kṣīrivṛkṣa).
Ghee prepared with *balā*, *vidārigandhā*, *vidārī*, and *madhuka*,
along with salt, is an unsurpassed nasal medication (*nasya*) for the voice.
Prapaunḍarīka, madhuka, pippalī, bṛhatī, and balā,
prepared with milk and ghee, constitute an excellent nasal medication (nāvana) that restores one's natural vigor.
One should lick the powder of the "sweet" (madhuraka) drugs mixed with honey and ghee;
likewise, [the powder of] śatāvarī, balā, payasyā, kākolī, and madhuka.
If it is not pacified in this manner, one should venesect the vein on the forehead;
in the case of a kaphaja disorder, one should drink pungent substances with urine while following a dry diet.
One should lick a paste of *kaṭphala*, *āmalaka*, and the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), saturated with oil and honey;
or alternatively, *vyoṣa*, alkali, *agni*, *cavikā*, *bhārgī*, *pathyā*, and honey.

One should drink barley gruel prepared with *yavānī*, *pippalī*, and *āmalakī* in a mixture of two parts water and one part milk; after eating, one should consume *pippalī* and *śuṇṭhī*, or undergo a strong emetic therapy.
One whose voice is impaired while speaking loudly should drink boiled milk mixed with sugar, honey, and sweet [medicinal] substances.
AS.Ci.7.66 Treatment for Anorexia:
In cases of anorexia, various foods prepared with wholesome ingredients are beneficial.
External and internal cleansing, and the nirvāṇa of the mind, are the heart-pleasing medicine. One should consume the tooth-stick at two times of day along with mouth-washes.
One should wash the mouth with astringent decoctions and inhale medicinal smoke. Tālīśa-leaf pills, combined with camphor and white sugar,
[should be used].
And those known as śaśāṅkakiraṇa are excellent edibles that stimulate the appetite; in cases of anorexia caused by vāta, one should drink them with *prasannā* wine.
Or [a powder] made from hareṇu, kṛṣṇā, kṛmijit, drākṣā, saindhava,
nāgara, elā, bhārṅgī, yavakṣāra, and hiṅgu, mixed with ghee.
One should induce vomiting with water decocted with *vacā*, or with molasses-water for cases involving *pitta*;
or one should lick a mixture of sugar, ghee, the best salt (*saindhava*), and honey.
In cases of *kapha*, one should vomit using water infused with *nimba*; one should drink *dīpyaka* and *āragvadha* decoctions, as well as sharp *ariṣṭas* mixed with honey and *mādhava* liquor.
One should drink the previously mentioned powder of hareṇu and other ingredients with warm water; likewise, one should take trikaṭu, triphalā, rāsnā, and yavakṣāra, saturated with honey.
And at the time of the morning meal, one should employ a mouthwash consisting of bida salt,
sauvarcala salt, kuṣṭha, ajājī, marica, and sugar. (AS.Ci.7.74)
Dhātrī, elā, padmaka, uśīra, pippalī, candana, utpala, lodhra,
tejovatī, pathyā, yavakṣāra, and the three pungents (kaṭutraya).
The juice of fresh pomegranate mixed with asafoetida and white sugar, combined with oil and honey—
these four types of gargles (kavalagraha) [are recommended].
Kāravī, ajājī, marica, drākṣā, vṛkṣāmla, and dāḍima destroy the four types of anorexia (arocaka), whether caused by a single doṣa or by all of them combined.
Sauvarcala salt, jaggery, and honey destroy all forms of anorexia. Cardamom, cinnamon, nagakesara, long pepper, black pepper, and ginger [are likewise effective].
This powder, increased by one part at a time and taken with an equal amount of sugar, gradually destroys excessive salivation,
anorexia, heart disease, pain in the flanks, cough, dyspnea, and diseases of the throat. (AS.Ci.7.79)
Having prepared a paste of *yavānī*, *tintiṇīka*, *amlavetasa*, *auṣadha*, and pomegranate, along with one *karṣa* each of *kola* and four *palas* of sugar—
Half a karṣa each of dhānyaka, sauvarcala salt, ajājī, and varāṅga,
along with one hundred pippalīs and two hundred maricas.

This powder is highly appetizing, beneficial for the heart, constipating, and it destroys obstructions, cough, diseases of the heart and flanks, splenic disorders, hemorrhoids, and ailments of the digestive tract (grahaṇī).
[It consists of] tālīśapatra, marica, nāgara, and auspicious pippalī.
In this powder,

the bark and the ginger each have one part, while the sugar is eight times the amount of long pepper (kaṇā); this is progressively increasing in its constituent parts, and it is pleasing to the palate and digestive-stimulating.
It conquers cough, dyspnea, anorexia, vomiting, splenic disorders, and pain in the heart and flanks;
it destroys anemia, fever, and diarrhea, and facilitates the downward movement of obstructed wind.
One *pala* each of *tālīśapatra*, *cavikā*, and black pepper; two *pala*s each of long pepper and its root; and three *pala*s of ginger.
Add four types of aromatic drugs and *uśīra*, each in the measure of one *karṣa*, finely powdered;
then, having added thirty *palas* of refined jaggery (*guḍa*) that has been boiled down, [mix them together].
One should prepare *modakas* (boluses) equal in number to the [number of] seeds; these also possess those same qualities.
This concludes the treatment for excessive salivation (*praseka*).

One who possesses strength should eat barley-meal (saktu) and other foods prepared with barley that has been soaked overnight in water containing the ashes of *arka*, *amṛtā*, and *kṣāra*, and then vomit.
One should eat pungent and bitter meat of wild animals roasted on a spit,
as well as dry foods that are very light, followed by a drink of chickpea soup and similar liquids.
When the wind (vāyu) expels the phlegm (śleṣman) due to excessive secretion of phlegm,
one should recognize that as kaphapraseka; it should be overcome by means that are unctuous and hot.
One should employ this same procedure for chronic rhinitis (pīnasa) and vomiting as well; specifically for chronic rhinitis,
one should habitually practice oil massages, unctuous applications, and sudation.
One should apply unctuous *anutkārikā* boluses to the head, sides, throat, and other areas,
along with savory juices that are salty, sour, pungent, and hot, combined with unctuous substances.
In cases of pain in the head, shoulders, and sides, one should apply the therapeutic measures according to the specific involved *doṣa*.
Well-prepared poultices made from the meat of aquatic and marshy animals should be used.
For those suffering from pain in the head, sides, or shoulders, applications mixed with ghee and oil are recommended;
likewise, a paste made of *nata*, *yaṣṭyāhva*, *śatāhvā*, *kuṣṭha*, and *candana* is beneficial.
Balā, rāsnā, sesame seeds, ghee, madhuka, blue lotus (nīlotpala),
palankaṣā, devadāru, sandalwood, madhuka, and ghee.
Kṛṣṇagandhā, balā, vīrā, vidārī, punarnavā,
abhīru, yaṣṭīmadhuka, payasyā, kattṛṇa, and ghee.
Thus, four types of plasters (pradeha) have been described using these half-formulas;
they are recommended for those with combined doṣas suffering from pain in the head, sides, and chest.
Nasal drops, medicinal smokes, unctuous substances taken after meals,
oils for massage, and likewise enema therapy (bastikarma).

Or, according to the specific dosha involved, one should remove their vitiated blood using horns and other such means; an external application (pradeha) with lotus, ushira, and sandalwood mixed with ghee is desired,
or one with durva, madhuka, manjishtha, and kesara soaked in ghee.

Anointing with oil prepared from sandalwood and other ingredients, or with clarified butter washed a hundred times, as well as sprinkling with milk or water infused with licorice (madhuka), is recommended.
Generally, due to the impairment of the digestive fire (*agni*), one suffers from diarrhea accompanied by mucus;
for such a person, the medicinal treatment prescribed for diarrhea and disorders of the *grahaṇī* is beneficial.
One should have [the patient] drink long pepper and indrayava with rice-water;
once these are digested, one should give gruel prepared with cāṅgerī, sour gruel, and pomegranate.
One should drink the powder of pāṭhā, nimba, and yavānī with buttermilk (takra), or one should drink pāṭhā soaked in wine (surā) along with nāgara and durālabhā.
One should prepare a gruel-scum (peyāmaṇḍa) containing the pulp of *jambu*, mango, and *bilva*, along with *kapittha* and ginger, using the three formulations beginning with *pāṭhā*.
One should prepare *khala* preparations from the pulses and grains, along with fats, *sālma* fruits, and salt, as well as from *vetasa*, *arjuna*, and *jambu*, from *mṛṇālī* and *kṛṣṇagandhā*,
and from the market-available varieties of *mātuluṅga*, *dhātakī*, and *dāḍima*.
One should employ the tender shoots of *cāṅgerī*, *madayantī*, and *yūthikā*,
as well as those of *kālaviddhugdhikā* and *cukrikā*.
One should administer parched grain flour mixed with whey, ghee, and pomegranate;
it is highly effective for curing diarrhea, being appetizing and digestive-stimulant.

One should carefully preserve the feces of a patient suffering from *rājayakṣman* who is wasting away; for one whose all constituent elements (*dhātu*) are depleted, his strength indeed resides in the strength of his stool.
One should also apply these treatments for fevers and other disorders according to the specific disease;
for consumption (*yakṣmā*) is a collection of many ailments and is therefore exceedingly difficult to endure.
Or, dwelling in a hut for six months, one should attend upon a she-goat, subsisting on its milk,
urine, and dung, and using them for sprinkling and rubbing the body.
Surrounded by these [women], he should sleep amidst the mixture of their dust and excrement;
this is the most excellent elixir (rasāyana) for the destruction of the king of diseases.

One suffering from wasting disease (kṣaya) should drink ghee boiled with goat dung, juice, milk, curd, and urine, along with the five salts and the five products of the goat, followed by a draught of milk.
For one who eats meat according to the proper method and subsequently drinks mṛdvīkā wine,
the disease does not find an opportunity to enter, provided its natural urges have not been suppressed.
While eating meat, one should drink, as appropriate for the purpose of a post-prandial draught, surā with its scum (maṇḍa), mṛdvīkā-liquor, ariṣṭas, śīdhu, and mādhava. (AS.Ci.7.111)
For the purpose of releasing obstructions in the channels and for the sake of strength, vitality, and nourishment,
one should cause the patient— who has been well-anointed with oil— to immerse themselves in vats filled with fat, milk, or water.

Once the patient has emerged from the bath with the mixed oils, one should again gently rub his body with pleasant hands; having been comfortably massaged, he should then be thoroughly rubbed with medicinal powders (udvartana).
[The ingredients for this are: *jīvantī*, *śatavīryā*, *vikasā*, and *punarnavā*.
Aśvagandhā, apāmārga, tarkārī, madhuka, bala, vidārī,
mustard seeds, kuṣṭha, rice grains, and the fruit of atasī.
One should grind together black gram, sesame seeds, and fermenting agent (kiṇva) into a single powder;
this should be combined with three times its amount of barley flour, mixed with curd and honey.
This rubbing (udvartana) should be performed; it bestows nourishment, complexion, and strength. It [should be done] with a paste of white mustard seeds and bathing herbs.
One should bathe in waters pleasant for the season, prepared with *jīvanīya* (vitalizing) herbs;
one should resort to ornaments such as perfumes and garlands, which destroy misfortune (*alakṣmī*).
The sight of friends, the hearing of songs, instrumental music, and festive sounds; enemas, milk, clarified butter, wine, meat, and good character.
Likewise, the therapy based on divine intervention (daivavyapāśraya) as declared in the Atharvaveda is honored;
it is that very sacrifice by which the Moon was formerly conquered of consumption (rājayakṣmā).
"The family priest should employ that [rite] prescribed in the Veda for one who has conquered his self.
Thus ends the seventh chapter.
Now begins the eighth chapter.
Hereafter, we shall explain the treatment of vomiting, heart disease, and thirst.
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and others: "Vomiting generally arises from the agitation of the stomach; therefore, [the following] is beneficial."
Fasting is indicated except in the case of Vāta; in that situation, one should employ emesis for a strong patient with abundant Doshas who vomits copiously and continuously.
Then, one should administer a pleasant purgative gradually with wines, fruit juices,
or milk; for that indeed brings down the morbid humors (doṣas) that have moved upward.
For one who is parched and weak, that same pacifying medicine is recommended; furthermore, food that is dried, agreeable, wholesome, and light is praised.
Likewise, fasting, vegetable soups, meat broths, *kāmbalika* preparations,
*khala* pastes, leafy vegetables, electuaries, solid foods, *rāga*, *ṣāḍava*, and drinks. (AS.Ci.8.6)
Edible foods, dry items, and various fruits; bathing and rubbing [the body];
fragrances, pleasant scents, and those derived from perfumes, fruits, flowers, food, and drinks.
The sudden sprinkling of cold water on the face immediately after eating cures vomiting caused by Vāta; likewise, clarified butter drunk with rock salt has the same effect.
One should administer something slightly warm, specifically that which causes the heart to melt with longing,
enriched with the three pungents (vyoṣa) and the three salts, or prepared with pomegranate juice.
Milk drunk with equal parts water, along with ginger, curd, and coriander; or ghee with rock salt; or the meat broth of wild fowl seasoned with sour fruits.

In this condition, unctuous food prepared with ginger, curd, and pomegranate, served lukewarm and with salt, is beneficial; likewise, unctuous purgation is indicated. In cases arising from Pitta, one should administer purgation using *trivṛt* processed with the expressed juices of grapes and sugarcane.
Clarified butter or oil from *Vr̥kṣaka* should be administered when [the disease] has increased and reached the seat of *śleṣman*.
One who has attained purification through sweet and bitter [drugs] should eliminate the *pitta* by means of upward evacuation alone.
One should drink a stirred potion (mantha) or gruel (yavāgū) with parched grain (lāja), honey, and sugar;
and one should eat Śāli or Ṣaṣṭika rice with side dishes made from the meat of domestic or wild animals.
One should drink very cold water produced from clay or a heated clod of earth,
or water that has been left to stand overnight with mung beans, ushira root, long pepper, and coriander.
The juice of grapes, the juice of sugarcane, guḍūcī water, and milk;
[and] that which arises from the shoots of jambū, mango, uśīra, vaṭa, and aśvattha.
This decoction, when drunk either warm or cold and combined with honey, subdues vomiting,
fever, diarrhea, fainting, and even difficult-to-conquer thirst. (AS.Ci.8.15)

One should drink it cold with the juice of *dhātrī*, or water boiled with the leaves of *mudga*. Or one may take the pulp of *kola*, *sita*, parched *lāja*, fly-dung (*makṣikāviṭ*), *kaṇā*, and *añjana*.
One should lick either the marrow of the kernel of the *kola* fruit mixed with the water of *ājā* lotus pollen, or *pathyā*, or *drākṣā*, or *badara* fruits, combined with honey.

One should drink the powder produced from *śāli* rice, gold, and red ochre (*gairika*) with cold water; or alternatively, one may drink *candana*, grapes, *māṃsī*, *sevyā*, water, and red ochre ground together with *śāli* rice-water and sugar-honey. (AS.Ci.8.18)
Madhūka, madhuka, grapes, lotus, āmalaka, and water; or sārivā, parūṣaka, akṣa, and mūrvā, combined with honey.

In the case of vomiting caused by *kapha*, one should administer madhuka or ātmaguptā, cooled with the juice of *dhātrī*; alternatively, one should induce emesis with nimba, *kṛṣṇā*, piṇḍīta, and mustard seeds.
One should administer a weak enema with lukewarm water mixed with appropriate substances;
furthermore, one should drink the cooled decoction of the *āragvadha* group of drugs combined with honey.
One should drink either a gruel (peyā) prepared with triphalā, kaṇā, and cavya, along with the leaves of karañja;
or one should consume various types of mantha made from barley that have been repeatedly impregnated (bhāvita) with emetic-destroying medicinal herbs.
Food that subdues *kapha* and is pleasing to the heart, as well as *rāga* condiments made with *sārjaka* and *bhūstṛṇa*;
