and *manaḥśilā*, *kṛṣṇā*, and *marica* licked together with *bījapūraka*.
One should conquer vomiting by means of *kapittha* with its natural juice and honey (AS.Ci.8.23),
or by *mustā*, *śṛṅgī*, and *madhu* (honey) (AS.Ci.8.24), or by sour *kola* fruit together with *jāmbava*.
In the same manner, one should eat viḍaṅga, triphalā, kṛmighna, and paripelava; likewise, one should consume durālabhā, or kapittha with the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa).
That which arises from an aversive object is pacified by favorable treatment; that born of worms is treated by the remedies prescribed for worms and heart disease.

AS.Ci.8.26 Just as the remaining [doshas] and the diseases caused by them are treated according to their respective natures, so too should one act. AS.Ci.8.27 One should quickly conquer persistent vomiting that is accompanied by complications.
For that [fever] causes greater pain to the vital organs (mahāmarmans) located within the abdominal cavity; moreover,
the body cannot exist even for a moment without food, as it is composed of that [food].

Exhaustion of the bodily constituents (*dhātu-kṣaya*) and excessive vomiting arise inevitably from the provocation of the wind (*samīraṇa*); therefore, one should quickly apply [remedies] for that condition.

The procedure for excessive vomiting described [previously], as well as methods for suppression and nourishment, [should be applied]; furthermore, ghee-boluses, meat soups, milk, clarified butter, and the *Kalyāṇajīvana* [medicinal compound] [are recommended].
Either the *dhānvantara* or *tryūṣaṇa* [medicinal preparations] should be administered according to the state of the humors (*doṣa*) and the body; this is the treatment for heart disease (*hṛdroga*).

In cases of heart disease caused by Vāta, one should drink oil that is pleasantly warm, mixed with buttermilk, Sauvīraka, buttermilk, and Viḍa salt; this also cures abdominal tumors, flatulence, and pain.
A paste prepared with salts, along with urine and sour liquids, possesses similar qualities;
likewise [one may use] bilva, rāsnā, barley, jujube, devadāru, and punarnavā.
Having boiled horse gram (*kulattha*) and the five roots (*pañcamūla*) in water,
one should cook oil in that same water; this [oil] should be employed for nasal administration (*nāvana*), internal drinking (*pāna*), and enema (*basti*).
Ghee boiled with ginger, *vayasthā*, salt, *kāyasthā*, asafoetida, *pauṣkara*, and *pathyā* conquers pain in the flanks and heart, as well as abdominal tumors (*gulma*).
Two palas of sauvarcala salt combined with fifty pathyā fruits,
cooked with one prastha of ghee, cures heart disease, dyspnea, and abdominal tumors.
Pomegranate, black salt, asafoetida, dry ginger, and sour vetiver—
this powder is an excellent remedy for hiccups, heart disease, and asthma.
Puṣkarāhvā, śaṭhī, śuṇṭhī, bījapūra, jaṭā, and abhayā,
when ground into a paste and drunk with alkali, ghee, sour liquids, and salt, [cure the aforementioned disorders].
A lukewarm decoction made from yavānī, salt, kṣāra, vacā, jīraka, and medicinal herbs relieves the pain of vikartikā and possesses those same qualities. (AS.Ci.8.38)
With *sapītadāru*, *bījāhva*, *palāśa*, *śaṭhī*, and *pauṣkara*; with *pañcakola*, *śaṭhī*, *pathyā*, jaggery (*guḍa*), *bījāhva*, and *pauṣkara*.

One should eat this preparation— fried in *yamaka* oil, processed with the paste of *vāruṇī*, and mixed with salt— to relieve pain in the heart, the sides, and the female reproductive organs, as well as abdominal tumors and disorders of the abdomen.

In this condition, unctuous sudations are beneficial, as are medicated ghees prepared with the light *pañcamūla* or with ginger. Water boiled with the light *pañcamūla* or with ginger [is also recommended].

In cases of thirst, one should drink either the supernatant liquid of curd (*vāruṇī-dadhimaṇḍa*), or fermented grain-water (*dhānyāmla*). When the heart is afflicted by wind (*māruta*), characterized by evening-onset stiffness and pain, [these remedies should be applied].
In the absence of delusion regarding the proper administration of therapeutic procedures, the following juices are beneficial:
those rich in fats, derived from the partridge (*tittiri*), the *krauñca* crane, the peacock (*śikhi*), the *vartaka* quail, and the *dakṣa* partridge.
One suffering from heart disease should drink either *balā-taila* or *sukumāraka*;
or likewise, the excellent *mahāsneha* cooked a hundred times with *yaṣṭyāhva*.
One should cook the mahāsneha with rāsnā, jīvaka, jīvantī, balā, vyāghrī, punarnavā, bhārṅgī, sthirā, vacā, and vyoṣa.

Likewise, curd-rice with sour substances, when consumed as available, is satiating, nourishing, strengthening, and a destroyer of vāta and heart disease (AS.Ci.8.46). [The powder of] tri-ūṣaṇa, tri-phalā, pāṭhā, madhūka, madhuka, and cūṭī...
The five roots (pañcamūla), balā, medā, ṛddhi, śatāvarī,
kaṇḍūkarī, tāmalakī, and jīvaka, each measured at one akṣa; AS.Ci.8.47 [these are used].
One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with those [drugs] and one *prastha* of buffalo curd;
once prepared, when consumed along with honey, it destroys [the disease].
When the digestive fire is kindled, [this therapy] is beneficial for heart disease, anemia, disorders of the *grahaṇī*, cough, dyspnea, and *halīmaka*,
as well as for *vātika* heart disease accompanied by discharge and physical exertion.
Milk, curd, molasses, ghee, the meat of aquatic and marshy animals, and even clarified butters— these should be avoided in all four types of hemorrhoids (hṛdroga).
In the remaining cases, as well as in Vāta disorders associated with stiffness, dullness,
and lassitude, one should employ dry and hot treatment, provided there is an association with Kapha.
In the case of pitta-type fever, a purgative combined with grapes, sugarcane juice, sugar, *akṣa*, *ārdra*, and *parūṣaka* is pleasing to the heart; once purified, this regimen alleviates pitta.
One should also employ the external and internal cleansing treatments prescribed for fever caused by *kṣata-pitta*,
and one should drink a paste of *kaṭvī* and *madhuka* with sugar and water.
A superior [milk] is that prepared with sugar, *drākṣā*, *jīvaka*, *ṛṣabhaka*, and *utpala*,
along with the two types of *balā*, *kharjūra*, *kākolī*, and the two types of *medā*.
Buffalo ghee mixed with milk destroys bile disorders and heart disease. [The following are also used:
*prapauṇḍarīka*, *madhuka*, lotus root joints (*bisagranthi*), and *śerukā*.
One should cook ghee with those [drugs] along with *śuṇṭhī* and *śaivalā*, together with milk;
when cooled, it should be taken with honey, as well as any [preparation] made from the group of sweet (*svādu*) substances.
And one should administer an enema consisting of oil prepared with madhuka and mixed with honey;
in the case of a disorder arising from kapha, one should induce emesis after fomentation, using a decoction of nimba and vacā.
One who eats horse gram, dhanvana, pungent substances, wine,
and barley should drink a powder made from vacā, asafoetida, the two salts, and ginger.
Sailā, yavānaka, kaṇā, and yavakṣāra should be taken with lukewarm water,
as well as with the soups of fruits, grains, and kaulattha, or with urine and āsava.
A decoction of *puṣkara*, *abhayā*, *śuṇṭhī*, *śaṭhī*, *rāsnā*, *vacā*, and *kaṇā*;
likewise, a decoction of *abhayā*, *śuṇṭhī*, *mādrī*, *pītadru*, and *kaṭphala*;
and a decoction of *rauhītaka*, *aśvattha*, *khadira*, *udumbara*, and *arjuna*.
A linctus prepared from a banyan tree with its leaves attached, combined with the powder of trikaṭu and trivṛt,
taken with lukewarm water as an after-drink, destroys disorders of kapha.

One should drink clarified butter prepared for the treatment of phlegm-based abdominal tumors (śleṣmagulma) and various types of alkaline preparations; or one should employ śilāhva and the brāhma rasāyana in this condition.
Likewise, one may consume either the *āmalaka* linctus or the *prāśa* prepared by Agastya;
this is for one who experiences colic after eating excessively, or whose food does not digest even when only a small amount has been consumed.
One should pacify [the condition] with kuṣṭha, kṛmijit, the two types of salt, and tilvaka;
one should drink a powder of these, along with devadāru and ativiṣā, with warm water.
One for whom the [unwholesome matter] has been digested by excessive unctuous substances should be purged again with fruits;
likewise, when food is being digested, one should use sharp roots if there is constant, excessive colic.
Since the wind (vāyu) generally becomes aggravated in the stomach (āmāśaya) when its movement is obstructed,
one should treat it by means of purification, fasting, and digestive (pācana) therapies to restore it to its natural downward course.
All anthelmintic medicines [are indicated] for heart disease caused by worms;
[this concludes] the treatment for thirst.
In all types of thirst, a regimen that subdues vāta and pitta is generally recommended; it should be cooling, both externally and internally, and consist of palliative and purificatory measures.
Divine water is cool and mixed with honey; likewise is terrestrial water of similar quality,
provided it has been cooled by heated clods of earth, potsherds, sand, and so forth.
Water boiled with sugar and the five roots (pañcamūla), or a churned drink (mantha) made with parched grain flour (lāja-saktu) and mixed with darbha grass, is recommended.
A cold gruel made with vāṭya and other grains, combined with sugar and honey,
as well as one made with old śāli rice or with kodrava, should be prepared in the same manner.
A meal prepared with cold substances and those of cooling potency,
served after one has been sprinkled with cold water, [should be taken] with milk mixed with sugar and honey.
And with juices that are neither sour nor salty, prepared from the meat of wild animals fried in ghee,
as well as with soups of mung beans and other pulses combined with the flavors of the *jīvanīya* (vitalizing) group of drugs.
Nasal therapy (nasya) with milk and ghee prepared with cooling [drugs], or likewise with sugarcane juice,
or camel bone ground with woman’s milk and mixed with sugar, is beneficial.
The gargles mentioned in the Sūtrasthāna are beneficial for cooling; likewise,
the ointments and other treatments prescribed for burning fever (dāhajvara) are useful, as is remaining motionless and finding delight in the mind.
The sight and recollection of great rivers, lakes, and the like,
as well as curd mixed with jaggery, are recommended when thirst arises from wind (vāta).
Tonic and cooling tastes, as well as water decocted with the Vidārigandhādi group [of herbs], are beneficial.
In the case of fever born of Pitta, the juice of ripe Udumbara fruit mixed with sugar should be administered.

Likewise, one may use a decoction or a cold infusion (himas) of that [same plant], or water boiled with the sārivādi group of drugs; or, with drugs of similar properties, one may administer cold infusions mixed with sugar and honey.
Likewise, [one should use] preparations made with sweet medicinal herbs and milky trees,
as well as the sprouts of *bījapūraka*, *mṛdvīkā*, *vaṭa*, and *vetasa*.
The roots of *kuśa* and *kāśa*, along with *yaṣṭyāhva*, boiled in water;
or water boiled with *apāmārga*, *śarkarā*, *chinnaruhā*, *lodhra*, and *añjana*.

Or one who eats food with sugar and milk should drink the paste of *kārpāsī* fruit; or one should drink the water prepared from the five essences (*pañcasāra*) beginning with *drākṣā*, as prescribed for fever.
In cases arising from *kapha*, emesis should be induced with water infused with *nimba* sprouts,
prepared with *bilva*, *āḍhakī*, the five spices (*pañcakola*), and the five types of *darbha*.
One should drink water prepared with *rajanī*, mixed with honey and sugar; or one may take mung bean soup along with *vyoṣa* and the tender leaves of *paṭolī* and *nimba*.
One should habitually consume barley-based foods, pungent gargles,
and electuaries; for all types of āma, treatments that destroy it are desired, as is emesis.

One who knows the proper time should administer a warm gruel made with *tryūṣaṇa*, *āruṣkara*, *vacā*, and sour fruits along with hot water and *mastu* for those suffering from the loss of appetite; otherwise, one should give a cold *mantha*.
In thirst due to fatigue, one should drink meat broth or a churned drink (mantha) with sugar;
from exposure to the sun, one should drink a churned drink with sugar made from the flour of barley and jujube fruits.
One should smear all the limbs with sesame paste, oil-cake,
and fermented rice-gruel; and if thirsty, one should drink cold wine diluted with water or molasses-water after taking a cold bath.

For one who has drunk wine, half water mixed with wine should be given; for one who has bathed, water combined with sour and salty substances; and for one whose digestive fire has become excessively sharp by oleation, water that is naturally cool should be used.
One who is thirsty after undigested food containing fats should drink warm water;
however, one who is thirsty after digesting such food should drink molasses-water that rivals snow in its coolness.
One who has become thirsty from eating the food of a guru or others should drink warm water and then induce vomiting;
in cases arising from wasting (kṣaya), all nourishing medicines beneficial for wasting should be administered.

For those who are emaciated, weak, or parched, milk or goat’s meat broth [is recommended]; and for one suffering from upward-moving wind (ūrdhvavāta), milk boiled with drugs that cure wasting cough (kṣayakāsa) [should be used].
For a fever arising as a complication of a disease, rice-water mixed with sugar and honey is prescribed.

Drinking [liquids] is recommended, and every therapeutic action should be performed with due regard for the disease and other factors. (AS.Ci.8.89) If one who is thirsty, or one previously weakened by illness, does not obtain water, [the consequences are grave]. (AS.Ci.8.90)
From that, he may quickly meet with death or suffer from a chronic disease; therefore,
one should first conquer his thirst with wholesome food, drink, and medicine.
When that [ignorance] has been conquered, even other diseases can be treated;
thus ends the eighth chapter.
Now begins the ninth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of intoxication (madātyaya).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:
"Whichever *doṣa* one perceives to be predominant, that one should treat first.
Or, in cases where the doshas are equal, [the treatment follows] the sequence of the seats of *kapha*;
for generally, in alcoholism (*madātyaya*), the condition culminates in *pitta* and *vāta*. Whatever disease arises from drinking [alcohol] in deficient, improper, or excessive amounts—
He is pacified by that very same liquor when it is drunk in equal measure;
for liquor is similar to poison, whereas poison acts with superior intensity.
Due to its association with qualities such as sharpness (tīkṣṇa) and others, it requires another poison [to neutralize it]. When drunk in excessive measure, it is sharp, hot, sour, and burning.
When the moisture of the food essence is corrupted by liquor and reaches a state of alkalinity (kṣāratā),
it produces intoxication, thirst, delusion, fever, internal burning, and confusion.
When the vital air (māruta) is obstructed within the channels by humors (doṣa) agitated by alcohol,
there arise extremely intense piercing pains (devanā) in the head, the bones, and the joints.
When the disorders of undigested food (āma) and alcohol have been digested, and there is a desire for food and lightness of the body, alcohol itself—
administered appropriately and according to rule— destroys those very disorders.
For alkali, when combined with sour substances, quickly attains sweetness;
and among sour substances, wine is the best, as it is fully capable of liquefying the bodily humors (doṣas).
Through the previously mentioned qualities such as sharpness and heat, as well as those beginning with digestive stimulation (dīpana),
and because of its suitability (sātmya), that very [diet] is the supreme means for restoring the equilibrium of his bodily constituents (dhātu).
One should administer the medicine for alcoholism (pānātyaya) for seven or eight nights;
within this time, the alcohol that has taken a wrong path will be digested.
Whatever subsequent disease then follows,
one should apply its appropriate remedy, having already administered the medicine for the alcoholism (pānātyaya).
In that case, when vāta is predominant, one should administer wine prepared from flour and combined with *bījapūraka*,
*vṛkṣāmla*, *kola*, *dāḍima*, and *dīpyaka*.
With *yavānī*, *īṣapuṣā*, *jīraka*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), the three salts, and fresh ginger;
with roasted meats on spits, green vegetables, and oily parched grain flour (*saktu*).
Warm, unctuous, sour, and salty foods, as well as rich meat broths, are beneficial;
likewise are rāgas and ṣāḍavas prepared with mangoes, hog-plums, and peśīs.
Preparations of wheat and mung beans that are soft, variegated, and pleasing to the palate;
and those containing *ārdikā*, ginger, fermented grain-porridge (*kulmāṣa*), vinegar, meat, and so forth.
Fragrant, salty, and cold, it is described as having the appearance of a reddish-brown liquid;
it is the juice of pomegranate and a decoction of the minor *pañcamūla*.
AS.Ci.9.17 Likewise, ginger, coriander, whey, fermented rice-gruel,
sour water, and sour gruel; warm massage, dry rubbing, bathing, and thick clothing.
Incense made of solid agarwood, and paste from agarwood and saffron;
[and] those women possessing beautiful breasts, thighs, and hips, their slender bodies heated by youth.
Beloved women are appropriate for embracing with joy and for massaging; in cases where pitta is predominant, one should administer honey mixed with sugar and plenty of water.
One should prepare a very cold drink made from the juices of pomegranate, date, bhavya, grape, and parūṣaka,
mixed with sugar and parched grain flour; such a beverage should be administered.
Or one may drink wine mixed with sweet and astringent substances along with honey;
one should eat *śāli* and *ṣaṣṭika* rice together with the meat of rabbit, deer, or grey partridge.
One suffering from thirst and burning sensations should eliminate the provoked *kapha* and *pitta* by means of *satīna*, *udga*, *āmalaka*, *paṭolī*, and pomegranate as well.
Having drunk cold water, or wine mixed with abundant sugarcane juice,
or grape juice, the *saṃsargī* [formula] consisting of nourishing (*tarpaṇa*) and other such substances is most beneficial.
In that way, his digestive fire blazes up, digesting the remnants of the bodily humors (doṣas) along with food,
in cases of cough with blood-stained expectoration and pain in the flanks and breasts.
When there is burning sensation and distress in the thirst, along with agitation in the heart and chest,
one should administer the juice of *guḍūcī*, *bhadramustā*, or *paṭola*.
One should administer a meal consisting of partridge meat along with ginger when there is excessive thirst and when vāta and pitta are intensely aggravated.
One should administer grape juice as a drink; it is cooling and facilitates the downward movement of the humors (doṣas).
Once it has been digested, one should eat with sweet and sour goat meat broth.
One who is thirsty should drink wine sparingly while guarding against intoxication, mixing it with plenty of water;
or one may drink water infused with *mustā*, pomegranate, parched grain, and *parṇinī* herbs, or water boiled with *parṇinī*.
Or [one may use] the tubers of the *pāṭalī* and the blue lotus, or even snow by its very nature,
when the water element has been depleted due to excessive drinking of alcohol and the fire element has become aggravated.
One whose throat, palate, and lips are parched and who moves the tongue out as if trying to lick it,
should be made to drink water according to his desire, cooled by the night breeze.
The juice of kola, dāḍima, vṛkṣāmla, cukrīkā, and ācūtṛkā—
this "five-sour" (pañcāmlaka) application to the face immediately subdues thirst. Furthermore, when the heat of the drink reaches the skin, it becomes aggravated by pitta and blood.
It produces a terrible burning by which the person becomes overwhelmed and faints;
for one thus afflicted by thirst and burning, this [remedy] removes the fever of burning.
One should employ the prescribed regimen for cleansing both externally and internally (AS.Ci.9.32).
At dawn, [the waters] are stirred by the breeze and shower down dewy water (AS.Ci.9.33).
Even when merely remembered, the sandalwood trees of Malaya alleviate the burning heat;
likewise do pearl necklaces, as white as moonbeams and as lovely as lotus stalks and the petals of the lotus and water-lily.
Sprinklings and immersions, water-bearing breezes moist with water, very cool gems of great value, and jars covered with lotus-petals, colored like coral and filled with snow-water;
AS.Ci.9.34–35 Sprinklings and immersions, water-bearing breezes moist with water, very cool gems of great value, and jars covered with lotus-petals, colored like coral and filled with snow-water.

Leaking large leather bags, beloved sons, mirrors as bright as circles, women with lotus-like eyes and ear-ornaments, and those who have barely touched the bloom of middle age— AS.Ci.9.35–36. These things flow away like water from leaking vessels. (The wise man should not grieve for them.)
Moist with yellow sandalwood, these [beds] are pleasing to the mind and conquer thirst, burning heat, fainting,
and exhaustion. Or, one may experience agitation caused by a leader of an elephant herd surrounded by female elephants.
Remembering the lashing waves and the showers of spray of the ocean— which are unapproachable for those suffering from heat and thirst—
and the rivers, lakes, mountain caves, moonrises, and lotus ponds; AS.Ci.9.38 [he remains there].
Even when engaged in delightful conversation, this [mixture] immediately destroys burning sensations and thirst;
it is called "the Cool," consisting of parched grain, blue lotus, ushira root, and sandalwood water, enriched with honey and sugar.

When drunk, [this preparation] consisting of priyaṅgu leaves, plava, lodhra, sevya, drībera, kāleyaka, and nāgapuṣpa, destroys thirst arising from alcohol as well as that caused by pitta, along with burning sensations and emaciation. (AS.Ci.9.39–40)

An application over the entire body with a paste made of cold water and placed in a new earthen vessel destroys thirst and burning sensations. Alternatively, if the burning sensation is not subsiding, one should use the meat juices of wild animals for one who has been satiated.
One should, according to the prescribed rule, venesect the *rohiṇī* vein located in the extremities;
one should overcome an excess of *kapha* through scraping and fasting.
One who is thirsty should drink water prepared with *mustā* or *parpaṭa*,
or with any one of the following: *sthirā*, *śuṇṭhī*, *balā*, *udīcya*, or *duḥsparśā*.
This [remedy] is established as effective and is recommended for all defects arising from drinking;
one should administer it at the proper time to a person who is free from undigested matter (āmadoṣa) and hungry, mixed with a large amount of honey.
Sugar-cane juice, honey, aged *ariṣṭa*, or even *sīdhu* liquor, combined with parching and nourishing substances and mixed with *yavānī* and ginger.
One should feed [the patient] barley and wheat with a thin,
small amount of broth that is warm, sour, pungent, and bitter, along with *kaulattha* pulse and a little clarified butter.
Or one may use the meat juices of goats or of animals that roam in arid lands, prepared with dried radish, along with sour vetasa,
vṛkṣāmla, paṭolī, the three pungents (vyoṣa), and pomegranate.
AS.Ci.9.47 A preparation containing abundant ginger, black pepper, green vegetables, and pieces of fresh ginger,
acidified with the juice of *bījapūra* and other sour fruits, fried and then made into a dry bolus (*vartita*).
AS.Ci.9.48 [This preparation] contains *karīra*, *karamarda*, and other shining,
abundant salts; it has clearly manifested eight-fold salt (*lavaṇa*) and is prepared with various types of *nimardaka*.
Just as one might eat meat with fire, [one should drink] Mādhava decoction;
[and take] sugar, sauvarcala salt, cumin, tamarind, and sour vetasa.
A beneficial eight-ingredient salt (aṣṭāṅgalavaṇa), containing one-eighth part each of cinnamon-bark,
cardamom, and black pepper, purifies the channels, stimulates the digestive fire, and is useful in cases of alcoholism (madātyaya) where kapha predominates.
One should also take white grapes (mṛdvīkā) from which the seeds have been removed, combined with pungent substances.
One should grind [the ingredients] with the juice of citron or pomegranate; prepared with this and mixed with honey, it becomes a *rāga* that is pleasing to the palate and stimulates digestion.
One should prepare *śukta* (fermented vinegar) in this same manner using *sauvarcala*, cardamom, black pepper, *dīpyaka*, cumin, and coriander, combined with unrefined sugar (*matsyaṇḍikā*).
One should take grains, sauvarcala salt, cumin, kāravī, and black pepper,
combined with jaggery, made distinctly sour with honey, and enriched with an abundance of black pepper.
By means of dry and hot unguents, rubbing, bathing, food, fasting,
and by staying awake with women who are full of desire, [the phlegm is subdued] through proper application.
This treatment prescribed for each according to the strength of the specific dosha causes an excess of kapha (madātyaya) to subside quickly.
In the case of the ten types of *sannipāta* (combined humors) and their remaining varieties,
one should likewise apply this formulation with *tvak*, *nāgapuṣpa*, *magadhā*, *marica*, *ajājī*, and *dhānyaka*.
A refreshing drink made from *parūṣaka*, *madhūka*, *elā*, and *surāhvā*, combined with sugar and the juice of *kapittha* and stirred with camphor, is pleasing to the heart.
In all cases of intoxication (madātyaya), that which is appetizing and stimulates the digestive fire (agni) should be drunk;
likewise [a preparation] with pomegranate, grapes, long pepper (kaṇā), kāśmarya, and Indian berberry (dāru).
[One may take] bījabhāraka fruits combined with biḍa and sauvarcala salts,
or various sour fruits together with the powder of trivṛt and sugar.
The sprouts of *kacchudāra*, grapes, *varṣābhū*, the two types of cumin (*jīraka*),
*madhūka*, the bark of *yaṣṭī*, *kṛṣṇā*, and *kesara*— these should be finely powdered. (AS.Ci.9.59)
One should drink it after stirring it with milk and filtering it through a fine cloth; for indeed, without agitating the mind or harming the body, one may consume wine.
For that reason, one should induce intoxication; therefore, exhilarating therapy is desired.
One should enjoy those things that bring pleasure to all the senses, which are the sprouts of the wish-fulfilling tree of Dharma.

The five objects of sense are the arrows of the flower-bowed god; even when the purification, pacification, and other remedies for the fault of intoxication have been applied, [the affliction remains].
And I do not desire this [treatment] when phlegm has been depleted and weakness and lightness have arisen;
for such a person whose [stomach] is corrupted by liquor and in whom vāta and pitta predominate.
Just as rain is to a tree scorched by the summer heat,
so is milk to one emaciated by alcohol; for milk quickly nourishes the body of one who has been depleted by liquor.

When the disease has been overcome by milk and strength has been restored, one should discontinue [the treatment], as it possesses all qualities equal to *ojas* and is contrary to the effects of alcohol.
One should gradually administer milk preparations and wine in very small quantities,
so that one is not afflicted by complications arising from wasting (kṣaya) or destruction (dhvaṃsa).
For those two, however, ghee, milk, nourishing enemas,
beneficial massages, dry rubs, baths, and food and drink that conquer Vata are appropriate; for one who drinks wine in moderation, no disease arising from wine occurs.
Therefore, the regimen for this [patient] will be described, which leads exclusively to happiness:
that splendor which belongs to Aśvinī, and that strength which belongs to Sārasvatī.
She who bestows the heroic power of Indra and the majestic influence of Viṣṇu;
she who is the weapon of the god whose banner is the dolphin, and she who is the purpose of man for Bala.
That which is offered into the fire in the mouth of the twice-born during the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice,
and that which was produced by the gods and demons while churning the ocean filled with all medicinal herbs; [these are the two types of surā].
Arising from the great ocean together with the nectar of the illustrious moon,
[it was joined] with honey-wine, spring-wine, maireya, sīdhu, gauḍa, āsava, and other such liquors.
That which does not abandon its power of intoxication, yet exists in many forms,
and by tasting which graceful women bear their name in its true sense; AS.Ci.9.72 [that is wine].
Even a woman of noble family, having drunk this, leads even the mind of a sage— her own heart being haughty— to some place where her limbs are embraced by the bodiless god of love.
By appeasing the mind of one proud woman with the frowns and threats of her wave-like eyebrows,
she brings satisfaction to both [her husband and her lover].
In that battle where the throngs of Apsarases are delighted by the acquisition of soldiers at will,
men, having tasted the joys of Yama, cast away their lives like blades of grass.
Even after practicing for a long time in many ways that which has many forms,
one constantly indulges in it as before due to the excessive force of passion.
Seeing her, one is not overcome by grief, agitation, discontent, or fear;
without her, social gatherings, great festivals, and gardens do not shine.
That [faith] by which one, having been separated [from it], grieves after remembering it again and again many times;
that which, though not yet clear, leads to joy; and that which, when clear, is indeed heaven itself.
Even Indra considers himself ill at ease because of that [meditative state] which abides in the heart;
it is the supreme experience, to be known only by oneself, consisting of the taste of an ineffable bliss.
Thus, she who imitates her beloved in various circumstances (AS.Ci.9.79–80) attains a state of being exceedingly dear to that beloved in particular.
That which is praised as joy, delight, and nourishment by the Vedas, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and humans— (AS.Ci.9.80–81)
But when there is a need for drinking, one should drink that liquor according to the prescribed rule;
then those diseases arising from fat, wind, and phlegm do not occur.
Without the application of medical prescriptions, even potent intoxicants and the like do not bring about [the desired] results;
there is a certain state of the body in which drinking is prohibited.
Except for liquor prepared from various medicinal herbs,
even meat from marshy or wild animals, though prepared according to the prescribed rules, [is not to be consumed].
Without obtaining a companion, how could liquor undergo proper digestion? And [how could it digest] garlic, which destroys diseases caused by excessively sharp winds?
What benefit would there be in the application [of this treatment] for one who abstains from wine and meat?
AS.Ci.9.86: [It is beneficial] in the extraction of deeply embedded foreign bodies, and in the surgical procedures of cauterization with instruments, alkalis, or fire.
One who has drunk wine endures the boastful talk of physicians with ease;
it stimulates the digestive fire, improves the appetite, and destroys grief and fatigue.
There is nothing else beyond this that produces health, strength, and nourishment; therefore,
one who values their own life should always drink it.

Having bathed, and having prostrated before the gods, Brahmins, and teachers according to their respective status, and having provided for the maintenance of all his dependents, he should perform the supreme means for attaining Dharma, which is beneficial to those who have sought refuge and those who have sought further refuge. (AS.Ci.9.88–89)
Then, one should resort to a drinking hall sprinkled with fragrant water, situated near the pavilion for food; there,
upon a comfortable and beautiful couch, one should be joined by friends, servants, and beloved women.
He heard his own world-transcending fame being extolled by throngs of storytellers and bards,
as well as the songs of playful women, beautified by their graceful charms and accompanied by dance and the resonant sounds of musical instruments.
Resounding with girdles of many bells and with pet birds,
[the women] had their limbs covered with various garments of watered silk and fine linen, adorned with diverse ornaments made of jewels and gold.
Moreover, [he was distracted] by beloved women who agitated the minds of even sages, with glances as tremulous as startled deer;
and [he was weary] from the excessive weight of their breasts and hips, rendered languid and overwhelmed by his reliance upon them as lords.
Thus it was described by those who possess a restless gait, whose very nature is the enchantment of youthful minds,
who are intoxicated by the wine of youth, and whose selves are presided over by amorous playfulness.
Being moved here and there simultaneously by slender-limbed maidens with fans of palm leaves and lotus petals, which were exceedingly cool with their breezes; AS.Ci.9.95.
Even in a mere glance, he brings one under his control; how much more so when tasted by the mind-born god of love?
He is perfumed by the mango, the moon, and the musk-deer, and graced by the radiant jasmine.

Having consumed a pleasing powder such as *tālīsa* and others, or *melā* and its companions— which, like a lovely body possessing waves upon a crystal oyster shell, bears the form of the bodiless god of love— or having taken a youth-preserving elixir suitable for one's age; AS.Ci.9.96–97.
Having caused those who seek it to receive water mixed with [the medicine] upon a well-swept patch of ground, the physician,
being steadfast and mindful, should always administer it neither deficiently nor in excess.
Cherishing everything with appropriate hospitality,
[he beheld] her whose splendor was increased by the reflection of her eyes, which were like full-blown blue lotuses.
One should drink wine like the face of a beloved, from which the swarms of bees have been drawn away by its fragrance.
Having thus drunk three cups and honored all the attendants, one should then—
Having first gone to the dining hall, the physician should eat again;

there, he should consume food combined with meat, cakes, ghee, fresh ginger, and green vegetables, along with *sauvarcala* salt, two or three times in small quantities, for the sake of union with his wife. He should also drink [liquor].

If a wise man, having taken his beloved onto his lap in private, does not impetuously make her drink wine— she whose body is thrilled with horripilation, who has broken into a sweat, and whose breasts tremble— then what does he experience other than a household life consisting mostly of hardship?
The *saraka* drink, made more fragrant by contact with the mouth of a beautiful woman and appearing like a ruby that has suddenly assumed the form of liquor,
becomes like wine through the exhaustion of lovemaking; even if one drinks only a little, intoxication arises, so one should avoid the depletion of vital energy (*ojas*) and sleep thereafter.
Thus, by drinking wine according to this method, one does not fall away from the three aims of life (trivarga) and attains the supreme happiness of this essence-less saṃsāra.
This enjoyment of sovereignty is desirable even to the gods;
for otherwise, in times of misfortune, wealth would become fuel for remorse.
One who possesses wealth but is deprived of its enjoyment is censured;
this miserly guardian of a treasure-trove was created by Fate for that very purpose.
Therefore, by means of disciplined regulation, the consumption of alcohol is always beneficial,
once one has overcome the independence of the senses that are greedy for their objects.

This is the rule for those who possess wealth; however, those who will possess wealth in the future should drink wine in the appropriate measure, as it is beneficial, according to their circumstances.
As long as there is no confusion of vision and as long as the mind is not disturbed,
for that long alone should a self-possessed person always abstain from intoxicants.
One whose vāta is predominant should drink [medicinal liquids] after being treated with oil massages, dry rubs, baths, perfumes, incense,
and ointments, and after having consumed unctuous and warm foods.

One who has been affected by pitta does not suffer when drinking wine, provided they have been treated with various cooling measures that are sweet, unctuous, and cold, and have been conditioned with such foods.
One of phlegmatic constitution (ślaiṣmika) who eats barley and wheat should drink wine with meat from arid regions (dhanvaja) seasoned with black pepper, accompanied by non-cooling treatments.
In that regard, wine made from flour or molasses is generally beneficial for Vāta;
for Pitta, honey with water; and for Kapha, Mārdvīka, Ariṣṭa, or Mādhava wine.
One with a predominance of phlegm (kapha) should drink alcohol before the meal; one with a predominance of bile (pitta) after the meal;
one with a predominance of wind (vāta) in between; and one with balanced humors may drink as they desire.
Among the intoxications (madas), that which subdues vāta and pitta is generally desired for cases of fainting (mūrchā);
indeed, in all instances, one should specifically observe the involvement of pitta.
Cool plasters, gems, affusions, and the breeze from fans;
the juices of sugar-candy, grapes, sugarcane, dates, and *kāśmarya*; and milk.
Soups prepared with the group of sweet substances (madhuravarga) along with pomegranate are proven [remedies]; likewise,
sixty-day rice (ṣaṣṭika), śāli rice, mung beans, barley, and ghee are life-sustaining.
Kalyāṇaka-pañcagavya with six palas of milk and processed with fire,
or long pepper, or realgar, according to the procedure for elixirs (rasāyana).
Or Triphalā should be administered with ghee, honey, and sugar;
when the morbid force is persistent, the occlusion of the mouth and nose is beneficial.

Or one should drink human milk, and with that, one should administer nasal drops (nāvana). Alternatively, one should lick a paste of lotus stalks, lotus roots, and black pepper, along with chebulic myrobalan and honey.
One should drink either *durālabhā* or *mustā* with cold water, or [a mixture of] black pepper, *kola* stones, marrow, *uśīra*, and *ahi-kesara*.
One should prepare ghee processed with the juice of *dhātrī* fruit or with a decoction of *pathyā*,
and one should also perform the treatments prescribed for fever according to the strength of the manifestation of the respective *doṣas*.
Five procedures are recommended, as well as bloodletting;
[the patient should have] confidence, knowledge of the objective, and lack of greed for sense objects.

When poisons have become excessively aggravated, and in cases of fainting, one should administer the sharp treatment prescribed for the induction of unconsciousness; and in cases arising from poison, one should employ anti-poisonous remedies.
In cases of fainting (saṃnyāsa), one should quickly employ a very sharp nasal drop (nasya) or collyrium (añjana),
as well as medicinal smoke (dhūma), blowing [medicine into the nose] (pradhamana), and pricking with needles between the nails.
Plucking out the hair, cauterization, being bitten by dogs or scorpions,
gargling with pungent and sour substances in the mouth, and rubbing with *kapikacchu* [are the treatments].
Once he has recovered consciousness and risen, he should drink the fresh juice of garlic;
he should also eat the seeds of the citron (bījapūraka) along with the filaments and the three pungent spices (vyoṣa) and salt.
One should eat light food that is pungent and sharp for the purification of the channels;
[one should also restore consciousness] by means of startling events, recollections, and the hearing or sight of beloved things.
By means of sharp sounds of song and musical instruments, physical exercises,
emetics and purgatives, medicinal smokes, and bloodletting—
One should attend to him constantly out of fear of complications; furthermore, his mind must be protected from the cause of dissolution.
Thus ends the ninth chapter.
Now begins the tenth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of hemorrhoids.
Thus indeed said the great seers, Ātreya and the others.

Now, indeed, for one who is strong and afflicted by hemorrhoids, who has been properly lubricated with oil and fomented, and who has eaten a small amount of unctuous, warm food consisting mostly of liquids—intended to pacify the increase of wind-pain—one who is pure, for whom auspicious rites have been performed, who has voided feces and urine and is free from distress, should be placed on a level bed or plank in a clean, secluded place during a moderate, cloudless season. With his buttocks facing the sun, he should sit upon the lap of another person with his upper body bent forward, supine with the region of his waist elevated. Having had his neck and hip joints encircled with a binding cloth and being well-supported by trustworthy attendants who are beyond reproach, one should then, once his anus is smeared with ghee, gently insert the ghee-smeared instrument straight and comfortably into the rectum.

Having observed that the hemorrhoid has entered the rectal canal (pravāhaṇa), one should press it with a probe covered by either a cotton pad (picu) or a cloth strip (plotaka), and treat it with fire or caustic according to the prescribed method, ensuring it is properly extinguished. Large hemorrhoids should be excised in a person of strong constitution and then cauterized.
Having tied umbrella-shaped [specula] that extend upward with an alkaline thread,
one should then remove the instrument and, having raised the patient, bathe him at the appropriate time in a tub of warm water after his anus, buttocks, and groin have been well-anointed.
Then, having led him into a windless chamber, one should instruct him in his conduct;
if any portion remains, one should cremate him again.
In this manner, one should proceed with each [vein] every seven nights;
however, when there are many [veins], one should first treat the right [side], then the left, and after the left, those located at the back and the head.
However, for one who cauterizes all [the vessels] in a single day, the fault described as "excessive application" (atiyoga) occurs;
in that case, one should treat dry [vessels] with fire or alkali,
and moist [vessels] with mild alkali alone.
This is the procedure for cauterization of hemorrhoids at all locations;
however, regarding the third fold of the anus, some authorities maintain that one should treat it after first declining to do so.

Now, when properly cauterized, there occurs downward movement of the *vāta*, a relish for food, stimulation of the digestive fire, lightness, clarity of the sense organs, cessation of the aforementioned complications, and the restoration of strength and complexion.
However, in the case of improper cauterization, one should observe the procedure for alkali and fire therapy.
AS.Ci.10.7: In the event of pain in the bladder, one should smear everything below the navel with a paste of kuṣṭha, śatapuṣpā, devadāru, surabhi, punarnavā, and agaru.

In the event of obstruction of urine and feces, one should apply a lukewarm decoction of *varaṇa*, *ālambusā*, *eraṇḍa*, *punarnavā*, *aśvadaṃṣṭrā*, *surabhī*, and *suṣavī* as a sprinkling (*pariṣeka*) or for downward irrigation (*avāha*), after well-anointing the back, waist, groins, and anus;
or one may use milk with unctuous substances, or even oil alone.
Once the hemorrhoids have been cauterized, one should eat food combined with *trivṛt*, *vāstūka*, *upodakā*, *cuñcuparṇī*, and leaf-vegetables for the purpose of softening the feces.
To protect and stimulate the digestive fire (*anila-anala*) and for the nourishment of the body, one should properly employ unctuous substances (*sneha*) and other such treatments.

Purificatory measures such as pastes, decoctions, and oil formulations should be applied to those [ulcers] that have healed, after considering the specific requirements of the ulcer treatment (vraṇādhikāra) (AS.Ci.10.9). Now, for those ulcers caused by the improper application of surgical instruments, alkali, or fire, which are aggravated by Vāta and Kapha, protruding due to the fullness of the humors, and accompanied by stiffness, itching, swelling, and pain— one should apply an ointment made of oil processed with *kṣāra*, *citraka*, *kuṣṭha*, and the root of *bilva*, or else with the fat of a black snake, a cat, a camel, a leech, or a pig.
One should foment [the patient] with a bolus or with liquid fomentation,
and should fumigate [the area] with ghee, *śamī* leaves, the root of *arka*, human hair, snake slough, and cat skin.
Or with the dung of elephants, boars, and bulls, and groats, and resin of *sarja*;
or with *surasā*, *bṛhatī*, *pippalī*, and *aśvagandhā* mixed with ghee;
or with *ariṣṭa*, leaves of *śigru*, *kulattha*, and *vacā*.
And after cauterization, [the area should be treated] with turmeric powder mixed with the milky sap of *snuhī*,
or with cock's dung, turmeric, long pepper, and roots of *guñjā* ground with cow’s urine,
or with *dantī*, *citraka*, and *suvarcikā* ground with cow’s bile.
Alternatively, one may use *sudhā* (Euphorbia) and milk ground together; or *guḍa*, *kṛṣṇā*, *saindhava*, *kuṣṭha*, and *śirīṣa* seeds;

or likewise, goat’s bone, *tuttha*, *bhallātaka*, *lāṅgalī*, *kulīraśṛṅgī*, *vacā*, *abhayā*, *hiṅgu*, *kuṣṭha*, *bilva*, *śigru*, the roots of *mūlaka*, the seeds of *nimba*, the leaves of *aśvamāra*, and the roots of *pīlu*, all ground with goat’s urine;
or *sudhā* stalks, *arka* latex, the fruit of *tumba*, *karañja*, and the *pippalyādi* group of substances used for oil enemas (*anuvāsana*).
For arrows smeared with these [substances], having discharged the accumulated vitiated blood and the slimy discharge, become pacified;
and with these one should prepare oils for the purpose of massage (abhyaṅga).

Likewise, oil cooked with four times as much urine along with kāsīsa, saindhava, long pepper (pippalī), kuṣṭha, ginger (śuṇṭhī), viḍaṅga, vidārī, lāṅgalī, karavīra, fresh ginger (ārdraka), svarṇakṣīrī, dantī, citraka, and the latex of alarka and sudhā, does not cause further corruption and, through massage of the anus, cuts away hemorrhoids like alkali.

Alternatively, having smeared the anal region with oil, one should apply heat by pressing it against pieces of baked brick with sharp points, heated to the color of fire and quenched in buffalo urine, twice a day for seven days;
and one should also perform the *anantā* bath as previously described.

Then, after seven nights have passed, one should prepare a suppository from a paste of *pūtīkarañja* sprouts mixed with rock salt (*saindhava*) and the milky sap of *snuhī*; this should be inserted into the anus while still slightly moist.
Once the patient has voided feces and urine, he should be placed in a sitz bath (*avagāha*).
This procedure should be performed every morning and evening, either daily or on alternate days, for up to three nights.
Then one should regularly consume *devadālī*, alkali, and *harītakī*;
in this way, hemorrhoids are destroyed.
(AS.Ci.10.11) Now follows the procedure for the preparation of *harītakī*.

One should burn *jīmūtaka* together with its roots and net-like fibers using the antardhūma method; from that ash, one should filter half an *āḍhaka* with two vessels (*pātra*) of cow’s urine twenty-one times.

Then, with that alkaline urine combined with three *prasṛta* measures of the powder of *kuṭaja*, *citraka*, and *vyādhighāta*, one should cook two hundred *pathyā* fruits until the mixture reaches a thick consistency.

Once that electuary has cooled, one should place it in a vessel smeared with ghee along with a *prasṛta* measure of the powder of the three pungents (*vyoṣa*). When this electuary is used in combination with *sāvaleha-vijayā*, its regular application cures hemorrhoids, abdominal diseases, pain in the loins and groin, artificial poisons, flatulence, abdominal tumors, anemia, urinary calculi, gravel, asthma, and cough.
Furthermore, one should always perform cleansing with lukewarm water infused with leaf-decoctions or plain warm water.
If blood does not flow from hemorrhoids that are swollen and hard, one should induce its flow using leeches or a brush of needles (sūcīkūrca).

In cases of loss of digestive fire (agnisāda), swelling and pain in the anus, one should administer a powder made by combining one-half karṣa of hiṅgu, one karṣa each of sauvarcala salt, yavakṣāra, indrayava, and pippalī, half a pala of mūrvā, one pala of pāṭhā, and two palas of śuṇṭhī; this should be taken with warm water, ghee, wine, or other suitable liquids.
One should administer either the powder of trilavaṇa and other ingredients, or asafoetida, ativiṣā, kuṣṭha, svarjikākṣāra, and biḍalavaṇa in increasing double proportions;
or one may give prāṇadā with molasses, followed by buttermilk as an after-drink.

In the morning, or before a meal, or while fasting, one should drink buttermilk every day; once that buttermilk has been digested, one should drink buttermilk-peyā (gruel) with rock salt in the evening, or lick parched grain flour (*lāja-saktu*) with buttermilk, or consume *pīlu* fruits with buttermilk as an after-drink;
this should be practiced for a fortnight or half a fortnight in the morning.
Alternatively, one may take a paste of *kaṭukikā* and *mūlaka* with buttermilk in the morning,
or milk boiled with a decoction of *śuṇṭhī*, *citraka*, and *punarnavā*.
Or, *harītakī* fruits that have been soaked many times in cow’s urine infused with the alkali of *jīmūtaka*;
or a hundred *abhayā* fruits boiled in half a *droṇa* of cow’s urine and mixed with honey;
or the *vāsiṣṭha-harītajīrva*.

Or one may take bhallātaka fruits according to the instructions for rejuvenation (rasāyana), or punarnavā and āmalakī according to the procedure prescribed for swelling (śopha), or jaggery and fresh ginger,
or barley-flour mash (mantha) mixed with bhallātaka powder and buttermilk, not too salty.

In any one of the months of Vaiśākha, Kārttika, or Mārgaśīrṣa, when the moon is in conjunction with the Puṣya asterism, one should extract the *citraka* root; or else, one should habitually consume the decoction of *citraka* root—which has been processed with buttermilk, whey, broth, milk, ghee, oil, or any one of these—either as a linctus mixed with honey and jaggery, while subsisting on buttermilk.
When curd has formed in a jar that has been dried after being smeared with a paste of the root-bark of *Citraka*, it is called *kālaśeya*; this may be used in drinks and foods.
Similarly, there is a procedure for buttermilk (*takra-kalpa*) using *bhārgī*, *āsphota*, *guḍūcī*, and *pañcakola*.

Alternatively, buttermilk produced in a jar of ghee that has been infused with the powders of *hapuṣā*, *upakuñcikā*, *dhānakā*, *ajamoda*, *ajājī*, *śaṭhī*, *kāravī*, *yavānī*, *citraka*, the two types of *pippalī*, and *pippalīmūla* is also used.

Alternatively, one whose digestive fire is extremely weak should practice the habit of consuming buttermilk (*takra*) for seven days— whether it be sour or non-sour, with or without food, and whether warm or cold. Thereafter, he should gradually consume gruels (*peyā*), soups (*āyūṣa*), meat broths (*rasa*), and side dishes (*vyañjana*) prepared from *arśoghna* (hemorrhoid-curing), light, and digestive-stimulating substances, along with grain-pastes (*dhānya*) and vegetable preparations (*śāka*).
Buttermilk is indeed the supreme medicine for ailments caused by vāta and kapha, especially those localized in the abdomen;
it is particularly effective against hemorrhoids.
For indeed, once those other hemorrhoids are destroyed, they do not sprout again;

moreover, that [medicine] being administered day after day eradicates the mass of grass even from the ground and the moss even from the water. Furthermore, when the channels of the body have been purified by it, the essence of food, accumulating therein, quickly conduces to the increase of nourishment, strength, complexion, and vitality.
And the drinker of intoxicants should consume *śīdhu* made from molasses, or *surā*, mixed with the powder of *cavya*, *citraka*, and *ajājī*,
along with *sauvarcala* salt and *hapuṣā*.

One should take eight palas of *abhayā*, double that amount of *āmalaka* (sixteen palas), five palas of *indravāruṇī*, and double that amount of the pulp of *kapittha* (ten palas); then add two palas each of *lodhra*, *viḍaṅga*, *elavāluka*, *pippalī*, and *marica*. Having crushed these and boiled them in one *bhāra* (ten thousand palas) of water until reduced to one-quarter, the strained and cooled decoction should be mixed with two *tulās* of jaggery (*guḍa*) and eight palas of *dhātakī*. This should be kept in a vessel smeared with ghee for half a month and then consumed either in the morning or at mealtime.

This *Abhayāriṣṭa* destroys hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*), anemia, heart disease, jaundice, consumption, intermittent fever, splenic disorders, abdominal tumors, abdominal enlargement, edema, skin diseases, worms, nodules, and tumors; it also promotes digestion, relieves hunger, and improves complexion. (AS.Ci.10.20) Having boiled one *pala* each of *dantī*, *citraka*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and the ten roots (*daśamūla*) in one *droṇa* of water until one-quarter remains, and having strained and cooled it, one should add half a *tulā* of jaggery and one *kuḍava* of *dhātakī*. After it has been kept in a vessel smeared with ghee for a month, this *Dantyariṣṭa* is equal in its effects to the previous one.

One *prastha* of *durālabhā*, two *palas* each of *abhayā*, *āmalaka*, *vṛṣa*, *pāṭhā*, *citraka*, *dantī*, and *mahauṣadhī*, should be boiled in one *droṇa* of water as previously described. Once prepared, strained, and cooled, it should be mixed with a *tulā* of sugar and placed for half a month in a jar of ghee that has been smeared with a paste of honey, ghee, *priyaṅgu*, *pippalī*, and *cavikā*. This *durālabhā-ariṣṭa* is identical in its effects to the previous one.

One hundred palas of fresh *āmalaka*, two *kuḍavas* of *pippalī* and *nāgapuṣpa*, one *pala* each of *cavya*, *citraka*, *kramuka*, *lodhra*, *pāṭhā*, *marica*, *viḍaṅga*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *elavāluka*, and *pippalīmūla*, and half a *pala* each of *dārvī*, *śatāhvā*, *indrāhvā*, the two types of *sārivā*, *musta*, and *kuṣṭha*, should be boiled together in two *droṇas* of water until one-half remains.

That juice, purified and cooled, combined with the fresh juice of grapes, two hundred *pala* of sugar, half a *prastha* of honey, and one *karṣa* each of the powders of cinnamon, cardamom, *lodhra*, *kuṭannaṭa*, *ambusevya*, betel nut, and *kesara*, should be placed in a ghee-smeared vessel fumigated with jaggery and sugar. Having been left to mature for a fortnight, this Āmalakāriṣṭa is equal to the previous one and also pacifies premature wrinkles, graying hair, and baldness.

AS.Ci.10.22: Four *pala*s of *guggulu*, one *prastha* of *āmalaka*, one *prastha* of *dhātakī*, one hundred *abhayā* fruits, and one hundred *akṣa* fruits; two hundred *pala*s of jaggery (*guḍa*); five *pala*s each of the five spices (*pañcakola*), *ajamodā*, the four aromatics (*caturjātaka*), *kaṭphala*, *musta*, and black pepper (*marica*); and ten *pala*s each of sugar candy (*khaṇḍa*), grapes (*drākṣā*), and pomegranate (*dāḍima*). Having soaked all these together in water and stirred them well, one should place them in an old vessel made of lac that can hold one *droṇa* and set it aside.
When the resulting *āsava* is observed to be endowed with the proper fragrance, color, and taste, one should fill that jar with sugarcane juice.
This Guggulu-āsava, prepared for six months, is equal to the previous one;
or, one who does not drink wine may drink it with a small amount of water that has been boiled and cooled, or with water boiled with coriander and ginger.

One should prepare soups, meat broths, meat juices, and the like, using either the minor *pañcamūla*, or *pañcakola*, cumin, *kāravī*, *gajaśauṇḍī*, unripe *bilva* fruits, *pāṭhā*, *tumburu*, and coriander;
these should be made sour with fruit-acids and enriched with the "yamaka" (a mixture of ghee and oil) and fats. (AS.Ci.10.24)
With these very same [substances], one should prepare ghee,
or drink buttermilk, fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla), honey-vinegar, or water.
One should boil two hundred palas of dried *pūtīkarañja* bark in one *droṇa* of water until reduced to one-fourth;

then, when it has been strained and cooled, one should add eighty palas of jaggery and half a *prastha* of the powder of the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), and place it in a jar of ghee within a heap of barley for one month.
This *karañja*-semen, when practiced regularly, generates fire and destroys hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), flatulence (*ānāha*), splenic disorders, poison, and abdominal diseases.
One should press one *tulā* of *pīlu* seeds with an equal amount of jaggery in a *droṇa* of buttermilk or whey.

Into that, having added one *pala* each of the powder of *abhayā*, *ativiṣā*, *pāṭhā*, *mustaka*, *kaṭukā*, *devadāru*, *hiṃsrā*, *jīraka*, *āruṣkara*, *cavya*, *ajamoda*, *elā*, *citraka*, *gajapippalī*, *vyoṣa*, *viḍaṅga*, *śatāhvā*, *hareṇu*, *cirabilva*, bark, *kuṣṭha*, *kuṭaja*-seeds, *trivṛt*, *pippalī*-root, and *upakuñcikā*, one should store it as before; this possesses superior qualities compared to the former.

One should press one *droṇa* of well-cut pieces of sugarcane into a vessel previously treated with ghee using one *droṇa* of water. Into this, one should add crushed *yavānī*, *yavānaka*, *kustumbarī*, and *pṛthavīkā*, each in the measure of one *kuḍava*; likewise, two *palas* each of *tejovatī*, the five *kolakas*, *ajājī*, the two types of *jīraka*, and *kāravī*. Having added one *kuḍava* of honey, one should drink from it after ten nights have passed, taking a dose that has been made fragrant with *sauvarcala*, fresh ginger, and *bhūstṛṇa*, while eating [the appropriate food].
Furthermore, one should repeatedly add water and ingredients such as pieces of sugarcane to this;

that fermented gruel known as *gaṇḍīra-kāñjika* is highly appetizing, stimulates the digestive fire, and cures hemorrhoids, disorders of the *grahaṇī*, abdominal enlargements, artificial poisons, worms, abdominal tumors, alcoholism, and anemia (AS.Ci.10.27).
Moreover, a person with hemorrhoids and a dry bowel should drink ghee mixed with sugar and sour fruits, containing *nāgara*, alkali, black cumin (*kṛṣṇājājī*), coriander (*dhānyaka*), and *āravī*.
Or the ghees mentioned for gulma, or [ghee] cooked with the decoction of *kiṃśuka* alkali and containing *vyoṣa*.

Ghee cooked with four times as much curd and containing *pāṭhā*, the five types of *marica*, alkali, *yavānī*, *kustumbaru*, *harītakī*, *bilva*, *viḍaṅga*, and rock salt (*saindhava*) cures dysentery (*pravāhikā*), prolapse of the rectum, slimy discharge, flatulence, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), pain in the anus, flanks, and groin, disorders of the digestive tract (*grahaṇī-doṣa*), heart disease, and difficulty in urination (*mūtrakṛcchra*).

(AS.Ci.10.28) One should cook forty *palas* of ghee with six times as much curd and an equal amount of *cāṅgerī* juice, adding a decoction of three *palas* each of *pippalī*, *pāṭhā*, *nāgara*, and *gokṣuraka*, along with a paste (*kalka*) consisting of half a *pala* each of *gaṇḍīra*, *marica*, and the five types of *kolaka*.
That clarified butter is identical to the previous [preparation],
and it cures swelling, abdominal enlargement, asthma, and hiccup.
Hemorrhoids with bound stools should be treated like udāvarta;
hemorrhoids with broken stools should be treated like atisāra.
When the [disorders] are excessively active and red, like the diarrhea of *raktapitta*,
one should disregard the flowing blood while considering the impurity and the strength of the time.
In both cases, phlegm (śleṣman) and wind (anila) are involved;
however, when pitta and phlegm are predominant, one should treat it by purifying with digestive and appetizing substances and through watchful care.
When pitta and wind are predominant, one should pacify them internally and externally, upwards and downwards, using fire-like therapies and unctuous substances as appropriate.

In cases where pitta alone is predominant, especially during the hot season, or in a weak patient, one should use astringent (stambhana) measures. Furthermore, in a condition where kapha is predominant, one should drink a decoction of *kuṭaja* bark and *viśvabheṣaja*.
Alternatively, one should boil the bark of *kuṭaja*, its fruit, *ativiṣā*, and *rasāñjana* with honey in rice-water.
Or, one should boil one hundred palas of fresh *kuṭaja* bark in rainwater;

when the decoction has been extracted and strained, one should add one pala each of finely ground *priyaṅgu*, *samaṅgā*, and *mocarasa*, along with three palas of *kuṭaja* seeds, and cook it again over a gentle fire until it reaches the consistency of a ladle-coating (*ādarvīlepa*).

This electuary, when administered with goat's milk or the scum of gruel by one who subsists on goat's milk, cures hemorrhoids born of blood, diarrhea, and Kapha-Pitta that has manifested either upward or downward.
One should boil one hundred palas of Kutaja bark in one droṇa of water until it is reduced to one-eighth.

Having strained that water, one should place it over the fire after mixing it with one *pala* each of the paste of *vyoṣa*, *rasāñjana*, *mocarasa*, *mustā*, *dhātakī* fruit, young *bilva* fruits, young pomegranate fruits, bark, *samaṅgā*, and the two types of *lodhra*; likewise, adding ten *palas* of *kuṭaja* bark, twenty *palas* of ghee, and thirty *palas* of jaggery.

Once it has reached the consistency of an electuary (*avaleha*), it should be removed from the heat and stored well-protected in a vessel of grain for seven days, half a month, or a full month. When consumed, it quickly cures all types of hemorrhoids, disorders of the *grahaṇī*, dyspnea, and cough.
Alternatively, one should drink mocarasa, samaṅgā, sesame, lodhra, sandalwood, and blue lotus with goat’s milk. In cases of colic (śūla), however,
one should take the powder of pāṭhā combined with any one of the following— bilva, yavānī, nāgara, rasāñjana, durālabhā, or the seeds of vatsaka— with warm boiled water or with buttermilk (takra).

In cases of colic and excessive bleeding, one should administer ghee prepared with a paste of *lodhra*, *dhātakī*, the bark of *kuṭaja*, *indrayava*, saffron, and blue lotus; or alternatively, ghee prepared with a paste of *dugdhikā* and *nidigdhikā*.

However, when the blood is dominated by *vāta*, one should cook one *prastha* of ghee with one *karṣa* each of *balā*, *atibalā*, *bilva*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *hastipippalī*, leaves of *nyagrodha* and *karañja*, *madhuka*, *tinduka*, and blue lotus, along with ten times the amount of goat’s milk.

That supreme ghee, which destroys bleeding hemorrhoids, prepared with a paste of pāṭhā, lodhra, hrīvera, utpala, cavya, candana, samaṅgā, ativiṣā, bilva, dhātakī, madhuka, devadāru, the bark of dārvī, mustā, māṃsī, nāgara, yavakṣāra, citraka, and the fresh juice of cāṅgerī, destroys three droṇas [of blood] and is to be employed in cases of hemorrhoids, diarrhea, dysentery, distension of the bladder, prolapse of the rectum, slimy discharge, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), anemia, fever, dysuria, anorexia, piles, and colic.

One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with a decoction of two *palas* each of *balā*, *ārvī*, *vākpuṣpī*, *gokṣuraka*, *pṛśniparṇī*, and the tender sprouts (*pravāla*) of *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *nyagrodha*, *plakṣa*, *badarī*, and *vetasa*; along with a paste (*kalka*) consisting of half a *karṣa* each of *jīvantī*, *kaṭukā*, the five spices (*pañcakola*), *indrayava*, *devadāru*, *śālmalī* flowers, *vīrā*, *candana*, *añjana*, *kaṭphala*, *musta*, *śyāmā*, *sthirā*, *ativiṣā*, *samaṅgā*, *vyāghrī*, *mocarasa*, *bilva*, *kamala*, *utpala*, and *kiñjalka*; and with two *prasthas* of the fresh juice of *aṅgerī* and *suniṣaṇṇaka*.
This [preparation] is equal to the previous one.
For the purpose of arresting hemorrhage, one should employ cold massages, plasters, affusions, immersions, and so forth.
If the bleeding is not pacified by these, one should administer the aforementioned medicated ghees while lukewarm, administered via the *avapīḍaka* (nasal drop) method.

Having fed him lukewarm ghee, oil, milk, or meat broth, or else with unctuous and warm meat juices, one should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) with lukewarm scum of ghee, or with an oil processed with drugs of cold potency according to the specific case. One should prepare a decoction by boiling two palas each of the flowers of *śālmali*, and the roots of *yavāsa*, *kuśa*, and *kāśa*, along with the shoots of *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, and *aśvattha*, in one prastha of milk and three times that amount of water; this should be removed from the heat once only the milk remains.

This enema (picchābasti), prepared with a decoction of *niryūha* mixed with the paste (*kalka*) of *śālmalī* resin, *samaṅgā*, sandalwood, blue lotus, *indrayava*, *priyaṅgu*, and lotus filaments, combined with ghee, honey, and sugar, cures prolapse of the rectum, dysentery, hemorrhaging, and fever.
Furthermore:
Gruel prepared with parched grain (*lāja*), *cukrīkā*, saffron, and blue lotus (*utpala*), or likewise with *balā* and *pṛśniparṇī*, when drunk, quickly destroys blood disorders.
[AS.Ci.10.36] Also, gruel prepared in a decoction of *hrīvera*, *bilva*, and *nāgara*, together with fresh butter (*navanīta*)...
One should administer a *peyā* (thin gruel) prepared with *vṛkṣāmla*, pomegranate, *amlīkā*, and *kola*, all acidic,
along with *gṛñjanaka* and *surasā*, fried in a mixture of two oils (*yamaka*).

It subdues blood-dysentery, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), dysentery with tenesmus, and swelling. [One should prepare] medicinal pastes (khalas) from *kāśmarya*, *āmalaka*, and *kacchurā*, along with sour fruits.
[One should prepare] pits of *gṛñjanaka*, *śālmalī*, *dugdhīkā*, and *cukrikā* (AS.Ci.10.38),
as well as pits of *nyagrodha-śṛṅgikā* and *kocidāra-puṣpa* (AS.Ci.10.39).
When excessive bleeding occurs, one should administer curd prepared with *sareṇa* (a type of plant);
likewise, one should give onion-vegetable, *upodakā*, and jujube fruits prepared with buttermilk.
In the event of blood discharge, one should administer lentil soup with sour gruel and *takra*;
or [soup] with milk boiled [with herbs], or soups made from *satīna*, mung beans, *āḍhakī*, and lentils.
One should eat food prepared from *śāli*, *śyāmāka*, and *kodrava* grains with sour substances,
along with well-prepared meats of rabbit, deer, quail, partridge, and antelope.
One should eat *śālī* rice with sweet or slightly sour soups seasoned with a little black pepper,
or with the meat of the peacock, partridge, francolin, or the *dvika* and *kulūpāka* birds, prepared with sweet and sour sauces.
In cases of excessively discharging hemorrhoids where vāta is predominant in the body,
one should eat with meat juices; goat’s milk administered along with the juice of vāstūka destroys the blood [discharge].
The meat broth of desert-dwelling birds and wild animals, prepared without sourness or with only slight sourness—
whether combined with meat-scum, leafy vegetables, barley gruel, and ghee, or taken alone— is victorious [over disease].
Onion, when consumed, overcomes blood and aggravated vāta; likewise,
goat meat cooked with young sprouts and blood, along with abundant onion, [achieves the same].

In cases of the depletion of feces and blood, one should administer sweet [substances] in reverse order; through the habitual use of fresh butter and sesame, and through the habitual use of saffron, fresh butter, and sugar.
By the habitual consumption of the cream of curd churned with water, hemorrhoidal diseases involving the flow of blood are pacified.
Goat's fresh butter, ghee, milk, meat, and *ṣaṣṭika* rice [are likewise beneficial].
Fresh surā-maṇḍa and fresh surā conquer hemorrhage like a young woman; generally, hemorrhoids become dominated by vāta when blood has been excessively lost.
For even when phlegm and bile are observed, vāta should be understood as predominant; likewise,
having seen that blood and bile are powerful while the signs of phlegm and vāta are slight.
Cooling treatments should be applied as prescribed for diseases caused by *pitta* (AS.Ci.10.50).

However, in the case of *udāvarta*, for the purpose of dissolving the morbid humors (*doṣa*), one should apply a cooling fever-alleviating oil and perform sudation. Then, having prepared a suppository shaped like a thumb from the powder of *śyāmā*, *trivṛt*, *pippalī*, *nikumbha*, and *nīlinī* soaked in cow’s urine and mixed with double the amount of salt and jaggery, one should insert it into the anus of the patient whose anus has been smeared with ghee, in order to facilitate the downward movement of flatus, feces, and urine (AS.Ci.10.50).
Or one may blow into the nose through a tube the powder of long pepper (pippalī), madanaphala, mustard (sarṣapa), and soot (agāradhūma) mixed with urine and jaggery;
or the powder of bottle gourd (tumbī), karaghāṭa, kaṇā, white mustard (siddhārthaka), rock salt (saindhava), and jīmūtaka.
Alternatively, the powder of these very same substances may be blown into the nose.
In the event of its obstruction, one should administer a very sharp non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) combined with emollient drugs, oils, urine, sour liquids, salts, and alkalis.
Triphalā, trikaṭu, the three salts, dantī, citraka, and bhallātaka—these should be crushed and cooked with fats and urine in a vessel smeared with clay, using a fire of cow-dung cakes.

This alkali known as *Kalyāṇaka*, when drunk with ghee or administered in food and drink by one who subsists on milk, meat, and broth, cures hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), anemia (*pāṇḍu*), heart disease, upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*), malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*), urinary obstruction, urinary calculi, worms, edema, hiccups, dyspnea, cough, colic, flatulence, splenic disorders, and urinary diseases.

The roots and fruits used for purgation, along with *sahiṃsrā*, *arkamūla*, the ten roots (*daśamūla*), jaggery, *dvīpi*, two types of *punarnavā*, and all five salts in equal parts—this alkali prepared as previously described is called *Kāṅkāyana*; it possesses superior qualities compared to the former.

Take one *karṣa* each of asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), *pāṭhā*, the three acrids (*tryūṣaṇa*), the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *kaṭabhī*, the pulp of *bilva*, iron filings (*ayaḥrajaḥ*), *kaṭukā*, the five spices (*pañcakola*), *musta*, *kuṣṭha*, the two types of alkali (*kṣāradvaya*), *muṣkaka*, *madhuka*, *ugragandhā*, *viḍaṅga*, *mūrvā*, *ajamoda*, *indrayava*, *guḍūcī*, and *devadāru*; and take one *pala* each of the five salts (*pañcalavaṇa*). Having crushed these together, mix them with two *kuḍavas* of ghee and oil and two *kuḍavas* of curd. Burn this according to the procedure for the *Kalyāṇaka* preparation; this is the "Great Alkali" (*Mahākṣāra*), which is equal in potency to that [preparation] and destroys all artificial and natural poisons.
One should administer it before a meal, or alternatively, provide ghee, jaggery, and barley-alkali.
Or pomegranate juice with *yavānī*, *pāṭhā*, *mahauṣadha*, salt, jaggery,
and *takra*; or the sprouts of *karañja* fried in a mixture of two fats (*yamakasneha*) and mixed with barley meal (*saktu*).
One should consume curd, pomegranate, sour jujube, tamarind, citron, salt, and wine prepared with a combination of two [ferments];

likewise, the sprouts of *trivṛt*, *dantī*, *guḍūcī*, *citraka*, *cāṅgerī*, young radish, *loṇīkā*, *suvarcalā*, *upodikā*, *cuñcuparṇī*, *vīra*, and *vāstuka*; as well as the meat of the cock, peacock, porcupine, iguana, cat, camel, jackal, tortoise, and *śalyaka*—using these for meat soups; for food, one should take a diet consisting mostly of barley;

and for drink, one should take *gauḍa* liquor, clear wine (*acchasurā*), salted *āsava* liquors, or fermented gruel (*āranāla*) and whey (*mastu*), all prepared with digestive stimulants (*dīpanīya*) and wind-alleviating (*vātahara*) agents.
If there is excessive after-effect, however, one should administer a purgative combined with wine, *āma*, and urine;
or else *harītakī* fried in ghee with *pippalī* and jaggery; or [a preparation] containing *kumbha* and *nikumbha*.
Or one may employ the satiating (tarpaṇa) formulations mentioned in the "Chapter on the Two Types of Therapeutic Procedures" (Upakramaṇīya),
or the powder of trivṛt mixed with the juice of triphalā, or the "Māṇibhadra" preparations consisting of abhayā, āmalaka, and viḍaṅga combined with trivṛt and jaggery.
One should administer mixed oils, *sukumāraka* ghee, *nīlinī* ghee, or purgatives prescribed in the Kalpa section.

For when the morbid humors (*doṣa*) localized in the rectum are removed, the diseases born of them are also pacified. Since colic and upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*) arise from dryness and the obstruction of feces and flatus, one should therefore quickly apply oleation or unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*) in that case.

Oil prepared with finely ground *pippalī*, *madana*, *bilva*, *vacā*, *madhuka*, *śatapuṣpā*, *śaṭhī*, *kuṣṭha*, *puṣkaramūla*, *dvīpi*, and *devadāru*, along with double the quantity of milk, cures hemorrhoids, prolapse of the rectum, pain in the female genital tract, distension of the groin, anal swelling, dysentery, slimy discharge, weakness in the thighs, waist, and back, discoloration, and dysuria; it also restores the downward movement of wind, urine, feces, pitta, and kapha. For when the wind moves downward, the digestive fire certainly becomes kindled, and consequently, the hemorrhoids undergo contraction.
And on this subject, there are these verses (AS.Ci.10.55): One should treat hemorrhoids with surgical instruments, alkaline applications, cauterization, medicinal pastes, and oil massages.
Furthermore, those [symptoms] that are visible and invisible [respectively] are [treated] by constant internal purification;
and for those [diseases] arisen in a short time, where the signs and defects are slight, medicine [is the remedy].
In cases where the swellings are not too high, are soft, and discharge blood, [cauterization with] alkali is indicated;
in cases where the swellings are elevated but have small roots, surgical instruments are recommended for those known as *kunāma*.
In cases where there is stability, hardness, and toughness, one should apply a blade or fire;
or, having incised or cut open large [abscesses], one should apply caustic alkali (kṣāra).
Likewise, a probe and a hook are the instruments used for them; however,
if the instrument is excessively thick or long, it will cause injury to the vital points (marmas).
In that which is slightly perforated, the great form remains in one part;
in that which is extremely perforated, the form has descended further due to the flow.
One should not excessively injure the large intestine; therefore, one should apply the treatment as prescribed.
For dry [disorders], bhallātaka is said to be the foremost medicine, whereas for moist [disorders], the bark of vatsaka is used.

In all seasons and at all times, whey (kālaśeya) is strengthening and removes impurities; it is used for clearing obstructions and for the downward movement of wind, as well as for increasing the strength of the digestive fire.

That food, drink, and medicine should be used by one suffering from hemorrhoids; the opposite of this should be avoided. Hemorrhoids, diarrhea, and disorders of the *grahaṇī* are generally causes for one another.
"While the fire is unkindled it exists, and when kindled it does not exist; therefore, one should guard the fire with special care.
Thus ends the tenth chapter.
Now begins the eleventh chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of diarrhea;
thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
For diarrhea generally occurs by first impairing the digestive fire and then taking its seat in the *āma* (undigested matter);
therefore, even in cases arising from *vāta*, one should initially treat with fasting (*laṅghana*) for the purpose of digesting the *āma*.

In that case, one who suffers from colic, constipation, or excessive salivation should be made to vomit with warm salt water; however, if the disease is still associated with undigested matter (āmadoṣa), one should not first employ astringent measures.
Or, when the feces are obstructed and the abdominal cavity is stiff, distended, heavy, and painful, one should administer the "life-giving" (*prāṇadā*) decoction with warm water.

Or [one may take] it with trikaṭu and hot water, or boiled with fermented rice-water (dhānyāmla), or any other medicine that is laxative and digestive-stimulant. Furthermore: AS.Ci.11.3. For when the channels have been purified and the remaining morbid humors (doṣas) have been drained away, it is easy to effect their consolidation (saṅgrahaṇa) by means of digestive (pācana) or astringent (stambhana) measures.
One with moderate doṣas, however, while drying up [the excess], should drink a decoction of māgadhī, nāgara, vacā, bhūtīka, dhanikā,
and harītakī; or alternatively, a decoction of jalaja, jalada, bilva-pesikā, śuṇṭhī, and dhānyaka.
Both of these are called *pramathyā*;
they consist of the group of drugs beginning with *vacā*, boiled or powdered; or likewise, *vacā*, *abhayā*, *viḍaṅga*, *pāṭhā*, dry ginger, and black salt.
Or *mustā*, *pippalī*, *indrayava*, *pāṭhā*, and *tejovatī*;
or *viḍaṅga*, *abhayā*, *kaṇā*, and the five salts; or *pippalī*, *indrayava*, *pāṭhā*, and *śuṇṭhī*.
If the *āma* (undigested matter) associated with blood has set in, one should administer *gajapippalī* sweetened with honey and sugar;
furthermore, if the *doṣas* are slight, one should fast.
For one suffering from diarrhea, the drink should be water boiled with *vacā* and *ativiṣā*,

or with *śuṇṭhī* and *ativiṣā*, or with *mustā* and *parpaṭaka*, or with *nāgara* and *dhānyaka*. However, for one who suffers from hunger, one should prepare food and drinks such as gruels (*yavāgū*) using the light *pañcamūla*, the five types of *kola*, *hastipippalī*, *balā*, *bilva*, *pāṭhā*, *hiṅgu*, *dhānyaka*, *jīraka*, *śaṭhī*, *gandhapalāśa*, *hapuṣā*, *yavānī*, *tintiṇīka*, *dāḍima*, *biḍa*, and *saindhava* salts.
For mūḍhavāta (obstructed wind), [one should use] unripe bilva fruit, harītakī, and pippalīmūla;
for that characterized by an excess of pitta, [one should use] the two types of aṃśumatī, balā, and unripe bilva fruit.
Having drunk buttermilk filtered through a cloth, or one of the following— honey-wine, fermented grain-sour, or the scum of gruel— the thirsty person should do so;
