this regimen destroys wind and phlegm, stimulates the digestive fire, promotes digestion, improves appetite, is constipating, and is strengthening.

Furthermore, when one with matured *doṣas* suffers from diarrhea that is frequent, obstructed by wind (*anila*), accompanied by mucus, froth, pain, cutting sensations, horripilation, and is devoid of feces, that condition is called *pravāhikā* or *bimbisī*. In that case,
one should administer goat meat juices prepared according to the same method prescribed for *udāvarta*.
In cases of loss of feces accompanied by thirst, one should provide soups made from barley, mung beans, black gram, and sesame; or else,
a *khalaka* (a thick gruel) prepared with an equal paste of sesame, *bālaka*, and *bilva*, combined with the liquid from curd and fat.

Alternatively, there is the preparation called *Ajita*, made from *citraka*, *śṛṅgavera*, *pūtīkarañja*, *bilva*, and *ajamoda*, enriched with buttermilk, pomegranate juice, and oil, and combined with rock salt (*saindhava*).

Or else, there is the *khalaka* (a medicinal bolus) known as *Aparājita*, prepared from equal parts of *śaṭhī*, *tintiṇīka*, *biḍa*, pomegranate, the five salts (*pañcakola*), black pepper, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *dhātakī*, *dhanikā*, *pāṭhā*, *ajamoda*, *ajājī*, cumin, *kapittha*, rose-apple (*jambu*), mango stone, and six times the amount of *bilva* pulp; this is cooked with jaggery, green gram broth, fat, and curd. It is digestive, carminative, appetizing, astringent, and destroys hemorrhoids (*bimbisi*). Or one may take the whey of curd (*dadhisara*) mixed with jaggery and pomegranate, fried in a mixture of two fats (*yamaka*).
Or one may take parched barley flour mixed with powdered dry ginger,
or well-cooked mung beans sprinkled with the scum of clarified butter and served with black pepper as a side dish.

One should consume a side dish or a drink prepared from the inner juice of goat or sheep meat, soured with pomegranate, combined with coriander and ginger, and cooked with fats; or likewise, one should drink *surā* liquor mixed with sour gruel and fats,
or a powder of dried ginger and jujube fruit combined with curd, ghee, oil, honey, and molasses.
One should lick a powder of asafoetida, pomegranate, ginger, and long pepper with ghee, milk, warm water, or wine as desired;
or one may take lodhra, young bilva fruits, and jaggery, combined with an abundance of the three pungents (trikaṭu), along with oil.

Alternatively, one should eat śāli rice prepared with a decoction of aśvattha and vātapota, combined with ghee, oil, and honey, followed by a drink of whey (dadhisara) produced from curd stirred with a churning stick.
Moreover: AS.Ci.11.11.

Curd is illuminating, appetizing, pleasing to the taste, and an excellent subduer of Vāta; it removes even long-standing Bimbisī (hemorrhoids) when combined with bound feces. However, one who suffers from excessive thirst, passes blood-stained mucus-like stools, and has abstained from drinks and food, should drink warm milk while maintaining a continuous flow.
Or that same [milk] boiled with the root of *gandharvahasta* or with the tender fruits of *bilva*; or,
for one with little thirst, that same [milk] with jaggery and oil.
One should eat rice with boiled milk mixed with a paste of black pepper and double the amount of sesame paste;
or with milk alone mixed with long pepper;
or with foods prepared with milk processed with the three pungents (vyoṣa).
In the event of excessive pain (śūla), however, one should administer a non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) with milk boiled with the ten roots (daśamūla) and mixed with honey;
or alternatively, a slimy enema (picchābasti) or an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) that alleviates either vāta or pitta.

In cases of prolapse of the rectum (gudabhraṃśa) and colic (śūla), one should administer sour ghee— boiled with the paste of sour jujube (amlabadara), cāṅgerī juice, curd, alkali (kṣāra), and ginger (nāgara)— to the patient once the morbid humors (āma) have been eliminated. Alternatively, as previously described, one may administer sour ghee containing black pepper, the five spices (pañcakola), cumin (ajājī), dhanikā, biḍa salt, and pomegranate (dāḍima).
One should administer an unctuous enema with oil prepared from the ten roots (daśamūla) or with the *pippalyādi* group of drugs;
then, having first anointed the rectum and softened it with fomentation, one should insert the enema.
One should also perform a bandage around the ankle using his skin with its holes intact;
having removed the entrails from the mouse, one should cook the decoction of the great five roots (*mahāpañcamūla*) in milk.

One should cook oil with that milk, adding a paste of drugs that subdue *vāta*; by means of its external application and internal consumption, it cures even a severe prolapse of the rectum (*gudabhraṃśa*). One should also treat *pitta*-dominant diarrhea accompanied by undigested matter (*sāma*) at the outset like *vāta*-dominant diarrhea, using medicines that avoid those which are too sharp.
In the event of thirst, one should administer water boiled with *sārivā*, *abhūmimba*, and *nimba*, prepared as a six-fold decoction (*ṣaḍaṅga*).

For one who has fasted, at the time of eating, one should provide—according to the season—gruels (*maṇḍa*), thin gruels (*peyā*), flour-pastes (*saktu*), soups (*yūṣa*), meat-broths (*rasa*), and so forth, combined with a decoction of *abhīru*, the two *pañcamūla* groups, the two types of *balā*, *śūrpaṇī*, and other mild, sweet, bitter, and digestive (*dīpana*) substances; these should be slightly sour or unsoured, tepid or cold, and mixed with honey.
However, if there is a persistent complication (*anubandha*), one should drink a decoction of *mūrvā*, *ativiṣā*, *indrayava*, *haridrā*, and *rasāñjana*.
Or simply the seed of the *vṛkṣaka* tree,
or *pāṭhā*, *guḍūcī*, *kaṭukā*, and *kirātatikta*.
Or one may take the group of drugs beginning with turmeric (haridrādi-gaṇa); or vatsaka seeds, ativiṣā, bilva, ambu, and mustā;
or ativiṣā, vṛkṣaka bark, and its fruit, mixed with honey and taken with rice-water.
Or *candana*, *uśīra*, *śuṇṭhī*, *lodhra*, and *nīlotpala*; or *nāgara*, *utpala*, *dhātakī* flowers, and the bark of *dāḍima*;
or *kamala*, *utpala*, *lodhra*, *mocarasa*, *samaṅgā*, and sesame seeds.
Alternatively, one may take the barks of *madhuka*, *śṛṅgavera*, and *dīrghavṛnta* mixed with honey; or *śarkarā*, lotus filaments, *mustā*, *āpayasī*, and *candana*;
or a cold infusion made from the stalks of *śālmali* combined with honey and *madhuka*.
Or one may take a gruel (yavāgū) or a thick porridge (khalaka) mixed with curd and a paste of madhuka, priyaṅgu, kaṭvaṅga bark, and pomegranate sprouts;
or [a gruel] made with the stones of bilva, kapittha, jambu, and mango.

One suffering from colic with a dry bowel should drink ghee mixed with alkali, or various groups of drugs such as *lodhra*, *ambaṣṭhā*, and *priyaṅgu* prepared separately as decoctions and so forth with honey, or the great decoction (*mahākaṣāya*) beginning with *śyāmā*. (AS.Ci.11.19)
Alternatively, milk prepared with the roots of *bṛhatī*, *balā*, *aṃśumatī*, and *kacchurā*, sprinkled with the powders of *madhuka*, *kaṭvaṅga*, *ajamodā*, and sugar, mixed with oil and honey;
or simply milk that is warm as it flows from the udder.

A strong person whose feces are obstructed should drink milk processed with the powder of *triphalā* or with a decoction of *palāśa* fruits for the purpose of purgation; thereafter, he should drink only lukewarm milk. In the same manner, [milk] boiled with *trāyamāṇā* may be used.

When the old feces have been discharged, the diarrhea comes to peace. If, during the period of dietary rehabilitation (*saṃsarjana*) for one whose morbid humors (*doṣa*) have been eliminated, colic should persist, then one should cook ghee with four times the amount of oil and milk, containing *bilva*, *madhuka*, and the two types of *śatāhvā* as its internal ingredients, and administer it as an unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*).
Then, even when the *saṃsargī* enema has been correctly administered, if diarrhea persists, *picchā-bastis* should be employed.
One should wrap the stalks of the *śālmali* tree with fresh *darbha* grass, coat them with black earth, and heat them over a fire of cow-dung.
Once the earth has dried and the stalks are known to be steamed, one should pound the stalks in a mortar and then macerate a ball of them, the size of a handful, in a *prastha* measure of milk.
Then, one should administer an enema with that purified milk mixed with ghee and oil, along with a paste of honey and madhuka.
Once the enema has returned, the patient should bathe and eat with milk boiled with *kacchurā* or with the juices of wild animals (*jāṅgala*).

This is the *picchā-basti*; it pacifies bilious and sanguineous diarrhea, malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*), abdominal tumors (*gulma*), emaciation, fever, and excessive administration of purgatives and non-unctuous enemas.
In the case of chronic diarrhea that has arisen long ago, which is painless, matured, yet remains unrelieved, one should treat it with *puṭapāka* preparations.
One should cook the paste of *aralu* bark, covered by *kāśmarya* leaves, according to the method of *puṭapāka*. One should drink its juice when well-cooled, mixed with honey.
One should prepare a paste of the bark and sprouts of the *vaṭa* tree and others in the same manner.

Alternatively, one may fill a plucked-out entrail of a partridge (*tittiri*) with a paste of the bark of the *nyagrodha* group or its sprouts, and then perform a *puṭapāka* as previously described. From that, having extracted the juice, one should administer it mixed with sugar and honey. By this, all wild animals (*jāṅgalasattva*) are explained.

However, if one suffering from pitta-type diarrhea should consume pitta-aggravating substances, his excessively increased pitta causes blood-type diarrhea (raktātisāra), as well as thirst, burning sensations, delusion, fever, colic, and inflammation of the anus. In that case,
one should prescribe goat’s milk boiled with the tender leaves of the Nyagrodhādi group, mixed with sugar and honey, for both food and for washing the rectum.
Or one should drink ghee of that same kind mixed with milk, or ghee produced from milk with milk as a post-drink (anupāna), while eating the meat-juice of the *kapiñjala* bird or subsisting on milk;
or one should lick [the paste] mixed with *sallakī*, *priyaṅgu*, *tiniśa*, *śālmalī*, and *plakṣa* bark, or drink milk prepared with these along with honey.
Alternatively, one may take [the milk] boiled with yaṣṭī, lodhra, and sārivā, mixed with honey and sugar; likewise, [it may be prepared] with black sesame, samaṅgā, utpala, and yaṣṭīmadhu.
One should consume the juices of rabbit, grey partridge, pigeon, *taṇḍulīyaka*, green gram, *kāśmarya* seeds, and so forth; or one may eat goat or deer meat fried in ghee;
or the previously mentioned *puṭapāka* preparations; or one should drink a paste of *madhuka*, black earth, and conch shell mixed with blood, using rice-water as the vehicle.
Or else, one may take the paste of *phalinī* with honey, or sandalwood with sugar and honey;
for these applications alleviate thirst and other symptoms, and they destroy excessive hemorrhaging.
But one with a predominance of Vāta should lick Śatāvarī-ghṛta mixed with sugar,
or fresh butter (navanīta) with sugar.
Alternatively, ghee prepared with slimy substances and juices,
or ghee processed with lac, long pepper, ginger, katuka, indrayava, and the bark of darvi, when drunk with the scum of gruel, wards off even diarrhea caused by all three doṣas (AS.Ci.11.26).

Furthermore, when stool mixed with blood is passed in small quantities, frothy, and with difficulty due to the action of vāyu, then one should administer the previously mentioned slimy enema (picchābasti).
One should administer an oil enema (anuvāsana) using ghee prepared with sweet medicinal herbs,
for generally those suffering from diseases localized in the rectum have weak anal canals.

Specifically, in cases of diarrhea that has persisted for a long time or where there is excessive discharge, the *vāyu*, having increased in strength at its own site and having gained the support of *pitta*, becomes exceedingly difficult to conquer; therefore, one should frequently administer oil enemas (*anuvāsana*) to such patients. Furthermore, in the event of burning in the rectum, one should sprinkle the anus and its surrounding areas with a decoction of *paṭola*, *madhuka*, *madhūka*, milk-yielding trees (*kṣīrivṛkṣa*), and so forth, mixed with ghee, sugar, and honey, or simply with milk.
One should apply medicinal plugs (picu) and massages with ghees such as *śatadhauta* and others; one should also apply an ointment made from the paste of *paṭola* and other herbs mixed with ghee,
and one should dust the anal opening with their powder, as well as with the powder of *dhātakī*, *lodhra*, and black gram (*māṣa*).
In the same way, one should treat a patient with a *śūla* by applying applications of oil that pacify *vāta*;
however, if one continues to consume *pitta*-increasing substances even after this, he will quickly perish once the anal folds have become suppurated.
As for *kapha*-type diarrhea (*śleṣmātīsāra*), one should first treat it with fasting (*laṅghana*) specifically to digest the undigested matter (*āma*).
And as a follow-up treatment, one should drink a decoction of *mustā*, *abhayā*, ginger, and young *bilva* fruits;
or alternatively, a decoction of *vacā*, *viḍaṅga*, *bhūtīka*, *dhanikā*, and *devadāru*.

Alternatively, one may take pāṭhā, ativiṣā, kuṣṭha, cavya, and kaṭurohiṇī; or citraka, the two types of pippalī, and pippalīmūla with warm water; or the compound beginning with hiṅgu as prescribed for alasaka; or a powder of harītakī, rock salt, and śuṇṭhī.
Or one should lick the powder of the three pungents (trikaṭu) combined with honey and sugar;
or the wood-apple (kapittha) with honey;
or the katphala; or long peppers (pippalī).
As before, one should determine the entire treatment by considering the respective combinations of wind (vāta), bile (pitta), phlegm (āmara), and blood;

and for one suffering from colic and dysentery who is free from undigested matter (nirāma) with a predominance of wind, one should administer a slimy enema (picchābasti) or an oil enema (anuvāsana) consisting of a paste of vacā, bilva, pippalī, kuṣṭha, and śatāhvā mixed with salt, along with warm bilva-oil, or repeatedly with an oil containing the paste of vacā and the other ingredients.
On this subject, there is also this verse:
In its own location, the wind (māruta) necessarily increases due to the depletion of phlegm (kapha). Once increased, it may suddenly kill; therefore, one should conquer it with haste.
Because the wind (marut) is also quickly provoked by fear and grief, one should therefore employ treatments that pacify the wind, as well as measures to gladden and reassure the patient.
If urine or flatus passes without the need for straining,
and if the digestive fire is kindled and the abdominal cavity is light, his abdominal disease has been pacified.
The digestion of undigested matter (āma) is followed by the retention of waste products; when there is retention, pain arises in the groin and the umbilical region.
This condition should be treated gradually with various procedures that involve fasting, digestive stimulants, and measures that eliminate wind.
There is no constipation for one with an empty stomach, nor for one whose abdomen is parched,
nor for one who has overeaten; except in cases other than those involving pitta and blood, it never occurs through [the use of] excessively cold, hot, or sharp [substances].
A preparation made from the juice of *khala-rasa* with *yāmaka* and pomegranate essence;
curd with jaggery; milk; and well-ground black sesame seeds.
Oil prepared with the group of drugs that subdue salt and wind,
or even clarified butter (ghṛta), is sufficient to conquer the pains caused by dysentery;
thus ends the eleventh chapter.
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of disorders of the *grahaṇī*.
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and others:

"One should first treat the disorder located in the *grahaṇī* according to its specific nature, following the principles of indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) and by means of the methods described in the chapter on 'The Proper Measure and Coolness' (*mātrāśītīya*)."
Then, according to the procedure for diarrhea,
one should drink a decoction of mustā, ativiṣā, and viśvabheṣaja for the purpose of digesting undigested matter (āma),
or that powder with lukewarm water.
Or, one may take ginger,

or similarly the group of drugs beginning with *vacā* along with rock salt, or the powder of the "three salts" (*trilavaṇa*) and other ingredients as prescribed for abdominal tumors (*gulma*), mixed with the scum of *vāruṇī* wine.
Or, when the stool is flowing excessively, one should take powdered *bilva* pulp, *nāgara*, and *citraka* mixed with *biḍalavaṇa* and water from a pomegranate, in cases associated with phlegm. Or,
in the case of excessive colic due to undigested matter (*āma*), one should drink the *hiṅgvādi* compound mentioned for *alasaka* with warm water.
In cases of vomiting, colic, flatulence, and tumors, one should administer black pepper, cumin, sauvarcala salt, and harītakī;
likewise, in cases of āma associated with pitta and kapha, one should use kaṭukā, indrayava, pāṭhā, pippalīmūla, vacā, harītakī, and ginger, either as a decoction or in powdered form (AS.Ci.12.4).
At the time of eating, one should prepare a thin gruel or similar food prepared with the five spices (pañcakola), which is sharp, light, and digestive-stimulant.

One should give a gruel prepared with ginger (*nāgara*) and ativiṣā, acidified with buttermilk, pomegranate juice, and sour wood-apple (*vṛkṣāmla*). For drinking, one should provide buttermilk, whey, *āranāla*, wine (*madirā*), and *ariṣṭa* as prescribed for diarrhea.

Furthermore, having powdered three *palas* each of bishop’s weed (*yavānī*), chebulic myrobalan (*pathyā*), emblic myrobalan (*āmalaka*), and black pepper (*marica*), along with one *pala* each of the five salts, one should pour this mixture into a jar of freshly churned buttermilk and allow it to ferment.
Then one should drink it once the sour and pungent flavors have become manifest;
this *takrāriṣṭa* is a supreme stimulator of the digestive fire and cures hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, abdominal enlargement, edema, worms, and urinary disorders.
Furthermore:
For those suffering from disorders of the *grahaṇī*, buttermilk is wholesome because it stimulates digestion,
is easily digestible, and is non-aggravating to *pitta* due to its sweet post-digestive transformation (*pāka*).
Because it is astringent, hot, and expansive, and because it dries up the body, it is beneficial for kapha;
however, when fresh, it is sweet, sour, and thick, and thus does not cause burning in cases of vāta.
Therefore, one should employ all those applications of buttermilk that have been prescribed for abdominal enlargements and hemorrhoids in cases of *grahaṇī* disorder.

AS.Ci.12.8: One *kuḍava* each of pomegranate, wood-apple, *vṛkṣāmla*, and *amlīkā*; one *kuḍava* of the five salts; three *palas* of the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*); and eight *palas* of sugar—these should be powdered together and administered with food or drink. This destroys indigestion, anorexia, dyspnea, cough, splenic disorders, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*), heart disease, and anemia.
Furthermore, for those suffering from *grahaṇī* due to wind (*māruta*) and for those with both matured and immature [doshas], one should administer ghee to kindle the digestive fire.

One should boil the two groups of five roots (*dvipañcamūla*), *pañcakola*, *sarala*, *suradāru*, *surabhi*, *gajapippalī*, *śaṇabīja*, barley, jujube, and horse gram with either curd-whey (*mastu*) or sour gruel (*āranāla*). When reduced to one-fourth, this decoction should be cooked with ghee along with the five salts, the two alkalis (*kṣāra*), sour fruits, and *badara*. Alternatively, ghee may be cooked with rock salt (*saindhava*), the three acrids (*vyoṣa*), the two alkalis, the five roots, *abhayā*, *rāsnā*, cumin, *granthika*, *śaṭhī*, and *viḍaṅga* as the inner ingredients; combined with the fresh juices of ginger, citron, jujube, *amlīkā*, and pomegranate, and with the decoctions of dried radish, curd-whey, buttermilk, fermented gruel (*śukta*), clear wine (*prasannā*), *sauvīraka*, *tuṣodaka*, and sour gruel—this is called *agnighṛta*, which is supremely kindling to the digestive fire.

Alternatively, one should boil one *kuḍava* each of *cavya*, *citraka*, *pāṭhā*, *tejovatī*, and *pippalīmūla*, along with two *kuḍavas* of *musta*, and one handful each—measured by the fingernail—of *āsphota*, *jātī*, *nimba*, *saptacchada*, *aśvamāraka*, *karkoṭaka*, and the tender leaves of *paṭola* in one *droṇa* of water; once reduced to one-fourth, it should be removed from the heat.

In this [preparation], one should add half a *pala* of *ativiṣā* made into a paste (*kalka*), two *palas* each of *kṛṣṇā*, *sārivā*, and *bhadrā*, as well as *saindhava*, *biḍa*, and *yavakṣāra*, four *palas* of *māgadhikā*, and one *pātra* of ghee. This formulation, devised by Agastya, is sufficient for generating digestive fire.
Once the fire has been somewhat kindled, one should administer a non-unctuous enema (*āsthāpana*) to clear obstructed waste (*vibaddha-mala*).
Then, once the wind (mātariśvan) has been conquered, one should administer a purgative using castor oil, or *tilvaka* ghee mixed with alkali, or *miśraka-sneha*.

Once the patient has undergone the sequence of digestive and restorative therapies (*saṃsarga-krama*) and their stools are bound, one should administer an unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*) with oil prepared from Vāta-alleviating, digestive-stimulating (*dīpanīya*), and sour substances.
Thereafter, while continuing on a light diet, one should again administer ghee in small quantities according to the strength of the digestive fire.
For one suffering from vomiting, constipation, colic, dyspnea, or cough, one should administer ghee processed with fire (citraka) and bījavṛkṣa (bījapūraka).
For the purpose of massage, one should prepare oil using the same medicinal substances used for the ghee and fire-processed preparations.
However, in cases of a combination of vāta and kapha, one should drink the powder of these medicinal herbs with warm water.

In the case of *grahaṇī* vitiated by *pitta*, one should eliminate the *pitta*— which has returned to its own site, become aggravated, and is liquefied— by means of a non-unctuous enema (*āsthāpana*) or emesis (*vamana*), using analgesic measures. For one who has undergone the process of dietary reintegration (*saṃsarjana*) with bitter and light substances, one should administer a linctus with honey or cause them to drink it with warm water for the purpose of pacifying the remaining morbid humor (*doṣa*).

The powder of *mūrvā*, *kirātatiktaka*, *parpaṭaka*, *vacā*, *candana*, *mustā*, the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), *trāyamāṇā*, *yavānī*, the bark and fruit of *kaliṅga*, *kaṭurohiṇī*, *devadāru*, the bark of *dārvī*, *padmaka*, *uśīra*, *ariṣṭa*, *paṭola* leaves, *ativiṣā*, *saurāṣṭrī* bark, cardamom (*elā*), honey, and the seeds of *śigru*—

this indeed destroys disorders of the digestive tract (*grahaṇī-doṣa*), colic, diarrhea, anemia, heart disease, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), fever, urinary disorders (*prameha*), jaundice, diseases of the mouth, and loss of appetite.

Equal parts of *bhūnimba*, the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), *kaṭukā*, *mustā*, and *indrayava*; two parts of *citraka*; and sixteen parts of *kuṭaja* bark—all these ground together and drunk with jaggery and cold water has an effect identical to the previous formulation.

*Nāgara*, *rasāñjana*, *ativiṣā*, *dhātakī*, *ghana*, *pāṭhā*, *kaliṅga* bark, its seeds, *bilva*, and *kaṭukā*, taken with honey and rice-water, eliminate disorders of the *grahaṇī* caused by *pitta*, blood-dysentery, hemorrhoids, tenesmus, and anal pain.

Then, for the stabilization of the digestive fire (*agni*) whose excess of *pitta* has thus been pacified, one should administer ghee for drinking, prepared with the previously mentioned decoction of *mūrvā* and others, along with a paste of *sārivā*, *āsphota*, *saptaparṇa*, *āṭarūṣaka*, *indrayava*, *vīrā*, *bhūnimba*, *dhānya*, *nyagrodha*, *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, *upakulyā*, and blue lotus (*nīlotpala*). Alternatively, one may use the bitter (*tikta*) formulation prescribed for skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*). Furthermore, in cases of *grahaṇī* disorder corrupted by *śleṣman*, one should repeatedly induce emesis using a sharp decoction of *madanaphala* mixed with a paste of *māgadhikā* and *siddhārthaka*.
For when the water element has increased, it extinguishes the fire;

therefore, once the sequence of administering liquid gruel (*peyā*) and so forth has been completed, one should stimulate the digestive fire with the aforementioned foods and drinks that are intensely salty, alkaline, sour, and pungent.

One should boil *mañjiṣṭhā*, *citraka*, *āruṣkara*, *kṛmighna*, and *madhūkapuṣpa* in three *droṇas* of water, using portions of two *kuḍavas*, half an *āḍhaka*, one *āḍhaka*, half a *droṇa*, and one *droṇa* respectively.

The dregs remaining from this decoction, purified and cooled, along with honey and a double portion of ghee, and scented with sandalwood, uśīra, small cardamom, and agallochum, is a fermented liquor (āsava) that has been infused in a jar of lac for a month.
It destroys all derangements, kindles the digestive fire, is nourishing, and cures consumption, leprosy, vitiligo, urinary disorders, abdominal distension, gulma, anemia, and heart disease.
Likewise, the juice of madhūka flowers boiled down to half its volume and mixed with a quarter part honey is in every respect identical to the former.
By this, the fermented liquors (*āsava*) made from the juices of *drākṣā* (grapes), *ikṣu* (sugarcane), and *kāśmarya* (gular fig) fruits are explained.

Having boiled five *pala* portions each of *daśamūla*, *vīrā*, *rajanī*, *triphalā*, *jīvaka*, and *ṛṣabhaka* separately in water until reduced to one-fourth, when the decoction has cooled, one should add two *tulās* of jaggery (*guḍa*), half a *kuḍava* of honey, and equal quantities of the following powdered ingredients: *mustā*, *priyaṅgu*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *madhuka*, *viḍaṅga*, *plava*, *śābara*, and *lodhra*. This *mūlāsava*, kept for half a month, is identical in its effects to the previous one.

Having burnt four *palas* of *mahāvṛkṣaka* stalks, double that amount (*eight palas*) of *arka* stalks, three *palas* each of the three salts, one *kuḍava* of ripe *vārtāka*, and two *palas* of *citraka* root, while under a smokeless fire (*antardhūmam*), one should prepare pills with the juice of *vārtāka*.

When consumed after a meal, they cure *grahaṇī*, hemorrhoids, cholera, intestinal torpor, cough, asthma, chronic catarrh, splenic disorders, anemia, edema, urinary disorders, anorexia, and abdominal tumors.

Having burnt ten-pala portions each of the roots of *daśamūla*, *arka*, *dantī*, *trivṛt*, *citraka*, *āsphota*, *pāṭhā*, *rāsnā*, and the stalks of *snuhī* inside a skull, one should boil them with four *droṇas* of water. When reduced to one-fourth, it should be strained; then, having boiled it again until reduced to one-fourth of that amount and removed from the heat, one should place it over the fire mixed with one hundred palas of jaggery.
When that has become solidified, one should add thirty palas each of very fine powder of the two types of *vṛścikālī* and *yavaśūka*,
thirty palas each of *vacā*, *abhayā*, *vyoṣa*, and *citraka*, and two palas each of *hiṅgu* and *amlavetasa*.
Then, having made pills the size of a jujube fruit and consumed them according to one's strength, one should— either as prescribed previously or in greater quantity—

utilize alkaline preparations, buttermilk, and fermented liquors (ariṣṭas) indicated for hemorrhoids; one should also employ medicated ghees, food, and drink, as well as the *Ṣaṭpala-bhallātaka-ghṛta* and the *Dhānvantara-ghṛta*.
In the case of a combination of all three doshas (sannipāta), however, one should perform the five therapeutic actions, or treat the grahaṇī according to the specific condition.
Regarding this, there is a verse here: "In the case of excessive salivation caused by kapha and weak digestive fire, one should administer stimulants for digestion that are dry and bitter."
In the case of one who is emaciated, the application should be reversed; when there is an increase of *kapha*, the treatment should be both unctuous and dry.
For one whose body is wasted and emaciated, a digestive stimulant combined with unctuous substances should be administered.
A digestive stimulant (dīpana) that is bitter combined with sweet substances is for one with an excess of bile;
an unctuous substance (sneha) combined with sour and salty substances is recommended for one with an excess of wind.
One should know that unctuousness (sneha) alone is the supreme stimulator of a weak digestive fire;
even very heavy food is not capable of pacifying a fire kindled by unctuousness.
One who has excessive discharge of feces during the month of Malimluca, whose kapha is diminished, and whose digestive fire is weak,
should drink a dose of ghee combined with digestive-stimulating (dīpanīya) medicinal herbs.
The wind (anila), being clear, having entered its own path, and being balanced by that [therapeutic procedure], quickly produces strength due to its proximity to the fire (agni).
A person who voids feces with difficulty due to its hardness should drink ghee mixed with salts while maintaining a restricted diet.

When the digestive fire is weak due to dryness, one should drink ghee or oil along with digestive stimulants; when it is weak due to excessive intake of fats, one should take alkaline preparations, powders, *āsava*, or *ariṣṭa*.
In cases of udāvarta, however, nirūha and sneha enemas should be administered;
when the digestive fire is weak due to the excessive increase of the doṣas, one who has been thoroughly purified should follow the dietary regimen.

For one who has been freed from disease but whose digestive fire is weak, ghee alone is the stimulant. Due to exhaustion from travel or fasting, one should cause such a person to drink ghee with gruel (yavāgū).
That [milk] pressed out after eating food is strengthening, digestive, and nourishing; however,
for men who are emaciated, wasted, and thin due to long-term indulgence in [sexual activity], [it is beneficial].
One should feed those who eat meat with the sour juices of carnivorous animals;
for they quickly stimulate the digestive fire due to their light, hot, pungent, and purifying qualities.
Because they cause the flesh to become well-nourished and further increase strength,
[these preparations]— along with unctuous substances, fermented liquors, *surā*, *ariṣṭa*, powders, decoctions, and wholesome food— are beneficial. (AS.Ci.12.28)
When applied correctly, the strength of the body and the digestive fire increase,
just as an external fire, when kindled with seasoned wood, becomes both bright and steady.
In the same way, the fire residing in the digestive tract is kindled by food that contains fats;
the bodily fire is not ignited by fasting, nor by overeating.
Just as a small fire, when devoid of fuel and covered by wind-blown embers, [blazes up],
so too when the phlegm is diminished, the bile follows the wind in its own location.
Then that fire, together with the wind, increases the already augmented fire;
having quickly digested the food, it withdraws all the bodily constituents (dhātus) and the vital essence (ojas).

He may die, or if he survives, he will not be healthy; when the food is digested, he suffers exhaustion, and diseases arising from excessive digestive fire—such as thirst, cough, burning sensations, and fainting—occur. One should treat that excessive fire with heavy, unctuous, mild, thick, cold, and stable [substances].
One should bring about pacification with foods and drinks, just as one quenches a blazing fire with water; even when there is no indigestion, one should repeatedly offer him edible foods.
Just as one might find an opportunity when the fuel is exhausted so as not to extinguish it,
[one should avoid] *kṛsarā*, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), oily foods, flour-based preparations, and products made from molasses.
One should eat the flesh of aquatic and marshy animals that have been properly prepared,
and especially fish that are tender and those that dwell in still waters.
One should eat well-prepared mutton, which wards off excessive digestive fire;
or, if thirsty, one should drink milk with beeswax or ghee.
One should drink wheat flour mixed with milk and saturated with abundant ghee; or one may take fats devoid of oil, combined with the juices of marshy animals.
One should administer milk boiled with *śyāmā* and *trivṛt* as a purgative; furthermore,
one should repeatedly take meals with milk to eliminate pitta.
Whatever food is heavy, nourishing, and increases phlegm— all that is beneficial for one with excessive digestive fire; furthermore, sleeping during the day after eating such food is recommended.
The digestive fire digests food; deprived of food, it digests the *doṣas*.
When the *doṣas* are exhausted, it digests the *dhātus*; when the *dhātus* are depleted, it consumes life itself.
The strength of men has its root in the digestive fire (agni), for life itself is rooted in strength;
this is the essence of medical treatment: the preservation of the digestive fire.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
Chapter 13: We shall now explain the treatment of urinary obstruction (mūtrāghāta).
Thus indeed said the great seers, Ātreya and others:

"In cases of dysuria caused by vāta, one should anoint the body with vāta-alleviating oils from the navel downwards, and then foment the entire limb with bolus-sweat (piṇḍasveda), affusion, immersion baths, and pot-sweat (kumbhīsveda) using vāta-subduing substances."

One should administer for drinking oil or ghee prepared with a decoction and paste of the ten roots (*daśamūla*), *eraṇḍa* root, *punarnavā*, *śatāvarī*, *vṛścīva*, *pattūra*, *pāṣāṇabheda*, *kola*, *kulattha*, and barley, combined with the five salts and the fat of a dog or a camel.
One should prepare these same medicinal herbs for food and drink, as well as for boluses, poultices, and fomentations, combined with oil, fruit-essences, fats, and sours;
one should also drink clear wine enriched with *sauvarcala* salt.
In cases arising from Pitta, one should employ cold affusions, immersions, and external ointments.
One should drink the cooled decoction of *tṛṇapañcamūla*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *abhīru*, *vidārī*, and *kaśeruka*, mixed with honey and sugar;
likewise, one may drink the decoction of the root of *kāṇḍekṣuraka*.

The seeds of *kamala*, *utpala*, *vidārī*, and *śṛṅgāṭaka* with grape juice; or a paste of *trapusa*, *kusumbha*, *urvāru* seeds, *vṛṣaka*, and saffron—all these destroy all types of urinary obstruction (*mūtrāghāta*).
Alternatively, *madhuka*, *dārvī*, and *urvāru* seeds may be taken with rice-wash water.
In cases arising from Kapha, one should administer Darvī with honey and the juice of Āmalaka,

or the paste of Mṛdvīkā with water that has stood overnight; furthermore, appropriate sudation, emesis, pungent, sharp, hot, and alkaline foods and drinks, barley-based meals, and buttermilk should be prescribed.
One should drink *sūkṣmailā* with wine, or with the juice of *āmalaka* mixed with honey; or *kaiḍarya* fruit with the juice of plantain; or the seeds of *śitivāraka* with buttermilk;
or the powder of coral with rice-water.
Alternatively, one may take a cooled decoction of dhava, kuṭaja, karañja, amṛtā, kebuka, elā, āragvadha, and saptacchada mixed with honey; or a gruel prepared with that same decoction;
or the fresh juice of kaṇṭakārī mixed with honey.
Alternatively, one may take the three pungents (vyoṣa), cardamom (elā), the pith of *gokṣuraka*, and the bones of a crane, combined with honey and urine;
or *pāṭalī* alkali, repeatedly strained and mixed with oil;
or clear wine (*prasannā*) infused with the alkaline water of sesame, *pāṭalī*, *pāribhadra*, and *yavaśūka*, combined with the powders of cinnamon-bark (*tvac*), cardamom (*elā*), and *uṣaka*.
Alternatively, one should eat the individual alkaline extracts of sesame and other such substances with molasses as an accompaniment,
and use oil processed with sharp and hot substances for drinking and massage.
In cases of *sannipāta* (combined humors), one should treat the *vāta* and other doshas according to their respective locations, starting from the nearest one.
Furthermore, one may consume barley-alkali (yavakṣāra) either in a predominant dose or in equal proportions when all [the humors] are equally aggravated.
Having drunk the powders of cardamom (*elā*), *aśmabheda*, *śilājatu*, and long pepper (*pippalī*) stirred with rice-water,
or having used them similarly combined with jaggery for one month, even one who is near death or suffering from dysuria (*mūtrakṛcchra*) lives.
One should drink a decoction of ela, upakulyā, madhuka, aśmabheda, kauntī, śvadaṃṣṭrā, vṛṣaka, and pūga,
saturated with sugar, in cases of dysuria accompanied by burning, pain, and constipation.
One should drink a decoction primarily of *aśmajatu* (bitumen) made from *harītakī*, *gokṣura*, *rājavṛkṣa*, *pāṣāṇabhida*, and *dhanvayavāsaka*, in cases of gravel,
urinary calculi, and dysuria.

In cases of urinary calculi (aśmarī) that have not been present for long, as well as in disorders of the vāta-basti and similar conditions, one should perform this same treatment according to the specific dosha involved.

Having boiled *pāṣāṇabheda*, *vasuka*, *vasira*, *aśmantaka*, *śatāvarī*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, *kapotavaṅkā*, *abalā*, *atibalā*, *kacchūra*, *uśīra*, *gundrā*, *vṛkṣādanī*, *bhallūka*, *varaṇa*, *yava*, *kola*, *kulattha*, *śāka*, *phala*, *kata*, and *kvātha* with clarified butter, adding *ūṣakādi* as a paste (*pratīvāpa*), and drinking it, one quickly breaks up a calculus caused by *vāta*.
One should prepare decoctions, alkalis, and food and drinks using these very same substances.
A paste of *siṃhī*, *vyāghrī*, *gokṣuraka*, *ikṣuraka*, and *eranda* roots, drunk with non-sweet curd, breaks up urinary calculi immediately upon ingestion.
A soup prepared with the paste of *śigru* root, curd, and salt, along with *yamaka*, [is beneficial].

Ghee cooked in a decoction of the *vīratarādi* group, *guṇḍrā*, *utkaṭa*, *pattūra*, *vārāhī*, *pāṭhā*, *pāṭalī*, *śirīṣa*, *śāli* root, *vidārī*, and the two types of *punarnavā*, with the addition of *trapusa*, *kusumbha*, cucumber seeds, *karkaru* seeds, *madhuka*, and *śilājatu*, when drunk, quickly breaks up *pitta*-type urinary calculi (*pittāśmarī*).
As before, one should prepare [the medicated ghee] with decoctions and other ingredients.

Ghee prepared with a paste (kalka) of varaṇa, bhadradāru, guggulu, the two types of elā, kuṣṭha, marica, citraka, mustā, and surasāhvaya, with the addition of musk (ūṣaka) and other substances as a secondary additive (pratīvāpa), breaks up phlegmatic urinary calculi (śleṣmāśmarī).
Thus, as before (AS.Ci.13.14),
having repeatedly strained the ash of *pāṭalī* through whey (mastu), one should discard the ash (AS.Ci.13.15).
Then, having taken that curd and boiled it together with horse gram (*kulattha*),
one should lick the powder of *gokṣuraka* root, cardamom (*elā*), *trapusa*, *kuraṇṭaka* seeds, and *pāṣāṇabheda* with honey, and subsequently drink that decoction.

In this way, the stone is quickly broken and expelled (AS.Ci.13.16). Having burnt the medicines for urinary calculi with clarified butter while suspended over a subterranean fire (antardhūma), one should filter that alkali along with the alkali of the dung of domestic animals many times through cow’s urine; then, one should cook that clear liquid over a fire (AS.Ci.13.16).
When that [mixture] has become thick, one should add the powder of trikaṭu, uṣaka, and so forth, and remove it while it is still sticky enough to be smeared with a ladle (*darvīpralepa*).

This alkaline electuary (*kṣārāvaleha*), when consumed by one who subsists on milk, breaks up urinary calculi (*aśmarī*) and causes gravel (*śarkarā*) to be expelled. (AS.Ci.13.17) The alkali of sesame, plantain, barley, *apāmārga*, and *palāśa*, when drunk with goat’s urine, produces an effect equal to the former.
A preparation consisting of the alkaline ash of *pāṭalī* and *karavīra* combined with asafoetida and the alkaline ash of *krauñca* bone,

or alternatively, a powder of *krauñca*, camel, donkey, and dog bones, along with *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, the root of *kadamba*, *tālapatrikā*, *ajamoda*, and *nāgara*, administered with either the scum of wine (*surāmaṇḍa*) or warm water, [is used] with a decoction of *ketaka* leaves.
A lukewarm decoction of picuka, aṅkola, śāka, kataka, and indīvara fruits mixed with jaggery;
and the powder of nṛtyakuṇḍaka seeds combined with honey and sheep’s milk.
One suffering from the pain of urinary calculi (aśmarī) should drink either wine prepared with the root of *kapotavaṅkā*, or milk boiled with that same [root].
Alternatively, it is prepared with *abhayā* seeds, bones, or *punarnavā*.
In other cases of urinary obstruction (*mūtrāghāta*), one should likewise differentiate the treatment based on these very same principles.

One should drink water prepared with *drākṣā* and the five roots (*pañcamūla*), along with twice the amount of *trikaṇṭaka*, or milk alone, or mixed with clarified butter; this cures all types of urinary obstruction (*mūtrāghāta*). Alternatively, one may take a gruel (*yavāgū*) made from *gokṣuraka* and *kaṇṭakārī*, combined with treacle (*phāṇita*).
Or [one may take] that which has been prepared with the juice of *tāmracūḍa*, or with a decoction of the *vīratarādi* group.
Or else, that bitumen has been processed by him,
or the juice of the dung of either a horse or a donkey, or the juice of *durālabhā*.
Or one may take the decoction of *kakubha*,
or the paste of *mūrvā*, *abhayā*, *mustā*, *devadāru*, and *madhuka*, with either *vāruṇī* wine, milk, or warm water, as desired.
One should drink either the paste of the three myrobalans (triphalā) with rock salt and warm water,

or the seeds of the bibhītaka alone; or one may drink wine accompanied by the meat of birds as a side dish, or the scum of fermented liquor (nigada-madirā-maṇḍa), or various kinds of mārdvīka and āsava spirits.
One who has drunk wine should travel by means of a chariot or on a horse with a swift gait;
in this way, the *aśmarī* (urinary calculus) and *śarkarā* (gravel) are expelled.
In all cases of urinary obstruction (*mūtrāghāta*), and especially in those caused by *aśmarī* and *śarkarā*, the *vīratarādi* group of drugs should be employed in every respect.
Tilvaka-ghṛta should be used for purgation,
and enema therapy (bastikarma) should be administered frequently, especially the urethral/vaginal enema (uttarabasti).
In that regard, a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) prepared with cow’s urine and consisting of half-and-half portions of the Śyāmādi group [of drugs] is prescribed.

An oil prepared with the roots of the *bilva* group and fermented liquors such as *surā* and *sauvīraka*, or with milk boiled with the five grasses (*tṛṇapañcamūla*), *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, and a paste of *trapusa*, *vāruka*, *śatāhvā*, *bīja*,
*karṣabhaka*, *yavānī*, and *pītadāru*, is used for an oily enema (*anuvāsana*).

In a decoction of *śatāvarī*, *gokṣuraka*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, *punarnavā*, *uśīra*, *madhuka*, the two types of *sārivā*, *śreyasī*, *lodhra*, and the five roots of grass (*tṛṇapañcamūla*), with four parts milk added, one should prepare an oil containing a paste of *balā*, *vṛkṣaka*, *kharāhvā*, *upakuñcikā*, *vatsaka*, the seeds of *trapusa* and *urvāru*, *śitivāraka*, *madhuka*, *ṣaḍgranthā*, *śatāhvā*, *aśmabheda*, *madana*, and *hapuṣā*; this oil is used as an uttarabasti (urethral/vaginal enema).

Furthermore, for one with a purified urinary tract who has been satiated with aphrodisiac meats and chicken meat in order to cleanse the seminal receptacle of *śukrāśmarī* (seminal calculi), a man should, according to the proper time, enjoy women who are agreeable, excellent, and beloved. If there is no relief from these proven treatments, then the physician [should proceed further].
Having thus taken leave of the king, one should properly apply the surgical instrument;
for in the absence of action death is certain, while in the presence of action there is uncertainty.
Even for a physician who is certain [in his diagnosis] and has many times achieved success in his practice.

AS.Ci.13.27 Then, having prepared the patient—who has been lubricated, whose humors have been eliminated, who is slightly emaciated, whose body has been anointed and fomented, and who has not yet eaten—and having performed the auspicious rites and recitation of blessings, and having arranged the necessary materials, the physician should encourage him. Then, once he is strong and composed, the patient should be seated facing east on a plank level with his knees; another man should sit upon his lap with his upper body well-settled, supine, and resting on a cloth or pad, while his knees and elbows are contracted and bound together with cords or a strip of cloth by that other man. Then, after massaging the unanointed region of the navel on the patient's left side, the physician should press it firmly with his fist.

When the stone has descended below the navel, the patient should be anointed with oil and his nails clipped. Then, having inserted the middle finger of the left hand into the anus and having reached the perineal raphe (*anusevanī*), one should, by means of effort and strength, bring the stone between the penis and the anus. Having positioned the bladder so that it is free of folds, not distended, and even, one should press firmly with both fingers until the foreign body (*śalya*) becomes prominent like a tumor. Then, on the left side of the raphe, leaving a space for the raphe itself the size of a barley grain, one should apply the surgical instrument to the extent of the stone.
Some say it should be placed to the south for the sake of convenience in performance;
one should exert effort so that it does not split or crumble,
for even a small amount of that powder, if kept stable, increases further.
Therefore, one should insert [the enema nozzle] with its tip directed straight ahead;
however, for women, the bladder is situated laterally and close to the uterus (garbhāśaya).
Therefore, one should cause the instrument to fall below [the bladder] like a lap;
otherwise, a wound that causes urinary leakage will occur in these women, and in the case of a man, due to the injury of the urethral meatus,
the bladder may be cured even when perforated on one side for the sake of removing a stone.
Due to the practice of medical procedures, the cutting and other interventions prescribed by the scriptures, and the increased mobility of the foreign body (śalya),

the bladder— even if split in two and the size of a stone— will not burst; however, once the foreign body has been extracted, one should have the patient immerse themselves in a large tub of warm water and apply fomentation (sveda).
Likewise, the bladder is not filled with blood;
however, when it is full, one should administer a decoction of milk-tree (kṣīrivṛkṣa) through the flower-tube (puṣpanetra).
For it thus expels the gravel powder and blood located in the bladder;
furthermore, for the sake of purifying the urine, one should have him consume his fill of jaggery (guḍa).

Having raised him up, and having smeared the wound with honey and ghee, one should have him drink warm gruel prepared with urine-purifying substances and mixed with ghee, twice daily for three nights.
After three nights, one should feed [the patient] a small amount of soft rice with milk thickened with jaggery until ten nights have passed;
after that, [he should be fed] with sour fruits and the meat-broths of wild animals.
Having washed the ulcer with a decoction of milky trees, one should apply an ointment made from the paste of *lodhra*, *madhuka*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, and *prapauṇḍarīka*.
One should carefully foment it for twelve nights.
Furthermore, oil cooked with these same ingredients combined with *haridrā* and others should be used as an ointment for the ulcer.
If, after seven nights, the urine does not return to its own path, one should cauterize the wound with fire as previously described.

Once it has returned to its own path, one should treat it with urethral enemas (uttarabasti), non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana), and unctuous enemas (anuvāsana) consisting primarily of sweet substances.
If a seminal stone (śukrāśmarī) or gravel (śarkarā) has entered the urinary tract by chance and become lodged within, one should remove it through the channel.
Alternatively, having opened a sinus with a hook, one should extract it;
and once the wound has healed, for one year he should not climb upon women, mountains, elephants, chariots, or trees.

One should not swim in water nor eat heavy foods (AS.Ci.13.32). Furthermore, during this procedure, eight structures must be avoided: the urinary duct, the seminal duct, the scrotal channels, the urethra, the perineal raphe, the vagina, the anus, and the bladder (AS.Ci.13.32).

In that regard, from the severing of the urine-carrying channels, death occurs due to the bladder being filled with urine; from the severing of the semen-carrying channels, death or impotence results;
and from the injury to the ducts of the scrotum, loss of virility (dhvajabhaṅga) occurs.
From the cutting of the urethra, there is urinary leakage;

from the cutting of the perineal raphe or the vagina, the manifestation of pain occurs; and for one whose anus or bladder has been pierced, instantaneous death is said to have been mentioned previously.
And there is a verse on this point:
"Without knowing these vital points (marmas) of embodied beings, which are born from the channels..."
"One who holds a weapon in hand surely kills through sheer recklessness, even if alone.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of *prameha* (urinary disorders).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.

For generally, because the body of a person suffering from prameha is excessively moistened and the digestive fire is impaired, even the five types of food, such as edibles and the rest, when consumed, are transformed into urine and fat. Therefore, for the increase of the fire element (*tejodhātu*) and for the pacification of the moisture and fat, one should administer strong purification therapies (*saṃśodhana*) to this patient.

For one who is weak, however, there are pacifying foods and drinks that bind the urine, do not increase fat, do not cause corpulence, kindle the digestive fire, and generate strength; for strength, when accumulated according to the prescribed method, leads to the destruction of all diseases without exception.

AS.Ci.14.3 Now, having first oleated a patient with prameha who is fit for purification (*saṃśodhana*) with oil derived from *bibhītaka*, *sarṣapa*, *iṅgudī*, *karañja*, *nimba*, or *nikumbha*, or with a fat (*sneha*) processed according to its specific requirements using the *trikaṇṭaka* group of drugs, or with clarified butter (*havis*) boiled with the *priyaṅvādi* group, one should cause him to vomit and purge by means of the formulations prescribed in the [relevant] chapters (*kalpa*).

AS.Ci.14.4 Thereafter, once his strength has been restored, one should administer an enema (*āsthāpana*) using a decoction of the *surasādi* group mixed with a paste (*prativāpa*) of *mustā*, *amaradāru*, and *nāgara*.
But when pitta is predominant, one should first treat with a decoction of the nyagrodhādi group and then gradually nourish the patient with the juices of wild animals.

For in a patient suffering from *prameha*, excessive depletion specifically gives rise to dysuria, pain in the bladder and penis, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), extreme emaciation, vertigo, and other such conditions; therefore, one should administer pacifying treatments for those who require pacification, while guarding against further complications (AS.Ci.14.5). In the morning, in all types of *prameha*, one should drink turmeric mixed with honey along with the juice of *āmalaka*.
Alternatively, one should lick the flowers of *sāla*, *saptaparṇa*, *kuṭaja*, *kapittha*, *kampillaka*, *bibhītaka*, and *rohitaka*, or their powder mixed with honey;
or else, the powder of *harītakī*.
Or one should drink a decoction of triphalā, mustā, devadāru, and haridrā;
or likewise, a decoction of asana, citraka, triphalā, dārvī, and kaliṅgaka mixed with honey;
or similarly, the fresh juice of guḍūcī or of āmalaka.
Specifically, however, in cases of kapha-type urinary disorders (kaphameha), one should administer a decoction of kaṭphala, mustā, lodhra, and abhayā mixed with honey;
or alternatively, a decoction of tagara, viḍaṅga, and the two types of haridrā.

In cases of urinary disorders caused by pitta (pittaprameha), one may use sandalwood, agallochum, costus, and deodar; or pāṭhā, agnimantha, cavya, and the three myrobalans; or lodhra, sevya, arjuna, and sandalwood.
Or [a paste] of nimba, amṛtā, āmalaka, and paṭolī; or of śirīṣa, sarja, arjuna, and kesarā; or of phalinī, kamala, utpala, and kiṃśuka.

Or one may use *kuṭaja*, *utpala*, and *kaṭaṅkaṭerī*; furthermore, specifically for those beginning with *udakameha*, one should drink in sequence a decoction of *pārijāta*, *vaijayantī*, *saptacchada*, *ariṣṭa*, *niśā*, *kakubha*, *candana*, *citraka*, *pāṭhā*, *joṅgaka*, *khadira*, *triphalā*, and *āragvadha*, mixed with honey.
Having drunk sand, Meha, asafoetida, coral, Kaila, and salt with wine, urine, or alkaline water;

and for the various types of urinary disorders beginning with *kṣārameha*, one should take Triphalā, or [the bark of] Asana and others, Nyagrodha and others, Śamyāka, Chandana, and Mañjiṣṭhā, as well as Guḍūcī, Tinduka seeds, Kāśmarya, and dates, mixed with honey; and for *śoṇitameha*, a paste of Madayantī leaves with honey and cold water.
In cases of vāta-type disorders as well, for the purpose of palliation, one should drink a decoction when kapha and pitta are predominant;
therein, in the case of vasāmeha, [the decoction] of agnimantha is used.
In *majjameha* (semen-like urine), [one should use] a decoction of *amṛta* and *citraka*;
in *kuṣṭhamēha*, a paste mixed with *kuṣṭha*, *kuṭaja*, *pāṭhā*, and *kaṭurohiṇī*; in *hastamēha*, the alkali from the bones of elephants, pigs, donkeys, and camels;
and in *madhumēha*, a decoction of *kadara*, *khadira*, and *pūtika*.
In cases of vasā-meha and others associated with kapha, one should employ oils prepared with their respective decoctions;
in those associated with pitta, one should employ ghee or a combination of both (yamaka).
By this, it should be understood that the same options regarding unctuous substances (*sneha*) are stated for the remaining types of urinary disorders (*meha*).
Likewise, the pacification of phlegm (*kapha*), bile (*pitta*), urine, fat (*medas*), and wind (*anila*) occurs through unctuous substances combined with decoctions (*kaṣāya*).

An oil cooked with trikaṇṭaka, ativiṣā, bhallātaka, lodhra, vacā, picumanda, ghana, niśā, jamodā, arjuna, aśmantaka, paṭola, somavalka, mañjiṣṭhā, padmaka, candana, and agaru destroys all types of meha (urinary disorders).

AS.Ci.14.13 One should boil ten *pala*s each of the roots of *daśamūla*, *harītakī*, *devadāru*, the two types of *karañja*, *dvivarṣābhū*, *dantī*, *bhūkadamba*, *bhallātaka*, *śaṭhī*, *puṣkaramūla*, *arkamūla*, *snuhīmūla*, *varaṇamūla*, and *pippalīmūla*, along with three *prastha*s each of *yava*, *kola*, and *kulattha*, in eight times the amount of water; one should then remove the decoction when reduced to one-fourth.

With that decoction, one should cook one *prastha* of ghee, adding as an after-throw (*pratīvāpa*) *vacā*, *viḍaṅga*, *kampillaka*, *bhallātaka*, *bhārṅgī*, *rohiṣa*, *cavikā*, the two types of *pippalī*, *trivṛt*, *nicula*, and *viśvabheṣaja*.

This *anvantara* ghee indeed cures all types of urinary disorders (*meha*), pustules, skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), poisons, swellings, hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), abscesses, splenic enlargement, abdominal dropsy, dyspnea, cough, intestinal obstruction (*vardhma*), anemia (*pāṇḍu-roga*), gout (*vāta-śoṇita*), insanity (*unmāda*), and epilepsy (*apasmāra*). For diet, one should consume preparations primarily of barley, combined with honey and *āmalaka*.

Having soaked barley many times with decoctions of various medicines that cure prameha, one should prepare various light foods such as flour-meals, parched grain cakes, stuffed cakes, parched grains, and *vāṭya*,
and likewise prepare wheat or barley that has been stored in the stomachs of cows, horses, or donkeys, or bamboo-barley.
One should consume barley, which binds the urine and removes fat, bile, and phlegm, as well as promotes stability;

likewise, one should utilize *śāli* rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, grass-grains, and pulses such as mung beans; bitter vegetables; meats from wild animals that are roasted on spits, dried, smeared with fat, or fried; along with roasted chickpeas as side dishes and various fermented liquors as after-drinks.

AS.Ci.14.15: Having boiled one *karṣa* each of *lodhra*, *mūrvā*, *śaṭhī*, *viḍaṅga*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *puṣkaramūla*, the four spices (*cāturjātaka*), *kramuka*, *cavikā*, *yavānī*, *śyāmā*, *bhārṅgī*, the two types of *viśālā*, *bhūnimba*, *tagara*, *citraka*, *pippalīmūla*, *kaṭurohiṇī*, *kuṣṭha*, *pāṭhā*, *indrayava*, *ativiṣā*, *plavana*, *nakha*, and black pepper in a jar of water, and when the decoction has been reduced to a quarter and strained, one should place it in a vessel containing aged ghee that has been heated with lac; after adding honey equal to half the quantity of the liquid and letting it sit for a fortnight, this *lodhrāsava* destroys all types of urinary disorders (*prameha*), skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), leucoderma (*kilāsa*), obesity, anorexia, worms, anemia, edema, hemorrhoids, and disorders of the digestive tract (*grahaṇī-doṣa*).

Take twenty-five palas each of daśamūla, dantī, trivṛt, śyāmā, śreyasī, citraka, punarnavā, sudhā, dhava, ekaṣikā, gaṇḍīra, and guḍūcī, along with one āḍhaka of triphalā; boil these with ten droṇas of water until reduced to one-fourth, and then remove the decoction.

In that [jar], once it has been purified and cooled, and placed in a clean vessel, one should add two *tulās* of old jaggery, one *āḍhaka* of cow’s urine, half an *āḍhaka* of iron filings, one *prastha* of *māgadhikā* (long pepper), and twelve *palas* each of *kuṭaja*, *arjuna*, *kuṣṭha*, *kṛmighna*, *vacā*, and *citraka* as an additive (*pratīvāpa*), and let it sit for a month.
This *daśamūlāriṣṭa* is similar to the previous one.
One should boil twenty *palas* each of the drugs beginning with *asanā* separately in eight jars (*ghaṭa*) of water.

One should take *parisruta* [fermented liquor] that has stood for four months, well-cooled, and mix it with two hundred *palas* of jaggery (*guḍa*), half an *āḍhaka* of honey, and one *pala* each of the finely ground powder of the *vatsakādi* group; having combined these, one should pour it into a ghee-pitcher lined internally with honey and *pippalī* powder, seal it with lac, and place it in a heap of barley for three or four months. This prepared *lohāriṣṭa*, when opened, possesses qualities superior to the former.
One who has ceased drinking liquor should drink *śīdhu*, *madhu*, and *mādhava* liquors along with *nigada*; furthermore,

he should consume syrups (*pānaka*) and *rāga-ṣāḍava* preparations mixed with the heartwood (*sāra*) of trees, water from *darbha* grass, and *madhuka*, *pittha*, *tinduka*, and black pepper, as well as mustard-based drinks and similar after-drinks (*anupāna*).

One should give him food mixed with the powder of the dung of camels, mules, and donkeys. Having powdered equal parts of *mustā*, *amṛtā*, *gaṇḍīra*, the two types of *haridrā*, the two types of *sārivā*, *āḍhakī*, *varṣābhū*, *trikaṇṭaka*, *vyoṣa*, *phalgu*, sprouts of *rohiṣa*, *śyāmā*, *suradāru*, *kāla*, *viḍaṅga*, *pāṭhā*, *kampillaka*, *bhārṅgī*, *nidigdhikā*, *dantī*, *citraka*, *kaṭukā*, and the roots of *eraṇḍa*, and having added twice as much fine powder of [the aforementioned] powder, one should lick it with honey followed by wine as a vehicle, or drink it with lukewarm water or a decoction of *triphalā*.

By this, urinary disorders, splenic enlargement, halīmaka, anemia, edema, hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, and abdominal enlargements are quickly pacified; one should also practice the formulations for excessive obesity and other diseases mentioned in the chapter on the two types of therapeutic procedures (dvividhopakramaṇīya).
Furthermore, those with increased fat should engage in strenuous exercise, dry massage (udvartana), bathing, and anointing with unctuous medicinal herbs.
But one who is without wealth, devoid of umbrella and footwear, and living according to the conduct of a sage, may travel a hundred yojanas or more;
or, subsisting on a diet of *śyāmāka*, *nīvāra*, *amatinduka*, *kapittha*, and *aśmantaka* fruits and roots, he may dwell together with wild animals.
Or, together with cows, he should wander about subsisting on their urine and dung;
or he should dig ponds;
or, if emaciated, he should nourish himself with non-conflicting foods.
One should treat undripped swellings such as *śarāvikā* and others like a swelling (*śopha*),
and once they have suppurated, like an ulcer (*vraṇa*).

However, during the premonitory stages (pūrvarūpa) of these [diseases], physicians prescribe the decoction of forest trees (vanaspati-kaṣāya) and goat's urine for drinking; furthermore, strong purification therapies are indicated,
for those suffering from prameha become difficult to purge due to their bodies being pervaded by fat (medas).
One should prepare oil from the elādi group for the purpose of healing wounds;
a decoction from the āragvadhādi group for rubbing the body (udvartana);
and [a decoction] from the asanādi group for sprinkling (pariṣecana).

For calves and others, [one should administer] powders of *pāṭhā*, *citraka*, *śārṅgeṣṭā*, *kṣudravṛhatī*, *sārivā*, *somavalka*, *saptaparṇa*, *āragvadha*, and the root of *kuṭaja* with honey to be licked, or fresh iron [powder], during their drinks and food (AS.Ci.14.22).

Having taken a quarter-remnant decoction of the group of drugs beginning with *āsana*, and having strained it, one should again add a powder of *priyaṅgu*, *āmalaka*, *lodhra*, *dantī*, *kṛṣṇā*, iron, and copper until it becomes thick enough to coat a ladle; this should be licked according to one's strength. Furthermore, a *tulā* of *śilājatu* processed with decoctions of drugs that cure specific types of *prameha*, when used, removes all types of *prameha* along with their associated pustules. Regarding this, there is also a verse: AS.Ci.14.23. bhavati cātra (And there is also a verse here) [The verse follows: "By the power of its taste, post-digestive effect, potency, and medicinal properties, *śilājatu* is like nectar; it conquers all diseases, especially those arising from deranged *pitta*. [The commentary continues: It is said that *śilājatu* is of six types, corresponding to the six metals: gold, silver, copper, iron, lead, and tin. Among these, the one derived from iron is the best for curing *prameha*. It is black, heavy, and has the smell of cow’s urine; it is beneficial for the eyes and the digestive fire (*agni*). One should use it after purifying it with the prescribed methods. The dosage is one *māṣaka* to be increased gradually up to one *karṣa*, to be taken with honey and ghee, or with the appropriate decoction of *prameha*-curing drugs. It should be consumed daily until the disease is cured, and then discontinued. This treatment is effective even for chronic cases. Thus ends the chapter on the treatment of *prameha*. (Note: The final portion of the provided text contains the concluding statement and the first line of the verse, which have been translated accordingly.)
Māgadhī, madhuka, ledhra, kuṣṭha, elā, hareṇu, samaṅgā, dhātakī flowers, sārivā, and the two types of rajanī.
Priyaṅgu, resin of the Sarja tree, Padmaka, the filaments of the lotus,
leaves of the Mātuluṅga, beeswax, and rock salt.
Oil prepared with these [drugs], when used for massage, purifies and heals malignant ulcers,
carbuncles, scrofulous swellings, cervical adenitis, and fistula-in-ano.
The physician should quickly treat the abscesses, for they destroy the life-breaths of the patient suffering from prameha;
he should likewise treat all remaining complications according to their strength.
Because it arises from all [the doshas], because it involves major vital spots (marmas),
because it is accompanied by complications, and because it possesses many secondary afflictions, prameha is a terrible disease.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter.
Hereafter, we shall explain the treatment of abscesses (vidradhi) and swellings (vṛddhi).
"Thus indeed said the great sages, such as Ātreya and others:
one should treat every kind of abscess while it is still in the raw (āmā) stage according to the procedure for swelling (śopha), in accordance with the specific doṣa involved."
One should repeatedly remove the blood;
once it is ready to suppurate, one should apply a poultice, and once it has suppurated, one should incise it and treat it like an ulcer.
In the case of an internal abscess (ābhyantara-vidradhi), one should drink a decoction of *varuṇa* and other drugs with an addition (*pratīvāpa*) of *mūṣaka* and others;
and from these same two groups, as well as with purgative substances, one should prepare clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) for drinking.

One should employ *madhuśigru* and *śilāhvaya* according to the prescribed methods of preparation for use as non-unctuous enemas (*āsthāpana*), unctuous enemas (*anuvāsana*), and for drinking, eating, and external applications.
Or one should administer guggulu according to the specific dosha, treating it in every respect like a gulma;
[one may also use] triphalā, picumanda, madhuka, kaṭukā, paṭola, and śāṇa, each in equal parts.

Having prepared a decoction by boiling one *karṣa* each of *trivṛt* and *trāyamāṇā*, along with one *pala* of *masūra*, together in eight times the amount of water, one should drink the strained liquid mixed with clarified butter (*ghṛta*).

By this, abscesses (*vidradhi*), abdominal tumors (*gulma*), fever, burning sensations, colic, thirst, heart disease, vertigo, restlessness, fainting, internal hemorrhaging (*raktapitta*), jaundice, skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), and erysipelas (*visarpa*) are pacified.

AS.Ci.15.5: One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with one *pala* each of *trāyamāṇā*, *mustaka*, *kaṭukā*, *tāmalakī*, *trāyamāṇā*, *candana*, *durālabhā*, *jīvantī*, *vīra*, and *utpala*, combined with two *prasthas* of milk and *āmalaka* juice; this is equivalent to the previous [recipe].

One should cook ghee in a decoction of *drākṣā*, *madhūka*, *kharjūra*, *abhīru*, *vidārī*, *parūṣaka*, and *triphalā*, together with milk, sugarcane juice, and *dhātrī* juice, with *abhayā* as the internal ingredient (*garbha*).
That [milk] should be cooled and mixed with honey, sugar, and so forth; it is the same as the previous [prescription],
and one should perform bloodletting with horns and other instruments according to what is most accessible.
One should pierce a vein in the middle of the arm, or apply a poultice to a suppurating abscess located in the trunk that has risen upward externally.

When the pain has become localized in that very spot and numbness is induced by pressing on its sides, one should recognize that it is ripe by the signs specified in the procedure for surgical intervention; having incised it, one should treat it like an ulcer.
If the pus has ripened internally and has begun to flow either upwards or downwards, one should wait for ten days at most, protecting the patient from complications.

If the *kleda* (morbid moisture) flows improperly, one should drink either sour wine (*surā*), fermented liquor (*āsava*), *maireya*, or warm water, along with *varaṇādi* or *madhuśigru*, in order to expel it;
or one should consume gruel (*yavāgū*) prepared with their roots, together with a soup of barley, jujube, and horse-gram (*kulattha*).
After ten days have passed, one should purify the patient with *tilvaka* ghee or *trāyamāṇā* ghee according to their strength (AS.Ci.15.10).
Once purified, they should consume a very small amount of bitter medicine combined with ghee and honey (AS.Ci.15.10).
One must strive so that it does not reach suppuration, because of its tendency to burst quickly; hence it is called *vidradhi*.
However, once it has suppurated, success depends on fate (*daiva*), and *vidradhi* is more rapidly cured than any other disease.
When prameha is present, one should observe the treatment for prameha;
one should also treat a breast abscess according to the procedure for ulcers.
When it is ripening, one should cause it to ripen with a diet of desired foods,
but one should not apply a poultice;
for if the breast is poulticed, because of its soft flesh, it would ripen too quickly, undergo putrefaction, and burst open.
When the abscess on the breast has ripened, one should treat it with a surgical instrument while avoiding the milk-carrying vessels and the dark circle (kṛṣṇamaṇḍala) including the nipple;

furthermore, in all stages—whether unripened, ripening, or fully ripened—one should have the breast milked out. Regarding abscesses of the teeth and other such locations, their specific characteristics and treatments will be described accordingly.
Thus ends the treatment of abscesses (vidradhi), AS.Ci.15.12.

However, in the case of a Vata-born enlargement (vṛddhi), one should first lubricate the patient with *trivṛt* and then apply sudation; thereafter, one should purge the patient using any one of the following oils: *miśraka*, *sukumāraka*, *tilvaka*, *eraṇḍa*, or the oil from *kośāmra* fruit, AS.Ci.15.12.

Then, one should administer a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) using decoctions and pastes that subdue Vāta; once the patient has been treated with the enema and fed with meat broth, one should perform an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) with Yaṣṭīmadhuka oil.
One should also employ fomentation (sveda), medicinal plasters (pralepa), and poultices (upanāha).
Once it has suppurated, one should incise it and treat it like an ulcer (vraṇa).
An increase of bile is treated like a swelling caused by bile,
and when it has suppurated, it is treated like a wound caused by bile.
In the case of an increase of *kapha*, one should also drink a decoction of *pītadāru* with urine, as in the treatment for *kapha*-type swelling.
One should treat everything like a kapha-granthi (kapha-nodule), with the exception of the *vimlāpana* procedure; once it has suppurated and been incised, it should be treated like a kapha-wound;
and that born of blood should be treated like an increase of pitta.

In this condition, one should repeatedly extract blood. For an increase of fat (medovṛddhi), one should apply fomentation using cow-dung, husks, fermenting agent (kiṇva), fermented gruel (surā), sour gruel (sukta), and similar substances mixed with urine— all of which are hot and dry— and then apply a warm, slightly elevated plaster made of the same materials.

Likewise, having fomented [the area] with head-purgative substances and avoiding the *phalasevanī* vessel, one should incise it with a *vṛddhipatra* blade, remove the fat, rub it with *kāsīsa*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and honey, and then suture it. Thereafter, one should prepare an oil for massage using *sumana* flowers, *granthi*, realgar (*manaḥśilā*), cardamom (*elā*), and *bhallātaka*.
One should apply oleation and fomentation for the purpose of healing a wound;
in the case of a scrotal enlargement (mūtravṛddhi), one should foment it with unctuous substances and then wrap it with a cloth bandage.
Then, below that, having incised along the suture like a belly-wound with a *vrīhimukha* instrument, one should drain it through a tube;
thereafter, one should apply a *sthagikā* bandage and perform the cleansing and healing of the wound.
One should treat intestinal hernia (*āntravṛddhi*) that has not yet reached the scrotum in the same manner as flatulent enlargement (*vātavṛddhi*).

One should boil one hundred *pala* of *punarnavā* and ten *pala* each of the roots of the ten-roots group (*daśamūla*), *payasyā*, *aśvagandhā*, *śatāvarī*, and *eraṇḍa* in water until eight parts remain.

When that decoction has been strained and cooled, one should add thirty palas of jaggery, one prastha of castor oil, two prasthas of ghee, two prasthas of milk, and the paste (kalka) consisting of two palas each of raisins, ginger, long pepper, long pepper root, yavānī, alkali of barley, citraka, licorice, and rock salt; having combined these together, one should cook them over a fire.

This preparation, known as *sukumāra*, is free from all restrictive constraints and afflictions; it is for delicate persons, lords, women, those with diminished semen, the childless, those with weak digestion, and those with irregular digestion. When used at will with food and drink, it destroys misfortune (*alakṣmī*), bestows luster, provides strength, promotes nourishment, stabilizes youth, and is a supreme medicine for goiter, abscesses, splenic disorders, abdominal tumors, upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*), edema, abdominal enlargements, hemorrhoids, diseases of the penis and vagina, and major Vata disorders.
To prepare it: one should boil one *tulā* of the root of *gandharvahasta*, one *āḍhaka* of barley, and half a *kuḍava* of *nāgara* (ginger) in one *droṇa* of water until one-fourth remains.
One should prepare one *prastha* of castor oil with twice as much milk, adding a paste ground from the following: one *kuḍava* of the root of *gandharvahasta* and one *pala* of *śuṇṭhī*.
This *gandharvahastataila* is equal in efficacy to the previous formulation.
And on this point there is a verse:
"If the swelling does not subside through oleation, unctuous enemas, and non-unctuous enemas, one should proceed [with surgery].

Having first performed enema therapy (bastikarma), one should then cauterize with fire the ligament located in the groin, which is yellowish and thin as a thread, using a crescent-shaped instrument to prevent the obstruction of the wind (māruta). This is situated above the thumb.
Having lifted [the skin] with a needle, one should cauterize it transversely where the disease is located after incising it;
others, however, say that one should cauterize on the other side of the [incision], or else at the ring finger.
This procedure is prescribed for gulma caused by vāta and kapha, as well as for splenic enlargement (plīhan) caused by the same factors.
"Since disease arises from the *viśva* [vitality] located in the little finger and the ring finger"—
thus ends the fifteenth chapter.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of gulma;
thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
For a gulma does not arise without vāta;
therefore, in all these cases, oleation and sudation— which alleviate vāta— should be administered first.
One should administer mild purgatives combined with oleation, as well as enemas of that same kind repeatedly, and meat soups that are sour, salty, and sweet, applying them judiciously;
for when the *vāta* has been conquered, even another *doṣa* in cases of *gulma* can be controlled with little effort.

Alternatively, if *vāta* is predominant, one should have the patient drink any oil prescribed for *anila*-related diseases, provided the patient is dry, suffers from obstructed flatus and feces, and experiences intense pain.

Alternatively, ghee cooked with milk and containing a paste (*kalka*) of *viḍaṅga*, the five *kola* spices (*pañcakola*), black pepper, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and coriander; or [ghee] prepared with the same paste combined with a decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūla*).

Or, for the treatment of consumption (rājayakṣman), one may use a six-pala preparation of asafoetida (hiṅgu), dhānyaka, amlavetasa, sauvarcala salt, cardamom (elā), biḍa salt, śaṭhī, pomegranate (dāḍima), yavakṣāra, trikaṭu, ajagandhā, ajamoda, cumin (ajājī), puṣkaramūla, vacā, citraka, and surasa, combined with curd. Alternatively, ghee prepared with hapuṣā, black pepper (marica), bāṣpikā, rock salt (saindhava), dīpyaka, cumin, and the five pungent spices (pañcakolaka), along with the juices of jujube (kola), radish (mūlaka), and pomegranate, as well as curd and milk, is effective when properly prepared in cases of colic (śūla), constipation (vibandha), hiccups (hidhmā), flatulence (ādhmāna), splenic disorders (plīha), heart disease (hṛdroga), malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), dyspepsia (hatanāma), worms (kṛmi), hemorrhoids (vardhma), anemia (pāṇḍu), consumption (kṣaya), asthma (śvāsa), cough (kāsa), gynecological diseases (yoniroga), abdominal enlargement (udara), fever (jvara), and anorexia (arocaka).
One pala of ginger, one pala of long pepper, one and a half palas of fried grain, two kuḍavas of pomegranate, and twenty palas of ghee should be cooked together with milk;
this ghee is identical to the previous one.
One should boil one *tulā* (ten *khārīs*) of garlic from which the skins have been removed, along with one *paṇa* each of the five great roots (*mahāpañcamūla*), in eight times that amount of water.

With that decoction, and with half as much of each of the following separately—wine (*surā*), curd-whey (*dadhimastu*), fermented rice-water (*dhānyāmla*), and pomegranate juice—one should cook one *prastha* of ghee with half a *palā* each of *yavānī*, *dīpyaka*, *amlavetasa*, asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), *cavikā*, rock salt (*saindhava*), the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and *amaradāru*. When boiled, this ghee, when drunk, has effects identical to the previous preparation.

One should boil two palas each of *varṣābhū* (two types), *daśamūla*, *aśvagandhā*, *suṣavī*, *chinnaruhā*, *bhārṅgī*, *rāsnā*, *eraṇḍa*, *balā*, *kālaśaṭhī*, *puṣkaramūla*, and *gandhapalāśa*, along with one *prastha* each of *yava*, *māṣa*, *kola*, and *kulattha*, in one *droṇa* of water until reduced to one-quarter.
AS.Ci.16.6
