One should prepare one *prastha* of ghee by cooking it separately with equal quantities of the juices of *mātuluṅga*, *dāḍima*, and *āmrātaka*, along with fermented rice-gruel (*śukta*), *tuṣodaka*, and *āranāla*, together with one *āḍhaka* of curd; this should be combined with *vacā*, *kāravī*, *śatāhvā*, the two types of alkali (*dvikṣāra*), the three salts (*trilavaṇa*), the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), *rāsnā*, *kumbha*, *nikumbha*, *yavānī*, *yavānaka*, *hiṃsrā*, *amlavetasa*, *nīlinī*, the fruit of *viḍaṅga*, *dāḍima*, *hiṅgu*, *pāṣāṇabheda*, *uṣaka*, *vṛṣaka*, *hapuṣā*, *bhārṅgī*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, the seeds of *trapusa* and *ervāru*, *jīraka*, *sārivā*, *upakuñcikā*, *granthika*, *kustumbarī*, *tumburu*, the fruit and root of *mūrvā*, *citraka*, *surasā*, and *gajapippalī*.
This ghee, known as *dādhika*, is similar to the previous one;
it removes urinary obstruction, insanity, epilepsy, and diseases caused by *vāta*.
Alternatively, one should drink ghee prepared with *vyoṣa*, *ṣaḍgranthā*, *kṛmighna*, *kaṭukā*, *citraka*, *sauvarcala*, *abhayā*, and *yavakṣāra* in ten parts, combined with milk.
For one who is unfit for milk, one should provide any one of the following: wine, liquor, grape juice, honey, curd, ghee, or pomegranate juice;
and one should always foment this patient after first applying an oil massage.

For oleation and sudation, when properly administered, produce softness in the channels, conquer the wind (vāyu), and having broken up the obstruction, quickly draw out the gulma. In that regard, they especially desire the drinking of oleaginous substances for a gulma arising in the heart.

In cases where both types of enema (basti) are indicated for those with obstructed flatus and feces localized in the umbilical region and sides, and who have a stimulated digestive fire, one should repeatedly administer unctuous, warm, and nourishing food and drink, as well as oil-drinking, non-unctuous enemas (nirūha), and unctuous enemas (anuvāsana), while taking care not to aggravate kapha and pitta;
otherwise, the increased kapha may cause drowsiness, heaviness, anorexia, nausea, and impairment of the digestive fire.

One should administer that [purgative] in cases of colic, distension, and constipation caused by it; furthermore, one should prepare powders, pills, and decoctions from the drugs of the aforementioned ghees, using any one of the following as the vehicle: water boiled with jujube (kola), pomegranate (dāḍima), citron (mātuluṅga), the scum of wine (surāmaṇḍa), fermented rice gruel (takra), sour gruel (mastu), sour grain-water (dhānyāmla), or warm water.

Furthermore, one who eats wholesome food with care and drinks for a month, at the time of breakfast or at mealtime, a powder made from all these ingredients— *trilavana*, *hapuṣā*, *ajamodā*, *ajagandhā*, *vacā*, *hiṅgu*, *pāṭhā*, *upakuñcī*, *śaṭhī*, *jīraka*, *ajājī*, *kustumburu*, *bāṣpikā*, *kāravī*, *tumburu*, *svarjikā*, *yāvaśūka*, *jaṭā*, *pauṣkarī*, *dāḍima*, *tintiṇīka*, *viḍaṅga*, *bhārṅgī*, *vara*, *vetasāmla*, *miśī*, *marica*, *gajakaṇā*, *abhayā*, *pañcakola*, *kumbha*, *nikumbha*, *viśālā*, *yavānī*, and *surāhva*— all ground together and repeatedly saturated with the juice of *bījapūra* fruit, shall [attain the desired results].
AS.Ci.16.10: "The [remedy] which is effective against the disease that has arisen from the three humors combined is also effective against those arising from two humors."

By drinking water that has been boiled and cooled, or by consuming aged wine, urine, buttermilk, water from *kola* fruits, whey, thin gruel (*peyā*), ghee, camel’s milk, or horse-gram soup; or by drinking alkaline water, or the juice of pomegranate seeds; or by consuming ghee prepared with these very same medicinal herbs—an individual who possesses self-control will find that the pain localized in the heart, anus, waist, liver, spleen, and genitals is destroyed. Likewise, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), constipation, hemorrhoids, urinary distress, abdominal enlargement, flatulence, hiccups, obstructions, dysentery, loss of appetite, asthma, and cough will be cured, and the digestive fire will become capable of digesting even swallowed stones.

Two palas of *abhayā*, two palas of *amlavetasa*, one pala each of *vacā*, *viśvabheṣaja*, *trivṛt*, *dantī*, *citraka*, *śaṭhī*, *puṣkaramūla*, and *yāvaśūka*; one karṣa each of *marica*, *ajājī*, *saindhava*, *upakuñcikā*, *śitivāraka*, *yavānī*, *dhātakī* flowers, and *viḍaṅga*; and three karṣas of *hiṅgu*—all these should be powdered, processed as previously described, and drunk; its effect is equal to that [of the preceding recipe].

AS.Ci.16.12: One part each of *yavānī*, *śatapuṣpā*, *nāgakeśara*, *vacā*, *mustā*, *vyoṣa*, *pāṭhā*, *guggulu*, *trivṛt*, *gajapippalī*, *tālīśa*, *elā*, the roots of *pāmārga*, *dravantī*, and *nidigdhikā*, along with one part of *amlavetasa*—this, reduced to a fine powder and drunk with either the juice of *mātuluṅga*, *dāḍima*, or *badara*; or with *śīdhu*, *sura*, or warm water, removes colic (*śūla*), abdominal tumors (*gulma*), hernia (*vaddhman*), flatulence (*ānāha*), abdominal enlargement (*udara*), stiffness of the trunk (*koṣṭhastaimitya*), hemorrhoids (*arśas*), urinary stones (*aśmarī*), retention of urine (*mūtragraha*), stiffness of the waist and back (*kaṭīpṛṣṭhagraha*), insanity (*unmāda*), epilepsy (*apasmāra*), loss of semen (*skannaśukratā*), and weak digestion (*agnisāda*).

One should repeatedly filter the alkali of seeds of *tila*, *kuṇṭala*, *palāśa*, mustard, barley, *yava-nāla*, and radish that have been burnt with smoke inside [an earthen vessel], using the urine of cows, goats, sheep, buffaloes, donkeys, and elephants. Then,
having added a powder of *śuṇṭhī*, rock salt (*saindhava*), *kuṣṭha*, and *kṛmighna* (vidanga) as an additive, one should boil it until it becomes a thick syrup and take it.

That oil, combined with the previously mentioned ingredients, should be cooked over indirect smoke (antardhūma) inside a jar after mixing half-pala portions each of mahauṣadha, devadāru, dantī, trivṛt, pāṭhā, the two types of kṣāra, triphalā, upakuñcikā, cavikā, the two types of dvīpippalī, pippalīmūla, sarpa-sugandhā, kuṣṭha, and kaṭurohiṇī, along with one pala each of the five salts, all ground together and saturated with curd and trivṛt. (AS.Ci.16.14)
Having removed the fire-colored jar, one should take the alkali;

this is the *kṣārāgada* prescribed by Bhela, which is equal to the previous [formula]. It cures snakebite, rat-bite, poisoning, epilepsy, insanity, urinary calculi, disorders of the female reproductive tract, and defects of the semen;
it also alleviates aggravated *pitta* that produces internal burning heat.
In that case, one who has excess phlegm (kapha) should drink castor oil with milk for the purpose of purgation,
mixed with the scum of *vāruṇī* wine.

One with excessively aggravated *pitta* should drink *triphalā* or *trāyamāṇā* with milk; even after purgation, if the burning sensation persists, one should perform bloodletting. In cases of constipation due to feces (*viḍvibandha*), one should employ the treatment protocol for upward-moving wind (*udāvarta*).
One should drink two palas of plucked sesame seeds and half a pala of ginger, ground together with one pala of jaggery and taken with warm milk;
this cures vāta-gulma, udāvarta, and pain in the female reproductive organs. Likewise, one may take realgar (śilāhvaya) with milk boiled with the great five roots (mahāpañcamūla).

Having drunk garlic boiled in milk, one conquers abdominal tumors (gulma), upward-moving wind (udāvarta), sciatica (gṛdhrasī), heart disease, abscesses, wasting, and irregular fevers. A decoction of the two types of *bṛhatī*, *bilva*, *gokṣura*, castor root, *mātuluṅgī* root, and *pāṣāṇabheda*, combined with *yavaśūka*, removes abdominal tumors and colic.

A decoction of *māṣaparṇī*, *mudgaparṇī*, *sahadevā*, the five minor roots (*laghupañcamūla*), castor root, and *ikṣuvālikā*, combined with alkali of barley (*yavakṣāra*), destroys all types of abdominal tumors (*gulma*) and colic in the digestive tract (*koṣṭha*).
A decoction of *devadāru*, *nāgara*, castor root, and *puṣkaramūla* destroys all types of abdominal tumors and colic;
or alternatively, [a decoction] of *puṣkaramūla*, *durālabhā*, barley, and ginger.
Oil, sour gruel, urine, wine, and *yavaśūka* drunk together cure abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, distension, and splenic disorders;
furthermore, one should repeatedly apply various types of sudation (*sveda*).
One who desires purgation should drink the aforementioned sacrificial foods mixed with the powder of *nīlinī* fruit.

Alternatively, one part of asafoetida (*rāmaṭha*), three parts of rock salt (*saindhava*), twenty-seven parts of fresh castor oil (*eraṇḍataila*), and twenty-seven parts of garlic juice (*laśunasvarasa*)— having combined these and drunk them— removes abdominal enlargement, gulma, hemorrhoids, and splenic pain.

One should prepare a decoction by boiling one *pala* each of *nīlinī*, *balā*, *vyāghrī*, *kaṭukā*, *phalā*, *tālapattrikā*, *rāsnā*, and *kṛmighna* in one *āḍhaka* of water, and then remove it when reduced to one-eighth.
One should cook one *prastha* of clarified butter with an equal amount of curd and the addition of one *pala* of *snuhī* latex.

This *nīlinī-ghṛta*, when drunk in a dose of one *pala* along with the scum of gruel while subsisting on meat broth, removes abdominal tumors (*gulma*), splenic enlargement, skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), vitiligo, abdominal dropsy, freckles, edema, fever, anemia (*pāṇḍu-roga*), insanity, and epilepsy.
Indeed, every patient suffering from an abdominal tumor is difficult to purge because their digestive tract is overwhelmed by wind (*māruta*).

Therefore, one should purify this [patient], who is excessively unctuous, with unctuous purgatives (snehavireka). However, when a pitta-gulma has arisen through the use of unctuous and hot substances, one should lick kampillaka with honey for the purpose of inducing laxation (sraṃsana).
One should drink the juice of grapes and *abhayā* with jaggery, or administer purgatives prescribed in the [relevant] treatises (kalpa). Furthermore,
when the condition arises from dryness and heat, one should drink bitter *vāsā*-ghṛta for the purpose of pacification.
Alternatively, ghee prepared with a decoction of *tṛṇapañcamūla* and a paste of the *jīvanīya* group;
or likewise, milk processed separately with the *nyagrodhādi* group or with *tṛṇapañcamūla* and the others.

In cases of an emergency arising from dryness (rūkṣa) or heat (uṣṇa), or when an abscess (vidradhi) has developed in general, one should drink any one of the following: a decoction of the triphalā group, trāyamāṇā-ghṛta, or drākṣā-ghṛta, as prescribed for abscesses.
Alternatively, having drunk lukewarm milk boiled with trāyamāṇā, one should subsequently drink warm milk.
If the gulma is located in the colon (pakvāśaya), one should purify it with milk enemas containing bitter substances; furthermore,
one should apply oil massages prepared with cooling drugs.

One should place vessels made of gems, gold, silver, and copper, filled with cold water, as well as very cool strings of pearls, over the region of the Gulma. If this fails, or if there are premonitory symptoms of internal burning (vidāha), one should perform bloodletting. Once the blood has flowed out and strength has been regained through the meat-broths of wild animals, one should again practice the administration of ghee to destroy the remaining pain.
One should apply poultices to a condition that is burning like an abscess (vidradhi);
likewise, having recognized it as having reached suppuration (paryāgata), one should treat it in every way accordingly.
One should first cause a patient with a kapha-gulma to undergo emesis according to the prescribed rules; those who cannot be made to vomit should be subjected to fasting.
For one who has fasted, one should administer a combination of hot, pungent, bitter, and digestive-stimulating substances.

Likewise, the sudations mentioned for vātagulma, as well as the ghees and other preparations containing double the amount of hiṅgu, kṣāra, and amlavetasa [should be used]. Ghee prepared with a decoction of daśamūla, combined with vyoṣa, dāḍima, hiṅgu, yavakṣāra, biḍa, and saindhava, cures śleṣmagulma.
One should boil two palas of *bhallātaka* and one *pālika* of the minor pentad of roots (*laghupañcamūla*) in one *āḍhaka* of water until one *prastha* remains;

then, adding one *prastha* of milk and one *prastha* of ghee, one should cook it with one *karṣa* each of asafoetida, *viḍaṅga*, *śaṭhī*, *biḍa* salt, rock salt, alkali, *rāsnā*, ginger, long pepper, *ṣaḍgranthā*, licorice, and *citraka*.
This *bhallātaka*-ghṛta destroys phlegmatic abdominal tumors, splenic disorders, cough, dyspnea, malabsorption syndrome, and anemia.
Alternatively, one should prepare and administer six palas of double the alkaline salt (dviguṇakṣāra) without milk, combined with two āḍhakas of whey, curd, sour gruel, and fresh ginger juice.

Then, a powder of asafoetida, chebulic myrobalan, puṣkara root, dry ginger, rock salt, biḍa salt, black salt, barley ash, and tumburu, soaked in a decoction of barley and fried in ghee, should be eaten; this destroys colic, abdominal tumors (gulma), and hardness.
Thereafter, one should repeatedly and extensively foment the entire body and the tumor—whether it be distended, obstructed, hard, elevated, deep-seated in the flesh, stable, or a large mass.
When the gulma has become loosened in one whose body has been lubricated and fomented, one should apply the aforementioned ghaṭī;
once the gulma has been seized by it, one should remove the ghaṭī or break it open.

Then, avoiding the heart and the rectum, one should press a gulma—separated from the skin by a cloth—using any one of the following: a *vimārga*, a *ajapada*, or a mirror; thereafter, one should wipe it clean.
Then, having applied a warm paste of *sālvaṇa* and other such substances, one should apply fomentation using iron vessels.
When the mass has thus been displaced from its site and rendered lax by this sequence, one should administer unctuous purgatives and enemas containing the ten roots (daśamūla).
One should cause the patient to drink this Nīlinī-ghṛta in double the usual quantity,
as well as the medicated ghees mentioned for abdominal diseases (udara).

AS.Ci.16.28: One should prepare a medicinal fat (*miśrakasneha*) by cooking together ghee, castor oil, and milk with a decoction of *triphalā*, *kumbhī*, *nikumbha*, and *daśamūla* reduced to one-sixteenth of its original volume.

This *miśrakasneha* eliminates phlegmatic abdominal tumors (*kaphagulma*), wind-related constipation, upward movement of gases (*udāvarta*), splenic enlargement, abdominal diseases, and pain in the female reproductive organs.

AS.Ci.16.29: One should cook one *pala* each of *pippalī*, *āmalaka*, *drākṣā*, *śyāmā*, and other such ingredients, along with two *prasthas* of castor oil and clarified butter, in six times the amount of milk. This *miśraka-sneha* is a laxative for those suffering from abdominal tumors (*gulma*), and it is like supreme nectar for cases of enlargement of the spleen or liver, abscesses, and wind-related diseases.

AS.Ci.16.30: Twenty-five *palas* of toothbrush tree (*dantī*), the same amount of *citraphala* (*citraka*), and the same number of *harītakī* fruits—one should boil all these together in a jar of water until one-eighth remains. Once that decoction has been strained, one should add those twenty-five *harītakī* fruits, five *palas* of jaggery, half a *kuḍava* of oil, one *kuḍava* of powdered *trivṛt*, half a *pala* of *māgadhikā*, and half a *pala* of *mahauṣadha* (ginger) to it.

Then, once it has become a semi-solid mass over a mild fire, one should remove it from the heat; when cooled, one should mix in honey equal in measure to the oil and a karṣa of powdered *caturjātaka*.

These *dantī-harītakīs*, taken as a linctus for twenty-five days, dispel abdominal tumors (*gulma*), hemorrhoids (*arśas*), edema (*śvayathu*), skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), jaundice (*kāmalā*), anorexia (*arocaka*), malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*), anemia (*pāṇḍu*), heart disease (*hṛdroga*), nausea (*utkleśa*), splenic enlargement (*plīhodara*), and irregular fevers (*viṣamajvara*); they provide a pleasant and comfortable purgation.
Alternatively, one should lick the powder of *trivṛt* soaked in jaggery and milk with clarified butter and honey;
or one should drink *guggulu* with cow’s urine.

Or, one should administer *śyāmā*, *trivṛt*, *kuṣṭha*, *dantī*, *guggulu*, alkali, and *harītakī*; or the juice of *pīlu* with honey, ghee, and salt; or various types of urine, enemas, and alkalis mentioned in their respective contexts. One should do so while consuming a diet of milk, meat broth, and unctuous foods, resting for either two days or one day between applications.
For alkaline substances, by cutting through the phlegm— which is unctuous, stable, and sweet from its seat— cause it to flow out (AS.Ci.16.33).
To purify the channels obstructed by phlegm, one should administer various powders, salts, buttermilk, *ariṣṭas*, and *āsavas* (AS.Ci.16.33).
And one should also administer aged wine mixed with the powders of *pippalī*, *pippalīmūla*, rock salt (*saindhava*), *ajājī*, and *citraka*;
furthermore, by means of emetics, fasting, sudation, the drinking of clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*), and purgatives.

If a gulma of kapha origin does not subside due to its having become deeply rooted, even by means of enemas, pills, powders, alkalis, fermented liquors (ariṣṭas), and spirits (āsavas); AS.Ci.16.35 [then further measures should be taken].
Once the blood has been removed, one should apply cauterization (dāha) to that area at the end with arrows or similar instruments.

Alternatively, having covered the mass of the tumor (gulma) along its margins with a cloth, one should rub it with a flaming arrow, iron, agnimantha, or tinduka wood— using any one of these— while carefully avoiding the navel, the bladder, the heart, the intestines, and the line of hair, and without pressing too firmly.
Then, having pacified the intensity of the digestive fire with decoctions that are sweet and cooling, one should undertake the treatment for improving the complexion (varṇopakrama).
However, in the case of a combination of doshas, one should apply this very same mixed treatment as previously described.
Furthermore,
in the case of a woman with a blood tumor (raktagulma) whose time for childbirth has passed, one should administer an unctuous purgative preceded by oleation and sudation.
A sharp and hot procedure consisting of *yamaka* (ghee and oil) prepared with water alkaline from *palāśa* leaves is for the purpose of breaking up abdominal tumors (*gulma*).
When the vagina remains thus unopened, a paste of sesame seeds mixed with alkali or the milky sap of the *mahāvṛkṣa* should be used for the purpose of purifying the vagina.

Or, one may take bitter fish prepared with those two [substances], or those prepared with their bile, or dried meat (naktaka) prepared with the bile of a boar, or with drugs that act as purgatives and emetics, along with jaggery, alkali, and fermenting agent (kiṇva).
One should administer an enema (basti) containing alkali, milk, and urine, along with a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla), and also apply a urethral/vaginal enema (uttarabasti).
However, once the bleeding has commenced, one should let it proceed while the patient consumes rice with meat broth.

However, if the blood has flowed excessively, one should treat it according to the procedure for *raktapitta*. In all cases of *gulma*, the physician who understands the true nature of food and drink should administer diet while taking into account the strength of the digestive fire (*agni*).

In cases of constipation (ānāha) and similar conditions, one should treat them like abdominal tumors (gulma), in accordance with the presence of undigested matter (āma), pure vāta, or upward movement of wind (udāvarta). Regarding this, there is a verse: AS.Ci.16.42 ānāhādiṣvapyāmaśuddhavātodāvartānurodhena gulmavat pratikuryāditi AS.Ci.16.42 bhavati cātra.
When the digestive fire (agni) is weak, the abdominal tumor (gulma) increases; when it is kindled, however, it subsides.
For the pacification and provocation of all the humors (doṣas) depend upon that [fire].
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
AS.Ci.17.1: Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of abdominal enlargements (udara).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and others:

"Since every type of abdominal enlargement (udara) arises from the obstruction of the openings of the channels due to the persistence of an excessive accumulation of morbid humors, resulting in the agitation of the vital wind (vāyu), therefore one suffering from abdominal enlargement should frequently employ purgatives."
One should take castor oil mixed with either urine or milk every day for one or two months while subsisting on a diet of milk; or one may consume cow's or buffalo's urine;
or one may subsist on camel's milk.
One afflicted by swelling, pain, oppression in the chest, thirst, and fainting should especially drink the life-giving *pippalī* with cow’s urine as an after-drink;
or one should consume a thousand *pippalī* fruits that have been saturated with the milk of the *snuhī* plant.
Or, with black *abhayā* powder impregnated with that [milk],
one may prepare *kāsarasa* mixed with *saindhava* salt and *ajamodā*, or *nimba* oil combined with the juice of fresh ginger.

Alternatively, one may prepare the following proven formulation: having melted an āḍhaka of ghee over charcoal embers together with a prastha of powdered *harītakī*, one should churn it with a churning-stick and store it well-protected in a barley heap for one month.
Then, having strained it and added a decoction of *harītakī* along with sour curd as an additive,

one should cook it. Alternatively, having added the milk of the *mahāvṛkṣa* (snuhī) to cow’s milk, having cooked it, and having churned it once it has cooled, one should process that butter together with the milk of the *mahāvṛkṣa* itself.

Alternatively, one should cook together one karṣa each of cavikā, citraka, dantī, ativiṣā, kuṣṭha, sārivā, viḍaṅga, triphalā, kaṭurohiṇī, the two types of haridrā, śāṅkhinī, trivṛt, and dīpyaka; two palas of the pulp of rājavṛkṣa fruit; two palas of the latex of snuhī (mahāvṛkṣa); and three kuḍavas each of cow’s urine, milk, and ghee.
This destroys abscesses, aṣṭhīlā, abdominal distension, skin diseases, insanity, and epilepsy.

One should administer one *prastha* of clarified butter prepared with five *palas* each of *yavaśūka* and *pañcakola*, along with two *āḍhakas* of the decoction of *mastu* and the ten roots (*daśamūla*).
Alternatively, one may use clarified butter combined with wine (*surā*) and fermented gruel (*sauvīraka*), along with a decoction of *yava*, *kola*, *kulattha*, and the five roots (*pañcamūla*).

When the morbid humors have been loosened by the drinking of ghee, a strong patient should habitually consume urine, fermented liquors (āsava), medicinal wines (ariṣṭa), and spirits (surā) mixed with the milky sap of the snuhī plant for the purpose of purgation.
A decoction of purgative substances strongly reinforced with ginger (*nāgara*) and *devadāru*,

or a powder of the "three salts" (*trilavaṇa*) and other ingredients combined with two or three times the quantity of a carminative substance; [or] one *karṣa* each of *paṭola* root, turmeric (*rajanī*), *viḍaṅga*, and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*).

Having powdered kampillaka, the fruit of nīlinī, and trivṛt combined respectively with two, three, and four karṣas, one should drink them with urine; once digested, one should consume thin gruel, scum, or meat broth.
Then, for six nights, one should eat with milk mixed with the three pungents (vyoṣa);
on the seventh day, one should drink the powder again.
By this method, this powder destroys abdominal enlargements, even those in which fluid has accumulated.

One should also employ the various formulations for breaking up *gulma* (AS.Ci.17.11): one should take one *pālika* each of the substances belonging to the groups beginning with *vatsaka*, *vacā*, and *haridrā*, which are used for emesis, purgation, and head-purgation; having ground them into a fine paste and added the salts and one *prastha* of the latex of the *vajravṛkṣa*, one should cook it over a gentle fire while stirring it in a collection of urines.

Having removed the unburnt residue from that preparation once it has been cooked and cooled, one should roll it into pills the size of a thumb and administer three or four pills according to one's strength for three or four months.

This "urine-pill" (*mūtravarti*) is a supreme remedy for major diseases, including dyspnea, cough, chronic rhinitis, excessive salivation, edema, abdominal tumors, anemia, intestinal worms, stomach disorders, anorexia, indigestion, and upward-moving wind (*udāvarta*).
Furthermore, after undergoing purgation and being emaciated, one should occasionally consume camel’s milk, or cow’s or goat’s milk mixed with the three pungents (*vyoṣa*).
And for the conquest of the remaining morbid humors (doṣas), one should habitually consume either *cavika* and *āragvadha* ground with milk,

or *suradāru* and *citraka*, or *suraṅgā* or *punarnavā*, or a decoction of *triphalā*, *dantī*, and *rauhītaka* combined with the three pungents (*vyoṣa*) and alkali (*kṣāra*), mixed with the milky sap of *snuhī* and clarified butter (*ghṛta*).

One should habitually consume old grain, buttermilk, various types of *ariṣṭas*, and milk combined with *dantī*, *citraka*, *viḍaṅga*, *cavikā*, and the three pungents (*trikaṭu*); or alternatively, one should consume milk mixed with an equal amount of fresh ginger juice.
Or one should consume pippalīvardhamāna, or śilājatu while subsisting on milk, or guggulu;
furthermore, one should repeatedly administer oleation and purgation.
In cases of emergency, one should treat with oleation and purgation alone,
while avoiding water; however, for abdominal distension (ānāha) and upward movement of wind (udāvarta), one should apply the respective specific treatments.
In cases of side pain, stiffness, and cardiac oppression caused by Vāta, one should cook oil with the alkaline water of *bilva*;
or alternatively, oil cooked with the alkali of any one of the following: *syonāka*, *agnimantha*, sesame, *kuntala*, *kadala*, or *apāmārga*.
When kapha or pitta is occluded by vāta, or when vāta is powerful due to those two, one should drink castor oil according to the procedure prescribed for vātagulma (AS.Ci.17.15).

Furthermore, one should apply a lukewarm plaster made of *śigru*, *palāśa*, *arka*, *aśvakarṇa*, *gajapippalī*, and *devadāru*, ground with urine, to the abdomen of those suffering from abdominal enlargement (AS.Ci.17.16).
One should sprinkle [the patient] with decoctions of vṛścikālī, kuṣṭha, ṣaḍgranthā, dvipunarnavā, dhānyaka, nāgara, and the five roots (pañcamūla), as well as with urines,
and should also apply fomentation continuously.
And for one who has been purged, if the abdomen remains constantly flaccid, one should wrap it with a thick cloth after applying a plaster of *sālvaṇa* and other such substances;
in this way, the wind, finding no space, will not cause the abdomen to distend again.
Nevertheless, if flatulence occurs after a person has been well-purged, one should administer non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) that are sour, salty, and very unctuous;
however, if the vāyu is obstructed, one should give sharp and hot enemas.

Then, for one suffering from abdominal enlargement due to vāta (vātodari), having lubricated the body with ghee prepared with the vidārī group of drugs and having sweated the limbs, one should repeatedly facilitate the downward movement of the wind (anulomana) using tilvaka-ghṛta.
Once the combined treatment (saṃsargī) has been administered, one should administer milk for the sake of strength,
and gradually discontinue it before the onset of nausea.

Then, for one suffering from upward-moving wind (udāvarta) whose digestive fire has been kindled by meat broth and similar substances that are mildly sour and salty, and who has undergone oleation and sudation, one should administer a non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) using a decoction of the vidārigandhādi group, enriched with oil from the fruit of *citrā* and combined with sharp, hot, downward-acting drugs; or, for one with a stimulated digestive fire, one may use a decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūlī*).

For one with obstructed feces who suffers from pain, throbbing, and convulsions in the bones, joints, sacrum, flanks, and so forth, and who is dry, one should administer an unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*) using sesame or castor oil prepared with Vāta-alleviating and sour substances.
One should feed him with the meat-juice of wild animals, or with milk boiled with the vidārigandhādi group of drugs;
furthermore, the oils of sarala, madhuśigru, and mūlaka seeds, when used for drinking or as an external massage, destroy colic pain.
One should repeatedly apply fomentation to the abdomen (AS.Ci.17.21).
However, for one who is not to be purged, one should pacify [the condition] with milk, ghee, vegetable broth, meat soup, enemas, massages, and medicines taken in equal quantities (AS.Ci.17.21).

In a patient suffering from *pittodara*, one should first provide oleation with ghee processed with sweet drugs, and then administer a non-unctuous enema (*āsthāpana*) and an unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*) using a decoction of the *nyagrodhādi* group enriched with honey, ghee, and sugar, which has been processed with *śyāmā*, *trivṛt*, and *triphalā* to ensure downward movement of the doshas. However, if the patient is weak, one should first administer an unctuous enema and then cleanse them with milk enemas (*kṣīrabasti*).
And when the digestive fire has regained its strength, one should again administer unctuous food with milk, or with milk boiled with trivṛt and eranda.

In the case of pitta associated with śleṣman, one should repeatedly administer purgation using *sātalā* and *trāyamāṇā*, or with *vārāhanda*; in the presence of vāta, one should use milk mixed with urine and bitter ghee (*tiktaghṛta*). One should also perform enema therapy (*bastikarma*).
Furthermore, one should feed the patient with these same milks, or with food prepared with the *vidārigandhādi* group of drugs boiled in milk.

One should cause the abdomen of a patient with *śleṣmodara* (edema caused by phlegm) to be fomented with milk-porridge (*pāyasa*). Having first applied oleation with ghee prepared from the *vatsaka*-group of drugs, and having induced downward movement of the bowels with ghee cooked with *snuhī* latex, one should then provide a transitional diet consisting of *kapha*-alleviating foods combined with pungent substances and alkalis. Finally, one should administer both non-unctuous enemas (*āsthāpana*) and unctuous enemas (*anuvāsana*) using a decoction of the *muṣkaka*-group of drugs, heavily fortified with the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), urine, and oil.
One should feed the patient with pea-soup (kulattha-yūṣa) mixed with the three pungents (vyoṣa), or with milk;
one should also administer alkaline preparations and sharp fermented liquors (ariṣṭas), and constantly apply sudation therapy (sveda) for styāna-kaphodara.
One should apply a poultice to the abdomen using a paste of fermenting agent (*kiṇva*), mustard seeds, and radish seeds;
having first declared the prognosis hopeless, one should treat a case of *sāṃnipātika* (tri-dosic) abdominal enlargement.

Some say that it is indeed everything, because everything consists of the nature of everything; however, one should counteract [the disease] due to the excess of the doshas by means of the most difficult [remedies]. One should administer purgation with ghee prepared from the exudations of *saptalā* and *śaṅkhinī* for a month or half a month.
Alternatively, one should administer an unctuous non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) prepared with the milk and urine of a large tree;

or else, with a decoction of *avājagandhā*, *ajaśṛṅgī*, *dantī*, *dravantī*, *svādukaṇṭaka*, *punarnavā*, *ajharasī*, *vṛścikālī*, *mūṣikaparṇī*, *mahāsahā*, *kṣudrasahā*, *vṛkṣādanī*, *bhārṅgī*, *gṛdhranakhī*, *taṇḍulīyaka*, pomegranate, citron, and radish, mixed with a paste of *madanaphala*, cardamom, costus, *kuṭila*, and *rāsnā*, combined with cow’s urine, rock salt, and oil.

If it does not subside in this manner, one should inform the patient's relatives that the abdominal swelling is of a chronic (nicaya) nature; then, one should have the patient drink a paste made from *aśvamāraka*, *guñjā*, and *kākādanī* roots mixed with wine.
Or one might introduce poison into his food and drink,
or have him eat a piece of sugarcane after being bitten by a black cobra, or give him vine-fruits or radish;
for in this way, his mass of humors (doṣas)— which had become stagnant, latent, and diverted from their natural course— is quickly shattered by the violently agitating poison and flows outwards.
Therefore, it either proceeds to another state of existence or becomes speechless.
Once the morbid humors have been eliminated, one should sprinkle the patient with cold water and have him drink milk-gruel (*kṣīrayavāgū*).

Then, for one month, while abstaining from solid food, he should eat any one of the following— *trivṛt*, *vāstuka*, *maṇḍūkaparṇī*, *kālaśāka*, or *yavaśāka*— prepared with their own juice, seasoned with non-sour, non-salty, and oily condiments, and served either warm or cold.
One who is thirsty should drink that very [milk] fresh from the udder;
then, once the morbid humors have been eliminated by means of leafy vegetables, one should subsequently administer camel’s milk to the weakened patient.

In the case of splenic enlargement (plīhodara), after the patient has been properly lubricated and fomented according to the specific humor involved and has eaten with curd, one should lance a vein in the left arm.
And for the purpose of causing the blood to flow, one should massage the spleen with the hand;
furthermore, once the patient has drunk oil and his body is purified, one should have him drink sea-pearl ash (samudraśuktikṣāra) with milk, or asafoetida (hiṅgu) and suvarcikā.
Or [one may use] water with the alkali of *palāśa*, or barley-alkali (*yavakṣāra*),
or the alkali of *pārijātaka*, *ikṣvāku*, and *apāmārga* mixed with oil.
One should drink a decoction of *Saubhañjana* mixed with the powder of *Pippalī*, *Citraka*, and rock salt;
or a sour-drained liquid enriched with *Biḍa* salt and *Māgadhikā*; or the alkali of *Pūtikarañja*.

However, in the case of loss of digestive fire (*agnisāda*), one should drink alkaline preparations such as the "three salts" (*trilavaṇa*) and other alkalis, as well as fermented medicinal liquors (*ariṣṭas*).
One should prepare *mahāṣaṭpala* ghee or *rohītaka-ṣaṭpala* ghee:

one should boil twenty-five palas of *rohītaka* bark and two *prasthas* of *kola* in water. With that decoction, along with one *pala* each of the five spices (*pañcakolaka*) and an equal amount of *rohītaka* bark all made into a paste, one should cook one *prastha* of ghee.
That is excellent for the spleen.
One should soak the shoots of *rohitaka* cut into pieces, along with *harītakī*, in water or cow’s urine for seven nights.

That medicated ghee cures splenic enlargement, abdominal tumors, abdominal diseases, worms, urinary disorders, jaundice, and hemorrhoids. If the condition does not subside in this manner, or if the stool has not yet become slimy, one should perform cauterization (agnikarma) according to the procedure for abdominal tumors when vāta and kapha are predominant. However, if pitta is predominant, one should administer *jīvanīya* ghee, milk enemas, and purgatives.
Furthermore, one should repeatedly bleed the blood even in the condition known as yakṛt; this same division of treatment applies there as well.

In the case of abdominal distension (baddhodara), once the patient has been fomented, one should administer a sharp non-unctuous enema (nirūha) containing oil, salt, and urine, as well as an unctuous enema (anuvāsana). Furthermore, one should provide laxating foods that alleviate upward movement of wind (udāvarta), and any sharp purgative or remedy that subdues vāta.
In the case of *chidrodara* (perforated abdomen), one should treat it like *kaphodara*, with the exception of applying sudation (*sveda*).

In *dakodara* (ascites), however, one should first employ dry and sharp medicines, along with decoctions, powders, alkalis, and urine, as well as food and drink that subdue *kapha* and stimulate digestion, for the purpose of eliminating the morbid water.

Thus, when [the condition] is not established [by other means], one should apply the surgical instrument after making it known to friends, as in the cases of *baddhodara*, *chidrodara*, and gallstones (*aśmarī*).

In those cases, for *baddhodara* and *chidrodara*, having anointed and fomented the patient, one should incise the abdomen four finger-breadths below the navel, avoiding four finger-breadths to the left; having opened the abdomen and extracted a portion of the intestines measuring four finger-breadths, one should examine them and, in the case of *baddhagudodara*, remove the hair, the accumulation of feces, or the stone that is causing the intestinal obstruction.

In the case of intestinal leakage (*parisrāvin*), having extracted the foreign body and cleansed the intestinal discharge, one should have the wound bitten by centipedes (*markoṭaka*). Once they have attached themselves, one should remove the abdominal wall.
Then, after anointing with honey and ghee and replacing the intestines in their proper place, one should suture the external abdominal wound.
Having smeared the ulcer with black earth mixed with *yaṣṭīmadhuka* (liquorice), one should bandage it;
then, having brought the patient into a windless room, one should have him subsist on a milk diet and stay in a tub of oil.

In cases of *dakodara* (ascites) and abdominal enlargements where fluid has accumulated, after the patient has been anointed with oil that alleviates *vāta* and fomented with hot water, he should be supported by attendants. Having wrapped his abdomen with a cloth up to the armpits, one should leave a space of four finger-breadths below the navel and, using a *vrīhimukha* instrument, pierce the abdomen to a depth of about one thumb's breadth. Having inserted a tube, one should drain half of the morbid fluid (*doṣodaka*).
Then, having extracted the vessel (nāḍī), one should treat the wound by anointing it with oil and salt and applying a bandage.
If all the lymph (sarvasnim) is drained too suddenly, thirst, fever, body ache, diarrhea, dyspnea, cough, or a burning sensation in the feet may arise.
And because it becomes even more filled,
one should therefore wait for an interval of either the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, eighth, twelfth, or sixteenth night, and then drain out a small amount of the morbid fluid (doṣodaka).
Once the morbid fluid has been discharged, one should massage the abdomen and wrap it tightly with either a woolen cloth, silk, or skin;
in this way, the wind will not cause distension.
After the patient has undergone fasting, one should administer a gruel containing little fat and salt in measured quantities.
Thereafter, for six months, one should subsist on milk;
then for three months, one should drink milk-gruel (peyā);
and for another three months, one should eat śyāmāka or koradūṣa grain with little salt and little milk.
And there is a verse on this point:
"By practicing thus for a year with self-restraint, one shall conquer ascites.
Restrained regarding things to be avoided, not over-indulging in what is prescribed, and having conquered the senses;
for almost all abdominal diseases arise from a combination of the humors (doṣas).
Therefore, therapeutic measures that pacify wind and the other [doshas] are recommended in all cases;
for when the abdomen is filled with the doshas, the digestive fire becomes weak.

Therefore, foods that are appetizing, digestive stimulants, and light should be prepared, along with the five roots (pañcamūla), and containing a small amount of sour, salty, oily, and pungent flavors. (AS.Ci.17.46)
One should feed the person as much as desired a gruel prepared with the urine of cows that have been treated [medicinally] and with sixty-day rice grains, using milk.
One should drink sugarcane juice following [the meal] for the cessation of abdominal enlargements; thus, their respective vāta, pitta, and kapha return to their own locations.
Excessively hot, sour, salty, dry, constipating, cold, and heavy; jaggery, sesame-based preparations, leafy vegetables, and water— these are [prohibited] for drinking and immersion baths.
One should avoid exertion, travel, sleeping during the day, and improper modes of transport;
but buttermilk that is neither too clear nor too thick and sweet is recommended as a drink.
In cases of *vāta* and *pitta*, [one should administer] with *kaṇā*, salt, and sugar; in *kaphodara*, with *yavānī*, *saindhava*, *ajājī*, honey, and the three pungents (*vyoṣa*).
In Nicayodara, [one should administer] a mixture of the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), alkali, and salts;
or [a mixture] of honey, oil, vacā, ginger, śatāhvā, kuṣṭha, and rock salt.
In the case of an obstructed spleen, [one should administer] hapuṣā, yavānī, paṭola, and jājī;
in the case of a perforation, [one should administer] kṛṣṇā and honey; and in the case of fluid in the abdomen, [one should administer] the three pungents (vyoṣa) with water.
For those suffering from loss of appetite, indigestion, weak digestive fire, diarrhea,
or afflictions caused by vāta and kapha, buttermilk serves as a nectar. Furthermore, after all medicinal formulations, one should administer milk.

Milk alone acts as a stabilizer for all the bodily tissues (dhātus), is strengthening, removes the persistence of the humors (doṣas), and for those whose limbs have been emaciated by medicine, it truly becomes like nectar.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter.
AS.Ci.18.1: Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of anemia (pāṇḍuroga).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and others:
one suffering from anemia (pāṇḍvāmaya) should first be made to drink one of the following ghees— Kalyāṇaka, Pañcagavya, or Tikta.

Having made a paste from one *kuḍava* of pomegranate essence, half a *kuḍava* of coriander, eight parts of long pepper (*pippalī*), and one *pala* each of ginger and *citraka*, and cooking this together with twenty *palas* of ghee in one *āḍhaka* of water, [this preparation] cures heart disease, anemia, abdominal tumors, splenic disorders, hemorrhoids, dyspnea, cough, and the afflictions of obstructed wind and wind-phlegm; it kindles the digestive fire and is highly regarded for barren women and those who suffer difficult labor.

One should prepare one prastha of ghee by boiling it with one karṣa each of durālabhā, candana, paṭola, trāyamāṇā, guḍūcī, kirātatiktaka, rohiṇī, ghanasāra, the two types of niśā, indrayava, devadāru, parpaṭaka, and ajamoda, along with one āḍhaka of milk.
This destroys jaundice, kāmalā, raktapitta, fever, burning sensations, menorrhagia, eruptive boils, swelling, fistula-in-ano, and edema.
Once he has been lubricated, one should emeticate him with a sharp [drug];
then, having lubricated him again, one should have him drink cow’s or buffalo’s milk mixed with urine for half a month.
Or one may take *triphalā* boiled in Magadha wine or prepared with urine;
or for seven days, one may take *harītakī* fruits ground into a paste with urine.
Alternatively, the roots of *svarṇakṣīrī*, *bhadradāru*, *nāgara*, *śyāmā*, and *trivṛt* may be boiled with that same [liquid], or milk may be boiled with these.

Having drunk equal parts of the seeds of *vatsaka*, *viśālā*, *kuṣṭha*, *kaṭukā*, *dāru*, and *mustā*, along with two parts of *mūrvā* and half a part of *ativiṣā*, all powdered together, one should lick honey over it with lukewarm water.

This [preparation] dispels anemia (pāṇḍu), jaundice (kāmalā), fever (jvara), loss of appetite (aruci), abdominal tumors (gulma), flatulence (ānāha), undigested matter (āmavāta), blood-bile disorders (raktapitta), cough (kāsa), and dyspnea (śvāsa). Alternatively, pills may be prepared from trikaṭu, black sesame, and iron, combined with an equal amount of honey-ore (mākṣikadhātu) and honey. Or, pills may be made with nine parts each of the three pungents (vyoṣa), salt (kāgni), and viḍaṅga, along with nine parts of iron powder. When consumed with honey and ghee, or with buttermilk or warm water, these remove heart disease, anemia, jaundice, skin diseases (kuṣṭha), hemorrhoids (arśas), edema (śopha), abdominal enlargement (udara), splenic disorders (plīha), and urinary disorders (meha).

Having finely powdered nine ingredients— mākṣika mineral, cavikā, dāru, bark of dārvī, granthika, and the three myrobalans (triphalā) etc.— one should add twice the amount of very fine maṇḍūra separately; then, having boiled cow's urine eight times the total quantity of these, one should throw that powder into it.
Immediately thereafter, one should prepare boluses (vaṭakas);

when practiced with buttermilk as an after-drink, these are the supreme medicine for those suffering from jaundice, as well as for those afflicted by edema, hemorrhoids, skin diseases, jaundice, urinary disorders, splenic enlargement, and disorders of wind and phlegm.

Five palas each of the impurities of *śilājatu*, gold, silver, and iron, along with the *triphalā* group and other ingredients, free from dregs, in the measure of one pala each, should be reduced to a fine powder and combined with eight palas of white sugar. When mixed with honey, this preparation is known as *Yogarāja*.
For one who eats soups of *kulattha* and other such pulses, [the medicine] is digested by the digestive fire in the same manner as before;
it removes consumption, poisons, toxic fevers, cough, dyspnea, and epilepsy.

AS.Ci.18.9: Eight *palas* of the substance called *śilā* (realgar), impregnated for a month or half a month with decoctions of *triphalā*, *kuṭaja* fruit, *ghana* (musta), *paṭola*, *picumanda* (nimba), and *mahauṣadha* (ginger), together with an equal amount of sugar; one *pala* each of *upakulyā* (pippalī), *tugākṣīrī*, *dhātrī* fruit, and *karkaṭakaśṛṅgī*; one *pala* each of the fruit and root of *nidigdhikā*; and three *karṣas* of the "three aromatics" (*trijātaka*)—these should be made into pills (*vaṭakas*) mixed with three *palas* of honey.

These, known as "Vajra" (the Thunderbolt), when taken with any one of the following vehicles—pomegranate juice, milk, meat broth, water, wine, or fermented liquor—shatter the aforementioned diseases like a thunderbolt.
It cures heart disease, throat diseases, abdominal tumors, menorrhagia, fistula-in-ano, abdominal enlargements, hernias, and disorders of semen and urine (AS.Ci.18.10).

Having powdered two *prastha*s of grapes and long pepper, half a *tulā* of sugar, and two *pala*s each of *tavakṣīrī*, ginger, and licorice, one should add them to a *droṇa* of *āmalaka* juice and cook over a mild fire (AS.Ci.18.10).
When that has become a linctus and has cooled,

one should add three karṣas of powdered *trisugandhika* (the "three aromatics") to the *madhuprastha*, stir it thoroughly with a ladle, and place it in an earthen vessel scented with jasmine flowers and other fragrances.

This grape linctus (*drākṣā-leha*), when consumed, forcibly removes diseases such as anemia (*pāṇḍvāmaya*), heart disease, jaundice, chlorosis, fever, abdominal tumors, abdominal enlargement, edema, and upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*), as well as other diseases curable by purgation, just as the wind disperses the clouds.

Regarding diet, however, one should consume what is wholesome: *śāli* rice, barley, wheat, mung beans, the meat of wild animals, milk, ghee, and the vegetables of vṛṣa, paṭola, vetra, and parpaṭa; as well as the juices of grapes, pomegranate, dates, and *āmalaka*.
For drinking, water boiled with the five roots (*pañcamūla*) should be used when wind (*vāta*) is predominant.

In cases where pitta predominates in kapha disorders, [the gruel] should be prepared with ginger, long pepper, and dry ginger; otherwise, arishta, sidhu, madhvika, or asava may be used in all cases, or buttermilk.
One prastha of the essence of *bījaka* and twenty-five palas of *varā*.

Having boiled five *tulās* of grapes and seven *tulās* of *balā* in one *droṇa* of water until reduced to one-fourth, one should take the juice from them. When this liquid has been strained and cooled, one should add one *tulā* of sugar, one *prastha* of honey, and one *karṣa* each of the powdered powders of *vyoṣa*, *vyāghranakha*, *uśīra*, *kramuka*, *elāvāluka*, *kuṣṭha*, and *madhuka*. Having placed all these together in a vessel smeared with ghee, one should store it for ten nights in a heap of barley during the summer, or for twenty nights in the cold season.
This *Bījakasārāriṣṭa* destroys anemia, jaundice, urinary disorders, heart disease, gout, irregular fevers, anorexia, cough, and asthma.
One should take one *tulā* of the *gaṇḍīra* tree, including its roots, flowers, and branches;
half a *tulā* of the ten roots (*daśamūla*); half a *prastha* each of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) and of *kuṭaja* bark.
One should take one *kuḍava* each of *mustā*, *aruṣkara*, *kṛmighna*, and *indrayava*;
one *pala* each of *pāṭhā*, *dantī*, *madhurasā*, *rāsnā*, *śaṭhī*, and *citraka*;
and half a *prastha* of *mṛdvīkā*. Having boiled these in sixteen times the amount of water until one-fourth remains, one should take the decoction.

Once purified and cooled, one should add two *tulās* of sugar, one *prastha* of iron powder, half a *prastha* of *māgadhikā*, and half a *pala* each of finely ground *granthika*, black pepper, *viḍaṅga*, and *elavāluka*. Having placed this in a jar smeared with clarified butter, one should store it for exactly one month; this *gaṇḍīrāriṣṭa* possesses superior qualities to the former and cures glandular swellings, tumors, and worms.

Alternatively, one should place a *droṇa* of whey (*mastu*), a *tulā* of jaggery, three *prasthas* of long pepper (*pippalī*), three *prasthas* of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), three *prasthas* of *viḍaṅga*, and one *kuḍava* each of black pepper, *parūṣaka*, grapes, *kāśmarya* fruit, and *indrayava*— along with two *palas* each of powdered *dantī*, *citraka*, and *bhallātaka*— into a vessel smeared with *cavya*, *kuṣṭha*, and *citraka*. Then, having left it for a fortnight in a heap of barley, one should drink it according to one's strength.
This [mixture] is swift-acting and destroys leucoderma, urinary disorders, obesity, morbid fat, malabsorption syndrome, splenic enlargement, edema, abdominal tumors, and fistula-in-ano;
it is also a supreme stimulator of the digestive fire.
Regarding this, there is also a verse here: AS.Ci.18.15 bhavati cātra (And there is also a verse here)
The medical treatment prescribed for the purpose of pacifying anemia (pāṇḍuroga) should be modified by the learned physician according to the relative strength of each individual doṣa.
In fever born of Vāta, it should consist mostly of unctuous substances; in that born of Pitta, bitter and cold;
in that born of Kapha, pungent, dry, and hot; and in that caused by all three combined (Sānnipātika), it should be a mixture of these.
First, one should expel the morbid matter from the body with sharp purificatory therapies;
once the gastrointestinal tract is purified, one should then administer strengthening medicated ghees.
AS.Ci.18.18 Vyoṣa, bilva, the two types of rajanī, triphalā, the two types of punarnavā,
mustā, iron filings, pāṭhā, viḍaṅga, and devadāru.
Ghee boiled with vṛścikālī, bhārṅgī,
and milk quickly pacifies all disorders caused by [ingesting] earth.

Similarly, for the purpose of softening [the wound] when there is a tendency toward excessive sensitivity, one should apply earth that has been infused with keśara, yaṣṭyāhva, pippalī, milk, and śādvala grass.
With viḍaṅga, ativiṣā, pāṭhā, and nimba shoots;
or with vārtāka, kaṭurohiṇī, kuṭaja, and mūrvā.

Medicines should be administered according to the persistence of defects that are not distinct from those of *mṛdbheda*; however, in cases of *kāmalā*, one should employ treatments that subdue *pitta* without contradicting the treatment for *pāṇḍuroga*.

One *prastha* of ghee prepared with the juice of one hundred *pathyā* fruits and the paste of fifty *pathyā* stalks conquers abdominal tumors (*gulma*), jaundice (*kāmalā*), and anemia (*pāṇḍuroga*). [A similar preparation] is made with the juice of four *pala* of *dantī* and the ground unripe fruits (*śalāṭu*) of *dantī*.
A *prastha* of ghee boiled in that same manner likewise conquers splenomegaly and edema.
A *prastha* of aged ghee prepared with half a *prastha* of grapes [is also effective].

This [decoction], prepared with *haridrā*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *nīlī*, *balā*, and *madhuka*, removes jaundice, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), anemia (*pāṇḍu*), fever, urinary disorders (*meha*), and ascites.
Buffalo ghee mixed with milk is an excellent remedy for jaundice. Half a pala of the paste of *dārvī* (barberry) should be prepared with twice the amount of cow’s urine.
In a decoction of five palas of *dārvī* with a paste of *kālīyaka*,
one should add a *prastha* of buffalo ghee— first [adding] the former [ingredients] first, and the latter [ingredients] last.
It is established that [this] is beneficial when combined with niśā in a decoction of kālīyaka,
and it is also beneficial for the uttaravasti (urethral/vaginal enema) when prepared with the juice of āragvadha, or of ikṣu, vidārī, or āmalaka.

One should cause [the patient] to drink a dose the size of a *bilva* fruit containing the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), which removes jaundice; or one should drink the paste of *nikumbha* with double the amount of jaggery and cold water.
One should administer the powder of *kumbha* with honey, or with the juice of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*),
or *tribhaṇḍī* with sugar, or *gavākṣī*.
One should administer the juice of triphalā, or of guḍūcī, or of dārvī, or of nimba,
mixed with honey every morning to one suffering from jaundice.
In one suffering from *kāmalā* who passes stool resembling ground sesame seeds,
the *pitta* has its path obstructed by *kapha*; this should be overcome with treatments that eliminate *kapha*.

When the wind (vāyu), congealed by phlegm (kapha) due to dry, cold, heavy, and sweet [foods], as well as the suppression of physical exercise and movement, casts the bile (pitta) outward; AS.Ci.18.32.
At that time, the person’s eyes, urine, and skin become yellowish, and his feces become white;
he suffers from flatulence and constipation, and his heart feels heavy.

When pitta has resorted to the peripheral tissues (śākhā), it should be known by its gradual association with weakness, low digestive fire, pain in the flanks, hiccups, dyspnea, anorexia, and fever, even when the dosha is present in small quantities.
One should feed him with soups made from the meat of peacock, partridge, and cock, seasoned with dry, pungent, and sour tastes,
as well as with soups made from dried radish and horse gram (kulattha).
Excessively sour, sharp, pungent, salty, and hot substances are recommended;
one should lick vyoṣa together with the juice of bījapūra according to the state of the internal receptacle (āśaya).
One's own pitta returns to its proper place, whereby even his feces become colored;
and the vāyu attains pacification along with complications such as flatulence (āṭopa).
For this [patient], once the complications have subsided, the treatment for *kāmalā* (jaundice) should be performed. In the case of *kumbhakāmalā*, one should drink *śilājatu* with cow's urine.
For one suffering from *halīmaka*, [one should administer] honey-ore (*mākṣikadhātu*) or the dross produced from gold for a month,
prepared with the fresh juice of *guḍūcī* and milk.
One who has been lubricated with buffalo ghee should drink the juice of *dhātrī* (myrobalan) mixed with *trivṛt*; once purged by that, he should eat sweet food that alleviates *pitta* and *vāyu*.
One should habitually employ the previously mentioned grape electuary, sweet medicated ghees,
sustaining enemas, and milk enemas along with oil enemas.

One should drink preparations of *mārdvīkāriṣṭa* according to the proper method for the increase of the digestive fire; likewise, one should take the electuary of *abhayā* for cough, as well as *pippalī*, *madhuka*, and *balā*.
An expert [physician] should administer milk according to the specific dosha and the patient's strength,
as well as the therapeutic regimen prescribed for edema (śopha) in cases of anemia (pāṇḍuroga).
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter.
Now begins the nineteenth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of swelling (śvayathu).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and others:

"In all cases of swelling born of the *doṣas* and spreading throughout the entire body that are associated with *āmadoṣa*, one should first employ fasting, digestive treatments, and purification therapies."
In cases arising from oleation, drying (virūkṣaṇa) medicines are indicated; in those arising from drying, oleating (snehana) measures are indicated.

Among these, for disorders born of phlegm (āmaja), one who has undergone fasting should eat light food with warm water mixed with *bhadradāru*, ginger, black pepper, *prativiṣā*, *viḍaṅga*, and *indrayava*;
or alternatively, *nāgara*, *devadāru*, *pathyā*, and *varṣābhū*.
One who has heavy, broken-down stools should take pañcakola, cumin, nidigdhikā, musta, pāṭhā, and turmeric;
or a suppository made of urine; or fresh iron;
or buttermilk with trikaṭu, sauvarcala salt, and honey.
Or one should habitually consume jaggery and *harītakī*;
otherwise, one should take *trivṛt*, the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), *kaṭurohiṇī*, and iron powder with a decoction of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*).
Or one may take vyoṣa, yavakṣāra, and iron powder with rice-water; or the paste of bibhītaka;
or guggulu with cow's urine.
One should consume either *harītakī* with an equal amount of jaggery, or *śuṇṭhī* with a decoction of *punarnavā* as an after-drink,
or fresh ginger with an equal amount of jaggery, increasing it by half a *pala* at a time until reaching a maximum dose of five *palas*.

This month-long regimen cures swelling, emaciation, hemorrhoids, dyspnea, cough, excessive salivation, chronic rhinitis, intestinal torpor, loss of digestive fire, abdominal tumors, abdominal enlargements, urinary disorders, anemia, jaundice, and mental disorders;
or one may drink the juice of fresh ginger while subsisting on a diet of śāli rice and milk,
once the complications of the morbid humors have subsided, consuming boiled milks and clarified butters.
Milk prepared with the three pungents (trikaṭu), castor root, and the roots of śyāmā,
or with the two roots of mahauṣadha and uruṅgī, [is beneficial].

Or one may take [the powder] of *varṣābhū*, *mayūra*, and the five pungents (*pañcakola*); or that of *kumbha*, *nikumbha*, the three acrids (*vyoṣa*), and *agni*. One should subsist on the milk of a female camel, or drink cow urine or the urine of a great bull (*maharṣi*) along with milk, while consuming only milk. Having boiled one *akṣa* each of pomegranate, *yavānī*, *yavānaka*, *dhanikā*, *pāṭhā*, *amlavetasa*, black pepper, the five pungents (*pañcakola*), and the fruit of *bilva* in one *āḍhaka* of water, one should prepare a *prastha* of ghee with that decoction; this cures edema, hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, urinary disorders, and loss of digestive fire.
One should take butter from *citraka* curd according to the procedure prescribed for hemorrhoids;
that [butter], containing the root of *citraka* and prepared with the paste of *citraka* and buttermilk, is the same as the previous [preparation].

AS.Ci.19.6 One should cause [the patient] to drink the *dhānvantara*, *kalyāṇaka*, *pañcagavya*, *tikta*, or *mahātikta* ghees according to the predominance of the respective *doṣas*, or the ghees mentioned for abdominal diseases (*udara*) with *tilvaka* as the fourth ingredient.
AS.Ci.19.7 One should place one hundred *pathyā* fruits mixed with one *tulā* of jaggery into a *kaṃsa* of decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūla*) and set it over the fire.
When it has become a linctus, one should add the powder of trikaṭu, trijātaka, and yavakṣāra, as well as half a prastha of honey.

These Daśamūla-harītakīs destroy even highly advanced edema, as well as abdominal enlargement, anorexia, indigestion, anemia, abdominal tumors, urinary disorders, dyspnea, cough, emaciation, āmavāta, acid gastritis, and defects of the urine and semen.

One should prepare foods such as gruels (*peyā*) and others, seasoned with a small amount of fat and salt, using *śaṭhī*, *puṣkaramūla*, *kāravī*, *citraka*, *ajājī*, *jīvantī*, the pulp of *bilva*, alkali of barley (*yavakṣāra*), *vṛkṣāmla*, and *daśamūla*, fried in ghee and oil;
one should also provide massages, ointments, and affusions that are pleasant to the touch.

One should cook oil for anointing with *śaileya*, *sthauṇeyaka*, *śrīveṣṭaka*, *agaru*, *devadāru*, *hareṇukā*, *kuṣṭha*, *dhyāmaka*, *padmaka*, *māṃsī*, *māgadhikā*, *vanyadhānya*, *tālīśapatra*, *caturjātaka*, *palāśa*, *ambuda*, *ambu*, *priyaṅgu*, *spṛkkā*, and *nakha*, finely ground together;
and one should also apply a poultice (*pradeha*) made from these same ingredients.

A paste made from mustard, sauvarcala salt, saindhava salt, śārṅgeṣṭā, and the marrow of various trees, or even the marrow alone, is recommended; specifically for those arising from a single limb, a plaster should be applied using *punarnavā*, *hiṃsrā*, *kośātakī*, *karavīra*, *kiṃśuka*, *ativiṣā*, *ṛddhi*, *vṛddhi*, *mūṣikaparṇī*, *hastikarṇa*, *nalikā*, *nākulī*, *sthūlakākādanī*, *sāla*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *devadāru*, *lodhra*, *tālaparṇī*, *daśapatrikā*, and *jayantī*.
A bath with lukewarm radish juice, or with a decoction of *vṛkṣaka*, *arka*, *naktamāla*, *nimba*, and *varṣābhū*.

Now, in the case of a swelling caused by Vāta, one should drink *trivṛt* or castor oil for half a month or for a full month. Furthermore, in cases of the obstruction of feces and flatus, one should take castor oil before a meal with milk or meat broths.
One should administer Vāta-alleviating massages, sudation, and poultices;
specifically, when the condition is localized to a single limb, an external application (pralepa) of mātuluṅga, agnimantha, śuṇṭhī, devadāru, and hiṃsrā should be used.
In the case of a Pitta-originated [Vātarakta], one should drink ghee prepared with the Nyagrodhādi group of drugs.
Or bitter milk may be used in cases of fainting, craving, thirst, and burning sensations.

However, for one seeking to induce purgation, a decoction of *abhayā*, *amaradāru*, *madhuka*, *kaṭukā*, *dantī*, *candana*, *nicula*, *paṭola*, *mūrvā*, *dārvī*, *trāyamāṇā*, *upakulyā*, and *viśālā*, mixed with cow’s urine and taken with ghee, pacifies swelling, poison, erysipelas (*visarpa*), fever, burning sensations, thirst, internal heat, and the disorders of the three humors (*sannipāta*). One should prepare massages and other treatments using substances of cold potency, such as ghee, milk, the milky trees (*kṣīrivṛkṣa*), *vetasa*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *mṛṇāla*, *candana*, and so forth.
In the case of [hemorrhoids] arising from kapha, however, one should drink oil prepared with the āragvadha group of drugs,
as well as alkali, urine, buttermilk, fermented gruel (āsava), and medicinal liquors (ariṣṭa).

Take one *prastha* each of *bhallātaka*, *citraka*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), *viḍaṅga*, and the fruits of *bṛhatī*. Place these in a *droṇa* of clear fermented grain-water (*dhānyāmla*) and boil them over a cow-dung fire until reduced to one-third.

Once it has been strained and cooled, mix it with a jar of whey (*mastu*) and one *tulā* of sugar candy (*sitopalā*). Pour this into a strong vessel smeared with a paste of *agnika* and *magadhikā*, and store it well-protected in the open air.

After ten days, this *bhallātakāriṣṭa*, when consumed, quickly cures swelling, abdominal enlargements, hemorrhoids, fistula-in-ano, malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*), worms, skin diseases, urinary disorders, emaciation, and edema.

Take one hundred palas each of triphalā, marica, drākṣā, pippalī, and kāśmarya fruit, along with one *tulā* of jaggery and one *droṇa* of water. Place these in a vessel smeared with honey and let it sit for seven days during the hot season, or for two weeks during the cold season.
This is the Aṣṭaśatariṣṭa, which is identical in its effects to the previous formulation.
One should apply a lukewarm paste made from old oil-cake, black *śigru*, bark, and sand, ground with urine,

for a localized application on a single limb; however, for a bath, one should use *kālā*, *sarala*, *lāja*, *śṛṅgī*, *ajagandhā*, *aśvagandhā*, *ekaiṣikā*, ginger, *kulattha*, *tarkārī*, *kuṣṭha*, *arjaka*, *citraka*, water, and urine.
Caṇḍāgaruṇī is for external application; this very same formulation is the remedy for both combined (saṃsarga) and complex (sannipāta) fevers, according to the manifestation of the respective doṣas.
In the case of swelling localized to a single region, one should administer emetics and other therapies as appropriate to the site, along with bloodletting.
Regarding this, there is a verse here (AS.Ci.19.17):
"Generally, due to trauma, the wind (vāyu), together with blood, produces a reddened swelling; in that case [the treatment should be applied]."

In cases of *visarpa* (erysipelas) caused by wind (*vāta*), blood (*rakta*), or poison (*viṣa*), one should perform anti-venomous treatments appropriate to the specific cause. One should avoid the meat of domestic, aquatic, and marshy animals, as well as weak meats, dried vegetables, and sesame-based foods.

Gauḍa liquor, flour-based foods, curd with salt, slimy substances, sour wine, parched grain, dried meat, eating in equal proportions [of incompatible items], heavy food, unwholesome food, and burning food.
One who suffers from swelling or disease should avoid sleep during the day and sexual intercourse at night.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter.
Now begins the twentieth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of visarpa;
thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
In the initial stages of all types of visarpa, one should administer fasting, drying therapies, venesection, emesis, and purgation; however,
under no circumstances should oleation be administered.

In those cases where there is no *āma* and the *kapha* has been diminished, one should administer ghees of cooling potency— such as *tiktaghṛta*, *trāyamāṇāghṛta*, and others— for drinking. In that context, for the purpose of emesis, one should employ *madana*, *indrayava*, *paṭola*, *picumanda*, *madhuka*, and sugarcane juice.
For purgation in cases arising from Vāta, one should use grapes, trivṛt, triphalā, and trāyamāṇā (AS.Ci.20.4).

For external applications and affusions in Vāta disorders, one should use musta, devadāru, kuṣṭha, śatāhvā, vārāhī, dhānyāka, kṛṣṇagandhā, vaṃśā, and ārtagalā, as well as the small pentaroots (hrasvapañcamūla), the large pentaroots (bṛhatpañcamūla), and the thorny pentaroots (kaṇṭakapañcamūla) (AS.Ci.20.4).

In the case of *pitta*, however, one should use lotus (*kamala*), blue water-lily (*utpala*), duckweed (*śaivāla*), mud, *dūrvā* grass, lotus-stalk (*mṛṇāla*), *śṛṅgāṭaka*, *kaśeruka*, sugar, *drībera*, red sandalwood (*kucandana*), pearl, gem, red ochre (*gairika*), *payasyā*, *prapauṇḍarīka*, *madhuka*, *padmaka*, ghee, milk, and the *nyagrodhādi* group. In the case of *śleṣman*, one should use *ajagandhā*, *aśvagandhā*, *sarala*, *kālakā*, *aiṣikā*, *agaru*, *uśīra*, *rāsnā*, *vacā*, *śītaśiva*, *indravallī*, cow’s urine, and the *varaṇādi* group. In cases of combined doshas (*saṃsarga*), one should formulate the treatment according to the relative strength of each dosha.

In that case, when [the fever] is located in the seat of kapha and is accompanied by āma, or when it has moved to the seat of pitta, unctuous and non-cold applications such as ointments (pralepa) and affusions (pariṣeka) should be used.
In cases of pitta, thin, very cold [poultices] mixed with ghee and separated by a cloth should be applied, and they should be removed and reapplied at every moment.
In cases arising from two doshas (dvandvaja), one should treat the doshas according to their respective natures.
Specifically for agnivisarpa (erysipelas), one should drink mahātiktaka;

for granthivisarpa (nodular erysipelas), having observed the association with raktapitta (blood-bile disorder), one should first employ pacifying treatments beginning with fasting and ending with purgation.
Then, for pain, one should perform treatments that remove wind and phlegm; furthermore, for glandular swellings, one should apply poultices that are unctuous, sour, and warm.
One should apply a plaster with those same pastes mentioned for *vāta-kapha-visarpa*, or perform an irrigation (*pariṣeka*) with oil or water prepared with them;
or one should smear it with the paste of dried radish, or with the bark of *naktamāla*, or with *bibhītaka*; or with *vijayā*, *akṣa*, *nāgabalā*, *agnimantha*, *bhūrja-granthi*, and bamboo leaves.

A warm plaster made from the roots and bark of *dantī* and *citraka*, *kāsīsa*, the milks of *arka* and *snuhī*, and the seeds of *bhallātaka* breaks even stone. However, when a tumor has persisted for a long time, one should administer *triphalā*.
Or honey and long pepper, or musta, roasted grain flour, and bhallātaka, or sidhu wine, honey, and sugar.
Or wine infused with the juice of citron, or mineral pitch, or a decoction that breaks up tumors,
or the application of heated iron, stones, and the like.
When [the disease] has ascended above the collarbone, one should employ sharp fumigations and emetics;
even so, if there is no resolution, one should cauterize with alkali or fire.
Alternatively, one should incise it with a surgical instrument and thoroughly cleanse it;
or, having repeatedly removed the vitiated blood, one should apply fomentation again and again.
In this manner, one should proceed by turns in cases of raktapitta as well as vāta-śleṣman.
In all cases of visarpa that have reached suppuration and been incised, one should treat it like a wound;
furthermore, one should prepare a medicated oil with dārvī, viḍaṅga, and kampillaka to cure the resulting granthi-wound.
In a case of *kardamaka* (slimy swelling), one should perform emesis and other purificatory therapies very quickly and thoroughly, and then repeatedly drain the blood with leeches;
for from the excessive moisture of the blood, there occurs the putrefaction of the skin, flesh, vessels, and ligaments.
One should drink the decoction of thick *paṭola*, *picumanda*,
*musta*, *uśīra*, *āmalaka*, and *sārivā*, as well as of *candana* and *utpala*.

Alternatively, one should administer a preparation of the *paṭola* group mixed with ghee; or, for the purpose of purgation, one should have the patient drink the powder of *trivṛt* with ghee, milk, grape juice, or warm water— using *dārvī* bark, *tiktā*, *paṭola*, *yaṣṭyāhvā*, *ariṣṭa*, *masūra*, *triphalā*, and *trāyamāṇā*.
Milk boiled with *trāyamāṇā* is for one whose *pitta* has been aggravated; and regarding this, there is also a verse here: AS.Ci.20.15 *trāyamāṇāśṛtaṃ pittodvṛtte kṣīramiti bhavati cātra*
In this condition, the excellent treatment is indeed the extraction of blood, for visarpa has blood as its substrate;
furthermore,
it arises when [the disease] is not associated with rakta-pitta.
Clarified butter should not be given to one with excessive morbid humors (*doṣa*) if it does not induce purgation; for by that [butter], the obstructed humor would cook the skin, blood, and flesh.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter.
Now begins the twenty-first chapter.
Herein we shall explain the treatment of skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and others:
"In the very stage of premonitory symptoms (pūrvarūpa), one should treat the patient suffering from leprosy (kuṣṭhin) with the internal administration of oleaginous substances (sneha)."

In that case, if vāta is predominant, one should administer for drinking or massage oil or ghee prepared with *meṣaśṛṅgī*, *śārṅgeṣṭā*, *eraṇḍa*, *guḍūcī*, and the two groups of five roots (*pañcamūla*). If pitta is predominant, [one should administer] ghee prepared with *dhava*, *aśvakarṇaka*, *kakubha*, *vacā*, *punarnavā*, *palāśa*, *picumanda*, *madhuka*, *lodhra*, and *samaṅgā*.
Alternatively, one should boil one *pala* each of *paṭola*, *picumanda*, *dārvī*, *durālabhā*, *tiktarohiṇī*, *pāṭhā*, *parpaṭaka*, and *trāyamāṇā* in two *āḍhakas* of water until eight parts remain;
with that decoction, one should prepare twelve *palas* of ghee by adding one *karṣa* each of the pastes of *candana*, *upakulyā*, *mustā*, *trāyantī*, *indrayava*, and *bhūnimba*.

This Tikṭaka-ghṛta removes leprosy (kuṣṭha), erysipelas (visarpa), eruptive boils (visphoṭa), glandular swellings (gaṇḍa), cervical adenitis (gaṇḍamālā), edema (śvayathu), pustules (piṭaka), internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta), hemorrhoids (durnāma), vātaśoṇita, jaundice (kāmalā), anemia (pāṇḍvāmaya), insanity (unmāda), burning sensations (dāha), thirst (tṛṣ), vertigo (bhrama), itching (kaṇḍū), leprosy (kuṣṭha), sinus ulcers (nāḍī), abdominal tumors (gulma), intoxication (mada), blindness (timira), facial freckles (vyaṅga), vitiligo (śvitra), epilepsy (apasmāra), fistula-in-ano (bhagaṇdara), abdominal enlargements (udara), menorrhagia (pradara), fever (jvara), artificial poison (gara), abscesses (vidradhi), malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), and heart disease (hṛdroga).

AS.Ci.21.4: Ghee cooked with saptacchada, kaṭukā, ativiṣā, śamyāka, pāṭhā, musta, triphalā, uśīra, paṭola, parpaṭaka, the two types of pippalī, the two types of rajanī, the two types of sārivā, candana, durālabhā, padmaka, vacā, śatāvarī, viśālā, kuṭaja seeds, vṛṣa, mūrvā, guḍūcī, bhūnimba, trāyamāṇā, and madhuka as the internal ingredients; with double the quantity of āmalaka juice and eight times the quantity of water—this ghee known as Mahātiktaka is superior in its qualities to the previous one.
Or, one should drink guggulu combined with the five bitter drugs (guggulupañcatikta).

In cases where *kapha* is predominant, one should prepare ghee by cooking it with *sāla*, *priyāla*, *śamyāka*, *ariṣṭa*, *saptaparṇa*, *citraka*, black pepper (*marica*), *vacā*, and *kuṣṭha*. Alternatively, one may prepare ghee by boiling it in a decoction of the two types of *bṛhatī*, *kākamācī*, and *śukanāsā*, along with a paste of black pepper, *viḍaṅga*, *śigru*, *jātī*, *devadāru*, *kṣavaka*, *haridrā*, and *abhayā*, and using horse urine as the liquid medium.
In all cases, one should use either oil prepared from any one of *bhallātaka*, *tuvaraka*,
or *siddhārthaka*, or clarified butter (*havis*) prepared with *bhallātaka*, *pathyā*, and *kṛmighna*.
Then, for one who has been oleated, one should administer purificatory therapies according to the specific doṣa and its proximity;
and,
considering the patient's strength, one should venesect one, two, three, four, or five veins.
Furthermore, from time to time, he should drink oil repeatedly;
for if the patient is weak and his internal cavities are empty, the wind (vāyu) will overcome him.
However, during the administration of emetics, one should provide him with liquorice, seeds of *kuṭaja*, and the tender leaves of *nimba* and *paṭola*.
Kumbha, nikumbha, and triphalā are used for purgation; one should also administer māṇibhadra pills (AS.Ci.21.8).

The roots of paṭola and viśālā, along with triphalā, each weighing three-quarters of a śāṇa; kaṭukā and trāyamāṇā, each weighing one śāṇa; and śuṇṭhī, weighing three-quarters of a śāṇa—this entire amount, totaling one pala, should be boiled together in water and administered for drinking (AS.Ci.21.8).
After being purged both upward and downward, one should eat meat broth from wild animals once the medicine has been digested.

By this six-night regimen, [this ghee] destroys Pitta, Kapha, swelling, skin diseases, malignant sinus ulcers, hemorrhoids, fistula-in-ano, malabsorption syndrome, anemia, chlorosis, jaundice, intermittent fevers, and pain in the heart and bladder (AS.Ci.21.9).
Alternatively, one may drink clarified butter prepared with the fresh juice of *Brāhmī*, which acts as a purgative for both channels.
Having boiled *āvartakī* to the consistency of a paste in eight parts of water until one-eighth remains, one should prepare a *prastha* of ghee with that decoction and its roots; then,
one should drink a dose of it once every day.
When purged both upwards and downwards, the patient becomes thirsty;
he should then drink cold salted *māranāla* (fermented gruel) once his oily substances have been digested. With that same [diet], he should eat *kodrava* rice.
By this means, leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), vitiligo (*śvitra*), scrofula (*apacī*), fistula-in-ano (*bhagaṃdara*), sinus ulcers (*nāḍīvraṇa*), and the poison of rats are cured.
This is purifying and promotes the birth of a male child.
An asthāpana enema prepared with dārvī, paṭola, bṛhatī, sevya, madana, nimba, kṛtamāla, ghanā, and indrayava, along with fats, [is also recommended].
When the oleation has been properly digested by these very means, an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) should be administered to one who is fit for it.

In cases of skin diseases (kuṣṭha) and parasites (kṛmi) located above the clavicles, head-evacuation (śirovireka) should be performed using dantī, marica, phaṇijjaka, ārdraka, karañja seeds, pippalī, viḍaṅga, and rock salt,
as well as the purgative smoke (vairecanika-dhūma) described in the Sūtrasthāna.
Then, for one who has been completely purified, one should apply pacifying treatments both internally and externally.

AS.Ci.21.12: One should take the heartwoods (sāra) of *khadira*, *kadara*, *tiniśa*, *asana*, *śirīṣa*, *śiṃśapā*, *śāka*, *sarja*, *arjuna*, *jambu*, *karavīra*, *dhava*, *āmalakī*, *muṣkaka*, *akṣika*, *badarī*, *vañjula*, *nimba*, *karañja*, *kadamba*, and *madhūka* while they are still moist; and having cut into pieces thirty *palas* each of the roots of *kṛtamāla*, *nicula*, *paṭola*, *aṅkola*, *balā*, *bilva*, *kuṭaja*, *kaṭabhī*, *pāribhadra*, *sahacara*, *gṛdhranakhī*, *varaṇa*, *vardhamāna*, *arka*, *saubhañjana*, *aṭarūṣaka*, *śatāvarī*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *himārā*, *aśvakarṇa*, *śrīparṇī*, *svayaṃguptā*, *agnimantha*, *indravāruṇī*, *kākodumbarikā*, *meṣaśṛṅgī*, *ṭuṇṭuka*, *guḍūcī*, *varṣābhū*, *vāyasī*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, *rohiṇī*, and *mūrvā*, as well as *śārṅgaṣṭā*, one should crush them separately and boil them in a large cauldron with eight times the amount of water.

Having removed the decoction when one-eighth remains and having strained it, one should cook three hundred palas of ghee in that [liquid]. When the decoction has been reduced to a small remainder, one should add three thousand pieces of *aruṣkara* fruit that have been split open and boil them again; once the juices of the *aruṣkara* fruits have evaporated, one should discard them and add well-powdered [medicinal substances] into that fat.
