Take three *palas* each of the following: *vyādhighāta*, *vyoṣa*, *nākulī*, *mārkava*, *arka*, *kākādanī*, *tagara*, *kaṭukā*, *kuṣṭha*, *bilva*, *hiṅgu*, *viḍaṅga*, *citraka*, *ativiṣā*, *mustā*, *indrayava*, *indravāruṇī*, silver ash, iron filings, *lohakānta*, *rasāñjana*, *abhra*, *śukanāsā*, *devadālī*, *triphalā*, *lāṅgalikī*, *viśālā*, *kumbha*, *nikumbha*, *vacā*, *vārāhī*, *mahādruma*, *kośātakī*, *prapunnāṭa*, *somaparṇī*, the two types of *nalikā*, *paṭolī*, *jātī* sprouts, *tāpya*, *kāravellī*, *kūlikā*, *kandaka*, *saptacchada*, *śārṅgeṣṭā*, *utpala*, *sārivā*, *guggulu*, *śilājatu*, *mūrvā*, *kustumbarī*, the two types of *jīvaka*, *pāṭhā*, *indurekhā*, *vajrakanda*, the two types of *haridrā*, and the five salts (*lavaṇapañcaka*). Then, having thoroughly stirred them all together with a ladle, one should bury it well-protected in the ground or in grain for one month.
Then, having performed the purification rites and auspicious ceremonies, the leper should take the dose in the morning;
once it has been digested, he may eat food as desired, whereby his limbs first experience pricking, splitting, swelling, throbbing, and bursting sensations.

Then, after seven nights, they become healthy again; moreover, by licking this entire King of Formulas (Yogarāja), which has been described as possessing supreme power through its very name, they are restored.
It completely destroys leprosy (kuṣṭha), even when the body has been cast down and nothing remains but a network of sinews;

it also cures dyspnea, loss of digestive fire, anorexia, cough, consumption (yakṣman), abdominal tumors (gulma), severe vāta disorders, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), and urinary disorders (prameha).
This foremost elixir (rasāyana) cures swelling, worms, anemia, and fevers.

One should habitually consume the powder of triphalā, daśamūla, mūrvā, musta, saptacchada, dāru, nimba bark, gavākṣī, citraka, and mañjiṣṭhā, along with vyoṣa, mixed with nine parts of roasted grain flour (saktu) and honey.
Alternatively, one should crush dehusked barley, soak it in cow urine overnight, and dry it on a mat during the day; in this manner, one should steep and dry it for seven days.

Then, having prepared those groats (saktu), one should have the patient drink them mixed with one-fourth part of the powder of bhallātaka, prapunnāṭa, avalguja, citraka, viḍaṅga, and musta, along with a decoction of asana and other such drugs. AS.Ci.21.18 In this manner, for those who have drunk the decoction of asana and others, or the decoction of āragvadha and others, or for those who have consumed old barley groats mixed with the powder of aruṣkara and agnimantha, one should have them drink [the mixture] stirred with a decoction of any one of khadira, asana-sāra, rohitaka, or guḍūcī; acidified with pomegranate and sour vetasa; seasoned with rock salt (saindhava); and sweetened with sugar and honey.
This is the ritual procedure for all types of *mantha*;
one should prepare barley-based foods such as *yāvaka*, as well as cakes, filled pastries, *śaṣkulī*, and so forth, using wheat just as one would with barley.

One should prepare *surā* with rice flour soaked in *palāśa* alkali and steamed with that same alkaline water, mixed with the powders of *priyaṅgu*, *gajapippalī*, *citraka*, *kebu*, *elāvāluka*, *paripelava*, *lodhra*, black pepper, and *viḍaṅga*. This should be placed in a new vessel smeared with lac, honey, and *pippalī*.
Then, once it has acquired the proper aroma and flavor, one should give it to the patient suffering from skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*) to drink.
One should boil the heartwood of *khadira* and *śiṃśapā*, along with *brahmī* and *kośavatī*— the best of medicinal ingredients— according to the method for preparing a decoction (*kaṣāya*).
With that decoction, one should soak rice grains.
One should heat the ground meal and press it as before (AS.Ci.21.21).

Having taken the juice of *trivṛt*, *śyāmā*, *agnimantha*, *saptalā*, *kebuka*, *śaṅkhinī*, *tilvaka*, *triphalā*, *palāśa*, and *śiṃśapā*, one should pour it into a trough made of *palāśa* wood. Then, having quenched an iron ball heated by *khadira* charcoal twenty-one times with that juice, one should pour it back into the juice and cook it in a pot over a fire of cow-dung cakes.

When it has been prepared, one should add two parts of powdered *pippalī*, as much honey, and as much clarified butter; then, when the liquid has boiled down until four parts remain and has been removed from the fire, one should again throw an iron ball heated in the fire into it. Once it has cooled, one should store it well-protected in an iron vessel.
This Ayaskṛti cures even difficult-to-treat leprosy or urinary disorders, reduces obesity, destroys edema, restores a weakened digestive fire,
and is especially prescribed for those afflicted by pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman).

By consuming this, a man attains a lifespan of one hundred years (AS.Ci.21.22). One should pour the decoction of *asanā* and other herbs into a Palāśa trough, heat it with iron hammers, and then extinguish the heat; having poured it into a consecrated jar, one should add the *vatsakādi* group of drugs and honey, store it very securely for a month, and then consume it (AS.Ci.21.22).
In this manner, one should prepare an iron preparation (*āyaskṛti*) from *nyagrodha* and other trees, as well as from *āragvadha* and others.

One should take one *prastha* each of a decoction of *khadira* and *suradāru*, one *prastha* of honey, one *prastha* of sugar-candy (*matsyaṇḍikā*), half a *prastha* of iron powder, and one *karṣa* each of *triphalā*, the four spices (*caturjātaka*), and black pepper; having added these into an iron vessel, it should be left for a month and then administered.

And by the application of *rasāyana*, one [should take] a *tulā* of iron, along with *tuvaraka* seeds, *bhallātaka* fruits, *alambuṣā*, *avalguja*, *guggulu*, and *citraka* according to the procedure prescribed for hemorrhoids. Regarding this, there is also a verse here: AS.Ci.21.24–25: *rasāyanaprayogeṇa ca lohatulāṃ tuvarakāsthīni bhallātakānyalambuṣāmavalgujaṃ guggulumarśovihitavidhānena vā citrakamiti*.
AS.Ci.21.24 AS.Ci.21.25: And there is also this [verse] here.

In cases of kilāsa, kuṣṭha, grahaṇī, prameha, obesity, hemorrhoids, and fistula-in-ano, as well as pallor, swelling, and diseases caused by kapha, the wise physician should prescribe formulations such as mantha and others.
Śāli rice, barley, wheat, koradūṣa, and priyaṅgu; mung beans,
lentils, tuvarī, bitter vegetables, and meat from the arid forest (jāṅgala).
The juice of *dhātrī*, *khadira*, and *nimba*, as well as that produced from *mudga* and *paṭola*, should be prepared by being infused with *triphalā*, *aruṣkara*, and *ariṣṭa*, combined with honey.
Alcoholic drinks containing medicinal herbs, as well as buttermilk (mathita) with a small amount of curd (indurājimat),
are beneficial food and drink in cases of kuṣṭha; however, sour, salty, and pungent substances are not.

One should strictly avoid curd, milk, molasses, products of marshy lands, sesame, and black gram. Likewise, one should take half a *tulā* of the five parts of the *nimba* tree and the heartwood of *khadira*.
One should boil one *tulā* each of *harītakī* leaves and *bhallātaka*,
along with one *kuḍava* each of *kṛṣṇā* and *viḍaṅga*, together in water.
Having strained that decoction, one should place it in a copper vessel;
after six months, one should drink it, and thus one is liberated from skin diseases, worms, and urinary disorders.
This is known as Nimbāriṣṭa, prepared by Varuṇa;
it consists of one pala each of the essence of viḍaṅga, āmalaka, and abhayā, and three palas from the decoction-pot (kumbha).
And this [preparation], when consumed for twelve months by one who has conquered his self,
destroys leprosy, vitiligo, asthma, cough, abdominal enlargement, hemorrhoids, urinary disorders, splenic disorders, tumors, pain, parasites, and abdominal masses.
Māṇibhadra, the Yakṣa, indeed taught this perfected yoga to the bewildered monk whose life was at stake:
[the roots] of kaṭukā, paṭola, uttamā, vacā, nimba, rātri, and mañjiṣṭhā.

A decoction of *kaṣāya* that has been repeatedly processed destroys skin diseases characterized by an excess of *śleṣman* and *pitta*. However, for those conditions where *vāta* is predominant, ghee should be cooked with the decoction and paste of the *kaṭukādi* group of drugs.
One should prepare these separately: khadira, ariṣṭa, guḍūcī, surataru, and dārvī.
Thus, a cold decoction of khadira, when drunk with honey and tārkṣya (rasāñjana), forcibly removes [the disease].
Like a fierce wind dispersing clouds, it [the medicine] destroys skin diseases, throat ailments, apacī, gulma,
and urinary disorders when combined with ghee, honey, the decoction of triphalā, and a paste of viḍaṅga. (AS.Ci.21.37)

The decoction of *kuṣṭha* and *khadira* destroys leprosy, just as righteousness destroys impurity when it dwells within the mind. [AS.Ci.21.38] From the root of a *khadira* tree that has been cut at its head and dug out, one should take the middle-sized root. [AS.Ci.21.38]
Having pierced the iron vessel below for the collection of the essence,
one should place it over a fire ignited by fuel of black earth smeared [with the liquid].

Therefore, the oil that distills from it, when drunk together with honey, clarified butter, and the juice of *dhātrī*, conquers leprosy, fistula-in-ano, skin diseases, scrofula, urinary disorders, and anemia;
one *prastha* of it also overcomes old age. However, in this case, as with *bhallātaka*, one must avoid solid food.
For one who drinks heartwood water (dhātrī-udaka), nimba, śiṃśapā, āragvadha, asana, rohitaka, and surāhvā should be applied in the same manner as khadira.
Either *dārvī* or *rasāñjana*, taken with cow’s urine, overcomes *kuṣṭha*; or else, *abhayā* administered for a month together with *vyoṣa*, jaggery, and oil [achieves the same].
A fine powder of *darvī*, *kaliṅga*, *kaṭukā*, *ativiṣā*, *agni*, and *pāṭhā*, measured at one *dharaṇa* each and taken with urine,
conquers hemorrhoids, abdominal enlargements, tumors, skin diseases, disorders of the internal cavities, vāta, excessive wind, *grahaṇī*, and urinary disorders.

Having drunk for a month the powder of lac, danti, madhurasā, varā, dvīpi, pāṭhā, viḍaṅga, pratyakpuṣpī, the three pungents (trikaṭu), rajanī, saptaparṇa, and āṭarūṣaka, along with raktā, nimba, surataru, and the two types of pañcamūlī, while consuming wholesome food with cow’s urine, one conquers leprosy (kuṣṭha).
Ten palas each of the sprouts, flowers, roots, bark, and fruits of the *ariṣṭa* tree, [to be taken] according to the season.
One should likewise collect the entire [powder] of the *kṛtamāla* tree and,
having ground it, soak it with a decoction of *asan* and *khadira*, and then dry it for use against *vāta*.
One pala each of citraka, ghanabhallātaka, gokṣuraka, mahauṣadha, triphalā, loha, viḍaṅga, avalguja, and sitopalā, having been ground into powder— AS.Ci.21.47.
Then, for one week, it should be processed with the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*.
Thereafter, it should be drunk in a dose of one *akṣa*, along with ghee, milk, or lukewarm water.
It quickly produces fire [of digestion], intellect, memory, dexterity, and intelligence;
it cures worms, skin diseases, scabies, anemia, urinary disorders, mouth diseases, loss of appetite, and vomiting.
It cures apacī, bhagaṃdara, sthaulya, malignant sinus ulcers, and facial freckles (vyaṅga),
as well as disorders born of kapha and pitta, especially those that are very difficult to treat.
By constant practice for a year, [this remedy] destroys the effects of poisons, artificial toxins, and sorcery, as well as baldness and graying hair.
A formulation consisting of the three pungents (trikaṭu), sesame seeds, *aruṣkara*, ghee, honey, and sugar is prepared.

This pill (guṭikā) is a rejuvenative (rasāyana), a cure for skin diseases (kuṣṭha), and a purgative; it consists of seven equal parts of candraśakala, agni, rajanī, viḍaṅga, tuvarāsthi, aruṣkara, and triphalā.
Pills (vaṭaka) prepared with one part jaggery, when practiced regularly, destroy all types of skin diseases (kuṣṭha),
[along with] viḍaṅga, bhallātaka, bākucī, dvīpi, vārāhī, and harītakī.
A bolus made from *salāṅgalī*, *kṛṣṇā*, *tikta*, and *kulyā* with jaggery (*guḍa*) overcomes leprosy (*kuṣṭha*).
[AS.Ci.21.54] [The same result is achieved] with *pathyā*, *kaliṅgaka*, *palāśa* fruit, *indurājī*, *bhallātaka* seeds, *caturaṅgula*, *citraka*, and *arka*.

Pills (*vaṭaka*) made from *sāvartakī*, *krimighna*, and *tuvara* in gradually increasing proportions, mixed with an equal amount of urine, are destroyers of disease. [AS.Ci.21.55] [The compound] *śaśāṅkalekhā* [consists of] *viḍaṅga* kernel, *pippalī*, and the root of *hutāśa*. [AS.Ci.21.55]

Licked with honey, oil, and *sāmalaka*, it destroys even difficult-to-cure skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*). [The powder of] *bhūnimba*, *nimba*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *padmaka*, *ativiṣā*, and *kaṇā* [is likewise effective].
Mūrvā, paṭolī, the two types of niśā (tagara and haridrā), pāṭhā, tiktā, indravāruṇī,
kaliṅga, and vacā— these should be taken in equal parts, with each subsequent substance being double the quantity of the preceding one.
One should lick the powder of dantī, trivṛt, and brāhmī mixed with honey and ghee;
this is the supreme medicine for leprosy, urinary disorders, and loss of sensation.
Or one should lick vārākaṇa and viḍaṅga with oil, ghee, and honey;
or the powder of khadira wood chips mixed with honey and ghee.
One who consumes [this] along with *giriñja*, *tuvaraka*, and *viḍaṅga* in the proper dosage,
eating light, measured, and wholesome food, practicing celibacy, and having conquered the self, shall destroy edema, *kiṭibha*, *koṭha*, vitiligo, and leprosy.
One should throw one *tulā* of the heartwood of *khadira* or *asanā* into a *droṇa* of water;
on the eighth day, that water should be boiled until it reaches the consistency of a paste that adheres to the ladle.
One should take half a *tulā* of powdered *triphalā*, one-quarter of that amount of *bākucī*,
half of that again of the root of *dvīpin*, and likewise equal parts of *brāhmī* and *arkavā*.
Having added two *prasthas* of *lohakrimighna* (copper-destroying iron) and formed it into pills,
this is highly esteemed for treating leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), urinary disorders (*meha*), malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*), hemorrhoids (*arśas*), and fistula-in-ano (*bhagaṃdara*).
One should take ten palas each of lāṅgalī, triphalā,
and iron powder; having soaked them in the juice of bhṛṅga, one should prepare three hundred and sixty pills.
Once it has been dried in the shade, one should eat half a pill there beforehand;
when that has been digested, one should eat a meal preceded by thin gruel with a dry meat broth.
Restrained by celibacy and other such disciplines, one should gradually consume even a pill; after a month, one will become able to act according to one's desire through this sequence.
In this way, one conquers all types of leprosy, even those that are extremely severe; endowed with wisdom, intellect, and memory, and free from disease, he shall live for a hundred years.
Ghee cooked with the paste of vāsā, amṛtā, nimba, varā, paṭola, vyāghrī, karañja,
and udaka is known as Vajraka; it destroys visarpa, fever, jaundice, hemorrhage, and skin diseases.
With one *picu* each of triphalā, trikaṭu, dvikaṇṭakārī, kaṭukā, kumbha, nikumbha, rājavṛkṣa,
vacā, ativiṣā, agni, and pāṭhā, along with a handful of fresh *vajra*-milk;
One *prastha* of ghee prepared with these ground ingredients serves as both an unctuous agent and a purgative for those with a hard bowel;
known as Mahāvajraka, it destroys leprosy, vitiligo, splenic disorders, abdominal tumors, urinary calculi, gulma, and other difficult-to-cure ailments.
The fat of a lizard (lelītaka), combined with honey and the juice of *jātī* flowers,
cures leprosy (*kuṣṭha*); alternatively, it may be taken with equal parts of ghee, *gāyatrī*, and a decoction of *asanā*.
Haridrā, prepared in urine, in the decoction of triphalā, in clarified butter, or in pure water,
acts as a rejuvenative for one who eats wholesome food; it destroys jaundice, skin diseases, and urinary disorders.
Or one should drink the fresh juice of amṛtavalī, pressed out by a mechanical press;
that is purifying and destroys skin diseases, urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, vomiting, and internal hemorrhaging caused by vāta.
For leprosy (kuṣṭha) that has become firm and hard in its patches, fomentation using cloth-packs (poṭṭala) is beneficial;
once the skin has been fomented and elevated, one should scarify the leprosy with a sharp instrument.
Alternatively, for the purpose of bringing out the blood, one should remove the blood using horns or gourds;
or one should scarify slightly with a scalpel or drain it with leeches.
Those ointments for skin diseases (kuṣṭha) which are prescribed for those whose blood and humors have been eliminated and whose internal cavities have been purified achieve success immediately.
In those cases of leprosy (kuṣṿha) where the surgical instrument does not penetrate because the sense of touch has been destroyed,
one should apply caustic (kṣāra) after draining the blood and the morbid humors (doṣa).
In cases of very hard, rough, chronic, stable, or long-standing kuṣṭha, as well as when the patient is asleep, an ointment should be applied after they have drunk an antidote (agada); furthermore,
it should be followed by poisons combined with mantras and antidotes.
In cases of kuṣṭha where the skin is stiff, numb, or characterized by a lack of perspiration and itching,
[one should apply] brushes made from dantī, trivṛtā, karavīra, karañja, and kuṭaja.
Alternatively, having rubbed [the area] with the leaves of *arka*, *nimba*, or *jāti*, or with weapons, or with sea-foam,
or with cow-dung, one should then apply medicinal plasters (*pradeha*).
Āragvadha, saiḍagaja, karañja, vāsā, guḍūcī, madana, the two types of haridrā,
śryāhva, surāhva, khadira, dhava, nimba, viḍaṅga, and karavīraka.
Granthi, bhūrja, garlic, śirīṣa, lomaśa, guggulu, kṛṣṇagandha,
phaṇijjaka, vatsaka, saptaparṇa, pīlu, kuṣṭha, and the young shoots of sumana.
Vacā, hareṇu, trivṛt, nikumbha, bhallātaka, gairika, añjana,
manaḥśilā, āla, gṛhadhūma, elā, kāsīsa, lodhra, arjuna, musta, and sarja.
These six, prepared in half-verse forms and further ground after being colored with cow-bile,
are proven to be excellent when combined with mustard oil; these powders should be applied as plasters in many ways.

When administered, these [medicines] quickly destroy for men skin diseases (kuṣṭha), difficult urinary disorders, fresh leucoderma (kilāsa), alopecia (surendralupta), kiṭibha, and sadadru; as well as fistula-in-ano (bhagaṃdara), hemorrhoids (arśas), scrofula (apacī), and scabies (pāmā).
One should prepare equal quantities of the powders of nimba, the two types of haridrā, surasa, paṭola, kuṣṭha, aśvagandhā, suradāru, śigru, along with sarṣapa, tumburu, dhānyaka, vanyaka, and caṇḍā.
One should first endeavor to rub the body, which has been anointed with oil, with those [herbs] ground with buttermilk;
by doing so, his itching, pustules, urticaria, skin diseases, and swellings will subside.
Mustā, amṛtā, saṅgā, kaṭaṅkaṭerī, kāsīsa, kampillaka,
kuṣṭha, lodhra, gandhopala, sarjarasa, viḍaṅga, manaḥśilā, āla, and the bark of karavīra.
For one whose body has been anointed with oil, these powders should be applied for the purpose of dusting;
thus, ringworm, itching, kiṭibha, scabies, and eczema no longer exist.

Hidden within a large tree trunk, one who has been perspiring in a kiln by means of the *puṭapāka* technique— such a person destroys *vicarcikā* (eczema) with a mass of mustard paste, just as a surge of passion destroys modesty.
Realgar, red ochre, black pepper, castor oil, and the milk of *arka* constitute a medicinal paste that cures leprosy (*kuṣṭha*).
Likewise, the seeds of *karañja* and *prapunāṭa*, ground with cow's urine, [cure] leprosy when applied.
With guggulu, marica, viḍaṅga, mustard seeds, kāsīsa, sarjarasa, musta,
śrīveṣṭaka, kālāguru, manaḥśilā, kuṣṭha, and kampilla;
When these [substances], combined with both types of *haridrā* and mixed with *ātrī-taila*,
are heated by the rays of the sun, they destroy both rubbed and internal leprosy (*kuṣṭha*).
Black pepper, *tamāla* leaf, costus, realgar,
and orpiment, combined with oil and kept in a copper vessel for seven days.
By that [ointment], when applied, sidhma departs within seven days for one who resorts to the heat;
new kilāsa [departs] within a month for one who is purified, even without bathing.
Having burnt a *mayūraka* plant that is withered and complete with its roots, and having strained it seven times,
oil extracted from *kaṅguṇī* seeds prepared with that water is supreme for the eradication of *sidhma*.
Jīvantī, mañjiṣṭhā, dārvī, kāmpillaka, milk, and tuttha—
this is the preparation for cooking ghee and oil; once it is cooked, resin (sarjarasa) is added.
It should be applied with beeswax; by this, Vipādikā is destroyed.
When smeared with the skins [of animals], Kuṣṭha, Kiṭibha, and Alasaka are pacified.
The root derived from *saptaparṇa*, *karañja*, *arka*, *mālatī*, and *karavīra*,
as well as from *snuhī*, *śirīṣa*, *citraka*, and *āsphota*.
Oil cooked with *karañja* seeds, the two types of *niśā*, *vyoṣa*, *aiḍagaja*, mustard, *varā*, and *vella*, along with cow's urine, [is used for an enema].

The Vajraka oil, when used for massage, specifically destroys skin diseases (kuṣṭha), malignant ulcers (duṣṭavraṇa), tumors (granthi), cervical adenitis (gaṇḍamālā), and fistula-in-ano (bhagaṃdara), as well as those arising from vāta and kapha.
With eraṇḍa, tārkṣya, ghana, nīpa, kadamba, bhārṅgī, kampilla, vella, phalinī,
suravāruṇī, nirguṇḍī, aruṣkara, surāhva, suvarṇadugdha, śrīveṣṭa, guggulu, śilā, haritāla, and viśva; AS.Ci.21.101.
Oil prepared with equal parts of snuhī and goat’s milk is known as Mahāvajra;
it possesses qualities superior even to the vajra and destroys vitiligo, hemorrhoids, and chains of glandular swellings.
Kanaka-kṣīrī, śailā, bhārṅgī, the fruits and root of dantī,
jātī sprouts, mustard, garlic, viḍaṅga, and the bark of karañja.
The roots, bark, and sprouts of *saptacchada*, *arka*, and *nimba*; *citraka*, *āsphota*, *guñjā*, *eraṇḍaka*, and the roots, bark, and resinous fruits of *bṛhatī* and *arjaka*.
Kuṣṭha, pāṭhā, mustā, ṣaḍgranthā, the bark of tumburu,
mūrvā, eḍagaja, kuṭaja, śigru, tryūṣaṇa, bhallātaka, and kṣavaka.
Haritāla, avākpuṣpī, tuttha, kampillaka, amṛtāsaṅga,
saurāṣṭrī, kāsīsa, bark of dārvī, and svarjikā salt.
Oil or mustard oil cooked with four times as much urine and with a decoction of the roots and tender leaves of *karavīra* conquers [the disease] by means of these [substances].
When applied as an ointment using bitter bottle-gourd (kaṭukālābu), it conquers skin diseases caused by vāta and kapha,
as well as maṇḍala, dadru, koṣṭha, worms, pāmā, and vicarcikā— these last especially.
Kaṭuka oil prepared with *sikthaka*, *tutthaka*, *guggulu*, *sindūra*,
and *rasāñjana* is excellent for massage in cases of *pāmā*, *kiṭibha*, and *vicarcī*.
Śaileya, kampillaka, paṭṭikāhvā, surāṣṭrajā, sarjarasa,
upala, and śilā— this powder, when combined with fresh butter, is highly recommended for kuṣṭha that is excessively discharging.
When smeared with *eḍagaja*, *kuṣṭha*, rock salt (*saindhava*), white mustard (*siddhārtha*), and *viḍaṅga* mixed with sour gruel (*kāñjika*),
worms, scabies (*pāmā*), ringworm (*sidhma*), *dadrū*, circular skin lesions (*maṇḍala*), and leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) are pacified.
Lac, the three pungents (vyoṣa), prapunnāṭa seed, śrīveṣṭaka, kuṣṭha, and white mustard seeds,
mixed with buttermilk and haridrā, constitute a plaster prescribed for ringworm (dadrū); likewise, the seed of the radish (mūlaka) may be used.
Dūrvā, abhayā, saindhava, cakramarda, and kuṣṭheraka, ground with kāñjika and buttermilk,
destroy even deeply rooted ringworm and itching when applied as three successive plasters.
Realgar, cinnamon bark, *kuṭaja*, along with *kuṣṭha*, *lomaśa*, *aiḍagaja*, *karañja*,
the knot of birch bark (*bhūrja*), and the root of *karavīra*— these powders should be prepared with *tuṣodaka*.

Alternatively, they prescribe a paste to be smeared with a ladle using the juice of the burnt *palāśa* wood, measured at one *karṣa* per *āḍhaka* of liquid; this application is supreme for the eradication of skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*).
Cardamom, *citraka*, neem, *vṛṣaka*, red piper, ginger, and arka—
these should be powdered and infused for eight days with the juice of *palāśa*.
When these circular patches (maṇḍala) are smeared with that alkali produced by cow's urine and heated by the sun, they are quickly broken and torn open.
Nardostachys, black pepper, salt, turmeric, Tagara, Sudhā,
house-soot, urine, bile, and Palāśa-alkali constitute a plaster that destroys Kuṣṭha.
Musta, triphalā, madana, karañja, āragvadha, kaliṅga-yavas,
saptāhva, kuṣṭha, phalinī, dārvī, and siddhārthaka constitute the bath [mixture].
This decoction is an emetic, a purgative, and a restorer of complexion; it is an exfoliant that overcomes skin disorders, leprosy, and swelling, and it destroys anemia.
A plaster made from the roots of *karavīra*, *nimba*, *kuṭaja*, *śamyāka*,
and *citraka* mixed with urine, or a decoction applied as a plaster, destroys skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*).
A paste consisting of the root of white karavīra, the fruit of kuṭaja and karañja, the bark of dārvī,
and the young shoots of sumana is proven to remove skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
The bark of *śirīṣa*, the flower of *kārpāsī*, the leaves of *rājavṛkṣa*,
and ground *kākamācī* constitute a fourfold ointment that destroys *kuṣṭha*.
Of dārvī, rasāñjana, nimba, paṭola, the heartwood of khadira,
āragvadha, vṛkṣaka, triphalā, and saptaparṇa.
Thus, there are six decoction formulations that cure skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*); the seventh is that of *tiniśa*,
which is beneficial for bathing and drinking, and the eighth is that of *aśvamāra*.
These same decoctions (kaṣāyas) are intended for use as ointments, rubbings, and dustings,
along with formulations for cooking oils and ghees, for the purpose of pacifying skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
Sesame, karañja, kośātaka, and iṅgudī oils are said to be beneficial for skin diseases (kuṣṭha), as is the oil from the heartwood of the khadira tree, which is considered the best of all.
Cold applications and affusions, bitter ghee, and venesection are indicated in cases of tissue sloughing,
burning sensations, excessive secretions, eruptive vesicles, and skin peeling.
A leper whose nails, hair, and flesh have fallen away, and who is infested with worms, should avoid food and water;
for six months, he should consume camel's milk mixed with honey.
Eḍagaja with viḍaṅga, the roots of āragvadha,
and the teeth of the cow, horse, boar, and camel cause the extraction of skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
The two types of *rajanī*, *kṛmighna*, *prapunāṭa*, and the root of *rājavṛkṣa*,
along with *pippalī* and *pākala*, should be employed as the foremost remedy for the eradication of *kuṣṭha*.
For vitiligo that is completely purified, a specific treatment should be applied in every respect; furthermore,
when the lesions have subsided, ointments for restoring the natural skin color and likewise massage oils should be employed.
Every fortnight one should resort to emetics, and every month one should also undergo purgation from below.
Cleansing of the head should occur every three nights, and bloodletting should take place every sixth month.

If a person has vomited or purged poorly, he may be afflicted by the aggravated *doṣas* and become a leper; such a case will undoubtedly reach a state of incurability. Therefore, one should eliminate all his *doṣas* completely.
The observance of vows, self-restraint, service, renunciation, and application to virtuous conduct; the worship of the twice-born, gurus, and deities; loving-kindness toward all sentient beings;
and the propitiation of the Jina, the sons of the Jina, Tārā, and the Sun—these uproot leprosy when its stains and sins have been made manifest.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter.
Now begins the twenty-second chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of vitiligo and parasites.
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and others:
"That which is more loathsome than even leprosy (kuṣṭha) and which reaches the state of incurability more rapidly..."
Therefore, for the pacification of vitiligo, one should strive as if in a burning house [to extinguish it],
using *madayantī*, *savāyasa*, *surabhī*, and *āragvadha*.
One hundred palas each of the best [drugs], and three āḍhakas of *varā*.
[The roots of] *vyāghrī*, *vahni*, *kapota*, *vatsaka*, *khadira*, *arka*, *dantī*, and *aindrī* [are used].
To a decoction of these [drugs] weighing ten palas along with two niśās, one should add, having ground them,
the seeds of karañja, iṅguda, śigru, nimba, nīlī, nīlotpala, and candralekhā.
Śyāmā, kirāta, and the three pungents (kaṭukatraya), five āḍhakas each, along with five parts of *pañcagavya*—
this "Great Blue" (*mahānīla*) ghee, prepared over a gentle fire, pacifies [the disease] in no time.
Indeed, it is said that *kḷāsa* alone, when practiced [therapeutically], cures *apacī*, worms, *kāsa*, and *kuṣṭha*,
as well as insanity (*unmāda*), epilepsy (*apasmāra*), hemorrhoids (*arśas*), abscesses (*vidradhi*), and diseases of the head.
It destroys goiters, abdominal tumors, swellings, tumors, edemas, urinary disorders, diseases of the throat,
erysipelas, wasting, wind-related diseases, and irregular fevers.
One should specifically employ purification therapy after the patient has consumed unctuous substances.
For vitiligo, the juice of *malayū* mixed with jaggery is considered the foremost laxative;
having drunk it and anointed one's body, one should expose oneself to the heat of the sun’s rays according to one's strength.
Having undergone purgation, one who is thirsty should drink *peyā* for three days (AS.Ci.22.11).
On the body parts affected by *śvitra*, those eruptions (*sphoṭa*) that arise should be lanced with a thorn (AS.Ci.22.11).
When the *sphoṭa* eruptions have emerged, one should drink every morning for a fortnight a decoction of *malayū*,
*amasa*, *priyaṅgu*, and *śatapuṣpā* prepared with water.
Or one may take the alkaline ash of *pālāśa* mixed with treacle according to one's strength; or the powder of dehusked *avalguja* seeds, repeatedly saturated with cow's urine.
One should drink a decoction of *kalitaru*, *kṛtamāla*, *madana*, and *phalgu* with a root-decoction (*mūlakvāha*).
Having drunk this, the patient suffering from *kilāsa* (vitiligo) should be smeared with sesame oil and, day after day, should attend upon the feet of the Sun.
When the meal is digested, he should eat kodrava grain soaked in buttermilk; this regimen is for three nights to bring about the eruption of pustules.
On the following day, having pierced those pustules with thorns, one should rub them with a wick made of *śukta* (fermented gruel) ground with goat’s urine.
If desired, for pain caused by a sticking sensation, a plaster should be applied; [this] plaster consists of conch-shell navel with water, combined with the three pungents (vyoṣa),
mustard, turmeric, house-soot, barley-alkali, salt, and citraka.

A medicinal paste containing one part of poison and pills equal in size to *kola* fruits is an excellent application for curing vitiligo and leprosy (AS.Ci.22.17). Cow’s urine mixed with *citraka*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), and honey, kept in a jar of clarified butter (AS.Ci.22.17).

After a fortnight, this should be drunk by those suffering from vitiligo; furthermore, the treatment prescribed for leprosy should be applied to him. Alternatively, one may eat the leaves of *mārkava* fried in oil and placed in an iron vessel.

And one should drink milk boiled with *bījaka* for the destruction of leucoderma (*śvitra*). The sprouts of *pūtīka*, *arka*, *vyādhighāta*, *snuhī*, and those born of the *jāti* plant, ground with urine, [should be applied].

By application as a paste, it destroys vitiligo, fistula-in-ano, dadrū, scabies, skin eruptions, and malignant sinus ulcers. For vitiligo, burnt elephant hide or the hide of a black antelope applied as a paste mixed with oil is the best remedy.

Even a single *pūtīkīṭa* worm, when smeared with the alkali derived from the *rājavṛkṣa*, destroys leucoderma. One should soak the causes of eruptions— those whose limbs are shattered— in cow urine at night and dry them in the shade during the day.
In this manner, one should apply a paste made from finely ground *snuhī* with its own milk three times for the destruction of vitiligo (*śvitra*). Alternatively,
there is an application of black snake-bone ash melted in *akṣa*-oil.
Likewise, peacock bile burnt [and applied], or ginger (drībera) soaked in that [bile],
should be given to a white cock for three meal-times while the patient observes a fast.
One should administer a powder of yaṣṭīmadhu, kuṣṭha, and seeds of iḍagaja mixed with ghee;
then, having scraped away the white leprosy (śvitra) with the patient's own feces, one should apply this [ointment] to it.
This plaster, containing *paṭu*, *vela*, *śilā*, *kāsīsa*, *rocanā*, and *kanakapuṣpī*, quickly destroys that *śvitra* (vitiligo), especially when it is located in the private parts.
Alternatively, one may take iron powder combined with cow-bile and the two types of *capalāñjana*;
or *kākodumbarikā* together with *avalguja*, *citraka*, and cow-urine.
Alternatively, donkey bone burnt with plantain-ash and mixed with cow's blood;
or blue lotus with kuṣṭha and rock salt, ground with elephant urine.
Alternatively, the alkaline ash of *mālatī* infused with elephant ichor;
or *siddhārthaka*, *bṛhatī*, the fruit of *karañja* and *kośātakī*, and *guñjā*.
Śukanāsā, sagavākṣī, svarṇakṣīrī, and nikumbha; lāṅgalikī, hayamāra, tilvaka, bhallātaka, and aśvamūtrī.
Mustā, snuhī, sahiṃsrā, suvarṇaśakalā with its fruit,
mūlaka seeds, vyoṣa, pīlu, viḍaṅga, and karṇikāra— AS.Ci.22.30.
Picumanda, jātī-kisalaya, bākucī, tuttha, kuṣṭha, kaṭurohiṇī, manohvā, and triphalā, well-ground together with cow's urine—

One should administer three vessels of the urine of elephants, horses, and donkeys, along with two *kuḍava*s each of the milks of *snuhī* and *arka*, and one *kuḍava* of mustard oil, for the fourth-day fever (*cāturthikajvara*).
The *rasakriyā* known as *mūtrikā*, prepared with a ladle-smeared consistency, cures vitiligo when rubbed and smeared; one does not exceed three applications of it.
It destroys moles, warts, skin-piercing nails, cysts, tumors, and all types of leprosy.
One *kuḍava* of *avalguja* seeds mixed with a fourth part of yellow orpiment [is used].
Ground with the urine of cows, it is an excellent means for restoring the natural color to vitiligo;
or, when elephant dung has been well-burnt and reduced to ash, it should be saturated with elephant urine.
Having taken a quantity of *avalguja* seeds equal to one-tenth of a *droṇa*, one should cook them;
when that [preparation] has become thick, it should be smeared repeatedly and rubbed onto *śvitra* (vitiligo) to overcome it.
Whether it be leprosy (kuṣṭha), a mole (maśa), a freckle (tilakālaka), or any excess flesh (adhimāṃsa) that has formed upon a wound,
[one should apply] the powder of bhallātaka, dvīpī, sudhā, the root of arka, guñjā fruit, the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), and conch-shell (śaṅkha). (AS.Ci.22.37)
Having boiled tuttha, kuṣṭha, the five salts, the two alkalis,
and lāṅgalikā in the milks of snuhī and arka, one should apply that as a paste.
In cases of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), vitiligo (*kilāsa*), freckles (*tilakālaka*), moles (*maśa*), hemorrhoids (*durnāman*), and warts (*carmakīla*),
purification is achieved through bloodletting, drying therapies, and the consumption of parched grain flour (*saktu*).
Leucoderma subsides only for someone whose sins have been exhausted; [this concludes] the treatment for worms.

When the abdomen has been lubricated and fomented with jaggery, milk, fish, and similar substances, and the worms and phlegm have been provoked, the patient should be made to rest comfortably for that night. Then, having boiled the *surasā* group of drugs in urine until it is reduced to half its original volume, [one should administer it].
On that day, one should administer an enema (basti) consisting of that decoction combined with a paste of pippalī, gālā, and kṛmijit, along with oil and svarjikākṣāra.
Once that [dosha] has been firmly established in that very place, one should administer a purgative consisting of a paste of *trivṛt* stirred with a decoction of *phala* and *kaṇā*.
Once the upper and lower parts have been purified, one should administer the sequential treatment combined with the five pungent fruits (pañcakola),
followed by sprinkling with decoctions of pungent, bitter, and astringent substances.

Then, at the appropriate time, one should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) using Viḍaṅga oil. For disorders localized in the head, one should follow the procedure prescribed in the "Refutation of Head Diseases" (Śiroroga-niṣedha).
Food that is excessively bitter and pungent, with little fat,
[should be consumed] along with viḍaṅga, kṛṣṇā, marica, pippalīmūla, and śigru.
One should drink gruel prepared with buttermilk along with the alkali of svarjikā;
or one may drink the juice of śirīṣa, kiṇihī, pāribhadraka, and kembuka.
One should drink separately the seeds of *palāśa*, *bījapūra*, or *pūtīka* with honey;
or one should lick separately the drugs of the *surasādi* group mixed with honey;
or one should take horse dung powder, processed a hundred times with a decoction of *viḍaṅga*.

One suffering from worms should lick [the powder] with honey, or [the powder] processed with the juices of *varā*; when worms have migrated to the head, that same powder should be administered as a nasal insufflation (*pradhamana*).
Having cooked small cakes (pūpalikā) made from well-ground sprouts of ākhukarṇī mixed with flour,
one should eat them and subsequently drink fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla).
Or one may take thin buttermilk mixed with *pañcakola* and salt;
this same procedure applies even to the tender leaves of *nīpa*, *mārkaava*, and *nirguṇḍī*.
Or one may prepare various foods mixed with the flour of *viḍaṅga* seeds; alternatively,
one may mix them with half-parts of *viḍaṅga* grains and keep them in the sun.
One should employ Aruṣkara oil for drinking and for enema (basti) for one day; likewise,
one should prepare the oils of Devadāru and Sarala separately in the same manner.
In two palas each of *tilvaka*, *uddālaka*, *trivṛt*, and *śyāmā*,
add half as much of *dantī* and *dravantī*, and half of that again of *cavya* and *citraka*.
Having ground sesame seeds with the juice of *viḍaṅga*,
one should prepare one *prastha* of oil from that [grain] which has been processed and pressed, using twice as much of the decoction of the anthelmintic drugs (*krimighna*).
One should drink that purificatory decoction at the proper time and administer an oil enema (anuvāsana).
[The preparation involves] the oils of *kośātakī*, *karañja*, *umā*, and mustard (*sarṣapa*).
Having prepared it according to that same procedure, one should cause the intestinal worms to drink it; in cases of worms born from feces, one should especially administer enemas and purgatives.
In cases arising from kapha, one should administer head-purgation (śirovireka), emesis (vamana), and palliative treatments (śamana);
for those born of blood, one should apply the remedies for skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
And in this case, the procedure for alopecia (indralupta) should be applied to those [conditions] that consume the body hair (romabhojin).
Milk, meats, ghee, molasses, curd, and leafy vegetables should be consumed.
In brief, one desiring to destroy worms should avoid sour and sweet tastes;
thus ends the twenty-second chapter.
Now begins the twenty-third chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of diseases caused by *vāta*.
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.

In all disorders caused solely by Vāta, one should employ internal and external oleation and sudation; poultices prepared with *sālvaṇa*; staying in a windless place; wearing warm coverings; meat soups from the heads of domestic, marshy, and aquatic animals, enriched with the "great fats" (*mahāsneha*), mixed with sour curd, ginger, and long pepper; milks, vegetable broths, and nourishing foods;
and frequent applications of bolus-sudation (*piṇḍasveda*) and other methods using those same meats mixed with the "great fats" and smeared with them.
Moreover, kola, kulattha, āmalaka, yava, misi, māṣa, atasī, vacā, and kuṣṭha.
Rāsnā oil and fruits, along with a warm, sour poultice (utkārikā) that subdues Vāta;
and bandaging with the skins of cats, mongooses, camels, jackals, and so forth.
Unctuous enemas and nasal drops should be administered,
and one should observe the treatment for the humors (doṣopakramaṇīya).
For in one who has been lubricated and fomented, disorders of Vāta such as pricking pain, piercing pain, stiffness, and colic are quickly pacified.
Unctuousness nourishes the bodily constituents and generates strength in the body;
therefore, one should repeatedly practice oleation and sudation.
When the internal cavity has been softened, wind-related disorders no longer persist. However,

if they do not subside due to the presence of residual humors (doṣas), then even when the vāyu pervades the entire body— specifically when it is localized in the colon (pakvāśaya)— one should administer mild unctuous purgatives such as *tilvaka* ghee, *sātalā* ghee, or castor oil, along with milk.
For in this way, the wind moving through the purified channels, being unobstructed, quickly attains tranquility;
moreover:

For when waste matter is accumulated by foods that are unctuous, sour, salty, hot, and so forth, it obstructs the channels and blocks the wind; therefore, one should restore that wind to its natural downward course. Now, in the case of a weak patient who requires purgation, one should administer a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) combined with digestive and appetizing substances, as well as food of a similar nature.

Or one should administer a laxative combined with food; and once the patient has been purified, one should repeatedly apply oleation and sudation over a well-kindled fire, along with food and drink that is sweet, sour, and salty.
Even if there is no cessation [of symptoms] in this way, one should administer enema therapy using unctuous substances that are not overly compressive.

For one who has undergone emesis when the disease is located in the stomach (āmāśaya), one should administer the *ṣaḍdharaṇa* powder, followed by unctuous substances and other treatments as appropriate.

If the disease is located in the region of the navel, one should administer fish prepared with unripe *bilva* fruits; if it has pervaded the entire digestive tract, one should employ the treatments prescribed for hemorrhoids and disorders of the *grahaṇī*, as well as the digestion of undigested food (*āma*) and the application of alkali (*kṣāra*) for internal tumors (*gulma*).
If it resides in the heart, milk boiled with *aṃśumatī* should be used.

When [the disease] has specifically reached the ears and other sense organs or the head, one should administer unctuous nasal medication (*nasya*), medicated smoke (*dhūma*), head-pouch therapy (*śirobasti*), massage, and ointments as appropriate, along with measures that nourish the channels (*srotas*). When it resides in the skin, one should employ oil massage (*abhyaṅga*), sudation (*sveda*), and avoidance of wind (*nivāta*).

In the case of blood disorders, cold applications, purgation, and bloodletting are indicated; for disorders of the muscle and fat tissues, purgation, non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana), and palliative treatments are prescribed.
The internal and external unctuous substances of the bones and marrow lead to exhilaration upon the attainment of semen; food and drink that increase semen are beneficial,
whereas if the semen is obstructed, purgation should be administered.
Then, following that sequence, one should perform the procedure mentioned immediately above; furthermore, one should observe the rite for those desiring a son.
However, if the fetus dries up or if there are complications involving the children, one should administer milk boiled with *yaṣṭīmadhuka*, the fruit of *kāśmarya*, *sārivā*, and sugar.
In cases where [the disease] has reached the vessels, ligaments, and joints, one should administer meat-eating, meat juices, nourishing substances combined with fats,
as well as massage, rubbing, fomentation, poultices, bandaging, and thermal cautery.
For contraction, an oil prepared with black gram (*māṣa*) and rock salt (*saindhava*) should be used for massage;
during sleep, bloodletting should be performed frequently,
provided there is no loss of skin luster, for fear of emaciation.

For one from whom blood has been drained, an external application (pradeha) with oil, salt, and soot (gṛhadhūma) should be used. Now, one should treat a patient suffering from apatānaka who does not have drooping eyes, stiff fingers, pain, perspiration, delirium, tossing about on the bed, or outward extension of the limbs.

In that case, having first lubricated and fomented the patient's body, one should administer nasal therapy (*nasya*) with *vyoṣa*, *viḍaṅga*, white pepper (*śvetamarica*), and other sharp head-purgatives (*śirovirecana*) for the purpose of purifying the channels. Immediately thereafter, one should have him drink clear ghee cooked with the decoction of the *vidārī* group, meat broth, milk, and curd;
in this way, the wind (*anila*) does not spread excessively.

Then, having collected the group of drugs beginning with *bhadradāru* which subdue Vāta, along with barley, jujube, horse-gram, and the meat of marshy animals, one should boil them; in that decoction, mixed with sour milk and supplemented with the sweet group of drugs, one should cook a great quantity of fat (*mahāsneha*).
This should be administered to the patient suffering from apatanaka through massage, affusion, immersion baths, drinking, food, non-unctuous enemas (*anuvāsana*), and nasal drops (*nāvana*).
If the wind is powerful, one should bury the patient up to the mouth in a pit filled with warm,
well-heated cow-dung; or, one should have him lie down on a heated blacksmith's hearth or on a stone slab sprinkled with wine, covered with straw.
Or one should foment with a bolus;

or a paste prepared with the fresh juices of *mūlaka*, *korubūka*, *sphūrjātaka*, *arka*, *saptalā*, and *śaṅkhinī* may be applied for massage and other treatments. Furthermore, this [preparation], when drunk by one who has not eaten, combined with sour curd, black pepper, and *vacā*, overcomes *ākṣepaka*.
One should crush the materials used in oil-pressing after they have been saturated with a small amount of oil, soak them in water in a large cauldron, and boil them until the oil is extracted.

Then, having taken that oil from above the water with either the hand or a shallow bowl, one should cook it according to the procedure for preparing medicated oils, adding a counter-infusion of wind-alleviating herbs;
this is Aṇutaila, which cures all disorders of Vāta.

It is called *aṇutaila* because it is produced from substances such as *aṇutaila*. Furthermore, during the intervals between the bouts [of vomiting], one should repeatedly administer sharp *avapīḍas* and *pradhamanas*.
Likewise, by the removal of phlegm through the release of breath, his consciousness will not be obstructed again and again;
one should have him drink the fats of a rooster, a crab, a porpoise, and a boar,
as well as barley gruel prepared with barley, jujube, horse gram, radish, curd, ghee, and oil.
One whose strength has returned should employ all forms of oleation therapy, as well as emesis, purgation, non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana), and unctuous enemas (anuvāsana).

Regarding Tilvaka-sarpis: take one akṣa each of the pastes of trivṛt, ṛntī, suvarṇakṣīrī, śaṅkhinī, viḍaṅga, and triphalā; one bilva-measure of tilvaka root; two pātras of triphalā juice and curd; and one pātra of ghee. Having combined all these together, cook them. This is Tilvaka-sarpis, an oleation therapy used for purgation in diseases caused by vāta.
The procedure for the *tilvaka* [oil] should be understood as applying to both the *aśoka* and *ramyaka* [oils];
this is the method for pure wind-diseases (*vātapātānaka*), whereas in cases of combined disorders, it should be applied according to the specific combination.

When Vāta is associated with phlegm (sakapha), one should drink the powder of *Tumburu*, *Phalābhayā*, *Hiṅgu*, *Puṣkaramūla*, and the three salts (*lavaṇatraya*) with barley decoction to alleviate pain in the flanks;
or else, the powder of *Hiṅgu*, *Nāgara*, *Dāḍima*, *Amlavetasa*, and *Sauvarcala*.
A powder of mustā, pippalī, nāgara, ativiṣā, bibhītaka, and bhārṅgī, taken with wine or warm water, cures apatantraka, cough, and heart disease.
Ghee prepared with sauvarcala salt, abhayā, and vyoṣa, or a paste of rāsnā, amlavetasa, saindhava, vacā, and harītakī fried in ghee, when consumed, [achieves the same].

One should prepare one *prastha* of ghee by cooking it with one *akṣa* each of *śuṇṭhī*, *citraka*, *bhārṅgī*, *śukanāsā*, *nicula*, *mahāvallī*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, *kākamācī*, and *punarnavā*. When drunk, this [ghee] is the supreme remedy for *patantraka*, dyspnea, hiccups, and heart disease.

One should cook one prastha of ghee with four times its quantity of milk, along with the paste of fifty pathyā fruits and two palas of sauvarcala salt; this destroys apatantraka, and for this condition, sharp enemas (bastis) should not be administered for the purpose of purification;
furthermore, one should observe the treatment prescribed for heart disease (hṛdroga).
One should effect the expansion of both the internal and external [dimensions] as in the case of a single dimension;
and in this case, the patient's bed should be placed in a vat of oil.
And the obstacle for these two is even more terrible; moreover,
his teeth and face become discolored, his limbs droop, and he loses consciousness.
One who perspires and has a trembling bow [in a dream] does not live for ten nights; however,
in cases of other [types of] morbid urges (vega), one may survive, whereas one who is stooped and dull-witted does not.
One who is lame, club-footed, suffering from hemiplegia, crippled, or otherwise deformed,
as well as one with lockjaw, should be treated in the same manner as one afflicted by facial paralysis (ardita).
Having applied fomentation, one should bring the stiff or drooping jaws back to their natural position and press them with both hands;
when the mouth is open, one should elevate the chin, and when the mouth is closed, one should depress it.
In cases of tongue-stiffness (jihvāstambha) and facial paralysis (ekāyāma), the general treatment prescribed [previously] applies.

Likewise, one should boil the Mahātṛṇapañcamūla, Vidārīgandhādi, and Jīvanīya groups, along with fatty meats and aquatic tubers, in two parts water until only the milk remains; having strained this, one should mix it with one prastha of oil and place it back on the fire.
Once the milk has been fully absorbed, one should remove it from the heat while it is still cool and churn it; then, having extracted the oil, one should cook it again as before.
This *kṣīrataila* (milk-oil) should be employed for drinking, massage, and other such purposes.
This very milk and ghee, devoid of oil, provides inexhaustible nourishment. One should prepare meat broths together with curd and milk processed with *tilvaka* fruits.
The aforementioned gruels, as well as unctuous nasal drops, medicated smokes, and gargles, should be employed.
One should burn a field of black soil with Rohiṇī wood that is not overly dry;
having smeared it with cow dung and burned it again with Khadira wood, one should remove the ashes and, once it has cooled, pour oil into it.
Having let it sit overnight, one should have that earth scraped out; then, taking that earth along with oil, one should boil it together with the five roots (*pañcamūla*).
Once that decoction has been strained, one should cook it with eight times as much milk until only the oil remains.
This *aṇutaila*, moreover, cures all wind-related diseases when used as nasal drops.

And likewise, having burned [the earth] with the wood of the *pañcamūla*, removed the ashes, and drenched it a hundred times with oil prepared with *vidārī* and other herbs, one should take clay as before and pour it into a cauldron containing hot water. Taking the oil with the hand or a cotton pad, one should prepare a "thousand-fold cooked" (*sahasrapāka*) preparation by adding a thousand parts of decoctions of wind-alleviating herbs, meat broth, milk, and sour liquids; this should be cooked for as long as it takes to complete the cooking. Furthermore, the additives (*prativāpa*) here are Himalayan and Southern-Indian *aśvagandhā*, as well as wind-alleviating substances.
And when this is accomplished, one should blow the conch shell,
sound the drums, cause the Brahmins to recite, and feed them.
One should hold an umbrella over it and fan it with yak-tail whisks;
once prepared, one should employ it for nasal administration, internal potions, massage, and enemas.
This oil, having been cooked a thousand times, possesses irresistible potency; likewise, that which has been cooked a hundred times is called *śatapāka*.
One should repeatedly apply fomentation (*sveda*).

Then, for the patient who has been lubricated and fomented, one should wrap him all over with strips of smooth, soft leather or cloth, four fingers wide, grasping the curved regions while binding them firmly.
Having bound it at night, one should release it during the day; or having bound it during the day, one should release it at night.

At the end of the release, one should apply fomentation using very unctuous *utkārikās* prepared with Vata-alleviating substances. Then, while massaging in an upward direction to relieve pain and straightening the limb, one should bind it again.
In this manner, if there is swelling, one should administer emesis for seven nights; however,
for a strong patient with fever and redness, one should perform venesection.
One should administer enemas and affusions of ghee and milk, as well as treatments that pacify Vāta and Pitta (AS.Ci.23.30).

For a patient suffering from a localized disease whose body is not emaciated, one should first treat him with oleation and sudation; then, having purified him with a mild cleansing therapy, one should administer an oil enema and a decoction enema, and subsequently treat him according to the protocol for Akṣepaka (convulsive disorders) (AS.Ci.23.30).
Specifically, for the purpose of an oil enema (anuvāsana) in cases of combined humors (doṣasaṃsarga), one should administer Balā-taila according to the respective combination,
or one should employ Kukkūṭī according to the procedure for rejuvenation (rasāyana).
In cases of *apabāhuka*, one should avoid massage and meals after the midday meal; in the absence of *āma*, one should administer a fatty enema (*sneha-pāna*).
In diseases beginning with *viśvabhī* and ending with *pādadāha*, one should pierce the vein as prescribed and treat them like *vātavyādhi*.
However, in *ūrustambha*, one should avoid the administration of fats, bloodletting, emesis, purgation, and enemas.

Because of their antagonism with undigested matter (*āma*) and phlegm (*śleṣman*), it is impossible— by means of emetics and other therapies— to lead upward those [doshas] that have settled in the thighs and become stiffened by wind (*vāyu*), just as it is impossible to lead water from a low place to high ground.
Then, having repeatedly observed the signs of pacification and drying there through clinical reasoning,

one should employ dry treatments; one should habitually consume barley, *śyāmāka*, *kodrava*, and *uddālaka* grains, vegetables prepared with little oil and salt, alkaline substances, *ariṣṭa*, honey, and water, along with rock salt (*saindhava*), the *vacā* group, the *haridrā* group, or the *vatsaka* group.
Alternatively, one may take six *dharaṇas* of *harītakī*, or *pippalī*,
or *śārṅgeṣṭā*, *madana*, *dantī*, and *vatsaka*.
Or one should drink the powder of *svādukaṇṭaka*, *āragvadha*, *dārvī*, *marubaka*, *pāṭhā*, *karañja*, and *kūlaka* with honey and buttermilk;
or lick *citraka*, *devadāru*, *kuṣṭha*, *pāṭhā*, and *tiktakarohiṇī* with honey;
or [lick] *triphalā*, *pippalī*, *musta*, *cavikā*, and *kaṭurohiṇī*.
One should administer dry sudations; however,
if the patient is excessively parched, emaciated, and sleepless, one should satisfy them with the meat-broths of wild animals and *śāli* rice.
One should drink mustard oil prepared with *sarala*, *kuṣṭha*, *śrīveṣṭaka*, *suradāru*, *nāgakeśara*, and *ajagandhā*, along with honey and one *pala* of rock salt (*saindhava*).

Alternatively, having ground two *palas* each of *śuṇṭhī*, *citraka*, and *pippalīmūla*, as well as ten *bhallātaka* seeds, one should cook one *prastha* of oil together with one *āḍhaka* of *āranāla* vinegar.
This is beneficial for all disorders of *vāta*, and it specifically cures stiffness of the thighs (*ūrustambha*), hemorrhoids, and sciatica (*gṛdhrasī*), while also promoting fertility.
Externally, for the purpose of exhausting phlegm (*śleṣman*), one should apply a warm plaster made of honey, mustard seeds, *karañja* fruit, anthill earth, and cow urine.
One should also perform applications, massages, and affusions using *saubhāñjana*, the two types of *tarkārī*, *sarala*, *arjuna*, *karañja*, *āḍhakī*, and *gokṣuraka*.
Furthermore, one should exhaust the fat (*medas*) through various forms of physical exercise.
One should cross dry land and ford a river free of predatory beasts against the current;
in this way, indeed, thigh-stiffness caused by dry phlegm is pacified.
And on this point, there is also [this verse]:
Devadāru together with āmalaka and nāgara, boiled in water and mixed with oil, [is used].
One whose bodily movement is oppressed by wind, drinking [this] at will with a rapid or slow gait,
[should take] rāsnā, mahauṣadha, dvīpī, pippalī, śaṭī, and pauṣkara.
Having ground these, one should cook ghee; this is the supreme remedy for diseases of Vāta.
One should boil ten palas each of nimba, amṛtā, vṛṣa, paṭola, and nidigdhikā in a droṇa of water.

Furthermore, one should cook one *prastha* of ghee with the decoction remaining from one-eighth part [of the previous ingredients], along with a paste (*kalka*) consisting of one *picu* each of *pāṭhā*,
*viḍaṅga*, *suradāru*, *gajopakuñcikā*, the two types of alkali (*dvikṣāra*), *nāgara*, *niśā*, *miśī*, *cavya*, and *kuṣṭha*. (AS.Ci.23.37)

With *tejovatī*, black pepper, *vatsaka*, *dīpyaka*, *agni*, *rohiṇī*, *aruṣkara*, *vacā*, and the root of *kaṇa*; with *mañjiṣṭhā*, *ativiṣā*, *viṣā*, and *yavānī*; and with five *pala* measures of purified *guggulu*.
When practiced, it dispels even powerful wind (vāta) that has reached the joints, bones, and marrow, as well as such skin diseases (kuṣṭha),

sinus ulcers (nāḍīvraṇa), tumors (arbuda), fistula-in-ano (bhagaṇḍara), cervical adenitis (gaṇḍamālā), all diseases above the clavicle, abdominal tumors (gulma), anal disorders, and urinary diseases (meha).
One should boil ten-pala portions of daśamūla in one droṇa of water to treat consumption, anorexia, dyspnea, coryza, cough, emaciation, heart disease, anemia, poison, abscesses, and vātarakta.
With one-prastha portions each of barley, jujube,
and horse-gram, when reduced to one-quarter in liquid, [the mixture] should be combined with the Jīvanīya drugs ground together with sugar.
Similarly, one *prastha* of ghee prepared with dates (*kharjūra*), *kāśmarya*, grapes (*drākṣā*), jujubes (*badara*), and *phalgu*, along with milk, cures pure *vāta*.
This faultless [preparation] should be employed for drinking, nasal administration, massage,
and enemas. One should cook the scum of ghee (*ghṛtamaṇḍa*) in milk that has been boiled with *balā* and *bilva*.

A dose of one *śukti* or a *prakuñca* of that [oil] should be used as nasal medication (*nasya*) when wind has reached the head; likewise, fat (*vasā*) prepared from the same ingredients, derived from the *nakra*, fish, tortoise, or owl, [is effective].
One should employ this fresh [oil] according to this procedure for nasal administration and internal drinking.

Having separately prepared a decoction of old oil-cake (*piṇyāka*) and the five roots (*pañcamūla*), one should cook oil with these two decoctions together, adding one-eighth part milk; by drinking it, Vāta disorders are destroyed, especially those associated with Kapha.
One should boil in water one *tulā* each of *sahācara* (including its roots and branches) and *daśamūla*,
along with half a *tulā* of *abhīru* roots; this should be reduced to one-eighth of its original volume over a fire.
In that case, [one should apply] a paste made from *sevya*, *nakha*, *kuṣṭha*, *himā*, *elā*, *spṛk*, *priyaṅgu*, *nalikā*, *ambu*, and *śilāja*;
or with *lohitā*, *analadala*, *loha*, *surāhva*, *kopanā*, *miśī*, *turuṣka*, and *nata*.
A vessel of oil prepared with one *pala* each of [the aforementioned drugs] and an equal amount of milk, when consumed regularly, overcomes difficult cases of Vāta disorders—
including tremors, convulsions, stiffness, and wasting— as well as abdominal tumors (*gulma*), insanity (*unmāda*), chronic catarrh (*pīnasa*), and gynecological diseases.
Oil cooked with a copious quantity of the juice of *ketakī* root, *balā*,
and *atibalā*, combined with no small amount of rice-water (*tuṣodaka*), shall dispel wind located within the bones.
One should boil one *tulā* of garlic bulbs, half a *tulā* of meat from wild animals (*jāṅgala*),
and five *pala* portions each of the ten roots (*daśamūla*).
In a water-based preparation for the feet, one should add oil, milk, and curd in equal parts,
along with one *pala* each of *rāsnā*, *madhuka*, and *jīvaka*.
Miśi, sthirā, mahāmedā, capalā, ativiṣā, balā, kākolī,
pauṣkara root, and aśvagandhā— these should be prepared [as a decoction].
That [preparation] is supreme for destroying diseases of the wind (vāta), and it relieves abdominal tumors (gulma), distension, pain, and colic;
it is beneficial for those with fractured or shattered limbs and stimulates the digestive fire.

One should boil one *tula* of *prasāriṇī*, including its roots and stalks, in a jar filled with one-quarter part water. One should then add an equal amount of curd together with oil, and an equal amount of *vijayā* to those two, and subsequently cook [the mixture].
With two palas each of well-ground *prasāriṇī*, *jīvaka*, *sindhujanman* (rock salt), *yaṣṭyāhva* (liquorice), *rāsnā*, *agnika* (citraka), *yavaśūka*,
and those known as *granthika*, along with thirty *bhallātaka* fruits;

Taken as a drink, nasal drops, and so forth, along with three *pala* of ginger, this [decoction] overcomes all disorders of the wind (*maruta*), as well as leprosy, urinary disorders, loss of strength, mental derangement, dyspnea, bone-splitting pain, abdominal worms, and defects of the seed.
One should boil one *tulā* of *sahācarā* in four *droṇas* of water.
When one *droṇa* of milk remains, one should cook one *āḍhaka* of oil there with ten *palas* of the root-paste of *sahācara*.
Alternatively, [one may prepare a paste] from nata, ṣaḍgrantha, asthi, kuṣṭha,
and surāhvaya, along with elā, nalada, śaileya, śatāhvā, and raktacandana.
When this has been prepared, one should add eighteen *pala* of sugar-candy powder;
that oil, approved by Bheda, [cures] difficult dysurias and diseases caused by Vāta.
It destroys vātakuṇḍalikā, insanity, possession by spirits, epilepsy, hernia, abdominal tumors, heart disease, chronic ulcers, and diseases of the female genital tract.
Two *prastha*s of the decoction of *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, equal in measure to two *prastha*s of milk,
six *palas* of fresh ginger, and eight *palas* of jaggery.
One should administer one *prastha* of that well-cooked oil in all afflictions caused by Vāta.
One hundred parts of *balā*, one part of *chinnaruhā*, and one-eighth part of *rāsnā* [are used].

Having boiled [the ingredients] in one hundred āḍhakas of water until the decoction remains as one-hundredth part, one should cook one āḍhaka of oil with equal quantities of curd-whey, sugarcane juice, and fermented gruel (śukta).
One should cook half a *dhara* of goat’s milk with these paste ingredients, each weighing one *pala*:
*śaṭhī*, *sarala*, *dāru*, *elā*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *agaru*, and *candana*.
With padmaka, atibalā, mustā, sūpyaparṇī, and hareṇu;
with yaṣṭyāhva, surasa, vyāghranakha, ṛṣabhaka, and jīvaka.
With the juice of *palāśa*, musk, *nalikā*, and *jātikośaka*;
with *spṛkkā*, saffron, *śaileya*, *jātī*, *kaṭuphala*, and water.
With cinnamon, kunduruka, camphor, turuṣka, and śrīnivāsaka; with cloves, nakha, kaṅkola, kuṣṭha, māṃsī, and priyaṅgu.
When [the oil] has been prepared with *sthauṇeya*, *tagara*, *dhyāma*, *vacā*, *madanaka*, *plava*,
and *nāgakesara*, one should add [these] once it has been removed from the heat.
Then, that filtered leaf-paste, when administered according to the prescribed method,
cures dyspnea, cough, fever, fainting, vomiting, thirst, chest wounds, and consumption.

This excellent Balā oil destroys splenic disorders, consumption, epilepsy, and misfortune; it is the foremost destroyer of Vāta diseases. One should boil five *tulās* of Amṛtā in two *vahana*s of water.
In the final quarter of verse 70, one should cook two āḍhakas of oil with an equal amount of milk.
In verses 71, [it is prepared] with ela, māṃsī, nata, uśīra, sārivā, kuṣṭha, and candana.
With śatapuṣpā, balā, medā, mahāmedā, ṛddhi, jīvaka,
kākolī, kṣīrakākolī, śrāvaṇī, atibalā, and nakhī; AS.Ci.23.72–73.
With mahāśrāvaṇī, jīvantī, vidārī, and kapikacchu;
with śatāvarī, tāmalakī, karkaṭāhvā, and hareṇu.
With one karṣa each of vacā, gokṣuraka, eraṇḍa, rāsnā, kālā,
sahācara, vīrā, mahā, ṛṣabhaka, and tridaśāhva.
With three karṣas of mañjiṣṭhā and eight palas of madhuka,
[one should prepare] a paste for those whose vitality, digestive fire, and strength are diminished, and whose minds are bewildered.
One should restore to their natural state those afflicted by insanity, aversion, and epilepsy;
this foremost oil, called Amṛta, is the best for removing diseases of Vāta.
One should cook one *droṇa* of oil in a decoction of a thousand parts of *rāsnā*;
when combined with ground Himalayan fragrances and the *elā* group [of spices], it cures ailments caused by *vāta*.
This same procedure applies to aśvagandhā and also to balā and atibalā;
alternatively, one may cook the drugs beginning with balā separately with decoctions, pastes, and milk.
Oil prepared with the juices of barley, jujube, horse gram, fish, drumstick, and bilva, combined with radish juice, curd, and milk;
One should prepare that supreme remedy for all wind-related diseases,
as well as the oil beginning with *agaru* which was previously described for cold-fever (*śītajvara*).

Having boiled one *prastha* of the three fruits (*phalatrika*) and two *kuḍavas* of horse gram (*kulattha*) a hundred thousand times, this prepared [decoction] removes diseases caused by wind (*vātāmaya*). (AS.Ci.23.80)
Five *pala*s each of *kṛṣṇagandhā* and *tvacāḍhakī*,
two *pala*s each of *rāsnā* and *citraka*, and one *pala* each from the *daśamūla*.
One should cook [the drugs] in one droṇa of water until one-fourth remains, adding separately one prastha each of *surā*,
*āranāla*, sour curd (*dadhyamla*), *sauvīraka*, and *tuṣodaka*.
The juice of *kola*, pomegranate, and *vṛkṣāmla*, milk, fresh fat, marrow, oil, clarified butter, and six *pala* of *jīvanīya* [drugs]. (AS.Ci.23.83)
That paste, when prepared together, is effective for disorders of pure Vāta located in the vessels,
joints, and bones, whether affecting the entire body or a single limb.
One should apply that oil massage in cases of trembling, convulsions, and colic. One should boil the bones of animals from marshy and arid regions in water.
One should cook that oil again with a decoction of daśamūla and with jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, āsphota, vidārī, and kapikacchu.
With pastes made from wind-alleviating and digestive-stimulating drugs mixed with two parts of milk,
one destroys that mobile [dosha] located in the vessels, joints, bones, and the visceral cavities through such means as drinking.
For those whose *ojas*, marrow, and semen are depleted, this [milk] is like nectar.
These unctuous substances (snehas), when properly administered at the right time through drinking, nasal drops, enemas, and massage, [bring about recovery]. (AS.Ci.23.88)
They would quickly bring the wicked humors (doṣas) to pacification and cause barren women to possess sons;
when the phlegm (śleṣman), liquefied by oleation and sudation, is situated in the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya).
Or if it manifests the symptoms of *pitta*, one should conquer it with enemas (*basti*).
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter;
now begins the twenty-fourth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of vātaśoṇita (gout/rheumatism);
thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.

In a patient suffering from *vātaśoṇita* (blood disorder caused by *vāta*) who has been treated with oleation (*snigdha*), one should repeatedly extract the vitiated blood in small quantities using leeches for burning, redness, pain, and swelling; or, in cases of itching, heat, numbness, tingling, and piercing pain, one should extract it using horns, gourds, or scarification (*pracchāna*) at intervals along the course of the vessel.
For, upon the depletion of blood, deep-seated swelling, stiffness, tremors, exhaustion, and contraction occur.
Furthermore,

one should not cause blood to flow if fainting and other such complications mentioned regarding venesection have occurred, nor in cases of bodily exhaustion, dryness, or when the blood is dominated by Vāta.

Thereafter, one should repeatedly administer purgatives that are either unctuous or dry, as well as enema therapy (bastikarma). Alternatively, if vāta is predominant, one should drink old ghee or śatāvarī-ghṛta.

One should boil two palas each of the ten roots (*daśamūla*), the two types of *punarnavā*, castor root (*airaṇḍa*), *mudgaparṇī*, *māṣaparṇī*, *mahāmedā*, *śatāvarī*, *rāsnā*, *vākpuṣpī*, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *balā*, and *atibalā* separately in one *droṇa* of water.
AS.Ci.24.5

When one-quarter remains, one should add equal quantities of goat meat, *āmalaka*, sugarcane juice, ghee, and milk; then, having prepared a paste (*kalka*) of long pepper (*pippalī*), black pepper (*marica*), *kāśmarya* fruit, blue lotus (*utpala*), the two types of *medā*, *viśrāvaṇī*, *vīrā*, *punarnavā*, ginger (*nāgara*), *samaṅgā*, *tugākṣīrī*, *kṣīrakākolī*, grapes (*drākṣā*), *kṣoḍa*, lotus seeds (*padmabīja*), *śṛṅgāṭaka*, *nikocaka*, *bhavya*, *ūrumāṇa*, date palm (*kharjūra*), *vātāma*, *muñjāta*, and *abhiṣuka*, one should cook it again.

This medicated ghee, known as Jīvanīya, specifically cures disorders of Vāta, as well as anemia, fever, epilepsy, fistula-in-ano, dyspnea, cough, hiccups, hoarseness of voice, pain in the flanks, diseases of the liver and spleen, urinary retention, calculi, gout, and all diseases affecting the whole body or a single limb.
It is strengthening, improves the complexion, is aphrodisiac, beneficial for the eyes, and bestows progeny.
Alternatively, one who is accustomed to oil may drink oil mixed with milk and sugar.

Alternatively, one may use *balā-taila* prepared with a decoction of *śatāvarī*, *mayūraka*, milk, *vidārī*, the two types of *balā*, and the five roots (*pañcamūla*), containing the *padmaka* group as an internal ingredient;
or the *balā-taila* mentioned in the treatment of wind diseases (*vātavyādhi*).

One should perform a lukewarm affusion with milk processed a hundred times or with milk prepared with Vātahara drugs, or with sour liquids (AS.Ci.24.7). For the purpose of poultices, one should prepare five types of *pāyasa* (milk-puddings) cooked with ghee, oil, muscle fat, marrow, and milk, each mixed individually with barley, wheat, sesame, mung bean, and black gram, along with the pastes of *kākolī*, *jīvaka*, *ṛṣabhaka*, *bala*, *atibala*, *mahābala*, *śṛgālavinnā*, *meṣaśṛṅgī*, *priyāla*, *sitopalā*, *surabhi*, *vacā*, and *kaśeruka*.

An unguent (upanāha) should be applied consisting of a poultice made from the marrow of oily fruits, or from the pulp of *bilva* combined with *tagara*, *devadāru*, *sarala*, *rāsnā*, *hareṇu*, *kuṣṭha*, and *śatapuṣpā*, mixed with curd-whey (*dadhimastu*).
A plaster made from barley, madhuka, castor seeds, and punarnavā, ground with rice-water;
or the root of śigru mixed with mātuluṅga, amlavetasa, rock salt, and ghee.

An oil massage with ghee prepared from the roots of *sahacara* and *jīvantī*, or from a paste of *rāsnā*, *madhuka*, *guḍūcī*, the two types of *balā*, *jīvaka*, and *ṛṣabha*, boiled with milk and containing beeswax,
[is indicated]. When pitta is predominant, one should administer a decoction of *drākṣā*, *revata* fruit, *payasyā*, *madhuka*, *candana*, and *kāśmarya*, sweetened with sugar and honey.
Or one may take a decoction of śatāvarī, paṭola, triphalā, guḍūcī, and kaṭukā,
or ghee and milk prepared with the sweet and bitter groups of drugs.
Or, for the purpose of purgation, one may take milk boiled with rāsnā, bhīru, daśamūla, and balā, either while it is still hot from the stream (dhāroṣṇa) or mixed with the powder of trivṛt.
Or, while subsisting on a milk diet, one should repeatedly drink castor oil with milk;
or one should administer milk enemas (kṣīrabasti) containing ghee along with a decoction of amṛtā, āragvadha, and āṭarūṣaka.
An affusion with milk boiled with cooling substances such as sandalwood (*candana*), *padmaka*, lotus stalks (*bisa*), and lotus roots (*mṛṇāla*),
or with rice-water mixed with milk, sugarcane juice, honey, and sugar, [is recommended].

Alternatively, one should apply a plaster made of grapes, licorice, and *kāśmarya* with fermented grain-water (*dhānyāmla*), or with clarified butter processed with the *jīvanīya* drugs, or with clarified butter washed a hundred times;

or a plaster consisting of lentils, *uśīra*, *prapauṇḍarīka*, *dārvī*, licorice, *mañjiṣṭhā*, sandalwood, blue lotus, and *padmaka*, along with powdered rice, ghee, milk, and sugar. This relieves burning sensations, redness, pain, erysipelas, and swelling.
Alternatively, wheat flour mixed with goat’s milk is an ointment; likewise,
sesame seeds ground with milk, roasted on a potsherd, and then re-immersed in milk until extinguished [of their heat].
In the case of a predominance of blood as well, one should likewise bleed frequently;
in a predominance of phlegm, one should drink a decoction of *dhātrī*, *niśā*, and *mustā*, sweetened with honey.
Or a decoction of triphalā, or a decoction of madhuka, śṛṅgavera, abhayā, and kaṭurohiṇī.
One should gently induce emesis with a drink containing an appropriate amount of oil, dry out the patient, and avoid excessive pouring of liquids or applications of ointments;
a lukewarm paste made of nimba, mustard, aśvagandhā, alkali, and sesame seeds should be applied.
Alternatively, [one may use] vacā, gāradhūma, dviniśā, kuṣṭha, śatapuṣpā, or punarnavā, together with ghee.

Alternatively, a powder of sesame, mustard, linseed, and barley, mixed with *śleṣmātaka*, *kapittha*, and *madhuśigru*, ground with alkali and urine, should be used; or there should be sprinkling with alkaline water, oil, and urine prepared with the drugs of the *kaṭuka* group.
In cases of combined disorders (*saṃsarga*), one should treat them according to the mixture or according to whichever is predominant.

In all these cases, one should habitually consume *guḍūcī*, *guḍaharītakī*, or the *pippalī-vardhamāna* regimen as appropriate, and perform enema therapy (*bastikarma*) frequently; and on this point, there is also this verse: AS.Ci.24.15: In all [these conditions], one should practice *guḍūcī*, *guḍaharītakī*, or the *pippalī-vardhamāna* [regimen] as appropriate, and repeatedly employ enema therapy (*bastikarma*). Thus it is said here.

One should treat the external [condition] with ointments, massages, affusions, and immersions; one should treat the internal [condition] with purgation, non-unctuous enemas, and the drinking of unctuous substances.

One should conquer a condition dominated by Vāta through the internal consumption, massage, and enemas of ghee, oil, muscle fat, and marrow, as well as through lukewarm medicinal pastes, poultices, and affusions.
Vātarakta in which pitta and blood predominate should be treated with purgatives, the drinking of ghee and milk, affusions, enemas, and cooling medicinal pastes.
In vātarakta where kapha is predominant, mild emesis— not excessive— and treatments such as oleation, affusion, and fasting, along with lukewarm medicinal pastes, are recommended.
In cases where vāta and kapha are predominant, or in vātarakta, if a cold ointment is applied,
there will be an increase in burning sensation, swelling, pain, and itching due to the obstructive (stambhana) nature of the treatment.
In Vatarakta where Pitta and blood predominate, cooling applications such as plasters are beneficial;
from hot treatments, there arises burning, pain, redness, sweating, and cracking of the skin.
To a decoction of one hundred palas of Madhuyaṣṭī reduced to one-fourth,
one should cook one āḍhaka of oil with an equal amount of milk and paste-ingredients measuring one pala each.
With śatapuṣpā, varī, mūrvā, payasyā, abhīru, and candana; with sthirā, haṃsapadī, māṃsī, the two types of medā, and madhuparṇī.
With *kākolī*, *kṣīrakākolī*, *tāmalakī*, *ṛddhi*, and *padmaka*; with *jīvantī*, *jīvaka*, *ṛṣabha*, bark, leaves, *nakha*, and *vālaka*.
Prapauṇḍarīka, mañjiṣṭhā, sārivā, aindrī, and vitunnaka— these,
when used in four ways of administration, alleviate vāta-rakta, burning sensations, fever, and pain.
Having added one *pala* of *madhuyaṣṭī* to a *prastha* of oil, one should cook it in four times as much milk for a hundred times; thus it is prepared from a hundred parts of *madhuka*.
This proven formulation should be applied, as before, in cases of thirst, insanity, dyspnea, cough, erysipelas, heart disease, anemia, and disorders of wind, blood, and bile.
When Vāta is aggravated due to the obstruction of its pathways by medas (fat) or kapha,
or because of their excessive increase, oleation and nourishing therapies are not recommended at the outset.
Having administered there the treatment prescribed for severe vāta disorders,
one should then apply vāta-śoṇita (vātarakta) remedies, as well as unctuous (snehana) treatments that purify the blood.
If the deep [wound] is invaded by blood and wind (vāta), one should avoid it;
however, due to the excessive increase of blood and bile (rakta-pitta), it quickly undergoes suppuration.
When it is ruptured, that blood flows out, or if it is suppurated, pus itself; for these two conditions,
one should apply treatment similar to that for ulcers, consisting of incision, purification, and healing.

Therefore, one should treat each of the complications with its respective therapy; however, when there is a simultaneous provocation of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, one should act according to the instructions given and according to the specific disease.
