Medicine should be prescribed according to proximity and according to one's strength; once the *āma* has been rendered free of *āma* through sweating, fasting, and digestive treatments,
[the remedy should be applied].
One should treat pure vāta with dry applications such as ointments and affusions;
when vāta is covered by pitta, one should repeatedly employ both cold and hot treatments.
One should administer ghee prepared with the *jīvanīya* drugs in alternating doses and cause the patient to drink it;
the diet should consist of the meat of desert animals, barley, and *śāli* rice, along with mild purgation using milk.
Enemas with milk, milk boiled with the five roots (pañcamūla) and balā,
and at the appropriate time, oil enemas (anuvāsana) prepared with oils processed with sweet medicinal herbs [are recommended].
In the case of [fever] obstructed by kapha, one should perform sprinkling with liquorice, balā-oil, ghee, milk,
or with water cooled after decoction of the five roots (pañcamūla);
[the diet should consist of] barley-based foods and the meat of wild animals and birds.
Strong sudation, non-unctuous enemas, emesis,
and purgation are beneficial, as are aged ghee and oils derived from sesame and mustard seeds.
When [the disease] is associated with both kapha and pitta, one should first conquer the pitta;
when associated with blood, one should employ the treatment prescribed for vātarakta.
Sudation, oil massage, meat soups, milk, and unctuous substances are beneficial in cases involving the obstruction of *māṃsa* (muscle/flesh).
In *āḍhyavāta* (obesity-associated vāta), the physician’s remedy consists of measures that destroy urinary disorders (*prameha*), fat (*medas*), and vāta.

In the case of excessive unctuousness (mahāsneha) when the [vitiated doshas] have reached the bones and marrow, the previously mentioned treatment applies; however, when they are obstructed by semen, one should administer purgation.
When obstructed by food, digestive stimulants (pācanīya), emesis, digestive fire stimulators (dīpana), and light [dietary measures] are indicated.
In obstruction by urine, diuretic drugs, sudations, and urethral enemas (uttarabasti) are indicated;
in obstruction by feces, castor oil and purgative enema oils are recommended.
Whatever is not antagonistic to kapha and pitta and which promotes the downward movement of vāta should be administered immediately,
even when vāta is obstructed in all locations.
The sustaining enemas (yāpanā-basti) are generally unobstructing, unctuous, sweet, and accompanied by oil enemas (anuvāsana); they are the cause of purification for the channels.
Having carefully considered the predominance of strength, a mild purgative should be administered;
the use of all types of rejuvenatives (rasāyana) is highly recommended.
A linctus made specifically of *śilāhvaya* with milk and purified *guggulu*,
or likewise that of Bhārgava with one hundred and eleven parts of sugar.
When the *apāna* wind is obstructed, all digestive stimulants and astringent medicines should be administered;
furthermore, measures that facilitate the downward movement of wind (*vātānulomana*) and cleanse the bladder (*mūtrāśaya*) should be performed.
Thus, the treatment for those whose vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and other functions are obstructed has been briefly described; the physician, having reflected upon it himself, should perform it.
The wise man should direct the *udāna* upward, cause the *apāna* to flow downward,
pacify the *samāna*, and employ the *vyāna* in its threefold manner.
The vital breath (*prāṇa*) must be protected from even these four [factors], for when it remains stable, the stability of the body is maintained; thus,
one should lead the winds that have strayed onto wrong paths back to their respective locations.
And all types of obstruction, provided they are free from the association of pitta and blood,
are destroyed by one who regularly practices this light elixir according to the prescribed method.
When [the vāyu] is occluded by pitta, one should administer treatments that alleviate pitta and promote the downward movement of vāyu;
when it is occluded by blood (rakta), the same applies, as well as the medicinal remedies mentioned for khuḍa.
Beneficial for pitta, rakta, and vāta, as well as various rejuvenative therapies (rasāyana),
have been correctly described according to their respective etiological factors.
This section on the fruits of Āyurveda is for the immediate destruction of suffering;
it consists of treatment, what is beneficial, wholesome regimens, expiation, and the physician's victory.
Medicine is praised as a pacifier; it is known by various synonyms as "auṣadha.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, the Section on Formulas (Kalpasthāna).
Now begins the first chapter. Now, therefore, we shall explain the procedure for emesis (vamana-kalpa).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and others:
among emetic substances, the fruits of *madana*, *jīmūtaka*, *ikṣvāku*, *dvikośātakī*, and *kuṭaja* are the best; and among those, the *madana* fruit is the most excellent.
The predominance of these formulations depends on the influence of the *doṣas*, the *dūṣyas*, and other factors.

Furthermore, because the *doṣas* and other elements possess an immense number of different states (*avasthābheda*), the formulations for emesis and other therapies, as well as their complications and their remedies, are innumerable. Therefore, this Section on Formulations (*Kalpasiddhisthāna*) will be taught as a mere illustration to show the path of variation to the intelligent.

Then, during the interval between spring and summer, on an auspicious day and at a favorable moment, one should take *madana* fruits that are neither too green nor too pale. Having wiped them clean and tied them in a bundle of *kuśa* grass roots, one should smear them with cow dung and leave them for eight nights in a heap of either barley chaff, *māṣa* beans, rice, *vrīhi* paddy, or *kulattha* or *mudga* beans. After removing them, one should dry them in the sun.

Having extracted well-dried *pippalī* fruits, rubbed them with curd, ghee, honey, and meat-fat (*palala*), dried them again, and filled a new, dust-free jar to the brim, one should store it in a well-protected place. Then, at the time of administration, one should crush an inner handful of those *phalapippalī* fruits— or as much as one deems appropriate— soak it overnight in a decoction of *yaṣṭīmadhuka*, or in a decoction of any one of *kovidāra*, *kacchurā*, *candana*, *nīpa*, *vidula*, *bimbī*, *śaṇapuṣpī*, *sadāpuṣpī*, or *pratyakpuṣpī*, and having muddled and strained it, one should have the patient drink it according to the procedure stated in the Sūtra.

In cases of fever caused by *kapha*, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), catarrh, and internal abscesses, one should induce vomiting repeatedly until the *pitta* appears, as this ensures effective emesis. Alternatively,

one should drink the powder of *phalapippalī* (long pepper) saturated with its own decoction, mixed with a third part of *triphalā* powder, along with a decoction of *kovidāra* and other such plants, in cases of excessive salivation due to strong *kapha*, scrofula (*apacī*), tumors (*arbuda*), glandular swellings (*granthi*), fever, abdominal enlargement, and loss of appetite.
Alternatively,
when pitta has moved to the seat of kapha, one may administer the powder of the fruit-pulp with a decoction of *jīmūta* and other such herbs.

Milk prepared with *phalamajja* (the marrow of fruits) or gruel made from that same milk should be administered in cases of downward-bleeding hemorrhage (*raktapitta*) and burning sensations in the heart.
Or, when pitta is aggravated and thin phlegm has coated the chest, throat, and heart, one *añjali* of the cold supernatant layer (*santānikā*) of that milk should be drunk.
Or,
in cases of phlegm, vomiting, excessive salivation, and asthma, one should administer curd produced from that [milk] or the whey of curd.

Therefore, when the digestive fire is overcome by *kapha* and the body is wasting away, one should consume fresh butter produced from milk that has been processed with a decoction of the six fruits (*phala-ṣaṭka*),

or a linctus prepared with the decoction of any one of the substances belonging to the *vāraṅgvadhādi* group— excluding *ghoṇṭā*, *nimba*, and *bāṇa*— together with *somavalka* and the five *kolakas*, mixed with the powder of fruit pulp.

Alternatively, one should consume a bolus (*utkārikā*) or a sweetmeat (*modaka*) prepared with the powder of the fruit-pulp mixed with a decoction of any one of these twenty-two substances: *reṇuka*, *elā*, *śatāhvā*, *kustumburu*, *tagara*, *kṛṣṭhatvac*, *coraka*, *marubaka*, *agaru*, *guggulu*, *vālaka*, *śrīveṣṭaka*, *paripelava*, *māṃsī*, *śaileya*, *sthauṇeyaka*, *surasā*, *revata*, *pūti*, *aśoka*, and *rohiṇī*.

AS.Ka.1.14 Or, having prepared *śaṣkulī* cakes, *apūpa* cakes, or other edible foods with flour of sesame and *śāli* rice that has been thoroughly saturated with the juice and decoction of *phala-pippalī*, or mixed with a decoction of any one of the drugs belonging to the *surasā* group, he should eat them. AS.Ka.1.15 Or, having cooked the juice of *phala-pippalī*— which has been strained according to the procedure for *bhallātaka*— until it reaches the consistency of a paste on a ladle, he should have the patient lick it.
Or one should administer that electuary with food and drinks,
and one should prepare the food and drinks using the decoctions of those very same [herbs].

Alternatively, a decoction of *phala* (myrobalan) and *majja* (kernel), with an addition (*prativāpa*) of the *vatsakādi* group, combined with a secondary decoction (*kaṣāya-upasarjana*) of either *nimba* or *rūpikā*, cures all diseases arising from *kapha* that result from over-nutrition (*santarpaṇa*).

Alternatively, one should sprinkle the pollen-like powder of *phalapippalī* seeds—well-impregnated twenty-one times with a decoction of the fruits and other ingredients—over a lotus in a pond during the late afternoon. Having left it overnight, one should scoop up the lotus at dawn once it has been sprinkled again. Then, having drunk up to the neck any one of the following—a preparation of turmeric, *kṛsara*, *akṣari*, or barley gruel—mixed with rock salt, jaggery, and molasses, one should inhale its fragrance. Thus, a person who is delicate, accustomed to fragrant scents, whose *kapha* and *pitta* are provoked by the excellence of those scents, and who has an aversion to medicine, will easily vomit.
By this, all garlands, perfumes, coverings, and cloths are explained.
And in the same way, in the absence of fruit, one should employ *madana* flowers and *śalaṭu* stalks.
Thus the prescription of the results has been stated;
and in this manner, one should also prepare [medicines] from *jīmūta* and other such substances.
Specifically, however, *jīmūtaka* is used in cases of fever, dyspnea, hiccups,
and so forth; among its parts, the latex is found in the flowers.
From the fruits, one should take milk-drink (kṣīrapeyā);
from those with hair, cream (santānikā); and from those without hair, curd or the whey of curd (dadhyuttara).

In cases of vāta and pitta, one should drink the powder of matured, aged, and dried *jīmūtaka* fruits— which have turned pale green or yellowish— either mixed with their own decoction or combined with milk, along with milk or sour curd. Alternatively, for a fever born of pitta and *śleṣman*, one should crush two or three seeds of any one of the fresh *āragvadha* group or of *paṭolī*, soak them in a decoction, churn them, and then drink the resulting mixture.
In cases born of pitta, one should take powdered or pasted *jīmūta* with cold water;
in those born of vāta and kapha, or kapha alone, that same substance should be taken with warm water.
In cases arising from vāta and pitta, [one should administer] either the fresh juice of one of the following— jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, ikṣu, or śatāvarī—
or ghee prepared as previously described.
Ikṣvāku, however, is especially to be employed in cases of cough, dyspnea, fever, vomiting, poisoning, and diseases of phlegm (kapha).
Milk boiled with the tender shoots (pravāla) of that plant when it has neither flowers nor fruit is [indicated] for fever arising from phlegm (kapha-jvara) when pitta is predominant.

Furthermore, applications [of these drugs] with flowers and other parts are even more effective than with the fruit, just as in the case of *jīmūta*. Or, one seeking to induce emesis in cases of *kapha* located in the chest, nasal catarrh (*pīnasa*), or loss of voice, should drink the fresh juice of *ikṣvāku* fruit prepared with three times its quantity of milk.
Alternatively, when the seeds have been digested or removed, one should add milk;
the curd produced therein is used for phlegm, cough, dyspnea, and vomiting.

Or, seeds of *ikṣvāku* soaked in goat’s milk are used for poison, abdominal tumors, intestinal obstruction, poisons, goiter, glandular swellings, tumors, and elephantiasis. Or, the pulp of the *ikṣvāku* fruit with whey is used for skin diseases, poison, and anemia.
Or one should consume that same buttermilk when it has been fermented, mixed with honey and rock salt; or one may eat that very same liquor (madhya) along with jaggery and meat paste.

Or one should drink the oil of *ikṣvāku* fruit, or a churned drink (*mantha*) made with roasted grain flour (*saktu*) saturated with the expressed juice of that same fruit, in cases of phlegm-fever, cough, throat diseases, and loss of appetite.
Alternatively, one may use a paste of *ikṣvāku* with meat broth for chronic fevers associated with *vāta* and *kapha* and abdominal tumors (*gulma*).
Or, one should boil *tumbī* seeds in a decoction of two *prastha*s of *bilva* root; then, one-third part of ghee should be added to that [decoction].

Having ground ghee-like seeds of *tumbī* in equal parts with half that amount each of *jīmūta*, *mahājālinī*, *vatsaka*, and *kṛtavedhana*, one should add *trikaṭu* in an amount equal to the decoction.
Having heated it again, one should prepare the linctus; having licked that, one should drink the *pramathyā*.
This same procedure is to be understood as prescribed individually for each of the four [groups] beginning with *kāśmarya*, which constitute parts of the great *pañcamūla*.

Dhāmārgava is especially indicated for diseases arising from stones, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, cough, and the accumulation of *kapha*, as well as for stable and heavy disorders, for *vāta* and *kapha* located in the seat of *kapha*, and for those localized in the throat.

One should prescribe linctuses made with the decoctions of that [dhāmārgava] combined with honey and sugar, along with the powder of any one of the *jīvanīya* (life-promoting) drugs, in cases of *kapha* associated with *pitta*.

In cases of mental derangement, one should administer one or two fruits of *dhāmārgava* with a decoction made from any one of the following: *sumanaḥ*, *saumanasyāyanī*, *haridrā*, *coraka*, *haimavatī*, *mahāsahā*, *kṣudrasahā*, *vṛścīva*, *bimbī*, *punarnavā*, or *kāsamarda*. For poison, abdominal tumors (*udara*), gulma, splenic disorders (*plīha*), anemia (*pāṇḍuroga*), and edema (*śvayathu*), one should prepare *kṛtavedhana*, which is exceedingly pungent, sharp, and hot.
Furthermore,
one should employ the fruit of *kuṭaja* in cases of delicate patients suffering from severe blood and pitta disorders, phlegm, vāta-rakta, erysipelas, fever, leprosy, and similar conditions.

Having processed the powder of *kuṭaja* fruit with *arka* milk for seven days, one should drink it with a decoction of *jīvaka*, or with a decoction of any one of *phala*, *jīmūtaka*, *ikṣvāku*, or the root of *jīvantī*, or with water infused with any one of mustard, honey, or salt; or one should prepare the powder of *kuṭaja* fruit for emesis with *kṛsarā*.
Regarding this, there is also a verse here:
"This is the direction for emetics that are most useful;
by means of this seed, the wise man should devise others as well."
Thus ends the first chapter.
Now begins the second chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the pharmaceutical preparations for purgation (virecana-kalpa).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and others:
among the substances used for purgation, *trivṛt* is foremost among the roots.
Among barks, *tilvaka* is the best;
among milks, *snuhī*.
Among fruits, *harītakī* is preeminent.
Indeed, the root of *trivṛtā* is of two kinds: reddish and dark-brown.

Among these, the reddish variety is astringent and sweet, pungent in its post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), dry, and it removes *śleṣman* and *pitta*; furthermore, through specific pharmaceutical preparations, it pacifies all diseases.
Because it is easily purgative, that which is designated by the term *trivṛt* (AS.Ka.2.3) is recommended for children, the elderly, the delicate, and those with soft bowels;

other [purgatives] are slightly inferior to it in their qualities. [That other variety] is sharp, draws upon the throat and heart, causes fainting and delusion, and acts quickly; because it removes the *doṣas*, it is recommended for those with many *doṣas*, for those who can endure affliction, and for those with hard bowels, and it is designated by the term *śyāmā* (AS.Ka.2.3).
Then, one should extract their root, which spreads horizontally, extends deep, and is smooth; thereafter,
having dried the bark, one should store it well-protected.
One should drink that powder, combined with ginger and rock salt, along with sour liquids or meat broth in cases of Vata disorders;
in cases arising from Pitta, it should be taken with milk, honey, grapes, sugarcane, the juice of *kāśmarya*, ghee, or decoctions of sweet substances, mixed with sugar.

In cases arising from *kapha*, one should prepare linctuses, pills, sweetmeats, and various foods mixed with powders of the three pungents (*tryoṣa*) along with decoctions of urine, honey, grapes, *ariṣṭa*, *pīlu* fruit, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and the five spices (*pañcakola*). Furthermore, using these same substances, one should prepare as appropriate: ghee, sugar, grape juice, sugarcane juice, and *tugākṣīrī*; sweet preparations; sour preparations made from the juices of citron, pomegranate, *āmalaka*, jujube, and *karamarda*, or from *kapittha* juice and buttermilk; salty preparations with rock salt (*saindhava*); and sharp preparations with the three pungents. These should be enriched with various types of minced meat (*veśavāra*) and rendered fragrant with mango juice, the three aromatics (*trijāta*), *nāgakeśara*, and camphor. Thus should one prepare the linctuses, pills, sweetmeats, and edible foods.
And there is a verse on this point:
A cold infusion prepared with the decoction and paste of trivṛt, mixed with sugar, [is beneficial].
A linctus combined with honey and the three aromatics (trijāta) is a heart-tonic purgative. Ajagandhā, tugākṣīrī, vidārī, sugar, and trivṛt [are also used for this purpose].
Having licked this powder mixed with honey and ghee,

one afflicted by the fever of *sannipāta*, as well as by stiffness, thirst, and burning sensations, is properly purged. One should split a stalk of sugarcane in two and smear the inside with *trivṛt*.
Having combined these and heated them by means of *puṭapāka*, one should consume them;
[the ingredients are] equal parts of cinnamon (*tvac*) and cardamom (*elā*), along with indigo (*nīlī*), trivṛt, and sugar.
One should drink a nourishing powder made from fruit juice, honey,
and roasted grain flour (saktu) in cases of diseases arising from vāta, pitta, and kapha, as well as in those with weak digestive fire.
For delicate persons,
*trivṛt* combined with *viḍaṅga*, *taṇḍula*, *varā*, *yavaśūka*, and *kaṇā* is a safe purgative.
Licked from all sides with half that amount of honey, clarified butter, or jaggery,
it cures abdominal tumors, splenic enlargement, cough, chlorosis, and loss of appetite.
And one should rub away many other diseases caused by phlegm and wind using viḍaṅga,
pippalī root, triphalā, coriander, and citraka.
Marica, indrayava, ajāji, pippalī, and hastipippalī;
dīpyaka and the five salts— each one karṣa in weight, powdered separately.
Take eight *pala*s each of sesame oil and the powder of *trivṛt*,
along with three *prastha*s of the juice of *dhātrī* fruits and half a *tulā* of jaggery.
Having cooked it over a mild fire, one should then eat it without restriction regarding the quantity.
It cures leprosy, hemorrhoids, jaundice, abdominal tumors, urinary disorders, enlargement of the abdomen, and fistula-in-ano.
It cures disorders of the *grahaṇī* and anemia, and it promotes virility;
this preparation known as Kalyāṇaka-guḍa is suitable for all seasons.
Equal parts of vyoṣa, trijātaka, ambhoda, kṛmighna, āmalaka, and trivṛt,
together with an equal amount of sugar, are made into pills with honey.
They are recommended in cases of dysuria, fever, vomiting, cough, emaciation, vertigo, wasting, burning sensations, anemia, and weak digestion, as well as for all types of poisoning.
Trivṛt, *koṭaja* seed, *pippalī*, and *viśvabheṣaja*,
combined with honey and grape juice, constitute a purgative for the rainy season.
Trivṛt, durālabhā, mustā, sugar, udīcya, and candana,
along with yaṣṭyāhva and sātala, [should be taken] with grape juice at the end of the rainy season.
In the winter season, one should drink a powder of trivṛt, citraka, pāṭhā, ajājī, sarala, vacā, and svarṇakṣīrī with warm water.
Trivṛt mixed with an equal amount of sugar is a purgative to be used during the summer season.
Trivṛt, trāyantī, hapuṣā, sātalā, and kaṭurohiṇī— [these are combined for purgation].

Having powdered *svarṇakṣīrī* and steeped it in cow’s urine for three days, this formulation is suitable for all seasons; it removes impurities and disorders for those who have undergone oleation therapy.
Śyāmā, trivṛt, durālabhā, hastipippalī,
vatsaka, nīlinī, kaṭukā, mustā, and śreṣṭhā— these, when combined and finely powdered, [are used].
For those who are dry (rūkṣa), it is always recommended to take [the powder] with meat broth, ghee, or warm water.
One karṣa each of the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), the three myrobalans (triphalā), and asafoetida (hiṅgu), along with one pala of trivṛt.
One should drink half a karṣa of sauvarcala salt and half a pala of amlavetasa,
this powder being equal in measure to sugar, with either maṇḍa or sour gruel.
This [mixture], proven effective for removing pain in the abdominal tumors (gulma) and the flanks, should be taken with meat broth and rice once it has been digested;
[it is prepared] with trivṛt, triphalā, dantī, sātalā, vyoṣa, and saindhava salt.
Having prepared the powder, it should be infused for seven days in the juice of *āmalaka*;
this is to be added to nourishing drinks (*tarpaṇa*), soups (*yūṣa*), meat dishes, and preparations with colored condiments (*rāgayukti*).
Ghee prepared with an equal amount of sour substances and a paste of *trivṛtā* is a destroyer of abdominal tumors (*gulma*).
Ghee prepared with a decoction of *śyāmā* and *trivṛt*, or even milk [prepared with them],
[is beneficial]. One should boil eight handfuls of *trivṛt*, including the nails, in one *droṇa* of water.
That decoction, reduced to one-quarter and strained,
should be combined with one *tulā* of jaggery and placed in a jar smeared with honey, *pippalī*, *phala*, and *citraka*.

When a month has passed since being smeared [with oil], drinking [this] cures anemia, edema, and abdominal tumors (gulma). Alternatively, one may drink *surā* liquor mixed with *trivṛt*, *pādākaṇvā*, and its decoction.
One should drink sauvīraka, which is prepared by steaming barley with a decoction of śyāmā and trivṛt, fermenting it with water as boiled grain (kulmāṣa) for six days in a vessel.
Or one may drink roasted, husked, and dried barley mixed with that powder and saturated with water;
thus,
*tuṣodaka* (barley-water) is produced.
For those suffering from fever, heart disease, disorders of wind (vāta), blood (asṛg), upward movement of gases (udāvarta), and similar ailments,
the *rājavṛkṣa* is especially beneficial; it is mild, sweet, and cooling.
In children, the elderly, those who are wounded or emaciated, and in persons of delicate constitution,
the four-finger-breadth (caturaṅgula) [enema] should be employed because it is mild and non-depleting; this is especially so for the former group.
When the time for fruit has arrived, one should gather its ripened fruit;
one should then cast the weight of those excellent fruits onto the sands.
After seven nights have passed, one should extract [the marrow] and dry it in the sun;
then, having extracted the marrow, one should place it in a clean vessel.
One should administer that with grape juice to a child suffering from burning sensations or upward movement of wind (udāvarta);
it is beneficial for children from four years of age up to twelve.
Alternatively, one should administer four finger-breadths of cold decoction with curd-whey (*dadhimanda*),
the supernatant of wine (*surāmāṇḍa*), or the juice of *dhātrī* fruit, each separately.
Or [one may take] ghee prepared with *sauvīraka* vinegar and a paste of *traivṛta*, or that ghee which arises from milk processed with *caturaṅgula*.
One should drink that very [preparation] prepared with the marrow-paste of emblic myrobalans (*dhātrī*) in their juice;
likewise, it may be prepared with *daśamūla*, horse gram (*kulattha*), and barley (*yava*).
One should drink [the decoction] prepared with a decoction of *śyāmā* and other plants along with their pastes;
into that decoction of *dantī*, one should add its marrow, jaggery, and aged [grain].
One should drink that *ariṣṭa* after it has stood for a month, or even for a fortnight,
having discarded the inner bark of the root of *tilvaka*.
Having dried it and reduced it to powder, one should then strain two parts;
the third part should be processed with a decoction of *lodhra* itself.
Having impregnated that portion with a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla) and dried it again,
one should then make it into a powder and drink a palmful (pāṇitala) of it.
In water boiled with mastu, urine, the scum of surā, kola, dhātrī fruit, and juice, along with meṣaśṛṅgī, abhayā, kṛṣṇā, and citraka; AS.Ka.2.46.
One should ferment that [grain] with desert soil to produce sauvīraka; when it has formed, one should drink a paste of *lodhra* made from an *añjali* of that liquid.
One should drink the *surā* that has been produced with a decoction of *lodhra* and allowed to stand for a fortnight.
A linctus prepared with the decoction and paste of *tilvaka*, along with sugar and ghee, is an excellent purgative.
Nectar destroys even a vast accumulation of defects; it brings about the swift removal of suffering. Therefore, one should never disregard it.

It is suitable for those with a soft bowel, the weak, children, the elderly, and those suffering from chronic illness; it is also indicated for abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, poisoning, skin diseases, and diabetes mellitus.
It is excellent for treating anemia, latent poison (dūṣīviṣa), swelling, and for those whose minds are deranged by the humors;
it is covered with many sharp thorns.
Having incised that [plant] which is two or three years old with a surgical instrument, especially at the end of the winter season, one should then extract the milky sap.
Having mixed the milk of *sudhā* with an equal amount of the decoction of either *bilva* and others or the two types of *bṛhatī*, one should then dry it over charcoal embers.
One should drink [the medicine] after making it into a pill with whey, urine, wine, and so forth;
[using] the nine beginning with Trivṛt, Varā, Svarṇakṣīrī, and Sātalā.
For seven days, one should drink [the juice] with milk or with ghee;
likewise, one should eat vyoṣa, uttamā, kumbha, nikumbha, and agni with jaggery-water.
One should also consume a decoction of śyāmā and trivṛt with snuhī-milk, ghee, and treacle.
Or one should drink the milk of *snuk* (Euphorbia) combined with the juice of *kāsāri*, vegetable broth, and so forth;
or the powder of *nikumbha*, *kumbha*, *śamyāka*, *śaṅkhinī*, and *saptalā*.
One should let it stand for seven days in urine at night and in the heat of the sun during the day;
then, having placed it in the milk of the *snuk* plant, one should sprinkle a garland or a garment with that [mixture].
One who strikes [the abdomen] and wraps [it with a cloth], having a soft bowel, is purged. The fruit of *śaṅkhinī* should be taken when not too dry and dehusked.

Likewise, one should employ the root of *saptalā*, for they are sharp and purgative; one should prescribe them in cases of phlegmatic diseases, abdominal enlargements, poisons, swellings, and the like.
A bolus of the size of an akṣa fruit, mixed with wine and salt,
should be administered for heart disease caused by vāta and kapha; one should apply it similarly for abdominal tumors (gulma) as well.
Two parts of conch-shell powder and one part of sesame paste should be pressed with a decoction of *harītakī* to produce oil, which one should then drink.
This same procedure applies to linseed, mustard, castor,
and *karañja* as well. The root of *dantī* and *dravantī* is firm and thick like an elephant’s tusk.
Slightly copper-colored, dark, sharp, hot, acting quickly, and causing dilation;
it pacifies the severely provoked vāta and dissolves yellow phlegm (pitta-śleṣman).
Having smeared that with honey and long pepper, one should steam it between layers of clay and kuśa grass and dry it in the sun;
for fire and the sun destroy its bitterness. One should drink it with whey, wine, buttermilk, the juice of *pīlu*, or fermented liquors.

One with a body afflicted by excessive secretions, one suffering from abdominal tumors (gulma), one with urinary disorders (prameha), one with abdominal enlargement (jaṭhara), one with edema (śotha), one with anemia (pāṇḍu), one with intestinal worms (kṛmikoṣṭha), and one with fistula-in-ano (bhagaṃdara) [should be treated with the meat juices of wild animals, goats, and sheep].
This ghee, prepared with the decoction and paste [of the aforementioned drugs] along with the juice of daśamūla,
conquers erysipelas (visarpa), abscesses (vidradhi), impetigo (alajī), burning sensations in the armpits (kakṣyādāha), and similar ailments.
Oil, however, [cures] abdominal tumors, urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, constipation, phlegm, and wind;
while the great unctuous substance (mahāsneha) [remedies] the obstruction of feces, semen, and flatus, as well as pain caused by wind.
A prepared linctus made from *dantī* and *ajaśṛṅgī*, combined with molasses, honey, and ghee,
is used for purgation and cures burning sensations, fever, and urinary disorders.
In fever characterized by excessive thirst and dominated by pitta, that same preparation should be made with ajagandhā;
then, one should boil the roots of dantī and dravantī in the juice of āmalakī.
This electuary, prepared with three parts of treacle and two parts of *śyāmā* and other drugs ground into a paste, fried in either oil or ghee, is an effective purgative.
Likewise, one may take the powders of *pathyā*, *akṣa*, and *daśamūla* separately with their respective juices;
the powder of these two, equal in measure to *biḍa* salt, should be saturated with that same juice.

In a gulma arising from vāta that is obstructed by feces (vibaddha), [food] combined with sour substances is beneficial; one should also prepare soups and other dishes using the roots of mudga and other pulses.
[One may also use] dantī, dravantī, marica, svarṇakṣīrī, and yavāsaka.

One should take a powder of dry ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), long pepper (*agnika*), and black cumin (*pṛthvīkā*), which has been soaked in urine for seven days; this should be consumed with clarified butter (*ājya*), and once it is digested, a satiating drink (*tarpaṇa*) should be taken.
This is beneficial at all times for all diseases, for the young and the old;
it is also useful in cases of indigestion from poor eating, abdominal pain due to dust, and in disorders of the gulma, spleen, and abdomen.
This is recommended for cervical adenitis (gaṇḍamālā), disorders of Vāta, and anemia (pāṇḍuroga).
In this formulation, there should be eight palas of jaggery and twenty palas of harītakī, one pala each [of the other ingredients].
Having prepared one *karṣa* each of *dantī* and *citraka*, and ten *karṣas* each of *pippalī* and *trivṛt*,
one should administer a single bolus (*modaka*) on every tenth day.
Drinking warm water after eating, one should consume all of these according to this procedure;
they are free from contraindications and are destroyers of all diseases.
These nine, beginning with trivṛt, are especially beneficial for grahaṇī, anemia, itching, urticaria, and hemorrhoids; they are considered the foremost among purgatives.
One should also prepare *harītakī* according to the method for *trivṛt*;
it specifically removes disorders of the *grahaṇī*, edema, anemia, urinary disorders, and abdominal enlargement.
One should drink *pathyā* (harītakī) together with rock salt (*saindhava*), *viḍaṅga*, black pepper (*uṣaṇa*), and ginger (*nāgara*) with urine;
or one should take *harītakī* with a decoction of the *vatsaka*-group of drugs.
Or one should consume a powder of *pathyā* and *nāgara* combined with the fruits of *nīlinī*,
along with jaggery; thereafter, one should drink lukewarm water.
Pills should be prepared from *pathyā* and *trivṛt*, soaked in grape juice;
when dried and made into a paste with ghee, they should be licked in the measure of a *māṣa* by one suffering from consumption.
Haritaki, trivṛt, and the two salts (sauvarcala and viḍa), taken with warm water, are desired as a purgative in all cases.
One should prepare boluses from powdered haritaki that has been processed with snuhī milk.
One should have the patient lick the dried kernels of the *kola* fruit, the size of a plum stone, with fresh butter;

this cures abdominal tumors (*gulma*), enlargement of the spleen or liver (*yakṛt-plīha*), colic, flatulence, and constipation. One should likewise lick *kuṣṭha* combined with the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*) along with castor oil.
One should drink lukewarm water; this is a pleasant purgative.
It ensures that even a small dose has great efficacy, while a large dose produces only a mild effect.
One should prepare [this] by means of the techniques of combination, separation, time,
and processing, using cinnamon, saffron, *āmrātaka*, pomegranate, cardamom, sugar candy, honey, and *mātuluṅga*.
Purgatives should be administered combined with wine and other substances that are pleasing to the mind;
thus ends the second chapter.
Now begins the third chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "The Successful Management of Complications Arising from Emesis and Purgation."
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and others:

"Emesis that is drunk by one who is excessively hungry, who has an extremely soft digestive tract, who has little phlegm, or who finds it difficult to vomit; or when taken in too small a dose, in too large a dose, with a sharp or very cold preparation, or during indigestion, goes downwards."
In that case, there is the failure to obtain the desired result and the aggravation of the doshas;
therefore, having quickly re-uncted him again with appropriate [medicines], one should induce emesis while considering the proper dose, time, and other factors,
and one should avoid those things previously mentioned that cause complications, keeping them in mind.

In one suffering from indigestion or having an excess of *śleṣman*, if a purgative or another medicine that is excessively hot, sharp, salty, or unpalatable is administered in an excessive dose, it moves upward; in that case,
the complications previously mentioned and their treatment apply.

After that, even if the medicine rises upward, one should not administer a third dose of medicine— excluding electuaries and boluses— for a person with a hard bowel (krūrakoṣṭha). For such a person, an extremely sharp-tipped medicine, whether of small or weak potency, administered for upward or downward evacuation, undergoes digestion like food.
In that case, the aggravated doshas, if not expelled at the proper time, cause confusion;
one should administer a large quantity of potent medicine to a person with unctuous bowels.

Alternatively, a decoction that is small in dose, not fresh, or dry, when drunk by one who has not undergone oleation and sudation, or due to a cold regimen, becomes stagnant and entangled with the doshas, resulting in inadequate administration (ayoga).
In that regard, if emesis has not occurred, one should induce emesis again;
if purgation has not occurred, one should administer oleation and sudation and then induce purgation once more.
Or, if many morbid humors (doṣas) are aggravated, on the third day one should foment both types of patients with salted oil and bolus-fomentation (piṇḍasveda) or bed-fomentation (prastarasveda).

For one who has been oleated and sweated, if purgation is administered without first performing emesis— whether the patient has ingested [purgative medicine] while still possessing undigested matter (sāma), or has been only mildly purged— the result is excessive heaviness and rigidity of the abdomen, colic, and obstruction of flatus, urine, and feces in the lower part of the body.

Having first treated even that non-yogic patient with sharp emetics and having fed him with meat-broths from wild animals (*jāṅgala*), one should administer an oil enema (*anuvāsana*) prepared with *phaladāru* and *pippalī*, and after lubricating him with unctuous substances that alleviate *vāta*, one should again purge him with sharp purgatives.

(AS.Ka.3.6) In a patient dominated by *kapha*, who has been excessively oleated, whose digestive tract (*koṣṭha*) is heavy, or whose digestive fire (*agni*) is weak, a mild medicine administered will greatly agitate the *doṣas* and produce numbness, drowsiness, debility, and a sense of physical exhaustion. (AS.Ka.3.7)
One should quickly scarify that [area],
and once the digestive fire has been stimulated by fasting, one should again cleanse it with sharp and hot unctuous substances.

If a cold or dry medicine is administered to one who has undigested food remaining, or who suffers from wind and phlegm, is parched, afflicted with upward-moving wind (udāvarta), or has weak digestion, it causes severe distension. In that condition,

due to the obstruction of the waste matter, the abdomen becomes distended, accompanied by internal pain like that of a leather bag being filled, fullness in the flanks, pain in the head and back, dyspnea, cough, and piercing pain in the anus and bladder.
One should treat that udāvarta with emesis, purgation, oleation, massage, sudation, suppositories, digestive stimulants, powders, and enema therapies (basti).

When a strong medicine is administered to one who is emaciated, weak, with a soft bowel and weak digestive fire, or who is dry, unoleated, or suffering from undigested toxins (sāma), it vitiates the pitta and vāyu, resulting in parikartikā (cutting pain).
In that condition, there is burning and cutting pain in the navel, bladder, anus, and penis, along with the retention of flatus and constipation;
one should treat this with picchā-basti enemas containing black sesame, madhuka, and honey.

Alternatively, once he has been sprinkled with cold water and has eaten with milk boiled from milky trees (kṣīrivṛkṣa), one should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) using the scum of ghee, or madhuka oil; and for one who is emaciated,
every sweet and nourishing (bṛṃhaṇa) procedure is desired.
In the presence of *sāma* (undigested toxins), fasting, digestive stimulants, and light, dry, and hot food and drink are indicated.
Once the residual *anubandha* has become free of *sāma*, light alkaline and sour substances are prescribed.

In cases of *savāta* (with wind), one should always employ curd-cream (*dadhisāra*) mixed with sour [substances] and pomegranate bark in food and drink; or one should drink ghee with pomegranate juice, or a paste of sesame and *devadāru* with warm water. In a person with a hard bowel (*krūrakoṣṭha*) and abundant morbid humors (*bahudoṣa*), a purificatory treatment (*śodhana*) that is mild, ununctuous, or of little potency, though it agitates the humors, does not eliminate them.

When it flows out in very small quantities mixed with pitta and kapha, it produces constipation, heaviness, swelling, itching, pallor, lassitude of the limbs, abdominal tumors (gulma), and colic; in such a case,
one should administer an asthapana enema using decoctions of tiniśa, dhava, aśvakarṇa, palāśa, and balā, combined with honey.
Furthermore, when the flow [of secretions] has been pacified and the body is moistened, one should purify it with sharp [medicines];
once purified, one should administer digestive stimulants such as powders, *āsava*, *ariṣṭa*, and so forth.
When one who has drunk medicine experiences a sudden impulse or suppresses it,
then diarrhea arises for him.
In that condition, the patient passes stool accompanied by a burning sensation and colic, with a copious discharge of phlegm that is white, black, or red;
one should treat this according to the procedure for *parisrava*.

When the medicine has been ingested, the suppression of its eructation, vomiting, and other such effects causes the Vāta and other doshas to become aggravated; having reached the heart, they bring about a terrible constriction of the heart (*hṛdgraha*).

Then, due to the affliction of the vital organs (*pradhāna-marma*), he is excessively tormented by pains; accompanied by delusion, hiccups, coughing, salivation, and pain in the flanks, he trembles, loses consciousness, grinds his teeth, and with upturned eyes, devours his own tongue.
They call that the "approach to the heart.

For this condition, the physician, acting quickly and without confusion, should first apply an oil massage, then foment the area with grain-sweat (dhānyasveda), and finally administer a sharp pressed-out snuff (avapīḍa).
One should induce emesis with rice-water mixed with yaṣṭīmadhuka or with pungent substances for one in whom kapha predominates;
thereafter, one should digest the remaining morbid humors with digestive (pācanīya) drugs according to the specific aggravation of each humor and administer enemas.

If a dry medicine is administered in excessive quantity by one who is ununctuous, whose body is not perspiring, who does not practice celibacy, who suppresses natural urges, or who has a soft digestive tract or is delicate, it provokes the *vāyu* due to excessive purgation;
by that, a seizing of all the limbs occurs.

Due to its specific aggravation, there may occur pain, fainting, giddiness, near-unconsciousness, stiffness, pricking, splitting, twisting, and loss of consciousness in the sides, back, hips, neck, and thighs.
Having anointed the patient and fomented him with grains, one should administer an oil enema (anuvāsana) using oil cooked with licorice (yaṣṭīmadhuka),
along with Vata-alleviating food and drink.

If medicine that is too sharp or administered in excessive quantity is given to one who has been lubricated and fomented, whose bowels are very soft, or who is hungry, it may expel all the impurities (malas) and, having liquefied the tissues (dhātus), cause them to flow out through over-action (atiyoga). In such a case,

one should massage the patient with *śatadhauta-ghṛta* (clarified butter washed a hundred times) and stabilize the discharge daily by means of pastes, affusions, immersions, food, and drinks that are astringent, sweet, and cold, and containing sugar and honey.
One should have the patient drink parched grain flour (lāja-saktu) mixed with sandalwood, añjana, uśīra, goat’s blood, and cold water;

one should also administer thick enemas (picchā-basti) to him, as well as milk-ghee prepared with the drugs of the sweet group (madhura-varga), and an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) consisting of the scum of ghee (sarpir-maṇḍa).
One should also apply the treatment for *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders),
especially in the case of excessive vomiting; in such instances, one should drink a *mantha* (gruel) made with fruit juices, ghee, sugar, and honey.

One should administer at the mealtime a gruel prepared with the sprouts of milky trees mixed with honey, or milk processed with astringent (saṃgrāhin) substances, or milk itself. In the case of vomiting accompanied by eructation, one should lick a paste of dhanika, madhūka, madhurasā, mustā, and añjana with honey.

In cases of obstruction of speech, lockjaw, and affliction by Vāta, one should drink a thin gruel (peyā) prepared with ghee, meat broth, and a small amount of rice; furthermore, one should apply oleation and sudation therapies.
In the event of the tongue being retracted, one should administer unctuous, sour, and salty gargles and mouth-rinses, as well as pleasing meat broths of goat.
And one should have him eat sour fruits in front of him.
Once his tongue has protruded, one should cause it to re-enter while it is smeared with a paste of sesame and grapes, or rubbed with a powder of the three pungents (vyoṣa) and salt.
If the eyes are turned back and have been smeared with ghee, one should press them while making the unconscious person hear the sounds of Sāman chants and the flute.

In the case of excessive purgation, one should induce vomiting with rice-water mixed with honey; or one should drink a powder of the *priyaṅgu* group with rice-water, or the juice of *rodhra*, *rasāñjana*, and the bark of *dāḍima*.
Alternatively, one may take *somavalkala*, *ṭphala*, *utpala*, *samaṅgā*, *padmakesara*,
or the bark of *kṣaudra*, *śarkarā*, *madhuka*, and *auḍumbara*.
One should also perform the treatment for bloody diarrhea;
having anointed the prolapsed rectum, fomented it, and stabilized it with decoctions, one should cause it to re-enter.
And as before, one should accomplish the obstruction of speech and so forth; furthermore,
in both cases for the purpose of knowing the living blood and the *rakta-pitta*, one should insert a white cotton wick or cloth into the blood.
In that vessel, which has been cleaned by washing with lukewarm water, one should recognize *jīvarakta* (living blood) as being discolored, whereas *raktapitta* (blood-bile) is of its natural color;
or one may give it to a dog or a crow to determine.

If he has eaten that [poison], one should diagnose it as *jīva*; if he has not eaten it, it is *pitta*. Until death, for one afflicted by thirst, fainting, and intoxication, one should administer treatments that subdue *pitta* and those prescribed for excessive administration (*atiyoga*).
One should quickly administer the blood of an antelope or other such animals, mixed with honey, according to the prescribed method;
for that indeed immediately joins together the vital breath (*jīva*).

Alternatively, one should administer a cold enema (*basti*) consisting of milk boiled with *śyāmāka*, *kāśmarya*, *madhuka*, *dūrvā*, and *uśīra*, combined with the scum of ghee (*ghṛtamaṇḍa*) and collyrium (*añjana*).

In the remaining cases as well— namely, the complications arising from improperly administered emesis and purgation— one should treat them by considering the disease, the *doṣas*, and other factors, and one should also consult the "Success in the Treatment of Enema Complications" (*Bastivyāpatsiddhi*).
Likewise, in the case of a dual-cleansing (*ubhayatobhāga*) procedure, one should act according to the specific condition.
Whatever cutting pain occurs in purgation is equivalent to the irritation of the throat in emesis;
whatever downward discharge occurs is equivalent to the expectoration of phlegm; and whatever downward gushing occurs is equivalent to dry eructation.
And in this regard, it is said:
"Excessive, untimely, deficient, or lacking in equal potency.
Medicine that is improperly prepared will certainly cause decay and harm; likewise,
an emetic that is difficult to induce vomiting with, or a purgative that is difficult to purge with, will fail to achieve its purpose.
If one administers the medicine again, it will indeed destroy those two;
for that which was drunk mixed with phlegm moves downward in a person who is subject to downward movement.

Once he has been purified by the emesis of mouthfuls and has undergone fasting, one should have him drink [the medicine]. If the doshas are obstructed, scanty, or take a long time to flow out, he should drink warm water.
By this, flatulence, vomiting, thirst, and constipation are quickly pacified;
however, if the medicine is obstructed by the *doṣas*, it does not move upward or downward.
In that case, one should apply sudation accompanied by eructation or pain in the limbs;
for one who has been properly purged, if eructation persists, one should quickly administer an emetic as medicine.
If there is no movement [of the medicine] due to indigestion, the physician should suppress it with very cold substances. Sometimes the medicine remains stuck in the chest, obstructed by phlegm.
When the phlegm (śleṣman) has been depleted, it flows forth in the evening or at night;
it also occurs when dry food has been digested, or when [the humors] remain stationary or have moved upward.

If the medicine is digested while accompanied by thirst, delusion, giddiness, fainting, and so forth, one should drink another medicine containing unctuous substances and salt under the influence of Vāyu.
In that condition, a medicine that is bitter, sweet, and cold is recommended.
When [the channels] are obstructed by kapha, there is salivation, nausea, constipation, and horripilation.

In that case, a medicine that is sharp, hot, pungent, and so forth is beneficial for subduing *kapha*. Its movement is contrary [to its nature], its digestion is heavy, and it is characterized by a sense of constriction and heaviness.
Aggravation of the humors, excessive flatulence, cutting pain,
discharge, dysentery, cardiac oppression, and the seizing of all the limbs.

Together with the outflow of the bodily constituents (*dhātu-srava*), these twelve complications (*vyāpad*) have been described along with their causes as arising from the failure of the prescribed procedure (*vidhi-vibhraṃśa*) in both types of purgation (*virecana*).
Furthermore, when those various complications arise through the failure of the purification process (*saṃśodhana-vibhrama*), [the following measures should be taken].
"By this very method, one should strive quickly for success; for the science of light [astrology] is the guide among right and wrong courses.
Thus ends the third chapter.
Now begins the fourth chapter. Now, therefore, we shall explain the pharmaceutical preparations for enemas (bastikalpa).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and others:
"Take one *pala* each of *balā*, *guḍūcī*, *triphalā*, *sārāsnā*, and the two sets of five roots (*pañcamūla*)."
One should boil eight fruits and half a *tulā* of goat meat in water until one-fourth remains; then,
having purified it with *yavānī*, fruit (*phala*), *bilva*, *kuṣṭha*, *vacā*, *śatāhvā*, *ghana*, and *pippalī*.
This enema, prepared with the pastes of [medicinal] drugs combined with jaggery, honey, ghee, oil, salt, and made pleasantly warm,
is supreme for crushing all diseases; it is beneficial for those in good health, promoting longevity and nourishment.
In whatever [case] the *kalka* is not prescribed, one should administer this very [mixture] everywhere;
it consists of the juice of the ten roots (*daśamūla*) combined with sour liquids, along with goat meat and the aforementioned pastes.

This excellent non-unctuous enema (nirūha), prepared from bala, paṭolī, the minor pentaroots (laghupañcamūla), trāyamāṇā, eraṇḍa, and barley, is declared to remove all diseases caused by vāyu when combined with the three unctuous substances (trisneha).
One *prastha* of the juice [of *priyaṅgu*] should be combined with half a *prastha* of goat’s milk and cooked until it reaches the volume of one *prastha* again;
this should then be mixed with a paste of *priyaṅgu*, black pepper (*kṛṣṇā*), and *ghana*, along with oil, ghee, honey, and rock salt (*saindhava*).

It is digestive, bestows strength to the flesh and muscles, and immediately imparts strength to the eyes. [One should take] three palas of *eraṇḍa* root, one pala of *palāśa*, and one pala each of the minor *pañcamūla*.
One should boil rāsnā, balā, chinnaruhā, aśvagandhā, punarnavā, āragvadha, devadāru,
and eight fruits in two āḍhakas of water until one-eighth remains.
One should administer vacā, śatāhvā, hapuṣā, priyaṅgu, yaṣṭī, kaṇā, vatsaka seeds, and musta,
well-ground together with tārkṣyaśaila, in a dose of one akṣa, combined with a portion of salt.
This enema, containing honey, oil, and urine, is scraping (lekhana) and digestive-stimulating (dīpana); it conquers pain in the calves,
thighs, feet, sacrum, back, abdomen, heart, and genitals, as well as heaviness and constipation.
It cures various diseases arising from phlegm and wind, such as abdominal tumors, urinary stones, scrotal enlargement, and disorders of the digestive tract and anus;
this preparation is fried in four palas of oil and ghee, and contains half a hundred [palas] of goat meat, curd, and sour pomegranate juice.

This juice, to be taken with a paste, is praised for strength, wounds, muscle tissue, semen, digestive fire, cataracts, and headache. Milk prepared with eight palas of liquorice (yaṣṭyāhvaya) along with dill seeds (śatāhvā), fruits, and long pepper (pippalī) [is likewise beneficial].

A decoction enema (nirūha) prepared with liquorice, *lodhra*, *abhaya*, sandalwood, and lotuses and blue water-lilies, mixed with ghee and honey, is beneficial for vātarakta, erysipelas, and loss of voice. Milk boiled with these same ingredients is also excellent.
Sugar, honey, and ghee, well-cooled and combined with the Jīvanīya group of drugs, destroy diseases caused by pitta.
[It is prepared] with cow-milk, gochandanā, śītapākī, grapes, kharjūra, kāśmarya, madhūka, and sevya.
Boiled milk, mixed with a paste of *śrāvaṇī*, *mudgaparṇī*, *balā*, *svaguptā*, and *madhuyaṣṭī*,
along with wheat flour in the quantity of a cotton-pick (*picu*), and combined with the juice of sugarcane and *vidārī*.
An enema prepared with oil processed with licorice (yaṣṭīmadhu), along with sugar, honey, and ghee,
is recommended when there is a burning sensation throughout the entire body, or when pain is localized in specific parts.
In cases of abdominal tumors, diarrhea, vertigo, dysuria, emaciation, injury, and the depletion of ojas and strength,
one should use kośātakī, āragvadha, devadāru, mūrvā, aśvadaṃṣṭrā, kuṭaja, arka, and pāṭhā. (AS.Ka.4.18)
Having boiled *kulattha* and *bṛhatī* in water, there should be ten *prasṛta*s of that decoction;
these, combined with one *akṣa* each of mustard, *elā*, *madana*, and *kuṣṭha*, and with one *prasṛta* [of other ingredients],
[should be administered].

One should administer an enema (nirūha) consisting of honey, oil, the oil of *phalāhvaya*, alkali, and mustard oil to one suffering from diseases of *kapha*, those with weak digestion, and those who have an aversion to food.
One pala each of punarnavā, eraṇḍa, vṛṣa, aśmabheda, vṛścīva, bhūtīka, balā, and palāśa,
as well as the two groups of five roots (daśamūla), should be crushed and washed; [to this] eight fruits [of harītakī] should be added.
One *prasṛta* each of *bilva*, barley, *aṅkola*, horse gram (*kulattha*),
and coriander seeds should be boiled with two *āḍhaka*s of water and milk; that [mixture], when only the milk remains, should be strained through a clean cloth.
A preparation made from the pastes of *vacā*, *śatāhvā*, *amaradāru*, *kuṣṭha*, *yaṣṭyāhva*, *siddhārthaka*, and *pippalī*,
combined with *yavānī* and *madana*, and mixed with jaggery and rock salt, should be neither too hot nor too cold.

One who knows the procedure should administer a Nirūha enema according to the rules, using three Prasṛtas each of honey, oil, and fresh clarified butter; this destroys all diseases arising from the combination of various humors.
Next, various enemas (bastis) prepared with half-and-half proportions will be described:
the two types of *kośātakī*, *ikṣvāku* fruit, *jīmūta*, and *vatsaka*.
The roots of śyāmā and trivṛt, as well as those produced from dantī and dravantī,
along with prakīryā, udakīryā, kṣīriṇī, and the fruit of nīlinī.
Saptaparṇa, pāṭhā, śaṅkhinī, lodhra, and the fruit of kampillaka,
combined with their own pastes and rock salt, are purgatives for the colon (pakvāśaya).
Ghātakī flower, tarkārī, the root of jīvantī,
vatsaka, pragraha, khadira, kuṣṭha, śamī, piṇḍītaka, and barley.
Priyaṅgu, arka-mūlī, taruṇī, jāti, yūthikā,
the vaṭa and other such trees, kiṃśuka, and lodhra are considered to be astringent (saṅgrāhika).
The *grāhin* (binding) [lepa] is prepared with the decoction and paste of priyaṅgu, ambaṣṭhā, and so forth, applied in sequence;
the scraping (*lekhan*) [lepa] is the juice of triphalā with an addition (*pratīvāpa*) of ūṣaka and other ingredients.
This is nourishing when prepared with the decoction and paste of Madhura drugs along with fresh ghee. The sprouts of Badarī, Airāvaṇī, Śelu, Śālmalī, and Dhanvana [are also used].
They are known to be mixed with honey, combined with milk, containing blood, and slimy;
[they are prepared] with *kola*, *kaṭaka*, stalks of sugarcane, *darbha* grass, *poṭa*, and *ikṣupālī*.
The first [application] for quelling burning sensations consists of *candana* and other ingredients with ghee and milk;
the second is a handful of *śālmalī* stalks boiled in milk and mixed with ghee.
Likewise, it is beneficial when prepared with a decoction of *pravāhaṇa*, as well as the stalks of *śālmalaka*, along with *karbudāra*, *āḍhakī*, *nīpa*, and *vidula*, boiled in milk.
Likewise, for *parikarta*, [one should use] stalks produced from *śrīparṇī* and *kovidāra*;
for *parisrava*, milk boiled with *vṛścīva* and *punarnavā*.
Likewise, with *ākhukarṇikā* combined with *taṇḍulīyaka*,
one becomes a rider of horses; [with] *kākanāsā*, *rājakaśerukā*, and [the others].

In cases of excessive hemorrhage, these proven formulations should be prepared with milk, combined with honey, collyrium, and ghee, along with the four drugs beginning with Nyagrodha; this is another method.
[The four drugs are: Bṛhatī, Kṣīrakākolī, Pṛśniparṇī, and Śatāvarī.
Kāśmarya, badarī, mūrvā, uśīra, and priyaṅgu; these,
along with jīvaka and ṛṣabhaka, should be boiled in milk and combined with two parts of ghee and collyrium.
The physician should administer two enemas that are cold and mixed with honey and sugar,
along with the milk of cows, goats, and buffaloes, combined with the drugs of the jīvanīya group.
An enema prepared with the freshly crushed blood of a rabbit, antelope, cock, cat, buffalo, sheep,
or goat is recommended for the extraction of a *jīvādāna* (living parasite).

Now, I shall describe these mild, unctuous non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) for those who are delicate and for those whose [bodily constituents] have been deranged by medical procedures, each prepared with one handful (prasṛta) of ingredients.
Two *prasṛta*s of milk should be used, along with three each of honey, oil, and ghee; this enema,
churned with a churning stick, destroys Vāta and promotes strength and complexion.
One *prasṛta* each of oil, clarified butter, honey, and ghee,
along with two *prasṛtas* of a decoction of the roots of the *bilva*-group and two *prasṛtas* of *kaulattha* pulse, conquers disorders of *vāta*.
An enema consisting of one *prasṛta* each of the decoction of *paṭola*, *nimba*, *pūtīka*, *rāsnā*, and *saptacchada*,
along with clarified butter and a paste of mustard seeds, [is effective].
Viḍaṅga, triphalā, śigru fruit, mustā, and ākhukarṇī, combined with pañcatikta, destroy excessive secretions, worms, skin diseases,
and urinary disorders.

Five [parts] are drawn from the decoction (kaṣāya), and one [part] from oil and the other substances; having churned these together, this non-unctuous enema (nirūha), combined with a paste of *vellaka* and *pippalī*, destroys worms.
[The paste consists of] *payasyā*, sugarcane, *sthirā*, *rāsnā*, *vidārī*, honey, and ghee.

Each of these, mixed with a paste of *kṛṣṇā*, administered as a single enema, produces virility. [Take] four parts each of oil, cow urine, whey from curd (*dadhimanda*), and sour gruel (*amlakāñjika*).
A fistula applied with ground mustard seeds breaks up the obstruction of feces and causes the splitting of abdominal tumors (ānāha).
[This is achieved] from a decoction of *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *aśmabhid*, and *eraṇḍa*, combined with oil, wine (*surā*), and fermented liquor (*āsava*).
An enema consisting of five *prasṛta* measures of the paste of *capalā*, *kauntī*, and *yaṣṭyāhvaka*,
administered lukewarm, is considered excellent for curing dysuria caused by *sāha*.
When the bladder has become numb due to a mild enema, another sharp enema is desired;
when it has been irritated by sharp enemas, a mild, sweet, and cold unctuous enema is prescribed.

Sharpness [of the enema] should be induced when appropriate by means of cow’s urine, bilva, fire (citraka), salt, alkali, and mustard; whereas softness should be achieved by means of milk, clarified butter, and similar substances.
An enema administered after carefully analyzing the factors of age, season, morbidity, disease, and constitution, when combined with its respective groups of medicinal substances,
cures each of its specific diseases.

Having carefully considered the case, one should administer enemas that are cool for those afflicted by heat, and comfortably warm for those afflicted by cold, combined with appropriate medicinal drugs.
One should not administer nourishing enemas (basti) in diseases requiring purification,
nor for those who are obese, nor for men afflicted with skin diseases (kuṣṭha) or urinary disorders (meha) who require purification.
One should not administer purificatory therapies to those whose bodies are emaciated, wounded, weak, fainting, thin, withered, or pure [of humors],
nor to those whose life-force is bound up within the *doṣas*.
Thus ends the fourth chapter.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the pharmaceutical preparations for the prepared enema (siddhabasti).
"Thus indeed said the great seers, Ātreya and others:
one should always employ perfected enemas for all embodied beings."
Free from harmful effects, yielding great fruit, providing strength and nourishment, and bringing happiness—
[one should take] equal parts honey and oil, one *karṣa* of rock salt, and two *palas* of *misi*.
A Nirūha enema prepared with a decoction of castor root and Madhutaila is a rejuvenative (rasāyana) that cures urinary disorders (prameha), hemorrhoids, worms, abdominal tumors (gulma),
and hernia; when combined with Yaṣṭimadhu, it is beneficial for the eyes and conquers bleeding disorders (raktapitta).
This enema, prepared with a thick paste and containing honey, oil, juice, and clarified butter,
provides relief and overcomes pain in the anus, knees, thighs, scrotum, bladder, and penis.
One should prepare a palliative enema (yāpana) with one prasṛta each of ghee, honey, muscle fat, and oil, combined with half an akṣa of rock salt and half a pala of hapuṣā.
A decoction of castor root, honey, oil, rock salt,
along with *vacā*, long pepper, and *phala*— this is the "Yuktaratha" enema.
Boiled with honey, ṣaḍgranthā, śatāhvā, hiṅgu, saindhava salt,
suradāru, and rāsnā, this enema (basti) removes the doṣas and is auspicious.
A decoction of the five roots (pañcamūla), oil, Māgadhikā (long pepper), honey,
rock salt (saindhava), and Madhuka— this is known as the Siddhabasti.
One should boil the two types of *pañcamūla*, the three *phalas*, and *bilva* in cow’s urine; then, with that [decoction], one should grind *pāṭhā*, *toyada*, and *vatsaka*.
An enema prepared with honey and oil, combined with alkali and salt,
is effective for diseases caused by phlegm (kapha), anemia, and cholera-like dysentery.
It is highly esteemed for obstructions of semen and flatus, as well as for abdominal distension caused by the bladder;
[the decoction of] Musta, Patha, Amrita, Eranda, Bala, Rasna, and Punarnava [is used].
One pala each of mañjiṣṭhā, āragvadha, uśīra, trāyamāṇā, akṣa, and rohiṇī,
along with the minor pentad of roots (kanīyapañcamūla) and eight palas of madana.
One should cook that [mixture] in one āḍhaka of water until reduced to one-fourth,
then strain it; having combined it with two prasthas of milk, one should cook it again until only the milk remains.
The juice of half a *jāṅgala* animal, together with ghee, honey, and rock salt,
[should be used] with the pastes of *yaṣṭī*, *misi*, *śyāmāka*, *kaliṅgaka*, and *rasāñjana*.

A comfortably warm enema increases muscle mass, digestive fire, strength, and semen; it cures disorders of wind and blood, fainting, urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, and the retention of feces and urine.
Intermittent fevers, erysipelas, abdominal tumors, flatulence, dysentery,
and pains in the groin, thighs, hips, abdomen, neck, ears, and head.
This king among rejuvenatives (rasāyana), which sustains life (yāpanā), destroys menorrhagia, insanity, edema, cough, urinary calculi, and earache; it is beneficial for the eyes and bestows sons.
One should boil one pala each of the five roots (pañcamūla) and gokṣura separately.
An enema prepared with one-fourth part of an āḍhaka of milk,
combined with the pastes of yaṣṭīmadhu and other ingredients, along with honey, oil, ghee, and rock salt, is highly esteemed.
Specifically for children, the elderly, women, and those who are delicate by nature,
[this preparation] should likewise be prepared with *sahācara*, *balā*, *sārivā*, and *darbha*.
Milk prepared as an enema (basti) with *abhīru*, *guḍūcī*, and the two types of *bṛhatī*, along with a paste (*kalka*) of *māgadhikā* and *yaṣṭīmadhuka*, is likewise effective.
One pala each of the five roots beginning with *bṛhatī*,
and two palas each of rice, wheat, barley, and *māṣa* beans, together with *yaṣṭimadhu*.
Goat's milk processed with these [herbs], along with the juice of hen's eggs,
sugar, ghee, honey, and the two salts— this enema (basti) is supreme for generating semen.
This elixir is also effective when prepared from the juices of the eggs of peacocks, cranes, fish, and other such creatures; likewise,
the juice of crab meat combined with the juice of sparrow eggs [is used].
An enema that is sweet with sugar, ghee, and honey is considered most aphrodisiac.
[It may also be prepared] with the testicles of a goat or a pig, and the flesh of a crab or a sparrow.
Milk, goat semen, uccaṭā, ikṣuraka, and honey—
these, combined with plenty of ghee and a small amount of salt, constitute an enema that is supremely aphrodisiac.
One should eat with prepared milk along with *ātmaguptā*, *uccaṭā*,
and sugarcane; he who thus employs these enemas for ten days at a time.

Like a well-nourished stallion, a bull goes unto a hundred women; these [medicines], when combined with honey, make a man exceedingly virile. They produce neither excessive application nor lack of application, and they act as aphrodisiacs.
Nirūha enemas are generally purgative (lekhanā), whereas oil enemas (snehabasti) are nourishing (bṛṃhaṇā).
In cases of maintenance therapy (*yāpana*), both [types of enema] are used; therefore, an oily enema (*anuvāsana*) is not desired for them.
However, if these [oily enemas] have been administered and the patient does not recover because they are too mild, [the procedure should be repeated].
He should be administered a sharp non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana-basti) with urine immediately;
this cures swelling, loss of digestive fire, pallor, colic, hemorrhoids, and cutting pain in the rectum.
Fever and diarrhea may arise from the excessive use of *yāpana* enemas;
in such cases, digestive-stimulating (*dīpanī*) treatments using *ariṣṭas*, alkalis, *śīdhu* liquor, and similar substances are desired.
Therefore, one should employ these palliative treatments with reason, not out of addiction;
[this is done] through the combination of mild and small doses of medicine, and by reducing the quantity by one-quarter.
And because they are used for a short duration, there is no contraindication regarding those substances that are merely palliative;
[one should administer] the proven unctuous preparations separately for each.
Or one may employ all types of enemas (basti) in all cases, provided they are free from restrictive dietary and behavioral precautions.
[One may also use] sahācara, abhīru, balā, rāsnā, and gokṣuraka, either individually—
AS.Ka.5.32 AS.Ka.5.32
One should boil one *tulā* [of the herb] in one hundred *droṇas* of water until one *droṇa* remains; when it has been strained and cooled, [one should add] *bisā*, grapes, *tāvakṣīrī*,
and *nidigdhikā*.
Mahāsahā, kṣudrasahā, yaṣṭīmadhu, and madhūlikā;
jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, udīcya, mṛṇāla, utpala, and candana.
Date-palm kernel, Tāla-palm kernel, Atmaguptā, Āmalakī,
Kaṇā; Paṭola, Medā, Tvak, Patra, Śītapākī, and Odanāhvaya.
Having made these into a paste, one should add to it separately one *prastha* each of the juices derived from the testicles of a boar, a buffalo,
and a goat.
Oil and clarified butter produced from the eggs of peacocks, cocks, and swans;
the fresh juice of *dhātrī* and *vidārī*; and two *āḍhaka* measures of cow’s milk.
And that [palanquin] was prepared with the resonant sounds of the *brahmabherī*, mṛdaṅga drums, and other instruments;
it was shaded by white umbrellas and draped with white cloth.
Having placed the bull-bannered deity upon the back of an elephant and honored him, one should perform a rite for well-being and administer an unrestrictive oil enema.
Having attained extreme virility through that [practice], he may tire a hundred women; moreover,
he shall become free from wrinkles and gray hair, handsome, and long-lived.

It is beneficial for those with depleted semen, those suffering from chest wounds, those who are emaciated, and those with irregular fevers; it bestows sons upon those with impaired menses or semen, and serves as a rejuvenative elixir (rasāyana).
In this manner, other enemas (bastis) should also be prepared and cooked in numerous ways.

One should cook [the oil] a hundred or a thousand times if possible; the unctuous enemas (snehabasti) that destroy the humors (doṣa), along with their contraindications (parihāra), will now be described.
Daśamūla, balā, rāsnā, aśvagandhā, and punarnavā.
One pala each of *guḍūcī*, *airaṇḍa*, *pūtīka*, *bhārṅgī*, *vṛṣaka*, *rohiṣa*,
*śatāvarī*, *sahacara*, and *kākanāsā*.
Having boiled barley, black gram, linseed, *kola*, and horse gram, measured by a handful (*prasṛta*), in water until one *droṇa* remains, and with that [decoction]—
One should cook one āḍhaka of oil with one pala each of the paste of the jīvanīya drugs; this is known as anuvasana, and it cures all disorders of vāta.
Similarly, the fat of marshy animals prepared with life-promoting (jīvanīya) drugs [is used];
oil processed with śatāhvā, yava, bilva, and sour substances is [used] for vāta.
Saindhava salt, agnivraṇa, and *tapta* (copper), which subdues *vāta*, should be taken; likewise, *jīvantī*, *madana*, *medā*, *śrāvaṇī*, *madhuka*, and *balā*.
Śatāvarī, ṛṣabhaka, kṛṣṇā, kākanāsā, śatāvarī,
svaguptā, kṣīrakākolī, karkaṭākhyā, śaṭhī, and vacā.
Having ground these, one should prepare oil and ghee in four times the quantity of milk;
this is nourishing, subdues wind and bile, and increases strength, semen, and digestive fire.
This nourishing oil, which removes disorders of the *rajas* and *śukra* and promotes the birth of sons,
should be prepared by grinding [the ingredients] with substances that have a cooling touch and potency, along with four times the amount of milk.
Ghee prepared with oil as a quarter-part is an effective non-unctuous enema (anuvāsana) that subdues pitta;
it contains rock salt, madana, kuṣṭha, śatāhvā, nicula, and vacā.
Drībera, madhuka, bhārṅgī, devadāru, kaṭphala,
nāgara, puṣkara, medā, cavikā, citraka, and śaṭhī.
Viḍaṅga, ativiṣā, śyāmā, hareṇu, nīlinī,
sthirā, bilva, ajamoda, capalā, dantī, and rāsnā— with these [ingredients]...
Castor oil or sesame oil, when prepared with *sādhya* drugs, cures diseases of *kapha*, as well as *vardhma*,
upward-moving wind (*udāvarta*), abdominal tumors (*gulma*), hemorrhoids (*arśas*), splenic disorders, urinary disorders (*meha*), and excessive *vāta*.

This oil, prepared with the *pañcamūla* or with the *bilvādi* group [of herbs], administered as an unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*), quickly destroys abdominal tumors (*ānāha*) and urinary calculi (*aśmarī*).
An oil enema (anvāsana) prepared with Kapha-subduing substances,
or with the eight-fold sour fruit-mixture (aṣṭaguṇa-amla), is effective for Kapha; however, in cases of colic and abdominal distension,
a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) combined with that [sour mixture] and containing strong urine is indicated.
Then the wise Agniveśa questioned the Sage: "In this matter, which fruit would be perpetually beneficial for the administration of enemas? Punarvasu instructed him as follows.
In this context, *garāgarī* is beneficial for skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), the fruit of *ikṣvāku* is beneficial for those suffering from urinary disorders (*pramehin*),
the fruit of *kuṭaja* is excellent for heart disease, and the *kośaphala* is best for anemia (*pāṇḍu*).
In the stomach, *kṛtavedhana* is beneficial; likewise, *madana* is not antagonistic to any disease.
It is sweet, slightly astringent and bitter, non-dry (*arūkṣa*), and possesses pungency, heat, and黏滑ness (*picchila*).
That which quickly removes kapha and pitta from the heart, is free from complications, and promotes the downward movement of vāyu—
among the various types of fruits and other substances, that is remembered as the most excellent for administration in non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana).
Then, when the bull among sages had finished speaking and stood silent, he,
standing upon the earth with his other disciples, placed his joined palms before him and addressed him once more regarding this most profound matter.
When administered by a teacher skilled in the qualities of painting, the enema does not go above the navel;
rather,
it quickly descends through the body and completely eliminates the humors (doṣas) from every part.

The Teacher said: This enema (basti) subdues even the most formidable clusters of diseases by bringing into harmony that which is corrupted— whether located within or external to the body— which is otherwise subject to the force of heavy and stagnant winds.
Diseases located in the branches, those situated in the trunk, and those arising from the vital points (marmans), the upper body, all the limbs, or the minor parts— of these,
there is no other cause for their birth than Vāyu.
Vāyu indeed performs the dispersal and reabsorption of the accumulated impurities such as feces, phlegm, bile, and so forth;
for the pacification of that excessively increased [vāyu], there is no medicine equal to enema (basti). This is because: [AS.Ka.5.65]
When the wind (vāyu) is conquered through effort, even the bile (pitta), phlegm (kapha), and other humors that are driven by it are pacified;
therefore, some declare that the enema (basti) is half of medical treatment, while others say it is the entirety of medical treatment.
And just as the sun situated in the sky draws up the juices of the earth, so too does the enema, even when located in the colon, draw up the morbid humors from the feet to the head by its potency.
Whatever medicinal potency is present there, it is quickly brought to full effect by the apāna wind and then received by the samāna wind.
After the Samāna, the Vyāna and the other vital airs follow in succession;
when they are satisfied, they return to their natural state and remain intent on the welfare of the body.
Having forcibly settled the *pitta* and *kapha* in their respective locations,
they thoroughly nourish their own respective elemental qualities throughout the body.
The *vyāna* moves transversely, the *apāna* downwards, and the *prāṇa* draws [the breath] upwards,
each through its own respective channels like water through channels that draw it up.
Thus, when the body and the bladder are well-prepared with the appropriate medicinal airs and channels,
it forcefully pervades the entire system and destroys even the most difficult cases of consumption (yakṣman).
Therefore, the enema (basti) is the foremost of all therapeutic procedures; it destroys all diseases without exception.
Having purified the internal channels, it brings about the restoration of ojas, tejas, semen, intellect, digestive fire, and physical vigor.
Thus ends the fifth chapter.
Now begins the sixth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the successful treatment of complications arising from enemas (*basti-vyāpad-siddhi*).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:
"Obstruction, heaviness, flatulence, headache, and upward-moving [vāyu] in the limbs..."

From deficient application (ayoga) and excessive application (atiyoga) of the enema (basti), there arise six complications each: abdominal pain, body ache, hiccups, cardiac distress, cutting pain, and discharge.
If administered to one whose body has not been lubricated or fomented, whose digestive tract is heavy,
or who has consumed only cold, low-fat, or salty substances— even if the enema is thick— it will fail to act properly.
If the enema agitates that morbid humor (doṣa) but fails to expel it due to the patient's weakness,
it causes a most severe obstruction of flatus, feces, and urine.
It causes burning in the navel and bladder, a coating sensation in the heart,
swelling in the anus, itching, eruptions, discoloration, restlessness, and weakness of the digestive fire.
When a patient suffering from diarrhea has an aggravation of the doshas in the middle [of the body], the two previously prescribed decoctions should be used;
in that case, the drinking of one of them while warm is recommended.
Likewise, fruit-candles, sudations, and purgation should be administered after considering the proper time;
[this involves] bilva root, trivṛt, devadāru, barley, jujube, and horse gram.

One should administer an enema containing wine, feces, and urine, along with the paste of the previously mentioned drugs; when a remnant of undigested food remains, the provoked dosha should be expelled by means of a mild non-unctuous enema (nirūha).
It causes fainting, obstructs the path of the wind (vāyu), impairs the digestive fire (agni),
and brings about heaviness, exhaustion, cardiac pain, burning sensations, delusion, and convulsions.
Then one should treat and manage him with dry sudation and digestive therapies;
water boiled with long pepper (pippalī), kattṛṇa, uśīra, devadāru, and mūrvā [should be used].
One should drink [this] mixed with sauvarcala salt, which stimulates digestion and cleanses the heart; or alternatively, vacā, nāgara, and śaṭī combined with the whey of curd (dadhi-maṇḍa).
The gruels may be prepared with *prasannā*, or with *ariṣṭa* or *āsava*. [One should take] *dāru*, the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), *pathyā*, *palāśa*, *citraka*, and *śaṭhī*.

Having ground kuṣṭha with urine, one should drink it along with digestive alkaline substances; furthermore, one should administer a *daśamūla* enema for him containing urine. If [the medicine] is administered when the patient has abundant doshas, is dry, or has a hard receptacle (āśaya), it will be of little potency.
When the bladder is enveloped by the *doṣas* and its passage is obstructed, it blocks the wind (*samīraṇa*).
