That wind, taking a deviant course, causes flatulence and pain in the vital organs (*marman*).
It causes a burning sensation in the rectum and abdomen, pain in the scrotum and groin, constricts the heart, and causes the patient to run here and there with piercing pains.
For one whose body has been well-anointed and fomented, one should apply an enema (varti) there;
the non-unctuous enema (nirūha) should consist of the Bilva group of drugs along with Pīlu, mustard seeds, and urine.

An oil enema (anuvāsana) prepared with *saralā* and *amaradāru* is indicated for those with abundant morbid humors (*doṣa*) who are weak and have a hard bowel (*krūra-koṣṭha*). For such a patient, the enema bladder should be small and soft.
Cold, slight, and obstructed by the doshas, it strikes against the vāyu;
moving upward through the body, that vāyu causes headache.
For stiffness of the neck, catarrh, deafness, and visual impairment,
one should apply warm oil and salt, and then perform sudation and massage.

One should quickly employ sharp fumigations, insufflations, nasal drops, mouth-cleansing agents, purgatives, and enemas that promote downward movement. When the great *doṣas* have been lubricated and fomented, an enema with mild and small-dose medication [is indicated].
If one extracts only a small amount of the morbid humor (doṣa) after it has been agitated, it may cause dysentery (pravāhikā),
swelling in the bladder and the anal region, and a sense of exhaustion in the thighs and shanks.
A person whose vital breaths (māruta) are obstructed frequently suffers from excessive discharge;
for such a case, one should administer sudation, oleation, and non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) that are purifying and carminative.
One should prescribe a diet for him after he has been purged, as if he were one who has undergone a cleansing; however,
if he suppresses the urges or is afflicted by excessive pain, [the treatment must be adjusted].
An enema that is ununctuous, salty, or hot, or one that is too small in quantity or contains insufficient medicinal ingredients,
or one that is too mild, may be driven upward by the Vāyu wind and expelled through the mouth and nostrils.
It emerges, bringing about fainting, nausea, thirst, burning sensations, and so forth;
having observed these symptoms of fainting, one should sprinkle his face with cold water.
And one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) for the sake of removing fatigue from the seed [of semen].
One should massage the back, sides, and abdomen with warm hands while facing downwards.

One should pull [the enema] out by the hair and shake it, or frighten it with beasts of prey and fanged animals, or with men carrying weapons, torches, and making loud noises; thus the enema flows downward.
One should apply pressure to the throat with the hands and a cloth so that [the victim] does not die;
for by the obstruction of the prāṇa and udāna breaths, the path [to death] becomes most well-established.
The downward-moving wind (apāna) quickly draws that [semen] back into the bladder;
one should then administer a paste of *kuṣṭha* and *kramuka* combined with sour substances.
Due to its heat, sharpness, and mobility, it (castor oil) should move the *basti* (urinary bladder) and *tasa* (feces) downward;
alternatively, a paste of *trivṛt* and *pathyā* with cow's urine acts as a downward purgative.
When [the patient] is located in the *pakvāśaya* (large intestine) and has been fomented, a *nirūha* enema prepared with the ten roots (*daśamūla*) should be administered.
An enema (basti) should be administered using barley, jujube, and horse-gram prepared with urine,
or with *amṛtā* and mango shoots processed in cow's urine.
A purgative preparation consisting of the paste of *pūtīkarañja* bark, leaves, *śaṭhī*, *devadāru*, and *rohiṣa*, combined with oil, jaggery, and rock salt.
An enema prepared with the five roots beginning with *bilva* is indicated for [kapha] located in the chest;
for [kapha] located in the head, nasal drops and medicinal smoke are used, and the head should be covered with mustard seeds.
An enema that is excessively hot, sharp, sour, or thick,
or one administered repeatedly to a person who has been over-sweated, or to one with few morbid humors (doṣas) and a soft bowel, [causes complications].
When it reaches the state of excessive administration (atiyoga), it causes pain in the abdomen;
by means of excessive purgation, it produces symptoms identical to those [of the disease].
Having ground pṛśniparṇī, sthirā, padma, kāśmarya, madhuka,
utpala, drākṣā, and madhūka with milk and rice-wash water, [one should apply it].

In the case of excessive discharge (atiyoga) resulting in burning sensations, one should administer an enema (basti) prepared by dissolving grapes, burnt clods of earth, the clear supernatant of water, or licorice (madhuka) along with ghee.
If an enema that is heavy, sharp, or administered in excessive quantity is applied to one who has not been prepared with oleation and sudation,
or to one who is in a poor physical state or has not been properly cleansed, it will cause complications.
When excessively active, it provokes the wind (vāta); moving along improper channels,
it causes pain in the limbs, yawning, stiffness, and a splitting sensation in the joints.
Having anointed that [patient] with oil and salt and having fomented him with heated stones and other such means,
[one should apply a paste] of *bilva*, *kola*, barley, *eraṇḍa*, *vaṣā*, *bhū*, and the two types of *bṛhatī*.
One should administer a non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) using meat broths from wild animals mixed with rock salt;
subsequently, one should perform an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) with oil cooked with drugs that subdue Vāta.
In a patient with a delicate digestive tract who is weak, an excessively sharp enema that causes over-evacuation may induce hiccups;
in such a case, that which is beneficial for curing hiccups and is nourishing should be administered.

Having cooked oil with *balā*, *bṛhatī* and other [herbs], *varā*, *kāśmarya* fruit, and rock salt (*saindhava*), along with *prasannā* and sour *āranāla*, one should administer an unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*).
One should apply warm water with long pepper (pippalī) mixed with salt to the eye;
furthermore, one should employ fumigation, medicinal pastes, meat juices, milk, sudation, and food that subdues vāta.

If the enema is too sharp, or if it is administered with air, or if it is not properly pressed, it may cause pain in the heart; in such a case, one should use a bladder made from *kāśa* or *kuśa* grass.

An enema prepared with boiled *sāmla*, *lavaṇa*, *skandha*, *karīra*, *badarī*, and *nala*, along with *vāta*-subduing drugs, is beneficial; likewise, an unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*) prepared with these same drugs is likewise indicated.
In a person with a soft bowel and few morbid humors,
a bladder enema that is excessively dry and sharp quickly expels the impurities but provokes vāta and pitta.
The umbilicus, bladder, and rectum are not [to be cut], for by cutting them repeatedly,
there would arise a pale, very slight discharge due to the scraping of the bladder.

There, for one whose diet consists of milk, an enema (basti) should be prepared with sweet and cooling medicinal herbs such as milk and sugarcane, boiled together, and mixed with a paste of licorice (*yaṣṭyāhva*) and sesame.
Having dissolved resin (*sarjarasa*), licorice (*yaṣṭyāhva*),
*jiṅgaṇī*, and *kardamāñjana* in milk, this should be administered as an enema (*basti*) to one who consumes food with a distinctly sour taste.
A slimy enema and an unctuous enema prepared with sweet [drugs] are beneficial; or for one with a pitta constitution, an enema that is alkaline, sour, sharp, hot, and salty is beneficial.
By scraping, burning, and lacerating the rectum, it causes a discharge of blood;
when it is burnt (vidagdha), it discharges blood and bile with many colors.
If one repeatedly applies it excessively, one frequently falls into a state of delusion. In that case, one should take fresh *śālmalī* leaves, crush them, and boil them in cow's milk.
One should administer a purified enema (basti) mixed with ghee, as well as other slimy (picchila) preparations;
this same method applies to the sprouts of the *vaṭa* tree and others, as well as to barley and sesame seeds.
The use of *suvarcalā* and *upodakā*, as well as *kacchūdarī*, is recommended; furthermore,
one should apply cold and sweet liquid infusions and plasters to the anus.
In this condition, treatment that cures hemorrhagic disorders, bile disorders, and diarrhea is recommended;
for burning sensations and similar symptoms, one should drink a paste of *trivṛt* with grape juice.
For that, having subdued bile, feces, and wind, overcomes burning sensations and other such ailments;
once purified, one should drink cold gruel mixed with sugar.
One should prescribe food for one who has been excessively purged or whose feces are diminished:
boiled grains with black gram soup, or curd, or wine as a drink.
For one who, suffering from pain, passes undigested matter that is putrid and accompanied by nausea— AS.Ka.6.55 [The physician should treat him accordingly.]
He who suffers from diarrhea characterized by feces, flatus, blood, bile, or phlegm should drink a decoction of *ghana*, *ativiṣā*, *kuṣṭha*, *nata*, *dāru*, and *vacā*.

In that case, an enema belonging to its own category [of the humor] for a matured condition is the best medical treatment. From the combination of two of these six [humors], there are thirty varieties.
One should know those [diseases] along with their complications to be thirty-six in total:
colic (śūla), dysentery (pravāhikā), flatulence (ādhmāna), cutting pain (parikarta), anorexia (aruci), and fever (jvara).
One should recognize thirst, delusion, burning sensations, fainting, and so forth as their complications (upadravas).
In that case of undigested matter (āma), an internal drink (antarapāna) combined with pungent, sour, and salty substances [is prescribed].
A digestive enema (pācana-basti) is recommended when there is undigested matter (āmā), for it is strictly prohibited in such a state;
however, an enema composed of drugs that subdue Vata and those that are astringent (grāhin) is recommended when the stool is present.
An unctuous enema that is sweet and sour, with a distinct salty taste, is indicated for vāta; for blood disorders,
it should contain blood, and for pitta, it should be astringent, sweet, and bitter.
When phlegm is being expelled, an enema consisting of decoctions that are astringent, pungent, and bitter [is indicated]; or,
when there is obstruction by feces or flatus, [an enema] containing those [substances] is used for the stool or the wind.
In the case of a combined disorder (*saṃsṛṣṭa*), there should be an intermediate drink mixed with pungent, sour, and salty substances;
likewise when *pitta* is combined with undigested matter (*āma*) or blood, or when those two are combined with *āma*.
When there is a combination [of doshas], the drink should be pungent, sweet, and bitter (AS.Ka.6.63). Likewise, when the āma is combined with kapha, it should be astringent, pungent, and bitter.
When combined with *āmadoṣa* and *kapha*, [the diet] should be astringent, salty, and pungent;
likewise when combined with *vāta*, *viṣ* (poison), *pitta*, or with feces, *pitta*, and blood, as well as with *anila* (wind).
When [the doshas] are combined, an enema that is astringent, sour, and sweet is the best; however,
when blood is affected by vata, an enema that is sweet, sour, and bitter should be administered.
In the case of mutual admixture of feces and blood, of bile and feces, or of blood and bile, an enema (basti) that is astringent, sweet, and bitter [is indicated].
When pitta is combined with kapha, or kapha with feces and pitta,
a decoction enema (basti) consisting of pungent, bitter, and astringent substances is the best treatment for these combinations.
When blood is combined with phlegm (kapha), [the treatment] should be sweet, pungent, and bitter;
when wind (vāta) is associated with phlegm, it should be pungent, sour, and salty.
The enema should consist of pungent, bitter, and sour substances when kapha is associated with vāyu;
one should formulate combinations of three, four, five, or six ingredients in this very same manner.

This principle stated regarding diarrhea is remembered as applicable to all diseases as well. When there is a combination of all six tastes simultaneously, it becomes a digestive (pācana) formulation.
For the five types of persons who are free from morbid humors (āmā), an enema containing all six tastes is beneficial.
[The ingredients include] the tender fruits of the *udumbara*, and the barks of the *jambu*, *āmra*, and *udumbara*.
Having ground one pala each of conch shell, sarja resin, lac, and kattṛṇa grass,
one should cook one prastha of ghee with twice that amount of milk using these ingredients.
In all cases of diarrhea, this should be drunk according to one's strength,
[prepared] with *kacchurā*, *dhātakī*, *bilva*, *samaṅgā*, and red roots.
A gruel should be prepared with the sprouts of *masūra* and *aśvattha* boiled in water,
along with the tender shoots of the *udumbara*, the bark of the *kaṭvaṅga*, and the leaves of the *plakṣa*.
Likewise, it may be prepared with masūra, dhātakī flowers, and balā.
Various types of complications arise from the misapplication of the enema (basti).
"One should perform their accomplishment according to each [individual] and according to their state.
Thus ends the sixth chapter.
Now begins the seventh chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the successful management of complications arising from oleation and other therapies;
thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.

In the case of an oil enema (snehabasti), eight complications are recognized when it is obstructed by an excess of vāta, pitta, or kapha; by feces (viḍāvṛta); or when administered on an empty stomach, or when the rectum is swollen.

When Vata is predominant, it is cold or slight; when Pitta, it is hot; and when Kapha, it is mild. When there is overeating, it is heavy; likewise, when there is an accumulation of feces, it is of little strength.
The unctuous substance administered by them does not reach its destination due to obstruction caused by stiffness,
heaviness, lassitude, flatulence, fever, colic, and body aches.
One should recognize that fat (sneha) is occluded by vāyu through pain and twisting in the sides;
this [occlusion] is treated with unctuous, sour, salty, and hot substances, along with rāsnā, pīta, druti, and tailika.
One should properly eliminate [the doshas] with decoction enemas (nirūha) prepared with sauvīraka, surā, kola, kulattha, and yava, along with cow's urine and the five roots (pañcamūla).
And with those very two oils, one should administer an oil enema (anuvāsana) after the evening meal.
[This is indicated] by thirst, burning sensations, redness, delusion, discoloration, excessive drowsiness, and fever.

One should recognize that [fever] covered by pitta by [the presence of] sweet and bitter [tastes in the mouth]; one should eliminate it with enemas (basti). With drowsiness, cold fever, lassitude, excessive salivation, anorexia, and heaviness—[one should know it as kapha-occluded].
One should know that [the oil] has been occluded by phlegm due to fainting or exhaustion;
it should be processed with astringent, bitter, and pungent substances, along with wine and urine.
One should eliminate that [dosha] with enemas (basti) containing fruit oils, sour substances, and salt;
[one should recognize it] by vomiting, fainting, anorexia, exhaustion, colic, drowsiness, and body aches.
One should recognize that condition as being caused by overeating when it is accompanied by symptoms such as burning sensations;
its treatment consists of digestive decoctions and powders made from pungent and salty substances.

A mild purgative is beneficial, and everything prescribed for *āmavāta* is wholesome there. [One should recognize the condition] by the obstruction of feces, urine, and flatus, pain, heaviness, flatulence, and cardiac oppression.
Having recognized that the oleaginous substance is obstructed by feces, one should treat it with oleation and sudation, along with enemas (basti),
as well as non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) prepared with the Śyāmā-bilvādi group of drugs, accompanied by oil enemas (anuvāsana).
One should properly eliminate [the disorder] by means of the method that removes upward-moving wind (udāvarta);
or, for one who has not eaten, or for one whose anus is swollen, or for one who has eaten only a small measure of food, [one should administer it].
Oil applied to the rectum, when unconfined, rushes upward with force;
from there, it reaches the upper body and even exits through the upper orifices starting from the throat.
[This occurs when] a decoction of *mūrvā*, *śyāmā*, and *trivṛt* has been prepared and administered along with barley, jujube, and horse gram.
Oil prepared with those [drugs] should be administered as a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) along with an unctuous enema (anuvāsana).
For stiffness or constriction of the throat occurring from the throat upward, one should employ treatments for throat-obstruction and emetics.
One should effect its cessation through emetic treatments;
one must not administer uncooked fat, for it will smear the rectum.
From that, pain, delusion, itching, swelling, and inflammation may arise; in such cases, a sharp enema (basti) as well as oil boiled with the juice of *arka* leaves should be administered.
One should avoid eight types of needles: those that are too short, too long, too thin, too thick, worn out, with loose joints, with a side-opening, and likewise crooked.
Non-attainment, excessive movement, agitation, extraction, and non-exudation;
the crushing of the bolus and crookedness of the passage— these are their respective defects.

One should avoid these eight types of bladder-bags for clinical procedures: those that are fleshy, greasy, unevenly webbed, thick-walled, or excessively windy; as well as those that are torn or moist.
Irregular movement, foul odor, crookedness, leakage, and difficulty of grasping;
frothiness, displacement, and inability to retain [the enema fluid]— these defects of the bladder occur due to morbidities of the bladder itself.

One should avoid these seven types of beds: those that are too high, those where one lies with the head hanging down, those where one is face down, those where one is curled up, those where one stands, and those where one lies on the back or the right side.
Obstruction of urine, excessive onset, non-onset, and improper movement; rapid onset, provocation of the wind (marut), and distension of the colon (pakvāśaya).
There may be defects in that; therefore, one should act here in a manner appropriate to the situation.
[The faults are: accompanied by wind, too rapid, thrown upward, horizontal, suppressed, and trembling.
The defects of being too slow, external, or having excessive force arise from the administrator;

If the enema enters and causes agitation, it may produce piercing pain like a spear;

This applies if the nozzle is inserted too quickly, withdrawn prematurely, or jerked upward with force.
There may be stiffness, pain, and piercing sensations in the waist, anus, calves, thighs, and bladder;
in such cases, wind-alleviating food, sudation, oil massages, and medicinal enemas (basti) should be administered.
If the eye does not enter because the door is blocked by a horizontal beam or is fastened shut,
one should pull the probe straight out, cleanse it, and then insert it again.
When the anus is pressed and then released, the powerful Vāyu, being obstructed there,

In that case, an enema (basti) containing bilva and other drugs, along with fruits, śyāmā and others, and urine, should be administered.

In that case, affusions and enemas should be prepared with astringent and sweet substances and applied cold;

There may be pain, burning, pricking, heaviness, and the discharge of stool;

in that case, an application of medicated ghee, milk, and a slimy enema (picchābasti) are recommended. However, if the [enema] is weak, it does not saturate [the channels], whereas an external [application] is quickly withdrawn.
In that case,
one who desires success should again properly administer an unctuous enema (sneha).
If administered with excessive force, it remains in the abdomen or moves up toward the throat.
In that case, enema therapy, purgation, procedures such as pressure on the throat,
and purification through emesis and other means [should be employed] for one whose body, strength, and digestive fire are emaciated.
Just as one would protect a fresh egg or a vessel full of oil, so should the physician, with great effort, guard [the patient] against every kind of mishap.
One should first give foods that are sweet and pleasing to the heart, then those of sour and salty tastes;
thereafter, those of sweet and bitter tastes, and finally, those of astringent and pungent tastes.
By using flavors that are mutual opposites, as well as the pairs of unctuous and dry substances in alternation, one should gradually restore the patient to their natural state.
One who endures everything and possesses steady strength should be known as having returned to his natural state.
In this interval, one should especially abandon the eight [faults], beginning with harsh speech (bhāṣya).
From speaking too loudly, there arise headache, visual impairment (timira), pain in the chest, and disorders of the voice;
in those cases, expectoration of blood, breathlessness (tamaka), fever, and so forth may also occur. The treatment for these is as follows:
Oil massage, sudation, consuming unctuous substances after meals,
silence, and Vata-alleviating procedures— each according to its specific requirement— conquer the disease.
From excessive sitting and improper riding, pain arises in the joints, the head, the sacrum (trika), and other regions.
From excessive walking, the feet, calves, and thighs become exhausted; for these conditions,
all wind-alleviating treatments such as oleation and sudation are recommended.
From eating when the previous meal is undigested, there arise disorders such as āma-viṣa, vomiting, and fever.
In that regard, the regimen prescribed in the chapter on "Eating in Proper Measure" (Mātrāśitīya) should be followed until the āma is eliminated.
Just as diseases arise from unwholesome food and drink, so too do medicines [become harmful]; likewise,
ailments such as *halīmaka* and others were previously described as resulting from sleeping during the day.
In those cases conquered by phlegm, one should prescribe smoking, dry food, and avoidance of [oily] substances.
From sexual intercourse, there is loss of life through various wind-related diseases caused by it.
The rectum feels as if it is being torn away, and consciousness seems to whirl;
the penis smokes, and the mind feels as if it is being cast into darkness.
The consumption of ghee boiled with milk that promotes longevity, nourishing food, aphrodisiacs, and those various enemas are indicated therein.

For those previously mentioned who are always afflicted due to the suppression of natural urges and the upward movement of wind (ūrdhvavāta), when that wind becomes obstructed, it causes suffering throughout the entire body.
First, one should administer a suppository (phalavarti), and then an enema (basti) that removes morbid humors (calāpaha).
[The ingredients for the enema are: Nikumbha, Kumbha, Agni, Urubūka, Dhāvanī, Punarnavā, and Mahādāru; this is the "Panchaka" group.
The fruits and roots boiled together with urine, combined with ghee, oil, and the five salts,
should be used as a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) along with the meat broth of desert animals; thereafter, one should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) using Nikumbha oil.
One should boil bala, sārasnā, the fruits of bilva and citraka, the two groups of five roots (pañcamūla),
the fruit of kṛtamālaka, barley, and kulattha in water; this decoction should be combined with a paste (kalka) of mustā, pāṭhā, and indrayava.

Oil, ghee, jaggery, and rock salt, combined together, are always beneficial for the sick, bestowing strength, nourishment, and a healthy complexion. Likewise, an oil prepared with licorice (madhuka), or with emetic nut (phala), or with wood apple (bilva), or with dill (śatāhvā) should be used for an oil enema (anuvāsana).

The vitalizing (sajīvanīya) oil, free from salt, is beneficial for children when used as both an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) and a decoction enema (nirūhaṇa). For the elderly and children, there is no other regimen more wholesome than the decoction enema (nirūhabasti).

In a dry (*jāṅgala*) or ordinary (*sādhāraṇa*) region, at the appropriate time, on ground that is served by cold, sun, wind, and water; which is level, clean, with water flowing clockwise; free from cremation grounds, sacred trees, altars for gods, houses, assembly halls, pits, groves, anthills, and saline soil; strewn with *kuśa* and *rohiṣa* grass; possessing soft, black, golden, sweet, and fragrant earth; and where the soil is gentle, unploughed, undisturbed, and not overshadowed by other more powerful trees—medicinal plants grown in such a place are praised. This is the general examination of the soil (*bhūmiparīkṣā*).
In particular, the Aśmavatī region is firm, heavy, and dark; it abounds in black soil, thick grass, trees, and crops, and is preeminent in its own [earthly] qualities.
The Srigdhā region is cool, situated near water, abounding in glossy grass, crops, and tender trees, and is preeminent in the qualities of water. It is white.

A land possessing flowers of various colors that are small and few, with sparse, pale growths of trees, and abounding in the qualities of fire (tejas) is dry; one consisting mostly of trees that are rough, thin, hollow, and of little sap, and abounding in the qualities of wind (vāyu), is also dry;
whereas a land that is soft, level, possessed of chasms, with water of indistinct taste, containing great mountains and trees, and dark in color, abounds in the qualities of space (ākāśa).
Among those, purgatives and nourishing (bṛṃhaṇa) drugs grown in soils abounding in the qualities of water and earth are recommended;
emetics are recommended in soils abounding in the qualities of fire, air, and ether; and drugs possessing all the qualities are recommended for both types of elimination.
In those [plants] in which the quality of space (*ākāśa*) predominates, pacifying (*śamana*) treatments are thus most powerful.

Among them, those that are seasonally appropriate, possess fully developed dimensions, taste, potency, and fragrance; whose fragrance, color, taste, touch, and efficacy have not been impaired by time, sun, fire, water, wind, weapons, or living beings; and which are deeply rooted and situated in the northern direction—[these are the best].
Of these, the branches and leaves that have recently sprouted should be gathered during the rainy season or spring;
the roots should be gathered in summer or winter from trees whose old leaves have fallen and new ones have grown.
In autumn, one should take the bark, tubers, and milky juices;
in winter, the heartwoods; and flowers and fruits according to their respective seasons.
Others, however, say that cooling medicinal herbs [should be used] during the cooling seasons, and fiery ones during the fiery seasons; in this way,
they remain undeteriorated and possess their full flavor and potency.

Now, regarding the auspicious conduct: one who is of virtuous character, pure, and dressed in white garments, having worshipped the deities—the two Aśvins—as well as cows and Brahmins, and having observed a fast, should take [the medicines] while facing either the east or the north.

Having taken them, he should place them in suitable, high-quality containers within inner rooms that have doors facing the east or north, in areas that are partly sheltered from wind and partly exposed to it, where there is a constant offering of flowers and ritual oblations (*bali*), and which are inaccessible to fire, water, steam, smoke, dust, mice, and quadrupeds; these should be kept well-covered and suspended on racks.
One should prepare those [plants] while they still contain their milky sap;
in the absence of such, those whose years have not yet elapsed [should be used].
Furthermore, aged long pepper, viḍaṅga, jaggery, honey, and ghee (AS.Ka.8.8).

The milk of a *bāṣkayaṇa* cow should be taken, as well as the feces and urine of those free from disease;
likewise, the feathers, bile, horns, hooves, and so forth of birds that are strong and vigorous.
Thus, there are five types of pharmaceutical preparations for medicinal drugs, beginning with the decoction (*kaṣāya*).
Exudate, paste, decoction, cold infusion, and hot infusion—
these are more potent in their respective order.
In that regard, the fresh juice (*svarasa*) is the extract obtained from [a plant] that has been immediately uprooted, washed, crushed, and squeezed through a cloth;
whereas a paste (*kalka*) is that which has been ground on a stone or with the teeth.
Powder (*cūrṇa*) is flour that has been dried and ground fine and passed through a fine cloth;

because it does not abandon any of its constituent substances and because it is used after being saturated with liquid, it is not distinct from a paste (*kalka*); [this same preparation] is called a decoction (*kvātha*) or an extract (*niryūha*).

In that regard, having broken down the medicinal substances that require splitting into minute pieces, having cut those that require cutting, and having washed them with water, one should place them in a clean, dry vessel made of copper, iron, or clay that has been smeared on the bottom. Having determined the proportion of water required by the medicinal substances—whether much or little—one should pour in as much water as will cause the essence to be released, and then allow it to evaporate. Then, having placed the vessel over the fire, sitting comfortably on a high seat and watching it constantly from all sides, one should cook it while stirring with a ladle, using a gentle fire that approaches from all directions.

Having strained the decoction, one should apply it with a touch appropriate to the patient's condition. Since a substance mixed with milk and other liquids does not properly release its essence, when that is prescribed along with milk and so forth, one should boil it first with water-decoctions until it is not scorched.
That which is steeped in cold water and purified by remaining overnight is *śīta*;
that which is crushed and extracted in hot water and purified is *phāṇṭa*.

In that regard, having carefully examined the proper taste, potency, and other qualities of the medicine, as well as the strength of the disease and the patient, one should employ the pharmaceutical preparation and dosage of the exudates and other ingredients.
And thus, some have said:
There is no fixed rule for dosage; having considered the disease, the constitution of the patient, strength, age, as well as place and time, one should apply the preparation accordingly.
Thus has this been taught for the awakening of knowledge in the wise; however,
it will now be taught in such a way that all physicians may understand it.
The medium dose of resin (niryāsa) is four *palas*;

for paste (*kalka*) and powder (*cūrṇa*), it is one *karṣa* and three *palas* respectively. When mixing, [one should use] these amounts. For a decoction (*niryūha*), one *pala* of medicine should be boiled in half a *prastha* of water until reduced to one-quarter, then removed from the heat.
For cold decoctions and *phāṇṭas*, one *pala* of medicinal herb is infused with six or four *palas* of water,
respectively.

In the cooking of medicated fats (sneha-pāka), when no specific measure is prescribed, the fat should be combined with one-quarter part of the total liquid, and the paste (kalka) with one-quarter of that [fat].

Regarding the cooking of medicated oils, Śaunaka further teaches that when no specific measure is mentioned, one should employ a paste, oil, and liquid in a ratio increased fourfold.
When the oil has been processed, one should gradually add a fourth, sixth, or eighth part of the paste (kalka) using pure water, decoctions, or fresh juices.
But from five onwards, one should add liquid ingredients separately in an amount equal to the fat; furthermore,
any medicinal substance for which no specific preparation has been determined should be made into a paste (kalka).
Then, having combined them together and placed them on the fire, one should cook them like a decoction (*niryūha*).

When the sound ceases, it attains clarity (*prasāda*), the oil (*sneha*) develops its respective color, smell, and taste, and when the medicinal substance is rubbed between the fingers, it should be neither too soft nor too hard, and it should not stick to the fingers.

Furthermore, regarding measurement: six *vaṃśya*s make one *marīci*.
Six of those [mustard seeds] make one *ṣaṭsarṣapa*; eight of those make one *taṇḍula*; two of those make one *dhānyamāṣa*.
Beyond that, barley-measures are calculated by a fourfold increase as the aṇḍikā, māṣaka, śāṇa, karṣa, pala, kuḍava, prastha, āḍhaka, droṇa, and vaha; however,
a *dharaṇa* is one-tenth of a *pala*.
Māṣaka has the synonyms hema and dhānaka; śāṇa has the synonyms draṅkṣaṇa, kola, and vaṭaka;
karṣa has the synonyms suvarṇa, akṣa, picu, biḍālapadaka, pāṇitala, tinduka, kavalagraha, and ṣoḍaśikā.
Two *karṣas* make a *śukti*; an *aṣṭamikā* and a *muṣṭi* make one *pala*; a *prakuñca* is a fourth part [of a *pala*]; an *āmra* and a *bilva* are two *palas*;
a *prasṛta* is an eighth measure [of a *pala*].
Two *kuḍavas* make one *añjali*; two *kuḍavas* make one *mānikā*;
and an *āḍhaka* is equal to a *pātra* or a *kaṃsa*.
A *droṇa* is [the measure] of a *nalvaṇa*, an *armaṇa*, an *unmāna*, a *ghaṭa*, a *kumbha*, and a *kalaśa*;
two *droṇas* make a *śūrpa*; furthermore, a *tulā* is one hundred *palas*, and twenty of those make a *bhāra*.
And on this point there is a verse: "This measurement applies to dry substances; however, for liquids and moist substances, it is double."

In cases of grinding, stirring, water-based preparations, and the cooking of fats where no specific quantity is mentioned, one should take equal parts of the ingredients, provided they are not liquid.
In the case of unmentioned or unknown substances such as bark and the like, the root should be taken.
The cooking of medicated oils (sneha-pāka) is of three kinds: mild (manda), sticky (cikkaṇa), and rough-sticky (kharacikkaṇa).
The mild stage occurs when the residue (kiṭṭa) is equal in consistency to a medicinal paste (kalka); the sticky stage occurs when it resembles the fruit of the Madana tree.
When a small portion of the black part has been consumed while the wick is being burned,
the remaining [black part] should be removed once it is burnt; however, the unburnt [part] causes the fire to go out.
A mild oil is used for nasal administration (nasya), a coarse oil for massage (abhyaṅga), and a viscous oil for drinking (pāna) and enema (basti).
The earth is generally pervaded by the Himalaya and Vindhya mountains.
In that regard, the first [type of] medicine is mild and wholesome, while the Vindhyan medicine is fiery;
thus ends this section on pharmaceutical preparations (Kalpasthāna), which serves as a general exposition (Paribhāṣā).
The technical rules (paribhāṣās) well-established for medical treatment shall now be proclaimed:
the physician should boil the medicinal substances in water possessing sixteen qualities.
AS.Ka.Paribh.2: It is desired that the fourth remaining part of the decoction, once strained, should be taken.

If urine, buttermilk, the scum of wine, or sour gruel are used as the liquid,
it should be sixteen times the quantity of the medicine; when boiled down, it should be reduced to one-fourth.

AS.Ka.Paribh.6: "When an instruction must be carried out, it should indeed be done exactly as instructed. However, this paribhāṣā is not applicable in cases such as the *ṣaḍaṅga* [section].
In that regard, relying upon established convention regarding medicinal substances and waters,
the constituent parts (bhāgas) should be prescribed in such a way that they correspond to the nature of the disease and other factors.
Therefore, this [dose] may be half a *pala*, or even one *karṣa*; for medicinal substances it may be a *pala*, but for water it shall be two *prasthas*.
Those skilled in reasoning through addition and subtraction should either add more than that,
or even reduce it; this same principle applies to the preparation of soups and beverages.

One should consider [the preparation] with respect to meat, rice, fermented liquor, decoctions, and gruel; for wherever a decoction (niryūha) is prescribed for the purpose of preparing fats and so forth, it applies there as well.
In that case as well, this sixteen-fold proportion is adopted:
in this alternative, the substance to be boiled is used in a quantity equal to the oil.
If it is astringent (kaṣāya) alone that serves as the liquid medium there,
or if another liquid such as milk and so forth is mentioned in that context, [it should be used].
AS.Ka.Paribh.13: Having calculated the quantity accordingly, one should prepare the substance with water;
the substance should be boiled in an amount equal to the oil, even when other liquids are present.
AS.Ka.Paribh.14 That [method] is not appropriate there; therefore, one should prepare it according to what is suitable.

In the case of a decoction (kvāthya), however, the medicinal drug should be twice the amount of the oil; likewise,

One should prepare it according to the appropriate method; some explain it thus:
one should boil the medicinal herbs with four times the amount of water.
The opinion of all the sages, such as Suśruta and others, is as follows;
however, there is this much distinction here: the remainder is just as before.
In this alternative method, the medicinal substance to be boiled should be four times the quantity of the oil; furthermore,
water should be four times the quantity of the drug, measured by weight (pala).
When water four times the quantity of the substance is used in relation to one *prastha*,
it should be boiled down to twice the quantity of the oil; from that, the oil is then applied.
For liquids, a *prastha* is considered double that of dry substances; however,
in medical practice here, the usage among physicians is indeed twofold.
Just as there is [a distinction] in relation to a *pala*, so too is there [one] in relation to a *prastha*;
however, that which was previously presented by Suśruta is the ancient [tradition].
"When there is a requirement for a specific reading, that [reading] is cited as the indicator"—
thus has the threefold [classification] regarding the inclusion of *kaṣāya* been declared.
