In this manner, in all other cases, the oil is four times the amount of the paste (kalka). Wherever a liquid is prescribed as being four times the oil or another base substance, that liquid is to be understood as such.

When no liquid is specified, water alone should be given in a fourfold quantity. Furthermore, the method for preparing medicinal pastes (kalka) from decoctions (kaṣāya) has not been described in the Caraka Saṃhitā.
The procedure for the cooking of medicated oils has already been stated; however, Caraka, having composed only half of the treatise, attained absorption into Brahman by means of Dṛḍhabala.
However, regarding a decoction that is to be drunk, or a paste or powder,
the dosage has been prescribed therein even by Dṛḍhabala.
Just as the measure (*mātrā*), though not explicitly stated, was established by me through inference from the words spoken by Caraka,
so too shall I explain it later.
In this *Kaṣāyakalpa*, the classification of these decoctions is prescribed:
among the three types of *kaṣāyakalpa*, that which has been boiled with four parts of water [is the first].
The decoction-proportion (kaṣāyakalpa) is generally adopted by physicians only when medicated fats (sneha) are to be prepared;
it is not so [applied] when water sixteen times the quantity [of the drug] is used.
AS.Ka.Paribh.30: When the water is four times the quantity [of the drug], the substance is four times the quantity of the oil;
AS.Ka.Paribh.30:
one hundred and twenty-eight palas of the decoction substance are produced.
If one prastha of oil is to be cooked and that [substance] should be dry,
or if it is moist, it should be removed immediately; from that, two hundred palas [are to be taken].
When a *sneha-prastha* (one prastha of oil or fat) is to be prepared, it should contain fifty-six additional *pala*s;
thus, because of the large quantity of the substance, [the rule] that there should be four times as much water applies.
In that context, the desired substance is the oil, which should be most potent;
oils are proclaimed to be those cooked a thousand times or even a hundred times.
Even a very small substance that has been well-prepared performs many functions;
therefore, it is the side upon which the greater amount of substance is employed [that prevails].
In the case of the cooking of medicated oils (*sneha-pāka*), the rule "that [which is the last] is superior" has been adopted by me; however,
its application is appropriate only within the specific procedure for cooking oils.
Those decoctions that have been prescribed for fevers and other ailments as being digestive (pācana) or pacifying (śamanīya),
these are again to be prepared from those very same decoctions.

Four times as much water should be used for drinking, and one *pala* of the decoction should be prepared; therefore, physicians employ one *pala* of the medicinal substance in the process of decoction.
Physicians, however, cause patients to drink four *pala* of the decoction's measure;
this is the well-known procedure handed down through tradition.
It cannot be set aside, for there is no indicative mark (jñāpaka) present here;
one should drink the juice after boiling the seeds of the *vatsaka* fruit.
Thus it was stated by the teacher Caraka regarding excessive diarrhea:
"In the *paṭolādi* decoction, one pala of the substance to be boiled is prepared."
When there is one pala of medicinal substance, one should cook it with four times as much water;
when one-fourth remains, that pala of decoction is ready to be drunk.
In medical treatises and regarding leprosy, that dose is declared to be large;
the dose of a decoction considered by physicians to be four *pala* is [the standard].
In water four times the quantity of the paste, that measure is not achieved;
this being the case, the medicinal drugs would have to be four *pala*s in total.
When four palas of a substance have been boiled in four times that amount of water,
the decoction remaining as one-fourth is called a "four-pala decoction" (catuṣpala-kvātha), which is to be drunk.
Bhaṭṭāra Haricandra has proclaimed in the *Kharaṇāda* that a dose (*mātrā*) of six *palas* is to be drunk; for that [dose], there are six *palas* of medicinal substance.
In the case of decoctions, [the ingredients] are combined with four times as much water as the substance; thus,
in the *paṭolādi* group, one pala of the decoction-substance is prepared.
The measure prepared with *kharaṇada* is a gruel (*peyā*); by that same [measure], there are six *palas*.
That which is mutually contradictory is also applied to this.
This prescription for a decoction (kaṣāya) regarding fevers and other ailments is not well-known;
neither are six palas boiled, nor is four times as much water used.
Therefore, the rule [of fourfold water] is not applicable here;
for that [rule] is intended only for decoctions (kaṣāya) and medicated fats (sneha) such as those used for fever and other ailments.
AS.Ka.Paribh.50: That decoction which was proclaimed by the sage Kṛṣṇātreya as containing sixteen-fold water is used for the administration of decoctions in cases of fever and other ailments.
Even regarding the rule taught that water should be four times [the amount of the substance],
some have relied upon this other distinction therein as well.
In those medicinal oils for which no specific measure in *pala*s is prescribed,
the quantity of water and medicinal herbs is to be determined here by reference to the *prastha*.
AS.Ka.Paribh.53: Even with respect to the *palā* [measure], the conventional practice (*samācāra*) is twofold;
that which was previously stated regarding the dependence on the *prastha* applies when there is an indicator (*vijñāpaka*).
AS.Ka.Paribh.54: Wherever a measurement in *palas* for substances is stated in the *Miśraka*,
here [in the *Kalpa*], water is likewise four times that amount, with reference to the *pala*.
Because it is specified in another section, it is inferred that even in the Caraka [Saṃhitā],
a decoction (kaṣāya) should be drunk even if its dosage has not been explicitly stated.
In the formulation beginning with *svarṇakṣīrī* for the treatment of jaundice (*pāṇḍuroga*),
the stated dose is to be drunk with four *pala* of cow’s urine.
In the treatment of pitta-type gulma using [decoctions of] *rohiṇī*, *kaṭuka*, and others,
the prescribed dose for the decoction— excluding ghee— is four palas.
From this inference, it is established in the Caraka Saṃhitā that the standard measure (mātrā) is four palas; furthermore,
one pala of substances such as paṭola and others is prescribed to be boiled [for a decoction].
One pala of vatsaka seeds is prescribed for one suffering from diarrhea;
if it is not boiled in sixteen times that amount of water, then [the remedy is ineffective].
In water that is four times [the quantity of] the medicinal substance, one pala of the decoction should be drunk;
this is where sixteen times the amount of water is employed.
This very same technical rule (paribhāṣā) of Caraka is also inferred for decoctions (kaṣāya) to be drunk, such as those made from musta, parpaṭaka, and other [herbs].
Another distinction is also stated regarding measurement based on dry and liquid substances:
having specified the measurement based on dry substances, that which was exemplified [is as follows].
AS.Ka.Paribh.63: For liquids, the measure is double, both when they are fresh and when they have been extracted.
This rule beginning with "the measure is double" applies starting from the *kuḍava*.
In the case of dry and liquid substances alike, the measurement below one *kuḍava* must be equal;
even when using a scale (*tulā*), a doubling of the measure is not desired.
One hundred palas of a scale are considered equal for both dry and liquid substances;
a pala is desired to be four times [the standard], as established by well-known authorities and the like.
In the case of the *sahācaratulā* (one *tulā* of *sahācara*), one should cook one *āḍhaka* of oil with the juice;
here, it is understood that exactly one hundred *palas* are taken.
This *pala* consists of four *suvarṇas*, not eight *suvarṇas*; however,
when the substance is doubled, the *pala* would consist of eight *suvarṇas*.
Neither in the hollowed palms, nor in the cupped hands, nor in a handful, nor below a handful;
for liquid medicinal substances, a double measure is prescribed.
AS.Ka.Paribh.69: In the case of doubling [the weight] for liquids, a *pala* consists of eight *suvarṇas*.
By that [rule], their method of calculation regarding doubling is contradicted.
In technical designations such as *kuḍava* and others, the rule for liquid substances is twofold;
and there exists an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this shown by the teacher Caraka.
This has been recited for the sake of clarity in the *Kuṣṭhacikitsita* (Chapter on the Treatment of Leprosy):
"When one-eighth remains of an *āḍhaka* of water, the strained decoction should be taken."
Those eight *palas* of decoction and four *palas* of ghee should be cooked until eight *palas* remain;
that lukewarm liquid should then be drunk.
But when two sets of eight *pala*s remain as an eighth part of the *pala*s,
it is not appropriate if the measurement is made at double the size of a *pala*.
For when the weight is doubled, that which was [originally] one *pala* becomes eight *palas*;
and that which was prescribed as four *palas* together with clarified butter should be given.
When the measure is double that of a *pala*, even that becomes eight *palas*;
for it is held that four *suvarṇas* constitute a *pala* of dried substances.
Because liquids are doubled in quantity, that [dose] would become eight suvarṇakas; and in this case, the specific instruction regarding the measure of the enema (nirūha) is contradicted.
Starting from half a *prasṛta*, up to twelve *prasṛtas* at the maximum—
this measure, when doubled, constitutes a double *prasṛta*.
The measure for an enema (nirūha) prescribed in the treatises is twelve *prasṛta*;
it should consist of forty-eight *pala*.
AS.Ka.Paribh.79: However, for diseases such as those in the middle category, one añjali of decoction is prescribed;
in this context, according to the Suśruta-nirdeśa, this decoction should be doubled.
One should drink six *pala* of a decoction that has been boiled until it is naturally cooled;
what was stated by Kharaṇāda should be twelve *pala*.
In the case of a bile-dominant (paittika) gulma, four palas of ghee are prescribed;
one should drink it after it has been thoroughly mixed, and by that, the bile-dominant gulma is pacified.
This [dose] of ghee shall be four *palas*, and the measure [of the liquid] shall be eight *palas*.
In formulations such as those beginning with *svarṇakṣīrī*, one *añjali* of cow’s urine is prescribed.
For because the añjali is doubled, its measure becomes eight palas;
this is recited in the context of the *gaulmika* and *trāyamāṇādi* ghees.
Having taken eight *pala* each of juice from *āmalaka* and sugarcane, and [eight] of milk and ghee, one should cook them thoroughly.
AS.Ka.Paribh.85: Each of these eight [units] should be sixteen *palas*;
therefore, it is contradicted in such instructions.
For liquids, the measure in *kuḍava*s and other such units should be doubled;
this applies even to moist substances, provided they have not all been recently extracted.
They maintain that the measure [of the drugs] should be doubled, and a distinction is prescribed here:
for the dried roots of the *daśamūla* group and others are indeed employed.
In those very cases where one might establish the conventional usage for things while they are still wet, the measurement is double, provided that not all of them have been removed.
In the case of *vāsāghṛta*, *vṛṣaghṛta*, oil, and likewise *sāhacara*,
as well as in cases such as "double the measure for fresh [substances]," this [rule] is not intended to apply.
For their application is recommended only when they are fresh; thus,
four *tulās* of the roots of *śatāvarī*, as they have been prescribed, [should be used].
In this matter, no doubling of the measurements has been adopted by any physicians;
therefore,
for the sake of expanding the intellect of those who are to be instructed, this other [system] is now being elucidated.
AS.Ka.Paribh.92: For where the measure of the medicinal herbs to be boiled has not been specified, a fourfold quantity is prescribed; likewise for other liquids such as milk and the like.
Indeed, in that case, a decoction (kaṣāya) of medicinal herbs should also be prepared with four times [the quantity of liquid];
the Mahākalyāṇaka ghee is intended here as the illustrative example.
In this very way, for medicinal substances where no specific measure has been stated,
it is prescribed that they should be doubled, as well as other liquids such as milk and the like.
For even a decoction of medicinal herbs is prescribed there in double measure;
the use of dyes and the like for fever has been mentioned, and this is recorded as an illustration here.
AS.Ka.Paribh.96: Where milk or another liquid is specified as being four times [the quantity],
the measure for the decoction herbs has been stated, but that of water has not been mentioned.
In that case, the quantity of the decoction is understood solely by virtue of the medicinal herbs;
if this rule is desired, it is the technical convention (*paribhāṣā*) that there is four times as much water.
Then, in that case, the medicinal decoction (kaṣāya) is prepared with the substances combined; however,
when the technical rule (paribhāṣā) is desired, it is [prepared] with sixteen times the amount of water.

AS.Ka.Paribh.99: The decoction (kvātha) should be four times the quantity of the medicinal substance; this is the remainder for the fourth [ingredient]. In this context, oil is intended as the example of that which accompanies [the decoction].

AS.Ka.Paribh.100: Where the medicinal drug, the decoction, and the liquid such as milk and so forth—these three—are present, yet their specific proportions have not been stated, or where the proportion of the oil has not been mentioned; [in such cases, the following rule applies].

AS.Ka.Paribh.101: Milk and other liquids should be added there in an amount equal to the decoction; furthermore, it should be prepared so that [the liquid] is four times the quantity of the fatty substance (sneha).
The *gaulmika* mixed oil is the example here;
for it is thus proclaimed as being twice and thrice the quantity of oil.
AS.Ka.Paribh.103: When a liquid such as milk is to be used,
it should be taken together with the decoction (kaṣāya) so that the liquid is four times the amount [of the powder].
An example of this is as follows:
where a decoction (kaṣāya) is prescribed as being four times the quantity of oil, yet its specific measure is not stated.
It is taught that liquids such as milk and the like may be fourfold or even more;
in that case as well, one should employ a decoction that is four times the quantity of the unctuous substance.
In the case of wind-disease (vātaroga), a decoction of the five roots with oil-cake of many years' standing is prescribed; this is indeed the illustrative example here.
AS.Ka.Paribh.107: Where many liquids are prescribed for a particular unctuous enema (sneha),
their specific quantity is not mentioned even though they are numerous.

AS.Ka.Paribh.108: In that case, there should be a collection of all [the ingredients], with the oil being four times [the quantity of the medicinal paste]. Some explain the procedure for cooking the oil in this manner.
Regarding the rule AS.Ka.Paribh.109, "In cases where there are many [substances], some desire one part each; therein, the liquid is equal"—
due to such differences of opinion, it is just as in the procedure for decoction (kvātha).
When the fourfold water decoction method is adopted there,
it is said that the oil contains many substances, is potent, and has been processed by a hundred-fold cooking.
By this very reasoning, however, some do not accept that the aggregate is fourfold; they say that each [ingredient] has a fluidity equal to its own oiliness.
In the case of unctuous substances used for the treatment of disorders of the *grahaṇī*, such as those containing the five roots (*pañcamūla*) or *abhayā* and others,
one should first [prepare them] with *śukta* or the fresh juice of *mātuluṅga*.
An example of this is found here: "Or whatever other [substance] is very liquid—
this procedure for the cooking of *oṇutaila* (mustard oil) is stated in these verses."
AS.Ka.Paribh.114: For whichever quantity of oil one desires to prepare,
having added that many medicinal herbs to it, one should add four times as much water.
They are cooked for the purpose of medicinal decoction (kaṣāya). Whatever decoction possesses four qualities,
one should give it such that only a quarter remains of the amount of oil.
AS.Ka.Paribh.116: As long as this decoction has not been extracted from the oil,
why is it here made fourfold instead of tenfold relative to the substance to be boiled?
According to the technical rule (paribhāṣā) at AS.Ka.Paribh.117, those substances which are to be boiled with four times the amount of water are here to be cooked in a hundredfold quantity of water.
"Paribhāṣās are boiled [overruled] by the statements of the technical treatise (śāstra);
thus, the complete purification of the 'subtle oil' (aṇutaila) must be performed."
When a meaning that has already been stated in prose is subsequently sung again in verses,
that repetition is not to be censured, as it serves the purpose of clarifying that specific point.
"The meaning which was previously stated by me has been elucidated here in verse form.
Thus ends the eighth chapter.
The Uttarasthāna, Chapter One:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter titled "The Management of Infants" (Bālopacaraṇīya).
Thus indeed said the great sages, beginning with Ātreya.
Now, as soon as a child is born, one should cleanse him from the amnion with Saindhava-salt ghee.

Then, for one whose entire body is overwhelmed by the fever of exceedingly powerful delusion, who is incapable even of crying out due to the corresponding pain, whose bodily constituents are entirely unstable, whose state of youth and so forth is inconceivable, who perceives contact with the bedding and garments as if it were the touch of a saw, who tosses his limbs about uncontrollably, experiencing death once again as it were, and whose consciousness is fading away— one should perform an effusion with *balā*-oil to restore the vital breath that has been crushed within the extremely narrow cavity of the womb.
And there should be a rubbing together of two stones at the root of the ear;
or, if he should indeed move, one should then winnow him over with a black potsherd and a winnowing basket.
And one should recite the mantra at the root of the right ear:
"You arise from limb after limb; you are born from the heart.
(AS.Utt.1.5)
"You are indeed the self named son; live for a hundred autumns. You are one with a hundred lives and a hundred years; may you attain long life."
May the constellations, the directions, night, and day protect you.

When his life-breath has returned and he has regained his natural state, one should tie the umbilical cord four finger-breadths above its attachment to the navel with a linen thread and then cut it with a sharp instrument.
One should hang this [medicinal substance] around the neck and sprinkle the navel with *kuṣṭha* oil (AS.Utt.1.8).

Thereafter, one should bathe the patient with a decoction of milk-tree barks or with water infused with all fragrant substances (*sarvagandha*), using water that is lukewarm— having cooled molten gold or silver— or with a decoction of *kapittha* leaves of a similar nature.

Then, with his right index finger— whose nail is well-trimmed, which has been thoroughly washed and lubricated, and which is wrapped in a cotton swab— he should gently wipe the tongue, lips, and throat.
Having raised the palate, one should cover it from above with a cotton swab soaked in oil.

Then, one should have the patient consume a paste of *aindrī*, *brāhmī*, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, and *vacā*, mixed with honey and ghee in a dose the size of a *hareṇu* seed, consecrated over the tips of *kuśa* grass, using a golden leaf of the *aśvattha* tree; this generates intelligence, longevity, and strength.
Similarly, one should induce vomiting with clarified butter mixed with rock salt, using either the powder of *brāhmī*, *balā*, *anantā*, or *śatāvarī*.
Likewise, through the purification of his chest and throat, lightness and desire arise.
Then, one should perform the birth-rite for him according to the Prājāpatya rite.
Moreover,
because the vessels situated in the heart are wide open at the time of birth, [the fetus does not die].
As.Utt.1.13.
On the third or fourth day, breast milk flows for women (AS.Utt.1.14);
therefore, on the first day, one should have her consume honey and ghee mixed with Anantā and purified by mantras at the three times of the day (AS.Utt.1.14).
In the second month, ghee prepared with lakṣmaṇā, and in the third month as well; thereafter,
for one whose breast milk has been withheld, one should have him take ghee in an amount equal to the palm of his own hand twice a day, and immediately after that, breast milk as desired.

Day after day, one should cover his ears and the junctions of the temples with a cloth soaked in oil. One should lay him down with his head toward the east upon a heap of linen, and place a water-pot consecrated with mantras at his head and at both sides of the door.
One should fan him with the branches of *ādārī*, *vidārī*, *badarī*, *khadira*, *nimba*, *pīlu*,
and *parūṣaka*.
And with those [threads], one should surround the maternity chamber on all sides; one should scatter mustard seeds, linseed, and *kaṇakaṇikā* both inside and outside,
and offer a sacrificial oblation (*bali*) every morning and evening.
One should offer incense made from guggulu and other substances mentioned in the context of wounds;
likewise, a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Atharvaveda should perform rites for pacification (śāntikarma) for ten days.
One should have the *Māyūrī*, the *Mahāmāyūrī*, and the *Āryā Ratnaketudhāriṇī* recited at both times of day. Furthermore,
one should hang a small pouch containing asafoetida, *vaca*, spikenard, and substances that destroy demons upon the northern door-lintel.
And one should have the noble Parṇaśabarī and the noble Aparājitā, inscribed with yellow orpiment, placed on the neck and at the head of the bed of the prince together with his mother;
and at the door, one should have a pestle placed across the threshold.
One should remain awake day and night like a fire fueled by the wood of *kaṇa*, *kaṇḍaka*, and *tinduka* trees; so too should women and friends who are devoted [to one].

And that house should be made full of joyful people (AS.Utt.1.22). Now, his wet-nurse (*dhātrī*) should be of the same caste as himself, middle-aged, pure, not greedy, modest, free from disease, whose calf is still living, affectionate, skillful, celibate, without physical defects, with abundant milk, dressed in white garments, free from the eight bodily defects such as being too tall or too short, without pendulous or upturned nipples, free from the defects of overly large breasts or nipples, and possessing well-proportioned nipples; he should drink her milk alone. (AS.Utt.1.22)

When that [milk] is being milked into a water-vessel and it becomes one with the water, provided it is free from the defects to be described hereafter, it is pure and generates health and strength. Now, the wet nurse— having bathed and anointed herself, wearing constant, unwashed garments, and being of cheerful mind— carrying on her head herbs that establish progeny, should face the east and cause the child to drink from her right breast, which has been washed and slightly drained.
Indeed,
because breast milk that is not uniform is unwholesome (*asātmya*), various disorders arise.

If the breast milk is not drained, the excessive drinking from breasts full of milk causes over-nutrition, leading to the occurrence of cough, dyspnea, fever, and vomiting (AS.Utt.1.26). The loss of breast milk occurs due to dry food and drink, emaciation, anger, grief, desire, and so forth (AS.Utt.1.26).

Substances that promote breast milk include liquors other than *śīdhu*, the meat of animals from marshy regions (*ānūpa*), foods consisting mostly of sweet, sour, and salty liquids, milky plants, drinking milk, lack of physical exertion, and cheerfulness.

However, one should not give breast milk to a child if the mother is hungry, afflicted by grief, exhausted, angry, or has vitiated bodily constituents (*dhātu*), nor if she is pregnant, has consumed incompatible food, or if the medicine has not yet been digested.
And regarding this, it is said in AS.Utt.1.28: "On the sixth night especially, having performed the rites of protection and offerings..."
His kinsmen should remain vigilant as he experiences supreme joy;
on the tenth or twelfth day, at an auspicious time, according to the auspicious traditions of his lineage,
[the funeral rites should be performed].
The father should perform the bathing festival for his child and give him a name on the hundredth day,
or when a full year has passed.
One who bears on his limbs manahśilā, rocanā, aguru, and sandalwood,
whose lineage of three ancestors is venerable, and whose first syllable is a sonant consonant—
[such a person is auspicious].
It is not increased, it has reached the end of the *uṣman* stage, it is not established in an enemy,
and it is joined with the lunar mansion deity; indeed, it is not merely that alone.

A name that is auspicious, containing a semi-vowel within it, neither harsh nor ending in a *taddhita* suffix, and for a man ending in the *visarjanīya* (the final *s*), while for a woman it should have a corresponding vowel;
AS.Utt.1.33.
It should consist of uneven syllables, be non-harsh, clear in meaning, and pleasing to the mind; it should be easy to pronounce, end in long vowels, and contain words of benediction.
Thereafter, the examination of the lifespan is performed using the forms described according to the divisions of the *prakṛti*.
A wise physician should have the child placed with its head toward the east or the north in a clean dwelling located on auspicious ground and well-equipped with necessary materials.
A place that is both sheltered from the wind and well-ventilated, frequented by elderly women and physicians, and free from bedbugs,
mice, mosquitoes, and darkness, is recommended.
The beds, coverlets, and garments should be clean, washed, free from wrinkles, soft, and fumigated with anti-demonic incense.
A crow, whether unslaughtered or slaughtered, combined with *trivṛt* for fumigation,
should always be fumigated with *vacā*, clarified butter, *kuṣṭha*, *śrīveṣṭa*, and mustard seeds.
One should not awaken a sleeping person suddenly, nor should one lift them up;
for in such cases, a sudden fright and the obstruction of natural urges may arise.

To alleviate excessive salivation, abdominal distension, and loss of appetite, one should rub the inside of the mouth with honey, *āmalaka*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), the root of *bṛhatī*, and rock salt.
One should wear auspicious gems set in the horns of living rhinoceroses and other such animals,
as well as the ten [herbs] beginning with aindri, along with jīvaka and ṛṣabhaka.
One should constantly recite it with the hands, the neck, and especially the head;
it bestows longevity, intelligence, memory, and health, and provides protection against malevolent spirits.
If the child develops diseases due to defects in the mother's milk, one should have him drink [medicines] as previously described;
for if he drinks excessively, it causes stiffness of the neck, and when moving upward, it may cause the eyes to roll upward.
Due to the suppression of breath, a woman with a pendulous or excessively large breast may face a risk to her life;
one should not drink the breast milk of a pregnant woman, for it causes harm to the fetus.
In the absence of breast milk, one should drink goat's milk or cow's milk possessing similar qualities;
or [one may drink] milk prepared with the roots of the *bṛhatī* group or with *sthirā*, combined with sugar.
In the fourth month, having properly adorned her, one should cause her— preceded by a mass of fire— to go out from the maternity chamber to pay homage to the gods.
In the fifth month, on an auspicious day, one should have the child placed upon the ground;
having smeared a patch of earth measuring two *kiṣkus* and offered an oblation in the four directions.
O Earth, you are the mother of all beings without exception, the fulfiller of desires;
you are ageless, immeasurable, and saluted by all creatures.
You are the eternal foundation of the worlds, both moving and unmoving;
protect Kumāra like a mother, and may Brahmā grant his approval to that.
Thereafter, every day, with this mantra "Svāhā," one should massage the waist and other areas, along with their supporting structures and attachments.
In the sixth month, one should gradually perform the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*);
by consuming food in this manner over time, the child does not suffer from disease.
To the extent that one consumes solid food, to that same extent must breast milk be abandoned.
During the sixth, seventh, or eighth month, on an auspicious day, for a child who is free from disease—
At the onset of winter, while consoling the child seated on his mother’s lap, the physician should pierce the right ear of a male child and the left ear of a female child.
Holding the needle with the right hand and the pincer with the other hand,
[he should apply it] at the center of the ear-piercing plate, slightly toward the region of the cheek.
Covered only by the fetal membrane, illuminated by the rays of the sun,
held perfectly still and marked with the juice of lac.
One should pierce once, straight and with lightness, at the opening created by fate;
for the veins there are not located above, nor on the sides, nor below. (AS.Utt.1.55)
From that [inhalation], there arise fever characterized by blackish, rust-colored, or reddish discoloration, as well as passion, pain,
and burning sensations; furthermore, swelling, a burning sensation, inflammation, stiffness of the neck, and facial paralysis may occur.

One should quickly perform their treatment by dividing it according to the specific disease; [in this way] there will be no bleeding from the puncture site, nor the occurrence of pain, redness, and so forth.
One should cause a thread soaked in oil and threaded on a needle to be placed along [the incision];
likewise, one should sprinkle thick [ointment] with raw oil (āmataila) and,
for one who eats wholesome food, pierce the ear-lobe after it has been moved to a thicker part.
Once the wick has healed from the discharge, one should gradually increase its size;
furthermore, the ear, having been fomented and treated with an errhine, should be massaged again with nourishing substances.
One should not increase [the dose] during indigestion, nor when there is an excess of morbid waste (mala), nor even when it is excessively hot;
and one should always employ the oil massages for the earlobes as described in the section on diseases of the ears.
When [the child] has been well-nourished and strengthened, resulting in growth and the production of strength and luster,
one should place jewels set in gold upon the ears.
In women, however, one should pierce the *pālī* (the fleshy fold) between the outer corner of the eye (*antara-pāṅga*) and the temple (*avṛddhi*),
but never outside the outer corner; otherwise, complications will certainly arise.
If, due to the oblique insertion of the needle, the application of the wick, excessive tightness, or by the morbid humors (malas),
a great swelling (saṃrambha) arises, one should immediately remove that wick.
One should apply a plaster made of barley, castor root, yaṣṭīmadhu, mañjiṣṭhā, and jyā;
once it has healed well, one should pierce it again with haste for the sake of its further expansion.
If the lobe of a pure patient is severed, the physician should join that pure-secreting [lobe] according to the procedure for joining described in the section on the treatment of ear diseases.
For one year, one should not show the prince anything outside his own residence—
neither a lamp, sunlight, fire, nor any other radiant object.
Then, once the child has cut its first teeth, one should gradually wean it from the breast;
one should provide the milk previously mentioned, along with light and nourishing solid food.
One should cause the child to cease nursing by applying unctuous substances to the breasts,
using loathsome methods such as pouring red lac juice upon them or displaying artificial wounds.
A nourishing *modaka* for an infant should be prepared by combining the pulp of *priyāla*, *madhuka*, honey, parched rice (*lāja*), and white sugar with water or breast milk.
The digestive stimulant [is prepared] with *bāla*, *bilva*, *elā*, sugar, parched rice (*lāja*), and roasted grain flour (*saktu*);
the astringent [is prepared] with *dhātakī* flowers, sugar, parched rice, and parched barley meal (*tarpaṇa*).
If the hunger of a woman who has ceased lactating becomes intense, the procedure for her,
as prescribed by Atreya, is that she should be treated with measures suitable for pregnancy.
One who is diligent, of good conduct, neither too corpulent nor greedy,
who understands the minds of children— such a person should first be appointed as the nurse for the prince.
One who is unrighteous and of evil conduct produces a person who is corpulent and moves with a staggering gait; one who is greedy and gluttonous produces a child who is diseased.
One should treat his diseases with mild, non-depressing medicines; however,
one should especially avoid administering purgation except in the case of a life-threatening illness.
One should not frighten a person who is not compliant, for the seizing spirits (grahas) take hold of one who is terrified;
one should protect such a person from the falling of garments, from physical contact with others, and from fasting.
The play-ground should be made level, free from weapons, stones,
and gravel, and sprinkled with water mixed with the powder of *vellī* plants or with neem water.
One should use a large, resonant, variegated, and non-terrifying wooden toy for play,
with a non-sharp point, or else an auspicious fruit such as that of the cow or horse.
Then, one should teach the science to a capable person according to their caste;
furthermore, one should always instruct them in dharma and in discipline.
Just as one is not carried away at the onset of youth by the wicked horses of the senses,
so should one perform daily anointing, massage, and bathing.
With sahadevā, asthirā, kauntī, kumuda, utpala, and candana;
with bṛhatī fruit, tarkārī, mustard, kuṣṭha, and rock salt.
Oil cooked with *aśvagandhā*, *balā*, castor root, sesame, *apāmārga* grain, and the fruit of *atmaguptā*, along with goat’s milk, [is used for this purpose].
Anointing with these [substances], as well as rubbing the body with them, destroys demons and bestows nourishment;
they should be combined with curd and honey, and mixed with three parts of chickpea flour.
An unguent made from the roots of *mūrvā*, the two types of *rajanī*, and *yava* is beneficial for massage; alternatively, either the powder of *kulattha* or the dust of *vājigandhā* may be used.

For bathing, a paste of all medicinal herbs (sarvauṣadhīkalka) and water boiled with the life-sustaining herbs (jīvanīya) are desired; [this] should be prepared in a decoction of the āragvadhādi group during the cool and spring seasons.
One should have the child consume ghee mixed with a paste of vatsaka and other ingredients;
for in the summer, a child becomes exhausted by wind, heat, and perspiration, and therefore [ghee] is cooling.
In the morning itself, one should drink milk boiled with the group of drugs known as the jīvanīya;
one may also lick barley flour (saktu) enriched with sugar and ghee, but never [drink] the decoction.
One who does not drink excessive water, or who is habituated to ghee, should lick boiled ghee prepared with *kākolī*, sugar, *medā*, *tugākṣīrī*, *yaṣṭimadhu*, and *jīvaka*. (AS.Utt.1.86)
One should smear the head with pungent substances and other cooling agents,
such as *rāsnā*, *sarala*, *varṣābhū*, asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), rock salt (*saindhava*), and *dāru*.
One should have the child lick ghee prepared with water boiled from vidārī and other such herbs;
[the decoction should contain] prapauṇḍarīka, madhuka, the two types of sūpyaparṇī, and durālabhā.
Priyāla, majjā, kākolī, vidārī, kaṭphala, amṛtā, drākṣā, ajaśṛṅgī, dugdhikā, kṣīraśuklā, and hayāhvayā.
A child at the end of the rainy season should lick milk-ghee prepared with śṛṅgī, madhūka flowers, medā, ṛṣabhaka, and jīvaka. (AS.Utt.1.90)
Ghee prepared with *brāhmī*, *siddhārthaka*, *vacā*, *sārivā*, *kuṣṭha*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and black pepper, when drunk, bestows eloquence, intelligence, and memory. (AS.Utt.1.91)
Triphalā, lakṣmaṇā, anantā, samaṅgā, sārivā, and vacā promote longevity, destroy evil spirits and demons, and subdue malevolent beings and insanity.
Brāhmī, pāṭhā, the two types of bṛhatī, the two types of sthirā, the two types of punarnavā,
sahadevā, ravervallī, payasyā, and girikarṇikā. (AS.Utt.1.93)
One should boil one pala of this [substance] in a water-pot until one-fourth remains;
with that decoction, [one should prepare a collyrium] using kauntī, vacā, kuṣṭha, kṛṣṇā, sarṣapa, and saindhava.
One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with the milk of a cow that has a healthy appearance and a healthy calf, combined with pieces of gold,
under the conjunction of the Puṣya asterism.
This Sārasvata ghee, when used for drinking or as an unguent, bestows intelligence, memory, longevity, nourishment, and wisdom; it destroys demons and neutralizes poison.

Or, Vacā and the powder of gold, taken in small quantities with ghee and honey for a year, are supremely purifying, destructive of demons, and increase eloquence (AS.Utt.1.97). Vayasthā, Pippalī, Kuṣṭha, Haridrā, Sārivā, and Vacā—
Having licked this powder of *māṃsī* and *kaiḍarya*, equal in measure to the dust of *brāhmī*,
with clarified butter, a child becomes free from gray hair and free from affliction for a year.
Strong, endowed with learning, destined for a hundred-year lifespan, and possessing stable youth,
one should have him consume this electuary every morning, and likewise cause him to lick *dhātrī*.
One should employ dūrvā, mūrvā, brahmasuvarcalā,
lakṣmaṇā, śvetatarkārī, avyaṇḍā, and white mustard seeds in the same manner as one would brāhmī.
Sahasravīryā, phalinī, ripe bṛhatī fruit,
and rohiṣa— these twelve are proclaimed as separate medicinal boluses (prāśas).
Even a man of great [strength], with his senses restrained, should always consume [earth] with [the prescribed measure];
for by eating earth constantly, he will certainly be protected from diseases.
Pallor, swelling, dyspnea, cough, diarrhea, parasites,
vomiting, fainting, loss of digestive fire, aversion to breast milk, body ache, and vertigo.
One should not eat a tooth-cleansing stick if one's teeth are loose or if the gums are not firm;
for by the friction of that stick, the wind (vāyu), becoming aggravated, may produce dental diseases.
Just as a city protected by brave warriors armed with weapons is unassailable by enemies, so too is the body of a child unassailable by the grahas when the prescribed rites are performed.
Thus ends the first chapter.
Now begins the second chapter:
We shall now expound the chapter titled "The Treatment of Diseases of Infants" (Bālāmayapratiṣedha).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:
"The child is of three types as previously described; among them, for one who subsists on milk, one should administer unvitiated milk."
Food is beneficial for one who subsists on food; both are beneficial for one who follows both ways of life.

AS.Utt.2.3 Indeed, when breast milk is vitiated by the aforementioned dietary and lifestyle factors that aggravate the *doṣas*, it leads to the arising of various diseases in the child. AS.Utt.2.4 Among these, milk corrupted by *vāta* is dark reddish-brown in color, has a bitter and astringent aftertaste, is clear, dry, and has an imperceptible smell; it is frothy, causes lack of satiety, and produces flatulence and obstruction of urine and feces. It causes emaciation, spreads on the surface of water, and floats in broken fragments.

That which has a black, blue, or coppery appearance, a bitter, sour, or pungent aftertaste, the smell of a corpse or blood, is extremely hot, leaves yellow streaks when placed in water, and causes a burning sensation, is vitiated by pitta.

Excessively white and sweet, with a salty after-taste, smelling of ghee, oil, fat, or marrow, slimy, thick, fibrous, heavy, and sinking in water; and characterized by excessive sleep—such is the stool when the *śleṣman* (phlegm) is vitiated.
When consumed, it produces diseases according to their respective symptoms.
If he frequently touches a particular area and cannot endure that touch, one should recognize pain there.
[One should recognize] pain in the head by the closing of the eyes;
[pain] in the heart by biting the tongue and lips, labored breathing, clenching the fists, and upward gazing.

In the abdomen, [symptoms arise] through the passage of feces, urine, and vomiting; distension; gurgling in the intestines; throbbing in the breasts; twisting; bending of the back; and upward heaving of the belly.

In the bladder and the private parts, as well as everywhere else, [the child suffers] from excessive crying and facial contortions beyond its natural disposition, along with urinary retention, thirst, fainting, fear, looking toward the directions, halitosis, and stiffness of the hands and feet, hunchbacking, and plucking out hair.
(AS.Utt.2.10) Then, according to the specific disease and the specific dosha involved, one should administer pacifying and purifying treatments to the wet-nurse.

In that case, when the breast milk is vitiated by *vāta*, one should have the mother drink for three nights a decoction of *devadāru*, *sarala*, *kaṭurohiṇī*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, *pāṭhā*, *bhārṅgī*, *māgadhikā*, *vṛścikālī*, *citraka*, *ajamodā*, *śuṇṭhī*, and *marīca*, or a decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūla*). Thereafter, one should administer one of the clarified butters prescribed for *vāta* disorders, followed by a non-fermented liquor (*nigada*) or wine as a post-drink, or a clarified butter prepared with *vāta*-alleviating substances.
Then, having gently administered an unctuous purgative, one should treat the patient with enema therapy (basti-karman),
as well as with Vata-alleviating massages, sudation, poultices, and rubbing.
One should have the child lick a powder of Sarala, Rasna, Jamoda, and Devadaru mixed with ghee.
And likewise, ghee cooked with these same [ingredients] along with sugar should be administered.
AS.Utt.2.12 Furthermore,
AS.Utt.2.12.
One should purify breast milk that has a bitter aftertaste with mudga, māṣa, palāśa, and the two types of kākolī; or,
if it has an astringent aftertaste, one should purify it with a ghee prepared with priyaṅgu, dhātakī flowers, padmaka, devadāru, and honey, along with hiṅgu and saindhava salt.

For a child with *pitta*-dominant diarrhea that is frothy, interrupted, and floating, one should administer milk boiled with *bilva* and *agnimantha*, along with an oblation of rice-porridge (*havis*) mixed with the fruits of *sūpyaparṇī*, *kākolī*, *bṛhatī*, and *avalguja*;
or, both the wet-nurse and the child should drink a decoction of *amṛtā*, *paṭola* leaves, *sārivā*, *śatāvarī*, *nimba*, and *candana*. (AS.Utt.2.13)
Or one may take a decoction of triphalā, bhūnimba, kaṭukā, and musta; or a decoction of jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, the two kākolīs, madhuka, kaṭphala, and karkaṭaśṛṅgī.
One should administer the Paṭolādi, Padmakādi, Sārivādi, or Nyagrodhādi groups along with honey; furthermore,
one should prepare ghees from these very same substances that alleviate pitta, as well as purgatives, and cold unguents, plasters, and affusions.
Moreover,
milk that has a coppery appearance causes the heart to twist.
One should purify that [milk] with priyaṅgu, mustā, śābara, and lodhra;
it then possesses a sour taste and produces amlapitta.
One should purify it with drākṣā, madhuka, payasyā, and śrīparṇī.
That which has a pungent aftertaste causes vomiting, diarrhea, cough, and dyspnea;

when combined with *kākolī*, *vidārī*, and *madhuparṇī*, it is extremely hot and causes fainting, burning sensations, and fever, yet acts as a purgative; and that same [milk] combined with sandalwood, blue lotus, and white lotus [has the opposite effect].
In the case of kapha, however, one should administer fresh ghee mixed with rock salt (*saindhava*) and long pepper (*pippalī*).
Alternatively, one should smear the breast and the lips of the infant with a paste of *madana* flowers combined with rock salt, licorice (*madhuka*), and honey.
If she vomits easily with that, one should then induce vomiting with sharp emetics;
once she has undergone the process of dietary rehabilitation (*saṃsarjana*), one should have her drink a decoction of the five roots (*pañcamūla*), *ghanā*, *vacā*, and *ativiṣā*.
Alternatively, one should habitually employ a decoction of *tagara*, *suradāru*, *surendrayava*, *pṛthvīkā*, and *vṛścikālī*;
or the *āragvadhādi* group, or the *mustādi* group;
as well as dry and hot treatments such as nasal drops (*nasya*), medicinal smoke (*dhūma*), gargles (*gaṇḍūṣa*), external applications (*pradeha*), and affusions (*pariṣeka*).
And one should administer food and drink that is non-contradictory [to the patient's condition],
moreover.
That which has a salty aftertaste causes erysipelas, urticaria, and itching;
one should purify it with *picumanda*, *paṭolī*, and *kṣīrīvṛkṣa*.
That which is fibrous causes debility, dyspnea, and cough.
That heavy, sinking-type [fever], which causes catarrh, nasal discharge, dyspepsia, and lassitude, should be treated with a powder of *pippalī* and *nāgara* mixed with honey and ghee;
or alternatively, with a paste of *pāṭhā* and *vyoṣa*, or with the powder of the five spices (*pañcakola*), all saturated with honey and ghee.
One should also consult the chapter on the treatment of the humors (doṣopakramaṇīya).

Furthermore, when a wet-nurse indulges in things that provoke the *sannipāta* (the combination of all three humors), her three impurities simultaneously reach the chest and, following the milk-carrying channels (*rasāyanī*), bring about breast milk characterized by the combined symptoms of all three humors.

If, however, due to lack of knowledge, constant failure to observe, or negligence, the child drinks the mother’s [discharge], then he suffers from diarrhea— feces that are watery, clear, undigested, foul-smelling, multicolored, and frothy— and there manifest in him symptoms such as pale urine, abdominal distension, thirst, fever, vomiting, yawning, dry eructations, loss of appetite, vertigo, body aches, convulsions, moaning, inflammation of the nose, eyes, mouth, and vision, and hoarseness of voice; this condition is called *kṣīrālasaka*.
In that case, one should first quickly cause the wet-nurse and the infant to vomit; then,
once they have been brought into contact with the treatment, one should give them a decoction of *mustā*, *pāṭhā*, *ativiṣā*, *kuṣṭha*, and *kaṭukā* for drinking.
Or [a decoction] of rāsnā, jamodā, priyaṅgu, and bhadradāru; or of pāṭhā, tejovatī, punarnavā, and vṛścikālī;
or of bhūnimba, amṛtā, kuṭaja fruit, and sārivā.
Or [one may use] the groups beginning with *vacā* and *haridrā*,
or the great decoction beginning with *pāṭhā*,
or the leaves of *jambu*, *āmra*, *tinduka*, and *kapittha*.
Or, in the event of complications from a *bilva* fracture,
one should treat it according to the specific disease;
furthermore, the eruption of teeth is the seat of all diseases.

Specifically, however, diseases rooted in that [vitiation] are fever, headache, burning sensation, thirst, giddiness, ophthalmia, kukūṇaka, pothakī, vomiting, cough, dyspnea, diarrhea, and erysipelas (visarpa).
That [disease] manifests after the eighth month of long life, or even later.
But for others, [the treatment] is from the fourth [month],
because they are excessively tormented by the pain of tooth eruption during extreme infancy and thus do not possess fully developed bodily constituents or strength.
In that regard, bone and marrow are the causes for the emergence of teeth.

At that time, because their potency is not yet fully developed, the teeth fall out again after a period of time; and because the constituent elements (dhātus) are being replenished, they emerge once more. For this very reason, teeth do not grow again in the elderly.

However, in cases where [the fetus] has fallen prematurely due to force, there is a non-regeneration of the vessels because of the sudden loss of the elements and seeds residing in their seats, the interruption of the continuity [of the embryo], excessive hemorrhage, and the discharge [of the fetus] due to trauma; by this,
those who have fallen from disease are also generally explained.

When those two elements, ripening in the course of time, reach the site of the teeth, then, due to their slight elevation and their friction against the gums of the upper and lower teeth, a horripilation of the limbs arises;
and by means of the phlegm associated with that [site], itching occurs, whereby the child bites its nipples.
Whatever he eats, that very thing he brings into his mouth;
the vital air (māruta) becomes obstructed at the roots of his teeth,

and then, permeated by phlegm (kapha), situated within the marrow of the bones, and spreading in all directions along with bile (pitta), it vitiates the tissues (dhātu) and the waste products (mala), thereby producing various complications as previously described.

Furthermore, when the powerful Vāyu alone, or Vāyu accompanied by Pitta, becomes disordered and localized in the gums and causes the drying up of the bone and marrow, then the emergence of teeth simply does not occur.
