In the case of a cat's backbreaking, a peacock's crest-sprouting,
or the eruption of teeth in children, there is indeed nothing that does not cause pain.
Having analyzed the specific dosha, the disease, the degree of aggravation, and the strength [of the patient],
as well as the place, time, and other factors, the physician should apply the appropriate medical treatment therein.
Since those very same doshas, dūṣyas, and diseases such as fever are [the objects of treatment],
therefore that very same medicine is used, though its dose should be smaller.
Due to their delicacy, small stature, and the fact that they do not consume all types of food,
children are always unctuous because of their consumption of ghee and milk.
Therefore, a wise physician should immediately administer mild emesis;
in cases requiring treatment, one should employ enemas, purgation, suppositories, and follow-up applications.

One should administer purgatives and other such treatments using *dhātrī* (myrobalan) alone as appropriate; [the decoction consists of] *mūrvā*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), *varākoṭaja*, jambū bark, *dāruharidrā*, and mustard seeds.
Pāṭhā licked with honey is an excellent remedy for defects of breast milk;
the body is purified by means of sugarcane root, kaśeruka, and yaṣṭimadhu.
It should be thickened with honey, *kāśmarya*, and *guḍūcī* along with rice-water; or alternatively, it may be prepared by boiling *surasa*, white mustard, and the two types of *bṛhatī*.
One should apply a powder made from *padmakośīra*, *phalinī*, and white sandalwood, mixed with honey,
to rub over the gums (*dantapālī*).
Or [it may be prepared] with long pepper, dhātakī flowers, and āmalaka fruit; or likewise, it may be combined with the dust raised from the hooves of a vādhrīṇasa and a kapota.
The powder of the flesh of the common quail (*lāva*) and the partridge (*tittiri*), mixed with honey and the juice of flowers,
quickly makes the mouths of children as beautiful as a forest of teeth-like filaments.
Ghee prepared with vacā, dvibṛhatī, pāṭhā, kaṭukā, ativiṣā, ghanā, and the sweet [drugs] is effective for the eruption of teeth.
Bhadradāru, ghanā, yaṣṭī, samaṅgā, along with sugar and candied sugar [are also used].
One whose limbs are afflicted by fever caused by Vāta should drink Antarapānaka,
consisting of Surāhvā, Ghanā, Yaṣṭyāhvā, Payasyā, and the two types of Aṃśumatī.
Nāgara, marica, bhārṅgī, vṛścikālī, and śatāvarī—
ghṛta prepared with the decoction and milk of these [herbs] cures fever caused by vāta.
For a child, drinking, massage with oil, and rubbing with these [substances] are beneficial.
(AS.Utt.2.38) [These consist of] turmeric, kuṣṭha, ṣaḍgranthā, śatapuṣpā, and hareṇu. (AS.Utt.2.39)
With *bhārgī*, *elā*, *suṣavī*, *rāsnā*, *varṣābhū*, *nata*, and *sarṣapa*,
each in one part (*akṣa*), ground with water, *sauvīra* (sour gruel), and *mastu* (whey), [this is used] for fever caused by wind (*marujvara*).
One should cook one *prastha* of oil with the scum of *surā* wine as an ointment,
adding parched grain (*lāja*), blue water-lily (*nīlotpala*), long pepper (*kaṇā*), licorice (*madhuka*), collyrium (*añjana*), and sugar.

Honey licked [with the powder] cures fever caused by pitta and diarrhea. A decoction of parched grain (lāja) and two types of long pepper (pippalī), combined with sugar and honey, [achieves the same].
When drunk, it destroys fever, diarrhea, thirst, and vomiting. In cases of diarrhea caused by undigested matter (āmātisāra) and blood, one should administer Gajapippalī as a paste.
One should have [the patient] drink [milk] mixed with sugar, or a powder made from *devadāru*;
in cases of headache, one should apply cold, ghee-soaked plasters to the head.
An application of the leaves of *kapittha*, *cāṅgerī*, *badarī*,
and *kākamācī* to the head destroys headache, vomiting, and diarrhea. (AS.Utt.2.44–45)
One suffering from thirst should drink *gavādanī* and pomegranate with lukewarm water.
For *kukūṇaka* and *pothakī*, one should apply their respective specific medicines as previously described.
Realgar, conch-shell navel, long pepper,
and liquorice, ground with honey into pills, conquer all eye diseases of an infant.
An excellent wick (varti) is prepared from one hundred parts each of long pepper seeds, rice, mung beans, jasmine buds, barley,
and blue lotus petals.
A powder of *priyaṅgu*, *añjana*, and *mustā*,
drunk with rice-water and honey, cures thirst, diarrhea, and vomiting.
Patola, nimba, kuṭaja, saptaparṇa, and dīpyaka;
devadāru, viḍaṅga, sarala, honey, and ghee.
When licked, it destroys fever, diarrhea, cough, anemia, and vomiting; it also cures disorders of the *mātṛkā* (fetal constituents) and other diseases of a similar nature.
One should cook ghee with madhuka, vyoṣa, ṣaḍgranthā, granthika, asparśarodikā, the young shoots of milk-exuding trees, and pāṭhā.
That, when drunk with honey, destroys phlegm-born fever and is an excellent digestive stimulant.
(AS.Utt.2.52) [It is prepared] with rāsnā, elā, nata, tarkārī, madhuśigru, and surāhvaya. (AS.Utt.2.52)
A plaster made from bilva, kuṣṭha, varaṇa, reṇukā,
and miśī removes fever caused by phlegm (śleṣman); oil prepared with these same ingredients serves as an ointment for massage.
One should smear the mandalas with elephant urine mixed with clarified butter.
[The ingredients are: turmeric, deodar, pine resin, śreyasī, and the two types of bṛhatī.

Pṛśniparṇī and śatāhvā, when licked with honey and ghee, are excellent for stimulating the digestive fire (grahaṇī), for regulating the downward movement of wind (māruta), and for conquering diarrhea,
fever, dyspnea, jaundice, anemia, and cough. (AS.Utt.2.55)
In all diseases of children, [this formulation] is honored as it bestows strength and complexion. [It consists of:
Bilva-peśī, gaja-kaṇā, dhātakī, lodhra, and vālaka.
This,
when licked and quickly mixed with honey, swiftly cures diarrhea in a child.
[It is prepared] with triphalā, dhātakī flowers, padma, and the tender fruits (śalāṭu) of bilva.
Ghee prepared with the six parts of the *sakṭu* (barley meal) cures abdominal diseases.
[This is done] with *pathyā*, *sauvarcala* salt, alkali, *vella*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), *agni*, and asafoetida (*hiṅgu*).
Ghee prepared with bitter herbs and an equal quantity of milk cures colic,
abdominal distension, prolapse of the rectum, dyspnea, cough, and chronic vomiting.
With *samaṅgā*, *dhātakī*, *lodhra*, *kuṭannaṭa*, the two types of *balā*,
*mahāsahā*, *kṣudrasahā*, *mudga*, and the tender fruits of *bilva*.
Ghee prepared with water boiled with the fruits of *kārpāsī*,
combined with alkali and whey, quickly destroys diseases arising from the eruption of teeth.
This [treatise] composed by the aged Kāśyapa provides remedies for various diseases;
regarding diseases arising from the eruption of teeth, one should not over-restrain a child.
The diseases of a child whose teeth have emerged subside by themselves;
a child who has been born for as many months as there are years [of age] is considered a *dvija*.

It generally falls [into one of] these eight; their occurrence is among the preceding ones. [This happens in one who] indulges in excessive sleep, cold water, phlegm-inducing substances, and breast milk.
When the channels carrying the nutrient fluid (rasa) are obstructed by phlegm (kapha) in an infant,
loss of appetite, catarrh, fever, and cough arise.
Then the child withers; his face and eyes become oily and pale. [One should administer] rock salt, trikaṭu, śāraṅgeṣṭā, pāṭhā, and girikadambaka.
For one who is wasting away due to loss of appetite and similar conditions, one should administer honey and ghee;
likewise, one should employ the powdered *pañcakola* combined with *aśoka* and *rohiṇī*.
Or, the powder of *badarī*, *dhātakī*, and *dhātrī* mixed with clarified butter;
or *madhuyaṣṭikā* combined with the juice of horse-dung and honey.
One should take either the juice of two vārtākī fruits alone, or the juice of horse-dung,
or [a paste of] ghanā, vyōṣa, pāṭhā, mūrvā, and śatāvarī with honey.
One should administer *saparyasā*, *pṛthakparṇī*, or ghee mixed with honey;

or [ghee] prepared with *sthirā*, the "immortal tree" (*amarataru*), the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), the two types of *punarnavā*, *sthirā*, *vacā*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, *kākolī*, *pippalī*, and *nata*.
Half a *prastha* of clarified butter,
prepared with one *karṣa* each of *nicula*, blue lotus, *varṣābhū*, *bhārṅgī*, and *musta*,
is the supreme purifier of the channels.
That [milk] which contains *siṃhī*, *aśvagandhā*, *surasā*, and *kaṇā* possesses those same qualities.
[One may also prepare it] with *yaṣṭyāhvā*, *pippalī*, *lodhra*, *padmaka*, *utpala*, and *candana*.
Ghee prepared with *tālīśa* and *sārivā* conquers wasting diseases (*śoṣa*). [Ghee] prepared with *rāsnā*, *madhūlikā*, *bhārṅgī*, *pippalī*, and *devadāru* [is likewise effective].
Ghee prepared with a paste of *aśvagandhā*, the two types of *kākolī*, *śṛṅgī*, *ṛṣabhaka*, *jīvaka*, *ṛddhi*, *sūpyaparṇī*, and *viḍaṅga* [is beneficial].
A decoction prepared with vācā,
vayasthā, tagara, kāyasthā, and coraka, boiled in the marrow extracted from the head of a rabbit, is supremely nourishing for one who is wasting away.
Oil prepared with goat's urine and *surā* liquor is beneficial for massage (*abhyañjana*). Two types of *balā*, *tumburu*, the bark of *challī*, *vacā*, and *girikadambaka* [are also used].
For those whose lower body is drying up, an ointment made from *surā* and flour should be applied.
[This is done] with *siṃhaskandī*, *siṃhavallī*, *karamardī*, and *trikaṇṭaka*.

A decoction made from these parts serves as a sprinkling for children who are wasting away. By licking a paste of *aśoka*, *rohiṇī*, and *kṛṣṇā* with honey and clarified butter, one may overcome [the disease].
A child suffering from emaciation of the body should consume goat’s milk mixed with sugar;
in cases of dry cough in a boy, this serves to purify the mother’s breast milk.
A soup of black gram (māṣa) should be administered, fried in ghee and mixed with black pepper;
one should also have the child lick a linctus made of ativiṣā, śṛṅgī, and pippalī with honey.
To one afflicted by cough, fever, and vomiting,
or one tormented by cough, thirst, vomiting, and diarrhea, one should administer a parching gruel (*lājatarpaṇa*) made with *ativiṣā* alone. (AS.Utt.2.79–80)
One should cause [the patient] to drink either parched grain and *tālīśapatra*, or the seeds of the lotus, or a paste of *lodhra* and *priyaṅgu*, with rice-water.
Powdered parched grain and *kustumburu* mixed with sugar and honey;
or a preparation made from the fruit, root, and bark of *bṛhatī*, along with *pippalī* and *granthika*.
A decoction prepared with *tavakṣīrī* and consumed with honey, when habitually used, destroys vomiting,
fainting, fever, dyspnea, cough, diarrhea, and chronic rhinitis.
The roots of pañcakola, dvivārtākī, bhārṅgī,
and tugāhvaya, when licked with honey and ghee, destroy asthma, cough, catarrh, and pain.
Ghee prepared with a decoction of *śyāmā*, *atimuktā*, and *tarkārī* flowers, and containing *yaṣṭīmadhu*, cures thirst, hiccups, dyspnea, and hemorrhagic disorders.
One who vomits breast milk after every time it is drunk should be made to lick the juice of two *vārtākī* fruits mixed with honey and ghee, along with the five spices (*pañcakola*).
One should lick a paste of long pepper (pippalī), the five salts, kṛmijit, and pāribhadraka;
likewise, one may lick trikaṭu (vyoṣa) or the soot of hair and skin.
From the perspective of the benefits, [the oil] of the porcupine, the hedgehog, the monitor lizard,
the iguana, and the peacock, along with a decoction produced from khadira, arjuna, tālīsa, kuṣṭha, and candana, [is recommended].
Ghee prepared with milk and [the paste of] the sprouts of milky trees (*kṣīrī*), madhuka, the root of darbha grass, lotus stalks (*bisā*), and blue lotuses (*utpala*) cures vomiting.
A decoction containing sugar and honey removes the fever of thirst and burning sensations. [Sugar, pomegranate, long pepper, nāgakeśara, and jīvaka.
A child who licks [this] with honey is freed from thirst and vomiting; [likewise,
one may lick] parched grain together with sandalwood, uśīra, yaṣṭīmadhuka, and padmaka.
Anointed, washed, and drunk, it destroys wandering, thirst, burning sensations, and delusion. Having drunk the prepared broth of common quail (lāva) without fat or salt...
A child conquers diseases born of fasting by means of sugar;
however, erysipelas (visarpa) arising in the bladder-head (bastiśīrṣa) is life-destroying for an infant.
Padmavarṇa, known by the name Mahāpadma, arises from the three defects;
it proceeds from the two arms to the heart, or from the heart it goes to the anus.
If a child is born with teeth, or whose upper teeth emerge before the lower ones,
one should perform a propitiatory rite for that portent and for a pair of Brahmins.
One should give a gift along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and worship the deity Naigameṣa;
facing eastward, one should fill the mouth of a calf with honey and parched grain (lāja).
A child should be made to kiss [the image] three times; this is the supreme expiation.
One should not cause a child who has bathed to mount a boat or the shoulder of an elephant.
In this case, one should feed the Brahmins milk-rice (pāyasa) with honey and clarified butter;
for even while drinking her breast milk, the child generally [remains] in the mother's womb.
That which is accompanied by cough, weak digestion, vomiting, drowsiness, emaciation, anorexia, and vertigo,
and is associated with enlargement of the abdominal cavity, is called *pārigarbhika*.
And for the disease known as *paribhava*, one should employ treatments that stimulate the digestive fire (*agni-dīpana*) with long pepper (*pippalī*),
long pepper root (*pippalīmūla*), katuka, and devadāru.
One should cook ghee with the two types of alkali (kṣāra), biḍa salt, cumin, the pulp of bilva, agni, and dīpyaka, along with curd, sauvīraka, and the scum of surā liquor.
When administered at the proper time after the child has finished drinking breast milk supplemented with food as prescribed, it destroys diseases rooted in the mother's body.
One should apply these very treatments for these [diseases], and one should apply those very [treatments] for them;
and he who, having drunk breast milk repeatedly, passes wind with excessive flatulence.
This is also the supreme wholesome regimen for him, acting as a digestive stimulant and promoting strength and complexion; however,
one should have a child who is excessively hungry or emaciated lick it.
One should cause [the patient] to drink the powder of vidārī, barley, wheat, and coriander soaked in ghee,
followed by boiled milk mixed with honey and sugar.
One should boil milk or clarified butter with *akṣamajjā*, *dvika*, *kākoli*, *yaṣṭimadhuka*, *moraṭa*, and the seeds of *ikṣuraka*.
That which was previously mentioned for those with excessive digestive fire— namely, heavy and unctuous food— should be administered; likewise,
[one may eat] the remnants of dogs, crows, and cats, or with water containing such remnants.
One should bathe him; if not, his hunger will not subside.
Then, having been bathed according to the prescribed rite while standing at the foot of a milk-exuding tree...
One should adorn the boy with white ornaments such as garments and jewels;
thereafter, one should perform an exchange of ornaments between him and the tree.
This auspicious ablution bestows longevity and conquers all diseases; it causes the hair, eyes, and eyelashes to become matted together and overcomes excessive greed.
One should bathe the patient, who smells like cow urine, at a sacred bathing place with the juices of cow dung,
along with *vacā*, *puṣpa*, *śilā*, *kuṣṭha*, *vayasthā*, *hiṅgu*, and *kaṭphala*.
One should cook oil for anointment with *sabastā*, *mūtra*, and *madira*,
along with *balā*, *vidārī*, the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), *kuṣṭha*, *uśīra*, and red sandalwood (*kucandana*). (AS.Utt.2.111)
The proven yellow oblation (pīta-havis) completely destroys that disorder.
[It cures] that which causes pain in the head, then the back, then the scrotum, and then the feet.
The wind arising from the two hands is known as *saparvānuplava*.
[It is prepared] with *gaurī*, *vacā*, *sadāpuṣpī*, *hayagandhā*, and the three pungent spices (*kaṭutraya*).
One should administer for him oil prepared with *sakṭphala*, the two types of *vārtāko*, *vayaḥsthā*, asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), and *rohiṣa*, combined with goat's urine and wine.
One should apply oil as an ointment and treat the remaining symptoms as in the treatment for wind-diseases (vātavyādhi). When kapha is provoked in the flesh of the palate, it produces tālukaṇṭaka.
By that, a depression at the top of the palate occurs;
there is falling from the palate, aversion to the breast, drinking with difficulty, and liquid feces (AS.Utt.2.116).
Thirst, itching of the mouth, pain in the eyes, stiffness of the neck,
and vomiting [occur]; in that case, having lifted [the patient's head], one should rub [the area] with barley-alkali and honey.
Likewise for the palate, [one should apply] a paste of long pepper, dry ginger, cow dung juice,
and rock salt; or a paste of ginger, turmeric, and kuṣṭha, along with the tender leaves of the *vaṭa* tree.
Having bound it and smeared it with cow dung, one should then foment it over a fire-pit; then,
one should smear the palate and mouth with its juice and sprinkle the eyes with it.

Having drunk a paste of *harītakī*, *vacā*, and *kuṣṭha* mixed with honey along with breast milk, a child is freed from *tālukaṇṭaka*. If, due to the depletion of the brain matter (*mastuluṅga*), the *vāyu* should cause the palate bone to bend, [this remedy should be applied].

For that patient afflicted by the misery of thirst, ghee boiled with sweet substances should be administered for drinking and for massage, and one should also provide relief with cold water to alleviate agitation.
Due to the accumulation of impurities or from sweating, a copper-colored ulcer arises within the rectum, produced by blood and phlegm,
accompanied by itching and many complications.
Some call that [disease] *mātṛkā-doṣa*, others *pautana*; some call it *pṛṣṭhāru* or *gudakuṭṭa*, and others call it by no specific name at all.
In that case, the nurse's milk should be purified with drugs that remove pitta and kapha;
it should be made white and cool, and an internal drink (antarapānaka) mixed with cold water should be given.
One should smear the wound with that [ointment] containing honey, *tārkṣya* (guggulu), and *śaila* (śilājatu),
and irrigate it with a decoction of *triphalā*, *badarī*, and *plakṣa* bark.
One should apply a plaster made of *kāsīsa*, *rocanā*, *tuttha*, *manohvā*,
and *rasāñjana* ground with sour liquids, or one should dust [the area] with these same substances in powdered form.
Or, with very fine powders of yaṣṭīmadhu, śaṅkha, sauvīrāñjana,
sāriva, śaṅkhanābhi, or the bark of asana; AS.Utt.2.126
When the itching caused by passion is intense, one should perform bloodletting with leeches; furthermore, all treatments that heal pitta-type ulcers are recommended for anal fissures.
In cases of indigestion, stiffness, disorders of pitta and blood, itching, swellings, diseases of the throat,
and excessive enlargement of the abdomen, the internal consumption of *tārkṣya* (mercury) is desired.
If [the infant] does not take the breast in the maternity room,
then one should touch its tongue with the powder of *pathyā* (yellow myrobalan), *dhātrī-phala* (emblic myrobalan), and *kaṇa* (black pepper), mixed with clarified butter and honey.
A powder of *pippalī* and *triphalā*, saturated with ghee and honey,
should be administered as a linctus to bring relief to one who is weeping or trembling.
On the fifth day, one should dust the inflamed area with the ash of burning charcoal once it has subsided, or one should apply a plaster of *apāmārga* stalks mixed with jaggery-water.
One should rub thick [powder] on the ground until it becomes smooth, and then, even when the stalks have fallen away,
one should sprinkle the elevated navel with burnt goat dung mixed within.
One should heal the umbilical region so that it is not elevated by applying a powder made from aśvagandhā, jana, ajāvi, viḍa, yaṣṭīmadhu, and other such ingredients, mixed with unctuous substances.

One should irrigate the navel with oil cooked with a paste of yaṣṭīmadhu, lodhra, niśā, and śyāmā; however, in the case of suppuration, one should sprinkle it with oil and dust it with the powder of those same drugs.
When the umbilical region is distended by Vāta and accompanied by pain, it is known as Tuṇḍi;
it should be pacified with Vāta-alleviating measures, oleation, sudation, and poultices.
From improper mental construction, yawning and stretching may arise from the navel;
in that case, one should perform treatments to remove wind and bile both internally and externally.
Due to the suppression of the amniotic fluids during gestation, or from contact with phlegm located in the throat,
the vitiated nutrient-fluid (rasa) obstructs the channels within the heart.
Then, with his fists clenched and his mind bewildered, the child is overcome by diseases such as heart disease,
convulsions, dyspnea, cough, vomiting, fever, and others.
One should say that it is a congenital disease characterized by swelling and fullness with water; in that case,
the internal drink in the morning should be a purifier of the channels.
One should apply goat's urine [as a wash], and one should avoid bathing and oil massage.
One should take one pala each of the roots of bilva and others, bṛhatī, and pañcakola.
One should cook eight palas of the flesh of a camel and eight palas of the head of a rabbit in sixteen times the quantity of water until one-eighth remains.
With that decoction, one should cook a *prastha* of ghee with portions of one *karṣa* each [of the medicinal herbs],
along with equal parts of goat’s urine, wine, curd, and milk.
With finely ground pastes of viḍaṅga, rock salt (saindhava), cumin (ajājī), long pepper (cavikā), devadāru, sahiṃsrā, vermilion (hiṅgula), garlic (laśuna),
and the three pungents (vyoṣa).

By drinking it, one destroys congenital gulma, hiccup, diseases of wind, and anemia caused by vāta; furthermore, it provides nourishment for maintaining health. One should apply a plaster of dūrvā, sesame, and utpala to a child whose skin is scorched.
One should drink the powder of śamī leaves, śirīṣa bark, sārivā, madhuka, abhayā, mūrvā,
dhātrī, and niśā, mixed with honey and cow's urine.
A patient suffering from anemia (pāṇḍuroga) should take clarified butter boiled with either chebulic myrobalan (*varā*) and *bhṛṅgarāja* juice,
or with *pāṭhā*, *vella*, the two types of *rajanī*, *mustā*, *bhārṅgī*, and *punarnavā*.
Ghee boiled with bilva, the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), and vṛścikālī, when consumed in the proper dose,
liberates one from diseases arising from the ingestion of earth.
Whichever medicine is prescribed for a particular disease, if one is smeared with it,
remains so for a moment, and then washes off and subsequently drinks it, that very medicine will conquer that specific ailment.
Indeed, diseases of children are also produced by the *grahas* (seizing spirits) when they remain hidden; therefore,
in their treatment, action based on divine means (*daivayukti*) is always recommended.
Thus ends the second chapter.
Now begins the third chapter.
Chapter 3 of the Uttara-tantra: We shall now expound the chapter entitled "Knowledge of the Seizers of Children" (Bālagrahavijñānīya).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:
"In ancient times, [these remedies] were created by the wielder of the trident (Śiva) for the protection of Guha."
There are five male spirits and seven female spirits that seize human beings.
These are Skanda, Viśākha, Meṣāsya, Śvagraha, and the one known as Pitṛgraha.
Śakunī, Pūtanā, Śītapūtanā, Dṛṣṭipūtanā,
Mukhamaṇḍitikā, and likewise Revatī and Śuṣkarevatī.
Those [gods], capable of assuming any form at will, attended upon Skanda with concentrated minds;
because Skanda was their protector (*bāladhāra*), Skanda became their leader.
Then, when Skanda had reached youth, Rudra favored those fierce grahas— who were humble and desirous of a livelihood— with the office of general.
Nor are guests, deities, or ancestors honored on sacred festival days in those houses where the path of right conduct has ceased.
In those households where offerings and oblations have ceased, and where broken bronze vessels are used for eating—
take away from them the health of their children, as well as their stability and happiness.
Appointed as "Wielders of the Trident," they long for offerings and worship;
yet they are angry, fearful, dejected, and wander alone in desolate places.
Those who wear flowers, garments, and ornaments already used by others; children who have unclean nurses; and those who weep during the twilights—these are impure.
Sometimes they terrify those who are sleeping, or even those who are awake, by assuming the forms of bears, owls, cats, and other such strange creatures.
Generally, during the lunar nodes (parvan), the seizing spirits (grahas), who strike at vulnerabilities,
take possession; they are perceived only by one whose eye is the scripture (śāstra).
They enter the bodies of children as Gandharvas enter those of women; their form is that of those who seize [the victim], characterized by constant weeping and fever.
The general symptoms are terror, yawning, knitting of the eyebrows,
dejection, salivation of foam, upward gaze, biting of the lips and teeth, and sleeplessness.
Crying, whimpering, aversion to breast milk, abnormality of voice,
and suddenly scratching all over the limbs of one's nurse with the nails.
In that condition, there is discharge from one eye, the head is frequently tossed about,
one side of the body is paralyzed, the limbs are rigid, there is perspiration, and the neck is bent.
One who bites his teeth, hates the breast, cries out discordantly in fear,
has a distorted face, vomits saliva, and stares intensely upward [suffers from this disease].
The infant smells of fat, garlands, and perfumes, is agitated, has clenched fists and passes stool,
moves one eye, cheek, or eyebrow, and has both eyes bloodshot.
Afflicted by the *skanda* [fever], he will certainly suffer either disability or death;
there is frequent loss of consciousness, plucking out of hair, and bending of the neck.
Bending forward while yawning, the discharge of feces and urine,
vomiting froth, looking upward, and the dancing of the hands, eyebrows, and feet.
Clinging to the breasts, biting with the tongue, agitation, fever, wakefulness,
and the smell of pus and blood are the symptoms of Skandāpasmāra (epilepsy caused by Skanda).
Bloating of the hands and feet, twitching, and vomiting of foam [are also its signs].
Thirst, clenching the fists, diarrhea, weakness of voice, discoloration of the complexion,
moaning, groaning, vomiting, cough, hiccups, and sleeplessness; (AS.Utt.3.20–21)
Biting the lips, contraction and stiffness of the shoulders, a smell like that of a goat,
looking upward, laughing, bending at the waist, and fever; (AS.Utt.3.21–22)
Fainting, swelling of one eye, and the symptoms of the Naigameṣa graha;
trembling, horripilation, perspiration, and closing of the eyes.
In a dog-like person, there is protrusion of the tongue, biting with the tongue, internal gurgling in the throat,
running about, foul-smelling excrement, and barking like a dog.
Horripilation, frequent terror, sudden weeping, fever, cough,
diarrhea, vomiting, yawning, thirst, and a foul odor of the body [are the symptoms].
In the case of a child afflicted by Pitṛgraha, there may be contraction, tossing about, emaciation, stiffness, discoloration of the limbs, clenching of the fists, and watering of the eyes.
There is drooping of the head, diarrhea, ulcers on the tongue, palate, and throat, and eruptions with burning,
pain, and suppuration that recur repeatedly in the joints.
Day and night they dissolve away; there is suppuration either in the mouth or even in the anus,
as well as fear, a bird-like odor, and fever during the seizure by Śakuni.
In *pūtanā*, there is vomiting, trembling, drowsiness, and wakefulness at night;
hiccups, flatulence, diarrhea, thirst, and suppression of urine.
The falling out of hair on the body along with horripilation, and a putrid odor like that of a crow,
occur through Śītapūtanā; trembling, weeping, and sidelong glancing also occur through her.
There is gurgling in the intestines due to thirst, diarrhea, a cadaverous smell like fat,
coldness in one side of the body and heat in the other; and through Andhapūtanā there is vomiting, fever, cough, and little sleep.
There is a breaking up of the feces, discoloration, foul odor, and emaciation of the limbs;
there is impairment of vision, pain and itching in the eyes, the appearance of pothakī eruptions, and swelling.
Agitation due to suppressed urine is characterized by distaste for the breasts, discoloration, harshness of voice,
trembling, a fishy odor, or an acidic odor.
Adornment of the face, loveliness of the hands, feet, and mouth,
an abdomen covered with dark-colored veins, and fever.
Loss of appetite, exhaustion of the limbs, and an odor like cow's urine occur under Revatī; there is a dark-blue discoloration and rubbing of the ears, nose, and eyes.
Cough, hiccup, twitching of the eyes, distortion of the face, and redness; a smell like that of a goat, fever, emaciation, and greenish, liquid stools.
In Śuṣkarevatī, there arises a gradual wasting away of all the limbs,
as well as loss of hair, aversion to food, weakness of voice, and discoloration.
The presence of multi-colored feces, knots and veins in the abdomen, crying, a vulture-like odor, and persistence for a long period [indicate the disease].
In one whose abdomen has circular knots and various kinds of stool...
One should abandon that child whose tongue is depressed in the middle and whose palate is dark-brown; likewise,
that child who, while eating various kinds of food, suffers emaciation.
One seized by thirst (tṛṣṇā), with sunken eyes, is killed by Śuṣkarevatī (AS.Utt.3.37).
Violence, aversion, and the desire for worship are the causes of being seized by the Grahas (AS.Utt.3.38).
In that case,
one who commits acts of violence— whether a child or an adult— becomes one with a drooping nose.
With a wounded tongue, groaning loudly, miserable, with tearful eyes, discolored, speaking with difficulty, and foul-smelling, he is born [in that state]. (AS.Utt.3.40)
Emaciated, he soils himself with urine and excrement without feeling disgust;
and, agitated, raising his hands, he strikes himself as well as others.
Likewise, one should enter a blazing fire using weapons, wood, or other such means;
one may drown in water, fall into a well, or perform other similar acts.

One should recognize the onset of thirst, burning sensations, delusion, vomiting of pus, and the discharge of blood from all the orifices; such a person, for whom these fatal signs (ariṣṭa) arise, should be abandoned. One who is fond of solitude, sexual intercourse with women, conversation, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments [is also to be avoided].
Exultant yet agitated, difficult to manage, and tormented by lust;
dejected, touching his face, with dry lips, throat, and palate.
He looks about apprehensively, cries out, broods, and falls into a state of fear;
even when food is offered at his desire for food, he does not wish to eat it.
One should know that a [demon] who has been seized by one desiring an offering (bali) is easily subdued;

"But the other two [may be used] according to one's desire through the giving of sexual pleasure, offerings, and so forth.
Thus ends the third chapter.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
Hereafter, we shall expound the chapter named "The Prevention of Seizures by Demons Affecting Children."
Thus indeed said the great seers, beginning with Ātreya: "When the planets are to be propitiated, one should place the child in a secluded shelter."
In a place that is cleansed and sprinkled three times a day, where fire is always present,
and which is strewn with earth, flowers, seeds, leaves, food, and mustard seeds.
In a place where evil has been destroyed by lamps burning with demon-slaying oil, and where attendants have abstained from sexual intercourse, wine, and meat;
AS.Utt.4.4 AS.Utt.4.4
Anointed with aged clarified butter and sprinkled with lukewarm water prepared with *balā*, *nimba*, *vaijayantī*, and *nṛpadruma*.
With *pāribhadraka*, *kaṭvaṅga*, *jambū*, *varaṇa*, and *kattṛṇa*; with *kapotavaṅkā*, *apāmārga*, *pāṭalī*, and *madhuśigru*.
For one who has bathed, one should perform incense fumigation with *kākajaṅghā*, *mahāśvetā*, *kapittha*, milky trees, along with *kadamba* and *karañja*.
With the skins of leopards, tigers, snakes, lions, and bears mixed with ghee, along with pūtī,
the ten-ingredient compound (daśāṅga), white mustard, vacā, bhallātaka, and dīpyaka.
An incense made of kuṣṭha with ghee brings liberation from all planetary influences (grahas). Mustard seeds, nimba leaves, aśvakharā root, and vacā— [these are used for fumigation].
Bhūrja bark, ghee, and incense destroy all planetary afflictions. Anantā, copper, bone, gara, black pepper, and the group of sweet (madhura) substances [are also used].

One should cook ghee with the pastes of *śṛgālavinnā* and *mustā*, combined with the decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūla*) and milk; that is supreme for overcoming seizure by Grahas. [From] *rāsnā*, the two types of *aṃśumatī*, *vaḍhra*, the five roots (*pañcamūla*), *balā*, and *ghanā*...
One should cook ghee in a decoction with the pastes of sārivā, vyoṣa, citraka,
pāṭhā, viḍaṅga, madhuka, payasyā, hiṅgu, and dāru.
For a child, this [mixture] with *sagranthika* and *indrayava* is always beneficial;
it removes all diseases and planetary influences (*graha*), stimulates digestion, and bestows strength and a healthy complexion.
One should cook ghee with sārivā, surabhī, brāhmī, śiṅkhinī, kuṣṭha,
and mustard seeds, combined with vacā, aśvagandhā, and surasā.
One should destroy all those planetary afflictions by means of drinking and anointing,
and one should employ the medicinal ghees that have been prescribed in the science of spirits (bhūtavidyā).
In a clean place, one should smear an area measuring one cubit with cow dung;

Smokeless fire, water, guggulu resin, and oblations of clarified butter;
white flowers, a sacrificial offering, incense, dūrvā grass, and white mustard seeds.
Then, facing east and being pure, the physician, having sat down and taken a cord of three strands or white in color, should wrap it around the *pratisarā*.
The *vidyā* inscribed on birch bark with yellow pigment, which is unconquered,

Accompanied by a retinue such as Lakṣmaṇa and others, and constantly served by mindfulness,

Markaṭī, karkaṭī, lambā, bṛhatī,
kaṇṭakārikā, kharanāsā, mṛgī, urvāru, mahāśvetā, and śatāvarī.
Then, while reciting this mantra, one should tie it around the neck of the child who is facing north; in its absence, one may use a strong linen thread.
Having paid homage to the Self-Existent One, I bind this auspicious *pratisarā*,
fashioned by the ancient seers, for the protection of children.
May Indra grant his approval to you, as well as those who are his followers—
beings who wield the thunderbolt and lightning and move in the company of the masses of clouds.
Those who follow Purandara as he rides upon the shoulders of Airāvata,
King Yama Vaivasvata, and those who are his attendants— [they all come].
Those with faces resembling a ram, a boar, a lion, a camel, a donkey, or a horse— black,
with eyes fixed by nooses of black iron, and with frowning faces— [are the messengers of Yama].
And those who hold spears and mallets in their hands, and those who carry swords and nooses;
King Varuṇa, the bearer of the noose, whose domain is the waters and whose abode is the ocean.
And those followers of his, with forms like dense autumn clouds,
violently agitate the lord of rivers, which is full of great waves.
Vaiśravaṇa, the lord of wealth and sovereign ruler of all yakṣas,
is indeed omnipresent; and those beings of various forms are always his attendants.
May the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Maruts, and also the two Aśvins—
all these together— grant their approval for this rite of the *pratisara*.
They will grant you long life and freedom from disease;
may it be well with you! May the Blessed Lord Brahmā grant you well-being, and may Nārada and Parvata grant you well-being.
May the Vedas and the sacrifices bring you well-being; may Agni and Soma bring you well-being.
May Śrī, Dhṛti, Kīrti, Lakṣmī, Medhā, Kṣamā, and Dyuti bring you well-being.
May Svasti, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Vapus, Drī, and Buddhi likewise grant you well-being; may Rudra, Viśākha, Skanda, and Śaktidhara protect you.
May Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, and the mighty Suparṇa, grant you well-being;
may the gods and yakṣas also grant you well-being, and may no evil come upon you.
Ill-omened sights, bad dreams, thoughts conceived by the mind,

This protective *pratisarā*, which destroys evil, has been bound for you. Live free from suffering and free from anxiety; may you live happily for a hundred years.
Apūpa, pūpa, saṃyāva, svastika, ālopikā, and so forth;

"O gentle ones of gentle form, I invite you;

Aulā, Nīlā, Khalā, Kālā, Nakulā, Grahakārikā, Senā, Susenā, Mātā, Mahāsenā, and Yaśasvinī. (AS.Utt.4.51)

The youth offers you perfume, incense, and garlands; having smelled them, you must not remain— go to your own destination without delay.
All the nurses of the prince gathered together on Mount Gandhamādana,
[who were] adorned with red banners and flags and clothed in red garments.
Go there to the prince's residence and release the boy; at that time, Śammukha, who indeed has twelve eyes, was chosen as the boon.
Let your son Vīra, the lord of the Kumāras, be consecrated;
and let the Brāhmaṇa, the best among all those who know the Vedas, be consecrated as the leader of the Brāhmaṇas.
He is the lord of the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and nāgas, as well as of the gandharvas and asuras, and of the hosts of piśācas and bhūtas, and of diseases.
Skanda commands you: "Go to Gandhamādana!
Any graha who violates the command of the illustrious Kumāra [shall be punished]."
Having fallen from that state, he will indeed quickly become an outsider to the assembly. One should perform the fire-oblation immediately after Bali, having worshipped the purifier (fire).
With various flowers, edible offerings, and red caru oblations,
as well as with fragrances, guggulu incense, and fuel-sticks of khadira wood.
One hundred and eight oblations of sandalwood wood should be offered; I shall now describe the "Fire-staff" rite, which grants liberation from all planetary afflictions.
One should invoke the god Anala, the receiver of sacrificial offerings (havya) and ancestral oblations (kavya),
facing eastward for the gods; he swiftly removes misfortune with "Svasti" and "Svāhā."
You are the thousand-fold knower, the burner, the purifier, and the consumer of all;
for you are indeed the sacrifice and the sacrificial post, and you are the refuge of those who possess righteousness.
O God, you are Hiraṇyaretas; for you are the refuge of those who know the Vedas.
You were brought forth by the gods for the destruction of the wicked.
This is the divinity of the fire-gathering [rite], for the subduing of the wicked: *agnaye svāhā*.
Svāhā to the Great Fire!
For you are the fire that brings peace; you are the wind, the remover of tears.
You possess the primary gait of Hari; having seized this Guhyaka, destroy him with your splendor. Make him subject to my will, and ward off evil planets and all calamities.
Through the oblation performed by you, peace is swiftly produced. Come, O Agni, for you are the ancient mouth of the gods.

By that truth, O Lord of Gods, accomplish this rite for me! Homage to you, O Havyavāhana! Display your staff! Burn, burn! Show, show! O Splendor, splendor! Crush, crush! Exorcise the epilepsy! O Youthful One, terrifier and shatterer by the weeping of the Piśāca Revatī, cause trembling, intense trembling, yawning, and terror among gods, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Bhūtas, Nāgas, and Rākṣasas! O Blessed One, Agni-staff, fire-power, homage to you! By your own splendor, utterly destroy what has been abandoned! Svāhā!
Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā!

There, in the fire—ruddy, copper-colored, with a luster like molten gold—"
Resembling a star or lapis lazuli, with a radiance like that of the moon or lightning,

If the fire has the luster of a *ketakī* flower, a blue lotus, or curd, one should certainly predict good health; however, if it is blue like fire, or tawny and lusterless like ashes, there will be ill-health.
When it is black, pigeon-colored, foul-smelling, smelling like fish, pus, or blood;

Now, therefore, we shall explain the chapter on ritual bathing (snāna).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:
[at] the confluence of rivers, at sacred fords on riverbanks, on the shoulders of lordly elephants, and in cow-pens.
And one should have a child bathed at a crossroads along with his breastfeeding mother;

A ground abounding in *dūrvā* grass and milky trees, sloping toward the northeast,
with trees rich in glossy, healthy, and flowering foliage, is auspicious for the ritual bathing.

The bathing of a child should be performed under the asterisms of Revatī, Śravaṇa, Svātī, Rohiṇī, the two Uttarās (Uttaraphalgunī and Uttarāṣāḍhā), and Mṛgaśiras, as well as under Puṣya and Mūla, and on auspicious festival days.
One should draw a three-colored mandala measuring four cubits, eight cubits, or thirty-two cubits, or even the size of a *nalva*.
A *nalva* is said to be threefold, measured by a cowhide, a bow, or an arrow;
it should be square, have four gates, and be adorned with banners.
It should be strewn all around with sprouts of *dūrvā* grass, white mustard, and barley;
and one should draw Indra mounted upon an elephant, starting from the east and proceeding in order through the directions.
Having passed beyond the station of Yama, [one sees] Dharmarāja mounted upon a buffalo, the Lord of Waters seated upon a ruddy goose, and Dhanada with mace in hand.
One should draw the Mātṛsthāna there, along with Nandikeśvara accompanied by his bull,
and first [draw] Vināyaka made of clay;
having passed beyond the abode of Varuṇa, one should establish the thousand-spoked [wheel].
The discus, the weapon of Viṣṇu, which wards off all obstacles;
and Śrī, who holds a lotus in her hand and whose abode is between the lords of the gods and the yakṣas.
The *nandyāvarta*, the elephant goad, the mirror, the fish, the *svastika*, the archway,

At the gate of Indra, those with pendulous breasts should be stationed; at the gate of Yama, the one with hanging hair; at the gate of Varuṇa, the one with no husband; and at the gate of Kubera, the one with a long nose.
The physician should prepare six stakes made of iron and seven made of the three metals;
among these, two should be stakes of khadira wood, sprinkled with sandalwood water.
Eight, sixteen, or even thirty-two jars,

Filled with pure water mixed with appropriate medicinal herbs,

From an elephant stable, from a horse stable, from a crossroads or a four-way junction, from the top of an anthill, from a riverbank, from the house of a courtesan, or from the palace of a king.

Then, one should have [the child] sit upon a lotus situated in the center, together with the nurse, along with unbroken rice grains, parched grain, five-colored boiled rice,
and sesame seeds.
On a seat made of *audumbara* wood or *pālāśa*, covered with green *darbha* grass, he should face north— not facing the east or any other direction—

With that [mixture], one should offer oblations into the fire established there in the northern direction;

Wiping the limbs with earth mixed with mustard seeds and *akṣata* grains,

"This auspicious jar of yours was produced from the nectar (amṛta) in the beginning."
May the Blessed Lord Indra grant victory by name;

Surrounded by hosts of gods and seated upon the shoulder of the lordly elephant,

Salutation to Indra, Svāhā!

By the power of virtuous women, of tawny cows,
and of perfected beings, and by the splendor of seers and brahmins, you have today been bathed by me.
