One should avoid meat, sexual intercourse, and sleeping during the day for five nights. Bathing is meritorious, it conquers evil, and it brings nourishment even to those who are free from disease.
It destroys all diseases of the sick and grants sons even to barren women; however,
if administered according to the prescribed rite or otherwise, it kills the child along with the physician.
This should not be applied to one who lacks faith, nor to one who does not approach [the teacher] properly;
it is more potent than the bark and leaves of the *pūtīkarañja*, or even than *barbara* from among the milk-exuding trees.
Having boiled the decoction of *tumbī*, *viśālā*, *āragvadha*, *śamī*, *bilva*,
and *kapittha* in a pot, that water is auspicious for the bathing of children.
At night, when the world is fast asleep, it bestows nourishment and conquers all diseases.
Thus ends the fifth chapter.
Now begins the sixth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "The Prohibition of Individual Grahas";
thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.

In cases of seizure by Skanda-graha (Skandapasmāra), a plaster should be applied using guggulu, elavāluka, manaḥśilā, haritāla, mañjiṣṭhā, uśīra, rāsnā, agaru, devadāru, śrīveṣṭaka, hareṇu, girikadambaka, and candana, all finely ground together. A lukewarm affusion should be performed with a decoction of the leaves of vāta-alleviating trees. Furthermore, an oil cooked with a decoction of the roots of those same trees, along with an addition of all the fragrant substances (sarvagandha), the supernatant of wine (surāmaṇḍa), and kaiḍarya, should be used for massage.

Alternatively, one may take ghee cooked with the paste of the two types of *bṛhatī*, *dvipuruṣa*, *nāgara*, *reṇuka*, *upakulyā*, *mustā*, *khadira*, *vacā*, conch-shell (*śaṅkhanābhi*), *sarala*, *sarpasugandhā*, and *surāhvā*.

Or, one may drink a *prastha* of ghee prepared with milk and the decoction of milky trees (*kṣīrivṛkṣa*), along with half-pala portions of the following ground ingredients: the two types of *sārivā*, the two types of *kākolī*, the two types of *balā*, the two types of *aṃśumatī*, and *hastikarṇaparṇa*.
Alternatively, ghee prepared with milk and a paste of either *rāsnā* or *devadāru* [is recommended].
An incense made of *vacā*, *kākādanī*, *sarpakañcuka*, and mustard seeds, together with the hair of a camel, goat, sheep, horse,
and cow mixed with ghee; or alternatively, an incense made of white mustard, resin of *sarja*, *kuṣṭha*, asafoetida, and *guggulu*.

One should wear the roots of *somavallī*, *indravallī*, *śamī*, *bilva*, *vṛndāka*, and *mṛgādinī*, strung together with a thread, around the neck or on the head. For the seizure by Kumāra (*kumāragraha*),

one who has fasted should offer a bali-oblation consisting of red garlands, ointments, garments, banners, various gems and seeds, and diverse foods— including curd, ghee, honey, parched grain, *kulmāṣa* porridge, meat, fish, *surā* liquor, and *āsava*— along with a peacock and a cock, accompanied by a bell, a winnowing basket, and a fan, and served with red rice.
And there, having kindled a fire at night, one should offer oblations of honey and clarified butter while reciting this mantra.
"To Agni and to the Kṛttikās, svāhā! Svāhā!"—thus at the end;
"Homage to Skanda, the god, the lord of the grahas; homage!"
I salute you with my head; please accept this offering from me.
May the child always remain free from disease and free from affliction.
In all planetary afflictions (*graha*), one should worship and offer libations to the fire at the three times of day; specifically,
in the case of Skanda-graha, one should perform the ritual bathing of the Dhātrī plant and the child at a crossroads every night for three nights with water consecrated by the *gāyatrī* mantra.
And one should wipe the child with this mantra three times a day and tie a *pratisarā* amulet upon him. [The mantra is:
"Of austerities, of splendors, of glories, and likewise of physical forms..."
May that immutable god Vidhātṛ, who is Skanda, be gracious to you. May the lord of the host of Grahas, the all-pervading god who is the commander of the divine army, [be gracious].
May the blessed Guha, the destroyer of the enemies of the divine army, protect you—
he who is the son of the great God of gods and of Agni.
May Gaṅgā, Umā, and Kṛttikā grant you protection.
Adorned with red garlands and garments, glorious, and embellished with red sandalwood paste—
"May the God, whose body is like the red sun, the destroyer of Krauñca, protect you.

(AS.Utt.6.17) Regarding the seizure by Skanda during the *viśākhā* asterism, a plaster mixed with *vacā* and *kuṣṭha* is prescribed; a sprinkling [of water] should be performed with a decoction of *golomī*, *bilva*, *śirīṣa*, *mustā*, *surasā*, and so forth. (AS.Utt.6.18)
Oil prepared with a paste of *sarpasugandhā*, *devadāru*, *kuṣṭha*, and *mustā*, along with cow’s urine and the urine of a urinary bladder (*bastamūtra*), should be used for massage.
Ghee prepared with a decoction of milk-exuding trees (*kṣīrivṛkṣa*), containing *jīvanīya* drugs as an internal additive, and mixed with milk, should be drunk.

Alternatively, one may use *jīvaka*, *ṛṣabhaka*, *kṣīriṇī*, *bṛhatī*, the two types of *haridrā*, the two types of *aṃśumatī*, and *madhuka*; or the two types of *vidārī*, *tālakṣīrī*, *mṛdvīkā*, *madhuka*, *rāsnā*, the root of blue lotus, *vacā*, and the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*).
Or, as an incense, one may use the excrement of vultures and owls, along with bull hair, human hair, and elephant claws, all soaked in clarified butter.
One should wear *anantā*, *kukkuṭī*, *markaṭī*, *bimbī*, *samaṅgā*, *śvetagirikarṇikā*, and those previously mentioned, as before.
A sacrificial offering (*bali*) consisting of cooked and raw meat, blood, curd, and *vāruṇī* wine should be placed at the foot of a *vaṭa* tree or at a crossroads; [then] one should bathe.
And the mantra [is prescribed] in AS.Utt.6.21;
that which is known as Skandāpasmāra is the beloved friend of Skanda.
May that one known as Viśākha, with his deformed face, be auspicious to the child.

For Naigameṣa, the application (pradeha) prescribed for Viśākha is made with agnimantha, varuṇa, nala, rohiṣa, pūtīka, and pāribhadraka; the sprinkling (pariṣeka) is done with fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla); and the massage (abhyaṅga) is with oil cooked with bīja, guggulu, aśvagandhā, mustard, uśīra, śvetā, kuṣṭha, and śatāhvā.
One should drink ghee prepared with a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla), containing the group of sweet drugs (madhuraskandha) as an internal ingredient, along with milk.
An incense made from *sarpagandhā*, cast-off skins, and body hair [is used];
one should carry seeds of *sarpagandhā*, *bastagandhā*, *tumbī*, *mṛgī*, *urvāru*, *śatāvarī*, *sahadevā*, and *punarnavā*.
An offering (*bali*) consisting of variegated garlands, fruits, white ointments, boiled rice, curd, ghee, molasses, and milk should be presented on a great road or at a milky tree.
Bathing at the riverbank and the mantra (AS.Utt.6.25);
one who is unborn, with moving eyes and eyebrows, capable of assuming any form at will, and of great renown (AS.Utt.6.26).
May the god Naigameṣa, who is devoted to children, protect the child;
svāhā!

For dog-bite, an ointment should be applied consisting of *gavākṣī*, *brahmadattā*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, *sārivā*, *uddrīvera*, *kuṣṭha*, *bhūmikadamba*, *surasamañjarī*, and *karavīra* flowers,
along with the feathers and dung of peacock, owl, horse, and buffalo.

An affusion with a decoction of *bilva*, *eraṇḍa*, *naktamāla*, and *āragvadha* leaves [is prescribed]. An oil prepared with the paste of *vayasthā*, *śatāvarī*, *sārivā*, *payasyā*, *eraṇḍa*, *sahadevā*, and the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), boiled with milk, is for massage.
Likewise, drinking ghee;
powdered dried fish processed with cow's urine and goat's urine as incense at midnight;
and one should wear *vacā*, *vayaḥsthā*, *brāhmī*, *jaṭilā*, *golomī*, *lambā*, *pūtanā*, *keśī*, *girikadambaka*, *ekaiṣikā*, and *sahadevī*.
An offering consisting of ghee, surā liquor, meat, curd, blood, and minced flesh should be presented at a crossroads.
The bath at Saṅkarakūṭa and the mantra for the protection of Kārttikeya by Kṛttikā, Umā, Agni, and Śūlin are [described] in AS.Utt.6.31.
May that deity who was created in the form of a dog protect you;
svāhā!

In the case of possession by a *pitṛ-graha*, the previously mentioned paste (*pradeha*) should be applied; alternatively, an oil prepared with *vacā*, *sthirā*, *jīvantī*, *dhātakī*, *priyaṅgu*, *guggulu*, *rāsnā*, *manaḥśilā*, and *alarka*— or with *vacā* and the others alone— should be used for massage (*abhyaṅga*).

In the night, an irrigation [of the head] should be performed with a decoction of the leaves of *bilva*, *kapittha*, *karañja*, *tarkārī*, *surasā*, *pāṭalī*, *varaṇa*, *pāribhadraka*, *pārijāta*, and *mātuluṅga*. Furthermore, an oil prepared from these same *bilva* and other ingredients, combined with wine, goat's urine, and cow's urine, should be used as an anointing massage (*abhyaṅga*).

An internal drink of ghee should be administered, having been cooked with a paste (*kalka*) of *triphalā*, the two types of *aṃśumatī*, *payasyā*, and *madhuka*, along with a decoction (*niryūha*) of the ten roots (*daśamūla*) and milk.
Alternatively, oil prepared with *devadāru*, *bhārgī*, *viḍaṅga*, *candana*, the two types of *kākolī*, *jīvaka*, and *ṛṣabhaka*,
along with alkalis (*kṣāra*), or oil prepared with *lakṣmī*, *puru*, *kuṣṭha*, *golomī*, *jaṭilā*, and *ugragandhā*, is used for nasal administration (*nāvana*).

And with these same ingredients ground with *surā* liquor, a plaster should be applied (AS.Utt.6.35). Alternatively, the feathers of a vulture, an owl, and a monkey mixed with clarified butter, or their excrement, or incense made of *vacā* and other drugs mentioned in the context of plasters— or the previously mentioned [fumigation]— should be used while the person is asleep (AS.Utt.6.36).
One should maintain those very [observances] previously mentioned (AS.Utt.6.36).

AS.Utt.6.37: At the foot of a tree, a sacrificial offering (*bali*) consisting of liquor, spirits, molasses, cakes, flour, sesame, and prepared foods, accompanied by a bull and a pair of golden-eyed [birds], must be presented by the father himself for the sake of the boy.
Bathing near a milky tree and the mantra.
He who is the father of all children, the most excellent one worshipped among the grahas,
who has made his dwelling at the foot of a tree— may that father protect you always.
Svāhā!
(AS.Utt.6.39) A medicinal plaster (pradeha) should be applied using śakunī, madhuka, drībera, uśīra, sārivā, padmaka, utpala, mañjiṣṭhā, loddhra, priyaṅgu, and gairika.
Alternatively, one may apply plasters mentioned for ulcers made from *lodhra*, *yaṣṭīmadhuka*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *harītakī*, and *devadāru*, ground with wine and urine;
or with *vetasa*, *amlaka*, *kapittha*, and the five roots (*pañcamūla*);
or oil cooked with the ashes of pearl-oyster shells, conch shells, and snails, along with *mañjiṣṭhā*, *abhayā*, and *madhuka*, which promotes the healing of ulcers.

AS.Utt.6.40: An irrigation with milky trees, or an oil cooked with milk and the following—*mārkava*, *mūlaka*, *āmalakī* bark, leaves, *priyaṅgu*, realgar (*manaḥśilā*), the two types of *elā*, *yaṣṭīmadhu*, *kramuka*, *lodhra*, *dhātakī*, *sārivā*, collyrium (*añjana*), *utpala*, *pataṅga*, *samaṅgā*, the two types of *haridrā*, *māṃsī*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *candana*, *padmaka*, gold, and *gaurika*—is an ointment that destroys seizures and promotes the healing of wounds.
AS.Utt.6.41:
A powder of *arjuna* fruit, *lodhra*, *madhuka*, *udumbara*, and *vacā*, mixed with honey, used as a rubbing on the mouth (*mukhodgharṣa*) cures inflammation of the mouth (*mukhapāka*).
The water for drinking as spoken by Viśākhā, and the incense as spoken by Skanda.

Or one should wear a crow’s feather, or cow-hair, or the pungent-smelling *ugragandhā*, or *rakṣoghnaghṛta* (ghee that destroys demons), or peacock eye-patches; or one should wear *kaṭambharā*, *kukkuṭī*, *markaṭī*, *lambā*, *sahadevī*, *hrīvera*, and *uśīra*.

Nāgadantī, lakṣmaṇā, the two types of bṛhatī, mṛgī, ervāru, śatāvarī, and sahadevī [are used for the bath]. AS.Utt.6.43. An offering (bali) consisting of sesame seeds, rice, fish, māṃsī, realgar, and mixed with sesame paste, should be made to the *śakunika* birds at the *karañja* tree in the garden; then the bath is performed.
AS.Utt.6.43.
And the mantra is:
"The goddess who moves through the intermediate space, adorned with all ornaments. (AS.Utt.6.44)
May that bird with an iron mouth and a sharp beak be gracious to you;
she who is difficult to behold, massive of body, tawny-eyed, and of terrifying voice.
May Lambodarī, Śaṅkukarṇī, and Śakunī be gracious to you. For in the case of Pūtanā, an external application (pradeha) should be made with hiṅgu, vacā, girikadamba, kuṣṭha, elā, dvaya, and surāhva.

A decoction made from the leaves of *kapittha*, *śirīṣa*, *nyagrodha*, *bilva*, *eraṇḍa*, *bakula*, *dhava*, *vaṃśa*, and *agnimantha*, mixed with water perfumed with all fragrant substances (*sarvagandha*), is used for sprinkling (*pariṣeka*). An oil prepared with *varaṇa*, *kaṭvaṅga*, *āsphota*, *kapotavaṅkā*, *pāribhadra*, *dārvī*, *kuṣṭha*, *sarjarasa*, *vacā*, *golomī*, *vayasthā*, *manaḥśilā*, and *ala* is used for massage (*abhyaṅga*).
One should drink ghee prepared with sweet medicinal herbs;
an incense made of the two types of *elā*, *kuṣṭha*, *vacā*, *hiṅgu*, *devadāru*, and *girikadambaka* should be used;
and one should wear *bimbī*, *guñjā*, *kākādanī*, *nadravāruṇī*, and *citrapālā*.
An offering (*bali*) consisting of variegated garlands, fish, boiled rice (*odana*), *kṛsara*, and meat should be placed on a heap of refuse;
likewise, when there is a seizure by a "void-grasper" (*śūnyagraha*), it should be thrown in the four directions from a pair of earthenware bowls.
And there, the ritual bathing with the remnants and the mantra [are prescribed];
she is clothed in soiled garments, soiled, and has coarse hair.
May the goddess Pūtanā, who dwells in empty houses, protect the child;
may Durdarśanā, Mahākāyā, Karālā, and Meghakālikā [protect him].
May the goddess Pūtanā, who dwells in a ruined house, protect the child.
Regarding the cold-Pūtanā, the medicinal paste and protective amulets prescribed by Pūtanā should be applied.

An irrigation (pariṣeka) should be performed with a decoction of the leaves of *varaṇaka*, *kapittha*, *tulasī*, *pāśikā*, *vaṃśī*, *bilva*, *pāṭalī*, *nandī*, and *bhallātaka*. An oil cooked with *mustā*, *amaradāru*, *kuṣṭha*, and *sarpagandhā*, combined with cow's urine and goat's urine, should be used for anointing (abhyaṅga).

Ghee boiled with *kāśmarya*, *pṛśniparṇī*, *lodhra*, *madhuka*, and the drugs of the sweet group (*madhuravarga*), along with an equal quantity of milk, when consumed, pacifies *śītapūtanā*, vomiting, hiccups, cough, and dyspnea.

(AS.Utt.6.52) In the case of diarrhea (*atisāra*), however, [ghee] should be prepared with an equal amount of milk and a decoction of the barks of *khadira*, *palāśa*, *sarja*, *arjuna*, and *rohiṇī*. (AS.Utt.6.53)

An incense [is prepared] from vulture, owl, human excrement, dog, the slough of a snake, and nimba leaves; or alternatively, from old cow-hide, mustard seeds, a monk’s patched robe, and a snake’s skin.
The offering should consist primarily of green gram and boiled rice, performed near a body of water; likewise, bathing should take place at that very spot,
as well as the recitation of mantras.
May Śītapūtanā protect you— she who eats mung-bean rice, who drinks wine and blood, and who delights in dwelling by reservoirs of water.
In the case of Andhapūtanā, an application (pradeha) of all fragrant substances should be made to the head and face;
a sprinkling (pariṣeka) with Varuṇa, Āsphota, Pāribhadraka, Vṛkṣādanī, Nāgabalā, Gairika, and Śatāvarī should also be administered.

Oil prepared with yellow orpiment (*haritāla*), realgar (*manaḥśilā*), kuṣṭha, resin of *sarja*, wine (*surā*), and *sauvīraka* should be used for massage (*abhyaṅga*). Ghee boiled with the decoction of *syandana*, *yūnāka*, *kāśmarya*, *khadira*, *kuṣṭha*, and the drugs of the sweet group (*madhuravarga*), along with milk and mixed with honey, should be consumed as a potion by those afflicted by disorders of the eyes.
For those suffering from vomiting and diarrhea, that same [milk] should be combined with a paste of *pippalī*, *pippalīmūla*, *sālaparṇī*, and *bṛhatī*; furthermore,
an incense made of *rakṣoghna*, *ruṣkara*, *sarjarasa*, and honey [should be used].

Or one should wear an endless number of worn-out monastic robes (saṅghāṭī), as well as the excrement of a cock, skin, hair, and hides; [or] one should wear [the skins of] the *kukkuṭī*, the *markaṭī*, and the *bimbī*.
One should offer an oblation of ripe *tumbī*, *citraphalā*, *mṛgī*, *urvāru*, *jālinī*, and *kākādanī* fruits,
along with raw meat and blood, at a crossroads; and one should bathe at home.
And the mantra is:
"Karālā, Piṅgalā, Muṇḍā, she who is clothed in saffron-colored garments. (AS.Utt.6.61)
"O Goddess Andhapūtanā, being pleased, protect this child. For Mukhamāṇḍitikā, there is an ointment made with all fragrant substances ground finely with Vāruṇī liquor.

A sprinkling [of the body] should be performed with a decoction of the leaves of *bilva*, *eraṇḍa*, *kapittha*, *agnimantha*, *vaṃśī*, and *kuberākṣī*, or with the expressed juice of those same plants. An oil and muscle fat (*vasā*), cooked together with *madhuka* and *vājigandhā*, should be used as an ointment. Furthermore, clarified butter prepared with the "small five roots" (*hrasvapañcamūla*) and the "sweet group" (*madhuravarga*) should be consumed along with honey and sugar.
Alternatively, one may drink a powder of *pāṭhā*, *ketaka*, *sūcī*, *nimba* fruit, *pippalī*, *viḍaṅga*, *harītakī* ash, *vacā*, and *coraka* with honey and ghee;

or a powder of bear-hair soot, *pāṭhā*, black pepper, and *pippalī* combined with *devadāru* ash; or a powder of *mūrvā*, the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), *musta*, *rāsnā*, *girikadamba*, *aśvagandhā*; or a powder of *aśoka* and *rohiṇī*.
One may also drink goat’s ghee or milk that has been cooked with these same ingredients.

With these same formulations, one should perform fumigation (dhūpa), medicinal paste application (upadeha), massage (abhyaṅga), nasal drops (nasya), oil enemas (taila), eye-filling (akṣipūraṇa), and affusion (pariṣeka). Fumigation should be made with barley, kuṣṭha, and resin (sarjarasa).
One should apply the tongues of a snake, a blue jay, a parrot, and a *rallaka* bird;
and for this mother, one should administer medicine that removes phlegm (*śleṣman*) for drinking, as well as for bathing her breasts and anointing them.

[AS.Utt.6.65] A sacrificial offering (*bali*) consisting of various perfumes, incense, garlands, collyrium, mercury, and realgar should be placed in the middle of a cow-pen, and she should bathe amidst the cows.
And the mantra (AS.Utt.6.65);
[she who is] adorned, beautiful, fortunate, and able to assume any form at will (AS.Utt.6.66).
May she who delights in dwelling in the midst of a cow-pen and adorns her face protect you.
In the case of Revatī, an external application (pradeha) should be made with all types of fragrant substances and the powder of *kulattha* and *māṣa* beans.

An irrigation (pariṣeka) should be performed with a decoction of aśvagandhā, ajaśṛṅgī, sārivā, dvipunarnavā, visahā, and vidārī. An oil prepared with kuṣṭha and sarjarasa should be used for massage (abhyaṅga).

One should consume ghee boiled with the ground *dhava*, *aśvakarṇa*, *dhātakī*, *kakubha*, *tinduka*, and *jīvanīya* herbs; and an incense made of the dung of a goat, a horse, a fruit-eating bird, an owl, and a vulture, mixed with ghee, should be used.

A plaster made of *varaṇa*, *ariṣṭa*, and *sinduka* mixed with sheep’s urine is for *kaṇḍu*. An offering at a river-crossing (*gotīrtha*) consisting of white garlands, ointments, parched grain, boiled rice, and milk-rice (*pāyasa*) [should be made].
The ritual bathing at a confluence of rivers or near a milk-producing tree,
as well as the mantra, is described in AS.Utt.6.70: "The goddess, wearing various garments and adorned with variegated garlands and ointments..."
May the dark-complexioned Revatī, with her swinging earrings, be gracious to you.
In the case of Śuṣkarevatī, the ritual procedure prescribed for Skanda-graha is to be followed, with the exception of incense.
Anointment with vacā, aśvagandhā, hiṅgu, lāja, and siddhārthaka;
and filling the eyes with mustard oil prepared with vacā [are the remedies].
An ointment made from the excrement of a crow, a vulture, and a donkey [is used for anointing].
An incense made from the claws of a crab, a tortoise-shell, a porcupine, a pearl-oyster, a ram's horn, a horse, a donkey, a jackal, an elephant, and a mongoose destroys all *grahas*.
An offering of groats, liquor, and dried meat should be made at a withered tree,
and one should bathe at that very spot.
And the mantra:
"The goddesses adorned with various ornaments who constantly worship [him]... (AS.Utt.6.74).
"May that goddess Lambā, Karālā, Vinatā, as well as Bahuputrikā, Revatī, and she named Śuṣkā, be gracious to you.
Thus it is said here: AS.Utt.6.75. And there is also this [verse]:

One should treat complications, difficult conditions, seizures, their disappearance, and secondary afflictions with the same medicines prescribed in the section on the prevention of childhood diseases.
Thus ends the sixth chapter;
the second section, the Kaumāra-tantra, is complete.
Now begins the seventh chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter titled "The Knowledge of Living Beings.
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
There are eighteen lords of beings (bhūtādhipati), namely:
AS.Utt.7.2 AS.Utt.7.2: tadyathā (as follows).
The gods, asuras, gandharvas, uragas, yakṣas, brahmarākṣasas, rākṣasas, piśācas, pretas, kūṣmāṇḍas, kākhordas, mauniraṇas, vetālas, and pitṛs, as well as the ṛṣis, gurus, elders, and siddhas—
each of these has a retinue of ten million,
and their retinues are likewise incalculable; thus, the world of beings is infinite.
Moreover, almost all of them generally wander about at midnight, driven by a craving for food; they are terrifying beings who feed on flesh, blood, and fat.
Furthermore:
AS.Utt.7.4 Through dwelling and association with gods, asuras, and others, and by adopting their character, conduct, and activities, they receive those respective names.
AS.Utt.7.5 Furthermore, the cause for their re-entry [into the womb] is either an immediate or a previously committed transgression of wisdom (prajñāparādha) in particular.

For by that [conduct], which is produced by desire, anger, greed, delusion, and so forth, one becomes defiled— having lost dharma and having violated vows, conduct, and purity— and by failing to honor those worthy of worship, one brings harm upon oneself.
Then, even the gods and other planetary spirits (*graha*), seeking an opportunity for descent, strike down that self-killer; likewise,
they strike one whose mind is overwhelmed by insanity or epilepsy, as well as one afflicted by diseases such as fever.
And especially for one suffering from a wound, [death occurs] due to the smell of pus, blood, and fat;
such persons approach these times of destruction.
For example,
at the commencement of an evil deed.
Or at the time of the transformation of what was previously performed,
or while dwelling in an empty house,
or stationed at a crossroads.

If one engages in sexual intercourse during the time of twilight, or while in a state of ritual impurity, or at the junctions of the fortnights; or if one approaches a woman in her menses, or performs the recitation of the Vedas, fire-oblations, offerings, or auspicious rites in a defective manner.
Or upon the violation of the rules of conduct, celibacy, or vows;
or in a great battle;
or in the destruction of one's country, city, or family.
Or when a great planet approaches,
or when a woman is in the throes of childbirth, or when there is contact with various impure beings;
Or when one has undergone emesis, purgation, or bloodletting; or when one is impure or lacks self-restraint; or when visiting a shrine or a temple of a deity;
or when one is defiled by the remnants of meat, honey, molasses, sesame, or liquor.
Or when one is naked at night; or when approaching the city crossroads, groves, or cremation grounds;
or when one commits an offense against Brahmins, gurus, deities, or ascetics who are worthy of worship.
There, the grahas of the gods and asuras produce mental disturbances by gazing [at them],
while the gandharvas do so by touching them.
The serpents entered [the chariot], the yakṣas made themselves smell their own fragrance,
and the rākṣasas, having mounted, drove it.
Likewise, Piśācas and others appear,

while Pitṛs revile [the patient], and Ṛṣis, Gurus, Elders, and Siddhas [manifest]. Among them, the gods generally seize one who is virtuous, of pure conduct, wearing white garments, and devoted to austerity and Vedic study, usually on the first, thirteenth, fourteenth, or full-moon day.
On the twelfth and thirteenth days of the dark fortnight, as well as at the two twilights, the Asuras [frequent] one who is wrathful, miserly, self-conceited, proud of his lineage and beauty,

fond of dance, song, instrumental music, perfumes, garlands, and fine garments, devoted to the wives of others, and of refined conduct; while on the fourth, eighth, twelfth, and fourteenth days, the Gandharvas [frequent] such a person.
Nāgas generally favor a Brāhmaṇa who is prone to sleep, fickle, unfriendly, irascible, and successful in his aims, during the two twilights and at midday;

Yakṣas generally favor one endowed with courage, strength, beauty, fragrance, wealth, and valor, who is fond of garlands, ointments, and laughter, and highly proficient in grammar, on the seventh and eleventh days of the bright fortnight.

Brahmarākṣasas generally seize one who is devoted to Vedic study, austerity, vows, religious observances, gods, and the worship of elders; or a Brāhmaṇa who has fallen away from purity, or even a non-Brāhmaṇa who professes the Veda, a hero, or one who is conceited; as well as one who delights in sporting in temples or in water, whose celibacy has lapsed, especially on the fifth day of the bright fortnight, on the eighth day, at the sight of the full moon, and during the twilights.

Rākṣasas, piśācas, and other such beings generally seize those who are of low character, slanderous, thievish, greedy, and deceitful on the second, third, and eighth lunar days. Furthermore, on the night of the ninth and twelfth lunar days of the dark fortnight, rākṣasas seize those who are fond of strife and drinking, envious, harsh-spoken, and gluttonous.
On the fourteenth day, Piśācas and other spirits seize one who praises himself, gives false testimony, or causes distress to others.
On the tenth and the new moon day, the ancestors generally seize one who serves his mother, father, elders, perfected ones (siddhas), and teachers.

Likewise, on the sixth and ninth [lunar days], those who have become perfected through their teachers and elders generally [attain] that very state; and likewise, sages [favor] one who practices bathing, remains pure, and frequents secluded places, and who is skilled in the Dharma-śāstras, the Vedas, and poetry.
The premonitory symptoms of those who are about to contract these [diseases] are as follows:
AS.Utt.7.16.
AS.Utt.7.16. That is to say:

A fondness for harming gods, cows, brahmins, and ascetics; a cruel disposition; irritability; and the affliction of one's luster, complexion, shadow, strength, and body; as well as being reviled or incited by gods and others in dreams.

In that regard, one should recognize a person seized by a divine spirit (*devagraha*) as having a gentle gaze, being profound, unassailable, free from anger, pure, sleepless, and having no desire for food; possessing little sweat, urine, feces, or speech, speaking refined language, and being devoted to gods, the twice-born, and teachers; fond of white garlands, garments, riverbanks, mountains, lofty mansions, curd, milk, and fragrant substances; closing his eyes after a long time, appearing like a granter of boons, having a pleasant fragrance, being radiant, with a face like a full-blown lotus.
There too, he saw him bellowing like a bull, with a blazing face and eyes, addressing everyone with a roaring voice— like the Lord Indra,
emitting clouds, thunder, lightning, and rain through his speech.
By Dhanada, who bestows wealth with his speech yet seizes it away;
and by Varuṇa, who considers everything from wood and grass to ropes to be a snare, smelling like the scent of divine liquor.

One who has a squinting gaze, is evil-minded, wrathful, and insatiable; whose limbs are perspiring; who hates the gods, Brahmins, and teachers; who is fearless and arrogant; who is a hero and resolute; who speaks such things as "I am Rudra," "I am Indra," "I am Upendra," "I am Skanda," or "I am Viśākha"; who speaks with distorted speech, laughs repeatedly, has a taste for liquor and meat, and harms others with his teeth and nails—such a person is possessed by an *asura*.

One who is of good conduct, joyful in spirit, fragrant, and of few worldly dealings; one who dances, sings, and plays wind instruments; one who delights in gardens, riverbanks, red garments, bathing, garlands, ointments, incense, food, drink, laughter, playfulness, amorous discourse, and music;

and one who, when confronted by a Gandharva, shakes his head there as well, engages in quarreling with agitation, remains wakeful, recites, laughs, and laughs with derision—[such a person is known as a Gandharva].

One who is prone to anger, constantly suspicious, wandering about while trembling under a parasol, with bloodshot eyes and a fixed gaze, flicking his tongue and licking the corners of his mouth, lying face-downward, moving restlessly and walking crookedly, looking for a hole like a snake and slithering upward upon seeing one, rejoicing at the sounds of water, rain-clouds, and drums, fond of bathing in milk, ghee, molasses, and honey, and of garlands, shaking his limbs, gnashing his teeth, and unwilling to emerge from the water—such a person is [seized] by a serpent.

One possessed by a *yakṣa* frequently experiences dreams of weeping, laughing, dancing, singing, reciting, storytelling, eating, drinking, bathing, wearing garlands, incense, perfumes, and red garments; he moves quickly with eyes reddened, terrified, or rolling, walking haughtily like one intoxicated, pulling up the hem of his garment, with the tips of his hands trembling, talking much, lustful for women, fond of wine and meat, armed with a weapon while searching for prey, possessing excessive strength and being free from pain, joyful, contented, and having little anger; he says, "What shall I give to whom?", possesses a pleasant fragrance, is radiant, treats Brahmins and physicians with contempt, and speaks in secret.
In that case as well,
one should [recognize] him by his bristling hair, his upward gaze, his wide-open eyes, his fierce and harsh nature, his loud roar, and his excellent jewel.

One who practices secret laughter, dancing, and singing in public, yet observes silence in private; who is fond of grotesque laughter and dancing, who is abusive and runs about restlessly; who hates gods, Brahmins, and physicians, yet professes knowledge of mantras, the Vedas, and the scriptures; who strikes himself with wood, weapons, and the like, who attacks at vulnerable points, who seeks out the physician's weaknesses, who habitually uses the word "Bhoḥ," who is harsh, of fierce disposition, and quick-moving—such a person is possessed by a *brahmarākṣasa*.
There too, he saw one who spoke with a distorted voice, terrifying the expounder of the Veda who spoke in refined Sanskrit, repeatedly begging for water from Yajñasena.

One should recognize a person possessed by a *rākṣasa* as one who looks with angry eyes, frowns, has a terrifying face, runs about swiftly, cries out, strikes about in agitation, loses sleep, wanders at night, hates food, and remains extremely strong even when fasting; who laughs at mealtime, is shameless, brave, irascible, speaks unpleasantly, is impure, and is fond of wine, meat, blood, and garlands; who licks his lips upon seeing red meat or blood; and who is dejected, suspicious, runs away, weeps suddenly, laughs, sings, dances, and utters meaningless chatter.

There too, he saw him striking the rough-skinned ground, weeping all of a sudden, his throat broken and faltering due to Viśākha, breaking his limbs, licking his tongue, muttering prayers with a rosary, and constantly performing purification rites with Saṅgama.

He was exhausted by the rising clouds and lightning, imagining on all sides a rain of water from one who was angry; he was crushed by carts by Vidyunmālin, and by Virūpākṣa, he was one who begged for raw meat, minced meat, radishes, cakes, and fine rice, while his own complexion was parched.

One who has an unsteady mind, who does not remain in one place but runs about, who delights in dancing, singing, laughter, and jesting, and who takes pleasure in eating leftovers, meat, and living in empty dwellings; who strikes at things before him, whose face becomes dejected and fearful upon being rebuked, who scratches his own body with his nails, who has lost his memory, who speaks both coherently and incoherently, who weeps suddenly and expresses his sorrows, whose body and voice are disheveled and harsh, who is foul-smelling, impure, naked, and filthy, who wears rags from the street or grass as ornaments, who climbs onto heaps of refuse, wood, or horses, who is restless and eats excessively—such a person is possessed by a *piśāca*.
Even there, one sees [the patient] laughing at the sight of food, crying out discordantly, constantly terrified,
making all his limbs tremble with dejection, running about again and again, and being frightened by a blade of kusha grass.

One should recognize a physician possessed by a *preta* as one who becomes angry upon seeing [the patient], eats erratically or excessively, sleeps covered in ashes, blocks the path for women, defiles himself with urine and feces, lacks luster, has the appearance, movements,

and odor of a corpse, cuts grass, is terrified, loathes food, speaks much and harshly, moves slowly, has a dark face, and has swollen, pendulous testicles— [these are the signs] of one possessed by a *kūṣmāṇḍa*.

One who runs about naked, suddenly seizing stones, wood, and the like, wandering about while wearing garments of grass, rags, or garlands; one whose gaze is terrified, who speaks harshly, who frequents cremation grounds, solitary trees, or deserted roads; and one whose eyes are fixed on sesame, food, liquor, or meat—such a person is [afflicted] by *kākhorda*.

One who speaks harshly, whose eyes are bloodshot and trembling, who desires food and begs for water [is afflicted] by a *maukiraṇa*; one who speaks the truth, shivers, delights in the scent of incense and garlands, and is excessively drowsy [is afflicted] by a *vetāla*.

One with a lackluster gaze, twitching eyelashes, suspicious eyes, a dejected face, a parched palate, drowsiness, and impaired speech; one whose clothing is disarranged to the right, who has diminished digestive fire and loss of appetite, yet craves sesame, jaggery, milk-rice, and meat— such a person is afflicted by the seizure of the Pitṛs (ancestors).

One should understand that the curses, meditations, and movements, as well as the speech and food of sages, teachers, elders, and perfected beings (siddhas), are taken up by their very influence. And there is a verse on this point: AS.Utt.7.32 One should know that the curses, meditations, and behaviors, as well as the speech and food of sages, teachers, elders, and perfected beings, are taken up through their influence.
And there is a verse here:
One should observe a person's knowledge, specialized insight, speech, gestures, strength, and prowess;
where these human qualities are absent, one should declare that there is possession by a spirit.
One should abandon a patient who is followed by a crowd of children, who is naked, has disheveled hair, possesses a distressed mind, suffers from chronic illness, and is possessed by a spirit.
Thus ends the seventh chapter.
Now begins the eighth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "The Prevention of Possession by Spirits."
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:
"One who desires non-violence should conquer the [demonic] being through recitation, burnt offerings, oblations, and vows."
Through austerity, virtuous conduct, meditative concentration, knowledge, generosity, compassion, and so forth; [and by using] asafoetida,
the three pungents (vyoṣa), rock salt, Nepalese black pepper, garlic, and the roots of the arka plant.
Ajalomī, golomī, bhūtakeśī, and vacā-latā;
kukkuṭī, sarpagandhā, tilā, kāṇavikā, and vikāṇikā.
Vajraprokta, vayasthā, śṛṅgī, and mohanavallī;
añjana produced from a stream, and another medicinal herb that destroys demons.
From the donkey, horse, dog, cat, camel, bear, monitor lizard,
mongoose, porcupine, leopard, cat, cow, lion, tiger, and marine creatures; AS.Utt.8.6 [from these, one should avoid meat].
One should prepare ghee from this group of ingredients— skin, bile,
teeth, nails— or alternatively, fresh oil, for use as a drink or as nasal drops.
Their powder should be used for massage and as an incense;
and with these one should employ pills for collyrium and for the *sāvapīḍana* procedure.
The paste of these [herbs] should be used as an ointment, and their decoction for sprinkling;
this application brings relief from seizures, insanity, and epilepsy.
Gaja-hvā, pippalī root, vyoṣa, āmalaka, and sarṣapa,
ground together with the bile of a monitor lizard, a mongoose, a cat, and a hare.
One should not employ [medicines] for sprinkling, massage, or unction that drive away the seizing spirits (grahāpahā),
which are produced from horses, dogs, mules, owls, herons, vultures, and jackals.
Oil cooked with the dung of a donkey, camel, and boar, along with that [powder], ground together with goat's urine, is highly recommended for nasal administration and other treatments (AS.Utt.8.11).
[One should also use] *śirīṣa* flowers, garlic, ginger, white mustard, and *vacā*.

One should grind mañjiṣṭhā, the two types of niśā, and kṛṣṇā with goat's urine; once this has been dried in the shade, it is made into a wick (varti) and liquefied with fish bile as an añjana collyrium.
A wick made from the fruit of *naktamāla*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), the roots of *bilva* and *syonāka*,
and the two types of *haridrā*, prepared as before, serves as an ointment for the eyes.
Vayasthā, hiṅgu, kaṭukā, ṣaḍgranthā, and likewise saindhava; siddhārthaka, vacā, hiṅgu, priyaṅgu, and the two types of rajanī. (AS.Utt.8.13)
Mañjiṣṭhā, śvetakaṭabhī, varā, śvetā, adrikarṇikā,
the leaf of nimba, and the seeds of naktamāla and śirīṣa. (AS.Utt.8.14)

Ghee prepared with *surāhvā*, the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), and four times as much cow’s urine, along with white mustard seeds (*siddhārthaka*), is known by the name Siddhārthaka; it is to be employed both for drinking and as a nasal medication (*nasya*).
It quickly destroys all planetary influences, especially those of the Asuras; it conquers malevolent spells, misfortune, poison, insanity, fever, epilepsy, and sin.
A medicinal preparation (agada) formulated with these very same herbs and bovine urine,
when employed for drinking, nasal administration, collyrium, external application, bathing, and rubbing, [cures the aforementioned ailments].
It is indicated by its qualities as before, and it brings success at the royal gate. Siddhārthaka, vyoṣa, vacā, aśvagandhā, the two types of niśā, hiṅgu, palāṇḍu, and kanda— AS.Utt.8.18.

The seed of *karañja*, the flower of *śirīṣa*, and the fruit, bark, and root-bark of the *kapittha* tree; *samaṅgā*, *mantha*, *nata*, *kuṣṭha*, the root of *syonāka*, *kiṇihī*, and sugar. (AS.Utt.8.19)
One should prepare jaggery balls well-impregnated with goat's urine and cow's bile for those afflicted by evil planetary influences,
insanity, darkness, blindness at night, or hanging, as well as for those whose bodies are submerged in water.
One should treat those who have been poisoned, struck down, or bitten by a proud serpent with collyrium,
snuff, and ointments made from cotton seeds, peacock feathers, *bṛhatī*, discarded flower-garlands, and *piṇḍītaka*.
An incense prepared from equal parts of bark, vāṃśī, vṛṣadaṃśaviṭ, chaff, vacā, hair, snake-skin slough, the horns of a great elephant and a twice-born man, asafoetida,
and black pepper is supreme for destroying the possession by Skanda, insanity, piśācas, rākṣasas, spirits, and grahas.

[One should prepare a medicinal preparation] with the three pungents (trikaṭuka), kadala, saffron (kuṅkuma), granthika, alkali (kṣāra), siṃhī, the two types of niśā, dāru, white mustard (siddhārtha), the pair [of salts],
ambu, śakra, sita, garlic (laśuna), the three fruits (phalatraya), uśīra, tiktā, vacā, tuttha, yaṣṭī, balā, red oil (lohitaila), elā, śilā, and padmaka.
Ghee prepared with the paste of viṣā, tārkṣya, śaila, cavya, and āmalaka, along with nine parts of cow's urine, is known as bhūtarāva; when drunk, it is the supreme destroyer of grahas.
With nata, madhuka, karañja, lākṣā, paṭolī,
samaṅgā, vacā, pāṭalī, hiṅgu, siddhārtha, siṃhī, the two types of niśā, latā, and rohiṇa;
With *badara*, *kaṭu-phala-trika*, *kāṇḍa-dāru*, *krimighna*, *ajagandhā*,
*amarā*, *aṅkola*, *kośātakī*, *śigru*, *nimba*, *ambuda*, and *indrāhvaya*.
Ghee prepared with a paste of gada, śuka, trapuṣa, bīja, ugrā, yaṣṭī, adrikarṇī, nikumbha, agni, and bilva, along with the group of urines (mūtravarga), [is used for enema].

That which is known as Mahābhūtarāva, when administered according to the prescribed rules and combined with all the sequential methods, quickly destroys all planetary seizures (graha), insanity, leprosy, and fevers. As for those specific planets that seize individuals in their respective [periods], they affect them particularly intensely.
On these days, the physician should perform offerings (bali), oblations (homa), and other such rites,
as well as provide baths, garments, fat, meat, wine, milk, molasses, and so forth.
Whatever is pleasing to whomsoever at whatever time, that one should bring for them then:
jewels, perfumes, garlands, seeds, honey, and clarified butter.
And all foods are for everyone; this is the general rule.
[This was taught] by the divine seers, the gurus, the elders, and the perfected ones (siddhas) in the abode of the gods.
One should offer a bali-oblation to the gods in the northern direction;
at the crossroads, one should offer it to the Daityas and Bhūtas in the western direction at the appropriate time.

For an affliction by a Gandharva, one should offer a bali-oblation with clothing and ornaments on the path of cattle. For an affliction by the Pitṛs or Nāgas, one should offer it to the Nāgas in a river located to the southeast.
To a Yakṣa at a Yakṣa shrine, or at the confluence of two rivers;
at a crossroads, or in terrifying, dense thickets inhabited by Rākṣasas.
One should offer to the *rakṣasas* in the south, to the *brahmarākṣasas* in the east,
to the *piśācas* in an empty dwelling, and to those situated in the western direction.
Pure white garlands, perfumes, milk-rice with sesame seeds,
curd, and a white umbrella are prescribed as the offering for the gods.
One should cook one prastha of ghee with half-pala measures each of asafoetida, mustard seeds, vacha,
and the three pungents (vyoṣa) in four times as much cow’s urine.
By means of drinking that [mixture], nasal drops (nāvana), and massage (abhyaṅga), one is liberated from possession by malevolent spirits (devagraha).
For nasal drops and collyrium, one should use *vacā*, realgar (*hiṅgula*), and garlic with goat’s urine.

To the Daityas, an offering of *balī* along with *uśīra*, white lotus, and blue lotus yields great fruit; to the Nāgas, an offering of *sumanā* flowers, parched grain, molasses, cakes, and rice mixed with molasses.
An offering (bali) should be made with fine rice, honey, milk, black earth, nāgakesara,
vacā, padma, pūga, uśīra, and the petals of the red lotus.
White lotus petals, *lodhra*, *tagara*, and *nāga-sarṣapa*—
ground with cold water, this is beneficial for nasal drops (*nāvana*) and collyrium (*añjana*).
For yakṣas, [the offering consists of] milk-rice mixed with curd, ghee, and guggulu;
for gods, deodar, blue lotus, lotus, uśīra, cloth, and gold.
Gold and a medicinal offering (bali) should be employed; urine, clarified butter, and milk,
prepared together in equal proportions, are beneficial for drinking, nasal administration, and massage.
Harītakī, the two types of haridrā, garlic, marica, vacā,
and nimba leaves— these, ground into a paste with goat's urine, are used as a nasal drop (nāvana) and as a collyrium (añjana).
The offering for the Brahma-rākṣasa is prepared as follows: a full āḍhaka measure of barley,
a jar of water, minced meat, an umbrella, a garment, and an ointment.
One should cook [this] in a decoction of twenty palas of *gāyatrī* with half-pala quantities of *tryūṣaṇa*,
*triphalā*, asafoetida, *ṣaḍgranthā*, *misī*, and mustard seeds.
Seven *kuḍava* measures of ghee, along with nimba leaves and garlic,
cooked in three times as much cow’s urine, is beneficial when used for drinking, nasal administration, and massage.
For the *rakṣasas*, the offering consists of raw flesh, white flowers, rice mixed with various ingredients,
cooked and raw meat, and *niṣpāva* beans sprinkled with blood.
The bark, roots, flowers, and fruits of *naktamāla* and *śirīṣa*,
as well as those of black *pāṭalī*, the root of *bilva*, and the three pungents (*kaṭutrika*).
This medicine— consisting of *hiṅgu*, *indrayava*, *siddhārtha*, garlic, and the fruit of *āmalakī*—
should be used for nasal drops (*nāvana*) and collyrium (*añjana*), having been dissolved in goat's urine.
Ghee prepared with these same [drugs] and four times as much cow's urine wards off Rakshasas and Grahas through drinking, massage, and nasal administration.

The offering for the Piśācas consists of fermented liquor (sīdhu), oil-cake (piṇyāka), minced meat (palala), curd, radish, salt, clarified butter, cooked rice accompanied by living beings, and barley gruel (yāvaka).
The two types of turmeric, mañjiṣṭhā, misi, rock salt, ginger,
asafoetida, priyaṅgu, the three pungents (trikaṭu), garlic, the three myrobalans (triphalā), and vacā.
Ghee prepared with the flowers of *pāṭalī*, white *kaṭabhī*, and *śirīṣa*,
with one-fourth part cow’s urine, is beneficial when used for drinking and as an ointment.
One should employ collyrium and nasal drops made from those same [substances] ground with goat's urine.
One should avoid strong nasal treatments and the like for gods, sages, ancestors, and gandharvas.
In this [condition], one should administer mild medicine such as the drinking of clarified butter (sarpiṣpāna) and so forth;
except for cases involving Piśācas, one should not employ any harsh measures against any of these [afflictions].
Together with the physician, they slay the patient, for they are wrathful and possess great power.
[One should worship] the Lord, the twelve-armed Protector, the Noble Avalokita.
By reciting this treatment for all diseases, one may conquer all planetary influences (*graha*), as well as insanity, epilepsy, or any other derangement of the mind.
One should always cause that pure person to hear the Mahāvidyā Māyūrī;
one should worship Sthāṇu, the Lord of Beings (Bhūteśa), and his attendants known as the Pramathas.
By reciting those perfected mantras, one repels all malevolent planets;
and whatever else is beneficial shall be taught in the two subsequent chapters.
"Whatever has been stated here, one should apply all of that mutually"—
thus ends the eighth chapter.
Now begins the ninth chapter. Hereafter, we shall explain the chapter titled "The Prevention of Insanity" (Unmādapratiṣedha).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and others: there are six types of insanity, caused by vāta, pitta, kapha, their combination (sannipāta), poison, and mental affliction.

Among these, what is called *unmāda* (insanity) is the intoxication of the mind caused by physical and mental defects that have strayed from their proper course. Furthermore, the cause for those [defects] straying from their proper course is: foodstuffs that are impure, corrupted, unwholesome, or unsuitable, consumed regardless of the rules for diet; sexual excess; the onset of disease or suppressed natural urges; the practice of irregular bodily movements; the transgression against gods, the twice-born, or teachers; mental affliction arising from the distresses born of passion and hatred; or the ingestion of poisons, secondary poisons (*upaviṣa*), and artificial toxins. (AS.Utt.9.3)

In one whose mental essence is thus diminished, when the mind is impaired and the intellect is agitated, the aggravated *doṣas*, due to their extreme intensity, reach the heart, obstruct the channels that carry the mind, and produce insanity.

AS.Utt.9.5: In that regard, the premonitory symptoms (*pūrvarūpa*) of insanity caused by the *doṣas* are: emptiness of the head; unsteadiness of the eyes; ringing in the ears; excessive respiration; salivation from the mouth; lack of desire for food; anorexia; indigestion; a gripping sensation in the heart; meditation, exhaustion, delusion, and agitation at inappropriate times; constant horripilation; fever; frequent mental derangement; the appearance of *ardita* (facial paralysis); the production of the form of *ardita*; and in dreams, the frequent vision of confused, agitated, unstable, and inauspicious forms; mounting a wheel like an oil-presser; being churned by whirlwinds of wind; sinking into whirlpools of turbid water; and the withdrawal of the eyes [from their sockets]. These are the premonitory symptoms of insanity caused by the *doṣas*.
Immediately following that, the manifestation of insanity itself is the general symptom: the loss of mind, intellect, memory, and so forth.

Consequently, the body— like a chariot whose charioteer has been slain, or like a boat upon the waters without a helmsman— wanders aimlessly and suddenly, its course subverted by pleasure and pain, and by conduct characterized as dharma and adharma.

Among these, the symptoms of [Vāta-type insanity] are: inappropriate smiling, laughing, dancing, singing, playing musical instruments, agitation of speech and limbs, incoherent speech, knitting of the eyebrows, weeping, shouting, and slapping; constant wandering about; frothing at the mouth; traveling by means that are not vehicles; adorning oneself with objects that are not ornaments; greed for food; contempt for what has been obtained; intense envy; emaciation; harshness; reddish eyes that are swollen or protruding; and excessive strength even when the food has been digested. (AS.Utt.9.8)

From *pitta* arise: anger; threatening suddenly with fists, clods of earth, sticks, or weapons; nakedness; a desire for shade, cool things, and water despite the heat; a sensation of burning; yellowish discoloration of the skin; falling off of hair without apparent cause; a fear of fire blazing up; seeing stars during the day; and eyes that are coppery, green, or turmeric-yellow and bloodshot. (AS.Utt.9.9)

From *kapha* (phlegm) arise: scantiness of speech, movement, and food; loss of appetite; vomiting; a fondness for warmth; salivation and discharge from the nose; a desire for solitude; a preference for women; excessive sleep; loathsomeness; aversion to cleanliness; swelling of the face; whiteness, stickiness, and turbidity of the eyes; and strength after eating or at night. When there is a combination of all the sense-bases and their structural configurations, one should recognize that as a severe form of insanity characterized by those very factors; the physician should avoid treating it.
Afflicted by the unbearable loss of wealth, a beloved wife, and so forth, the pale and dejected patient, repeatedly fainting, laments, "Alas! Alas! (AS.Utt.9.12).
He weeps for no apparent reason, laughs, and holds those qualities in high esteem;
with a mind afflicted by grief, he broods, remains wakeful, and acts restlessly.
One whose face has turned dark from poison, whose luster is lost, whose senses are weak,
who is agitated even during the intervals between paroxysms, and whose eyes are bloodshot— such a person one should avoid.
Now, in insanity caused by Vāta, one should administer the drinking of oleaginous substances; however,
when the channels are previously obstructed, mild purification combined with oleation should be employed.
In cases arising from kapha and pitta as well, emesis along with purgation should first be administered to one who has been oleated and sudated,
followed by enemas and head-purgation (errhines).
In this way, the mind of one whose body has been purified attains clarity; and during the period of oleation for disorders arising from Vata, sesame oil mixed with Shariṣa is desired.

In cases of Pitta, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are highly beneficial; in cases arising from Kapha, even when this [diet] continues, sharp nasal drops (nāvana) and collyrium (añjana) should be used.
Gladdening, consoling, frightening, causing fear, beating, and threatening; as well as massage, rubbing with unguents, ointments, incense, and the drinking of clarified butter.
One should employ these, for they lead the mind of the pure person back to its natural state. Two palas each of asafoetida, sauvarcala salt, and vyoṣa [are added] to one āḍhaka of ghee.
This proven preparation, along with its accompanying urine, is supreme for curing insanity, possession by spirits,
and epilepsy. Two *prasthas* of the fresh juice of *brāhmī* and one *prastha* of ghee should be cooked together.
With one akṣa each of the paste made from vyoṣa, śyāmā, trivṛt, bimbī, śaṅkhapuṣpī, nṛpadruma, saptalā, and kṛmihara;
AS.Utt.9.22 AS.Utt.9.22
One should administer it by increasing the dose by one pala up to a maximum of four palas;
this cures insanity, skin diseases, and epilepsy, and bestows sons upon barren women.
Brāhmī-ghṛta is known to be beneficial for speech, voice, memory, and intelligence. It is prepared with varā, viśālā, vaḍhra, elā, devadāru, and elavāluka.
With dvisārivā, dvirajanī, dvisthirā, phalinī,
nata, bṛhatī, kuṣṭha, mañjiṣṭhā, nāgakeśara, and dāḍima.
One should cook ghee with one karṣa each of vella, tālīsa, patra, elā, mālatī buds, utpala, dantī, padmaka, and hima.
AS.Utt.9.26 AS.Utt.9.26
One *prastha* [of this preparation] destroys spirits, seizures, insanity, cough,
epilepsy, anemia, itching, poison, consumption, urinary disorders, delusion, fever, and artificial poisons. (AS.Utt.9.27)

In one who is devoid of merit, whose passion is slight, whose mind is afflicted by fate, who is dull-witted, whose speech falters, who merely desires memory, and whose digestive fire is weak— A.S.Utt.9.28.
This ghee is strengthening, auspicious, life-prolonging, and bestows luster, good fortune, and nourishment; it grants all that is desirable and is excellent for the *puṃsavana* rite.
Having boiled these twenty-one [drugs], beginning with the two types of *sārivā*, in water— AS.Utt.9.29.
In that water, one should cook ghee with four times the amount of milk from a cow that has recently calved,
along with *vīrā*, *dvimēdā*, *kākolī*, *kapikacchū*, and *viṣāṇī*.
This supreme Mahākalyāṇaka [mixture], combined with *sūpyaparṇī*,
is highly nourishing, destroys the *sannipāta* disorder, and is superior to the previous one in its qualities.
Jaṭilā, pūtanā, keśī, cāraṭī, markaṭī, vacā,
trāyamāṇā, jayā, vīrā, coraka, and kaṭurohiṇī.
Kāyasthā, sūkarī, chatrā, sāticchatrā, palaṅkaṣā,
mahāpuruṣadantā, vayasthā, and the two types of nākulī.
Ghee prepared with *kaṭaṃbhārā*, *vṛścikālī*, and *śāliparṇī* destroys insanity, seizures,
and epilepsy occurring on the fourth day.
This ghee, named Mahāpaiśācaka, is like nectar;
it produces intelligence, intellect, and memory, and promotes the growth of the limbs of children.
One hundred bulbs of garlic, thirty *palas* of *abhayā* and the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*),
one *prastha* of the soot of cow-hide, and two *āḍhakas* each of milk and urine.
One should administer one prastha of old ghee prepared with these [drugs];
once it has cooled, one should add one pala of asafoetida powder and one mānikā of honey.

It quickly destroys unmādas (insanities) arising from those [three] doṣas and from spirits, as well as viṣamajvaras (irregular fevers) and apasmāras (epilepsy), through drinking, massage, and nasal drops.
Alternatively, having made him drink an excellent quantity of pure, prepared ghee that has been aged, one should confine him in a pit or in a house.
Or, when these groups of medicinal substances have become available,
one should employ them in applications such as collyrium, dry massage, ointments, and nasal drops.
Oil cooked with *aśvagandhā*, *ajagandhā*, *ugragandhā*, garlic, mustard, *rāsnā*, *kāyasthā*, and *golomī* [is used for massage].
Like cow's urine, when used for drinking, nasal administration, massage, and oil enemas,
it destroys all forms of insanity, possession by spirits, misfortune, sin, and epilepsy.
Śirīṣa, madhuka, hiṅgu, garlic, tagara, vacā,
and kuṣṭha, ground with goat's urine, should be used as a nasal drop and as a collyrium.
Similarly, vyoṣa, the two types of haridrā, mañjiṣṭhā, asafoetida, mustard seeds,
and the seeds of śirīṣa destroy unmāda, graha, and apasmāra.
Brāhmī, aindrī, viḍaṅga, trikaṭu, hiṅgu, jaṭā, murā,
rāsnā, viṣaghnā, laśuna, viśalyā, surasa, and vacā.
Having ground jyotiṣmatī, nāgavin, anantā, along with harītakī and kāmlī, in elephant urine, one should dry them in the shade.

For one suffering from insanity, the *unmādasūdanī* (insanity-destroying) preparation is made by grinding the fruits of *apāmārga*, vermilion (*hiṅgula*), and *hiṅgupatrikā*, along with collyrium, ointments, and incense. (AS.Utt.9.46)
A wick (varti) made with the bile of a cow or a jackal, combined with an eighth part of black pepper as a collyrium,
[is used] in cases of insanity, possession by spirits, and epilepsy in men and cattle within its range.
Various types of expressed juices (avapīḍas), combined with mustard oil, [should also be administered].

Anointing with pungent oil (kaṭutaila) and blowing its powder into the nose are beneficial; likewise, the sharp fumigation (dhūma) containing asafoetida (hiṅgu), as described in the Sūtrasthāna, is recommended.
One should prepare [a medicinal application] from the urine, bile, feces, hair, nails, and skin derived from a jackal, porcupine, owl, bat, wolf,
and goat.
Incense, collyrium, oil massage, medicinal paste, and sprinkling [of water] should be administered;
one should also constantly fumigate the patient with the highly putrid flesh of dogs, cows, and fish.
In cases primarily characterized by vāta and śleṣman, [the aforementioned treatments] are generally recommended; however, in the paittika type,
tikta-ghṛta, jīvanīya-ghṛta, and miśraka-sneha are praised.
Cold foods and drinks that are sweet and light [are beneficial].
Or one should venesection the vein as previously described, or [administer] fatty meat to one who is satiated;
having thus laid him down in a windless place, he is freed from mental confusion. Or, having thrown him into a well without water, one should cause him to wither away through hunger.
One should console that friend with words consistent with dharma and artha;
or one should speak of the destruction of desired objects, or show him wonders.
Having bound it and smeared it with mustard oil, one should place it face upwards in the sun;
or else, one should touch it with *kapikacchu* or with heated iron, oil, or water.
Having beaten them with whips, or having bound them, one should cast them into a pit;
or else, into a house that is dark and devoid of weapons or stones.
One should frighten him with a snake whose fangs have been extracted, or with tamed lions and elephants,
or with Kirātas, enemies, and thieves holding weapons in their hands.
Alternatively, by the king's command, royal officers may take him well-restrained outside and terrify him with threats of execution.
For the fear for one's life is considered superior to the fear of bodily suffering;
by that [fear], his mind, which was agitated in every way, attains tranquility.
This effective treatment should be applied with due regard for place, time, and other factors;
however, if one's mind is afflicted by the loss of a cherished object, [it must be treated accordingly].
One should pacify that [distress] through attainments similar to it, consolations, and reassurances,
[as well as those arising from] desire, grief, fear, anger, joy, envy, and greed.
One should bring these very [doshas], which are mutually antagonistic, to a state of equilibrium;
one should observe the persistence of the [diseased] elements, noting any manifestation that exceeds the described symptoms.
If [the condition] is insanity, then one should administer the medicine prescribed for spirits;
and one should offer a bali-oblation consisting of minced meat, barley gruel, and balls of parched grain flour.
Unctuous and sweet food, rice soaked in blood, meat that is both cooked and raw, *surā*, *maireya*, and *āsava* liquors.

One who has desisted from meat and wine, who eats wholesome food, and is self-restrained and pure, [should offer] the flowers of the *atimukta*, the *jāti*, and the *sahacara* at crossroads, at watering places for cattle, and at the confluences of rivers. (AS.Utt.9.64)
A person of strong constitution is not afflicted by endogenous or exogenous forms of insanity;
likewise, there is clarity regarding the objects of the senses, as well as the intellect, self, and mind.
The state of the bodily constituents (dhātus) being established in their natural condition is the characteristic of freedom from insanity;
thus ends the ninth chapter.
Now begins the tenth chapter. Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "The Prohibition of Epilepsy" (Apasmārapratiṣedha).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and others:
"Apasmāra is indeed the loss of memory, arising from the confusion of the intellect and the mind."
It arises when the mind is struck by anxiety, grief, fear, and the like,
or when the impurities residing in the mind and body become agitated, leading to a state resembling insanity.
When hatred pervades the heart, the channels that carry consciousness, and the bodily cavities,
the person of deluded mind enters into darkness and performs loathsome actions.
Chewing his teeth, vomiting foam, tossing his hands and feet,
seeing non-existent forms, he stumbles and falls to the ground.
When the force of the disorder has passed, one whose eyes and eyebrows are distorted awakens;
after some time, he again behaves in this very same way.

Apasmāra is of four types, caused by Vāta and the others, and by their combination (nicaya). Its premonitory symptoms, when it is about to arise, are cardiac tremor, a sense of emptiness, and vertigo.
Seeing darkness, meditative absorption, the raising of the eyebrows, and distortion of the eyes;
hearing sounds that do not exist, perspiration, and the flowing of saliva and mucus. (AS.Utt.10.8)
Lack of digestion, aversion to food, fainting, abdominal distension,
loss of strength, insomnia, body aches, thirst, and singing or dancing in dreams.
The drinking of oil or liquor, or the voiding of urine from those very substances [is the cause];
therein, due to Vāta, the thighs throb and twitch repeatedly and continuously.
He loses consciousness and regains it while crying out in discordant tones;
with eyes bulging, he pants, vomits foam, and trembles. (AS.Utt.10.11)
He shakes his head, bites his teeth, and his neck becomes distended;
he tosses his limbs about in all directions, and his fingers become crooked and bent.
One whose eyes, skin, nails, and face are rough, dark-brown, or reddish, who perceives black objects, and who repeatedly sees flickering, harsh, ugly, or deformed faces,
suffers from epilepsy due to pitta and frequently regains consciousness.
With yellow-foaming eyes, mouth, and skin, he strikes the earth; possessed by thirst, he displays a form that is terrifying and blazing with rage.
Due to kapha, there is slow grasping [of objects] and slow awakening; one sees white forms and colors. However, if all these symptoms are present, one should avoid [treating] the patient.

AS.Utt.10.15 Furthermore, for those whose intellect, mind, heart, and consciousness are obstructed, one should first induce awakening through sharp procedures such as emesis and other therapies in cases of epilepsy (apasmāra).
One should treat epilepsy caused by vāta primarily with enemas, that caused by pitta mostly with purgatives,
and that caused by kapha mainly with emetics.
Madana, Lambā, Viśālā, Ariṣṭaka, and Koṭaja are used for emesis;
Trivṛt, Śyāmā, Dravantī, Saptalā, and Snuhī, along with cow’s urine, are used for purgation.
With the ten roots (*daśamūla*), *balā*, *rāsnā*, *saralā*, and *devadāru*,
along with barley, jujube, and horse gram, together with urine, alkali, and rock salt.

One should administer an enema (āsthāpana) prepared with these and other wind-alleviating (vātaghna) substances combined with asafoetida (hiṅgu) and fats, having duly processed mustard oil (kaṭutaila).
It pacifies epilepsy caused by Vāta through nasal medication, massage, and oil enemas,
provided the patient has been thoroughly purified and properly reassured.
Listen to the pacifying yogas for the purpose of liberation from epilepsy:
clarified butter boiled with cow-dung juice, milk, curd, and urine.

One should drink [a decoction of] the two groups of five roots (pañcamūla), triphalā, the two types of niśā, and the bark of kuṭaja to bring an end to epilepsy, fever, insanity, and jaundice. (AS.Utt.10.22)
Saptaparṇa, apāmārga, nīlinī, kaṭurohiṇī, śamyāka, the root of puṣkara, phalgu, and durālabhā.
Having boiled two palas of each [of these] in one droṇa of water until reduced to one-fourth,
[one should add] bhārṅgī, pāṭhā, āḍhakī, kumbha, nikumbha, vyoṣa, and rohiṣa.
One should cook ghee with one-eighth parts each of mūrvā, bhūtīka, bhūnimba, śreyasī, the two types of sārivā, madayantī, agni, and nicula. (AS.Utt.10.25)
Likewise, one *prastha* of this with the aforementioned liquids constitutes this great *pañcagavya*,
which is supreme for curing fever, epilepsy, abdominal diseases, and fistula-in-ano.
This [decoction] cures swelling, hemorrhoids, jaundice, anemia, abdominal tumors, asthma, and urinary retention.
Two *tulās* each of the flowers, leaves, bark, pith, and roots of the *śirīṣa* tree [are used].
Varaṇa, eraṇḍa, śamyāka, daśamūla,
and āṭarūṣaka; śatāvarī, bala, rāsnā, suṣavī, and pāribhadraka.
Muruṅgī, vañcula, dantī, kakubha, along with punarnavā, the root-tuft of rohiṣa, its flower, karaghāṭa, and mayūraka.
One should take fifty parts each of grapes, lac, misī, excellent barley,
kola, and kulattha, measuring half an āḍhaka for each.
One should cook two hundred palas of beef or goat meat in water;
when reduced to one-eighth by thirty-two *droṇas* of water, it should be boiled down further.
One should prepare a mixture of one droṇa of oil and a vaha of curd, along with one pālika each of finely ground pāṭhā, samaṅgā, suṣavī, the two types of haridrā (dviniśā), and candana.
With cardamom, water-lily, balā, aśvadaṃṣṭrā, sārivā, and ghanā;
with mañjiṣṭhā, kuṣṭha, madhuka, lodhra, rāsnā, and kuṭannaṭa.
With śaṭhī, śirīṣa flowers, nata, nāga, and amarāhvaya; with varāṅga, joṅgaka, pattaṅga, viḍaṅga, and priyaṅgu.
With muruṅgī, patra, nalada, sevyaka, kunda, and nakha,
along with tilaparṇī— by means of these, through drinking, enemas, massage, and nasal drops.

Epilepsy, possession by spirits, insanity, consumption, and irregular fevers; diseases of the female reproductive tract and semen, abdominal tumors, urinary disorders, anemia, and intoxication—[these are cured]. It [cures] all diseases born of wind (māruta), such as vātaśoṇita, visarpa, pakṣāghāta, ardita, and others,
especially those arising from poison and wind.

This ghee, boiled with the juice of *brāhmī*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, and *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, destroys the effects of sorcery, spells, poisons from roots and fangs, and artificial poisons; it is the best among elixirs (*rasāyana*), promotes intelligence, and is a supreme aphrodisiac. (AS.Utt.10.38)

Ancient [clarified butter] is pure and conquers insanity, misfortune, epilepsy, and sin. One *prastha* of oil and one *prastha* of clarified butter, with one *pala* each of the *jīvanīya* (life-promoting) drugs, [should be cooked].
One should cook [the herbs] in one *droṇa* of milk; when prepared, it is a liberation from epilepsy.
[One should also cook them] in a bronze vessel with milk, sugarcane juice, and eight times as much decoction of *kāśmarya*.
One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with the *kārṣika* and *jīvanīya* drugs;
that quickly destroys epilepsy arising from *vāta* and *pitta*.
In the same way, milk boiled with a decoction of *kāśa*, *vidārī*, sugarcane, and *kuśa* grass,
along with two *pala* of *madhuka* paste and one *droṇa* of *āmalaka* juice, [is beneficial].

This prepared *ghṛta* (clarified butter), a measure of one *prastha*, is a proven remedy for *pitta*-type epilepsy. Ghee is boiled with the fresh juice of *kūṣmāṇḍa* (bottle gourd) that is eighteen times its quantity.
A paste of yaṣṭīmadhu removes epilepsy and bestows intelligence, speech, and a clear voice. The bile of tawny cows is an excellent and highly beneficial nasal medication (nāvana).
It is honored [as a remedy] for dogs, jackals, and cats, as well as for lions and other such beasts;
and also for monitor lizards, mongooses, snakes, spotted deer, bears, and cattle.
Oil prepared with pitta-alleviating substances is recommended for use as nasal drops (nasya) and for massage (abhyaṅga).
[This is done] with triphalā, vyoṣa, pītadru, yavakṣāra, and phaṇijjaka.
Oil prepared with the seeds of *śrī*, *apāmārga*, and *kārañja*,
along with goat’s urine, is beneficial as a nasal drop (*nasya*); or the physician should blow it into the nose as a powder (*cūrṇa*).
Vṛścikālī, balā, kuṣṭha, bhārgī, the five salts,
kāyasthā, śāradā, mudga, uśīra, jalada, and barley.
One should grind trikaṭu with goat's urine and prepare a medicinal wick (varti) for those afflicted by epilepsy,
poisoning from artificial poisons, insanity, or the venom of snakebites.
Musta, vayasthā, triphalā, kāyasthā, hiṅgu, śādvala,
vyoṣa, māṣa, and barley, along with the urine of a goat, a sheep, and a bull.
This wick (varti) destroys epilepsy, vitiligo, and irregular fevers;
ghee extracted under the Puṣya constellation, along with dog’s bile, is an ointment that cures epilepsy.
That same [mixture], combined with clarified butter (sarpiṣ), is an excellent fumigation (dhūpana).
[It is prepared] from the juice of kaṭabhī, nimba, kaṭvaṅga, madhuśigru, and bark (tvac).
The prepared oil, equal in quantity to the urine, is recommended for massage.
[It is prepared] with *piṇḍakharjūra*, *vacā*, *pathyā*, *vṛścikālī*, *arka*, and mustard seeds.
With *jaṭilā*, *pūtanā*, *keśī*, *nākulī*, *hiṅgu*, and *coraka*; with garlic, *atirasā*, *chatrā*, *kuṣṭha*, and the excrement of birds;

Oil cooked in goat's urine with whatever meat-eating animals are available—such as those born from mongooses, owls, cats, vultures, insects, snakes, and crows—should be used for anointment; they should also be employed for fumigation and as a paste. (AS.Utt.10.54)
One should apply smoke to it using its beak, wings, and excrement;
[as well as] *kākolī*, *śigru*, salt, *hiṅgu*, and *śivāṭikā*.
One should grind together kaiḍarya, sandalwood, black kākanāsā, mustard seeds,
and the shoulder, eyes, claws, and ribs of a dog.
Under the Puṣya asterism, one should apply an ointment made from these [substances] with goat's urine and fumigate [the area] with them;
or alternatively, with the burnt hair of a cow's tail or the hair of a goat.

One should always perform anointment with the bones of a donkey or the claws of an elephant, ground into a paste with urine; likewise, one should perform sprinkling with decoctions that have been boiled.
By these successful therapeutic measures, the heart is thoroughly cleansed;
his channels are purified, and he regains memory and consciousness.
In cases of epilepsy associated with a persistent possession by spirits (bhūtānubandha), where the symptoms of the humors (doṣas) are predominant,
one should employ the aforementioned spiritual therapies (daivavyapāśraya) appropriate for each specific spirit.
One should habitually consume garlic with oil, or śatāvarī with milk,
or the juice of brāhmī, or the juice of kuṣṭha, or vacā combined with honey.
Apasmāra arises from the simultaneous provocation of the bodily and mental *doṣas* when they are enraged; it occurs because it takes its seat in the great vital organs (*mahāmarmans*).
Therefore, one should treat this difficult-to-cure condition with rejuvenative therapies (rasāyana); furthermore,
one must always protect the afflicted person from dangerous substances such as fire and water.
One should not say to him who is free from mental agitation, "You have done such a thing," nor should one cause his mind, which is afflicted by desirable objects, to swell with passion.
For those whose bodies are afflicted by planetary influences and whose memory and consciousness are deranged,
physicians praise the administration of strong unctuous substances through oral intake, massage, and enemas.
Thus ends the tenth chapter (the third section on the elements, *bhūtatantra*, is complete).
Now begins the eleventh chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter entitled "The Knowledge of Diseases of the Eyelids.
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
The humors (malas), aggravated by unwholesome things described in the etiology of all diseases—
especially by those harmful to the eyes— are generally accompanied by pitta.
The vessels that extend upward and take refuge in the parts of the eye— whether the eyelid margin,
the junction, the white part, the black part, the pupil, or the entire eye— [are affected].
The diseases, having reached the unstable vessels located within the eyelid margins, produce [afflictions];
in one who has just awakened from sleep, they cause a painful stiffness of the eyelid margin.
When the eyes appear as if filled with dust, there is difficulty in opening them and the shedding of tears;
because they subside upon massage, physicians call that condition *kṛcchronmīla*.
The wind, repeatedly agitating the two eyelids,
causes their constant blinking; this disease is called Arun-nimesha, wherein the eyelid is closed.
With its joints loosened, motionless, and drooping, it is indeed struck by Vāta. Due to Pitta, many black spots appear on the inner eyelid like the seeds of the *kumbhīka* plant.
Furthermore, the boils known as *kumbhī* swell and then burst;
they are accompanied by burning, moistening, and piercing pain, appear red, and cannot endure being touched.
The eyelid is produced by pitta; they call that *pittotkliṣṭa*. Pitta, having taken refuge at the edge of the eyelashes, causes itching and burning.
The falling out of the eyelashes is called *pakṣmaśāta*. White pustules, resembling mustard seeds and dense, arising from phlegm (*kapha*), are known as *pothakya*.
Accompanied by swelling, coating, pain, itching, and slimy discharge,
the eyelid (vartman) becomes afflicted by phlegm (kapha), characterized by stiffness, moisture, and coating.
A hard, whitish swelling that suppurates and is itchy arises from kapha; this is called granthi.
That *lagaṇa* is the size of a *kola*, or perhaps slightly smaller than that; it is red, and with blood, it is covered with pustules similar to itself.

The type called *utsaṅga* (pouch-like), as well as *utkliṣṭa* (elevated), *rājimat* (striped), and *sparśanākṣama* (insensitive to touch); these are fleshy growths (*adhimāṃsa*) within the eyelid that are stiff, oily, and always accompanied by burning and pain.
It is red, exuding blood, and it grows larger each time it is cut;
whether in the middle or at the edge of the eyelid, it is firm and characterized by itching and pain.
AS.Utt.11.17 A copper-colored pustule the size of a mung bean, located at the base of the eyelashes, is called añjana-piṭaka.
AS.Utt.11.18 When the eyelid is swollen externally due to the [vitiated] humors (doṣas) but is covered with fine [pustules] internally, it is [known as] vartma-saṃplava.

AS.Utt.11.18 That which has discharge, with water inside, resembling a lotus stalk, is *bisavartman*. AS.Utt.11.19 That path which, being displaced, becomes suddenly swollen and then undergoes a state of withering is [also *bisavartman*].
From the provocation of the three doshas along with blood, *utkliṣṭavartma* arises.
*Śyāvavartma* is characterized by a dark-brown discoloration due to the impurities and blood, accompanied by pain, discharge, and swelling.
The condition known as Śliṣṭa (adherent) is characterized by the two eyelids being stuck together, accompanied by itching, swelling,
and redness.
Pustules at the edge of the eyelid that are dry, rough, and resemble sand are [known as] *sikatā*. A black path on the eyelid that resembles mud is [known as] *kardama*.
It becomes thick, covered with abundant, uniform, and fleshy growths of the same color as the skin.
Kukūṇaka occurs only in an infant and is caused by the eruption of teeth; because of it,
the child has swollen, copper-colored eyes and is unable to see.
In Pakṣmoparodha, there is pain along the eyelids, sliminess, and rubbing of the ears, nose, and eyes; subsequently, a contraction of the two eyelids occurs.
Furthermore, there is roughness and inward-turning of the eyelashes; or else,
as if rubbed by sharp-pointed thorns, the eye swells because of them.
It is treated with the previously extracted [medicines] that counteract wind and other humors;
it is a hard, elevated nodule on the outer eyelid near the corner of the eye, characterized by slight pain and subsiding [with treatment].
Copper-colored, discharging mature pus and blood, it repeatedly distends; appearing like a mass of flesh within the eyelid, the swelling is knotted and painless.
Accompanied by tears, with the humors (doṣas) being uneven, it is arbuda; externally it is mobile.
These twenty-four diseases are located in the eyelids (vartman).
Among these, the first is curable with medicines; the next two, as well as arśas (pterygium), should be rejected [as incurable];
pakṣmoparodha (trichiasis) is palliable; and the remaining types should be conquered with surgery and drugs.
One should scrape the eyelashes, excise the *arbuda* even among them,
and incise the *lagana*, *kumbhīkā*, *bisotsaṅga*, *añjana*, and *alajī*.
One should scrape away the four types of soil— namely, that covered with *pothakī* plants, black earth, sand, and clods— as well as mud and thick dregs, in the case of *sukukūṇaka*.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter.
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the chapter named "The Treatment of Diseases of the Eyelids" (Vartmarogapratiṣedha).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:
