in cases of difficult awakening, one should administer at night ghee prepared from ancient [sources], processed with a paste and decoction of grapes, and sprinkled with sugar.
One should administer unctuous nasal drops (nasya), medicated smoke (dhūma), collyrium (añjana), eye-filling therapy (tarpaṇa), and poultice-cooking (puṭapāka),
as well as enemas (basti) prepared with Vata-alleviating substances; furthermore, one should apply fomentation (sveda) to the eyelids using castor leaves steamed with milk.
If there is no subsiding [of the swelling] in this way, one should perform cauterization with fire using drops on the skin at intervals of the size of a mung bean.

In cases of *kumbhīkā* pustules, after scraping the eyelid, one should rub it with rock salt (*saindhava*) and sprinkle it with a decoction of *paṭola*, *āmalaka*, and *madhuka*, as well as with clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
In the case of those afflicted by *pitta* and blood, one should pierce a vein after the patient has been lubricated with ghee prepared with sweet medicinal herbs;
furthermore, one should administer a purgative using a paste of *triphalā* mixed with a decoction of *trivṛt*.
Or, one may apply *brāhmī* powder mixed with a decoction of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*).
Furthermore, one should administer an oil prepared with sandalwood, *uśīra*, *madhuka*, *mṛdvīkā*, *punarnavā*, and the roots of *bṛhatī*.
Once the eyelid has been incised and the blood has flowed out, the area should be washed with a decoction of *yaṣṭyāhva*.
Sprinkling with milk boiled with sandalwood,

and cold, unctuous ointments applied to the head and face [are indicated]. In the case of falling eyelashes, one should prick the hair follicles with the tip of a needle or cause leeches to feed there.
Emesis may be induced with milk or sugarcane juice; an errhine (nāvana) consisting of ghee prepared with the sweet and cold groups of drugs [is also indicated].
One should prepare a powder for collyrium by burning *kākajaṅghā*, the flesh of the *rohita* fish, and crow's blood together in a smokeless fire,
then pulverizing them; alternatively, one should grind *puṣpakāsīsa* and saturate it with the juice of *surasā*.
That collyrium should be kept for ten days in a copper vessel; it is most effective when the eyelashes have fallen out.

Having scraped off the *pothakī* [lesion] and rubbed it with a powder of ginger, rock salt, and long pepper, one should wash it with warm water and then sprinkle it with a decoction made from the heartwood of *khadira*, *āḍhakī*, and the leaves of *śigru*.
Then, one should perform eye-drops with a decoction of *āmrā*, *jambū*, and *pravāla*, or with water from *triphalā* and the heartwood of *khadira*;
or one should apply a collyrium consisting of the powder of *viḍaṅga*, *lākṣā*, the bark of *dārvī*, *gairika*, and *manohvā*, mixed with honey.
If there is still no relief even thus,
one should apply leeches or scarify the area again and again.
One should perform an irrigation with a decoction of triphalā, madhuka, and the two types of haridrā mixed with honey;
or alternatively, with water boiled with musta, sugar, and kapittha leaves.
Once the eyelid (vartman) has been scarified due to being aggravated by kapha, one should rub it with a powder of saindhava, kāsīsa, pippalī, manaḥśilā, and rasāñjana, combined with honey.

In cases of *vartmāpakleda* (excessive moisture of the eyelids), one should employ phlegm-alleviating treatments such as emesis, medicated smoking (*dhūma*), nasal drops (*nāvana*), and collyrium (*añjana*), as well as dietary regulations. Furthermore,
an ointment stick (*varti*) for application as collyrium should be prepared from *kāsīsa*, salt, jasmine buds (*sumanomukula*), and *rasāñjana*.
One should treat *lagaṇa* like [the condition] caused by the provocation of *kapha*. If it does not subside, one should apply cauterization with fire, emesis, and purgation.

One should administer oil prepared with *pippalī*, *madhuka*, *nimba*, *jyotiṣmatī*, *devadāru*, *viḍaṅga*, *priyaṅgu*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *kuṣṭha*, *śatāhvā*, and rock salt as nasal drops (*nāvayet*);
one should also apply sharp pressed-out ointments (*avapīḍa*), collyria (*añjana*), gargles (*kavala*), and employ warm treatments.
Having incised, squeezed, and scraped a *utsaṅgapiṭaka* or an *añjananāmikā*, one should rub it (*pratisārayet*) with a powder of *tagara*, *elā*, rock salt, and *nepālī*, mixed with honey.
A sprinkling (pariṣeka) with turmeric, licorice, patola, and lodhra mixed with honey [is indicated];
for conditions beginning with bisavartman and ending with bahalavartman, rubbing with rock salt (pratisāraṇa) is prescribed.
In cases where the eyelids are adherent (*bisa-śliṣṭa-vartman*), if there is no relief through other means, one should cauterize with fire or alkali (*kṣāra*).

In *kukūṇaka*, one should have the mother drink ghee prepared with a paste of *nimba* leaves, *triphalā*, and the root of *khadira*; thereafter, she should be made to vomit using warm water mixed with rock salt (*saindhava*), mustard, *upakulyā*, and *yaṣṭyāhva*.
One should administer a purgative using a decoction of pippalī, drākṣā, and abhayā; furthermore, one should smear her breasts with a paste of māgadhikā, mustā, and dvirajana, and then rub them.
One should fumigate with white mustard seeds mixed with ghee,

and have her drink a decoction of *paṭola*, *musta*, *mṛdvīkā*, *guḍūcī*, and *triphalā*. Having scarified the eyelids of the child, one should rub them with honey, rock salt (*saindhava*), and *rasāñjana*, and then wash them with a decoction of *āmalakī*, *aśmantaka*, and the sprouts of *jambu*.
Or one should have the blood extracted by leeches;

however, in the event of pain, one should perform a sprinkling over the head with a decoction of *kuṣṭha* and *guḍūcī* mixed with jaggery and honey, after having anointed the head with pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*) and smeared it with a paste of *pāṭhā*. Then, one should sprinkle [the area] with a decoction of the leaves of *arjuna*, *bilva*, *nirguṇḍī*, *mārkava*, *tarkārī*, *sairyaka*, *kārpāsī*, and *mālatī*.
Oil prepared with a paste of *marica*, *viḍaṅga*, and *haridrā* is used as a *pratimarśa*. A bolus collyrium (*piṇḍāñjana*) is made from *mūrvā* and copper dust ground with breast milk.
Alternatively, a medicinal extract (*rasakriyā*) may be prepared from conch shell, realgar, rock salt, and *rasāñjana* mixed with honey;
or, iron filings, *śivāṭikā*, and clay, repeatedly heated in a skull-cup and quenched with breast milk, may be ground into a fine powder for use as a collyrium (*añjana*).
Or, one may use lac, *vella*, realgar, red ochre, and the bark of *dārvī*.

Furthermore, one should repeatedly treat the *dhātrī* with emetics and purgatives. In the case of *pakṣmoparodha*, blood that has accumulated in the eyelid (*vartman*) should be removed by scraping; if it is elevated, it should be drained; and if accompanied by swelling, it should be treated with head-purgatives, gargles, and emetics.

When the hair has grown long, for a patient whose body is purified and who is capable of enduring the procedure, one should cut off two parts below the eyebrows and one part from the edge of the eyelashes, making an oblique incision the size of a barley grain; then, using a moist cloth, one should catch the blood. When the bleeding has subsided, one should suture it with a linen thread or hair using a curved needle, with stitches spaced at intervals the size of a mung bean.
Then, having bound a bandage over his forehead, one should apply the suturing thread there with needle-stitches that are neither too tight nor too loose;
and one should place a medicinal poultice (kavalikā) mixed with honey upon it, using clarified butter that has been washed a hundred times.
And one should not bandage this; rather,
for the pain of the ulcer, one should apply a pouring of clarified butter processed with powdered yaṣṭīmadhuka bound in a cloth, as well as decoctions of the vaṭa tree and others mixed with milk.
On the fifth or sixth day, once the edges of the wound have become firm, one should cut away the suturing thread from its supports and remove it;
the wound should then be dusted with the powder of golden ochre (svarṇagairika) and treated with sharp nasal drops and collyriums.
If the thread is raised too high, swelling will occur;
in that case, mild fomentation and unctuous nasal medication (nasya) should be administered.

Alternatively, having everted the eyelid and scraped away the fold damaged by the defects of the eyelid, one should rub it with a paste of any one of *tumburu*, *vakra*, *kuśa*, or *abhayā* seeds, or cauterize it with alkali or with a heated probe. However, for the eyelashes, one should mark them with lac-dye, extract them with forceps, and cauterize the hair follicles with the tip of a fine needle made red-hot.

Then, as before, there should be sprinkling and nasal medication (nāvana). For an external alaji that has burst or been incised, there should be cauterization with alkali or fire, and treatment should be conducted like that for a wound.
And regarding an *arbuda* that has been fomented, excised from its base, scraped, and rubbed with medicinal paste, there are these verses here:
For one who has been placed in a windless place by trusted attendants, who is pure and lying on his back,
the eyelid should be fomented with a cloth warmed by slightly warm water from the outside.
Having bent it and held it between the left thumb and fingers with a cloth interposed,
the eyelid does not slip down or move; thus, it remains fixed in its place on all sides.
Having made a transverse incision at the edge of the circle, marked with the point of the surgical instrument,
one should scrape [the area] using that very same instrument or with leaves derived from plants such as *śāka* and *śephālikā*.
If blood continues to flow, one should wipe it away with foam from the surface of the water or with a cotton wick; once the bleeding has ceased, one should rub the well-incised wound with honey.
After washing with warm water as prescribed for each case,
one should sprinkle it with ghee, anoint it, and bandage it with honey and clarified butter.
Having applied a bolus of barley flour to the upper and lower parts of the ear,
one should perform an appropriate irrigation on the third day once the patient has been released from the bandage.
On the fourth day, one should administer nasal therapy (nasya) and other treatments; on the fifth day, one should release [the bandage].
It should be even, resembling the color of a fingernail, and free from the afflictions of swelling, itching, or friction.
One should know that the eyelid is properly incised when it is well-marked; one should incise it again if there is a contrary result.
From excessive scraping, pain, irritation of the lashes, tearing, and flaking of the eyelid occur.
In that case, the desired procedure is one that removes Vāta, beginning with oleation (sneha) and sudation (sveda).
Having anointed [the area] with fresh butter, one should apply a plaster of white Lodhra.
Then, one should cook it using a *puṭapāka* method with a paste of castor root;
once steamed, washed, dried, and powdered, it should be made into a small cloth packet (*poṭṭalī*).
An eye-wash prepared by crushing [the plant] in the milk of a woman or a she-goat, or similarly processed and smeared with a paste of *śāli* rice, [is used for the same purpose]. AS.Utt.12.35.
If the eyes have been excessively scarified, one should apply a massage with curd-whey alone,
or even a wash with whey for a patient who eats meat from wild animals;
however, in the case of fatty, hard, and elevated growths, one should excise them using a *vrīhivaktra* instrument.
The procedure for squeezing [the bladder] follows; the remaining [instructions] therein shall be as previously stated.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter. Hereafter, we shall expound the chapter entitled "The Knowledge of Diseases of the Conjunctions, White [Parts], and Black [Parts]."
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:
"Vāyu, when provoked, reaches the vessels that resemble water and carry water."

When tears flow from the junction of the eyelid and the sclera, or from the corner of the eye (kanīnaka), causing redness, swelling, and pain in the eye, that is *jalāsrava*. In *kaphāsrava* caused by *kapha*, one should expect a white, slimy, and thick discharge to flow.
Due to *kapha*, there is swelling with sharp points, resembling an alkaline bubble.
An upanāha (concretion) that has a broad base, is unstable, glossy, matching the color of the skin, soft, slimy, large, non-suppurating, itchy, and painless [is of the vāta type].
In the case of blood-origined discharge, copper-colored, very hot tears flow out.
A pustule located at the junction of the eyelid margins on the white part [of the eye], accompanied by burning and pain, [is called Śuktikā].
The *parvanī* [disease] is copper-colored, resembles a mung bean when split open, and discharges blood;
in *pūyāsrāva*, the impurities flow from the junction of the eyelids and the inner corner of the eye.
Due to the suppuration of the skin and flesh, they repeatedly discharge pus mixed with blood;
such a wound is characterized by a thin layer of putrid slough, preceded by swelling and inflammation.
In the junction of the *kanīna*, there is a swelling that distends, discharges pus and blood, and is painful;
in the interior of the *kanīna*, there is a swelling characterized by pain, pricking, and burning.
In the outer corner or the pupil, characterized by itching and falling eyelashes,
discharging pus, and infested with worms, it is a *kṛmigranthi*— a glandular swelling accompanied by worms and pain.

One should treat with a surgical instrument the five types of abscesses— namely *upanāha*, *kṛmigranthi*, *pūya*, *alasaka*, and *parvaṇī*— but one should avoid incising those that have a flow of *sālajīna*.
Pitta produces white spots that are blackish, dark-brown,
or yellow; or else, the entire eye becomes like a mirror smeared with filth, characterized by whiteness, burning, and pain.
This disease, known as śuktikā, is accompanied by diarrhea, thirst, and fever;
due to kapha, it is white and equal in size to a conch shell, consisting of an adhimāṃsa growth that increases over a long period.
Śuklārma-śopha is known to be painless, matching the color of the surrounding tissue, thick, soft,
heavy, unctuous, resembling a drop of water, and composed of congealed phlegm (balāsa).
One should diagnose *piṣṭaka* by the presence of abundant white specks resembling flour. That which is white, covered with red streaks, and accompanied by pain is called *ūṣya*.
Accompanied by swelling, lacrimation, and exudation, that sirōtpāta arises from blood;
if neglected, the sirōtpāta causes those very streaks to increase further.
It causes bleeding and twitching of the vessels, whereby the eye becomes incapable of looking upward. The network of vessels becomes extensive, red, thick, and elevated.
Śoṇitārma is even and smooth, resembling the color of a lotus; ādhimāṃsaka is characterized by an excess of flesh.
A *bindu* that is painless, smooth, and vigorous, and which is red like the blood of a rabbit,
is healthy; whereas a spreading (*prastāri*) ulcer that is soft, rapidly increasing, and dark-red is diseased.
Prastāryarman is characterized by impurities mixed with blood, while snāvarman resembles the appearance of a ligament.
That which is dark brown like a clod of dried blood, thick and broad,
is known as *adhimāṃsārma*; it is covered by vessels and characterized by burning and friction.

Pustules resembling mustard seeds, dark and situated near the vessels, are known as *sirāsaṃjñā*. [The conditions] *śukti*, *harṣa*, *sirotpāta*, *piṣṭaka*, *grathita*, and *arjuna* [are also described].
One should treat six types [of hemorrhoids] with medicines, and the remaining seven with surgery;
even that which arises from a recent cause is treated with substances, as has been stated by Aruṇadatta in five ways.
That which has reached the black part (asita) and is covered with flesh, sinews, and vessels should be excised; however,
one should avoid [excising] that which is elevated like a flayed skin and has reached the pupil of the eye.
When the *pitta* [is located] in the black portion of the eye, it produces a white [spot] accompanied by pricking pain, tearing,
and redness; having pierced the skin, it thus causes the black circle (*kṛṣṇamaṇḍala*) to become white.
That which resembles a ripe jambu fruit, is slightly depressed, and has its vitreous humor (śukra) injured,
is difficult to cure; however, it is palliable when there is a perforation of the second layer (paṭala).
In that case, there is an abundance of pricking pain and other symptoms, a sensation as if pierced by needles, and blackness;
when the third layer is cut through and the condition is consolidated by ulcers, it is incurable.
That which is white like a conch shell due to *kapha*, easily curable, and characterized by pure semen, is [the *śukra* type].
That which flows with blood that is coppery and slimy, accompanied by copper-colored pustules and intense pain, is [the *asṛj* type].
The blood of goats, sheep, and wild ruminants (viṭsa) is to be rejected because it possesses an elevation and blackness similar to that [of the diseased eye].
The black circle (kṛṣṇamaṇḍala) is composed of veins, semen, and impurities along with blood; when afflicted by these, it becomes black.
If it is pierced by veins that are painful, burning, and copper-colored,
and if blood flows out that is causeless, hot, cold, or thick and turbid, one should abandon that [vein].
By the humors (doṣas) along with blood, the black portion is transformed into a white appearance;
it has the luster of being smeared with white blood and the shape of half a flat bean (niṣpāva).
One should avoid that semen which is afflicted by extremely intense pain, redness, burning, and swelling due to the complication of suppuration, and which is characterized by severe agony.
Or that which has the destruction of the penis-marks (liṅga), or is dark-brown or reddish internally,
or is excessively elevated or depressed, or is covered by a wound with discharging channels.
AS.Utt.13.36: Old, uneven, interrupted in the middle, and that which is "śukraka"—
these five types of *gada* (club-like swellings) have been described in the *Kṛṣṇa* [chapter], according to the classification of those that are curable and those that are incurable.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "The Treatment of Diseases of the Joints and the White and Black [Parts] of the Eye."
Thus indeed said the great seers, Ātreya and the others:
"The physician, having fomented the *upanāha* (abscess) and incised it with a *vrīhimukha* instrument, should scarify it all around with a *maṇḍalāgra* blade."
Then, one should rub the area with a powder of rock salt and long pepper mixed with honey, and bandage it as previously described.

One should irrigate [the wound] with a decoction of *paṭola* leaves and *āmalaka*. Having suspended it at the upper junction of the joints using a hook (*baḍiśa*), one should cut it to the depth of half a finger-breadth with a curved blade (*vṛddhipatra*).
Otherwise, it would become a *śruṇāḍī*;
one should treat it like a corneal ulcer (*arma*) after applying honey and rock salt as a rubbing agent.
In the case of *pūyālasa*, one should perform venesection and then apply a poultice (*upanāha*), observing the procedure described for *akṣipāka*.
An ointment made from finely ground rock salt (*saindhava*), fresh ginger (*ārdraka*), green vitriol (*kāsīsa*), iron, and copper, mixed with honey, [should be applied].
Having steamed a *krimigranthi* tumor with dried cow dung, one should incise it, scrape it, and then rub it with a paste of green vitriol, rock salt, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and honey.
One should treat *śuktikā* in the same manner as *pittābhiṣyanda*.
Balāsagrathita and Piṣṭaka should be treated like Kaphābhiṣyanda, with the exception of venesection (sirāvyadha). Specifically,
one should soak sesame stalks or barley stalks in green shoots for half a month with goat’s milk, dry them, and then burn them.
Then, having strained that ash according to the method for alkaline preparations, one should cook it until it reaches the consistency of a paste spread with a ladle;
this *rasakriyā* removes phlegm-induced knots, swellings, and coatings.

This same procedure should be performed separately with the flowers of *phaṇijjaka*, *arjaka*, *āsphota*, *bilvaka*, *kapittha*, *nirguṇḍī*, *eraṇḍa*, *kumuda*, *utpala*, and *jātī*. A wick made from rock salt (*saindhava*), *ālābu*, black pepper (*marica*), *kaṭphala*, conch shell, and sea foam (*samudraphena*) serves as a collyrium for the eye-paste (*piṣṭaka*).
A powder of ginger, *śigru* fruit, long pepper, and rock salt, saturated with the juice of *bījapūraka*, when used as a collyrium, removes *piṣṭaka* (pustules);
likewise, a powder of the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*) and *kaṭphala* removes *balāsagrathita*.
One should cook a *bṛhatī* fruit filled with long pepper seeds by the *puṭapāka* method.

A powder-collyrium made from those same rice grains destroys *balāsa* and obstructed swellings; for excessive swelling, a *biḍālaka* (a medicinal paste) should be prepared with yellow orpiment, rock salt, dry ginger, *devadāru*, and *punarnavā*.
In cases of *sirotpāta*, *sirāharṣa*, *jālārjuna*, and *raktābhiṣyanda*, one should treat them as one would [treat] *raktābhiṣyanda*;
specifically for *sirāharṣa*, gold-ore (*svarṇagairika*) mixed with honey should be used as an ointment (*añjana*).

Or *kāsīsa* mixed with breast milk; or *kāsīsa* and rock salt melted with honey; for *arjuna*, an eye-drop (*āścyotana*) consisting of *kāsīsa* and rock salt with the juice of *mātuluṅga* and sugar; or with buttermilk;
or *śaṅkhanābhi* combined with honey or with sugar and sea-foam (*samudraphena*) and *añjana*.
Alternatively, one may apply rock crystal, saffron, conch-shell navel, or licorice moistened with honey; or likewise, *rasāñjana* or *kāsīsa*.
Regarding the five types of *arma* that are slightly reddish, smoky-colored, or resemble curd, one should treat them like *śukra* with emetics for the body and head, scarification, and collyrium.

Now, in the other case, for a patient who has been oleated and has eaten one of the following—liquid gruel (*peyā*), thick gruel (*avilepī*), or the meat-broth of wild animals (*jāṅgalarasā*)—and for whom propitiatory rites have been performed, the physician should proceed as follows: while the patient lies on a comfortable bed with the body supine, the head slightly lowered, and the eyes moistened with lukewarm water and wiped with a fine linen cloth, he should apply *saindhava* salt with the juice of *bījapūraka* to the eyes. Then, using the thumb, he should massage the closed eye until the morbid growth (*arbuda*) appears as a stiffened, knotted mass.
When the eye has been thus provoked and the fleshy growth (*adhimāṃsaka*) has become mobile, the attendant should hold the head steady.
Furthermore, another person, standing comfortably on either the left or right side, should press the eyelids with the two thumbs whose palms are covered with firm cloth.

Then, once the *arman* has grown from the pupil toward the outer corner (*apāṅga*) of the eye, the physician should grasp it—not too tightly—with a hook (*baḍiśa*) or forceps (*mucuṭī*), lift it slightly, and release it from all sides using the tip of a needle at the junctions of the black and white circles (*kṛṣṇa-śukla-maṇḍala*); having done so, he should pull it out slightly.

Then, having scraped with a sharp circular blade or a lancet and having drawn out the *kanīnaka* (the inner corner of the eye), one should cut [the flesh] so that it remains at a fourth part, level with the *kanīnaka*;
and one must avoid the *kanīnaka* and the tear-carrying vessels (*sirā*), for in this way the eye will not be damaged.
As for that network-like vessel which is pervasive, one should follow it as far as the pupil with the probe, release it, and lift it up, then cut it as before.

Similarly, when [the vessel] has extended from the outer corner (apāṅga), while the patient is looking at the pupil, one should bring [the probe] as far as the outer corner; then, keeping it level with the outer corner, one should avoid the outer corner and the vessels, and so forth.

Then, having thoroughly cleansed the blood with a cloth and ensured it is properly severed, one should repeatedly rub the wound with powdered rock salt (saindhava) or the ashes of *yava-nāla*. Once purified by the cloth, it should again be treated with honey.
Then, after sprinkling cold water and bathing the area with lukewarm ghee, one should bandage it as before, smeared with honey and ghee.
Furthermore, one should apply *śatadhauta-ghṛta* to his head and feet, and provide cooling poultices.
One should prescribe the regimen mentioned for oleation therapy;
on the second day, one should sprinkle the head and the eye with lukewarm honey and ghee in the evening and in the morning, while they remain bandaged.

For five days, one should drink ghee with warm water as an after-drink; once it has been digested, one should eat wholesome food. On the third day, having released [the bandage], one should foment the eye with milk prepared with *karañja* seeds.

On the seventh day, one should irrigate [the eye] with a decoction of *lodhra*, *madhuka*, *kiṃśuka*, *paṭola*, the two types of *haridrā*, and the buds of *koraṇḍa*, mixed with honey; at all times, one should avoid exposure to the sun and looking into open space. If there is swelling in the eye, however, [one should apply] medicated smoke (*dhūma*) and head-purgation (*śirovirecana*).
For one whose passion has not subsided, bloodletting by venesection is prescribed; for one with nasal discharge, nasal medication (nasya) is used.

Sesame seeds, well-scrubbed, should be soaked for seven days in milk that has been boiled with madhuka, kākolī, suniṣaṇṇaka, the five roots (pañcamūla), and sugar, and then strained while cold; these seeds should then be pressed using that same milk.
When [the eye] is being pressed, one should add a powder of madhuka, śatāhvā, sārivā, anantā, agaru, kākolī, hareṇukā, elā, and vāluka in a sixteenth part [of the oil].

That oil, prepared with these same medicinal herbs and eight times the amount of milk, destroys redness from tearing when used as a nasal drop (nāvana) and clarifies the vision. However, if the ulcer has reached the black portion (kṛṣṇagata), the treatment should be like that for an ulcer of the cornea (śukra).
And when only the scar remains, there are applications of medicinal ointments and collyriums;
therein, when properly incised, there is purification of the complexion.

Health [of the eyes] results from moderate cutting; however, from excessive cutting, there occurs further swelling, an inability to endure the appearance of tears of passion, and so forth, as well as inflammation of the eye,
stiffness, throbbing, discharge of blood, cataracts, agitation, and obstruction of the eyelids.
In those cases, one should treat them according to the specific aggravation of the respective *doṣas*.

One should apply *rasāñjana* (half a *pala*) mixed with half-*karṣa* portions each of *nāgara*, *manaḥśilā*, *lailā*, *saindhava*, and sugar, melted in honey; this collyrium (*añjana*) destroys the diseases of *adharma*, residual phlegm, *timira*, and *pillā*.
Regarding the network of vessels (*sirājāla*), those which are thick and hard should be seized with a hook (*baḍiśa*) and scraped away with a circular blade (*maṇḍalāgra*).
One should cut the varicose veins (sirāpiṭaka), having suspended them with the point of a needle, while avoiding injury to the black [portion].
One should scrape [the growth] with a fine instrument like a crescent moon and perform the remaining procedures for these two as appropriate.

In cases of *śukra*, one should administer the drinking of *triphalā* ghee, bloodletting, purgation, eye-drops, facial ointments, bathing, and saturation-poultices according to the specific dosha involved. (AS.Utt.14.24)
One should administer these decoctions.
In that regard, for a wound with pus (vraṇaśukra), one should have the patient drink ghee that has been cooked three times with a decoction of trivṛt.
One should also puncture the vein and,
with leeches, remove the remaining vitiated blood that has become clotted and is localized in the eye.

One should perform eye-drops with a decoction of madhuka, kākolī, mṛdvīkā, utpala, and vidārī, or with goat’s milk boiled with mañjiṣṭhā, kṣīrakākolī, and madhuka, mixed with sugar. One should also apply cold poultices to his head and face and sprinkle them with cold water.
If the pain persists even thus, one should administer an oil enema (anuvāsana) using the scum of ghee prepared with śatāhvā and yaṣṭyāhvā.
This should be done whenever one observes that the patient's tearing, redness, and pain have subsided.
At those respective times, one should treat the *śukra* with scraping collyriums.

An ointment-stick (*varti*) made from lapis lazuli, crystal, conch-shell, pearl, coral, silver, iron, copper, tin, lead, *ālāmanaḥśilā*, the shell of a hen’s egg, sea-foam, *rasāñjana*, and rock salt— all ground together with goat’s milk, dried in the shade, and rubbed with honey— when applied in the morning and evening, removes ulcerous *śukra*.

The teeth of the best of elephants, boars, cows, donkeys, horses, goats, and camels, along with conch-shell, pearl-oyster, and sea-foam, ground with water and mixed with one-fourth part black pepper, form a medicinal paste (*varti*) that removes blood and semen from wounds.
A paste made from lac, gold-stone (*suvarṇagairika*), red sandalwood, and jasmine buds clarifies the blood and bile, and removes blood and semen from ulcers.
One should elevate the sunken and painful semen by means of drinking medicated fats (sneha), nasal medication (nasya), and the meat-broths of wild animals (jāṅgalarasa); however,
if it is painless, one should treat it with saturating drops (tarpaṇa) and eye-poultices (puṭapāka).

In that case, for the purpose of satiation (*tarpaṇa*), one should cook the flesh of wild animals and gallinaceous birds with *kāśmarya*, *suniṣaṇṇā*, blue lotus, lotus stalks, *śṛṅgāṭaka*, *śera*, *drākṣā*, *akṣīravidārī*, and the *jīvanīya* drugs in milk. Having extracted the butter (*navanīta*) from that, one should cook it with the paste of sandalwood, honey-sugar, *anantā*, and blue lotus, along with eight times as much milk, and administer it as previously described.

One should prepare a *puṭapāka* using a cock with its intestines removed, having turned it into *veśavāra*, and mixing it with the pastes of *candana*, *sārivā*, *madhuka*, sugar, *anantā*, blue lotus, *prapauṇḍarīka*, and the *jīvanīya* drugs, along with honey and ghee; one should administer this as previously described.
In this manner, one should treat a case of *dvitvacchinna*.
In the case of pure semen (śuddha-śukra), one should perform eye-drops (āścyotana) with a decoction of haridrā, madhuka, sārivā, and lodhra;
or alternatively, with a cloth-bound bolus of powdered lodhra moistened with warm water.
For one with a purified bowel, a paste of *dantī* and *jyotiṣmatī* should be used as an *avapīḍaka*;
or oil cooked with drugs for head-purgation (*śirovirecana*) should be administered as an enema (*marśa*) or a secondary enema (*pratimarśa*).
One should smear a copper vessel with a paste made from ginger, rock salt, licorice, the roots of *bṛhatī*, copper dust, and the juice of *āmalaka*.
One should repeatedly fumigate that [instrument] with barley mixed with ghee and with *āmalaka* leaves;
this wick, known as Mahānīlā, when rubbed with honey-water and ghee, destroys pure semen (or seminal impurity).

If the previously mentioned tooth-cotton application does not subside when the semen is involved, one should repeatedly apply it everywhere according to the aforementioned sequence; and from time to time, one should drain the blood.
One should observe the prevention of excessive secretions;
then, for the purpose of stimulation when the semen is pure, one should administer aphrodisiacs.
One should apply an ointment of rock salt (saindhava) processed for three days with the juice of the three myrobalans (triphalā),
or likewise with long pepper (pippalī), or with a compound consisting of black pepper, long pepper, seeds of śirīṣa, balā, and the alkali mentioned in the section on "grathita."
AS.Utt.14.34: To alleviate pain caused by excessive weeping due to joy, one should apply a collyrium for the joining of the lids (*sandhāvāñjana*).

One should rub a conch shell with breast milk on copper and fumigate it with *yava* grains mixed with ghee and *śamī* leaves; with this collyrium for the joining of the lids, one should apply it as an ointment.
Similarly, gold or silver rubbed together with ghee-soaked jujube leaves and fumigated serves as an ointment;
or powdered conch-shell, dehusked green mung beans, or a paste or powder mixed with honey acts as an ointment that removes the friction of the *śukra* (corneal opacity).
Likewise, the resin of *madhūka* with honey, or the marrow of the *bibhītaka* seed, [may be used].

Dehusked lentils ground with breast milk, young sprouts of *darbha* grass, ghee, goat’s fat, cow’s milk, and *śara* grass rubbed together on an iron or copper plate serve as a counter-collyrium (*pratyañjana*) that destroys pain.

A poultice (*utkārikā*) made from the powder of barley, wheat, *jīvanīya* herbs, and *māṃsī*, combined with ghee and sugar, when applied as a warm compress (*upanāha*), removes pain and promotes the flow of semen.

In the same way, a prepared mixture of meat from marshy animals, vesavāra, muscle fat, milk, and ghee is [to be used]; then, for one whose condition has been aggravated by such an external application (upanāha), an ointment (añjana) is prescribed.
The teeth of a cow, donkey, horse, and camel, sea-foam, and conch shell, ground with the decoction of *arjuna*, form a scraping collyrium (*lekhanī-varti*).

Alternatively, sea-foam, conch shell, potsherds, parrot bone, the horn of an elephant, the hair of a horse and a cow, ground with the decoction of *tinduka*, may be used as a counter-collyrium (*pratyañjana*);
likewise, the powder of the bones of young jujube, *khadira*, and *tinduka*, burnt with internal smoke.
One should scrape out the vitiated or foreign-body-containing semen with instruments such as a probe, or by means of *puṭapāka*,
or by means of an alkaline preparation or medicinal paste as described for *balāsagrathita*.

In the case of *sirāśukra* that destroys vision when it is recent, one should treat it like *vraṇaśukra*. Furthermore, for this condition, a medicinal wick (*varti*) should be prepared by grinding together *prapauṇḍarīka*, *madhuka*, *haridrā*, iron filings, collyrium (*añjana*), *bṛhatī*, *kṣīrakākolī*, and goat’s milk; this wick should then be fumigated alternately with barley grains mixed with ghee and with *āmalakī* leaves.
One should treat even an unsubsided condition as if it were a vital organ (marman).
Rasāñjana mixed with honey should be used as a rubbing application.
On the seventh day, one should apply collyrium using a wick (varti) made from the shell of a hen’s egg, rock crystal, sandalwood, realgar, lac, and the teeth of a horse and a boar.

A wick made from the froth of the ocean, conch-shell, and sandalwood, ground with goat’s milk and rubbed with honey and ghee, serves as a counter-collyrium (pratyañjana) that conquers [disorders of] the vessels and semen.

When one observes that the patient finds no relief, one should repeatedly perform this very treatment. One should cure [the condition] caused by the obstruction of the *ajakāmā* [disorder] with bloodletting from the black vein (*kṛṣṇānta*), sweet purgatives, and milk enemas (AS.Utt.14.41).

And like [the treatment for] *sirāśukra*, it is performed according to the procedure for surgical intervention (*śastrakarman*) and so forth; regarding this, there is a verse here (AS.Utt.14.42): "In the case of *ajakā* that is incurable, and in *śukra* and other conditions of that same type..."
One should alleviate the pain through the drinking of medicated fats, bloodletting, and other such measures, in order to overcome the feeling of loathsomeness and to achieve the increase of semen.
One should cause the ashes produced from coconut husks, *bhallātaka*, palm, bamboo,
and *karīra* shoots to be washed with water, and then one should saturate the ashes produced from camel bones with that same liquid.

This powder is an effective collyrium for removing discoloration and tearing in cases of śukra that are incurable; and when practiced regularly, it is also sufficient for the treatment of those cases that are curable.
Having pierced the goat's bladder at its side with a needle and drained the water,
one should press it evenly with the thumb and fill it with fat moistened with water.
Having bound the wound with powdered beef and releasing it after each binding,
once the wound has healed after seven nights, it becomes even and free of black discoloration.
An unguent of fats and nasal medication (nasya) with milk-ghee should be administered; nevertheless, if there is further distension, procedures such as incision and excision must be performed.

One should apply this with skill so that there is no excessive cutting and no submersion [of the instrument]. Furthermore, in cases of seminal disorders, one should regularly administer ghee boiled with the appropriate medicinal herbs for both internal drinking and as an enema (marśa).
For the vision, once its power is gained, does not diminish even when sharp collyriums are applied continuously;
thus ends the fourteenth chapter.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter entitled "The Diagnosis of Diseases of the Vision.
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
When the morbid matter (mala) follows the channels and has first reached the [first] layer (paṭala),
one perceives forms indistinctly, even those that are distinct, due to the absence of a causal basis.
When the second stage is reached, one sees even that which is non-existent;
however, one does not perceive with effort what is real, whether it be nearby, distant, or subtle.
One perceives forms situated at a distance or nearby as being reversed; when the humors are arranged in circular formations, one sees things as if they were circles.
When [the humors] are located in the middle of the vision, one [object] appears as two; when they are located in many ways, it appears as many.
When they have entered inside the vision, there is the reversal of short and long.
One does not see what is near when [the eye] is situated below, nor what is distant when it is situated above;
one does not see what is at the side when [the eye] is situated at the side— this is the disease known as *timira*.
When the defect reaches the third layer [of the eye], it acquires the nature of glass (kāca);
by means of that, one looks upward but not downward, resembling [a person] covered by a cloth on the body.
Just as one becomes attached to colors, the vision gradually deteriorates;
even so, for one who remains indifferent, [the disease] reaches the fourth layer.

The morbid humor (mala), causing the destruction of the visual mark (liṅganāśa), covers the circle of vision (dṛṣṭimaṇḍala). Among these, in the case of *timira* caused by Vāta, one sees things as if they were distorted.
One repeatedly sees things that are moving, agitated, and reddish in appearance, as well as clear objects;
furthermore, one perceives webs, hair, gnats, and flies even where they do not exist.
When the eyes have become turbid, one sees the face as lacking a nose;
one perceives the moon, lamps, and so forth as multiple, and considers even that which is straight to be crooked.
Advanced cataract (kāca) impairs vision so that it appears as if veiled by dust or smoke; it may appear clear, reddish, wide, or narrow, thereby destroying the power of sight.

In Vāta-type [Timira], there is loss of the eye's characteristic marks; it contracts the vessels of the vision, and the orb of the eye enters inwardly; this is known as the deep-seated (gambhīrā) eye. In Pittaja Timira, the eye is illuminated by the flashes of lightning and the glow of fireflies.
In *kāca*, one generally sees things with the luster of a peacock’s tail or a partridge’s feather, or as blue;
and it appears exactly like that.
Halos around the sun and moon, fire, rays of light, and rainbows;
as well as [seeing] bees or dark blue forms, loss of vision, or a lack of light, yet with eyes appearing glossy— these are signs of *liṅganāśa*.

Vision affected by *pitta* is called "short-sighted" (*drasvā*); it is short-sighted and sees things as short. That which is known as "vitiated by *pitta*" (*pittavidagdha*) is yellow and perceives objects as yellowish.
In cases of *timira* caused by *kapha*, one generally sees things as oily and white,
as if covered with conch shells, the moon, jasmine flowers, and white water-lilies.
In the case of *kāca*, however, the vision appears white and lusterless, as if covered by the moon, the sun, or lamps;
this is observed in the destruction of the visual faculty (*liṅganāśa*).
Mūrtaka-kapha, when localized in the vision, is glossy and destroys sight;
it moves like a drop of water resting upon a lotus leaf.
In the heat it contracts, and in the shade it spreads;
its whiteness is like that of a conch shell, kunda jasmine, kumuda lily, or crystal.
In *timira* caused by blood, one sees red or as if enveloped in darkness; in *kāca*, the vision is reddish or blackish, and one perceives objects accordingly.
Even when the *liṅganāśa* occurs, vision becomes such that it is lusterless and its power of seeing is destroyed;
one should recognize the symptoms of combined or aggregated disorders as being a mixture of these characteristics.
Due to *timira* and other causes, one may suddenly have eyes that perceive objects clearly yet confusedly;
in *timira*, a variegated discoloration arises in the vision of the remaining two [eyes].
This occurs in one whose sight is obstructed by impurities, appearing like the vision of a mongoose.
On that day, the man blinded by *nakula* sees various forms, but not at night;
when the sun has set its rays upon the western mountain peak, he perceives them as if they were pillars.
Defects obscure the vision; one blinded by defects is subject to disease. When touched by the rays of the sun, those impurities fall away from the path of sight.
When a person who has been heated by heat suddenly immerses himself in cold water, the [doshas] that were dissolved and latent manifest their visible effects on that very day. (AS.Utt.15.24–25)
When the three *doṣas* are combined with blood and the heat moves upward, it afflicts the two eyes;
there is burning pain, the pupil becomes turbid, and during the day there is a blurred vision.

If blindness occurs at night due to the excessive heating of the vitiated humors, it is known as *vidagdhā* (burnt). That vision which is covered by the humors along with blood due to the consumption of excessively sour food is [known as *raktā*].
When it is moist, itchy, and turbid due to burning from sour substances, it is known as *vidagdha*.
In one afflicted by grief, fever, or headache, the [doshas] beginning with vāyu become aggravated.
It makes the vision turbid with smoke and gives it a smoky appearance; that is *dhūmara*.
It causes one of little strength who suddenly beholds a wondrous form [to experience this].
The [doshas] beginning with vāta, residing in the eyes, dry up the brilliance of the sun and other luminous objects,
thereby causing the vision to lose its clarity.
When the eyes have the color of lapis lazuli, are steady, appear as if in their natural state, and are free from pain—
this is the destruction of vision caused by an external affliction; in such a case, one should avoid treatment.
Except for the loss of vision caused by *kapha*, those [types of blindness] arising from deep-seated [vitiation] or from trauma,
as well as *ṣaṭkāca* and *nakulāndhya*, are palliable; the remaining types should be treated curatively.
Twelve [types] are described in the examination of the mallet (gadā), and twenty-seven [in that of the staff (yaṣṭī)];
thus ends the fifteenth chapter.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter. Hereafter, we shall expound the chapter named "The Treatment of Timira" (the cure for blindness).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:
"Timira turns into Kāca, and Kāca, through neglect, leads to blindness.
Therefore, among eye diseases, one should quickly treat the most severe condition, timira.
One should boil one *tulā* of *jīvantī* in a *droṇa* of water until one-quarter remains. AS.Utt.16.3 AS.Utt.16.3
One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with twice as much milk in a decoction of those [herbs],
along with *prapauṇḍarīka*, *kākolī*, *pippalī*, *lodhra*, and rock salt.
One karṣa each of śatāhvā, madhuka, drākṣā, sitā, dāru, and the three fruits (phalatraya), when drunk at night, is an excellent remedy for removing timira.
[Likewise, a preparation] with drākṣā, candana, mañjiṣṭhā, the two kinds of kākolī, and jīvaka...
One should cook an equal quantity of old ghee with milk, using one *picu* each of white *śatāvarī*, *medā*, *puṇḍrāhva*, *madhuka*, and blue lotus (*utpala*).
It destroys the darkness of the ears, red streaks, and headaches.
[One should take] paṭola, nimba, kaṭukā, dārvī, sevya, vara, and vṛṣa.
One should boil one *pala* each of *sadhanvayāsa*, *trāyantī*,
and *parpaṭa*, along with one *prastha* of *āmalaka* fruits, in eight *āḍhaka* of water.
Then, one should cook one *prastha* of ghee with half a *pala* each of the following ground ingredients:
*musta*, *bhūnimba*, *yaṣṭyāhva*, *kuṭī*, *udīcya*, and *candana*.
That ghee, prepared with trikaṭu and cavya, conquers diseases of the nose, ears, and eyes; it also cures abscesses,
fever, malignant ulcers, erysipelas, apacī, and leprosy.

Specifically, it removes cataracts, night-blindness, and burning sensations caused by heat or sour substances. One should boil eight *pala* of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) in one *āḍhaka* of water until one-quarter remains.
With that same quantity of milk, half a *prastha* of ghee prepared with one *pala* of the paste of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) should be taken, either with sugar or with honey.
One suffering from timira (blindness) should drink that [milk] prepared with [the aforementioned drugs], or else the juice of *varā* prepared with *yaṣṭīmadhu*,
the two types of *kākolī*, *vyāghrī*, *kṛṣṇā*, *amṛtā*, and *utpala*.

One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with equal parts of sugar and grapes using small cooking vessels (*pālikaiḥ*). [This should be done] separately with goat’s milk, excellent *vāsā*, and the fresh juice of *mārkava*.
This is known as Mahātraiphala; it is supreme for overcoming disorders of vision.
Then, at night, one should lick Triphalā along with the sacrificial oblation (havis) of Traiphala.
One who follows a wholesome diet should drink the water of *āmalaka* for one month, combined with *yaṣṭīmadhuka* and saturated with honey.
"One obtains the vision of Suparṇa," so said the venerable Nimi. Cow's ghee and iron filings placed in a vessel made of *bādara* wood [should be used].
Taken with the powder of triphalā, it destroys timira;
likewise, aged [ghee] taken with the powder of sugar, abhīru, and yaṣṭīmadhuka.
Alternatively, one may administer clarified butter that has been infused with iron balls heated to the color of fire until it is digested;
or, one may take the three myrobalans (triphalā) separately, combined with the powders of gold, silver, and iron.
One should eat this powder either mixed with ghee and honey or by itself; likewise,
one should take the powder of tāpya, ayas, and triphalā, stirred with honey and aged ghee.
One should eat meat kept in an iron vessel for a month, and one should eat a heap of mung beans;
or one should eat groats mixed with ghee and combined with the powder of the three myrobalans (triphalā).
Or one may eat well-prepared soup together with *āmalaka* fruits;
or, before the morning meal, one should eat *pathyā* (harītakī) separately from each [of the other ingredients].
A person suffering from *timira* should constantly consume raisins, sugar, and honey;
likewise, oil produced from black sesame seeds should be prepared with the decoction and juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*.
That [mixture], prepared together in a single iron vessel, is beneficial as a nasal medication (nāvana).
[One should take] sixty-four parts of conch-shell [powder] along with gold, iron, silver, and copper.

Having placed each of these, joined with their respective single parts, inside a blind crucible (andhamūṣā) and having blown upon them [with fire], one should then pour out that which has been completely liquefied.
Having been processed seven times separately with the decoction of the group of juices (rasaskandha),
it is then combined with three parts each of beryl, pearl, and conch shell.
One should apply this as a powdered collyrium; it removes all types of *timira*.
Tuttha [copper sulfate] that has been scorched by the embers of *badara* fruit and thus processed should be used in this manner.
From that [milk], two *pala* of ghee should be prepared by gradually adding goat’s milk, honey, and [the following]:
one *karṣa* each of *tāpya*, black pepper, *srotoñjana*, *kaṭukā*, and *ananta*.
Powdered *paṭola*, *lodhra*, *śilājatu*, *pathyā*, *kaṇā*, *elā*, *añjana*, and *phenaka*,
combined with one *pala* of *yaṣṭimadhu*, should be roasted inside a crucible (*mūṣā*).
When well-regularized, this powder— known as Bhāskara— destroys ophthalmia, night-blindness, and red streaks in the eye, and especially cataracts (timira), just as the sun destroys darkness.
Realgar, rock salt, the three pungents (vyoṣa), conch-shell navel,
rasāñjana, kataka, sandalwood, sea-foam, viḍaṅga, and white sugar.
A paste made from a hen’s eggshell ground with water is called *sukhāvatī*; when rubbed with honey, it destroys *kāca*, *timira*, and *śuklakā*.
Triphalā, the shell of a hen’s egg, kāsīsa, iron filings,
blue lotus, viḍaṅga, and the foam of the lord of rivers (sea-foam).
Having ground [the ingredients] with goat's milk, one should smear a copper vessel;
when seven nights have passed, one should again grind [the mixture] with milk and form it into a paste.
This wick, when applied, may restore sight even to one whose vision is impaired.
As for the collyrium: it is placed within the mouth of a black snake and wrapped in *kuśa* grass.
Then, having stirred it thoroughly for a month, one should grind it together with dried *sumanā* flower-alkali and half as much rock salt (*saindhava*).
One should apply that excellent collyrium for night-blindness caused by passion;
these three, having been well-impregnated, should be ground with milk.
This, however, is the general treatment; now hear the specific remedies for each individual dosha. In the case of vāta-born timira, ghee [should be prepared] with the decoction of daśamūla.
Then, one should drink [the medicine] cooked with four times the amount of milk and the paste of the best [drugs]; thereafter,
one should take a decoction of triphalā and pañcamūla combined with milk.
One should administer a purgative combined with castor oil (eraṇḍataila),
or alternatively, having decocted śaṅkhinī, tilvaka, śyāmā, and dantī in water.
One should drink ghee cooked with that [mixture] using a paste of *trivṛt* as an additive;
[this is prepared] with *prapauṇḍarīka*, *bṛhatī*, *balā*, *nalada*, and rock salt.
One should administer an ear-drop consisting of oil prepared with *dāru*, *bilva*, *āḍakī*, *kṛṣṇā*, *haridrā*, and *madhuyaṣṭi*, along with four parts of milk.
Oil cooked with white *eraṇḍa*, *jaṭā*, *siṃhī* fruit, *dāruniśā*, *nata*, *śatāhvā*,
and the roots of *bilva*, combined with milk, [is used for massage].

Nasal medication (nasya) is indicated for all diseases of the upper torso arising from wind (vāta) and phlegm (śleṣman); for the purpose of ointment (añjana), the fat of a tiger or a boar is highly recommended.

Alternatively, [one may use] the [flesh] of a vulture, a snake, or a cock, each combined separately with honey; and as a counter-anointing (praty añjana), [one may use] *srotoja* (antimony) mixed sequentially with meat-broth, milk, and clarified butter.

The application [of the ointment] should be performed as previously described; this is the unsurpassed destroyer of darkness (timira). If it does not thus subside, one should then perform a satiation therapy (tarpaṇa).
With śatāhvā, kuṣṭha, nalada, the two types of kākolī,
yaṣṭi, prapauṇḍarīka, sarala, pippalī, and devadāru.
Ghee cooked with eight times its weight of milk is an excellent nourishing (tarpaṇa) treatment;
one should employ this as a soothing (prasādana) and oleating (snehana) puṭapāka.

In this case, as in the treatment for vāta-type chronic rhinitis (pīnasa), one should administer a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) along with an unctuous enema (anuvāsana). In the case of timira caused by pitta, [one should use] ghee prepared with the jīvanīya group of drugs and the three myrobalans (phalatraya).
After administering the cooked [mixture], one should perform venesection on the patient once he has been oleated; then,
one should purge him with a powder of sugar, *elā*, and *trivṛt* mixed with honey.
Water boiled with mañjiṣṭhā, lodhra, madhuka, sārivā, and candana,
mixed with sugar and breast milk, is recommended for eye irrigation.
Alternatively, breast milk boiled with *padmaka*, *uśīra*, and sprouts of milk-exuding trees,
or ghee repeatedly quenched with heated iron balls [should be used].
One should apply crushed white sugar and grapes as a cold wash for the eyes;
one should also practice cold ointments, washes, and other such treatments on the face and the head.
A wick (varti) made from sārivā, padmaka, uśīra, mustā, śābara, and candana is recommended for collyrium; likewise, a powder made from padma, utpala, and añjana is beneficial.
With nāgapuṣpa, karpūra, yaṣṭyāhva, svarṇagairika, lodhra, mūrvā, prapuṇḍrāhva, māṃsī, yaṣṭyāhva, and candana;
(AS.Utt.16.54) with lodhra, mūrvā, prapuṇḍrāhva, māṃsī, yaṣṭyāhva, and candana.
Ghee prepared with these same drugs, along with milk, is beneficial as a nourishing tonic;
likewise, it is beneficial when cooked in goat liver and its juice using these very same medicinal herbs.
As before, a *puṭapāka* preparation should be made to destroy *timira*;
when [the disease] arises from phlegm (*śleṣman*), ghee boiled with a decoction of *amṛtā*, *varā*, and *kaṇā* should be used.
For one who has drunk [the medicine], one should pierce a vein and subsequently administer a purgative;
[this consists of] a decoction made from pūga, abhayā, śuṇṭhī, kṛṣṇā, kumbha, and nikumbha,
along with karañja, kaṭphala, vacā, triphalā, and pañcakola.
Oil prepared with *sadarvīka* and milk,
along with conch shell, *priyaṅgu*, *naipālī*, the three pungents (*kaṭutrika*), and the three aromatics (*phatrika*), should be used as nasal drops (*nāvana*).
For the purification of vision, a clean wick should be prepared with *kokilā*,
black iron filings, the three pungent spices (*vyoṣa*), rock salt, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and collyrium.
The preparation known as *pīta* (yellow) is made with the two types of *niśā* (turmeric), *kuṣṭha*, *natapatraka*, *kaṇa* (black pepper), and *uṣaṇa* (long pepper);
the *patrapīta* variety is made with *varā*, *tryoṣa* (the three pungents), *śilājatu*, *alambuṣā*, and *saindhava* salt.
One should conquer timira (blindness) with realgar, conch-shell, rock salt, and black pepper.
A wick (varti) made from tālīsa, pāṭhā, kiṇihī, vella, māṃsī, niśā, and abhayā quickly cures even severe śukra, pillā, āmaya, and arma.
Ghee prepared with the pastes [of drugs] in a decoction of milky trees provides nourishment; likewise,
*puṭapāka* should be performed using the meat of wild animals mixed with rock salt.
One should proceed as before with a paste made of long pepper, honey, and ghee;
furthermore, sudation should be performed in the proper measure using *śigru* leaves steamed in water.

In cases born of blood (raktaja), one should act as in the case of pitta; in cases of *sannipāta*, one should act according to whichever [dosha] is most predominant. Tiger, bear, and cow-bile, combined with a decoction of barley and milk, [should be used].
A tarpaṇa prepared with a paste of dūrvā and madhuka is beneficial;
likewise one prepared with yaṣṭī, anantā, dvivṛhatī, pippalī, and the two types of salt.
One should prepare a *puṭapāka* cooked with iron filings, sandalwood, liver,
and the flesh of the porcupine, the monitor lizard, and the rabbit.
One should add powdered *kaṇa* and rock salt (*saindhava*) to a decoction of *uśīra*; once that has been strained,
one should cook it again with ghee and add honey when it has become thick.
In this cold [season], this collyrium is beneficial for all types of *timira*:
either *kuṣṭha* combined with sugar, or with rainwater. (AS.Utt.16.69)
The decoction should be processed with ghee and honey,
and applied as an ointment as previously described; likewise, *srotoñjana* mixed with *sauvīra* [salt] should be wrapped in buffalo fat.

Likewise, a powder cooked over a fire of cow-dung and black earth, along with *vaṭa* leaves and *darbha* grass, is recommended as a collyrium (*añjana*). [This is prepared] from the dung of a ram, a porcupine, a dog, a cat, and a peacock.
By this method, the formulations with the various fats should be applied individually:
[using] the shoots of the *vaṭa* tree, *madhuka*, *dūrvā*, *lodhra*, sesame, and blue lotus.
One should smear the head and face with a paste made from the flour of *vaya* seeds mixed with ghee;
one should also perform an affusion (pariṣeka) on the head using these same ingredients boiled in milk.
In the case of a *sannipāta* (combined disorder), one should treat it by analyzing the specific excess of each *doṣa* that has been described.

Even when there is a confluence [of diseases], one should apply the treatment as in the case of *kāca* or *timira*; however, one must not pierce the vein located in the eye, due to the risk of injury from the pressure of the instrument.
Impurities may cause blindness; leeches should be applied for bleeding in cases of smoky vision, sour eructation, pitta disorders, heat, and burning sensations, using aged ghee.
One should administer an unctuous purgative with cold substances and apply cold plasters all over the body;
an ointment prepared by cooking cow-dung juice, milk, and clarified butter is recommended.
A medicinal extract (rasakriyā) prepared by adding a powder of gold, gaurika, and tālīśa; [and] the dust of old jaggery, kāsīsa, pippalī, and kaṭphala.
A pill prepared from Triphala fruit soaked in water, dried, and then saturated with the liquid of cow dung,
immediately destroys night-blindness and cataracts. Black pepper rubbed with curd is an excellent collyrium for night-blindness.
Ghee fried with the leaves of the *kumbhayoni* (Arka) plant is highly esteemed for internal consumption; likewise,
[ghee] prepared with *kārañjika*, blue lotus, *svarṇagaurī*, and the filaments of the white lotus [is also praised].
This wick, ground with cow-dung juice, destroys night-blindness;
or else [a wick made] from the two types of turmeric (*haridrā*) and *añjana* mixed with honey and the juice of the *jātī* flower.
Or [one may use] goat’s urine with *kauntī*, black salt, *strotoja*, and rock salt;
or [a paste] ground with cow dung juice, combined with the two types of turmeric and long pepper.
With *kālānusāri*, *tālīśapatra*, *yaṣṭyāhva*, and *nāgara*, or with *kaṇā* (long pepper) soaked for half a month in the bile of a tawny cow (*kāpila-pitta*).
In cases of liver or bile disorders, one should eat the liver of the monitor lizard, rabbit, rṣya, ruru deer, or peacock;
and one should also consume the spleen and liver of a buffalo with oil and ghee.
One should eat the sprouts of *jīvantī* prepared in ghee,
as well as those of *atimuktaka*, *eraṇḍa*, *sahā*, and *abhīru*.

In cases of eye diseases, one should prescribe foods that are wholesome or unwholesome just as one does for wounds. For one who uses collyrium and nasal drops without suppressing natural urges, [the disease will not be cured].
For one who abandons anger and grief, darkness does not enter within;
for one who eats triphalā at night and drinks clarified butter that has been duly prepared.
Having eaten this and drunk water, darkness (timira) is quickly pacified.
[One should worship] Suṣabhavya, Sukanyā, Skanda, Cyavana, and the two Aśvins.
He who constantly remembers these six [verses] does not lose his sight.
[Vision is impaired] by anxiety, physical assault, fear, grief, roughness, and sitting on uneven ground.
From errors in purgation, nasal therapy, emesis, and *puṭapāka* procedures;
from vomiting undigested food; and from the suppression of hunger, thirst, and other natural urges.
And even after the conclusion of eye diseases, one may see as if suffering from the disease of *timira*,
as in the case of one whose vision is impaired by looking at a solar eclipse, fire, lightning, and so forth.

Satiation with unctuous and cooling substances should be employed, as well as collyrium made by rubbing gold with ghee. For the protection of the eyes, men should exert effort at all times, for as long as there is a desire for life.
This world is useless for those blind men whose days and nights are equal, even though wealth exists [for them].

(AS.Utt.16.92) The purification by the flow of blood from the *triphalā* [remedy], the tranquility of the mind, and the application of collyrium are [the means for] the healing of the eyes. (AS.Utt.16.93)

Eating birds, worshipping trees, and constantly drinking ghee provide protection for the eyes. One should always abstain from eating unwholesome food and from staring intensely at objects that are extremely bright, moving, or minute.
This supreme protection for the eyes of men was taught by the sage Nimi:
*tamāla*, *tṛṭi*, saffron, blue lotus, long pepper, white antimony, iron filings, black pepper, *kākamācī*, and cinnamon bark.
Yashṭimadhu, añjana, and udadhiphena are unsurpassed for eye diseases; therefore, this pure collyrium quickly removes blurred vision.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter. Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "The Prohibition of Liṅganāśa."
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and others:
"In the case of *liṅganāśa*, *nīlikā*, *paṭala*, and *āndhya* are synonyms.
That [condition] caused by phlegm (ślaiṣmika) was previously described as curable; furthermore, it has six complications, the first of which is āvartakī.
Śarkarā,
Rājīmatī,
and Chinnāṃśukā.
"Candrakī and Chatrakī" (AS.Utt.17.3): therein, the *āvartakī* gaze is one that is white and reddish, whirling, and unstable.
Covered with a small amount of sun-milk (*arka-kṣīra*) like a mass of inspissated milk (*kūrcikā*),
and surrounded by rice-awn-ghee (*śāli-śūka-ājya*), it is called *rājīmatī*.
The *chinnaviṣamā* has the luster of burnt [substances] and is painful; the *chinnāṃśukā* has a color like bell-metal (*kāṃsya*); the *candrakī* is shaped like a moon;
the *naikavarṇā* is of many colors; and the *chatrakī* resembles an umbrella.
One should not pierce them;
furthermore,
one should not pierce those who are unfit for venesection, nor those suffering from thirst, catarrh, or cough.

One should not [administer it] to those fearing indigestion, nor to those with undigested food, nor to those suffering from pain in the head, ears, or eyes; nor when the weather is excessively hot, cold, windy, or cloudy, nor when the *nīlikā* (the dark cloud) has not fully cleared.
For if it has not yet formed, being uneven, thin like curd or whey,
even when scraped with a probe, it rises up again.
It produces intense pain and further obstructs the vision;
it is quickly filled with phlegm, wind, and bile.
After a long time, it becomes accompanied by complications; therefore, one should extract the foreign body without delay.

AS.Utt.17.7 Now, when the patient has been lubricated, purged, and nourished with ghee; when his head has been refreshed at night with meat broth; when he has not yet eaten; when his equipment is ready; on a clear day; when the practitioner has performed the rites for well-being (*svastyayana*); when he has paid homage to the Sun and the Lord of Videha; in the forenoon; seated in a place sheltered from wind and well-lit; facing the sun upon a mat that has acquired softness from the ground; with both feet extended; with both hands placed flat upon the surface of the earth; with his head held steady by the two hands of an attendant seated comfortably behind him; with his face slightly tilted upward; looking at his own nose with one eye while the other is closed; the physician, seated on a seat not too high above the patient's shins, should—using his right hand to gently open the slightly moistened, closed eye (which has been massaged on the cornea by the tip of the thumb)—and having opened it with the left thumb and index finger, hold the probe steadily with the right middle finger, index finger, and thumb. He should then pierce the eye-socket at the junction of the two parts [of the eyelid] starting from the black portion, extending from the outer corner (*apāṅga*) to one part [of the pupil], ensuring the needle is straight and neither too high nor too low, at the natural joint of the eye.
In this very manner, having stood on the right side of the patient, one should open the right thumb and index finger with the other hand.
Now, one should know that the needle has been correctly pierced when there is a sound like that of a word, a lack of sensation, and the oozing of drops of water;
and as soon as it has entered, one should hold the needle steady.
And for the purpose of preventing the flow of tears caused by passion, one should sprinkle [the eye] with breast milk;
then, having again comforted the patient, one should move the probe and insert it from the center of the vision.
As the patient looks downward, one should remove the *liṅganāśa*—not too quickly and not too slowly—comfortably and facing downward, and then cause the patient to exhale.
For in this way, the vision of one whose phlegm has been eliminated becomes purified;
and when the vision is purified, one may perceive fingers, threads, kinsmen, and lineages.

While the patient is looking [at the eye] with eyes that are not yet closed, one should gradually remove the probe while still rotating it. Then, for one whose defect has been removed and who is seeing properly, one should place a cotton pad soaked in lukewarm ghee over the eye and bandage it.

Thereafter, having led him into a windless room and laid him down on a soft bed provided with a pillow, one should attend to him with pleasant conversation if the right eye was pierced—lying on the left side—or if the left eye was pierced—lying on the right side—or if both were pierced—lying on his back.
One should fasten it on him according to one's ability;
and for three days he should avoid belching, sneezing, coughing, spitting, and stretching;
for seven days he should avoid bathing, drinking water, brushing his teeth, and remaining with his face downward.
One should observe the procedure for oleation and apply an anointing of ghee to the head and the feet.
On the third day, after eating, one should sprinkle the eye with milk boiled with castor leaves and heated,
or with milk prepared with the *jīvanīya* drugs, or with clarified butter, or likewise with a light broth prepared with the five roots (*pañcamūla*).
Then one should bind it as before (AS.Utt.17.12); from that time onwards, one should do exactly thus every day for seven days (AS.Utt.17.12).
On the seventh day, however, he should release him from all restrictions, or on the tenth day,
he should feed him a gruel (vilepī) or a thick porridge (vāṭya) combined with the three pungents (vyoṣa) and āmalaka, slightly oily and salty, accompanied by warm water.

For one who practices in this manner, pain, passion, and other such afflictions do not persist (AS.Utt.17.13). However, if they do persist, one should apply eye-drops consisting of liquorice (*yaṣṭīmadhu*), *lodhra*, raisins (*mṛdvīkā*), rock salt (*saindhava*), and sugar, prepared with goat’s milk (AS.Utt.17.13).
Or one should apply a paste to the head and face made of madhuka, kuṣṭha, utpala, drākṣā, lākṣā, and sugar;
or with pṛśniparṇī, musta, madhuka, śatāvarī, padmaka, and rock salt;
or one should apply a paste of sārivā, gairika, barley, dūrvā grass, and ghee.
Or with sesame seeds and mustard seeds, slightly fried and saturated with the juice of *mātuluṅga*;
or with sesame seeds and mustard seeds, slightly fried and mixed with goat’s milk.

Alternatively, a plaster made of *payasyā*, *sārivā*, leaves, *mañjiṣṭhā*, and *yaṣṭyāhva*, ground with goat’s milk, applied cold or lukewarm, [is beneficial]; likewise, one may apply a plaster of *devadāru*, ginger, and *madhuka*. Furthermore, one should feed the patient meat broth from wild animals (*jāṅgala*) mixed with a decoction of the *jīvanīya* group of drugs.

One should administer ghee prepared with milk processed with the vāta-alleviating group of drugs and containing the *padmakādi* group as an internal potion, for nasal drops (*nāvana*), or for affusion (*seka*).
If there is no subsiding [of the symptoms], one should lance the vein and observe the treatment for *adhimantha*;
however, due to the transgression of the prescribed regimen, the lancing leads to suppuration.
Abhiṣyanda, adhimantha, and other such conditions may arise from the defects of improper venesection; one should treat them according to their respective [therapeutic] measures.
Furthermore, the defects of venesection are: [incision] too low, too high, too close to the black part (kṛṣṇa), too close to the outer corner (apāṅga), or improper venepuncture.

Among these, from a puncture that is too low, there occurs excessive pain, discharge of blood, and redness; there is a thick, slimy coating on the probe, the black part is covered with folds, and the eye weeps; one should avoid such a case.
From piercing too high, there is excessive pain.
In that case, an affusion of very warm ghee and treatments that alleviate *vāta* should be employed; by piercing the black part adjacent [to the pupil], the *paṭala* is removed with ease.
In Kṛṣṇa, there is pain and the vision is covered by redness; the appearance of the black circle (kṛṣṇamaṇḍala) becomes obscured.
In that case, success is achieved through the application of ghee, purgation, and bloodletting.

From piercing near the outer corners [of the eyes], there arise swelling, pain, pricking, and tearing sensations, along with lacrimation and discharge; in that case, treatment consists of pouring ghee [into the eyes], fasting, and cauterization between the eyebrows.
From the venesection, there may be discharge of blood and various types of pain;
in that case, an affusion with ghee prepared from breast milk and madhuka, or cauterization at the outer corner of the eye (apāṅga), should be performed.
If the eyes are covered with a network of veins, one should first remove that network of veins; then,
once the patient has regained strength and has been treated with oleation, one should perform the venesection.
Now, the defects arising from the improper rotation of the probe (śalākā):
agitation, upward or excessive downward movement, friction against the vision, and excessive pressure upon the sight.
From the agitation caused by the probe, there arise swelling, throbbing, piercing pain, tearing, and distress;
in such a case, one should apply an infusion of a bag of *yaṣṭīmadhuka* soaked in ghee, and employ leeches;
furthermore, from drawing [the blood] upward, redness and excessive pain occur.
In that case, fasting and the application of ghee provide tactile pleasure; however,
from downward movement there arises pain and the discharge of blood,
wherein success is achieved through agitation as previously described.
From excessive friction of the vision, there arises agitation of the sight;

in that case, the application of ghee-sediment (*sarpirmaṇḍa*), oil enemas (*anuvāsana*), and nasal drops (*nāvana*) are indicated. Furthermore, from the insertion of the probe beyond the visual field, there occurs the flow of blood and the perception of forms as being tinged with red.
In that condition, the treatments are ghee application, fasting, and leeches;
the defects of the *liṅganāśa* (blindness) are bursting, oozing, spreading, swelling, and subsidence.

In that case, if the *liṅganāśa* (blindness) probed with a lancet bursts open, one should cleanse it in pieces after applying a fomentation (*sveda*) using castor leaves. Then, an expressed juice (*avapīḍana*) made of *kṛṣṇā*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and honey should be applied.
However, if it exudes [pus], one should remove the lancet, apply breast-milk washes, and administer an expressed juice of ginger and jaggery, as well as leeches.
When [the swelling] is expanding, a massage with a cloth soaked in pleasantly warm water and the scum of clarified butter (ghṛtamaṇḍa) should be applied;
likewise, when it is floating up, one should employ frightening and continuous splashing with cold water.
In cases where the doshas are either stable or mobile, fomentation with leaf-paste (patrabhaṅgasveda) is indicated.

Even so, if the probe does not come out, or if it rises up again, one should treat the patient with the administration of oil, nasal drops, and other such measures, and then pierce [the area] again; if it still rises up in this manner, one should apply cauterization between the eyebrows.
If, however, [the pupil] being pulled out dissolves within the visual circle (*dṛṣṭimaṇḍala*), one should apply fomentation to the channels (*nāḍīsveda*) with milk;
furthermore, ghee mixed with the powders of *śatāhvā* and *madhuka* should be used as a nasal application (*pratimarśa*).
And on this point there is a verse: "In the case of an immediately pierced [vessel], however, one should apply fomentation, cauterization, massage, and sprinkling.
On the third day, one should apply a pressed-out extract (avapīḍa), and likewise bloodletting with leeches; at the end of seven days, one should perform venesection, purgation, and enema therapy.
One should observe restraint until stability of vision is attained;
one should not suddenly look at subtle or dazzling forms.

If the probe is thick at the tip, it causes the wound to become enlarged; if thin, it causes the lifting of the membrane (paṭala); if sharp, it causes injury within; and if rough, it causes intense pain.
The *kaṇṭhā* [fever] has irregular tears; it is short and difficult to grasp.
[It is treated] with the roots of *āḍhakī*, black pepper, yellow orpiment, and *rasāñjana*.
When the eye is pierced, a wick mixed with jaggery and ground with celestial water (divyāmbu) should be applied.
Jātī, śirīṣa, dhava, the horn of a sheep, flowers, vaidūrya, pearls, and fruit should be well-ground with milk.

Copper that has been thinly smeared with this goat’s fat and ground again with milk for seven days makes a beneficial medicinal collyrium (piṇḍāñjana) when dried in the shade; it restores clarity and provides strength to the vision in an eye that has been pierced.
It is said that [the diamond] is equal to this very [iron] in its qualities and applications, being like the *srotoñjana*, coral, stone, sea-foam, and *tīkṣṇa* [iron].
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter titled "The Knowledge of All Eye Diseases.
Thus said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
When the eyes are afflicted by Vāta, there is nasal obstruction and slight swelling; there is also a pricking pain,
throbbing, and splitting sensation in the temples, eyes, eyebrows, forehead, and mouth.
The eye-secretion is dry and scanty, the tears are few and cold, and the pains are shifting;
opening and closing the eyes is difficult, as if crawling among living creatures.
The eye appears swollen as if filled with fine thorns; this is *abhiṣyanda*,
which is pacified by unctuous and warm treatments, but if neglected, it leads to [further complications].
In that condition, there occurs a severe eye-pain (adhimantha), ringing in the ears,
and vertigo; moreover, the forehead, eyes, eyebrows, and other parts feel as if they are being churned like fire-sticks in a forest.
Even one whose *adhimantha* has been destroyed may experience various kinds of pain due to negligence; consequently,
ulcers arise in the eye and there is loss of vision.
The wind (vāyu), moving from the neck, the eyes, or the temples, or from another location,
causes intense pain, a lack of lubrication, redness, and swelling in the eye.
In the condition known as *anyatovāta*, the eye contracts and tears flow;
likewise, in the disorder of wind (*vātaparyaya*), the eye becomes distorted or sunken.
Burning, smoking sensation, swelling, and a dark-brown discoloration of the eyelids externally; internal moisture, yellowish-hot tears, redness, and yellowish vision— these are the signs.
The state of having eyes wounded and smeared with alkaline matter is the characteristic of *pitta*-induced ophthalmia (*abhiṣyanda*);
it has the appearance of being strewn with glowing embers and possesses a luster similar to a mass of liver.
In Adhimantha, the eye becomes [red]; in Syanda caused by Kapha, however, [the same occurs].
In Adhimantha, there is dullness, great swelling, itching, drowsiness, and a lack of desire for food;
the eyelids are thick, oily, and profusely coated with white, slimy, and sticky secretions;
and the black portion of the eye is sunken while the white circle is elevated. (AS.Utt.18.12)
AS.Utt.18.12 There is discharge, inflation of the nose, and eyes feeling as if filled with dust;
AS.Utt.18.13 red streaks and filaments in the tears, and the appearance of red circles.

Due to the flow of blood along with pitta, the eye exhibits the symptoms of a discharge; AS.Utt.18.14: in the Mantha type, the eye is copper-colored at its margins and has a pain similar to that of Utpātana.
Due to redness, it resembles a bandhūka flower, becomes exhausted and incapable of touch,
appears like a blood-soaked ariṣṭa fruit, turns black, and its vision is like fire.
In cases of *adhimantha*, all the symptoms of *syanda* occur according to their respective types, along with excessive pain in the temples,
teeth, cheeks, and the skull.
In one afflicted by vāta and pitta, there is itching, pricking, tearing,
and discharge; the eyelids are dry and rough, and the opening and closing of the eyes is difficult.

AS.Utt.18.17: Characterized by contraction, dryness, a desire for cold, piercing pain, and suppuration, this condition is called *śuṣkākṣipāka* (dry eye inflammation); it occurs with swelling when caused by all three *malas*.
In that condition, there is swelling accompanied by blood, characterized by excessive pain, burning, spitting, and so forth;
and tears that are repeatedly hot, cold, clear, slimy, transparent, or thick.
When there is little swelling and little swelling, yet it ripens with other symptoms as well, [it is known as *alpaśopha-alpaśopha*].
