In the stage beyond akṣipāka (akṣipākātyaya), there is swelling, inflammation, turbid tearing,
and the black portion of the eye becomes coated with phlegm, appearing white and characterized by moisture and redness.
There is a burning sensation, obstruction of vision, and unstable pains;
the essence of food is rendered sour by the humors when pitta and blood are predominant.
Having ascended to the eye through the vessels, it makes the eye dark-red,
accompanied by swelling, burning, suppuration, and tearing, and causes extremely blurred vision.
Having stated that "this is amlōṣita," sixteen diseases affecting all parts [of the eye] have been described.
Among these, one should abandon the treatment of adhimantha when it is accompanied by sākṣipāka and atyaya.
Adhimantha arising from vāta [destroys vision] in five nights, that born of śleṣman in seven days,
and that produced by rakta likewise destroys it in three nights; however, that caused by pitta destroys it immediately through improper conduct.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter.
Now begins the nineteenth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the chapter named "The Treatment of Abhiṣyanda" (Ophthalmia).

Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others. Now, for all eye diseases, one should employ head-purification (śirovirecana), gargles, medicinal smoke, and fasting at the very onset of the premonitory symptoms, except in cases where there is an excess of Vāta.

In all cases, however, one should prepare a *biḍālaka* (a medicinal paste) using sandalwood, black pepper, cinnamon leaves, *elā*, gold-stone (*svarṇagairika*), *tagara*, *rasāñjana*, salt, and liquorice.
Likewise, in cases of vāta-pitta, [one should use] dārvī,
tuttha, and harītakī; but in kapha, [one should use] harītakī, nāgara, rasāñjana, and svarṇagairika.
Moreover,
*biḍālaka* [ointment] made with *kuṣṭha*, *amiṣī*, *pippalī*, *candana*, and *utpala* destroys pain.

Mustā, aguru, and candana, combined with honey, destroy pain, burning sensations, and redness. [Likewise,] sandhava, aguru, trijātaka, trikaṭuka, svarṇagairika, kuṣṭha, tagara, and śaileya remove pain, swelling, burning sensations, and redness. One should dust the eye with the fine powder of śigru fruit, manohvā, śābara, and lodhra—each increasing fourfold in sequence—which has been ground into a smooth paste and placed upon a fine silk cloth.

One should sprinkle into the eyes a powder made from half a *pala* of the bark of white *lodhra*, which has been scraped on the outside, smeared with a paste of *nimba* leaves, cooked by the *puṭapāka* method, mixed with four *marica* peppers, ground into a fine dust, and bound in a cloth. (AS.Utt.19.6–7)

This bandage removes piercing pain, burning, tearing, swelling, itching, suppuration, discharge, and exudation. At the time of administering eye-drops, one should drip [the medicine] using that same pouch soaked in *avantisoma*.

Alternatively, as before, one should prepare a paste of *lodhra* bark mixed with the same quantity of two parts black pepper (*marica*), one-quarter part realgar (*manaḥśilā*), one-eighth part each of licorice (*yaṣṭīmadhuka*), *śatapuṣpā*, and collyrium (*añjana*).
Moreover,
wild *kulattha* beans, bound in a cloth, well-steamed in the juice of goat dung, and dehusked by the fingernails; AS.Utt.19.9.
That powder, when applied once at midnight with the sound of snapping fingers, immediately dispels the inflammation of the eyes.
Then, one should prepare an eye-drop by boiling one pala of *dāruharidrā* in half a prastha of water until one-eighth remains, and mixing it with honey.

If there is no relief in this way, one should first treat the patient with meat soups of wild animals (*jāṅgala-rasa*) for those suffering from *vātābhiṣyanda*, and then administer either freshly prepared ghee or old ghee that has been processed with a decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūla*), *rāsnā*, and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), along with a paste of the *jīvanīya* drugs, mixed with milk.
One should prepare an eye-drop (āścyotana) consisting of goat’s milk boiled with the roots and tender leaves of *eraṇḍa*,
or alternatively with *sālaparṇī*, *pṛśniparṇī*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, *madhuka*, and *urupūga*.
Similarly, one may use the roots of tagara, drīvera, śārṅgeṣṭhā, udumbara, madhuka, pippalī, and the two types of bṛhatī, along with eraṇḍa;

or the two types of aṃśumatī, bṛhatī, and kaṇṭakārikā—bound together with cloth and soaked in any one of *surā*, *madya*, or fermented grain-water (*dhānyāmla*), or in a decoction of the meat of marshy animals mixed with sour liquids.

AS.Utt.19.14: With those same meats, having been made into *veśavāra*, steamed, and mixed with a large quantity of fat, one should prepare a thick poultice (*utkārikā*) enriched with barley flour and salt, and apply it to the forehead, cheeks, and other areas to induce sudation (*sveda*).
Alternatively, one may use the steam from *rāsnā*, *abhīru*, the ten roots (*daśamūla*), *balā*, *kola*, horse gram (*kulattha*), and barley, which have been steamed in goat’s milk.
Oil or ghee prepared with *rāsnā* and the other aforementioned drugs should be used for nasal administration (*nāvana*);
likewise, one should perform tube-sudation (*nāḍī-sveda*) using these same ingredients.

AS.Utt.19.16 A facial paste made from *sarala*, *surabhi*, *ghana*, *devadāru*, *hiṃsrā*, *karañja* fruit, *bilva*, and *sarṣapa*, along with roasted sesame seeds ground with milk and applied lukewarm, pacifies eye pain and stiffness.
AS.Utt.19.16 AS.Utt.19.17 If the pain is not thus relieved, one should perform venesection on this patient.

For blood vitiated by Vāta, once it has been purified by oleation, sudation, and drainage, should not again provoke the Vāta; therefore, one should administer a purgative of ghee combined with *tilvaka* for oleation, or ghee followed by a decoction of *tilvaka* as a post-drink (*anupāna*).

One should administer a decoction enema (āsthāpana) and an oil enema (anuvāsana) using pure [oil] as in the treatment for wind-induced coryza (vātapratiśyāya). Then, one should soak husked sesame seeds overnight in a decoction of bilva fruit and dry them during the day; this process should be repeated for five days.
Having taken oil from these [plants], one should cook it with boar fat along with a paste of bilva root and madhuyaṣṭikā, and with milk;
with this, one should administer nasal drops (nasya) and a head-poultice (śirobasti).
Alternatively, one may prepare oil containing madhuka, mixed with milk, using a decoction of all the fragrant substances (sarvagandha).
One should inhale unctuous smoke, and once his pain has subsided, he should receive a satiating treatment.

One should prepare milk with *kāśmarya*, *madhuka*, *kumuda*, *utpala*, *urupūga*, *kuṣṭha*, *bṛhatī*, *tamāla*, *māṃsī*, *sārivā*, *prapauṇḍarīka*, *darbhamūla*, and *kaśerukā*; this should be administered as a saturating drink (*tarpaṇa*), nasal drops (*nasya*), or an unguent (*abhyaṅga*). Alternatively, one should boil the head of a black cobra in milk.
Then, having extracted the oil, one should cook a *tarpaṇa* with a paste of sandalwood, *uśīra*, sugar, and blue lotus, along with milk;
or alternatively, one should boil milk with the five roots (*pañcamūla*), the life-promoting drugs (*jīvanīya*), and chicken meat.
From that, one should prepare fresh butter (*navanīta*) by cooking it with *ghanā*, *anantā*, *sārivā*, *uśīra*, and sandalwood, together with milk.
One should prepare a *puṭapāka* using the liver of either a goat, a sheep, or a boar, combined with long pepper (*pippalī*), rock salt (*saindhava*), honey, and ghee;
this should be used as a collyrium (*añjana*) for the purpose of clarifying the vision.
Having husked black sesame seeds, one should soak them in breast milk for seven days and then dry them.

Having made a powder of these, equal in amount to sugar candy, mixed with half a part of *madhuka*, a portion of rock salt, and a portion of the head of a black cobra burnt by internal smoke, one should form pills by grinding them with celestial water (*divyodaka*).

One should add the powder of *saindhava* salt and long pepper (*pippalī*), as well as *rasāñjana*, to the fat of a monitor lizard (*godhā*) and a snake, and to the fat of a horse. This medicinal extract (*rasakriyā*), having been kept for a month, clarifies the vision and alleviates pain.
One should smear a silver vessel with cow’s curd from which the cream has been removed and which is slightly sour;
when that [vessel] has turned blue and is thoroughly dried, wicks made from it and dried in the shade conquer diseases of the eyes caused by wind (vātākṣiroga).

One should grind together the roots and bark of the two types of *māgadhikā* and *kaṇṭakārikā*, along with *madhuka*, white sugar, rock salt, and copper dust, with goat’s milk, and smear a copper vessel with it.
Every seven days, one should remove [the coating], grind [the ingredients] again in the same manner, and re-smear.

After seven such periods of seven nights, pills (*guṭikā*) are prepared; these are supreme for removing pain, redness, swelling, cataracts (*timira*), *kāca*, night-blindness, burning sensations, *adhimantha*, and injuries caused by trauma in diseases of the eyes due to Vāta.
And for counter-application (pratyañjana) in this case, a wick (varti) should be prepared from rock crystal, conch-shell navel, madhuka, and red ochre, ground with sugarcane juice.
This entire procedure should also be employed for adhimanth and other similar conditions.
Specifically, in the case of *adhimantha*, one should drink clarified butter prepared with milk and a decoction of *sahacara*, *sphūrjātaka*, *kataka* seeds, *bilva*, and *vṛkṣādanī*. AS.Utt.19.27

If there is no relief with ghee, one should apply oil, muscle fat (vasā), or marrow, alternating them according to the previously mentioned procedure. If there is no relief by any means, one should perform the cauterization (dāha) above the eyebrows as previously described.
In cases of *pittābhiṣyanda* and *adhimantha*, one should drink ghee sprinkled with sugar,
or any one of the bitter (*tikta*) [decoctions].

A decoction of *prapauṇḍarīka*, *āmalaka*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, *darbha*, the ten roots (*daśamūla*), *śatāvarī*, *tālīśapatra*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, and blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), mixed with sugar and breast milk, is used as an eye-drop; or else, a decoction of *madhuka* and *kaṭaṅkaṭerī*.

A decoction of sandalwood, madhuka, lodhra, mañjiṣṭhā, and svarṇagairika, mixed with honey, removes severe pain and burning sensations. Lodhra, dārvī, madhuka, and prapauṇḍarīka should be crushed and bound with a cloth.
Sprinkling with that [decoction] soaked in honey-water destroys pain;
likewise, that same [decoction], mixed with sugar and either human breast milk or goat's milk, destroys burning sensations and redness.
Having fried white *lodhra* and *madhuka* in equal parts with ghee, one should reduce them to powder.
Then, a poultice bound in a cloth and softened with breast milk or water, quickly removes pain, burning, redness,
and swelling; or likewise, one prepared with sandalwood, lotus, water-lily, nalada, and other such ingredients processed with milk.

With these, one should perform applications as head-pastes and facial ointments, as well as affusions (AS.Utt.19.33). If there is still no success, venesection should be performed; furthermore, for one who has been oleated, purgation should be induced with the powder of *triphalā*, *kāśmarya*, sugar, and *trivṛt* mixed with a decoction of *triphalā* and *kāśmarya* (AS.Utt.19.33).
Having ground conch shell, madhuka, rock salt, and the root-bark of bṛhatī with goat’s milk, one should smear it on the outside of a copper vessel.
After repeating this for seven days— thus over seven periods of seven nights— one should fashion pills from it.
Rubbed with breast milk, these [substances] remove pain from bile-related diseases when used as an eye-salve (añjana).

One should dry gold-ochre (*suvarṇagairika*) and turmeric (*niśā*) that has been placed in divine water for seven days; likewise, one should saturate it with a very cold decoction of the sweet group (*madhuravarga*). This powdered eye-salve destroys burning sensations and redness.

One should boil fifty *dārvi* pieces and one *pala* each of *sārivā*, *madhuka*, the two types of *kākolī*, the two types of *niśā*, *mṛdvīkā*, *kāśmarya*, *suniṣaṇṇaka*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *lodhra*, *uśīra*, and *candana* in eight *droṇas* of water until one-eighth remains. Once strained,
it should be removed from the fire while still thick enough to coat a ladle, and then one should add an equal portion of white sugar and two *palas* each of honey and ghee.
This sweet medicinal preparation (rasakriyā) is beneficial for all eye diseases.
A paste of *sārivā* and sugar ground with the fresh juice of *kāśmarya*, or liquorice (*yaṣṭyāhva*) ground with sugarcane juice, may be used as a nasal medication (*nasya*).
In this regard, the satiation (tarpaṇa) and the eye-cupping (puṭapāka) prescribed for Kṣataśukra should be employed; furthermore,
in cases of Śleṣmābhiṣyanda and Adhimantha, one should observe a fast for three days and apply sharp medicinal fumigations, gargles, and nasal drops.
A collyrium prepared from śārṅgeṣṭhā, kuṣṭha, tagara, muruṅgī, vyoṣa, elā, dāru, and biḍālaka,
boiled with cow’s urine along with the root-barks of tilvaka, bṛhatī, nidigdhikā, lodhra, and āragvadha, destroys swelling, exudation, and itching.

Alternatively, one may apply a paste of *nimba* leaves smeared with powdered *lodhra* that has been heated over embers, bound in a cloth, and moistened with warm water; likewise, one may use powders of *abhayā*, *āmalaka*, *upakulyā*, and *pāṭalī*.

Either the juice of *śigru* sprouts mixed with honey, or a decoction of *madhuśigru*, *pāṭalī*, the roots of *bilva*, and *śuṇṭhī*; or a sprinkling (*seka*) with honey and jaggery-based liquor (*gauḍasīdhu*), in which *nimba*, *paṭola*, *jātī* leaves, the two types of *lodhra*, and *mahauṣadha* have been cut into pieces, tied in a cloth, and steeped— these are supreme for destroying phlegm-induced colic.
Fomentation (sveda) should be applied using the leaves of rohiṣa, pūtīka, karañja, kapittha, āsphota, pīlu, bilva, śigru, surasa, arka, and nimba, boiled in cow’s urine.
Nevertheless, if there is persistence of swelling and friction, one should fumigate the eye with a tube using barley, madana, birch bark, and *śamī* leaves mixed with ghee,
or with ghee alone. On the following morning, after the patient has eaten light food, one should have him drink ghee prepared with the three pungents (*vyoṣa*) and sprinkled with barley ash.
Then, venesection and purgation [should be administered] (AS.Utt.19.44).
Having ground the bark of *bṛhatī*, dry ginger, and the dust of copper and bell-metal with the whey of curd (*dadhimastu*), one should smear it upon a vessel made of that [copper].
In the same manner, when seven days have passed,
or after seven weeks, suppositories (vartis) should be prepared; either a suppository made of black pepper, turmeric, and chebulic myrobalan ground with water,
or one made of the three pungents (trikaṭu), the three fruits (triphalā), the heartwood of *viḍaṅga*, and turmeric.
Equal parts of *harītakī* and *tuttha*, with black pepper added in an eighth part of the *tuttha*, form this *kumārī* wick, which destroys all eye diseases caused by *śleṣman*.

Alternatively, powdered *viḍaṅga* saturated with *vāruṇī* wine; or conch-shell with *madhuka* and *triphalā* juice, either separately or combined; or a powder collyrium (*cūrṇāñjana*) or a paste (*piṇḍa*)—these remove *pothakī*, excessive *kapha*, agitation, and *abhiṣyanda*.

A wick made from gold, red ochre, rock salt, realgar, lac, *nata*, *karañjikā*, *surasa*, conch shell, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), *tālīsa*, costus, *kaliṅgaka*, *devadāru*, *nalada*, jasmine buds, and *rasāñjana*, ground with the scum of wine (*surāmaṇḍa*), cures all disorders of the eyes caused by *śleṣman*.
One should soak the powder of *puṣpakāsīsa* for seven days in the juice of *surasā* leaves within a copper vessel;
this powder used as a collyrium (*añjana*) destroys swelling of the eyelids and the falling out of eyelashes.

A wick (*varti*) made from rock salt, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), *varā*, *viḍaṅga*, *lodhra*, *prapauṇḍarīka*, *madhuka*, *tutthaka*, *tārkṣyaśaila*, and copper filings, ground with goat’s milk and saturated with the fresh juice of *mārkava*, is called *kāṇḍacitrā*; it conquers all eye diseases. (AS.Utt.19.49) In cases of itching (*kaṇḍū*), a wick should be prepared from realgar (*manaḥśilā*), rock salt, and white pepper, ground with the juice of *mātuluṅga*. (AS.Utt.19.50)
In the case of swelling (śopha), a medicinal paste (rasakriyā) should be prepared with nagara, devadāru, saindhava, jāti, and kṣāra, ground with the scum of wine (surāmaṇḍa);
or alternatively, with naktamāla, laśuna, śigru, and the seeds of śigruka.
AS.Utt.19.51 [One should administer] a satiation draught (tarpaṇa).

AS.Utt.19.52 One should boil together liver, *agaru*, *priyaṅgu*, *nalada*, and *devadāru* in milk; when that has cooled, it should be churned with a whisk (*khaja*), and the butter (*navanīta*) thus produced should be cooked again with these very same medicinal herbs.

AS.Utt.19.52 Furthermore, a *puṭapāka* (herb-pot) should be prepared with *kuṣṭha*, *tagara*, *dārvī*, the *sarvagandha* group, and *rājavṛkṣa*, ground together with liver, and combined with honey and ghee. AS.Utt.19.53 Moreover, one should treat *raktaja-abhiṣyanda* and *adhimantha* in the same manner as *pittaja* [conditions].
One should cause [the child] to drink either breast milk, sugarcane juice, sugar-water, or any one of these,
and one should repeatedly let his blood flow out by means of venesection or leeches.

In the case of intense pain, one should administer a large dose of ghee (AS.Utt.19.54). A pill collyrium (*guṭikāñjana*) made from the roots of *āḍhakī*, *kuryaṭa*, *pāṭalī*, *śrīparṇī*, *vidula*, *arjuna*, *bṛhatī*, *campaka*, and *mālatī*, ground with the juice of dates, [should also be used] (AS.Utt.19.54).

One should rub bell-metal with hair moistened with water; having burned that [hair] smeared with the impurities of the bell-metal in a smokeless fire, one should saturate the resulting ash for five days in a decoction of triphalā, the fresh juice of *surasā*, and goat’s milk.
This powder, equal in quantity to *srotoñjana*, is a counter-collyrium (*pratyañjana*).

One should boil a black cobra in milk; then, from that [milk] which has been strained, cooled, and churned, one should give the fat to a fasted cock. Its excrement is the medicinal collyrium (snehāñjana).

AS.Utt.19.57: Having filled the mouth of a black cobra with collyrium and clarified butter, wrapped it in *darbha* grass, smeared it with clay, turned it face-downward, and roasted it over a fire of cow-dung; then, taking the collyrium—which resembles the leaf of *nalada* or the blue lotus—and reducing it to powder, this is a supreme collyrium that produces clarity of vision.
Furthermore, the scum of clarified butter (*ghṛtamaṇḍa*), prepared with sugar, *madhuka*, and blue lotus combined with human milk, serves as an effective nasal medication (*nasya*).
And on this point there is a verse:
"Almost all eye diseases arise preceded by *syanda* (ophthalmia)."
Therefore, one should quickly conquer [the disease] after it has vitiated the blood.
It is called *syanda* because it flows through all the channels above the clavicle (*urdhvajatruga*).
For those located in that [region] and for the limbs likewise, there is excessive inflammation due to over-churning.
In the case of Vata, an eye-wash (akṣiseka) should be prepared with castor oil, bṛhatī, and madhuśigru.
With the five roots (pañcamūla) prepared with sugar, [one treats] pitta and rakta;
likewise with dārvī, lākṣā, utpala, drākṣā, mañjiṣṭhā, and the two types of madhuka.
In cases of eye inflammation (syanda) arising from phlegm (kapha), one should perform eye irrigation with a combination of triphalā, ginger (śuṇṭhī), nimba, lodhra, and āṭarūṣaka;
in cases arising from the combination of all three humors (sannipāta), one should use all these together.
A sprinkling with *tuttha*, *vyoṣa*, *abhayā*, *lodhra*, and *yaṣṭyāhva* kept in copper vessels and ground with fermented grain-water (*dhānyāmla*) removes all pains caused by *abhiṣyanda*.
Similarly, an irrigation with *utpala*, *abhayā*, *lodhra*, *yaṣṭīmadhu*, and *rasāñjana*,
combined with half-parts of *śatāhvā*, conquers all eye pains.
Sprinkling [the eyes] with a mixture of *puṣpāñjana*, white [sugar], and honey, placed in a copper vessel and combined with sesame-water,
destroys pain, redness, burning, swelling, and irritation.
An irrigation with the paste of the two types of *niśā*, *triphalā*, and *musta*,
ground together with the milk of a young woman and mixed with sugar and honey, removes the pain caused by injury.
Tutthaka, having been infused twenty-five times in cow's urine,
or in breast milk, or in goat's milk, is an immediate remedy for sudden inflammation (sadyaḥkopa).
Equal parts of *badarī* leaves, *yaṣṭyāhva*, *tuttha*, and *dhātrī* fruits,
heated within a *puṭa* by a fire of *badara* wood, constitute a collyrium that destroys inflammation of the eyes.
A wick (varti) made from the bark of the roots of *bṛhatī* and *eraṇḍa*, along with the roots of *śigru* and rock salt (*saindhava*),
ground with cow’s milk, cures all eye diseases caused by *vāta*.
Sumana, kṣāraka, śaṅkha, triphalā, madhuka, and balā— these,
ground with celestial water (cow’s urine), form a medicinal wick that removes pitta and blood disorders.
A wick (varti) made from rock salt, the three myrobalans, the three pungents (vyoṣa), conch-shell,
sea-foam, śaileyaka, and sarjarasa overcomes diseases of the eyes caused by kapha.
A medicinal wick (varti) made from conch-shell, coral, lapis lazuli, red coral, the bone of a porpoise, antimony,
and white pepper overcomes all eye diseases.
Pippalī, the juice of kiṃśuka, snake fat, rock salt,
and aged ghee— this medicinal extract (rasakriyā) destroys all disorders of the eyes.

The fat of a black cobra, honey, and the juice of *dhātrī* prepared as a medicinal extract (*rasakriyā*) are recommended for all eye diseases, as well as for cataracts (*kāca*), pterygium (*arman*), and opacities (*paṭala*).
Rasāñjana, śṛ� invēra, abhayā, and auspicious tutthaka—
this other varti, called Aparājitā, is prepared with these ingredients in successively doubling proportions.
Except for abhiṣyanda caused by vāta, it cures timira, kukūṇaka,
pothakī, piṭakā, pillāna, and arma.
Tutthaka rubbed with whey on copper until it turns black is a collyrium that cures all types of abhiṣyanda, śukrārma, and sirājāla.
One part of excellent salt-marsh salt (*marica-vara-lavaṇa*), two parts each of black salt (*kaṇa*) and sea-foam (*samudra-phena*),
and nine parts of *sauvīra* salt, ground together under the asterism Citrā, conquers diseases caused by phlegm (*kapha*).

The formulation known as *ṣaṇmākṣika*, consisting of long pepper (*marica*), myrobalan (*āmalaka*), mineral pitch (*jalodbhava*), blue vitriol (*tuttha*), antimony collyrium (*añjana*), and iron pyrite (*tāpyadhātu*), increased in successive order,
destroys cataracts (*timira*), pterygium (*arma*), moisture in the eye (*kleda*), opacities (*kāca*), itching (*kaṇḍū*), and pain.
One should prepare a wick (varti) from long pepper, *saptagaru*, blue lotus petals, licorice, and turmeric;
he who desires eyes equal to those of Suparṇa should constantly apply collyrium made from this.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter.
Now begins the twentieth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "The Prohibition of Akṣipāka and Pilla."
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:
in the case of *śuṣkākṣipāka*, one should drink ghee prepared according to the procedure for *vātābhiṣyanda*.
Alternatively, an eye-drop prepared from crab meat and milk,
or a decoction of *dārvī* and *prapauṇḍarīka*, destroys eye inflammation (*akṣipāka*).
A paste of mañjiṣṭhā, madhuka, kālānusārī, sārivā, lodhra, lākṣā, and prapauṇḍarīka,
strained through rice-water and mixed with honey, cures inflammation of the eyes, red streaks, tearing, and burning sensations.
A decoction of *lodhra* and *koraṇḍaka* flowers relieves pain;
*aṇu-taila* used as nasal drops [is likewise effective].
AS.Utt.20.4 AS.Utt.20.4

Oil prepared with *sārivā*, *vidārī*, *balā*, *madhuka*, *utpala*, *drākṣā*, *āṭarūṣaka*, *jīvaka*, and *candana*, combined with the meat-broth of wild animals and milk, destroys all diseases of the regions above the clavicle caused by an excess of *vāta* and *pitta* when used as nasal drops (*nāvana*). Furthermore, in this condition, nourishing *puṭapāka* applications that are unctuous are beneficial.
And according to the predominance of either vāta or pitta, the procedure for *abhiṣyanda* should be applied accordingly (AS.Utt.20.6).

Having rubbed hair smeared with ghee upon the surface of a mirror, one should burn it while inhaling the smoke; that soot, ground with ghee and placed in an iron vessel, removes eye inflammation when used as a collyrium (añjana) (AS.Utt.20.6).
One should cook the powder of *loha* (iron) and *srotoñjana* in a decoction of *mañjiṣṭhā*, the three fruits (*phalatrika*), and *kaṭaṅkaṭerī* until it reaches a thick consistency.
This powdered collyrium, known as *abhaya*, removes burning, stinging, redness, and tearing.
Copper filings, *sairya*, *puṣpakuṇḍa*, *madhuka*, *kālānusārī*, and *sārivā*, ground with goat’s milk, constitute a bolus collyrium (*piṇḍāñjana*).
A fatty substance mixed with the fat of aquatic animals and the powder of *śuṇṭhī* and rock salt constitutes an oily collyrium (*snehāñjana*).
If there is still no relief even thus, an enema consisting of the scum of ghee prepared with madhuka and mixed with the powder of śatāhvā, or milk, should be administered. Furthermore,
in cases of swelling or slight swelling, after the patient has been lubricated and fomented, one should perform venesection.
A purgative consisting of a decoction of grapes and *abhayā* with the paste of *trivṛt* and ghee is [recommended].
AS.Utt.20.11
For one who has undergone purgation, a non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) should be administered according to the manifestation of the specific dosha.
Thereafter, for one whose head has been fomented with a bolus, head-purgation (śirovireka) should be performed using mustard oil mixed with rock salt, or ghee mixed with *phaṇijjaka*, or *aṇu-taila*.
After the head has been purged, one should administer an unctuous enema with milk-ghee and smoke-inhalation; furthermore,
one should foment the head and eyes of the patient with well-seated *sunisannaka*, *pattūra*, and castor leaves, which have been steamed in milk and water.
Powdered *lodhra* fried in ghee, placed in a fine cloth and rubbed with warm water, serves as an eye-drop (*āścyotana*);
it also relieves pain as prescribed for dry eye-inflammation (*śuṣkākṣipāka*).

In this way, one should treat the non-pacified pain with *sandhāva*. The skull of a rabbit's head mixed with rock salt and rubbed with breast milk on a bronze vessel is a *sandhāva* that destroys the pain.
Likewise, copper and iron [should be treated] by being rubbed with cow’s urine and fumigated with ghee;
and the juice of *śigru* sprouts, rubbed on copper and fumigated with ghee, [is similarly used].

A conch shell rubbed with breast milk on copper, fumigated with *śamī* leaves smeared with ghee, cures the pain of rubbing [during eye application]. (AS.Utt.20.17) An *udumbara* fruit rubbed with breast milk on iron, fumigated with *śamī* leaves smeared with ghee, cures colic, redness, tearing, and the sensation of rubbing. (AS.Utt.20.18)
The cream of curd mixed with long pepper and rock salt, rubbed in a copper vessel, destroys swelling, rubbing sensations, tearing pain, and lachrymation.

(AS.Utt.20.18) A fragment of a clay pot rubbed in a bronze vessel with sesame-water and ghee, and fumigated with neem leaves smeared in ghee, destroys swelling, itching, rubbing sensations, lachrymation, pain, and redness. (AS.Utt.20.19)
If the eye is affected by *saṃdhāva*, one should irrigate it with breast milk.
One should not apply collyrium more than three times with those [previously mentioned substances].
Now, for the collyriums (añjanas):

the bark of *madhuka* and *bṛhatī*, copper filings, and [the ash of] cow-dung, ground with goat’s milk and repeatedly fumigated with the leaves of *śamī* and *āmalaka* soaked in ghee, constitute a ball-collyrium (*piṇḍāñjana*) that destroys swelling and pain.

Tālīśapatra, pippalī, iron powder, añjana, kāsīsa, tagara, jātīmukula, and saindhava—these, ground with cow’s urine and smeared upon copper, should be left for seven nights; then, having ground them again in the same manner, pills should be prepared. When rubbed with breast milk, they destroy stiffness, swelling, erection, friction, lacrimation, and itching.

Having ground together unbound bone, mango fruit, and meat, along with skinless copper powder, a small amount of rock salt, and cow’s curd, one should smear it onto copper. As it dries, one should grind the same ingredients again and apply another layer.

This *piṇḍāñjana* (poultice-collyrium), prepared over seven periods of seven days, destroys all types of ocular suppuration (*akṣipāka*), tearing, itching, swelling, redness, and growths of the eyelids (*vartmopacaya*).

A medicinal extract (*rasakriyā*) made from *aśmantaka*, *amlavetasa*, *parūṣaka*, *kola*, and pomegranate destroys swelling, slight swelling, suppuration, and *alasā*. Even if the swelling persists in this manner, blood-letting and head-purgation (*śirovireka*) should be performed again.
One should treat *amloṣita* in the same manner as *pittābhiṣyanda*,
and one should also observe the therapeutic measures for *pilla*.

AS.Utt.20.25: Pitta, kapha, and blood, when accumulated and aggravated, cause eighteen diseases known as *vartma-pothakī*, *visākhya*, *kukūṇaka*, *pakṣmoparodha*, *pūyālasa*, *śuṣkākṣipāka*, *alpaśopha*, *amlādita*, and *asryandādhimantha*—all of which, excluding those caused by Vāta, are chronic conditions designated as *pilla*.
Their treatment has already been taught according to their respective natures.
Furthermore, for those whose eyes have become *pillī*, a general treatment is taught:
now, one should first administer oleation and then induce emesis in a patient suffering from *pillākṣi* disease.
After the sequence has been performed, one should perform venesection; thereafter, for one who has undergone purgation,
one should scarify the two eyelids.
If it is not purified by a single application, one should apply it again and have leeches take hold of it;
a *biḍālaka* (ointment) should be made with a paste of *priyaṅgu*, *lodhra*, lotus filaments, sandalwood, and *madhuka*, mixed with honey.

One should always perform washing with a honeyed decoction of *tuvarikā*, the three fruits (*phalatrika*), and *rocanā* in the morning and evening, following the application of collyrium; and for those who dislike heat, one should apply fomentation intermittently using the decoction of the tender leaves of astringent trees (*kaṣāyavṛkṣa*) and those very same leaves.

AS.Utt.20.30 Twenty palas of *tutthaka* and twenty white peppercorns, ground with fermented rice-water (*dhānyāmla*) and stirred in a copper vessel with thirty palas of that same liquid, constitute the supreme eye-drop (*āścyotana*) for even multi-colored corneal opacities (*pillā*).

AS.Utt.20.31 For collyrium (*añjana*), one should prepare a wick (*varti*) from the paste of mango, *dhātakī* flowers, and *tilaparṇī*. Furthermore, one should boil eight *āḍhakas* of *harītakī* in water until reduced to one-eighth; having strained it again, this medicinal extract (*rasakriyā*) made from the residue adhering to the ladle serves to heal corneal opacities (*pillā*).
When the fresh juice of *palāśa* branches is being boiled, one should add the powder of *bṛhatī* and *uśīra*; once it has thickened and cooled, it becomes a collyrium (*añjana*).
Alternatively, [one may prepare it] with *vacā*, *devadāru*, and the juices of *surasā*, all ground together.
Alternatively, [an ointment] may be prepared from cow-bile and *piṣṭa*, or from the juices of the three pungents (*vyoṣa*) and *rasāñjana*;
or, as an ointment, copper powder mixed in equal parts with *haritāla*, *sauvīrāñjana*, and *kāñjana*.

Having internally smeared a copper vessel with a paste of *paripelava*, *kāsīsa*, the two types of *haridrā*, mustard seeds, *priyaṅgu*, *tagara*, and long pepper (*pippalī*), one should let it remain for seven days with its opening facing downward inside a jar of fermented gruel (*sauvīraka*). Thereafter, one may prepare pills or powder from it.
A pill made of the powder of *tuttha* and red ochre (*gairika*) ground with goat’s milk serves as an eye-salve (*añjana*).
Alternatively, that same powder, when infused with divine water (divyodaka),
or that same [liquid] when sprinkled [with it], serves as eye-drops; and regarding this,
there is a verse:
One suffering from eye-pillar disease (pillārōga) should repeatedly undergo scraping of the eyelids, bloodletting in the same manner,
and frequent purgation.
When the discharge of pus has not subsided, one should apply cauterization with a fine probe; thus, by means of etiology,
symptoms, and therapeutic measures, there are ninety-four eye diseases.
The various types of *gadā* (pains), described in their entirety without mutual confusion,
should always be attended to; even one who is healthy should practice that which is pleasing to the eyes.
Ancient barley, wheat, śāli rice, ṣaṣṭika rice, and kodrava,
as well as mung beans and other such grains that destroy kapha and pitta, should be thoroughly saturated with abundant ghee.
Likewise, one should take such vegetables, meat from wild animals,
pomegranate, sugar, rock salt, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), grapes, and celestial water for drinking.

One should use an umbrella and footwear, and perform purification of the bodily humors according to the prescribed rules. One should avoid suppressing natural urges, as well as eating before the previous meal is digested or overeating.
Anger, grief, sleeping during the day, staying awake at night, exposure to the sun, and any food or medicine here that causes burning sensations or constipation— [these should be avoided].
The two vessels that extend from the middle of the feet with a broad distribution reach the eyes in many ways;
they lead the eye [to receive] applications such as copper-based collyrium, rubbing powders, ointments, and so forth, when applied to the feet.
The eyes are corrupted by the contact with dust, heat, pressure,
and so forth; therefore, one who desires the welfare of his vision should always employ shoes, ointments, and cleansing.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter.
Now begins the twenty-first chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter entitled "The Diagnosis of Ear Diseases."
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:
"By nasal catarrh, playing in water, and scratching the ears, the wind [is provoked]."
Due to improper application of sound, or by other aggravating factors, the [doshas], becoming provoked,
reach the vessels of the ear and produce a forceful pain within the auditory canal.
Hemiplegia (ardhāvabhedaka), rigidity, and a lack of desire for cold things [occur];
after a long time, suppuration sets in, and when it is ripe, lymph (lasīkā) flows out only in small quantities.
The ear suddenly becomes empty, accompanied by a sense of movement and shifting;
there is piercing pain from bile with a burning sensation and distress, a desire for cold, and tremors with fever.
That which is quickly ripening or fully ripened, discharging a flow of pus and lymph,
and whatever comes into contact with that lymph, undergoes putrefaction.
From *kapha*, there is heaviness of the head, jaw, and neck, as well as dullness,
pain, itching, swelling, a desire for warmth, and, upon suppuration, a thick white discharge.
It causes pain in the ear when it is afflicted by trauma and the like;
the blood and pitta produce symptoms similar to those [of the previous type], though perhaps slightly more severe.
Shula (piercing pain) arises from the aggravated doshas, accompanied by swelling, fever, and intense pain;
it alternately desires heat and cold and is associated with dullness of hearing.
When located in a sound-carrying vessel, the wind repeatedly causes one to hear a discharge of pus that is ripe and thick, white, black,
or red.
They say that various sounds in the ears arise not from an external cause; rather,
it is the wind accompanied by phlegm, or the sound itself, which has been neglected.
If one speaks loudly with great effort, it causes deafness gradually; furthermore, Kapha, dried up by the heat, coats the channels, and from that, deafness arises.
Heaviness and swelling of the ear are known as *pratīnāha*; itching and swelling caused by *kapha* that are firm in the ear are designated by that same name (*pratīnāha*).
Kapha, when vitiated by pitta,
produces pūtikarṇaka (putrefying ear disease), which may be painful or painless and is characterized by thick, putrid, and profuse discharge.
When the ear is vitiated by Vāta and other humors, organisms that feed upon the flesh, blood, and moisture cause a sharp pain; this is known as Kṛmikarṇaka (earworm).

An abscess (vidradhi) characterized by the aforementioned symptoms arises from an injury caused by scratching the ear; another type is called a swelling (śopha), while a tumor (arśobuda) is described as follows.
In those cases, there occurs, respectively, suppuration and putrefaction of the ear, as well as deafness; furthermore,
when the ear-canal is constricted in the womb due to *vāta*, it results in *kūrcikarṇaka*.
Whether alone or accompanied by disease, this single mass of flesh, like a sprout, becomes firm within the womb.
Pippalī and pippalīmāna arise from the derangement of all three humors (sannipāta); that swelling (śvayathu), which is accompanied by pain, is stiff, and is called vidārikā when neglected.
When mature, it exudes a secretion resembling pungent oil and heals with difficulty;
once healed, it certainly causes the ear-passage to contract.
When the Vāyu located in the vessels causes the drying up of the earlobe, it is called Pālīśoṣa. When the earlobe becomes thin and firm like a string due to Vāta, it is known as Tantrikā.
In one who is delicate, [the disease] increases suddenly due to long-term neglect.

AS.Utt.2
Inflammation of the ear accompanied by pain, redness, and cracking occurs;
this cracking arises from vāta, while swelling with tearing pain arises from pitta and blood.

A swelling caused by the weight of heavy ornaments and the like is dark-brown in color, accompanied by pain, burning, and suppuration; it is characterized by eruptions, pustules, redness, heat, and moisture.
In the jaw (pālyāṃ), a swelling arising from vāta, pitta, and kapha is painless, firm, fixed,
of the same color as the surrounding skin, itchy, and is known as unmāntha or gallira.
When the ear is improperly pierced or has grown too large, there occurs itching, burning, suppuration,
and pain; this swelling arising from the derangement of all three humors (sannipāta) is known by the name Duḥkhavardhana.
Those small pustules arising from phlegm, blood, and worms, accompanied by itching, moisture, and pain,
are called *lihya*; for if neglected, they lick away the earlobe.
Pippalī, sarvaja-śūla, vidārī, and kūcikarṇaka— among these, one (kūcikarṇaka) is incurable, one (vidārī) is palliable, while the others may be cured.
Thus, twenty-five diseases of the ear have been described according to their classification.
This concludes the twenty-first chapter.
The twenty-second chapter: The Treatment of Diseases of the Ear (Karṇarogapratiṣedha).
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter titled "The Treatment of Diseases of the Ear."
"Thus said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:

in the case of earache caused by Vāta, one should drink at night after every meal of meat-broth (rasa) ghee prepared with Vāta-alleviating substances, either on an empty stomach or with milk as an after-drink."
Then,
when goat’s milk has been processed with the ten roots (daśamūla) and a cow’s horn has been placed therein, one should take red-hot stones with tongs and throw them into it.
One should thoroughly anoint the area with that heat and foment it using steam from a tube (*nāḍīsveda*).
Alternatively, one may foment it with boiled leaves of *bilva*, barley, jujube, horse-gram, black gram, *arka*, and *śigru*, along with the meat of marshy animals.

Once the patient has been sweated, one should fill the cavity with oil cooked with *kuṣṭha*, *rāsnā*, *madhuka*, bamboo scrapings, ginger, peacock feathers, *candraka*, black gram, *sarala*, and milk.
Or [an oil] prepared with milk eight times the quantity of a paste of *jīvaka*, *madhuka*, *kuṣṭha*, *maṇḍūkī*, *devadāru*, and *mahauṣadha*;

or with oil and muscle fat processed with a paste of peacock feathers, horse gram (*kulattha*), *aguru*, black gram (*māṣa*), and *devadāru*, along with alkali, fermented gruel (*śukta*), and sour liquids.
Or with the fat of a boar cooked with milk and a paste of madhuka, kṣīrakākoli, māṣa, śatāvarī, and all the aromatic substances (sarvagandha);
or with the fat of a porpoise cooked with milk and a paste of rāsnā, madhuka, kākoli, and devadāru.
One should administer the fat of a monitor lizard cooked with māṃsī, kuṣṭha, medā, sarala, surabhi, madhuka, and milk;
or one should employ the fat of a cock or a peacock prepared with jīvaka, śatāhvā, madhuka, and māṃsī along with milk, for filling the ears, as nasal drops, or for massage.

Alternatively, one may use oil prepared with a paste of madhuka, kṣīrakākolī, and śigru, along with four parts of the juice of the small *pañcamūla* and eight parts of the juice of castor leaves, boiled with milk.
Or, fresh leaves of the *aśvattha* tree, smeared with ghee, oil, and muscle fat, should be cooked by the *puṭapāka* method; once squeezed, one should fill the ear with that expressed juice.
And likewise, one should apply oil and salt to the leaves of any one of the following: arka, uru, pūga, mūlaka, kāraluka, bilva,
or mahāvṛkṣa.

AS.Utt.22.10: One should take a piece of wood eighteen finger-breadths long from either the great five roots (*mahāpañcamūla*), *sarala*, *agaru*, or *devadāru*; wrap it at one-third [of its length] with linen cloth, drench it with oil, and set fire to the tip.
Then, the first oil that drips from it while burning shall immediately remove earache.

AS.Utt.22.11 One should smear a linen cloth—having the dimensions and thickness of a smoking wick—with finely ground *madhūcchiṣṭa*, *kaḍarya*, the fruit of *madhuśigru*, *vacā*, *yavānala*, *elā*, and *guggulu*; then, having wrapped it with thread, one should give it to the patient to inhale smoke through a *ḍuṇḍuka* tube.
AS.Utt.22.12 Alternatively, one may apply this paste to the *ḍuṇḍuka* tube itself, dry it, and then administer the smoke.
One should apply an external ointment to the ear using *śreyasī*, *devadāru*, *kākoli*, *kuṣṭha*, and the seeds of *nicula*, ground with milk and mixed with sesame seeds.
One should apply a poultice (*utkārikā*) prepared with all types of grains, fats, and cow’s milk over the ear covered with castor leaves for the purpose of fomentation; furthermore,

one should repeatedly employ tube-fomentations (*nāḍīsveda*) and bolus-fomentations (*piṇḍasveda*), and perform the treatments prescribed for wind-diseases (*vātavyādhi*), coryza (*pratiśyāya*), and facial paralysis (*ardita*), including both non-unctuous and unctuous enemas (*nirūha* and *anuvāsana*).
One should especially avoid things that ought to be avoided, namely exposure to strong winds, drinking cold water, and bathing the head.
In the case of a colic arising from Pitta, one should administer ghee mixed with sugar in the morning.
Thereafter, one should administer an unctuous purgative;
furthermore, breast milk processed with *drākṣā* and *madhuka* should be used as an ear-drop.
Honey, or ghee prepared with a paste of madhuka and padmaka,

or ghee cooked with sugar, madhuka, dates, and grapes along with milk and sugarcane juice, or priyāla oil boiled with these, when used for massage, nasal drops, or ear-filling, destroys pain and burning sensations.

Having prepared one kuḍava of madhuka with sixteen times its weight of water until eight parts remain, one should cook half a kuḍava of oil with eight times its weight of milk and the paste consisting of yaṣṭīmadhu, uśīra, sārivā, kākolī, jīvaka, anantā, mṛṇāla, mañjiṣṭhā, lodhra, candana, and bisa;
this should be administered as previously described.
One should smear the area around the ear with a paste of these very same ingredients mixed with ghee,
and then apply fomentation.
Likewise, nasal drops of milk and clarified butter (sarpiḥ) and anointing of the head should be administered; if there is still no relief, however, a purgative should be given again.
In the case of a kaphaja [headache], one should induce vomiting after having the patient drink either ghee cooked with long pepper (pippalī) or ghee mixed with honey.
Then one should administer strong smoke and fill his ear with oil prepared with *sarala*, *devadāru*, *hiṃsrā*, and the leaves of *paṭola*, along with sour gruel (*surasā*).
Alternatively, [the eye] may be treated with oil prepared from the decoction and paste of *devadāru*, *pippalī*, *mālatī* leaves, *haridrā*, *kuṣṭha*, *triphalā*, and *elā*;
or with the juice of *rasāñjana*, *mārkava*, *vaijayantī*, *śigru*, garlic, fresh ginger, radish, banana, or *kadala*—either individually or all together; or with honey; or with *rakṣoghnataila*.
Likewise, piercing pain, swelling, and heaviness are pacified;
one should apply tube-sudation (nāḍīsveda) using the steam from a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla) boiled in fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla).
One should fill [the ear] with oil prepared with boiled *kuśa*, *āmrātaka*, *trivṛt*, *nalada*, *śuṇṭhī*, and *musta*,
and one should hold gargles (gaṇḍūṣa) consisting of drugs that subdue *kapha*.
In cases arising from blood (*raktaja*) or *pitta*, the treatment is successful as in the *paittika* type, and venesection (*sirāvyadha*) should also be performed.
In cases of suppurated earaches accompanied by the discharge of pus, one should administer, as appropriate, medicated smoking, nasal drops, gargles, and emetics.

When the canal is smeared, one should wipe it morning and evening with cotton-wool swabs (*picuvarti*), fumigate it with a mixture of *yava*, *aguru*, and *madanaka* along with clarified butter or with *guggulu*, and then fill it with honey.

Having thoroughly lubricated a cotton-wool swab with a medicinal extract (*rasakriyā*) prepared from a decoction of the barks of *palāśa*, *dhava*, *tiniśa*, *kakubha*, and *sarja*, one should insert it into the canal.

Likewise, with a decoction of *badarī*, *sallakī*, *jambū*, *dhātakī*, *vaṭa*, *plakṣa*, *udumbara*, and by means of a medicinal extract (*rasakriyā*) prepared from a decoction of *haridrā*, *dhātakī*, *triphalā*, *jambū*, *sallakī*, and *kiṃśuka*.
Likewise, by means of a decoction of *saurāṣṭrikā*, *padmaka*, *dhātakī*, *samaṅgā*, *aśvattha*, *dhavala-udumbara*, and *rasāñjana*,
and by sprinkling the channels with the fine powder of these very same medicinal herbs, moisture, pain, and heaviness are pacified. (AS.Utt.22.25)

Washing with the decoction of these very same [herbs] mixed with honey, or with the fresh juice of *kapittha*, as well as the application of the *surasā* group [of herbs] for washing and dusting, should be employed; furthermore,
the entire procedure prescribed for earache due to *vāta* is also indicated for deafness caused by *nāda*.
If there is an association with phlegm (kapha), one should first eliminate the phlegm by means of emesis, nasal medication (nasya), and strong medicinal smokes. Furthermore,
deafness should be avoided [as a treatment] in children, the elderly, the emaciated, those suffering from cough or wasting (śoṣa), and when it has been present for a long time.
However,
the other [type] should be treated by means of oleation, sudation, head-pouch enemas (śirobasti), rectal enemas (bastikarma), and so forth, after considering the persistence of the humors (doṣas).
In that case, one should first administer a purgative using either aged ghee or vāta-alleviating oil after the patient has been lubricated with unctuous substances;
once the process of dietary rehabilitation (saṃsarjana) is complete and the patient is again lubricated, one should then extract the blood.

Then, one should apply leeches close to the ear, followed by enemas, head-oil massage, nasal drops, medicinal smoke, and ear-drops; one should habitually employ these treatments. One should boil young *bilva* fruits in cow’s urine, and with that decoction, along with a paste of sugar, *madhuka*, and *bījaka* seeds, one should cook oil mixed with milk.

That oil, while warm, should be poured into a cold decoction of *bilva* and stirred until it forms a solid mass; having removed it, one should stir it again in another *bilva* decoction. Then, having removed it and cooked it in eight times its quantity of milk containing *madhuka*, *gandha*, and *candana*, its application as an ear-drop quickly destroys deafness.
Freshly harvested sesame seeds, bound in a cloth, should be kept overnight in flowing water and dried during the day for five nights.

When five nights have passed in this manner, one should soak and dry [the material] for another five days in milk boiled with liquorice (*madhuyaṣṭikā*), *kṣīrakākolī*, the great pentad of roots (*mahāpañcamūla*), *devadāru*, *śatāhvā*, and *jīvaka*. Then,
one should press it together with a measured amount of the powder of these very same substances mixed with that same milk.

One should cook that oil with a paste of blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), *anantā*, sandalwood, agallochum, licorice, *jīvaka*, *kākolī*, *suniṣaṇṇaka*, and radish, along with eight times the amount of milk.

When administered as a nasal drop, an ear-drop, or an external massage for the head, it quickly removes pain, piercing aches, and deafness, as well as all disorders of Vāta associated with Pitta; it also promotes the healing of fractured bones.

Oil prepared with dried radish, ash, the two types of alkali (kṣāra), asafoetida, dry ginger, misī, vacā, kuṣṭha, devadāru, saubhāñjana, the nodes of birch bark, mustā, the three salts, and udbhida, combined with fermented gruel (śukta), plantain juice, and citron juice, is effective for earache, ringing in the ears, deafness, itching, swelling, discharge, exudation, worms,
and putrefaction of the ear. Now, if the ears feel as if they are numb, one should venesect a vein in that vicinity as previously described.
In cases of swelling and discharge associated with impaired hearing, one should administer emesis.

In *pratīnāha* (obstruction of the ear canal), after the ear has been moistened with oleation and sudation and cleansed with an ear-cleansing instrument (*karṇaśodhana*), one should fill it with oil, or with the juice of *mātuluṅga*, or with vinegar, honey, and rock salt (*saindhava*).
If,
while being cleansed, there is pain or the emergence of blood, then one should fill [the cavity] with the scum of clarified butter (ghṛtamaṇḍa) and practice nasal medication (nasya).
This same procedure applies even when the ear is full of pus;
in cases of itching, one should apply sharp nasal drops, medicated smoke, and other remedies that subdue *kapha*.
Food that is dry, bitter,
and pungent is likewise prescribed for swelling; so too are poultices and affusions that are pungent, sharp, and hot.

In cases of putrid ear (pūtikarṇa) and worm-infested ear (kṛmikarṇa), the procedure prescribed for ear discharge (karṇasrāva) should be applied; however, in this specific instance, anti-worm remedies are particularly required.
Likewise, filling [the cavity] with mustard oil,
or with cow's urine mixed with yellow orpiment powder,
or fumigating it with the seed of a bitter gourd (vārtāka).
One should treat ear abscess (*karṇavidradhi*)— both its raw and suppurated stages— like [the treatment for] an abscess (*vidradhi*), preceded by emesis.
One should treat wound abscess (*kṣatavidradhi*), ear pain caused by *pitta*, hemorrhoids, nasal polyps, and tumors (*arbuda*) in the same manner.

One should treat the unripe *vidārikā* like a carbuncle of the ear (*karṇavidradhi*), according to the manifestation of the respective doshas. In the case of atrophy of the earlobe (*pālīśoṣa*), one should apply nasal drops (*nasya*), ointments (*ālepa*), and fomentation (*sveda*), as in the treatment for Vata-type pain.
When the patient has sweated, one should rub the body with a paste made of sesame, *priyāla* seeds, *madhuka*, barley, and *aśvagandhā*. Once rubbed,

one should massage the body with oil prepared by boiling it with a paste of *madhuka*, *payasyā*, *śatapuṣpā*, *aśvagandhā*, and eight times as much of a decoction of *vājigandhā*, *bṛhatī*, and *abhīru*.
Alternatively, one should cook [an oil] with *śatāvarī*, *aśvagandhā*, *eraṇḍa*, *payasyā*, and *jīvakā* prepared with milk;

or, having collected the fat, marrow, ghee, and mustard oil from the meat of iguanas (*godhā*), birds of prey (*pratuda*), gallinaceous birds (*viṣkira*), marsh-dwellers (*ānūpa*), and aquatic animals (*audaka*) as available, one should boil it with an addition (*pratīvāpa*) of *arka*, *alarka*, *balā*, *atibalā*, *anantā*, *vidārigandhā*, *jalaśūka*, and the drugs of the sweet group (*madhuravarga*). This massage is supreme for generating flesh in a sore.

Even so, however, whatever portion of the earlobe (pālī) has been destroyed, one should cut away what is diseased, join it according to the prescribed rule, and treat it according to the stated sequence.
One should manage a *tantrikā* in exactly the same way, by means of nasal medication (*nasya*), massage (*abhyaṅga*), and so forth. This same procedure applies to *paripoṭaka* as well.

Likewise, a great unctuous preparation (*mahāsneha*) is prepared for massage (*abhyaṅga*) from *madhuka*, *kharamañjarī*, rock salt (*saindhava*), *aśvagandhā*, the roots of *devadāru*, *avalguja* fruit and root, and beeswax (*madhūcchiṣṭa*), combined with milk.
A poultice (*upanāha*) is prepared from a bolus (*utkārikā*) made of sesame, *madhuka*, *prapauṇḍarīka*, white mustard (*siddhārthaka*), ghee, and milk.

When bleeding has been removed by leeches during an emergency (utpāta), a cold medicinal paste should be applied. Oil prepared with sesame, madhuka, sārivā, utpala, lodhra, kadamba, balā, and the tender leaves of āmra and jambu, along with fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla), should be used for massage.
Likewise, the ghees mentioned in the treatment of visarpa (erysipelas) involving milk and clarified butter [should be used]; in cases of unmantha, head-purgation with strong drugs is indicated.

For an earlobe that has been rubbed with sesame, mustard, *lodhra*, and the two types of *haridrā*, an ointment should be applied consisting of *tālīsa*, *tamāla*, cardamom, *kaṭphala*, and *rasāñjana*. Alternatively, oil cooked with *tālapattrī*, *aśvagandhā*, *arka*, rock salt (*saindhava*), seeds of *avalguja*, *surasā*, and *lāṅgalikā*, combined with the fat of a monitor lizard (*godhā*) and a crab (*kulīra*), should be used as an unguent; or simply oil [cooked] with *paṭola*, *kaṭurohiṇī*, *rasāñjanī*, and *śarīṣa*.

In the case of an increase in pain, one should sprinkle the earlobe with a decoction of the leaves of *jambu*, mango (*āmra*), and *aśmantaka*; then, having anointed it with oil, one should dust it with the powder of licorice (*yaṣṭīmadhuka*), turmeric (*haridrā*), *prapauṇḍarīka*, and *mañjiṣṭhā*.
One should also anoint it with oil cooked with lac (*lākṣā*) and *viḍaṅga*.

In cases of *lehikā* and *piṭaka*, one should repeatedly apply a paste made of *kṛmighna* (vermifuge) drugs ground with the urine of a sheep to the earlobe that has been softened by fomentation with cow dung and *āpaṇḍa*;
or alternatively, a paste made from the bark of *kuṭaja*, *karañja*, *iṅguda* seeds, and *āragvadha*.

Furthermore, mustard oil prepared with all these—sugar, nimba leaves, and beeswax—is an ointment for massage that destroys ulcerated sores; in cases of burning sensations, one should cause blood to flow by means of lotus flowers and apply cold poultices.
In all diseases of the earlobes, one should appropriately employ oleation, sudation, purification, massage, external application, nasal drops, and bloodletting.
One should avoid the causes of provocation; furthermore,
when a fistula-in-ano (pāli) is developing, an ointment should be applied consisting of the barks of *sarjarasa*, *apāmārga*, *paṭola*, *nimba*, and *nicula*.

When [the wound] is ulcerating, [one should apply] the bile of a hog and the fat and marrow of a monitor lizard along with *śigru*, *śamyāka*, and *pūtīka*; when it is dark-brown, [one should apply] the roots of *gaurī*, *sugandhā*, *śyāmā*, *anantā*, and *taṇḍulīyaka*.
In the case of itching (kaṇḍūmatī), after incision, [one should apply] pāṭhā, tārkṣya, śaileya, and honey;
in the case of burning (dahyamānā), a paste of milk-exuding trees and jīvanīya drugs with honey and ghee;
and in the case of ulceration (vraṇitā), honey and jīvanīya drugs.

In the case of a thin ulcer, after breaking open the knots and scraping it with the fats of a monitor lizard and a boar, one should rub it with black salt, rock salt, and honey; for an ulcer containing sinews,
an ointment should be applied consisting of honey, licorice, madhūka, and madhuparṇī.

One should prepare these very substances for their respective purposes as unctuous applications and massages; then, depending on the disease or the strength [of the patient], one should rejoin an ear that has been severed.
In brief, there are fifteen ear-joints (karṇasandhi), which generally occur according to their specific names, shapes, and locations. They are as follows:
One with both eyelashes broad, long, and even is called *cakranemi*. One with both eyelashes round, long, and even is called *utpalabhedaka*.
A door with long inner panels. AS.Utt.22.56. A door.
AS.Utt.22.57: The *viparītorddhakavāṭa* (inverted upper-lid).
The *vallūraka* (leather-like), which has both eyelids short, round, and even.
The hair-whorls (pāli) may be minute, thick, regular, or irregular; this is the vyāyojima [type].
The outer rim is the support for the cheeks; that which is contrary to this, however, is the *āsaṅgima*.
Apālī said:
"He should be brought here.
That very fleshy seat is pierced;
it is like a dried fish-cake with its edges swollen up.
One with small earlobes is "contracted" (saṅkṣipta);
one with no earlobe attachment and with flesh wasted away at the edges is "deficient" (hīna).
With a body possessing uneven, small,
and long hairs.
A *yaṣṭī* (stick-like) ulcer is characterized by knotted, fleshless, stiff,
and vein-covered narrow edges; a *kākauṣṭha* (crow-beak) ulcer has fleshless, contracted tips and blood-stained edges.
Among these,
the first ten are curable.
But in that case, when the external sheath is long, the internal joint is not [so].
Likewise, in the other [direction], the external [wind] is equal when the two [winds] are equal;
however, when they are unequal, such as in the case of the subtle [wind] and so forth, there is a mutual reversal.
If, however,
there should be only a single suture that is thick, broad, and firm, one should split it in two, cut the upper part, and join them together.
One should fashion the earlobe using flesh cut from a goitre, along with blood and its connective tissue;
this same procedure applies even for one who lacks both earlobes.

Alternatively, having transferred [the ear] to the ear-ornament due to defects such as being of equal age, one should place it evenly in the middle and perform the augmentation. Furthermore, regarding the procedure for joining: when the hair at the edge of the ear has been bound and the wound is healed, one should prepare the ear with appropriate instruments for excision, incision, or scraping, and then examine the blood to see whether it is vitiated or not.

AS.Utt.22.75 Then, having washed a fracture vitiated by Vāta with fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla) and warm water, one vitiated by Pitta with milk and cold water, or one vitiated by Śleṣman with *vāruṇī* wine and water, and having scraped it again so that the joint is placed without being elevated, depressed, or uneven; then, having anointed it with honey and ghee and wrapped it with either a cotton pad (*picu*) or a cloth (*plota*), one should bind it with a thread neither too tight nor too loose, scatter it with the powder of a skull as prescribed for venesection, and instruct the patient on the regimen.
AS.Utt.22.76 One should suture a joint that does not close together with a linen thread (*kṣauma-sūtra*).
Or, if the lip is excessively thinned, one should wrap it with a cotton pad soaked in blood and treat it like an ulcer.

After three or four days, having sprinkled it with water, one should remove the cotton and the thread; however, one should not join an ear that is impure, bleeding excessively, or where the blood has become depleted (AS.Utt.22.77). For in such a case, even if joined by itself, the union will separate, the ear will swell, turn dark-brown, suppurate, dry up, heal slowly, and even when healed, it will not tolerate ornaments.
In that case, there occurs swelling, itching, burning, and nodular growths;
one should treat it according to its specific nature.
In the case of vitiated blood, one should perform bloodletting;

in the case of depleted blood, one should nourish it with the drinking of fats, nasal medication (nasya), meat broth, and massage. In all such cases, even when the joint is accompanied by complications, one should release the joint and, having restored the memory of previous treatments, set it correctly.
And there is a verse on this point:
One should not perform the suturing of an ear that is afflicted with swelling, redness, and other such symptoms.
It should not be applied to one who is gluttonous, nor when it is excessively hot, nor to one whose body is impure; rather,
it should be applied when the wound is well-healed, hair has grown back, the joints are joined, and it is even and firm.
One should gradually enlarge the ear so that it becomes well-formed and free from disease;
otherwise, burning sensations, pain, piercing, and swelling will occur, for which one must provide treatment.
Cold applications, affusions, and the like, as well as purification that destroys moisture, [should be used]; likewise,
oil from fatty animals or marshy regions, ghee, and lac-resin in equal parts.
One should prepare a paste from the sweet group of drugs (madhuraskandha), horse-gram (hayagandhā),
and peacock flesh, ground with ten times the amount of milk; this is the supreme means for increasing the size of the ears.
Hard, painful, and emaciated ulcers, when treated with poultices, massaged, anointed with oil,
and fomented, become soft, painless, and stable.
Bṛhatī, the two types of bṛhatī, kacchurā, vāriśūka, arka-jaṭā,
ghee, honey, śaṅkhinī, and oil [should be kept] for seven days in a copper vessel.
One should fix that [instrument] at the ear and nourish what is emaciated until it reaches the size of a leech;
the lizard-skin, the leech, the horse-tether, and the *śabara-kandaka* are equal [in application].

One should apply a plaster of *kapittha* fruit combined with buffalo butter for the purpose of increasing the ears; these methods of anointing and plastering are proclaimed for cases of facial wasting (*pali-śoṣa*).
Now, one should restore the severed nose of a healthy person.
One should cut the skin flap equal in size to the nose, and likewise from the cheek;
one should preserve the skin and flesh near the nose and bring it to a state of thinness.
Then one should suture the swelling with a needle and a suture combined with a wick (picu). After the nose has been incised and the flesh scraped away, one should turn the skin upward.
One should join the cheek-flap and diligently sew the nose; one should draw it inward through two tubes for the sake of facilitating easy respiration.
Having sprinkled it with raw oil (āmataila), one should subsequently dust it with a very fine powder of pataṅga, madhuka, añjana, and other blood-stasis-inducing substances.
Then, having bound it after anointing it with honey and ghee, one should prescribe the regimen;
once the subsequent stage has been recognized, one should thereafter perform the treatment for fresh wounds.
One should excise any excess flesh that has grown over and the skin from the edge of the nose; then,
having sutured it very smoothly, one should again increase any deficient portion.

This same procedure applies even to a nose that has been recently severed, provided it is repositioned according to its original placement. For one whose nostrils have failed due to the joining of the channels, the procedure is like that for the restoration of the nasal bridge.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter.
Now begins the twenty-third chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter titled "The Diagnosis of Diseases of the Nose.
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
Through exposure to dew, wind, and dust; through excessive talking, sleeping, or staying awake;
by using a pillow that is too low or too high; or by drinking other [unwholesome] water.
Due to excessive drinking of water, sexual indulgence, vomiting, suppression of tears, and other such factors, the humors (doṣas),
with vāta predominating, become aggravated and reach a state of thickening within the nose.
They produce catarrh that increases and brings about wasting. Among these, in the case of a vāta-type catarrh, there is extreme dryness of the mouth and frequent sneezing.
There is obstruction and piercing pain in the nose, as well as distress in the teeth, temples, and head;
one feels as if insects are crawling all around the eyebrows.
From *kapha*, there is a natural loss of taste, delayed suppuration, and the discharge of cold,
clear phlegm; from *pitta*, there is thirst, fever, nasal inflammation, the appearance of pustules, and vertigo.
From *kapha*, there is inflammation of the tip of the nose, dryness, heat, and a discharge of copper-colored or yellow phlegm;
cough, loss of appetite, dyspnea, vomiting, and heaviness of the limbs arise from *kapha*.
Sweetness in the mouth, itching, and the discharge of unctuous, white phlegm;
the type caused by all three doshas (sarvaja) possesses all these symptoms and is characterized by sudden onset and subsidence.
When vitiated blood reaches the nasal vessels, it causes rhinitis (pratiśyāya),
numbness of the chest, reddish-brown eyes, and foul-smelling breath.
There is itching in the ears, eyes, and nose, and the symptoms mentioned for pitta are also present here. All types of catarrh (pratiśyāya) become malignant if neglected.

Due to the excess of the aforementioned complications, it causes affliction to all the sense organs; it is accompanied by fever with a burning sensation as if from fire, dyspnea, cough, and pain in the chest and flanks.
It causes frequent and sudden anger, foul breath, and dryness;
it repeatedly produces moisture, dryness, purification, and obstruction in the nose.
There is a discharge of phlegm mixed with pus-like white and red matter;
furthermore, worms that are long, glossy, and minute in size multiply therein.
The signs of their maturation include lightness of the limbs and the cessation of sneezing.
Phlegm (śleṣman) is very黏稠 (viscid), yellow, and the [source of] cognition regarding taste and smell.
It is pierced by sharp points, such as the application of sunbeams, threads, grass, and so forth.
When the cartilaginous bone of the nose is struck by those things that provoke vāta or by other causes,
the agitated vāta, being obstructed, enters the junction of the nasal septum (śṛṅgāṭaka).
When it has subsided, that wind causes excessive sneezing known as *bhṛśakṣava*; drying up the nasal passages, it produces phlegm.

When the nose has the appearance of being filled with porcupine quills and there is labored breathing, that is known as *nāsikāśoṣa* (nasal dryness); however, *nāsānāha* (nasal constriction) arises [from a different cause].
AS.Utt.23.17 When the wind is obstructed by phlegm, it is as if there were a binding of the nose;
due to the obstruction of inhalation and exhalation, the two channels seem as if they were closed.
When pitta cooks within the nostrils, causing burning and pain in the skin and flesh,
that is *ghrāṇapāka* (inflammation of the nose); the discharge resulting from it is known by the same name when it arises from *śleṣman*.
AS.Utt.23.19: It is clear, resembling water, and arises incessantly, especially at night.
Kapha, having increased in the nose, obstructs the channels and causes avīnasa.
One should recognize [this condition] by a rattling sound in the breath and excessive pain in the nose;
because of it, the nose becomes excessively moistened and discharges like that of a goat.
Constantly oozing, slimy, cold, thick, and like cooked mucus;
when the nose is burned by blood, it becomes unable to endure touch, both internally and externally.
When the root of the palate is afflicted by impurities, the breath becomes like smoke, and the wind (māruta) seems to burn as it exits through the mouth and nose.
If phlegm and pus should issue forth, they call it *pūtināsa* (putrid nose). Due to the accumulation [of humors] or from injury, pus and blood may flow from the nose.

That is declared to be *pūyarakta* (pus-blood), which causes burning and pain in the head. When the wind (*marut*), obstructed by bile (*pitta*) and phlegm (*śleṣman*), dries up [the secretions] within the nose, [it produces this condition].

When that [kapha] dries up, it attains the state of a *puṭa*; that is indeed a *puṭaka*. One should distinguish the hemorrhoids (*arśas*) and tumors (*arbuda*) according to their respective symptoms of the [doshas].
In all [these conditions], there is difficult breathing, chronic rhinitis, and persistent sneezing.
Hoarseness with nasal resonance, fetid nose, and headache— by treating these eighteen [conditions], one may cure malignant chronic rhinitis (duṣṭapīnasa).
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter.
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter.
Hereafter, we shall expound the chapter named "The Treatment of Diseases of the Nose."
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and others:

"In all cases of *pīnasa* (nasal catarrh), one should first employ oleation, sudation, emesis, medicated smoking, gargling, unctuous and warm food, and lying or sitting in a windless place. (AS.Utt.24.2)
For the purpose of ripening [the doshas], one should consume jaggery, fresh ginger, milk, the three pungents (trikaṭu), goat meat, wine, and sour foods. Furthermore,
one should repeatedly inhale the powder of rohiṣa, ajājī, vacā, coraka, upakuñcikā, tarkārī, and the four aromatics (cāturjātaka), bound in a cloth.
Having placed barley meal mixed with ghee inside a hollowed-out gourd shell, one should inhale the smoke;
once it has cooked, one should employ head-evacuants (śirovirecana) and nasal drops (avapīḍa).
And one should avoid those things mentioned in the section on etiology (nidāna).

Specifically, one should avoid bathing in cold water, drinking [cold water], very high pillows, lack of pillows, anger, and grief (AS.Utt.24.7). Furthermore, in the case of vāta-type coryza, one should first drink ghee processed with vāta-alleviating substances and rock salt in the morning, or the Mahāṣaṭpala ghee (AS.Utt.24.7).

Ghee prepared with *daśamūla*, horse gram (*kulattha*), jujube (*kola*), barley, dried radish, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), the five salts, curd, and fermented grain-water (*dhānyāmla*), when administered in food and drink, cures catarrh, consumption, cough, dyspnea, malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*), abdominal tumors (*gulma*), and constipation.

Once the oil has been digested, one should feed the patient meat broth from wild animals seasoned with the three pungents, pomegranate, and rock salt; or with the juice of young radishes; or with a soup made from all types of grains.
One should drink *nāgara* with milk; or,
one should foment the head with milk prepared from a decoction of *kṛṣṇā*, *daśamūla*, *śuṇṭhī*, barley, and *eraṇḍa* roots.
One should prescribe that very same [diet] for drinks and food,
as well as the sudations described for those suffering from ardita (facial paralysis).

If [the swelling] does not ripen in this manner, one should repeatedly apply tube-sudation (nāḍīsvēda), vāta-alleviating non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana), unctuous enemas (anuvāsana), and head-pouches (śirobasti). Once it has ripened, however, one should administer head-purgatives (śirovirecana) consisting of oil mixed with the powder of *kṣavaka* and rock salt, or clarified butter.

In the case of *pitta-pratiśyāya* (pitte-based coryza), one should boil half a *ḍhaka* of each of the following—*padmaka*, *uśīra*, *paṭola*, *sārivā*, *vidārī*, *śatāvarī*, sprouts of milk-exuding trees (*kṣīridruma*), *śaṭhī*, *karkaṭākhyā*, and *durālabhā*—in eight times that amount of water until one-fourth remains. Then, adding one *mātrā* each of *madhuka*, *mṛdvīkā*, *candana*, *śṛṅgāṭaka*, *kaśeruka*, and *śvetapākā*, one should cook one *prastha* of ghee with milk.
This should be administered for drinking in the morning.
Once the [medicine] has been digested, one should feed the patient a very unctuous meal with meat-broth seasoned with rock salt and sprinkled with lukewarm water;

then, one should administer a purgative using a decoction of *drākṣā*, *paṭola*, *śrīparṇī*, *mūrvā*, and *trivṛt*, combined with the powder of *trivṛt*, *pathyā*, and *pūgaphala*. After the patient has been purged and has eaten, one should apply cool pastes and affusions to the head and face, and provide gargles.
And fanned by the breeze from a fan, he should resort to houses cooled by the spray of water and the rays of the moon, as well as groves of dark-green grass and gardens.
In that case, when the *doṣa* has matured, one should administer head-purgation (*śirovireka*) using aged ghee with rock salt, or with the scum of ghee (*ghṛtamaṇḍa*) combined with *kaṭphala*.
Once the channels have been purified, the diet should consist of meat broth from wild animals or cold milk.
In the case of [diarrhea] born of *kapha*, however, one should have the patient drink ghee dusted with *yavakṣāra* (barley-alkali) followed by warm water;
once that is digested, one should give him gruel containing sesame, *māṣa* beans, and meat-paste.

Then, one should induce emesis with a warm decoction of emetic medicinal herbs, prepared with ghee, enriched with a paste of *saindhava* salt and black gram (*māṣa*), and administered with warm water. Thereafter, one should treat the patient with sharp medicinal smoke, gargles, and a diet consisting primarily of barley, chickpeas, and vetch, as well as nasal drops and bloodletting.
In cases of anorexia and heaviness, one should purify [the head];
when [the doshas] have ripened, nasal medication (nasya) should be administered with kṣavaka, viḍaṅga, saindhava, and other such substances.
Food consisting of mung beans soaked in oil and mixed with powdered ginger, along with dry, sharp, and hot items according to one's constitution;
and for one whose nasal passages have been cleared, an errhine (nasya) of oil cooked with *devadāru*, *sarala*, *kākolī*, *jīvaka*, *madhuka*, *pippalī*, and *anantā* mixed with milk.
In the case of a sannipātika (combined) disorder, one should treat it according to the strength of the involved doshas;
furthermore, oil prepared with rasāñjana, ativiṣā, musta, and bhadradāru should be used here as nasal drops (nāvana).
In cases arising from blood (raktaja), the Pittic treatment and the regimen prescribed for Raktapitta should be followed.

In the case of malignant coryza (duṣṭapratiśyāya), one should administer ghee cooked with Trikaṭu, Citraka, Yavakṣāra, Bījaka, Viḍaṅga, the bark of Pūtīkarañja, and the three salts, with meat broth added as a post-decoction (pratīvāpa), and mixed with honey.
Once the ghee has been digested, one should feed the patient a meal with a base of meat broth from wild animals and sprinkle it with ghee;
furthermore, one should treat him as in the case of kaphaja coryza (pratiśyāya).
When [the swelling] has ripened, one should apply an *avapīḍa* (pressed snuff) made from *vyoṣa*, *indrayava*, *viḍaṅga*, *sāra*, *jīraka*, and *saindhava*, ground with goat’s urine.
Once the nasal passages have been purified, one should again lubricate them and administer a purgative (*virecana*).
One should boil fried barley grains together with *bhūstṛṇa*, *āmrātaka*, cumin, and *trivṛt* in cow’s urine; this decoction,
mixed with the powders of *abhayā*, ginger, black pepper, *kramuka*, rock salt, and *yāvaśūka*, along with the juice of *bījapūraka*, should be administered,
and lukewarm water should be given to swallow it down.

Once the patient has been purged, at the appropriate time, one should administer ghee prepared with *mustā*, *haridrā*, *nāgara*, *yavakṣāra*, *pūtīkarañja*, *reṇukā*, and the curd from the milk of goats, sheep, or cows;
as well as sharp *nirūha* and *anuvāsana* enemas.

And for the purpose of drinking, one should take *ariṣṭas*. If [the disease] is still not pacified even by this, one should drink ghee prepared with asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), alkali (*kṣāra*), and *amaradāru*, followed by meat broth as a post-drink (*anupāna*).

AS.Utt.24.26 Having made a smoking wick (*dhūmavarti*) from the following ingredients— *kośāmra*, *pallava*, *mūrvā*, *tarkārī*, the fruits of *iṅgudī*, *phaṇijjaka*, the great five roots (*mahāpañcamūla*), *kaṇṭakārikā*, *sāriva*, *urupūga*, *hiṃsrā*, *nimba*, *śigru*, the fruits of *rakṣoghnā* and *kṛmighna*, *dantī*, *pūtikarañja*, *pippalī*, the seeds of *vārtāka*, *ahimāraka*, and the root-bark-leaves-flowers-fruits [of these]— ground with goat’s urine and mixed with the liquid from goat and horse dung— one should give it to the patient to inhale after it has been smeared with ghee. AS.Utt.24.27 Furthermore, one should employ the *pippalī-vardhamāna* regimen.
One should treat [the patient] with vermifugal formulations (AS.Utt.24.27).

In cases of excessive sneezing and *puṭaka*, one should administer a blowing-in (pradhamana) of the powder of nimba, kaṭphala, kuṣṭha, and marica for the purpose of moistening (kledana) (AS.Utt.24.28).

Oil or ghee cooked with a decoction and paste of pippalī, kuṣṭha, śuṇṭhī, viḍaṅga, and mṛdvīkā should be used as nasal drops (nāvana) for dryness of the nose (nāsāśoṣa). For dryness of the nose, balā-taila should be administered both as a drink and as a head-poultice (śirobasti).
For one who has been treated with oleation, sudation is indicated, as well as nasal drops (nasya) of milk or ghee, or oil prepared with the sweet group of drugs (madhuravarga).
Likewise, when there is obstruction of the nose, medicated smoke is used;
if this does not alleviate it, cranial purgation (śirovireka) should be administered.
In cases of inflammation of the nose (nāsāpāka) and burning sensations, blood should be drained using leeches;
furthermore, cold emetics, purgatives, medicinal pastes, and affusions should be administered.
