In cases of nasal discharge, a strong nasal medication (nasya) and medicinal smoke (dhūma) should be administered.
In cases of non-flowing or putrid nose (pūtināsa), a nasal medication should be prepared from jaggery, black pepper, asafoetida, śivāṭikā, and viḍaṅga, ground together with goat’s urine.

As in the case of kaphaja coryza, one should administer oleation, sudation, and emesis (AS.Utt.24.32). For one who has been made to vomit, one should prepare mustard or *pīlu* oil by cooking it with the fresh juice of the leaves of *nirguṇḍī*, *śigru*, *tarkārī*, *phaṇijjaka*, *kṣavaka*, *surasā*, and *arjaka*, and then apply it as a nasal drop (*nasya*) (AS.Utt.24.32).
Alternatively, sesame oil may be prepared with a paste of lac, viḍaṅga, pippalī, lavaṅga, kṣavaka, niśā, kuṣṭha, vacā, and karañjikā;
or with śigru, bṛhatī, the roots of dantī, bilva, vyoṣa, surasa, and saindhava.
AS.Utt.24.34 One should treat pus and blood as soon as they appear like [the treatment for] bloody catarrh;
when it has increased, one should treat it like a sinus ulcer (nāḍī-vraṇa).
Once he has undergone emesis, one should administer nasal medication and medicated smoke;
furthermore, one should cauterize the hemorrhoids according to the prescribed rules with either alkali or fire.
In the case of large [foreign bodies], however, after touching them with a surgical instrument and performing cauterization, one should subsequently apply cooling measures.

One should also insert into the nose a wick (varti) smeared with a paste of kumbha, nikumbha, agnika, rock salt (saindhava), long pepper (pippalī), realgar (manaḥśilā), and orpiment (ala), mixed with honey and ghee.

Oil cooked with a paste of *tuvarikā*, *bibhītaka*, *haridrā*, *lodhra*, *priyaṅgu*, and *karañjikā*, along with jaggery and water, is used for nasal administration (*nāvana*). Oil cooked with a paste of *karañja*, *lodhra*, *utpala*, *madhuka*, seeds of *tinduka*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and the heartwood of *khadira* [is also used for this purpose].
One should administer oleation, emesis, purgation, and other therapies according to the specific dosha involved.
Having seized the tumor with a hook, one should cut it off evenly at its base using a circular blade.
A wound that has been cut, torn, or wiped by a moving object should be cauterized with a probe or with oil.

Once it has been cauterized with fire, one should then apply cooling plasters. When the ulcer has healed, a nasal medication (*nāvana*) consisting of mustard or *kārañja* oil mixed with *lodhra*, pungent, hot, and salty substances, and cow’s urine should be administered.

In cases of arbuda arising from pitta or blood, an application (ālepa) should be made with godanta, saindhava, ālaka, kāsīsa, kāṃsya, and nīla, ground together with water; thereafter, cooling plasters and affusions,
as well as medicated ghees prepared with the same cooling substances, should be used for massage, nasal administration, and internal consumption.

One should treat cases of hemorrhoids caused by the combination of muscle and fat, as well as tumors (arbuda), in this same manner. Regarding this, there is also a verse here: AS.Utt.24.41 One should treat hemorrhoids arising from the combination of muscle and fat, and likewise tumors, in this way.
And there is a verse on this point:
He summarizes:
From cutting too little there is regrowth; from excessive cutting, loss of voice.
One should likewise cut away [the skin] in cases of loss of smell, erysipelas, and fainting.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter;
now begins the twenty-fifth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter titled "The Diagnosis of Diseases of the Mouth.
Thus spoke the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
The flesh of fish, buffalo, and boar; raw roots;
bean soup, curd, milk, sour gruel, sugarcane juice, and molasses.
For one who sleeps on the ground and hates the cleaning of the teeth,
as well as for one unaccustomed to medicinal smoke, emesis, gargles, and venesection— AS.Utt.25.3.
When the humors (doṣas), aggravated by phlegm (śleṣman) and provoked by anger, produce diseases directed inwardly,
among them is that which is called Khaṇḍauṣṭha, wherein the lip is split in two by Vāta.
In the case of lip disease caused by Vāta, however, the lips become stiff and extremely painful;
they crack, peel away, and become rough, black, and coarse.
Due to pitta, the two [ears] become intolerant of sharp objects; they are covered with eruptions shaped like mustard seeds, characterized by excessive discharge and rapid suppuration.
Furthermore, due to phlegm (kapha),
[the scrotum] is intolerant of cold, heavy, swollen, and covered with eruptions of the same color as the skin.
In the case of a *sannipāta* (combined) disorder, the two [ears] appear multicolored, foul-smelling, with slimy discharges;
they suddenly become flaccid, painful, and characterized by irregular suppuration.
In the case of affliction by Rakta (blood), they discharge blood and have the luster of blood;
when the blood is depleted, a tumor (arbuda) resembling a date palm fruit arises there.
Resembling lumps of flesh, they arise from muscle tissue; gradually, worms emerge from them.
With fat as the cause, there is swelling resembling oil, accompanied by discharge, itching, and softness.
They are repeatedly torn apart by blood, and they are lacerated again and again.
Furthermore, the lips may become knotted and itchy; when wind and phlegm produce a swelling on the lip resembling a water bubble, it is called *jalārbuda*.
Gaṇḍālajī is a firm swelling on the cheek accompanied by burning and pain. Due to Vāta, the teeth cannot tolerate heat and experience excessive agony from cold contact.
AS.Utt.25.15 It feels as if the teeth are being pierced by a spear; that is the disease called *śīta* (cold), also known as *dālana* (tearing).
AS.Utt.25.16 In *dantaharṣa* (trembling of the teeth), the teeth are unable to endure drafts, sour things, or cold food.
By eating only withered leaves, they become afflicted with disease as if they were trembling;
when there is a splitting of the teeth, the teeth are accompanied by pricking pain, splitting, aching, and cracking.
Cāla causes excessive pain due to the gnashing of moving teeth;
Karāla, however, is characterized by the emergence of jagged teeth.
Dantodhikodhi is known as Dantākhya, and it is said to increase the teeth.
When it erupts, it causes extreme pain, but once born,
the pain subsides there; however, due to lack of cleaning, impurity or phlegm dried by the wind remains on the tooth.
Foul-smelling and hardened, it becomes gravel; even that, if neglected,
[leads to further complications].

The *kapālikā* tooth-decay causes the tooth-sockets to crumble into fine particles; the *śyāva* tooth-decay occurs when the teeth turn blackish-brown due to the combined action of blood, bile, and wind.
When the marrow within the hollow of the tooth has been dried up by the aggravated humors (doṣas), primarily the vāta, which have taken hold of the root of the tooth,
and the tooth becomes filled with impurities; this is [the condition known as] dantaśarkarā.
Due to putrefaction, minute worms are born; from that,
there arises an intense pain without apparent cause, accompanied by swelling, discoloration, and throbbing.

When it is destroyed and discharges pus and blood, that is called *kṛmidantaka* (worm-infested tooth). When the teeth discharge foul-smelling blood due to phlegm and blood without any apparent cause, [that is also a form of dental disease].
The gums decay, becoming soft, moist, and black;
this is the disorder caused by cold (śītadoṣa). Upakuśa and Pāka arise from pitta and blood.
When the blood is located in the gums, the gums and the flesh are burned, they become red and swollen,
itchy, discharge blood, and become distended.
The teeth become loose and mildly painful, and a foul odor arises from the mouth. Furthermore, a swelling resembling a jujube stone (badara-phala) or a hard pebble forms upon two or three teeth.
Due to phlegm and blood, the gums (dantapuppuṭa) become intensely painful and suppurate quickly;
when the gums are affected by impurities mixed with blood, a heavy swelling occurs both externally and internally.
When it bursts open, the tooth abscess (dantavidradhi) discharges pus and blood accompanied by pain and burning;
it is a swelling at the roots of the teeth, painful and born from blood and bile (raktapitta).
That [disease] is characterized by the flow of saliva, it is hollow, and it erodes the gums;
it is accompanied by a fever of the *sannipāta* type and involves the discharge of pus and blood.
That which is called Mahāsuṣira is characterized by the loosening of the attachment of the teeth;
it is a swelling at the edge of the teeth resembling a peg, causing pain in the jaw and the ears.
The *adhimāṃsaka* [growth] obstructs the swallowing of food due to the presence of phlegm;
when the gums are rubbed, a great swelling arises.
That condition in which the teeth waver is called Vidarbha, born from injury. That [condition] which neglects diseases localized in the gums, even those that are curable, [is fatal].
The morbid humor (doṣa) leaking internally within it produces a subtle course;
it repeatedly discharges pus that penetrates the skin, flesh, and bone.
Furthermore, those [five types] are to be recognized by their own characteristics as previously described:
that which is rough like a leaf, that which is withered, that which is cracked, and that which is vitiated by Vāta.

Due to pitta, the tongue is characterized by a constant burning sensation and pain; due to blood, it is covered with fleshy sprouts resembling the thorns of the śālmali tree; and due to kapha, it becomes thick and heavy.
Due to kapha and pitta, there arises an elevated swelling below [the tongue] that causes stiffness of the tongue;
when ripened, it has the odor of fish, and this ulcerative condition (ulso) destroys the flesh.
When the tongue is pressed down, there is a swelling resembling the tip of the tongue at its base;
accompanied by sprouts, it is caused by kapha, pitta, and blood, and is characterized by excessive salivation, numbness, and roughness.
Adhijihva causes pain and itching, and it obstructs speech and the intake of food;
upajihva is similar to that, but it is situated upon the tongue.
When the palate is afflicted by vitiated vāta, numerous painful and rough pustules arise accompanied by thick discharge;
these are known as tālupiṭaka.
At the root of the palate, due to phlegm mixed with blood, there arises a soft, hanging, slimy swelling resembling a fish-bladder,
which obstructs the passage of food through the nose.
Throat obstruction, thirst, cough, vomiting, and tonsillitis (galashuṇḍikā);
a painless, firm mass of flesh in the middle of the palate is called tālusaṃhati.
An arbuda is a red swelling in the middle of the palate, shaped like a lotus. A kacchapa is a painless, long-standing growth caused by kapha, shaped like a tortoise.
A *kolābha* is caused by phlegm and fat; a *puppuṭa* is painless and firm.

Due to pitta, there is suppuration known as *pāka*, which exudes pus and is accompanied by great pain. Due to vāta and pitta, fever, and exhaustion, there occurs dryness of the palate, which is named after that [condition].
Those arising from the attachment of the tongue in the throat are severe and obstruct the passage.
The *māṃsāṅkura* (flesh-sprout) grows rapidly; *rohiṇī* acts swiftly.
Caused by *vāta*, it causes dryness of the throat and mouth, and produces pain in the jaw and ears.

From pitta, [the ulcer] is accompanied by fever, burning sensation, thirst, delusion, and a sensation of smoke rising from the throat; it arises quickly, suppurates quickly, is excessively red, and cannot bear being touched.
Due to phlegm (kapha), it is slimy; due to pale blood, it is covered with pustules;
resembling a heated charcoal, it causes earache and possesses the characteristics of a pitta-born [disease].
Due to the accumulation of humors with a deep-seated maturation, accompanied by all their characteristic signs,
a swelling arises from a predominance of kapha, knotted and elevated like a jujube fruit.
A *śālūka* is like a bristle-thorn in the throat, obstructing the passage;
a *vṛnda*, located on the side of the neck, is round and elevated, causing burning fever.
Located at the joint of the jaw in the throat, resembling the fruit of the *kārpāsī* plant,
slimy, slightly painful, swollen, and hard, it is called *tuṇḍikerikā*.
The external and internal swelling (*śvayathu*) is terrible, like a bolt barring the passage of the throat;
this "throat-flood" (*galaugha*) causes heaviness in the head, lassitude, salivation, and fever.

A *valaya* (ring-like swelling) is characterized by little pain and swelling; likewise, an elongated and elevated *māṃsakīla* (flesh-tumor) in the throat, caused by the *doṣas*, may be single or multiple and is associated with slight pain.
Kṛcchra, ucchvāsa, abhyavahṛti, pṛthumūla, and gilāyuka;
bhūrimāṃsa, ākhu-vṛtā, tīvra-tṛṣ, jvara, and mūrdha-ruj.
The *śataghnī* is a swelling that resembles a *śataghnī* weapon; it is covered with circular patches (*vartī*), extremely painful,
spreads throughout the entire throat, develops rapidly, suppurates quickly, and is accompanied by great agony.
A swelling resembling putrid pus in the vessels is *galavidradhi* (throat abscess).
The impurities cause a non-suppurating swelling at the tip of the tongue, the throat, and other such locations.
When it produces firm, painless blood, that is a *galārbuda* (throat tumor). A *galagaṇḍa* (goiter) occurs externally due to the combination of wind (*pavana*), phlegm (*śleṣman*), and fat (*medas*).
Increasing over time, it hangs down like a scrotum;
it is blackish-red and intensely pruritic due to Vāta, marked by black streaks.
In the Vṛddha type, it causes dryness in the palate and throat as well as a bad taste in the mouth.
From Kapha, it is firm, the same color as the surrounding tissue, itchy, cold to the touch, and heavy.
In the case of an increase [of phlegm], one should apply a paste to the palate and throat to produce a sweet taste in the mouth.
It follows the same principles as the decrease and increase of phlegm when [the treatment] involves fat (medas).
In an old person, it causes a sound in the throat and a diminution of voice;
with the movement of wind obstructed by phlegm, the throat becomes dry and the voice is lost.
Fainting and breathing with great effort due to the loss of voice caused by wind (anila),
the wind pervading all the channels produces ulcers within the mouth.
The lips are moving, reddish-brown, rough, copper-colored, and have trembling skin; the tongue cannot endure cold, is heavy, cracked, and covered with papillae.
And that ripening of the mouth causes the mouth to open with difficulty; furthermore,
the downward-moving wind (vāyu) is obstructed by hemorrhoids, gulma, phlegm, and other such conditions.

He who passes upward, causing foul odor from the mouth, is one with an upward-opening anus (ūrdhvaguda). In a Pitta-type inflammation of the mouth, there is burning, heat, and a bitter taste in the mouth.
Ulcers caused by blood are like wounds smeared with alkali;
those born of phlegm have a sweet taste in the mouth and are itchy and slimy.
An internal, dark-yellowish or pale tumor of phlegm (kapha) arising within the cheek.
That [condition] increases when it is rubbed, cut, or pressed;
facial suppuration occurs with all types of secretions and impurities accompanied by tears.
And by those very same [faults], one suffers from foul-smelling breath; furthermore, for those who are averse to using tooth-sticks and the like,
there is disease in the lips, the cheeks, the teeth, their roots, the tongue, the palate, and the throat.
Thus, it is stated that there are seventy-five diseases in total, including those of the mouth; specifically,
eleven, one, ten, thirteen, and six respectively.
Among them, eight, eighteen, and eight respectively are incurable;
Karāla, Māṃsa, and Raktoṣṭha are arbudas, excluding those arising from water.
The tortoise, the palate-tumor, the throat-obstruction, the large perforation, the voice-destroyer, the upward-moving anus, the dark-colored, the hundred-killer, the ring-worm, and the lassitude.
From the accumulation of blood, the diseases *nāḍī*, *oṣṭhakopa*, and *rohiṇī* arise from all [the humors].
One who suffers from voice loss (*svarabhraṃśin*) due to [a disorder of] the teeth will find relief only after more than a year, provided there is difficult breathing (*kṛcchrocchvāsa*).
Excitement and diarrhea should be palliated, while the remaining complications should be conquered with surgical instruments and medicinal drugs.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter.
Now begins the twenty-sixth chapter.
Hereafter, we shall expound the chapter named "The Treatment of Diseases of the Mouth."
Thus indeed said the great seers, Ātreya and others:
"In the case of one who has been lubricated and fomented and whose lips are cracked, one should scrape the edges of the lips and sew them together tightly with a linen thread."
One should apply a medicinal plug (*kavalikā*) smeared with clarified butter purified a hundred times over the ulcer,
and one should treat a moist ulcer according to the procedures for ulcer therapy.
Oil cooked with *jyotiṣmatī*, *lodhra*, *madhuka*, *paṭola*, *utpala*, *kākamācī*, *śrāvaṇī*, and *sārivā* serves as an ointment for cleansing and healing.

Likewise, oil prepared with wind-alleviating and sweet medicinal herbs should be used as nasal drops (nasya) [for vāta-type lip swelling]. In cases of lip swelling caused by vāta, anointment (abhyaṅga) should be performed with a "great unctuous substance" (mahāsneha) processed with devadāru, guggulu, sarjarasa, and beeswax.
One should apply a rubbing with that same powder of *samadhuka*, and cover it with a cotton pad (*picu*) smeared with that same substance.

In cases arising from pitta or caused by injury, one should apply tube-sudation (nāḍīsveda) using castor leaf tips boiled in milk, as well as nasal drops and head massage as prescribed for Khaṇḍauṣṭha; furthermore, bloodletting should be performed using leeches.
Ghee cooked with *pattaṅga*, *yaṣṭīmadhu*, and *chinnaruhā* should be used for massage;
a rubbing application (*pratisāraṇa*) should be made with honey, *madhuka*, *lodhra*, and the resin of *sarja*;
and the treatment is the same as that for a *pitta*-type abscess (*vidradhi*).
In cases of [skin diseases] arising from blood that have not been long-standing, one should treat them as in the case of those arising from pitta.

In cases arising from kapha, one should extract the blood using leeches or leaves of the *śāka* plant and others; then, one should rub the area with a paste of the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), *pāṭhā*, alkali of barley (*yavakṣāra*), and alkali of *svarjika*, mixed with honey.
Or one should administer sudation, fumigation, and gargles that subdue *kapha* using *kuṣṭha*, *tagara*, *dantī*, *śyāmā*, *viḍa*, *haritāla*, and *viḍaṅga*.
In the case of [disease] arising from fat (*medoja*), one should foment the gums, incise them with a *vṛddhipatra* scalpel, and once the fat is purified, treat it with fire.
There should be rubbing with the remedies prescribed for kaphaja [tumors],
and healing with the oil prescribed for *jalārbuda*.

Having burst open a *jalārbuda* and purified it, one should rub it with a powder of the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), *kaṭukā*, *tejovatī*, alkali of barley (*yavakṣāra*), *svarjikā*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and *kāsīsa*, mixed with honey.

If it is deeply seated or excessively enlarged, one should cauterize it with alkali or fire. An oil cooked with *haridrā*, *lodhra*, *madhuka*, *mālatī*, *hareṇu*, and *tagara* serves as a healing agent for healing.

In the case of a *gaṇḍālajī* (gum-boil) that is not yet suppurated, one should treat it like a swelling (*śopha*) that has reached the stage of suppuration; once it has ripened, one should incise it and treat it like a wound (*vraṇa*).

In the case of *śītadanta* (sensitive teeth), after the patient has been fomented with warm water, one should scratch the gingival margin (*pālī*) with a *vrīhimukha* instrument and cauterize it with *picu-taila*.

One should also apply a powder of priyaṅgu, jambu seeds, dāḍima bark, triphalā, rasāñjana, saindhava salt, śuṇṭhī, and musta, mixed with honey and ghee; furthermore, a gargle made from a decoction of milk-exuding trees (kṣīrivṛkṣa) should be used.

In cases of sensitivity and splitting of the teeth, *aṇutaila* prepared with Vāta-alleviating drugs should be used as a nasal drop (*nasya*); alternatively, oil cooked with cardamom (*elā*), costus (*kuṣṭha*), trumpet-flower (*pāṭalī*), and bark, or marrow cooked with these, should be used as a mouth-rinse (*gaṇḍūṣa*).

In cases of loose teeth, unctuous treatments such as nasal drops (nasya) and others should be administered; furthermore, gargles (kavala) should be prepared with a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla) along with oil, ghee, muscle fat (vasā), and honey.
Pippalī, saindhava, tuttha, lodhra, pataṅga, srotoja, mustā, and triphalā should be used for rubbing (pratisāraṇa).
One should regularly inhale unctuous medicated smoke (snaihika-dhūma), consume unctuous and sweet food, and be intent on bloodletting (visrāvaṇa).

One should cook one *prastha* of oil with one *pala* each of candana, padmaka, madhuka, vidārī, kaśeruka, nīlotpala, mṛdvīkā, jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, and sugar, along with milk and twice as much meat broth.
This [medicated oil], when used as a nasal drop or a mouth-rinse, is supremely beneficial for strengthening the teeth, eyes, ears, and strength.
Having smeared a decayed tooth with alkali and recognized it as such, one should extract it according to the procedure for carious teeth and treat it in the same manner.

Having cauterized unstable blood, one should treat it like a wound. Having scraped dental calculus from the roots of the teeth with a toothpick without causing pain, one should sprinkle it with alkaline oil.
One should apply a powder made from the rind of *mūṣā*, *kūrpa*, and *pāṭalī* for rubbing the teeth, and should always practice tooth-cleaning and other such habits,
as well as follow the regimen prescribed for tooth-aversion (*dantaharṣa*).
In the case of *kapālikā*, one should specifically practice this same treatment.
In *kṛmidantaka* (worm-eaten tooth), having filled the cavity with jaggery, beeswax, or clarified butter, one should cauterize it with a heated curved probe.
Or, for filling [the ear], one may use the milk of a seven-vomiter,
or mustard oil mixed with *karañja* oil.
A powder of hiṅgu, viḍaṅga, svarjikā, kaṭphala, kāsīsa, and kuṣṭha, bound in a cloth and placed upon the tooth, removes pain; or alternatively,
a powder of kunduruṣka may be used.
Oil prepared with these same [ingredients] serves as a gargle;

for a swelling with firm and deep-seated flesh that is painful, there should be bloodletting; and for one that is fractured, cracked, discolored, numb, unstable, or painful, [bloodletting is likewise indicated].
If there is no such subsidence, one should grasp the protruding tooth with a forceps, move it, release it from its sides with a surgical instrument,
and extract it; or, having pressed it out by striking the tooth, one should strike it out with a mallet or a stone.
But one should not extract an upper tooth;
from its extraction there is excessive bleeding, and from that follows either loss of sensory function or a wind disease.

Having washed the mouth, one should hold a gargle (*gaṇḍūṣa*) consisting of oil mixed with the powder of *madhuka* or honey. Oil prepared by boiling it ten times in milk along with *vidārī*, *madhuka*, *śṛṅgāṭaka*, and *kaśerukā* should be used as a nasal drop (*nasya*).
In the case of the extraction of an upper tooth as well, this very same remedy is to be applied.
Cold treatments are especially recommended for cold-originated [bleeding];
having drained the blood, one should hold a gargle (gaṇḍūṣa) consisting of a decoction of rasāñjana, musta, triphalā, arjunatvak, priyaṅgu, and mahauṣadha.
With these same [substances] mixed with honey, an ointment (pratisāraṇa) should be applied; oil prepared with the sweet group of drugs (madhuravarga) should be used as nasal drops (nasya).

An ointment made from tejovatī, vyoṣa, the two types of haridrā, kuṣṭha, pāṭhā, kaṭurohiṇī, lodhra, samaṅgā, and musta removes itching, swelling, pain, and bleeding in all diseases of the gums and teeth.

Likewise, pills made from these same salts— vit (bitumen), kṣāra (alkali), manaḥśilā (realgar), saindhava (rock salt), and the bark of dārvī— cure all diseases of the mouth. In the case of upakuśa, one should foment the swollen gums with lukewarm water and then scrape them with a round-tipped instrument or with leaves such as those of the śāka plant.
Then, a lukewarm gargle of clarified butter-scum (ghṛtamaṇḍa) or oil should be administered.
For rubbing (pratisāraṇa), one should use black pepper, kuṣṭha, madhuka, priyaṅgu, lākṣā, pataṅga, gairika, rasāñjana, śuṇṭhī, and rock salt, combined with honey and clarified butter-scum.
Furthermore, oil cooked with pṛthakparṇī, viḍaṅga, vidārī, madhuka, payasyā, and suradāru should be used as a gargle and for nasal administration (nasya).
Alternatively, one may repeatedly apply ghee prepared with the sweet group of drugs (madhuravarga) and perform bloodletting.

In the case of *dantapuppuṭaka*, after it has been fomented, incised, split, or scraped, one should apply a rubbing powder (*pratisāraṇa*) consisting of *svarjikā*, *madhuka*, ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), and rock salt (*saindhava*).
In the case of dental abscess (dantavidradhi), gargles and topical applications should be made with bitter, pungent, astringent, and hot substances mixed with urine; furthermore,
rubbing (pratisāraṇa) should be performed with vṛścikālī, kuṣṭha, kaṭukā, and alkali of barley (yavakṣāra).

One should ward off that [inflammation] when it is ripening by applying dry and cold treatments internally and externally; however, once it is ripe, one should perform incision, and if it is deep-seated, apply cauterization. A decoction of triphalā, sumana, and iṣṭakā should be used as a gargle.

Clarified butter scum prepared with yaṣṭīmadhuka should be used as nasal drops (nasya). When a sinus has been incised or scarified, one should apply a rubbing powder consisting of lodhra, musta, triphalā, kiṃśuka, pataṅga, tārkṣya, śaila, śatapuṣpā, and kaṭphala.
The decoction of those same [plants] used as a gargle,
or that of milk-exuding trees, *kiṃśuka*, and *āmalaka*;
or oil prepared with *gairika*, *utpala*, *madhūka*, *sārivā*, *candana*, *prapauṇḍarīka*, sugar, *anantā*, *lodhra*, and *agaru*— this oil is for nasal administration (*nāvana*).
One should drain an adhimāṃsaka that has arisen recently;
however, if it has grown large, one should seize it with a hook or forceps, excise it with a round-tipped blade (maṇḍalāgra), and rub it with sharp instruments.

In the case of *vidarbha*, one should cleanse the roots of the teeth with a sharp instrument, apply alkali (*kṣāra*) mixed with pungent and acrid substances, or oil sprinkled with *yavakṣāra* as a gargle; thereafter, one should administer the scum of clarified butter (*ghṛtamaṇḍa*) as a mouth-rinse.

A powder of *lodhra*, *pataṅga*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, and *madhuka* is for rubbing; oil cooked with *kākolī*, *yaṣṭīmadhu*, and sugar is for nasal drops. Having incised the dental sinus with a surgical instrument, opened it, and extracted the entire tooth situated therein, one should cauterize it with a probe.
In the case of a deep-seated fistula with multiple openings, one should fill it with either jaggery, honey,
or beeswax, and then hold a mouthful (gaṇḍūṣa) of a decoction of milk-exuding trees.
Or, with oil prepared from those [same ingredients],

one should use oil cooked in a decoction of *dantī*, heartwood of *khadira*, *madana*, and *svādukaṇṭaka*, along with a paste of *lodhra*, *vālaka*, *uśīra*, *devadāru*, and *mañjiṣṭhā*, or mustard oil, for the cleansing and healing of the sinus tract.

Alternatively, one may use *prapauṇḍarīka*, the two types of *haridrā*, *madhuka*, beeswax (*madhūcchiṣṭa*), *lodhra*, *kaṭukī*, sugar, *padmaka*, sandalwood, *mūrvā*, *upodikā*, *vāstūka*, *taṇḍulīyaka*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *amlīkā*, and the leaves of *kapittha*. Or,
one may administer as nasal drops (*nasya*) oil prepared with *viḍaṅga*, *madhuka*, *musta*, *nirguṇḍī*, *khadira*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *uśīra*, and *surataru*.
One should practice fuming, bloodletting, and nasal drops, and one should observe the application of tubular instruments.

In cases of *jihvākaṇṭaka* (fissured tongue) caused by *vāta*, the procedure prescribed for *vāta*-afflicted lips should be followed. In those caused by *pitta*, where blood has been released through friction, one should perform rubbing with sweet substances, as well as gargling (*gaṇḍūṣa*) and nasal medication (*nāvana*).

Similarly, in cases of *jihvālāsa* (tongue-lassitude) arising from *kapha*, when it has recently manifested, sharp treatments such as rubbing with medicinal powders (*pratisāraṇa*) and so forth should be employed.
One should not apply a sharp instrument here,
but rather one should pierce the vein;
having lifted up the *adhijihvā* and grasped it with a hook, one should excise it with a circular blade (*maṇḍalāgra*).
Strong nasal medications and other treatments should be administered;
having drained the sublingual swelling by means of a leaf from a vegetable or a finger-scraper, one should rub it with barley-alkali (yavakṣāra).
One should treat *galaśuṇḍikā* with therapies that alleviate *kapha*.

However, in the case of the enlarged [tumor], one should grasp it—using either a hook (*baḍiśa*) or a forceps (*mucuṭī*) wrapped in cloth—with the left thumb and index finger; its tip resembles the seed of a *urvāru* (cucumber) and is located above the tongue, free of visible vessels. One should then excise it with a circular blade (*maṇḍalāgra*), neither too near the tip nor too close to the root.
If the incision is insufficient, there is no subsiding of the swelling, or an increase in saliva and other secretions;
if it is excessively deep, death may occur due to the loss of blood.
When the incision is properly made, the procedures such as rubbing with medicinal paste (pratisāraṇa) and so forth are to be performed as previously described.
In cases of *tālusaṅghāta*, *puppuṭa*, and *kacchapa* occurring in a new [patient], this procedure is [the same];
however, there is a specific distinction regarding surgical intervention (*śastrakarman*).
For in this case,
regarding inflammation of the palate (tālupāka), there should be scraping of the unripened swelling, followed by rubbing with kāsīsa, rasāñjana, and honey.
For a ripened [abscess], one should perform gargling with sweet and astringent cold decoctions; incision with a scalpel in a checkered pattern; rubbing with sharp substances;
and a gargle consisting of a decoction of paṭola, ariṣṭa, jātī, karavīra, guḍūcī, vṛṣa, kaṭukā, the two types of haridrā, vetrāgra, and kaṇṭakārikā, along with honey and oil.
In the case of dryness of the palate, one who suffers from thirst should drink ghee prepared with licorice (*madhuka*), long pepper (*pippalī*), and ginger (*nāgara*) after a meal; furthermore,
he should perform gargling with sour liquids.
Nasal drops (nasya) prepared from milk-butter cooked with *payasyā*, *madhūka*, and *madhūlikā*; unctuous medicated smoke (*dhūma*);
and food and drink that alleviate thirst.

In cases of throat diseases not complicated by fever and other such conditions, pungent and sharp substances should be used for nasal drops (*nasya*), rubbing (*avagharṣaṇa*), gargles (*gaṇḍūṣa*), and so forth; venesection (*sirāvyadha*) may also be performed. A decoction of *rasāñjana*, *indrayava*, *dārvī*, and *nimba* should be drunk.

A gargle (*kavala*) or medicinal bolus (*guṭikā*) for rubbing the affected area should be prepared from *vyoṣa*, *yavakṣāra*, *dārvī*, *rasāñjana*, *tejovatī*, *pāṭhā*, *nimba* bark, *triphalā*, and *citraka*, boiled with fermented gruel (*śukta*) and cow’s urine.

Pills made from *tālīsapatra*, *gṛhadhūma*, the five spices (*pañcakola*), *kailā*, black pepper, the exudation of *palāśa* and *muṣkaka*, and alkali of barley, mixed with a decoction of barley, are like nectar for all diseases of the throat (AS.Utt.26.42). Alternatively, in the case of internal or external *vātarohiṇīkā*, after applying fomentation (*sveda*) and draining it with a finger-sword or a fingernail containing honey and salt, one should rub the area with sharp [medicinal] agents (AS.Utt.26.42).
A gargle of a decoction of the five great roots (mahāpañcamūla),

and oil cooked with milk and a paste of cardamom (elā), punarnavā, siṃhī, and kapittha, should be used as a gargle and for nasal drops. In cases born of pitta, one should likewise drain [the abscess] and then rub it with pataṅga, sugar, lodhra, and priyaṅgu.
An astringent gargle made from these same [ingredients], or a decoction of grapes, *parūṣaka*, *uśīra*, *madhuka*, and sandalwood, [is also used].
Ghee prepared with triphalā, tilvaka, śyāmā, the bark of śrīparṇī, and madhuyaṣṭikā in ten times the amount of milk should be used for nasal drops, gargles, and food;
in cases of blood-born [diseases], one should likewise treat them after having first rejected [the patient] [if incurable].
In the case of a kaphaja [type], after fomenting and scraping [the area], one should rub it with a mixture of the *kaṭukavarga* (pungent group of drugs), house-soot, *triphalā*, and rock salt;
gargles of the same composition should also be employed.
Oil cooked with nimba, jāti, apāmārga, and viḍaṅga should be used as a nasal medication (nasya). This same procedure is also prescribed for cases of śālūka, vṛnda, tuṇḍikerī, and gilāyu.

In the case of a throat abscess (galavidradhi) that has been drained, there should be rubbing with a powder of *lodhra*, *varā*, *rasāñjana*, *pataṅga*, *gairika*, *rocanā*, *pippalī*, and *saindhava*.
A gargle should also be made from these same ingredients boiled together.

Oil prepared from the decoction and paste of *kirātatiktaka*, *lodhra*, *darvī*, *śatapuṣpā*, *nimba* leaves, *kuṣṭha*, *elā*, *guḍūcī*, *citraka*, *tagara*, *mustā*, and *taila* should be used for nasal administration (*nāvana*). Having applied fomentation (*sveda*) to a wind-born goiter (*galagaṇḍa*), one should drain it; once the wound has healed, one should apply a poultice (*upanāha*) made of sesame, *priyāla*, *laṭvā*, radish, hemp, and *atasī* seeds.

One should repeatedly apply a paste made from *tilvaka*, *agnimantha*, *punarnavā*, *kālamṛtā*, *saubhāñjanaka*, *gajapippalī*, *ekaiṣikā*, the roots of *arka*, and the flowers of *karaghāṭaka*, ground with wine (*surā*) and sour gruel (*amlapiṣṭa*).
One should also administer oil prepared with *nimba*, *guḍūcī*, *kuṭaja*, *haṃsapādī*, *kṛṣṇā*, the two types of *balā*, and *devadāru*.
This same procedure applies even in cases of *ślaiṣmika* (phlegmatic) disorders, though the sudation, external applications, and other treatments should be more intense.
A comfortably warm plaster made from *viśalyā*, *ativiṣā*, *viṣāṇikā*, *śukanāsā*, *jagandhā*, *guñjā* fruit, *kaṭukālābu*, and *palāśa* alkali, ground together with water, [is applied].
One should drink oil prepared with the *vatsakādi* group of drugs combined with the five salts,
practice sharp emetics and other such therapies, and apply fomentation and bloodletting in rotation.
If there is no subsiding in this way, one should treat both [the patient and the wound] like a common ulcer after it has been ripened;
one should prescribe barley-based food and soups of mung beans and other pulses made pungent with the three acrids (vyoṣa) for both drink and meal.
Once the fat has been fomented, one should lance a vein.
The previously mentioned pastes [should be applied]; furthermore, every morning one should drink the powder of the heartwood (sāra) of the *āsana* and other trees along with cow's urine.
If there is still no relief even by this means, one should incise it with a surgical instrument, cleanse the fat (*medas*), and suture it.
Alternatively, if it is fit for cauterization, one should cauterize it properly with any one of muscle fat, clarified butter, or honey.
Oil mixed with the powders of *rocanā*, *kāsīsa*, and *tutthaka* cleanses and heals the ulcer; or oil combined with the heartwood of the *asanā* group and the ashes of cow dung.
In cases of stomatitis (mukhapāka), a decoction of triphalā mixed with honey is generally recommended; other mouth-washes consisting of bitter, pungent, and astringent substances are also indicated.
For those who do not eat, the chewing of grapes, pāṭhā, jasmine, citron, the leaves of arjuna, and the tender shoots of jīvaka is advised.

Having boiled half a *tulā* of *dāruharidrā* in twenty parts of water, one should prepare this decoction along with red ochre (*gairika*) until it reaches the consistency of a paste that adheres to the ladle; when finished, it should be mixed with honey and stored in a vessel of clarified butter.
This gargle destroys all diseases of the mouth and the channels of the oral cavity.

This is another distinct formulation: take seven parts each of the barks of *yaṣṭīmadhuka*, *paṭolī*, *nimba*, *āṭarūṣaka*, *jātī*, *lodhra*, *arimeda*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *jambū*, and *khadira*; two parts of *suvarṇagairika*; and one part each of *mūrvā*, *kaṭukā*, *ativiṣā*, and *āmalaka*. Grind all these together with the alkaline water of *kutaja* and form them into pills. One should eat them and then spit them out. (AS.Utt.26.53)

One should boil one *tulā* of *khadira* heartwood and two *tulās* of *āmalaka* in water until only one-eighth remains; having removed it from the heat and strained it, one should boil it again until it becomes thick.

When it has thickened and cooled, one should add one *karṣa* each of the following finely ground ingredients: sandalwood, *padmaka*, *uśīra*, *vālaka*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *dhātakī*, *musta*, *prapauṇḍarīka*, *madhuka*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), the four spices (*cāturjātaka*), lac, *nalada*, *tārkṣyaśaila*, *lodhra*, the two types of turmeric (*dvirajanī*), *samaṅgā*, *pāṭhā*, *kaṭphala*, *elā*, *pataṅga*, agallochum, red ochre, and collyrium.
Pālikās of nutmeg, cloves, kaṅkola, and kebuka,
along with half a kuḍava of camphor—
these pills, when held in the mouth, conquer all diseases of the oral cavity.
These [substances] produce fragrance, cheerfulness, and relish;
furthermore, oil prepared with the paste (kalka) and decoction (kaṣāya) of these very same [substances] should be employed as a gargle (kavala).

In that case, for mouth ulcers caused by Vāta, oil prepared with a decoction of daśamūla, kākolī, rāsnā, madhuka, and sārivā, along with a paste of kuṣṭha, should be used as nasal drops (nasya) and gargle (gaṇḍūṣa),
as well as for unctuous smoking (snaihika dhūma).
In the case of a Pitta-type disorder, one should rub [the area] with long pepper (pippalī), cardamom (elā),
and the best salts; for gargling, one should use milk, sugarcane juice, grape juice, and sugar-water.
Milk prepared with sweet substances should be used for drinking, gargling, and nasal administration; likewise,
the scum of ghee cooked with *padmaka*, *samaṅgā*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *lodhra*, and *dhātakī* should be used as a nasal drop (*nāvana*), and a mouthwash made from the petals of *madayantikā*.
In cases arising from *kapha*, one should apply a rubbing (*pratisāraṇa*) with pungent, alkaline, and salty substances; however,
for firm pustules (*piṭaka*), one should first perform scarification (*lekhanam*) using the leaf of a vegetable such as *śāka*.
A gargle should be prepared with the alkali of *muṣkaka*, *palāśa*, and *āmalakī*, along with cow’s urine; likewise, oil cooked with these [substances] is used.
For spitting out [the medicine], one should use *nirguṇḍī*, *phaṇijjaka*, *ārjaka*, and the leaves of *surasā*.

Devadāru, pāṭhā, ativiṣā, dantī, indrayava, and kaṭukā, prepared as a paste or a decoction and drunk with cow’s urine, destroy all diseases caused by kapha. In cases arising from blood, the treatment is successful as in the case of pitta.

In cases of *sarvaja* (all-cause) [arbuda], one should prepare a paste by cooking together *rocanā*, *kāsīsa*, *saurāṣṭrī*, *rasāñjana*, *mocarasa*, and honey; once cooked and placed in an iron vessel, it should be dried and powdered. This powder should then be applied as an ointment to the ulcer with honey. Now, if an *arbuda* that is *sarvasara* (pervading all tissues), not long-standing, and not enlarged, is cut with a scalpel (*maṇḍalāgra*), one should rub the site with the ashes of *muṣkaka* mixed with honey, or with the powder of *svarjikā* and *śuṇṭhī*.
A gargle consisting of honey, oil, and a decoction of nimba and guḍūcī should be used;
one should eat barley-based food and employ sharp gargles, massages, and nasal drops.
In the case of *pūtimukha* (fetid mouth), after applying oleation and sudation, one should treat the patient with head-purgatives (*śirovireka*).

Then, having prepared pills from *svarjikā*, asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), house-soot (*gṛhadhūma*), realgar (*manaḥśilā*), cardamom (*elā*), dry ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), *viḍaṅga*, and *tejovatī*, mixed with honey, one should administer them for the purpose of cleansing the mouth.
One should use water sprinkled with the powders of *samaṅgā*, *dhātakī*, *padma*, *lodhra*, and *priyaṅgu* for rinsing the mouth;
one should also employ the treatments prescribed for *śītāda* and *opakuśa*, and regularly practice nasal drops, medicinal smoking, and gargles.
On this subject, there is also a verse:
Diseases arising from the mouth, the roots of the teeth, and the throat are generally characterized by a predominance of phlegm and blood;
therefore, one should repeatedly drain the vitiated blood from them.
Purgation of the body and head, emesis, and gargles containing pungent and bitter substances are generally recommended for them; likewise, any treatment that removes phlegm and blood is beneficial.
Gruels made from grasses and grains that have been soaked in alkaline solutions and are free of oil,
as well as soups and foods beneficial for the destruction of phlegm— whatever else is suitable— are wholesome.
Diseases of the throat, situated in the path of the vital breaths, even arrest the breath of one who is negligent; therefore,
one should perform their treatment swiftly.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter.
Now begins the twenty-seventh chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter entitled "The Diagnosis of Diseases of the Head."
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:
"By smoke, heat, frost, water, sporting, excessive sleep, and wakefulness..."
By excessive sweating, exposure to the east wind, suppression of tears, and weeping;
by drinking too much water or liquor, by worms, and by the suppression of natural urges— AS.Utt.27.2–3.
Head diseases [are indicated] by the presence of pillows, by cleanliness, by oil massage, by aversion [to food], by downward-looking eyes,
by unpleasant odors, by foul-smelling breath, by improper speech, and so forth.
The humors (doṣas) generate diseases;
among these, [the following occurs] due to the provocation of wind (māruta).
The temples are pierced intensely, the fontanelle likewise splits apart, and the space between the eyebrows and the forehead feel as if they are falling away due to extreme pain.
The ears are oppressed by their own sounds, as if the eyes were being pulled out;
the entire head seems to reel, and one feels as if released from all the joints.
The network of veins throbs excessively, there is constriction of the neck and jaw,
intolerance to light, nasal discharge, and sudden bouts of pain and relief.
Softness arises from massage, oleation, sudation, and bandaging;
this is known as *śirastāpa*.
When it occurs on one half of the head, it is called *ardhāvabhedaka*;
it becomes aggravated after a fortnight or a month, and subsides by itself.
If administered excessively, it may destroy the eyes or the ears. In a fever arising from pitta with a burning sensation in the head, there is a sensation of smoke rising from the head.
In the case of [fever] born of phlegm (kaphaja), there is sweating, burning of the eyes, fainting, softness from cold things at night,
loss of appetite, and heaviness, stiffness, and coldness of the head.
Lassitude due to the lack of pulsation in the vessels, mild pain that increases at night,

drowsiness, swelling of the eye-sockets, itching of the ears, and vomiting; from blood there is excessive pain, from pitta the pain is predominant, and from all [three] combined, it possesses all the symptoms.
When the blood and flesh in the head are moistened by mixed foods and the *sannipāta* is provoked, living organisms are born in the head.
Drinking the blood from your head, those terrible [demons] cause agonizing pains that produce mental derangement, fever, cough, and loss of strength.
Roughness, swelling, pain, cutting, burning, throbbing, and putrefaction [occur];
in the *kapāla* stage, there is itching, swelling, and stupor in the palate and head.
The morbid humors (malas), aggravated by Vāta, produce copper-colored nasal discharge, ear-ringing, and head-shaking in a living being; this condition is known as Śirahkampana.
When vāta and the other [doshas], dominated by pitta and accompanied by blood, affect the temple region (śaṅkha),
there occurs swelling along with intense burning, pain, redness, delirium, fever, thirst, and vertigo.
One with a bitter mouth and a yellow face who acts with haste is a *śaṅkhaka*;
he destroys life within three nights, yet if properly treated, he may also be cured quickly.
When vāta is associated with pitta, it causes throbbing pain in the temples, eyes, eyebrows,
and forehead, arising in accordance with the rising of the sun.
In one who is hungry, that [thirst] increases especially until midday;
it is characterized by unstable sensations of cold and heat, and thus subsides when one is satiated.
Thus, including Sūryāvarta,
these ten diseases located in the head have been described.
Furthermore, nine diseases will be described as occurring specifically in the skull;
when the wind (vāyu) in the skull is vitiated, they arise even in one still within the womb.

A swelling that is the same color as the skin and free from pain— one should know that as upaśīrṣaka. One should describe piṭakas, arbudas, and vidradhis according to the manifestation of the respective doṣas.
In a skull, those [worms] abound in moisture due to bile, blood, phlegm, and parasites.
Pustules resembling millet or mustard seeds are *arūṃṣikā*;
they cause itching, loss of hair, sleeplessness, and roughness, and result in the cracking of the skin.
One should know that *dāraṇaka* is extremely subtle and caused by both *kapha* and *vāta*; it is *pitta*, accompanied by *vāta*, that has spread into the hair follicles.
It causes the body hairs to fall out; then the phlegm, along with blood,
obstructs his hair follicles, whereby the growth of others becomes impossible.
Some call that indralupta, others ruj,
and still others āceti; the origin of khālitya is likewise, but its gradual wearing away occurs there in sequence.
That [eruption], due to vāta, has the appearance of being burnt by fire; due to pitta, it is covered with sweat and dilated vessels;
and due to kapha, one should observe the thickness and color of the skin according to their respective characteristics.

That [leprosy] which possesses all forms due to all the humors (doṣas) is incurable; it is called *nakhaprabhā*. That which is burnt as if by fire, devoid of hair, and accompanied by burning sensations, is likewise incurable.
The bodily heat produced by grief, fatigue, and anger, when it reaches the head along with the humors (doṣas),
cooks the hair; from this, gray hair (pālita) arises.
From vāta, it is cracked, dark-brown, rough, dry, and has a flaming luster;
from pitta, it is accompanied by burning, yellowish in appearance; and from kapha, it is unctuous and increases in size.
One should recognize that which is thick and very white as having mixed characteristics;
another, arising from headache, is discolored and cannot bear being touched.
Baldness and premature graying caused by the derangement of the three humors (sannipāta) are incurable;
however, those arising from the natural transformation of the body may respond to rejuvenative therapy (rasāyana).
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter.
Now begins the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Diseases of the Head. Now, therefore, we shall explain the chapter named "The Treatment of Diseases of the Head."
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:
in the case of headache caused by Vāta, one should apply the treatments prescribed for Vāta diseases.
At night, while staying in a windless place, one should have the patient drink either oil or clarified butter after anointing the head, followed by a draught of milk;
or one should have them eat black gram mixed with clarified butter, followed by a warm draught of milk.

Or similarly, having given a poultice (utkārikā) made of mung beans with minced meat from marshy animals seasoned with salt, or with barley, sesame, mung beans, black gram, horse gram, kuṣṭha, dāruharidrā, linseed, rock salt, and a large quantity of fat, one should wrap the head.

Then at dawn, one should perform a sprinkling with lukewarm milk processed with the ten roots (*daśamūla*), and apply either bolus-sudation (*piṇḍasveda*) or an external paste made from milk-porridges prepared with those same roots. Furthermore, the fat of a tortoise, buffalo, boar, cock, or porcupine, mixed with rock salt (*saindhava*), should be used as nasal medication (*nasya*) and for filling the ears.

In the same manner, ghee and oil cooked together with a decoction of the five roots (*pañcamūla*), *balā*, and the two types of *sārivā*, containing an infusion of *madhuka*, *jīvaka*, *ṛṣabhaka*, and *punarnavā*, along with milk,
[should be used]. Furthermore, cotton-seed marrow, bark, *mustā*, and jasmine buds ground with warm water constitute a nasal drop (*nāvana*) that destroys all headaches.
Similarly, a plaster consisting of cinnamon bark, sugar, and the seeds of *śigru* and *karañja*, along with sandalwood, blue lotus, *tagara*, and *kuṣṭha*, mixed with clarified butter, [is applied].
Clarified butter prepared with *devadāru*, *kuṣṭha*, *coraka*, *yaṣṭīmadhuka*, *kamala*, *nīlotpala*, *elā*, *prapauṇḍarīka*,
saffron, and sugar, administered as an enema (*marśa*), is for cases where *raktapitta* is persistent.
In this condition, one should not apply bloodletting for fear of aggravating the Vāta;
rather, one should inhale unctuous medicinal smoke and regularly employ head-poultices (śirobasti).
One should perform enema therapy (bastikarma). If [the disease] is not thus cured, then for the vāta-born and kapha-born types, the aforementioned cauterization (dāha) should be applied.
This same procedure is also prescribed for hemiplegia (ardhāvabhedaka).
Furthermore, the juice of *nirguṇḍī* leaves, combined with the scum of clarified butter (*ghṛtamaṇḍa*) and rock salt (*saindhava*), should be used as a nasal medication (*nasya*).
Alternatively, a plaster consisting of the roots and fruits of *śirīṣa* with *sārivā*, *utpala*, *kuṣṭha*, *vacā*, *madhuka*, and *pippalī*, mixed with oil and sour liquids,
[should be applied]; if it does not subside, one should treat it after considering the persistence of the underlying *doṣas*.
AS.Utt.28.9: This same procedure applies to *sūryāvarta*, with the specific addition of venesection.
In cases of headache arising from *pitta* or blood, one should perform venesection on the patient after he has been treated with oleation (*snigdha*).
One should purge the body with very cold [substances] mixed with ghee washed a hundred times, and one should sprinkle and anoint the head and face.

Ghee prepared with *candana*, *sārivā*, *madhuka*, *dūrvā*, *utpala*, *prapauṇḍarīka*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, and *vidārī*, along with milk, should be used as nasal drops (*nāvana*) and as a head-pouch enema (*śirobasti*).

Butter extracted from milk boiled with the *jīvanīya* group of drugs, and then cooked again with the decoction and paste of those same *jīvanīya* drugs, cures all disorders arising from *pitta* and blood when administered through drinking, food, nasal drops, massage, and enemas.
Alternatively, ghee prepared with a *jīvanīya* (life-promoting) decoction in sixteen times its quantity of milk may be used;
or, a scum of ghee (*sarpirmaṇḍa*) processed with milk, sugarcane juice, meat broth, dates, grapes, *kaśeruka*, and lotus stalks may be used as an unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*).

Milk boiled with the group of drugs beginning with *añjana* should be used as a non-unctuous enema (*āsthāpana*). In the case of *śaṅkhaka*, one should treat it in this very same manner after first declaring the prognosis.
Like [the treatment for] visarpa, but specifically, a paste of black sesame, śatāvarī, nīlotpala, mūrvā, and punarnavā should be applied;
in cases of head-ache born of kapha, one should first undergo fasting (laṅghana).
Or one should induce emesis with old ghee that has been made unctuous; if the patient is dry, one should apply sudation with a dry bolus.
Alternatively, tube-sudation (nāḍīsveda) may be performed with a decoction of śigru,
nimba, and eraṇḍa; or a lukewarm poultice (ālepa) made of devadāru, kuṣṭha, śārṅgeṣṭā, sarala, and rohiṣa, combined with salt, may be applied.

A poultice (upanāha) should be prepared with barley flour, madhuka, sandalwood, turmeric, kuṣṭha, priyaṅgu, śatapuṣpā, and suradāru, combined with oil, goat’s milk, and rock salt. For nasal administration (nasya), one should use either viḍaṅga oil or mustard oil processed with the three pungents (vyoṣa). Alternatively, a paste of madhūka pith mixed with honey, or the bark of meṣaśṛṅgī or iṅguda [may be used].
And by means of these very substances used for smoking, or with the drugs for head-evacuation (śirovirecana) mentioned in the Sūtrasthāna, one should perform insufflation (pradhamana).

Oil cooked with those same [ingredients] is used as a *marśa* or *pratimarśa*; following a head-purgative (*śirovirecana*), an unctuous nasal therapy (*snehanasya*) is administered as prescribed for ear-ache (*karṇanāda*).
Sharp gargles, a fumigation consisting of the powder of realgar (*manaḥśilā*), *analada*, *tuttha*, and *kāsīsa* mixed with ghee,
and the repeated inhalation of the powder of *nalada*—
in cases of *sannipāta*, these combined procedures are prescribed. (AS.Utt.28.19)

For worms, ghee cooked with *durālabhā*, *suradāru*, *rohiṣa*, *pūtīka*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *kaṭphala*, *vacā*, and the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), along with goat’s urine, should be administered as a drink.
For one who has been lubricated and fomented, one should apply oil cooked with *devadāru*, *pūtīka*, *kaṭabhī*, mustard seeds, *viḍaṅga*, sesame, and *kaṇṭaka* to the head and ears,
and then administer sudation. Thereafter, one should administer bloodletting via ear-drops (*nastaḥ*) for the purpose of stupefying the parasites.

Then, driven by the intoxication of the smell of blood, worms emerge; they fall when the sap of the bark of the *saptacchada* tree or its flower-nectar has been recently poured [upon them]. A powder made from *sarala*, *devadāru*, *kaṭphala*, mustard, *apāmārga*, *kṣavaka*, bitter gourd, *surasa*, seeds of long pepper, and rice, or oil cooked with these, instantly expels the worms.
Viḍaṅga seeds ground with horse urine, or śirīṣa seeds ground with goat urine,
or the seeds from the interior of the puṣkara lotus;
having prepared a gruel (yavāgū) with beef or goat meat mixed with fat, one should smear it on the head.
Then one should sprinkle [the area] with a decoction of the leaves of *nimbārka*, *vaṃśa*, *surasa*, *kuṭaja*, *karañja*, and *karavīra*,
or with lukewarm goat’s urine.
And when the worms have been eliminated, one should appropriately administer as nasal drops (*nāvana*) either mustard oil,

*aiṅguda* oil, or *pailuka* oil, cooked with a paste consisting of *tejovatī*, *pūtīka*, *bimbī*, *surasa*, *naktamāla*, *viḍaṅga*, *harītakī*, mustard roots, *arkakaravīra* roots, *mālatī*, *devadāru*, *kṣavaka*, *musta*, *phaṇijjaka*, *pippalī*, *śatapuṣpā*, *madhūka*, hemp, and the heartwood (*sāra*) of *nimba*, combined with goat’s urine. (AS.Utt.28.24)
One must never let blood flow [from the head],
for if blood has been drunk by insects in the head, premature death may occur from the further discharge of blood.

One should also examine the treatment for worms (AS.Utt.28.26). In a case of head-shaking occurring in one who is not emaciated and is not afflicted by other diseases, one should treat it according to the procedures for Vata, with the exception of cauterization (AS.Utt.28.26).

In cases of *upaśīrṣaka* occurring after birth, whether newly arisen or chronic, one should employ the unctuous substances prescribed for wind disorders (*vātavyādhi*) via oral intake, nasal drops (*nāvana*), and massage (*abhyañjana*).
After massaging the patient, one should apply fomentation (*sveda*) and then poultices (*upanāha*), taking care that no burning sensation occurs.
In cases of suppuration,
the treatment is the same as for an abscess (vidradhi); in cases of pustules, tumors, and abscesses, one should apply the respective specific treatments.
When the carbuncles have become ulcerated, oil cooked with nimba, niśā, madhuka, and dhātrī fruit serves as both a purifier and a healer (AS.Utt.28.29).
For abscesses (vidradhi), [oil cooked] with the roots of mūrvā, candana, sārivā, dhātakī, kāntā, lodhra, madhuka, samaṅgā, padmakesara, and śataparvaka [is used] (AS.Utt.28.29).
Ghee prepared with these same [drugs] is established as a nasal medication (nasya).
However, if the skin over a healed abscess becomes as if numb, one should then induce emesis and, after applying mild oleation, administer a purgative.

In cases of *aruṃṣikā*, blood should be extracted by means of leeches; or, after the head has been scraped with a razor, it should be sprinkled with *nimba* water and then smeared with the juice of horse dung mixed with an abundance of salt.

After it has remained for a short time, it should be washed with either warm water or sour *kāñjika*, and then smeared with a paste consisting of *viḍaṅga*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), lac, soot (*gāradhūma*), *manohvā*, *lavaṇa*, *rasāñjana*, and the two types of *haridrā*.
Or with sesame paste mixed with the milky sap of *snuhī*;
or with *madhuka*, blue lotus, sesame, castor seeds, and leaves of *mārkava*; or with the roots of *śigru* and *mūlaka* and mustard seeds, all ground together with cow’s urine.
Or with the seeds of *vālaka*, *āmalaka*, *nāgara*, *mūlaka*, and mustard, ground with milk;
or with the bark of *śirīṣa* and *yaṣṭīmadhuka*;
or with old oil-cake and chicken dung.
Powdered kuṣṭha roasted in a skull, combined with oil, destroys itching, exudation, burning, sweating,
and pain; likewise, the oil beginning with citraka has been prescribed for massage.

Oil prepared with *dantī*, *pāṭhā*, *kośātakī*, *citraka*, *ativiṣā*, and *mahālāṅgalakī* should be used for the anointing of wounds (AS.Utt.28.32). Oil cooked in the sun (*ādityapāka*), containing a paste of *manaḥśilā*, *elā*, *haritāla*, *pippalī*, *kuṣṭha*, *kāsīsa*, *haridrā*, *karañja*, *mustā*, *tagara*, *viḍaṅga*, *citraka*, *siddhārthaka*, and the root of *karavīra*, promotes the healing of wounds (AS.Utt.28.32).
If there is no such pacification, one should administer emetics, fumigation, and purgation of the body and head;
in the case of *dāraṇaka*, one should lance a vein on the forehead.

One should practice oil massage, bathing, and nasal drops; an ointment made of *priyaṅgu* seeds, *madhuka*, *kuṣṭha*, black gram, and mustard seeds mixed with honey should be applied, followed by washing with water containing the alkali of *kodrava* grass.
In cases of *indralupta* (alopecia), one should pierce a vein near the affected area and apply an ointment of *tuttha*, *kāsīsa*, realgar, and black pepper.
One should apply an ointment made from *bhadradāru*, *kuṭannaṭa*, or oil prepared with *citraka*, *karavīra*, *naktamāla*, and *mālatī*. Alternatively,
having scarified the deeply seated [abscess] with a needle-brush, one should repeatedly apply an ointment made from the root of *kapotapāṅkā* or the root of *lāṅgalikā*, ground with buffalo milk.
Having rubbed and smeared [the substance] and covered it with castor leaves, one should let it remain overnight and then smear it with buffalo butter.

Alternatively, oil cooked with the flowers of *mārkava* and *patrasa*, or with *vārtāka* fruits, applied as an ointment combined with honey; or the juice of small *vārtāka* mixed with honey may be used as an application.
Alternatively, a thick decoction of *palāśa* alkaline water mixed with *jalaśūla*,
or *indralupta* ground with cow dung, should be smeared [on the scalp] and then dusted with the soot of a tortoise burnt in a smokeless fire (*antardhūma*) mixed with the juice of *aruṣkara*.
One should apply an ointment of tortoise-shell ash moistened with the juice of *surasā*, or a paste of elephant-tusk soot mixed with oil,
or a plaster of *pūtīkarañja* leaves combined with rock salt.

Alternatively, one may apply long pepper (*pippalī*), antimony (*añjana*), mineral antimony (*rasāñjana*), *bākucī* fruit, and iron filings, ground with cow’s urine, as prescribed for the treatment of *khalati* (alopecia); furthermore,
one should avoid sprinkling water until the hair begins to grow.
In cases of *khalati* (baldness) and *indralupta* (alopecia), the procedure is as described, along with purification according to the specific dosha.

The powder of the bark, flowers, and fruits of *triphalā*, *arjuna*, and *sairyaka*; the roots of *kṛṣṇapiṇḍītaka*; *nīlotpala*; iron filings; *kāsīsa*; *jambu*; *mārkava*; *mañjiṣṭhā*; *meṣaśṛṅgī*; and the dust of *khadira*—all these should be ground together with mud. This paste, combined with *aṇutaila* as previously mentioned, should be placed inside a hollowed-out *asana* heartwood and buried in mud for one month. Once extracted, it should be applied as a plaster to the bald spot after it has been scraped with a needle and brush; this is an excellent means for the regrowth of hair.
A paste made from the ashes of red agnimantha flowers, kiṃśuka, the root of nalada, madhuka, and hastidanta, ground with goat’s milk, is for external application.

One should prepare sesame oil and *akṣa* oil together with a paste (*kalka*) of the bark and leaves of the two types of *jambū*, *madhuka*, *bhṛṅgaraja*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *śleṣmātaka*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *phaṇijjaka*, *balā*, grapes (*drākṣā*), *ajaśṛṅgī*, *capalā*, *ativiṣā*, and *kaṭphala*, along with a decoction (*kvātha*) of the milky trees (*kṣīrivṛkṣa*). This should be employed for both nasal administration (*nasya*) and massage (*abhyaṅga*).
In the same manner, it may be prepared with a paste of the sweet group (*madhuravarga*).
One should apply treatments for baldness and gray hair to each other [as appropriate].
In cases of premature graying, one should administer oleation, sudation, purification, bloodletting, and depleting therapies after considering the involvement of Vāta and the other doshas.
Then, for this [condition], one should administer *maṇutaila* as nasal drops (*nasya*) and an ointment (*abhyañjana*), as prescribed by Ātreya; furthermore,
one should smear the roots of the hair with *madhuka*, *āmalaka*, and honey.
Or [one may use] sesame, āmalaka, honey, and oil; or tutthaka,
the stones of the āmra and jambu fruits, kāsīsa, iron dross, and sugar.
Alternatively, oil ground with *sairyaka*, blue lotus, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and *bhṛṅgarāja*, mixed with black antimony and goat’s urine,

should be placed in a vessel made of *asanā* flowers and leaves, which has been externally smeared with a paste of *āmalakī*. Kept for six months in a heap of rice, this oil, when used for massage and nasal drops (*nāvana*), overcomes graying hair (*palita*).

This same procedure applies to *sairīyaka* as well: oil prepared with the fruit and root of *kapikacchū* in an iron vessel is identical to the previous [preparation], provided it is processed and stored in the same manner.

Two *pala*s of the root of *rāmataraṇī*, one *pala* of *yaṣṭīmadhuka*, and half a *pala* of *sārivā*, all crushed together and saturated with ten *pala*s of sesame oil, should be heated in an iron vessel for ten days under the rays of the sun. When used as an errhine (*nāvana*), it destroys graying hair and brings firmness to all the sense organs. (AS.Utt.28.47) Black sesame, *tilaparṇī*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *madhuka*, *kāsīsa*, *padmaka*, clay, *māṃsī*, *mārkava*, and the leaves of *asanā*—these should be ground with their own juices and kept in an iron vessel for three nights. (AS.Utt.28.48)
Then, one should smear the hair and the skull with the previously mentioned liquid extract mixed with lotus-mud that has been washed seven times;
thereafter, having covered them with lotus-mud, one should wrap them in silk cloth.
On the third day, having washed [the head] in this very same manner, one should act accordingly;
thus the hair, dark as a swarm of bees, adorns the head.
And there is a verse on this point:
In cases of baldness, graying hair, wrinkles, and discolored body hair, one should administer purified [medicines] through nasal drops,
mouth-washes, head-massages, and external plasters.

When the oil has been prepared with the *bṛhatyādi* group and the *jīvanīya* group, it is used as a nasal medication (*nāvana*). [This is done] with milk, *sāhacara*, *bhṛṅgaraja*, and the juice of *saurasa*.
Nasal medication (nasya) should consist of *dugdhikā* and *karavīra* ground with milk.
Having plucked out gray hair, one should apply [the following] into the hair-follicles to remove the grayness:
the roots of *ādityavalī* and of black *sairēyaka*.

Take ten *pala* each of the fruit of black hemp (*kṛṣṇa-śaṇa*), the leaf of *surasā*, *yaṣṭimadhu*, *mārkava*, *surāhva*, and *kākamācī*. Prapauṇḍarīka, mañjiṣṭhā, lodhra, kṛṣṇāguru, and utpala; the black mud from the stones of the mango fruit, mṛṇālī, and red sandalwood.
Nīlī, the seeds of bhallātaka, madayantī, somarājī, asana, śastra, kṛṣṇa, piṇḍīta, and citraka [are used] for coughs.

Five palas each of the flowers of *arjuna* and *kāśmarya*, and the pulp of unripe *jambu* fruit, along with the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) and long pepper (*kaṇā*), should be ground together. (AS.Utt.28.57–58)
One should cook one āḍhaka of oil with unhusked grains (akṣataila) using that [decoction] along with the juice of āmalaka;
or one should prepare it by solar cooking (ādityapāka) until the juice has dried up.
Then,

for one who is pure and self-controlled, purified *mahānīla* [soma] that has been processed in an iron vessel should be employed for drinking, nasal administration (*nāvana*), and massage (*abhyaṅga*).
This destroys diseases of all parts of the body and the upper regions, and especially removes gray hair; one should also apply these same medicinal substances as an ointment to the head and face.
Milk, *priyāla*, *yaṣṭyāhva*, the *jīvanīya* group of drugs, and black sesame seeds— this facial paste is beneficial for removing tawny body hair and wrinkles.
Sesame seeds, *āmalaka* fruits, lotus filaments, licorice, and honey— this mixture,
when applied as an ointment to the head, promotes the growth of hair and dyes it.
One should cook iron powder with rock salt, fermented gruel, sour liquids, and rice;
having smeared the head with this, it should be kept overnight while the head is cleansed and not anointed with oil.

In the morning, one should apply a paste of the three myrobalans (triphalā) to achieve black and glossy hair. Iron powder ground with sour liquids, combined with the three myrobalans, is an excellent cosmetic preparation (rāga).
For a maiden, a powder made from sesame, nimba seeds, madhuka, śreṣṭhā, vacā,
and mārkava should be saturated with a pala-measure of goat, cow, or buffalo fat.
If one places iron filings in an iron vessel, sets it on the ground for a month, and then extracts them, this application—
when used as an ointment by one who is grey-haired or bald— destroys those conditions. Furthermore,

when an iron rod is smeared with the fine paste of *śleṣmātaka* seeds from which the husks have been removed and soaked in sour gruel (*kāñjika*), and is heated by the rays of the sun, [the resulting substance] shall fall away [from the hair].
That oil produces supreme blackness of the hair through nasal medication and massage; it destroys, without exception, pain in the head, nose, eyes, teeth, ears, and throat.
[It is prepared] with *balā*, *madhūka*, *madhuka*, *vidārī*, *candana*, and *utpala*.
One *prastha* of oil, prepared with *jīvaka*, *ṛṣabhaka*, grapes, and sugar, along with milk, in the decoction of half a *tulā* of the meat of wild animals; AS.Utt.28.68–69.
Nasal medication (nasya) removes all diseases of the upper trunk arising from vāta and pitta.
[One should use] a peacock, excluding its feathers, bile, intestines, feet, excrement, and beak.
Having boiled the ten roots (*daśamūla*), *balā*, *rāsnā*, *madhuka*, and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) together in water,
one should cook one *prastha* of ghee with that decoction along with an equal amount of milk.
Pulverized sweet substances (madhuradravya) cure all diseases located in the entire body and those in the upper parts;
when practiced habitually through drinking, enemas, massage, and nasal drops, they achieve this.
With this very decoction, one should cook one *prastha* of ghee with four times as much milk and these [drugs] in the measure of one *karṣa* each as a paste.
Jīvantī, triphalā, medā, mṛdvīkā, ṛddhi, parūpaka,
samaṅgā, cavikā, bhārṅgī, kāśmarī, and karkaṭāhvaya.
With *ātmaguptā*, *mahāmedā*, the tops of *tāla* and *kharjūra*,
with *mṛṇāla*, *bisā*, *kharjūra*, *yaṣṭīmadhuka*, and *jīvaka*.
With *śatāvarī*, *vidārī*, *ikṣu*, the two types of *bṛhatī*,
and *sārivā*; with *mūrvā*, *aśvadaṃṣṭrā*, *ṛṣabhaka*, *śṛṅgāṭaka*, and *kaśeruka*.
With rāsnā, sthirā, āmalakī, sūkṣmailā, śaṭhī, pauṣkara,
punarnavā, tāvakṣīrī, kākolī, and dhanvayāsaka.
Madhuka, akṣoḍa, vātāma, muñja, ātābhiṣuka,
and also mahāmādhūra— this [group] possesses qualities superior even to māyūra.
It cures disorders of the bodily tissues (dhātu), the sense organs (indriya), and the voice (svara), as well as dyspnea, cough, and facial paralysis.
It is recommended for defects of the female reproductive tract, blood, and semen, and it bestows sons upon barren women.
One should prepare [medicines] with mice, cocks, swans,
and hares; these constitute two hundred and thirty-one diseases located above the collarbone (jatrūrdhva).
This has been explained at length, without mutual confusion.
The sages know the Puruṣa as having its roots above and its branches below.
Therefore, one should conquer those diseases that strike at the very root even more swiftly;
for upon them all the sense organs depend, and upon them the vital breaths (prāṇas) are sustained.
"Therefore, one should be diligent in protecting that supreme limb.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter.
Now begins the twenty-ninth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter entitled "The Thorough Knowledge of the Classification of Ulcers."
Thus indeed said the great seers, Ātreya and the others:
"As long as one chooses life, or as long as the body remains unexposed, it is called a *vraṇa* (wound)."
And that [fever] is of two kinds: endogenous (nija) and exogenous (āgantu).
Among these, the endogenous arises from the [deranged] humors (doṣa).
An exogenous wound (*āgantuvraṇa*) is caused by weapons, secondary weapons, stones, clubs, nails, teeth, horns, poison, *aruṣkara* (marking-nut), and so forth;
furthermore, when that too is presided over by the *vāta* and other [humors], it acquires the nature of an endogenous wound.
Moreover, a wound is of two kinds: vitiated (*duṣṭa*) and pure (*śuddha*).

In that case, [the ulcer] vitiated by the *doṣas* is considered "corrupted" (*duṣṭa*). Its general signs are: being excessively constricted or dilated; excessive softness or hardness; excessive elevation or depression; an excessive state of coldness or heat; excessive redness, blackness, or pallor; being covered with putrid flesh, vessels, and ligaments; a discharge of putrid pus; the presence of sinuses; and being afflicted by complications such as burning, suppuration, itching, swelling, pain, inflammation, and pustules, as well as persistence for a long duration.
Specifically, however, it is divided into fifteen types.

Among these, the ulcer caused by *vāta* is dark-brown, reddish, black, or has a color like ash, bone, a dove, or the throat; its discharge is slight, resembling curd-whey, alkaline water, meat-washings, or the liquid from boiled rice-grains; it is dry, characterized by a crackling sound, and suddenly experiences various types of piercing pain, throbbing, stretching, pricking, breaking pain, and numbness; furthermore, it is devoid of flesh.

The ulcer arising from Pitta is quick to develop; it is yellow, blue, green, black, tawny, or reddish-brown in color, resembling cow’s urine, ashes, a conch shell, the water of the *kiṃśuka* flower, or *mārdvīka* wine, as well as oil or hot substances; it is characterized by excessive moisture, burning, thirst, fever, redness, suppuration, bursting, and a sensation of fuming; its pain is like that of a wound sprinkled with caustic alkali (*kṣāra*), and it is afflicted with pustules.

Due to *kapha*, [the swelling] is unctuous, with thick lips, pale, intensely itchy, and resembles butter, muscle fat, marrow, flour, sesame, or coconut water; it is white, cold, copious, slimy, and moist; it is associated with numbness, stiffness, heaviness, and a coating sensation; it is covered with a network of vessels and ligaments, characterized by mild pain, hardness, and is due to *kapha*.
Due to *rakta* (blood), it is red like coral, covered with a network of black vesicles and pustules, and has the odor of a horse stable.

That which discharges blood and pus and exhibits the symptoms of pitta arises from blood (rakta). One should recognize a wound as vitiated by two, three, or all [the humors] when there is a combination of their respective symptoms.
Moreover,
[the disease] arising from pitta and rakta has the appearance of ghee-scum, smells like fish-washing water, is soft, spreads, and is blackish-pus-like.
AS.Utt.29.12 Furthermore, the absence of affliction by wind and the other [doshas] is the purification of the ulcer (vraṇa).

In that regard, due to the absence of the aforementioned signs of corruption, it is characterized by being free from inflammation, having the color of the tongue, smoothness, painlessness, absence of discharge, dark margins, evenness in the middle of the lips, or a slightly elevated center.
Skin, flesh, vessels, ligaments, joints, bones, the abdominal cavities, and the vital points— these eight are the locations of ulcers. Furthermore,
due to the specific nature of the underlying cavity, there is a corresponding variation in the discharge.
In that case, when the skin has been rubbed or when the pustules have burst, the discharge is clear like water, slightly fetid,
and yellowish in appearance.
When located in the flesh, it resembles clarified butter, is thick, and slimy;
when located in the vessels, however, there is excessive bleeding from the vessels that have been recently cut.
And when they are suppurated, pus flows out through the channels as water does;
it is thin, severed, slimy, hanging, and dark brown.
When located in the sinews, it is unctuous, dense, resembling nasal mucus, and mixed with blood.

When located in the joints, it does not flow even when the joint is pressed from all sides; likewise, during contraction, extension, elevation, depression, or movement, it flows as a slimy, hanging discharge mixed with frothy blood.
Bone that is struck, cracked, shattered, split open by the *doṣas*, or devoured by the *doṣas* becomes devoid of essence (*niḥsāra*) because it has been consumed by them.
In this case, the discharge is mixed with marrow, accompanied by blood, and unctuous; however,
when the ulcer is located in the visceral cavity (koṣṭha), it discharges urine, feces, blood, pus, and serous fluid.
However, [the condition] located in the vital points (*marman*) is not mentioned separately, because it is already included within the skin and other [tissues]. Among these,
the ease of cure increases in the order listed above.
Likewise, ulcers that are elongated, square, circular, or triangular,
as well as those that are dry and deformed in shape, are difficult to treat.

And these [ulcers] are generally either exogenous or spontaneous, arising from the [vitiated] humors, but not produced by medical intervention. Ulcers in those who are in their prime, firm, vital, courageous, self-controlled, and possessing a keen digestive fire, are easily curable.
In that regard,
for those in the prime of youth, because their bodily constituents (dhātus) are fresh, the healing of wounds occurs rapidly.
In those who are firm, because of their abundant and stable flesh, the surgical instrument does not reach the veins, ligaments, and so forth;
in those endowed with vitality, there is no exhaustion due to the constraints of pain, diet, and movement;
and in those endowed with courage, no distress arises even from particularly harsh medical procedures.

For those who possess self-control, [the healing] occurs through instructions such as well-regulated diet and lifestyle, and not otherwise; for those with a stimulated digestive fire (*dīptāgni*), the body becomes excessively moistened, whereas for those whose bodies are naturally non-moistening, and during those specific places and times where there is an absence of discharge and foul odor, the wound is quickly filled with pure flesh without complication (AS.Utt.29.25). These very same qualities are reversed in cases of the elderly, the emaciated, those with little strength, the timid, those with weak digestion, and in persons with a moistened body, or during unsuitable places and times; furthermore, one should examine whether the patient is fit to be initiated as a disciple.
Likewise, those located in the buttocks, anus, generative organs, forehead, cheeks, lips, back, ears, scrotum, abdomen, collarbone, and the interior of the mouth are easily healed.

Those [fistulas] that are inverted, located at the skin, eyes, teeth, nose, outer corners of the eyes, ears, navel, abdomen, suture (sevanī), buttocks, sides, flanks, chest, armpits, breasts, or joints; those discharging frothy pus, blood, and wind; those containing internal foreign bodies; those discharging from the lower part upward; those situated at the hairline, nails, vital points (marmans), calves, thighs, or nose; and those fistulas with an internal opening located at the suture or the pelvic bone—[these are incurable].
Moreover, [it is contraindicated] for those suffering from skin diseases, those afflicted by poison, those with consumption, and those with diabetes mellitus.
Wounds that heal with great difficulty, or those in which further wounds have formed within the original wound,
are palliative; as are avapāṭikā, niruddhaprakaśa, niruddhaguda, wounds from fistula-in-ano, granthi, and all injuries to the bones.
