Furthermore, those [fistulas] that are incurable are: those protruding like a lump of flesh; those with internal suppuration and discharge; those with pain; those with lips turned upward like the anus; those with hard, horn-like elevations of flesh; those discharging vitiated blood or thin, slimy secretions; those elevated in the center with depressed, hollow margins; those covered with a network of fibers like hemp-cotton; those of hideous appearance; those discharging fat, marrow, muscle-fat, or brain-matter; those arising from the *doṣas* (humors); those located in the trunk (*koṣṭha*) which carry yellow or black urine, feces, and flatus; those born in the receptacle of blood (*raktaśaya*) which have a discharge like alkaline water; those born in the receptacle of digested food (*pakvāśaya*) which flow like the water of fermented rice-grains; those occurring in patients with wasted muscles, spreading in all directions, having small openings, and appearing like fleshy bubbles; those carrying sound-accompanied flatus; those located in the head or skull; those associated with erysipelas, fever, thirst, anorexia, indigestion, cough, dyspnea, diarrhea, and vomiting; and those where, upon the splitting of the cranial bone, brain-matter is visible or where the symptoms of the three *doṣas* manifest.
And there is a verse on this:
"Due to the moistening of the ligaments, the cutting of the vessels, depth, and being devoured by worms..."
Due to the breaking of bone, the presence of a foreign body (śalya), the presence of poison, or being unexpected;
due to improper bandaging, excessive unctuousness, dryness, or the rubbing of hair and other such factors.
Due to agitation, impurity of the digestive tract, over-satiety, or excessive emaciation;
due to the drinking of wine, sleeping during the day, physical exercise, or staying awake at night.
Even a wound that is curable does not heal if it is treated improperly. When the edges of a wound resemble the color of a pigeon and are free from moisture, [it is considered healed].
"One should diagnose it as 'it is healing' when [the wound] is firm and covered with pustules.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter.
Now begins the thirtieth chapter. Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "The Treatment of Ulcers."
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and others: "The procedure for surgical intervention during the stage of swelling of a wound, as well as the treatment for edema, has been indicated."
In that regard, fasting alone is taught as the most important treatment at the outset,
according to the specific case, for the purpose of pacifying the excessive increase of the humors (doṣas).
Having considered the body, the vital breaths, and so forth, one should apply fasting therapy (apatarpaṇa).
Those [humors] that are free from passion and agitation, withered, and deprived of their support [should be treated thus].
The wounds and swellings of pure-bodied persons are pacified immediately;
one should also apply the aforementioned medicinal pastes, massages, and affusions.
Just as fire, when drenched with water, attains tranquility,
so too does the fire of the bodily humors (doṣa) when external applications such as plasters are suddenly employed.
One should apply the ointment only in the reverse direction, not in the natural direction;
for in this way, the medicine remains properly in place.
It enters through the pores of the skin, but it must not be neglected while drying; otherwise, it should be pressed out,
for if it dries up, it increases burning sensations, heat, redness, blackish discoloration, and pain.

That which is applied cool and repeatedly in small quantities is a *pradeha* (massage paste); it clarifies the blood, pitta, and skin. A *pralepa* (plaster), however, whether warm or cold and applied thickly, pacifies vāta and kapha; its application is indicated for both wounds and non-wounds.
That which is applied to wounds receives the designation "kalka" (paste); thus,
in brief, there are ten types of ālepa (plasters).

They are as follows: emollient (*snaihika*), pacifying (*nirvāpaṇa*), clarifying (*prasādana*), stabilizing (*stambhana*), liquefying (*vilāyana*), digestive (*pācana*), compressive (*pīḍana*), purificatory (*śodhana*), healing (*ropaṇa*), and color-restoring (*savarṇīkaraṇa*).
Among these, the emollient treatment for wind (*vāta*) consists of unctuous substances rich in oil, or indeed oil itself.

In cases of swelling caused by pitta or dominated by pitta, as well as in those burnt by poison, fire, or alkali, that same [application] is cooling; furthermore, when the blood is internally vitiated, it acts as a purifier.
Furthermore, that same [unctuous substance] is designated as "stambhana" (astringent/fixing) when there is excessive discharge;

it is used for "vilayana" (liquefying) with cold substances when the condition is dominated by *śleṣman* and *medas*, is uncooked (*avidagdha*), flour-like, or knotted; and with those same [cold substances], it is used for "pācana" (digestive/digestion-promoting) when the condition is cooked (*vidagdha*).
In a small-mouthed ulcer, compression should be applied with dry and slimy substances;
if it is impure, purification should be performed with the appropriate purifying agents as prescribed;
once purified, healing should be induced.
Once healed, their natural form is described by names that indicate their coloration; furthermore,
one should not apply a medicinal paste at night.
"Let there not be an increase in the morbid transformation due to the heat being confined within and unable to escape externally," so says Puṣkalāvata.
As.Utt.30.11 Puṣkalāvata, however, recites:
For the heat, being shrouded by darkness, [emerges] through the unobstructed pores of the skin.
One does not emerge from it without the plaster; therefore, one should not apply it at night.
Nor should one apply a plaster that has been kept overnight, nor should one apply the same plaster again.
For that which has become sour is indeed stale, and likewise, the other [type] has lost its potency;
[it should be applied] to a swelling, an ulcer, one that is hard, discolored, and accompanied by pain.
In cases of poisoning, one should especially extract the blood using leeches and other such means,
both for the purpose of pacifying the pain and to prevent suppuration;
furthermore, in this case, cooling applications should be made with the *nyagrodha* group and others.
One should apply plasters, affusions, and other treatments mixed with ghee, milk, and sugar,
using the bark of *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *plakṣa*, and *vetasa*.

An application (pradeha) with abundant clarified butter is excellent for cooling inflammation; likewise, an application of roasted grain flour (saktu), madhuka, and ghee mixed with sugar has the same effect.
For swellings and even such ulcers that are dominated by vāta, are stiff, hard, accompanied by great pain, and from which blood has flowed; AS.Utt.30.17.

Fomentation (sveda) should be applied using village meat, marshland meat, aquatic meat, veśavāra, kṛsarā, pāyasa, and utkārikā. However, for those suffering from burning sensations and pain, one should roast sesame and linseed, quench them in milk, grind them with that same milk, and apply it as a plaster.

A lukewarm *utkārikā* (poultice) prepared with *balā*, *madhuka*, *pṛśniparṇī*, *chinnaruhā*, *abhīru*, *jīvantī*, sugar, *madanaka*, milk, and *mahāsneha* (the five fats), when applied, removes colic and burning sensations.
Similarly, a lukewarm poultice made of honey, barley powder, oil, and ghee is [recommended],
as is a warm compress consisting of sesame seeds and mung-bean porridge.
AS.Utt.30.22: A pouring (pariṣeka) with lukewarm water prepared with the ten roots (daśamūla), or with milk, or with ghee and oil, relieves burning and pain in cases of swelling or an ulcer.
For swellings that are firm and characterized by mild pain, a process of softening (vimlāpana) should be performed.
Having anointed and then fomented [the area], one should then slowly [extract the foreign body] by means of a bamboo tube.
One should massage it with the palm or the thumb for the purpose of softening; likewise, an ointment made from the paste of *āsphota* leaves and *asūra* should be applied.
If it does not dissolve by means of well-prepared flour mixed with ghee, or with mung beans, barley, or wheat, then one should apply a poultice (upanāhana) to it.
Likewise, the undigested [dosha] attains pacification, while the digested undergoes maturation.

(AS.Utt.30.27) Having prepared a poultice (*utkārikā*) from *śigru*, *śaṇa* fruit, *citraka*, *kiṇva*, *niṣpāva*, mustard seeds, sesame, *atasī*, roasted flour (*saktu*), and soot (*gṛhadhūma*), ground with sour liquids, made lukewarm, unctuous, and salted, one should apply it and bind it after covering it with an *eraṇḍa* leaf.

When the swelling is ready for suppuration, one should feed the patient as desired for the purpose of promoting maturation, and so that he may endure the pain of ripening and the surgical procedure. Once it has suppurated, one should apply the knife according to the prescribed method.
When a swelling is well-matured, consolidated, and compressed by pressure,
incision is beneficial for that which requires incision, once the aggravated doshas have reached full suppuration.

With the roots of *citraka*, *cirabilva*, *dantī*, and *karavīra*; with *kapota-paṅka* and *gṛdhra-purīṣa*; with *guggulu*, *atasī*, the milky sap of *snuhī*, the alkali of *palāśa*, *suvarṇakṣīrī*, the dung of a cock, and *mukūlaka*; or with alkaline medicinal herbs, or with alkali alone—one should treat abscesses containing pus that have small openings, those with raised edges, or even those located in vital parts (*marman*).
One should apply squeezing substances that are devoid of oiliness and press them all around;
one should then observe the application as it dries during the process of squeezing.
One should not smear this [medicated oil] into the mouth, for in that way the defect is aggravated.
Kalāya, barley, wheat, mudga, māṣa, and hareṇu [beans are beneficial].
In the case of substances that are slimy, the bark and roots should be used for squeezing.
[One should avoid] those that are discolored, slimy, foul-smelling, and characterized by moisture and pain.
Having recognized that wounds are impure, one should treat them with these purifying agents:
*śaṅkhinī*, *aṅkola*, *sumanā*, *karavīra*, and *suvarcalā*.
Triphalā, khadira, dārvī, the leaf of kola, palankaṣā,
and the decoctions of the āragvadhādi group are used for washing.
A paste consisting of *paṭolī*, sesame, *yaṣṭyāhva*, *trivṛt*, *dantī*, the two types of *niśā* (turmeric and long pepper),
and *nimba* leaves mixed with *pāṭu* (salt) is a purifier of ulcers.
Ajagandhā, ajaśṛṅgī, gavākṣī, lāṅgalī, niśā, pūtīka,
citraka, pāṭhā, paṭolī, vella, and reṇukā.
The three pungents (kaṭutraya), alkali of barley (yavakṣāra), salts, and the mineral surāṣṭrajā;
nikumbha, kumbha, kāsīsa, haritāla, and manaḥśilā.
Regarding the medicinal paste, ghee, oil, juice, powder, and wick:
in those deep ulcers of a pitta-nature that involve burning and suppuration, one should prepare and apply a paste and ghee— neither too sharp nor too hot— mixed with the fruit of the *kārpāsī* plant.

In cases where the flesh has been destroyed, the discharge is slight, and the area is dry, one should apply the previously mentioned *pūtīka* and other substances combined with sesame and *apāmārga*, along with the two types of *bṛhatī*, and mustard oil. In cases arising from unstable regions that are excessively moist, characterized by raised and firm flesh, and which do not succeed with oil, one should employ a medicinal extract (*rasakriyā*).

When the decoction of the aforementioned purificatory drugs has been strained and boiled again, one should employ it— once it is prepared by adding a powder of realgar (*manaḥśilā*), *tuvarī*, and copper sulfate (*kāsīsa*) as a post-decoction additive (*pratīvāpa*), combined with the juice of *mātuluṅga* and honey—
in cases where the disease is associated with fat (*medas*), is deep-seated, exuding moisture, or is difficult to cure with pastes (*kalka*).
In vacā, rock salt, fermenting agent, ferrous sulfate, and the two types of turmeric;

One should prepare a cleansing powder for other excellent purificatory treatments [to be used] for deep-seated wounds that have internal foreign bodies, minute openings, and are embedded in the flesh.

One should cleanse with medicated wicks those ulcers located at joints or vital spots (marman) that are overwhelmed by Vāta, accompanied by discharge, and characterized by severe pain; such ulcers should be fumigated.

One should thoroughly extinguish [the heat] with very cold applications of śrīveṣṭaka, sarjarasa, sāla, devadāru, śiṃśapā, khadira, āsana, kaiḍarya, the heartwood of yava, beeswax, birch bark, silk-cotton, and ghee, for those cases where pitta, blood, and poison are predominant.

In a deep ulcer with little or no flesh, filling it up (utsādana) is beneficial. A paste made from aśvagandhā, apāmārga, tālapatrī, suvarcalā, balā, atibalā, anantā, dhātakī flowers, samaṅgā, the padmakādi group, and the nyagrodhādi group, as well as medicated ghees, should be used for the purpose of anointing.
Today, one should eat the meats of meat-eaters, properly prepared according to the prescribed rules.
The flesh of one with a pure mind increases through the flesh of a meat-eater;
it is used for the healing of wounds where the soft flesh has been destroyed.
The powders of *manthā*, *dantī*, *śirīṣa*, the fruits of *karañja*, *bhūrja* knots, *kukkuṭāṇḍatvac*, pigeon dung, sparrow dung, *nepālī*, and *haritāla*, mixed with honey,
[are used] for a wound that is painful, hard, stiff, dry, and parched.
For the purpose of producing softness and without harming the wound, one should drink ghee prepared with Vāta-alleviating drugs.
Oil prepared with those same [medicinal] substances is used for massage; the aforementioned sudations should also be employed.

Likewise, fumigations with clarified butter, marrow, and muscle fat; and frequent applications of slightly warm pastes made from well-oiled roasted grain flour (*saktu*), rock salt, yeast, ground sesame, *kṛsara* (rice and pulse mixture), milk-porridge (*pāyasa*), and meat-broth from marshy animals (*veśavāra*).
The medicated ghees for treating pitta-type abscesses, erysipelas, swellings,
and skin diseases (kuṣṭha) should be employed in all types of wounds for drinking, sprinkling, and external application.
In wounds with excessively soft flesh, for the purpose of making them firm (dāruṇīkaraṇa), one should apply the bark of triphalā, lodhra, āmra, sarja, jambū, priyaṅgu, and aśoka,
along with a powder of saurāṣṭrī, kāsīsa, and rocanā.
With heartwood and fragrant substances,
one should apply incense to those [wounds] that have lost their flesh, are hard, itchy,
and long-standing.
One should cleanse those wounds that are very difficult to purify by means of caustic application (kṣārakarman),
as well as those discharging urine from urinary stones (aśmarī) or others that discharge blood.

Those whose joints have been severed, or those for whom the healing is not accomplished despite being treated with the prescribed methods, should be purified by means of thermal cautery (agnikarman). Then, once the wounds are purified, one should apply healing agents (ropaṇa).

The barks of the *asanā*, *nyagrodha* group, *dhava*, *sallakī*, and *kuṭaja*; *mañjiṣṭhā*, *samaṅgā*, *amṛtā*, *aśvagandhā*, *āragvadha*, and the flowers of *dhātakī*; and the *padmaka* group—these are to be employed in the seven procedures beginning with washing (*prakṣālana*). Regarding this, there are these verses: [AS.Utt.30.58] Asanādinyagrodhādivargadhavasallakīkuṭajatvaco mañjiṣṭhāsamaṅgāmṛtāśvagandhāragvadhadhātakīpuṣpāṇi padmakādiśca prakṣālanādiṣu saptasu prayojyā iti bhavanti cātra.
In a wound where putrid flesh has been removed and the blood is turbid and afflicted,
emesis is recommended, especially when the wound is corrupted by *kapha*.
Purgation is indicated when pitta is vitiated and has persisted for a long time; enema is indicated when there is dryness and pain, especially in the lower part of the body.

In cases of swelling occurring above the collarbone that is characterized by excessive itching, strong nasal medication (nasya) should be administered; however, if the swelling arising from that same cause is dominated by Vāta, unctuous nasal medication should be used.

Likewise, in cases of swelling, pain, and discharge, or when the mouth is afflicted by disorders dominated by Vāta and Kapha accompanied by pain and other symptoms, medicinal gargling (kavala) is beneficial according to the specific requirements of each case.
The two groups known as the first two *pañcamūla*s and that which subdues *vāta*—
these should be employed in the seven forms of treatment, beginning with decoctions (*kaṣāya*), for wounds caused by *vāta*.
The Nyagrodha-padmaka group and the Pitta-subduing group are for Pitta-type [fever];
the Aragvadha group destroys Kapha and is for Kapha-type; however, mixed groups are for fever arising from a combination of doshas.

In cases of Vātika disorders, a thick, lukewarm paste made from flour mixed with water and combined with oil, ghee, and muscle fat should be applied; however, in Paittika cases, the paste should be ground with milk and mixed with ghee.
A thick paste made from cow’s urine and ground with [medicinal herbs], kept constantly warm between thin layers of cloth,
is beneficial for Kaphaja [piles]; it may be dry with oil or unctuous, depending on the case.
For wounds from which putrid flesh has been removed, where the site for flesh growth remains unhealed,
one should apply a paste of sesame seeds combined with madhuka to promote healing.
Being unctuous, hot, bitter, sweet, and astringent, it conquers all [doshas]; when combined with honey and nimba leaves, it is an excellent purifier.
Combined with the two aforementioned [substances] and ghee, this becomes a swift healer; however,
experts in the field maintain that some desire a paste of barley to be used like sesame seeds for deep wounds caused by blood, bile, poison, or external trauma, provided they are accompanied by heat.
One should heal wounds caused by *kapha* and *vāta* with clarified butter (*ājya*) boiled with milk and healing medicinal herbs, or with oil prepared with those same healing herbs.
For wounds that are not caused by trauma, which are unstable or stable, and whether they are pure or become contaminated,
one should treat them with appropriate healing agents containing the two types of harītakī (niśādvaya) for those caused by [vitiated] rasa.
A powder is prescribed for those [wounds] that are even, have firm flesh, and are located in the skin; for those that are painless, deep-seated, and purified, medicated plugs (varti) are beneficial.
A paste (kalka) consisting of samaṅgā, mocarasa, sarala, somavalka,
candana, and padmaka, etc., is a supreme healer for wound healing.
Puṇḍrāhvā, tila, jīvantī, gojihvā, dhātakī, balā,
prapauṇḍarīka, madhuka, the two types of kākolī, and candana.
Oil or clarified butter prepared in the same manner with *kampillaka*,

or with the juice of *dūrvā*, or with the bark of *dārvī*, promotes the healing of wounds. [Likewise,] the leaves of *paṭola* and *nimba*, along with *lodhra*, *mustā*, and *priyaṅgu* [are used for this purpose].
Sūkṣmailā, dhātakī, sarja, khadira, agaru, candana, kampillaka,
viḍaṅga, vatsaka, triphalā, and balā.
Ghee or oil prepared with these pastes is an excellent healer for promoting wound healing.
Padmaka, lotus stamens, dārvī, mūrvā, sesame, and utpala [are used].
An ointment made of *medā*, *samaṅgā*, and *yaṣṭyāhva* is a means for restoring the complexion.
[An ointment] produced from *kakubha*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *jambū*, *kaṭphala*, and *lodhra* [is likewise beneficial].
Wounds powdered with the ashes of bark quickly contract their skin when treated with lac, realgar,
madder, yellow orpiment, and the two types of turmeric.
An ointment consisting of ghee and honey is supreme for purifying the skin.
[The roots of] *dhyāmaka*, *aśvattha*, and *nicula*, along with lac and red ochre, [are used for this purpose].
Gold, amṛtāsaṅga, and kāsīsa are color-imparting agents.
[These are used] with kāleyaka, latā, copper, bone, gold, and the finest kālārasa.
A plaster consisting of cow-dung juice is the best for restoring one's natural complexion; likewise,
iron filings, green vitriol (kāsīsa), and the flowers of the three myrobalans (triphalā) [are effective].
An ointment made from the finely powdered skin of burnt marsh-dwelling animals produces blackness on fresh skin immediately.
One should apply a white plaster made from the fruit of *rohiṇī* soaked in oil of *bhallātaka* to the ulcer. This should remain for seven nights in goat's milk.
Having ground that very [substance] until it is very fine, one should apply a black ointment to the ulcer. [The substances are: the root of *kapālikā* (fresh), *vaidula*, and *sthirā*.
A paste of kāsīsa and madhuka applied to a black wound, mixed with honey, [is effective]; having removed the flesh from a *kapittha* fruit, one should fill it with urine and clarified butter.
One should add to this realgar, bamboo scrapings,
and ox-gallstone; after a month, one should place kāsīsa and prapunāṭa upon the ground.
Below the *arjuna* tree, that white ointment applied to the wound restores the natural skin color. An elephant tusk burnt with smokeless fire, along with oil and *rasāñjana*, [is likewise effective].
A plaster for the growth of hair is likewise [prepared] with soot derived from the hooves, hair, bones, skin, horns, and hoofs of quadrupeds, saturated with oil.
One who eats aged śāli rice that is unctuous and in small quantities, followed by plenty of warm water,
along with the meat of wild animals, quickly heals the wound.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter.
Now begins the thirty-first chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "The Prevention of Acute Wounds" (Sadyovraṇapratiṣedha).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and others:
the origin of an exogenous wound has already been taught.
In each respective case, the remedy should be applied accordingly.
Furthermore, a limb afflicted by fresh wounds of many diverse forms produced by various types of trauma is, in brief, of three kinds: incised (chinna), pierced (viddha), and lacerated (piccita).
All three of these are called "wounded" because they involve the cutting of the skin and so forth;
among them, the "severed" is divided into five types.
For example, it is like a small amount of flesh that has been scraped when the skin was cut; yet,
that very same [flesh] is deeply penetrated, specifically severed, and made wide and long.
When some of the bones, sinews, and so forth remain, it is called "delayed";
when all the limbs have been severed, it is "cast down";
and when pierced, it is of eight kinds.
In that case, when the shaft has reached the flesh and is displaced,
one should elevate the skin on the second side and push it upward.
When [the weapon] has exited slightly, it is called *atividdha*; when it has exited completely, it is called *nirviddha*.

This same fourfold classification receives the designations *anubhinna*, *bhinnottuṇḍita*, *atibhinna*, and *nirbhinna* when pierced by broad-mouthed weapons such as spears (*kunta*) and the like within the cavity.
Furthermore, when a limb containing bone, drenched in blood and marrow, becomes swollen due to a blow or pressure, that is *piccita*;
it is of two kinds.

Therein, fractures are both with wound (savraṇa) and without wound (avraṇa); of these, the one with wound has been described, while the one without wound will be taught among the types of fracture (bhaṅga).
And on this point, it is said in AS.Utt.31.6: "One should immediately sprinkle a fresh wound with ghee mixed with yaṣṭīmadhuka."
Or again, for one suffering intense pain, [the wound] should be treated with lukewarm balā oil to suppress the heat of the injury and to prevent its spreading at that time.
Astringent, cold, sweet, and unctuous applications, such as ointments and the like,
are beneficial for fresh wounds, especially for the purpose of promoting healing.
One should administer honey and ghee, as well as cooling treatments that alleviate pitta;
in cases accompanied by swelling (saṃrambha), purification therapies for both the upper and lower tracts should be performed.
Fasting, wholesome food, and the continuous bloodletting prescribed for those with rubbing and itching are especially recommended in these cases.
For from those two [wounds], blood flows only slightly, and thus suppuration arises quickly;
whereas elsewhere, except in the case of a traumatic wound, blood generally flows excessively.
Then, when the wind (vāyu) is provoked by the loss of blood and causes excessive pain, [one should employ] the drinking of oleaginous substances, affusion, fomentation, ointment, and poultice.
One should also administer an unctuous enema prepared with Vata-alleviating drugs;
thus has been declared the seven-day regimen beneficial for fresh wounds.

When the force [of the poison] has subsided after seven days, one should follow the previously mentioned procedure; if that [affected area] remains vitiated, one should employ washing, massage, and ointments.
The group beginning with *āragvadha* and the *surasā* group are used for purification;
a paste (*kalka*) should be prepared from *trivṛt*, sesame, castor leaves, and rock salt.
In cases of Vātika ulcers, [one should use] Kumbha, Yaṣṭyāhva, and Rajanī with sesame;
in Ślaiṣmika ulcers, sesame, Tejohvā, Nikumbha, Svarjikā, and Agnika.
This procedure for treating malignant ulcers applies also to those caused by Kuṣṭha and Meha.
Generally, this is a common procedure; however, it will now be explained separately for each case.

When [the skin] has been rubbed, one should quickly apply powders to suppress the pain and restore the color; however, for those [wounds] that have not been incised, or for those that are fissured or hanging, one should apply pastes (kalka) and the like.
Suturing according to the prescribed method, as well as bandaging and non-compression; [however,] an eye that is ruptured, protruded, or hanging down is incurable.
Having positioned it in its proper place so that the veins are not displaced,
the physician should press it with his hand covered by a lotus leaf.
Then, for him, clarified butter prepared with liquorice (*yaṣṭyāhva*), *jīvaka*, *ṛṣabha*, and blue lotus (*utpala*) is beneficial for sprinkling, nasal administration, and saturation. (AS.Utt.31.21)
Indeed, that [oil] with milk is supreme for conquering all injuries to the eyes;
when the eyes are failing due to pressure on the neck, emesis, eructation, vomiting,
or sneezing [should be employed].

Alternatively, breath control (prāṇāyāma) should be performed, and treatment like that for a wounded eye should be applied; if the ear has been displaced from its position and sutured, one should fill the canal with oil.
If the *kṛkāṭikā* (the nape of the neck) is severed and air is escaping,
one should quickly suture it without leaving any gaps, aligning the parts evenly and then bind them.
In this case, sprinkling with clarified butter mixed with goat’s meat is recommended;
the patient should eat with his head raised and lie down well-restrained.
If the fracture is oblique in the limbs or well-aligned in the trunk,
one should sew it with a twisted suture (vellitabandha) and bind it with a thick cloth.
A binding of the scrotum with a leather strap should be performed when the wound has healed;
for one whose scrotum is hanging down, the feet and eyes should be sprinkled with water.
Having inserted the testicles, one should suture them with a stitch known as the *tunna*;
then, having applied a cloth bandage around the waist, a *goṣphaṇā* bandage should be performed.
One should not apply an oil enema, for by that the wound becomes moistened.
[One should instead use] kālānusāri, aguru, elā, jātī, candana, and parpaṭa.

Oil prepared with stone, wood, *amṛta*, and *tuttha* is a healing agent for wound closure. Having thoroughly cauterized a severed branch with oil according to the proper method, [one should apply it].

One should bind it with a sheath-like bandage and then treat it like a wound. In the case of a perforation from which the foreign body has been extracted, the procedure for a fracture should be followed; however, in the case of a crushed injury, [the same applies].
Once the foreign body has been extracted from the head, one should insert a cotton wick;
for if the brain matter flows out, the patient will die in anger, otherwise he may survive as it is unstable.
As the wound heals, one should gradually remove the hair one by one; in the case of a discharge of brain matter, one should consume the brains of other living beings.

Once the foreign body has been removed from another part of the body, one should apply a medicated oil-soaked wick (snehavarti). This applies to those wounds that are deeply seated, narrow-mouthed, and have discharged blood.
One should irrigate those [wounds] with *cakrataila* applied through a fine nozzle;
when the abdominal cavity is ruptured and filled with blood, fainting, pain in the heart, and pain in the flanks occur.
Fever, burning sensation, thirst, flatulence, aversion to food,
retention of feces, urine, and flatus, dyspnea, perspiration, and redness of the eyes.
There will be a metallic odor in his mouth and a foul smell on his body;
when the blood is located in the stomach, he even vomits blood.
When blood is located in the colon (pakvāśaya), one suffers from excessive distension and piercing pain, and there is heaviness accompanied by colic.
Below the navel there is coldness, and blood flows out from the orifices;
even though the receptacle is not ruptured, it becomes filled by means of subtle channels.
With blood flowing from the flanks like urine from the bladder,
there occurs internal hemorrhaging, coldness of the feet, labored breathing, and a distorted facial expression.
One should avoid [treating] a patient with bloodshot eyes, a pale face, and a distended abdomen.
If the [vitiated humor] is located in the stomach (āmāśaya), emesis is beneficial; if it has reached the large intestine (pakvāśaya), [purgation is beneficial].
Purgation and non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) should be administered with cleansing agents that are ununctuous and hot,
using the decoctions of barley, jujube, and horse gram, devoid of any fats.
One should eat food or drink gruel mixed with rock salt; however,
one whose blood has flowed excessively and whose abdominal cavity is ruptured should drink blood.
The perforation of the visceral cavity (koṣṭhabheda) is considered to be of two types: that involving the intestines (kliṣṭa) and that involving the rupture of the intestines (chinna).
In the first type, fainting and other symptoms are mild; in the second, however, they are extremely distressing.

A person whose intestines are afflicted by disease lives in a state of uncertainty, whereas one whose intestines are severed does not live at all. He whose excrement, urine, and flatus have returned to their respective natural channels [is saved].

One who is free from complications will undoubtedly survive even if the abdominal cavity is ruptured. If the intestines have come out with the abdomen intact, they should be reinserted; otherwise, it is not so.
Some, however, say that even that [wound] which has been seized by the head of a *uluṅgila* fish should be washed with milk and then smeared with grass, blood, and dust.
One whose nails have been trimmed should insert it very slowly, anointed with ghee;
having moistened the dry [speculum] with milk and soaked it thoroughly in abundant clarified butter,
one should touch the throat with a finger and agitate the patient with water.
Likewise, they enter into the intestines and cause pain at that time;
however, due to the narrowness of the wound or because of their great number, they may not enter the abdominal cavity or the intestines.
Having incised the abdomen with that same measurement, one should insert [the intestines];
once the intestine is properly restored to its place, one should suture the wound.
It draws out the life-force that has departed from its place, even if it is well-guarded. Having wrapped it with a secondary bandage, one should sprinkle it with clarified butter.
Then, for the sake of softening the stool and ensuring the downward movement of the wind (vāyu), one should have the patient drink lukewarm milk mixed with *citrā* oil.
Oil prepared from the paste of *tvak*, *aśvakarṇaka*, *kakubha*, *badarī*, *sallakī*, and *dhava* is the foremost for healing wounds.
One should observe the rainy season and maintain the prescribed regimen for the bandaging of the wound. From the abdomen, a wick made of fat should be drawn out using ashes or clay.
Having sprinkled the root with mild astringent decoctions and then wrapped it evenly and firmly with a thread, the skilled physician should cause it to grow.
With a sharp instrument heated by fire, one should cut [the vessel] all at once; otherwise, there may be intense pain, swelling, or death as it is being severed.
When the wound has been bound with honey and well-digested food has been consumed, one should drink ghee.

Milk boiled with sugar, citrā, lac, gokṣura, and yaṣṭyāhva conquers pain and burning; the previously mentioned regimen is also excellent. Furthermore, the oil prescribed for fatty glandular swellings (medogranthi) is beneficial here as an unguent.
Tālīsa, padmaka, māṃsī, hareṇu, agaru, and candana.
Oil cooked with the two types of *haridrā*, lotus seeds, *uśīra*, and *madhuka* is declared to be the best healer for fresh wounds;
it is also indicated for those struck by a blow while unconscious, or who have fallen from a high place in an uneven manner.
One should provide treatment that overcomes wind and hemorrhage, consisting of satiation, massage, oil application, and affusion,
for a patient whose body is disjointed, agitated, emaciated, struck in the vital organs (marmans), or wounded.
One should have the patient stay in a vat filled with oil while feeding him meat broth.
Fresh wounds of various forms may occur on the limbs due to the blows from the weapons and efforts of the assailant.
"Nevertheless, they do not transcend the state of being three, just as the winds and other elements do not exceed their nature despite the distinctions of accumulation and so forth.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter.
Now begins the thirty-second chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "The Prevention of Fractures."
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and others:
"They teach that fractures of the bones are of many kinds, caused by specific types of trauma such as falling, being crushed, blows, dislocation, and the bites of wild beasts.
That collection of fractures has two locations: at a joint and not at a joint.

Among these, those occurring outside of a joint are of six types: crushed (utpiṣṭa), separated (viśliṣṭa), depressed (avakṣipta), displaced (atikṣipta), obliquely displaced (tiryakkṣipta), and rotated (vivartita).
Its general characteristics are: inability to extend, contract, rotate, or flex; intense pain; and intolerance to touch.
Furthermore, in the case of a crushed joint (utpiṣṭa), there is swelling on both sides at the very site of the joint, along with pain that is particularly severe at night.
In *viśliṣṭa* (dislocated), there is slight swelling, constant pain, and displacement of the joint;
in *avakṣipta* (dropped), there is separation of the joint and intense pain.
In *atikṣipta* (over-extended), both joints have moved beyond their limit and there is pain;
in *tiryak-kṣipta* (lateral displacement), one joint has moved to the side and there is extreme pain;
in *vivartita* (rotated), because the joint has moved to the side, the limb becomes deformed and there is pain.
Furthermore, a fracture not involving the joint is of twelve types,
namely:

The types of fractures are: *karkaṭaka* (crab-like), *vakra* (curved), *sthūṭita* (crushed), *vellita* (twisted), *asthicchallikā* (bone-skin), *aśvakarṇa* (horse-ear), *piccita* (pressed), *dārita* (split), *cūrṇita* (powdered), *atipātita* (displaced), *śeṣita* (partially remaining), and *majjānugata* (penetrating the marrow).

The general symptoms of a fracture not involving a joint (*asandhibhagna*) are: excessive swelling, throbbing, shifting, intolerance to touch, a cracking sound when pressed, drooping of the limbs, intense pain, and an inability to find relief in any position. These constitute the common characteristics of a fracture not involving a joint.

The *vaiśeṇika* fracture is one that is well-displaced with the bone broken at both ends, elevated like a knot, and resembling a crab; it is called *karkaṭaka*. The *ābhugna* fracture is one where the bone is bent but not separated, being curved.
AS.Utt.32.9 Like a bladder filled with porcupine quills, swollen and ruptured in one large opening;
AS.Utt.32.10 split in two, it undulates while trembling— this is the vellitaka [type of hemorrhoid].
The *pārśvataḥ* [type] is characterized by a deficiency of bone on the side, while the *asthicchallikā* [type] is characterized by protruding bones.
Aśvakarṇa is so called because it protrudes like the ear of a horse. Piccita is characterized by broadness and significant swelling.
It is torn apart by minute, manifold, and piercing pains.
When being touched, it sounds like a grinding powder;
when entering into the interior of a bone fragment, it is called *atipātita*.
That which remains on one side is called "residual" (śeṣita).

A wound that is fractured, elevated, or where the marrow sinks into the marrow— these last five types are difficult to cure, as are those occurring in emaciated persons, children, the elderly, the weak, those who overeat, those whose disorder is dominated by Vāta, lepers, and those with complications.

However, the following cases are incurable: a fractured hip-bone (kaṭīkapāla), a dislocated joint, a crushed pelvis, a dislocated elbow, a shattered forehead, a skull with non-approximated bone fragments, and fractures of the temporal bone, the spine, or the space between the breasts.
And there are verses on this point:
"Now, one should raise what is depressed and press down what is elevated.
One should stretch what is compressed and elevate what has sunk downward by means of stretching, pressing upward, lifting, contracting the skin, and binding;
thus one treats all the joints of the body, whether they are mobile or immobile. (AS.Utt.32.22)
Having thus properly stabilized [the patient] by these means of stabilization so that he is motionless,
one should then wrap him comfortably with cloths soaked in abundant ghee.
[The nozzle] should be made from the wood of the kadamba, udumbara, aśvattha, sarja, arjuna, or palāśa trees,
or from bamboo; it should be broad at the base, tapering toward the tip, and well-fashioned.
One should apply a binding made of very smooth, supportive bark or even wood-shavings called *kuśa*,
together with a cloth bandage.
For with a loose bandage, stability of the joint is not achieved;
whereas with a tight one, there arises excessive pain, burning, suppuration, and swelling.
In the hot season during the menstrual period, one should cause [the blood] to be released every three days; in the cold season, every seven days;
but in the moderate season, every five days, or according to the requirements of the specific disorder.
Then one should sprinkle that [wound], if it is painful, with a cooled decoction of *nyagrodha* and other [trees],
or with milk boiled with the five roots (*pañcamūla*).
The wise physician, having considered the location and the time, should administer lukewarm *cakrataila* combined with Vata-alleviating drugs.
One should frequently apply very cold ointments and affusions;
[one should also give] the milk of a cow that has recently calved, mixed with ghee and prepared with sweet medicinal herbs.

One who has suffered a fracture should drink cold water mixed with lac every morning. However, for one whose fracture is accompanied by an ulcer, the ulcer should be treated with substances in which honey and ghee predominate.
Then, having rubbed [the area] with astringent decoctions, the remaining procedure described for fractures should be followed;
protruding wound-flesh should be smeared with honey and ghee.
The physician should close the wounds and treat them with bandages;
once he knows they have become even and well-settled, he should apply *phalinī*, *lodhra*, and *kaṭphala*.
One should dust [the wound] with the powdered *samaṅgā* and *dhātakī*,
or with the powder of the five barks (*pañcavalkala*) combined with honey and fermented gruel (*madhuśukta*).
Alternatively, wounds heal quickly with the powders of *dhātakī* and *lodhra*; likewise,
one should keep the joint of a dislocated or crushed bone from being disturbed in this very manner.
One should treat complications such as visarpa according to their respective [specifics],
when the patient's bodily constituents (dhātu) are stable and during the winter season. Thus has the section on "fracture" been commenced.
For one who is stout, has few defects, and is easy to treat, [the treatment] is otherwise severe;
for those in the first, middle, and final stages of life, it is applied in one, two, and threefold doses respectively.
For those who follow the prescribed rule, stability of the joint occurs within months; this is the general method, whereas the specific treatment will be described hereafter.
When a nail joint is crushed and filled with blood,
one should crush it with a lancet; once the blood has flowed out, one should apply a plaster of ground śāli rice.
Having set the fractured fingers and those that were dislocated as before,
one should wrap them with a thin cloth bandage and apply an irrigation of clarified butter.
The wise physician, using a wheel-like mechanism, should extract a protruding bone from the thigh; he should then excise it both above and below in the case of a fractured hip.
One should lift the arm with a mace when the joint of the armpit and shoulder is dislocated.
Being composed, one should bind it while it remains in its place with a cross-shaped bandage;
then the physician should rub the elbow joint with the thumb.
Then, having gently rubbed the joint, one should press it as it slips from the elbow; one should extend and flex it, and cause it to be treated with oleation.
This same sequence of treatment applies to the wrist, the knee, and the ankle.
Having made both surfaces even for one who has milked the udder and broken the surface,
[one should proceed].
One should apply a bandage with raw oil and perform a sprinkling (pariṣeka);
first, one should hold a ball made of cow dung, and thereafter one made of clay.
Once strength has been generated in the hand, one should gradually practice holding stones. One should then raise up the drooping eye with a mallet after it has been fomented.
In that manner, one should press the elevated part and then bind it firmly; the treatment for a dislocation of the arm should be performed in the same way as for the thigh.
When the neck is twisted, or when it has gone downward,
one should grasp the hollow of the nape and the two jaws and raise the head upward.
One should bind it evenly with *kuśa* grass and lay the patient on his back; likewise, when the jawbones are dislocated at the jaw-joint, one should bring them back into alignment.
Having applied fomentation properly while the patient remains still, one should perform the binding of the five limbs (*pañcāṅgībandha*).
An errhine (*nasya*) prepared with ghee and sweet drugs that subdue Vāta is highly recommended.
One should press upon teeth that are loose, bleeding, or displaced, provided they are not fractured.
Having sprinkled the patient with cold water, one should apply an ointment;
one should treat him with external cooling measures and internal unifying remedies.

Ghee boiled with milk that has been processed with *lādvaya* and ghee boiled with the *padmakādi* group of drugs should be employed for nasal drops (*nasya*) and gargles (*gaṇḍūṣa*), as well as for those suffering from loose teeth.
One should smear his gums with these [medicinal substances] ground into a paste and prepared as electuaries;
for three months he should eat soft food consisting of meat broth and rice, and avoid all hard foods.
Having straightened the nose, whether it is twisted or sunken, one should then insert a double-ended tube into each nostril using a probe.
Then, having wrapped it with a cloth, one should apply an irrigation of ghee.
Having applied ghee to a fractured ear, one should set it in place and secure it with a bandage.
Thereafter, one should perform the treatment for fresh wounds;
for those with fractures of the waist, calves, or thighs, a bed with a door-panel (kavāṭa-śayana) is beneficial.
Then, for the purpose of restraint, five binding pegs (kīla) should be applied:
two each on the sides of the thighs, one peg on the sole,
and likewise one in the pelvis, the spinal column, the chest, or the collarbones.

In the case of dislocations where the joints have been shattered, one should perform this procedure for liberation; however, for joints that have been dislocated for a long time, they should first be treated with oleation, sudation, and softening.
One should bring [the fracture] back to its proper place according to the prescribed methods and one's own intelligence; however,
in the case of a fracture without a joint that has healed, it must be treated with great care due to the irregularity of the union.
Having crushed the fracture, one should restrain it; thereafter, one should treat it as a case of fracture.
The physician should strive in such a way that the fracture does not undergo suppuration.

When the flesh, vessels, and ligaments have matured, the joint does not achieve proper cohesion. For one with a fracture, one should administer the oleation therapies prescribed for wind-diseases (vātavyādhi).
One should practice the four types of applications, strengthening therapies, and enema treatments (basti),
using nourishing substances such as rice, milk, meat broth, and ghee, which are non-burning (non-acidic) in nature.
One should treat the fracture with appropriate measures that promote the union of the joints;
for exhaustion is not recommended in such a case, as it causes the separation of the joints.
Salt, pungent substances, alkaline matter, sourness, sexual intercourse, and exposure to the sun.
One should avoid physical exertion and dry medicinal remedies for one who has suffered a fracture; even a bone that has been properly set may become displaced due to improper positioning or binding.
One should avoid that which undergoes transformation even from slight agitation;
likewise, one should avoid from the outset any bone or joint that is poorly formed.
Young bones are crushed, while long tubular bones (nalaka) are broken.
The skull plates split apart, and others mostly burst open;
[the fetus] is not distorted, not pierced, and remains situated in its own place.
One should recognize a fracture as well-healed when there is no pain during movement. One should soak black sesame seeds that are free of dust and tied in a firm cloth for seven nights in water.

One should dry them up day after day, rubbing them with milk as well as with water boiled with *madhuka*. Then, once they have again drunk milk and been thoroughly dried out as before, [one should proceed].
Having crushed the husks and dust away from these [seeds], one should employ them as a powder along with *nalada*,
*vālaka*, red *yaṣṭikā*, *nakha*, *misī*, *plava*, *kuṣṭha*, and the three types of *balā*.
Then,
that paste of sesame flour is combined with agallochum, saffron, sandalwood, sārivā, sarala, resin of the *sarja* tree, and *amaradāru*, along with the group of drugs beginning with *padmaka*.
One should press [the juice] with milk that has been prepared with all types of fragrant medicinal herbs (gandhabhaiṣajya) and siddha-milk;
[one should also use] śaileya, rāsnā, śumatī, kaśeruka, kālānusārī, natapatra, and lodhra.
One should cook oil with milk, white flowers, milk, dūrvā grass, and the *nalada* group of drugs;
this is an excellent fragrant oil (*gandhataila*) that provides stability to the bones and quickly conquers diseases.
"Those [fevers] born of vāta and pitta, even when they are pervasive and of extreme potency, [are cured] by various applications.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter.
Now begins the thirty-third chapter. Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "The Treatment of Fistula-in-ano."
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:
"By riding on the backs of elephants or horses, and by sitting in hard or elevated postures..."
By indulging in other factors described as the etiology of hemorrhoids (arśas),
or by the immediate effects of undesirable or desirable digestion, or by the censures of virtuous people, [the disease arises].
Generally, a wound in the anus— either internal or external— occurring at a distance of one or two finger-breadths from the preceding anal folds, may involve corrupted blood and flesh.
Because it is located near the bladder and the receptacle of urine, it is of a liquid nature; when the vulva, bladder, and anus are being torn apart by many [instruments], [the blood flows].
As.Utt.33.5 As.Utt.33.5

It carries flatus, urine, feces, and semen through its minute openings in succession; it is known as the eighth [type], caused by the humors (doṣas) individually, in combination, or all together, as well as by external factors (āgantuka).

They say that when it is unripe, it is a *piṭaka* (boil), and when it has reached suppuration, it is a *bhagaṇḍara* (fistula-in-ano). It has deep-seated roots, is accompanied by swelling, is rich in granulation tissue, and causes irritation even after healing.
One should recognize a carbuncle that causes fistula-in-ano as such, and not otherwise. In that case, it is dark-brown or reddish, and characterized by pricking, piercing, throbbing, and aching pain.
From wind,
there are boils; from bile, they are elevated like the neck of a camel.
A tumor that is reddish, rich in heat, accompanied by a sensation of fuming due to fever,
firm, unctuous, deeply rooted, pale, and itchy arises from kapha.
That which is dark-brownish red, accompanied by burning and severe pain, arises from vāta and pitta.
Pale and slightly dusky, it suppurates with difficulty due to *kapha* and *vāta*. When equal to [the size of] the big toe, it possesses various kinds of pain caused by all the *doṣas*.
Those [afflictions] that are afflicted by piercing pain, loss of appetite, thirst, burning sensation, fever,
and diarrhea become ulcerated through negligence; among them, those born of Vāta [are as follows].
It gradually accumulates through minute openings like a *śataponaka* fish,
with a clear discharge flowing incessantly and mixed with foam.
This condition known as śataponaka is characterized by a camel-like neck and arises from pitta;
whereas parisrāva is characterized by the discharge of abundant mucus and arises from kapha.
Due to vāta and pitta, the *parikṣepī* [fistula] has a course that encircles the anus.
There, a wall and a moat are formed all around;
due to vāta and kapha, the rectum is torn open by a straight path of discharge.
In the case of *kapha* and *pitta*, however, when they become aggravated by relying on hemorrhoids that have previously arisen,
a swelling accompanied by itching, burning, and other symptoms occurs at the base of the hemorrhoids.
When it has quickly become suppurated and burst open, it moistens the root of the hemorrhoid; this *arśobhagaṇḍara* flows incessantly through its various channels.
The *sarvaja* hemorrhoid is characterized by a whorl resembling a conch shell (*śambūkāvarta*). In this condition,
the hemorrhoids tear the anus with violent, agonizing pains.
When a fragment of bone, swallowed out of greed for meat,
pierces the rectum as it passes obliquely, its movement then follows an abnormal path.
Then, when it has become putrid and burst open,
worms are born there from the rotting flesh; they consume his anus on all sides.
Those following the wrong path soon tear [the body] apart, and that blood [flows];
one should recognize pain, burning, itching, and so forth in those [wounds] according to the classification of ulcers.
Six of these are curable with difficulty; one should avoid treating those caused by trauma or blood,
as well as those that have reached the *pravāhiṇī* vessel, the *balinī*, or are located at the *sevanī*.

Now, one should quickly treat a patient with fistula-in-ano (bhagaṇdara) who has an unripe abscess by means of fasting, as prescribed in the treatment of wounds, for the purpose of preventing suppuration. However, when the abscess is ripe, one should first administer oleation, purify the patient with a decoction of *arka* and other plants, apply oil, and perform fomentation through immersion (*avagāha*). Then, having fed the patient and placed him on a bed, one should restrain him as in the case of hemorrhoids. Thereafter, one should carefully examine the fistula—whether it is directed outward, inward, externally opening, or internally opening.
Then,
having applied the instrument into the anal opening and having carefully observed the fistula that has entered the channel, one should search it thoroughly and incise it with a surgical blade.

Having directed this probe toward the exterior opening, one should extract the foreign body with a surgical instrument; immediately thereafter, one should treat both [the wound and the foreign body] with fire, alkali, and bandaging. However, for a wound at the lip or the neck, one should treat it with alkali alone.
Thereafter, one should heal it at the appropriate times through cooling, cleansing, and healing measures. This is the general procedure.
Now, in the case of *śataponaka*, one should incise the channels at intervals of one finger-breadth and apply healing measures; once they have healed,
one should treat the remaining ones.
Otherwise, however, when the wound has opened wide due to the tearing of the anal canal, wind, feces, and urine enter it;
consequently, the wind moving out of its proper path produces distension, flatulence, pain in the rectum, and other such symptoms.

In that case, one should apply unctuous bolus-sweats (*piṇḍasveda*), tube-sweats (*nāḍīsveda*), or jar-sweats (*kumbhīsveda*) to the anus after it has been smeared with oil, or one may employ immersion-baths (*avagāha*).

Once the patient has sweated, one should have him drink asafoetida, kuṣṭha, vyoṣa, the five salts, and ajamodā, mixed with any one of the following: clarified butter, wine, sour gruel, or horse-gram soup;
furthermore, one should sprinkle his ulcer with warm madhuka oil and his anus with vāta-alleviating oils such as balā-taila.

By this method, the wind and other humors enter their own proper channels, and the disorders caused by them are eliminated. In the same manner, in the case of a circular incision (parikṣepiṇī), one should gradually cut the path with an alkaline thread applied to the vessels, dividing it into two or three parts.
For if one attempts to excise both at once, there may be either incurability or a condition requiring lifelong management.
In the case of fistula-in-ano (bhagandara) accompanied by hemorrhoids (arśas), one should first excise the hemorrhoids, and thereafter treat the fistula according to its course.
However,
one should treat a patient who has strayed from the right path after first refusing to accept them as a patient.

One should extract the splinter even if it is not protruding, and likewise employ a vermifuge regimen through both topical applications and oral intake; furthermore, in cases of pain, the previously mentioned sudations should be applied.

One should apply a poultice of *vacā* and other digestive herbs, or one smeared with *sālvala*, to a wound, and then bandage it with the skins of a plantain tree, a deer, a jackal, a goat, silk, or wool; and regarding this, there is also a verse: [The verse follows: "Bandaging with the skin of a plantain tree, a deer, a jackal, a goat, silk, or wool, and applying a poultice of *vacā* and other digestive herbs, or one smeared with *sālvala*, [is prescribed for wounds]."
In the case of a fistula-in-ano with many openings, one should determine the locations of the incisions and apply the *gotīrtha*,
*sarvatomadra*, *ardhalāṅgala*, and *lāṅgala* incision techniques.
A cut made with a blade applied from the side is considered a *gotīrthaka*;
one made on all sides is a *sarvatobhadra*, while a cut on the side is an *ardhalāṅgala*.
One should cauterize the entire *lāṅgalaka* on both sides with fire; by doing so,
one completely eliminates the channels of discharge so that they do not recur.
The physician should also strive for the purification of the patient's digestive tract from time to time; he should have the patient drink ghee prepared with the juice or the paste of fresh ginger.
In cases of fistula-in-ano caused by Vāta, whether suppurated or unsuppurated, one should administer purgation using jyotiṣmatī,
lāṅgalikā, śyāmā, dantī, trivṛt, and sesame seeds.
Kuṣṭha, śatahvā, golomī, tilvaka, girikarṇikā,
and hemakṣīrī— this group [of drugs] purifies ulcers when used as a paste and other such applications.
Tila, kumbha, varadanti, tuttha, sindhūttha, mākṣika,
along with kṛṣṇa, rocanā, and kuṣṭha, constitute a purifying formulation that further promotes the growth of flesh.
Mañjiṣṭhā, saindhava salt, honey, nāgadantī, trivṛt, and sesame seeds;
rasāñjana, the two types of rajanī (turmeric), tejohvā, and nimba leaves.
A paste of *nikumbha*, *kumbha*, and *raktāhvā* removes sinus ulcers (*nāḍī-vraṇa*). [With] *sudhā*, *śelu*, *trivṛt*, *pāṭhā*, *malayū*, and *hayamāraka*...
One should cook a taila known as Viṣyandana with jyotiṣmatī, lāṅgalikā, svarjikā, arka, vacā, and agnika; it is both purifying and healing.
With trivṛt, dantī, haridrā, the root of arka, iron, and aśvamāraka;
with the essence of viḍaṅga, triphalā, snuh, the milk of arka, and honey.
Oil prepared with madana fruits brings about the healing of fistula-in-ano; likewise,
oil prepared with rock salt, arka, trivṛt, pāṭhā, samaṅgā, pūtikā, and agnika [achieves the same].
Oil prepared with *mātuluṅga* leaves serves for cleansing and healing.
Viḍaṅga-sāra, triphalā, pippalī, and marica, when licked together with honey and oil, heal worms, skin diseases, fistula-in-ano, urinary disorders, wounds, sinus tracts, and ulcers.
Amṛtā, truṭi, vella, vatsaka, kali, pathyā, āmalaka, and nāgaramodha— this [mixture],
increased in sequence and saturated with honey, conquers boils, enlargement of the scrotum, and fistula-in-ano.
Five *pala*s of *guggulu*, one *pala* each of *māgadhikā* and *triphalā* separately,

along with one *karṣa* each of cinnamon (*tvak*) and *tvaktruṭi*, when licked with honey, destroys leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), fistula-in-ano (*bhagaṇḍara*), abdominal tumors (*gulma*), and diseases of the lower abdomen (*gati*).
That same [medicinal preparation], well-processed and combined with the powder of *śṛṅgavera*,
especially when taken with a decoction of *daśamūla*, conquers diseases of the wind (*vāta*).
The best [remedy] is the powder produced from the heartwood of *khadira*, processed with goat’s urine;
when taken together with buffalo horn, honey, and *kuṣṭha*, it destroys skin diseases, urinary disorders, pustules, and fistulas.
This specific [treatment] has been described for fistulas-in-ano; however, regarding the remaining [diseases],
one should understand the appropriate means correctly through the section on wounds and by careful study, and then apply the remedies.
One should avoid riding on horseback, suppressing natural urges, alcohol, sexual intercourse, indigestion, unwholesome food,
and various types of rash acts for one year or more once [the hemorrhoid] has healed.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter.
Now begins the thirty-fourth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "The Diagnosis of Granthi, Arbuda, Ślīpada, Apacī, and Nāḍī."
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:
"The impurities (mala), when dominated by phlegm (kapha), affect the fat, muscle, and blood."
A swelling that is rounded and elevated is known as a *granthi* (node) because of its knotted nature.
There are nine types [of *granthi*], arising from the *doṣas*, blood, muscle, fat, bone, vessels, and wounds.
Therein, [the swelling] caused by Vāta is accompanied by stretching, piercing pain, and tearing; it is dark-colored,
moves from one place to another, and undergoes sudden decrease and increase in size.
AS.Utt.34.4 Like an unbaked clay bladder, when it is pierced, it discharges blood. AS.Utt.34.5 Due to pitta, it quickly suppurates, appearing yellowish with a burning sensation or red.
When pierced, a cold abscess discharges warm fluid mixed with phlegm and is painless;
when thick, cold, and of the same color as the skin, it is itchy; when suppurated, it discharges thick pus.
When the *sṛj* (semen) is vitiated by the *doṣas* in a person who is fainting, a nodular growth (*granthi*) arises,
localized in the vessels and flesh, accompanied by numbness and exhibiting the characteristics of *pitta*.
Flesh corrupted by fleshy foods may produce a tumor (granthi) that is unctuous,
large, hard, covered with veins, and shaped like phlegm (kapha).
When the fat (medas), increased by sedative [or cooling] factors,
is displaced into the muscle or the skin by the wind (vāyu), it forms a tumor (granthi) that is extremely oily, soft, and mobile.
When it is punctured, that thick fat— which has the appearance of phlegm and whose increase or decrease corresponds to the body's own growth or decline— flows out coppery, black, or white.
That which becomes elevated or depressed due to a fracture of the bone or a blow is an *asthigranthi* (bone-knot); it may also occur in a pedestrian from suddenly plunging into deep water.
In one who is exhausted by physical exertion,
the Vāyu, having compressed, contracted, bent, and dried up the network of vessels along with the blood, [causes the following].
That which is called *sirā* produces a painless, non-pulsating knot;
this occurs when one who eats all kinds of savory foods consumes food while a wound is either unhealed or only just beginning to heal.
Furthermore, when the moist or unbound limb is struck by stones,
the vitiated wind (vāta), having dried up the blood that has not flowed out, causes the wound to become knotted and constricted.
It should always be treated with cauterization; this is known as *vraṇagranthi*. Those born from the humors (*doṣa*), blood, and fat are curable, but those that are thick, hard, and mobile are not.
And [tumors] located in the vital points, throat, or abdomen— namely the *mahat*, *tuga*, *granthi*, and *toruda*—
their characteristics are sixfold according to the distinctions of the *doṣas* and other factors, ending with those arising from fat (*medas*).
Generally, because it is rich in fat and phlegm and is stable, it does not suppurate;
the dosha, having constricted and compressed the blood residing in the vessels, [causes this].
Then that swelling, filled with pus and consisting of a mass of flesh, ripens;
covered with sprouts of flesh, it increases rapidly and subsequently discharges [pus].
That large tumor of blood (śoṇitārbuḍa) constantly discharges foul blood;
among those [tumors], the two born of blood and flesh should be rejected, while the other four should be treated.
The doshas, dominated by kapha and located in the flesh and blood, having moved from the groin, thighs, and other parts of the lower body, eventually reach the feet and produce [the disease].
That which is a dense swelling that gradually increases is called Ślīpada; it is characterized by cracking, is blackish, painful without apparent cause,
and rough.
That caused by Vāta is rough; that by Pitta is yellow and accompanied by burning sensations and fever;
that by Kapha is heavy, unctuous, painless, and large with fleshy sprouts.
One should avoid that which has been kept for two years or more, as it is excessively prone to leakage;
others, however, say this applies to the hands, thumbs, and ears, just as it does to the feet.
Elephantiasis (ślīpada) arises from that [vitiation], and it occurs most frequently in marshy regions due to wandering [of the humors].
The impurities located in the fat-tissue (medas) reach the throat, the neck, the eyes, the armpits, and the groins.
They produce numerous swellings that are of the same color as the skin, firm, smooth, shaped like eggplants or *āmalaka* fruits, deeply seated, and slow to suppurate.
Some are cooked with intense pain, others ooze, and others are itchy; some perish, others arise, and still others persist for a long duration.
This gaṇḍamālā and apacī fluctuate in their decline and growth like the dūrvā grass;
one should abandon it when accompanied by fever, vomiting, pain in the flanks, cough, and rhinitis.
Due to the lack of distinction between the ripened swelling and the ulcer, and because of the patient's indulgence in unwholesome things,
the pus enters deep into the flesh and other tissues and spreads far away.
That movement is called *nāḍī* because it travels far; it is like a channel (*nāḍī*) due to its continuous flow.
For others, it is a single straight channel, while for this [system], that very same movement has many paths.

That [disorder] is caused by the humors (doṣas) individually or combined, with a foreign body (śalya) as the fifth cause. From vāta, it is painful, has a narrow opening, is discolored, and emits frothy matter.

In the case of a Pitta-type discharge, it flows excessively at night, causing thirst, fever, and burning sensations; it is yellow, hot, and foul-smelling pus that gushes out during the day and continues to flow even when one lies down.

Due to *kapha*, the ulcer has a thick, slimy discharge, is itchy, and is hard; at night, it has excessive moisture. One should avoid [treating] an ulcer that exhibits all these characteristics when they are present together.
A foreign body (śalya) remaining inside, if not extracted, causes a sinus tract (nāḍī);
and this [tract] of his constantly discharges pus that is mixed with foam, thin, scanty, warm, bloody, and painful.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter.
Now begins the thirty-fifth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "The Prevention of Tumors and Other Growths" (Granthyādipratiṣedha).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:

in all cases of abdominal tumors (*granthi*), one should first cause the patient to vomit after they have been lubricated with aged ghee prepared with two *bṛhatī*, long pepper (*pippalī*), and *citraka*.
One should administer purgation after the patient has undergone the process of gradual dietary rehabilitation (*saṃsarjana*).

For tumors located in the head, one should perform head-purgation (*śirovirecana*) using lac, the two types of turmeric, *viḍaṅga*, ginger, and *pūtīdāru*; furthermore, the patient should employ medicinal smoking (*dhūma*), gargles (*kavala*), and mouth-washes (*gaṇḍūṣa*).
An ointment should be prepared from *aṅkola*, *madhuka*, *mātuluṅga*, *hiṃsrā*, *pūtīdāru*, the root of *bilva*, *sarala*, *kuṣṭha*, *vacā*, the bark of *varuṇa*, *kālātiviṣā*, and *jagandhā*;
or alternatively, from *śyāmā*, *suradāru*, *samaṅgā*, *kośātakī*, *punarnavā*, and *sarṣapa*.
In cases of swelling, pain, and stiffness, a poultice (upanāha) should be applied made of barley flour, madhuka, kuṣṭha, śatapuṣpā, udīcya, and devadāru mixed with ghee;
or alternatively, with the flesh of cow, goat, sheep, donkey, camel, horse, elephant, and rat, prepared as *veśavāra* and combined with muscle fat (*vasā*) and oil.
Having repeatedly steamed it with a paste of *palāśa* stalks, fire-drill wood (*agnimantha*), and bark, or with balls of meat,
one should gently and repeatedly massage it with the thumb or a bamboo joint.
One should apply treatment according to the specific condition, as in the case of swelling (AS.Utt.35.6).
Now, for a tumor caused by Vāta, one should drink the "great unctuous substance" (mahāsneha) prepared with the ten roots (daśamūla) (AS.Utt.35.6).
An application of Amṛtā, Nimba seeds, Bhārgī, Syonāka, Bāṇa, Tālapatrī, Kṛṣṇagandhā, and Aguru, ground with milk and applied lukewarm;
as well as various oleation, sudation, and poultices prescribed for Vāta diseases;
and, if there is no relief, venesection.

Once the abscess has ripened, one should incise it, remove the pus, wash it with water prepared from the *arka* group of plants, and apply a paste of sesame mixed with *citraka* and rock salt (*saindhava*).
One should then prepare a healing oil processed with *rāsnā*, *sarala*, *uśīra*, *viḍaṅga*, *madhuka*, and milk.

In cases arising from *pitta* and blood, leeches should be applied; *nyagrodhādi* [gana] is used for ointments and affusions, while *padmakādi* [gana] is used for drinking along with grape juice and sugarcane juice. *Harītakī* administered as a purgative is also indicated.
Once the ulcer has ripened and been incised, the procedure prescribed for *pitta*-type ulcers should be followed.

In a case of [diseases] born of *kapha* in one who has been thoroughly purified internally, one should apply intense sudation and cause the area to soften; then one should apply a plaster made of the roots of *kākādanī*, *vikaṅkata*, *kākanandī*, *āragvadha*, and *iṅguda*, along with *madana* fruit and *bhārṅgī*, and *karañja*;
or alternatively, a plaster made of *nāgara*, *viḍaṅga*, *elavāluka*, *cavya*, the stalks of *palāśa*, and *citraka*.
Or, with bhallātaka, saindhava, ajagandhā, and sarṣapa;
even if it is not being cooked [by these], one should incise it when it is located away from a vital spot (amarmastha) and burn the remaining blood completely with fire.
For that which remains with residual tissue is replenished again;
therefore, once it has been cauterized, one should heal the purified wound with ointments consisting primarily of alkali, honey, and jaggery.
One should treat muscular swellings and ulcers in this very same manner.

This same procedure applies to fat as well. Furthermore, having smeared a fatty tumor with sesame paste and placed it between two layers of double-folded cloth, one should repeatedly rub it with a heated iron plate or a ladle smeared with lac.
Then, after applying the surgical instrument, one should cauterize the fat as previously described.

Alternatively, having fully cooked [the ulcer] and incised it, one should wash it with urine and apply an ointment made of sesame seeds mixed with honey, rock salt (*saindhava*), *suvarcikā*, *kāñcanakṣīrī*, and *haritāla*, along with an abundance of *kṣīrabaka*. An oil prepared with *guñjā*, the two types of *karaja*, *tāpasavṛkṣa*, bamboo scrapings, and urine should be used for massage (*abhyaṅga*).

One should apply this [ointment] properly once it is purified. However, in the case of a fresh vascular knot (*sirāgranthi*), one should drink *sāhacara* oil; furthermore, one should administer poultices (*upanāha*) with Vata-alleviating substances and perform enema therapy (*bastikarma*).
One should perform venesection (AS.Utt.35.14) and apply a poultice made of the marrow of *airaṇḍa*, *priyāla*, coconut, cucumber, *arka*, or *kaurubīja* to a vata-tumor (AS.Utt.35.14).
One should administer tube-sudation (nāḍīsveda) using marshy meat and vesavāra; furthermore, one should repeatedly perform bloodletting here with a horn.
One should drink trivṛt processed with a decoction of drugs from the vāta-alleviating group, milk, and sour liquids.
In cases arising from pitta, one should apply mild sudation and poultices, as well as purgation of the body. Furthermore,
after rubbing with the leaves of *śāka* and *kākodumbarikā*, an ointment should be applied consisting of *priyaṅgu*, *pataṅga*, resin of *sarja*, *arjuna*, *lodhra*, honey, and *madhuka*.

Ghee prepared with the juice of any one of the following— *śyāmā*, *agrikarṇikā*, *añjana*, *klītaka*, *nakha*, *drākṣā*, or *saptalā*— when drunk, destroys *pitta*-originated tumors (*arbuda*), elephantiasis (*ślīpada*), and abdominal enlargements (*udara*). In cases arising from *kapha*, however, after the humors have been removed from above and below and blood has been let, a plaster should be applied using emetic and purgative substances.
Or he should smear [the area] with the roots of *kākādanī*, *śukabarha*, *agnijihvā*, *dakṣa*, *kapota*, and *gṛdhra-purīṣa*, along with the root of *kāśa*, all ground with the milky sap of *palāśa*;
or he should smear it with oil-cakes, horse-gram, and flat beans mixed with meat and ground curd.
He should then wait, observing the flies as they settle there out of greed for the taste of the ointment.
When it is being eaten by worms— either those already released from it or others—

one should scrape off the remainder of what has been consumed by the worms using leaves of vegetables and the like, and then cauterize it with fire; or, if the root is small, one should wrap it in a band of tin, copper, iron, or lead.

Furthermore, one should repeatedly apply alkaline substances according to the stage of the disease, as well as the tender leaves of *jātī*, *āsphota*, and *karavīra* for the purification of the ulcer;
and for massage, an oil prepared with a decoction of *pāṭhā*, *viḍaṅga*, *bhārṅgī*, and *triphalā* should be used.
In the case of a fatty tumor (medo-budbuda), once it has been fomented, incised, its fat thoroughly cleansed, and the bleeding subsided, one should immediately suture it. Then,
one should rub the area with a powder of house-soot, *lodhra*, realgar (*manaḥśilā*), turmeric (*haridrā*), and *pataṅga*, mixed with honey and clarified butter.
One should employ Karañja oil for the purpose of anointing,
and one should heal all tumors that have spontaneously matured, provided they have been thoroughly cleansed;
furthermore—
However, for those ulcers that leave behind residual morbid humors (doṣas), they quickly recur; therefore,
their complete extraction by means of alkali, surgery, or fire is recommended.
In the case of elephantiasis (ślīpada) caused by vāta, one should apply oleation, sudation, and poultices, and then venesect a vein two finger-breadths above the ankle; furthermore,
one should drink castor oil with cow urine for a month.
When it has been digested, one should eat old grains with milk boiled with ginger and should administer trivṛt;
one should also employ enemas.
If it does not subside even thus, one should cauterize with fire.

In the case of a Pitta-type [gulma], a mild poultice should be applied below the ankle, followed by venesection; furthermore, unctuous purgatives and Pitta-alleviating plasters as described for Pitta-type tumors (pittārbuda) should be employed.
In the case of a kapha-type disorder, one should venesect the dorsal vein at the thumb;
furthermore, one should repeatedly administer kapha-alleviating decoctions mixed with honey,
or administer increasing doses of *harītakī* according to the patient's strength.
In the case of a phlegmatic (ślaiṣmika) condition, one should venesect the vein at the thumb; furthermore,
one should repeatedly administer phlegm-subduing decoctions mixed with honey.
Alternatively, one may take increasing doses of *harītakī* according to one's strength.

Having burnt *ādārī*, *kākajaṅghā*, *kākādanī*, *śukanāsā*, *kadambapuṣpa*, and the two types of *bṛhatī* with internal smoke (*mantardhūma*), one should repeatedly strain them with cow’s urine. Then, that alkaline water (*kṣārodaka*) should be cooked according to the procedure for preparing alkalis (*kṣārakalpa*).

In this case, one should add a secondary decoction consisting of the juice of *madanaphala* known as *phalguśuka*. This alkali, when practiced with a sweet diet, cures elephantiasis (*ślīpada*), scrofula (*apacī*), disorders of the *grahaṇī*, loss of appetite, and all types of poisons.
Alternatively, one should drink oil prepared with *viḍaṅga*, *arka*, black pepper, *citraka*, ginger, *devadāru*, *elā*, *vāluka*, and the five salts.

One should apply an ointment made of *nāgara*, *amṛtā*, *viḍaṅga*, *kaṭukā*, and *bhadradāru* ground with urine, as well as the medicinal substances prescribed for *ūrustambha*. One should also habitually consume barley-based food (*yavānna*).

In the case of *maṇḍalamālā*, one should drink ghee cooked with the fruits of *kumbha*, *nikumbha*, *dravantī*, *jīmūtaka*, and *kośātakī*; this acts as a purgative and a carminative for both upper and lower tracts.

Alternatively, for the purpose of inducing emesis, one may administer the root of *śārṅgeṣṭā* ground with buttermilk or with warm water; or a powder of the roots and bark of *jātī*, *barhiṣṭha*, *nirguṇḍī*, *jīmūtaka*, and *kottuṇḍakī*;
and one should also venesect this patient.
However, if the internal [doshas] remain with a residue,
one should administer the nine-fold *rasāñjana* with either cow’s urine or rice-water.

One should cause that very [wound] to suppurate, or apply the essence of *madhūka*, or the fruits of *śigru*, or oil prepared with *nimba*, *karañja*, and *karavīra*; one should also inhale purgative smoke (*vairecanika-dhūma*).
Furthermore, one should apply a plaster of *nākulī*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and ginger (*nāgara*) to unripe swellings (*gaṇḍa*).

Oil cooked ten times with *guñjā*, *karavīra*, *arka*, *śyāmā*, and *siddhārthaka* mixed with goat’s urine, and combined with the powder of the five salts (*pañcalavaṇa*), *pippalī*, and black pepper, removes, when used as an ointment, all types of *apacī*, hemorrhoids, *budana*, sinus tracts (*nāḍī*), malignant ulcers, and *valmīka*. Oil prepared with a paste of *sauvarcala*, *saindhava*, *audbhida*, *dantī*, *bhallātaka*, and *citraka* is an ointment for *apacī*.

Oil prepared with the fresh juice of *taṇḍulīyaka* or with the juice of *sanirguṇḍī*, when used for massage, drinking, and nasal administration, removes scrofula (*gaṇḍamālā*), sinus ulcers (*nāḍīvraṇa*), skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), and the afflictions of wind (*anila*).

One should cook one *prastha* of *karañja* oil with half-pala portions each of the seeds of *kākādanī*, *nalikā*, *agnijihvā*, *vandhyākarkoṭakī*, *viśālā*, *pāṭhā*, *uttuṇḍakī*, *jīmūtaka*, and *kośātakī*, along with one *karṣa* of poison and the fresh juice of *nirguṇḍī*. When administered as previously described, it is a supreme remedy for *apacī*.
One should extract even unripe goiters that do not arise from vital spots (marmas) and treat them with fire or caustic (kṣāra).
The wound should be washed with decoctions of *sarṣapa*, *vṛkṣādanī*, and *kvātha*. A lukewarm plaster made from ground sesame seeds and *tilakuntala* should be applied.

Alternatively, one may perform an oil massage using *iṅguda* oil saturated with the soot (*maṣī*) of any one of the following—crow, lizard, iguana, snake slough, or tortoise—burnt in the absence of smoke.

Oil cooked with *māṃsī*, *sarjarasa*, cotton seeds, and rock salt, ground with breast milk, should be used as an ointment to destroy hardness of the ulcer. Oil and the fat of a cobra (*sarpa-ajagara*)—these three in equal parts—destroy *apacī*.

One should also employ the oils mentioned for *ślīpada*.
