If there is no improvement in this way, for a [tumour] arising on the left side, one should make an incision of the size of an eye with a surgical instrument at the middle of the back of the right calf, or above or below the *indrabasti*, and having removed the fat which resembles a net of fish eggs, one should cauterize it with fire.
By this,
those arising on the other side are explained;
likewise, for those arising on both sides, [the treatment is] from both sides.

In cases of gaṇḍamālā, the diet should consist primarily of barley and mung beans. For a sinus tract (nāḍī) caused by vāta, one should apply a poultice, drain the pus completely, and then incise it with a surgical instrument.
Then, having filled it with a paste of sesame and *apāmārga* fruits mixed with rock salt, one should bind it;
for a [wound] born of *pitta*, one should apply a poultice (*upanāha*) made of *utpala* and other drugs prepared with ghee and milk.

Once it has been incised, one should fill it with a paste of *tila*, *nāgadantī*, and *mañjiṣṭhā*. Ghee processed with the paste of *śyāmā*, *tribhaṇḍī*, *triphalā*, *tilvaka*, and the two types of *haridrā*, along with milk, is an excellent ointment for destroying sinus tracts (*nāḍī*). For a sinus tract born of *śleṣman* (phlegm), one should apply a poultice of *saktu*, *kulattha*, *kiṇva*, and mustard seeds, and after incising it, smear it with a paste of *nimba*, *tila*, rock salt (*saindhava*), *saurāṣṭrī*, and *nikumbha*.

Oil cooked with *dantī*, *citraka*, *svarjikā*, rock salt (*saindhava*), *tālīsa*, *nalada*, *pūtīka*, and the fruit of *apāmārga*, along with urine, should be used as an ointment for massage (AS.Utt.35.33).

Having incised [the wound] caused by a foreign body and having completely cleared away the foreign body, one should bandage it after covering it with a paste of honey, ghee, and sesame. (AS.Utt.35.34)

Oil prepared with a decoction of the unripe fruits (*śalāṭu*) of the *bilva*, *kapittha*, *kumbhī*, date palm (*kharjūra*), and *vanaspati* trees, containing *priyaṅgu*, *mustā*, large betel nut (*urupūga*), *śakuna-sugandhika*, *lodhra*, *mocarasa*, and *dhātakī* flowers, quickly heals a wound born of a foreign body (*śalyaja*).
In a sinus (*nāḍī*) that cannot be treated with a surgical instrument, one should pierce it at the end of the opening with a probe (*eṣiṇī*) and insert a thread smeared with caustic (*kṣāra*).

In the absence of that [primary opening], however, for one seeking another [opening] and when it has not been opened by him, one should pass another alkaline thread (kṣārasūtra) threaded through it, until the differentiation of the tracks is reached; this is an infallible method for fistulas with subtle or multiple tracks, and for the roots of perforated nodes (granthi) and tumors (arbuda).
And there is a verse on this point:
regarding ulcers that are malignant, minute-mouthed, deep-seated, and so forth, the following is the means of treatment.
One should also prepare wicks and oils for those channels using *vibhītaka*,
mango stones, *vaṭa* sprouts, *hareṇukā*, and seeds of the *śālmali*.
Soot from the dung of a boar, well-burnt and saturated with oil, destroys all [unwanted] growths. Dhattūraka, the seeds of Madana and Kodrava, Kośātakī, Śukanasā, and Mṛgabhojanī [are likewise used].
Having prepared a powder from *Aṅkola* flowers, it should be applied once the defects have been removed by means of lac-water; oil mixed with that [powder] is a supreme healing agent for wounds.
[Oil] prepared with Sauvarchala salts and tubers known as Vajra;
and [oil] processed with Bhallātaka, Arka, Marica, the best salt (Saindhava), Viḍaṅga, the two types of Rajanī, and Citraka.
Oil prepared with the juices of *samārka* (the sun-plant) cures difficult *nāḍī* (sinus), as well as ulcers caused by *kapha* and *vāta*, and severe *apacī* (scrofula).
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter;
now begins the thirty-sixth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter titled "The Knowledge of Minor Diseases" (Kṣudrarogavijñānīya).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
Glossy, uniform, clustered, painless, and resembling mung beans—
such pustules caused by kapha and vāta in children are called ajagallikā.
Resembling barley, dense, and situated within the flesh— these are the *alajī* ulcers;
they are mouthless, circular, slightly suppurating, and thickly elevated.
There are five or six knots, shaped like tortoises and elevated like tortoises;
or there may be pustules all around the upper part of the ear that are hard and intensely painful.

A swelling resembling a lotus root (śālūka), located at the joint of the jaw, which is firm and slightly painful, is called Pāṣāṇagardabha; it arises from those two [doṣas]. Eruptions shaped like the thorns of the Śālmali tree, which are painful and dense, [are known as Śālmalīpiṭaka].

AS.Utt.36.5 Medogarbha: there is swelling in the mouth, and from those two [conditions], there is foulness of the mouth. AS.Utt.36.6 Those should be known as Padmakaṇṭaka, by which [the mouth] is like a lotus with thorns.
The body is covered with painless, white eruptions arising from phlegm and wind; by bile,
there are circular pustules resembling ripe udumbara fruits.
Vivṛtā causes a high fever with great burning; she has a wide-open mouth,
and she is accompanied by fever and pain from burning within the limbs and the mouth.
Dense pustules the size of lentils, having the same color and name as that [disease],
arise; thereafter, even more painful eruptions known as visphoṭaka (boils) appear, accompanied by great agony.
A carbuncle shaped like the pericarp of a lotus, covered with pustules; this is [the disease called] Piṭakācitā.
That [wound], pierced by both wind and bile, becomes a gardabhī; it is circular, extensive and elevated, and covered with reddish pustules.
In regions near the armpits,
these pustules generally arise from pitta combined with vāta; they are small, thick, and resemble parched grain.
Such a great single disease is celebrated as Gandhanāma;
when the limbs are overwhelmed by heat and perspiration, painful and dense pustules appear.
Named after the *rājikā* seed, they have the color, shape, and size of a *rājikā*;
spreading like erysipelas (*visarpa*), they are caused by the humors with a predominance of bile (*pitta*) that has become sluggish.

Jālagardabha is a thin, copper-colored swelling that causes fever and does not suppurate (AS.Utt.36.15). In one suffering from fever, eruptions caused by the humors with an excess of pitta tear through the flesh (AS.Utt.36.15).
Those eruptions resembling fire that arise on the sides of the armpits, along with Rohiṇī accompanied by Agni,
destroy life within five days, seven nights, or a fortnight. A circular swelling above the collarbone, possessing the three symptoms, is called Irivellikā.
The *vidārī* is hard like a tuber; it occurs in the armpits and the groin.
A glandular swelling (granthi) formed by fat, lymph, and phlegm, resting upon the ligaments, flesh, and vessels, when incised,
exudes a secretion resembling marrow, clarified butter, or honey; in that condition, the wind (vāyu) is predominant.
Having dried up the flesh, one should apply a medicinal paste (granthi) containing sugar;
then the impurities— foul-smelling, moist blood of various colors— will emerge.
One should know that when they discharge this accumulated [pus], it is called *śarkarārbuda*;
it accumulates on the palms and soles, at the joints, or above the collarbone.

An anthill (valmīka) is characterized by a gradual swelling with many small openings, abounding in pain, burning, itching, and discharge; this [type] arises from all [three doshas]. When the foot is crushed by a stone or wounded by thorns and the like, [an anthill may form].
A knot that arises elevated like a wedge is called *kadara*.
Due to the suppression of natural urges, the apāna vāyu, residing in the region of the anus, [causes this].
It narrows the internal and external passages of this [patient], and consequently, the stool emerges with great difficulty; this disease is known as ruddhaguda (obstructed anus).
One should know that when pitta and vāta cause suppuration in the flesh of the nail accompanied by pain and fever,
it is called *cippa*, *akṣataroga*, and *upanakha*.
Due to injury from a black [creature], the nail becomes rough, harsh,
and deformed; due to contact with foul mud, it becomes characterized by itching and moisture within.
They call the fingers *alasaka*; the black, painless spots located in the skin are *tilakālaka*, while those same [spots] when raised are called *masa*.
A *jatumaṇi* is a slightly elevated, painless, white or black mole; however, that which is red is painful.
A *lāñchana* is a congenital, uniform circular mark that is either black or white.
From vāta and pitta aggravated by grief, anger, and so forth, there arises a thin [eruption] on the face.
A dark, blemished patch other than on the face is called *nīlikā*;
a rough, rough-to-the-touch, and dusky blemish arises from wind (*māruta*).

From pitta, it has a copper-colored edge and a bluish interior; from kapha, it has a white edge and is itchy; from blood, it has a red edge and a slightly coppery color; the remaining types have a tingling sensation. Driven by vāyu, the phlegm reaches the skin and becomes parched.
Thereupon,
the skin becomes pale and gradually loses sensation;
being slightly itchy and without discharge, that state is called *prasupti*, arising from numbness.
Due to improper emesis, the provocation of pitta and kapha, and the suppression of natural urges, many circular patches appear that are intensely itchy and reddish.
Utkoṭha accompanied by its sequel is designated as Koṭha. Thus, these thirty-six minor diseases (kṣudraroga) have been described according to their classification.
"Knowing which [factors], the physician shall not be deluded in his treatment"—
thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter.
Now begins the thirty-seventh chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter titled "The Treatment of Minor Diseases" (Kṣudraroga-pratiṣedha).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
One should have leeches applied to an unripe *ajagallikā* and then apply a paste made of *yavakṣāra*, *śukti*, and *saurāṣṭrī*.
Having fomented the conditions beginning with *yavaprakhya* and ending with *pāṣāṇagardabha*, one should apply a paste of *suradāru*, *kuṣṭha*, *manaḥśilā*, and *ālāla*.
Once they have suppurated, including *hājagallikā*, one should treat them like a wound.
Or one should apply a plaster of *lodhra* and *tuvarikā* to the impurities of the mouth.
Alternatively, one may administer [the medicine] with *vaṭa* leaves and coconut shells, or with rock salt, *vacā*, *akṣi-bheṣaja*, and white mustard seeds;
if [the fever] is still not pacified in this way, one should induce vomiting and pierce a vein in the forehead.
In cases of *padmakaṇṭaka*, one should administer ghee prepared with *nimba* water and boiled with *nimba* water, mixed with honey;
and an ointment for rubbing the body (*udvartana*) should be made with a decoction of *nimba* and *āragvadha*.
One should treat *vivṛta* and the other [types of erysipelas] up to *jālagardabha*, as well as *nirivellikā*, in the same manner as *pittavisarpa*. Specifically,
one should apply a plaster made of *rājikā*, *apākaśarkarā*, *mūrvā*, and *kaṇṭakaśarkarā*, ground with milk.
One should practice frequent cleansing and consume dhātrī fruits in the case of jālagardabha.

One should treat *agni-rohiṇī* even after rejecting [other measures], using [remedies for] *pitta-visarpa*; once it has suppurated, however, one should heal it with ghee prepared with the sweet group (*madhura-varga*) of drugs.
Having caused *vidārikā* to be seized by aquatic creatures, one should smear it with a paste of *bilva* root, *naga-vṛttika*, *varṣābhū*, *ajakarṇa*, and *palāśa*.
If it does not subside, one should massage it, apply fomentation, and cause it to soften; once it has suppurated,
one should incise it with a surgical instrument, cover it with a paste of nimba, sesame, and paṭola, and bandage it.

A decoction of milky trees, *kadara*, and *khadira* should be used for washing the ulcer; once it is purified, one should heal it with oil processed with sweet and astringent drugs. One should treat a tumor of sugar (*śarkarārbuda*) in the same manner as a tumor of fat (*medobuda*).
One should avoid treating an anthill (balīmīka) that has grown upon the hand, the foot, or over a vital point (marman), which is extensive, covered with many holes, and accompanied by swelling.
Otherwise, however, one should remove the blood before purification has been performed;
one should then plaster the area with a paste of sugar, sesamum, salt, *guḍūcī*, *ārevata*, *śyāmā*, *dantī*, *kulatthikā*, and *mūrvā*.
When it has suppurated, one should thoroughly excise all the corrupted tissues with a surgical instrument and then cauterize it with fire or alkali.
Once the wound is well-cleansed, one should cook nimba oil with bhallātaka, realgar, lākṣā, kālānusārya, aguru, and sandalwood for the purpose of healing.
Having excised with a surgical instrument, one should cauterize with an oily substance.
Regarding the treatment for obstructed feces and suppressed flatus:
one should treat hemorrhoids with bloodletting and purification therapies.
Once its heat has subsided, one should sprinkle it with warm water, incise it appropriately with a surgical instrument,

and remove [the foreign body]. Then, having cleansed it with a paste of *rasāñjana*, *rocanā*, *nepālī*, and *tejohvā* ground with sour liquids, one should heal it with oil prepared with *kāleyaka*, *agaru*, *haridrā*, and *rasāñjana*.
Or, one may fill it with the decoction prepared from sweet and astringent [drugs] when only a small amount remains, along with powdered resin of *sarjarasa*.

One should treat a corrupted *kunakha* (ungual warts) in exactly this same manner. Having sprinkled the feet with sour gruel (*amlakāñjika*) due to their sluggishness, one should apply an ointment made from a paste of *nimba*, sesame, *paṭolī*, *kāsīsa*, and *rocanā*.
Having anointed [the area] with mustard oil prepared with the juice of *nidigdhikā*, one should rub it with the powders of *rocanā*, *kāsīsa*, and *manaḥśilā*.
One should cauterize *tilaka*, *alaka*, and *maṣa* moles with a *sūryakānta* gem, fire, or an alkali (*kṣāra*).
In the case of a skin-wart (*carmakali*) and a mole (*jatumaṇi*), one should likewise excise them with a surgical instrument;
in cases of moles (*lāñchana*), freckles (*vyaṅga*), and dark spots (*nīlikā*), one should pierce a vein as close as possible to the lesion.
One should apply a paste made from the bark of milky trees ground with milk, or alternatively, a paste of *balā*, *atibalā*, *madhuka*, and *haridrā* ground with milk.
Or with madhuka, agaru, payasyā, and kālīyaka;
or with young kapittha, tinduka, and rajanī; or with the root of amlikā.
Alternatively, one may use a boar’s tusk smeared with honey and ghee; specifically for facial blemishes (*vyaṅga*), an application of *arjuna* bark after first inducing the flow of blood.
Alternatively, mañjiṣṭhā ground with honey;
or fresh dāḍima bark with goat’s milk;
or young āmalaka fruit soaked for seven days in cow urine.
Or [one may use] the cream of curd (*dadhimanda*) with *kāleyaka*, *lodhra*, and the filaments of the blue lotus; or fresh butter (*navanīta*) with the soot of a white horse's hoof.

Furthermore, for disorders born of Vāta, one should administer at night—after the meal—a ghee cooked in a decoction of *devadāru*, *durālabhā*, *bṛhatī*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *mūrvā*, *apāmārga*, *trāyantī*, *trāyamāṇā*, *śukanāsā*, *balā*, *vidārī*, barley, jujube, horse gram (*kulattha*), *bilva*, blue lotus, *śatāvarī*, and the roots of *darbha*, containing *śṛṅgī* and *viḍaṅga* as internal ingredients; this should be used for drinking, massage, and nasal drops.
And one should apply a plaster made from the powders of *nyagrodha*, *devadāru*, *harītakī*, *pūtīkarañja*, and *madanaphala*, mixed with clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
In cases of Pittaja disorders, one should administer either jujube-pulp, *kodo* grain, or parched rice flour mixed with ghee;
or the milk of the white yak, *tālapatrī*, honey, and ghee.
Alternatively, as before, one should employ ghee prepared with milk and a decoction of *balā*, *madhuka*, *māgadhikā*, *kṣīrakākolī*, *svaguptā* fruit, *kākamācī*, and *tugāhvā*.

Alternatively, one may use grapes, white-pāka dates, wild dates, *parūṣaka*, *sauvīra* jujube, the two types of *medā*, *punarnavā*, *kaśeruka*, young shoots, coral, and lotus stalks, together with milk.

Once the patient has been lubricated, one should administer a purgative using sugarcane juice on both sides [of the body]. After these patients with vitiligo have undergone bloodletting, one should apply an ointment consisting of madhuka, sārivā, balā, candana, lodhra, and utpala, mixed with ghee.

Or, one should consume cool, sweet food and drink prepared with *prapauṇḍarīka*, *madhuka*, *padmaka*, blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), *sārivā*, the roots and sprouts of plantain (*kadalī*), and golden ochre (*suvarṇagairika*); and one should resort to a breezy place, daytime sleep, and a state of mental cheerfulness.

In cases arising from *kapha*, one should prepare ghee by boiling it in a decoction of *daśamūla*, *devadāru*, *harītakī*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, and *āmalakī*, with the paste (*kalka*) of *mustā*, *kuṣṭha*, *haridrā*, and *amarataru*; this ghee should be used in the same manner as before.
A plaster (*lepa*) made of *tuttha*, *rocanā*, *lodhra*, *priyaṅgu*, and *kāleyaka*, combined with honey and ghee, [should also be applied].
Or with the roots of *devadāru*, *sarala*, *balā*, and *śigru*; or with realgar (*manaḥśilā*), blue vitriol (*tuttha*), and *rasāñjana*.
Alternatively, for ten measures, a plaster of mild alkali should be applied.
In cases arising from blood, one who has been lubricated with milk and ghee should have a vein opened.
One should administer emesis and purgation as in the case of pitta; furthermore, an ointment for this [condition] should be made with a paste of *candana* and *madhuka* mixed with ghee,
or alternatively, with a paste of *sarjarasa*, *nīlotpala*, conch-shell, *vetasa*, the roots of *kadali*, *mūrvā*, and *madhuka*.

In the case of *prasupti*, one should follow the procedure prescribed for *vātakuṣṭha* and finally apply cauterization with fire. For *utkoṭha*, the treatment consists of measures that remove *pitta* and *kapha*, as well as massage with oil containing alkaline salts and salt.
One should observe the treatment for skin diseases (kuṣṭha) in the abdominal cavity (koṣṭha);
thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter.
Now begins the thirty-eighth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "The Knowledge of Secret Diseases."
Thus indeed said the great seers, Ātreya and the others:
"For one who has abstained from sexual intercourse with women, yet suddenly indulges in it again..."
One whose path of subtle dust is defiled, mixed, and impure with faults; one who is of another species, unwilling, unapproachable, or has recently given birth.
Or one who touches water while thirsty, or even during sexual intercourse,
or one who administers sharp ointments and the like with the desire to increase [the virility].
By the crushing of fists, teeth, and nails; by poison, [sharp] thorns, and falls; by the suppression of natural urges, and by long, excessively harsh contact with young grass.
The vitiated doshas, having entered the secret region, produce twenty-three diseases beginning with upadaṃśa; here, upadaṃśa is fivefold.

In this condition, there is swelling of the penis along with various pains, stiffness, and cracking of the skin due to the individual humors (doṣas) and blood, both separately and combined; when caused by vāta,
it resembles a ripe udumbara fruit, while with pitta there is swelling and fever.
That which is caused by phlegm (śleṣman) is hard, unctuous, itchy, cold, and heavy.
From blood arises the appearance of black vesicles, discharge of blood, fever, intense pain,
rapid suppuration, cracking, and the emergence of worms.
Among those [types of piles], that which arises from blood is palliable, whereas that born of the combination of the three humors (sannipāta) leads to death.
Due to aggravated *doṣas* localized in the secretions, blood,
and flesh, fleshy nodules (*māṃsakīlakas*) arise, accompanied by itching, either internally or externally on the penis.
When there is a discharge of slimy blood from the vagina, and likewise when it resembles an umbrella (in shape),
these, if neglected, destroy the penis, virility, and the female generative organ.
Pustules caused by phlegm and blood, occurring either externally or internally on the penis,
which are shaped like mustard seeds and are dense, are known as *sarṣapikā*.
When many long abscesses burst open from the middle, that condition is called avamantha; it arises from phlegm and blood and is accompanied by pain and horripilation.
Kumbhīkā arises from rakta-pitta and resembles the bone of a jambu fruit, appearing red. One should know that Alajī is like Meha, while Uttamā is born from rakta-pitta.
A carbuncle (piṭaka) resembling black gram or mung bean, covered with many small pustules,
and shaped like the pericarp of a lotus, should be known as puṣkarikā.
When [the area] is excessively compressed by both hands, it becomes a *saṃvyūḍhapiṭaka* (a tumor formed by compression).
An object that has been repeatedly crushed or violently agitated due to the provocation of *vāta* [becomes a *mṛditapiṭaka*].
Irregular, hard, and curved due to wind, this condition is known as aṣṭhīlikā.
Due to wind vitiated by excessive massage and other factors, the skin of the penis becomes retracted, accompanied by pain and burning, and in some cases, it undergoes suppuration.
That which is clotted, putrid, and flaccid below the navel,
devoid of sensation, accompanied by phlegm, and characterized by itching and hardness, is [the disease known as] carma.
A wound that has healed poorly and the skin has burst is designated as *avapāṭikā*.
If the skin, vitiated by *vāta*, becomes adhered to the glans and obstructs it, [it is likewise so called].
Then the urine flows out with a slow stream from the opening;
the dilation of the glans penis is obstructed, and this disease is known as Niruddhamani.

The condition in which the penis is covered as if strewn with awns is called Granthi; it arises from Kapha. That which arises from blood vitiated by Śūka (the awn) and is characterized by loss of sensation is named after that [Śūkadūṣita].
That which is the urethra, covered on all sides by minute-mouthed openings; AS.Utt.38.27. AS.Utt.38.26.

One should recognize that as *śataponaka* when it arises from the provocation of *vāta* and blood (*śoṇita*). However, *tvakpāka*, characterized by fever and burning sensations, is the suppuration of the skin caused by *pitta* and blood.
Māṃsapāka is caused by all [three doṣas], characterized by all types of pain, and involves the sloughing off of flesh;
it is afflicted by dark, reddish eruptions and intense pains.

One should recognize as *asṛgarbuda* (blood tumor) the presence of urination and severe pain; the *māṃsārbuda* (flesh tumor) has been described previously, as have abscesses (*vidradhi*) arising from the three *doṣas*.
Having turned black, the flesh falls away on all sides.
One should recognize those *tilakālaka* moles as being caused by the vitiation of all three *doṣas* (*sannipāta*).
Tumors arising from the flesh (*māṃsottha-arbuda*), abscesses (*pāka*), fistulas (*vidradhi*), and *tilakālaka* moles [should be treated accordingly].
One should avoid the four defects and treat the remaining ones quickly;
twenty complications of the female genital tract arise from unwholesome diet.

Due to sleeping on uneven limbs, excessive sexual indulgence, vitiated menstrual blood, unwholesome substances, defects of the seed, or by fate, the provoked Vāyu in the womb causes pain, pricking, stretching, and numbness.
A pillar-like swelling that feels as if crawled over by ants, roughness, and a ringing sound;
the discharge of *ārta* (menstrual/seminal) fluid that is frothy, reddish, black, scanty, thin, and dry.
Dropping [of the fetus], pain in the groin, flanks, and so forth, abdominal tumors (gulma), and various other diseases occurring in succession— this is known as the complication called Vātikī.
That same condition, known as *aticaraṇā*, results from excessive sexual intercourse with a woman who has swelling,
or from intercourse with one who is too young; it affects the back, calves, thighs, and groins.
The Vāyu, moving upward from the feet, causes pain and corrupts the womb;
by reversing its natural flow, that Māruta afflicts the womb.
When, with great difficulty, she discharges frothy menstrual blood that has been turned upward,
this is the complication known as *udāvṛttā*. However, when the wind (*anila*) is the cause, it is called *jātaghnī*.
Due to harshness arising from a vitiated menstrual flow (*duṣṭārtava*), she kills every son born; likewise,
when she has overeaten or is in an irregular position during sexual intercourse, the vital wind (*marut*) [causes the same].
When the fetus, compressed by another [fetus] in the womb,
remains in the birth canal and turns its face with bone and flesh toward the orifice, causing intense pain within, that is called *antarmukhī*.
In a mother who consumes a diet that increases *vāta*, the aggravated wind may cause the woman's vaginal opening to become narrow; this condition is known as *sūcimukhī*.

Due to the suppression of natural urges during the menstrual period, the vitiated *vāyu* causes retention of feces and urine, as well as vaginal dryness; this condition, characterized by intense pain, is called *śuṣkā*.
If, within six days or seven nights, the wind expels the *śukra* (semen/fetal matter) from the uterus,
whether accompanied by pain or free from it, that condition is considered *vāminī*.
When the womb is afflicted by Vāta due to defects in the seed within the woman's womb,
she becomes one who hates men, lacks breasts, and follows the characteristics known as a eunuch (ṣaṇḍa).
The vitiated wind (māruta), having become obstructed within the vagina, the mouth, and the uterine cavity,
causes it to become dilated or prolapsed, making the woman suffer as if from a vātika disorder.
They call that [condition] Mahāyoni, which has wasted flesh and is accompanied by great pain;
it occurs when pitta, vitiated by its own specific corrupting factors, has taken refuge in the female reproductive tract.
It causes burning, suppuration, pain, a putrid odor, fever, and is accompanied by an excessively hot, copious, cadaverous, blue, yellow,
or black menstrual flow; this disorder is the Pitta-type complication known as *raktayoni* due to excessive discharge of blood.
Kapha,
aggravated by obstructive substances, may cause a painless discharge from the vagina.
That which is accompanied by a discharge of slimy, itchy, pale, and slippery mucus is the ślaiṣmikī complication;
in cases of vāta and pitta, the menstrual flow (rajas) becomes diminished.
That [menorrhagia] in which there is constant burning, emaciation, and discoloration is *lohitakṣaya* (loss of blood),
occurring in a woman of bilious temperament (*pittalā*) due to the suppression of sneezing and eructation during sexual intercourse with a man.
When the womb is vitiated by wind combined with bile (pitta),
it becomes swollen, intolerant to touch, and discharges ghee-like, blue, or yellow fluids.
Pariplutā causes heaviness in the bladder and abdomen, diarrhea, and loss of appetite; it produces pain and throbbing in the groins and inguinal regions, as well as fever.
A vagina pervaded by disorders of vāta and śleṣman, discharging white and slimy secretions,
is known as *upaplutā*; that which is called *viplutā* results from improper cleansing.
When a living being has been formed, itching arises, and scratching is exceedingly dear to it.
Due to riding at an improper time, the wind (vāyu), combined with phlegm (śleṣman) and blood (rakta), becomes agitated.
It produces a protuberance (karṇikā) in the birth canal that obstructs the path of the menses;
this condition is called *karṇinī*, caused by the three doṣas localized in the womb and the uterus.

When the disorder is caused by factors that produce their respective complications, it is a sannipātika (combined) condition. Thus, these are the vaginal diseases by which a woman does not accept the semen.
Consequently, she does not conceive, and she suffers from severe diseases such as menorrhagia,
hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, and other afflictions caused by the derangement of vāta and the other doshas.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter.
Now begins the thirty-ninth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "The Treatment of Secret Diseases."
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and others:
in cases of *upadaṃśa* (venereal sores), as soon as they have appeared, one should pierce a vein in the middle of the penis to prevent suppuration.

One should properly eliminate his humors from both sides, especially by means of purgation; however, for one who is unfit for that, one should eliminate the excessively elevated humors by means of non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana).
One should apply ointments, affusions, and other treatments incessantly according to the specific dosha;
in this way, pain, piercing sensation, swelling, redness, and inflammation are immediately relieved.
Once they have ripened, one should apply the surgical instrument;
then, one should apply an ointment made of sesame paste mixed with ghee, honey, and sugar.
Moreover,
[one should use] the sprouts of the Jambu, Amra, Sumanas, Nīpa, Śveta, Kāmbojika,
and Aṅkura.
One should boil in water the barks derived from *sallakī*, *badarī*, *bilva*, *palāśa*, and *tiniśa*, as well as those of the milky trees (*kṣīridruma*) and *triphalā*.
That decoction is for washing; oil cooked with it is for healing,
along with *gojī*, *viḍaṅga*, *madhuka*, and the *sarvagandha* group ground together,
as well as *tuttha*, *gaurī*, *lodhra*, *elā*, *manohvā*, and *rasāñjana*.

A fine paste made from mercury, flowers (of the *kubjaka* tree), green vitriol, *saurāṣṭrī*, and the best salt, mixed with honey and applied while still warm, cures ulcers caused by venereal disease (*upadaṃśa*).

Alternatively, an excellent plaster for a wound consists of the bark of *dārvī*, conch shell, *tārkṣya* (guggulu), lac, cow's milk, and the juice of *viḍa* salt, combined with honey, oil, and clarified butter.
Lac, grapes, linseed, honey, honey, śaileya, and the product of *tārkṣya*,
along with *triphalā* burnt in a skull and mixed with ghee, is the supreme healer for promoting wound healing.
This general remedy for vāta-type [skin diseases] should be applied as a paste using unripe *kuṣṭha*, *yaṣṭyāhva*, *suradāru*, and *punarnavā*.
With unctuous and warm substances combined with iron filings, sarala, rāsnā, and puṇḍrāhvā;
or alternatively, with nicula, castor seeds, wheat, and parched grain flour.
For [fever] arising from pitta, one should use a cooling application rich in ghee, consisting of red ochre, collyrium, madder, madhuka, uśīra, padmaka, sandalwood, and blue lotuses.
One should irrigate with lotus, blue lotus, and lotus stalks, or with *sarja*, *arjuna*, and cane;
and one should sprinkle with ghee, milk, sugar, sugarcane juice, honey, and water.
One should apply a warm plaster made of the bark of *dhava*, *sāla*, *aśvakarṇa*, and *ajakarṇa*, ground with *surā* liquor and mixed with oil, for a swelling arising from *kapha*.
Alternatively, [a decoction] made from *rajanī*, *ativiṣā*, *mustā*, *saralā*, and *devadāru*, together with *sapattrā*,
*pāṭhā*, and *pattūra*, [is used for] that which arises from phlegm (*śleṣman*).
One should strive intensely so that [the penis] does not undergo putrefaction;
for when the ligaments, vessels, and flesh have become putrid, the organ is generally destroyed.

When two types of secondary hemorrhages (upadaṃśa) remain, one should abandon [the patient] and perform the treatment [only for those who can be cured]. For one whose body has been purified, one should treat the hemorrhoids (arśāṃsi) with surgery, caustics, or thermal cautery as appropriate.
The medicinal preparation (rasakriyā) and the ointment mentioned here for upadaṃśa should also be used. After scarifying sarṣapikā, one should dust it with astringent powders (kaṣāya).
With those very same [ingredients], one should prepare an oil for the healing of the wound; in cases of *avamanya*,
one should apply leeches.
When it has ripened and burst open, one should treat it with oil prepared from *dhava*, *tinduka*, *sallakī*, *pataṅga*, and *sarja*.
One should treat *kumbhīkā* in the same manner.
A paste made from *lodhra*, *tinduka*, and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), along with oil, is for healing; one should dust an *alajī* ulcer that has had its blood drained with astringent powders.

One should also prepare oil from those very same [ingredients] for the purpose of healing the wound. Having incised a severe carbuncle (*piṭakā*) with a surgical instrument, one should treat it with astringent decoctions, powders, and plasters mixed with honey and wine.
In cases of *puṣkarikāsaṃvyūḍha*, loss of sensation (*sparśahāni*), and inflammation of the skin (*tvakpāka*), the treatment prescribed for *pittavisarpa* should be applied.
One should sprinkle the crushed area with lukewarm *balā*-oil and apply a poultice (*upanāha*) made from the pastes of sweet substances mixed with ghee, applied while still comfortably warm.
One should cause leeches to take hold of the *aṣṭhīlikā*;
if there is no relief in that way, one should extract it with a surgical instrument like a phlegm-granule (*śleṣmagranthi*).
Once the discharge has ceased, one should anoint the area with clarified butter (sarpiḥ) and apply fomentation;
once it has been fomented, one should apply a poultice (upanāhana) made of sālvala for three or five nights.
Then, having sweated it further and anointed it with ghee, one should gradually bring the skin together and press upon the stone;
after pressing it, one should apply a poultice again and provide unctuous, warm food and drink.
This same procedure applies to *avapāṭikā* as well.

In the case of a constricted urethra (*niruddhamaṇi*), one should insert a tube made of gold or other metals, or made of wood, or coated with lac, with openings at both ends and lubricated with oil, into the channel and irrigate it with the fat or marrow of a boar or a porpoise.
Or with castor oil,
or with trivṛt processed with vāta-alleviating drugs.
On every third day, one should insert a larger cannula;
in this way, one should enlarge the opening of his channels and feed him unctuous food.
If [the swelling] does not subside in this manner, one should avoid the *sevanī* (median raphe) with a surgical instrument, incise it, and treat it like a fresh wound (*sadyaḥkṣata*).
Having treated a *grathita* (knotted swelling) with fomentation by means of a tube (*nāḍī-sveda*), one should apply a warm, unctuous poultice (*upanāha*).
Having scarified a *śataponaka* (boil), one should apply a paste of decoctions and powders mixed with honey.
One should treat a sugar-tumor (*śarkarārbuda*) with oil prepared from *vidārī* and other ingredients, and its management is like that of a blood-abscess (*raktavidradhi*).

In all cases, one should administer internal purification according to the specific condition, as well as decoctions, medicinal pastes, ghee, oils, *rasakriyā*, powders, and agents for cleansing and healing.

In the case of a vaginal disorder caused by *vāta*, one should foment the vagina— lubricated with salted oil— using bolus-fomentation (*piṇḍa-sveda*), tube-fomentation (*nāḍī-sveda*), or pot-fomentation (*kumbhī-sveda*). Thereafter,
having sprinkled all her limbs with lukewarm water, one should feed her with the meat-broths of wild animals.

One should prepare one āḍhaka each of ghee and oil by boiling them with two droṇas of a decoction of bala, along with milk four times the quantity of the liquid, and adding as internal ingredients (garbha) payasyā, sālaparṇī, māgadhikā, śatāvarī, kākanāsā, śrāvaṇī, sugar, and the drugs of the jīvanīya group. By drinking this, one dispels all disorders of vāta and pitta and promotes conception.

A *prastha* of ghee prepared with one *karṣa* each of *śatāvarī*, *triphalā*, *guḍūcī*, *kāśmarya*, *mṛdvīkā*, *kāsamardaka*, *parūṣaka*, the two types of *haridrā*, *sahacara*, *śukanāsā*, and *punarnavā*, when drunk, cures Vata-originated gynecological diseases and promotes conception. The powder of *saindhava*, *vacā*, *upakuñcikā*, *pippalī*, *vṛṣaka*, *yavakṣāra*, *ajamodā*, *ajājī*, *sitopalā*, and *citraka*, mixed with wine and made into a *saṃyāva* (sweet cake) with ghee, when eaten, removes pain in the vagina, flanks, and bladder, as well as hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), and heart disease.
In cases of *śūla*, one should drink milk boiled with *vṛṣaka*, *rāsnā*, and *agokṣuraka*.
Alternatively, one may take a paste of *vṛṣaka*, the root of *mātuluṅga*, *madayantikā*, rock salt (*saindhava*), long pepper (*pippalī*), and black cumin (*kṛṣṇajīraka*) with that same liquor;
or the root of *arjaka* combined with *bilva* or long pepper with that same liquor;
or *sauvarcala* salt, *upakuñcikā*, and long pepper with liquor or *avantisoma*.

A lukewarm decoction of *dantī*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and *guḍūcī* should be used for pouring over the vagina (*pariṣeka*). One should apply oil prepared with *kuṣṭha*, *tagara*, *devadāru*, *vārtākinī*, and rock salt (*saindhava*) using a tampon (*picu*).

A *prastha* of oil cooked with one *karṣa* each of the roots of *rāsnā*, *mālatī*, *chinnaruhā*, *madhuka*, *balā*, *vyāghrī*, *devadāru*, *citraka*, and *yūthikā*, along with cow’s urine and double the quantity of milk, when applied with a cotton swab (*picu*), removes the afflictions caused by *vāta*.

One should apply enema therapy (basti) repeatedly and sudation (sveda), especially with oils that alleviate Vāta, such as Sukumāra-bala-taila and Śirīṣa-taila, as well as oils processed a hundred or a thousand times for oil enemas (anuvāsana) and urethral/vaginal enemas (uttara-basti). This regimen specifically destroys pain, hardness, stiffness, prolapse, and loss of sensation in the female genital tract (yoni).

In all conditions arising from Vāta, such as *aticaraṇa* (excessive walking) and others, this same procedure should be followed. For the treatment of *aticaraṇa*, one should apply a poultice (*utkārikā*) made from the paste of barley, wheat, *kiṇva* (ferment), *kuṣṭha*, *śatapuṣpā*, *śryāhvī*, *priyaṅgu*, *balā*, and *khukarṇī*.
When the feet have first been dried and the oil has not yet spread upward, one should administer an uttarabasti (urethral/vaginal enema) using an arrow-shaft (karṇinī) that is not too long.

In the case of *viplutā*, one should apply linen or cotton cloth that has been soaked twenty-one times with the bile of either a cow or a fish; or alternatively, one may apply fermenting yeast (*kiṇva*) mixed with honey. In this way, her channels are purified, and itching, discharge, and swelling are eliminated. In the case of *karṇinī*, however, one should prepare a wick (*varti*) by grinding together *kuṣṭha*, the tender leaves of *arka*, long pepper (*pippalī*), and rock salt with goat’s urine, and then insert it.

One should administer everything that alleviates *śleṣman* (phlegm). In the case of upward movement of the wind (*udāvarta*), meat broth from marshy animals, milk, sudation, and oil prepared with a decoction and paste of *daśamūla* and *trivṛt* should be used for drinking, unctuous enemas (*anuvāsana*), and urethral/vaginal enemas (*uttarabasti*).
In cases of uterine prolapse (yoni-sraṃsa) and conditions such as mahāyoni, this same procedure is prescribed.
For women suffering from jātaghnī, raktayoni, or raktakṣaya, one should administer ghee prepared with a decoction of kuṭaja and kāśmarya via an uttarabasti enema.

Alternatively, [the substances are] the blood of deer, goats, and boars, sour curd, honey, and ghee; and there is a verse on this point: AS.Utt.39.47 athavā mṛgājāvivarāharudhirāmladadhimadhughṛtānīti bhavati cātra.
In cases of disorders caused by Vāta, one should administer oleation, sudation, enemas, and other such therapies that alleviate Vāta;
in those caused by Pitta, one should employ cooling measures that cure blood-bile (rakta-pitta).
In cases involving phlegm (śleṣman), one should perform dry and hot treatments as appropriate; however,
in cases of combined humors (saṃnipāta) or associated disorders, one should employ a mixed regimen.

Having lubricated and fomented the vagina, one should thus restore it to its proper position if it is displaced; with the hand, one should straighten it if it is crooked, and expand it if it is constricted.
One should cause that which has protruded to re-enter and turn back that which is everted;
for a uterus displaced from its position is considered a source of pain like a foreign body for a woman.
One should treat a woman with all types of obstructed labor by first administering mild emesis and other purificatory measures (pañcakarma), after she has been lubricated and fomented.
For one who has been thoroughly purified in every respect, the remaining treatment is prescribed as enemas,
massage, affusion, ointments, and the application of medicinal plugs.
In cases of suffering from Vāta, one should massage with a lukewarm paste of Hiṃsrā and apply it;
in cases of Pitta, with the five barks (pañcavalka); and in cases of Kapha, with Śyāmā and other such herbs.
In cases of *vāminī* and *āpluta*, one should apply sudation and then administer nourishing therapy (*tarpaṇa*) with oil-soaked cotton plugs (*sneha-picu*),
as well as food that pacifies Vāta.
From an oil prepared with the decoctions of the barks of *sallakī*, *jiṅgiṇī*, *jambū*, *dhava*, and the five types of *valkala*,
one should apply a cotton pad (*picu*) soaked in it to both eyes.
Having filled the large vaginal canal with crab fat, pig fat, ghee, and sweet decoctions, one should bind it with linen and *naktaka* cloth.
Having anointed the prolapsed organ with ghee and steamed it with milk,
one should reinsert it and bind it with a bolus of *veśavāra* until the time of urination.

Furthermore, the wise physician should perform whatever treatment for disorders of Vāta has been prescribed, especially in all calamities and particularly in the case of a major vaginal prolapse (mahāyoni).
Indeed, the female reproductive tract is not corrupted except by wind;
therefore, having conquered that [wind], one should apply the remedy for the other dosha.

For female reproductive tracts characterized by an excess of pitta, cooling treatments such as irrigation (sekā), massage (abhyaṅga), and the application of cotton swabs (picu) should be performed to overcome pitta; furthermore, ghees (ghṛta) should be used for the purpose of oleation.
From four *tulās* of crushed and squeezed *śatāvarī* root,
one should cook one *āḍhaka* of ghee with an equal amount of milk using the resulting juice.
With the life-promoting (jīvanīya) drugs, śatāvarī, grapes, parūṣaka,
and priyāla— each ground in one akṣa measure— and combined with half a pala of madhuka;
When the [mixture] has been prepared and cooled, one should add eight palas of honey, eight palas of long pepper (pippalī),
and ten palas of sugar; from this, one should lick a dose of one picu.
It destroys defects of the vaginal tract, blood, and semen; it is aphrodisiac and a supreme promoter of male progeny.
It cures chest wounds, consumption, hemorrhagic disorders, cough, dyspnea, and chlorosis.
It destroys kāmalā, vātarakta, visarpa, and stiffness of the heart and head; it also cures epilepsy, facial paralysis, intoxication, and insanity.
In this very same way, milk processed with ghee and life-promoting (jīvanīya) herbs bestows conception and is supremely beneficial for diseases born of pitta.
In the case of *raktayoni*, having observed the persistence [of the disorder] through the colors of the blood,
one should administer blood-stabilizing (*raktasthāpana*) medicine according to the manifestation of the specific *doṣas*.
Sesame powder, curd, ghee, treacle, and hog’s fat,
when drunk mixed with honey, overcome menstrual disorders (asṛgdara) in which vāta is predominant.
The juice of the boar (*varāha*) is pure (*medhya*), as is that of the *kaulattha* pulse; it possesses similar qualities.
A paste of the leaves of the *rājādana* and *kapittha* trees, fried in ghee, [is likewise beneficial].
Curd combined with sugar, honey, liquorice, and ginger; and milk-pudding (payasyā) along with blue lotus, white lotus root, lotus stalk, kālīya, and water-lily.
In cases where blood is predominant and pitta is excessive, one should drink [the juice of] *saparyaś* with sugar and honey;
or alternatively, one may take the root of *taṇḍulīyaka* with honey and rice-water.
One should drink lac along with goat's milk and *tārkṣyaśaila*,
or take *vāsāghṛta* and *mahātikta*, which are beneficial for *raktapitta*. [One should also take] *madhuka*, *triphalā*, *lodhra*, *musta*, *saurāṣṭrikā*, and honey.
In cases of *asṛgdara* caused by *kapha*, one should drink *nīpa*, *guḍūcī*, and *madya*; likewise,
one should take *pāṭhā*, the stones of *jambū* and *āmra*, *śilodbheda*, and *rasāñjana*.
Ambaṣṭhā, the pulp of the śālmalī fruit, samaṅgā, the bark of vatsaka,
bālhīka, bilva, ativiṣā, lodhra, toyada, and gairika.
Dry ginger, madhūka, mācīka, red sandalwood, and kaṭphala; kaṭvaṅga, vatsaka, anantā, dhātakī, madhuka, and arjuna.
Having taken [the drug] under the Puṣya asterism and having powdered it, one should drink it with honey and rice-water in cases of hemorrhoids and dysentery,
as well as for blood that is passed in the stool.
It shall destroy those defects caused by insects that afflict children,
as well as disorders of the female reproductive tract (*yonidoṣa*), disorders of the menses (*rajodoṣa*), and [skin conditions] that are dark-brown, white, reddish, or black.
The powder known as Puṣyānuga, praised by Ātreya, is beneficial;
it is recommended for all types of pradara and is prescribed for cases where miscarriage has been mentioned.
In the case of a depletion of blood, one should drink milk boiled with the drugs of the jīvanīya group.
When the vaginal canal is afflicted by *balāsa* (mucous phlegm), a cleansing suppository is beneficial;
it should be prepared from *naktaka* fibers repeatedly saturated with the bile of a boar.
Barley-meal powder mixed with rock salt and soaked in the milk of the arka plant should be made into a wick;
it should be applied for a moment and then washed off with lukewarm water.
A wick (varti) made from long pepper, black gram, black pepper, śatāhvā, kuṣṭha, and rock salt,
with a thickness equal to the index finger, cleanses the vagina.
One should boil one *droṇa* of unripe *udumbara* fruits in one *droṇa* of water, together with the five barks (*pañcavalkala*), sesame, *mālatī*, and neem sprouts.
When that water has stood overnight, one should cook one prastha of oil with the barks and decoctions of *palāśa*,
*śālmalī*, and *lākṣā*.
Then, one should insert a tampon (picu) soaked in oil mixed with these ground powders into the vagina; furthermore, one should perform irrigation with cold decoctions containing *śakra*.
The *picchilā* and *vivṛtā* types of vaginal disorders, as well as those that have been chronically afflicted and are severe (*dāruṇā*),
are quickly purified within seven days, and one obtains offspring accordingly.
Oil should be prepared from sesame seeds that have been infused six times with the milk of the *udumbara* tree using its decoction, and it should be administered as previously described.
With *dhātakī*, *āmalakī* leaves, *srotoñjana*, *madhuka*, and *utpala*;
with the heartwood of *jambu* and *āmra*, *kāsīsa*, *lodhra*, *kaṭphala*, and *tinduka*.
One should cook [the paste] of *saurāṣṭrika* (borax), pomegranate bark, and unripe *udumbara* fruits— each in the quantity of an *akṣa*— in goat’s urine and twice as much milk.
One should employ one prastha of that oil for massage, cotton swabs, and enemas. Furthermore,
[the vagina] may be swollen, elevated, protruding, stiff, slimy, or discharging.
A vaginal canal that is overflowing, submerged, or accompanied by eruptions and pain may be cured with a decoction derived from arka,
nimba, āmra, kośāmra, bilva, būka, and dhava.
An excellent cleansing wash (dhāvana) is prepared from the decoctions (kaṣāya) of karīra, jiṅgiṇī, nambū, karañja, arjuna, śigru, palāśa,
and sidhraka.
One should effect the cessation of vaginal discharge using a mixture of fermented gruel,
sidhu wine, and honey; or alternatively, with sour gruel, cow’s urine, fermented gruel, or the juices of the three myrobalans (triphalā).
One should habitually consume barley-based food, abhayā, ariṣṭa, sīdhu, and oil;
as well as preparations of pippalī, iron powder (ayaḥrajaḥ), and pathyā mixed with honey.
In cases of anemia (pāṇḍu) or menorrhagia (asṛgdara), one should drink the paste of the root-bark of *rohitaka*,
or else the paste of the marrow of *dhātrī* combined with sugar and honey.
In the bright fortnight, one should have [the patient] consume honey with the powder of *āmalakī* or its juice;
one should also rinse the teeth with a decoction of *vaṭa* bark mixed with *lodhra* wood.
In cases of discharge (āsrāva), one should apply linen cloths or bandages impregnated with that [medicinal decoction],
or one should apply a bolus made from a paste of *plakṣa* bark powder mixed with honey.
The vaginal canal should be lubricated with oil, and a suppository made of *lodhra*, *priyaṅgu*, and *madhuka*, or one prepared from *madhuka* and various decoctions, should be inserted repeatedly.
For the purpose of cutting the discharge, one should fumigate the anointed area with *sarala*,
*aguru*, and barley soaked in ghee, along with sesame seeds and pungent fish.
A powder consisting of kāsīsa, triphalā, kāṅkṣī, the stones of mango and jambu, and ghātakī,
combined with honey, produces clarity when there is excessive sliminess.
A powder derived from *palāśa*, *dhātakī*, *jambū*, *samaṅgā*, *moca*,
and *sarja* is desired as a styptic for foul-smelling, slimy, and discharging wounds.
A decoction of the group of drugs beginning with *āragvadha* should be used for sprinkling;
it acts as a softener for those [limbs] that are stiff and rough.
One should administer vesavāra, or kṛsarā,
or pāyasa; for those with foul odors, a decoction, oil, or even a paste should be used.
Or a powder of all fragrant substances removes foul odors; for those with phlegmatic disorders, enemas consisting mostly of pungent substances mixed with urine are beneficial.

In cases of pitta, [the treatment] combined with madhuka and milk is beneficial; in cases of vāta, it is combined with oil and sour substances; for those arising from sannipāta, general treatment is beneficial.
Thus, when the female reproductive tracts are purified, women conceive.
When the natural seed is not defective and the process of impregnation has occurred,
even for a man who has been purified by the five medical procedures (pañcakarma), the [reproductive] organ [may fail].
Having examined [the condition] by the colors of the humors (doṣas), one should treat that which is afflicted with remedies that destroy them.

Mañjiṣṭhā, kuṣṭha, tagara, triphalā, śarkarā, and vacā— AS.Utt.39.107 Having examined [the condition] by the colors of the humors (doṣas), one should treat that which is afflicted with remedies that destroy them. AS.Utt.39.108 Mañjiṣṭhā, kuṣṭha, tagara, triphalā, śarkarā, and vacā—
The two types of niśā, madhuka, medā, dīpyaka, kaṭurohiṇī,
payasyā, hiṅgu, kākolī, vājigandhā, and śatāvarī.
Having ground one part of Aksha seeds, one should cook it with one prastha of ghee and four times as much milk;
this is recommended for all disorders of the female reproductive tract and the semen.
This is known as *phalasarpiḥ* (fruit-ghee), which bestows longevity, nourishment, purity, prosperity, and is supremely effective for ensuring male progeny;
it is drunk during the menstrual period to ensure conception.
This is honored for those whose offspring are dying and for pregnant women;
it is supreme for children, destroying the influence of seizing spirits (grahas) and promoting bodily growth.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter; the fifth limb, known as the Śalyatantra, is completed.
Now begins the fortieth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "The Prevention of Poisoning.
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.

Formerly, indeed, while the ocean was being churned by the gods and the asuras for the sake of the nectar of immortality, a being emerged like wrath incarnate— black in color, with eyes of fire and hair blazing upward, formidable with fangs and possessing a terrifying roar and form. Because the gods and the dānavas were despondent at the mere sight of it, it therefore obtained the name "poison" (*viṣa*).

Then, wishing to consume all living beings by its very force, [the poison] was appeased by Brahmā through specific applications and rendered into the state of ambrosia; he then deposited it within medicinal herbs.
Consequently, because it dwells within stationary forms, it is called "sthāvara" (stationary).
Furthermore,
for the purpose of removing the burden from the earth, Viṣṇu created mobile beings in the form of serpents and others.
Of those two [types of poison], the stationary (sthāvara) has ten bases (*adhiṣṭhāna*), distinguished by root, leaf, flower, fruit, bark, pith, resin, latex,
mineral, and tuber. Among these, the root-poisons include *klītanaka*, *aśvamāraka*, *guñjā*, *sugandhaka*, *gargaka*, *karkara*, *karaghāṭaka*, and so forth.
The leaf-poison consists of *kālapattrikā*, *lambā*, *varadakarabhā*, *arka*, and so forth;
the flower-poison consists of *vallī*, *reṇuka*, *karambha*, *mahākarambha*, and so forth.
The fruits of *kumudvatī*, *reṇukā*, *karambha*, *mahākarambha*, *madana*, *katuvaraka*, and so forth;
the inner bark and exudations of *karaka*, *karaghāṭaka*, *karambha*, *mahākarambha*, *nārācaka*, and so forth;
and the milky sap of *kumudvatī*, *dantī*, *snuhī*, *arka*, *jālinī*, *vyāla*, and so forth [are used].
Minerals (*dhātu*) include yellow orpiment, rock-foam, stone-ash, red ochre, and so forth;

whereas those produced from tubers (*kandaja*) include *hālāhala*, *kālakūṭa*, *vatsanābha*, *śṛṅgī*, *sāṣarpa*, *jālakaka*, *kardamaka*, *vairāṭaka*, *mustaka*, *muṣkaka*, *sāktuka*, *krauñcaka*, *vālaka*, *mahāviṣa*, *puṇḍarīka*, *gālava*, *mūlaka*, *markaṭa*, *karkaṭaka*, *karavīraka*, *indrāyudha*, *saṃkoca*, *lāṅgalaka*, *tailapeya*, *kuśapuṣpaka*, *puṣpaka*, *rohiṣa*, *añjanābhaka*, and others. Among these, when root-poisons (*mūlaviṣa*) are consumed, convulsions, delirium, and fainting occur.
From leaf-poisons there arise yawning, twisting of the body, and labored breathing;
from flower-poisons, vomiting, flatulence, and delusion.
From poisons found in fruits, there arise burning sensations and swelling of the scrotum;
from poisons found in the sap and resin of trees, there arise excessive salivation, foul odor of the mouth, roughness of the skin, and headache;
and from poisons found in milk, there arise heaviness of the tongue and diarrhea.

Poisons derived from the mineral elements (dhātu) cause burning of the palate, fainting, and pain in the heart; they produce all stationary poisons (sthāvara), as well as fever, hiccups, horripilation, lockjaw, throat obstruction, frothing at the mouth, vomiting, loss of appetite, dyspnea, and fainting— especially those born from bulbs (kandaja),
for these, due to their extreme acuity, act most rapidly.
The other [type], however, generally takes life at a later time (AS.Utt.40.9); and all of this is called "fundamental" (*maula*) because leaves and the other parts depend upon the root (AS.Utt.40.9).
The sixteen sources of danger from mobile beings are:
sight, breath, touch, fangs, mouth, nails, bones, urine, feces, semen, menstrual blood, saliva, hair, bile, blood, and corpses.

Furthermore, those [poisons] residing in snakes, insects, *kaṇabha* beetles, and so forth, produce their respective diseases and means of treatment, which he will describe later; and for the most part, all mobile poisons cause sleepiness, lethargy, exhaustion, burning sensations, horripilation, swelling, suppuration, and diarrhea.

Both types of this poison are endowed with ten qualities— sharpness, heat, dryness, clarity, subtlety, pervasiveness, rapid action, diffusiveness, lightness, and unmanifested taste— and they are undigested.
In that regard, due to its sharpness and heat, it aggravates pitta and blood;
due to its dryness, it aggravates vāyu.
Due to its clarity, it flows with unimpeded force;
due to its subtlety and penetrative nature, it enters all the bodily constituents, tissues, waste products, and every part of the body;
and due to its rapid action, it brings about destruction swiftly.
Because it causes expansion and cuts into the vital points (marmans), it deludes the intellect;
because it is difficult to extract due to its lightness and its unmanifest taste, it provokes phlegm (śleṣman) and pervades all components of food essence.
For this very reason, it has been said that one should protect foods from poison with great effort.
Because it is undigested, it does not undergo transformation;
therefore, what has been ingested necessarily kills.
Even if it has been pacified by the power of mantras and medicines, it may flare up again upon encountering the appropriate conditions.
And in this regard, it is said:
"Poison is declared to be of two kinds—static and mobile—and is natural (akṛtrima).
That which is known as artificial poison (*garasaṃjñam*) is prepared from various medicinal herbs;
it kills quickly, after a long time, or even after a very long period, according to the nature of its application.
Or it may cause swelling, anemia, abdominal enlargements, insanity, chronic diarrhea,
and so forth; furthermore, all this poison is endowed with qualities such as sharpness (tīkṣṇa) and others.
In persons where vāta and pitta predominate, poison takes away life instantly;
for once it has reached the body, the poison first vitiates the blood.
Following the kapha, pitta, and vāta, along with their respective seats (āśaya) and when the humors are in equilibrium,
[the wind] then takes refuge in the heart and leads to the destruction of the body.
When the blood is vitiated, the entire body experiences a tingling or pricking sensation.
A circular eruption (koṭha) arises, accompanied by sweating and horripilation;
one feels as though small insects are crawling over the limbs.
He bends his limbs and yawns, being fond of cold;
this is due to the pervasive, corrupted, and swift energy of that poison.
Even those who are powerful fall under the control of wind and the other [humors], like the weak;
poison first attacks whichever humor is most predominant.
In whichever receptacle (āśaya) a particular substance resides, it remains there and produces those transformations which [the author] will describe for all [of them].
Likewise, when located in the seat of vāta, it produces diseases of kapha;
similarly, when it has entered the seats of pitta and kapha, it produces those arising from pitta and kapha.
Furthermore, when it is located in the head, the head becomes swollen with a localized swelling (koṭha),
and specifically, there is horripilation of the eye-sockets, lips, nose, and mouth, as well as sensitivity of the teeth.
Drying up of the palate, pain in the head, a tingling sensation in the mouth,
non-functioning of the eyes and other senses toward their objects, and lockjaw (AS.Utt.40.24).
Thus, one should also recognize that poison situated elsewhere in the body;
having thus pervaded the entire body and obstructed the channels, it remains there.
Poison, like poison itself, swiftly expels the vital breaths from him who has drunk it, or from one whose heart is struck by a poisoned arrow or bitten by a venomous creature.
In a stinging insect (daṃśa), the poison is for the most part concentrated throughout the entire body;
therefore, one should especially not eat their flesh, as it serves as its substrate.
When [such flesh] is eaten according to its own nature, there is pain according to its own nature, and the course of treatment is likewise according to its own nature.
"Punarvasu says that there are seven stages of poison, though some say there are eight."
In the first stage, the vitiated rasa becomes corrupted, causing vomiting and excessive salivation.
In the second stage, it causes a tingling sensation, yawning, and trembling; in the third stage, it produces fleshiness, itching, urticaria, circular patches, and swelling.
In the fourth stage, the humors (doṣas) become aggravated, and corresponding complications (upadravas) arise;
in the fifth stage, there is a distortion of vision; and in the sixth stage, hiccups (hidhmā) manifest.
In the seventh [day], the breaking of his limbs occurs; in the eighth, death. In the first [day], the blood becomes vitiated; in the second, swelling arises.
In the third stage there is a tingling sensation; in the fourth, fever and fainting;
in the fifth, the tongue and mouth become pale and dry; and in the sixth, pain in the heart.
In the seventh stage, death occurs with the onset of the paroxysm; this is the opinion of Gajanita.
There is fainting, extreme pain in the heart, headache, and facial paralysis.
Hiccup, severe cutting pain in the vital organs (marmaccheda), and the danger to life—
these seven, beginning with fainting, are recorded as the stages of onset by the Lord of Videha.
Blood, flesh, fat, sinew, bone, and so forth— these three [groups] are respectively the substrates for the [seven] humors;
thus Ālambāyana declared there to be seven [substrates] for the seven [humors].
In the same way, Dhanvantari considers the toxic impulses (vega) of one bitten by a snake; however,
he maintains that in those locations, the humors (doṣas) reside in the visceral cavity (koṣṭha), excluding the tendons (snāyu).
Having passed beyond each one of those seven stages (*kalā*) previously proclaimed in relation to the other bodily constituents (*dhātu*), the poison produces its effect.
The duration of time required for it to reach even a fraction of its distance is considered to be the interval of its velocity as it is carried along by the wind.
Whatever has been taught by the Sage has all been demonstrated here. [The poison] may be digested, or destroyed by anti-poisonous herbs, or dried up by forest fire, wind, or heat.
Poison known as *dūṣīviṣa* does not acquire its specific name because of its inherent nature nor because it is well-endowed with [other] qualities;
due to the smallness of its potency (*vīrya*), it remains unperceived.
When [the disease] is obstructed by phlegm (kapha), it persists for many years.
Afflicted by that, the patient has discolored stool, suffers from vitiated blood disorders, and is tormented by thirst and loss of appetite.

Fainting, vomiting, stammering speech, and delusion occur, and the patient exhibits the symptoms of *dūṣyodara*. When located in the *āmāśaya*, there is disease of *kapha* and *vāta*; when located in the *pittāśaya*, there is disease of *vāta* and *pitta*.
A man whose bones, body, and hair have perished would be like a bird with its wings clipped;
or else, he remains within the fluids and other elements, experiencing various states.
It produces disorders arising from the bodily elements (dhātu) due to prior exposure to wind, indigestion, cold, clouds, daytime sleep,
and unwholesome food.

Because it vitiates the bodily constituents (dhātus), it is known as *dūṣīviṣa* (corrosive poison). When the stationary (*sthāvara*) poison has been ingested, the following symptoms arise during the first stage (*vega*).
In the first stage, there is blackishness of the tongue, stiffness, fainting, terror,
exhaustion, and vomiting; in the second stage, there is trembling, perspiration, and pain in the throat.
Poison that has reached the stomach causes pain in the heart;
in the third stage, however, there is dryness of the palate and intense colic in the stomach.
When it has reached the small intestine (pakvāśaya), piercing pain, hiccups, coughing, and rumbling in the intestines arise, and his eyes become weak, greenish, and sunken.
In the fourth stage, there arises excessive heaviness of the head;
in the fifth, there is salivation of phlegm, discoloration, and a breaking sensation in the joints.
There is an aggravation of all the doṣas and pain in the colon (pakvādhāna); in the sixth stage, there is loss of consciousness and one suffers from very severe diarrhea.
There will be a breaking pain in the shoulders, back, and waist, and death occurs on the seventh day;
in this case, when the first poison-impulse has been vomited up, one should be sprinkled with cold water.
One should quickly administer an anti-poisonous medicine mixed with ghee and honey;
on the second day, one should administer it again after the patient has vomited or been purged as previously described.
In the third stage, the drinking of medicine, as well as nasal drops (nasya) and collyrium (añjana), are beneficial;
in the fourth stage, one should administer medicine mixed with unctuous substances (sneha) along with food.
In the fifth [stage], a decoction of madhuka mixed with honey is beneficial;
in the sixth, the treatment is like that for diarrhea; but in the seventh, an avapīḍa [nasal drop] is used.
Having made a crow’s-foot mark on the head, one should apply blood or flesh;
[the drugs] are kośātakī, agnika, pāṭhā, sūryavalī, amṛtā, and abhayā.
Śelu, śirīṣa, kiṇihī, the two types of haridrā, the two known as kṣudrā, the two types of punarnavā, trikaṭu, the two types of bṛhatī, sārivā, and the two types of balā—
having prepared a gruel from these in a decoction, one should serve it cold with ghee and honey.
One should administer a remedy that destroys all poisons during the intervals between the paroxysms for one who has completed the ritual;
likewise, with madhūka, madhuka, padmakesara, and candana.
Hereafter, we shall describe the proven medicinal formulations (agadas) composed by the ancient seers.
Sandalwood, saffron, costus, orpiment, lac, and priyaṅgu— these are supremely beneficial against all poisons in every condition.
Mustā, sthauṇeya, śaileya, rocanā, madana, plava,
śrīveṣṭakī, vaḍa, iṅgudā, viśālā, ālamanas, and śilā.
Surasā, prasava, spṛkkā, the two types of rajanī,
vālaka, hiṅgu, siddhārthaka, padmacāriṇī, and padmakesara.
The flower of the *jāti* plant, as well as the sprouts and flowers of the *arka* and *śirīṣa*,
*dvirodhra*, *bṛhatī*, *kauntī*, *madhuka*, and *gandhanākulī*.
Mudgaparṇī, kaṇā, śyāmā, dhyāmaka, nalada, nata,
sinduvāraka, śamyāka, devadāru, and mayūraka.

This supreme medicine, Sañjīvana, should be prepared with those [herbs] ground together and collected under the Puṣya asterism; it was ordained by the Self-Existent One (Brahmā) before the appearance of the nectar of immortality.
Through drinking, nasal medication, collyrium, snuffing, fumigation, ointment, and wearing [the drug],
Jīvana brings victory at the king's gate for those who have been rendered unconscious by poison.

Situated in the house, it bestows fortune, grain, wealth, long life, prosperity, security, nourishment, and happiness; it destroys great misfortune, spells, fever, poison, and the influence of malevolent planets.
[It wards off] sorcery, malevolent spells, *kākhorda*, fierce beasts, crawling creatures, and reptiles; [it protects against] the afflictions of dreams, bad dreams, water, fire, enemies, and thieves.
Sandalwood, vālaka, musta, dhyāmaka, kaṭukā, and nata destroy untimely death, epidemics, lightning,
and strife.
Pomegranate, saffron, ginger, wood-apple, the fruit of *vatsaka*,
seeds of *karañja*, black pepper, blue lotus, and the petals of the white lotus.
Nala root, apāmārga, karavīraka,
añjana, lac, mālatī, ahicchatra, nāgapuṣpa, and amlavetasa.
Viśālā, rocanā, śyāmā, śaṅkhapuṣpī, priyaṅgukā,
ajājī, sārivā, kuṣṭha, ajamoda, and kuraṇḍaka.
Vayasthā, sinduvāra, elā, kāyasthā, cāraṭī, vacā,
karkaṭī, pūtanā, keśī, śvetā, and girikarṇikā.
Golomī, siṃhalomī, varṣābhū, and gajapippalī constitute this antidote known as Yāpana, which is similar in its qualities to the preceding one.
Śrīveṣṭaka, the two types of haridrā, kovidāra, and manaḥśilā [are used for the following].
Pippalī, pāṭalī, padmā, śvetā, and girikarṇikā;
mañjiṣṭhā, bṛhatī, vakra, yaṣṭī, marica, and keśara.
One should saturate *phalinī* and *kiṇihī* with the bile of cows;
this "sunrise" destroys poison, just as the rising sun destroys darkness.
Nimba leaves, house-soot, treacle, and the fruit of bṛhatī,
combined with cow’s bile, constitute a supreme medicine that restores life to the dead.
Cow’s bile, kuṣṭha, surasa, madhuka, the two types of niśā,
as well as viśālā, rajanī, kuṣṭha, dog’s bile, vyoṣa, and tumburu.
Vacā with the five parts of śirīṣa is a medicine that restores life to the dead;
the five parts of śirīṣa together with dog’s bile are an excellent medicine.
Priyaṅgu, tagara, lac, mañjiṣṭhā, madhuka, honey,
and haridrā— this is the excellent medicine favored by Kauṭilya.
It restores consciousness to those who are unconscious due to terrible poisons or fatal blows,
and it brings back the senses to those who have died by hanging or by drowning in a flood of water.
A medicinal preparation (agada) made from śirīṣa, phalaka, kāka, surasā, and agrapuṇarnavā,
combined with kakṣyā and vāyasī, possesses qualities as previously described.
One should grind the roots of *kaṭukālābu* with the bile of cows; this medicinal preparation (*agada*), known as *brāhma*, is to be worn and is honored for all ritual actions.
House-soot, trivṛt, cow-bile, trikaṭu,
and vacā— this is the Prājāpatya antidote, which destroys all demons and poisons.
A gem made from equal parts of white lotus and the flowers of *jīvantī*,
ground with gold and worn as an ornament, is held by Cāṇakya to be a destroyer of poison.
Māṃsī, tvak, patra, surasa, manaḥśilā, śīta, kuṅkuma,
niśā, vyāghranakha, and śuṇṭhī— this is the ten-ingredient (daśāṅga) formulation that destroys poison.
It removes the poison of eruptions, swellings, pustules, and the like, as well as that from bites and wounds.
[This is prepared] with the bark of the *udumbara*, the seeds of the *jambū*, *madhuka*, blue lotus, and red ochre.

Sandalwood, uśīra, nalada, nāgakeśara, and padmaka specifically destroy poison, eruptive boils, erysipelas, fever, and burning sensations. [Likewise, one may use] the bark of śirīṣa, udumbara, plakṣa, nyagrodha, and aśvattha.
Taken with ghee, it cures burning sensations, thirst, secretions, poisons, erysipelas, and disorders of pitta.
Gajapippalī, kāsīsa, alkali, yaṣṭīmadhu, and mayūraka— AS.Utt.40.86 saghṛto dāhatṛṣṇāsraviṣavīsarpapittahā AS.Utt.40.87 gajapippalikāsīsakṣārayaṣṭīmayūrakam
Raktā, nata, vacā, dantī, śiva, and śivakṛt constitute the *agada* (medicine) called Śiva.
Surālā, pāvakī, somā, bhogavatī, amṛtā, and nata [constitute the medicine] called Nata.
Āḍhakī, kiṇihī, somarājī, and the fourfold medicinal preparation of Śaunaka;
śleṣmātaka, arka flowers, taṇḍulīya, and mayūraka.
Surasā, mañjarī, and kākamācī are the best remedies when drunk for poison.
Curd, ghee, honey, and salt, when drunk together, remove root-poison.
One should mix turmeric, rock salt, honey, and ghee,
and administer it to those suffering from the terrible root-poisons, especially those who have been pierced by poisoned arrows.
Haridrā is recommended both internally and externally for a patient suffering from the toxic effects of poison. [It is prepared] with niśā, aśvamāra, surasa, karañja, vyoṣa, and dāru.
Collyrium made from [these] ground with goat's urine overcomes obstruction of the eyes;
it is used as nasal drops for diseases of the ears, eyes, nose, throat, and tongue.
[The oil] prepared with bījapūra, āryā, bṛhatī-phala, and jyotiṣmatī; [the powder] consisting of śvetā, vacā, hiṅgu, amṛtā, sugandhā, kuṣṭha, and saindhava.
Śirīṣa flowers, the two types of niśā (haridrā and dāruharidrā), vyoṣa, ṭuṇṭuka, and sarṣapa;
the pulp of kapittha, garlic, karañja, and bamboo scrapings.
Having ground [the substance] with cow's urine and then processed it with its own bile for seven days alternately, one destroys [the disease] by applying it as a collyrium.
Poison located in the head [causes] headache, fever, chronic poisoning, and cholera; it also causes epilepsy, possession by spirits, insanity, anemia, urinary disorders, and alcoholism.
[It cures] diseases of the eyes, dryness of the eyes, diseases of the head, tumors of the palate and throat, cataracts, darkness of vision, films over the eyes, itching, debility, and consumption.
By its application as a plaster, one may conquer the poisons of those who have been smeared, wounded, licked, bitten, or poisoned by arrows;
it also overcomes vitiligo, difficult diseases, leprosy, malignant sinus tracts, and large ulcers.
By applying an ointment to the anus, it cures anal fissures; applied to the forehead, it treats malignant chronic rhinitis.
By applying it to the vagina, it facilitates the downward movement of a dead fetus in women.
This [formula] uproots poison, just as a scent-elephant uproots a forest.
Viḍaṅga, pāṭhā, triphalā, ajamodā, hiṅgu, agnivakra, and the group of salts.
The antidote named Ajita, combined with the three pungents (vyoṣa), is the conqueror of all poisons, both stationary and mobile. [It consists of] realgar,
yellow orpiment, caṇḍā, bark, cardamom, and black mustard.
This medicinal preparation, ground with *spṛkkā*, vermilion, saffron, and *kāntā*,
is a destroyer of poisons; it is called "the Rising Sun" (*bālasūrya*), and it bestows prosperity, protection, victory, and success.
Ajagandhā with cow's urine, house-soot, and suguggulu—
this is the Māheśvara formulation; it is never obstructed by anything.
One pierced by a poisoned [arrow] faints again and again;
he assumes a pale complexion and quickly falls into despondency.
His body feels as if covered with insects and experiences a pricking sensation;
the joints of the hips, back, head, and shoulders become painful.
It discharges black, foul, and bloody secretions, and is accompanied by thirst, fainting, fever, and burning sensations;
it causes turbidity of vision, vomiting, dyspnea, and cough in an instant.
The flesh swells and suppurates immediately upon being reached; it becomes black,
constantly moist, putrid, and exudes a slimy discharge.
One should quickly apply a covering over the heart of a patient whose vital spots (marmans) have not been pierced;
having extracted the foreign body (śalya), one should cauterize the wound with heated iron.
Alternatively, one should rub [the area] with the alkali of *muṣkaka*, white *soma* bark, *tāmravallī*, *śirīṣa*, and *gṛdhranakhī*.
One should apply a plaster made from the roots of śukanāsā, prativiṣā, and vyāghrī; furthermore, one should administer the appropriate treatment for that person who has been bitten by a snake.
In the case of a wound containing putrid flesh, the treatment is like that for *pitta*-visarpa.
Women, urged by their enemies, may [administer it] to their husbands or to the king for the sake of securing good fortune.
Those standing nearby offer food mixed with hot substances,
as well as the ashes of various medicinal plants, animal parts, and impurities.
The administration of poisons of low potency is known as *gara*.
By this, one becomes pale, emaciated, and weak in digestion, afflicted by cough, dyspnea, and fever.

When the *vāyu* moves in a contrary direction, the patient becomes intent on dreams and anxieties; he suffers from enlargement of the abdomen, liver, and spleen, and is dejected in speech, weak, and lethargic.
One who suffers from swelling, constant distension, dryness of the hands and feet,
and wasting, sees in dreams jackals, cats, mongooses, serpents, and monkeys.
Generally, one perceives trees and reservoirs as dry; a fair-skinned person considers themselves dark, and a dark-skinned person considers themselves fair.
One whose senses are impaired would see [beings] with distorted ears, noses, and eyes;
afflicted by these and many other terrible, dreadful portents.
One afflicted by *gara* (poisoning) meets with destruction immediately if left untreated. One afflicted by *gara* who has vomited should eat that which is wholesome as food and drink.
One with a pure heart should practice this while recollecting the rules of the Sūtrasthāna:
a powder of *tāpya* (copper pyrite) and gold, combined with sugar and honey. (AS.Utt.40.119)
This linctus pacifies all severe poisons produced by yoga:
mūrvā, amṛtā, nata, kaṇā, paṭolī, cavya, and citraka.
One whose digestive fire has been impaired by poison should drink vacā, musta, and viḍaṅga with buttermilk,
warm water, or curd-cream; or one should drink the cooled decoction of pigeon meat, śaṭhī, and puṣkaramūla with sour juice.
Vāyasī, fried in ghee and taken with a decoction of triphalā, removes chronic thirst, disease, cough, dyspnea, hiccups, and fever. (AS.Utt.40.121–122)
A decoction of *bhārṅgī* and *nāgara*, cooled and mixed with honey;
and *hareṇu*, *candana*, *śyāmā*, and *nalada*, finely ground together.
An ointment should be applied to one whose skin has been afflicted by poison:
[an ointment made] with mañjiṣṭhā, kiṇihī, nimba, rajanī, aśvattha, and candana.
For those who are emaciated and whose vital energy has been depleted by poison,
the habitual consumption of milk and ghee is declared to be the supreme wholesome regimen.
One should cook ghee with a decoction of vṛṣa, nimba, and paṭolī. AS.Utt.40.126
One should cook haridrā, nākulī, and jātī, having ground them separately; this is the best [remedy] for the womb, providing fearlessness and destroying the embryo-poison (gara).
This "Triple Ghee" is the supreme bestower of health for those afflicted by poison.
[One should prepare it] with the root of *taṇḍulīyaka* and house-soot combined together.
Ghee prepared with milk conquers all diseases caused by poisons. [One should also use] nāgadantī, trivṛt, dantī, dravantī, and the latex of snuhī, each in the measure of one pala.
Buffalo ghee prepared with one āḍhaka of cow urine is beneficial for the pacification of those afflicted by the venom of snakes and insects, as well as those suffering from artificial poisons (gara).
[The following herbs are used: madhuka, tagara, kuṣṭha, bhadradāru, and hareṇu.
Mañjiṣṭhā, elā, ilavālu, nāgapuṣpa, utpala, plava, viḍaṅga,
candana, patra, priyaṅgu, dhyāmaka, and balā.
The two types of *aṃśumatī*, the two types of *haridrā*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, and the two types of *sārivā*—
clarified butter prepared with the pastes of these is renowned by the name Ajeya.
When administered quickly, this destroys all poisons.
[One should take] seeds of *śvetā*, *kapotā*, *pratyakpuṣpī*, and *śirīṣa*.
Ghee prepared with these [herbs] ground with cow’s urine is a supreme destroyer of poison;
renowned by the name Amṛta, it can even restore the dead to life.
Śirīṣa bark, the three pungents (trikaṭuka), vidārī, sandalwood, utpala,
the two types of bala, sārivā, āsphota, and the sprouts of bṛhatī and nimba.
Bandhujīva, āḍhakī, mūrvā, vāsā,
surasa, vatsaka, pāṭhā, aṅkola, aśvagandhā, the root of arka, yaṣṭyāhva, and padmaka.
Viśālā, bṛhatī, lākṣā, kovidāra, śatāvarī,
kaṭabhī, dantī, apāmārga, pṛśniparṇī, and rasāñjana.
