The two white [substances], bāṇa, aśvakharaka, kuṣṭha, dāru, priyaṅgukā,
the heartwood [of śiṃśapā], madhūka, triphalā, the fruit of karañja, and vacā.

Having ground two *rajanya* plants and one part of *lodhra*, one *āḍhaka* of ghee should be prepared with an equal amount of water and three *āḍhakas* each of goat’s urine and cow’s urine; this destroys poison.
Epilepsy, consumption, insanity, possession by spirits or planets,
abdominal diseases, jaundice, worms, splenic disorders, abdominal tumors, stiffness of the thighs, and hemorrhoids.
Through drinking, massage, and nasal drops, it cures lockjaw, seizures, and other such ailments; it restores life to men who have died from poison or hanging.
When green vitriol (haritāla) has been ingested, there is burning pain in the heart, a sensation of constriction in the chest,
flatulence, vomiting of sour matter, and the passage of turmeric-yellow feces.
Likewise, one should apply the symptoms and the remedies described for the Maṇḍali snake after making a distinction, and having purified the patient through emesis and purgation.

One should have the patient lick a paste of *aṅkola*, *jālinī*, seeds of *śukanāsā*, *priyaṅgukā*, *lodhra*, *dhyāmaka*, *tālīsa*, *natā*, *yaṣṭyāhva*, *guggulu*, *hībera*, and *bhadrakāṣṭha*, mixed with honey and ghee. (AS.Utt.40.143)

One should administer that [substance], combined with the bile of a mongoose and a cow, as a nasal drop (nasya) and as a collyrium (añjana). By the application of *dhurdhūraka*, one sees everything as yellow.
One afflicted by trembling, salivation, intoxication, vomiting, loss of memory,
and vertigo should be made to vomit with sweet substances, or should be given sugar-water to drink.
Gadas caused by *koradūṣa*, *madanaka*, and especially *dhurdhūra* result in insanity and the destruction of cattle; in those cases as well, emesis is beneficial.
One should frequently eat *kūṣmāṇḍaka* with jaggery there; likewise,
various types of *kodrava* prepared with diverse combinations are causes of intoxication.

Having classified them according to the specific dosha, one should treat them with non-contradictory remedies. One afflicted by *dūṣīviṣa* should be well-sudated and purified through both upper and lower routes.
One should have the patient lick a medicine that is an enemy to *dūṣīviṣa* poison, saturated with honey;
[the ingredients are] long pepper (*pippalī*), *odhyāmaka*, spikenard (*māṃsī*), *lodhra*, cardamom (*elā*), and *suvarcikā*.
Kuṭannaṭa, nata, kuṣṭha, yaṣṭī, candana, and gairika—this group is known by the name Dūṣīviṣāri; it is not prohibited for use elsewhere either.
Harītakī with salt, māgadhī, and black pepper [are also used].

This purgative prescribed by Kāśyapa for those afflicted by *dūṣī-viṣa* should be employed by the physician in cases of poisoning when a purgative is indicated, or one containing *vyoṣa* (the three pungents) and other such ingredients.
One should boil the alkaline water that has been squeezed from the fresh leaves of the *palāśa* tree.
Into that decoction, one should add as a post-throw (pratīvāpa) the finely powdered vyoṣa,
śirīṣa flowers, madhuka, sārivā, and misi.
Kuṣṭha, vella, the two types of niśā, lākṣā, white surasa,
mañjarī, rock salt, red earth, māṃsī, reṇukā, hiṅgu, and bālhika.
That which has been produced should be smeared with a ladle and placed within a cow’s horn;
it cures consumption, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, hemorrhoids, urinary disorders, weak digestion, and fever.
Skin diseases, cough, epilepsy, possession by spirits, insanity, fistula-in-ano, anemia, hoarseness of voice, splenic disorders, edema, and worms.
By eating only a kola-sized portion from this, one shall conquer all poisons;
for poison, though composed of fiery energy, is overcome by mantras consisting of truth, sacred knowledge, and austerity.
It cannot be warded off so quickly by medicines as it is by [the aforementioned means]; moreover,
not all human beings possess the abundance of medicines.

When the actual presence of a disease is unknown, the [proper] fitness for treatment is extremely difficult to find; moreover, poison that has been conquered by medicinal herbs alone may break out again.
Therefore, a physician should strive for the acquisition of perfected mantras;
yet even those [mantras] fail for one who is deficient in his vows or impaired in his voice and complexion.
Since they do not achieve success, therefore a course of treatment with medicines should be applied when there is a combination of poison, constitution, season, food, humors, and affected tissues.
This is declared to be a perilous situation involving poison, where only one out of a hundred survives;
[it is further afflicted] by hunger, thirst, heat, weakness, anger, grief, fear, and exhaustion.
Indigestion, loose stools, and liquidity [of the stool] arise from the aggravation of pitta and vāta,
as well as from smelling the flowers and fruits of the sesame plant, exposure to ground mist, and the thundering of clouds.
Poison increases through the sounds of elephants, mice, and musical instruments, as well as through the dangers of poisonous substances;
it is further increased by the fragrance of blue lotuses carried by the east wind and by intoxicants.
During the rainy season, because its origin is from water, it becomes moistened like molasses.

At the end of the rainy season, when the clouds have vanished, that poison spreads; it is destroyed by the star Agastya, and therefore, at the departure of the clouds, the poison becomes weak in potency.

Having carefully examined the constitution, suitability, season, location, the force of the urges, and the relative strength [of the patient], one should perform the medical procedure with an intelligent mind immediately thereafter.
One should pacify phlegmatic poison (ślaiṣmikaviṣa) with emetics that are hot, dry, and sharp; with external applications (pralepana);
and with foods that are astringent, pungent, and bitter.
A Pitta-type [eye disease] should be treated with purgatives, and with very cold affusions and plasters,
as well as with foods combined with ghee that are astringent, bitter, and sweet.
One should conquer disorders of the wind (vāta) with foods and ointments that are sweet, unctuous, sour,
and salty, combined with ghee, as well as with the consumption of meat.
Clarified butter (ghṛta) is not recommended as a laxative, nor as an external paste, nor as a medicinal food,
in any case or at any stage of all types of poisoning; indeed, there is nothing equal to clarified butter [for countering poison].
If there is some specific remedy for a condition where the wind (vāyu) is particularly strong,
one should cause the blood to flow out when it has entered the blood; the course of treatment is the same as that for pitta.
Furthermore, when *dūṣīviṣa* is located there, one should perform the five purificatory procedures (pañcakarma),
using sharp gargles, mouthfuls, ingestions, insufflations, and collyriums.

One should pacify that which has reached the head by means of the transference of poison; for when the wind is obstructed by the channels of phlegm corrupted by poison, it becomes like one who is dead.
For one who is devoid of the signs of incurability,
one should apply a paste derived from *carmaka* after making a "crow's foot" incision on the head.
And for its incision, *kaṭabhī*, *jālinī*, and pungent substances are beneficial; furthermore,
whichever humor (*doṣa*) the poison resides in within the body cavity, that [should be treated].

The wise physician should administer the alkaline antidote (kṣārāgada) without causing harm to the site and its contents; when [the poison] is located in the seat of phlegm (kapha), one should employ sudation and venesection.

In cases of pitta, one should administer honey, milk, sour liquids, ghee, drinking, affusion, and immersion; for the seat of vāta, fomentation with curd and the drinking of nata and kuṣṭha with milk containing an anti-venom and the fruit of madana [are indicated]. AS.Utt.40.175.
One should administer non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) when the poison has reached the seat of Vata. One should cook oil with four times the amount of milk in a decoction of yaṣṭīmadhu.
Triphalā, sarpavetālī, śatapuṣpā, indurājī,
and anantā— these, when used for drinking, nasal drops, massage, and enemas, [cure the aforementioned conditions].
Poison residing in the food destroys the wind (vāta) when it is consumed from the stomach;
one should cook it with *valayā*, *somarājī*, or *pāṭalā*.
Oil for an oil enema (anuvāsana) that is like the scum of clarified butter is supreme;
having considered it beneficial even for complications from poison, one should employ it according to the specific disease.
That which resides in the phlegm (kapha) is curable without effort; that which is situated in the seat of bile (pitta) is curable with effort.
The fortieth chapter: On poison located in the seat of Vāta, which is very difficult to pacify or even incurable.
Now begins the forty-first chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "The Knowledge of Snake Venom.
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
Serpents are recorded as being of two kinds, distinguished by their celestial and terrestrial natures:
Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Ananta, Sagara, and Sāgarālaya.
Likewise, Nanda, Upananda, and the others, possessing a radiance equal to a blazing fire,
roar, rain down, flash, and illuminate as divine beings.

They sustain the entire world, and when enraged, they could reduce it to ashes with their very glance and breath; salutations to them, for there is no medical treatment for those who have bowed down to them.

The terrestrial snakes are, in brief, divided into three types— the hooded (darvīkara), the circular-spotted (maṇḍalin), and the striped (rājīmant)— and these are further subdivided into many varieties.
They are not described in detail according to their specific origins because they are of no practical use;
[the tastes] are specifically dry, pungent, sour, hot, sweet, and cold.
The venom of hooded snakes (*darvīkara*) and other species sequentially provokes *vāta* and the other [doshas],
during youth, middle age, and old age, and in conditions of rain, cold, and heat.
These Vyantara deities become fierce with poison during the transitions between seasons;
they bear the emblems of the wheel, the plow, the parasol, the svastika, and the goad.
The *phaṇinaḥ* are known as snakes of swift movement, while the *darvīkarāḥ* are those with hoods; the *maṇḍalinaḥ* are to be known as those with coils, variegated with various circular spots.
Those that are tall-bodied have slow movement; those with stripes are marked with streaks that are glossy and variegated, appearing obliquely as well as vertically.
The *godhera*, the offspring of the *godhā* (iguana), is equal to the *darvīkara* snakes in its venom.
The Vyantara [spirits] are four-footed; they are known from the mixture of those very [classes].
For they possess mixed characteristics and provoke the derangement of the humors (sannipāta). The celestial snake is the *kojagara*, and the *patāka* is the one that lies in trees.
Śakalī, Puṣpaka, Kṣīrī, Lāsinī, Sārasāhika, Varṣāhika, Jyotiratha, Śukavaktra, and Balāhaka.
The elephant-eater, the one who carries the raft, and the sixteen non-venomous horses; generally, the female serpent remains in heat for the month of Jyeṣṭha.

In the month of Āṣāḍha, due to its conjunction with the serpent [constellation], she gives birth to two hundred and twenty staffs; in the month of Kārttika, she gives birth to two hundred and twenty more, and there he is born.
When an egg the color of a karketana gem has burst open, a male serpent emerges; when it is variegated with long red stripes, it is a female or a hermaphrodite.
On the seventh day, four fangs resembling *śirīṣa* flowers appear on the snake; on the fourteenth day, venom is present in them.
The lower left fang is black, while the one above it is yellow; the lower right fang, however, is white.
Red, or with one, two, three, or four dark-brown spots,
these [pustules] are respectively the size of a mung bean; this is indeed the mark of serpents.

One should know that there is no variation in poison [other than that of the snake]; likewise, there are other [creatures] with fangs. Of the serpent, there are forty-four types that are devoid of venom.
The lifespan is one hundred and twenty years for those with a five-hundred-year life span;
these [leeches] are called *gonasā*, originating from the noses of cows scorched by the heat.
In that case, one with upward-looking eyes, a large body, long tongue, head, and voice,
possessing manifest enjoyments and being wise, would be a man; by the opposite of these traits, she would be a woman.
Long, fickle, impotent, delicate, and dull in appearance;
with slow speed, voice, and anger; white-hued, and with a head bent sideways.
They are powerful during the day, at night, and at twilight respectively;
however,
the female serpent (pannagī) is always harmful at all times.
The Brāhmaṇas are prone to anger, with hair that is dark-brown or tawny, and complexions that are white or reddish;
they have red faces and tawny eyes, and they roam through sacred regions.
In their enjoyment, they are distinguished by the marks and insignia of the twice-born, such as the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*),
and possess the fragrance of *bilva* flowers, camphor, *uśīra*, lotus, and *guggulu*.
Kṣatriyas are proud, wise, red-eyed, and extremely irascible;
their luster is like that of ripe jambu, dates, grapes, or split collyrium.
Marked with the signs of the half-moon, śrīvatsa, conch, discus, and plow,
and possessing the fragrance of jasmine, campaka, punnāga, patra, and joṅgaka flowers, they are destined for enjoyment.
The Vaiśyas have the luster of pigeons, the brilliance of diamonds and cowries,
their bodies variegated with circles of spots, and they are smoky, pale-red, or crimson.
Equal parts of the scents of castor oil, kuṣṭha, vikaṅkata,
milk, and ghee; Śūdras of the same caste [should be used] with wheat, buffalo, elephant, and mud.
Coated with streaks of droplets, rough, and smelling of wine and blood,
they roam during the forenoon, midday, and afternoon; these are the [omens] pertaining to the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes.
When the sun has set, the Śūdras bite; the Brāhmaṇas stand in front, the Kṣatriyas on the right side, and the Vaiśyas on the left.
But the Śūdras [bite] from behind, and the Vipras [drive away] even the three [poisons] beginning with that which is caused by wind.
The three [castes] beginning with the Kṣatriya gradually provoke the three doṣas;
their respective scents should be known by the odor of the bite and the odor of their bodies.
The wind, the rat, the frog, and the omnivore— these are [the sources of the humors] in their respective order.
[The bite occurs] for the sake of food, out of fear, from the touch of a foot, from extreme poison, from anger,
due to wicked conduct, from enmity, or by the instigation of gods, sages, or Yama.
Snakes bite them; it is stated that their venom increases progressively. Having understood the cause for one who has been possessed, one should treat him accordingly.
Due to his evil nature, the *vyantara* demon stands blocking the path;
there,
on the body, only the moisture of saliva is visible.
One should not, however, designate a bite made by the fangs as one struck by the snout. A single or double fang-mark that is bloodless is called *vyālīḍha*.

If two tooth-marks with blood are present, it is *vyālupta*; if three such marks are present, it is *daṣṭaka*, characterized by the cutting of flesh and the continuous flow of blood. (AS.Utt.41.37–38)
There are four types of fang-marks; likewise, there is that which is bitten and pressed. Among these, the first two are rendered venomless, while one should declare the last to be incurable.
Poison does not corrupt the body's blood without first reaching it.
Even a minute amount of blood, once reached, increases like a drop of oil;
in one who is timid, the wind (vāyu) becomes provoked by fear upon contact with the body of a snake.
Sometimes it causes swelling when struck by the body of a snake; or when someone pierced in a dark, difficult place suspects they have been bitten by a snake.
Agitation from poison, fever, vomiting, fainting, or even a burning sensation,
as well as exhaustion, delusion, or diarrhea— this is called "suspicion-poison" (śaṅkā-viṣa).
Furthermore, every bite by a venomous [insect] is accompanied by swelling and pain.
When it is knotted, it pricks slightly; when it is itchy, it burns intensely.
A non-venomous [swelling] is the opposite of this.
Among those, the bite of hooded snakes (phaṇāvat) is raised like the back of a tortoise, rough, and marked with the impressions of fine fangs.
The morbid changes consist of a dark discoloration of the face, nails, urine, eyes,
feces, and skin; cold fever, pain in the joints, loss of sleep, and yawning.
Stiffness of the neck, distension of the vessels, stiffness of the back, waist, and bones, impairment of speech,
heaviness of the head, loss of appetite, cough, dyspnea, and lockjaw [are the symptoms].
Twisting pain in the abdomen, dryness and obstruction of the bowels due to the retention of waste products,
indistinct speech, lack of movement, and unconsciousness like that of a dead person; AS.Utt.41.47.
The emergence of froth and mucus, hiccups,
a rattling sound in the throat, and frequent dry belching— these and other diseases are born of Vāta.
The bite of a maṇḍalī snake is hot and causes desiccation; it is yellowish-red, broad,
and is characterized by spreading inflammation, burning, moisture, and sloughing.
The symptoms [of pitta] are discoloration of the face, teeth, and so forth; thirst, fatigue, and giddiness;
burning sensation, fainting, fever, a bitter taste in the mouth, and a yellowish vision.
The discharge of blood from the upper and lower openings, a desire for cold things, a sensation of fumes, intoxication,
rapid spreading throughout all the limbs, and various diseases— these are born of pitta.
The bite of the *rājīmat* [snakes] produces a glossy, firm, and slimy swelling;
it is accompanied by thick blood, feels cold, and is pale in color. Its complications include headache.
Loss of appetite, vomiting, lassitude, nausea, sweetness in the mouth,
a gurgling sound in the throat, indigestion, itching in the eyes, and fever accompanied by cold sensations [are the symptoms].
Labored breathing, sleepiness, coughing, whitening of the nails and teeth,
stiffness, heaviness of the limbs, and discharge from the nose, eyes, and mouth [are the symptoms].
Horripilation, darkness, dyspnea, and other diseases arising from phlegm occur;
when bitten by an intermediate creature, there is a mixture of symptoms, and the victim looks upward.
Raising the upper body, he should place his right foot forward;
being resolute and with diminished vigor during the night, but the opposite when with a woman.
One afflicted by diarrhea with a weak voice trembles and is terrified; one suffering from fever has a sidelong gaze, lacks fortitude, and is excessively fond of sexual intercourse.
In the elderly, there is much speaking and the pains are slow;
in the young, they are sharp and quick; and in children, they occur in the right eye.
If a patient, a maiden, or a pregnant woman has a black tongue and eyes,
yawns, suffers from anger and an upturned tongue, and has swollen lips and a pale face, [he or she will die].
One bitten by a *sūta* suffers from an enlarged abdomen and headache;
afflicted by painful urination and sharp pains as if being pierced by needles, he passes blood.
Blood, flesh, and so forth have been previously mentioned as the seven locations for these bites.
Furthermore,
in one bitten by a *darvīkṛta* [snake], the blood becomes vitiated and turns dark-brown.
By that [fever], a dark discoloration appears on the face and other parts, and it feels as if insects are crawling over them;
in the second stage there are knots [in the limbs], and in the third stage there is heaviness of the head.
In the fourth [stage], there is obstruction of vision, swelling of the bite,
spitting, and vomiting; in the fifth, there is loosening of the joints, drowsiness, and splitting pain in the limbs.
In the sixth [week], however, there is burning, hiccups, pain in the heart, and heaviness of the limbs; upon reaching the semen in the seventh [week], fainting, indigestion, and diarrhea occur.
There is a breaking pain in the shoulders, back, and waist, and all physical movements cease;
furthermore, in one bitten by a *maṇḍalin* snake, the blood becomes foul and turns yellow.
By that [poison], yellowness of the limbs and a burning sensation occur in the second stage;
in the third stage, swelling of the bite site, perspiration, and thirst arise.
On the fourth day there is fever and burning; on the fifth day, it pervades all the limbs. In one bitten by striped snakes (*rājila*), the blood becomes vitiated and turns pale.

By that [poison], paleness of the limbs occurs in the second stage, and heaviness in the third; in the third stage, there is also the sloughing of the bite site and discharge from the nose, eyes, and mouth.
In the fourth stage, there is heaviness of the head and stiffness of the neck; in the fifth, obstruction of speech and cold fever. For the remaining two stages, one should speak as before.
One should administer treatment during the five stages of the poison's course, but not beyond that.
Those submerged in water, those exhausted by sexual exertion, those who are terrified, and those overcome by mongooses—
[these should not be treated].
Those afflicted by cold, wind, heat, disease, hunger, thirst, and fatigue, who have arrived quickly from other lands and are freed from the cloak of poison; AS.Utt.41.71.
Those who roam the forest like thorns on a medicinal herb, and those considered to have mild poison, frequent cremation grounds, sacred trees, anthills, sacrificial sites, and temples.
At a crossroads, in a body of water, in ruined gardens,
in a hollow; at a milky tree, a neem tree, a waterfall, or in a mountain cave.
Those who bear matted hair marked with the wheel, vajra, club, spear, and trident,
and whose mouths and eyes are red, are like venomous serpents.
For these [diseases], there is no fixed rule regarding time, nor is there a sequential order in their onset;
furthermore, they cannot be forcibly turned back by the power of mantras or tantric rituals.
One who is devoted to offerings, salutations, recitation, and rites of pacification may live even when bitten by them, though he may become deformed or maimed.
In cremation grounds, funeral pyres, shrines, and the like, during the fifth lunar day, the junctions of the fortnights,
on the eighth and ninth days, at the twilights, and at midnight; and on those days.
One should avoid [administering treatment] when bitten during the muhūrtas known as Yāmya, Āgneya, Māgha, Śleṣā, Viśākhā, Pūrva, Nairṛta,
and Nairṛtākhya, as well as when the bite occurs on the vital points (marmans).
Immediately upon being bitten, one whose face and eyes turn white, whose hair falls out,
whose tongue becomes stiff, who faints repeatedly, and whose breath becomes cold, does not survive.
Hiccup, dyspnea, vomiting, and cough arise simultaneously in a person as soon as he is bitten; such a person suffering from pain in the heart does not survive.
Trembling, intense pain, a broken neck, redness of the eyes,
fainting, throat obstruction, and vomiting— these are the servants of the King of the Dead.
The bite resembles a jujube fruit and is elevated like the back of a tortoise;
blood flows from all the orifices of the body, but not from the site of the bite itself.
One should abandon that patient who experiences no horripilation from cold applications on the hair, who has swelling that is reddish-black,
and whose penis is erect and whose mouth is distorted.
He vomits froth, is unconscious, and has darkened feet, hands, and face;
there is drooping of the nose, breaking pain in the limbs, diarrhea, and looseness of the joints.
These symptoms appear when the end of life has arrived for one who has drunk poison, been bitten by a venomous creature, or struck by a poisoned weapon.
There is no consciousness from sharp nasal medications, nor the flow of blood from a wound;
there is no mark from being struck by a staff for one who has departed to the presence of Yama.
Otherwise, a physician, acting with haste as if his own house were on fire,
must preserve the life-breaths residing in the throat and quickly pacify the poison.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter.
Now begins the forty-second chapter.
Hereafter, we shall expound the chapter named "The Prevention of Snake Venom."
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:
"Having remained for one hundred *mātrās* at the site of the bite of the bitten creature, the poison [spreads]."
It invades the body, vitiating the constituent elements (dhātus) such as blood and the rest;
in the meantime, one should perform the excision and other procedures upon the bite.
One should act quickly so that the poisonous creeper does not take root in the body. As soon as bitten, one should immediately bite that very wind-eater (the snake).
Having quickly bitten a clod of earth or a piece of soil with his teeth,
he should smear the bite with spittle or earwax.
The knower of mantras should bind an amulet four finger-breadths above the bite with linen or similar materials in a braided fashion, using proven mantras.
The binding should be applied according to the location, neither too tight nor too loose;
for if it is pressed too hard, it causes putrefaction of the bite, swelling, and other such ailments.
If one is unable to restrain it, the poison becomes lax and moves to another part of the body; by means of a binding, like a dam across water, the poison is held back.
The veins, being compressed by the binding, do not carry the poison;
likewise, one should extract the bite after squeezing it out, provided it is not located at a vital organ (marman) or a joint.
The force of the poison does not arise [again], like a sprout from the destruction of its seed;
if it reaches a vital point (*marman*), one meets death, but if it stays at a joint (*sandhi*), one suffers deformity of the limbs.
Having avoided the bite of the *maṇḍalin* snakes, one should then avoid others because of their bilious nature (*pittala*).
With heated gold, iron, and the like, or with a firebrand,
fire instantly reduces everything to ashes; what indeed cannot it accomplish in an instant?
Or one should suck it with the mouth full of mud, ashes, anti-poisonous drugs (agada), and cow dung; or,
having shaded it, one should especially apply these to a fleshy part of the *antarariṣṭa* ulcer.
One should repeatedly smear the limb, along with the insect sting, with anti-venomous medicines,
and sprinkle it with water mixed with sandalwood and uśīra.
When the poison has spread, one should venesect; this is the supreme treatment. For while the blood is being drawn out, the entire poison is indeed extracted.
For if [the blood] flows into a corrupted limb, death will certainly occur; therefore,
one should cause the blood that has not flowed out to flow by means of the methods prescribed for venesection.
One should arrest an excessive [hemorrhage] by those very means for the sake of preserving life;
foul-smelling, toxic blood crackles with a "caṭacaṭā" sound when placed in fire.
One should observe that the blood is purified according to the [specific] dosha as before;
when the vessels are not visible, horn-leeches (śṛṅga-jalaukas) should be employed.
And the blood that remains after being drained becomes liquefied by the heat of the poison.

One should staunch [the bleeding] very frequently with extremely cold applications of medicinal pastes; for if it does not stop, fainting, intoxication, heart-failure, and diarrhea may arise from the force of the poison.
One should conquer those [symptoms] with cold applications and sprinkle [the patient] until the hair stands on end;
because of its sharpness, the poison draws [the consciousness] toward the heart, and for its protection—
One should drink ghee, or ghee mixed with honey, or an anti-venom medicine (agada) saturated with ghee; likewise, marrow, cow-dung juice, water mixed with ashes, or water mixed with black earth.

One should consume at once either the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), or curd, or water mixed with red ochre (*gairika*), or the leaves of the *kovidāra*, *arka*, *śirīṣa*, and *kaṭabhī* plants.
Goats, sheep, and boars, as well as children, the elderly, women,
and pregnant women, should drink these [medicines] which are cold and sweet, along with milk, for their diseases.
Likewise, fainting and other such symptoms would not occur, nor would poison act [if the heart were protected]; however,
by obstructing the heart, his phlegm accumulates there.
Then,

one should cause the patient to vomit using liquids that exclude sour gruel (*kāñjika*), horse-gram (*kaulattha*), oil, wine, and the like, provided there is nausea, agitation, and a sense of heaviness resulting from the onset of the disorder.
And by means of emetics that remove poison, his body is not pervaded in this manner,
due to the specific differences in the snake's defect, its nature, its location, and its intensity.
Having carefully examined [the patient] very minutely,
one should perform the specific treatment; one should grind the roots of *sinduvāra* with its own juice.
This medicine mixed with honey is a drink for [neutralizing] the poison of *darvīkṛta* (crawling) snakes. The roots of *sinduvāra*, *śvetā*, and *girikarṇikā* [are also used].

When bitten by a hooded snake (*darvīkara*), honey mixed with *pākala* should be administered as a potion and as a nasal drop (*nasya*). For one bitten by a black cobra (*kṛṣṇasarpa*), after the blood has been removed, one should apply [the paste] to the site of the bite.
Or [one may use] cāraṭī and nākulī, or a sharp root-poison;
and for drinking, ghee mixed with honey, mañjiṣṭhā, and soot from a house.
Tanduliyaka, Kashmarya, Kinihi, Girikarnika,
Matulungi, sugar, and Shelu are beneficial when used as a drink, an errhine, or an ointment.
This is an antidote for the terrible venom of hooded serpents and even for those with striped hoods; likewise,
*sugandhā*, *mṛdvīkā*, the one called *śvetā*, and *gajakarṇikā* are equal [in efficacy].

A decoction consisting of half a part each of *saurasa*, *patra*, *kapittha*, *bilva*, and *dāḍima*, taken with honey, is especially beneficial as an antidote for the poison of a cobra (*maṇḍalin*). [Likewise,] *pañcavalka*, *varā*, *yaṣṭī*, *nāgapuṣpa*, and *elavāluka* [are also used].
Jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, sugar, white lotus, and blue lotus—
this cold preparation known as Himavat, taken with honey, destroys the poison of the maṇḍalī snakes.
An ointment made from these destroys swelling, erysipelas, eruptive boils, fever, and burning sensations.
[One should use] kāśmarya, banyan shoots, jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, and sugar.
One bitten by a maṇḍalin snake should drink mañjiṣṭhā and madhuka; [likewise,
one should take] bamboo bark, bījaka, kaṭukā, pāṭalī seeds, and nāgara.
Śirīṣa seeds, ativiṣā, the root of gāvedhukā, and vacā— this eight-ingredient formulation, ground with cow's urine, destroys the poison of the gonasa snake.
Kaṭukā, ativiṣā, kuṣṭha, gṛhadhūma, hareṇukā,
along with honey, vyōṣa, and tagara, destroy the poison known as rājamitā.
One should bury the bite of a *kāṇḍacitrā* [scorpion] in the ground for two watches;
having extracted it, one should cauterize the wound and apply an ointment of ghee mixed with grain-dust and clay.
One should drink aged ghee mixed with the powder of varā;
once it has been digested, having undergone purgation, one should eat barley-food prepared with soup.
One should make a paste of *karavīra*, the root of *arka*, *lāṅgalikā*, and *kaṇā*,
combined with *pāṭhā* and black pepper, using fermented rice-gruel (*āranāla*).
This is a universal remedy for those bitten by *vyantara* spirits:
white pepper [soaked] in the juice of *śirīṣa* flowers for seven days.
This prepared [mixture] is beneficial for those bitten by snakes when used as a drink, an errhine, or an eye-salve.
Two palas each of vakra and kuṣṭha, along with four palas of ghee and honey [are the ingredients].
This drink bestows happiness even upon those bitten by Takṣaka;
it consists of house-soot, the two types of Haridrā, and Taṇḍulīyaka with its roots.
Even one bitten by Vāsuki may drink [the potion] soaked in honey and ghee; likewise,
the dried and powdered meat and blood of a monitor lizard (godhā) is beneficial.
When the poison has entered the rasa-dhātu, one should administer a drink combined with the juice of kapittha; likewise, the root-bark and tips of śelu, along with those of bādara and udumbara.
When [the blood] has reached the blood, one should drink [a decoction of] *kaṭabhī*; furthermore, when it has reached the flesh,
one should drink the roots of *khadira*, *ariṣṭa*, and *kuṭaja* with honey and water.

In all cases where the poison has reached the head, one should employ a double dose of *balā*, along with *madhuka*, *madana*, and *nata*, as well as the root [of these], for the administration of nasal therapy (*nasya*).
Of *bandhujīva*, *bhāṅgī*, *surasā*, and *asitā*;
or alternatively, *pippalī*, *hiṅgu*, *vṛścikālī*, and *manaḥśilā*.

The seeds of *śirīṣa*, *apāmārga*, and salt, whether as a paste (*kalka*) or a powder (*cūrṇa*), are stimulants of consciousness; likewise are *kṛṣṇā*, *akṣaka*, *ativiṣā*, and *uṣaṇa*; and *pippalī*, *marica*, alkali (*kṣāra*), *vacā*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and *śigru*.
Ground with the bile of a red deer (*rohitapitta*), these applied as a collyrium (*añjana*) destroy [eye diseases] located in the eye.
Sandalwood, licorice (*madhuka*), spikenard (*māṃsī*), long pepper (*pippalī*), black pepper (*marica*), and blue lotus (*utpala*) [are used for this purpose].
Saindhava salt and añjana, ground into a paste with the bile of cows, are excellent;
likewise are the fruit of *naktamāla*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), the root of *bilva*, and the two types of *niśā*.
Flowers of *saurasa* ground with collyrium and mixed with goat's urine—
this is prescribed as the *bhoja-vaitaraṇa* remedy for awakening one who has fallen asleep due to poison.
Water, guñjā fruit, and uśīra, ground with water as a collyrium for eyes afflicted by poison, is "Gāruḍa," resembling Garuḍa himself.
Sea-foam, black pepper, *kaṇā*, *sauvīraka*,
and *añjana*, along with powdered *sindhūttha*, constitute a collyrium for those whose vision has been impaired by poison.
When the poison has reached the throat, one should lick the flesh of the wood-apple (kapittha) with sugar and honey;
when it has reached the stomach (āmāśaya), one should take a pala of the powder of those two [wood-apple and honey] mixed with nāgakeśara.
When the poison has reached the colon (pakvāśaya), one should grind equal parts of mañjiṣṭhā, the two types of rajanī,
and pippalī, and administer them with cow’s bile.
Long pepper, ginger, and alkali, mixed with fresh butter,
should be administered as a local application for excessive phlegm located in the throat.
One should quickly conquer the poison located in the head by means of transference;
one should apply it below the bite after making a "crow's foot" incision on the top of the head.
For one bitten by a snake with fangs pointing upward, [one should apply] the flesh and fat of a crow, a peacock, a goat, a cow, a buffalo, or a cock,
in the size of a *bilva* fruit, to the two feet.
In that case, the poison spreads; otherwise, it would quickly kill.
At the conclusion of the sharp nasal drops and collyrium, one should drink a large quantity of ghee.
For the poison of a person with dry (rūkṣa) eyes, when provoked by sharp [substances], destroys the vision; therefore,
one should induce emesis in such a person for the sake of pacifying the remaining poison.
A bite by a phlegmatic [snake] on a phlegmatic person, especially above the navel,
[is treated with] *dhāmārgava*, *śakrayava*, mustard seeds, *madana*, and honey.
Saindhava salt with lukewarm emetic therapy is used when poison has taken refuge in phlegm (kapha). Surasa, sarpavetālī, īśvarā, and white mustard (gaurasarṣapa) [are also used].
One should drink the leaves of *paṭola* and *nimba* along with honey and rock salt; likewise, [one should take] *śukāhvā*, *jālinī*, *dantī*, *madana*, *ikṣvāku*, and *kauṭaja*.
Kālā and lāṅgalikā are bitter; emesis with rice-water [is indicated] for a bite by a pitta-dominant [snake], especially one that has bitten below the navel.
When the poison has reached the seat of bile (pittāśaya),
one should administer a purgative consisting of *dantī* with *nīlī* fruit, along with milk or buttermilk.
One should mix fine powder of *trivṛt*, *śyāmā*, *surasā*, and *nīlinī* with either a decoction of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) or milk;
likewise, *piṇḍītaka* fruit, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), *trivṛt*, *vella*, and *harītakī*.
Purgation with salt mixed with urine is indicated when phlegm (kapha) predominates; when wind (vāta) predominates, it should be with the fruit of *nīlinī* mixed with ghee and salt.
One afflicted by poison should be purged while lying on a bed with holes.
For one who rises up even for a moment, the poison corrupts the vital air (vāyu);
having vomited or been purged, he should drink a medicinal gruel (yavāgū) that destroys poison.
When the poison has reached the seat of the wind (vātāśaya), the drinking of clarified butter (sarpiḥ) is prescribed.

That which was taught regarding the first and the last [sections] concerning poison and its suppression— now, in the case of the acute onset of *darvikṛta* [poison], having first drained the blood, [one should proceed].
One should quickly drink the medicine mixed with honey and clarified butter;
on the second day, having performed emesis, one should drink the medicine in the same manner.
One should employ the poison-removing [remedies] during the third stage, using collyrium and nasal drops;
in the fourth stage, once emesis has been performed, one should drink the previously mentioned gruel.

In the sixth and fifth stages, one should repeatedly administer a sharp emetic using cold substances after the patient has been smeared and sprinkled; then one should have him drink the gruel as previously described.
On the seventh day, one should administer a potent medicine as an ointment or nasal drop;
then, having made a deep incision on the head with a surgical instrument in the shape of a crow’s foot (kākapada), [one should apply it].
One should place his flesh, blood, or skin there;
or, during the third stage of the *vega* of *maṇḍalins*, one should drink *peyā* from the left.
In the sixth stage of a bite by a *rājila* snake, one should apply a non-pungent antidote or the *padmaka*-group of drugs; in the first stage, after providing shade, one should perform scarification.
One should extract the blood using a gourd and drink the antidote as previously described;
during the sixth stage of the impulse, one should apply sharp collyrium and an avapīḍa.
In cases where the specific courses (vega) have not been mentioned, one should employ the treatment prescribed for the Darvīkara [poison]; however,
in pregnant women, children, and the elderly, one should perform venesection only mildly.
Realgar, manaḥśilā, niśā, vakra, the juice [of madana], and tiger’s claw;
Tamāla and kesarā, when drunk cold with rice-water, destroy all poisons; this is like a thunderbolt against the asuras. Prapauṇḍarīka, kaṭukā, devadāru, and suvarcikā—
Kālānusārī, sthauṇeya, śaileya, ghana, padmaka, kuṭannaṭa,
elā, punnāga, nata, kuṣṭha, and priyaṅgu.
Lodhra, guggulu, tālīsa, pippalī, svarṇagairika,
white sinduvāra, śuṇṭhī, dhyāmaka, and the best of salts (saindhava).
One should place the finely ground powder in a horn and liquefy it with honey.
Tārkṣya, who is like Tārkṣya himself, [acts as a remedy] through drinking, nasal drops, massage, and collyrium.
This medicine would even counteract the force of the poison of Takṣaka;
[the ingredients are] lodhra, śirīṣa flowers, samaṅgā, hiṅgu, and reṇukā.
Kaṇoṣa, naileya, nepālī, vacā, yaṣṭīmadhu, utpala,
sinduvāraka, mandāra root, and karañja seed.
Jyotiṣmatī, nata, kuṣṭha, and white girikarṇikā,
ground into a powder by a maiden and made into a wick with honey and cow’s bile— AS.Utt.42.85 [this wick] should be used.
This medicine destroys the poison of snakes, rats, insects, and jackals;
it also neutralizes the venom arising from cats and *kāṇḍacitra* spiders, as well as the afflictions caused by spirits, possession, and fever.
For epilepsy, seizure disorders, insanity, abdominal tumors, indigestion, and cholera,
[one should use] the root of *bilva*, the flower of *surasā*, the fruit of *karañja*, *nata*, and *surāhva*.
The three fruits, the three pungents (vyoṣa), and the two types of niśā, finely ground with the urine of a goat,
[cure] the poisons of snakes, spiders, rats, scorpions, and the like, as well as cholera, indigestion, fainting, and fever.
It restores to health afflicted men and those tormented by malevolent spirits through the application of collyrium, potions, and nasal drops.
[The ingredients are: Trivṛt, Viśalyā, Madhuka, Niśā, and the five salts.
Likewise, one should grind together mañjiṣṭhā and tryūṣaṇa; that is the "Great Medicine" (mahāgada).
[Also included are] māṃsī, hareṇu, triphalā, muruṅgī, and madhuyaṣṭikā.
Mañjiṣṭhā, padmaka, aśoka, kuṣṭha, tālīsa, candana,
sugandhika, elā, kiṇihī, tvak, paṭolī, and mṛgādinī.
Bhāṅgī, viḍaṅga, pālindī, pāṭhā, kroṣṭukamekhalā,
the flower of māruṣkara, the leaf of saurasa, kramuka, and pura.
One should collect bile from a mongoose, a cat, an iguana, a scorpion, a boar,
a spotted deer, and a peacock; these are kept in a cow-horn as previously described.
In whatever house this [medicine] is present, no fear arises there from snakes, insects, and the like;
by means of this, kettledrums, war-drums, and banners are smeared.
They destroy poison by means of the *ārṣabha* [mantra] through touch, hearing, and sight;
and by means of ointments and other applications, they extract the poison from the bite entirely.

The poison may arise again with increased force, or as residual *dūṣīviṣa*; when the wind (*vāta*) has been provoked by the departure of the poison, one should treat it with oleation (*sneha*) and other such measures.
One should treat [the patient] with wind-alleviating measures, excluding oil, wine, horse-gram, and acidic substances;
and for pitta, with decoction enemas (kaṣāya-basti) and unctuous enemas (sneha-basti) that cure pitta-type fever.
One should [treat] kapha with the group beginning with āragvadha, combined with honey.
Sugar, fragrant substances, grapes, payasyā, madhuka, and honey—
this is the drink; it should be accompanied by sprinkling with water purified by mantras, as well as soothing words and encouragement.

One should employ [these remedies] for one struck by the limbs of a serpent, as well as for one afflicted by the poison of fear; likewise for those who are enemies of men, such as Pūtana, Upatakūṣmāṇḍa, Piśāca, and others.
Unrestrained [spirits] may destroy the potencies of medicinal herbs;
therefore, one should employ a protective rite that wards off hosts of *rakṣasas*.
On ground well-swept with cow dung and thoroughly perfumed with the incense of *agaru*, [one should perform this].
In a house where the deities have been worshipped with perfumes, garlands, offerings, and the like,
one should honor the authors of the Sūtras, as well as Śaṅkara, Āstika, and Kāśyapa.
Having gratified the blazing fires and the twice-born with offerings to the gods and ancestors,
the physician [should attend] to the patient afflicted by poison who is seated facing the east.
Facing north, one should employ the knowledge, mantras,
and medicinal herbs with green darbha grass of equal length that has been consecrated with mantras facing east.
One should perform its cleansing with blades of grass that have uncut tips and their roots;
one should also constantly anoint it with medicinal herbs beginning with the Brāhma-herb.
One should employ Sañjīvana and other such [medicines] in drinks and the like, as well as for application to the bite.
[One should also use] a full pitcher containing flowers, mustard seeds, and goat’s milk.
One should apply a blade of dūrvā grass, honey, and ghee to the head of the person bitten;
thus, for one who is self-controlled, the poison is pacified within seven days.
Karketana, emerald, diamond, elephant pearl,
lapis lazuli, gardabhamaṇi, picukā, and viṣamuṣṭikā.
Sōmarājī and punarnavā produced on the Himavat mountain,
as well as droṇa, mahādroṇa, mānasī, and the sarpaja maṇi.
One should carry potent antidotes for the purpose of neutralizing poisons; moreover,
one should especially wander at night carrying an umbrella and a rattle-drum in hand.
"The serpents flee, terrified by its shadow and its sound.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter.
Now begins the forty-third chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter titled "The Prevention of Poison from Insects.
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
AS.Utt.43.2: From the feces, urine, semen, eggs, and carcasses of snakes themselves,
four kinds of insects arise, produced by the humors (doṣas) either individually or in combination.
Kumbhīnasa, tuṇḍikerī, śṛṅgī, śatakulīraka,
ucciṭiṅga, agnināman, cicciṭāṅga, and mayūraka.
The ahijorabhrakābarta, the śārikāmukha, the vaidala,
the śarāva, the kūrda, the paruṣa, and the citraśīrṣa are indeed the jārakas.
There are eighteen types of wind-born insects that aggravate the bodily wind (*vāta*):
the *kauṇḍinyaka*, the *kaṇabhaka*, the *varaṭī*, and the leaf-scorpion (*patravṛścika*).
Vināsikā, Brāhmaṇikā, Vindula, and likewise Bhramara; Bāhyakī, Picciṭa, Kumbhī, Varcaḥkīṭa, and Urimedaka.
The *dundubhi*, the *padmakīṭa*, the *makara*, the *śatapādaka*, the *pañcāla*, the *pākamatsya*, the *sūkṣmatuṇḍa*, and the *gardabhi*.
The *klīta*, the *kṛmiśarārī*, and that which is known as the *utkleśaka*—
these twenty-four insects are fiery (*āgneya*) and cause disorders of bile (*pitta*).
The *viśvambhara*, the *pañcaśuṣka*, the *pañcakṛṣṇa*, and the *kokila*...
Sthairyaka, Pracalāka, Vaṭabha, Kiṭibha, Jaṭī,
Sūcīmukha, Kṛṣṇagodhā, Dabhra, and Kāṣāyavāsika.
These thirteen are specified as being mild and provocative of phlegm (śleṣman). [They are:
Tuṅganāsa, Cipilaka, Tālaka, and likewise Vāhaka; AS.Utt.43.10 [and others].
The Koṣṭhāgārī, the Kṛmikara, and the Maṇḍalapucchaka;
the Tuṇḍanābha, the Sarṣapaka, the Madguli, and likewise the Śambuka.
The fire-insect (*agnikīṭa*) and the mixed-insects (*saṅkīrṇa*); these twelve are destroyers of life.
When bitten by wind-insects (*vāyavya-kīṭa*), the bite is characterized by intense itching and pain in the abdomen.
From the fiery (āgneya) type, there is little discharge, accompanied by a burning sensation, redness, and spreading inflammation;
it resembles a ripe *pīlu* fruit or is like a *kharjūra* fruit.
A bite caused by the combined action of all three doshas (sānnipātika) is characterized by a predominance of kapha, resulting in mild pain, a resemblance to a ripe udumbara fruit,
an abundance of discharge, and the presence of all [the aforementioned] symptoms.
The symptoms include forceful onsets like those of a snake, swelling that increases, a foul-smelling redness,
heaviness of the head and eyes, fainting, giddiness, dyspnea, and intense pain.
In all cases, there is swelling of the calyx, fever, itching,
and anorexia. The vātika [scorpion] bites upon contact with its wings, while the paittika [scorpion] bites by touch.
A bite by a *śleṣmika* insect [causes symptoms] through the mouth; a bite by a *sānnipātika* insect [causes them] in every way.
When bitten by *kaṇabha* insects, there is swelling, erysipelas, vomiting, and fever.
The bite from a *daṃśa* is shaped like a *karṇikā*, dark red, and sloughs off;
whereas for one bitten by the *trikaṇṭaka* [scorpions], the bite is multicolored or white.
The bite of a *daṃśa* is characterized by swelling, delusion, and a breaking pain in the feces;
that of a *kṛkalāsa* resembles a half-moon and is intensely red due to the discharge.

The bite caused by *daṃbha* is characterized by red eruptions (*sphoṭa*) accompanied by pain. That which is inflicted by one with a single fang is yellowish, itchy, and painful; it is called *dārdura*.
A person bitten by a *daṃśa* (gadfly) suffers from thirst, sleepiness, fainting, and vomits green matter.
A bite by a *mātsya* (fish-like leech) is characterized by pain and burning; the symptoms of water-leeches (*jalaukas*) have already been described previously.
A bite inflicted by a Viśvambharaka spider is accompanied by swelling, itching, and pain;
it causes vomiting of phlegm, diarrhea, and the eruption of skin rashes (koṭha).

A bite by a centipede (śatapadī) is yellowish, accompanied by sweating, pain, discoloration, and swelling; it may be the color of linseed flowers (atasīpuṣpa), or it may be characterized by pustules, vertigo, and a burning sensation.
A bite by a house lizard (gṛhagodhikā) causes discharge, pricking pain, swelling, burning, and moisture; in one bitten, there is cardiac distress and the appearance of nodules.
Itching, slight swelling caused by mosquitoes, and mild pain— these are the signs of an incurable mosquito bite, resembling that of an incurable insect.
Generally, flies bite the eyes, causing prominent swelling;
their bite is characterized by burning and itching, and one should avoid those [flies] that frequent cooking pots.
Upon its appearance, the pustule becomes dark, exuding fluid, and accompanied by many complications; it is painful,
resembling the bite of an ant, and burns as if with fire.
One should recognize that body as afflicted by avamūtrita when it is covered with eruptions resembling drops of water, accompanied by burning, itching, and pain, and characterized by heat.
The venom of a scorpion is sharp; initially it burns like fire,
then it quickly ascends upward, and finally it remains localized at the site of the sting.
The *daṃśa* bite is characterized by immediate inflammation, a dark discoloration, pricking pain, and a sensation as if it were bursting;
it results from the putrefaction of cow dung and similar substances smeared on the site of the bite.
Born from the nests of snakes, these [scorpions] possess mild, moderate, or great venom.
Those with mild venom are yellow, white, dark-brown, rough, variegated, or blackish-blue.
Those that are hairy, many-jointed, red, and pale-bellied;
those that are smoke-colored in the belly, three-jointed, and tawny or reddish in the middle— these are the intermediate [types].
Tawny, brindled, variegated, and blood-colored, these are highly venomous;
they resemble fire, have two or one saddle-like markings, and possess red, black, or white bellies.
Bitten by them, one has a swollen tongue, stiff limbs, and is afflicted with pain.
Passing dark, scanty urine, unable to perceive the objects of the senses,
perspiring, fainting, with a parched mouth, agitated, and afflicted by pain.
When the flesh is being torn away, the patient generally loses consciousness;
however, the ucchiṭiṅga [insect] bites with its mouth, causing excessive pain.
From a scorpion sting that is curable, there occurs stiffness of the penis and horripilation,
as well as a sprinkling of the limbs as if by cold water.
Because of its camel-like color, it is called *uṣṭradhūmaka*; it is nocturnal due to its wandering at night, though it is distinct from [the poison] found in insects such as the *kaṇabha*.
Because there is no difference in the means of treatment for their disorders, even though they exist as distinct types, they have not been enumerated;
[namely] insects where vāta and pitta predominate, and those such as the *kaṇabha* and the rat which are characterized by *śleṣman*.
Scorpions whose venom is predominantly dominated by wind (vāta), along with those of the *uṣṭradhūmaka* species,
are generally [to be treated] according to whichever humor (*doṣa*) one perceives to have an excess of symptoms.
In that case, one should administer a treatment with medicines possessing qualities opposite to those [of the disease],
for there are chest pain, upward-moving wind (ūrdhvānila), stiffness, constriction of the vessels, and pain in the bones and joints.
In poisoning by vāta, there is rolling of the body, writhing, and a dark discoloration of the limbs;
there is loss of consciousness, hot breath, burning in the heart, and a pungent taste in the mouth.
In the Pittaja type, there is tearing of the flesh, swelling, and hemorrhagic fever (raktapitta),
accompanied by vomiting, anorexia, nausea, salivation, distress, and catarrh.
One should recognize an excess of phlegm (*śleṣman*) by its coldness, sweetness of the mouth,
and so forth; for a wind (*vāta*)-dominant fever, one should apply a paste of oil-cake (*piṇyāka*) to the wound and perform an oil massage.
For a fever caused by pitta, sweating induced by means such as tubular channels or parched grain, and nourishing therapy are beneficial;
one should arrest it with very cold affusions and medicinal pastes.
One should conquer disorders caused by *kapha* through scraping, excision, fomentation, and emesis;
for the three types of insects, a threefold therapeutic procedure is beneficial.
One should generally employ lukewarm fomentation, ointments, and affusions.
Except in cases of fainting, inflammation from a bite, or suppuration,
human hair, mustard seeds, and aged molasses, when drunk or used as an incense fumigation, [are effective]. (AS.Utt.43.49)
Kāśyapa declared that for every case of venomous bite,
one should perform the entire procedure for neutralizing poison as well as the various purificatory treatments.
One should treat those bitten by snakes or afflicted by fierce poisons from insects and scorpions [with this].
One should drink *trivṛt* mixed with ghee in portions equal to those of *taṇḍulīyaka*.
It suffers trembling from the poisons of insects, yet it is not shaken by them like Mount Kailāsa by the winds.
An ointment made from the bark of milky trees, applied once the area is cleansed, removes the poison of insects.
An ointment of pearls is excellent for removing swelling, pricking pain, burning sensation, and fever. Vacā, hiṅgu, viḍaṅga, rock salt, and gajapippalī [are used for this purpose].
Having drunk this ten-ingredient antidote prepared by Kāśyapa— consisting of pāṭhā, prativiṣā, and vyoṣa— one shall conquer all poisons of insects.
A great unguent that overcomes insect poison is prepared by combining these together: milk, honey,
the feathers of a peacock and a cock, oil, and excellent salt.
Incense prepared [from these] quickly destroys the poison of insects and scorpions. In the case of *kaṇabha* poison, one should employ the treatment prescribed for rats.

A paste made from *śirīṣa* seeds and the milky sap (*kṣīra*) of *snuhī*, mixed with honey, applied to a frog [bite]; likewise, for a fish-bite, *trikaṭu*, the root of white *piṇḍā*, *vacā*, bamboo bark, *pāṭhā*, *nata*, and the flower-cluster of *surasā*. (AS.Utt.43.57)
The two types of *bala*, *nākulī*, *kuṣṭha*, *śirīṣa*, the two types of *rajanī*, *guhā*, *matiguhā*, *śvetā*, *ajagandhā*, and *śilājatu*.
One should grind together kattṛṇa, kaṭabhī, kṣāra, gṛhadhūma, manaḥśilā,
and rohītaka with bile; this is an excellent medicine (agada).
Through the application of ointments, powders, collyriums, and potions derived from Viśvambharā and other substances,
as well as the alkali of *svarjika* and goat dung, *surasa* acts as a pain-reliever for the eyes.
Combined with the scum of wine (*madirāmaṇḍa*), it is beneficial for the poison of a centipede (*śatapadī*).
For eye pain caused by *kapittha*, one should use sun-seeds (*arkabīja*) combined with the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*).
Karañja, the two types of haridrā, and gṛhagodhī remove poison;
taṇḍulīyaka combined with kākāṇḍa removes all poisons.
A peacock’s egg is praised [as a remedy], as is a crow’s *pīluka* fruit; likewise,
*tagara*, ginger, *nāgakesara*, and black pepper.
When applied as a drink or as an ointment, it destroys the poison of flies. White and black salts, along with black pepper and ginger, [are likewise effective].
Phaṇijjaka combined with the juice of kara removes the poison of varaṭī insects.
One should immediately sprinkle the bite caused by a scorpion with cakrataila.
Or again, one should repeatedly apply lukewarm clarified butter prepared with vidārigandhā, or otherwise with the other [medicinal group],
combined with the best salt (saindhava).
One should sprinkle [the area] with warm *āranāla* juice, or with milk mixed with salt; or an ointment (*upanāha*) consisting of ground *ajājī* seeds with rock salt, fried in ghee, should be applied.
One should foment the bite, cover it, and then rub it with powders derived from *rajanī*,
rock salt (*saindhava*), the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), and the fruits and flowers of the *śirīṣa*.
A lukewarm plaster made from the tips of *surasā* ground with *mātuluṅga*, sour substances, and cow’s urine is beneficial; likewise, a plaster of oil-cake or cow dung is also helpful.
For drinking, one should take milk mixed with ghee and honey, or milk with abundant sugar,
or very cold jaggery-water scented with the four aromatic spices (cāturjātaka).

The seed of *palāśa*, smeared with the milk of a she-goat and processed with *arkakṣīra*, destroys the *śūla* (piercing pain). [Likewise,] the droppings of a pigeon, *pathyā*, *tagara*, and *viśvabheṣaja* [are used].
This excellent remedy for scorpion stings consists of bīja-pūra juice mixed with rock salt,
asafoetida, and the tender leaves of mālatī.
AS.Utt.43.71 AS.Utt.43.71
This pill, ground with the juice of cow dung, [is used] for one afflicted by a scorpion sting. Garlic, black pepper, asafoetida, surasa, and ginger— AS.Utt.43.72.
A pill made with the milk of the *arka* plant cures one afflicted by a scorpion; likewise,
[a preparation] containing moss, a clod of earth, and a dog’s tooth destroys poison born of a scorpion.
A pill made from asafoetida, yellow orpiment, and the juice of citron,
when used as both an ointment and a collyrium, is the supreme remedy for removing the effects of a scorpion sting.
The flowers of karañja, arjuna, śelu, kaṭabhī, kuṭaja,
and śirīṣa, applied as a paste with buttermilk, are for the treatment of stings.
One should grind together pippalī, marica, yaṣṭi, śvetā, the flower-cluster of surasa,
sahadevā, apāmārga, and taṇḍulīya into a paste.
An ointment made with the alkaline water of Kutaja destroys the poison of spiders;
for one who faints, breathes heavily, and raves in intense agony.

For one whose bite is characterized by itching, suppuration, and severe *koṭha* eruptions, a plaster consisting of *pathyā*, *aniśā*, *kṛṣṇā*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *ativiṣā*, and *uṣaṇa*, along with the stalks of *sālābu*, ground together with the juice of *vārtāka*, should be applied. (AS.Utt.43.78)
For that [condition], the medicinal paste consists of trikaṭu, yavakṣāra, and ukṣipīḍaka;
as well as pigeon droppings, kāntā, svarjikā, agni, and hareṇu.
If [the metals] are melted with the juice of *mātuluṅga* or with the milk of the *arka* plant,
for one whose heart is oppressed, fainting and a tingling sensation occur.
The biting of the teeth and lips and the bristling of the body hair cease for that person after five days, or else [the poison's] force does not subside at all without medical treatment.
In that case, one should apply a plaster to the bite made from white *pāṭalī*,
*ativiṣā*, *haridrā*, *harītakī*, and *nata*, ground with whey.
With [a paste] combined with bilva root, yavakṣāra, and sūkṣmamāgadhikā,
the bite— swollen, moist, and discolored— is as if it were being excised.
One who vomits blood resembling the fruit of the Jambu tree, makes moaning sounds, and writhes;
one who does not perceive the objects of the senses and perspires repeatedly— [such a person is near death].
Having ground together svarjikā, kuṣṭha, tagara, nākulī, pīlu, pippalī, and bṛhatī with clear surā, one should apply it as an ointment; furthermore,
in all cases of the virulent poison of a rat, one should cause [the patient] to drink honey and ghee.
One should venesect, and administer emesis, collyrium, and nasal drops;
the diet should consist of warm, unctuous, sour, and sweet foods that pacify Vāta.
This medicinal preparation— consisting of asafoetida, the excrement of a domestic pigeon, the juice of *bījapūraka*,
yellow orpiment, and rock salt— swiftly destroys the poison produced by bees when applied as an ointment.
In cases of those bitten by scorpions when the poison has become intensely aggravated,
one should apply a suitable quantity of stable (sthāvara) poison to the site of the bite.
This procedure may also be applied to *ucciṭiṅga* (scabies), using dust in the reverse order;
likewise, one should perform massage with pleasant, sour, and warm substances, as well as covering with thick layers.
The fruit of *kuṭaja*, *kuṣṭha*, *mālatī*, *phalinī*, *nata*,
and bitter *ikṣvāku*, ground together, [are used] for drinking, nasal drops, and other such applications.
This [remedy] is equal to nectar for neutralizing the poison of scorpions, mongooses, spiders, and snakes, and it destroys even the remnants of artificial poison (gara).
Śirīṣa seed and long pepper powder, processed three times with the milk of the *arka* plant,
constitute this medicine which destroys the poisons of insects, snakes, spiders, rats, and scorpions.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter.
Now begins the forty-fourth chapter.
1. Hereafter, we shall explain the chapter titled "The Prevention of Spider Bites" (Lūtā-pratiṣedha).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others,
regarding those born from the forehead of Vasiṣṭha when he was enraged by Viśvāmitra.
The drops of sweat that fell upon the grass when it was being cut are known as *lūtās*;
they originated from the bodies of the Asuras while they were being consumed by fire in the Khāṇḍava forest.
Some say that those sparks which issued forth are *lūtā*;
others state they arise from the coagulation of spoiled food that has been consumed.
Those which produce poisonous eruptions and possess the characteristics of spiders or insects,
and which bear their respective [names], are designated as spiders (lūtā) and insects (kīṭa).
Among those, the most terrible spiders are divided into three types— superior, middling, and inferior— and they kill [their victims] unless treated with medical care.
In seven days, ten days, or a fortnight, respectively, [the poison] becomes yellow-faced like fire, yellow, lotus-colored, urine-colored, white, or black.
The seven spider species born from sweat and originating from the fire element cause disorders of bile:
the pale (pāṇḍurā), the red-footed (raktapadikā), the bhr̥ṅgā, the tawny (piṅgā), and the three-ringed (trimaṇḍalā).
The seven *pūtivīra* and *aṇḍaja* spiders are mild and cause disorders of phlegm (*śleṣman*). The *kumuda*, *ālaviṣā*, *raktā*, *citrā*, *santānī*, and *mecakā* [are also among them].
The seven types of *kasanā* and *udbhidā* are caused by Vāyu and produce diseases of the wind-humor (*vāyu-roga*).
These are: *kākāṇḍī*, *eṇapadī*, *lājā*, *vaidehī*, and *jālinī*.
Golden in hue and adorned with garlands, these seven spontaneously born beings,
resembling blazing fire, swiftly pervade the limbs.
Those caused by the combination [of all three humors] are incurable; the others are curable with difficulty.
They bite during the bright fortnight, during the dark fortnight, and always at the junction [of the two].
In general, their bite resembles a ring of ringworm (dadru-maṇḍala);
it is white, black, reddish, yellow, or dark-brown, soft, and elevated.
In its center it is black or dark-brown, covered with a network of vessels at the periphery;
accompanied by erysipelas and swelling, it is characterized by great pain and intense burning.
Accompanied by fever, rapid suppuration, moistening, sloughing,
and bursting, it produces an ulcer wherever it touches a limb with its discharge.
These [venomous creatures] vomit poison from their mouths specifically through eight substances: breath, fangs, feces, urine, semen, saliva, nails, and menstrual blood.
A bite by a snake causes sudden swelling accompanied by fever and a burning sensation; however,
a bite made with its fangs is more severe, characterized by discoloration, hardness, and rigidity.
Accompanied by deep swelling, distension, pain,
and burning; foul-smelling, it is characterized by burning, itching, and a tingling sensation, along with the discharge of feces.
It ripens quickly, and once ripe, it becomes pale like the fruit of the pilu tree;
its edges are red with urine, while the center is black and it disintegrates.
Resembling a whirlpool, swollen, putrid, it creeps along and burns;
caused by semen (śukra), it has the shape of a knot, is hard, and characterized by intense pain.
It has shallow roots, slight pain, and small openings; it is itchy, soft,
and characterized by sucking with the nails, pustules, itching, and a sensation of fuming.
The *kiṃśuka* insect, which has the color of the interior of a *kiṃśuka* flower and is covered with dust on its proboscis,
bites from the navel upward; other insects bite both upward and downward.
Clothing and other items contaminated by that [poison], when in contact with the body, cause a transformation; however,
for half a day, no bite resulting from the poison of a *lūtā* spider is visible.
On the first day, it appears like the prick of a needle;
its color is indistinct, it is slightly mobile, and is accompanied by some itching and pain.
In the second [type], it is excessively elevated at its edges as if covered with pustules,
has distinct coloration, is depressed in the center, and is itchy like a glandular swelling.
In the third stage, it is accompanied by fever, causes horripilation, and features red circular patches;
it has the shape of a quiver, is characterized by intense pricking pains, and exudes secretions from the pores of the skin.
In the fourth stage, there is a great swelling that causes fever, labored breathing,
and vertigo; in the fifth stage, it produces various disorders arising from the provocation of the poison.
In the sixth [stage], it pervades the vital points (marmāṇi); in the seventh, it destroys life. Thus, one should distinguish between poison that is extremely sharp and others.
The poison is pacified for all [of these] after twenty-one nights.
A bite caused by a Pitta-dominant insect is characterized by burning, thirst, eruptions, fever, and a burning sensation;
it is accompanied by swelling, is hard, pale, and itchy, with little pain. A bite caused by a Kapha-dominant insect is characterized by itching and slight pain.

The vātika type is rough, dark-brown, and causes pain characterized by the splitting of joints; one should also observe the aggravation of the doṣas through the signs arising from the knowledge of snakes.

Generally, all spiders (lūtā) possess the three doṣas, with pitta and kapha being predominant. In those [bites] that are fatal, there occur delusion of the heart, dyspnea, hiccups, and stiffness of the head.
White, black, yellow, and red pustules arise from swelling (śvayathu). There is piercing pain, vomiting, burning sensation, thirst, blindness, and a crooked nose.
The lips, face, and teeth become dark-brown; there is a breaking pain in the back and neck;
and from the bite, blood flows out with the color of ripe jambū fruit.
Now, in the case of one bitten by a spider (lūtā), one should quickly excise the bite with a surgical instrument;
one should cauterize it with *jāmbavoṣṭha* and other [medicines], but one should not cauterize if pitta is predominant.
One should not cut a bite that is hard, has broken hairs, is located on vital spots (marmans), joints, and so forth, or is spread in all directions; rather, one should cauterize it.
One should apply a plaster of *dagdhāgadaka* mixed with honey and rock salt,
and subsequently irrigate it with very cold decoctions of the milk-exuding trees (*kṣīrivṛkṣa*).
One should extract blood from all sides using horns or other instruments, or even by means of venesection;
once the blood has flowed out, an affusion with ghee, milk, and similar substances is beneficial.
Prapauṇḍarīka, drībera, sārivā, uśīra, and jīvaka;
lodhra, candana, jīvantī, mañjiṣṭhā, sarja, and vañjula.
Lotus stalks, lotus roots, water moss, white and blue water lilies,
red ochre; banyan, udumbara, aśvattha, nicula, plakṣa, and vetasa trees.
Samaṅgā, pāṭalī, gundrā, kākolī, śataparvikā,
śirīṣa, dhātakī, mūrvā, vidārī, padma, and kiṃśuka.
Śṛṅgāṭaka, kośavatī, vāyasī,
somarājī, madhuka, aṃśumatī, and mūrvā— these should be collected as they are available.

A plaster composed of *śyāmā*, the two types of *dvaya*, *niśā*, *mustā*, *nakha*, *rāsnā*, and *mahāsahā*, mixed with clarified butter, is recommended for a yellowish (pittaja) discoloration after it has been left to stand overnight.
Vāsā, pattaṅga, suvahā, nākulī, girikarṇikā,
sarpagandhā, ayavaphalā, nirguṇḍī, aśmantaka, and sthirā.
Śukākhyā, mahiṣakrāntā, kuṣṭha, indrayava, saffron, karavīra, aguru, nata, sugandhā, and sinduvāraka.
Āsphoṭa and gundrā are beneficial as a paste for poisoning caused by phlegm (ślaiṣmika-viṣa). Bimbī, vidula, bandhūka, kovidāra, and palāśa [are likewise used].
Suvahā, iṣṭakābrāhmī, guḍūcī, viśvā,
and sairyaka; siddhārthaka, devadāru, viḍaṅga, and indravāruṇī.
Śatāvarī, lāṅgalikī, rājavṛkṣa, punarnavā,
jīvantī, vāyasī, bhārṅgī, kataka, indrayava, and arjuna.
Misī, vyāghrapadī, siṃhapucchī, maṇḍalaparnikā, śvadaṃṣṭrā, kolabṛhatī, revatī, and śvetapuṣpikā.
Prapunnāṭa and kuravaka as a paste are recommended for poison caused by Vāta; furthermore, bodhi, śleṣmātaka, and akṣaka are praised in all cases.
For those whose humors are aggravated, who are strong, or who have been bitten by a large snake or are terrified,
[one should treat them] with *kākaṇḍakī*, *kośavatī*, *lodhra*, *indrayava*, and rock salt.
With patola leaves, black pepper, karaghāṭa, and priyaṅgu; with pippalī, śukanāsā, nīpa, nimba, saptāhvaya, and yaṣṭi.
One should induce purgation with triphalā, trivṛt, trikaṭu, and rock salt;
or alternatively, one may cook [the medicine] with dantī, pūga, mṛdvīkā, and viḍaṅga.
With these [ingredients] weighing half a pala each, one should prepare one *prastha* of equal parts of *brāhmī* juice, ghee,
milk boiled with the five roots (*pañcamūla*), or water, along with purifying medicinal herbs.
One should administer a purgative separately, combined with its respective medicinal pastes:
[using] long pepper (pippalī), long pepper root (pippalīmūla), dry ginger (śuṇṭhī), indrayava, and rock salt (saindhava).
A decoction prepared with pāṭhā, ajamodā, yaṣṭyāhva, mustā, sarṣapa, dāru,
the minor pentaroots (laghupañcamūla), and sarala [is used].
This gruel, prepared with ghee and mixed [with other ingredients], destroys poison; it is to be employed in cases of flatulence,
hiccups, dyspnea, and stiffness of the back and neck.
In cases of contraction, stiffness, and tremors; in colic pains and hemicrania; and in other wind-related diseases such as joint-splitting pain and facial paralysis (ardita).
One should boil eraṇḍa, bilva, sarala, ciribilva, arka, pāṭalī, śigru, pāṭhā, kuśa, vṛṣa, and vidula in water.
One should cook a decoction of the minor pentad (kanīyaḥ-pañcamūla) in that [mixture] with double the amount of ghee and an equal amount of cow’s milk, using the pastes of yaṣṭīmadhu, niśā,
and nata.
With *surāhva*, *vella*, *sarala*, *śatāhvā*, *lodhra*, and *gairika*; with *payasyā*, *kuṣṭha*, *agāṅgeyī*, *kṛṣṇā*, *madana*, and *saindhava*.

Once the enema has returned, one should eat with broths prepared with the five roots (*pañcamūla*). Nasal drops (*nāvana*) should be used in cases of heaviness, swelling, excessive salivation, and lockjaw.
Girikarṇī, phala-sara, bandhūka, kiṇihī, sugar, ṣaḍgranthā, garlic, vyoṣa, bṛhatī, vella, and rock salt; AS.Utt.44.63.
Apāmārga fruit, bhārṅgī, nākulī, sarpagandhikā,
śyāmā, yavaphalā, and the seeds of phaṇijjaka and śirīṣa.

The juices of vārtāka ground with a paste [of other ingredients] are an excellent nasal medication for removing poison. For one whose head has been purged, the scum of clarified butter (sarpirmaṇḍa) should be used as a nasal drop.
In cases of obstruction of the eyes, swelling, itching, and excessive sleepiness,
[the physician should administer] vacā, manohvā, trikaṭu, triphalā, lodhra, and gairika.
Conch shell, blue lotus, copper, gold, coral, *jīvantī*, garlic, *kuṣṭha*, *kataka*, *mārkava*, and *nata*.
Prapauṇḍarīka, madhuka, karañja fruit, rock salt,
the two types of niśā, phaṇijjaka, tuttha, srotoñjana, and rasāñjana.
The flower of *meṣaśṛṅgī* ground with cow's urine is an ointment (*añjana*). [Also used are] the fruit of *surasā*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), the root of *vilva*, and *surāhvaya*.
Turmeric and goat’s urine are an ointment that destroys spider-bites. Śirīṣa, padmaka, uśīra, pāṭalī, and sinduvāra [are used for the same].
This medicinal preparation— consisting of milk, bamboo shoots, nata, udīcya, sārivā, kuṣṭha, and candana— ground with the fresh juice of śelu, is used for nasal administration and as an ointment.
Payasyā, madhu, mṛdvīkā, aśvadaṃṣṭrā, kṣīra, and moraṭā are most beneficial when used for drinking, as a paste, or for sprinkling in cases of spider-bites.
Goji, vidārī, yaṣṭyāhva, and madhuka possess those same qualities;
likewise do the flowers of śirīṣa and the fruit produced from candralekha.
One should likewise employ surālā, kaṭabhī, jāti, śvetā, and girikarṇikā, as well as tagara, kuṣṭha, nāgabalā, and balā.
The two types of *haridrā*, *nāgadantī*, *lodhra*, *śābara*,
*śirīṣa* flower, *tagara*, *sahadevā*, and *śatāvarī*.
Punarnavā, nāgabalā, sarpagandhā,
kuṭannaṭa, gavādanī, dantaśaṭha, somavalka, and indurājī.
This antidote (*agada*), combined with honey, acts as a remedy for all poisons and performs every therapeutic function.
It consists of *sarpākṣī*, *candana*, *vakra*, *mṛgākṣī*, and *gandhanākulī*.
Cardamom and *mahāsugandhā* ground into a paste with goat’s urine, used as an ointment or taken internally, is a remedy for spider-bites; there is no disease equal to it.
[Likewise, a paste] of *kaṭabhī* root, *tagara*, *samaṅgā*, *udavarta*, and *dāru*...
Ghee prepared with the two types of *bṛhatī*, *gāṅgeyī*, *rocanā*, and *candana*,
along with four times the amount of milk, is beneficial for both drinking and external massage.
When the extremely virulent poison of spiders, *kaṇa*-insects, and *bhakīṭa* insects has subsided,
once the burning sensation, swelling, and other symptoms have ceased, one should extract the *karṇikā* (the central core) from the ulcer.
Safflower, cow’s tooth, golden milk tree, and pigeon dung.
Trivṛt, saindhava salt, dantī, and likewise karṇikā cause the falling of [the ear-wax]; also haridrā, guggulu, fermenting agent (kiṇva), bamboo scrapings, and pigeon dung.

Similarly, at the time of applying the earplug (karṇikā), one should strengthen [the patient] with anti-poisonous substances such as rock salt (saindhava), kuṣṭha, dantī, kaṭuka, daugdhi, the root of rājakrośātakī, or ferment (kiṇva) produced from churning curdled milk.
And during the fertile period, however many drops of semen there are from spiders, [so many offspring will be born].
As many [drops] fall upon the body, that many pericarp-like eruptions arise simultaneously.
[The ingredients are]: cow's tooth (godanta), dantī, trivṛtā, the two types of haridrā, rock salt (saindhava), and sesame seeds.
Madhuka, nimba leaves, and ghee purify wounds. [One may also use] kāntā, viḍaṅga, khadira, nimba, kampillaka, and ambuda.
Ghee prepared with *sarja*, *elā*, *dhātakī*, and *loha* cures wounds. [One should also use] the bark of *śirīṣa*, *kaṭabhī*, *śelu*, *kṣīrivṛkṣa*, and *arjuna*.
Through the application of pastes, powders, and washes, these [remedies] remove wounds caused by insects and spiders:
*śatāhvā*, *lodhra*, *kāsīsa*, *dārvī*, *jambū*, and *rocanā*.
This powder of *harītakī* and *pūgaphala* promotes the healing of wounds. *Lākṣā*, the two types of *rajanī*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *haritāla*, and *manaḥśilā* [are used for the same purpose].
This application of ghee and honey is supreme for purifying the skin;
it also promotes the growth of hair, as described in the treatment of wounds.
One should perform every oleation therapy using ghee alone;
oil, however, increases poison just as grass and weeds increase a fire.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter.
Now begins the forty-fifth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "The Treatment of Individual Lūtās" (Insect Bites).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:
"At the site of the bite, there will be a copper-colored, firm pustule caused by *kapilā*."
When *lasīkā* [vitiated], there is burning in the hair follicles and heaviness in the eyes and head;
in this condition, one should employ drinking, nasal medication, collyrium, ointment, and affusion.
Niśā, padmaka, kuṣṭha, elā, karañja, and the bark of kakubha;
sthirā, arka-parṇī, apāmārga, brāhmī, jvalana, and nākulī.
Alternatively, from Kuṣṭha, Pattaṅga, Nakha, Joṅgaka, and Kuṅkuma,
there arises an extremely severe eruption (sphoṭa) resembling a burn by fire, as if one has been scorched by flames.
By the heat of the poison, which is like a flame of fire, the patient perspires;
afflicted by thirst, burning sensations, tremors, and fainting, he suffers from diarrhea caused by pitta and blood.
One should apply [the treatment] there as previously described, having first rejected [the patient's refusal], acting with urgency;
[using] kuṣṭha, lāmajjaka, uśīra, madhūka, madhuka, and honey.
AS.Utt.45.7 By way of their medicinal properties, tālīsa and gopakanyā possess a cooling potency.
AS.Utt.45.8 When drunk, they cause the passage of yellow feces and urine, as well as the subsiding of bites, moisture, and eye inflammation.
One suffering from fainting, vomiting, headache, fever, anorexia, and colic—
for such a person, *kaṭabhī*, *uśīra*, *muñja*, *vañjula*, and *padmaka* are desired.
Vaṃśa, kāśa, arjuna, kuśa, the bark of śirīṣa and kiṇihī;
or else, vanya, bālhīka, kuṣṭha, kesara, and joṅgaka.
A pustule resembling a lotus, caused by *padmābha*, may burst and then close again;
it quickly becomes moist, exudes warm discharge, and is extremely painful to the touch.
In that regard, lotuses, blue water-lilies, stalks, Himalayan cane,
*vañjula* reeds, lotus fibers, and white water-lilies, combined with honey, ghee, and sugar, [are beneficial].
The bite is putrid, accompanied by urine and poison, spreading, and characterized by black blood;
it is attended by dyspnea, cough, fever, vomiting, fainting, burning sensations, and giddiness.
Realgar, orpiment, madhuka, madhūka, blue lotus,
sandalwood, kuṣṭha, lāmajjaka, uśīra, and padmaka are the medicinal ingredients for that [ointment].
At the site of the bite, there appears a white pustule that is intensely itchy and causes burning,
fainting, fever, pain, erysipelas, and discharge.
In that regard, the following are recommended: cold-pressed *rāsnā*, *elā*, *hareṇu*, *nalada*, and *vañjula*;
as well as *kuṣṭha*, *māṃsī*, *nata*, *uśīra*, *kāntā*, *adhyāmaka*, and *padmaka*.
A bite by a black [snake] results in a black wound, foul-smelling, with discharge and swelling;
corrupted black blood arises there, and this is the remedy for it.
There is a great fragrance, snakes, milk, cardamom, and *gandhanākulī*;
