the bite is swollen and pale-yellow, with swelling of the face and heaviness.
Fever, vertigo, yawning, and headache are the symptoms; the remedy for that is the root of *vāruṇapuṣpā*, yellow orpiment (*rocanā*), and the juice of cow dung.
A bite by a *raktapādī* spider produces pale, pitted eruptions accompanied by swelling.
In that case where there is discharge of blood, *nalada*, *sevyā*, *udīcya*, *himā*, and honey should be used.
A bite by a *bhṛṅgī* is blackish like a bee; it causes pustules (*piṭakā*) and is characterized by burning and pain.
When the body is covered with boils, medical treatment is recommended there;
[the remedy consists of] the essence of *aṅkola*, *phalinī*, cow’s bile, and *misirgada*.
From the Piṅgā [serpent], the bite has the appearance of being burnt by fire; it is characterized by eruptions that exude much fluid,
and is accompanied by intense swelling, fever, pain, cardiac distress, burning sensations, and thirst.
In that case, the medicine consists of sugar, *gundrā*, jasmine, licorice, blue lotus, *jīvaṅka*,
the sprouts of milky trees, double snow (camphor), and *nāgakeśara*.
In the *trimandala* type, the bite is thick and black blood flows;
there is loss of appetite, burning of the eyes, turbid discharge, and blurred vision.
And by various medicinal circles (maṇḍalas), his body is nourished;
therein [are used] arka-root, the two niśās, surālā, and pṛśniparṇikā.
A medicinal preparation of *dadhittha*, *nākulī*, *brāhmī*, and *jyotiṣmatī* is beneficial. A bite from a *pūtigandhā* [snake] causes erysipelas (*visarpa*), discharge, and burning sensations.
Resembling alajī, it is painful and covered with obstructed pustules;
[the treatment involves] bhārṅgī, nidigdhikā, nimba, pāṭalī, and sinduvāraka.
Dūrvā grass, the two types of Haridrā, and Vāsā remove the poison of the Pūtigandha; a bite by this [insect] is characterized by variegated circular patches and is covered with a network of pustules.
In a woman suffering from *vīra* fever, there is headache accompanied by cold fever and aversion to food.
[The remedy consists of] *haridrā*, *nalada*, *kuṣṭha*, *elā*, and the flower-buds of *surasā*.
Tagara ground with dog bile destroys the poison of the vīrā spider. A bite by a kumudā spider is characterized by burning, eruptions, throbbing, and piercing pain.

In this case, one should reject [the bite] if it exudes a slimy discharge, is accompanied by dyspnea and lockjaw; otherwise, one should perform the course of treatment as generally prescribed. In the region of the lower jaw, yellow or red circular patches appear.
Pustules resembling mustard seeds, dryness of the palate,
pain, fever, vomiting, burning sensations, and trembling of the head [occur]; in that condition, [a preparation] with honey should be used.
The bite is accompanied by a smell of tin and hrīvera, and is marked by pippalī and vaṭa sprouts;
the extremities are red, the bite site is red, and it is associated with pale pustules and fever.
In cases of white-colored diarrhea (śvetatisāra), labored breathing, burning sensation, and blood-stained discharge,
the bark and root of śelu, arjuna, āmrātaka, and sinduvāra are recommended.
At the site of the bite, there is a variegated, red, spreading, and firm pustule;
it is accompanied by cracking of the joints, headache, fever, swelling, and is highly contagious.
When [the wound] is cracked, it turns black, becomes yellowish with discharge, and develops large ulcers;
in that case, kuṣṭha, nalada, śirīṣa, nala, and reṇukā are desired.
In the case of a bite by a *daṃśa* spider, there is a film over the eyes, piercing pain, agitation,
and lacrimation; in that condition, one should apply *kesara*, the barks of milky trees, and [other remedies].
The roots of the mango, the sinduvāra, and the aśmantaka [should be used]; black pustules resembling bird droppings appear in the center of the bite.
There is fever and swelling from the Vāruṇī; from the Rājimān, there is a bite marked by streaks, accompanied by headache, dyspnea, and coughing, along with Rocanā and the two types of Rajanī.
The remedy for that [poison] is the flow of cold, slimy blood;
the *kākāṇḍī* [poison] is known to cause pale-red discoloration, extreme pain at the site of the bite, and loss of memory.
Hiccups, labored breathing, thirst, fainting, sleepiness, convulsions, and heart disease [occur];
the bite of a *tveṇapādā* is red at its edges and shaped like a black sesame seed.
Accompanied by burning, delusion, spreading fire-like heat, thirst, vomiting, dyspnea, and cough;
it is putrid, dark-brown, extremely painful, bloody, and has a bite-mark the color of parched grain.
The bite of Vaidehī was accompanied by the onset of a cold fever, burning sensations, fainting, and diarrhea; it resembled a burn from fire and was extremely painful.
The bite of Jālinī is deep, accompanied by fever, sharp delusion, and pain in the heart;
it is marked by upward-pointing lines and characterized by intense swelling and pain.
The bite [of a spider] is characterized by an intense throbbing, delirium, labored breathing,
stiffness, and fainting; it is red, resembles a string of garlands, has a smoky odor, and is accompanied by severe pain.
It is torn from the sides by various enraged circular formations;
there is internal burning, external coldness, flatulence, and difficulty in urination.
Fainting, delirium, diarrhea, and fever are life-ending;
a bite from a *sauvarṇika* snake causes swelling and exudes a fish-like odor.
Headache, eye pain, fever, cough, thirst, swelling, vomiting, and vertigo— [these are signs];
even for those [diseases] considered incurable, one should quickly administer beneficial treatment after having informed [the patient and family] of the prognosis.
Depending on the specific aggravation of the humors (doṣas), [the bite] is devoid of cutting, burning, and other such symptoms;
there, the fire bites the nose and the collarbones.
The yellow Padmā is on the cheeks;
then the white Lūtā, whose venom is urine, is on the right shoulder and in the armpits; and the Kālikā is on the chin and in the eyes.
A pale-colored *bhṛṅgī* bites on the right shoulder, one with red feet on the hands; a *piṅgalā* bites on the left side and the left shoulder.
Pūti is in the interior of the three circles (trimaṇḍala), Vīrā on the back,
and on the right arm is Kumudikā at the navel; on the left shoulder is the one known as Alasā.
In the throat it is red; on the forehead, however, it is variegated; on the palate and the lips it is dark;
on the head, from coughing, it appears blackish; and on the hands and the roots of the armpits, it is black.
Kākāṇḍyenyā resides in the heart, Lājavarṇā between the breasts, Vaidehī at the joints of the arms, and Jālinī at the outer corners of the eyes.
"A golden necklace-like cord around the neck and at the roots of the ears"—these are the fixed locations [for the application of poison];
however, those whose poisons are extremely potent [may spread elsewhere].
"Even in another's field, kings prevail like those of great strength"—
thus ends the forty-fifth chapter.
Now begins the forty-sixth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "The Prevention of Rat and Fox Bites.
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
Lālana, Capala, Putra,
Hasira, Cikiru, Ajina, Kaṣāyadanta, Kulaka, Kokila, Kapila, and Asita.
The Aruṇa, Śabala, Śveta, Kapota, Palita,
Unduru, and Cūcundara— known as Rasāla— these eighteen are the varieties of mice.
Whichever limb this semen falls upon, or whichever limbs they touch with their semen-smeared hands,
that blood becomes vitiated and turns pale.
Knots, swelling, urticaria, circular patches, vertigo,
loss of appetite, cold fever, thirst, pain, malaise, shivering, and a splitting sensation in the joints.
Horripilation, perspiration, fainting, persistence for a long duration,
and vomiting mixed with phlegm resembling many mouse-young at a single time; AS.Utt.46.6.
The rat poison (ākhuviṣa) spreads diffusely, is difficult to treat, and recurs again and again.
It causes fainting, swelling of the limbs, discoloration, discharge, loss of hearing, and fever.
Heaviness of the head, salivation, and vomiting of blood are signs of incurability.
One whose bladder is swollen, whose lips are discolored, and who is covered with nodules resembling rats is likewise incurable.

One should avoid meat with the smell of a muskrat and that which has been defiled by a rat. In a dog, the humors (doṣas) are dominated by phlegm (śleṣman), and they affect the consciousness (saṃjñā) located in the channels of consciousness (saṃjñāvaha).
Stealing away [the vital essence], they cause an extremely violent agitation of the bodily constituents (dhātus).
One who possesses excessive saliva becomes blind and deaf, and runs about in every direction.
With his tail, jaw, and shoulders drooping, suffering from pain in the head, and with his face bent down,
the person bitten by that [insect] falls asleep and exudes black blood.
Subsequently, there arises pain in the heart and head, fever, stiffness, thirst, and fainting;
by this [description], other beasts of prey that strike with their fangs should also be understood.
Jackals, mules, horses, bears, leopards, tigers, wolves, and the like [are the signs];
itching, pricking, discoloration, numbness, moisture, fever, and vertigo [are the symptoms].
Burning sensation, redness, heaviness, suppuration, swelling, glandular swellings, contraction,
tearing at the site of the bite, eruptions, pustules, and circular patches.
In all cases, the symptoms of a venomous bite are the opposite in a non-venomous one; however,
one who has been bitten perishes by imitating the movements and cries of the creature that bit him.

And he who, seeing that very same [reflection] suddenly in mirrors, water, and so forth, becomes terrified due to the sight, touch, or sound of water; ||| AS.Utt.46.17 ||| and he who becomes terrified because of the sight, touch, or sound of water.
One should abandon even that patient who has not been bitten, if they suffer from a water-fright (hydrophobia).
Immediately after being bitten by a rat, one should cauterize the bite with a reed.
Alternatively, by using a mirror, one may detect a *karṇikā* (a localized swelling) that would otherwise cause intense pain.
Once it is identified, one should cauterize the bite, drain it, and apply a medicinal paste to the incised area.
With *śirīṣa*, *rajanī*, *vakra*, *kuṅkuma*, and *amṛtavallī*;
with soot from the house, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *rajanī*, and the best salt; [these are used].
The ointment overcomes the poison of a rat and causes the *karṇikā* to fall away;
then, having washed it with sour liquids, one should subsequently apply a medicinal paste with water.
One should quickly apply a vein-bleed using *pālindī*, white *kaṭabhī*, the roots of *bilva*, *guḍūcī*, and other [herbs] that destroy poison and swelling.
Emetics should be administered with decoctions of *jālinī*, as well as those of *śukākhyā* and *aṅkola*; likewise,
the fruit of *kośavatī*, *śukākhyā*, and *jīmūtaka*.
Having powdered madana and drunk it with curd, one should vomit the poison;
or else, vacā, madana, jīmūta, and kuṣṭha, ground with urine,
[should be drunk].
It should be drunk according to the previous method; it removes all poison from rats.
Nishpava beans, the root of the plantain, and the fruits of the bandhujīva—AS.Utt.46.24.
Suvarcalā, rāmaṭha, svarjikā, the two types of ativiṣā,
the roots of śyāmā and drikarṇikā, and mūrvā— these three emetics,
when the heart has been purified after vomiting, [cure] colic, hiccup, anorexia, and vomiting.
If there is a continuous succession of hot eructations, then this is the remedy: cumin,
the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), kuṣṭha, the plant called tuṅga, and nāgakeśara.
Having ground the two *rajani* herbs, *saindhava* salt, *yaṣṭīmadhu*, *suvarcalā*,
and the sweet group (*madhuragaṇa*) with the juices of *bījapūraka* and *kapittha*, [one should apply it].
One should prepare a *ṣāḍava* with juice, combined with honey and sugar; when drunk, it—
endowed with fragrance, color, and taste— overcomes the defects of poison.

A gruel prepared with a decoction of two parts each of *pippalī* and *aṃśumatī* possesses the same qualities [as the preceding formulation]. For purgation, a paste of *trivṛt*, *nīlī*, and *triphalā* is recommended.
In head-purgation (śirovirecana), the pith of the śirīṣa tree and its fruits are used;
for collyrium (añjana), the juice of cow dung mixed with the fine powder of the three pungents (vyoṣa) is employed.
A linctus made from the juice of *kapittha* and cow dung mixed with honey is beneficial when licked; ghee prepared with the root of *taṇḍulīyaka* is beneficial when drunk.
[One may use] *dviniśā*, *kaṭabhī*, *raktā*, and *yaṣṭyāhva* combined with *amṛtā*;
or [a decoction] prepared from the root of *āsphota*; or indeed the "five kapittha" formulation.
If pain occurs in the lower part of the body after purification,
or if there is an obstruction of feces at the navel, or if there is a cutting sensation in the anus;
In that case, one should drink cold liquid gruel (peyā) mixed with sugar and honey,
along with pippalī, pippalīmūla, sārivā, and kaṭukāhvaya.
Boiled with *balā*, *samaṅgā*, and *viśvabheṣaja*, it is prepared; likewise with *nalada*, *dhyāmaka*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), *lodhra*, *citraka*, and *dīpyaka*.
One should have [the patient] consume honey and ghee ground with alkaline water from Kutaja,
or honey along with barley-alkali, milk, and curd.
Treacle, oil, and clarified butter, when drunk together, are a remedy for poison. Sinduvāra, nata, śigru, the root of bilva, and punarnavā [are likewise used].
One afflicted by rat-bite should drink the decoction of vacā, śvadaṃṣṭrā, jīmūta, and meṣa mixed with honey, while eating rice with curd;
or alternatively, one may drink the seeds of śarapuṅkhā ground into a powder with buttermilk (takra).
Alternatively, the bark of the root of the *Aṅkola* tree, ground into a paste with goat's urine,
is effective when used for drinking or as an external application to eliminate all types of rat poison.
Milk combined with *payasyā*, sugar, and licorice;
and *kirātatikta*, *amṛtā*, *samaṅgā*, and the bark of *kakubha*.
Bāṇa, palāśa, kāśmarya, payasyā, taṇḍulīyaka,
ākhuvinnā, mahānimba, saptaparṇa, and madhūlikā.
A patient suffering from fever should drink either the juice of *kapittha* or *rājavṛkṣa*.
One should excise a stable, slightly painful *karṇikā* (pustule) or cause it to fall off.
Śyāmā, lāṅgalikā, dantī, kiṇihī, girikarṇikā,
ākhuvṛkṣa, mahāvṛkṣa, trivṛt, añjanakī, and snuhī.
The removal of the *karṇikā* (the central plug) and each type of paste (*kalka*) should be prepared like sesame paste.
[The ingredients are: milk-exuding sprouts, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *balā*, *dārvī*, and *hayāhvaya*.
For healing purposes, a paste should be prepared, or likewise, oil or ghee should be cooked with the two types of turmeric (dviniśā), sesame, licorice (yaṣṭyāhva), tagara, ushira, and padmaka.
The general treatment for the defects of action has been indicated; specifically,
by over-indulgence, vomiting, fainting, and salivation arise.
In that case, one should lick powdered *taṇḍulīyaka* mixed with honey.
If there is vomiting, fainting, or thirst due to the *capala* poison, one should administer this as an electuary.
By using *sadarū*, *mustā*, *triphalā*, and *putraka*, one cures *pāṇḍutā* (anemia),
exhaustion throughout the limbs, and the appearance of nodes resembling those of rats.
One should have the patient lick the seeds of *śirīṣa* and *kuṣṭha* with honey. [In this condition,
there is] aversion to food due to *hasira*, yawning, and horripilation.
One should cause the patient, who has been well-purged, to drink a decoction of *āragvadha* and other such herbs;
by this, headache, swelling, hiccups, vomiting, and vertigo are cured.
In this case, after vomiting with decoctions of *jālinī*, one should drink the essence of *aṅkola*.
Blackness of the limbs, fainting, vomiting, and cardiac oppression [are the symptoms].
In that case, one should lick mañjiṣṭhā mixed with honey and a paste of snuhī milk.
Sleep, astringent teeth, dryness of the heart, and emaciation [are also symptoms].

One should have the patient lick the pith, bark, and seeds of the *śirīṣa* tree mixed with honey; by means of this, the pain and discharge, as well as the streaks (*rājayaḥ*) on the site of the bite, are cured.
One should lick two *sinduvāraka* fruits together with sugar and honey there;
[this cures] severe glandular swellings (*granthi*), fever, and a terrible burning sensation caused by the *kokila* [fever].
One should drink ghee prepared in a decoction of *nīlī* and *punarnavā*.
In a wound caused by a brown (*kapila*) snake, there occurs suppuration, fever, glandular swelling, vertigo, and thirst.
One should have the patient lick white *punarnavā* with honey; furthermore,
one should drink red [punarnavā] with black [honey], especially on a cloudy day, when blood is being vomited.
In that regard, water mixed with the ashes of *kiṃśuka*, *śirīṣa* fruit, and *vālaka*,
along with [the drugs] beginning with *aruṇā*, [are used] for those [afflictions] arising from the individual doṣas, from their combination (*sannipāta*), and from blood.
All these [lesions], including those with knots and ear-like protrusions, gradually produce diseases from the *karañja*,
*āragvadha*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), the two types of *bṛhatī*, and *aṃśumatī*.
In the decoction [of the aforementioned drugs], one should cook one *prastha* each of curd, milk, and ghee,
along with *kapittha*, *dāḍima*, *varī*, *viśālā*, and the three aromatics (*trisugandhika*).
Trivṛt, clay, and crooked guḍūcī, ground into a paste with these,
should be added to the [milk] of the five [animals] beginning with the Aruṇa; this destroys poison.

Ghee prepared with the fresh juice of *kākādanī* and *kākamācī* [is used for these]. Severe exhaustion caused by a muskrat, stiffness of the neck, and choleraic illness (viṣūcikā) [are also treated thus].
One should administer a decoction of *yavānala*, *ṛṣabha*, and alkali, or alternatively, the two types of *bṛhatī*.
In cases of stiffness of the neck, one should apply *rasālā* (mango pulp) to the site of the bite to relieve the pain.
In that case, one should lick a great remedy consisting of ghee mixed with honey;
for the remaining mouse-poison becomes aggravated at the sight of clouds.
Or, according to the specific circumstances in the various worlds, when there are causes for the increase of the doshas,
all therapeutic measures should be applied there according to their respective conditions.

Those remedies which have been specified for their respective [poisons] likewise remove *dūṣīviṣa*. For one bitten by a *tvalarka* (mad dog), the bite should be cauterized with warm clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*).
One should apply various medicinal pastes and drink aged ghee;
or else, having pressed [the juice] of *pratyakpuṣpī* over the ulcer, one should apply it.
A paste made from *tila*, *guggulu*, *dūrvā*, pomegranate, and jaggery,
applied repeatedly as an ointment, is the supreme remedy for neutralizing the venom of dog bites.
The root of the *nala* grass, ground with water, is beneficial for drinking and as an external application;
one should bind a bite with the leaves of the *mātuluṅga* fruit, crushed between the teeth.
Furthermore, a quick purgative should be administered to him using *arka* latex;
he should drink white *punarnavā* combined with the fruits of *dhurdhūra*.
The fruit of the *dhurdhūraka* and the root arising from the *kākodumbarikā*.
Śīdhu liquor drunk with rice-water destroys the poison of a dog;
likewise, minced meat, oil, the milk of the Rūpikā plant, and jaggery taken together [have this effect].
It destroys the *viṣamālarka* poison like the wind disperses a dense mass of clouds. Garlic, black pepper, and long pepper, mixed with a paste of cow bile,
[are effective].
Drinking, nasal drops, collyrium, and ointments made from these are the supreme remedies for one bitten by a dog. One should boil the crushed leaves, bark, and roots of *jalavetasa* in water.
That decoction, when cooled and drunk, is a supreme remedy for the poison of dogs; likewise, ghee prepared with it may be used for drinking, nasal administration, massage, and external application.
In all cases of fear of water and of poison, that [oil] is like Garuḍa;
it should be prepared in water containing barley, māṣa, kulattha, and the five roots (pañcamūla).
One should prepare clarified butter with twice the amount of milk,
using the finely ground pastes of *aśvagandhā*, *sahā*, *kuṣṭha*, *bṛhatī*, and the two types of *rajanī*.
With vidārī, nata, kaṭvaṅga, payasyā,
and sinduvāraka; with sarpagandhā, nakhī, abhīru, sugar, and red sandalwood.
It destroys all complications arising from phlegm through drinking and massage;
it is highly effective for burning sensations in the heart, excessive salivation, purgation, and emesis.

Once the patient has been purified and the toxic effects have been removed, the process of gradual dietary rehabilitation (saṃsarjana-krama) should be employed. One must certainly administer a potent purificatory therapy (saṃśodhana) that destroys the poison.
Even when the ulcer has healed, the poison of an impure person flares up again;
[this is treated] with herbs that have seeds which flow [out], using jars filled with cold water.
One hundred and eight times consecrated with the perfected mantra,
[the patient should be sprinkled] with one hundred and eight measures [of water] wrapped in a garland of flowers.

O Lord of Alarka, O Yakṣa, O Lord of the pack of dogs! Having bathed on the bank of a river at a crossroads, he should smear a sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) the size of a cow-hide with [cow-dung], spread it with kuśa grass, and perform the rite upon that blazing fire. (AS.Utt.46.81)
"Make this [wound] afflicted by *alarka* free from poison for me without delay; *svāhā*!"— this mantra is recommended for all rites performed for one suffering from *alarka*.
A wound inflicted by the claws or teeth of four-footed or two-footed animals becomes swollen and suppurated,
accompanied by redness, fever, discharge, and pain.
Somavalka, aśvakarṇa, gojihvā, haṃsapādikā,
the two types of rajanī, and gairika— this ointment removes the poison from nails and teeth.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter.
Now begins the forty-seventh chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the chapter named "The Prevention of Complications Arising from Poison."
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others:
fever, cough, vomiting, dyspnea, hiccups, thirst, and fainting; AS.Utt.47.2 [these are the complications].
Loss of luster, excessive hardness, flatulence, pain in the head of the bladder,
swelling, a foul-smelling bite, bleeding, and toxic wind (viṣānila) [are the symptoms].
Thus, sixteen complications of those afflicted by poison have been specified;
possessed by these, patients suffering from poison meet their destruction even when treated.
A decoction made from *rājavṛkṣa*, *phala*, *uśīra*, *kāśmarya*, *ghana*, and *padmaka*,
combined with sugar and honey, is an excellent remedy for poison-induced fever.
Kaṭukā, along with sugar and candied sugar, taken with rice-water,
as well as ajājī, jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, and utpala, remove poison and fever.
The combination of kola, majja, sitā, dhānyaka, bhārṅgī, yaṣṭyāhva,
and kesara destroys poison, fever, vomiting, dyspnea, cough, and thirst.
A decoction of triphalā, āragvadha, and vyāghrī overcomes fever and constipation;
likewise, a decoction of bālabilva, vacā, mustā, and punarnavā [achieves the same].
It destroys fever, loss of digestive fire, and swelling caused by poisons. [The remedy consists of] Vaidehika, Ārāmaṭhaka, the juice of Kapittha, and rock salt.
Licked with sugar and honey, it removes dyspnea, cough, and fever; or else, long pepper (kṛṣṇā) combined with grapes, ginger, and varāghana.
Having licked clarified butter mixed with honey, one is freed from poison originating from insects;
likewise, [one should lick] pāṭhā, añjana, mañjiṣṭhā, the two types of niśā, and madhuka.
Having drunk yaṣṭyāhva with water and sprinkled it with powdered marica,
one should drink a decoction during the vomiting of poison; or else, one should drink the powder of bilva root.
Amalaki, sugar, grapes, and licorice, quickly ground with milk;
likewise, cardamom, the best añjana, ushira, liquorice, ela, kankola, and kesara.

One should lick either a jar of black pepper melted with ghee and the juice of *puṣpa* flowers, or [a preparation of] sprouts of milk-exuding trees with honey and sugar; these destroy thirst and vomiting.
One should eat aged *śāli* rice with honey and drink milk prepared with sandalwood while it is cold; after eating, this removes vomiting caused by poison.
One suffering from dyspnea should lick a paste of *kṛṣṇā*, *priyaṅgu*, and sugar with oil,
cow dung, *rasa*, and honey; or alternatively, one should take *drākṣā*, *śṛṅgī*, *māgadhikā*, and sugar with honey.
Or, in the case of hiccup (hidhmā), one may take jaggery, ginger, long pepper (vaidehī), vijayā, and āmalaka; or conch-shell, gold, katukā, and golden ochre (svarṇagairika).
Or one should lick a paste of vella, śuṇṭhī, kaṇa, uśīra, and the two types of rajanī; or one may lick vyoṣa and mṛdvīkā with the juice of bījapūra.
One should drink either a decoction of *bālaka* and *rajaḥ* with honey,
or a decoction of *viśvabheṣaja*, *gāyatrī*, *haridrā*, and *amaradāru* with jaggery.
Alternatively, a paste of *dantī*, *indravāruṇī*, and *dvīpī* with *sauvīraka* vinegar,
or cold applications and sprinklings, are beneficial for thirst and fainting when the head is not involved.
With lotus stalks, flowers, sandalwood, ushira root, and pearls,
soaked in the waters of the sky, white water, milk, ghee, and sugarcane juice;
Fanning with a palm-leaf fan, staying upon cool, sandy ground,
and [bathing] in waters covered by masses of filaments from lotuses and water-lilies.
Immersion in lakes cures thirst, burning sensations, and fainting caused by poison.
When thirst arises from the onset of a toxic impulse, parched grain (lāja) mixed with water should be used for satiation.
One should drink water infused with sugar, pomegranate,
and honey, as well as the cool water from the Vaṭa, Vetasa, Jambu, Āmra, and Sevya trees.
One should drink equal parts of bhūnimba, mustaka, kaṭukā, trāyantī, and indrayava,
along with two parts of citraka and eight parts of kuṭaja, with water.
Lodhra, mocarasa, ambastha, and dhātakī, taken with rice-water, remove poisoning, diarrhea, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), cough, dyspnea, and fever. (AS.Utt.47.25)
Likewise, one should drink ginger, ativiṣā, and abhayā with honey; or dhātakī, kuṭaja, and añjana, finely powdered together.

Alternatively, one may administer a powder of *pāṭhā* and *nāgara* mixed with curd and honey; in cases of pain in the bladder (*basti*), upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*), and constipation, one should employ a medicinal suppository (*phalavarti*).

One should drink *sāragvadha*, *trivṛt*, *upakulyā*, and *harītakī* with ghee and honey, which destroys pain in the bladder and other ailments. [One should also use] house-soot, *nata*, *śyāmā*, *nīlinī*, and *taṇḍulīyaka*.
Clarified butter prepared with *trivṛt* decoction is effective, as is unprepared [milk] mixed with *trivṛt*.
[Also beneficial are: *kākolī*, the bark of milk-exuding trees (*kṣīrivṛkṣa*), grapes, *yaṣṭimadhu*, and sugar.

This nasal medication (nasya), which destroys poison and headache, should be administered with cold water. For one whose bowels have been purified, boiled milk is beneficial for drinking when there is swelling (śvayathu).
Or one may take goat’s milk boiled with *pippalī*, or goat’s milk boiled with *viśvabheṣaja*, *vaidehī*, *kaṭukā*, and *devadāru*, or with the pastes of *surasā* and *amlavetasa*.
Trivṛt, processed for three days with a decoction of triphalā and stirred with ghee, when drunk, destroys poison-induced swelling.
A medicinal paste made from madhu, vellaja, vyoṣa, surāhvā, uśīra, padmaka,
and sweet and astringent decoctions likewise overcomes poison and swelling.
An incense composed of *śirīṣa* flowers, *ahiśira*, *nata*, and *kuṣṭha*, mixed with clarified butter,
is a medicinal fumigation that conquers swelling and destroys all poisons.
Even with only slight neglect, the bite becomes putrid;
generally, it does not tolerate sharp or hot medicine, nor poison.
Therefore, in the case of a poison-wound, one should apply sweet, unctuous, and cold substances; furthermore,
one should employ affusions and plasters made from the decoctions of milk-exuding trees mixed with milk.
The combination of *nyagrodha* shoots, *madhuka*, sesame, mustard, rock salt, *abhayā*,
neem leaves, and clarified butter destroys the foul odor caused by insect bites.
The removal of the calyx is the best treatment for destroying poison-induced ulcers. When blood flows excessively, one should drink ghee mixed with black pepper.
One should apply a plaster of the root of *taṇḍulīyaka* combined with sugar,
or well-ground *dārvī*, to the bite.
One should administer snuff consisting of sugar, salt, honey, ghee,
and goat's milk; one should drink a fine paste of *śamī* and anoint the body with *viśālā*.

In cases of excessive bleeding from the nose, blood is pacified by the application of honey and clarified butter, as well as by white [substances]; however, when blood flows excessively due to the overuse of drying (rukṣa) substances, [it must be treated accordingly].
Furthermore, by the very nature of the poison, the vital wind (mātariśvan) becomes aggravated;
from that [aggravation] arise insanity (unmāda), convulsions (akṣepaka), loss of mental faculties (manobhraṃśa), and epilepsy (apasmṛti).
In that case, the desired unctuous enema (snehana-basti), nasal drops (nasya), insufflation (pradhamana), and collyrium (añjana) [should be used].
[The ingredients are] nāgadantī, abhayā, kuṣṭha, pippalī, vṛṣa, and kaṭphala.
Ghee prepared with the seeds of *bhallātaka*, *kaṭukā*, *bilva*, *prativiṣā*, and *agnikā* along with milk conquers disorders caused by poison and wind;
one should drink either castor oil combined with goat meat broth.
One who consumes ghee or oil together with the juice of pure meat should take the root of *karpāsa*, black pepper, the two types of *haridrā*, *nalada*, and *nala*.
One should cause a person who is insane from toxic wind (viṣavāta) or afflicted with epilepsy to drink long pepper (pippalī), natron (svarjikā), and costus (kuṣṭha) stirred with water.
Vacā, haṃsapadī, vyōṣa, dadhittha, hastipippalī,
devadāru, balā, bilva, kṛmijit, kuṣṭha, and ṭuṇṭuka.
One should administer lodhra, ākhukarṇī, ativiṣā, milk,
and ghee; that ghee, when used for drinking and massage, destroys all poisons.
One should treat diseases among others in the same manner as one treats them in oneself,
after considering the persistence of the *doṣas* and ensuring there is no contradiction with the principles of toxicology (*viṣatantra*).
One should eliminate the remaining portion of the poison from this [patient] by means of visible [antidotes], sounds,
and medicines; for even a tiny remnant may lead to disease or death.
Dhavā, aśvakarṇa, tiniśa, karañja,
kapītanā, palāśa, āmrātaka, kuba, pāribhadraka, and tilvaka.
Kapittha, kuṭaja, aṅkola, pragraha, āmalakī,
bhujā, śamī, śleṣmātaka, aśmantaka, gojī, yamalaka, and kaṇṭaka.
Having reduced ciribilva, arka, kaṭvaṅga, samaṅgā, madhuśigru,
gopaghoṇṭā, and himārī to ashes, [one should mix them] with cow's urine.

Having caused the discharge [of pus] according to the procedure for alkaline preparations, one should cook it after adding and sprinkling with two parts of long pepper (*pippalī*), *kośātakī*, blood, *saptaparṇa*, and *elavāluka*.
Varāṅga, coca, mañjiṣṭhā, kuṣṭha, vañjula,
and tuṇṭuka; viḍaṅga, ativiṣā, anantā, sarṣapa, and taṇḍulīyaka.
Surāhva, sarala, plakṣa, gṛhadhūma, karañjaka,
nāgadantī, sutaśreṇī, nicula, varuṇa, and vacā.
A *bilva* fruit that has grown large and reached a state of alkaline ripening should be placed in an iron vessel and kept ready at all times.
With that [substance], one should smear the drum, as well as the banners and coverings;
through sight, hearing, and touch, these render [the poison] non-toxic.
When drunk, this alkaline antidote (kṣārāgada) destroys all poisons, both stationary and mobile,
as well as colic, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, consumption, dyspnea, cough, urinary calculi, and gravel.
It cures swelling, hemorrhoids, disorders of the digestive tract, and loss of appetite;
it even destroys the pride of snakes as venomous as the Takṣaka.
Śrīveṣṭaka, manohvā, sarjarasa, and vālaka—one karṣa each;
one prakuñca of nāgapuṣpa; and twenty parts of truṭi.
Sixty-four *hareṇu* seeds, four *kuṭannaṭa* fruits,
and sixteen *śatāhvā* flowers— one should collect these under the Puṣya asterism and grind them into a paste.
Under the asterism Āśleṣā, in the midst of cows, [the child] should be protected by weapons and mantras;
there, this mantra composed by Viṣṇu is to be recited by a maiden who has bathed.
My mother is named Vijayā, my father is named Jaya;
I am the son of Ajaya, and through Vijayā, I shall conquer you all.
This medicinal preparation called Sugandha, when used for constant anointing of the body,
prevents exhaustion in battle and brings victory in disputes.
Parasols, drums, banners, and archways smeared with this [substance] destroy all poison, whether stationary or mobile, merely by being seen, touched, or heard.
Even while staying at home, one should ward off possession by spirits, children’s diseases,
and insanity with *prapauṇḍarīka*, *sarala*, *devadāru*, and *kuṭannaṭa*.
Jaṭā, śatāhvā, ativiṣā, tilaparṇī, sugandhikā,
nīlī, yivaphala, bhārṅgī, madhuyaṣṭī, and elavāluka.
Toya, toyada, kālīya, tagara, dhyāmaka, and tvac;
nakha, padmaka, punnāga, patra, and kālānusārivā.
Tālīsapatra, marica, joṅgaka, the two types of candana, the two types of elā, viṣa, sevya, the two types of tā, the two types of niśā, and the two types of nalada.
Lākṣā, śītaśiva, vyoṣa, phalinī, dhānya, gairika,
śaileyaka, śilāpuṣpa, granthila, coraka, and abhayā.
Arka, sthauṇeya, pṛthvīkā, kaṭukā, candrarāja,
kaliṅgaka, sarjarasa, kuṣṭha, and the five salts (lavaṇapañcaka).
[The oils] produced from śrīparṇikā, aśmarī, śelu, and śiṃśapā; those originating from sinduvāra, campaka, aśoka, surasa, sumana, and tilvaka.
The blossoms of the *pāṭalī* and *tṛṇaśūlya*, as well as the *kumuda* and *utpala* lotuses, and the flowers of the *tiniśa*, *arjuna*, *śamyāka*, and *dhava* trees, together with the *paṅkaja* lotus.
This powder of eighty-five ingredients, combined with cow's urine, ghee, and honey,
should be placed inside a cow's horn; then, one should bring back the person [who had been taken away] and restore them to life by means of it.
With its shoulders broken and eyes rolled back, it has entered between the fangs of Death;
this one, known by the name Mahāsugandha, possesses extreme heroism and blazing splendor.
It wards off even the most difficult-to-restrain poison-fire of Vāsuki;
a king whose limbs are anointed with this shall become beloved by all people.
Even when standing in the midst of a royal assembly, he attains brilliance; furthermore,
he should provide cooling treatment for those afflicted by poison.
Having released that insect poison, it indeed increases greatly through cold.
[The following grains are beneficial]: aged *śāli* rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, *koradūṣa*, and *priyaṅgu*.
Mudga, hareṇu, tuvarī, paṭola, and cane sprouts;
taṇḍulīyaka, jīvantī, vārtāka, and suniṣaṇṇaka.
Jāṅgala meat, pomegranate, āmalakī, wood-apple, rock salt, sugar,
and whatever else is known not to cause a burning sensation (avidāhin) by its very nature [should be used].

One should give those various [remedies] to those afflicted by poison; the seasoning and preparation of the food should be done with decoctions of anti-poisonous herbs, with ghees such as Kalyāṇaka, and so forth.
One afflicted by poison should drink water that has been drawn from a celestial lake or a well, or otherwise boiled and cooled, combined with honey and *āmalaka*.
Water from rivers and ponds should be avoided, especially at the onset of the rainy season; well-prepared barley flour (saktu) should be consumed by those dressed in white garments.
Taken with buttermilk and ghee, these are supreme destroyers of poison.
One should avoid sesame, liquor, horse gram, hunger, anger, fear, exertion, and sexual intercourse [after consuming them].
Even one who has been freed from poison should especially avoid sleeping during the day—
one whose humors are pacified, whose bodily constituents are in their natural state, who desires food, and whose urine and feces are balanced.
The physician should recognize that a person whose complexion, senses, mind, and movements are clear and serene is not poisoned.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter.
Now begins the forty-eighth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter titled "The Application of Antidotes to Poisons. Thus said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
Regarding poison, an antidote should be administered; if it is not successful, one should employ mantras and ritual procedures (*tantra*).
In the past, during the fifth surge and before the seventh had passed,
while the Lord was in the state of nirvāṇa, he, being self-restrained, did not explain it to anyone;
having first performed the binding of the earth, he became a holder of perfected mantras.
Indeed, poison does not become uncontrollable when accompanied by mantras.
Generally, poison possesses qualities similar to phlegm (śleṣman); it is stable and tends to move upwards.
Generally, that which is endowed with the qualities of pitta moves downward;
when these [qualities] are reversed, they strike one another down.
Therefore, one should administer root-poison (mūlaviṣa) for both drinking and as an ointment for those who have been bitten; furthermore,
an expert should bite one who has swallowed poison with snakes that subsist on air.
There is nothing that neutralizes poison like poison itself.
[The dose] is low, medium, or high, measured by four, six, or eight barley grains respectively.
One should administer the appropriate dose of primary poison as follows:
two barley-corns for one bitten by insects, but the size of a sesame seed for one stung by scorpions.
In the case of one bitten by a spider, a drink placed on the sister [plant] is not desired at all.
When it is poisonous, even nectar is like poison; when it is non-poisonous, poison is like nectar.
In a weak person, or when there is excessive morbidity due to the mode of administration,
one should administer antidotes even when there is suspicion of poison or non-poison.
For even a non-poisonous medicine, when administered in contradiction [to the rules], becomes poison;
and likewise, even a poisonous one does so through the transgression of the proper time for action.
Therefore, a physician should diligently ascertain the presence of poison.
[One should use] *sāktuka*, *mustaka*, *śṛṅgī*, *vālaka*, and that which is called *sarṣapa*.
Poison that resembles the navel of a calf, which is functional, unctuous, dense, and heavy—
never another kind should be employed, especially not *kālakūṭa*.
When a potent poison has been administered, ghee mixed with bhārgī, curd, the smoke [of the aforementioned substances], sārivā, and taṇḍulīyaka should be drunk immediately thereafter.
Or one should lick the powdered bark of *Arjuna* combined with house-soot,
*mañjiṣṭhā*, and *yaṣṭīmadhu*, mixed with honey and ghee.
Taken with milk, honey, and ghee, it destroys even the most virulent poison. This "reviver of the dead" poison, combined with *sinduvāra* and *tagara*, [is likewise effective].
The curved flower of the *śirīṣa* tree removes the poison of rats and other poisons.

Devadāru, nata, māṃsī, drāmilī, bākucī, viṣa, and kuṣṭha— these, through both drinking and external application, are the pacifiers of all poisons. Manaḥśilā, añjana, elā, sinduvāra, and amarāhvaya [likewise serve this purpose].

Poison mixed with saffron and blood, when blown [into the nostrils], awakens one who is unconscious. For a burning sensation arising from poison, an application of roasted grain flour (saktu), milk, and ghee is beneficial.
But when a serpent, being provoked to anger, emits smoke from its mouth, [it is a sign of death].
Having tied a piece of flesh to the tip of a staff, the physician should have the patient bite it many times;
this is impossible to treat with any other medicines once the poison has been drunk.
One should have him drink that powder of meat, having ascertained the strength or weakness of the poison;
and in other diseases as well, when all remaining remedies have been exhausted.
One who seeks an elixir (*rasāyana*) should always employ poison [under controlled conditions] for one whose body is prepared with ghee, who is purified, and who eats wholesome food.
When the sun has risen for one of a sattvic constitution, [the treatment] should be applied during the cool season and spring;
it may also be used in summer in cases of urgent illness, but not during the rainy season when the weather is foul.
One should not [administer] it to one who is angry, nor to one afflicted by bile, nor to a eunuch, nor to a king, nor to a twice-born man,
nor to one oppressed by hunger, thirst, fatigue, heat, travel, or internal disease.

One should carefully avoid administering poison to pregnant women, children, the elderly, those who are emaciated, or those whose vital organs (*marmans*) are vulnerable, even if one is practiced in its administration.
One should always avoid pungent, sour, oily, and salty foods, sleeping during the day, exposure to the sun, and fire; especially dry food, fear, and indigestion [are to be avoided],
as they cause disorders of vision, earache, and other diseases born of wind (vāta).
In one who eats dry food, poison may cause death due to indigestion. It is sufficient to dry [the medicine] for three days in the sun, combined with cow urine.
This poison is indeed nourishing and is recommended at the very beginning of poisoning.
One should drink it with whey in a fever caused by Vāta, or with milk in one caused by Pitta.
In cases arising from *kapha* or from all three *doṣas*, [the enema] should be prepared with urine or with the decoction of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*).
It should contain *lodhra*, sandalwood, *ṣaḍgranthā*, sugar, ghee, and honey.
Poison combined with milk is an excellent remedy for chronic fever. A preparation made from Nikumbha, Kumbha, Triphalā, ghee, honey, and poison [is likewise effective].
The *modaka* (sweetmeat), when combined with the juice of *śikhī* and *karka*, destroys chronic fever, urinary disorders,
and skin diseases; it is an unequalled conqueror of intermittent fevers.
Viṣa, yaṣṭyāhvaya, rāsnā, sevya, and utpalakandaka,
when drunk with rice-water, are the remedy for raktapitta.
Visha, rasāñjana, bhārṅgī, vṛścikālī,
and mahāsahā constitute a medicinal paste for foul ulcers that are painful and characterized by suppuration.
The tender shoots of the white *aviṣa* and *kṣīra* trees, melted with honey and licked,
cure dyspnea and hiccups; when combined with poison, they destroy vomiting.
Honey, uśīra, madhuyaṣṭi, alkali, turmeric, and the bark of kuṭaja;
vijayā, pippalīmūla, the two types of pippalī, and citraka— [these should be used].
One should cook one *pala* each of the following: *puṣkarāhvā*, *śaṭhī*, *drākṣā*, *yavānī*, *kṣāra*, *dīpyaka*, sugar, *yaṣṭī*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, and *saindhava*.
One should drink one *prastha* of ghee prepared with half a *pala* each of [the aforementioned] ingredients along with poison; having digested it, one should eat food.
This cures hemorrhoids, urinary disorders, abdominal tumors, cataracts, blindness, worms, and anemia.
It cures throat-obstruction, seizures, insanity, and leprosy;
it destroys difficult dysuria, and [the drugs] viṣa, pathyā, agni, dantī, drākṣā, niśā, and viṣā are [also] effective against poison.
Bitumen, poison, and cow’s urine remove upward-moving wind (udāvarta), urinary calculi, and stones. Cow’s urine, alkali, rock salt, poison, and *pāṣāṇabheda* [are also used for this].
Like a thunderbolt, this single yellow substance tears away the stone; likewise, long pepper with its root, urine, and poison destroy colic.
Viṣadravantī, madhuka, drākṣā, rāsnā, śaṭhī, kaṇā,
castor oil, triphalā, cow’s urine, citraka, and viṣa.
When drunk together with clarified butter, it cures *vātāṇḍatva* (scrotal enlargement caused by Vāta). Triphalā, svarjikākṣāra, and poison are a means for breaking up abdominal tumors (*gulma*).

The milk of a cow that has licked poison or a *vellami* plant destroys abdominal tumors (*gulma*) and the spleen (*plīha*). *Śatāhvā* taken with milk cures splenic enlargement (*plīhodara*), and poison kills worms.
A decoction of the roots of *vāyasī* drunk [with honey] removes leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) and poison. [It is prepared] from the bark of *vāyasī*, *rājavṛkṣa*, *trāyantī*, and the fruit of *bākucī*.

Poison [taken] with a decoction of *plīhaghna*, *ibha*, and *kaṇā* conquers *kuṣṭha*. The seeds of *avalguja* and *aiḍagaja*, along with the two types of alkali (*kṣāra*) and poison, [are used for the same].
A paste made by grinding these with water along with rock salt (saindhava) destroys skin diseases (kuṣṭha). [It is prepared] from citraka, the root of arka, hastipippalī, bākucī, and viṣa.
With *manaḥśilā*,
realgar, *snuk*-milk, and poisons ground with cow’s urine; and with *candralekhā*, the fruit of *iḍagaja* and *karañja*, and rock salt.
With the paste made from trikaṭu, svarjīkṣāra, yavakṣāra, the two types of niśā, and soot (agāradhūma), all combined with goat's urine; AS.Utt.48.47.

An ointment made from *bhallātaka*, *agni*, and *śamyāka* mixed with poison and ground with cow’s urine cures *vicarcikā*, *dadru*, *śatāru*, and *kiṭibha*. Similarly, the leaves, bark, and root of *śamyāka*, along with poison and buttermilk, possess the same therapeutic properties.
One may conquer vitiligo and the severe *puṇḍarīka* leprosy with a plaster made from the fruits of *viṣa*, *bhallātaka*, *dvīpi*, *guñjā*, and *nimba*, ground together with sour liquids.
One should drink vakra, kuṣṭha, rasā, dvīpi, spṛkkā, patra,
and elavāluka, ground with khadira water and allowed to steep for three nights.

In the case of a person with vitiligo (śvitrin) who has been affected by poison, one should incise the eruptions arising from the skin disease (kilāsa) with a thorn and then apply ointments prepared from kuṣṭha.
Alternatively, [one may prepare a paste] with karavīra, the root of arka, bākucikā, and viṣa,
ground with cow’s urine, together with vīpi, dvipa, pippalī, and aruṣkara.
Lākṣā, surāhvā, mañjiṣṭhā, kuṣṭha, padmaka, sārivā,
the fruit of guñjā, kurabaka, lāṅgalī, and vajrakandaka.
Vārāhīkanda, Kāsphota, Saptāhva, Girikarṇikā, the roots of Arka and Aśvamāra, Nāgapuṣpa, Nata, and the two Niśās.
One should cook danti, ativiṣā, pippalī,
and marica with either oil or mustard oil to prepare an ointment for the application on vitiligo (śvitra).
Equalizing the color [of the urine] is the best method, as is the word of a believer;
[the herbs used are] vīrā, lāṅgalikī, dantī, and viṣapāṣāṇabhedaka.
A plaster made from the fresh juice of *bījapūra*,
*vacā*, the juice of *brāhmī*, and ghee is to be applied for the delivery of obstructed fetuses.
A barren woman drinking [the milk] mixed with poison is surrounded by many sons;
one whose semen is lost [is cured by] milk, grapes, *kapikacchū*, and *vacā* mixed with poison.
Poison, ghee, sugar, and honey applied as a collyrium remove *timira*. Furthermore,
poison alone, ground with goat's milk and fumigated with ghee, [achieves the same].
Poison that has been repeatedly processed with the juice of *dhātrī* fruits,
combined with conch shell as a collyrium, destroys even deep-seated darkness of vision.
Poison rubbed on breast milk acts as a collyrium that removes cataracts;
likewise, poison rubbed with the juice of *bījapūra* and combined with sugar has the same effect.

Poison, long pepper, the two types of *niśā* (turmeric and black turmeric), and glass-like collyrium [are used]; poison combined with black [turmeric] and processed with cow’s urine cures white *arma*.
Sea-foam, crystal, kuruvinda, lime, collyrium,
and tortoise-shell are equal [in potency]; from these, realgar (manaḥśilā) is one part more.
One should add half as much black pepper, rock salt, and the dust of iron filings;
thereafter,
one should add mercury in an amount equal to the iron.
This medicinal preparation (rasakriyā), taken with honey, removes white pilla and arma;
the eyes affected by poison should be repeatedly sprinkled with cold water.
First, the *pilla* (eye disease) should be scraped with a probe and then treated with a paste made from garlic bulbs, black pepper, poison, mustard seeds, rock salt,
and the juice of *surasā*.
One should fill [the vessel] with ghee and subsequently cause the patient to drink that very ghee,
which has been prepared with the essence of *madhūka*, *madhuka*, *viṣa*, milk, and water.
In cases of long-standing night-blindness, a cooked, nourishing diet is best; for headache, an errhine (nasya) consisting of *pratyakpuṣpī*, sugar, and *viṣa* alleviates the pain.
Alternatively, ghee, licorice, and sugar combined with poison [cure it]; likewise, ginger, harītakī, poison, pāṭhā, and dravantī overcome putrid rhinitis.
Pungent oil (kaṭutaila) and poison used as a nasal drop (nasya) remove gray hair and facial eruptions.
Poison combined with svarjikākṣāra, rock salt (sindhūttha), and fermented gruel (śukta) is supreme [for this purpose].
Filling the ears with [an oil prepared from] prapauṇḍarīka, mañjiṣṭhā, viṣa, and sindhusamudbhava destroys severe earache.
Oil prepared with these [ingredients], used as a gargle, destroys diseases of the mouth.
Devadāru, viṣa, ghee, cow’s urine, and kaṇṭakārikā [are also used].
Kāśyapa has said that when it is drunk, it destroys the stammering of speech,
[as well as] poison or *gara* administered by an enemy.
From spiders, serpents, and swarms of mice, from old age, untimely death, or the affliction of malevolent planets;
"For a man who consumes poison, there is no fear"—
thus ends the forty-eighth chapter;
thus the sixth limb, named the *Viṣatantra*, is completed.
Now begins the forty-ninth chapter.
Hereafter, we shall expound the chapter named "The Procedure for Rasāyana."
Thus indeed have the great sages, Ātreya and others, declared:
[it bestows] long life, memory, intelligence, health, youthfulness,
luster, complexion, nobility of voice, and the arising of strength in the body and the senses.
Through this elixir (rasāyana), one attains perfection of speech, virility, and splendor;
for rasāyana is indeed the means for obtaining the excellence of grains, juices, and other such things.
This should be administered in early or middle age to one who has conquered their self,
whose body is unctuous, whose blood has been drained, and who is thoroughly purified in every respect.
For when the body is impure, the procedure for rejuvenation (rāsaāyana) does not shine forth,
just as a dye applied to a garment stained with dirt does not appear.
Even for one who is disciplined, free from the defects of improper preparation, and perfectly vigilant,
the elixir does not succeed through human effort alone, just as it would otherwise fail.

Moreover, all the *doṣas* arise in those who consume village-derived foods that are sour, salty, pungent, alkaline, incompatible, unwholesome, dry, obstructive, moist, heavy, putrid, impure, stale, new grain, dried vegetables, raw meat, sesame, horse-gram, curd, fermented vinegar, sour gruel, flour-based foods, sprouted grains; who are constantly addicted to daytime sleep, women, and alcohol; whose bodies are agitated by irregular and excessive exercise and physical exertion; who abound in anger, greed, fear, grief, and fatigue; who perform evil deeds; and who are devoted to improper diet, conduct, and excretion.

For this reason, the rasa becomes impure; it undergoes inflammation, the blood is vitiated, the muscles become flaccid, the fat liquefies, the bodily constituents (doṣas) are corrupted, the joints become loose, the marrow in the bones does not nourish, and there is no semen, no vitality, no strength, and no vigor.

Then, having become thus, he languishes and sinks, overcome by sleep, drowsiness, and laziness; he becomes distressed and despondent, lacking enthusiasm and incapable of performing specific physical or mental activities. With his complexion faded, his memory lost, and his intellect diminished, his desired ends remain unaccomplished; sighing incessantly day and night, he becomes the very seat of diseases and does not attain even the full lifespan he has acquired.

Therefore, a wise person, having abandoned the aforementioned defects regarding food and other factors, and having eliminated those previously accumulated, should practice *rasāyana* as prescribed by rule.
That [practice] is of two kinds: *kuṭīprāveśika* (entering a small chamber) and *vātātapika* (exposure to wind and sun).
In that regard, because it involves the application and avoidance of the power of vigor with greater intensity, the "entering-the-hut" (kuṭīprāveśika) [practice] yields far greater fruit.

The method for its construction is as follows: in a village or city that provides security, abundant food, righteous people, faith, and a king, physician, and Brahmins; where great medicines, ghee, milk, wholesome food, and medical equipment are easily available; in a region sloping toward the northeast with well-divided quarters for recreation; one should have a small hut built in such a place, with walls that are firm, thick, and well-polished, possessing adequate height and width, with narrow windows, consisting of three chambers, comfortable according to the seasons, free from drafts yet with one side providing ventilation, with its door facing either east or north, surrounded by *śamī*, *bilva*, or milky trees, inaccessible to undesirable objects of the senses, wind, heat, dust, smoke, sweat, moisture, gadflies, mosquitoes, reptiles, predatory beasts, children, women, slaves, and outcasts, and situated near a qualified physician, attendants, and medical supplies.

In that [autumn], one seeking a *rasāyana* should enter [the treatment] during autumn or spring, in the bright fortnight, on an auspicious day; having honored the gods, teachers, and Brahmins as is appropriate, having bowed to Brahmā, Dakṣa, Aśvin, and others, having touched gold, ghee, honey, white mustard, *priyaṅgu*, and yellow pigment (*rocanā*), and having circumambulated cows and Brahmins, he should enter.
There, having been purified by cleansing therapies, happy, and having regained his strength, he should again observe celibacy, be endowed with fortitude, full of faith, and have conquered his senses.
Devoted to generosity, ethical conduct, compassion, truthfulness, vows, and righteousness,
he is intent on the recollection of the deities and disciplined in his sleep and wakefulness.
One who loves medicine and possesses eloquent speech should undertake this elixir (rasāyana):
Harītakī, Āmalaka, Saindhava salt, Nāgara, and Vacā.

A person who has first been lubricated and fomented should drink turmeric, long pepper, vella, and jaggery with warm water; by this means, he is properly purged. Then, for one whose body is purified and who has undergone the process of gradual dietary restoration (saṃsarjana), [the following treatment should be administered].
For three nights, five nights, or seven days, one should consume barley-gruel mixed with ghee until purification is achieved,
or else until one's excrement becomes old.
Having thus prepared the vessel,
one who knows what is wholesome for each individual should administer the elixir (rasāyana) after considering everything appropriate for that person.
That which is called *harītakī* because it removes all diseases,
is called *pathyā* because it is wholesome for all the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), and is called *śivā* because of its auspiciousness.
Because it conquers all diseases, it is called Vijayā;
from it comes freedom from fear of all ailments and eternal life.
Because it is practiced by those who cultivate it, it is known as "Fearless" (Abhayā). That which is new, round, dense, smooth, and heavy sinks in the water.
That [enema] should be administered to a child combined with fresh butter;
in cases of Vāta it should contain ghee and salt, and in Pitta it should contain jaggery and sugar.

In cases of *kapha*, that [preparation] with long pepper (*pippalī*) and honey is always recommended. (AS.Utt.49.22) Now, one should take one *āḍhaka* of *harītakī* fruits grown on the Himālaya mountains, harvested at the proper time, fully matured in juice and potency, healthy, and free of stones; these should be split into two or three pieces. Having steamed them with four times as much milk until they become soft, one should remove them from the heat. When cooled, one should mix them with one *āḍhaka* each of clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) and honey, and store the mixture well-protected.
Thereafter, after three nights have passed, one should consume daily a measured amount that does not obstruct the intake of food; for life, one should eat *śāli* and *ṣaṣṭika* rice with milk.

At the conclusion of the regimen, for that same duration of time, by virtue of this practice, a person becomes free from old age, wrinkles, baldness, graying hair, and disease for a hundred years, endowed with the wisdom of the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, and possessed of a kindled digestive fire.

One who diligently partakes of this yoga attains a large body as strong as the essence of a mountain, a voice that resembles the thundering of a mass of clouds, and offspring that are numerous and stable.
One thousand *pathyā* fruits combined with three times that amount of *dhātrī* fruits,
along with two hundred and fifty palas of the five groups of five roots (*pañcapañcamūla*).
Having boiled [the fruits] in ten parts of water until the liquid remains as one-tenth,
and having then crushed the *vijayā* and *āmalaka* fruits so that their seeds are removed;
Having strained that decoction, one should add one *kuḍava* each of cinnamon,
cardamom, nut-grass, turmeric, long pepper, eaglewood, and sandalwood.
Maṇḍūkaparṇī, kanaka, śaṅkhapuṣpī, vacā, plava, yaṣṭyāhvaya,
and viḍaṅga— these, powdered together, should be taken in a quantity exceeding one tula.
One should cook half a bhāra of sugar, three prasthas of clarified butter,
and two [prasthas] of oil; when all that has reached the state of a thick consistency on the fire, it is ready.
One should add melted snow to three hundred parts of honey;
then, having stirred it with a churning rod, one should place it in a vessel of clarified butter.
This Brahma elixir is in every respect equal to the previous one;
by consuming it, the Vaikhānasas and Bālakhilyas attained youthful vigor once again.
In a decoction made from the fivefold *pañcamūla* consisting of *abhayā*, *āmalaka*, and *vibhītaka*, one attains boundless health, longevity, and freedom from drowsiness,
fatigue, and exhaustion.
One should cook one *kumbha* of ghee with twice the amount of the juice of *vallī* and *palāśa* leaves, and eight times the amount of milk,
along with *madhuka*, *madhūka*, the two types of *kākoli*, *balā*, and *svaguptā*.
One should drink the milk of a white bull that still has its calf, along with water; this is rich in qualities.
One should grind one thousand *āmalaka* fruits according to the procedure for steaming ground substances, thoroughly steamed by the heat of milk, dried in the shade, and then deprived of their seeds.

Then, one should take one thousand fresh *āmalaka* fruits and soak them in their own juice. To this, one should add a powder consisting of one-eighth part each of *sthira*, *jīvantī*, *punarnavā*, *nāgabalā*, *maṇḍūkaparṇī*, *brahmasuvarcalā*, *bhīru*, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *vacā*, *pippalī*, *viḍaṅga*, *svaguptā*, *amṛtā*, *aguru*, *candana*, *madhuka*, *madhūkapuṣpa*, *padma*, *utpala*, *navamālikā*, *yuvatī*, and *yūthikā*. This mixture should then be soaked for a day in the juice of one thousand palas of *nāgabalā* and dried in the shade. Having mixed it with double the amount of clarified butter and honey, it should be formed into the shape of small lumps of jaggery, placed in a vessel of clarified butter, and buried beneath a heap of ashes in the ground for a fortnight, protected by one who knows the *Atharvaveda*. At the end of the fortnight, having extracted it and added one-eighth part each of the powders of gold, silver, copper, coral, and black iron, one should administer it in the morning according to one's digestive fire, increasing the dose by half a *karṣa* as before; the results are the same as previously described.

One should steam one thousand fresh *āmalaka* fruits in a covered trough made of *palāśa* wood, ensuring that no steam escapes, using fires of wild cow dung. Once they are well-steamed and cooled, they should be removed, de-seeded, and crushed. Then, one should combine them with one *āḍhaka* each of long pepper (*pippalī*) and *viḍaṅga* seeds, one and a half *āḍhakas* of sugar, and six parts each of honey, ghee, and oil. This mixture should be placed in a jar of ghee and stored for twenty nights; thereafter, it may be used, as previously described.

One should soak one thousand *abhayā* and *āmalaka* fruits together with one thousand *pippalī* seeds in the alkaline water of young *palāśa* leaves, and place them in a clean vessel. Then, once the alkaline liquid has been absorbed and the mixture has dried out of the sun's heat, it should be ground into a powder, freed of its husks, and combined with a quarter-part of sugar-candy and four parts each of honey and ghee. This should be placed in a ghee-pot and buried underground for six months; thereafter, one should consume it according to one’s digestive strength. The rest is the same as previously described.

One *āḍhaka* of *āmalaka* powder, saturated with *āmalaka* juice for twenty-one nights, should be mixed with one *āḍhaka* each of honey and ghee, along with an eighth part of *pippalī* powder and a fourth part of sugar. Placed in a vessel of ghee, it should be buried in a heap of ashes during the rainy season; it should be used in the autumn, as previously described.

One *āḍhaka* of *viḍaṅga* seeds, one *āḍhaka* of *pippalī* seeds, and one and a half *āḍhakas* of white sugar, combined with six *āḍhakas* each of honey, ghee, and oil, and placed in a vessel of ghee during the rainy season upon a heap of ashes—this is identical to the previous [preparation].

One should take one thousand *pala* of *abhayā*, *āmalaka*, and *bibhītaka* fruits—combined in pairs or triplets, wrapped in *palāśa* bark, coated with clay, roasted in a pit of embers (*kukūla*), and de-seeded. Having crushed these in a mortar, one should consume them mixed with curd, honey, ghee, oil, sesame paste (*palala*), and sugar, while abstaining from other food according to the prescribed regimen. At the conclusion of the treatment, for twice the duration, one’s diet should consist of gruel, broth, milk, ghee, and *ṣaṣṭika* rice; likewise, the use of ghee as an ointment, *yava* powder for rubbing the body, and so forth, is the same as previously described, yielding even greater results.
Daśamūla, balā, musta, jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, and utpala.
Parṇinī, pippalī, śṛṅgī, medā, tāmalakī, and truṭi;
jīvantī, joṅgaka, drākṣā, pauṣkara, candana, and śaṭhī. (AS.Utt.49.40)
Furthermore, one pala each of punarnavā, the two types of kākolī, kākanāsā, the two types of amṛtā, vidārī, and the root of vṛṣa should be taken together.
One should boil five hundred myrobalan fruits in one droṇa of water; from that,
when one-fourth remains, one should remove the seeds and the rinds of the myrobalans.
Having taken [the ingredients], one should fry them with twelve palas of oil or ghee;
mixed with half a tulā of granulated sugar (matsyaṇḍikā), one should cook it like a linctus (leha).
When it has cooled, one should add half a pala of ghee, four palas of tugākṣīrī,
two palas of pippalī, and half a pala each of the four aromatics (caturjāta) and kaṇā.
Therefore, one should lick this in the proper dose while staying in a small room and eating wholesome food.
This is the Cyavanaprāśa, by consuming which the sage Cyavana [attained his longevity].
Though worn out by old age, he remained a delight to the eyes of women;
[he was free from] cough, dyspnea, fever, consumption, heart disease, and gout.
It removes disorders of the urine, semen, and the internal heat (uṣman), as well as hoarseness of voice;

it promotes the growth of the limbs for children, the elderly, those with chest wounds, the emaciated, and the lean; and it bestows intelligence, memory, luster, freedom from disease, longevity, and the downward movement of the wind (vāta).

When used according to the prescribed method with madhuka, tālakṣīrī, pippalī, and saindhava salt, it produces exhilaration toward women, strength, and vigor of the senses, as well as [vitality] like that of fire.
Combined with various metals, gold, lac, honey, clarified butter,
or sugar, it constitutes an elixir (*rasāyana*).
Triphalā destroys all diseases and bestows intelligence, longevity, memory, and wisdom.
One should smear a new iron vessel with a paste of triphalā.
One should drink that plaster, prepared for a day and night, dissolved in honey-water;
once it has been digested, the administration of abundant fats is recommended as a pacifier.

By the regular practice of this for a year, one lives for a hundred years free from disease and old age. One should eat *prāṇadā* for a year, consuming one dose every morning before food, and two doses at other times.
At the end of a meal, one should take four fruits of the *dhātrī* (myrobalan) tree along with clarified butter and honey; this is sufficient for maintaining youthfulness.
Now, one should have iron leaves made, four finger-breadths in length and breadth, and one *tila* (sesame seed) in thickness.

Having heated those [iron balls] until they are the color of fire, one should quench them twenty-one times in the fresh juice of *āmalaka* fruits. Having placed one hundred palas of such [quenched iron] in an iron vessel, adding an excess of *āmalaka* juice, and having sealed it well, one should bury it in a heap of ash.
Every month, one should extract [the essence] and stir it with an iron rod;
as it dries, one should pour in the fresh juice of *āmalaka* as before.
In this manner, those iron plates become liquefied after one year.

Thereafter, having undergone emesis and purgation, while his body is still in a state of oleation, he should take a single spoonful (*sruva*) from that paste using an iron spoon with a mouth the size of a thumb-joint, into an iron vessel; having mixed it separately with honey and clarified butter using the spoon, he should consume it. Once digested, he should eat fresh *ṣaṣṭika* rice mixed with clarified butter along with milk, meat broth, or vegetable soup. By following this regimen for one year, and for another year as well, eating the prescribed diet and restraining his senses, he should reside within the chamber (*kuṭī*).

Then, having conquered all afflictions, he lives for two thousand years, unassailable by disease, old age, death, weapons, fire, water, or poison; transcending the senses regarding all phenomena, he possesses the speed of a horse and the strength of an elephant, and is endowed with mindfulness and intelligence.
He becomes eloquent, a bull among men, a retainer of what he has heard, possessed of great enjoyments and great wealth;
this indeed is the specific rule regarding copper, silver, and gold.
One should know that its excellence of qualities increases twofold in each successive stage. Gold, *dhātrī* fruit, and honey, consecrated with the *gāyatrī* mantra—
One who licks and drinks milk survives even when faced with fatal signs.
Gold, lotus seeds, honey, parched grain, and *priyaṅgu* [are the remedy].
Drunk with milk, it is the supreme remover of misfortune. Those who lick gold mixed with lotus seeds, *āmalaka*, and *abhayā*, along with clarified butter and honey, [attain prosperity].
Those who eat honey, māgadhikā, the essence of viḍaṅga, triphalā, gold, ghee, and sugar become long-lived, with diminished aging and affliction, and they become unapproachable even to reptiles.
One whose bodily luster is untouched by old age and whose humors are balanced shall live for a hundred years if gold, bilva,
vacā, and ṛṣabhaka are used together in a single preparation.
Śatāvarī ghee, when licked along with gold and honey, bestows purity, longevity, health, splendor, good fortune, and nourishment.

One who desires long life should take it together with *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, and one who desires intelligence should take it with gold and strong-smelling substances; this makes one live for a long time and brings kings under one's control.

One desiring prosperity should eat [the powder] mixed with lotus filaments; one desiring love should consume the fresh juice of *vidārī* and *maṇḍūkaparṇī*; and one should take the powder of *yaṣṭīmadhuka* with milk according to one's digestive capacity.
One should employ the juice of *guḍūcī* along with its roots and flowers, and also the paste of *śaṅkhapuṣpī*.
These [remedies] bestow longevity, destroy diseases, and increase strength, digestive fire, complexion, and voice.
These are purifying elixirs (*rasāyana*); among them, *śaṅkhapuṣpī* is especially purifying.
[Also] *nalada*, *kaṭurohiṇī*, *payasyā*, *madhuka*, *candana*, *sārivā*, and *ugragandhā*.
Triphalā, the three pungents (kaṭutraya), the two types of haridrā, paṭola, and salt— these, well-ground,
should be cooked with three times as much juice of śaṅkhapuṣpī, along with milk, ghee, and salt. AS.Utt.49.66
By using this, even a dull-witted person becomes eloquent, a retainer of what he has heard, possessed of genius, and free from disease.
Ghee prepared with milk and the paste of lotus stalks, lotus filaments, leaves, and seeds, along with pieces of gold, [achieves these results].
That which is celebrated on earth as the "five-lotus" (pañcāravinda), which is to be cultivated by those whose human strength and prowess have faded;
that which, like the stalk, bulb, petal, and filament of a blue lotus, ripens— this too is renowned upon the earth.

Clarified butter mixed with four *kuvalaya* fruits and gold leaf is purifying even for cows, let alone for humans. *Brāhmī*, *vacā*, rock salt (*saindhava*), *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *matsyākṣaka*, *brahmasuvarcalā*, and *aindrī* [are likewise beneficial].

Three barley grains of *vaidehī*, two barley grains of gold, and three of poison— these should be combined with one *pala* of clarified butter; once this has been digested, one should administer a meal rich in ghee.
By practicing this regimen of food with honey for a year, one gains superior intelligence, memory, and mental acuity,
and transcends old age, disease, drowsiness, laziness, fatigue, and exhaustion.
One lives for a full hundred years, endowed with splendor, vigor, beauty, and radiance; specifically, [this cures] leprosy, vitiligo, abdominal tumors, poison, fever, insanity, and dropsy.

By this [herb], magical spells (kṛtyā) performed through Atharvan mantras and the like are pacified, as are exceedingly powerful winds. One should uproot the Nāgabala plant together with its roots during the month of Tapas or Tapasya, under the constellation Puṣya and at an auspicious moment, according to the prescribed rite; it should be grown in soil possessing the aforementioned qualities, be neither too young nor overripe, have its old leaves decayed and no new leaves yet emerged, and be free from other vegetation.

One should drink a paste of its roots, the size of an *āmra* fruit or an *akṣa* fruit, either finely ground or mixed with powder, along with milk; or one should lick it with honey and ghee. Once it is digested, one should subsist solely on milk, or eat *śāli* and *ṣaṣṭika* rice with ghee and milk.
Thus, by practicing this for one year, one remains free from decay for a hundred years; the rest is the same as previously stated.

The ten medicinal herbs mentioned for maintaining youth—balā, atibalā, candana, aguru, dhava, tiniśa, khadira, kadara, śāka, and śiṃśapā—as well as asana, surasā, punarnavā, and anantā, are explained in the same manner as vidārī, śvadaṃṣṭrā, aśvagandhā, vārāhī, śatāvarī, and nāgabalā.
In that regard, for all heartwood trees when seeking their expressed juice (*svarasa*) for the treatment of *kuṣṭha*, one should observe the procedure for *khadira*.

However, if fresh heartwood is unavailable, one should take thin chips of heartwood two or three finger-breadths long, soak them in four times the amount of water, and leave them in the sun for three nights.
Then, having removed those [juices], one should pour others into that [vessel];
after three nights, again others [should be added]. In this manner, by pouring and removing [the juices] nine times, the natural juice (*svarasa*) is prepared.
Furthermore, for fruits, creepers, and medicinal herbs, one should crush them with a press or a mortar, squeeze them, and extract the natural juice.
Of those that have been completely dried and reduced to powder, one āḍhaka each should be placed in water for a day and night; once stirred and strained, it should be used like a fresh juice.
Furthermore, there is a separate instruction regarding *tuvaraka*, *bhallātaka*, and others:
"The trees known as *tuvaraka* grow on the shores of the western ocean.
When the clouds arrive, one should gather from them well-ripened fruits, whose sprouts are shaken by the wind and tossed by the agitation of ripples and waves.
Having taken the seeds from the fruits, dried them, and ground them into powder,
one should press them in a mill like sesame seeds, or boil them like safflower.

That oil, having been collected again, should be cooked until the water is completely evaporated; then, having removed it from the fire, one should store it in a heap of dried cow-dung for exactly one fortnight.
Having been well-anointed with oil and having his impurities removed, the diligent person should,
after a period of one fortnight, drink a palmful [of the medicine] in the morning, skipping the fourth meal.
With this mantra, on an auspicious day, [one should use] this oil: "O essence of marrow, of great potency, purify all the bodily constituents!"
"Acyuta, who holds the conch, discus, and mace in his hands, commands you: by this [procedure],
the humors (doṣas) shall repeatedly depart from him, both upward and downward."
In the evening, one should drink cold gruel (yavāgū) prepared without oil or salt;
for five days one should drink oil, and in this manner, one should avoid things that are prohibited.
One who eats food with *mudgara* juice for a fortnight is liberated from all types of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*).
That same [preparation], well-cooked in three times as much *khadira* decoction, [achieves the same].
Restraining oneself well, one should drink the previously described decoction for a month; having anointed the body with that [oil], one should take the prescribed diet.
By this application, one may quickly cure a man suffering from leprosy who has a broken voice, bloodshot eyes, withered limbs, and is infested with worms—
even if he is treated without the *khadira* [bark], provided that [the medicine] is drunk combined with clarified butter and honey. (AS.Utt.49.88)
If one consumes meat broth as food for a fortnight, it results in a lifespan of two hundred years;
that same [substance], when used as nasal drops (nasya) for fifty days, [yields the same result].
It makes one free from wrinkles and graying hair, with firm memory and lustrous teeth; it bestows a beautiful body, the retention of what has been heard, and a lifespan of three hundred years.
Its marrow, well-burnt with smokeless fire and mixed with rock salt heated to the color of fire,
when applied as a collyrium in equal parts, destroys *arman*, night-blindness, *kāca*, *nīlī* disease, and *timira*.
One who eats wholesome food and follows the regimen should drink *tauvaraka* oil at intervals of one day for a month; thus,
with the digestive tract opened and the regions of the limbs softened, he will quickly cast off his skin like a snake shedding its old slough.
One should boil one *āḍhaka* of *tuvara* in sixteen times its quantity of water;
when reduced to one-eighth, it should be strained and then crushed in a mortar.
One should mix powdered dried *āragvadha* bark with its own paste,
and from that, using the decoction water, prepare jaggery balls (*guḍa*) the size of *udumbara* fruits, which should be dried in the shade.
A person suffering from leprosy should take one of these [medicines] together with cow’s urine or stirred with water; remaining without food on that day, he should drink it when the sun has set.

At that very time and in that same manner, one who knows the defects and strength of the person should administer the medicine again at the time of sunrise, regardless of whether the previous dose has been digested or whether vomiting has occurred.
At midday, one should eat a large quantity of *niṣpāva* beans with oil, along with *kaṅgu* grain porridge accompanied by a side dish of *śigru* roots;
this should be served with curd mixed with a small amount of powdered sea salt (*sindhūttha*), followed by a small quantity of cow’s buttermilk and water.
Having anointed his body with oil and having rubbed it with a powder of *kaṅgu* and *viṣṭikā* for the duration of a day,
he should bathe with pleasant water; avoiding liquor, meat, and sexual intercourse, the benefit from this practice shall be threefold.
By applying the entire formulation twice daily with diligent effort,
even a leper whose ears, lips, and nose are shattered can cast off the disease.

Now, one should collect bhallātaka fruits that are unblemished, free from disease, full of juice, size, and potency, and resembling a ripe jambu fruit, during the month of Śuci or Śukra; having stored them in a heap of barley or a heap of mung beans,
one should begin to use them after they have been kept for four months, in the month of Sahas or Sahasya.

Having prepared the body with cold, unctuous, and sweet substances, one should first crush ten *bhallātaka* fruits and boil them thoroughly in eight times their weight of water. When the decoction is reduced to one-eighth, it should be cooled, mixed with milk, and drunk in the morning after an oil gargle (*gaṇḍūṣa*) has been applied to the lips, palate, and tongue.
In this manner, these ten *bhallātaka* fruits should be used for thirty days, increasing and decreasing the dose by one fruit at a time.

By this method, the application is performed a thousand times, and the duration is threefold. One should consume *śāli* and *ṣaṣṭika* rice with ghee and milk. Thus, specifically, one becomes free from leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), hemorrhoids (*durnāmaka*), worms, urinary disorders (*prameha*), and defects of the fat (*medas-doṣa*), remaining free from decay for a hundred years; the rest is the same as previously stated (AS.Utt.49.100).
Previously, one should drink a decoction of one *bhallātaka* fruit with milk, and increase the number of *bhallātaka* fruits by one each time until they reach five (AS.Utt.49.100).
Then one should increase by five [units] up to seventy,
and having reached seventy, one should decrease [by five] again until reaching five;
