from five, one should decrease by one each time until reaching one.
By this procedure, one thousand [applications] and so forth are the same as previously described;
one should consume one hundred and seventy.
And likewise, the application of two thousand [years] and so forth is the same as before;
however, the duration of life is doubled.

Having filled a vessel for steaming with crushed *bhallātaka* fruits, one should place it upon a sturdy jar smeared with oil that has been buried in the ground up to its neck; having sealed it with a lid and smeared it with black clay, one should apply heat using a fire of cow dung.
Of those fruits, the juice which enters the jar should be consumed mixed with one-eighth part honey and double the amount of clarified butter.
Time is composed of the three qualities (*triguṇa*). [The procedure] beginning with "with ghee and milk" is the same as the previous one.
By this very method, having extracted the juice of *bhallātaka*, one should employ it alone for one month.
Time consists of the three qualities (guṇas), and so forth, as previously described;
month by month, there is an increase of a hundred years in lifespan.
Thus, by consuming [the elixir] for ten months, the lifespan becomes one thousand years.
One should consume a vessel of *bhallātaka* oil with milk, processed a hundred times (*śatapāka*) with a quantity of *madhuka* equal to one *akṣa*;
the duration of time, being threefold, and so forth, is the same as previously stated.

One *droṇa* each of bhallātaka oil, black sesame oil, ghee, and the juice of *āmalaka*, along with a decoction of the heartwood of the *asanādi* group—these being mixed together with one *pala* portion each of *triphalā*, *trikaṭu*, *viḍaṅga* heartwood, *citraka*, the two types of *haridrā*, *trivṛt*, *dantī*, *indrayava*, *yaṣṭīmadhuka*, *viṣā*, *ativiṣā*, *rasāñjana*, and *priyaṅgu*—should be cooked according to the procedure for preparing medicated oils. Having removed it from the heat and strained it thoroughly, one should store it in a well-protected place.
Then, having prepared the body [through oleation and purification], one should consume it every morning, mixing a measure of one *pāṇiśukti* with honey.
When that [mudga] soup has been digested, one should eat soft boiled rice prepared with *khadira* water and mixed with unsalted ghee and *āmalaka* soup.

All water-related needs should be met with *khadira* water. Having thus consumed one *droṇa* [of this preparation], one becomes free from skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), hemorrhoids (*durnāman*), and so forth; the rest is the same as previously described.
Mature *bhallātaka* fruits, fallen naturally through ripening and measuring one *āḍhaka*, [should be used].
Having ground it with fine brick powder, washed it with water, and dried it with air,
one should boil the shattered pieces in a jar of water until one-fourth remains; this should then be strained, clarified with ghee, and cooled.
One should boil that juice again with a jar of milk over a low fire;
once the ghee is cooked, one should add an equal measure of it, along with sugar powder as desired.
Having unified that [mixture], it should be kept well-protected for seven nights in grain while being stirred with a ladle.
He who consumes this "elixir of immortality" (*amṛtarasa-pāka*) in the morning, and afterwards drinks water, milk, or meat-broth as desired, [attains the desired result].
Endowed with memory, intelligence, strength, wisdom, courage, and vitality, and possessing a complexion as bright as gold on a touchstone, he enjoys a long life.
From three hundred *droṇas* of water boiled down to one *āḍhaka*, one *pātra* of sesame oil should be cooked with one *pala* each of the [following] ingredients.

A preparation made of *tikta*, *aviṣā*, the two types of *varā*, *girijanman*, and *tārkṣya*, processed with *āmalaka*, *śukti*, curd-serum (*dadhisara*), or oil, is supreme for the destruction of all skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*).
With jaggery, milk, ghee, or barley flour, together with sesame, honey, meat paste, or soup.
Bhallātaka fruits bestow a beautiful body, remove anger, are supremely purifying, and promote longevity; they are sharp, digestive, and like fire in their potency.
When administered according to the prescribed rules, these [medicines] become almost like nectar;
there is no disease born of phlegm (kapha) nor any kind of constipation that they do not cure.
One should especially avoid *bhallātaka* even when following the regimen for wind and heat, for it may cause death and does not quickly bestow digestive fire and strength.
Kulattha beans, curd, and vinegar; oil massage and exposure to fire;
five, eight, seven, or ten long peppers (pippalī) with honey and ghee.
One seeking the qualities of rejuvenation (rasāyana) should employ it for one year; specifically,
three [measures] in the forenoon, and three after having eaten, at the beginning of the meal.
Long peppers (pippalyaḥ) that have been saturated with the alkali of *kiṃśuka* and fried in ghee should be consumed mixed with honey by one desiring the qualities of a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*).
For ten days, they should be increased in dose by one daily, until on the tenth day one consumes ten long peppers.
One should increase the dose together with milk and likewise decrease it again;
once the medicine has been digested, one should eat ṣaṣṭika rice with milk and ghee.

This application of a thousand *pippalī* fruits is a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*). Those [fruits] should be ground into a paste and drunk by those of strong constitution, or boiled and drunk by men of moderate strength.
These [medicines], having been cooled, should be administered against the humors (doṣa) and diseases by those with weak strength;
likewise, one should administer two thousand [drops] with goat's milk.
By these applications, long pepper (pippalī) cures cough, dyspnea, and throat obstructions.
It destroys consumption, urinary disorders, malabsorption syndrome, hemorrhoids, anemia, irregular fevers,
edema, vomiting, hiccups, splenic enlargement, and gout.
One should consume an equal portion of powdered *viḍaṅga* mixed with powdered *yaṣṭīmadhuka* along with cold water.
When the mudga-soup has been digested, one should eat boiled rice with ghee and saltless soup;

by this, especially, worms, hemorrhoids, skin diseases, urinary disorders, and defects of the fat are eliminated, and one remains free from decay for a hundred years— the rest is the same as previously stated.

One should employ these four formulations for one month: *viḍaṅga* powder with honey and a decoction of *bhallātaka*; honey and the juice of *āmalaka*; and a decoction of *guḍūcī*. This is the same as previously described for all of them;
and in every month, there is an increase of a hundred years in lifespan.
*Alambuṣā*, having been processed (*bhāvita*) with its own juice, [should be taken] separately with ghee, milk, honey, and warm water.
Likewise, one suffering from fistula-in-ano, pain, abdominal tumors, or cough should drink *kāñjika* with buttermilk and *mastu*.
It is hot in its post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), pungent, and astringent-sweet in taste.
It is an extreme stimulant, pure, and it removes wind and phlegm;
by its use during the rainy season, it makes a man live for a hundred years.
One who possesses firm sense organs and the strength of fire, and is free from wrinkles, grey hair, and disease,

should take white *avalguja* fruits dried in the sun, grind them into a powder, mix it with an equal amount of jaggery, knead the mixture, place it in a jar of ghee, and bury it for seven nights in a heap of grain.
Then, before the sun has risen, one should consume the dose according to one's strength, followed by a drink of warm water.
Once it has been digested, having bathed with warm water, one should eat rice or *ṣaṣṭika* rice with milk mixed with sugar.

By using this for one month, one becomes especially free from leprosy (kuṣṭha), possesses the capacity for retention and memorization, and remains free from aging for a hundred years; the rest is the same as previously described.
Furthermore, after the course of treatment, the regimen of avoidance is doubled.
One should drink one karṣa of the powder of *vākucī* with lukewarm water.
Having drunk [the medicine], one should stay in the shade, or in a windless and warm inner chamber during the afternoon; likewise, one should bathe and eat with vegetable broth or meat broth.
By practicing this for twenty-one nights, one becomes free from leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) and so forth, as described previously;
however, excluding the skin, hair, body hair, teeth, and nails, one obtains them again renewed.
One attains excellence of voice, complexion, strength, and energy, as well as renewed youth and the removal of gray hair. Ten *palas* of *bākucī* and ten *palas* of the three fruits [should be used].
One should take three *pala*s each of the seven [drugs] beginning with *krimighna*, two *pala*s of *girisambhava* (realgar),
and one *pala* each of *purā* and *puṣkaramūla*.
Half a pala each of small cardamom, the three pungents (vyoṣa), bamboo manna, saffron, lodhra, cinnamon bark, leaves, liquorice, and leadwort; one karṣa each of the others.
One hundred bhallātaka fruits, together with all their kernels and flesh,
should be ground into powder; one should then consume a maximum dose of one pala of that.
Acting as one desires, one obtains the benefits of rejuvenation (rasāyana) after a year;
one conquers all diseases, especially skin disorders.

It [cures] hemorrhoids, fistula-in-ano, dyspnea, cough, anemia, and worms; it increases [the size of] abdominal tumors, splenic disorders, urinary stones, urinary disorders, anorexia, and chronic rhinitis.
One should soak the fruits of *vākucī* in cow urine for seven nights to treat sluggish digestion, emaciation, as well as swellings, nodules, and tumors.

Then, having removed the husks, dried it in the shade, and ground it into a very fine powder, one should successively saturate it every three days with the decoction of triphalā, and separately with the fresh juices of kāravellī, vāsā, brāhmī, guḍūcī, and bhṛṅgarāja, as well as with the decoctions of khadira, asana, rājavṛkṣa, and picumanda. When this [powder] is drunk daily, saturated with the juice of āmalaka fruit, [it bestows the desired results].
One karṣa [of this] destroys all diseases, especially skin disorders,
when the *somarājī* has been processed with the decoctions of *asana* and *khadira*.
One who consumes a linctus composed of honey, ghee, long pepper, chebulic myrobalan, and iron powder,
while eating sparingly and wholesomely, abandons disorders arising from the transformation of food (pāriṇāmika) as well as those born of diet.
He whose body is afflicted by severe leprosy, if he should eat *somarājī* according to the prescribed rule for one year,
accompanied by black sesame seeds, will surpass others in beauty of form.
Those who extract the essence from well-prepared milk mixed with the dehusked powder of *somarājī*,
lick it with honey, and subsequently drink that very same buttermilk at the end;
Those lepers have eyes with sparse eyelashes,
or their ears, fingers, and noses are shattered.
Having abandoned their deformity and cast off their [former] form,
the trees appear as if they have sprouted anew;
one who attends to the sun should drink that with water of the *khadira* tree, or that gruel (*yavāgū*) with it.
One suffering from leprosy who has mastered the *gāyatrī* water and performs its prescribed rites [is cured]; likewise,
one who drinks the alkali of elephant dung and eats only gruel [is freed from the disease].
*Somarājī* forcibly destroys vitiligo when applied as a paste; likewise,
one should soak the fruit of *śaśiśakala* in cow’s urine for seven nights and then grind it.

One should dry the *prapuṇāṭa* fruit separately in the shade; once dried, a portion of each of these two, along with a portion of *kṛmighna*, *agni*, and *sphoṭakṛt*, should be made into a powder. When this powder is consumed with cow’s urine by one who eats measured and wholesome food, it quickly destroys skin diseases (*śvitra*).
Iksu, agokṣura, siṃhī, vyāghrī, and pañcāṅgulā, when drunk with water, [act as a remedy].

Bākucī, when ground with hot water and drunk mixed with ghee, destroys even a stone-like or dense *gulma* caused by those who consume [only] liquids. Once it has been digested, one should consume gruel prepared with the light *pañcamūla*.

Bākucī, when processed with the soups of kaṭvaṅga and kuṭaja, destroys hemorrhoids and fistula-in-ano; when processed with fermented liquors (madya) and nigada, it overcomes powerful urinary disorders.
If drunk with the juice of *viṣkira* birds, or with the decoction of *daśamūla*, or with *guḍūcī*,
it destroys *apatantraka* or *āyāma* in one who consumes meat broth and rice.
In cases of abdominal enlargement, one should drink *avalguja* with urine; in dropsy, with *traivṛta* ghee;
in swelling, with vegetable broth; and in the disease of jaundice, with *śīghra* and *ariṣṭa*.
A poultice made with decoctions of *ikṣuraka* and other plants, mixed with cow urine or warm milk, is recommended for the *vardhana* stage;
it destroys swelling and fever.

In cases of bites by spiders, insects, rats, and snakes, a decoction of *kṛmighna* and *caturaṅgula* should be applied with warm water; in cases of worm-infested ulcers, the lukewarm decoction of *kṛmighna* and *caturaṅgula* should be used.

By drinking the crescent of the moon mixed with ghee and lukewarm water at the time of the rising of the Puṣya constellation, a woman becomes possessed of sons; and by eating [with] milk boiled with *aśvagandhā*,
even a barren woman who performs this regimen for seven days becomes fragrant and joyful.
A woman who speaks kindly, is devoted to virtuous vows and purity, and observes these restraints, gives birth to sons rich in excellent qualities.
When combined with unctuous, warm, and sweet substances, she removes diseases born of Vāta, as well as those associated with Pitta.
Those caused by *kapha* are treated with bitter, sweet, and astringent [drugs], as well as with the juice of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) and honey.
Thus, this auspicious pacifying [therapy] destroys poison, artificial poisons, possession by spirits, and sinful influences.
Even a line of the moon’s rays, though situated within a house, [destroys darkness], how much more so when it is within a vessel?
Even a man who has come under the decree of death, whose intellect and senses are lost and whose mind is diminished— [is likewise overcome].
The *avalguja* plant delivers one from great fear and bestows abundant prosperity and intelligence.
One should drink a bolus of Himalayan *vacā* the size of an *āmalaka* fruit, stirred with milk; once it is digested, the diet should consist of milk, ghee, and boiled rice.
Thus, by seven nights one becomes intelligent;
by seven times seven nights, one becomes a retainer of what has been heard (*śrutadhara*) and remains free from decay for a hundred years, and so forth, as described previously.
One should also drink a decoction of two palas of the other *vacā* (Acorus calamus); when that has been digested, one should take milk, ghee, and so forth, as described previously.
Alternatively, one should lick that powder with honey and ghee according to one's strength.
When it has been digested, milk, ghee, and so forth are the same as previously described.

By consuming one *droṇa* of ghee that has been processed a hundred times with a paste of *vacā*, one is specifically freed from seizures (*graha*), insanity (*unmāda*), epilepsy (*apasmāra*), goiter (*galagaṇḍa*), cervical lymphadenitis (*gaṇḍamālā*), elephantiasis (*ślīpada*), and hoarseness of voice; one becomes successful in all undertakings and attains a lifespan of a hundred years.
For those whose bodies have been scorched by cold winds and frost, whose bones are stiff, broken, crooked, or afflicted,
and who are overcome by disorders of Vāta, the procedure for garlic as a medicine shall now be described.
From the throat of Rāhu, who had stolen the nectar, when it was severed,
drops of that nectar fell upon the earth and attained the state of garlic.
The twice-born eat that which arises from the body of a Daitya;
it is the leader of elixirs, produced directly from nectar itself.
One who has a predominance of phlegm (kapha) should consume garlic during the cold season and spring;
one afflicted by wind (vāta) may do so even at the onset of the rainy season, or always, as if for the pleasure of summer.
Diseases arising from *rakta-pitta* occur in those suffering from *rakta-pitta*.
For one month thereafter, they prescribe the consumption of meat juices and medicinal pastes at will; however, this applies only to those who have undergone the *vimardaka* treatment.
They say that a regimen of six months according to another method is not recommended, nor even a fortnightly application, for it is inferior in the case of *rasāyana*.
One whose body has been lubricated and purified, and whose internal constitution has been prepared with cooling and sweet substances,
[should proceed].
His courtyard was graced by attendants adorned with those very flowers as their ear-ornaments and head-crests;
at the end of spring, he [gathered] the tubers of that [mountain] growing in the region of the Himavat and Śaka.
At night, one should remove the bark and soak it with wine and other liquids; in the morning, its paste and expressed juice should be strained through a clean cloth.
Combined with one-third of well-fermented liquor (*madirā*),
or with another type of intoxicant, buttermilk (*takra*), whey (*mastu*), or sour gruel (*kañjika*).
Or, at that very time, having considered what is appropriate, one should administer oil, ghee, muscle fat, marrow, milk, and meat broth, each separately in the proper measure.
One should drink either a decoction according to the specific disease, or the juice alone,
in the quantity of a mouthful (gaṇḍūṣa) beforehand, for the purpose of purifying the throat and the channels.
Continuous fomentation is recommended during the stage of pain; however,
in cases of sudden vomiting or fainting, sprinkling the face with cold water is advised.
One should drink the remainder when fatigue has subsided and the *ojas* has attained stability;
for the avoidance of burning heat (*vidāha*), one should apply a cooling ointment.
One should wear drops of water, strings of pearls and camphor, lotus stalks as white as the moon containing cold water, garlands of blue lily petals, and swaying strands of pearls.
Women of lovely limbs, reclining upon the slopes of their breasts and anointed with thin, fragrant unguents, should embrace him firmly;
[he should be fanned] with winds from lotus leaves and palm-leaf fans, with trickling drops of water, and with a cloth moistened by water.

And with the cool sprout-like hands of their beloveds, they may remove the exhaustion caused by the heat of perspiration. A *kuḍava* is its maximum dose, while half of that is for the pure [substance] alone.
One should first practice consuming one *pala* of ground marrow along with boiled rice;
for the digestive fire becomes like that of Agni, being both mild and endowed with vitality.
If administered too hastily,
it may cause burning sensations, diarrhea, loss of appetite, and mental confusion; therefore, one should not administer it in haste.

When the previous meal has been digested, one should eat old *śāli* rice— which is as white as a conch shell, a jasmine flower, or the moon— along with soups, milk, or the meat-broths of animals that roam in arid lands.
One with a stimulated digestive fire should eat *maṇḍaka* cakes,
sprinkled with clarified butter and adorned with pieces of white lotus that possess the luster of the full moon.
Bound with leather straps that have lost their stiffness through contact with mustard seeds and vinegar,
When there is a continuous flow of thirst, one should drink a single measure of that wine mixed with water,
which is as fragrant as a buzzing bee intoxicated by scent and awakened by the moon-like face of a beloved woman.
He who does not drink intoxicants may drink fruit water, *tuṣodaka*, *vāruṇī*, *soma*, fragrant and cool liquids, *sauvīraka*,
the meat broth of wild animals, *tuṣodaka* (rice-water), or *parisikthikā*.

Or one may take that paste mixed with an equal amount of ghee, stirred with a churning-stick in a vessel of ghee; after it has stood for ten days, one should consume it, or likewise [consume it] together with animal fat.

One may administer this immediately ground [drug] combined with clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*), or as desired, combined with its own resin (*niryāsa*). It should be taken with the aforementioned drinks or with lukewarm water; for this preparation is exceedingly potent.
A paste of garlic mixed with fresh ghee, buried in the ground for six months,
destroys mental disorders and irregular fevers when used as an ointment, for drinking, as a collyrium, or as nasal drops.
Or, having kept equal parts of oil and fermented gruel (śukta) for a long time within a heap of barley,
one may conquer wind diseases by eating them while consuming a diet rich in ghee and meat.
One should take one *tula* each of oil, ghee, jaggery, and sugar;
two *tulās* of cleaned garlic; and three *kuḍavas* of the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*).
One pala of the bark, finely ground and placed in a vessel of ghee,
along with two palas each of the other two ingredients, when situated in the middle of barley, possesses qualities superior to the former.
One should throw one *tulā* of crushed *kanda* into twenty *palas* of buttermilk;
after seven nights have passed, [one should add] half a *tulā* of black sesame.
From the washed and crushed [mixture], one should separately take four palas each of honey, ghee, and ginger, along with cumin,
chaba pepper, coriander, the two types of black pepper, bael fruit, and bishop’s weed.
One *pala* each of the four aromatic spices (*caturjātaka*), finely ground;
one *pala* of oil; eight *palas* of ghee; and crushed mustard seeds.
One should add five pungent substances and two alkalis in the measure of one *akṣa* each; having kept that in grain for eleven days, one should consume it every morning.
Free from disease, he obtains all the rejuvenating qualities [of these herbs]. One *āḍhaka* of garlic should be added to a strong decoction of the two groups of five roots (*dvipañcamūla*).
The flour of this plant, when soaked overnight for a year, destroys diseases caused by Vāta and Kapha.
One should cook ghee and oil separately with the paste and the fresh juice of its tuber.
One afflicted by the pain of a severe fire should apply [the remedy] according to what is suitable; or, having ground it into a paste with an equal portion of fresh butter, one should rub it on.
One may eat to one's heart's content various meats on spits accompanied by diverse side dishes, containing abundant juices free from husks,
or *nimardaka* preparations mixed with ghee and vinegar, while consuming only light and insubstantial food.
With dishes featuring cumin, coriander, and fried green gram, sprinkled with the fine powder of black salt, and variegated with the bulbs,

One who fears an excess of phlegm, bile, or wind should drink, in due order, soups, milk, and meat broths prepared from the roots of those [plants], processed with their respective medicinal drugs.
One with a weak voice should consume a preparation of *yaṣṭimadhu* mixed with the powder of *uśīra* and *aśvagandhā*.

One suffering from abdominal tumors (*gulma*) should take it with oil; one with skin disease (*kuṣṭha*) with *khadira*; and one afflicted by worms should eat garlic (*rasana*) with anthelmintic drugs.

One cures consumption with the flesh of carnivorous animals, hemorrhoids with the bark of *kuṭaja*, and [furthermore] urinary disorders, cough, asthma, and dyspnea with the best [medicinal substances].
Having understood the true nature of food and having perceived its specific characteristics,
one should apply it appropriately for each respective disease.
From thirty-two *prasthas* of garlic juice, thirty-two from sesame oil,
two from fermented yeast (*kiṇva*) free of impurities, eight from flour, and six from barley.
From one *droṇa* of the decoction of *meṣaśṛṅgī*, once it has been strained and cooled,
one should place it together with an equal amount of oil in a clean and sturdy vessel.
Thereafter, one should gradually administer four *prasthas* of flour paste;
after a fortnight, this gruel or wine may be consumed by those suffering from disorders of *vāta*.
Then, after the cow has been kept for three nights, one should feed it garlic;
even for a Brāhmaṇa, milk, curd, and churned butter produced from that are recommended.
In pure air, which is free from bile and blood and devoid of all obstructions, there exists no substance superior to garlic.
Garlic liquor (laśunāsava) is especially to be employed for those whose nature is characterized by suffering;
this was prepared by Nārada for Uddhava, who had been paralyzed by wind (vātabhagna).
In this condition, one should avoid undigested food, drinking water, products of sugarcane, fish, traveling by vehicle, walking on foot, exposure to wind and sun,
excessive talking, worry, sleeping during the day, staying awake at night, flour-based foods, sexual intercourse, and curd.
One should administer garlic prepared with fats according to the rules for the preparation of oleaginous substances; indeed,
through its combination with fats, it becomes more potent.
At the end, one should employ mild purgation out of fear of provoking the *pitta*;
in this way, one enjoys the full benefits of the *rasāyana*.
Garlic (rasuna) certainly leads to complications for one who loves water, jaggery, milk, meat, wine,
and sour flavors, and for one who lacks digestive endurance and suffers from indigestion.
In cases of jaundice, abdominal enlargement, internal hemorrhage, swelling, thirst, alcoholism, vomiting, poisoning, and wounds;
in Pitta-type disorders, eye diseases, diarrhea, and emaciation of the body— he [the purgative] should be avoided.
When practiced, this [rite] produces a body and strength as difficult to attain as fire, equal [in power],
for a man and woman who desire a son rich in intelligence, beauty, and virtues, provided there is purity of seed.
He who always eats garlic during the cold season, prepared according to the prescribed method and arising from drops of nectar (*amṛtakaṇa*),
shall live for a hundred years accompanied by women; he will possess a complexion as beautiful as gold, be free from disease, and be filled with contentment until the end of old age.
Immediately after garlic, onion is the supreme medicine for wind disorders;
it is as if the very life of the Lord of the Śakas were present therein.

By the use of which, the moon— vanquished by the radiance of the cheeks of Śaka women who were fashioned from the very essence of beauty— descends to the subterranean realm as if out of sheer despondency.
Through the practice of which one attains smoothness of limbs, fairness of complexion, luster, radiance, robustness of body, and virility—
freed from the distress of restraint— one obtains enduring and pleasant happiness.
On account of having been habitually consumed as food for a long time, this onion— strengthening, beneficial for the eyes, satiating, and stabilizing—
is joined with various formulations and eradicates those various ailments of those suffering from urinary disorders.
Having drunk its juice like that of garlic, one should eat [garlic] in the same manner; likewise for one who drinks the fresh juice of *bījapūra*, wine, or *madhuśīdhu* liquor.
Its stalk is as blue as an emerald gem, its seed is exceedingly tender and white as the full moon, well-ground;
it takes on form when combined with *surasā* and *sumukhā*, abundant meat, sour gruel (*śukta*), and soft, white, well-rounded *maṇḍakas*.
It was repeatedly adorned with white *ghārikā*, *iṇḍarikā*, and creepers, which resembled fragments of the moon and appeared like portions of the Ocean of Milk.
Various kinds of foods prepared from barley, mung beans, black gram, and wheat;
*kāmbalika*, *rāga-ṣāḍava*, *saṭṭaka*, *khalaka*, and the essence of fruits.
One should habitually consume drinks made from dates, pomegranates, sugar, and grapes, which possess a sharp, fragrant, and sweet aroma and contain an abundance of white, clear, and thick juices.
By drinking that juice like garlic, even one whose feces and blood have been depleted obtains strength, complexion, vitality, vigor, voice, cheerfulness, and luster.
It is said that in ancient times, when the gods and asuras churned the ocean of milk, there were drops of nectar that fell upon the shore;
from them the *kukkuṭī* plant arose, by which humans today attain a state like that of the deities.
With bulbs resembling hen’s eggs, slightly pungent and slimy,
glossy with the luster of emeralds, and with leaves like those of the date palm;
This [medicinal formulation] specifically conquers even severe wind-disorders (*vātavyādhi*),
removes hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, darkness [of vision], and poisons, and produces supreme firmness of the body.
Having entered a hut, one should eat those tubers fried in ghee;
milk, fresh warm water, or rainwater is desired as a drink in that case.
One who consumes only those [specific] substances for ten days, or eats only sweet foods for twenty days without negligence,
shall overcome disorders of the wind (*vāta*) in the clavicles, the upper trunk, and the *trika* joint, as well as anemia (*pāṇḍu*), hemorrhoids (*arśas*), and cataracts (*timira*).
Free from wrinkles and graying hair, with firm hair, teeth, and ears,
and endowed with intelligence, understanding, and memory, he shall live for two hundred years.
Starting from the first day of the waxing moon,
one should gradually increase the dose of the bulb by one each day; fried in ghee, it should be eaten before a meal by one who follows a wholesome diet.

The sage should eat very little for half a day; at the end of the fortnight, by consuming milk, *bījakā* water, or buttermilk, he may maintain his existence. Likewise, by eating meat [made from] nails, teeth, and hair that have fallen out and grown back, he becomes radiant and lives for three hundred years, adorned with fortitude, intelligence, memory, and other such qualities.
Drinking the powder of the bulb with milk and barley gruel for a month after it has been digested,
one who avoids salt and fats, possessing firm vision, shall live for two hundred autumns.
One who eats wholesome food (pathya) will conquer *timira* and its dust (*rajas*) within a month by using honey and ghee; likewise,
one who eats the three tubers fried in ghee will overcome the *vāta* disorders.
Having cooked those *kanda* roots with fine flour mixed with one-third part of wheat flour in milk,
one should eat these *ghṛtapūra* cakes, which remove inguinal hernia (*āntravṛddhi*).
One should eat three *kandaka* bulbs fried in ghee at night, along with the juice of *dhātrī* fruit mixed with sugar, or the milk of a *cangalī* cow;
this should be consumed for the sake of conquering eye diseases, and it may be used as desired by those whose only aim is the alleviation of the ailment.
That plant which possesses milky sap, has a bulb equal in size to a radish, seven or eight leaves, and black or red stalks,
and which bears a sprout at the sound of the year (i.e., once a year), is the excellent *kañcukī* with its white body.
In the months of Āṣāḍha or Kārttika, that tuber remains cool;
it measures two joint-lengths of a thumb and, when ground, [is mixed] with eight palas of milk.
Having drunk that [mixture] while entering the hut, one should drink only milk afterwards;
and when that too is digested, one should drink gruel fried with oil.
One should touch water that is slightly warm, pure, and unsalted; one should not use cold water.
In this manner, within seven nights, one subdues even the skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
By the second [mantra] one casts off all diseases, and by the third, like a snake casting its worn-out skin, one likewise casts off hair, teeth, and nails.
One who possesses wisdom, intelligence, and beauty shall live for five hundred years;
or [one may take] the powder of the *kañcukī* tuber, processed with its own milk.
One karṣa of [the powder] mixed with one pala of sugar,
taken in a kuḍava of cow’s milk, destroys all fears— even those residing in the nails and hair.
Likewise, its own juice, or its powder combined with honey and ghee, should be drunk.
By eating this for seven days while consuming wholesome food, one conquers skin diseases and blindness.
[The powder consists of] viḍaṅga, tāpya, triphalā, iron, and kañcuki.
Restraining the senses, one should lick [the medicine] with honey for twenty-one days;
when it has been digested, one should take a meal of *śāli* rice with milk or with the juice of *labā*.
Likewise, for such a person, the severe eye diseases caused by *kāca* and *timira*, as well as ailments of the head,
are destroyed; the intelligent man regains his senses, and his numb body awakens.
This powder of the seven nectars (saptāmṛta) is honored for all diseases. One pala of the powder of kañcukī should be added to one prastha of milk.
Then, having conquered the self, one should lick the fat of curd mixed with sugar and honey;
for one month, one should consume Śāli rice and drink milk, practicing this regimen.
The avoidance [of these] possesses fourfold merit; with a radiance equal to that of the moon,
one shall live for five hundred years, as powerful as a god.
One should boil twenty-five palas of kañcukī in one droṇa of these [liquids];
when one-eighth remains, one should cook a prastha of ghee with an equal amount of milk.
With *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, *trivṛtā*, and *amaradāru*, along with *varā*, *yaṣṭī*, sugar, *drākṣā*, and *mahiṣākṣa*, each taken in a measure of one *pala*.
In this winter season, one should take three palas of lotus filaments mixed with honey and add four palas of honey; this is called Martyāmṛta (the nectar for mortals).

One should boil three palas of kañcukī and three well-powdered palas of iron; [this preparation] is beneficial for the eyes, nourishing, promotes intelligence, improves the complexion, and bestows a lifespan of a hundred years.
Four from the seed of *palāśa*, ten from two fruits,
eighteen from *śatāvarī*, and twenty-one from *bījaka*.

One should cook sixteen parts of fresh [medicinal substances] together with one part on the full moon day; when the decoction has been reduced to one-fourth in the water, [one should add] separately half an āḍhaka each.
One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with *kāñjika* and curd-whey,
along with a *picu*-measure each of *śatāhvā*, *aruṣkara*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, *elā*, *biḍa*, and *hiṅgu*.
With three palas each of sauvarcala salt and lotus filaments,
five palas of lotus seeds, and twelve lotuses.
Having drunk this nectar of Soma, that Soma who still shines even today—
by using this ghee of exceeding potency and noble qualities, one becomes eloquent, wise, very firm and strong, and fortunate.
With a body invincible against the fears of planets, spirits, calamities, and poisons, and having conquered the fever of old age, he shall live for two hundred years.
O Lord of the Dānavas, in former times, the gods were defeated by you, and their beauty, fortitude, patience, and splendor fell away.

Having beheld it, Viṣṇu indeed created amṛta, as well as guggulu, which bestows strength, a beautiful body, and victory; even today, for this reason, the hosts of gods, having set aside their primary incenses— agaru, turuṣka, hima, and indudarpa— rely upon these.
He whose fragrance, when drunk by those whose bodies are being consumed by fire, causes them to rejoice and attain serenity—
he is the bearer of yoga, he is Śiva, he is the All-pervading One, he is to be served in all seasons, and he is to be cultivated for happiness.
It is the destroyer of old age, sin, impurities, and diseases; the creator of fire, intellect, memory, and sharpness;
it is intensely fragrant, unctuous, liquid, and slimy, and it is free from any foreign matter.
Mahiṣākṣa has the luster of a topaz, a ruby, crystal, or a white cloud; it may have the redness of a lotus-gem or the pale-pink hue of a cut of gold.
This mantra, praised by the sage Ātreya, brings success in ritual action; it triumphs like a stainless sapphire that, though broken, possesses radiant luster in its proximity.
The Blessed One, the lotus-eyed one, and the gods together with Purandara—
just as those deities have arisen from the sufferings of old age and death.
O you of great strength, likewise become a consumer of this; indeed,
[prepare it] with a decoction of the great *pañcamūla* for one who eats wholesome food.
Guggulu, when habitually consumed, destroys all diseases caused by Vāta and Kapha;
likewise, it does so even more effectively when taken with lukewarm water.

Or one may use sour gruel made from mastu-grains, wine, or water boiled with vacā and other herbs; likewise, [medicines] from the varana group cure deafness and alleviate pain in the teeth, ears, and head.
It is desired for disorders of voice, abdominal enlargement, dyspnea, hernia, internal tumors, and abscesses,
as well as in diseases of vāta, pitta, and blood (rakta), and for one who desires nourishment.
With a decoction of *vājigandhā* or of the *jīvanīya* group,
or with a decoction produced from blue lotus, grapes, and red sandalwood.
This [mixture] destroys vāta and pitta, whether it consists of the padmakādi group, or of cavya, kuṣṭha, and viḍaṅga, or of nāgara.

Guggulu taken with the decoction of *prasāriṇī* conquers *kapha* and *vāta*. One should consume *mahiṣākṣa* mixed with equal parts of *tryūṣaṇa*, *agni*, *ghana*, *vella*, and *varā*, along with clarified butter.
Patola, nimba, triphalā, guḍūcī, gāyatrī, the two types of arka, and bījaka quickly destroy even powerful disorders arising from the humors of kapha, vāta, fat, and marrow.

For one who is devoted to wholesome diet, these decoctions taken separately destroy even the most terrible diseases of *kapha* and *pitta* within a month; they are especially effective against swelling, erysipelas, malignant ulcers, and fistula-in-ano.
[It cures] defects of semen, menstrual blood, and the mind, as well as urinary disorders (prameha), leucoderma (śvitra), and anemia (pāṇḍutā).
Paṭola, ariṣṭa, and rasāñjana— equal parts of these, ground into a paste with a decoction [of the same drugs],
[are used].
Śilājatu, when drunk with milk in equal measure, cures galagaṇḍa, apacī, tumors, enlargement of the glands, and worms, as well as vātaśoṇita (gout).
It turns back even the most powerful [disease] in one who consumes milk,
meat, and ghee; it removes vāta, pitta, and kapha through its juice, milk, or urine.
With the juices of *brāhmī*, frog, and conch— which separately produce intelligence and other qualities—
along with *māgadhikā*, *agni*, *kaliṅga*, and *biḍa* salts, and ghee prepared with *bilva*, together with six *palas* of *varā*.

By consuming one hundred palas of this [preparation] according to the prescribed method, combined with guggulu of similar quality and mixed with honey, a disciplined ascetic shall achieve the destruction of all diseases.
For him there is no fear of untimely death, nor of disease, nor of old age;
one should treat his various diseases with their respective medicines that destroy those ailments.
The entire procedure for *śilājatu* and *guggulu* is prescribed; however,
even that storehouse of qualities, if used in excessive measure, may cause blindness, facial dryness, emaciation, delusion, and fainting.

Therefore, one who frequents those regions inhabited by night-prowlers will experience a loosening of impurities and dryness of the body; these [conditions] do not occur among such diseases. Just as mountains heated by the summer sun vomit forth substances resembling lac.
That which is called *śilājatu* is said to be the essence of the six metals, such as gold and others;
it pacifies all *doṣas* and destroys all diseases.

One should state that whatever is produced from a particular mineral possesses the specific qualities of that mineral. Furthermore, all such substances are bitter and pungent, not excessively hot, and pungent in their post-digestive transformation (pāka).
And for excision specifically, an instrument made of iron is recommended there;
[the best resin] is black, smells like cow urine, resembles guggulu, is free from gravel, and is smooth.
Śilājatu that is unctuous, not sour or astringent, soft, and heavy is the best.
[It is prepared with] rāsnā, daśamūla, balā, punarnavā, eraṇḍa, śuṇṭhī, and madhuka.
That [mixture],
especially when processed with a decoction of grapes (drākṣā), abhīru, paṭola, trāyamāṇā, guḍūcī, and the jīvanīya group [of herbs], is a destroyer of wind diseases (vātaroga).
In cases of pitta disorders, a decoction that is well-filtered by means of a strainer (niryūha) is highly recommended;
[specifically] one prepared with *krimijit*, *vacā*, the three fruits (*phalatraya*), *karañja*, *ghana*, and the principal *pañcamūla*.
In diseases of *kapha*, one should saturate [the medicine] with a decoction of the five pungent fruits (*pañcakola*) (AS.Utt.49.287),
or with a decoction of the light pentad of roots (*laghupañcamūla*), ginger, grapes, *kāśmarya*, and *vājigandhā* (AS.Utt.49.288).
In diseases caused by pitta and vāta, [one should use] the decoction of guḍūcī, śara, and balā; [and] ghanā,
kuṣṭha, vacā, triphalā, suradāru, viḍaṅga, and pañcakola.
In cases of [fevers] arising from Vata and Kapha, [the decoction] of Rajani, Marica, and Ativisha is used;
or [the decoction] of Patha, Patola, Nimba, Triphala, Ghana, Kutaja, and Saptaparna.
In cases of disorders arising from pitta and kapha, as well as in their combined state (nicaya), one should administer these formulations— consisting of trāyantī, amṛtā, and ativiṣā—
after modifying them according to the relative strength of the doṣas.

One should prepare iron in an iron vessel, following the specific requirements of the disease and the patient, using those various groups of substances mentioned for the collection of diverse minerals from the essence of the mountains.
First, it should be washed with pure water and dried; then it should be processed with decoctions.
Having boiled the medicinal substance for saturation together with eight parts of mountain-ash (gairika) in water, [the liquid should be strained].
One should add the mountain-born [iron] to that decoction when it is reduced to one-eighth and is pure and warm;
once it has reached a state of uniform consistency and is dried, one should add it again to the liquid.
In this manner, it should be processed seven times with decoctions of its own respective [herbs].
Then, for one who has been oleated and purified, ghee prepared with bitter [herbs] should be administered.

One should administer the mountain-born (girikarṇika) for three days with each [of the following] in turn: for three days with the decoction of the three fruits (triphalā), for three days with that of paṭolī, and for three days with that of madhuka.
Then, one should administer that which is suitable for yoga to him, taking the proper time into account;
thus, the substance derived from *śilāja* becomes exceedingly beneficial for the body.
It produces all the [therapeutic] qualities instantaneously and prevents complications.
One should administer one karṣa, half a pala, or one pala for one, three, or seven weeks respectively.

The inferior, middling, and superior qualities of *śilāja* (bitumen) are considered to follow this sequence. When the substance called *girija* is properly processed and administered into a well-prepared body, it [yields its full benefit].
Combined either individually or all together with copper, iron, silver,
and gold, and stirred with milk, it quickly yields the fruit of rejuvenation (*rāsa-āyana*).
It destroys all diseases without exception for one who eats wholesome and moderate food once it has been digested;
[it also counteracts] physical exercise, exposure to the sun, wind, mental distress, heavy foods, and pungent or burning substances.
One should avoid [these] for twice as long as the duration of their consumption;
one should always renounce horse gram (*kulattha*), *kākamācī*, and pigeons.

One suffering from fever should drink water from a large reservoir, well-water, or spring water; or, for the destruction of fever, one should take a dose of liquorice (madhuyaṣṭikā) with a decoction of parpaṭa and other fever-destroying herbs.

One suffering from wasting should take the meat of carnivorous animals arising from flesh, along with peacock meat and milk, for emaciation; when fat has increased excessively, one whose mind and mental faculties are agitated by milk should take honey with water.

One suffering from jaundice (pāṇḍvāmaya) with abdominal swelling should drink *śilāja* with buffalo milk; for urinary calculi (*aśmarī*), one should take it with a decoction of *vīrataru* and other herbs; and for skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), with a decoction of *khadira*.
Just as poison is destroyed by anti-poisonous medicines, so too is that disease [destroyed]. One should consume realgar, the three pungents (trikaṭu), honey, and the mineral honey (kṣaudradhātu).
He who eats rice cooked in milk once the [medicine] has been digested is not afflicted by consumption (*yakṣman*),
provided he has drunk a *tulā* measure of mica (*śilodbhava*) processed with groups of strengthening (*sāra*) substances.
Consuming rice with its own essence-water and with juices derived from wild animals,
one casts off the fatal mixture of diseases known as madhumeha.
Endowed with a beautiful form, complexion, and strength, one lives for a hundred years free from disease.
One should infuse sixteen palas of the substance called Śilāhvā into a single vessel three times daily.
In the decoction of varā, daśamūla, guḍūcī,
karkaśa, balā, and madhuyaṣṭī, along with cow's milk and water, [one should prepare the medicine].
In this manner, one should take [the powder] seven times with milk, both at once and sequentially; likewise again,
[one should take it] of the pair of Kākoli, Ghana, Puṣkara, Vahni, Rāsnā, the pair of Medā, Ṛddhi, Cavyā, and Gajapippalī.
In one droṇa of water, one pala each of pāṭhā, dvijīvaka, nikumbha, the two types of vidārī, vīrā, avarī, madhuphalā,
and the two types of aṃśumatī are boiled until the decoction is reduced to one-quarter.
Having thus processed the mountain-born [iron] (magnetite), one should combine it with two *pala*s of powdered *karkaṭaśṛṅgī*, *dhātrī*, *vyoṣa*, and one *kuḍuba* of *tālīśapatra*.
With one pala of powdered vidārī, two karṣas of akṣīrī bark,
and two palas of the four aromatics (caturjāta), [one should prepare] oil along with ghee, honey, and sugar.
From two palas [of the powder], pills twice that size should be made, equal to the size of an akṣa fruit. Once dried, they should be placed in a new jar that has been perfumed with jasmine flowers.
One should eat one of these every day as a supplement to the prescribed regimen of drinking,
along with either milk, meat broth, pomegranate juice, grape wine (*mārdvīka*), or spirituous liquor (*surā-āsava*).
When the food has been digested, one should eat light food consisting of vegetable soups, milk, and meat broths;
for exactly seven days one should follow this regimen, and thereafter, one should gradually resume all types of food.

This pill, taken either at the end of a meal or before it, is not contraindicated; when administered easily with the avoidance of complications, it is beneficial, free from harm, and yields abundant results. It is victorious.
It cures even severe ūrustambha (stiffness of the thighs) caused by vāta and blood, chronic fever,
disorders of the female reproductive tract, urine, and semen, as well as splenic enlargement, liver disease, anemia, and heart disease.
It cures enlargement of the scrotum, abdominal tumors, gulma, chronic rhinitis, hiccup, cough,
anorexia, dyspnea, abscesses, abdominal enlargements, leprosy, vitiligo, stiffness, consumption, intoxication, and fainting.
[It cures] insanity, epilepsy, various diseases of the mouth, eyes, and head, as well as constipation,
diarrhea, chlorosis, jaundice, and disorders of the digestive tract.
[One should treat] knots, tumors, pustules, fistula-in-ano, scrofula,
excessive emaciation, excessive obesity, sweating, elephantiasis, and polyps in the anus.
It [destroys] the poison of fangs along with its root, the application of terrible poisons,
malevolent sorcery performed by enemies, bad dreams, and likewise afflictions caused by elemental spirits.
This auspicious pill named Śivā pacifies sin and misfortune; it is aphrodisiac, promotes longevity, brings wealth, awakens beauty, fame, and prosperity, and is conducive to the intellect.
Situated in the mouth, it brings about favor with kings, victory in debate, and the conquest of the wicked,
as well as the overcoming of wrinkles and gray hair; it grants a life of two hundred autumns lived in happiness.
By practicing this for two years, one may live for four hundred years;
there is no disease on earth that is curable which this [medicine] made from *jatu* and stone does not forcibly conquer.
When properly administered according to the rules at the appropriate times, it bestows abundant vigor upon one who is healthy. Therefore,
consume a hundred palas of this mountain-born substance originating from Mount Mandara in the abode of the Immortals.
If you desire a continuous stream of life for a very long time, free from the suffering of old age,
then one who avoids things that ought to be avoided should consume [the medicine] ten times a day for a hundred years, eating light, wholesome, and moderate food derived from the mountains.
He dispels the floods of diseases that are constantly afflicting those who have been abandoned by groups of physicians, yet he does not behold the end of their lifespan.
This nectar-like sweat, arising from the churning of the mountain, formerly emerged from the rocks of the mountain as if it were nectar itself.

That golden elixir, which was placed by the Self-born Lord upon Mount Mandara for the benefit of all, exists in the form of a stone among the mountains; it originates from the Golden Mountain and was brought forth by Viṣṇu.
The *tāpī* is produced among the Kirātas, the Cīnas, and the Yavanas;
heated by the rays of the sun in the month of Mādhava, it is seen in the *tāpī*.
Sweet and golden-hued, sour and resembling silver,
slightly astringent in both [sweet and sour] varieties, it is cold, pungent in its post-digestive effect (pāka), and light.
In this regard, one should avoid *kulattha* beans and the like, which are like the exudation from stone;
one who consumes them is not overcome by old age, nor by serpents, nor by poisons, nor by scorpions.
One is not afflicted by urinary disorders characterized by pale urine, fever, swelling, or consumption (yakṣman), nor by diseases of the throat, eyes, ears, or skin,
if one consumes the mineral honey (mākṣikadhātu) with boiled milk, or with ghee, or with honey, or combined with both honey and ghee.
Whether prepared with fermented gruel or mixed with oil, this [medicinal paste] destroys skin diseases, all types of poisons, and those accompanied by *sagara* toxins.
It consists of *akṣa*, grapes, iron rust, *mustā*, and *āmalaka*, combined with the three pungents (*vyoṣa*) and mountain resin (*parvataniryāsa*).

Having taken an equal amount of honey-ore (*mākṣikadhātu*) mixed with honey, one who is afflicted by jaundice and desires well-being should lick it. One part of ginger, one part of iron-rust, one part of jujube (*badara*), one part of long pepper (*pippalī*), and two parts of honey-ore [should be combined].
Honey, as desired, along with a portion of black sesame seeds, forms an excellent bolus that destroys disorders of jaundice and swelling.
Likewise, honey, mineral pitch (mākṣika-dhātu), the three pungents (vyoṣa), and mountain resin (parvata-niryāsa) mixed together with honey [is beneficial].
One who subsists on a diet of milk, licking [the powder] while self-restrained, quickly eliminates wasting and diarrhea;
likewise, iron, ghee, honey, mineral [oxides], honey-measure, *dhātrī* powder, and the resin of aquatic plants [achieve this].
This formulation, mixed with white [sugar], brings about the awakening of vision, smell, hearing, and the sense of taste.
Having roasted *mākṣika* mineral and *triphalā* together in a frying pan, those who lick them while they are still hot [attain these results].
Just as children who have ceased nursing are not affected by the defects of their mother’s milk, so too those who consume honey,
mineral powder, and the powder of *triphalā* with ghee and honey do not suffer from the defects of the food they eat. (AS.Utt.49.339–340)
Old age gradually approaches destruction, like the course of worldly life for one living near a borderland;
it has three joints, many branches, is yellow in its fruits, and red in its flowers.
With leaves that have milky sap and soft down, resembling betel-leaves, and possessing thick tubers and roots;
moving at will through wind, sunlight, women, and other [objects], it effects the cessation of various diseases of the mind and body.
On earth, there is a supreme medicinal herb known as *mahiṣavallarī*, which in some places is called *vṛddhadāraka* and in others *vellarikā*.
These should be collected during the spring and dried in the shade.
Having ground one *tulā* of the roots of *vṛddhadāraka*, one should steep it in clarified butter,
place it in a vessel of ghee, and let it sit among grain for a fortnight.
One should lick [the medicine] and afterwards drink milk; once it is digested, one should subsist on milk and ghee.
By its use, even those aged by old age attain the state of a youth.
One becomes broken-limbed, stammers, becomes lame, emaciated, short,
or deformed; moreover, all the complications arising from defects such as splitting of the nails are cast away.
Free from epilepsy, possession by spirits, insanity, sin, and misfortune,
with a blazing digestive fire, strong, and eloquent, he shall live for six hundred years.
Having consumed thirty palas of powdered *aśvagandhā* mixed with an equal amount of *dāraka*, along with milk or clarified butter;
One who eats [this] when it is digested, as previously described, shall live for a hundred years;
possessing the speed of a horse, the strength of an elephant, handsome, and radiant like the sun.
Aśvagandha should be combined separately with varī and gokṣuraka;
one who licks the powder derived from the root of vṛddhadāraka with clarified butter [attains success].

For seven days, one should subsist on barley gruel with broth; such a person’s speech becomes equal to that of a *kiṃnara*. Furthermore, that [gruel] should be infused for seven days with the fresh juice of *śatāvarī*.
Licking [it] as before for one month, the highly intelligent person shall live for a hundred years;
or he may lick [it] with honey and ghee, having been processed with the fresh juice of *dhātrī*.
Or, by drinking milk for a month, one who is healthy and wise shall live for a hundred years;
so too for one who drinks the juice of the roots of *vṛddhadāraka* with milk.
Ghee prepared with the paste of that [plant] will enable one who drinks it to live for a hundred years free from disease. Likewise,
the root of *Vellarikā*, soaked overnight in cow’s urine, when drunk, produces the same effect.
One may conquer leprosy, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, chronic poisoning, elephantiasis, hemorrhoids, and goiter by using long pepper,
the three myrobalans, barberry, ginger, and punarnava.
Take ten palas each of [the other ingredients] and an equal portion of vṛddhadāraka;
this powder, when drunk with fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla), allows for eating whatever one desires once it has been digested.
Śauṇḍī, along with equal parts of viśva, varā, dvīpi, vella, and mustā, removes elephantiasis, disorders of wind, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, poisons, and chronic fevers.
The roots of *vellarikā* taken with clarified butter and honey possess the same qualities [as the preceding remedies].
Likewise, one should lick one *karṣa* of the fresh juice of its fruit mixed with equal parts of clarified butter and honey.
One who eats as desired should drink cow’s milk followed by buffalo milk;
in five days he shall conquer coughs, and in seven days skin diseases.
Within one month, the great leprosies shall be cured; within two months,
one shall possess a lifespan of five hundred years and be endowed with intelligence, wisdom, strength, and beauty.
One should take equal quantities of the powder of vellarī fruit and root, and of pippalī,
and macerate it with the fresh juice extracted from the fruit and root of vellarī.
Then, having moistened the dried [powder] with the juice of *amṛtā* and saturated it with ghee,
one should bury it in a heap of abundant cow-dung while placed inside a jar of ghee.
He who extracts that electuary after one month and consumes it for a year shall live for a thousand years and will not be suddenly overcome by old age.
One should take one *tulā* of *kuṣṭha* powder combined with two *tulās* of honey and ghee,
place it within a heap of grain for one hundred days, and then administer it.
With a fragrant body, possessing qualities of sight, hearing, voice, and complexion that transcend the senses,
and free from disease and old age, he shall live for seven hundred years.
Entering a hut is beneficial for those who possess attendants and personal belongings;
however, for those who are otherwise, the regimen consists of exposure to the sun and wind.
From here on, we shall describe in detail those yogic practices that endure wind and sun,
which are easy to perform and do not cause distress to the body even in the event of a lapse.
Cold water, milk, honey, and ghee— each taken individually,
in pairs, in threes, or all together— if drunk beforehand, will preserve one's youth.
Harītakī, māgadhikā, and akṣa-dhātrī, reduced to powder and mixed with iron filings,
when consumed with ghee and honey, ensure that old age does not afflict the body like a messenger sent by Time.
Diseases do not attack one who licks a preparation of *harītakī*, *māgadhikā*, *viḍaṅga*, *śaśāṅkalekhā*, and *āmalaka* bark, combined with sugar, honey, and clarified butter.

Having ground turmeric with water decocted from the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) and *asanā*, and having let it sit overnight on an iron vessel, one who licks that sweetened preparation with honey destroys obesity, old age, and all diseases.
If men regularly consume *triphalā* that has been infused with a decoction of *khadira* and *āsana*, and saturated with ghee and honey, what wonder is it if they live free from old age?
Diseases do not indeed attack one who licks abhayā fruits processed with the juice of *āsana*, along with viḍaṅga seeds and rice, soaked in honey, iron powder, and ghee.
In men who habitually consume the juice of *bījaka* extract taken with a finger-measure (*aṅgulihārya*), along with sugar, honey, ghee, and *triphalā*, even advanced old age is indeed turned back.
A decoction of *darvī*, *pralepa*, *asr̥j* (madder), and *triphalā*, thickened with sugar-candy and abundant oil and honey,
and containing *pippalī*, *nāgara*, and iron filings, destroys old age for the body along with its companion, decrepitude.
Men who lick grapes mixed with the powder of the three fruits (triphalā) and the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), along with ghee, honey, and sugar,
and follow this with milk as an after-drink, live free from the transformations of old age.
Having heated a harītakī fruit in ghee, for one who eats it and drinks that ghee,
strength will become long-lasting in the body, just as a good deed performed once remains with a grateful person.
One who consumes an old pitcher filled with *dhātrī* fruits and honey,
which was kept at a distance for half a year among barley, overcomes old age.
For a man who consumes the powder of *dhātrī*, *kṛmighna*, and the heartwood of *asana*, along with oil, ghee, honey, and iron filings,
even his lost youth and beauty shall be restored.
Fresh *āmalaka* fruits, fermented rice-gruel (*śukta*), honey, ghee, and iron filings— these four, ground together and placed in an earthen jar for a year;
for one who licks this mixture in gradual doses, drinks milk, and eats wholesome food, life becomes long-lasting and the decay of the earth (old age) comes to an end.
One who licks the powder of *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *āmalaka*, and *amṛtā* combined with portions of ghee and honey [is cured].
One who is as firm as a bull, free from the suffering of physical transformations, and possesses black hair, lives for a hundred years.
[One should take] the essence of *viḍaṅga* and *madhuka* ground together, mixed with a decoction of *bhallātaka* and an abundance of honey.
It conquers hemorrhoids and even virulent parasites, and instantly kindles the digestive fire—
this preparation consisting of *viḍaṅga*, *bhallātaka*, and *citraka*, combined with *abhayā* and a predominance of jaggery.
Diseases do not afflict those embodied beings who consume medicinal powders with oil; likewise,
those who eat viḍaṅga, bhallātaka, and ginger combined with ghee and honey [are free from disease].
Those men endowed with beauty cross over the river of old age, which has disease for its waves;
and that man who drinks a paste of *viḍaṅga* mixed with the juice of *dhātrī* and honey [shall likewise do so].

Or, having conquered diseases, he shall live for a hundred years by consuming a powder consisting of equal parts of powdered *māgadhikā* and *kaṇā*, along with powdered *viḍaṅga* and *citraka*, soaked in grape juice and honey.
One who consumes [this] mixed with honey and oil shall not sink into the waters of the decline of age.
He who drinks half a *pala* or one *pala* of *punarnavā*, ground and taken with milk for half a month, [attains this].
For two months, or three times that, or for a year, even one who has reached old age shall become young again.
[This applies to] mūrvā, bṛhatī, aṃśumatī, balā, uśīra, pāṭhā, asana, and sārivā.

They say that for black aloe-wood, agaru, and sandalwood, the preparation is exactly the same as for punarnavā; those who consume ghee prepared with a paste and decoction of śatavarī, accompanied by sugar,
[attain longevity].
The thieves of transformation do not plunder those who have entered upon the path of life,
provided they drink Ashvagandha for half a month with milk, ghee, oil, or lukewarm water.
It brings nourishment to the body of one who is emaciated, just as a good rain does for young crops;
for one who eats a handful of black sesame seeds every day with cold water as an after-drink.
There is abundant nourishment for the body, and the teeth remain firm until death,
for one who consumes *śilājatu*, honey, *viḍaṅga*, ghee, iron, *abhayā*, mercury, and gold.
The bodily tissues of one with a weak constitution are replenished in fifteen nights, just like the moon;
[this is achieved by] honey, sweet juices, parched grain, bhārṅgī, madhūka, and śatāvarī.
Having licked a linctus made of lac from the Pārvatī tree together with the bark of the *kamalaka* flower and the *kṣīrī* plant, along with abundant clarified butter and plenty of sugar candy,
those whose old age has been weakened become long-lived.
Having ground together eight parts each of *gāyatrī*, *śikhi*, *śiṃśapā*, *asana*, *śivā*, *vellā*, *akṣa*, and *āruṣkara*, and having soaked them for three days in water six times their weight,

one should boil them in an iron vessel over a mild fire for three days, stirring with the rays of the sun; thereafter, one should cook that preparation until it stands at one-quarter [its original volume], along with pieces of iron.
One part of *pūta*, one part of milk, two parts of the resin of *bhārṅgī*, and three parts [of the decoction] should be drunk;
there, four parts of *hayyaṅgavīna* should be added, and having combined these, one should prepare this in a black iron vessel.

Whether combined with pure white sugar or honey, or even with ghee— whether this [medicine] is used appropriately or not— one who consumes it by the pala-portion becomes possessed of a natural appetite for food, drink, and activity.
Glorious, cleansed of sin, possessing the strength of a forest buffalo and the speed of a horse, with firm limbs, hair as dark as female bees, a face fragrant with honey, and attended by many women;

enriched with eloquence, intellect, and learning, and possessing a most sharp digestive fire— one attains a body resembling Narasimha, shining like gold heated by the flames of fire, through the consumption of this for just one month.
This oblation of exceeding power has been fashioned by Nṛsiṃha like his own body;
from it, the demons of disease, mental anguish, and old age perish, fleeing far away in fear.
One who, with self-restraint, eats *bhṛṅga* and *pravāla* fried in this very [oil] with ghee,
having purified the digestive tract, and whose meal is prepared with milk processed with the essence of *asanā*, attains success.
By consuming it for one month, he lives happily for three hundred years;
even if he takes it only once as prescribed, his memory and sensory faculties remain unimpaired.
And whoever should employ oil according to this very same method obtains those same benefits and becomes one with black hair.
Having consumed for a month one *tulā* of *kāśmarya* fruits that have been soaked and sprinkled with honey and ghee,
and subsisting on milk and rice, one lives for a long time, endowed with beauty.

The Rasāyanas that are feasible, productive of results, and suited to the respective Yugas have been described; furthermore, other Rasāyanas of great benefit, though difficult to obtain and so forth, have not been mentioned.
Although those superhuman and most wonderful meritorious deeds are indeed the cause [of such powers],
they utterly uproot the body by causing the destruction of the [divine] ordinance; therefore, they are devoid of that [power].
If the efficacy of medicinal herbs in therapeutic actions is considered to be diminished due to the nature of the current age,
then that same diminution applies to lifespan, strength, and other qualities; therefore, one should diligently employ rejuvenative therapies (*rasāyana*).
Nor should one imagine that the potency of medicinal herbs is entirely lost; for it is evident to everyone that *trivṛt* moves its fruit both upward and downward— how could this not be established?
Just as medicines that are administered at the wrong place and time, or are unwholesome, excessively hot, or too sharp,
bring about the destruction of the body all at once, so too do those correctly applied lead to its growth.
Therefore, having conquered the senses and other faculties that are extremely difficult to subdue,

one who is endowed with the proper timing and is purified in the correct manner should practice that medicinal therapy which is possessed of potency for the sake of increasing longevity, wisdom, and vitality.

The far shores of these elixirs— which are like great oceans difficult to cross— are inaccessible at all times even to men who are heroic in their zeal, if they are destitute of austerity; thus, they remain both unattainable and beyond reach.
By the excellence of the administration of elixirs (rasāyana), when the impurities, defects, and constituent elements (dhātu) have been rendered pure,
the bodies of embodied beings are made firm, just as a lineage is stabilized when presided over by virtuous men.
For one who has subdued the senses and practices the meaning of the scriptures exactly as they are,
how great must be their far-sightedness that even the status of Indra would not be difficult to attain?
If diseases should arise due to a failure in the procedure for rejuvenation therapy (rasāyana),
one should administer their respective specific medicines, setting aside the rejuvenation therapy itself.
Those [doshas] which have been overcome by substances that are sour, salty, alkaline, pungent, hot, and sharp, and which are present [in the body], undergo a state of decay;

they are kindled by those [substances], and when [the fire] has arisen, one should avoid formulations [containing them], for that [fire] is the root of the increase of the bodily constituents (dhātus).
Even well-administered medicinal formulations reach futility when applied to a weak digestive fire, just as favors rendered to an ungrateful person go to waste. Yet,
when the fire is blazing, even a mere trifle is expanded by the multitude of its qualities, like enjoyments bestowed upon a worthy recipient.
One should know that a person who speaks the truth, is free from anger, whose senses are inclined toward the inner self,
who is tranquil, and devoted to virtuous conduct, is a constant elixir.
He who, endowed with these qualities, practices *rasāyana* with a tranquil mind,
attains long life and rejoices both in this world and in the hereafter.
Conduct that follows the scriptures, attendants who understand one's mind,
and an intellect unerring regarding its objects— this is the complete elixir (rasāyana).

In places attended by very aged cowherds who were of excellent character, whose senses, lifespan, and digestive fires were stable, and who imitated the cows’ straightness through their speech, intentions, bodies, and movements, being entirely focused on them.
In cow-pens where there are trees laden with abundant ghee, milk, and medicinal herbs,
and where calves frolic with lowing sounds, elixirs achieve perfection even without entering a monastery.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter; thus the seventh limb, known as Rasāyana, is completed.
Now begins the fiftieth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter titled "The Procedure for Aphrodisiacs" (Vājīkaraṇavidhi).
Thus indeed said the great sages, Ātreya and the others.
A man who indulges in the objects of the senses should constantly seek aphrodisiacs (*vājīkaraṇa*),
for within them depend satisfaction, nourishment, and progeny endowed with excellent qualities.
That which produces offspring and ensures the continuity of the lineage, which brings immediate delight,
by means of which a man becomes as exceedingly strong as a stallion and approaches women unimpeded.

Whatever increases one's great affection for women is *vājīkaraṇa* (aphrodisiac), for it is the supreme vitalizer of the body's vigor. Indeed, a woman endowed with feminine qualities is the very essence of the world of living beings. (AS.Utt.50.4)
Virtuous women give birth to men who are as if composed of excellence;
for these householders increase their lineage and are the deities of the home.
For even a house that is magnificent does not shine if it is dilapidated by these [defects];
nor do those [ornaments] shine when they are as if overtaken by old age.
For women, indeed, that [practice] is the supreme means of attraction without union with a man,
for one who constantly employs aphrodisiacs and desires to enjoy every object of desire.
Neither does he obtain a body, nor does his delight in pleasure suffer decay;
he is like a tree without shadow, with rotten flowers, and devoid of fruit.
Just as a tree that has only one trunk and only one branch is without offspring,
so too is a man who has seen neither son nor grandson, and whose lineage is on the verge of extinction.
What indeed is the life of one who is excluded from the pleasures of saṃsāra? For one who has no son, every subsequent generation is forever a stranger.
At the end of his life, even if he remains in good health, his home falls into disorder if it is without a leader;
therefore, aphrodisiac formulations that increase the semen should be practiced.
For one who is healthy, of vigorous age, and who practices aphrodisiacs (vājīkaraṇa),
sexual intercourse every day throughout all seasons is not prohibited.
Semen is diminished by anxiety and old age; it is depleted by diseases, by physical exhaustion from labor,
by fasting, and by excessive indulgence with women.
Due to the depletion of semen, fear, grief, lack of confidence, non-observance [of the regimen],
excessive joy, extreme corpulence, accumulation of waste products, and exhaustion;
Due to the lack of skill of women, from the observation of defects, from malevolent magic (abhicāra), from severe diseases of the penis,
from anger, and from the proclamation of unrighteousness—
Even for one who is satiated, the power to approach a woman does not arise; nor indeed are all men endowed with vigor such that they possess offspring.
Some are large-bodied and strong, yet weak with regard to women;
others have small constitutions, yet are powerful with women and procreate many offspring.
Some men approach women repeatedly like sparrows;
others, like elephants, do not frequent them often but pour forth their seed.
Some bulls are driven by efforts, while others [are driven] by their own nature;
therefore, I shall describe the applications that bestow strength upon the weak.

Then, for those who have been lubricated and purified, one should administer non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) along with unctuous enemas (anuvāsana), which provide pleasant enjoyment for the strong and further increase their strength.
One skilled in formulations should first administer these combined with ghee, oil, meat broth, milk, sugar, and honey to those who subsist on milk and meat broth.
Then follow aphrodisiac formulations that bestow semen, progeny, and strength:
[the roots] of *śara*, *ikṣu*, *kuśa*, *kāśa*, *vidārī*, and *vīraṇa*.
The roots of Kaṇṭakārī, Jīvaka, Ṛṣabhaka, Balā,
the two types of Medā, the two types of Kākolī, Sūpyaparṇī, and Śatāvarī.
Aśvagandhā, atibalā, ātmaguptā, punarnavā,
vīrā, payasyā, jīvantī, ṛddhi, rāsnā, and trikaṇṭaka.
One should cook three palas each of madhuka and śāliparṇī, along with one āḍhaka of masha beans, in two droṇas of water.
When one āḍhaka remains of the decoction, one should add one āḍhaka of ghee and one āḍhaka each of the juices of vidārī,
dhātrī, and sugarcane, and cook it.
One should add four times as much milk as ghee and incorporate these paste ingredients:
vīrā, svaguptā, the two types of kākolī, yaṣṭīmadhu, phalgu, and the two types of pippalī.
One should add one *prastha* each of the powders of raisins (*drākṣā*), *vidārī*, dates (*kharjūra*), *madhuka*, and *śatāvarī* to that [decoction] once it has been prepared and strained.
With one *kuḍava* each of sugar, *tugākṣīrī*, and long pepper (*pippalī*), and with half a *pala* each of black pepper (*marica*) and the other [ingredients], taken separately.
One should then consume one pala daily of finely ground cinnamon, cardamom, and saffron, along with two kuḍavas of honey, while taking meat broth or milk as the vehicle.
By this, one mounts like a horse and rejoices like a sparrow;
[one should take] an āḍhaka of the seeds of māṣa and ātmaguptā, measured by a handful (prasṛta).
One should boil Medā, Aśvagandhā, Ṛddhi, Varī, Vīrā, Yaṣṭī,
and the two Jīvakas in a winnowing-basket (śūrpa) with water; when reduced to one-fourth, one should cook [the remaining ingredients] with that decoction.

With two *prasthas* each of the juices of *vidārī* and sugarcane, and an equal amount of all [the aforementioned] milks, one should cook one *prastha* of fresh clarified butter (*havis*) in this [mixture].
One should give four palas each of sugar, honey, and the substance called sitā separately; then, before a meal, one should lick a pala of *kaṇā* (long pepper), beginning with that same quantity.
While young women remain unsatisfied, [the patient] behaves like a donkey;
milk boiled with marrow and other parts weighing one-eighth part [of the milk] is the *bāṣkayaṇa* preparation.
Sugar, honey, and ghee together are an excellent means for increasing semen;
likewise, milk-porridge prepared with that [milk] and the fruits of *māṣa* and *kaṇḍūkarī* [is beneficial].

This preparation, containing ghee, honey, and sugar, is aphrodisiac and increases the vital energy; it is prepared with the juice of *śvadaṃṣṭrā* and *vidārī*, along with four times the amount of milk.
Māṣa-ṣaṣṭika milk-porridge (pāyasa), prepared with plenty of ghee,
is aphrodisiac; so too are madhūlikā, māṣaparṇī, sugar, water-chestnuts (śṛṅgāṭaka), and barley.
Equal parts of *svaguptā*, *mūlayaṣṭyāhva*, *vidārī*, and *ikṣuraka*,
along with *priyāla*, should be made into a powder; this should be taken separately with honey and ghee in a sixfold proportion.
By not touching the ground with his feet and licking the morning sun,
one obtains strength and enthusiasm like a *kuliṅga* bird and approaches women.
[The herbs] *svaguptā*, *kṣīrakākolī*, *vidārī*, and the two types of *jīvaka*— AS.Utt.50.39 svaguptā kṣīrakākolī vidārī jīvakadvayam
Having licked one *prasṛta* measure of powdered sesame seeds that have been plucked, roasted, and soaked in sugar, ghee, and honey, one approaches a hundred women.
Licking one *prasṛta* of either black gram (*māṣa*) powder saturated with the juice of *dhātrī*,
or the powder of *vidārī*, mixed with honey and ghee; AS.Utt.50.40.
One should approach women ten times like a sparrow following after milk; [one should take] the powder of *vidārī*, repeatedly saturated with its own juice.
Having licked a mixture of honey and clarified butter, a woman can go to ten men. Long pepper and the powder of *dhātrī* fruit, processed with its own juice, [achieves the same].
Having licked a mixture of sugar, honey, and clarified butter, he who subsequently drinks milk—
even a man of eighty years— rejoices like a youth.
(One *karṣa* of Madhuka powder, combined with clarified butter and honey, [should be taken].)
He who, suffering from constant diarrhea, licks [the powder] while drinking milk as an after-drink shall be cured;
likewise, he who drinks the paste of *kulīraśṛṅgī* stirred with milk [shall be cured].
One who eats white substances, ghee, milk, and rice becomes virile among women.
Grain-bean juice, milk, honey, sugarcane juice, and ghee [are likewise beneficial].
A decoction of two parts of *medā* and one part of *jīvaka*, when combined and drunk together, makes a man capable of approaching a hundred women.
One should cook half an āḍhaka of milk with four bhallātaka fruits;
when drunk, it produces virility even in a person whose digestion is already well-established.
A man who drinks the powder of the seeds of *svayaṅguptā* and *ikṣuraka* mixed with sugar and warm milk will act like a donkey.
One should likewise employ the powder of uccaṭā and śatāvarī;
[and] that which is boiled with sūpyaparṇī, the two types of kākolī, jīvaka, and ṛṣabhaka.
By practicing the use of milk with the "small five roots" (laghupañcamūla) combined with the two types of *kākolī*, even an old man becomes like a youth;
so too with *kṣīriṇī*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, treacle, sugar, and honey.
Fresh milk from a cow that has calved for the first time and fresh clarified butter— this is the supreme means for ensuring the birth of a male child.
A man [should drink] milk prepared with the fruit, root, and bark of the *aśvattha* tree and with [cow's] horn.
Having drunk it cold with sugar, one rejoices like a *kuliṅga* bird;
milk prepared with *payasyā*, along with ghee and honey, increases semen.
Take the juice of *śatāvarī* and *karkaṭa*, with ten times the amount of milk and ghee. AS.Utt.50.52;
Boiled with long pepper, honey, and sugar, this is an excellent aphrodisiac. One *prastha* of *śatāvarī* juice and four *prasthas* of milk [should be boiled].
