One *prastha* of clarified butter, along with one-eighth part (*śukti*) each of grapes, *māṃsī*, *parūṣaka*,
*jīvaka*, *ṛṣabha*, *yaṣṭyāhvā*, *balā*, *medā*, and *kaśeruka*.
One should cook priyāla seeds and the two types of kākolī together in one place;
once cooked and strained, one should add sugar-candy in the measure of one kuḍava to this.
Having drunk milk from a cow that has calved for the first time, one becomes virile toward women and conquers disorders of wind-blood (vātāsra), blood-bile (pittāsra), chest wounds,
and consumption; likewise, [the decoction of] jīvaka, kṣīrakākolī, sthirā, haṃsapadī, and ghana [is effective].
One should cook one *karṣa* each of *śaṭhī*, sugar-cane stalks, *yaṣṭī*,
and lotus stalks in one *prastha* of ghee with ten times as much milk; this promotes strength and nourishment.
This brings about the birth of sons for barren women and serves to increase and purify the semen.
One should boil five palas of *svayaṃguptā* root, starting from the base, in one āḍhaka of water.
Having ground these into a fine powder, one should add one *kuḍava* each of the following separately:
the root of *svaguptā*, wheat, black gram (*māṣa*), *ikṣuraka*, and long pepper (*pippalī*).
One should prepare those *modakas* (sweetmeats) using half a *prastha* of fresh ghee mixed with priyāla fruit and honey, along with a quarter-tulā of white sugar.
Having eaten a single modaka [prepared with this], one approaches sixty women.
[The ingredients are] palāṃśa, bṛhatī, vyāghrī, pṛśniparṇī, and trikaṇṭaka.
Having boiled [the ingredients] with two āḍhakas of water until one-quarter of the liquid remains,
one should add five palas of kṣīrakākoli and one pala of māgadhikā.
One should add one *kuḍava* each of the fruits and roots of *svaguptā*, *māṣa* beans, sugarcane, *vidārī*,
and honey.
Having separately prepared two types of *śaṣkulikā* cakes from mung beans and sesame seeds in ghee, one should cook them; then, by eating one [cake], a man approaches a hundred women.
Prepared with the powder of *svaguptā* roots mixed with fresh milk,
and cooked in ghee with sugar and honey, these confections provide a hundred sexual emissions when consumed.
The flours of black gram, *ātmaguptā*, wheat, *śāli* rice, and *ṣaṣṭika* rice,
as well as the powders of sugar, *vidārī*, and *ikṣuraka*.
Having mixed [the ingredients] with milk and ghee, one should fry cakes (pūpalikā) in clarified butter;
when taken with a draught of milk as an after-drink, they quickly produce supreme virility.
A powder made from black gram, sesame, śāli rice, and vidārī, along with rock salt,
should be soaked in the juice of red sugarcane and then applied to the fat of a boar.
Having cooked them, one who eats *śaṣkulī* cakes may ascend sixty women; likewise,
those who eat smooth, sweet-tasting fruits that are pleasing to the palate.
One *kuḍava* each of the fruits of *ātmaguptā*, rice, mung beans, sesame, ghee, green gram, and wheat, taken separately.
By eating cooked *pūpalikā* cakes made from those same [grains] which have been dehusked, ground into powder, stirred with milk, and kneaded,
one becomes as vigorous as a stallion among women. [This is prepared] with sugar,
black gram, wheat, *tugākṣīrī*, milk, and ghee.
One should eat cooked *utkārikā* and drink the meat-broth of a cock;
likewise, one should drink the broth of peacock, partridge, or swan.
By this means, like a spirited horse, the strong man shall offer his virility;
having ground the meat of a boar and added black pepper and rock salt.
Having made pills the size of jujube fruits, one should roll them in hot clarified butter;
once they have been rolled and solidified, they should be thrown into chicken broth.
In a mixture rich with ghee, fragrant with perfumes, and containing curd and pomegranate juice,
one should prepare that medicinal extract so that the pills do not break apart.
Drinking that [milk] and eating those [meats], one who possesses strength should proceed like a young elephant;
likewise, one should prepare other meats endowed with strength.
One should take pure, dehusked, sprouted *māṣa* beans along with *sājāhā* fruits,
and cook them in buffalo meat broth enriched with ghee, together with curd and pomegranate juice.
Having added *dhānya*, *jīraka*, and *nāgara*, one should prepare it according to the proper method;
when this juice is drunk or eaten, it produces inexhaustible semen.
He who eats the roasted eggs of swans, peacocks, and cocks with heated ghee,
drinking wine as an after-drink, being satisfied himself, shall satisfy women.
He who eats fresh fish-flesh or well-fried *śapharī* fish in heated clarified butter shall never suffer decline in sexual vigor with women.
One desiring offspring should consume rohita fish fried in ghee with goat meat broth and seasoned with fruit juices, taking the prepared broth as an after-drink.
One should cook ghee with black gram, goat testicles, and sour fruits in the flavorful meat broth of buffalo;
once purified, one should fry that broth in ghee.
This broth, seasoned slightly with salt and combined with coriander and ginger,
when drunk, is an excellent aphrodisiac, strengthening, and nourishing.
In the same way, one should prepare sparrows in the juice of partridge, and partridges in chicken broth;
one should prepare peacock in swan broth, or swans in peacock broth.
Having attained satisfaction from the flesh of sparrows,
the woman who then drinks milk satisfies her husbands even when they have been restrained for a long time.
One who desires inexhaustible semen should eat a roasted cock, rich in ghee, cooled, and mixed with honey; immediately thereafter, he should drink milk.
He who eats the testicles of a goat, prepared with milk and ghee along with long pepper and salt, may approach a hundred women.
If one eats sesame seeds that have been repeatedly soaked in cow's milk prepared with goat testicles and mixed with sugar, he may approach a hundred women as if they were virgins.
He who, having eaten sixty-day rice (*ṣaṣṭikaudana*) enriched with ghee along with black gram soup (*māṣasūpa*),
drinks milk, remains awake throughout the entire night, being full of vitality.
One should cook one *prasṛta* measure each of the fruits of *ātmaguptā*, *māṣa* beans, dates, *śatāvarī*, *śṛṅgāṭaka*, and grapes.
One prastha of milk and one prastha of water— this being boiled down until only the milk remains—
should be strained through a clean cloth and combined with three prasṛtas [of medicinal powder].
One should drink that [mixture] of sugar, *tugākṣīrī*, and fresh clarified butter,
combined with honey, while eating *ṣaṣṭika* rice.
Likewise, though overcome by old age, he is surrounded by his sons;
[he eats] the tops of grapes, *kharjūra* trees, and date palms, as well as the fruit of the *ajahā*.
One should prepare *payasyā*, *abhīru*, *māṣa*, and *madhuka*—
each weighing one *pala*— in one *āḍhaka* of water; when reduced to one-fourth, with that decoction...
One should cook one prastha of milk until only the milk remains; with this, one should eat ṣaṣṭika rice mixed with ghee and sugar. This formulation is supreme for increasing semen.
[The ingredients are: jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, medā, jīvantī, and the two types of śrāvaṇī.
Date-palm, licorice, grapes, vidārī, ginger,
water-chestnuts, cardamom, fresh ghee, milk, and water.
One should consume, according to one's strength, the prepared residue of ghee mixed with sugar and honey, along with sixty-day rice.
That [milk] is aphrodisiac, strength-promoting, complexion-enhancing, beneficial for the throat, and nourishing to the body.
A cow that has calved once, whose calf is still with her, who is healthy, whose horns point upward, and who has four teats— [her milk is especially so].
[That cow] which yields thick, delicious, and abundant milk, and is endowed with beauty and good character—
whether she is nourished by sugarcane, māṣa-parṇa, or well-nourished *arjuna* [leaves].
That milk, combined with sugar, honey, and ghee, produces a son and bestows sexual pleasure;
it is prepared with substances that increase semen, those known as vitalizers (jīvanīya), those that nourish, and those that augment strength.
This milk, prepared separately with each of these for the purpose of stabilizing one's age,
should be mixed with wheat flour, ghee, honey, and sugar.
For one desiring that the semen remain inexhaustible, it should be used in rotation with *medā*,
*payasyā*, *jīvantī*, *vidārī*, and *kaṇṭakārikā*.
One should cook one *karṣa* each of black gram (*māṣa*), *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *kṣīrīkā*, wheat (*godhūma*), *śāli* rice,
and *ṣaṣṭika* rice in half an *āḍhaka* of their respective milks and water.
One should discard the remainder of the milk; that purified portion, when combined with honey, ghee,
and sugar, causes even an old man to become like a youth upon drinking it.
This milk, boiled with well-heated discs of gold,
is prepared as a *puṃsavana* (fertilizing) tonic; it is aphrodisiac when combined with sugar, ghee, and honey.
This same distinct procedure applies to silver, iron, copper, and lead. Thirty powdered pippalī fruits [should be added] to a prakūñca each of oil and ghee.
One should drink [these] fried [grains], mixed with sugar and honey, stirred with milk;
and by eating *ṣaṣṭika* rice with milk and ghee, one becomes like a horse.
[One should eat] *ṣaṣṭika* rice, as white as moonbeams, enriched with milk and ghee.
A man who eats [this] combined with sugar and honey does not lose his virility; likewise,
sixty-day rice (ṣaṣṭikaudana) eaten with curd-cream and ghee [has the same effect].
Sailā, tugā, goṣaṇa, and honey, combined with a large amount of sugar, produce semen. Likewise, adhyaṇḍā, mārṣabhī, and the fruits of svayaṅguptā [are used for this purpose].
Having applied a foot-ointment at night, a man is not overtaken by fatigue.
[The ointment consists of] the root of *varṣābhū*, grapes, and the fruit of *svayaṅguptā*.
This ointment for the feet is perfected; one who applies it shall not touch the ground with his feet.
Constantly consuming ghee and milk, he remains free from disease, ever-moving, and eternally young.
A man whose mind is thus inclined toward women behaves like a bull among them. [The aphrodisiacs are:
the fruit of *ātmaguptā*, black gram, wheat, *śāli* rice, and *ṣaṣṭika* rice.
Sugarcane, *ikṣuraka*, milk, honey, grapes, white sugar, *uccaṭā*, the roots of *śara*, *vidārī*, and *śatāvarī*.
The vitalizing [substances] are *svarjūra*, the fruits of the *moca* and *coca* trees;
with these, one should prepare foods to be eaten, drinks, linctuses, and medicated ghees.
For one who constantly indulges in women,
sexual excitement increases through the consumption of vitalizing ghee, milk, honey, oil, and sugar-cane juice.
Enemas that consist of meat broth and milk quickly produce virility; those prepared according to the formulations described for the *siddhabasti* bestow strength, semen, and progeny.
One desiring a son should employ enemas with those substances prescribed for the desire for a son;
whatever is sweet, unctuous, nourishing, and strength-increasing [should also be used].
Whatever causes exhilaration of the mind is called aphrodisiac (*vṛṣya*). Therefore, one should approach a woman after having been fortified by such substances.
Impelled by his own momentum and gladdened by the qualities of women,
even individual desirable objects produce supreme joy and delight.
How much more so, then, regarding the female body, which is established through the destruction of the [male] assembly,
due to the diverse tastes of the world and the destiny of women?
Having encountered such and such a man, qualities such as beauty and the like flourish in him;
therefore, whichever woman seems to enter a man's heart, [she is his].
She whose nature is uniform, endowed with the qualities of charm, cleanliness,
and beauty, carries— through her limbs that have become like snares— an embodied form of loveliness itself.
She who bathes the limbs as if with nectar,
who drinks as it were while looking, and who touches as if she were anointing them.
She who is a constant festival, whose desires are identical to one's own,
and who always draws the heart toward longing even when she is ever-present; (50.120–121)
Separated from which, a man considers the world devoid of women and lacking delight;
she who is bold in the encounter of love, yet composed and full of modesty.
Even after going there many times, one returns as if it were for the first time;
she who is free from change through her conduct appears as if fashioned from changes.

A woman who is devoted above all to following her husband's will is considered the most excellent of wives. [She should attend to] the various types of ointments, powders, sprinklings, perfumes, garlands, and colorful garments and ornaments.
A bed that is wide, soft, and pleasing, strewn with the pollen from heaps of fragrant flowers; and companions who are wise, skilled in the arts, submissive, disciplined, sweet-spoken, and delightful.

Because of their shared intimacy, their common nature, and their identical activities, the forest regions resounding with the songs of cuckoos, and the delightful rivers flowing constantly, appear as if they were distinct entities from her mere body alone.
Wine produces intoxication and fragrance; specifically, *prasannā* is heart-pleasing and fragrant.
*Prasannā* is like the betel leaf, pale as the cheek of a Śaka woman, and beautiful when surrounded by its accessories.
The adornment of the lotus-faces of women is like the personified weapon of the Son of the Self-born (Kāma),
as white as the mass of foam produced from the Ocean of Milk when churned by the Himalayas.
The palace and the rays of the moon, exceedingly bright with plaster, produce a supreme state of virility;
for a man exhausted by a previously contracted bond, there is relief through another means.
With hands that bring pleasure through touch, she performs a massage that seems to fulfill my most extraordinary desire;
her heart is moistened by the intense passion arising from the practice of the various movements taught in the manual on sexual union.

One whose bodily constituents (*dhātu*) are nourished by the consumption of aphrodisiacs (*vṛṣya*) forcibly brings the minds of women under his control. Therefore, a lover who desires constant favor from women should employ aphrodisiac formulations even when his desire has already been aroused.
Having understood the constitution, suitability, place, and time, one should engage in the sixty-four arts;
[therein] there is the sound of bracelets, the clatter of fists, and the doubled resonance of girdles.
Even the sound of moving anklets does not repeatedly bring about the excellence of pleasure; rather,
it is the attainment of all goals, the first passion, and specific stories of love and music [that do so].
Laughing with a whistling sound and accompanied by sighs, singing with broken syllables and confusion;
glances at beloved ones that reveal beautiful limbs under some pretext, and their manner of conduct.

Mango sprouts, flowers, and fruits according to the season; clouds illuminated by lightning and accompanied by thunder; the warbling of birds and bees, followed by the humming of ornaments and the cooing of women.

When, at the proper time, there is purity of the body according to its own nature, those born of volition bear their burden; when the channels are purified and the body is stainless, he who eats a moderate amount of aphrodisiac food at the right time [attains success].
By means of that, a man becomes exceedingly virile; it is nourishing and bestows strength to the body.
Therefore, purification (śodhana) should first be performed according to one's strength, and not aphrodisiac formulations (vṛṣyayoga).
Just as dyes do not take hold on a soiled garment when applied to a defiled body, [so too] these [therapies] fail;
yet, within this diverse instruction, [the methods] have been taught in accordance with the requirements of the subject matter to be explained.
That which ought to be done must indeed be done, even at the cost of one's life, and nothing else;
this is the essential nature of the scripture as it is described through its pervasive scope.
A great fault of deficiency certainly touches that which does not pervade,
even if it is adorned with applications that are devoid of potency and incomplete.
How can that which is not dependent on its own essence attain the state of being dependent?
Even though the eggs of the swan, the peacock, and the cock are exceedingly rich in semen, [they do not produce their respective offspring].
Compassionate sages would say: "How could these [practices] be otherwise than [obstacles] to yoga? Or how is it that all these yogas are merely inflammers of the fire of passion?"
Those who give rise to afflicted intentions are said by the divine seers— who perceive the three times and are free from the defects of sentient beings— to be the increasers of saṃsāra.
Who would wish to transgress the path established by the ancient teachers?
When it has been set forth in every way, everything becomes explained and resolved.
For it is not possible to encompass all subjects by means of a mere fragmentary mention;
likewise [the prohibitions apply to] the milk of a female donkey, the meat of a horse, and that of elephants.
The ocean of my teachings has been declared to be useless even now,
yet it remains especially so because it contains a vast collection of the meanings of many tantras.
That knowledge by which one may understand the means of integration (*saṅgraha*) and so forth is exceedingly difficult to attain; thus,
this Veda, as promised, has been composed in due order as a treasury of the eight branches (*aṣṭāṅga*).
For one who practices the Noble Truths as if they were a path, the accomplishment of one's own welfare and the welfare of others arises;
such is the corpus of Ayurveda uttered from the mouth of the Grandfather (Brahmā).
It bestows longevity, health, dharma, wealth, happiness, dignity, and fame;
it is adorned with logical phrases like gold set with excellent jewels.
Among the thirty-six difficult points regarding meaning, like bridges for physicians,
there are therein the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), the application (*yoga*), the causal meaning (*hetvartha*), and the meaning of the word (*padārtha*).
The purpose [of the treatise] consists of the brief statement (pradeśa), the detailed exposition (uddeśa), the specific explanation (nirdeśa), and the completion of the sentence (vākyaśeṣa);
as well as instruction (upadeśa), reference (apadeśa), extension (atideśa), implication (arthāpatti), and determination (nirṇaya).
Prasaṅga, ekānta, anaikānta, sāpavarga, viparyaya, pūrvapakṣa, vidhāna, anumata, vyākhyāna, and saṃśaya.
Consideration of the past and the future, one's own perception, inference, and synthesis; illustration, etymological definition, application, and then alternative classification.
Pratyutsāra, uddhāra, and sambhava are the technical formulations (tantrayukti) [of this chapter],
just as the rays of the sun [awaken] a lotus pond full of blossoming lotuses.
Just as there is no light in a house without a lamp, so too there is no understanding of the treatise without its methodological principles (tantrayukti).
Even one who has studied the treatises, if he is unskilled in the methodological principles of the treatise [will fail to grasp its true meaning].
Just as one does not attain wealth when fortune is exhausted, one does not grasp the meaning of the treatise; however,
the logical arguments provided for the application of the meaning of the sentences grant the attainment of the desired goal.
They are the refuters of the statements employed by those who speak what is false; they are the illuminators of that which is expressed through hesitation, reversal, or subtle speech.
Having thus extracted the essence from the ocean of the logic of statements, they have established [this doctrine],
because it is proven by scripture and because its results are perceived directly.
This imperishable tantra should be applied like a mantra by those who are experts in the knowledge of tantras,
having recollected it from the Grandfather of the world.
To protect against untimely death, an armor made of non-metal has been fashioned;
this nectar is well-known as the abode of happiness for both the healthy and the unwell.
This treatise accomplishes all human goals, including their desired fruits; likewise, for those lacking vision, it acts as a source of illumination.
Just as the orb of the sun does not fail to shine, so too,
welfare is certain among physicians who follow the teachings of Āyurveda.
In other cases, for other acts such as warding off an umbrella or setting fire [to an enemy],
one should employ weapons and the like; even if the patient has only partially recovered, [the treatment] should be applied.

But medicine that is applied out of delusion without careful consideration is not so; rather, one should always examine the twelve factors, such as the humors and the drugs, according to their true nature.
A wise person should not administer treatment by means of medicinal formulations alone,
if they have not correctly understood the dosage and other factors, and have merely applied it by chance.
A medicinal formulation kills the diseased person just as [the mixture of] ghee and honey [kills].
Having observed that poison possesses the nature of nectar, one should observe that ghee and other substances possess the nature of death.
That evil-minded person who practices medicine without having understood the true principles of the science—
this great verse of a certain high-souled being is well sung.
Physicians who have not studied the meaning of the scriptures, yet are fools and full of arrogance—
these are indeed untimely deaths wandering upon the surface of the earth.
Those fools who entice a patient with various clever techniques—
one should always protect oneself from them, for the self is exceedingly difficult to attain.
Having extracted some [humors] that are fixed in duration like stable syllables,
those physicians, through their pride in their medical knowledge, kill hundreds of those whose lifespan is not fixed.
For one afflicted by disease, despondent, and whose happiness and life are obtained only with great effort,
that physician who performs a medical treatment while being unlearned, merciless, and cruel— [he is a destroyer].
By even conversing with that evil-minded messenger of Death, who has abandoned righteousness, a man shall fall into hell.
Those who have disregarded the meaning of the treatises and subsist on the scriptures alone,
acting like hunters, roam through the kingdoms due to the negligence of kings.
One should avoid those who revile the scriptures, for they are like the noose of Death; instead,
one should serve the best of physicians, who are filled with tranquility, discernment, and knowledge.
Wholesome food and drink, medicine for the eradication of disease,
rejuvenatives, and aphrodisiacs are obtained by relying upon a physician.
Just as countries without a king and houses without a master,
so too the limbs of a patient are to be pitied when they are not attended by a physician.
Therefore, a wise person should always respectfully honor a compassionate physician who has conquered his senses, just as Indra honored the two Aśvins.
Indeed, the severed head of the sacrifice was joined back together by the Aśvins; likewise,
the fallen teeth of Pūṣan and the eyes of Bhaga were restored by them.
The Moon, afflicted by consumption (*rājayakṣmā*), was treated by those very two; likewise,
the wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrin*) who had fallen from Soma, and [Indra] in his terrible paralysis of the arm (*bhujastambha*).
The descendant of Bhṛgu, Cyavana, though old and having undergone transformation due to desire,
was made young again by those two, endowed with vigor, complexion, and strength.
Through these and many other such meritorious deeds, those two supreme physicians became highly honored by the great-souled ones, beginning with Indra.
Vāsava drinks Soma together with the two Aśvins at dawn;
and in the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, the Blessed One rejoices together with the two Aśvins.
A portion for the Aśvins is assigned even by Brahmins in the sacrifices; moreover,
the Aśvins, Agni, and Indra are highly praised in the Vedas.
Therefore, the physicians Aśvinīkumāras are always honored by the gods, the ageless, the immortal, the blissful, and those who are thus esteemed.
How much more, then, should physicians be honored by mortals who are seized by disease, death, and old age, who are beset by suffering, and who seek happiness— to the best of their ability?
One who is virtuous, wise, disciplined, a twice-born,
and a master of the Vedas is to be honored by living beings like a father; for he is remembered as the teacher of life (prāṇācārya).
Upon the completion of their studies, physicians are said to possess a second birth;
for a physician does not truly acquire the title of "physician" by virtue of his previous birth alone.
Upon the completion of his studies, whether he is a Brahmin or a physician,
knowledge certainly enters him; because of that knowledge, the physician is remembered as a twice-born (dvija).
A wise person, desiring imperishable life, should never despise, revile, or act harmfully toward the teacher of life (the physician).
The physician, mindful of the Dharma and exerting himself, should protect all patients from their ailments just like his own children, keeping knowledge in mind.
But those who, for the sake of their livelihood, engage in the trade of selling medical treatments—
having abandoned a heap of gold, they pursue a heap of dust.
There is no donor at all equal to him who, having severed the terrible snares called diseases that drag one toward the presence of Death, bestows his own life.
Indeed, no gift excels the gift of life; therefore,
one should treat with one's own resources those who are destitute and ascetics.
For a physician of great intelligence who strives for the welfare of sentient beings in this manner,
the deities of success certainly abide in his presence.
In some cases it is dharma, in some a friend, in some wealth, in some fame,
and in some the practice of past actions; thus, medical treatment is never fruitless.
Therefore, a physician should always attend to the sick with great care;
for by neglecting them, he destroys his own life and his reputation.
In all cases, loving-kindness toward those afflicted by suffering, sympathetic joy toward men whose bodies are free from disease,
and equanimity toward those whose minds are heading toward harm— this fully extends the noble conduct of the physician.
Even that physician who eradicates diseases with a mind still attached to worldly gain— who can compare him to anyone else?
How much more so when, with a mind free from worldly desire and softened by compassion, he maintains equal respect for both the lowly and the exalted?
Constantly performing the exceedingly weighty conduct of a Bodhisattva, he pacifies even the web of diseases that are otherwise mutually incompatible.
Burning sensation, pain, thirst, flatulence, hunger, emaciation,
and loss of appetite— what ordinary person could conquer these diseases that are constantly obstructing one another?

Who could know how to treat those who have swallowed the *māruta* poison, which possesses a brilliance like that of lightning and assumes forms identical to its source, especially since its course of action is difficult to discern?
One should always honor a physician who has reached the further shore of the Vedas and is endowed with wisdom;
for who would consider it wealth-giving to bestow riches upon one to whom one's very livelihood is bound?
In the past, Brahmā taught Āyurveda in a hundred thousand verses; however, Agniveśa and others,
having mastered the essence of all that is to be known, independently expanded each of its single parts in many ways.
The best of physicians was Vāgbhaṭa; he was my grandfather, whose name I bear. His son was Siṃhagupta, and I am his [son], born in the Sindhu lands.
Having acquired from my teacher Avalokita and from my even more venerable father an inspired intuition,
and through the study of many medical treatises, I have properly established this determination of the divisions of the body.
What could have been said that was not already stated previously which would not produce faith and satisfaction?
For this entire mass of meaning— whether concise, doubtful, extensive, or scattered— is now clearly seen as a single whole.
Who can reach the further shore of the boundless ocean of Āyurveda? Yet,
this essence of the knowledge of medicines for all diseases has been here collected.
Having remembered this which was previously spoken, and having heard it again now from both [the speaker and the listener],
for whom is it more appropriate to have faith— namely, the rememberer or the hearer?
Alternatively, even if this has been heard as it has come down in sequence to the rememberer himself,
what purpose is served by the specific identity of the speaker?
If one like me, or even Atri, were to state that *madana* moves upward while *trivṛt* reaches only the bladder, what difference would there be in the action [of these two drugs]? Please explain.
Devoid of the discrimination between what is right and what is wrong, and showing a particular devotion based merely on worldly custom,
such a person is a fool; indeed, the wise man does not do so, for his mind delights only in that which is well-spoken.

May the merit that has been generated here by following these words of the Sage— which provide a refuge for life and are like wish-fulfilling trees for the attainment of one's desires— bring about a world free from disease and established in nirvāṇa.
Thus ends the fifth chapter;
thus the sixth section, the Uttarasthāna, in the Aṣṭāṅgasaṅgraha composed by the venerable teacher Vāgbhaṭācārya, son of the venerable Siṃhagupta, is complete.
